consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether, and when, a description made in the cadastre of a certain thing proves dominion, or something that is included in said description, distinguishes. Where damage is discussed, error is presumed, by proving the thing to be otherwise.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Having considered the aforementioned point, it must be known that sometimes the designation of a thing in the cadastre is made by one who is not the owner, and then the assessment does not prove ownership: nor is prejudice generated for the true owner by such assignment, as in l. solennibus, C. de rei vend., and ff. de acquirendo dominio, l. quae quisque, unless the true owner knowingly consents, as in l. censualis, C. de dominio, and l. si praeses, eodem titulo. Sometimes such designation is made by the true owner, and then it is either done knowingly, or ignorantly, or it is doubtful. In the first case, namely, when knowingly, knowing that his property is held in common, he causes it to be described in the assessment as common with another, and prejudices himself, according to the notes in the laws cited above and in l. circa, C. de omni agro deserto; nor can it be revoked after an interval, as noted there by Accursius, ff. de probationibus, l. cum de lege. And this is the opinion of some. But others say that it can be revoked, because no right has been acquired by another thereby, as in ff. familiae erciscundae, l. qui familiae. And it supports what is noted in C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, l. illud, and ff. de pollutione, l. 2. In the second case, namely, when ignorantly, it is doubtful, and then it does not prejudice him, provided that it is proven that the truth is otherwise, as in l. cum falsa, ff. de iure et facto ignorato. Since, therefore, it does not appear that the said Rentius made the said assignment with certain knowledge, it does not prejudice him, the error being proven, which in contracts can be proven at any time, although in judgment it is otherwise, as in l. error, C. de iure et facto ignorato. And error is presumed by the very fact that it is proven that the matter is otherwise. And this for two reasons.

† because where the matter concerns avoiding damage, error is presumed upon proof that the matter stands otherwise. As noted by Bartolus in *l. Celsus*, column 2, near the end, *Digestum*, *De usucapione*. Secondly, because this is not a question of fact, but of law, namely concerning dominion, which is a matter of written law: in which knowledge is presumed, whereas in private law based on reason, ignorance is presumed. As stated in *l. Ultra*, *Digestum*, *Pro socio*. Furthermore, it does not appear that the signs and distinctive boundaries were placed by him. For it may be that they were placed long ago; and men who are not skilled in the art do not understand these distinctions, but only architects or masters. As in the *Authenticum*, *De non alienando*, § *Quod autem*, which indicates that such signs are rather of a masterful nature than declared by open letters. As in *Digestum*, *De institutione*, *l. Sed et si pupillus*, § *Prosunt vitae*. And thus I say and advise, I, Francesco, of Lord Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When there is doubt regarding jurisdiction in a given case: or if there is an opinion among the doctors, the sentence of the judge shall be valid.
2. Custom is established from pronouncements frequently made in court.
3. Whether a statute providing that no appeal may be taken from a sentence in which the judge declares himself to be the competent judge is valid; and what if it provides that no appeal may be taken from a definitive sentence.
4. Whether an official who purchases something without expressly stating the office, purchases in the name of the office or in his own name, and whether he binds the office or himself.
5. The period for proving his exception does not run against the defendant before the plaintiff has proved his claim.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Having examined the petition of my lord against Gulielmucius, and having considered the exceptions raised by the said Gulielmucius regarding the jurisdiction of the lord chamberlain of the butchers, as well as other exceptions produced against the petition; and having reviewed the positions and articles of the said Dominic, and having diligently discussed and examined the testimonies of the witnesses; and having considered all other acts and proceedings in the said case: it remains now to be seen what are the rights of the said lord chamberlain in the aforementioned cause. And although several objections are raised against the jurisdiction of the said lord chamberlain on this point: there is no need to insist upon them. Because concerning all matters pertaining to the art of the craft, the chamberlain is the competent judge against anyone. There are also other chamberlains, in those matters which pertain to their own art, according to the reform of the commune of Perugia issued on this point, and which is continuously practiced. And because judgment has thus been pronounced on the jurisdiction, and no appeal has been taken.

And when there is doubt about jurisdiction in fact: or it is the opinion of the doctors, the sentence is valid. As in the Digest, "On Judicial Matters," law "When the Daughter"; and in the Digest, "If Anyone is Summoned to Court," law "From Whatever"; and what is not in the Code, "That a Son Should Not Be Sued for His Father," authority "Habit."

And from such pronouncements frequently made in contradictory examination, custom is induced, as in the Digest, *De legibus*, l. *Si de interpretatione*; and in the Extravagant, *De fide instrumentorum*, c. *Pastoralis*. And it supports what is noted by Innocentius, *De rescindenda donatione*, c. *Ceterum*, and c. *Si*. And the reason is evident: because whenever there is doubt about the law or about the fact concerning jurisdiction, the judge approached on this matter has the duty to cognize; therefore also to pronounce, as in the Code, *De dilationibus*, a. *A precedente*. Therefore the pronouncement is valid; otherwise he would have the authority to cognize and pronounce in vain, which is absurd, because litigants are not deceived by the authority of the law, as in the Code, *De his qui vel etate impediti sunt*, l. 1.

But suppose that the statute states that no appeal may be taken from a sentence in which the judge declares himself to be the competent judge; does the gloss in the aforementioned *Authentica Habita* apply in this case? I answer that this gloss does not apply in this case, as far as permitting an appeal is concerned, because the statute prohibits appealing, and the statute is valid in interlocutory matters. Likewise, in indefinite cases, where the legislator has principal jurisdiction and jurisdiction over appeals. But if there were principal jurisdiction and not jurisdiction over appeals, the statute would not be valid so as to prevent an appeal from a definitive judgment, as in *Extra*, *De iureiurando*, chapter *Venientes*; and note this through Bartolus in *Digestum*, *De aqua pluviali arcenda*, law *Is cuius*. But it would be valid in interlocutory matters, as in *Codex*, *De senatusconsultis et interlocutionibus omnium iudicum*, law *Si*. In the text and gloss, it is said that those who have the right to enact statutes can commit a matter with appeal removed from an interlocutory decision. But they cannot commit a cause with appeal removed from a definitive judgment, which is notable and is not found elsewhere. I therefore say that a statute prohibiting appeal is made in honor of the judge and in favor of the litigants. And so that lawsuits may be shortened, as in *Codex*, *De fructibus et litis expensis*, law *Honorem*; and *De appellationibus*, chapter *Ut debitus*. And that this strengthens the sentence, as in *Codex*, *Si de momento possessorii*, law 1. And it immediately becomes res judicata, as in *Digestum*, *De appellationibus*, law *Quoniam*. And therefore this statute favors the sentence, and is to be alleged for the sentence, not against the sentence; because whenever appeal is prohibited, the judge’s sentence passes into the status of law, and is a sentence of law, and by law. For from a sentence arises a presumption, as in *Digestum*, *De re iudicata*, in the beginning; *De probationibus*, chapter *Quia contra falsam*; *De evictione*, law *Herennius*, section *Cayo*; *Codex*, *De administratione tutorum*, law *Si bonum*. But when a statute is joined to it, then it is a presumption of law and by law, as in *Digestum*, *De regulis iuris*, law *Res iudicata*. Having therefore presupposed the foundation of jurisdiction, descending to the petitions and proofs. And because from the body of the petition it is necessary that positions and articles arise, as in *Digestum*, *De petitione hereditatis*, law *Si quis libertatem*, section *Si*. Considering that in the petition it is alleged that the said Dominic sold, gave, and delivered to the said Guilielmucio Porcastros for a price, and in the name of the price, 31 florins; the said Guilielmucio promised to the said Dominic to give and pay. And in the articles it is said that the said Guilielmucio bought in his own name, etc.

† On these points, the witnesses testify, namely regarding the purchase and sale, that Dominic sold with delivery; they state that he brought the champions to the houses in the article of Gulielmucius. As for the promise, two witnesses testify, namely Martin on the 4th article and Thietus Ange. on the first, where it says, "he sold and delivered to the said Gulielmucius for the price of 30 or 31 gold florins, which florins the said Guliel. promised to give and pay to the said Dominic, etc." Thus, three things are proven: the sale, the delivery, and the promise made without any mention of the office of the said Guliel. Therefore, although in truth the said Guliel. was the Fancellus (Chancellor) of the champion, and perhaps had another purpose in mind, namely not to bind himself but the champion or the commune of Perugia, nevertheless no mention was made of this quality of office. Nor are these Fancelli necessary officials, but hired ones. And therefore, they promise simply, bind their own faith, and can be sued, as in D. de procuratoribus, l. procreatio, which prefaces that he followed the faith of the city and of the administration promising simply, expressing his own name and not that of the office, even with prior knowledge of the matter in which the contract was made, provided it was without mention of the office, as noted in D. de negotiorum gestis, l. si pupilli, in principio, and by Bartolus in l. civitas, si certum petatur, non obstantibus what is noted in l. post mortem, D. quando ex facto tutoris, because there it speaks of a true administrator and when it stood for the benefit of the master that the contract was made. But here it is not proven that it was turned to the benefit of the city. And even if it were proven, nevertheless what I said would be true, because he bound his own faith, since he did not name the master in the contract. And thus l. Grisogonus and there by Bartolus do not obstruct. And see what is noted by Bartolus in D. iudicium solutum, 3, § si procurator, ver. sed si curator, where he notably speaks of that matter. By the proofs, nothing else is established than what I have said above; nor can I judge according to conscience, according to the acts and proofs. And because conscience tells me that since Dominic gave the pigs, he ought to have the price, and this the said Guliel. ought to do and ensure by law and by honesty. Therefore, concluding, I say by law that the said Guliel. is obliged to pay the said sum. And because the defense is proven on his part, let the Lord Camerarius take heed, that if it is paid, he does not have it paid again. And this especially the Camerarius ought to take heed of, who has to judge according to truth and equity, according to the reforms which speak of this matter. And thus I say and counsel, I, Franciscus, son of Baldus.

After the contradictory opinion was given, before the Camerarius knew the sentence, the defendant made new articles, and among others made an article of payment, namely that the plaintiff had confessed to him being satisfied of the said quantity on the faith of several credible witnesses. The plaintiff said that he ought not to be admitted to prove this, because the acts were public. Also because the term given to him for proving had elapsed. I say the contrary: because this is a new article, of which there was no knowledge; nor does the lapse of the term obstruct, and if it was assigned several times according to the form of l. in pecuniariis and l. oratione, D. de feriis.

† because the defendant is not bound to prove this exception before the plaintiff has established his claim. C. de exce. l. si quidem, which is to this effect, note. And the same applies to any peremptory exception, such as an exception based on a pact not to sue, a compromise, or res judicata, as is the gloss, note, and expressly stated in C. de testib. extra de testa. tene menti.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a substitution made by these words, "if the said nephews should die before reaching puberty, all that remains after the legacies have been deducted shall be, and ought to be, of the said hospital, etc.," is direct, and an express pupillary substitution excluding the mother from the Trebellianic and the legitimate portion.
2. That which is expressed is said to be not only that which is apprehended from express words, but also that which is deduced from presumptions.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The agreement is as follows: A certain man named Paulutius of Assisi made his last will and testament, in which, among other things, he disposed as follows: In all his movable and immovable goods, rights, actions, names, and debts, wherever they are, may be found, or discovered, and may be in the future, he instituted and made Ciacharello and Angelo, sons of the late Andrea, son of the said testator Paulutius, and nephews of the said testator, his universal heirs, and for an equal share. And the said testator willed that if any of his said nephews and heirs should die in pupillary age, or later at any time without legitimate children descending from their body, that succession should pass to the other survivor; and if both should die in the aforementioned manner without legitimate children descending from their body, that the said inheritance and goods should remain and succeed, and ought to remain and succeed, to the persons and places written below, in this manner, namely: First, he left, in the event of the said case occurring, from his said goods to Dame Vitalucia, his daughter, and wife of Francis, son of John, one house with all the customary furnishings and utensils to be placed in the said house in the city of Assisi and its territory. Furthermore, he left to the same Dame Vitalucia three plots of land described in the said testament, namely, during the life of the said Dame Vitalucia, the said goods left to her should remain and ought to remain freely to the Hospital of Saint Rufinus and the Hospital of the Fraternity of Saint George of Assisi, for an equal share. Finally, he thus disposed: Furthermore, he left, ordered, willed, and expressly commanded that the entire residue of his said inheritance, after the said legacies made, should be and ought to be for the said Dame Vitalucia, his daughter mentioned above, and for the said hospitals of Saint Rufinus and the Fraternity of George, for a share, and he left to the said hospitals with this condition, that the said goods thus left to the said hospitals should always be and ought to be for the perpetual use of the poor of Christ, who come to lodge in the said hospitals. And that they cannot be sold, alienated, or exchanged for any cause, and if the superior rectors of the said hospitals in any way attempted to sell, alienate, or exchange the said goods, or part of the said goods, that from now, as from then, they should freely, without contradiction of any person, devolve and ought to devolve to the Church of Saint Francis of Assisi, the Church of Saint Clare of Assisi, and the Church of Saint Mary of the Angels of the Castle of Assisi, for an equal share. Finally, the said testator Paulutius died, with the said Ciacharello and Angelo, his nephews and instituted heirs, surviving him, and with the said Dame Vitalucia and Dame Lipolla, wife of the late Andrea, son of the said testator, and mother of the said Ciacharello and Angelo, surviving him. Then the said Angelo and Ciacharello died in pupillary age within a year after the death of the said testator Paulutius, with the same said Dame Lipolla, their mother, and the said Dame Vitalucia, their aunt, surviving them. Now it is asked whether the said Dame Lipolla, mother of the said Angelo and Ciacharello, ought to have any part of the goods and inheritance of Paulutius, or of the said Ciacharello and Angelo, on account of any succession, having seen the said point. Invoking the names of Christ and his glorious Virgin Mother, having seen the point and the testament, of which mention is made,

† I hold that in the case of the Trebellianic quarter there is no doubt, because the mother is excluded from it, as when the last of the aforementioned nephews to die had a substitution made in favor of pious causes, as appears in the will. And thus the Trebellianic quarter ceases to apply in the first example, as noted in the Authentica *Similiter*, Codex, *Ad legem Falcidiam*; and in the law *Marcellus*, Digest, *Ad Senatusconsultum Trebellianum*; in the Authentica *De ecclesiasticis titulis*, § *Si autem haeres*; and fully by the doctors in the Authentica *De hereditatibus et Falcidia*, § *Si vero expressim*. And this is the truth, although some hold the contrary, as noted in the law *Si arctatur ad legitimam* from the person of the last one to die; for there is no doubt regarding the first, as noted in the law *Penultima*, Codex, *De impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus*; and the law *Cum acutissimi*, Codex, *De fideicommissis*; the law *Generaliter*, Digest, *De institutionibus et substitutionibus sub conditione factis*; and fully by Bartolus in the law *Heredes mei*, § *Cum ita*, Digest, *Ad Senatusconsultum Trebellianum*. Although this is also clear from the words of the will at the beginning, or is excluded. And I say that in this case the mother is also excluded from the legitime, because the substitutes take by direct right, especially since it is stated that the aforementioned nephews died while still minors. Nor does it matter if it is said that a tacit pupillary substitution does not exclude the mother, as noted in the law *In testamento*, Codex, *De testamento militis*; and in the law *Precibus*, Codex, *De impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus*; and the law *Centurio*, Digest, *De vulgaribus et pupillaribus substitutionibus*. For I answer that here it was not tacit but express, and inferred from the words from the mind of the testator, due to the words appended in the will which import that the substitutes take by direct right upon the nephews dying in their minority, as is fully stated by Bartolus in the law *Centurio*, Digest, *De vulgaribus et pupillaribus substitutionibus*. This is proven by the words of the will, where it is said that the entire residue of the inheritance, after the other legacies made, is and ought to be of the said hospitals. Note: "the entire," and thus without diminution, as in the law *2*, § *Ad filiorum*, Codex, *Quoniam et quibus quarta pars debetur*.

† because it is said to be expressed, not however that it is expressed from the words themselves, but that it is also ascertained from presumptions. L. licet Imperator, de legibus, 1. and de manumissionibus testamentis, L. si quis locuples, thus as if by a direct pupillary substitution, and expressly excludes the mother, so that in pupillary age, or afterwards at any time, etc. And thus, upon their dying in pupillary age, there was a direct pupillary substitution, which excludes the mother. As noted in the gloss in the aforementioned L. precibus, on the word "in fideicommissum" at the end. And especially since the testator used direct words in the said substitution, namely: "and others shall be due," which are direct words, and thus the substitutes are admitted by direct right within the time of pupillary age, as noted in the aforementioned L. precibus, and L. centurio, and in L. in pupillaris, and L. verbis, cum si. And if it is said that in the will he substituted in the first place in this manner. I answer that he also substituted in the second place for them succeeding in this way. As is clear, because he said: "and if both shall have died in the aforesaid manner, etc." And thus he substituted directly in both cases before puberty: because from the first he takes it as direct, and in the subsequent substitution. D. de legibus, 3. L. si servus, §. si. First, this is clear from the word "the whole remainder." As fully in the aforementioned L. centurio, noted by Bartolus. Nor does it avail that the testator in the substitution left certain particular legacies, wishing the remainder to come to the substitutes: because such particular legacies do not alter the substitution, when it is direct, as above, and in the remainder, as L. 2, C. de hereditatibus instituendis, and in the aforementioned L. centurio, vera. The conclusion is therefore that the mother is entirely excluded from the legitime and the Trebellian portion, and [the estate] devolves by direct right to the substitutes, except for the legacies, and does not depart in any respect from the words, mind, and presumptions of his aforementioned sons, etc. And thus I say and advise, I, Peter of Asti, doctor of laws, subscribed with my own hand to the faith [of this document], and signed with my usual seal.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
0. One summoned to one matter is not in contempt for another matter to which he was not summoned.
1. Whether a summons to all acts of the case up to the definitive judgment is valid.
2. If, while a case is pending, new jurisdiction accrues to the judge, and a new summons is required while that case is pending; otherwise, the sentence will be null.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A certain A. obtained from our Lord the Pope the assignment of a case of injuries, which he intended to bring against B., to be committed to a certain Lord Auditor in the Apostolic Palace, with the power to summon in court and to the parties, namely the said B., although the aforementioned case had not been devolved to the Roman Curia. The said Lord Auditor, at the instance of the said A., summoned and ordered the said B. to be cited for the entire case, so that he should appear, either in person or through his procurator, for all acts up to and including the definitive sentence; otherwise, the Auditor threatened to proceed further, as justice might deem just, through the medium of justice. After these things, the said B. not appearing, at the instance of the said A., our Lord the Pope committed to the same Lord Auditor that he could proceed summarily and de plano, etc., in the said case. By virtue of this commission, the said Lord Auditor proceeded in the case in the absence of the said B., citing the said B. by contradictory hearing, and [rendered] a definitive sentence for the said A. However, this commission was not otherwise intimated to the said B. Now it is asked whether this sentence deserves execution.

† He who is summoned to one matter is not in contempt for another, to which he has not been summoned, as noted by Innocentius in *de officio delegati*, chapter *Consuluit*; in *de procuratoribus*, chapter *Auditis*; in *de electione*, chapter *Ecclesia vestra*; in *de testibus*, chapter *Cum omnibus*; at the end of *de accusationibus*, chapter *Ad petitionem*.

But one summoned to the cause is summoned up to the sentence, inclusive, for all things, according to Innocentius, as noted in the question and quantity of the judge, and the authority *qui semel*. This must be understood as being summoned to the sentence, if the case was contested; otherwise, the judge would be foolish, who would thus summon to that which is impossible by law. Argument from the Digest, *de iudiciis*, *solui*, l. *vir bonus*; argument from the Digest, *ne quis eum*, l. 1, at the end. For if a present person could not be definitively condemned without the case being contested, therefore neither could he be summoned to that. And this is most clear.

Let us therefore assume that at the time of the citation the case could not be definitively adjudicated, and that a rescript supervened, whereby it could be, without the cause having been joined in issue. I say that by the force and foundation of that citation nothing could be done definitively; but a new citation is required. Because a new power, a new jurisdiction, a new order, indeed a new judge himself, is new by reason of office. And therefore, as a new judge, he ought to act according to new law. See Digest, *De iudicibus*, law *Edictum*. And therefore, perhaps it would not suffice to notify the state of the case of nullity without a new citation. And the reason is: because that clause, “as shall seem just, etc.,” operates according to the intention of the judge as he then was, and ought not to be according to the intention of which he could not then think and divine. And it is certain that recourse must be had to the intention of the judge as he then was, and not according to the intention of which he could not then think and divine. And it is certain that recourse must be had to the intention of the judge. Digest, *De arbitris*, law *Quolibet*; Digest, *De praetoria stipulatione*, law *I*, in the end.

Furthermore, just as it is not valid without the expressed quality of extraordinary jurisdiction, so also here, since it could not be expressed what was not [yet] so, this is supported by the aforementioned authority *Qui semel*, from the word *cognitus*. For with regard to future jurisdiction, at the time of the citation he was like a private person: see law *Observare*, § *Si*, *De officio proconsulis et legati*. And he did not know, nor could he know, that he was a judge. To this effect: Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, law *Multum interest*; through Bartolus to the same effect in law *Hoc autem*, § *I*, *Quibus ex causis in possessionem*; Digest, *De iudiciis solutis*, law *3*, § *Sed si quidem*; Digest, *De eo qui pro tutore*, law *Quaero*. It is certain that in an action civilly commenced, joinder of issue is required. Digest, *Si quis*, authority *Si eum*, § *Qui iniuriarum*; and noted in law *Cum emancipati*, § *Emancipatus filius*, *De collatione bonorum*. And therefore the Papal rescript changed the nature of the case. On account of which it seems to me that the said sentence does not merit execution.

Furthermore, just as the edict must be notified, otherwise the sentence is not valid: see law *I*, § *Item cum ex edicto*, so that which is by reason of the edict, otherwise the party is not bound to appear; because he knows his right to endure everywhere. Digest, *Si quis in ius vocatus non ierit*, law *Ex quacunque*; *De fideiussoribus conprehensis*, chapter *Cum sit generale*, through Innocentius; and better and more clearly, *De dilationibus*, chapter *I*, through Innocentius. But if the old and new power tended to the same state of the case: as always in summary proceedings, one should not believe that the process to sentence is vitiated; because power is added to power, argument from Digest, *De militum testamento*, law *Quod dicitur*, § *Ultra*. And supporting the above, in the same title, law *Titius* and law *Tribunus*, § *Ultimo*.

Whenever common law does not permit non-appearance to the definitive judgment without joinder of issue, I ought not to be called contumacious; because I ought not to have suspected that the judge would do something null and against justice to me. Argument from Digest, *De arboribus caedendis*, law *Videtur*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A wife may bind herself by oath for the release of her husband from prison.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The case having been considered, for which the wife bound herself: because for the release of her husband from prison,

† It appears that the obligation is binding. D. de solutione matrimonii, l. quamvis; and l. si ideo. To the contrary is a special reason, which dictates that a woman cannot bind herself for her husband. C. ad Velleianum, auth. si qua mulier; because she is presumed to have been seduced by her husband. In Auth. ut immobilia ante nuptias, near the middle; and lest she strip herself of her property due to immoderate love: as noted by Azo in his Summa ad Velleianum; Master Federicus de Senis in his consilia, consilium 135, which begins: “The point of the question is this: given that there is a marriage between spouses, it holds that an oath taken in such a case is binding; because it contains no turpitude, nor is it prohibited by divine law. The authorities are: D. de iureiurando, c. cum contingat; and c. 2, de pace, lib. 6. And this is true according to canon law, according to him whose authority I have followed, and I hold the same opinion, saving the more just opinion. I, Baldus.”

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What exceptions may be raised against a husband accusing of adultery.
2. A husband cannot criminally accuse the adulterer and the adulteress in the same bill of indictment; otherwise, in a civil action. No. 4.
3. If a husband accuses the adulterer in one bill and the adulteress in another, the case proceeds on the first.
4. Whether one can be definitively acquitted when adultery is not proven.
5. A statute providing that one may be tortured for adultery does not apply to the adulteress.
6. A disposition made regarding one of two correlated parties does not apply to the other when they are unequal.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The facts are as follows. A certain person named Blasius Paulutii accused Cionum one day of adultery committed with his wife, Lady Cathelina. Then, on another day, he accused the said Lady Cathelina of adultery, in order that, according to the form of the statute, he might recover her dowry. Thereupon, the accused appeared and denied the contents of the accusation. They raised their exceptions, both general and special, stating that the said Blasius should not be heard, and that the right of accusation did not belong to him. Then, a term being given for proof, it is presupposed without prejudice to the truth: that the indications of the said adultery are proven. Afterwards, the process is published with assignments, and it is said that the said accusation against the said Lady Cathelina proceeds; and that the said Lady Cathelina ought to be absolved in two ways, for the reasons set forth below.

† When adultery is alleged, an exception based on the husband’s own conduct is raised: sometimes the adulteress herself objects to him, having married after the divorce, without a prior protestation forbidding her to marry. D. de adulteriis, l. 2, in principio; and l. denuntiasse, §. quaeritur. This exception has no place today: because by divorce the first marriage is not dissolved, except as regards the act, not as regards the bond and the root of the marriage.

† However, the exception of duplicity stands in the way: because they accuse two persons simultaneously in the same bill of indictment, namely the adulterer and the adulteress. And in such a case, the accusation proceeds against neither person. D. de adulteriis, l. si maritus, §. si; and l. vim passam, §. duos. And this is a special rule in adultery, according to Bartolus.

† Sometimes the exception of numeration is an obstacle, when one person is accused in one libel, another in another. And then part of the libel is rejected, and the case proceeds only on the first. D. de adulteriis, l. nihil, §. si. And the reason is: because the accuser of adultery should not be peculiar. Just as he cannot suffer two penalties from the inscription: because one penalty is consumed; since under the common law the penalty for adultery is death. As C. de adulteriis, l. quamvis, in fine. And conversely, for one who subscribes to the penalty of talion and does not prove it. And it supports what is noted, D. de furtis, l. vulgaris, in principio, in its own reasoning.

And these laws speak when it is a matter of capital punishment. But when a woman is accused with the effect of losing her dowry, these laws do not speak. And therefore, recourse must then be had to the law of the Authentica, by which law it is provided that the adulterer be accused. And one may begin with the wife, and she loses her dowry. For she loses it entirely, unless she herself is sued. However, one cannot sue both by the same libel, or by different ones proceeding simultaneously. Hence, the woman cannot be accused together with you on the ground of delay. Text, ordinary, in Auth. ut liceat matri, et aviae, § quia non plurimas, Coll. 8, in the word "mulierem" or "adulterium." But this exception also impedes only the process.

But can one be absolved definitively when adultery is not proven? I believe that yes: because it is permissible for the party raising an exception, having omitted a dilatory exception, to proceed to a peremptory exception, or to full victory; since he may renounce his dilatory exception. Codex, De pace, l. pe.

But whether a statute, which provides for the torture of an adulterer, applies to an adulteress, I answer: no. For in D. 50, 17, l. Si vero, §. De viro, the law speaks. And because milder treatment is accorded to an adulteress than to an adulterer, C. de adulteriis, Auth. Hodie; and in Auth. Ut nulli iudici, §. Adulteram, Coll. 8. And because the law speaks of the torture of a minister, not of this woman, D. 49, 1, l. Prospexit. And because, with regard to recovering the dowry, which pertains to family affairs and is in a sense a civil cause, Extr. de procuratoribus, c. Tua; and because for private interest one cannot proceed to torture on the basis of presumptions, as noted in D. 48, 18, l. Maritus; and in the aforementioned §. Quia vero plurimas, in the word "natura" it is shown; and in §. Si vir, in the word "non probauerit" and in the word "non probatam." It is not safe to generalize from these points to other matters.

† The argument from correlatives does not stand in the way: because that argument applies to equal correlatives, and not to unequal ones. But here they are unequal, as is evident from the nature of the penalty, and from the different formal and final effect, etc. And so I say and advise, I, Baldus of Perugia. And so forth.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Contracts that are made formally, preceded by public auctions, are said to be made in writing: and they are not perfected unless the writing is executed.
2. A promise made to a notary does not bind the promisor: but it must be made to the official appointed for this purpose, so that it may bind the community which appointed him.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The matter on which counsel is sought is as follows: The salt tax of the city of Casti, having been repeatedly put up for auction by the Lords Priors of the people of the said city in the usual manner, was secured by a promise made by Iouanlisius Io. for the sum of eight hundred and sixty-six gold florins. As appears from the hand of Nicolaus, notary of the said Lords Priors, it is stated that Vinc., father of Nicolaus, after the aforementioned promise of Iouanlisius, promised the said notary the said tax of eight hundred and sixty-six gold florins, of which promise there is simple evidence in the hand of the said notary. After the promise of Vincentius, as it is said, was made, the aforementioned Lords Priors came to the bench, where the said tax is accustomed to be auctioned, and together with the said notary, they auctioned the said tax in the presence of, and without objection from, the said Vincentius, solely on the basis of the promise of the said Iouanlisius, although the said Iouanlisius was absent. The said Iouanlisius, perceiving this, claims to be absolved from the said promise and denies that the said Vincentius is bound. Vincentius denies that he made any promise regarding the said tax after the promise of the said Iouanlisius, even though the said notary wrote it thus. On this matter, the aforementioned Lords Priors, desiring to be more fully informed, had certain witnesses examined; their testimonies, along with the present documents and the statute speaking on this matter, are transmitted. Now it is asked whether, from the foregoing, the said tax should be granted or remain so. Otherwise, no one is found who will promise more.

† These contracts, which are made so solemnly after preceding auctions, are said to be made in writing, as noted by Bartolus in the Digest, *De liberis et posthumis*, and in the law *Gallus*, § *Idem credendum*. Such contracts are not perfected unless written documentation is drawn up, and until such writing is stipulated, it is permissible to withdraw; beware, do not write. For repentance is allowed, as stated in the Code, *De fidei instrumentis*, law *Contractus*.

† Moreover, a promise made to a notary does not bind the promisor. Rather, it must be made to the official appointed for the purpose of selling, who can bind the community of that territory. For if the community is not bound, the promise is not binding. Indeed, the notary has the office of writing, not of contracting. And therefore, a promise made in the absence of the officials is not valid, as noted in C. de sacrosan. ecc. l. illud; C. de liber. causa. l. iubemus; ff. iudic. sol. l. 2 and 3. From which it clearly appears that the said Vincentius is not bound to this. ff. de testa. mil. l. diuus; §. si. de act. et obl. l. obligationum substantia. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a woman may be a witness in codicils, although not in wills.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen.

† Although women cannot serve as witnesses in a will, where formal witnesses are required, they may nevertheless serve as witnesses in codicils, even those tacitly or expressly confirmed by a will; this is established in the Digest, *De testamentis*, l. *Qui testamento*, § *Mulier*; and in the Code, *De codicillis*, l. *Si*, § *In omni*. And therefore the said last will of the said legacy was valid. It must, however, be proved by five witnesses, because the words “for the soul” have no legal effect, since they appear to have been added merely to color the legacy left to the wife. Digest, *De castrensi peculio*, l. *Si forte*; and see the note in the Code, *De sacrosanctis ecclesiis*, l. *Illud*.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a will made before entering a monastery is valid: if the testatrix dies within the year of probation after entering with an express donation of her goods.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen.

† A woman made a will, afterwards she entered a monastery with an express donation of her goods: and she died within a year, whether her will is valid. This lady Margaret began with a donation of her goods, and finally made an express profession: and she renounced during the year of probation; for which reasons, if, as to the conscience of the monastery, the reception of nuns and oblates pertained to the abbess alone: this lady Margaret became a nun, or a lay sister of the monastery: and her goods were transferred to the monastery, as in the Authent. ingressi, C. de sac. san. ecc. and they were transferred by express concession. And even if there had been no express statement, they would have been transferred by operation of law by the force of the profession, as in D. de prec. l. si adoptauero. And the will is revoked: because, having entered, she retained no goods of which she could dispose by will. Or because, being revoked, it is as if by subsequent agnation, as noted by the gloss, Petrus, and Cynus in the said Authent. And because the renunciation of the will, which tends to pious causes, as here, is sufficiently proved by witnesses, at least according to canonical equity. And therefore I hold that the goods pertain to the monastery: since the monastery was passed over, and nothing was left to it in the will. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The dowry is proved by extrajudicial confession.
1. 2 How and when a confession made regarding the dowry outside of court is said to be proved. And nos. 3, 4, 5, and 6.
2. Extrajudicial confession, in order to effect a release, does not require the presence of the party.
3. A brother or blood relative is admitted as a witness.
4. A witness to whom the benefit or detriment pertains: whether he is to be admitted.
5. A witness stating that the contents of the article are true, proves.
6. How possession is proved: and whether the word "possession" is understood as possession in law or in fact.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. In the case at issue between Philip on one side, and Bartholomew and Dame Accha on the other, several matters must be considered. First, whether it has been proved according to law that Dame Accha is entitled in such a way that an action for recovery or retention of the goods pledged for the said dowry may be brought; for there is no doubt concerning the dowry of Dame Constantia, and this appears from the instrument of the legate. Solution: If it has been sufficiently proved concerning the aforementioned dowry, whether the possession of the said ladies has been proved, and by what right, if it has been proved; first, what is the effect of the said possession.

And as to the first point, that it has been proven, concerning the dowry of the said do. Accha, it is shown first from the confession of the said brothers, namely Philip, Bartholomew, and Magius, who confessed in the presence of several credible witnesses, and sometimes in the presence of the said ladies do. Accha and do. Constantia, that the said ladies, being satisfied with their dowries as set forth in the instrument of do. Accha and in the instrument of the legacy of do. Constantia, ought to receive them from and out of the goods and inheritance of John, their father and husband of the said do. Accha; which confession is legally proven, as I shall show below, and prejudices those who made the confession; because an extrajudicial confession, made in the presence of the opposing party and for a cause, prejudices the confessor, as stated in D. de interrog. et respons. act., l. 1, in fine; D. de pos. l. Publicus, in fine; indeed, for the purpose of releasing [a debtor], the presence of the party is not required, D. de lib. leg., l. Non solum, § Liberationis verba. Since, therefore, this confession was sometimes made in the presence of the party and on account of the dowry, it prejudices those who made the confession, according to the above-mentioned laws; indeed, even if it had been made in the absence of the party, because for the purpose of releasing [a debtor], as I shall prove below, it would prejudice [the confessor], as stated in the said § Liberationis verba.

† But that the said confession is sufficiently proven, it appears evidently from the depositions of the witnesses. For on this article, concerning the confession of these brothers, three witnesses, Giouanchinus, Iac., and Nico., testify. I therefore come to the first witness, namely Giouanchinus: and from his deposition the said confession is proven. For this witness, examined on the 29th article of the aforementioned confession, which begins: “Item that the aforementioned Philip, etc.,” says that he heard and was present when the aforementioned Philip, Barth., and Magius confessed that the said ladies were to receive their due dowries, declaring the dowry of the said lady Accha to be as contained in the instrument of her dowry; and thus he refers to something certain, namely to the instrument of promise. As is stated in D. de re iudicata, l. in summa, and C. de senatusconsulto, quod sine certa quantitate, l. hæc sententia. Nor do the jurists object if it is said that it is an instrument of promise of dowry; for to this I respond by interpretation, and according to the same title, l. si dotali instrumento, where it is said that a dowry instrument is any one in which is contained a dowry given or a promised possession. There are two kinds of dowry instruments, namely for constituting and for restoring the dowry; and this is an instrument of promise and of restoration of the dowry. And thus, whatever the reference may be, the conclusion follows from the words of the witness, as stated above. Furthermore, it is not an objection if it is said that from the deposition of the aforementioned witness it is not proven that the said confession emanated with the opposing party present, and thus does not seem valid, since it is an extrajudicial confession.

† because where a confession is made for the purpose of releasing [a party], the presence of the party is not required: as stated in the aforementioned § liberationis verba; but here it was made for the purpose of releasing, namely, to release the heir of the promisor. It therefore appears that the said confession is sufficiently proven by the said witness, according to Bartolus in l. certis, § si quis absente, ff. de confessionibus, who holds that although when made for the purpose of releasing [a party] the presence of the party is required, this applies to a pact, as in l. idem in duobus, § si, de pactis, but not to a confession. Now I come to another witness, namely, to La. Ciucii, who testifies on the same article concerning the confession of the said brothers. And he also clearly proves the said confession, since he states that in his presence and hearing, the aforementioned brothers, named in the article, confessed in the presence of the said ladies that they owed to receive their dowries from said ladies. And that the goods formerly belonging to the said Io. were pledged for the dowries of said ladies.

† Since he testifies regarding the confession, and the party is present, he undoubtedly proves the fact. And if it is said that this witness should not be believed: because he is a blood relative of the said Do. Accha; also because he has an interest in the matter, either for gain or loss; thirdly, because he does not specify the amount of the aforementioned dowries; I say that these objections do not prevail. And first, that which was said about kinship does not constitute an obstacle: because although a brother is not compelled to testify against his will for his brother, he is admitted if he is willing, as noted by Jacobus de Arena and Cynus in l. parentes, C. de testibus; and by Innocentius in c. si nuntius, de officio delegati; and by Bartolus in l. qui testamento, §. si, ff. de testamentis. And if it is said that, although a brother may be a witness for his brother, nevertheless on account of brotherhood he will not make entirely as much faith as an outsider would: this is true when he testifies alone; because in such a case he should not be believed by means of an oath in lieu of proof. But when he has a co-witness, his statement is supplemented by another co-witness, as in l. si quis ex argentariis, §. 2, ff. de edendo, where an incomplete witness is supplemented by a witness of the required number, which is a notable text to this effect. Moreover, there are other presumptions here in his favor: because he testifies between the parties, with respect to whom he is, as it were, equally affectionate, as in l. non solum, §. 1, ff. de re iudicata [sic: de re nuptiali], in which case he would make faith not only in civil but also in criminal matters, as another witness, as noted by Bartolus in the aforementioned l. qui testamento, §. si.

† As to the second point, which ought to be rejected because it concerns him who bears the benefit or detriment, it is answered, as has often been said, that this does not apply when it is a matter of prescription. Likewise, as to the third point, that it does not declare the quantity of the dowry, this is not an obstacle, because on the contrary it does declare it: for the witness is understood to refer to the article upon which he testifies, when he states that they are true. It would be otherwise if he were to say that he nevertheless knows them. And the reason is: because such are the subjects as the predicates demonstrate, as in l. si defensor, ff. de inter. act. Since therefore the aforementioned witness is understood to refer to the article upon which he testifies, and the article, by reference to the instrument of the promise of dowry, contains a certain quantity, therefore also the said witness, who is understood to refer to the article. From all of which I conclude that the said witness sufficiently proves the said confession. And thus we now have two concurring witnesses.

† The third witness, namely Nic., brother of Biancholo, testifying on the aforementioned article concerning the confession of the said brothers, clearly proves it without any doubt. For he states that the contents of the said article are true; since I say that they are true, the article is proved in form. And he gives a sufficient reason, because according to the sense by which he most perceives that about which he testifies, as is noted by Innocentius in the chapter Cum causae, De testibus, where he says that a witness ought to testify according to the sense by which he most perceives that about which he testifies. Since here he is questioned about the act of the word, that is, about the confession, and he testifies about hearing, just as the aforementioned two other witnesses, therefore he testifies according to the more appropriate sense, as is noted by Decius in law 2, in fine, Digest, De aqua pluvia arcenda. This witness also testifies about sight, which is the common sense for every sense, as in the Code, De testibus, law Testium, according to Jacobus de Arena. And one should consider what Bartolus says in law Item apud Labeonem, section Si quis sic fecerit, Digest, De iniuriis, where he says that the word "seems" refers to another understanding. Therefore, it appears from the above that the said confession is sufficiently proved, and clearly by three witnesses, who are in agreement and above all exception.

Secondly, it appears that the said dowry is proved by the aforementioned witnesses testifying on article 25, which begins: "Item, that at the time of the said etc." where they prove the said dowries to the said ladies. And thus the said brothers made an agreement together with the said ladies, declaring the quantity of the said dowries by reference to the dowry instrument; because a declaration suffices, as I proved above, and by reference to the instrument of the legacy of the said lady Constantia, as is evident, especially from the testimony of Iacobus Ciucius and Nic., brother of Biancholo, on the said article 25, which strongly corroborates the confession of the said John, which appears sufficiently proved. Having disposed of the first point, I come to the second, etc.

† namely, whether the possession of the said lords has been proven, I demonstrate: because the witnesses state, when examined on the 30th article, which begins: moreover, the said ladies had and possessed the said goods. But the word "possession" is understood as civil, unless it conflicts with the condition of the person: as holds Petrus and Raynerius in l. stipulatio ista, §. hi quoque, ff. de verbis obligatorum; and the same holds there Ancharanus of Pisa. To this effect, the law ob carmen, §. si, de testibus. Notwithstanding the gloss which is in the said §. hi quoque, which says that the word "poss." simply uttered is understood as possession of fact and a certain natural detention, which can be with anyone, because that is there due to the condition of the person stipulating, namely, the second, in whom possession of law cannot fall. And thus, so that the thing may rather have effect than perish, it is understood there as possession of fact according to the aforementioned doctors, presupposing that only possession of fact was proven, although a certain detention would suffice: because he who detains is presumed to possess, unless the contrary is proven. As expressly noted by Innocentius in c. cum olim, el. 2, de privilegiis; in the gloss on the word "dederat" at the end. And otherwise Innocentius says that if a witness says: I saw such a one, in fact, holding such a thing, he proves true possession: as he himself notes in the said c. cum causam, de testibus, on the word "de causis." And if it is said, although possession is proven, nevertheless it is not proven by what right they possess. I say that this is not necessary to be proven by witnesses: because the law provides that wherever he who is found in possession of any thing has a title, he is presumed to possess from the preceding title. This is the express gloss in l. quaedam mulier, in fine, ff. de re vendicata; and less instructed would be he who said the contrary. As l. minus instructus, C. de acquisitione possessionis; and l. Titia, de solutionibus. And this expressly holds Bartolus, ff. de usucapione pro emptore, l. 2, §. si sub conditione, in fine, where he says that it suffices if it appears that I had a title and possessed. And even if it does not appear that I knew of the title at the beginning of possession, which is to be noted according to Bartolus. To this optimally serves ff. si servus venditus, l. si a te. Since therefore these ladies have a title, that is, a right of pledge, or cause, they are presumed to possess from the preceding title, i.e., from the right, or from the cause of the pledge: because title is the same as cause: because there is no other meaning in saying "by what title you possess" than "from what cause, or by what right you possess," as C. de petitione hereditatis, l. cogi. Notwithstanding if it is said, rather by right of familiarity, or friendship. As l. qui iure, ff. de acquirenda possessione. Because that is true right of possessing, otherwise otherwise, as in our case. And thus it must be understood. The said l. qui iure. Otherwise they would be badly understood. And it would be contrary to the aforementioned laws. And to this I see no response. Moreover, the witnesses expressly depose on this, saying: that they saw the said ladies possessing for their right of dowries: and they give the reason. Because they saw, and were present. And although law cannot be seen, nevertheless the reason of the witness regards that which is seen. And therefore it proves: because in a witness the reason founds the statement, not the contrary. As C. de testibus, l. solam. Finally, it is certain that our possession was prior than the possession of them, namely, of the adverse party, whence their possession is presumed clandestine. As c. licet causam, de probatibus, where the text. And to such a clandestine possessor is not given a judgment of division. The text is to the letter. ff. communi dividundo, l. communi dividundo, §. inter praedones. Rather, such an occupier falls from the right of demanding division, if he had any. C. si regnum, l. si constiterit. From all of which I conclude, and as to the third, that the said ladies may use retention. ff. de damno infecto, l. utique. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A man having a daughter from his first marriage, if he confessed that he had received a dowry from his second wife, whom he later bequeathed to her in his will, such confession is of no effect.
2. A confession between husband and wife does not imply a gift with regard to the expectation of future payment.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† This woman ought to have her simple dowry: because the confession of the dowry was not valid to the prejudice of the children of the first marriage, unless a true payment appeared. C. de sec. nup. l. hac edictali. and on account of the statute prohibiting it.

† For a confession made between husband and wife, not in the hope of a future payment, has the character of a donation, as is stated in the Code, *De donationibus causa mortis*, in law 2. Due to the prohibition of the law or statute, simulation is presumed. Digest, *De probationibus*, law *Qui testamentum*. And therefore, unless it appears that such confession was made regarding a natural obligation, it is regarded as a donation, which is invalid. Digest, *De verbis obligatorum*, law *Si diuortio*. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. What precaution a father should take when he wishes to provide a dowry for his daughter and have her renounce her mother's goods.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† When a father wishes to provide a dowry for his daughter, and wishes that the daughter, who is an adult, renounce the maternal estate, the following procedure should be observed: namely, that the daughter make a renunciation of the maternal dowry, and of all the mother’s goods, and of everything that she could claim or obtain from the maternal succession. And she should do this on the ground that she has acknowledged that she has been fully satisfied, especially by the constitution and provision of the dowry made by the father for her husband, etc., and she should swear not to contravene this; and this should be done with the consent of other relatives. However, it would be more advisable and safer for the aforementioned daughter to be emancipated by the father, because obligations do not subsist between a father and a son in his power, as stated in l. si qui pro eo, § 1, ff. de fide. And that afterwards a curator be appointed for her, and with the consent of the curator, and with a second oath interposed, she should make the aforementioned renunciation.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. For a mandate is never extended to prohibited or penal matters, unless they are expressly stated in the mandate.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. To the most noble knight, I have learned that Domenico, son of Messer Blandisali of the Piccoli family of Siena, and Archenuccio have been captured, and that you lent them 300 florins, for which you wish to have security; and therefore I stand as security for him regarding his good faith, until he shall be brought to you with the band of men which I have promised you; and for the clarity of this matter, I have made this writing with my own hand on the 20th day of May 1386, to you, Messer Pietro degli Gaiettani of Pisa, in Perugia. It is now asked, from the above words: whether the said Master Fran. is bound for the said sum, on the ground that the said lord did not observe what was promised above, presupposing that the said writing bears the subscription of three witnesses.

† If a procurator is appointed so specifically that it appears he is appointed against a certain person, and to plead on that cause of expressed nullity, a penal article: then he is said to have a special mandate: and it causes the principal to incur the penalty. But if one penal case is expressed: then it does not cause the principal to incur the penalty. D. Quod quisque iure, l. 3, § Si procurator; Ad prohibita, n. And a mandate is never extended to penalties, unless they are expressed in the mandate. As in l. Si pater, Q. In fraudem creditorum; and note, per Guillaume in l. Sed et si quis, § Quaesitum, Si quis cautionem. And therefore, since there are many nullities, some penal, some not penal, it is not said that he has a special mandate, unless the penal one is expressed by itself, or by reference to another, for example, in a cause with such persons concerning nullity, and he has no other than the nullity of the award. Argument, D. De liberis et posthumis, l. Nominatim; and in c. 2, De procuratoribus, in such a case he then has a special mandate, otherwise it does not seem to be the sense of a prohibited and penal act. This point was proposed to me, and I have otherwise advised the same as now: but the point was not the same as this point. Because in that one it was said that he had a special mandate. And truly, understanding special mandate, there is no doubt: that it causes the principal to incur the penalty; otherwise not, unless the principal has ratified it. As C. De cohaereditatibus, l. Si apparitor, lib. 12. And therefore he said with himself according to what is proposed. It makes. D. De transactionibus, l. Ut responsum. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the person in whose name money is paid before ratification is subject to the statute of limitations; and whether he is deemed to ratify by the very fact that he acts on the basis of the contract itself.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Point. Whether prescription runs against the person in whose name the money is counted before ratification; and whether he is understood to ratify by the very fact that he acts on the basis of the contract itself. By acting on the basis of the aforementioned contract, the said Silvester appears to have ratified, as in *l. cum queritur*, D. de administratione tutorum; and D. si certum non petatur, *l. periculum*; and D. de rebus ratis habitis, *l. Paulus respondit*. And from that day on which it was held ratified, the statutory prescription appears to begin, and not before; because before ratification, action could not be taken. For prescription does not run when one is impeded from acting, as in C. de annali exceptione, *l. 1*, in fine. But certainly with regard to contracts: because ratification is drawn back retroactively, as in c. *Ratum*, de regulis iuris, lib. 6; and when an action is available solely by the will of the actor, it is imputed to him if he does not act. Hence, if you promised me ten, if I demand it immediately, prescription runs, because I could have demanded it immediately, according to Guillaume de Coucy. And even for ratifying, prescription runs, as in D. de rebus ratis habitis, *l. bonorum*. Wherefore it seems to me that in our case there is prescription, and that action cannot be brought. And so I say, and I advise, I, Baldus de Ubaldis, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A concession granted to someone, that he may build near the land of Clusa through the land of a certain N. and beyond through the same land, by these words, and beyond does not extend to other properties not belonging to the said N., nor does it establish a servitude. The same in the following opinion.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Point. The words of a certain contract state thus, that Peter may build near the land of Clusa through the land of a certain Lucia, and beyond through the same land, as much as is necessary by the retention of waters for his own mill for grinding.

It is asked whether the term "beyond" extends to other properties of the said Lucia not contiguous to the said Sluice, and whether the said words create a servitude, such that one may build adjacent to the said properties, and whether a new purchaser from the said Lucia of one of the said non-contiguous properties may prohibit that structures be made adjacent to the purchased property, and what is the law. The doubt lies in those extensive words, "and beyond through that very land, as much as will be necessary for the retention of waters, for the mill grinding." Whether these extensive words comprehend any places whatsoever, and those not contiguous to the said Sluice. And I believe that the said words, although they are extensive, nevertheless do not comprehend places distant from the Sluice, because those words "for the retention of waters" must be understood with reference to the Sluice. And because, according to what is contained in the point, the said structures were not made in the land of the said Lucia, but adjacent to the said land, hence the agreement concerning such structures does not speak. As in D. de contrahenda emptione, l. ruralia. And to the above it contributes that ambiguous words are interpreted against him who wishes to extend them to his own manner. As in D. de pactis, l. veteribus with its material. And from the above it follows that the said purchaser is not bound to suffer the said structures to stand thus, because they cannot be said to have been made by right of servitude outside the land of the said Lucia. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, etc. The same as above.

CONSILIVM XVI.

In the Name of Christ, Amen.

It seems to me for two reasons that those words "and beyond through that very land" refer only to the land where the head of the Sluice is built; and this is conveyed by the term "that very." For this term is relative and restrictive. And every relation of "that very" refers to the species, not to the genus, unless the writing could not otherwise be saved. As in D. de hereditatibus instituendis, l. Iulia. Furthermore, because the words are ambiguous, for they must be interpreted against the proferens, i.e., against him who wishes to extend them to his own advantage, as is read and noted in D. de pactis, l. veteribus. Although it is not permitted to restrict against the nature of the words, nevertheless doubtful words are to be strictly interpreted, as in D. de verborum obligatione, l. quicquid astringendae. Therefore, in another land of Lucia than the land where the head of the Sluice is, it is not permitted to build by virtue of the said words. And for this reason, it is lawful for the purchaser of another land, to which indeed no servitude has been imposed, to prohibit that building take place. And if building has taken place, that it be demolished; because on a free estate nothing can be rebuilt against the will of the owner. As in l. 1, D. quod vi aut clam. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The person presented by the greater part of the patrons is preferred to the person presented by the lesser part. See also nos. 3 and 4.
2. The collation of a patronal benefice is invalid if the presentation by the patrons has not been awaited.
3. Whether the person presented by the lesser part of the patrons may oppose the election made in favor of the person presented by the greater part.
4. When only one person is presented, he ought to be instituted; but if two are chosen in discord, then he who is presented by the greater part shall prevail. And if the patron first presents one person and afterwards another, the condition of the one who is instituted shall be stronger.
5. In the collation or confirmation to be made regarding the person presented by the greater part, whether the person instituted or elected by the lesser part must be cited; and consequently, whether the subsequent institution is valid without citing the aforementioned person. And what if the person elected by the lesser part has stated extrajudicially, in the presence of witnesses, to the collator that he is content for another person elected by the greater part to be instituted: whether in that case also the citation of the said person elected by the greater part is required.
body:
In the Name of Christ. Amen. The case is stated as follows. The parish of Saint Mary of the Castle of Fructa in the diocese of Fano became vacant through the death of Master Bartolomeo, its rector. The abbot of the monastery of Saint Apollinaris of Classe of the Camaldolese Order, to whom the institution of the parish priest pertains, instituted Master Augustine of the said Castle as parish priest of the said parish. However, the election and nomination of the said parish priest pertains to the parishioners, and the right of presenting the rector for the governance of the said parish belongs to them. Yet the collation of the said parish to the said Master Augustine was made without any election or presentation of the said Master Augustine having been made by the said parishioners. Finally, the aforementioned abbot, to whose knowledge the injury to the rights of the said parishioners subsequently came, decreed and declared the said collation of the said parish to the said Master Augustine to be null and void, without citing the said Master Augustine. When the said parishioners wished to preserve their rights and elect a rector, they fell into discord: the majority of the parishioners elected Master George Crestis, while the minority elected Master Augustine. Moreover, the said elections were made before the said abbot conferred the said church upon the said Master Augustine. Furthermore, the said elections were made within the four-month period granted to lay patrons for electing. It is further stated in the case that the aforementioned election of the said Master George, or the presentation made on behalf of those who elected him to the said lord abbot, to whom the institution of the elected person pertains, nevertheless the said elected person was not then instituted, but the said abbot suspended the institution. Moreover, the said Master Augustine was not presented to the said abbot within the said four-month period.

Therefore, the case is stated as follows: after the provision made to the said Master Augustine of the said parish, and even after the said abbot had declared the said provision to be null, the said parishioners made new elections. The majority of the parishioners elected the said Master George, and the minority elected the said Master Augustine. The abbot, however, confirmed the election made of the said Master George. Consequently, it is stated in the case that the said last elections were made within the four-month period from the day of the vacation of the said rectory, but no presentation was made within the four-month period because the monastery was then vacant; thus there was no abbot to whom presentation could be made. Presentation of the said Master George was made to the said abbot after the said four-month period, and the said Master George was instituted as parish priest of the said parish. Now, from the aforementioned facts, many doubts arise.

First, because two elections were held, one of Lord George by the greater part of the parishioners, and another of Lord Augustine by the greater part of the parishioners, which of these is void. I answer, that which was made of Lord George by the greater part of the parishioners. From the law of patrons, chapter "When," where the case is.

† The second doubt is whether the provision made by the abbot in favor of Lord Augustine is valid. I answer that such provision is null by operation of law; because when a church has a patron, the superior to whom the right of institution belongs cannot institute a person who has not been elected and presented by the patron. But the aforementioned abbot provided for the said vicarage in favor of Lord Augustine without any presentation or election of the said Lord Augustine having been made to him, as stated in *de officio*, *de legibus*, c. *Dilectus*; *de iure patronatus*, c. *Cum dilectus*; and 16 q. 7, c. *Decernimus*. It must also be observed that, although before the provision made to Lord Augustine regarding the said church, the said Lord Augustine had been elected, nevertheless the election was null by operation of law, because it was made by a minority of the parishioners, as stated in the aforementioned chapter *Quam*. Moreover, that abbot did not provide for that Lord Augustine as an elected person; rather, he provided for him by way of collation, and at the time of the provision the abbot did not believe that the church had patrons; indeed, he was ignorant of this fact. And thus the provision itself appears to be null, as is clear from the aforementioned laws.

The third doubt concerns the rights of declaration regarding the nullity of the said provision made to the said Lord Augustine, because the abbot declared that provision null. I answer that he could declare it null, because it was null. But it must be noted that this declaration is certainly judicial, because it was not made in the form of a judgment; but if the matter were litigated in court, the declaration would be made in a similar manner. And what is obtained by means of the nullity of the said provision and collation, whatever it may be concerning the said declaration made by the abbot alone, as I have said above, the said election made of the said Lord Augustine is null by operation of law, and furthermore the collation made of the said church to the said Lord Augustine is null by operation of law.

The fourth doubt concerns the last elections made for the aforementioned Lord George and Lord Augustine. And it must be noted: that by law no election was made for Lord Augustine, because it was made by the lesser part of the patrons. As stated in the cited chapter *Quam ergo*. Therefore, it is inferred from this that the election made for Lord George by the greater part of the patrons is valid. However, it must be said that since the said Lord George was elected by the said parishioners, namely, first before the abbot provided for the said church to the said Lord Augustine, and secondly he was elected after the provision made for Lord Augustine, that the said Lord George has the choice whether he wishes to rely on the first or the second election made for him. The case is found in the chapter *Quis duas*, on elections, Book 6.

The fifth doubt is whether the aforementioned Lord Augustine can oppose the election made of the said Lord George. Answer: Either he wishes to oppose on the ground that he claims the said parish was collated to him by the said abbot; and on this ground he cannot, because the said provision was null by operation of law. Or he wishes to oppose on the ground that he claims to have been elected. Again, on this ground he cannot, because the election itself is null by operation of law. Thus, on these grounds, it does not avail him to oppose, because he has no right. And thus, by opposing, he is repelled. The case is from the chapter Cum inter, in the title De electione. R. Senior.

† Nevertheless, it is doubtful whether the aforementioned Lord George ought to be instituted as the parish priest of the said parish by the said abbot. I set forth three cases: first, when a single person is presented by the patron; and he ought to be instituted, according to the exception in *c. Significavit*. For the right to request institution competes tacitly to the possessor, according to *de re iudicata*, *c. Cum Bertoldus*. The second case is when two are elected in discord. And then he ought to be instituted who is presented by the greater part of the patrons, as stated in the aforementioned *c. Quam*. The third case is when the patron presents one person in the first place, and after the first presentation, presents a second; and then it is doubtful to whom the right of instituting the first or the second pertains; and the condition of him who is instituted is the stronger. And this applies when the presentation pertains to the patrons, according to *de iure patronatus*, *c. Pastoralis*, where the case appears to be found. In our case, however, two were elected in discord. Thirdly, he ought to be instituted who is elected by the greater part, as was the case with the aforementioned Lord George.

† Thus far, certain doubts have been resolved; it remains to determine others, namely whether it was necessary to issue an edict or to make a specific citation of the said coheir by the minority party, such that, if the said citation is omitted while the adversary is certain and specifically citable, the confirmation of the said election is rendered void. Indeed, so that the institution made to the election of the patrons is null by operation of law. This is determined by the text and gloss of c. ult. de electione, lib. 6. Nevertheless, it must be considered that before the said Abbot proceeded to the confirmation or institution of the said Lord Georgius, the said Lord Augustinus presented himself before the said Lord Abbot. And the said Lord Abbot notified him that, as a matter of law, he was obliged to institute the said Lord Georgius; and the said Lord Augustinus had the opportunity to respond, stating that, since this was the case, he was content. However, no instrument was drawn up regarding this, but it can be testified to by three or four witnesses. The question now arises whether the said confirmation or subsequent institution is valid without another citation of the said Lord Augustinus. It must be said that it is valid; because such knowledge, especially when consent intervenes, has the force of a peremptory edict, as stated in C. quoniam et quando iudex, l. cessante, and as noted by Innocentius in de officio delegati, c. consuluit. Furthermore, since the purpose of citation is for the party to appear, it follows that one who has appeared is considered cited, as noted in the argument of c. ult. de electione, lib. 6, and in Novella ventilatum, de iure patronatus. Since the merits of both parties have been heard and intimated to the parties, and there was no objection, but rather concession, as in C. si per vim vel alio modo, l. fin. Moreover, because it is established before the judge, i.e., the said Abbot, if I may say he holds the part of the cognitor under whatever name, it is considered by law that the said Lord Georgius upheld justice, and the said Lord Augustinus could not object except through calumny. Therefore, the truth being known and examined, he could proceed to the said institution, because just as an irregular plaintiff should not be heard, so too a calumnious defendant, whose calumny is notorious, should not be cited further. Supporting the above is what is noted by Innocentius in de filiis presbyterorum, constitutio de officio vicarii, c. 1; C. de falsis, aperte; ff. de pactis, l. tale pactum, §. qui provocante; ff. de carborum edicto, l. 3, §. causae, and §. dicunt causae; ff. ad exhibendum, l. 3, §. ibidem. It must also be known that witness proofs operate in the same manner as documentary proofs, as in C. de fideiussoribus, l. in exercendis, and C. de pactis, l. pactum quod bona fide, and as noted in C. de haereticis, l. quoniam, and 25. q. 2, c. institutionis. Hence, from these it is clearly concluded that the affirmation of the said Lord Georgius was ultimately valid and effective, and the above can be proven by witnesses. Many other things could be alleged and said, which it is not expedient to allege, because it seems to me that this is the truth, especially since subsequently, after the said institution and collation made to the said Lord Georgius, the above were notified to him by the same Lord Abbot verbally. And the said Lord Augustinus did not object. For I say this, that if the institution had not held due to omitted citation, the subsequent notification would suffice due to the irregular procedure. But I say, and have said, that the preceding notification made by the Abbot at that time, without any fixed term, since the said Lord Augustinus did not request a term to oppose, nor did he oppose anything, having been certified both of the fact and of the intention of the said Lord Abbot, was valid both under ancient law and under the newest law, c. ult. de electione, lib. 6.
