And supporting this is c. eum qui certus, de regulis iuris, lib. 6, and in c. non praestat impedimentum, and there noted in ff. de re iudicata, l. de unoquoque, §. scientibus, and noted in c. quamvis, de re iudicata, by Innocentius. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A person appointed to an office by a superior may be removed by a subordinate on account of his own fault or negligence.
2. What right an appointee has to serve in a certain chapel.
3. Whether an appointment may be made by laymen.
1. The action for an inofficious will cannot be brought whenever the will... 2. Regarding this first point. † Now I come to the records, and I say that it is declared null, since they are contradictory.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen. Assuming as established that in the general assembly a certain Lord Thomas was elected and presented as the officiator of the lower chapel of Sant'Ercolano situated in Porta San Pietro; and assuming as established that the lords prior and the chamberlains, on account of the asserted bad morals and misrule of Lord Thomas, removed him from the said officiating of the said chapel and appointed the religious and honest man Lord Antonio; it is asked to whom are owed the civic loaves, the six baskets of grain, and the 25 pounds of pennies assigned annually by the ordinance of the commune of Perugia: whether to the said Brother Thomas, who has been removed from the act of administration, or to the said Lord Antonio, the officiator. I answer that they are owed to the said Lord Antonio, the officiator, and not to the said Lord Thomas, who was removed from office, as in ff. de excu. tut. l. quid autem. in the last response, joined with l. sed reprobari. in princi. of the same title; for the authority of the general assembly is no obstacle, because here nothing is done against the authority, nor against the power of the people by an inferior authority. For [if this were not so], that would be possible, but rather justice is administered to the chapel of Sant'Ercolano on account of the negligence of the governor. And it is similar to when the Emperor has appointed someone as tutor, and that tutor subsequently abandons his duty by negligence or renders himself suspect, incapable, or unworthy, the municipal magistrate can remove him—I say this on the supposition that the municipal magistrate has some general jurisdiction over removing tutors disregarded under negligence; whence here it is not the authority of the tutor that is weighed, but the vice of the administration; arg. C. de adop. l. adoptatum. Although here it is that, even if someone is apostolic [i.e., appointed by papal provision] and has obtained it, nevertheless through his own defects and neglects he can be removed by the diocesan [bishop]; to conclude against the said Lord Thomas that he could be removed, as in ff. de iniu. test. l. centurio. and ff. de solu. l. dispensatori; for the benefits are owed to the administrator, not to him who is removed from the act, as noted in C. de ser. fug. l. emancipia. and in l. vnica. C. de primipillo. li. 12. And it must also be known that the officiator of this chapel is not the rector of the chapel, because the canonical title of rector cannot be conferred except by the diocesan bishop, but he is the officiator of the chapel, and the office lasts as long as it pleases the lord and the one holding the place of the lordship. Likewise, he can revoke the act of the lord for cause, as in ff. mandati. l. hominem; and therefore it is finally concluded that the said baskets of grain and the said money are owed at their due time to the said Brother Antonio, the officiator, and not to the said Lord Thomas, who is alleged to be an erring and removed person. And therefore, having seen the petition of the said Lord Thomas and the response of the said Lord Antonio, and considering that labor and money admit of division, as in ff. de annu. lega. l. Seyo., payment ought to be made to each according to the proportion of the time during which he was in the service of the said chapel; so that, if payment was made to the said Lord Thomas for the time during which he served, nothing more is owed to him, but rather to the said Lord Antonio. And thus I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Both Laws, etc., state and advise. And the allegation is first, because the querela inofficiosi testamenti cannot be brought whenever the will is said to be void, because these things are contrary at their origin. For if the will is void, the inheritance cannot be entered upon; and if the inheritance cannot be entered upon, the querela inofficiosi requires that the inheritance be entered upon; but in the said petition it is concluded that the will is void: therefore, the petition is inept, self-contradictory, and consequently incompatible, which is explained as follows: for in the said disinheritance it is stated that the causes are not sufficient for disinheritance, and from this it is concluded that the will is void. Likewise, from the fact that an action is brought by the querela inofficiosi testamenti, from this it is concluded that the will is valid, and that the inheritance from the will was entered upon; and these things are entirely contrary, wherefore the petition is void by operation of law and inept, because he who puts forward contradictory claims defeats himself, as the laws say. Likewise, the said petition is inept for another reason: because the said Bartolomeo acts by a petition of inheritance before he is or can be an heir, even if the causes of disinheritance do not cease, which are nevertheless true and formal. Finally, it is set forth, etc., and to which [...] of the aforesaid let articles of ingratitude be framed both with the place and the time preceding the will, so that the causes conclude from the matter and from the time.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If there is a dispute as to whether someone died in the age of a pupillus or in adulthood, the burden of proof falls either on the mother bringing the action or on the other party in possession.
2. How age is proved, and no. 4.
3. A witness testifying about age using the word "I believe" proves nothing.
4. In proving age, presumptive evidence is sufficient.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen. The fact is as follows. A certain Vannus died in Rome having made a testament, in which he instituted his son Franciscus, and Petrus and Franciscus, his grandsons by another predeceased son, as his universal heirs in equal shares: so that the share of whoever should predecease would revert to the others. The testator died: next, it is stated that his grandson Franciscus died during pupillary age, while his paternal uncle Franciscus, his own full brother, and Lady Santessa, his mother, were still surviving: then the said Petrus died. Now there is a dispute concerning the succession between the said Lady Santessa and the said Franciscus. For the said Franciscus says that the entire inheritance pertains to him, on the ground that he asserts the said Petrus died during pupillary age; which the mother denies, saying that he died at adult age. Whence the first question remains, upon whom lies the burden of proving age, whether upon the mother as plaintiff, or upon the said Franciscus as possessor. The second question is: whether from the court records the pupillary age of the said Petrus who died last has been proved, so that the mother is barred because she did not seek a tutor by virtue of that substitution, since it is a fideicommissary one. It is established that the substitution does not exclude the mother entirely, but she would be excluded on account of her negligence in failing to request a tutor if the son died during pupillary age: otherwise if he died at adult age, as in C. ad Tertu. l. matris.

† Concerning the first question, I consider that it seems the proof lies upon the plaintiff, namely that she must prove the age that supports her, as noted in ff. de mino. l. 1. And so says Jacobus de Arena, that whoever sues or raises an exception concerning age must prove that age which is the cause of their action or exception; and to the same effect is ff. de proba. l. cum de aetate. I say the contrary by another rule: for whenever anyone wishes to exclude another from any right that belongs to them by natural or civil law, they must prove that by which the other is excluded; otherwise they fail in the suit, as in ff. de proba. l. ab ea parte. Whence he who wishes to exclude a mother from the succession, which is owed to her by natural affection and reason, as in ff. de inof. test. l. nam et si parentibus, must prove it by the said rule of the said law. Furthermore, he who says that the mother is excluded by reason of not having requested a tutor alleges a delict of the mother, as in C. si aduer. delic. l. fi., although it is not properly a crime, as noted there, yet because by the argument from effect it is regarded as a crime, since it deprives the mother of goods owed to her by quasi-natural law. Likewise he alleges presumed fraud and negligence; therefore the burden of proof lies on him, as in ff. de proba. l. quotiens ergo qui dolo. And therefore I say that he who alleges pupillary age against the mother must prove this, namely that the son died during pupillary age. And this concerning the first point.
† Now I come to the court records, and I say that Joannes does not prove the minor age, because a witness who deposes using the word

† "believes" proves nothing, as noted in ff. de arbi. l. diem proferre. §. si plures. Likewise Lady Jacoba does not prove it: because in order to prove age it is required to prove the beginning and the end of the time, since age is nothing other than a certain measure of time running from birth until death. To this effect is what is noted by Jac. de Are. on C. de testibus. l. testium; but see especially what is noted in consilia 51 and 52. She does not state in which year he was born, but only an uncertain month. And therefore the computation of time does not appear from her testimony: because the computation of the period is made with respect to years, months, days, and hours; and therefore certainty concerning these must be established through the statement of the witness, so that the witnesses depose conclusively and render a reason based upon bodily sense. In this manner the other witnesses do not seem to prove it, because they do not render a sufficient cause based upon bodily sense, nor through a certain division of time, since they do not depose concerning the year; and thus certainty of time cannot be had. For to prove time it is required that the year be proved, as in Auth. vt praeponatur nomen imperatoris. §. 1.

† It is true that in proving age conjectural proofs are sufficient, as in ff. de proba. l. cum de aetate, and maternal testimony or assertion would be worth much, as in l. etiam matris. in the same title, unless the mother herself were an adversary; for one would not believe a father in the case of l. vltima, C. de fideius. Whence it seems that by reason of uncertainty and of the cause not being rendered based upon bodily sense, the said witnesses do not prove sufficiently, although they establish a strong conjecture. And that age must be conclusively proved is clear in extra de proba. c. cum in praesentiam. But because the aforesaid matters are somewhat difficult, I say that the said mother has the right, because she has moreover proved by sufficient proof the adult age of the said Petrus. And therefore she succeeds him ab intestato; however, by virtue of the said substitution, the said Franciscus, [the son] of the said testator, ought to have half of the said inheritance and goods, as in c. Ray. and in c. Raynaldus and c. si pater. de testa. And so I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Both Laws, etc., state and advise.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a legacy for pious causes is proved by three witnesses.
2. In legacies for pious causes, acceptance by the heir is not required, nor is the Falcidian deduction taken.
3. How the title is proved.
4. How good faith is proved.
5. How possession and its continuity are proved.
6. The longest possession is never presumed to be clandestine.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† On the first point, which asks whether a legacy to pious causes is proved by three witnesses who are consistent in effect, although they do not refer to the words in one and the same immediate speech. I answer, as regards the number of witnesses, and I say that, according to civil law, three witnesses are not sufficient, as C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, l. generali. But according to canon law, three witnesses are sufficient, indeed even two: because a testament to pious causes is judged by divine law, not human law, as in c. de testibus, c. cum esses and c. relatum. And therefore, if it is necessary that the witnesses be rogated: because the rogation of witnesses was not introduced by divine law, but by human law, as Inst. de testamento ordinando, §. j. But it is far from the case that divine law, disposing of divine matters, is collated by human law, as noted in C. de usuris, auth. ad haec. Because a slave cannot abrogate the law of his master, and especially in those things that induce a legacy, such as to deny to churches and pious places under the pretext of knowledge of civil law, for interest, not before error is committed, as ff. de verborum obligatione, l. si servum, §. sequitur non ob. The glossators say that divine law is distinguished by human law, and an example is given in testaments, as noted in C. si contra ius vel utilitatem publicam, l. fi. and ff. de constitutionibus principum, l. 1. Because that is wonderful among laymen, but not as regards churches, as extra de constitutionibus, c. ecclesia sanctae Mariae.

† Since they here doubt whether, in such bequests, acceptance of the inheritance is required for their confirmation, and it seems that it is, as in the case of a legate in a military testament, in which the ordinatorial solemnity is not required, but only the confirmatory one, as in D. de stipulationibus servorum, l. si servus communis vicini, and D. de peculio castrensi, at the end of the principle, and l. si nemo, D. de regulis iuris; but the contrary is true: because for the confirmation of legacies which partake of piety, from which the Falcidian deduction is not made, the testator being prohibited, acceptance of the inheritance is not required, as in Auth. de haereditate et fideicommissis, l. § si non expressum, and there by Jacobus de Belvis, consilium. In the third place, if the Falcidian law prohibits, and the extension of the legacy is meritorious: and this is held by the Speculum in the title de instrumentis edicti. Moreover, acceptance of the inheritance is required so that an action arising from the testament and a hypothecary action with its consequences may arise. For such an action consists in the subject of the obligation, but an obligation requires persons; yet before the inheritance is accepted, there is no person who is bound; but in bequests for the soul, actions are acquired to the office of the judge, with every obligation circumscribed, as in D. de petitione hereditatis, l. hereditas, at the end; and therefore it pertains to the authority of the judge, just as a legacy for expenses, and similar things, as in D. de annuis legatis, l. Quintus Pomponius. Moreover, it must be considered that sometimes solemnity is remitted in favor of the testator: as in the soldier; sometimes in favor of him to whom it is bequeathed, as in § ex imperfecto; sometimes in favor of the cause for which it is bequeathed, as in C. ad pios usus, pro dimidia testatoris. And this case is more favorable according to canon law; hence I hold that the legacy made to the said church of Saint Bartholomew, equity of canon law being considered, is sufficiently proved. Nor does the objection hold regarding the diversity of narration, where the same conclusion arises: because the statements of witnesses should not be cavilled at, as in Extr. de verborum obligatione, l. quae extrinsecus. Nor can anyone say otherwise, saving conscience, nor even saving the rigor of canon law, as in the cited c. cum esses, and c. relatum. And this is the first point. On the second point, which is very prolix in effect, although concise in words, namely, whether, the acts being considered, it is proved

† As to the intention of the acquirer, it must be said that, with regard to the first principle of the Publician claim for recovery of property, which is peculiar to the defendant, it is undoubtedly proven: because the defendant asserts that he possesses. See Codex, On Alienation by Judgment, l. ex donatione. But as to the action on the part of the plaintiff, it must be considered first whether it is proven, yet, that it suffices in the Publician action, considering for Bartolus that the plaintiff has no foundational intention, and considering the proving and the obstacles thereto, and the difficulty of the instrument arises due to the variety of witnesses on this side and that. And it must be considered: that the principle of prescription of long time is title, good faith, and acquired possession, vacant naturally and not impeded, as in c. siue potest. and c. malaefidei. and de usuc. trans. l. 1. §. 1. and Pet. and noted by Dy. Codex, On Proof, l. cum res. The estimation of prescription begun in its principles is substantial; nor is continued good faith required by civil law or by canon law. The Publician action does not have its principles, and requires prescription begun, and not continued. See Institutes, On Actions, §. alia. For error caused by probable and plausible conjectures, and those which seem to conclude to the substance of the truth, is held as title, to found the beginning of prescription, and also to bring it to consummation by the passage of time, as in Digest, On Usucaption, l. celsus. Nevertheless, it is not required that it suffice in the Publician action, because in the Publician action the buyer requires title at the beginning: because by it a thing not usucapted is claimed, and in this it exceeds the claim for recovery of property, and therefore it must be put to consummation. These things being premised, let us come individually to the substantial articles of the plaintiff: and to the proofs, and depositions of witnesses thereon. The article of the abbot says that the thing claimed pertained to the saint. Another article says that after the death of the said saint it pertained to Marcus, his son. Another article says that the inheritance of the son pertained to Lady Agnes, his mother. Another article says that the said Lady Agnes bequeathed the said fund, concerning which there is question, to the church, and possessed it for a long time. And in the said articles it is said how the said saint possessed for many years, and then Marcus, and then Lady Agnes, and then the said church as legatee, and if the times are numbered and joined: because they ought to be joined. See Digest, On Acquisition of Possession, l. Pompo. §. cum quis.

† It is certain that it has been pleaded concerning a very long period of time, in which prescription of a very long time suffices with good faith without title, as in C. de praescri. 30. an. l. si quis emptiones. Such good faith is presumed in so long and undisturbed possession. Innocentius, extra de restitutione in integrum, c. 2. even if no other cause from which good faith arises is proved, although the rule is different in the pact of long time, as noted by Jacobus de Aretio, C. de acquisitione possessionis, l. in proba. and by Cynus in l. placet, C. de praescriptione longi temporis. If, however, these articles have been proved and not disproved, the plaintiff has founded the origin of his petition and ought to prevail, as in C. de exceptionibus, l. siquidem videamus. Thirdly, whether the articles are proved and placed in proof, namely that he possessed for ten years, and of the possession of Marcus for three years, and of the possession of Lady Agnes for ten years, and of the possession of the church of Saint Bartholomew for a period of twelve years and more; and the benefit of continuing possession passes to the one having a subordinate title, and whether without interruption of possession, and immediately from the said periods taken cumulatively results a very long prescription; thirdly, however, the plaintiff proved useful dominion, and thus he ought to obtain judgment. And if it is said that prescription does not run against a church, even by another church, in a shorter time than forty years, nevertheless, when one intends to prescribe a thing of the church, but here the time of prescription is that which is in question, and therefore the intention of the said abbot seems well-founded from subordinate titles: and if many things together at the end were proved to be substantive or interruptive, I say it is true: that the intention of the plaintiff is proved as regards the first chapters concerning the filiation of the said Marcus.

† Furthermore, regarding the fact that the said Marcus possessed: because the witness who testifies concerning acts concluding possession, as in the law and note, C. finium regum; l. si quis supra and ff. de sol. l. Titia; and C. de agri. et cen. l. litibus. §. hoc de redditibus. li. 10, it is remarkable that concerning the quantity of time the prior witness speaks of some title dubiously: because memory easily fails regarding punctual time: because there is someone who remembers the point of time, as ff. de acqui. poss. l. peregre. in prin. and note in c. qualiter, et quando. extra de accu. per Inn. Moreover, although the witness says it is so according to his sight, yet if he afterwards subjoins the sense of sight, it is certain that the addition of sight proves, insofar as the words of the witness allow: because the reason which attends the statement is more considered, as ff. de leg. 2. l. cum pater. §. dulcissimis. From that possession of the saint arises the possession of Marcus and the son, and it is quasi continued in him, as noted ff. de acqui. pos. l. cum haeredes. and l. cum mili. ff. quibus ex causis maio. not that actual possession passes without pension. sometimes the son would not be entitled to the benefit of acquiring possession, which is false. ar. in l. credo. and de edicto diui Adria. tol. But it passes, and is continued for the effect: which is to usucapt and to take the fruits his own: which he himself, or another for him, perceived. I say to take from some special putative title, for example as a buyer: because he presumed to have anticipated, or to have had another title by probable assumption. for the title as heir does not fall upon his own, as C. de vsucapione pro haerede. l. nihil. But another title well falls upon him even from the person of the father, as ff. de acqui. pos. l. 3. §. ex pluribus. and fully noted ff. de vsuca. l. celsus. And if it is said, and further inquired, whether actual possession of Marcus is proved. I answer thus, nor is it remarkable that for proving the prior proof of some age is required: because he who wishes to say another cannot possess by reason of age: must prove the impeding age. in any permissible act age conferring to the act is presumed, unless the contrary is proved, as noted ff. de arbi. l. 3. Furthermore I say. that although the witness by judgment of reason alone does not prove. by reason from all sense the act, yet by reason joined to sense he proves, hence the witness, who has knowledge of law, and fact, proves also those things which are of law, as in Auth. de non alienan. §. quod autem and ff. de ventre inspicien. l. 1. in prin. and ff. de ver. ob. l. 1. in fi. and therefore the witness, who saw first the father, then the son possess: could prove that he possessed as an hereditary thing, as C. de repu. hęredi. l. 1. because this happens to be, that reason supports the sense. And therefore not insisting on many words, I think the intention of the plaintiff founded on title, and possession, not only long, but very long, is proved, nor is anything obstructive to the plaintiff, or repulsive to the plaintiff, or repulsive sufficiently, or conclusively proved. For just as on the part of the plaintiff the proofs of the plaintiff must be conclusive, or strongly supporting with supplements of those proofs, as extra de succes. abintesta. c. cum dilectus. Furthermore much more strongly repulsive proofs, and exclusive of the daughters sufficient proofs, as I will say, and conclude, that those who must win, who prove, and conclusively as C. de edicto diui Adria. l. edicto. §. pe. and noted by Cy. C. de rebus creditis. l. in bonę fidei.

† It must be known that the longest possession is never presumed to be clandestine, even if another person possessed it at an earlier time: because that earlier possession is considered abolished, it is deemed lawful. D. de usucap. l. fur. § fundum and l. quaero. de usucap. § quod autem ad eas. and C. de serv. fugit. l. 1. and by Dynus in c. sine possessione. and after Innocentius in c. 2. de restit. in integr. From all of which the final conclusion clearly emerges, namely that when the plaintiff proves his case, the defendant is to be condemned, as stated in the aforementioned l. si quidem. C. de except. and C. de probat. l. siue possidetis. By which law the continuity of right, and also of possession, is proven, and even the supreme authority affirms that he who previously possessed is presumed to have possessed at the time of his death, if his son or heir asserts this, unless the contrary is proven. For to prove possession at the extreme moment of death, when memory and understanding are lacking, as in C. de his qui test. facere poss. l. hac consultissima. § at cum humana, would be in a manner impossible, or at least difficult: but how does one dying retain possession? How does one sleeping retain it? Sufficiently. Therefore, I openly conclude that judgment should be rendered in favor of the plaintiff, notwithstanding the most subtle allegations made to the contrary, which I believe were made rather to display the power of wit by arguing and subtletizing than to support the final conclusion. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Both Laws, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an omission or nullity of citation renders the proceeding null.
2. And whether, if a statute prohibits raising an objection of nullity, such nullity is understood to be excluded, or that which arises from a defect of jurisdiction.
3. One who is to be registered ought not to be considered as registered, but as cancelled, since one who is about to be cancelled forthwith ought to be considered as cancelled.
4. A defect which is easily proven by the records to be evident and notorious ought to be so regarded.
5. The crime of falsity is sometimes ambition, and yet it is not punished as falsity.
6. What barataria is.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

A proceeding conducted against a person not cited is null by natural law, as in the chapter *Pasto*, *De re iudicata*, in the Clementines. Moreover, if you have not been cited by him, because a citation that does not hold good effects nothing, as noted in the Code, *De accusationibus*, law *Si quis accusatoribus*. And citation is the beginning of extraordinary jurisdiction, as in the Institutes, *De periculis temere litigantium*, § *Finis*. And where there is no beginning, it is not possible, with the order overturned, to proceed from the substantial matters to further steps, as in the law *De uno quoque* and the law *Prolatam*.

† and therefore if it is not established that there was a citation, or if the nullity of the citation is established, and even if the nullity could not be opposed by virtue of some statute, nevertheless the judge must supply this ex officio by denying execution, not as a cognizant judge, but as a good man and mere minister of the law. To this effect serves what is noted in C. de transactionibus, l. ubi pater. For the law itself is read, and he speaks as written law, not as a disputant. Hence this ought to be called a supply of the law, rather than of the judge, as elegantly noted by Innocentius in c. Raynaldus, in fine, de testamentis. Hence, assuming such a statute, and even if he could not pronounce [a judgment], nevertheless he ought to cease from the grievance in the principal matter, rather than in the execution. To this effect, ff. de iudiciis solutis, l. vir bonus. For that which is null in itself is null in its accessory. ff. de re iudicata, l. si cum nulla. Moreover, this process, when it is established that there was no citation, or not, or before [proper citation], has no validity nor form, as ff. de falsis, l. si quis legatum. And if this applies, I say that if someone is registered among the accused, whose registration has no substance, it is held as unwritten, which ought to have been written, nor could it be. C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, l. iubemus, §. his tabellionibus; in Auth. de non alienando, §. quia vero Leonis; C. de donationibus, l. sancimus, in principio. Hence neither the stain of the act, nor infamy, ought to be imposed. C. de famosis libellis, l. 1. The character, namely the marrow, lies beneath, and the truth which is usurped from incongruous sources. As C. de testamentis, l. consulta diualia. Hence registration, which is not made by the authority of law, lacks name and effect. C. de probationibus, l. cum precibus. And also cancellation, unless it is made by due authority, is null by the evidence of the thing, and the evidence of the thing is the same as that which is notorious, impressed upon its knowledge, plainly displaying itself to the eyes of those who look, as l. emptorem, in principio, de actione empti. And that which is notorious by public office cannot be concealed by any tergiversation. C. qui et adversus quos, l. 1, in glossa. Just as a candelabrum placed on a mountain cannot be concealed, nor a circle placed at an inn. For writing placed before the rostra, l. 2, de origine iuris; de institoria, l. sed et si pupillus, n. proscribere. Hence the office of the inquisitor, once found, could not ignore it, nor the statutes of Florence, which he had sworn to observe; for by not observing them, the inquisitor himself incurs perjury. Nevertheless, by this he does not lose his effects, unless he is deposed. C. ad legem Iuliam repetundarum, l. si; C. de falsis, l. si quis decurio. And note ff. de infa, l. 2, §. nullorum. For all things which require the cognition of the cause demand the sentence of the judging authority. As ff. de poenis, l. quod ad statutum; and l. iubemus, §. economus, cum si.

Having premised these things, let us first consider jurisdiction, upon which the power of judgments is founded. As C. si a non competente iudice, per totum. Hence a sentence given by a non-judge is rather a famous libel, i.e., a writing, than a sentence, since it does not even merit having the name of sentence, as ff. de in ius vocando, l. si quis filio exheredato, §. quod si quis. And even if it had some name, it nevertheless does not have the effect of the name, whenever it ought to be invalidated from the beginning, as there noted very elegantly. Who is this prince? The Magnificent and Illustrious Commune of the Florentines. This jurisdiction is sometimes withdrawn on account of forum privilege, sometimes removed on account of prohibition. Sometimes it is suspended; in our case it is prohibited and suspended in favor of a certain person, but in favor of the entire principal order, i.e., the prior lords. Hence that which is attempted to the contrary does not become valid. As C. quoniam provocatio non est necessaria, l. veteribus; and C. de quaestionibus, l. decuriones. To this effect serves C. ad legem Falcidiam, de plagio, l. non valet; ff. de poenis, l. 2; and C. de poenis, l. partium. And wherever the law or statute makes mention of a sentence, it is necessary to presuppose jurisdiction in habit and act. As noted in c. 1, de sequestro possessionis; and de restitutione spoliati, c. olim, 3. Innocentius says that he who does not have jurisdiction cannot assign a delay, de rescriptis, c. cum contingat, per Innocentius. What more is there? Let him stop; he proceeds beyond by annulling, and the nullity itself, as an inseparable defect in its being, adheres just as to white and to the register, so that the registration is null. And when we speak of the nullity of the act, we do not consider the act materially, as in §. factae, but substantively, with regard to the substance of the law and its effect. The law says "let such a thing not be heard"; do the ears of the judge not hear? Certainly, indeed they hear, but the gloss explains: "with effect." C. de abolitione, fallaciously on the word "is not sought." And l. abolitio, there "the voice is in no way heard," in the text. And the registered person,

† who is the cancellation. It ought not to be considered as registered. In the Authentica "Qui semel" according to Iacobus de Belvisio, because those proximate to the cancellation ought to be considered as cancelled. Argument from the Digest, De iure, l. "Qui se dicit," and l. penultimate, De testamento militis. Nor does the shadow of the writing harm anyone, but the truth. L. 1, De his quae in testamento delentur; and noted in l. "Acta," De re iudicata, by Bartolus, because civil law does not consist in ciphers, but in substances. L. 1, Codex, De formidone. Hence, it does not provide an impediment, that from which no effect is felt in law, as in the rule of law. And it must be known that the register does not have being in itself, but through its cause and relation to the acts, as in l. "Cancellauerat," De his quae in testamento delentur. And the defect which appears in the acts represents its visible defect also in the register, as noted by Cynus in l. 1, Codex, De errore calculi. And it is known that it is said that "registered" ought to be understood more broadly, not that the register has a visible defect in the first figure, or by relation to the acts to which it expressly refers, as in l. "Edicto divi Adriani" and the aforementioned l. "Si quis legatum," because the same reason applies, and it does not obstruct.

† For a defect, which is easily proven by the records, ought to be considered evident and notorious, as noted in l. 1 and l. 2, C. de edicto divi Adriani; and in l. ille a quo, § si testamento, ad Trebellianum; and in l. is a quo, as in the position of l. Amplius. He who has jurisdiction in habit, but not in exercise: and although he is not reduced entirely to the status of a private person, nevertheless the inquiry is similar to his, just as one having a dignity or a formal administration. He does not have jurisdiction, although he has a causal [basis], as in C. ubi senatus vel clarissimi; l. si non. It is said that he who does not have operation has no form; because operation is that which leads us to the knowledge of formal qualities, and also of substantial form, according to Aristotle. And therefore, one interdicted from office is not considered an official, although the office has not been totally removed from him, as noted in ff. de auctoritate tutorum; and l. si pluribus; and it is clear in l. 2, ff. de curatore. Therefore, the registration of the said [act] is null, because the cause of the effect is lacking, and the material and subject potentia cause, along with the formal and constitutive final justificatory cause, i.e., the reason of the statute, as in ff. de falsis, l. divus Claudius, § Item sciat.

† Let us furthermore consider, for God’s sake, the matter about which this person was initially inquired. Certainly, regarding peculation, the gloss on the singular in the Code, to the Julian Law on Ambition, in the rubric, states that the crime of falsehood is sometimes ambition, yet it is not punished as falsehood, because it is not punished. L. Eorum, De falsis; nor is it treated as falsity. And thus we follow the gloss, which says the same regarding peculation. It states that, if one takes “falsehood” in a broad sense, for perjury or for a future inofficious act, but speaking strictly and according to the nature of judicial proceedings, this is not falsehood; because it is not punished by any law as falsehood, nor does the outcome of the controversy resemble a complaint of falsehood. D. 6, De falsis; L. Quid sit falsum.

† Moreover, this is not barataria, because barataria is that whereby a judge is corrupted by money or otherwise. C. de pec. iud. de eo. But it is settled. It does not speak, however, of theft. Therefore, we cannot speak of it either, because a point can be added or subtracted from the form of the law. ff. de ver. ob. l. punctus. and de acq. her. l. si servum. §. non dicitur postea. Now, this inquisitor alleged that falsehood had been committed, but because he did not impose the penalty for falsehood in the sentence, it does not appear that he condemned for falsehood. Hence, it is not stated expressly, nor perhaps tacitly by inference from the effect: because it is not a genus of crime, but the sentence is examined, and the sentence does not contain the penalty for falsehood: therefore, this person is not registered as condemned for falsehood: therefore, since nullity is established, it is not to be torn up: because we are not in the excepted cases. I believe that what is sufficient, which he exempts from exemption, has no place in obligation, except insofar as the obligation extends; therefore, it has no place in criminal judgment, which is for vengeance, because such a part does not consist in the bonds of obligation. C. de pec. fiscalibus creditores praeferri. l. 2. and ff. de don. post contract. And therefore, concluding from the first to the last, the aforementioned person found for offices ought to be admitted. And the extract from the register cannot be torn up. And thus I approve the most subtle allegations made above by another doctor, by his reasons and laws, adding what I have said. And so I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, Juris Utriusque Doctor and Consul.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A mother entering into a second marriage cannot give to her second husband as a dowry whatever she pleases.
2. A mother cannot give or bequeath more to the children of the second marriage than to those of the first.
3. On the interpretation of l. hac edictali, C. de secundis nuptiis.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen. A certain lady Nicolina, from her husband Leporino, bore two sons; and when she was marrying a second time to a certain Ser Donato, she promised to Orlando, father of the said Ser Donato, three hundred in the name of dowry, on this condition: that the same Orlando, if the said Nicolina should die in the said marriage with the children, would not be bound to restore the said dowry, but the dowry itself would remain in full to the same Orlando, Ser Donato, for the common children of the said Ser Donato and the said Nicolina. And it is true that a certain son from the said first marriage, though a minor, with the authority of his tutor, and the tutor himself, consented to the said agreements. Finally, the case arose: because the said Nicolina died in the second marriage, with two children surviving from the said second marriage. For the heirs of the children of the first marriage are opposing the heirs of the said Orlando. And it is said that, since the said Nicolina left nothing to the said children of the first marriage, either during her life or at her death, that to the said children of the first marriage, and consequently to their inheritance, is owed the giving of the dowry to the second husband. And of the remaining part, the legitime due by natural law is owed to them, with the fruits therefrom collected from the day of the death of the said Nicolina. And they demand from the heir of the said Orlando the said half, and the part of the dowry due by natural law, with the aforesaid fruits. But the heirs of the said Orlando object, among other things: that the agreement for the acquisition of the dowry was made with the said Orlando, not with the said Ser Donato, the second husband. Furthermore, they say that the aforementioned agreement was made between strangers. Furthermore, they say that, if a division of the aforementioned dowry ought to be made, it ought to be made per capita of the children. Furthermore, they object the prescription of thirty years. Now the question is: what is the law concerning the aforementioned points, and each of the aforementioned matters? As to the first point, it must be known:

† That one who proceeds to a second marriage cannot give to the second spouse more than to one of the children of the first marriage, neither to the spouse receiving it in his own person, nor through an interposed person: because all fraud ought to cease, so that the children of the first marriage are not defrauded. As in C. de secundis nuptiis, l. hac edictali; but here the fraud appears manifest. For the father-in-law received this pact and this stipulation of the dowry to be acquired for his son and for his sons. And it would be absurd to say that what is prohibited from being done could lawfully be done through an interposed person. As in C. quod metus causa, l. si per impressionem, ver. simili poena. Moreover, if the second husband did not receive it by himself, therefore neither through another. As in ff. de auctoritate tutorum, l. pupillus, §. per interpositam. Moreover, the absurdity would follow that the children of the first marriage would be entirely defrauded of the maternal dowry: if the pact were valid, and thus an open way would be laid for frauds, which ought not to be, as in the said l. hac edictali, there in the words omni circumscriptione. And therefore the law is actiua [i.e., giving rise to an action], so that even by oath one does not cease to come against that law. As in ff. de libellis et legibus, l. Aurelius, §. quidem; and ff. de legatis tertio, l. cum quis, §. Titia. Moreover, fraud is presumed on account of the interdiction of the law, as is read and noted in ff. de probationibus, l. qui testamento. Moreover, a color is presumed to have been sought against the interdiction of the law. As in ff. ad legem Velleianam, l. quamvis, §. cum enim; and noted in l. in uxorem, §. si; and ff. ad legem Maiestatis, l. si filius, §. quod ita; and ff. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. mulier, otherwise beginning Sulpitius. When this question was a matter of fact in the city of Cortona: I said that this case did not pertain to the law hac edictali, but pertained to the matter of the inofficious dowry. As in C. de inofficiosis dotibus, l. 1. The complaint of the inofficious dowry is available for the third part of that share which the plaintiff would have had intestate, and not for more, as in C. de inofficiosis testamentis, l. cum quaeritur; and auth. unde si parens. And it is not available after five years. As in C. de donationibus, l. fin. And if not prepared, it is not transmitted to extraneous heirs. As in ff. de inofficioso testamento, l. quemadmodum; and to this I was moved to say by such reasoning.

† For it must be known that a mother may give and bequeath more to the children of her second marriage than to those of her first; for she is not bound, when disposing among her children, to leave to any of them more than their legitimate portion, as in the Authentica *De nuptiis*, § *Illud quoque*, on this point, column 4. And this is because, although it is permitted regarding those born, it is lawful regarding posthumous children. Hence, a mother may give all her goods to one stranger, claiming on behalf of a child of her second marriage, whether born or to be born, reserving the legitimate portion of the child of her first marriage. Just as a stranger may intervene for this purpose, so too may a grandfather and the father of the future posthumous child intervene, because he acts not as father or grandfather, but as a bare minister, or as any other person. For we do not examine the person of the minister stipulating, but rather consider the persons for whom the benefit is sought in effect. As in D. *Ad legem Falcidiam*, l. *Cum dote*; and D. *Si quis aliquem testari prohibuerit*, l. 1, § *Sed si legatum*. For although the second husband could not take for himself to retain, he may nevertheless take for his son as heir of his mother. As in D. *De pactis et transactionibus*, l. *Inter socerum*, § *Cum inter patrem*. And it seemed to me that this would have no doubt for a learned person, because this edictal law condemns only excessive liberality toward the husband, and restrains the harms which women marrying a second time easily inflict upon their first offspring with respect to their husbands. As in C. *De administratione tutorum*, l. *Lex quae tutores*, where it is said: "It perceived that immoderate and intemperate women, in many cases, add not only the property of their children but also their lives to new husbands." Moreover, by such a pact, nothing is conferred upon the second husband in ownership, as in C. *De bonis quae liberis*, l. *Cum oportet*. And if we say it is conferred in usufruct, l. *Hac edictali*, it would have place in this usufruct, as we expressly note in a similar case in D. *De auctoritate tutorum*, l. 1, in the gloss beginning *I. acquirente*, in the last word of the gloss. On this question, Master Francis de Albergotis advised in the first part that it would not be valid. This question was submitted to Master Richard de Servete, who, with all due respect, without seeing the marrow of the aforementioned reason, immediately struck down the argument, but erroneously. And if you say that the children of the first marriage are defrauded, I answer that this fraud pertains to the complaint of an undutiful donation, as I said, in the aforementioned l. *Vnde si parens*, and D. *De legatis* 2, l. *Titia*, l. *Imperator*. And this edictal law has nothing to do with this crime, nor does its subject matter. Now, let us assume, without prejudice to the truth, that we are in the case of the law *Hac edictali*.

† I ask whether the *condictio* from that law is available against the heirs of the aforementioned father-in-law, who possesses nothing of the dowry, and it must be said that it is not, because the *condictio* in personam ought to be brought against him, or his heirs, to whom, or to whomsoever, the dowry remains according to the said pact; but this dowry does not remain with the heirs of the said Orlando as with the heirs of the same person, because, as I said, even if they intervened as ministers stipulating for future nephews, just as for the heirs of their mother. For the *condictio* from this edictal law strips profit from him to whom the profit is directed, whether the pact of gaining is in effect. For if a procurator made a pact for a husband, the procurator would not be bound by the *condictio* from that law, but the husband himself and his heirs would be bound, against whom also one can sue by *condictio sine causa*, with whom it remains, since the law itself by right forbids the pact. Argument: Codex, On the Right of Deliberation, Law Final, § If indeed heirs; and Codex, On the Sacred Sanctity of the Church, Law We decree. And in this *condictio* from the law, fruits before the contestation of the lawsuit do not come in, but in that part which ought to be due in place of the legitime, so that Law Papinianus, § Fourth, On the Inofficious Will; but in that which ought to be due by complaint of inofficious donation, fruits before the proposal would not come in, because before that the possessor is not in default. Also, in quantities you ought to demand something beyond the principal, unless it were proved that interest accrues as usury. As Digest, On Solutions, Law Titia; On Prescription of Thirty Years, there is no doubt. However, because during the mother’s lifetime the benefit of this edictal law has no place, nor the right of demanding the legitime, prescription does not run unless the mother is dead, concerning whose dowry and goods it is treated. Argument: Codex, On Donations, Law In things, § If, as is gathered in Authentic, On Marriages, § Optimely; Law Ne forte propter spem etc. While the mother lives, children are in hope, but not in act, that they can rescind dotal pacts, or demand that they be declared not binding, because they could commit ingratitude, while the mother lives, who will repel them. Consider that the *condictio* from this edictal law is a certain revocatory action, and the nature of revocatory actions is this, that it follows him with whom the thing is, and who has become richer. As Institutes, On Actions, § If anyone in fraud; and Law 1, § If anything in fraud of the patron. Since therefore the father-in-law received the dowry and did not restore it, the heirs of the father-in-law ought to be sued by the revocatory action, that is, by the *condictio* from this edictal law. Nor is it strange that the father-in-law, i.e., the father of the husband, is the true minister; rather, he is the owner of the dowry for the burdens of marriage. As noted, Digest, On the Dissolution of Marriage, Law If constant, in the beginning; and Digest, On the Division of an Estate, Law If the husband. Also it is to be known that sons of the first marriage, defrauded, do not compute into the legitime that which they acquire by this edictal law; but they can claim that as a principal thing as having suffered injury, and nevertheless they have the legitime from the remaining goods by natural right. As noted in the said § Optimely in Authentic, On Marriages. And therefore in this it must be rested for the final conclusion, that if we are in the case of this edictal law, which I do not believe: the said sons of the first marriage ought first to have half. For this edictal law is demanded without fruits before the contestation of the lawsuit, because the *condictio* from the law is a personal action and of strict right. And it is not properly a restitutory action, but an instituting one. And thus it does not object, Digest, On Usury, Law Let us see, § In the Faunian. And in it, the plaintiff does not demand his own from the performance. But into the legitime fruits would well come, if something other than money were demanded; but fruits of money do not come in, because they are not fruits perceptible by nature or goodness, but because they are perceived from mere denial. Argument: Digest, On the Law Falcidia, Law Or if the heir. And by this certain things declared concerning this edictal law appear, namely against whom the libel is founded in the *condictio* from that law. But these, according to my opinion, are not necessary in our case; because I said that they are not in the matter of that law, but if anyone held the contrary opinion, the aforementioned are necessary and true. And thus I say, and I counsel, I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Civil Law.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that a woman may not contract without consent and presence, etc., as here, whether a daughter and her father, by accepting a legacy, prejudice themselves, since the consent required by the statute was not given.
2. The words "I bequeath" do not pertain to a contract.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Given the statute of the city of Spoleto, which provides that no woman may contract, alienate, or make a donation mortis causa or inter vivos, nor make a will or last will, in the city or county of Spoleto, or elsewhere, without the presence of her husband, father, and sons over the age of fourteen, if she has all the aforementioned and they are present in the city of Spoleto or its territory; and if any of the aforementioned should be lacking due to death or absence, or because the heir does not have such persons in place of those lacking due to death or absence, or because the woman otherwise does not have the aforementioned persons, then two of the nearest relatives must be and ought to be present. And if she acts otherwise, it shall not be valid nor binding by operation of law. The fact is proposed that a certain Venantius promised to John Francis 300 livres as the dowry of his daughter Allegratia, of which he paid the said dowry to the said John, excepting 192 livres. Then, coming to the point of death, he made a will, in which will he left to the said his daughter, for the said 192 livres of money and for 15 livres more, one and a half measures of a certain plot of land, described in the said will; and this especially with the willing acceptance of the said John and the said Allegratia.

† It is now asked whether the said acceptance is valid or not. And it seems that it is not valid: because by the giving and promise of the dowry, the right of the daughter is acquired. Although the dowry is profectitious, nevertheless upon the death of the father, the action consolidates in favor of the daughter herself, as in C. rem in praesenti, §. videamus. Hence, the said woman, without observing the form of the statute, could not change or resolve the right she had acquired for herself; whether we say this is a contract, as if of the same exchange, as in ff. de iure dotium, l. ita constituit, or whether we say it is a novation of the cause, of the future obligation of the dowry to be restored, this cannot be done without observing the form of the statute: because when the form is given to be of the thing, it is necessary that the form of the statute be observed, as in ff. de transactionibus, l. cum hi, §. si praetor, and l. certa forma, C. de iure fisci, lib. 10. And this is true as regards the woman herself, but as regards one, such acceptance is valid: if the husband after death persisted in the same will, unless I say that rather he did not persist: because in the last will among those present, a contract can be made and exchanged, as noted in l. haeredes palam, §. si, ff. de testamento. And because the father consented, it seems that the prohibitive statute ceases in the person of the woman. But the first part seems safer, that it is not valid as regards the woman, but it is valid to the prejudice of the husband:

† Because the father used the word, he made a legacy. That word does not pertain to a contract, as in l. 1, in fine, ff. de tabulis exhibendis; and ff. de verborum significatione, l. verba cum esset, together with l. verbis. And although much time later it was permitted: from this it is not presumed that the solemnity of persons required by the example of the possessor is present, but if any solemnity is required, it would sometimes be presumed by that, as in C. de petitione hereditatis, l. si filius. And therefore the continuation of consent by the former does not make prohibited consent valid, as in C. de agricolis et censitis, l. quemadmodum, lib. 11. The solution seems sufficiently valid, which is also from the daughter: because she can well consent to him in a last will, as in l. 1, ff. de rebus eorum. And thus I say, and I advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of both laws, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a legatee must demand that the heir have entered upon the inheritance in the customary manner, with respect to the thing bequeathed; and whether the heir may impose a new servitude on the thing bequeathed.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A certain Vannes of Spoleto left to a certain Zarcharo a certain house, together with a courtyard, with its entrances and exits. And he instituted as universal heirs the Poor of Christ: who sold their rights to the ladies Matthea and Cicilia. Now, the same testator had another house: to which they had access through the said house. It is asked whether this is due to the said purchasers. And here it must be considered,

† That the testator, having access, had it by virtue of a certain custom, not by right of servitude: because one’s own thing is subject to servitude for no one. It therefore appears that the testator’s custom should be observed, as in l. nulla, D. de alimentis et cibus legatis, and D. de vino, tritico et oleo legato, l. ex usu. To the contrary, it appears that the testator bequeathed the house to the said Zarcharo without imposing any servitude; but if the said heir could have a way through the said house, this would be a certain servitude, and the heir cannot impose a new servitude on the bequeathed thing. Hence it does not appear that the legatee, through the bequeathed house, ought to grant any access to the heirs, unless perhaps at times there were no access to the heir’s house. As in D. de servitutibus urbanis praediorum, l. qui binas aedes. Nevertheless, the law seems expressly to state that the legatee must suffer the heir to have accustomed access, as in D. de servitutibus urbanis praediorum, l. olim. But to this it could be answered that, namely, there the heirs have passage through houses which were their own, although they have usufruct. But in our case, the legatee had ownership with his uses and accesses; therefore he is not to be burdened with a servitude with which the testator did not burden him. Argument from those who, D. de usufructu, l. 1, sed et si quis, § proprietatis. Unless one says that access is a part even without donation; although it is not an intrinsic and formal part, it is nevertheless a necessary and quasi-substantial part, as in D. de annuis legatis, l. quod conclauis. And argument from D. de contrahenda emptione, l. si aquaeductus consuetus heredi debet permitti. Access is to be allowed as accessory, but not such that one goes through the middle of the bequeathed house. Argument from D. quando et quibus quarta pars in bonis debetur, l. 2, lib. 10, and D. de usufructu legato, l. Sempronio, in principio. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How the release of a burden and benefit is to be made among brothers holding property in common.
1. Whether the fruits of a dotal fund are to be divided among brothers holding property in common.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† On the first point, it must be said that the aforementioned Jacob is not bound to contribute the aforementioned sums paid by the aforementioned Augustine, and the reason is that they were not partners in all goods, even though they held the paternal property in undivided shares, as stated in D. 17.2.1 (*Cum duobus*), § *Si fratres*; and D. 10.1.1 (*Licet indivisa*), Book 10.

† On the second point, it must be said that if the land was indeed designated as a dowry fund, all the fruits would belong to the said Jacob. If, however, it was not simply for the dowry, then up to the amount corresponding to the dowry, the fruits belong to the said Jacob and his wife for the burdens of marriage, as stated in C. de iure dotis, l. ubi adhuc; but from that point onward, they must be divided between the said brothers in equal shares, because the profit from the fruits should not exceed the amount of the dowry, and this is supported by ff. de donationibus excusationibus, l. pater, in principio. It is remarkable that if this Jacob worked the fields, he should receive half of the fruits, according to I. laboratoris, just as anyone cultivating them, as stated in extra de decimis, c. tua. The other half is divided, as I said first, into two parts, and one part should belong to the said Jacob, while the other should be divided into two parts: one part belongs to Jacob, and the other to his brother, and thus in effect, the said Jacob should receive seven parts of the said fruits, and the other part of the said fruits belongs to the said Augustinus. CASE. The point of the question is as follows: a certain person named Angelus died having made his will, in which he left several legacies. For he left his mother as usufructuary of all his goods during her lifetime, and after the death of his said mother, he wished the said goods to pass to Simon, Licita, and Florutia, as his heirs, and he instituted Simon, Licita, and Florutia as heirs. Finally, Simon died, leaving behind one only son named Colla, while the said mother of the testator, who was the usufructuary of all the goods of the said testator during her lifetime, also died, with the said Licita, Florutia, and the said Colla, son of Simon, surviving. Now the question arises whether the said Colla succeeds together with the said other heirs or not.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If a person is instituted as heir after the death of someone who was left as usufructuary of all the goods during his lifetime, and if such instituted heir dies before the death of the usufructuary, whether he transmits the inheritance to his heir.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

It would seem to be said that the lord Simodo, as instituted after the aforementioned certainty, i.e., after the death of the mother, does not transmit anything to his heir, as in D. 35.1.1 (Digest, On Conditions and Demonstrations, "My heir"). To the contrary, it seems, because it matters greatly whether someone is instituted after the death of another, and then he does not transmit, as in the said law; or whether the testator first bequeaths the usufruct, and then institutes under the aforementioned form, namely that after the death of the usufructuary he wished the said goods to pass to certain heirs: and then death is not understood to be attached to the ownership, but to the usufruct, which is proved by this reasoning. For he who bequeaths a usufruct wishes to enter upon the inheritance, otherwise the usufruct would not be due, as in C. 6.52.1 (Code, On the Abolition of the Falcidian Law, "Except even"). Since therefore he wishes to enter upon the inheritance, he seems to have purely instituted those instituted in the ownership of the inheritance, because he should not be understood to have attached a condition which would vitiate the legacies, as in D. 28.5.1 (Digest, On the Manumission of Testators, "If for this purpose"). Also contributing to this is that the testator added the word "as to his heirs," therefore he wished them to be able to enter upon the inheritance. Also contributing to this is that caution is to be given to them for using the land according to the discretion of a good man; therefore they are heirs immediately upon the death of the testator. If Simon, by word or deed, declared that he wished to be heir, or acted as heir, or took possession of the said inheritance and goods, he transmits the said inheritance; otherwise it would not be transmitted, except in the mind of one deliberating, and this seems to me to be the truth. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether, and when, a debtor is discharged by paying the assignor.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Above, in a certain point concerning the donation, it was omitted to state that, after the donation made to the said L. and the daughters, and the vindication made by the said daughters to Peter, the said mother made an end and renunciation with her legitimate and natural son of the said fruits and usufructs reserved to herself, the mother, during her lifetime. Now the question arises whether the said renunciation prejudices the said daughters and the said Peter, who derives his title from the said daughters.

† On this point, the common opinion of the doctors is that a debtor may be freed by payment to the holder of the actions, except in the three cases set forth in l. 3, C. de donat. and thus in our ff. de pact. l. si cum emptore. But here there is no payment, but a pact or transaction; a fourth case is added, namely, the knowledge of the debtor. For if the debtor is not thus freed by such pact or transaction, but is freed through ignorance by means of an exception. For he imputes the matter to himself through ignorance; he did not notify the one who knew, nor was he bound to notify: because wherever mere knowledge suffices, there is no need for a certificatory notification: because since the notification has no operative effect, it is not of the substance, but produces another effect. Thus says Cynus in l. ult., ff. de transact. But Jacobus de Arena says otherwise in l. 1, ff. ad Trebellianam, and Bartolus in the same title, l. facta, §. si haeres. The opinion of Cynus seems to me the more correct, because to receive payment is to preserve the nature of the obligation; but to free by pact or transaction is a certain new act separated from the primordial nature of the obligation. If the liberation was not made by reason of a contract of hire, for example, it is necessary for the cessionary, except in the said three cases. Likewise in the usufruct retained by the cessionary; because by the law itself it removes the substance and c. de qua quaeritur. Argument from ff. de legat. 3, l. 11, §. si reus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a statute providing that acknowledged instruments shall be put into execution, whether a compromise may be sought on a hypothecary claim.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. This matter is very intricate; nevertheless, I have been asked about two points.

First, whether the petition for arbitration has place in a hypothecary action when the hypothecary action is based on a confessed instrument. Second, whether, for the said mandate or for the said judgment, but without giving the adversary the opportunity to contradict, the judge may choose an arbitrator in place of the absent party. And the first point, which is the one in question in the city of Perugia, raises the doubt: if it were to be submitted to arbitration, could the arbitrators pronounce against the confessed instrument, i.e., declare it invalid, which would be contrary to the statute on the execution of confessed instruments? The hypothecary action is not distinguished in the first place as to whether someone is obligated. In principle, ff. de probat. l. ante omnia. Moreover, because the statute on summary proceedings removes the mode of arbitration: for it requires something to be paid, and the removal of the mode is the removal of the whole. de verb. oblig. l. qui Romae. §. Fauius. Moreover, because the case accords with those in which it is certain that one cannot arbitrate: and the nature of binding agreements is a uniform conclusion of them. As C. de sentent. et interloc. l. cum solum. Moreover, the special derogates from the general: for the exception derogates from the rule. But nevertheless, because §. ult. of the statute under the title de summaria cognitione speaks taxatively, I say that arbitration ought to take place: because the hypothecary action is not merely the execution of a confessed instrument. And because the defendant is bound by a new cause in the hypothecary action, i.e., that he possesses the thing. l. 1. de alien. iudic. ff. de pign. l. si fundus. §. in venditione. l. procurator. rem. rat. haec loquitur, because the hypothecary action is brought against an external possessor. But if the action is brought against the debtor, then the hypothecary action has something of a personal character, de pact. l. si tibi. §. de pignore. For it is seen that the debtor tacitly promised to deliver, or tacitly agreed on the possession to be delivered. And therefore, in that case, perhaps arbitration would not have place.

† Furthermore, on another point, I state that, since the procurator’s mandate was not produced upon the judge’s request, he could not choose a third arbitrator against the absent party; because it was not established to him that there was a mandate for the deposit. L. Si quis in fin. And thus I say, and I, Baldus of Perugia, advise. V. L. Doctor.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. An agreement that someone is to be treated as true and original has the force of law.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† There is an ordinance in the city of Todi, whereby men, whether from the city or from the county and district, if they are killed or injured, and also in civil cases which they may hereafter have in the court of the commune of Todi, shall be treated and regarded as true and original citizens of the city of Todi. There is no doubt that, while the said contract is in force, Perugians in Todi are to be treated as Todi citizens, and conversely; for so does the pact speak, having the force of law, as in D. de publicanis, l. Caesar; and C. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. pen.; D. de verbis oblig., l. quidam cum filium. And therefore the said Nicolaus Francischini of Perugia must, in the case proposed, in all respects and in every way, be treated by the judge of Todi in the same manner and form as Todi citizens are treated, and under the same law as applies to Todi citizens, D. de captivis, l. non dubito. And although they are not citizens of Perugia, one by the union of bodies, whereby diverse bodies are nevertheless considered as one by reason of friendship and the pact of equality. And so I say and advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Both Laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A testament in which the father stated that he was leaving [property] to his sons by right of restitution, when he ought to have said by right of institution, is valid at least as regards the substitution for minors and legacies.
2. The wife, who has been left as owner and also as usufructuary of the testator's daughters until she remains a widow, and together with the said daughters, what she ought to have.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Having examined the will of a certain illustrious citizen, in which he left his wife, Ciam, as mistress and usufructuary, together with the daughters of the said testator, the said Do. Ciam, so long as she remains a widow, and cohabits with her daughters, and has not reclaimed her dowries; and in which will, by way of institution, he wished Francisca to have, and beyond that, when she shall marry. Furthermore, he left to his said daughters the usufruct of the income, revenue, and term, and the ownership of the usufruct, income, and revenue of all his goods during their lives, and the life of each of them, until they shall marry. And if any of his said daughters should die in pupillary age, or afterwards at any time, he substituted as heirs of the said testator those whom he later named in the will, presupposing that the said testator has died, and that the said Blanche has married.

† It is asked what the said Do. Cia ought to have, and what she ought to have because nothing was left to the said daughters by way of institution. For the words of the testament say "by way of restitution"; these words are merely oblique, as in D. ad Trebellianum, l. Restituta; and Inst. de fideicommissis hereditatibus, § Restituta. And it is considered that this was an error of the scribe. I answer: I believe that he erred; nevertheless, this error cannot be corrected, because it is not established as such, as in C. de testamento, l. Ambiguitatem and l. Errore. Yet it is equitable to say that the said daughters were not understood to be passed over, and that the testament would be valid; because not all testators know how to speak of institution, as noted in C. familiae erciscundae, l. Quotiens. And we ought rather to interpret the words improprietly than to invalidate the testament. Moreover, if the words were used properly, such words would effect nothing; and words ought to effect something, as in l. Si quando de legatis. Let us therefore assume as certain, saving the substance of the truth, that the said testament is valid, at least as regards the pupillary substitution and the legacies for the aforementioned reason, or at least by the authority Ex causa, to whom the said 450 livres left to the said Francisco pertain. Answer: They pertain to the said pupillary substitutes, as in C. de impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus, l. Precibus; and C. de inofficioso testamento, l. Papiniana, § Sed nec impuberis.

But it is doubted what the said Dame Cia ought to have. Answer: If she wishes for maintenance, she ought to have it, and more abundant, and even more abundant, than if the girl were to marry. I do not say that she ought to have double maintenance, as in D. de usufr. l. dominus; but nevertheless simple maintenance, more plentiful, namely food and clothing at the discretion of a reasonable man, and as she had during the life of her husband, with the saving that she ought not to have such fine clothing, because they are not fitting for a widow, as in C. si secundo nupserit mulier l. 1 and l. Titia §. si de leg. 2. And if it should happen that the said Blanche dies, she ought to have full usufruct during her lifetime, according to what is noted in the said laws, namely, observing widowhood and the conditions appended in the said testament; for debts and legacies are said to be paid by universal heirs, and not by Blanche, nor by the said Dame Cia, as in C. de hær. inst. l. quot. cum forte. Since Blanche ought not to have usufruct after she marries, it would not be absurd to say that Dame Cia ought to have them, as the word sounds, because when the reason of custom ceases, custom ceases.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether, if a testator prohibits the sale of a thing except to his own sons, the sons have a claim for recovery if it is sold to another. Likewise, whether the same applies if the testator prohibits the sale except to Peter.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A certain Peter of Collio bequeathed a certain sum of money to his nephew Cechus, prohibiting him from alienating it, except to the sons of the testator. Now, the aforementioned Cechus has sold it to another.

† It is asked whether the sons of the testator can claim the said thing sold. I answer in the affirmative, because this precept is not naked, but made in favor of the sons of the testator himself. D. de leg. 1, l. filius, §. diuus; and D. de leg. 2, l. codicillis, §. pe. And as is noted, C. de fideic., l. quotiens. This. For indeed, the testator’s precept has a tacit cause within it, namely, the favor of the testator’s sons. But what if the testator had said, “I forbid it to be sold except to Peter,” and the legatee had sold it to another? Could the party bring an action for vindication of the thing? The solution is gathered from l. vxorem, §. agri plagam, D. de leg. 3, because the thing was not bequeathed to Peter, but rather the heir was also ordered to sell it, namely, in the case where he forbade selling to Peter and not to another. As is noted, D. de peti. haer., l. in aestimationibus; and D. de contrahen. empt., l. 1. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A statute providing that a creditor, upon payment or tender of the debt, is not bound to return the pledged property, is invalid, because it gives rise to usury.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† A statute that introduces the evil of usury is invalid, as noted in the Digest, De usufructu, and the Authentica Ad hoc. Therefore, a statute is invalid if it provides that a creditor, upon payment of the debt or its tender, need not return the pledged property; for the fruits, if they do not reduce the principal, would introduce the evil of usury. Moreover, the creditor would be penalized for committing a wrong. Thus I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Both Laws, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If a simple postponement for proof has been granted, it suffices, according to the common opinion, that the witnesses take their oath within the term. And number 3 of the said Blanca of the said widows. And it appears that the said testament is not valid: and 2 Whether a second postponement can be granted to one who was impeded in the first by oath alone. The opinion reports and afterwards distinguishes.
2. Instruments may be produced, even if witnesses are not [produced] after the term granted for proof, and it is to be considered as proved by every species of proof.
3. Witnesses received after the term, and having taken their oath, do not prove.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The statute provides that, in a contested lawsuit, the judge shall assign to the parties a term for proving and having proof established by every species of proof, of 15 useful days. Within this term, the plaintiff produced witnesses who took an oath in the case, but did not give their depositions. Then, the judge, upon the plaintiff alleging an impediment and proving it in general terms without specifying the kind of impediment, solely on the basis of the plaintiff’s oath, set a new term of 5 useful days in this manner, namely, if and to the extent permitted by the form of the statute. Within this term, the defendant, objecting and alleging that his probative evidence to impeach the plaintiff’s witnesses had arrived due to the delay of time, now raises the following questions: First, whether the aforementioned depositions made by the witnesses after the first extension and before the second extension given are valid or not. Second, whether the said extension could be granted without proving any other impediment except by the sole oath. Third, whether these could be produced if the extension granted secondarily was not valid. Whether it suffices for witnesses to take an oath within the term is fully discussed here.

† Regarding the first point, the doctors commonly state that if a delay is granted simply for the purpose of proving, it suffices for the witnesses to take their oath within the term, because the testimony is drawn back to the day of the oath, according to the noted rule in c. 1, de officio delegati. Others say that either the delay can be imputed to the party producing the evidence, for having failed to have the witnesses examined; and then they could not be examined after the term. Or it is doubtful whether the producing party was in delay or not; and then the impediment is proved by oath, as I will say immediately. But the ancient Perugian advocates said that there a term is established for proving and for having the proof completed; the oath alone without the deposition does not suffice; because these words require perfect proof, and where there is no deposition, there is no perfect proof. Arch. in c. Pia, de exceptionibus, lib. 6, and Io. And. in the novella say that publication is not required; however, it is well required that the plaintiff, or the one producing the witnesses, has done according to his ability, and that they also be published by requesting this before the judge, that they be compelled to testify by praetorian remedies.

But here it must be observed, for either the doubt is continuous, as in C. de dilat. l. siue parens; then certainly it prevents a new dilatio from being granted, as in ff. de fer. l. oratione. Or it concerns the last days; then, if one is impeded, whether on account of an impediment in his own person, or that of the judge, or of the adversary, or of the witnesses produced—for perhaps they were absent, cf. those things which are not, ff. de feriis, l. in prin.—the useful time does not run, as in ff. de diuer. et temp. pręscr. l. 1. For to one who is impeded, useful days for proving do not run. For the same reason applies to the impediment of witnesses as to the impediment of one’s own person, since in the witnesses consists the substance of the litigation, i.e., the obtaining of victory. Nevertheless, whether an impediment can be proved by oath, Dominus Federicus de Senis in his consilia, consilium 109, which is on the point committed, holds that proof by oath suffices.
