He then cites Spec. in tit. de dila. §. vlti. ad fi. and in tit. de appel. §. nunc breuiter, versi. quid ergo si appellatur; and that which is noted in qu. 5, c. 1, in the last gloss; and de elec. c. propter; and de resc. c. statu. §. 1, lib. 6; and de testi. c. pręsentia; and de exce. c. pasto. But the contrary is held by Iac. de Are. ff. de excu. tu. l. scire oportet. §. sufficit, by l. in exce. §. 1, ff. de prob.; and ff. de re mil. l. 3. §. si ad diem; and l. qui commeatus; and ff. si quis cau. l. 2. §. quod diximus. Guli. de Cu. says that credence will be given to the oath, considering the quality of the person, as in l. quo. de naufragiis, lib. 10; de re mil. non omnes. §. a barbaris. I say that either a matter of slight prejudice is at issue: and then it is proved by oath, cf. ff. ad exhiben. l. thesaurus. Or a matter of great prejudice is at issue, and then either the proof of the impediment is difficult, and credence is given to the oath, considering the quality of the person, as in ff. de re milit. l. non omnes. §. a barbaris. Or other proofs can easily be had, if the impediment is true; then credence is not given to the oath, unless several dilations ought to be granted in order. For then, after the first, a second dilatio is granted, the impediment being proved by oath alone, as is noted in ff. de fer. l. in pecuniariis, because that which is granted by common law is easily proved, cf. C. quondio mulier tu. off. fun. potest. l. 2; and that which is noted in ff. qui satisd. cog. l. 1.

Now, returning to our case, considering that the term of 15 days is single and peremptory, I do not believe that a simple oath suffices when the impediment is not alleged specifically. For causes must be specified, because the quality of the causes must be just and true, as in D. de in integrum restitutione, l. omnes; and l. 1, de pręd. curia, lib. 10; and D. de transactionibus, l. cum hi, § si prętor. Since, therefore, the judge did not grant a second adjournment simply, but under a condition, namely, if, and insofar as, and to the extent that it is permitted by the form of the statute, and the form of the statute does not state, nor does the statute provide that any other adjournment be given after the lapse of 15 useful days, it must be said that the depositions of the witnesses are invalid. And even if it were considered that the depositions of the witnesses who swore within the first adjournment were valid, the statements of the witnesses who swore afterwards would not be valid. Argument: D. de excusationibus tutorum, l. scire oportet, § consequens. For that which is done after the term is invalid, because what is permitted before the time is considered to be prohibited after the time, as in D. de legibus 2, l. statu liberum, § Stichum. Nevertheless, the statute seems to hold, and if the right of the adversary has not been made worse by the delay, because although they were not produced after the term, the instrument was nevertheless executed before the term, and because an instrument is a proven proof, as noted in c. saepe, de veritate sigilli, in the Clementines. And thus I hold, always saving the opinion of a more authoritative counsel. And to this effect it is made that what is noted in c. 1, de exceptionibus, in the Clementines, in the gloss, Hostiensis holds. Someone might say: if the witnesses prove the truth, why is the truth not believed? As in D. de officio pręsidentis, l. illicitas, § iuncta.

But to this it is answered that instruments may be produced after the term given for proving and having the matter proved by every species of proof, otherwise as regards witnesses, so that the rigor of judicial proceedings and the authority of the judge may be fully observed here. For the judge who fixed the term was to be obeyed. As in C. qui accus. non pos. l. si ea; ff. de adop. lega. l. mancipiorum; C. de ingenuis et manumis. l. diffamari; ff. de accu. l. cum Titiae; and de excep. ca. pastor; and no. Dy. in c. in regula indultum, de reg. iu. lib. 6. For this is proved, namely that it is certain that the term assigned makes one deemed and to be considered contumacious. As in C. quo. et quan. iud. l. cessante. But against the contumacious person the opportunity of judicial proceedings is closed, unless he has excused his contumacy by a probable reason. As in ff. de in integ. rest. l. 1; and C. de iudi. l. sancimus; ad hoc, ff. de arbi. l. celsus. Moreover, the term given for proving on the principal matter of the case tends to the decision of the cause; in which, unless equity suggests otherwise, no purgation of delay is admitted. As in ff. si quis cau. l. et si post tres.

I therefore state that, although witnesses were received after the deadline with the opposing party objecting, nevertheless their testimony should not be believed, because they were not duly received, having been admitted after the excluding deadline, as in c. Testibus, in the Clementines; and see the argument in D. De re iudicata, l. Donat. And although the said witnesses were called to take an oath, this is true only when the deposition was duly received; otherwise, it is not so, by virtue of the oath, and since the examination was impeded, the examination already conducted does not have the necessary consequence from the oath, and therefore it does not operate retroactively. And therefore I advised that the one who causes the witnesses to swear should urge the judge to examine them, so that time does not run against him, as in D. De usuris, l. Mora, and C. De temporibus appellandi, l. Aliter sed lex, and what is noted there. And thus I state and advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Both Laws, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether one who did not declare to the customs officer the goods he was carrying, or falsely declared them, may correct himself so as to avoid the penalty; and within what time; and nos. 10 and 11.
2. A congruent interpretation must be observed.
3. Rubrics have the force of text if they are authentically written by the legislators. Where a day is assigned as a term, it is said to be done within the term when it is done at the last moment of the term; examples. nos. 5 and 6.
4. He who wishes to exclude the presumption of fraud must allege and prove a just cause.
5. Indicia are proved by two witnesses.
6. Whether one who denies, but confesses after a short interval, before the adversary has been burdened with the onus of proof, may correct himself so as to avoid the penalty.
7. How the word "immediately" is to be understood, both in pacts and in other dispositions.
8. The law must be understood as referring to the first act.
9. The omission of gain repels fraud.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen. In a statute, or chapter, of the Commune of Faenza it is provided that anyone bringing and selling merchandise in the city and district of Faenza is bound to assign or declare the merchandise itself to the officials appointed for this purpose, or within the third day from the day of the bringing to pay the duty on it. But in another clause of the statute it is contained that whoever brings any merchandise into the city or district of Faenza is bound and ought to bring it openly and without fraud through the ports and public roads, and to show and present it to the guards appointed for this purpose, and to declare to them what goods he has, and whose they are, and to consign and deliver sufficient pledges to those guards; thereafter, to pay the duty for those goods within the term already stated in the preceding chapter, etc.; and if anyone fails in bringing them, and in not declaring them, not assigning them, or not presenting them, etc., or by defrauding in any manner, he shall pay double duty, and five shillings per pound, etc. In a third statute it is provided, among other things, that for a load of wool brought to the mill 15 shillings are to be paid, and for a load, etc., three pounds and 15 shillings are to be paid, etc. In a fourth statute it is provided that in cases of excise taxes against those defrauding taxes or concealing merchandise, the judge may hear, determine, and condemn summarily, on the basis of probable returns, with writing and without writing, with sworn witnesses, notwithstanding any statute, or canon or civil law providing to the contrary. Now it happened that a certain merchant from Sala Mona arrived at the port of Faenza on a certain boat or ship, having four bales of silk packed in the form of bales of wool; and when the boat was drawn to land near the walls of the city, the said merchant entered the city, and when asked by the guard appointed to record merchandise and goods brought to the said city lest frauds be committed whether he had anything of his own on which he ought to pay taxes, he replied that he did not. And immediately, when asked what he had in the boat, he replied that he had four bales of wool. And warned by the guard to be careful what he said, he said, "I have nothing else there." Then the said merchant went to the warehouse in which the said bales of silk were also to be warehoused, and declared to the warehouse keeper the goods he had brought; and then, before the said merchant returned to obtain the permit, the said guard wrote in his book, in which he recorded all other merchandise and goods brought to Faenza, that the said merchant had brought four bales of wool. And having done this, he touched and felt the said bales, and from the touch perceived that they were bales of silk; after these occurrences, within the space of one quarter of an hour, the said merchant returned with the said warehouse keeper to the said guard so that he might issue him the permit, and he then declared and confessed that he had the aforesaid four bales of silk in the boat; but the said toll-collector refused to issue him the permit, because he had written down four bales of wool, and because the said merchant had incurred the penalty of the statute and wished to defraud the duty. To this the said merchant replies that he did not speak with fraudulent intent, but because he was apprehensive, since he wished to send the said silk overland and had learned that the road was not secure, and was afraid to declare that the said bales were bales of silk.
† Now it is asked, first and principally, concerning the penalty: whether it has been incurred. In investigating this, having recited the words of the chapters of the statute,

† a harmonious interpretation must be observed, as in ff. de pe. hae. l. ita veniunt. §. praeter haec, where it says: It is best to make the interpretation of the senatusconsultum itself having recited its words; and in §. aptanda, where it says: an interpretation suited to the individual words. And on behalf of the merchant, that he has not incurred the penalty, it is proved: because where there is a day and a penalty, before the day the penalty is not incurred, as in ff. de verb. ob. l. illa stipulatio si calendis and l. cum stipulatus fuero mihi a Proculo and insulam intra biennium, and c. in commissa, de elect., in Sext. But here a penalty has been attached. Likewise, a day has been attached, namely three days; therefore, if within the three days the notification and declaration of assessment is made, the person notifying and declaring does not incur the penalty of forfeiture or of the statute. Moreover, that three days were set for the assignment and notification to be made to the officials appointed for this purpose is expressed in the first chapter of the statute. Whence it suffices to have obeyed the law within the three days, which speaks of the assignment and notification. Furthermore, the rubric of the statute says that notification must be made within the third day.

† But no one doubts that rubrics have the force of text if they are authentic, recorded by the lawmakers in the volume, as in l. 2, ff. de sta. hom. and C. etiam ob chirogr. pecu. in rub., and as noted in the proem of the sixth book, in that note which begins with the rubric being authentic; and where the text is doubtful, it is clarified by the rubric, which at times extends the black letter, that is, the text, and at times restricts it. For the rubric is, as it were, the beginning of the law, and the interpretation is made through the whole law, as in ff. de iur. et fac. igno. l. regula. §. fi. and as noted in C. ne fide. do. dem. in l. j.

† Since, therefore, the statute says that within the third day he must notify, and within ten pay, it is sufficiently clear that if notification is made within the term, the law has been complied with. But it is certain that he who obeys the law does not fall under the penalty of the law. And it is enough that he obeys at the final point of the term, because whatever is within the term is at the free choice of the debtor, as in ff. si quis cau. l. si eum. §. homo si.sti. And there are two precepts of the law: namely, that notification be made, and that it be made within the term; nor is the penalty incurred before the term has elapsed, as in ff. de arbi. l. Celsus. §. idem ait. And the reason is: because the day does not make a demand except at the very last moment, as in C. de contrahen. et com. stipn. l. magnam and ff. de act. et obli. l. traiecti. §. de illo. Where, however, the space of the last moment remains, there is no default; and therefore no penalty, as in ff. si cer. peta. l. lucri. §. dicebam.

† Furthermore, we see this in many cases expressed in the law: first, in the term given to draw up an inventory, as in C. de iure delibe. l. fi. §. donec; second, in the period that is given to judgment debtors, as in C. de vsuris, in l. 2 and l. fin.; third, in the term that is given to a woman to request a guardian for her son, as in Inst. ad Tertul. in fi. and ff. ad Tertul. l. 2. §. si mater; fourth, in the term that is given to accept a prebend, as is fully noted in cap. eum ei quem, de concess. praeben., in Clem.; fifth, this appears generally through infinite chapters, as in C. qui accu. non poss. l. si ea and ff. de adult. miles. §. sexaginta, and ff. de lega. 2. l. statuliberum. §. Stichum, and l. si ita sit scriptum. §. sub conditione, and ff. de pe. lega. l. 1, and ff. de succ. edic. l. j. §. quod dicimus.

† From which it is inferentially concluded that where a day is assigned as a term, the term is said to be complied with whenever it is done before the term has passed, even at the very last moment, as is fully read and noted in Inst. de ver. ob. §. omnis, and in c. consuluit, de off. composita iudi. de leg., and ff. quod vi aut clam. l. si vitem. §. fi., and in c. quamdiu, de app., in Clem.; for the benefit of delay must be taken away from no one, as in C. de dilationibus. l. siue pars, and ff. solu. ma. l. si constante. §. quotiens. Furthermore, where there is no default, there is no fault, as in C. de his quib. vt indig. l. sororem, and ff. de iure fis. l. edicto. §. cum autem. Moreover, that there is a day here appears expressly from the conjunction of the heads or chapters of the statute itself, as in ff. de lib. et posth. l. Gallus. §. ille casus, and the said l. 2 de statu ho., and by the argument of ff. de fun. instr. l. cum delanionis. §. asinam, and l. Seiae. §. Caio, and ff. de lega. 1. l. talis scriptura, and ff. de coniungen. cum eman. lib. l. nihil in hac parte. And ff. de libe. agno. l. 1. §. eleganter supports the aforesaid exceedingly well. To the contrary it seems: for he who denies is similar to a defrauder; the text is noted in ff. ad l. Fal. l. haereditatum. §. fi., where it says that it makes no difference whether it is passed over or whether he denied that it was hereditary. But it is certain that a defrauder incurs the penalty of the statute. Furthermore, in completed delicts repentance has no place, whether it is completed by word or by deed, as in ff. de fur. l. qui ea mente, unless time is given to seek it, as in C. de his quibus vt indign. l. alia; C. ad l. Corn. de fal. l. si falsos; and it is agreed, as noted in l. si quis non dicam rapere. Furthermore, this merchant is not excused by the fact that he dissembled out of fear; for he could have told the truth in secret to the guard, concerning which guard there was no sinister suspicion, by the argument of C. ad l. Iul. repe. l. fin.; for it is not lawful to deceive a public official, even though it may be lawful to deceive a robber and an ambusher, as in ff. de dolo. l. 1. §. non fuit, and ff. de infa. l. debuit. Furthermore, this delict also carries with it an execution, that is, a judicial sentence is not necessary, but the penalty follows immediately ipso facto; whence repentance has no place, as in C. loc. l. fi., and ff. quod quisque iur. l. 3. §. quod autem, and ff. de pub. l. commissa. Whence just as it is not permitted to purge a delict after condemnation, so it is not permitted to purge it once someone has been condemned ipso facto, as in c. ab eo, de elec., in Sext., and by the argument of C. de don. ante nup. l. si constante. §. exceptis. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that a period of three days was set, because that time was not set for the presentation to be made to the guards, but for paying. And it is certain that a term operates only regarding that for which it is set; the text is noted in ff. de contrahen. emp. l. qui fundum. Furthermore, the office of the guard of the passage is distinct from the office of the officials who collect the excise tax; whence the term of the statute regarding the collectors does not look to the act to be done before the guards, because a statute concerning one office is not enacted concerning another, in which the same is not found to have been enacted, unless the law proceeds further by declaring or extending itself, as in ff. de dam. infect. l. 4. §. dies, and ff. ad Tertu. l. 2. §. antepen., and ff. si quis ius dicen. non obtem. l. 1. in prin., just as is stated there in the text, "not however," and C. ne liceat potentioribus. l. 1. in fi.; for different offices have a different rationale and statutory provision, as in ff. de offi. eius cui man. est iur. l. 1. in prin. It must therefore be considered that the declaration before the guard ought to be made immediately, which is not apparent; because the letter of the statute says, "anyone who brings," therefore it denotes the act as it is in the course of being done, and consequently the place and time, as in c. abbate, de re iu., in Sext.; for the place of the buyer circumscribes the act, as in ff. de nox. l. in delictis. §. si extraneus. If therefore the promise was not made at that time, lest an opportunity for fraud be left, the statutory penalty seems to have been incurred, not so much by reason of default as by reason of fault, and thus by reason of the formal disposition of the statute itself, by the argument of ff. de act. emp. l. ratio. §. si per venditorem, and what is noted there according to the second solution of the gloss. Likewise, it does not stand in the way if it is said that this fault was not proved because it was not established to the merchant that he was a guard, by l. si quis inficiatus, ff. depo., and by l. prohibiti, C. de iu. fis. lib. 10; because those laws speak of an official of some lord who discharges his office in the presence of the lord, or in the city whose official he is, residing in that city, as in ff. de exercitoria. l. 1. §. magistrum. Likewise, it does not stand in the way if it is said that this was proved only by a qualified confession, and if the qualification is true, the penalty ceases, and therefore the confession cannot be accepted in part and rejected in part, as is noted in C. de dona. ante nup. l. 1 and C. de excep. l. si quidam; because I have said that this is an alleged qualification that does not deny the delict, because it does not conclusively lead to the merchant's excuse. And granted that such an excuse were true and just, nevertheless I say that since it is not an intrinsic but an extrinsic excuse, it is not presumed unless proved, as in C. ad l. Cor. de sica. l. 1 and C. de iniur. l. si non conuicii.

† Likewise, according to Bartolus, the gloss which is in l. si quaedam has no place in malfeasances, in which fraud is presumed; for he who wishes to exclude the presumption of fraud must allege and prove a just cause, as in ff. de abigeis. l. 1. in fi. And granted that the doctors distinguish: either the same utterance or several, which distinction is grammatical rather than substantive; yet in our case the delict seems proved by the official himself, to whose testimony credit must apparently be given in that which is committed to him, as in Extra, de app. c. cum parati, and l. magna, c. puto. §. ne tamen, de rebus eorum. But that allegation is of little value, by l. diuus, ff. de cust. reo; for the official is not believed so that a condemnation may be founded upon his statement, though he is certainly believed for the purpose of inquiring, as in l. 1, C. de iud. Nor does it stand in the way that the statute says proceedings may be taken on the basis of general indications,

† for the indications are not proved by the report of the official alone, because two witnesses are required to prove indications, as noted in C. fam. er. l. fi. Others offer the reason that for credit to be given to a single witness is against natural law; but this is not true, because if it were against natural law, the doctrine handed down in l. admonendi, ff. de iure iu., would be false, as is proved in the rationale of its own law, ff. de quaest. l. maritus. Having examined the premises alleged pro and con,

† we must now come to the decision of the question; and first, it must be seen whether he who denies, if after a short time has elapsed he confesses before his adversary has to be burdened with the onus of proof, can correct himself so as to avoid the penalty. And it seems that from equity it is granted to him, as in ff. de iureiu. l. eum, in prin. Furthermore, I see that a witness can immediately correct his statement, as noted by Speculator in the title de testi. §. quia vero. This word

† "immediately" ought not to be taken as strictly as it is taken in the matter of pacts, but ought to be understood as it is taken in the matter of purging default or fault, as it is taken in the matter of correction, by the argument of ff. de interro. l. de aetate. §. fi.; or "immediately" is understood as speedily, as in ff. de in integ. res.; or "immediately" is understood according to the judgment of an upright man, as in ff. de ver. obl. l. si ita quis. §. 1; or "immediately" is understood as on the same day, as in ff. de re. iu. l. Paulus; elsewhere "immediately" is set down as within three days, as in C. de errore aduo. l. 3 and C. de iudi. l. pe.; elsewhere "immediately" is used for forthwith. But in our case I believe it is sufficient that the space of a quarter of an hour is not a bad interval such as to impede the lawful sufficiency of the one declaring; rather, as it were ex post facto, it appears that earlier there was no intention of defrauding, by the argument of C. de incest. nup. l. cum ancillis and ff. de adult. l. cum incestu.

† Secondly, it must be seen whether—even granting that the purging of fault would not have place based on general equity, l. ex edic. §. placet, ff. de alienatione iudi.—nonetheless the penalty is not incurred because the three days had not elapsed. And in brief I think that not declaring to the guard in that transfer, or falsely declaring, is a fault or fraud; yet I do not believe that the penalty of five shillings is incurred in the meantime before the three days, because the statute sets three days for notification, designation, assignment, and declaration. And therefore it suffices that it was done within the term; the case is in the said l. qui fundum. And so I hold, namely that the penalty was not incurred by the said merchant, because by a negative act the delay of three days was not consumed. For however much he may deny, as long as time remains, he can declare and alter his statement;

† and if it is said that the law must be understood of the first act, that is true when through the first act the benefit is consumed; it is otherwise if the delay continues, by the argument of ff. de act. empt. l. si sterilis. §. fi., and the case is in the said l. qui fundum vendebat. Likewise, fraud is understood as damage; but here there is no damage, therefore neither is there fraud.

† Likewise, the omission of gain repels fraud, as in C. de his qui sibi ascri. l. 1. C. de crimine stell. l. 1, in the last response, and l. 1, C. ne tu. vel cu. vectigalia condu., there, "nevertheless since voluntarily," etc., support this excellently, which text is very notable for our question. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that to a person convicted, money is not granted, nor the abolition of the offense, as in C. de abol. l. fallaciter, and C. de non nu. pe., in the authentic contra qui propriam, and what is noted in Inst. de actio. §. item an ista est actio contra eos; but this merchant was not convicted on the ground that the guard had recognized it to be silk by touch. For with another immediate sensible object interposed, touch did not result in a clear sensation through an object removed from the touch, but through mere belief; and that is not properly a sensation, for example, if through the medium of a rough surface the sense perceives smoothness, it does not properly know its quality, but through belief, as in ff. de ven. in spi. l. i. in prin.; because sight is also required to perceive through touch. Whence the Patriarch was deceived, because the hands seemed to be Esau's; and note in ff. de testamen. l. haeredes palam. Likewise, he is not convicted who is not convicted before a judge, because proof must be made to a judge. Likewise, it does not stand in the way that the guard wrote "bales of wool" in his book, because it does not follow: "he wrote it down, therefore the merchant ought to be punished"; but rather the error ought to be corrected, as in C. de testam. l. errore. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that no appeal shall lie from the pronouncement or execution of an instrument of guarantee, no appeal may be taken from the renewal of a license.
2. Whether new acts are necessary before the successor.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The aforementioned words of the statute stating that no one may appeal from the pronouncement or execution of a *guarentigia* being set forth, the question arises concerning such a case. Suppose that the judge pronounced that a certain instrument, which is not *saboli*, nor vitiated, nor deferred from a date, nor suspended by a condition, but pure and liquid, or purified by an existing condition, is to be executed. Finally, the successor in office renewed this license, as is customary. L. de stilo curiae in certain places, as is the case in the city of Perugia, where such renewals are made even without the party being cited.

† It is asked whether an appeal may be taken from this renewal. And it seems at first that, if the party was not cited, this interlocutory renewal is void by operation of law. And first, on account of the successor, who ought to propose a new edict, as in D. de iudicatis, l. Edictum. Second, because due to the passage of time, an oblique defense might have accrued to the defendant in the meantime, which ought to be examined; therefore, the party ought to be cited, as noted by Cynus in l. 1, C. de iudicibus, and in D. de conditione sine causa, l. Si filio. Third, because it is necessary that the prior acts be produced before the new judge; therefore, in such production, the party ought to be cited, as in C. de testibus, l. Si quando. Fourth, because nothing is said to be clear to the judge unless the party is cited, as in C. si per vim vel alio modo, l. final. Fifth, because whatever is necessary in a cession is likewise necessary in a renewal, as in C. de nuptiis, l. In copulandis.

On the contrary, it seems that this renewal is not made for any other reason than because the mandate granted to the messenger for execution appears to have expired by the death of the principal, as in D. de iudicatis, cod., l. Iudex et quia. But judicial commissions may be issued without citing the adversary, because the commission precedes the citation, as in C. de exhibendis rebus, l. Neminem. Therefore, such renewal is valid against the party not cited. Second, because this renewal is an execution of law; therefore, the party ought not to be cited, as noted by Innocentius in Extra, de appellationibus, c. Ex ratione. For he who performs mere execution is not said to cause a grievance, so that an appeal may be taken therefrom, as in D. de appellationibus, ab executore; Extra, de appellationibus, c. Non novit ille; and C. quorum appellatio non recipitur, l. Ab executione, unless an appeal is taken within ten days from the day the first sentence was pronounced, as noted in D. quod mei causa, l. Si cum exceptione, §. Hæc autem actio. Fourth, because even without renewal, the license to plead exceptions appears to endure, as noted by Bartolus in D. de aqua pluviae arcendae, l. Fundum, §. 1. For this may be called a precept with regard to the matter, as noted in the said law, l. et quia. Fifth

† When it is said, whether a certain successor is in the same tribunal or in a different one. For in the first case new acts are not necessary, but in the second case they are necessary, according to the noted rule in the Digest, *De probationibus*, law *Quo*, § *Si*, and in the Digest, *De re iudicata*, law *A Diuo Pio*. Solution: Considering the beginning and the statute, and assuming that the first license holds by law: I say that an appeal cannot be taken from its renewal. For he who renews does not make a new thing, but executes an old one. Just as one could not appeal from the execution of an instrument renewed due to its age, because it is one and the same instrument. And it supports what is noted in the Authenticum, *De hereditatibus et falsis*, after the beginning, column 1. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. How a father may institute his daughter, legitimated by him, as his heir in the lands of the church, by one having authority from the emperor.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A certain Salnolinus Pelloli of Cerqueto, having a certain daughter born out of wedlock, who is called Agnesola, whom he had legitimated through the Bishop of Perugia, Count Palatine, and having authority on this matter from the Emperor. This Salnolinus, not having legitimate sons, nor hoping to have any, nor brothers, nor carnal nephews, wishes to institute this his daughter as his universal heir.

† It is asked how this woman may make a will, so that this daughter may have her own goods, or those of any friend of the testator. I answer that many have given various cautions: as appears through D. ff. de iure fideicommissorum, l. ita fidei; § patronus, de vulgari substitutione; si is qui, de his quibus ut indigitatis; l. si, per Bartolus; and in l. Gallus, per Bartolus. I say that if this legitimation is valid, there is no doubt that the said Salnolinus may make a will as he wishes, as in Auth. quibus modis naturales efficiuntur sui, § si, col. 7, and there noted. But if it is not valid, because some say that the Emperor cannot legitimize in the lands of the Pope, on which there are contrary opinions, nevertheless every such caution ought to be observed, namely, that the said Salnolinus institute the said Agnesola alone as his heir. And if the said Agnesola were not capable, he should institute her as heir when she shall be able to take; and if she were not capable, nor able to take with effect, he should institute and substitute as his universal heirs the legitimate and natural sons of the said do. Agnesola, whenever born and supervening to the said do. Agnesola. And if she had no sons, one or more, or had them but they died before the death of the said Agnesola, then he should institute and substitute simply and freely his friend, as C. de heredibus instituendis, l. 2. And this is my counsel. And thus I say and counsel, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If the plaintiff fails to prove his case, the defendant must be absolved.
2. Whether a judgment rendered without any proof against a contumacious defendant is null.
3. Whether one who accuses another of causing damage in his forest is required to prove ownership or possession.
4. If two persons hold a forest in undivided co-ownership, whether one may cut down the forest against the will of the other.
5. Whether a common valuation proves ownership.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A certain Nerius accused Benedict of a certain wood, which he claimed belonged to him, and that the said Benedict had no right in it. On the other hand, the said Benedict says that he has a certain share in the said wood as an undivided portion. And to prove this, he had evidence of that land, in which the said property was described as belonging to the said Benedict, as owner and possessor in undivided share with the said Nerius. The judge, without any other proofs being made, condemned the said Benedict, from whose sentence there was an appeal.

† Now the question arises as to what is the law. I answer that there is no doubt that if the plaintiff fails to prove his case, the defendant must be absolved. As stated in C. de eden. l. qui accusare; and 2. q. i. c. nos in quemquam; C. de proba. l. actor; C. de cal. l. nostris. Indeed, even more so, because no proof has been made, neither certain nor by circumstantial evidence: for instance, because all the plaintiff's witnesses say that they know nothing.

† Certain glossators say that the sentence is void by operation of law, as noted in Codex, De sententiis et interlocutionibus, l. proba; and in Extra, De constitutionibus, c. Ecclesia S. Mariae, on the ground that the order of law was not observed and the intermediate stage of proof was omitted. Others say that it is valid, because it was rendered through manifest bias and favoritism, and it is rescinded without appeal by way of restitution in integrum, as noted in Digest, Ad Trebellianum, l. servo invito, §. praetor. A third group distinguishes: either the sentence was rendered against an absent party not in true contempt, in which case it is void by operation of law, Codex, De accusationibus, l. absentem; or it was rendered against a present party, in which case it is of some effect, but may be overturned by the ordinary remedy of appeal and by the remedy of restitution in integrum under the general clause. On this matter, see fully the notes of Guillaume de Coucy and Cynus in l. pen., Digest, De iustitia et iure. Whatever the case may be, there is no doubt that if an appeal is brought by one who is not in true contempt for failing to appear, the defendant prevails, unless the plaintiff demonstrates that the sentence was rightly rendered, as in Authentica, De his qui ingrati sunt ad appellandum, §. illud quoque; and see Codex, De appellationibus, l. hi qui ad civilia.

† Furthermore, there is no doubt that if the plaintiff has proven those matters which are sufficient for the plaintiff’s victory against the defendant, and the defendant has not proven his possession, the defendant is absolved from the accusation, unless the defendant holds possession from the plaintiff, for example, clandestinely or by precarious title. See Codex, *Uti possidetis*, l. unica. For I say that, to ground this accusation regarding the cutting of a forest, the plaintiff’s possession suffices, to which possession injury and disturbance are caused by the cutting. See Digest, *De iniuriis*, l. *Iniuriarum*, § *Si*. And because, conversely, if he were to claim to be owner and possessor, nevertheless, since ownership arises incidentally due to another matter, possession is therefore taken as noted in l. *Sicuti*, § *Si quaeratur*, *Si serui venditi*; and Digest, *De conditione instituta*, l. *Pe*. And because a coppice forest is in fruit, and fruits pertain to the possessor, as noted in Digest, *De acquirenda possessione*, l. 3, § *Ex contrario*, unless it is said that the forest is a fruit by natural law, whereby the possessor does not make such fruit his own. For the reason ceases: it is asked whether the possessor makes fruits his own, namely, cultivation and care, as noted in Digest, *De rei venditione*, l. *Fructus*; and Institutes, *De rerum divisione*, § *Si quis domino*. Briefly, whatever the case may be, because the possessor ought not to suffer violent disturbance and must be protected in possession, another could not, against his will, cut such a forest, and this applies when only the actor possesses.

But when two persons have possessed as undivided co-owners, whether one may fell the woodland against the will of the other, it must be said that he may, if the woodland is coppice. For the negligence of the one who does not fell does not usually prejudice the vigilant party, nor the one who uses the thing for its intended use. See Digest 7.1.13 § 1 (Arboribus) and Digest 7.1.13 § 2 (Navis). And therefore in such a case the accused ought to be acquitted, see Digest 16.3.1 (Merito). The objection from Sabinus in Digest 10.3 (Communi dividundo), where the condition of the prohibiting party is the stronger, does not apply, because that rule is true only where the prohibited party was attempting to do something which he could not do by law, because it was not for the natural use of the thing. And thus the objection does not apply.

† Now it is doubted whether the valuation of a common thing proves ownership or possession, and that not necessarily; nevertheless, the valuation creates a certain presumption regarding ownership: and possession is proved, as in D. de acquirenda rerum dominium, l. quisque; D. de censibus, l. forma; C. de donationibus, l. censualis; C. communi diviso, l. si maior; C. de rei venditione, l. solennibus pensionibus. And therefore, according to what is proposed, the condemnatory sentence against the said Benedict was wrongly given, and it ought to be corrected by the appellate judge. L. eos, in principio; and D. de appellationibus, l. 1, in principio. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a fee is owed to the arbitrator who rendered his award.
2. How much the arbitrator's fee ought to be, and by whom it ought to be paid.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen.

† On this point, a distinction must be made as to whether these arbitrators rendered their award based on the first compromise, which preceded the aforementioned petition made before the judge; and in that case, the said salary ought not to be paid, because the statute does not speak of an extrajudicial compromise made without any petition having been filed, nor of the arbitral composition ensuing therefrom. Nor does the law speak to this effect; rather, it states that no salary ought to be paid for the fee arising from such a mutable compromise and award, as provided in the Code, *De episcopis et clericis*, in the authority *Generaliter*, at the end. For if a settlement were made by the parties themselves transacting upon the aforementioned petition, then the salary would be due, because so determines the statute, since such a settlement succeeds to the thing adjudicated, as stated in the Digest, *De manumis.*, l. *Si*. But if this statute did not so determine, it is certain that no salary is due for a transaction between the parties, because the reason set forth in the Authenticum *De iudicibus*, § *Ne autem laborando*, ceases to apply.

Let us suppose that the case is one in which a fee is due: I ask, what should be the amount of this fee, whether it should be calculated on the full valuation of the things, or on the half part, or whether it should not be estimated as merely half of the half. And that it should be on the whole thing, as in D. de iudiciis omnium iudicum, l. si idem cum eodem, §. fin. I say the contrary, because by division it does not happen that half of the half part is paid, as noted in D. de verbis obligatorum, l. qui Romae, § duo fratres. For division takes the place of exchange. And that which is exchanged is of value. The action is for the other party’s share and for my share: because dominion is transferred by exchange to that extent, and therefore the fee, or the tenth, i.e., the fourth part, i.e., half of the half, should be paid to that extent, namely because each one would be bound to pay in this manner. But between both parties it is properly paid up to the full half of the entire thing, calculating, i.e., computing, as aforesaid. And from the foregoing it appears that if the parties chose new arbitrators, just as the judge would do, or as they would do in a concord, then the fee should be due, because he who seeks division seeks that the thing be adjudicated to him for the part to be divided, as in Inst. de officio iudicis, §. fin. But if the matter proceeded from an old compromise, then the said fee should not be paid. I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a bishop, instituted as heir, transmits the inheritance to his successor or to his heir; and whether the successor is at least admitted as a legitimate executor.
2. In legacies for pious causes, acceptance of the inheritance is not required. Whether a bishop has a quarter share of what is left for the marriage of girls.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Having seen the testament of Bonaventure, the Dean, in which he disposes as follows, namely, that he left his wife, Bellaflora, as usufructuary of all the goods of the said testator, provided she lives chastely; and in all his other goods he instituted as heir the venerable father, Lord Luca Redolse of Camerino, with this condition, that the said Lord Luca, after the death of the said Bellaflora, is bound to marry those women who seem appropriate and pleasing to him, if the said Lord Luca were then alive. And if he were unwilling to accept the said inheritance, certain executors appointed and to be appointed by them are bound to marry the aforementioned women from the said goods. And that from then on, the aforementioned to-be-appointed persons are to be understood and are instituted heirs, and he instituted the said executors as his universal heirs from now, that is, from then, with the aforementioned condition of always marrying women from the said inheritance. Having seen, therefore, and considering the point formulated, in which it is proposed on behalf of the said Lady Bellaflora that the said Lord Luca died having accepted the aforementioned inheritance; and that the said executors were not appointed; and that the Lord Bishop of Camerino, as diocesan, wishes to enter into the custody and possession of the goods of the said inheritance, since the executors of the said testament are dead, and died before the said Lord Luca, and the legitimate diocesan executor succeeds in the place of the testamentary executor. But on the other side, the heirs of the said Lord Luca oppose themselves; and they say that the said execution ought to pertain to them as heirs of the heir; because since Lord Luca died before the inheritance was accepted, he transmitted it to his heirs with its burden, as is noted. The said Lady Bellaflora says that during her lifetime the said virgins are not to be married.

† Now it is asked, since the lord bishop wishes to take cognizance of the said lady Bellaflor regarding the payment of the legacy, whether he can, and whether, as diocesan, he can draw to himself the administration of the goods and exclude the heirs of the said lord Luca or not. I answer that it clearly appears from the series of the testament that the testator did not wish the said lord Luca to be heir of the fideicommissa solely during his lifetime, not for the purpose of possessing, but for the purpose of distributing, as in Extra, de testamento, c. Cum tibi. For he was appointed as a minister for a work of piety, as in Digest, de usuris, l. In fideicommissi, § Cum Pollidius. And in this, his singular fidelity and diligence were chosen. And therefore this does not transmit to his heir, as in Digest, de cura furiosi, l. Cuius bonis. Nor does it even acquire for the Bishopric of Camerino, because it was not left in contemplation of the bishopric, as in Extra, de testamento, c. Requisti. And because the testator openly disposed that after his death the witnesses should succeed for pious causes, one can institute heirs for a time, and even directly for a time, as we say in the case of a soldier, as in Digest, de vulgari et pupillari substitutione, l. Centurio. Although this is not expedient according to civil law: nevertheless, whether one can directly substitute or not, the benefit can nevertheless be transferred to the heir, and is transferred by the law itself without restitution under the Trebellian, according to Bartolus, who thus notes in l. Si, Codex, de sacrosanctis ecclesiis. And even if restitution under the Trebellian were necessary, nevertheless in this case it is not necessary: because, as I said, lord Luca was instituted so that he might be a bare minister during his lifetime.

And because such legacies to pious causes, whether particular or universal, do not require the acceptance of the inheritance according to the opinion of Speculum, since they are committed to execution by the office of the judge; and if the acceptance of the inheritance is not required, therefore neither is the restitution under the Trebellian law. Hence it is concluded with necessity that in place of the deceased executors the diocesan bishop succeeds, who shall order the will to be executed, as in C. de episcopis et clericis, l. nulli tamen. The girls should not be married while the lady of the house is alive, Bellaflo, unless she herself consents, as in C. de fideicommissis, l. post mortem. And because the lady of the house, Bellaflo, possesses everything, she can be compelled by the office of the diocesan bishop to pay the legacies, if any are to be paid during her lifetime, as noted according to one reading in ff. de usufructu legato, l. si. And regarding what remains, until the said lady Bellaflo is alive, she ought to have full usufruct; because there are no children, as in l. uxori, de usufructu legato, and as noted in C. si secundo nupserit mulier, l. 1.

But whether the diocesan bishop ought to have the fourth part of that which is left for the marriage of girls. I answer: not by law, although in fact it is so; because it is left to lay persons. And because the aforesaid testator expressly says that the said women were to be those specified by the said testator. And if the testator had said so, the fourth part would not be due, as noted in c. 2, Extra, de sepulturis. Therefore, the same applies if the testamentary executor, or the legitimate one, namely the diocesan bishop, specifies them. On the same title, c. Dudum, § Verum, in the Clementine; and de legatis, 2, l. Vnum ex familia, in principio.

Moreover, certain Bertinus and Nicolutius, natural brothers, donated a certain palace to Charles, who Charles had a natural brother with whom he had made no division. Indeed, although they held everything in common and lived together, and in return for the said donation, he delivered to the said donors one piece of land, which he held together with his brother, who brother was not sued regarding the said remuneration of the said land; rather, for his part, the said donors delivered the said palace to themselves for his part for 75 pounds. Then, when they wished to come to a division with the son of the said Charles. Now the said Charles and his brother have died, leaving one male son surviving from each. And it is said on behalf of the son of the brother of the said Charles, and not the said Charles, that he did not wish for profit or loss from the said palace, but that he wants a part of the said palace donated to the said Charles, just as from the other goods, since his father and Charles held everything in common and possessed it together. The son of Charles says that he ought not to have the said part of the palace, because it was donated only to the said Charles. The question is: what is the law? I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A thing given as a gift is not subject to sharing by an action for partnership.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Considering the first point, it must be said that whether we consider the simple nature of partnership, the said palace was given to the said Charles as his sole property; because donated things do not come to be shared through the action for partnership, as stated in D. 17,2,1, *nec adiecit*. For partnership regards only those things which are sought through care and industry, which can be common, because one contributes money, the other labor. But where nothing is sought from property or labor, but rather from the simple benefit of the giver, this does not pertain to partnership, but only to the affection of the donor, as stated in D. 17,2,1, *socium*, in the section *qui in eo*, § *si*, l. 3. Or, if we consider that the brother of the said Charles, in reward for his service, redeemed the property by exercising the right of preemption at the price, which succeeds in place of consent, and did not consent, but rather expressly renounced, nothing was acquired for him from the said donation, nor should anything be sought for his heirs, as noted in D. 3,5,1, *si ex duobus*. And therefore it is clearly concluded that the son of Charles ought to have the said palace as his exclusive property, and is not bound to share it with the other. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given the statute, which provides that once a crime is proven by one witness of truth, the accused ought to be subjected to torture: if it is proven by one witness who is said to be a capital enemy, will there be room for torture?
2. Whether capital enmity is induced by the fact that the brother of the accused was brought to kill the brother of the cousin of the witness produced to prove the crime, and from what sources it arises.
3. Capital enmity is said to exist wherever the offended party could vindicate himself directly or indirectly.
4. Capital enmity is proven by presumptions.
5. Associating with someone is not a crime, unless he is an outlaw or a murderer: then the knowledge of that associate must be proven.
6. If the accused or the inquisitio defendant did not protest against the opposition of exceptions against the witnesses, whether the exception of enmity can be raised to invalidate their testimony.
7. Whether, after the term assigned for proving according to the form of the statute, proof can be made by public instruments.
8. One witness, who provides an indication for torture, must be such that he is an undisputed witness.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Assuming the statute provides that, upon proof of a felony by one witness of truth, the accused ought to be subjected to torture, the question arises whether, if the proof is given by one witness who is said to be a capital enemy on the ground that the accused’s natural brother had been indicted for killing the said witness’s first cousin, and thus there is a capital enmity between them, there is room for torture.

And this question turns on whether from this it follows that there is capital enmity, such that the witnesses are entirely rejected, or such that the testimony of the witness is so weakened that from such testimony one should not proceed to torture. And it is certain that the natural brother of the said Bart., who was present to kill the cousin-brother of the said witness, is an enemy of the said witness. But doubt is raised concerning Bart. himself, because the said Bart. was not a principal in the said homicide; therefore he ought not to be called an enemy, because where there is no fault, there ought to be no hatred. Therefore neither enmity, because it would be irrational hatred, since it is not presumed unless it is proved, as in C. de testibus, auth. Si dicatur. But the contrary is true: because with regard to the contracting of enmity, he is presumed to be an enemy whose brother is an enemy, indeed even all of the kin, as in C. si quacunque praed. po. l. 1, and ff. de inimicitia, l. Lex Cornelia. And it supports what is noted in extra de officio delegati, c. Si pro debilitate, in the 10th column, concerning him who killed the brother of his lord, c. 1, and C. de excusationibus tuendis, l. Humanitatis, and extra de arbitris, c. Cum oporteat, and what is there stated by Innocentius, and ff. de liberatione causae, l. 2 and 3. For I say that if it appears that the brother of the said Bartholomew killed the cousin-brother of the said witness, from this it is presumed that there is capital enmity between them.

† because capital enmity is that in which, wherever the offense is avenged directly or indirectly, if possible. Also, because one suspected of enmity must be considered as an enemy, as in the Digest, On Witnesses, l. 3, in the word "suspicion." For, as Innocentius elegantly says, enemies are not only divided with regard to repelling from testimony those who harbor hatred in their minds, but also those who have causes of enmity, or are presumed to have them, and who, without malice in mind, bear hatred, as in the Decretals, On Matters Judged, c. Cum L. et A., through Innocentius. And therefore this witness is suspect as malevolent: because the connection of kinship of the offender on one side, and the connection of blood of the offended on the other, induce a valid suspicion for repelling the testimony of the testifying witness, or for invalidating it, so that he is not considered an impartial witness. Hence, the judge, who has discretion on this matter, as in the Digest, On Which Causes One Is Presumed a Capital Enemy, l. Licet; Digest, On Deprivation of Legacies, l. 2, at the end; and noted through Innocentius in the Decretals, On Accusations, c. Cum Oporteat, must judge that those who were once an enemy, or ought to have been, or were accustomed to be according to the custom of the country, are also presently an enemy, or elegantly noted by Innocentius in the said c. Cum Oporteat. And the gloss notes.

† That capital enmity is proven by presumptions. And from this it is presumed that he changed his mind towards his enemy, so as to take vengeance upon him, as noted in the Digest, On Excuses, title, l. athletae, §. dat remissionem. Therefore, these things being considered, faith should not be given to such a witness for the purpose of torture, unless perhaps the witness himself had been examined under torture. For tortures increase the credibility of a witness regarding another, and decrease the credibility of one confessing against himself, so that they increase it in the witness, but in the part that was tortured, they decrease it, as in the Authentica, On Witnesses, §. si, noted in ignoti, and in the Digest, On Questions, l. 1, §. quaestionum. From these it appears that the testimony given against the said Bartholomew, brother of the murderer, is not valid, to such an extent that from such a single witness, about whom there is suspicion of enmity, the said Bartholomew ought to be subjected to torture. And to this effect it is said in the Digest, On the Law of All Judges, l. qui iurisdictioni, and in the Digest, On Inofficious Wills, l. liberi, §. si, and in the Digest, On the Office of the President, l. 1, §. cum patronus, and what is noted there. And this is the truth, that from the statement of this sole witness one cannot proceed to torture. One must proceed to other witnesses: and in this it must be considered whether the statements of the other witnesses refer to the inquisition; because the inquisition alleges that the said Antonio was taken from the hands, etc.

But the other witnesses do not say this: and it is one thing to remove, i.e., to take away from the hands; another thing is to associate with a fugitive, as in D. 4.2.1 (ne quis eum, qui in ius vocatus est, vi eximat). Moreover, the said other witnesses do not say anything about knowledge, i.e., that the said Bartolus knew anything about the said homicide. And therefore, since knowledge is not proven, ignorance is presumed: and no one is punished for that which is not in itself a delict, but only with some adjunct, unless knowledge of that adjunct is proven. For associating with someone is not in itself a delict, but it becomes so with the adjunct that he was an outlaw or a murderer; then a wrong results. Now the law says that it is necessary to allege and prove knowledge of this adjunct, as in D. 48.19.1 and 2 (de receptatoribus) and D. 48.6.2 (de his qui latrones) and C. 9.13.1 (cum ancillis, de incestis nuptiis). And it is expressly stated in the case of one who associates with a fugitive that certain knowledge must be proven, in C. 9.13.1 (de raptu virginum) and C. 10.35.1 (de episcopis et clericis, raptores). Therefore, since they say nothing about knowledge, they do not prove the wrong, as in D. 47.10.1 (vi bonorum raptorum, Praetor, § Decretum) and D. 48.5.1 (de adulteriis, Denunciasse, § Quid tamen).

It remains to consider two doubts which are plausibly raised in court. The first doubt is: since the accused did not protest exceptions against the witnesses, can the exception of enmity be raised to invalidate or weaken the testimony? It seems that it cannot, because he who does not object against the person appears to consent to the witness, since the witness swears to tell the truth for both parties. Nevertheless, he may well object against the deposition if it is false testimony: for he was not produced or approved for giving false testimony, except by the party who produced him on the false article, as in C. de testib. l. si quis testibus. The contrary view seems correct, because it is one thing for a witness to be challenged on account of his person, and another on account of suspicion regarding what he deposes. Hence the exception of enmity is mixed, because it is presumed that he deposes out of enmity, and thus not the true testimony. Therefore, since the exception of enmity is a mixed exception as to both person and statement, it may properly be raised even though it was not protested; for although one does not protest, he nevertheless knows that his exception will endure. Hence he does not truly renounce it. To this effect, see extra de testib. c. praesentiam, and C. de testib. auth. si dicatur.

The second doubt arises because a time limit was assigned according to the form of the statute for proving the case; whether after the expiration of that term proof may be made by public and clear instruments, which do not require certification by witnesses: and I say that it may. For, with respect to the matter itself, even if the defendant is undefended, the judge ought to supply [the proof] from something notorious, of which he has knowledge, and the plaintiff’s instruments have the force of notoriety; therefore, etc., as in D. de quaestionibus, l. universalis, §. cogniturum; and D. de poenis, l. si non defendantur. Moreover, because as long as the deceptive instance lasts, instruments may be produced, as noted in c. Pastoralis, de re iudicata, in the Clementines. From all of which I firmly hold that the said accused ought not to be tortured.

† Because one witness, who provides evidence sufficient for torture, must be such that he is an undisputed witness, as in the Digest, De quaestionibus, l. Milites, § Oportet. The other witnesses, as being irrelevant, and consequently as not having been tendered, i.e., not produced nor sworn, do not establish proof, as in the Digest, De petitione hereditatis, l. Si quis libertatem, with its similar provisions. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A manifold species of conditions is found.
2. Whether a legacy made to someone, if she remains a widow, requires perpetual widowhood. Likewise, whether and when in the fulfillment of a condition perseverance is required, or whether a momentary fulfillment suffices.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

It must be premised for clarity that some conditions are instantaneous, for example, “I bequeath to Titius if he ascends the Capitol,” “if he certainly marries,” and the like. In such cases, it suffices that they were perfectly fulfilled at a specific moment in time. Codex, On Institutions and Substitutions, law *Si quis hereditatem*. Some conditions are successive, acquiring the persistence of a certain period of time; in such cases, it does not suffice that the condition began to exist, but its persistence is required. Argument, Digest, On Manumission by Will, law *Vicina*; Digest, On Alimony and Food Legacies, law *Servos ad custodiam templi*. Some conditions are susceptible to either interpretation, and in such cases, in wills, a liberal interpretation applies, unless something else is gathered from the tacit will of the testator. The case is found in the aforementioned law *Si quis hereditatem*, namely, that it suffices for the condition to have been fulfilled once, so that the legacy is owed perpetually. Hence, if a testator bequeaths to Berta if she marries Titius, and she does marry him, but later separates from him, and whether she marries another or not, I do not care, she must have the legacy, as in Digest, On Legacies, Title 3, law *Cum pater*, section *Pater certam*.

† Now let us consider this legacy: “I bequeath to my niece, if she remains a widow.” In this matter, I distinguish as follows: either this legacy is of all things, or of one thing. In the first case, it is immediately due to her that she is a widow, the whole legacy being owed to her; for it is understood to refer to the first and immediate widowhood, by argument from ff. qui et a quibus, l. matrimonii; ff. de verborum obligationibus, l. bonus, §. huius sermone; ff. solutione matrimonii, l. filiae meae. In the second case, it is due to her for that year or years during which she remained a widow for some part of that year. ff. de legatis 3, l. qui concubinam, §. uxori meae. And the reason is this: because in the beginning of any year it is examined whether the condition is true. For the condition must be true; then the day of the legacy ought to arrive, as noted in l. ex facto, in principio, ff. de vulgari substitutione, according to Bartolus. And therefore, since in our case it is presupposed that there was one legacy, I say that the said condition existed at the moment of widowhood and purified the said legacy. And although others marry, nevertheless the legacy is not thereby considered to have been revoked, because the testator did not say so. And I say that those words, “if she should remain a widow,” are verified immediately when the case exists, by argument from extra qui clerici vel vouentes, c. insinuante. For it is of her marriage that she is understood to have been widowed, that is, released from her marriage, and even if new marriages are contracted, she would remain so, although with respect to the woman herself she becomes married again. And if this reason displeases, because it would include that she ought to be a widow, which is false: nevertheless, other prior reasons conclude effectively in favor of the legatee. Hence, I make a distinction whether the testator says, “if she should remain a widow,” or “if she has remained a widow,” or whether he says, “if she has remained a widow,” or “if she should remain widowed.” For then the legacy would not be received unless caution had been provided, as in C. de indicio vidui, auth. cui relictum. Or whether he says, “as long as she remains a widow,” or “remains,” in which case, while she is a widow, she has the legacy, but afterwards not, as noted by Cyriacus, C. de indicio vidui, l. si, and in Authen. de nuptiis, §. quae, noted by Jacobus de Belvisio. And therefore, the counsel of the excellent doctor, my brother of the same name, is dismissed. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Laws, saving the sounder judgment. In my own hand.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A confession made by the principal debtor, acknowledging a certain debt, prejudices him who, by a formal stipulation, constituted himself debtor for that person and assumed all of his debt.
2. By what words one becomes a co-debtor.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A certain Ser Cechus constituted himself a debtor by solemn stipulation, and upon himself he assumed the entire debt of a certain Ser Nicolaus, according to the receipt of the said Ser Nicolaus at the time when he administered the affairs of a certain toll to a certain legitimate heir, so that the said legitimate heir might suffer no damage, etc. Finally, the said Ser Nicolaus confessed, in the absence of the said Ser Cechus, or against the present, that he was a debtor to the said Ser Nicolaus for the aforementioned toll in the sum of ninety-seven ducats.

† Now it is asked whether the confession of the said Ser Nicolaus, made in the absence or presence of the said Ser Cech, induces proof against the said Ser Cech, the aforementioned obligor and promisor, or not. And it seems that it induces proof against the said Ser Cech. For if the said Ser Cech was present, he ought to have contradicted; and if he did not contradict, let it be imputed to him, as in D. de fideiussoribus, l. cum ostendimus, §. si. For silence or express consent is equivalent to that of a guarantor, as in D. de re iudicata, l. quo enim, §. 1, and there noted; and D. ad Macedonianam, l. si filius. Moreover, even if the said Ser Cech had been absent, the principal debtor, i.e., the said Ser Nicolaus, could and ought to acknowledge good faith and confess the debt, even to the prejudice of another, as in D. de manumis., l. pariter; and D. de administratione tutorum, l. quotiens, §. sicut. And it is similar to the case of a procurator in rem suam constituted by the debtor. For the principal debtor can confess, and such confession prejudices the said procurator, as noted in D. de procuratoribus, l. procuratore in rem suam dato, in the solution of the contrary from l. si actor malitiose, eodem titulo.

To the contrary, it seems first by the general rule, res inter alios acta, etc. Second, by the law D. de pignoribus, l. si superatus. Third, because the confession of the debtor does not prejudice the contract of the guarantor, who guaranteed before the confession of the debtor, according to the note in D. de solutionibus, l. cum quis, §. si quis pro reo, in fine, the gloss beginning s. utilis. For just as a sentence passed against the debtor harms the guarantor, so that he retains exceptions even from the person of the debtor. And for this purpose, l. nec curandum, de non numerata pecunia, is most apt, regarding presence or absence; for, on the contrary, if the principal debtor, while the other is present but not consenting, cannot prejudice him; because he knew his right, according to the disposition of the law, to endure everywhere, according to those things fully noted in D. de actionibus pigneraticiis, l. Caius; and D. quibus modis pignus vel hypotheca solvitur, l. sicut, §. non videro.

The objection from l. quintus does not hold, because there it speaks conversely, namely that the guarantor can acknowledge good faith to the prejudice of the debtor, because he seems to have had a mandate from the very beginning to pay and fulfill his obligation, as noted in D. de condictione indebiti, l. indebitam; and D. de usufructu earum rerum, quas usu consumuntur, l. tribus. Likewise, the objection from the said l. quotiens, §. sicut, does not hold, because there it speaks of a tutor, who has a mandate to choose and who represents the ward, hence he is bound to acknowledge good faith by virtue of the office he administers, as in D. de inofficioso testamento, l. qui filium. Likewise, the objection from what is noted in the said l. procuratore, in the words scia dato, does not hold, because that is in a procurator who claims the cause from the confessor. It is different when interceding. And because that gloss must be understood when one confesses in court not spontaneously, but by way of necessary jurisdiction, as in the said l. si actor. The solution of the question lies in this,

† namely, whether the said *constitutor*, who bound himself by stipulation to pay, becomes a co-obligor (*correus*) in the debt of the primary debtor. For in the case of two co-obligors in debt, the rule is that the acknowledgment of the debt made by one prejudices the other, as in C. de duobus reis, l. si; and noted in ff. mandati, l. si fideiussor, §. si. But if they are not co-obligors in debt, certainly a simple *constitutor* by bare pact would be an intercessor, not a co-obligor. He is equally principal, as noted in ff. de pactis, l. in personam, §. qui pecuniam. But when he binds himself by stipulation, even with an interval of time, it might be doubted whether they are two co-obligors *insolidum*, who can be constituted against each other with an interval, as in ff. de duobus reis, l. in duobus, second response. But the truth is that neither are these two co-obligors, but the *constitutor* is an intercessor, because he is bound for another. And even assuming that they were two co-obligors *insolidum*, nevertheless the acknowledgment of one, or confession, does not prejudice the other regarding the proof of the debt, but only as to the interruption of prescription. And thus is understood the last law, C. de duobus reis. Hence one co-obligor can confess the debt, and the other deny it, and the one confessing is condemned, and the other is absolved, if it is not proved; nevertheless, he cannot oppose the exception of prescription. Argument from ff. de usuris, l. mora; ff. de negotiis gestis, l. si ex duobus. Hence against any intercessor contacted who denies, it must be proved that the debt exists, and the confession which the debtor made after the guarantee was given does not prejudice him. Since therefore the said promise was not liquid, nor of a certain quantity, it must be liquidated otherwise than by the sole confession of the principal debtor; otherwise it would follow that the principal debtor could confess in hundreds of thousands, charging the entire patrimony of the *constitutor*, which is false, as in ff. de iure et facto ignoto, l. 3, §. commissivum. And it is expressed in the said l. si cui. But if we were speaking of a guarantor (*fideiussor*), or a *constitutor* of judgment or sentence, then recourse must be had to the notes in l. si, C. de usu rei iudicatae, and to the notes by the modern jurists in l. 1, ff. iudicium solutum. Regarding that, however, about which I am asked, namely, if power was given to arbitrators (*arbitris*) and umpires (*arbitratoribus*) so that they could look into the law and the facts, but determine according to law, and the said compromissaries did not begin to proceed by the judicial way in the form of law, having nevertheless received proofs, whether their sentence can be reduced to the discretion of a good man. For if it is said that the procedure of the *arbitri* could not be reduced, but that of the *arbitratores* could. I answer, in doubt it is presumed that they chose the way of equity, i.e., the way of the *arbitri*; because in obscure matters, we must follow what is more humane, as in ff. de regulis iuris, l. semper in dubiis benigniora. Also because this appears from the mode of proceeding, as in the cited ff. de furtis, l. si dominium. Also I say one thing, which is notable, that when the judge judged as if strictly according to law, in this case a reduction to the discretion of a good man could be requested; namely, when it was added by pact that he should judge according to law, he acts against the intention of both committing parties, and against the quality of the power; I do not say against the form of his mandate, because then the award would be null by law itself. Since therefore from such a pact arises an argument from the contrary sense, namely, that if judgment is given against justice, recourse can be had, argument from ff. de pactis, l. inter socerum, §. cum inter, recourse can rightly be had by virtue of tacit consent, as in ff. de appellationibus, l. ex consensu, first response. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a vicinal way can be acquired by prescription, and whether one may lawfully build upon it, notwithstanding a statute that ways must be cleared of obstructions.
2. Whether a statute or agreement can remove any and all prescriptions.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Against a certain person who has built and possesses a building in a vicinal way, and it is sought that the building be removed, namely a certain house, which is said to impede the neighbors, and especially the neighbor who is bringing the action, so that he cannot go through the said vicinal way and use the said way. Hence, the said building, or the said house, is sought to be demolished, and for the part of the plaintiff it is proved that he has neighboring houses. It is also proved that for forty years past the said way was vicinal. But for the part of the defendant it is proved that for a period of forty years and more his predecessors, and he himself, held and possessed the place where the said house was built, just as one holds and possesses his own thing for a period of forty years and more. Now a sentence of acquittal has been pronounced in favor of the defendant, and the plaintiff was condemned in costs. But from this sentence an appeal was taken on the ground that by the statute of the said city it is provided that the authority of the said territory is bound, at the petition of anyone, to cause all vicinal ways to be cleared of stones, wood, earth, and of any obstruction, notwithstanding any prescription of time by which anyone might have held or possessed the said things in the said vicinal ways. And this chapter is precise. Now the question is, what is the law?

† namely, whether judgment was rightly given. For the plaintiff’s claim appears to be proven by certain responses of the defendant, and almost by all the witnesses, who prove that formerly, where the said house stands, there was a vicinal way: therefore, notwithstanding any prescription of time, the said house ought to be demolished. For so the statute of the city determines, to which statute one must adhere; for just as a statute may permit that something be built contrary to the common law, so conversely it may provide that, notwithstanding the common law providing for prescription of time, the building be removed, as in D. Ne quid in loco publico, l. 2, in principio, in gloss. 2, which begins “statuto municipali.”

† For a statute can remove all prescriptions, just as an agreement can, as is stated in the Digest, *de aedilicio edicto*, law *quod si nolit*, section *si quid*. And this is even stronger in the case of an agreement, because according to some, an agreement could not remove the prescription of long time, as noted by modern commentators in the Digest, *de legibus*, book 1, law *nemo potest*, and by Bartolus in the Digest, *de usucapione*, laws 1 and 1. Nevertheless, this could be done by statute, as is shown in the Code, *de sacrosanctis ecclesiis*, law *si*, and *autem*, and *quas actiones*.

To the contrary, it seems that the statute speaks of obstructing a vicinal way. But by this building of this house, held and possessed for a very long time by one’s own right and in good faith, that ground where the building stands ceased to be a vicinal way, and became the property of the possessor, as is stated in the Code, *de praescriptione triginta annorum*, laws *omnes* and *quod notissimi*. Therefore, the statute has no application, because the statute speaks of a vicinal way; but as soon as the way ceased to be vicinal, and that part of the way became the private property of the possessor, the words of the statute fail, and the authority of the statute ends, according to the argument in the Digest, *de divortio*, law *quod ait lex*. And this is especially so when it is a house, so that the city may not be disfigured by ruins, as is stated in the Digest, *ne quid in loco publico*, law *si*.

It does not obstruct the argument that the statute says that the obstruction of buildings must be removed notwithstanding the passage of time, and that such a statute is precise, that is, by its nature. However, no matter what words the statute uses, it must receive a sound interpretation, as is stated in the Digest, *de verborum obligatione*, law *stipulatus sum*, according to Dyachenko, Jacobus de Arena, and Raymondus; and in the Digest, *de arbitris*, law *licet statutum*. Therefore, it must be understood as referring to an obstruction that is not affixed to the ground, which does not induce prescription of time due to its natural or easy movability, such as piles of mortar and heaps of unattached stones, and similar things, as is stated in the Digest, *de servitutibus urbanorum praediorum*, law *quod autem*.

Furthermore, the law states that the property of temples is not prescribed by any long-time prescription; nevertheless, the law is never understood to remove the prescription of the longest time, as is stated in the Code, *ne rei donatae vel templi*, law *universas*, and there it is noted.

Furthermore, the plaintiff in our inquiry bound himself to those things which he did not prove, from which results a different mode of proceeding and a different action, as is stated in the Digest, *si servus venditus*, law 2, section *Pomponius*. Therefore, if he did not prove them, he must succumb, as is stated in the Digest, *de institoria*, law *habebat*. Nor does it obstruct the argument if it is said that the intention was acted upon, although the action tacitly intended was inept; for rather I say that both were part of the act, but not proven. Therefore, we are under the rule of the law *qui accusare* in the Code, *de edendo*, section *quod reus debet absolvi*.

Solution: Consider the aforementioned and other considerations, I say and advise that it was judged most correctly, and appealed against wrongly, and the loser should be condemned to pay the expenses to the winner. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the toleration or admission of an ineligible person to any act, made by him who has the power to dispense, is held as a dispensation and renders that person eligible.
2. Whether a statute excluding a married man from any act is understood also of one who has contracted marriage by words of the present, but has not yet consummated it.
3. Whether an uncanonical, but surreptitious election is confirmed by the mere lapse of time.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen. By the fullness of power which lord Micerinus possessed by the grant of the foundation whereof mention is made, the said two married men are to be tolerated in the said house, and they ought not to be expelled: because he is deemed to have dispensed with them out of certain knowledge; ff. de re iudi. l. quidam consulebat; ff. de offic. praeto. l. Barbarius at the end, in the rationale. For he was able, and chose not, to enter into possession through a corporal investiture made from certain knowledge in the one case, and from certain sufferance in the other; and these men have not yet brought home their wives, and they still retain the clerical honor; in c. 1. de cle. coniuga. lib. 6.
