But no married cleric can be admitted, and one admitted prior to the clerical state would be deemed tacitly to renounce by contracting matrimony through words of the present, as in c. gratiae. de rescriptis. in cle. Because henceforth no one exists who can dispense against the constitution, since the lord has closed his final day. Baldus. Join the following consilium, because it speaks on the same matter.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether tolerance, or the admission of an incompetent person to perform a certain act, made by one who has the power to dispense, is to be considered as a dispensation, and renders him competent.
2. Whether a statute excluding a married man from a certain act is to be understood as also applying to one who contracted by words in the present tense, but has not yet consummated the marriage.
3. Whether an election not canonical, but surreptitious, is confirmed solely by the passage of time.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen. In the constitutions of the House of Wisdom it is provided that married men cannot be in the aforesaid house. Yet in the same constitutions it is provided among other things in these words: ‘To myself, however, as long as I shall live, and to the said Lord Luca Rodulfi, Cardinal Deacon, as long as he shall live, I give and grant, and to each of them in solidum, the provision and governance of the said house or its college, and the admission and expulsion of such sort, and I reserve and retain plenary power to correct, supply, and amend, and to add to them, and to alter them, all and singular the aforesaid, as it shall please me and the said Lord Luca to do and ordain.’ Subsequently it happened that the aforesaid Lord Cardinal Luca knowingly admitted, made, and ordered to be received Master Giovanni of Aspello, a married man studying civil law; and although it was objected before the said Luca that he was ineligible because he was married, nevertheless the said Lord Luca, having considered the virtue and aptitude of the said Master Giovanni, willed that he be and remain in the house. Now the said Lord Luca is dead, wherefore the rector of the said house wishes to expel the said Master Giovanni from the said house, on the grounds that he asserts he is bound by the duty of his office to observe the aforesaid constitutions. To the contrary it is answered that the said Lord Luca, by knowingly causing the said Master Giovanni to be admitted and by granting him a singular favor, tacitly dispensed, contrary to the said constitutions, with respect to the said Master Giovanni so admitted.

† Now it is asked what the law is. I answer that, since the intention of the said Lord Micerino was that, notwithstanding the marriage, the said Master Giovanni should be a student in the said house, he is understood to have dispensed in the case of the said Master Giovanni, as in ff. de re iudi. l. quidam consulebat; arg. ff. de offi. praeto. l. Barbarius. in fi. by its reasoning; for it is advantageous to the commonwealth that suitable scholars study and have aid to study, by whose knowledge the world is illuminated, as in C. ne filius pro patre. auth. habita. Hence it is no wonder if a tacit dispensation is understood with the said Master Giovanni and others who might be in a similar case, because the cause of studies deserves special favor, as noted in l. j. ff. sol. mat. and ff. de in inte. rest. l. fi.; and the knowledge of him who has the power to dispense in those matters which are not prohibited by natural law is held to be equivalent to an express dispensation, as noted by Inn. extra de filiis presby. c. quotiens. And although Inn. says that for a dispensation to be so understood, circumstances must precede which cause this to be presumed—namely, that the necessary judicial inquiry into the cause of the dispensation preceded, otherwise the admission is reckless—a distinction must be drawn among those dispensing. For he who can dispense at his will and pleasure can also admit someone otherwise unqualified, as in the said l. quidam consulebat and arg. ff. de lega. 2. l. cum quidam and ff. de lega. 3. l. fideicommissum. w. qq.; it is otherwise in one who has power to dispense according to law alone, and thus the statement of Inn. ought to be understood. But it is certain that Lord Luca possessed plenitude of power, just as the founder of the house did. For the Lord Cardinal who founded the house was able to impose upon his property whatever law he wished, and to grant his power to another, as in ff. de dote pręleg. l. theopompus and ff. de serui. ru. prœ. l. cum esset. w. fi. Whence an act done by Lord Luca is understood to have been done by the founder himself; rightly, therefore, it ought not and cannot be retracted, as in ff. de manu. vindi. l. pater ex prouincia and ff. manda. l. si homine enim and ff. quod cuiusque vni. noted in l. item eorum. w. si decuriones; nor can a successor revoke such an act to the prejudice of the said Giovanni, to whom a right has been acquired. And the said Master Giovanni, being simply admitted, is understood to be included for the term of the constitution, arg. ff. de aedil. edic. l. quod si velit. w. qui assidua. For that which by custom was to be expressed seems tacitly provided, as in C. de fideius. l. fi. Indeed, I say further that even if the said admission seemed reckless, looking at the rule, nonetheless one cannot speak of such recklessness when considering the plenitude of power that resided in Lord Luca, as is apparent from the aforesaid. Subsequently it is asked what the law is concerning Master Giovanni de Aetate, for the fact is presented under this form: namely, that the said Master Giovanni was admitted into the said House of Wisdom, it being kept silent by the said Master Giovanni de Aetate that he was a cleric married by words of the present tense, although he had not yet brought home, nor has he brought home, his wife, nor was the marriage carnally consummated. When this later came to the notice of the said Lord Luca and was ventilated before him, the said Master Giovanni de Aetate was tolerated in the said house through sufferance and held as a student; and with the said Lord Cardinal’s knowledge he was held and treated just as others lawfully admitted into the said house were held and treated; which Master Giovanni was elected by the chapter as Bishop of Rieti, silence being kept, however, concerning the marriage.

† Now it is asked whether the said Master Giovanni ought to remain in the said house and complete the customary time, or whether in strict justice he ought to be expelled, considering that he is married by mutual consent expressed through words of the present tense, although the marriage has not been carnally consummated. I answer that this rests upon two questions: first, whether by the contracted marriage this Master Giovanni de Aetate is truly said to be married, since the matter is still so untouched that he could withdraw entirely from the marriage by receiving holy orders or through monastic profession, as noted in the Auth. de nup. w. distrahuntur. And on this point I first believe that he is called married by l. nuptias. de reg. iu. and as noted in C. de ince. nup. l. cum ancillis. in prin. and extra de cleri. coniug. throughout; it would be otherwise if there were only a betrothal for the future, because such a person would not be called married, as in ff. de his, qui no. infa. l. solet. w. fin.

† Second, whether, since his election was not canonical but rather surreptitious, it is confirmed by the mere lapse of time; and it must be said that it is not, as in c. si eo tempore. de rescrip. lib. 6. But since here not merely the lapse of time intervened, but the knowledge of Lord Martino, etc., and the provision of food and other things which are provided to students was made to the said Master Giovanni de Aetate with the knowledge and consent of the said Lord Martino, it is asked whether from this the said Master Giovanni is understood to have been tacitly and with certain knowledge admitted among the students; and it is said not, because stipends do not make someone a decurion, as in ff. de decur. l. Herennius modestinus. To the contrary, it seems that the favor of alimony or sustenance furnished for a three-year period induces consent and confirms what was invalid, not only for the past time but also for the future, as in C. de fidei. l. 1; but that law could be adduced for the opposite view, because there it is a special case by favor of maintenance in a last will: therefore, where we are not dealing with a last will, the contrary seems true. Likewise, an election that was void from the beginning does not gain strength later, because from nothing nothing can be made, unless a retroactive and solemn act similar to the first is performed, as in the rule of law quod ab initio with its parallels. Likewise, this seems to be tolerance rather than an obligation; therefore, whenever this Master Giovanni de Aetate can be dismissed, since he was not duly admitted, neither is the house bound to him in anything. But to the contrary makes the fact that the said Luca persevered with certain knowledge, as in C. si rector prouin. l. 1. vers. impleri autem; to which is added that ratification is retroactive and is compared to a mandate, as in the rule of law and C. ad Macedonianum. l. fi. But Lord Luca seems tacitly to have ratified that act by the acts executing it, as in ff. rem ra. hab. l. 3. w. fina. and l. non tantum verbis. Furthermore, this election ought not properly to be called surreptitious, because when he who is elected is capable of confirmation, even if according to the rigor of justice he ought not to be confirmed, yet if he can be confirmed by the simple will of the superior, these elections have the force of a kind of postulation; whence it suffices that the superior then or thereafter admit such a postulation and postulated candidate, whether by words or by facts and deeds themselves, arg. ff. de l. non quibus. w. fina.; and this is supported by what is noted in fina. in c. 1. de despon. impub. lib. 6. and ff. ad Macedonia. l. si filius and l. quo enim. w. 1. ff. rem rat. hab. In the aforesaid matters, however, it is necessary that knowledge be proved, because of legato. l. cum dominus. Furthermore, for those possessing absolute power, their will stands for reason, whence: ‘Thus I will, thus I command,’ as noted in C. de secun. nup. auth. vers. si quis and arg. ff. de adimen. leg. l. 3. w. fina. Wherefore it can be said that the said Giovanni de Aetate also—and especially because he is not incommutably married—ought to complete his time in the said House of Wisdom, just like the other students there, the sufferance and will of the said Lord Luca having been proven through indications and signs, arg. ff. loca. l. qui ad certi. and ff. de pac. l. item quia conuentiones. And thus I, Baldus de Perusio, state and advise.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that a statute speaking in the masculine gender includes the feminine, it may likewise be applied to her.
2. Given a statute providing that paternal cousins exclude the mother from the succession of the son, whether paternal cousins will exclude him.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The case is as follows: by a statute of the commune of Arezzo, under the heading “On Intestate Successions,” among other things it is provided that a mother, or any ascendant in the maternal line, shall not be admitted to the intestate succession of a son or daughter, or of descendants issuing from them, if there exists a brother or sister of the deceased, or the children of such siblings, or paternal uncles, or cousins on the father’s side. By another statute of the said commune it is provided that wherever the statute of the commune of Arezzo mentions creditors, it shall be understood to refer to both creditors and debtors, and that every chapter of the statute,

† That which is stated in the masculine gender shall be extended also to the feminine, if that which is contained in the aforementioned chapter can be suitably adapted to the feminine gender. It has recently happened in fact that a certain reverend son of Rencarius of St. Paul, of the commune of Arezzo, died intestate, with Domina Sanctina and Domina Cathelina, his sisters and daughters of his paternal uncle Boasna, surviving, and with Domina Angela, the mother of the said Rencarius, also surviving. Now it is asked, considering the aforementioned statutes, whether the said Domina Sanctina and Cathelina, in the succession of the said Rencarius, who died intestate as stated, exclude the said Domina Angela, his mother, or rather the contrary. And whether the inheritance of the said Rencarius pertains to the said Domina Angela, his mother, or to the aforementioned Domina Sanctina and Cathelina, his paternal cousins. It is therefore doubted whether paternal cousins exclude the mother from the succession of a son dying intestate: and it seems that they do not, because the statute has two exclusive clauses. The first is when there is a brother or sister of the deceased, or of the deceased woman, or children of theirs. The second is when there is an uncle, or paternal cousins, or a paternal cousin of the deceased. Here it must be considered that in the second clause no mention is made of a sister. For if the statute had intended that only a paternal cousin should exclude the mother, it would have spoken of a paternal cousin sister just as it spoke of a carnal sister. Since it did not say this, therefore it did not dispose of this, because it was easy for the legislator to express it if he had wished to do so, as in C. de caducis tollendis, §. si autem ad deficientes, and ff. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. si servum enim non dixit. Moreover, the statute enumerates the excluding persons, namely the paternal cousin brother, and thus six persons are comprehended by the statutory edict. Hence, by the argument from sufficient enumeration of persons, other persons who are not enumerated do not exclude the mother, as in Inst. ad Tertullianam, post principium, and Inst. de bonis possidendis, §. 4. Furthermore, this statute is odious, as in Inst. ad Tertullianam, §. sed si fuerat, and ff. de inofficioso testamento, l. nam et si parentibus; therefore it should not be extended, as in the cited chapter Hodie. Moreover, this statute is contrary to natural equity, as in C. qui potiores in pignore habeant, l. assiduis, there: "for who indeed etc." For nature is common to father and mother, as in Extra de conversatione in fide, c. fin. Moreover, the general rule is that a statute contrary to the common law should not be heard. Moreover, in that which is established contrary to natural equity, or contrary to natural reason, the masculine does not comprehend the feminine, as in ff. de venditionibus in possessione mittendis, l. quaeritur, and arg. ff. de liberis et posthumis, l. cum quidam. Hence it seems to be said that a paternal cousin sister does not exclude the mother. To the contrary it seems, because the appellation of brother contains sister, as in ff. de legatis 3, l. Lucius, §. quaesitum, and ff. de pactis, l. tres fratres. Moreover, the statute considers here agnation, as noted by Cynus, C. de adulteriis, l. publico; but paternal cousin sisters are of agnation, just as paternal cousin brothers, therefore they ought to exclude the mother in the same way, who is not agnate but cognate. Moreover, the statute expressly says that the masculine gender shall be extended to the feminine, against itself it can be restricted, i.e., if the natural reason is equal, or even if the civil reason is the same. But since only the reason of agnation seems to be weighed by the statute, therefore, since the reason of agnation is entirely the same, the mother is excluded, as in C. de revocatione donationum, l. his solis. And in the writing transmitted to me it is said that I advised on the part [of the mother]. I remember that he who came to me for counsel said that it had always been observed in the city of Arezzo, where there is a question, that they were by no means to be changed, etc., as in ff. de legibus, l. minime. However, I do not remember the point on which I advised. And therefore, with due respect, now I cannot advise unless the point on which I advised is first sent to me. And then I will answer the questions: to anyone rightly observing, the truth appears from what has been said. I, Baldus.

† It is doubted whether paternal aunts exclude the mother from the intestate succession of a son. It appears that they do, for since, according to the form of the statute on intestate successions, paternal uncles exclude the mother from the succession of a son, therefore, by the same reasoning, paternal aunts exclude her, having regard to the words of another statute which dictates that wherever a statute speaks in the masculine gender, it is to be extended also to the feminine: if that which is contained in the chapter can be suitably adapted to the feminine gender; but in the case proposed, the facts made concerning brothers can be suitably adapted to sisters, for in intestate succession, as stated in §. j. igitur and c. Qui enim, those who introduce a distinction between males and females are accusers of nature, as in l. maximum vicium, C. de lib. praete. And thus no distinction ought to be introduced between brother and sister with regard to the succession of a paternal uncle. Moreover, by the common law, the term "brother" includes the sister, even if the word "brother" is used by the law, as in l. tres fratres, ff. de pact. And the same holds if used by a testator, as in l. Lucius, §. quaesitum, ff. de lega. 3, where if the testator burdened his heir to restore the inheritance to his brothers, it had to be restored to the sisters as well, since the same reason applies for restoring to sisters as to brothers. Thus, in the present case, since according to the form of the statute the paternal uncle is admitted to the succession of the brother, removing the mother of the deceased, by the same reasoning the sister is admitted, since the term "brother" includes the sister, as in the aforementioned l. Lucius, §. quaesitum. Moreover, by the common law, even if it were not sufficient that the masculine gender comprehended in the law includes the feminine, in indifferent matters, i.e., in matters which suit both the masculine and the feminine, as in l. i, ff. de verb. signi. and l. si quis id, quod, ff. de iurisd. om. iudi. Hence, if a statute says that if anyone kills a man, he shall be punished with a fine of a thousand pounds, a woman is also included, because the same reason applies, therefore, etc. And thus it appears that the paternal aunt excludes the mother. And so I say and advise, I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an inventory commenced less legitimately benefits the person who compiled it.
2. Whether delay incurred in one term can be purged in another, when multiple terms are established regarding the same matter.
3. Likewise, whether an heir who does not know how to write may have it written in the inventory by a public notary, and thus subscribe himself to the said inventory, and whether such subscription is valid.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The case is stated as follows. The heir began to draw up an inventory within one month in the presence of two witnesses, and thus not in due form, because the lawful number of witnesses was not present, nor were the legatees and creditors summoned; nevertheless, after one month and within the following two months, those who were to be summoned having been duly summoned and legally required, and the requisite number and quality of witnesses being present, together with the subscription of the said witnesses, he completed the inventory.

† It is asked whether the inventory subsists by law. The doctors formulate this question in C. de iure delib. l. sin. §. cum igitur, and §. si vero postquam. And they say that it suffices if it has been legitimately completed, even if it was not begun within the present month, or not begun at all. And the reason is that both the first month and the other two months are assigned by law for the benefit of the heir. Hence, this entire period ought to be free. And what is not done at the beginning may be done at the end of the time, as long as the delay lasts, as in ff. si certum petatur, l. lecta; and ff. de pignoribus et hypothecis, l. si necessarias, and §. si annua; and what is read and noted in Inst. de verbis oblig., §. omnes; and Inst. de exceptionibus, §. temporales, with the following.

† Moreover, when several terms are established regarding the same matter, delay incurred in one term may be purged in another, as in D. de iudiciis, l. ad petitorium; and C. quomodo et quando iudex, auth. qui semel, with its subject matter. Furthermore, the reason why the inventory was introduced is so that the heir may not act maliciously or steal, as in Auth. de hereditate et falcidia, § sancimus. Therefore, if it is established that the inventory was made in good faith and formally before a judge, all fraud and suspicion cease, as in C. de praediis curiae, l. 1, lib. 10; and by argument from C. qui testamentum facere possint, l. hac consultissima. Hence, rightly, both by law and by equity, the said inventory ought to benefit [the heir]. And I hold this opinion in the aforementioned l. si, de iure delibandi, following the reasoning and equity of other doctors.

† Subsequently, it is asked: if an heir, being unable to write, employs another notary who subscribes in the name of the heir, and that notary does subscribe, yet in another subscription makes no mention of the quantity of movable and immovable things listed in the said inventory, whether such subscription is valid. I answer thus: because a simple subscription refers to all matters, so that all preceding items are considered as expressly stated, as in D. de pignoribus, l. fideiussor, § si pater; and D. de militum testamento, l. tribunus, § ult. For an indefinite and universal subscription regularly has as much force as a special enumeration. Moreover, since the subscription was made by a public notary, it is presumed that all things were done solemnly, according to the notes in C. de usuris, l. 1, cum si. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a statute providing that a mother who enters into a second marriage shall not succeed to her intestate son, if the son, by making a will, institutes his mother—who has entered into a second marriage—as heir to one-tenth of his estate and stipulates that she may not claim anything more from his goods, can she bring an action to supplement her legitime?
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The statute provides that a mother who enters into a second marriage shall not succeed intestate to the child of her prior marriage. Now, the son has died testate, and he left 10 to his mother by way of institution, or simply, and he forbade that she could demand or have more.

† Now it is asked whether this mother can bring an action for the supplement of her legitime. And it seems that she can: because the right to sue for the supplement ought to be said to arise from the will, and not from intestacy, since it tends toward the preservation of the will, as in C. de inofficioso testamento, l. omni modo. Furthermore, because the testator seems to have wished this tacitly by legal fiction, in the same title, l. sancimus. Moreover, we have a similar case, where an action contra tabulas is said to arise from the will. Hence it seems that a statute concerning intestacy does not exclude him from the will, if according to the common law he can bring an action contra tabulas, as in C. de collationibus, l. ex liberis. Moreover, this case seems to have been omitted by the statute; therefore, it is left to the disposition of the common law, as in ff. de solutione matrimonii, l. si cum dotem, in principio, and l. si vero, §. de viro. Moreover, a statute correcting the common law in another case, in which it does not speak, and even if in that case it were an equal or greater part of the statute, as noted in C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, auth. quas actiones. On the contrary, it seems that whenever something is statutorily provided in one matter, which requires the presence of another, it seems that both are statutorily provided, as in C. de fideicommissis, l. quamvis. It is certain that the cause of intestacy measures the legitime portion, as in C. de inofficioso testamento, l. cum quaeritur. Therefore, if the cause of intestacy is removed, there is no question of a legitime. Hence, no legitime is due to this mother, because she would not succeed intestate due to her remarriage. For the penalties of those who remarry are valid both under the common law and under municipal law in favor of the children, as noted by Innocentius in c. pe. et fi. de secundis nuptiis. Therefore, if the antecedent is destroyed, the consequent is destroyed. Moreover, the text expressly states that the mother does not succeed intestate upon remarriage, if something is left to her in the will, she succeeds as any stranger: therefore, not as a mother. Hence, no legitime is due to her, as in C. de secundis nuptiis, auth. ex testamento, and there I said. Moreover, this mother can be passed over and disinherited, assuming the said statute; because any injury is done to her by the law, not by the testator, as in ff. de contratabulis, l. si post mortem, §. liberi. And this seems to me to be the truth. And thus I hold, Balde of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Within what time period prescription runs for the right of complaint and for the right to claim the legitime, or its supplement. And number 3.
2. For the universal possessor of the testator’s heir, the time for claiming the supplement does not run: because prescription does not run against the possessor.
3. Notwithstanding the testator’s prohibition, whether donations can be alienated for the purpose of constituting or restoring dowries to the persons of children or others. And number 7.
4. Dowries can be deducted from a universal fideicommissum.
5. Whether one can recover expenses or maintenance which he made for someone, and what applies regarding a mother towards her daughters.
6. Whether, just as alienation of goods prohibited from alienation can be made on account of a dowry, so too it can be made on account of maintenance.
7. Whether a wife who has been left as a usufructuary ought to have the entire usufruct after the death of her children: because during their lives she ought to have only maintenance, according to customary interpretation.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Having examined the will of the late Lord Bonintendi of Matelica, doctor of both laws, in which, among other things, after the institution of heirs and substitutions, it is thus provided: namely, I order and wish that my present and future goods be preserved in my family and among my sons and children, and that my goods do not pass to others. And if all my children, or those to be born in the future from them, should die without male children, I wish that all my goods pass to the pious work of the priory, hospital, and place of Saint Mary. And that nothing from them ought to be sold or alienated, except the legitime portion, which cannot be burdened. It is presupposed that all the children and descendants of the testator have died, with only Lady Francesca, daughter of Lady Nicolina, daughter of Francis Berti, the last surviving male among the children of the said Lord Bonintendi, remaining. Now

† It is asked whether the said Lady Francesca, by successive inheritances made in the order of degrees and successively devolving upon the said Berto from the goods of the said Lord Bonintendo, presupposing in fact that the said [Lord Bonintendo] had endowed the said Lady Francesca with a certain amount not reaching the portion of her legitime; and whether the said Lady Francesca, who now lives, on behalf of the said Lady Francesca, her grandmother, through the said Lady Nicolina, may seek the fulfillment of the said legitime. I answer

† It must be premised for the sake of clarity that the time for claiming the supplement does not run against the heir who possesses the estate universally, because prescription does not run against the possessor, as stated in C. de praescri. 30. ann. l. cum notissimi, and ff. quibus ex cau. maio. l. si is, cuius rem. And therefore, as long as the aforementioned Bertus, who was the universal successor to the said inheritance, lived, the time for claiming the legitime did not run. No burden was attached to the legitime itself by the said Lord Boninten, both because he did not wish it, and because even if he had wished it, he could not have done so, as is fully read and noted in C. de inoffi. test. l. ex tribus, and l. quam in prioribus. Therefore, speaking of the legitime, and referring ourselves to the testament of Lord Boninten, and to the legitime dependent on his testament, there is no question that this legitime was free and remained with the said Bertus by virtue of his persons, the Pergomis, who succeeded to it. And it is of this legitime that the testament of Lord Boninten speaks. For the legitime is in a manner a thing alien; and thus it is not included in a universal fideicommissum, because, as I said, neither could the testator nor did he wish it, arg. ff. de vulg. l. cohaeredi, §. cum filiae, ver. nec fideicom., and ff. ad l. falc. l. Titia, and fully noted in C. fami. erci. l. filium, quem habentem. And in this legitime, the said hospital, or the brothers, by virtue of the testament of the said Lord Boninten, have no right, nor can they have any.

It remains to consider another point, namely that the said Bertus had one male child and two female children, and he instituted the male child as universal heir, while he provided dowries for the female children; and one of the female children was the said Francisca, grandmother of the present said Francisca. And the statute states that a dowried daughter shall not succeed in anything other than her dowry. Now the question arises: since the male child has died, along with all the descendants of said male child, whether the aforementioned Francisca can claim any supplement to her legitime, and whether the lapse of time prejudices the legitime. And thus the question consists in the common law regarding the time of prescription, and in the municipal law regarding the exclusion of the dowried female. And I answer the first point that the five-year period is an obstacle according to Bartolus, as in C. de inofficiosa testamento, l. Si quis filium, in fine; and this is held by many doctors who follow his opinion. But I believe the contrary, because the addition of the five-year period pertains only to the querela inofficiosi testamenti, which is odious; but it does not pertain to the supplement of the legitime, which is favorable; and thus by the law itself, as in C. de inofficiosa testamento, l. Sancimus. Regarding the point of the statute, it is necessary to examine the words of the statute. For the statute can prohibit the supplement, as is fully noted by Cynus and others in C. de nuptiis, l. Sancimus.

† Furthermore, it is asked whether, notwithstanding that the testator prohibited alienation, the property could be alienated for the purpose of constituting or restoring a dowry: and I speak concerning the persons of children. And it must be said that yes, up to the contrary, which is odious, as in C. com. de leg. auth. res quae. But if it were concerning the dowries of others than children, alienation could not be made, as noted in C. de iu. do. l. nulla. These things are true, and especially in our case, because the testator prefixed necessary alienations for cause. But the cause of a dowry is necessary, just, and honest, as in ff. ad Trebel. l. mulier. §. cum proponeretur. Now it is asked concerning dowries, namely whether the present d. Francisca can claim maternal and avuncular dowries in the said properties. And it must be said that yes, according to the note in the said auth. res.

† And similarly it is asked whether the lady Lisia can recover her dowry, which she gave to the same Berto. And similarly it must be answered that yes, from the said universal fideicommissum the said dowries ought to be deducted, having regard to and considering the form of the said testament of the said lord Bulmendi, that is to say, to confirm by natural reason. For the testator, who burdens his descendants, if they died without sons, prefers children to the universal fideicommissary, as in D. de hered. institu. l. Lucius. Therefore, out of affection he desires that sons be born; but to preserve the dowry for his daughters accords with the law, if legitimate sons are not born, as in Auth. de nupt. in princi. col. 4. Therefore, it is the mind of the testator that his descendants have the inheritance, and give dowries, and that they be restored, and that they bind themselves for restitution. For these are certain consequential matters, as in C. de donat. ante nupt. l. fina. and especially because the favor of the dowry and of children receives this interpretation, arg. D. sol. matr. l. 1. Moreover, we see that goods prohibited from being alienated by law can be alienated for the sake of a dowry, as in C. de prædiis mino. l. ob ęs. Therefore, concluding from the first to the last, it follows that concerning the dowries, of which it has been said, both of the said lady Francisca and of the lady Lisia, action may be brought against the said hospital, which is the universal successor of the said goods.

† Subsequently it is asked whether the said lady Lisia can recover from the said goods certain sums which she spent on the said Berto and the common children, sums which the said lady Lisia advanced from her own property outside the dowry, no agreement having intervened with the said [husband] regarding the restitution of those paraphernalia. And although much can be said on this point, and there are contrary glosses, namely whether it is understood that giving out of a certain profuse affection of charity constitutes making a gift, or rather acting with the intention of recovering [the sums]. And it must be said that either she provided for those in need for their sustenance, and then she cannot recover, as in C. de captivis et postliminio reversis, l. liber captus; or she otherwise expended [funds] on their affairs, and she cannot [recover], as is fully read and noted in C. de negotiorum gestorum, l. 1 and l. alimenta, and in D. de negotiorum gestorum, l. Necessarius. In matters of sustenance, it is also sometimes presumed that one acts as a negotiorum gestor out of liberality, as noted there, and in D. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. Si stipulatus. I therefore say that if the need was so great that the mother was bound by necessity to provide sustenance for the children, then the mother does not recover, because she paid a debt. But if for another reason the goods of the household were being consumed, so that she might preserve the husband’s goods intact, then it seems more that she is managing a business [negotium gerere] than making a gift. And therefore she can recover from the husband’s own goods, which were not subject to restitution.

But it is doubtful whether he can recover in excess of the goods restored. And the question turns on this: whether, just as alienation and obligation may be made on account of a dowry, so too may they be made on account of maintenance. The gloss says that they may not, in the Authentica *Res quæ*, and this is the noted gloss. But Oldradus says the contrary in the case of children, because if one may leave property for the cause of dowry and donations on account of marriage, much more so for the cause of maintenance, as is noted in a similar case in the Codex, *De sacris sanctis ecclesiis*, law *Sancimus*. According to Oldradus, Jacobus de Arena holds the same view. Cynus, however, raises the question and does not determine it in the said Authentica *Res quæ*. I say the same as Jacobus and Oldradus, especially since consideration must be given to the testament of the said Bonintendi, who promised what was necessary for the purpose of obligation and alienation, in accordance with this rule in the Digest, *De operis liberto*, law *Liber qui operarum*, second response. From this it follows that the lady Lisia could be kept indemnified from the said expenses by her son John, and could also receive payment from the said goods, notwithstanding the said burden of the fideicommissum, as in the Digest, *De fideicommissis liberis*, law *Cum prœdii*; and in the Digest, *De legatis secundis*, law *Peto*, section *Prœdium*, namely, up to a reasonable amount, not beyond. Argument from the Digest, *De exercitu*, law *Lucius*.

It is also asked, if the testator left his mistress and a usufructuary during his lifetime, which is by custom interpreted as being for the support of living children. What will be the law, if the children lived for some time and then died, whether she ought to have full usufruct after the death of the children. But Bartolus says that even after the death of the children she ought to have full usufruct, which is true if it is not a legacy. But it will be distributed over time: because the testator said, as long as she lives chastely and honorably. Because then more things are interpreted to be bequeathed. And in the beginning, any time is instituted. And how much the legatee ought to have, see the argument from the Digest, title "Who lose the usufruct," law "If, however, for years." And because custom interprets it thus, for besides the meaning of the words, in favor of the children, therefore, the children ceasing, the favor ceases, as in the Digest, title "On legacies," book 2, law "When the patron." I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a dispensation made against the common law, or municipal law, by one having authority over two heads, in favor of someone, if not accepted in one, nevertheless holds in the other.
2. A provision made in a determined manner does not exceed its limits.
3. It is one thing to extend, another to reaffirm.
4. An office reaffirmed is not called a new office, if the form has not been changed.
5. Once qualified, always is qualified.
6. The argument from a qualified statement to an unqualified one does not proceed.
7. The proems of laws and statutes have the force of laws and statutes.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. It is provided by general statute that officials may not be reappointed. Likewise, that foreign officials have a three-year vacation. Finally, in the general assembly it was provided in this form, namely that for this time only, in the present council, derogation be made and is made, and is to be understood as singularly established, regarding the non-reappointment of officials. Likewise, regarding the statute on the vacations of foreign officials. And finally it was provided that a certain Lord Jaco Autho be understood as having the aforementioned dispensation, although he was reappointed in the office he held for the semester then immediately following, beginning on the Kalends of November next following, and ending as follows. This Lord Jaco did not accept the reappointment, and the said semester of the said reappointment has elapsed.

† Now it is asked whether, by virtue of the aforementioned derogatory provision regarding the vacation of offices, the said Lord Jacob is simply enabled, to such an extent that the said statute concerning vacation is understood to be abrogated in his case, so that he may be newly elected notwithstanding the statute on vacations. And it seems that he is not, because the lapse of time induces the consumption of a temporal benefit, as in C. de legibus, l. si; ff. de legibus, l. nemo potest; ff. de pace, l. epistola, §. si; ff. de usufructu, leg. l. si usus fructus mihi in biennium; ff. de verbis obligatorum, l. eum qui ita, §. qui ita.

† Moreover, a provision made in a determined manner does not exceed its limits, whether it is a legal provision or a provision of a man, as in D. de institutionibus, l. cuicunque, § non tamen omne; and D. de exercendo, l. 1, § si plures; D. de negotiis gestis, l. qui aliena, § libertos; D. de transactionibus, l. cum hi, § modus generalis. Hence it does not accept a different definition, nor the substitution of another time, as in D. de vulgaribus substitutionibus, l. ex facto, § item quaero; and what is noted in D. de legatis 1, l. sicut legatur; and D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. si iam facta. But with regard to the statement of Master Jacob, by reformation it was entirely about the conjunct half-year: therefore it is not understood to be about the disjunct half-year. Moreover, a provision concerning one of the incompatible things does not include the other, but rather entirely excludes it, as in D. de legatis 1, l. legata inutiliter; and l. legata inutiliter, D. de alimentis legatis. But conjunct time and separate time formally contradict each other. Therefore, one mode being limited and granted, the other appears to be denied. That is, that thing to which time is granted appears to be denied after the time, as in D. de legatis 2, l. statuliberum, § Stichum. Moreover, a temporal dispensation should not be extended to perpetuity, as in c. nemo deinceps, de electione, lib. 6.

† Moreover, these three things are distinct. Namely, to prorogue, which is to extend an office that is pending, as in D. de verb. oblig. l. cum stipulatus sim mihi a Proculo; and D. de praec. l. sed si manente; and to reaffirm, which occurs when a time that has passed is imperfectly completed by the time immediately following, as in D. l. item quaeritur § qui impleto; C. loc. l. si cum Hermes; and D. de offic. praesid. l. meminisse. And if indeed this reformation is made by the same law by which the office was originally established, the whole is understood as one and the same office, as in D. de arb. l. si cum duo in princ. But if it proceeds by a different law or different right, it is not understood to be the same office, by argument from D. de bon. poss. l. sed cum patrono. And the aforementioned statements are true if the reaffirmation is made without changing the form of the office?

For if the form of the office were changed, it would always be a new office, as is argued from the Digest, title *Locatio conductio*, law *Cum in plures*, section *Lege dicta*; and from the Digest, title *De praetoria stipulatione*, law *Valerianus*; and from the Digest, title *De iustitia et iure*, law *Ius civile*, in the verse *Itaque*; and from the Digest, title *De verbis obligatis*, law 1, section *Cum adijcit*; and law *Qui usumfructum*. For wherever the form is changed, of necessity another thing comes into being, as in the Digest, title *De acquirendo possesione*, law *Si quis ante*; and as noted in the Decretals, chapter *Hi qui*, title *De praebendis*, Book 6. Hence, that which is not a prorogation, nor a reaffirmation—which denotes necessity—is called an office entirely separated by an interval of time, which is never the same as the first, neither by accession of time nor by aggregation of time. For the reason of separated things is itself separated, as in the Code, title *De donationibus inter virum et uxorem*, law *Si maritus*. Furthermore, this is supported by the Digest, title *De aqua pluviali arcenda*, law *Si prius*; and by the Digest, title *Quomodo servi amittantur*, law *Si communem*, section *Finis*; and law *Si sic*. The same applies if the offices are not of the same nature, such as guardianship and curatorship, as in the Digest, title *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, law *Pater Seuerinam*, section *Conditionum*. From these it appears that this office, to which the said Lord Jacob wishes now to be appointed, concerns an act and an office to be held anew after an interval of time, but does not concern an act pending and not yet finished, and which, upon its completion, is to be confirmed or immediately joined, regarding which the dispensatory provision concerning his person speaks. Moreover, the law speaks of the next and immediate office; therefore, with another intervening office, different and intermediate, the authority of the dispensation has ended, as in the Digest, title *Qui et a quibus*, law 2, where it is expressly clear. Likewise, by another reason, the authority of the statute has ended, because Lord Jacob, what he did not wish, he could not fulfill, as in the Digest, title *De officio delegati*, law *Ut de diuortiis*, law *Quod ait lex*, according to that maxim: "What I did not wish, I could; what I wished, I could not fulfill," as in the Decretals, title *De officio delegati*, chapter *Cum olim*. The Abbot says that something here was derogated to the intervals of time. Therefore, from the law derogated, as regards the person of the said Lord Jacob, nothing can be alleged for the inhabilitation of the said Lord Jacob, as in the Code, title *De latronibus et latrociniis*, law 1, in the beginning.

† For it suffices that one has been enabled once, so that he remains perpetually enabled, as in C. de nupt. l. imperialis § tales, and ff. de re iudicata l. quidam consulebat. For to these points it is replied by way of interruption, because dispositions are not to be extended, so that, given one inconvenience, another inconvenience should not be added, as in C. de dotis promissione l. 1. And although derogation was made by prorogation, and also to the intervals themselves with regard to the power of establishing: for the same assembly could have provided for both, nevertheless, he who has much power, if he brings such his power into act in a determined manner, such power does not extend beyond the act performed, as in ff. de liberis et posthumis l. commodissime, and ff. de verbis obligatis l. stipulationes commodissimum est ita componere. For power does not operate unless it is brought into act and the will of the disposing party, as in C. de mandato l. in re mandata.

And because a disposition made in a qualified sense ought not to operate in an absolute sense, nor does an argument from a qualified sense proceed to an absolute sense, the grace granted to the said Lord Jacob in a qualified sense, that is, in a determined manner, does not equate to an indefinite or universal grace, as stated in the Digest, *De rebus dubiis*, law *Si is qui ducenta*, section *Utrum ita*. And therefore it appears that the said Lord Jacob ought to have a vacation, and to observe the sorrow of those individuals, because the form of the dispensation, speaking of him, speaks of a certain semester, not of every one. Therefore, this case falls under the law *Si usus fructus mihi in biennium*. Moreover, in the said assembly, the said Lord Jacob was reformed with the same salary, and thus he promised to be bound to the said assembly as an obligor of the city, having regard to a certain time. And otherwise an obligation is contracted, unless according to that time, as stated in the law *Si cum Hermes*. Since the said Lord Jacob did not ratify the dissolution, the bond of obligation either remains, or it is as if it had not been contracted, as stated in the Digest, *De solutionibus*, law *Ratum*, and law *Dispensatorem*, in the law *Quo enim*, section 1, Digest, *Rem ratam habere*. For these reasons, it appears that the said Lord Jacob has no right, because the said grace appears to have been consumed regarding his act in time, and especially considering those words, "for this right," which words are introduced by the strictness of the statute. For the law speaks of a single act and restricts and limits itself in a determined manner to a single act, as stated in the Digest, *De verborum significatione*, law *Bonus*, section *Hoc sermone*. And to the decision of this question, the text determining the matter in the Digest, *De iureiurando*, law *Non erit*, section *Finalis*, can be introduced almost formally. Because by virtue of a general arbiter, they determined only one species. Code, *De appellationibus*, law *Praecipimus*, at the end.

On the contrary, it appears. And I premise that when a law disposes of several things, several effects arise therefrom, whether it disposes by prohibiting or by permitting, as stated in the Digest, *De hereditate instituenda*, law *Si non lex*, and Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, law *Haec scriptura*. Secondly, I premise that a derogatory disposition sometimes derogates absolutely, and sometimes also tacitly confers. For the law says that if a testator derogates from his will by canceling it, wishing to die intestate, he appears tacitly to leave his goods to those succeeding intestate, or, speaking more properly, to open them to them. For if they succeed intestate, but if one considers or ought to consider a canceled will as having instituted an unworthy heir, then it appears to open the way to the fiscus, as stated in the Digest, *De his quae in testamento delentur*, law *Cancellavit*, and law *Propria*, and law *Si*, and what is read and noted in the Code, *De testamentis*, law *Nostram*. Furthermore, I premise that favorable dispositions, and those made for the sake of public utility, are interpreted in law, as stated in the Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, law *Hoc modo*. Furthermore, I premise that sometimes the final reason comprehends more by the mind than by the words of the disposer, as stated in the Digest, *De legatis tertio*, law *Fideicommissa*. But sometimes the providence of the law supplies what is lacking in human provision, as stated in the Digest, *De vulgari substitutione*, law *Iam hoc iure*, taking the interpretation and presumed will, as stated in the Code, *De institutionibus et substitutionibus*, law *Si*.

† I do not omit that which follows, namely that the preambles of laws and statutes have the force of a statute, as argued in D. de haereditatibus instituendis, l. finalis. For through these preambles one arrives at the sense of the law, as in D. de origine iuris, l. 1. Having thus premised these matters, I consider that the said reform has two parts. One pertains to the office in continuation, i.e., upon the completion of one term of office, one may immediately be reassumed to a new office of the same kind and form. The other is simply derogatory to the statute speaking of vacations. The first part has been consumed, as argued in D. de procuratoribus, l. si is qui Stichum. The second, however, being derogatory, has not been consumed, because it has not been executed, nor expired, nor even commenced, unless it is commenced by a new election distant from the first by a time that is more than perfectly past. Therefore, by the force of the said absolute derogation, the said Lord James, having completed the vacation of time, may be reassumed to him for one time only. For this derogation must have some effect, because every word of the law and every word of a privilege must have some weight and be drawn to some effect, as in D. de legatis 1, l. si quando; and D. de petitione hereditatis, l. Item veniunt, § aptanda; and D. ad municipalia, l. prima, and in the first constitution C., § quibus. Having considered the aforesaid, and considering that by reason of the multitude of merits it is fitting to make a derogation from general statutes, as in D. ad Sillanum, l. si quis in gravi, § hi quoque, I say that the said Lord James may be reassumed to enter such office for one time only, without observing the interval of time. And those words, "this time," are explained as meaning "one time," as in D. de legatis 3, l. fideicommissum, § si quis decem.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What knowledge is.
2. From the past, it is presumed in the present in affirmative qualities.
3. Whether one having a privilege of the prince to do something, if he first uses the common law to do it, can return to the privilege and use it.
4. Witnesses ought first to know the truth by sense, before they testify.
5. One judge having been approached, another cannot be approached.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. To a certain religious, who had not yet completed the temporal course fixed by general custom, the apostolic authority granted, by special grace and indulgence, a privilege in effect under this form, namely: “To our beloved brother Antonius de Cassia, professed of the Order of Friars Minor of the Province of St. Francis, health and [greeting], and further: To the venerable brother Angelus of Perugia, Minister of the Province of St. Francis, Master in Sacred Theology, we commit and command that, if through diligent inquiry you shall find him to be thirty years of age or more, born of legitimate marriage, not tainted by any criminal infamy, nor marked by any grave crime, nor lacking any limb, and that he has studied and read in the general studies as aforesaid, then, after responses made by you before five masters in the said faculty, to be chosen by the said Master Angelus for this purpose, each individually on individual theological questions, at different times solemnly, as is customary in other general studies, if through the said masters, by means of an oath secretly taken by them in the hands of the said Master Angelus, he shall be found worthy to obtain the said mastership, of which we burden the conscience of the said Master Angelus, let it be conferred upon you, keeping the solemnities customary in such cases, by the aforesaid authority. Nevertheless, we will that you, the master to be obtained, if three of the masters shall depose against you concerning insufficiency and dishonesty of life, and if the multitude of the other masters shall deem you worthy of approval, notwithstanding etc. Finally, the said brother Antonius presented himself to the Chancellor of the University of Perugia, who has authority over those taking the degree in Sacred Scripture, and having obtained from him license to enter the private examination, he was examined by five masters, two of whom gave disapproving reports, the third gave no report. Now the said brother Antonius, seeing himself thus circumvented, because the said masters who disapproved him before any examination had drawn up the said disapproving reports, wishing to provide for his fame and honor, and for the honor of the Order and religion, wishes to undergo the examination again, so that the procedure shall follow the form of the said letters in the presence of the said Chancellor. Now it is asked whether he ought to be admitted to a new examination or not. And it is argued first for the negative part, namely, that he ought not to be admitted to the examination again. And I presuppose,

† that knowledge is a habit of the mind difficult to acquire, and once acquired, difficult to change. Hence it requires a long time to learn, especially theological knowledge, which is the highest of all arts and sciences: and all arts and sciences serve it by reason of its nobility, loftiness, and depth, as stated in Extra, de Clericis vel Monachis, c. Super specula. And this is naturally evident, because no science is learned except in a great length of time, as appears in the Proemium, ff.; § Discipuli, and C., de Advocatis diversorum iudiciorum, l. Nemini, § Iuris peritos; and C., de Advocatis diversorum iudiciorum, l. Iubemus, vers. Necessario; and C., de Professoribus qui in urbe Constantia, l. Unica, lib. 12, with many similar authorities. Solution, presupposing,

† That which is presumed in the present from the past in affirmative qualities, whence a learned man is once presumed to be such today, otherwise in negative qualities. For he who was unlearned three days ago is therefore presumed to be unlearned today, since learning, as I said, is a habit which is not acquired in a short time, and the rule of law is that an exception is presumed in the present in those things which are not easily narrated, as is read and noted in D. de probationibus, l. ex persona and l. siue possidetis; and C. de in integrum restitutione, in l. si minorem te; and D. de excusatione tutorum, l. spadonem, §. qui absolu. And therefore, unless he has shown that he has learned anew by reading and disputing with a suitable interval of time interposed, he ought not to be admitted to the examination again, for the exception of reproach is like an exception of res iudicata, as in D. de iureiurando, l. qui iurasse, §. pater; and what is noted in l. eum qui, §. in pupillaribus; and D. de excusatione tutorum, l. sed reprobari.

† Moreover, the grace of this brother Antonius appears to have been consumed, and tacitly renounced, because he chose another way, namely, so to speak, the way of the common law, and not the way of privilege or dispensation; and therefore his choice prejudiced him, as in C. de iure dominii impetrando, l. 2; and ff. de iureiurando, l. 2; and ff. quod metus causa, l. si mulier, §. fina., where it says, “so that whichever way I have chosen, this way shall remain open to me for the same purpose.” ff. de separatione bonorum, l. si creditores hereditarii, in principio, where it says, “but they must abide by what they have once demanded.”

To the contrary is the truth, namely, that the grace was not consumed by the act of the examination celebrated without observing the legitimate form. For neither according to the general forms nor according to the special form was the procedure followed in this examination, as I will prove. Therefore, the procedure was not rightly conducted. And it immediately follows that neither were the witnesses rightly received, nor was any act legitimately performed, and therefore the form must be repeated anew with due observance, as in ff. de iureiurando, l. qui per salutem. Nor is it surprising that the grace was consumed by the choice of an incompetent way. For the law says that if one who can testify under military law wishes to make a testament under common law, he is not thereby considered to have renounced the military privilege, as in ff. de testamento militis, l. simplex, qui destinaverat. Likewise, another law says that a certain Clodianus died having made two testaments: the first validly, the second invalidly. The heir, believing the later testament to be valid, entered upon the inheritance. Certainly, by choosing the invalid way, he did not thereby appear to renounce the solemn testament, as in ff. de acquirenda hereditate, l. Clodianus.

Moreover, one who has two ways, although he loses one, retains the other, because he comes by another right than that which he lost, as in ff. de bonis liberis, l. si filius, qui patri. Moreover, the law says that if a husband, who can accuse of adultery by the right of the husband and by public right, although excluded from one right, is not excluded from the other, from which he is not found to be excluded, as in ff. de adulteriis, l. si maritus, §. fina. We certainly have a similar case in possessio bonorum. For one who is excluded as a son can be admitted as any agnate, as in ff. de successionibus edictalibus, l. 1, §. sed videndum. We have another similar case, because a marriage that does not hold does not constitute an impediment to one that holds, according to the constitution Militis matrimonii, and a legacy is taken, as in ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. haec conditio, in principio.

Since therefore the way of privilege was not attempted, nor executed, it follows that the grace was not consumed, as in ff. qui et a quibus, l. si optio. Let there be added that rule of law: that which does not obtain effect in law does not constitute an impediment. Likewise, the law provides that a witness not received must be rightly received, as in c. Testibus, in Clementina, and note extra de testibus, c. Cum causam. Likewise, another law provides that if a disinherited son demands an invalid legacy, he is not understood thereby to renounce the querela inofficiosi testamenti, as in ff. de inofficioso testamento, l. nihil, §. si filius. To the same effect is l. Filius, ver. et quaerebatur, in the same title.

Moreover, another reason does not obstruct: the perfunctory examination of the said masters is invalid because they did not swear in the hands of the person in whose hands they ought to have sworn; therefore, their oath is not valid, as in C. de testamentis, l. hac consultissima, §. pe. For that which is boldly usurped from incongruous sources is invalid, as in C. de testibus, l. consulta diualia. Likewise, the chancellor of the bishop, in this regard, is reduced to the status of a private person; with his ordinary power of jurisdiction, he cannot execute letters that were not directed to him, as in extra de officio delegati, c. Studuisti, and de rescriptis, c. Ante, ver. cum itaque.

Moreover, the said masters, with all due respect to them, appear rather to have been conspirators, and to have come to testify according to a premeditated plan, rather than as witnesses; because they did not first know and examine the cause before stating, in their schedules, the grounds for reproach. And thus the deposition of the witness preceded the sense. For to examine consists in sense and understanding. And it is impossible that a witness should first depose before he knows or perceives the truth by sense, as in C. de testibus, l. testium, and ff. de testamentis, l. qui testamento, §. fi.

† Moreover, I do not call such persons witnesses, because they are not properly to be called witnesses; rather, they should be termed adversaries, and no credence ought in any way to be given to their statements, as is stated in the Digest, *De testibus*, in the law *Testium*, in the beginning; and in the Decretals, *De accusationibus*, in the chapter *Cum P. Manconella*. For one must first see, and then judge, according to that passage: “I will go down,” he says, “and I will see”; and in the chapter *Qualiter et quando*, in the Decretals, *De accusationibus*. Hence, such a testament is not merely testamentary, but is highly suspect, because merits arise before examination, as is stated in the Code, *Si per vim vel alio modo*, in the final law; and in the Code, *De falsis*, in the law *Ubi*; and in the Decretum, Question 2, Cause 1, noted by me; and in the chapter *In primis*; and noted in the Decretals, *De constitutionibus*, in the chapter *Ecclesia sanctae Mariae*. To this effect serves the Digest, *De acquisitione hereditatis*, in the law *Eum qui duobus*, section *Filiis*. There, when it says that one ought to investigate more diligently and thus approach the matter; and there, when it follows, “but it is more probable,” etc., which text is noted for this purpose. All things therefore having been seen and considered diligently, the said Brother Antonius is to be subjected to examination according to the form of his privilege. Notwithstanding the ineptly alleged objections. Nor do the laws alleged to the contrary stand in the way, because they speak when someone has chosen an incompatible course. Hence, by reason of contrariety, it appears that he has renounced the other, as is stated in the Code, *De furtis*, in law 1 and in the unique law; and in the Code, *Si servus exterritus*. Moreover, an action ought to be brought among several [options]. And therefore those laws speak when one of several remedies has been chosen, and due process has been carried out thereon. But here no due form has been observed, and therefore nothing appears to have been done, as is stated in the Digest, *De verbis obligatis*, in the law *Qui Romae*, section *Flavius Hermea*. It therefore rightly remains that what was attempted informally must now be done formally. The case is found in the aforementioned law *Qui per salutem*.

† It is objected that, once one judge has been approached, another cannot be approached, as stated in C. de assertionibus tollendis, l. 1, in fine; for that rule holds true only while the judicial proceeding is duly initiated. Otherwise, if it does not continue, as in C. quomodo et quando iudex, l. si ut proponis. That provision was established so that the continuity of the case is not divided; for nothing depends on acts performed improperly. To “depend” means that something is not yet concluded, but must be concluded from what has been begun; to “depend” from something means that it depends on that which has been concluded, though not yet executed, as in C. de iudicibus, l. nulli, and ff. de bonis autem iudicis positis, l. cum his, §. his qui. Therefore, concluding from the first to the last, it is true that it necessarily follows that Brother Antonius must be admitted to the formal examination, and that things useless to him do not obstruct him. For he who could not be approved in a perfunctory examination, because that examination depended on letters, rightly could not be reproved either, as in C. ubi senatores vel clarissimi, l. quot. The power of dispensing merely confers authority upon the person to whom the letters are directed, as has been proven above. To this effect is ff. de dote prælegata, l. Theopompus, in the words “Polianus will provide.” For where the ministry of a certain person is committed, one cannot depart from the person, just as one cannot depart from the form, as in ff. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. si quis mihi bona, §. pater filio, and §. si coram, and l. eum qui duobus, §. filius, and ff. de exercitoria, l. 1, §. si plures. I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The husband acquires the dowry, or a portion of the dowry, by agreement or by statute. And if the wife lives separately from him, this rule fails, unless the husband did not provide medicines or physicians for her illness, for then he acquires neither the dowry nor the fruits of the dowry. nu. 2.
2. A wife living separately from her husband cannot sell the dotal estate for the necessity of famine or sustenance; however, if she has sold it, and upon the wife's death the dowry remains with her, such sale is confirmed. nu. 4.
3. The statute of the husband's domicile is to be observed rather than that of the wife's origin.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A certain lady Richabella once married a man named Cecho, and gave him in dowry a certain house and some other of her goods. Then, returning from her husband, she lived apart and did not receive maintenance from her husband; and since she was suffering from poverty, in order to support herself, she sold the said house. It is true that the husband had a mandate issued on his behalf that she should return to him, i.e., that she should cohabit with him, and in contempt he had her excommunicated. Finally, the said lady Richabella fell ill, did not employ a physician, nor take medicine; she died without children. By the statute of the city where the husband has his domicile, although he is not a native of that place, it is provided that if the wife dies in marriage without children, the husband shall acquire half of the dowry. But in the place of the husband’s origin this statute does not apply, nor in the place of the wife’s origin, but it does apply in the place of domicile, and there the marriage was contracted. Now it is asked whether the husband ought to acquire the said half. And whether the said sale was valid from the beginning, or was later confirmed. And whether the statute should be considered according to the domicile, and not according to the origin, or the contrary. And whether the place of contract should be regarded concerning the said statute, or which place should be examined.

I answer that, whether the wife lives with her husband or not, if the husband bears the real burdens of the marriage, he must gain the dowry according to the form of the statute. And if an agreement is made to gain according to the form of the statute, by this agreement the effect is neither increased nor diminished; because this word "according to" has three functions. For it is a relative, declarative, and modifying word, as in Extra, De verbis significatis, chapter Abbate.

† If, however, the husband did not assume the real burdens of marriage, such as the burden of supporting his wife from the fruits of the dowry, while the dowry was in his possession, or, when she was dying, he did not care for her, but rather despised her, nor did he provide physicians or medicines, then he does not acquire the dowry, nor ought he to acquire the fruits of the dowry, although the law states that the husband acquires the fruits of the dowry, as in D. 23.3.16 (*Si ab hostibus*), § *Si vir uxorem*, and there the commentators note, and D. 23.3.10 (*Si cum dotem*), § *Si autem in seuissimo*. And this holds unless this occurs through the fault of the woman. And because she withdrew from her husband without cause, and refused to work for him, for then it is imputed to the fault of the woman, as in C. 3.10.1 (*Consensu*) and C. 3.10.2 (*Sicut*), and D. 38.1.1 (*Meuia*), § *Si*, and D. 36.1.1 (*De annuis legatis*). Someone might say: the husband, who does not bear the burdens of marriage, is deprived as unworthy; therefore, it is applied to the fisc. I answer: some are unworthy to take, in such a way that they do not take in any manner, and then the fisc does not succeed in their place, because they have no place in acquiring. Others do take, but possess unworthily, and in the place of these the fisc succeeds, as in D. 29.1.1 (*Papinianus*), § *Meminisse*. Hence, either acquisition ceases, and the fisc does not succeed; or deprivation is threatened, and then the fisc succeeds. Or I say otherwise, that here the husband does not acquire due to the defect of a tacit condition. For there is tacitly a condition, if the husband, from his side, fulfills the law of marriage and D. 23.3.10 (*Dotis patris*), as in D. 19.2.1 (*Quaero*), § *Inter locatorem*. Or at least the final cause fails, the defect of which reduces the acquisition of the dowry to no cause. By which is resolved what otherwise would not be resolved, as in D. 39.5.2, § *Finalis*. Now let us see in our question to whom the defect is imputed. And I say, to the husband, according to what is proposed: for just as the last delay harms, so also does the last fault, which the husband committed by abandoning his wife in her mortal illness, as in D. 18.1.1 (*Si per emptorem*). Nor is he excused on the ground that the wife was excommunicated, for an excommunicated wife must nevertheless be nourished by her husband, as part of his own body, as in c. *Admonere te cum lacrimis* etc. Hence, because the husband did not offer sustenance, nor medicines at the time of necessity, he ought not to derive benefit from the contract: which he attempted to contradict by the very things and facts. Moreover, necessity sometimes speaks for a person, as in D. 36.2.1 (*Nec semel*), § *Si in habitatione*.

It remains to be seen whether a woman may alienate a dotal estate on account of famine. And it seems that she may. For, on account of this cause, the wife possessed the property with the husband’s acquiescence; thus, it appears that the dowry was restored to her during the subsistence of the marriage, as stated in D. de divortio (Soluto matrimonio), l. quamvis and l. sed si ideo. And therefore it seems that the said house ceased to be dotal, and thus it could be alleged. This is supported by the principle that necessity knows no law, as stated in C. de praediis minorum, l. obesse and l. 1, and D. de officiis consulum. On the contrary, because the estate or house is dotal as long as the marriage endures, therefore, by the Julian law, it is prohibited from being alienated. Moreover, because the ownership belongs to the husband, therefore the woman cannot alienate the husband’s property, as stated in C. de rei venditione, l. dote ancillam and l. 1, C. de fundo dotali, and C. de iure dotium, l. si praesidium.

Next it remains to be seen whether the delivery and sale are confirmed upon the death of the woman, with the dowry remaining in his possession. And I say that they are, as in the Authentica de nuptiis, § infirmas; and as in the Digest, de usucapione, l. cum vir praedium.

† On another point, I say that the domicile of the husband must be considered, as is read and noted in the Digest, *De iudiciis*, law *Exigere dotem*. And this is supported by what is read and noted in the chapter *Statutum*, section *In his*, in the gloss beginning *Olim dicebamus*, at the end of the title *De rescriptis*, Book 6. And note what is stated by Archidamus, Distinction 12, chapter *Illud*. And it is supported by what is noted in the *Speculum*, *De senatu*, section *Qualiter*, in the verse *Item pone*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that a marriage cannot be contracted with a woman without the consent of such-and-such person, etc., whether his consent is required if he is under a ban, and whether, if it has been given, it is valid.
2. Natural reason prevails over civil law, and the words of a statute must be understood in their natural sense.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The statute of the territory of Nursia provides that no one shall contract marriage with a woman who has neither father nor mother without the consent of her carnal brother, under a certain penalty; and it is sufficient that the carnal brother interpose his authority and consent, and that one single brother [suffice], even if she had several brothers. Now the case has arisen that two carnal brothers of a certain woman have been excommunicated and condemned in person for contumacy.

† Now it is asked whether the consent of these brothers, or of one of them, suffices for contracting marriage with the sister. And it seems that it does not, because one banned to death from his city must be considered as dead with regard to the municipal rights of that city, namely that the statutes of that city speaking of citizens or natives do not apply to those banned, as noted by Jacobus de Aretino and Bartolus after him in D. ad Trebellianum, l. Ex facto, §. Ex facto; and to this effect in D. de captivis et postliminio, l. Admissione, §. Qui deficiunt. For those condemned to death are not only said to be equated with deportees, but also with enemies: since war has been declared against them by the form of the statute, §. Qui impune permittuntur occidi. Hence they leave no remnants of their status in the city, as in D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Intercidit; and in D. ad Trebellianum, l. Ex facto, §. Si quis rogatus. For they are not only equated with deportees, as noted in Inst. Qui modo ius patronatus solvitur, §. Relegati; but on the contrary, those condemned to the mines, or even to the ultimate penalty, are held as if present, because contumacy deems them to be present to their own prejudice, as in Auth. Qua in provincia, and in the Corpus from which it is taken, and cf. C. de poenis, l. Ne diu.

On the contrary, it seems that the statute does not consider that which is a matter of law in contracting marriages. Moreover, the consent of these brothers is not required as a matter of necessity; therefore, even if obtained, it does not provide support. To this effect, D. de tutela et rationibus distrahendis, l. Si tutor rei publicae, §. Pe. Furthermore, by the very fact that someone is confiscated, he is considered dead, as appears there, and in D. de contrahenda tutela, l. 1, §. Filium, according to natural affection, which the banned retain; for nature is common, as in D. de accusationibus, l. Hos accusari, §. Fi. For they retain affection, although agnation is not retained. And the statute speaks by the natural name, not by the artificial name, as in D. de captivis et postliminio, l. Tutelas. Moreover, a statute cannot remove natural affection; therefore, neither can it remove what follows in consequence, as argued in D. de capite diminuto, l. Eas. And although a banned person is said to be a vile person, because he is infamous by infamia facti, and the consent of vile persons is not required as a matter of necessity, and much less is authority required, as in D. de solutione matrimonii, l. Si cum dotem, §. Eo autem tempore; and in C. de repudiis, l. Dubium; and as noted in C. de iure dotium, l. Si a socero; nevertheless, because the statute does not distinguish what kind of brother he is, I understand the statute simply and indistinctly, so that whether he is of good fame or not, the consent of the same brother suffices. Nor does it avail to object that the banned ceases to be a tutor, therefore he ceases to be an actor. This is not true: he does not cease to be a tutor unless he is removed by the judge, as in D. de solutione, l. Quod si forte, §. 1.

† Hence, in this point, natural reason prevails over civil law, and the words of the statute are to be understood according to natural reason, as in C. de his, qui ve. aeta. impe. l. si. And therefore I believe that the consent of the excommunicated brother suffices for the said marriage to be contracted without penalty; such consent may be given by letters of notification and of procuratorship, as in ff. de procu. l. 1. §. usus. And it is provided in Auth. de nup. §. deportatio. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A statute excluding a dowried daughter from succession is not deemed to exclude a nun.
2. A nun to whom an inheritance has devolved is not barred from bringing an action by the lapse of thirty years.
3. A nun transmits to the monastery an inheritance not yet accepted.
4. Whether a will made in articulo mortis, and when, revokes a prior one.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A certain Lillus of Foligno died intestate, survived by his son Master Angelo and two women, one of whom was dowried and the other a nun. Thereafter, the said Master Angelo possessed the said inheritance for the space of twenty years and died having made two wills, one prior, in which he had instituted his son Francis as heir; and he ordered that, whenever the said Francis should die, after certain legacies, the residue be distributed to the fabric of the church of the brothers of Saint James. And because the aforementioned Francis died while the testator was still alive, it is said that he made another will, albeit at a time when he could not speak articulately, being weighed down by excessive illness, in which he is said to have instituted a certain nephew of his as heir.

† Now the question arises, first concerning the inheritance of the said Lilli: whether the monastery is admitted in the person of the said nun, his daughter. And it must be said that yes, for one-third part according to the number of children. For although the statute excludes a dowried daughter, such a statute provides nothing regarding a nun. Moreover, because the statute speaks of excluding a dowried daughter who survives a male, but here no male survives; although, the statute being set aside, we are in the common law, according to the note by the doctors in D. ad Tertullianum, l. 2. See there the commentary by Bartolus, and C. de adulteriis, l. 1. and D. de legatis 2, l. cum patronus. and D. de contrahenda tutela, l. si post mortem, § liberi. Moreover, as I said, a nun is not included in a statute that does not exclude her, as in C. de episcopis et clericis, l. Deo nobis.

† Nor does it avail that the nun has acquired prescription by thirty years, as in C. de sac. san. eccle., auth. quas actiones; and extra de praescrip., c. de quarta; and in Auth. de eccle., tit. eod., § 1.
