And this is clear if this nun is alive. I say the same if she died after the death of Francis and Master Angelus.

† For the monastery is transmitted by two reasons. First, on account of the existence of its heir, as in C. de suis, and the law l. apud hostes. Second, because the monastery is considered in the place of its heir, i.e., in the place of the heir of the son: it also has the same privileges which the son has, as in extra de proba, c. in praesentia, and in Auth. de sanctis epis., §. sed hoc praesenti.

† Now I come to the inheritance of the said Master Angelus, and I say that either the said Master Angelus could not speak intelligibly when he is said to have made his last will: and the first will remains valid, since the second will does not deserve to be called a will, because in such a sick person, who cannot speak articulately, there is not understood to be the deliberation of the mind, as C. de testat. l. iubemus. But if he could speak, so that he was clearly understood, this does not prejudice the will of one laboring in extremis, as ff. de fideicom. liber. l. si pater duos. §. fin. and C. de testamento milit. l. militis in expeditione. in fi. and ff. de leg. 3. l. Pamphilo. §. propositum. In doubt, however, it is presumed that soundness of mind continues in one who speaks sanely, otherwise if he spoke as though insane, as ff. de testam. l. in adversa. and ff. de cond. instit. l. quidam in suo. and C. de codicill. l. nec codicillos. Hence, he who impugns the will must prove the impediment; otherwise, the provision in the will regarding substitution. The aforementioned notes, since it is a substitution requiring the act of the commissioners, and it was not made by direct, express, or tacit, or implied words, the common opinion is that it should be regarded as fideicommissary. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a prescription runs against a complaint of an undutiful will.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. It is alleged that one of the said brothers is still alive, namely Paulutius. It is also alleged that John Cechi purchased a certain piece of land from the said goods from the late Ser Jaco, who had purchased the said piece of land from the bishop, now twenty years and more ago.

† Now it is asked whether the said Thomasia, one of the said daughters of the said Paulutius, who was dowered, yet was passed over in the will, can claim anything from the aforementioned piece of land. I answer that she cannot, notwithstanding the will, as stated in the Digest, *De in iustum testamentum*, l. *Filio praeterito*, and this is according to the common law. Likewise, notwithstanding the statute, as noted in the Code, *De adulteriis*, l. *Publicatio*, according to Cynus, and this is according to the common law. Likewise, notwithstanding the passage of time. For he who, by the authority of the praetor and the bishop, is deemed to have had good faith, and in whom dominion was transferred, or at least the condition for usucaption was established, as stated in the Digest, *De noxalibus actionibus*, l. *Cum generaliter*; and in the Digest, *De regulis iuris*, l. *Qui auctore praetore*; and in the Digest, *De acquisitione possessionis*, l. *Qui universas*, § *Item cum praetor*; and l. *Pomponius*, § *Si iussit*, with the *si* clauses: if the brother who is living opposes her, she is barred from bringing an action by the form of the statute; if he does not oppose her, she is barred from bringing an action by the common law; because the will, in which she was passed over, is deemed confirmed, since she suffered her brothers to possess for a long time, as stated in the aforementioned l. *Filio praeterito*, Digest, *De probationibus*, since she never protested according to her own mind, namely that she did not wish the will to be valid, but to challenge it as having been passed over, as stated in the Digest, *De acquisitione hereditatis*, l. *Pro haerede*, in the beginning. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The will of a usurer, if the required security was not provided when he died while the matter of providing it was still being discussed, is revived if the security is provided after death, and nos. 5 and 8.
2. An excommunicated person cannot be absolved after death.
3. A defect, or delay, must be cured at the time when the act can be performed.
4. A person who is impeded is excused, where the impediment was not sought out.
5. Whether the will of a usurer, who wished to provide security but could not find a priest or a notary, is null.
6. That which would have been reasonably enacted is held to be in accordance with the statute.
7. A mandate is not revoked by death, where the effect concerns matters that are confirmed by death.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The point of the question is as follows: A certain manifest usurer, coming to his death, instituted an heir universally and left certain legacies before the security had been provided. Foreseeing the will of the bishop, which was that ecclesiastical sacraments should not be administered to him unless he provided security, he sent a message to the bishop saying that he was prepared to solemnly provide the said security, and that it would please him to send his official or to entrust someone to receive the said security, because he wished to provide security. The bishop responded that he wanted security of five hundred florins, or at least that amount. Whereupon the messenger returned to the said usurer and spoke these words to him, who commanded his mother and other blood relatives present to immediately make the said security. And at that time it was dark night, and the lord bishop was in bed, so it was necessary to defer the matter. Fortunately, it happened that before the said security was made, the said usurer died. Immediately after his death, the mother executed the said command, had the solemn security provided, and the said usurer was handed over for ecclesiastical burial.

† Now it is asked whether the said testament recovers validity by canonical equity. And it seems that it does not, because the said testament was from the beginning null by law itself, as in c. *Quamquam*, § *Si*, *De usu*, lib. 6. And this occurred due to a defect of the testator; therefore, possession does not recover validity, as in D. *De se. ta.*, l. 1, § *Exigit*. For this testator was at the time of the testament incapacitated; therefore, the testament is null, as in D. *De leg. 1.*, l. 1, § *Si filius*. Before the time of death, this testament could not be confirmed; therefore, a subsequently arising caution cannot confer firmness upon it, as in D. *De vul. sub.*, l. *Lex Cornelia*. Indeed, if he had not been a usurer at the time of the testament, but was a usurer at the time of death, and the testament was interrupted, as if by diminution of status, as in Inst. *Qui mo. test. infir.*, § *Posteriora*. Furthermore, after the death of the said testator, he cannot be restored to his former position (*in integrum restitui*), nor can he be feigned to have had capacity, as in D. *Ad l. Aquil.*, l. *Huic scripturae*; and D. *De ope. li.*, l. *Libertinus, et posthumus*. Moreover, the gloss in the aforementioned c. *Quamquam* states that this caution must be provided before death. To this is added the Cato rule, because capacity must intervene at least at the time of death, or that which draws itself to the time of death, as in D. *De reg. Cato.*, l. 1. It accords with what is noted in C. *De sent. pas.* in the question of the testament; and D. *De haere. insti.*, l. *Sed si in conditione*, § *Solemus*; and l. *Si alienum*, § *In extraneis*.

† Moreover, just as an excommunicated person cannot be absolved after death, nor can one condemned to the mines be restored to full rights after natural death—because absolution and restoration require a person to receive them, and cannot exist without such a person; for, as stated in the Digest, *De stipulationibus servorum*, law *Usufructus*, regarding the end of the subject matter—so too does no one become incapacitated after death, just as no one becomes just or willing after death; because death dissolves all capacities, as in the Authenticum *De nuptiis*, § *Soluto*. Hence it follows that, since incapacity preceded and no capacity followed, it is impossible for the will to become valid. For whether a manifest usurer is prohibited from making a will on account of his guilt, or on account of bad morals, or so that others may be deterred by his example, or on account of the detestation of the wickedness of usury, they are not permitted to make a will. Given an impossible premise, it seems impossible that an effect should follow, especially since the defect was not purged during his lifetime, as in the Digest, *De servorum expositione*, law *Si minor*.

† Moreover, the defect must be purged at the time when the act can be performed, just as we say in the matter which must be purged at the time when the act can be performed, as in D. de appellationibus recipiendis, l. 1, in principio. But after death the act of making a will cannot be performed; therefore, after death a will cannot be reconciled, as argued in D. de rerum divisione, l. bonorum. Furthermore, the decretal *Quanquam* seems to require the act of the usurer himself, where it says, “or let them provide suitable security for satisfaction.” And note that the word *praestent* (let them provide) requires a completed act, not merely an attempted one. Otherwise, many things could be feigned against the intent of the said chapter, which is absurd, lest the law be circumvented, as argued in D. de transactionibus, l. cum hi, § si cum lis. Moreover, where the law speaks in a determined manner, we ought not to imply anything else, because it is for the one who establishes the law to gloss it, as in C. de legibus, l. si. Hence, where the law or decretal sets its feet, we must stop there, as noted in D. pro socio, l. si non fuerunt, in the last gloss. And we must observe the words of the law, even if the law is harsh, where it is a question of claiming faults: as in D. qui et a quibus, l. prospexit. And the law could have made one intestate on account of an ecclesiastical offense. For by reason of such an offense it has temporal jurisdiction, as is read and noted in C. de episcopis et clericis, aut h. Item nulla. and D. de fideiussoribus, c. cum sit generale.

On the contrary, the truth seems to be that the said will does not so much become valid after death as is declared to have been valid from the beginning. And this for multiple reasons. First, because it did not rest with the usurer that he did not provide security, but with the diocesan bishop, who raised difficulties concerning the amount of the security. For the law provides that whenever it does not rest with the party, but with the judge, no prejudice shall be caused to the party, as in D. de temporibus appellationum, auth. Item si pro alia. And by another law it is provided that if it rests with the Praetor that justice is not rendered, that the party shall be aided, as in D. quibus ex causis maioribus, l. sed et si per Praetorem. And by another law it is provided that when someone is hindered,

† from doing that which he is ready to do, and this impediment is not feigned, but causal, because the time and hour cannot be produced: for the thing that was to be done is in a manner considered as done, as in the Digest, title *Si quis cautio*, law 2, section *Quod diximus*.

Suppose that the usurer wished to make a will, but no priest or notary could be found. Shall we say that his will is void? Certainly not, because the case excuses him, as in D. de usur. l. sciendum; and D. quibus ex caus. ma. l. in ea causa; l. Item si. For we must come to the aid of one who is hindered, and especially in obligations and precepts of doing, as in D. de publ. l. Caesar; and note, Petrus de Bellapertica, D. de verb. oblig. l. continuus, § illud. For the law provides that he who is bound to do something at a certain time, if he was hindered by a just impediment, deserves forgiveness, as in D. de re mil. l. desertorem, § si ad diem; and l. qui commeatus. Moreover, a sudden case is to be corrected by the presumption of inequity and maternal piety, as in C. de inoff. test. l. si mater pia; auth. mater est ecclesia.

† Moreover, if he had been questioned on this point, through no fault of his own, it is likely that he would have declared the will valid. And the law provides that that which is likely to have certainly been decreed by the Legislator, had he been questioned on this matter, is considered as decreed, as noted in ff. de pactis, l. tale pactum, §. sin. For one who is prepared to give security for this reason is similar to one who gives security, or equal, as in Auth. vt exacti, inst. dotis, near the end, col. 7. For account must be taken of one who did not provide security not out of contumacy, but due to impediment, as in ff. de collationibus bonorum, l. 1, §. cum nobis. For not all things are within my power, nor is time available for certain matters. For deaths suddenly befall men, as in Auth. vt factae nouae constitutiones, §. fin., coll. 5, and ff. de donationibus causa mortis, l. senatus, §. 2. Suppose that a manifest usurer dies in a place where there is no notary nor priest, such that time and place did not permit the form to be observed. The cited chapter, although it itself provided by the word "before honest persons," and he did whatever he could. It would be harsh to say that his will is invalid, arg. C. de annalibus exceptionibus, l. vt perfectius, and that noted in ff. de nouis operibus nuntiandis, l. de pupillo, §. si quis ipsi praetori. Moreover, even from the strictness of the law, it seems to be said that the said will is reconciled; because whenever one act is performed first, and another afterwards, the latter act, by the ordered necessity of consequence from the prior act, is drawn back to the time of the first act, as in ff. de minoribus, l. 3, §. scio. Therefore, the execution of the mandate, so that it may seem that he himself did it who commanded it, as in ff. vi armatorum, l. 1, §. deiecisse. But if the usurer had provided, he would have made a will: therefore it is valid now.

† Nor should anyone say that the said mandate was revoked by death, since the effect of the mandate concerns those things which are confirmed by death, as in D. de mand. l. si vero non remunerandi, §. fin.; and D. de leg. 2, l. cum cum pater, §. meus; and D. de sol. l. fin. Moreover, this mandate was necessary, and therefore it does not terminate upon the death of the mandator, as in D. de acq. poss. l. fundi, §. Item si amicus. For the usurer is bound to provide security to the creditors regarding those usuries which they say they receive from him for payment, as in D. de iud. l. in omnibus; and D. de privil. cred. si creditores. Therefore, such a mandate was necessary and did not expire by death. Furthermore, a case occurring in the person of the procurator is excused, as in C. qui pet. tut. l. cum a matribus; and C. de app. l. praeses. Moreover, I judge specially for this part, C. de naturalib. lib. Auth. item si quis, where it is said that the father designated in his will that his son be made legitimate, and afterwards the Prince legitimated him, so that by such an act he is seen to have been legitimate and capable retroactively, and he succeeds. And the same is held by Bartolus in spurio: although a spurious child cannot be instituted due to double incapacity, namely that of the father and his own. Although it could be said that this is not a good analogy, because it is not sufficient that the usurer orders in his will that the usuries be satisfied, or that security be given for satisfaction, as is clear in the aforementioned c. quamquam, in principio.

But I answer that, in our question, the matter did not rest with him alone, and he merely commanded, although he could have provided the caution solemnly, and did not do so. And thus the aforementioned chapter does not apply. Someone might say: although he could not have an bishop or a vicar, nevertheless he could have had a priest and a notary, as stated in the aforementioned chapter *Quamquam*. Therefore, he is not excused, because he could have provided for himself by another means. Moreover, this usurer ought not to have constrained himself to the point of death, as in the Digest, *Si quis cautio*, law 2, § *Si quis tamen*, where it is possible; and in the Digest, *Ad legem Rhodiam de iactura*, law *Si nequenda*, § *Idem iuris*. What then, if someone were mortally wounded, such that he did not have time to provide the caution, and thus, since he could not do it himself, he entrusted it to another out of necessity, as in the Digest, *De verbis obligatis*, law *Continuus*, § *Cum quis sub hac*; and in the Code, *Qui testamento facere possunt*, law *Hac consultissima*, § *At cum humana fragilitas*? Furthermore, what if, while the caution was being dictated, the sick person died? It is certain that this person did not provide the caution, but intended to provide it. And as far as his mind was concerned, he purged the defect, although the words did not have obligatory effect, as in the Code, *De fidei instrumentis*, law *Contractus*; and in the Digest, *De testamento*, law *Iubemus*; and in the Digest, *Eodem*, law *Ex hac scriptura*; and law *Siis qui*; and in the Digest, *De testamento militis*, law *Lucius*; and in the Digest, *De legatis tertio*, law *Fideicommissa*, § 1; and in the Digest, *De condictione indebiti*, law *Eleganter*, near the beginning.

Should we therefore say that the testament previously made in health, and especially according to natural piety, or for parents, as in the Digest, *De bonis damnatorum*, law *Eum*; and in the Digest, *De inofficioso testamento*, law *Nam si parentibus*, is invalid? Certainly this seems harsh, and contrary to natural equity. Nor is it true that the Church, both militant and triumphant, imputes to anyone the fact that he bound himself, provided that he returns to the Church, because the Church never closes its bosom to the returning, as in the law *Inter claras*, Code, *De summa Trinitate et fide catholica*, near the end. And therefore, what the Church does, the statute of the Church ought to do. Considering therefore the indigence of the said usurer testator, about whom it is asked, and because the bishop imposed difficulty rather out of the blindness of avarice than out of care, I think that provision should be made for the said testament. I say that it is valid by equity. And from this I specially induce that the note of John of Andrea in the aforementioned chapter *Quamquam*, at the end, in the novella, where he says: "And there is a third cause which vitiates the testament, namely the defect of institution." This, however, does not apply to this case. Nevertheless, by him it is well argued towards the aforementioned, by the law *Filio praeterito*, *De inofficioso testamento*; and by the law *Qui solvendo*, *De hereditate instituenda*. By which laws it is proved by equity that a null testament convalesces upon the removal of the cause of impediment which induced nullity, not only before death, but also after. These are the words of John of Andrea. And he adds: "It is certain, however, that our law is based on equity." *De transactionibus*, chapter *Fidei*; *De rerum permutatione*, chapter *Unico*; *De appellationibus*, chapter *Quamvis*, in the principle. To this he induces the Code, *De precibus imperatoris offerendis*, law *Universa*. Notwithstanding the Digest, *De legatis tertio*, law 1, § *Si filius*, because there the testator was not *sui iuris*, here he is. Moreover, there was an impediment which could not be removed by the act of the testator, here it is. Moreover, there the testator was intestable, here, however, he was testable, with certain things being observed, which could come separately from the act of testing itself. And by this they were not of the intrinsic form of the testament, nor of the substance of the persons; but they were certain accidental things, which could be present or not present, by providing or following the ordinance of the testament. Argument to this effect: *De testamento militis*, law *Titius*, by contrary sense. To this it contributes, because certain conditions can be fulfilled by the heir in last wills, when it did not rest with the testator, which otherwise could not be fulfilled, as in the Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, law *Cui fundus*, at the end. Moreover, the right of cautioning is of such a nature that it passes actively and passively to the heir, as in the Code, *De colonis*, law *Si soror*. Hence it is not adhering to the first point, that it cannot be explained by the heir, equity persuading. These matters needed declaration: nevertheless, it seems to me that by equity it should be said that the testament is valid. And so I hold, saving the substance of the truth. Baldus

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. When and whether one who has title and license to enter possession is said to disturb or not to disturb possession, so that he may be criminally accused and condemned of the crime of violent disturbance.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A certain person is accused of having disturbed possession, inasmuch as he acted against a prohibition and protestation made so that he might not disturb it, as is stated in the Digest, title *Quod vi aut clam*, law *Prohibere*. And this accuser, in his articles of charge, adduced the title and possession of his client: namely, with regard to the possession derived from his title, and the protestation made upon the other party’s entry into the possession, from which the disturbance arose. But the accused says that he has an earlier title, descending through an intermediate author from the author of the said accuser, together with a precarial grant, and with license to enter the possession by his own authority, and by the union of time. Now, these things being presupposed, it is asked

Whether this accused, by his own authority, committed the crime of violent disturbance, such that the accused ought to be criminally condemned, as noted in the title and the constitution on precarious tenure. And although what is contained in the instruments of the imperial information might excuse him, assuming that the accuser has proven his bodily possession at the time of the disturbance. I answer: whenever succession is taken from the same author, and regarding what is said in the law *traditio*, the principle is that he is stronger in property and possession who has the title and possession prior in time, as is fully read and noted in D. de publiciana, l. *si a te autem*, § *si duobus*; and C. de rei venditione, l. *quotiens*. And in doubt, if both prove possession, the learned man of Arezzo notes there that priority of possession is presumed from priority of title. Therefore, if one who is prior in possession comes against another who is posterior, he does not commit violence, but suffers it; and he does not disturb, but is disturbed: because he who is understood to disturb, since he does not have the right of the posterior, does not have possession. Finally, the posterior is presumed to have entered clandestinely, and it does not pertain to the vigor of active judgment, neither by acting civilly, as in X. de probat., c. *licet causam*, nor by accusing criminally, because criminal judgments, which descend from the same source as civil judgments, imitate those civil judgments as to impugning and defending, as in C. ad legem Flaviam de plagio, l. *praeses*; and C. de adulteriis, l. *quoniam Alexandrum*; and it is made clear in D. de liberis causis, l. *liberis*, § final; and C. quando civilis actio praeiudicat criminali, l. 1; and C. de fide instrumentorum, l. final, in the end; and C. ad legem Iuliam de vi, l. *si quis ad se fundum*, in the verse *quis ad quem venit possidentem*.

Moreover, where someone has a title and license to enter possession, it is lawful for him to use such license against any possessor who derives his title from the same author, as is read and noted in l. 3, C. de pignoribus. And such license induces legal possession. And thus it would be an accusation, because what is done lawfully does not deserve punishment, as in C. de adulteriis, l. *Gracchus*. And this is proven in D. de pignoratitia actione, l. *qui ratio*; and D. de legatis 2, l. *Titia cum testamento*, § 1; and D. de servorum expositione, l. *Titius*; and it is made clear in C. de acquirenda possessione, l. final; and D. de furtis, l. *cum credito*.

Moreover, this accused believed, and ought to have believed, that his cause was aided by the laws: when it is the same in true or presumed fraud. And therefore he ought to be absolved, as in C. ad legem Flaviam de plagio, l. *plagii*; and D. de abigeis, l. 1, in the end; and what is noted by Bartolus in l. 1, § 1, D. si quis testamento liberum esse iussus fuerit; and D. de liberis causis, l. *igitur*. And therefore I conclude that the accused ought to be absolved, by the laws alleged above, and by many others which can be adduced to this effect in the case itself, namely, because it appears that he has a just cause for possessing, which is a legitimate defense, as noted in C. de rei venditione, l. *si fundum*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, in a legacy of a house made to friars for lodging, service, and utility, ownership is transferred to the legatees, or only the right of habitation, service, and utility is owed.
2. An inclusion, and the expression of a mode and a final cause, made in the same sentence, operates restrictively.
3. Whether the friars have an approved college.
4. The content is designated by the designation of the container.
5. What these words import: "I bequeath to Titius a house for his habitation."
6. A college requires the approval of the bishop.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A certain woman made a will, in which, among other things, she made such a legacy, namely: Furthermore, she left her house situated in the territory of Pavia, near the road, near the house of the fraternity, and near the property of John Line, for the lodging, service, and benefit of all the friars who are now, and will be in the future, residing and having their place in the district of Pavia, with one letter. Furthermore, for her soul. Now

† It is asked whether the ownership and possession of the said house ought to belong to the said friars, or whether it ought to remain with the heir of the said testatrix, subject to the burden contained in the said will, namely for the lodging, service, and benefit of all the friars, etc. And it seems at first that the ownership and property do not appear to have been bequeathed, but only the lodging, service, and benefit. For these words, “for the lodging, service, and benefit,” appear to have been added by way of limitation, so that nothing else appears to have been bequeathed than the lodging, service, and benefit.

† For inclusion, and the express mention of the mode and the final cause made in the same sentence, restricts [the interpretation] by virtue of what is noted in the Digest, *de transactionibus*, l. *cum his si uni*; and in the Digest, *de legibus* 1, l. *si fundum*, § *qui fundum*. For the final cause ought to be taken into account, as in the Digest, *de legibus* 2, l. *cum pater*, § *dulcissimis*; l. *epistola*, in the beginning, ad Trebatium. For this final cause does not regard the favor of the legatee only, but the favor of the testator; because for the soul, as is noted in the Digest, *de legibus* 2, l. *si quis*, where it appears that if the ownership had been bequeathed, these words, "for the office, service, and utility," would have no effect, which is a true absurdity, as in l. *si quando*, Digest, *de legibus* 1; and what is noted in the Digest, *de inofficioso testamento*, l. *si quando*, in the beginning. Therefore it would follow that the university of the said friars could sell and alienate the said house, if it were understood that full ownership was left to them; this is openly contrary to the mind of the testator, because it is absurd, because thus the intention of the testator, which must be observed, as in the Code, *communis de legatis*, l. 2, at the end, would not be preserved. Moreover, that the testator understood only the use and hospitality, and not ownership, appears from that word "service," and from that word "utility," and from that word "hospitality"; for the testator willed that the said friars should be received there for hospitality and for dwelling, but not that they should acquire any dominion. Nor is it customary to leave them dominion, but to leave to them charitable hospitality. Hence from the quality of the persons, and from the general custom, it ought to be presumed: that the testator did not wish to make them owners, but possessors, argument from the Digest, *de usu et habitando*, l. *plenum*, § *aequius*. For not only is the person speaking to be considered, but also the person to whom he speaks. Hence, since the testator speaks to friars who wander about begging: it is not understood that he leaves to them as patrimony, but for simple use of fact, argument from the Code, *de munere patrimonii*, l. *professio*; and Code, *de mendicantibus valentibus*, l. 1. Moreover, since the testator left [the bequest] to all the friars who are now, and will be in the future, dwelling and having their place inside, and the future friars are uncertain, and can be infinite in number: now no certain portion is found which can belong to them as owners. For what part will the present friars claim? It is impossible to designate, therefore it is impossible to sue for ownership, as in the Digest, *de iudiciis*, l. *sed et si restituatur*, § *fin.*; and Digest, *si pars haeredi petatur*, l. *antiqui*; and Digest, *de solutionibus*, l. *si pater*. Hence no friars are understood to be legatees, except according to the contingency of cases, i.e., those finally: and when they will dwell in the district of Ticinum, and not otherwise, as in the Digest, *de legibus* 3, l. *qui concubinam*, § *uxori*; Digest, *de manumissionibus*, l. *Meuia*; Digest, *de legibus* 3, l. *pater filium*, § *tusculanus*. And thus it would seem absurd that ownership be understood to be bequeathed in such a variable and uncertain manner. On the contrary, the laws seem to be expressed, and I premise,

† That the head of the Fraticelli, if they have no other head, is the bishop of the place; and since they are under one head, they are understood as such, and their college is approved with respect to piety and regards a spiritual life, like a congregation of the poor: as in D. de episcopis et clericis, l. Nulli; and l. Si quis ad declinandam; and note that in D. de universitatibus, l. Personam. Moreover, it is established that a college acts in place of a person: as in D. de fideicommissis, l. Mortuo. But it is so that if something had been left to a certain person under the aforementioned form, it would be understood that ownership was left; because the word “bequeaths” is in a certain house. For he who says house or field designates full dominion over the thing.

† For the thing contained is designated by the designation of the container. This is proven by the texts and reasons, and also by the doctors of the law: ff. de auro et argento legato, l. species; ff. de donationibus, l. donationes concubinam, § species; C. de iureiurando, l. si mulier; ff. de usufructu earum rerum quae usu consumuntur, l. fin.; ff. de alimentis et cibariis legatis, l. quartae; ff. de usufructu legato, l. si alii. This is also supported by the fact that in wills a broad interpretation ought to be made, as in ff. de usufructu, l. Proculus, and ff. de regulis iuris, l. in testamentis. This opinion is held by Cynus in the said § species, and by the gloss and Cynus in the said l. si mulier. And Bartolus examines this in the said l. 4, de alimentis et cibariis legatis, and there, disputing in favor of this side, determines accordingly.

† For if anyone says, “I leave to Titius the house for his habitation,” this addition, “for his habitation,” does not diminish the legacy, nor does it cause the house, if not inhabited, to revert to the heir, as is expressly proven by the said § species. Thus the word “for” operates in the same way as the word “in.” And whether the testator says “for habitation,” or “for dwelling,” or “for habitation,” such words indeed demonstrate the testator’s intent, but they do not diminish the substance of the legacy. Oldradus says that, on the contrary, they do diminish it, because they are placed in the same sentence; otherwise, if they are appended in a different sentence, as a certain mode. For example, “I leave to Titius the house, so that he may dwell in it.” For when the testator says, “I leave to Titius the house,” the sentence is complete, signifying a full legacy; but when it is in the same sentence, otherwise, for example, “I leave to Titius the house for dwelling, or for habitation,” however the testator speaks, it causes the damages to pass with the legacy, while the habitation of the house, according to Oldradus, makes a similar difference. D. de legatis 1, l. quidam in testamento; and C. de exceptionibus, l. si quidem. For it matters greatly whether there are two precepts of the testator, or one to be restricted, arg. D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. hæc scriptura; and D. de arbitrio, l. Celsus, § item ait. This question is doubtful, and the doubt is greatly caused by the quality of the persons of the legatees; because from the quality of the persons it seems that the legacy is rather referred to the fact than to the right. For to the said legacy even those incapable would be admitted, who would not be admitted to a legacy of right, as D. de capite diminutione, l. legatum; D. de alimentis et cibariis legatis, l. servus ad custodiam templi; and C. de necessariis servis hæredi institutis, l. quidem, § illa. And this consideration moves me, that the property is not understood to be left to the said friars. Also, because the said friars seem to be acephalous, i.e., without a head; as C. de curia, l. quidam iuuamen, lib. 11, whence they do not form a college. In which, in the approval of any spiritual college, or reduced to the likeness

† Proof is required of the bishop, because many could feign religion, as argued in ff. de extraordinariis criminibus, l. 3; and on this point, de excessibus praeparatorum, c. Dilecta, according to Innocentius. Hence, the writings of such Fraticelli appear to be rejected, and thus they cannot be considered as constituting a sect: as in C. de haereticis, instituta, l. Collegium; and C. de Iudaeis, l. 1. But as individuals, they are certainly capable [of receiving the legacy], unless they were heretics or schismatics; yet even then, they should be specially named, as in Inst. de legatis, §. Incertus. But to this it is answered, that it is the same as if they had been named, since they are designated by those words, “who dwell,” as in ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Illis libertis. For the fact designates the person, as in the said laws with their glosses. And this, that it is not understood that ownership is left, is not without doubt, since the said Fraticelli can receive, and it is a pious legacy, and should be enlarged in favor of the testator’s soul. Hence, in the said house, the heir ought not, nor can, dwell, but the said Fraticelli, who are and shall be for the time having their place in the district of Pavia, as contained in the testament, are said to have full and entire benefit. And this should be defended more strictly according to the rigor of law; nevertheless, for the heir, it seems expressly determined in l. Cum hi, §. Si uni certe. And that gloss says that it seems that dominion is left, yet not alienable or transferable to another, but always serving the burdens of hospitality, etc. And this part seems true. And thus I say, and I counsel, I, Baldus de Perusio, doctor of both laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a contract, which cannot be celebrated in one place due to a statute, may be celebrated elsewhere, where such a statute is not in force, and this by persons subject to the enacting authority.
2. Whether a statute prohibiting a woman from contracting, unless under a certain form, includes sisters of the Third Order.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A certain sister of the Order of Friars Minor of the presence, with the presence of the custodian of the said order, made a donation of certain possessions to another sister of the said order. This donation was made in the county of Foligno, while the sisters are from Assisi, and the donated possessions are located in the commune of Assisi. However, in the city of Assisi there is a certain ordinance that contracts of women are not valid by law itself unless the presence and consent of certain blood relatives intervene, whose consent and presence did not intervene here.

† Now it is asked whether the said donation subsists in law or not. On this point, two matters must be considered: the first is whether a contract that cannot be celebrated in Assisi, given such a statute, can be celebrated elsewhere, where such a statute is not in force. And it seems that it can: because just as with regard to the ordering and form of judicial proceedings, the place of the court is considered, so with regard to the ordering and formal solemnity of a contract, the place where it is contracted must be considered. For this argumentation proceeds from contracts to judgments, and conversely, as in D. de iudiciis, l. omnem. And for this, the common law, D. de evictionibus, l. si fundus; and C. de emancipatis liberis, l. 1; and the noted authorities in l. cunctos populos, with its subject matter. And on this, the ordinary gloss seems to hold in l. 2; and D. de eo quod certo loco.

To the contrary, it seems, because this statute disposes concerning the person, consulting the fragility of women and the like, and those who have the prospect of succeeding to these women, so that the goods may be preserved. And it is certain that this statute is valid. Furthermore, it is certain that this statute does not dispose with respect to the person in a place, but with respect to the person simply. And therefore, wherever a subject woman contracts, the contract is not valid unless the form is observed, which pertains to the capacity and incapacity of the person. Just as if a curator were appointed in Assisi to a person born in the city of Assisi: such an adult could not contract without the authority of his curator in any part of the world, as in C. de in integrum restitutionem minorum, l. si curatorem habens. Furthermore, the state of the law should not vary due to the difference of places, as in C. de temporibus in integrum restitutionis, l. fin. Furthermore, this statute is favorable, as in D. de conditionibus indebiti, l. qui exceptionem. Therefore, it extends its force even outside the territory; although we say otherwise in penal or odious statutes, as in c. animarum, de constitutionibus, lib. 6; and l. relegatorum, de interdictis. Furthermore, a subject is bound by municipal law, as in D. de postulando, l. ex ea. To this effect, what the noted authorities teach against the gloss in l. 2, D. de eo quod certo loco. Furthermore, to this effect, C. de testamentis, l. si non speciali; and l. fin. Otherwise, an absurdity would follow, because such contracts would always be made outside the territory, and the statute would be a mockery, which is absurd, arg. C. de commercio et mercatoribus, l. mercatores; and C. de eunuchis, l. 2. Now another doubt follows,

† namely, whether this statute binds these sisters of the Third Order, or whether they are ecclesiastical persons, or exempt, and subject to secular jurisdiction and power, or not: as is a certain order similar to it, which is called the order of the Knights of Joy. As noted by Bartolus in the Digest, *de iure immunitatis*, law *Semper*. And briefly, Master John of Legnano consulted very diffusely, holding that such persons were ecclesiastical persons, free from all secular jurisdiction. But the common gloss says that the order of the said continent women is not properly an order, but a certain mode of living. As noted in the chapter *Cum ex eo*, *de sententia excommunicationis*, in the Clementines. I say that they are not entirely ecclesiastical persons, nor are they entirely secular persons: but that as regards certain matters they ought to be considered as ecclesiastical persons, namely, in their free disposal of their goods, and in the alienation of their goods by those in possession of them; and that they are not compelled to swear, except in cases of calumny. This speaks of the status of the said brothers and sisters, which I have seen exemplified in public form. Moreover, they have superior persons, by whose authority they are governed and protected. Moreover, it is permitted to them to make a will, as appears in the privilege of Nicholas, in which the order of brothers and sisters of penance, confirmed by Blessed Francis in his statutes, and the rule given to them by Blessed Francis, is confirmed, as I likewise saw in public form. Nevertheless, they are not ecclesiastical persons if they commit a delict, nor are they persons who can be sued for their delicts and contracts, as appears from the said privilege of the said George. Therefore, as far as the proposition is concerned, I say that in contracting, the authority of their own superior suffices for the said donor. For as regards these statutes, which directly touch persons, these sisters of penance are not included in the statute. It would suffice for them to have the authority of their own superior. Argument from the Digest, *de legibus*, law *Quod in rerum*, section *Si quis post*, at the end; and what is noted there by Jacobus de Aretino; and from the Code, *de iurisdictione omnium iudicum*, law *Magisteria*; and law *Finis*. And therefore I conclude and say that the said donation was valid, considering the status of the said continent women and sisters of the Third Order. This is supported by the fact that continent women, especially widows, have their own privileges, as in the Code, *quando Imperator inter puellas et viduas*, law 1. Hence, if the Apostolic See granted privileges to such sisters. Moreover, since the said persons are capable of making a will, they are therefore capable of contracting; for it is lawful to argue from last wills to contracts, as in the Digest, *de legatis*, law *Servum filii*, section *Eum, qui chirographum*; and in the Digest, *de pactis*, law *Pactum inter haeredem*. Moreover, because a general statute is not understood to apply to persons specifically privileged by a superior, as noted in the Code, *ad Senatusconsultum Silanianum*, law *Decurionibus*, book 12; and in the Code, *ubi quis curiae vel coarctatione aliaque conditione*, law *Finis*, section *Exceptio*. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, doctor of both laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether, and when, a judge is liable for one who died under torture, or was tortured.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The case is stated as follows. When a certain person was defamed for having committed perjury, the judge had him arrested, and after preliminary interrogations conducted in ordinary form, since the arrested man denied the charge, the judge, informed by the testimony of credible men and considering that in cases of perjury the investigation must be most rigorous, as stated in the Code, *De falsis*, in the law *Ubi dictum*, had the aforementioned defamed man subjected to the torture of the rope. There, in the first pull of the rope, when he confessed nothing, he was raised up and lowered down a second time. And when he still confessed nothing, the same was done a third time, without the judges having reason to believe that the said tortured man would die so easily. However, unable to bear the pain, he breathed his last during the said third torture. And so, the torturers, believing that the said tortured man had expired, still gave him a little water to test for signs of life; yet in truth he had completely expired. Now it is asked whether the said judge is liable to the penalty of the Cornelian Law on murder, or another penalty, and which one; or whether he is excused by virtue of his office and by virtue of the reputation [of the accused]. And because not only three times, but often and repeatedly, suspects of such a crime are accustomed to be tortured.

† Solution. It must be said that either the aforementioned defamed person was tortured in a case permitted by law or by custom, or in a case prohibited, or not granted. In the first case, it matters whether the judge acted fraudulently in the manner of torturing, or in the quality of the torture; and then he is liable to the penalty of the Lex Cornelia de sicariis, as in D. ad l. Iul. pecul. l. lege, §. si. Or he acted strictly, but not fraudulently, and then he is liable to a milder penalty on account of fault, as in D. de poenis, l. respiciendum, §. delinquunt. Or he was neither fraudulent nor at fault, because he did what any diligent judge would have done; and then he is in no way punished, as noted in C. de adulteriis, l. Gracchus. In the second case, i.e., when he subjected someone to torture against the prohibition of law, or where it was not permitted, he is punished with the penalty of the Lex Cornelia, because he provided the cause of death. Nor is he excused on account of his office, since he sinned against the office itself, and contrary to the nature of the office, and fraud is presumed from the quality of the act, as in C. de emptione servorum, in l. 1. For when he does not observe the order of law, or due custom, he is reduced to the status of a private person. Therefore, he must be punished, and the aforementioned laws prove this to be true in our case: because the custom is to torture those defamed of falsehood, in order to form an inquiry against them based on reputation and certain indications. I say that if it can be made clear that there is infamy and certain indications, the said judge is in no way to be punished, or only for fault and not for fraud, as noted by Cynus in the said l. Gracchus. And thus says Jacobus de Aretino in D. de poenis, l. quaestionibus modum aliquando habent; and in D. de poenis, l. aut damnum, §. solent. This, however, lies within the discretion of the superior, or the syndicator, as to whether he is to be punished with some pecuniary penalty, or with none, according to what is presented. For he is entirely excused from corporal punishment, presupposing reputation and indications.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The entire age of pupils is secure by the law itself against the previously lapsed prescription.
2. The wife acquires the forum of her husband.
3. The son may cede his rights to his father, provided the solemnity is observed, which supplies for his age.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The point is as follows. Peter of the city of Castello died intestate in the year of our Lord 1248, with surviving him Catherine, his legitimate and natural daughter, aged two years, and also surviving him John, his carnal brother, who said John married the said Catherine, his niece, to Cecho in Mercatello, and gave her a dowry. Because Catherine, thus married, lived in marriage during her pupillary age, and up to the day of her death sixteen years had elapsed, there survived to Catherine Francisca, her daughter, and daughter of the said Cecho, who at the time of the death of her said mother was eight years of age. Now the said Francisca wishes to bring an action against Antonia and Philippa, nieces of the said John, and in their person the heirs of the aforementioned John, in the forum of spouses, outside the territory of the said city of Castello, in order to obtain the goods and inheritance of the said Peter, her grandfather, situated in the territory of the said city of Castello, which the said John, and Francisca his son, and the said Antonia and Philippa have possessed from the said year 1358 and around that time. Now it is asked whether she can do so, and whether the passage of time is an obstacle to her; and whether her minority, and that of her mother, benefits her, so that prescription has not run, and whether it runs in bringing the action in the said forum of spouses, and in the penalty established by the statute of the said city, placed under the heading that no one shall draw anyone to judgment outside the court of the officials of the commune; and that no person may obtain any rescript against the commune; and that no one shall draw any person to judgment outside the city of Castello. Furthermore, it is asked how a contract could be made by which the said Francisca could transfer the rights of the said inheritance to the said Cecho, her father, who wishes to marry her off and give her a dowry, and to retain or obtain for himself the said rights of his said daughter, and to give her nothing of the maternal goods. And whether such a contract can be made between the said father and daughter unless she is first emancipated. And whether by doing so he incurs the penalty of the statute of the said city placed under the heading concerning the non-acceptance of cession of rights, all of which statutes, together with the point, are transmitted to you. Three matters are in question: namely, prescription, forum, and cession.

† As to the first point, I say that the entire period of minority of pupils is secure by operation of law against the previously running prescription. C. de praescrip. xxx. ann. l. sicut. and there noted. C. in quib. cau. in integ. rest. non est neces. l. si. and ff. de mino. l. emilius. And therefore, having made the computation of time, the prescription of thirty years is not completed, because against a claim for inheritance without title, prescription does not run in less than thirty years for a minor, as C. de petit. haered. l. haereditatis.

† As to the second point, I say that a woman acquires jurisdiction in the forum of her husband, and it is not said that she is drawn there, but rather that she draws [jurisdiction]. L. Origine, and D. ad municipalia; L. De iure, and D. de iudicibus; L. Exigere dotem, and L. Cum quaedam puella, D. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum. Hence, the statute in question does not apply to our case. It supports what is noted in C. Statutum, § Cum autem, de rescriptis, Book 6. For the matter at hand concerns not a prohibition, but a necessary examination.

† As to the third point, I say that a son may cede his rights to his father, even if he is under his father's power, provided that he is of lawful age, or that the solemnities which supply for age are observed. This is supported by D. de fideiussoribus, l. si dubitetur, § 1; and by what is noted by Bartolus in D. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. actiones; and especially on account of a dowry, D. de familia erciscunda, l. Pomponius Philadelphus. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, doctor of both laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Where the form by which the order is given is not observed, the proceeding is null.
1. A messenger cannot summon without a mandate from the judge, nor is he appealed from.
2. A messenger is not believed regarding the commission, although he is regarding the summons.
3. Those under ban are considered as dead with respect to the forum of that city.
4. A person under ban does not suffer according to the decree.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Having been questioned solely on the matter of the subscription, I shall briefly conclude. It must be known that where the form by which the order is given is not observed, the proceeding is null. On rescripts, c. Cum dilecta; On restitution of spoliation, Pisanis. So much so that the omission of the mode or form, even in a favorable act, vitiates the disposition, as in the Digest, On verbal obligations, l. Qui Romae, §. Flavius Hermes. Since therefore the form prescribed by the statute was not observed, both with respect to the citation not made against the aforementioned Andrea and Bartholomew according to the form of the statute, and by reason of the petition omitted, which ought not to have been omitted according to the form of the statute speaking under the rubric "On precepts to be put into execution," as was shown by the first consultant in l. 4, §. Hoc iudicium, On damage threatened: therefore, the proceeding conducted against the aforementioned parties on behalf of the said Lord Vanna was null.

† Moreover, a messenger cannot summon without the judge’s mandate, C. de dila. l. 1. per Cyn. in 2. col. and l. neminem. C. de exhibend. reis. And the reason is manifest, because the messenger can say nothing on his own authority, but only that which he heard his lord speaking can he report, like a magpie and an instrument, as is read and noted, C. si quis alteri, vel sibi. l. multis. And therefore no appeal lies from a messenger, since he is not said to cause prejudice, de appel. c. peruenit. Moreover, a summons is the execution of an interlocutory order regarding the summoning, and therefore it must be preceded by a true judge, as C. de epi. et cleri. l. cum clericis. there, “warned by the authority of your sentences.” where the text is noted.

† Nor is credence given to a messenger regarding a commission, although credence is given regarding a citation, *de appellationibus*, c. *Cum parati*. For credence is given to an official in his own act, and to one whose report is entrusted to him by public authority, but not regarding another’s act or statement, according to Jacobus de Arena in the said law *Ea quidem*, on which point there, nor is such a commission presumed unless it is proved, because such extraneous matters are not presumed, c. *Quod sicut*. Since, therefore, the commission is not established, the citation is null: and if null, or less than legitimate, the procedure conducted by means of it does not hold. Gloss, note, in l. *Si accusationibus*, C. *de accusationibus*, and note, *de constitutionibus*, c. *Ecclesia sanctae Mariae*.

† Moreover, these individuals were banned with the deprivation of all their goods: because, with respect to the forum of that city, they are considered as dead. Hence, they cannot be summoned in a civil case, according to the chapter *Dimidium*, law *Tutor*, § 1. Nor is a summons to their dwelling valid, since they have abandoned their residence, as stated in the Clementine constitution *Cum causam*, on Elections; and see chapter *Cum olim*, in the same title; otherwise you will not understand the matter. On causing impending damage, law 3, § *Verecundum*, and § *Totius* there, where it says "nor shall he inhabit"; and see there Baldus and Bartolus in law 4, on causing impending damage.

† Moreover, an outlawed person does not suffer [legal disability] according to the decree during the outlawry, unless the statute provided otherwise. And the glossa ordinaria notes Bartolus in l. ad cognitionem, ex quibus causis in possessionem eatur. From all of which, I, Francesco, Doctor of Both Laws of the Lord Baldus of Perugia, advise, as concluded above, and as advised by the most learned Doctor John Bandini and the other Consulting Lords. And therefore, for the sake of faith, I have subscribed and sealed, saving the judgment of a better sentence, as in l. Claudius Felix, qui potiores in pignore habentur.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether restitution to a right lost, or from which one has been deprived, is drawn back to the time of the loss or deprivation.
2. How manyfold a city is.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Point. Paulutius and John petitioned the Lords Priors and the Commune. Whereas their father had formerly paid an imposed levy of 40 gold florins, and therefore, according to the form of the ordinances of the Commune of Perugia, had become a citizen of Perugia, had been enrolled, and described in the possession of the citizens; finally, by virtue of a certain mandate or decree made by the Abbot Major of the monastery, he was struck from the register of citizens of the Commune of Perugia and attached to the county in the village of Casale. Wherefore it was petitioned that the said Lords Priors and the Commune, in favor of justice and from the arbitrators granted to them by the general assembly, should cause them to be described among the citizens of Perugia in the said priories and parts. Certain Priors, considering that the aforementioned petitioners were obtaining justice, and that the administration of justice pertains to them, heard the aforesaid petition and solemnly ordered and decreed that, upon making faith of the payment of the said levy to the officials of the armory, the aforementioned Paulutius and John be restored and attached in the said priories and parts, just as their father had first been described. Finally, most recently, after the description and liberation made by virtue of the said ordinance, after many years, the Priors and the Commune decreed that whoever of the county of Perugia, or of the said county, however hitherto created or made a citizen by any reason, cause, right, or mode within the last ten years, has been a citizen of Perugia or enrolled in citizenship, shall be and be understood to be revoked from the said benefit of citizenship and restored to the county. It is asked whether the said Paulutius and John are comprehended under this law. Invoking the name of Christ, I say they are not comprehended, as is proven by the said law. These men were created citizens twenty years ago and more. And although they were struck from the register, there is no force in this, because they were unjustly struck from the register. For, since they acquired citizenship through the contract initiated with the commune, the aforementioned Abbot could not deprive them of the benefit of citizenship without the consent of the Priors, as noted by the doctors in the law *Omnes populi*, *De iustitia et iure*. Moreover, that they were unjustly struck from the register, and thus always remained after the acquisition of the benefit of citizenship and were citizens, the Lords Priors and the Commune declared, as is mentioned above in the point. And if anyone should wish to say that the said benefit of citizenship was extinguished by the said striking from the register made by mandate of the said Abbot, and afterwards resurrected or restored by the restitution made in the way of justice by the aforementioned Lords Priors and Commune, in the manner declared in the point,

† I state that the aforementioned persons are not included in the aforementioned newly enacted law: because the restoration made to the status of citizen, which is drawn back by way of grace, not merely by way of justice, to the time when the restoration was made, with respect to all matters provided for in the disposition of the aforementioned law. This is the notable gloss in *l. in quaestione*, *de sententiam passis*, in gloss 4, at the end, where it is said that if the son of a deported person made a will and died, and afterwards the father was restored, the father recovers the usufruct of the adventitious property, which had passed with the ownership to the heirs. This notable gloss and its true reasoning, from which I do not depart. Moreover, that he who is restored to civil status is always considered a citizen retroactively, is an ancient case in *l. intercidit*, *ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus*. It is well supported by *l. filio, quem pater*, *de liberis et posthumis*. I do not pursue this point further, because it is not expedient here. Therefore, I conclude that the aforementioned Paulutius and John are not comprehended under the law disposing concerning citizens of ten years ago, mentioned above. And so I say and advise, I, Rogerius of Perugia. Because it has been subtly concluded and advised by my lord, Lord Rogerius, such that in effect nothing more seems to be able to be said; and also, being asked only about the subscription, I briefly conclude: and I consider,

† That a certain kind of civility is one which cannot be induced except by nature, as is original civility: and concerning such statutes, it cannot feign; this is what the law does in *in nupta*, which it draws back to the origin of the husband. C. de muni. et origi. l. pen. There is a certain kind of civility which can be induced by human constitution, and this one is truly induced by statute: because where there is truth, there is fiction. One must hold to what is possible, ff. de lib. et posthu. l. filio, quem patri. according to Bartolus, and in l. si is, qui. pro empto. And it is of this last civility that ours is: because either it is presupposed in the point, because the aforementioned Bartholomew, by the benefit of the decree and the ordinance of the former lords, and by the act of the beneficiary himself, through the payment imposed, had civility made for him, and now twenty years have passed, he has the effect of a citizen of Perugia, and is described and enrolled among the citizens of Perugia. Hence, since his civility was acquired for him by statute or decree, it has the force of a contract, or not only by the vigor of the statute, but also on account of the act of the beneficiary, without consent or fault, it was unjustly annulled by the said Abbot of the greater monastery, or by decree, or struck off from the register of citizens and enrolled among foreigners, as noted, ff. de decret. ab or. fa. l. quod semel. and there expressly by Bartolus and Baldus in l. omnes populi, where they determine this literally regarding the Comitatenses. and de excu. tut. l. sed reprobari. de pact. l. fi. and l. si cum hermes. and de donat. inter vir. et vxor. l. pen. de fideicom. lib. l. si filius. §. aere rubiciano. Hence, it does not hinder that Bartolus notes in l. antiochensium, siue de priuile. cred., where he says that by a general statute against a certain person, a superior can take away the right of a subject: because it does not follow: therefore he can rescind a contract celebrated with that same superior: as noted in d. l. semel. and d. l. omnes populi. and Cynus in l. digna vox. And therefore the aforementioned civility remained unshaken, and the civility remained, as it was later declared by the former lords and the commune, by fact and not by the right of the officials, removing what was done, which is retroactive to the time of the aforementioned civility granted, as ff. de testa. l. haeredes palam. §. sed si notam. for he who declares does not induce, but reveals what is, as l. adeo. §. item cum quis. de acque rer. do. and by l. j. ff. de in integ. resti. and it is expressed that restitution is retroactive, so that they may appear rather to have been restored to the aforementioned civility than transferred. Moreover, if we say that the aforementioned mandate, i.e., that they be replaced and enrolled, as is expressed above, contains restitution, perhaps the same seems to be said by the laws subtly induced by the said Doctor Rogerius: or when a new and juridical fact intervenes after deportation, a right is acquired; otherwise, otherwise, according to Cynus, de decur. l. 2. and de iure patro. l. si patronus. for he restores who reduces to the former state, taking away what was done, or putting back what was taken away. ff. ne quid in loco publ. l. 2. §. vt restituas. and in the meantime, the one restored to obtain the effects of grace is rehabilitated. ff. de manu. testa. l. Aristo. ff. de iniusto test. l. si quis filio. §. pen. This last part, however, concerning restitution is more doubtful. And much could be alleged for and against. Nevertheless, all the above being considered, as concluded above by the eminent and perspicuous doctor of civil law, Master Rogerius, I say and counsel, I, Francis.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether illicitly acquired things are shared among partners, what things are to be shared, and from what sources partnership arises.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† If one of the brothers acquired money from fruits or from military pay. If indeed he acquired it illicitly, he is not bound to share it with his brother: for the sharing of crimes is base and foul, D. de fideiussoribus, l. Si Aristo, §. Si; D. de familia erciscunda, l. Caetera, §. 1; D. pro socio, l. Quod autem, and the following law. But if the pay was lawful, then he is not bound to share it: for castrense property is not contributed to brothers, whether it was acquired during the father’s lifetime or not, D. de collatione bonorum, l. 1, §. Nec castrense; C. de bonis quae liberis, l. Cum oportet; D. pro socio, l. Cum duobus, §. Si fratres. For these brothers were conducting business separately: and although they later returned to live together, nevertheless for this reason a community of their separate earnings is not established. Common to both judgments, D. l. Si cum patruo. But if they purchased certain goods in common, such goods are common, just as they were purchased, whether the money was common or belonged to only one of them. C. Si quis alteri vel sibi, l. Multum, with similar cases. However, when the money was common, if it was a small amount, a donation between brothers is presumed, D. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. Si servus communis. But if it was a large amount, it is not presumed to have been donated. But it may be recovered, insofar as one paid for the other, D. de negotiis gestis, l. Nesennius, unless there were other grounds for presuming remuneration, D. de mandato, l. Si vero non remunerandi, §. Idem Papinianus; and what is noted, D. de solutione matrimonii, l. Quae dotis, and l. Cum quid; D. si certum petatur. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the legatee is bound to have the bequeathed thing removed from the testator’s estate and placed in his own.
2. How and in what manner it is understood that a woman is presumed to acquire from her husband’s money; and see below in the following counsel.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The point is as follows: In the tax register of the community of the castle of Plebs, among others enrolled and assessed in the said estimate, or tax register, is found enrolled and assessed Faustinus Petri of the said land of the castle of Plebs, and in the book of the said Faustinus, among other things, it is found thus: namely, that the said Faustinus has immovable property, and for movable property eight hundred pounds, which, when reduced to the gross according to the custom of others of the said land having immovable property, amount to 17 pounds of denarii: at the rate of 2 pounds for every hundred pounds. Now it happens that the said Faustinus died having made a will, in which, among other things, he instituted Gaspar and Pelegrina, daughters of Antonius Nardi, as his heirs for one half, and certain others for the other half: and to Do. Antonia Angela, his wife, he left all and each of the dwelling houses of the said testator with their cloisters, cisterns, cellars, and with their appurtenances, situated in the castle of Plebs, within their boundaries, with all and each of the things, goods, and household effects existing in the said houses: and which were found, and which were, or of which he had knowledge. Furthermore, he left to the said Do. Angela a farm with a palace, etc., and a certain other piece of land, as in the said his will. Now the said Gaspar and Pelegrina, or their curator, are proceeding against the said Do. Angela: and they demand that the said lady, for the half of the estate touching the said movable property, cause to be removed and struck from the tax register, and from the book of the said lady, and to be alienated, annulled, and taken from the book of the said Faustinus.

† Now it is asked whether the said lady ought, by right, to be compelled to this, having regard to the legacies made to her in the aforementioned testament and the bequests left to her. And first it seems that she should: because he who receives the fruits, advantages, or profits from the allotted goods ought to pay and bear the burdens incumbent upon the common estate, as is stated in l. omnes, C. sine censu, or in reliquis, C. de alluvione, compared with l. 2, ff. de impensis, together with similar authorities. But this lady appears to be innocent, and that she is innocent is apparent: because the husband bequeathed to her the houses for habitation together with all and each of the things existing therein, which goods and household effects are said to have come into the hands of the said lady. Since, therefore, the said movable property came to her, and she receives fruits and profits from it, the burden also follows, as is noted in the legal maxim, "He who feels the burden," etc., de regulis iuris, lib. 6. What more? It appears that the said lady Angela, after some time following the death of the said Faustinus, her husband, deposited a certain sum of money, namely five hundred gold florins, with a certain money-lender, and furthermore provided a certain sum of money for the redemption of her brother Bartholomew, etc., and gave a dowry to her daughter. From these facts it seems to be proven that the said movable property of the said Faustinus came into the hands of the said lady.

† For that which a woman has is presumed to have been had from the husband’s goods, unless the contrary is proved, in l. Quintus and l. Etiam, D. and C. de donis inter virum et uxorem. Therefore, she ought to place it in her own estimate, or account, according to the above-mentioned laws to the contrary. And I believe this to be true, namely, that the said lady is not bound by the aforementioned [provision]. For he does not prove that this is so, which is absent for this purpose. l. Neque natales, C. de probationibus. Although the testator bequeathed to himself houses with all and each of the things existing in them: it does not follow conclusively and necessarily: therefore, all his movable property; for he could have had money and other things, and the aforementioned houses, and things moving, such as oxen and cattle, and similar items, which are commonly kept in rural estates, which would not be included in the legacy. Nor does it follow: the testator had 8 pounds in movables; therefore, all of it was in all the aforementioned things of the said lady’s legacies. For it could be that there was little or nothing in them; therefore, it does not conclude necessarily, l. Non omnium, D. de legatis.

† Nor does it matter if it is said that it appears that the said lady has in the hands of the money-changer five hundred gold florins: therefore, from the husband's goods, according to the aforementioned law *quintus*. For this is true, that what the woman seeks is presumed to have been acquired from the husband's goods while the husband was alive. It is otherwise when he is dead. For the law speaks of a wife, and not of a widow, as in the law *si vero*, § *de viro*, *solutis matris*. But if, after the death of the husband, it were presumed that what was acquired came from the husband's money, and it were presumed that the woman had taken that money from the husband, and thus fraud would be presumed, which ought not to be presumed, as in the law *Marcellus*, *de rebus donatis*. But while the husband is alive, she is not said to take away, if she were to accumulate, and it is sought for the husband as a supplement through administration, not simply. Law *multum*; law *si quis alteri, vel sibi*; law 1, *de institutionibus*; law *si ut proponis*, *de donis inter virum et uxorem*. From which I conclude that the said lady, regarding the aforementioned matters, namely, to deposit the said movable property, or pounds, for the aforementioned reasons contrary to those first adduced against her, must absolutely be compelled by the laws and reasons recently alleged above. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether property purchased by the wife is presumed to have been purchased with the husband’s money.
2. Property purchased by the wife in the wife’s name, which she stated was paid for from her own money, and which the husband also confessed, is acquired by the wife herself, and the husband’s heirs could not claim it after his death; but whether they can sue for the price, or to the extent that the wife has been enriched, no. 3.
1. The husband’s confession that the property was purchased by the wife from the wife’s funds has the force of a donation.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The point is as follows. During the subsisting marriage, Magdalene Pelegrini purchased a certain piece of land, and in the instrument it is stated that she purchased it with her own money, proceeds thereof beyond her dowries. And so too, in her presence, the husband confessed and asserted this. Now, the husband having died, leaving alien heirs, with his said wife surviving. Now it is asked, what is the law regarding the said purchased property, whether it pertains to the said woman or to the heirs of the husband? Regarding the above-narrated matters, two things must be considered. First, from whose money it is presumed that the said piece of land was purchased: whether from the husband’s money or from the wife’s money, namely, the said Magdalene’s. Second, if from the husband’s money, whether the ownership of the said thing is acquired by the wife or by the husband; and thus, whether, upon the husband’s death, an action for the said thing, or for the price, or for neither of the aforementioned, namely, neither for the thing nor for the price, belongs to the husband’s heirs.

† And as to the first point, it is certain in law that a thing purchased by a wife during the subsistence of the marriage is presumed to have been purchased with the husband’s money, in order to avoid the suspicion of illicit gain: as in l. Papin., ff. de donis inter virum et uxorem; l. et etiam, C. eodem titulo; according to Innocentius, de testamento, cap. cum in officiis. And there is no need to dwell on this, because it is so by law, unless the woman proves that she had the money from another source. Regarding this, however, it should be known that there are two cases: whenever a thing is purchased by the husband in the name of his wife, and sometimes the wife herself purchases in her own name, i.e., in the name of the wife herself. In the first case, if the husband purchases a thing in the name of his wife from his own money, and receives it by delivery in that name, ownership is acquired by the wife, C. si quis alteri, vel sibi; l. multum, § 2, responso. Unless it is proven that the name of the wife was fictitiously added to the instrument, as noted in ff. de donis inter virum et uxorem, l. uxori marito. However, such simulation is not presumed, because in case of doubt the instrument is upheld, C. de probationibus, l. cum precibus; and C. de donis inter virum et uxorem, l. si filii tui, unless it was expressly stated. In the second case, when the wife herself purchases for herself and in her own name, even though from the husband’s money, truly or presumptively, nevertheless ownership of the thing is acquired by her, and the thing becomes hers: she is, however, bound to the husband insofar as she has been enriched: as in the aforementioned l. multum, in principio; and l. 1, eodem titulo. For a thing purchased with my money is not mine, but that of the purchaser, and therefore cannot be claimed by me, as in l. si ex ea, C. de rei venditione, except in a subsidiary action, i.e., when the purchaser is insolvent. And thus the gloss in l. si ut proponis, C. de rei venditione, should be understood. The same applies to husband and wife, because otherwise, simply understood, it would not be true, in the aforementioned l. si ut proponis; and l. multum, cited above. From the foregoing, therefore, I infer two points relevant to our proposition.

First, that the said plots of land purchased from the aforementioned Doña Magdalena are presumed to have been purchased with the husband’s money, as stated in the aforementioned law *Papiens*, together with the similar provisions cited above. Second, that the said property, having been acquired by her and thus become her own, cannot be claimed by the husband’s heirs, as has been shown above.
But it is doubtful whether they can sue for the price, or insofar as she is enriched, by the aforementioned law *uxor marito* and the other laws cited above.

And briefly I say that this is not the case in our situation: because since the aforementioned John, her husband, confessed in her presence and at her urging that the said price had come from the wife’s own money, the said confession, by virtue of the prohibition of the law, has the force of a donation. See D. 22.5.10 (Qui testamentum); D. 23.5.1 (Vir uxori); D. 39.5.1 § 1 (Si quis in fundum). But a donation between husband and wife, if delivery intervenes, or something else that is regarded as equivalent to delivery, is confirmed by the death of the donor. See C. 8.53.1 (Quod de suo); D. 23.5.1 (Res); D. 23.5.1 (Donatio). Since therefore such price appears to have been presumptively donated by the aforementioned John, her husband, to the aforementioned Magdalene, and delivered there, which is apparent because it was paid to the sellers through her, therefore such donation was confirmed by the death of the aforementioned husband according to the laws cited above. And thus the aforementioned lady is secure against the heirs of the aforementioned husband, nor is she bound to restore either the said piece of land or the price, but it is hers and under her own dominion. But if the aforementioned husband had sworn an oath, then there would be no doubt that such donation would have been valid from the beginning. See D. 22.5.1 (Seius et Augerius). I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A natural son is said to be so in three ways.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† For the investigation of the truth, it must be known that a natural son is said to be so in three ways. In one way, as he differs from a spurious son: and then it suffices that he be born of a free man and a free woman, from a clandestine union; as appears in the extrajudicial decree *Innotuit* on elections. In the text there, "he snatched away the flower of her virginity, as if by stealth." The gloss supports this in the final law of the Code on natural children. In another way, with regard to intestate succession: and then it is required that the mother be retained in the household, not dismissed to wander the streets and alleys, as stated in the Authenticum *De triennio et semisse*, § *Consideremus*. Hence, with regard to this effect, namely succession, those are called natural children who are born of a free man and a free woman, the latter being the only one retained in the household. If, however, anyone had several concubines at the same time, with whom he fornicated, the sons are not called natural, but they succeed their father. For just as one cannot have several wives at the same time, so too one cannot have several concubines, lest greater license be given to fornicators than to those living chastely, as stated in the Authenticum *Quibus modis naturales efficiuntur sui*, § *Si quis autem*, Collatio 7.
