Therefore, it is necessary for a son to be called natural that three things concur, namely, that the parents be free, and that the woman be the only one. And these two are of the essence of natural status considered in a civil manner. Furthermore, that she be in the household; and this is more of the essence of the presumption for proving filiation than of the essence of the truth, just as in marriage, as stated in the law *Filium diffinimus*. It supports what Innocent noted regarding the children of priests, chapter *Michael*, and regarding elections, chapter *Innotuit*. In the Digest, on concubines, law *In concubinatu*. In the Extravagantes, on renunciation, chapter *Cum pridem*. Thanks be to God.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether greater credence should be given to four witnesses testifying that the boy was extracted from his mother’s womb dead, than to two stating that he was alive; and how both these and those give their testimony, and how they assign their reasons.
2. Goods are presumed to be paraphernal.
3. The son-in-law is not bound to make restitution of the fruits consumed.
4. No one is presumed to be born dead. A just cause for litigation excuses one from costs.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The case is as follows: a mother claims the inheritance of her daughter from her son-in-law. The husband, however, asserts that the inheritance belongs to him, because his wife died after the birth of a certain son, who was extracted from his mother’s womb. On this point, several witnesses were heard. Four of them state that the child was extracted from the mother’s womb dead, and they give their reason based on sight, and also provide a rational reason, namely that the child did not perform any act of a living child. On the contrary, two witnesses testify that the child was born alive, and in the matter of knowledge they give their reason based on sight: but they do not provide a rational reason, such as having heard the child’s cry. Rather, they say that they saw the child move his lips and arms, and that he drew breath and exhaled three times.

† Now it is asked whether judgment should be given that the said boy was born alive or dead. And it must be said that the testimony of four witnesses prevails, because although this testimony, that he was dead, is privative, it is not properly negative: because it falls within the sense of the witness through sight, and immediately: and therefore more witnesses are to be believed, as is fully noted by Cynus in l. 2, C. de errore aduocati, and de testibus, c. In nostra, and l. Ob carmen, §. Si, de testibus, by Cynus in l. In exercendis, C. de fide instrumentorum. And this is proved by another reason: because when witnesses are contrary and in equal number, those are more to be believed who give a specific reason for the cause of their knowledge, than those who simply say that they saw or were present; indeed, there are some cases in which, unless the reason for the reason is given, witnesses are not to be believed, as noted by Innocentius de testibus, ca. Cum causam, and these are those cases in which witnesses can be deceived in sight. Hence Bartolus in this matter says that life is not proved by the motion of limbs, in his Tractatus de testibus. For it happens in animals and in men that the dead move some limbs: because after death there remains a certain momentary impulse of preceding life, as appears in those condemned to the last penalty of the head. Nevertheless, the reason is that some are born entirely dead, some entirely alive, and also that they emit a voice. Some are in such weakness of spirit that they do not have the power to emit a voice, nor to make any signs of life. And these are understood to be born dead, not alive, as in C. de posthumis haeredibus instituendis, l. Quod creatum. Hence all witnesses can be reconciled with one another, and no one proves life. And even if it were assumed that they proved life, those two who speak of aspiration and respiration, which are instruments and signs of life according to Aristotle, nevertheless the four witnesses so tightly assert the opposite, that even if it were negative, one must still adhere to the greater number, and this is the truth. Hence the said mother has no right in the petition for inheritance: but because it appears from the confession of the said mother that the goods were dowry, the husband is said to have a third part of the goods, which are claimed according to the form of the statute: although where nothing had been proved or confessed regarding the dowry, it would be otherwise:

† because goods are presumed to be paraphernal and not dowry, unless a prior promise exists, as in D. de iure dotis, l. in stipulatione and l. mulier bona, unless something else were to be presumed from the quality of the persons. And thus is understood the gloss placed there, and the statement of Ariston.
† On another point concerning consumed fruits, I say that the said son-in-law is not bound to their restitution:

†because since no one is presumed to be born dead, and especially where the prior party has in his favor the presumption of certain witnesses, good faith is presumed. Hence, he acquires the industrial fruits, since this is the most just error of fact, namely the consumption of nature, as noted in D. de rei vend. l. vsus fructus. But if there were a dispute in law, although he would make the fruits his own, he would nevertheless not acquire them to the extent that he has been enriched by the consumption. And thus must be understood what is read and noted in D. de pet. haere. l. sed si lege. § scire. And therefore this person, concerning whom the question is asked, ought to be condemned to the restitution of two parts. From the restitution of the third part, and of the fruits of the aforementioned things, he ought to be absolved: and whether the fruits have been consumed or not, this is presumed from the time, as noted in l. vnica. C. si aduersus vsucapionem. de expensis

I say that, on account of a just cause for litigation, neither party is condemned against the other, according to the law *Properandum*, section *Si autem*, in the Code on Judges. And because each prevailed in part, as stated in the law *Qui solidum*, in the Digest on Legacies, Book 2. And thus I say, and I advise, I, Francesco, doctor of both laws of Lord Baldus, and I have subscribed and sealed this to attest to its truth.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether an acknowledgment of receipt with a promise to repay creates an obligation after two years have passed from the date of the acknowledgment.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen.

† The point: a certain person acknowledged that he had had and received one hundred from Titius, which he promised to repay him upon his demand and at a term, and he renounced the exception of money not counted. Now it is asked whether he is obligated by such an acknowledgment, since two years have elapsed from the day of the acknowledgment. Moreover, the exception of money not counted was renounced, and it seems that he is not, since he stated [or: did not state?] for what cause he had and received them, as in l. 2. §. circa. de excep. do. The contrary is true, because the cause is presumed once he acknowledges that money was counted out to him; the gloss is noteworthy in l. cum quid. It is one thing to acknowledge that money was counted out to oneself [and another to acknowledge that one owes]. For in the first case it would not suffice if from such an acknowledgment it were not inferred from what cause he acknowledges that he owes, because such an acknowledgment relates to law; and thus the gloss can be understood in the said §. circa. But in the second case it does suffice, because such an acknowledgment looks to the fact, that is, the counting out. I saw in another first book of consilia on the last folio, where you have a similar consilium in a similar matter in my own hand, and it is by lord Baldus; and thus there is a natural loan, whence it cannot be said to be without cause [or: sub causa?]. Franciscus Baldi.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If the heir in his will commands that legacies be paid, it appears that by this he has accepted the inheritance.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Titius appointed Martin as his heir and left a certain sum for his burial. Now, this appointed Martin made a will, appointed Sempronius as his heir, and commanded him to pay the legacies left by Titius, etc. The question is whether, by this act, he is deemed to have accepted the inheritance.

† He who ordered the heir that the legacies of another testator, to whom he himself could succeed, be paid, is thereby deemed to have accepted the inheritance. This is the reasoning, because unless the inheritance of the first testator has been accepted, legacies do not regularly take effect: as in l. eam, quam, C. de fideicommissis. Hence, whoever wishes them to take effect and be executed, thereby wishes to be an heir. Nor can he do this unless as an heir; therefore, etc., ff. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. pro herede, §. Papinianus, and C. de iure deliberandi, l. si auia. Moreover, he who binds his heir to the burdens of the inheritance of the first testator assumes the burden of the inheritance upon himself, and he too, even if he should recover, could be sued; because he involves himself in this inheritance with intent, as in the aforementioned l. pro herede. And there it is also clear that by possessing the goods he acts as heir. But possession has been proven; therefore, etc. Moreover, this is supported by the appraisal and the confession of the party, which prejudices only the confessor, provided it is public before public officials in the archive: C. de donationibus, l. censualis. All things considered, therefore, I hold that the acceptance and the management as heir have been sufficiently proven, even if there were no legacies or judgments to be paid, because not the effect, but the affection, the consideration of the mind, and the will are examined, as is fully noted in C. de iure deliberandi, l. potuit, and ff. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. gerit. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. How a spurious son may succeed to his father.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A certain person instituted his daughter as heir in the following manner: and if she could not accept the inheritance at the time of the testator’s death, he instituted the same daughter as heir when she would be able to accept it; and if she could not accept it, nor would be able to, he instituted as his universal heirs the legitimate and natural daughters descending from her; and if she had no daughters, or if they died while she was still living, he instituted and substituted Peter, his friend, etc. He did not, however, name the friend, etc., in the will, because fraud would thereby be detected. And this is the best course that can be found,

† that a spurious son may succeed his father. For here many intermediate cases are simultaneously joined. And this is clear from the notes by Bartolus in l. Gallus, § quidem tamen, de liberis et posthumis; by the same author in l. si, de his quibus ut indigis; and by Decius and Bartolus in l. is qui, de vulgari et pupillari substitutione; and in ff. de iure fisci, l. ita fidei, § patronus, by Decius and Bartolus. And thus beautifully advised Lord Baldus in the case of Castro Cerqueti. The same aforementioned Lord Baldus ordained in the testament of Gerolanus, that here at the beginning of this document Lord B. in the son of Gerolanus, Peter, who is called Herculanus, also known as Belfante, used these words: because the said Gerolanus instituted his said son in this form: In all his goods and so forth, he instituted, made, and left Herculanus, also known as Belfante, his son, as his universal heir; and if the said Herculanus, his son, cannot, or should not be able, to take the said inheritance, he substituted himself to himself, when he could, or can, or will be able, to take the said inheritance, and his sons, grandsons, and other descendants, whoever they may be, up to the end. Again, he left his said son as curator, administrator, and governor of the said inheritance; and that no account of the aforementioned administration may be demanded from him at any time or in any manner, nor is he in any way bound to provide a surety on account of the aforementioned matter, from which obligation to provide a surety and to render an account he expressly freed and absolved him. And if the said Herculanus, his son, should die at any time without children descending from him, he substituted, etc. I, Francis.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a conveyance made on account of a dowry is to be regarded as made to prove a preceding actual payment, or rather a future hope of payment.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Sometimes a confession arises in a contract of loan or dowry, sometimes in other contracts. In the first case, one who has confessed to having had and received in a loan and dowry is presumed to have done so in contemplation of the future. On the interpretation of words, law *Si ita stipulatus*, section *Grisogo*, through Bartolus, Digest, *Si certum petatur*, law *Singularia*, through the same. For by those words, namely, "he confessed to having had and received from such a giver and payer, etc.," the right of actual payment is not proven. Code, *Si certum petatur*, law *Si ex pretio*. Because the ablative placed in consequence signifies according to the antecedent to which it refers. But these ablatives refer to the confession and follow it, according to Jacobus Butrigarius, who thus disputed, and noted by the gloss and doctrine in law *Si ex cautione*, Code, *De non numerata pecunia*. And this is true, unless there has been a renunciation of the exception of non-payment of money; for then true payment is presumed to have preceded: as noted in the said law. See entirely Baldus there in law *Ex cautione*, and in law *§ 1*, *De dote causa non numeratae*. In other contracts, however, a confession is held for truth. Digest, *De postulando*, law *Publia*, at the end.

Now, to the point, I say that although in the fact, in which Mechus, formerly of Crechi, confessed to having had and received, and to have with him without any diminution, from Luca, the said Buono, giving and paying, and in the name of the dowry of the lady Paschola, his carnal sister, for the marriage contracted between the said Mechus on one part and the said lady Paschola on the other, 40 gold florins, etc., true payment is presumed to have intervened because of the renunciation of the exception of non-receipt of the said florins, which is added in the aforementioned instrument; and because of the lapse of two years; the subsequent refutation of the same quantity, reported by the hand of another notary, refers to the said quantity of dowry and confessed. It does not imply another dowry newly given; otherwise it would follow that the said Cechus had received a double dowry for the same marriage, which is not presumed, because this repugns the law, and it appears from the cause of the refutation itself, inasmuch as for 40 gold florins he received a certain holding of land in dowry. Moreover, when the same thing is promised twice from the same cause, it is owed only once, as in law *Qui bis idem*, *De verbis obligatis*. I, Francis.

CASE. In the name of Christ, Amen. The fact is as follows: Simbaldus Gitandelli of Perugia gave and paid at the *fondico de pecore* of Perugia to Stephanus Thomasini of Florence, residing in Perugia, 1300 florins. And the said Stephanus, partner of the said partnership, in the person of the partners and his own, promised the said Simbaldus that his partners from Florence would write themselves to be debtors of the said Simbaldus in the said quantity, which they will pay to him at his request. And furthermore, it was agreed between the said Simbaldus and Stephanus, after those from Florence had written that they owe the said quantity, that they will bring one *apodissa* [acknowledgment], once the others from Florence had written in their books that they owe the said quantity; and this being done, Simbaldus must return to the said Stephanus the written document which he has from the hand of the said Stephanus. Now it is asked whether the said quantity can be claimed here by the heirs of the said Simbaldus from the *fondico de pecore*, which is here; or whether it must be claimed in Florence.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Novation occurs in many ways.
2. Whether the addition of a new place or person to a prior obligation induces novation.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen.

† Sometimes novation occurs with respect to both the person and the place. For example, that which Titius owes in Perugia, Seius promises in Florence. Sometimes there is novation with respect to the place, but not with respect to the person; for example, that which I owe to pay in Perugia, I must pay in Florence. Sometimes there is novation with respect to the person, but not with respect to the place; for example, that which I owe to pay in Perugia, Titius must pay in Perugia. Sometimes there is no doubt whether this is novation or not.

In the first case, either some condition or final cause of the named obligation intended to novate the old obligation is inserted, which has not been fulfilled, and no novation has occurred; or the novating party is purely and freely content, and no novation has occurred, *l. pecuniam*, D. *si certum petatur*; *l. si*, C. *de novatione*.

In the second case, there is not properly novation; hence the debt can be sued upon in either place, if otherwise the place is suitable; for example, because he has a certain domicile in the place where he is sued. Nevertheless, it is an arbitrary action with respect to the place, D. *de eo quod certo loco*. It is otherwise if the place of the contract is not a suitable place, as in *l. 2*, C. *de bonis auctoris iudicis possessis*; and *l. quaero*, D. *de solutionibus*.

In the third case, the same applies as in the first, namely, that either the cause or condition of the novating obligation exists, or it does not, etc. See Bartolus in *l. quod traditur*, D. *de constitutione pecuniae*.

In the fourth case, either the person is added in favor of the debtor to release the first debtor, and novation is presumed by way of exception, not by operation of law, when it is not expressly stated that this is the case, as noted by Odofredus and others in the aforementioned *l. si*, C. *de novatione*. The same applies if it is for the purpose of reducing the obligation, as in D. *de actionibus*, *l. cum in plures*, § *lege dicta*; and C. *de praetoria stipulatione*, *l. penult.*; and noted in D. *de novatione*, *l. omnes*. Or, if it is in favor of the stipulation, no novation occurs; nevertheless, a single collection releases the whole, as in D. *de verbis obligationum*, *l. qui bis idem*; and *l. qui usus fructus*; and the aforementioned *l. si*. See Bartolus in the aforementioned *l. quod traditur*.

Now, to the point at hand: as regards Stephen, there is a change of person and place; but as regards the other partners of the society, it is an addition, not a novation, because they remain the same debtors; hence no novation has occurred. For the Florentine place was added in favor of Simbaldo Cudibono, so that he might have a more effective collection, and things introduced in favor should not be turned to injury, *l. quod favore*. And it seems to be an express law: if a testator bequeaths to me ten, and designates to me a place where I can conveniently receive it, nevertheless I may demand and receive it elsewhere, as in D. *de legatis 1*, *l. quidam testamento*.

Furthermore, the *mensa* [banking house/branch] acts in place of the person; and the *mensa* is that which is sued here, and can be sued, D. *de legatis 2*, *l. cum pater*, § *mense*. And if it is said that there are different *mensae*, this one and that one which is in Florence, they stand in relation to each other as principal and accessory.

Furthermore, the letters should come from the Florentine merchants, in the manner in which they had written in their books that the said Simbaldo should have the said quantity. But since they have become insolvent and fugitives, the letter which came first is not said to have come to the merchants, because they have changed their status for the worse, D. *de tutoribus et curatoribus datis ab his*, *l. debitor*, according to one reading which is not correct; and D. *de conditione indebiti*, *l. ante cessationem*. Nevertheless, since it was not presented, it has no effect, D. *de acquirenda possessione*, *l. qui absenti*; nor can delay be imputed, since the right of the creditor has become worse; and thus it is his own loss, *l. et si post tres*.

I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a father, who provides a dowry for his daughter and stipulates that it be returned to him if the daughter dies during the marriage without issue, may claim anything if there are surviving children.
2. What if the woman herself stipulates for herself and her heirs that the dowry be returned to her if she dies during the marriage without issue: whether these words are deemed to have been added in favor of the children, or of the husband, or of the father.
3. A limited case is understood to be repeated in the general clause that follows.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The words state that Philip, by himself and his heirs, promised and agreed with Lady Catherine, stipulating and receiving for herself and her heirs, the said dowry after the separation of the said marriage by death, divorce, or other just cause, without children legitimately and commonly descending from them; and the reason for restoring the dowry in another case and event is that the woman died in marriage with children.

† Therefore, whether the said dowry remained with the husband by his own right, or for the children as heirs of the mother, such that if they do not succeed, it remains with the consanguineous relatives of the woman. And this question is much named, and is alleged and consulted upon subtly, and is alleged for and against: for the husband, the case in §. cum inter, the opinions of Ricardus and Cynus in c. quod ob gratiam, and in l. quod fauore. Against this, the case in l. si cum dotem in the beginning, and de pactis dotalibus l. Bebius, and the disputation of Jacobus de Belvis, the opinion of Bartolus, and the observance of the world are alleged. Let us see what the authorities say: secondly, what the reasons say; thirdly, what is the truth. And I begin with §. cum intra, where the case is as follows: the father gave a dowry for his daughter, and stipulated that it be returned to him if the daughter died in the marriage without issue. It is asked whether the father can demand the dowry from the son-in-law. It is answered that he cannot, because it appears that it was agreed that the dowry be retained for the surviving children. Let us see what was the reason for doubting, and what the reason for restoring: and certainly the reason for doubting was that the dowry, having proceeded from the father, ought to return to him, and according to the subject matter, when children exist. And this is the nature of the dowry, which is consolidated to the father when the daughter is removed from the scene, as l. 2, ff. sol. matr. But it is so that in the hypothetical case, and omitting [the specific agreement], we recur to the subject matter of the contract: therefore it seemed that an action should be given to the father, even if the children remained. But the Jurisconsult decided the contrary: because that condition must have some effect, and although the case is tacit, it is not omitted, because it appears expressed from the contrary sense, and by a tacit reason, which reason can be thus adduced. For when the marriage is dissolved with children still existing, the father of these children sustains the burdens of the marriage; because the education of the children is from the remnants of those burdens. ff. fami. erc. l. si maritus. Therefore, if as from the day the remnants of the marriage consist, the husband has a just cause for retaining the dowry, which the contracting parties appear to have preserved. Also, there is another reason, because when the father-in-law had an action by common law, and by stipulating in one case only when children exist, he appears to have renounced in his own favor, and appended a pact in favor of the son-in-law, so that the son-in-law profits. d. l. inter socerum §. 1, according to Ricardus Malus and Cynus there. Because therefore the cause for retaining the dowry, and the tacit pact on account of the remnants of the burdens of marriage: and because a pact in favor of the husband appears to have been appended. Thus he profits, as if an express pact had been appended that the husband would profit; I do not say that for the children, but on account of the children, as is fully noted in Auth. de non eligendo secundo nubente §. Gregoria. And this the text says there, when it says, unless the action for restoring is due to the absence of children. Because now, positing the opposite of the antecedent, the opposite of the consequent immediately follows. ff. de manum. testa. si quis locuples. ff. de haered. inst. l. Lucius. But from these things it seems to contradict l. cum dotem mulieris. Namely, because the father appears to have preferred her, d. l. Bebius, as for the heirs of his mother, according to Jacobus and Bartolus. Which response is not true. First, because by law ff. filia familias did not have an heir even in the dowry, as is noted ff. sol. matr. l. filiae meae. For if she could have an heir in the dowry, the laws would never have consolidated the action to the father upon the death of the daughter, which is false, as l. fi. C. communia vtriusque iudicii. Second, because if she had an heir, therefore if the children do not succeed, extraneous successors would come. And this by tacit pact, which is false, because pacts concerning strangers are not understood, nor can they be understood, as in §. alteri, and in d. l. inter §. pe. Also, a tacit pact sounds the same as an express one: and of the express one there is no doubt, therefore neither of the tacit one. Nor does l. si cum dotem object, because it is one thing to tacitly agree, another to agree on nothing in that case. And this is most true, if we are in the mere terms of common law. But if we mix in custom, which dictates that when an express stipulation for restoring in the case of children ceases, then the tacit pact is to be interpreted in the same way; because then that condition, if without children, expresses its case for the caution of the stipulator, not in favor of the husband; nor is a tacit pact understood strictly for a third party, when the daughter's dowry is naturally due, as ff. de ritu nuptiarum l. qui liberos, according to Martinus Sillimanus, whose words I will subjoin below. And this being considered, the practice of the world is sustained, when the father stipulates the dowry to be returned to himself. But if he stipulates it to be returned to himself for the daughter, I do not examine now.

But I come to our case, when the woman herself stipulates for herself and her heirs that the dowry be returned upon her death in the marriage without children. Here I consider the common opinion of Martinus de Silliis, which is the reasoning of §. cum inter. For certainly there, under the common law, the donor had an action in either case. Hence, if she restricts herself to one case, she appears to have renounced her right in the other; because a pact is added to diminish, and in diminishing it must have some effect. Now this reasoning applies to the woman who endowed simply, and to whom the case of surviving children is attributed by law. Therefore, the children do not come as heirs; but it is a profit for the husband by the reasoning of l. si cum dotem and d. §. cum inter. For those words hold the place of a limitation when the woman endows herself; because the way of women’s simplicity is precluded, that they cannot make a will regarding their dowry, and thus they live as endowed and die as unendowed, which is very inhumane. And these prejudices are not considered by the simplicity of notaries. But still this is not our case. For either the stipulation is conceived in the case of non-existing children, and beyond that it does not proceed by a general clause comprehending all cases, as was the reasoning here, when he added, and the reason of another case, and the discovery of returning the dowry, and it is also doubtful whether by this general clause that condition, without children, is always seen as repeated. And it seems that it is. First, from the nature of the conjunction: as l. seiae, §. Gaio, de fun. instru. de leg. 3; l. in reputandis. Second, from the nature of the genus, which is limited by species. ff. fami. ercis. l. quotiens; ff. de leg. 3. l. haeres meus, §. duę statuę, de hęr. instit.; l. qui non militabat, §. Lucio, ff. de legat. 2; l. legatorum, §. qui plures, de vulga. substi.; l. cohaeredi, §. qui in diseretas. Third, because words must have some effect, as l. si quando, de legat. 1. But if we said the contrary, those words, without children, would have no effect; therefore, etc. Fourth, because it matters greatly whether the marriage is dissolved by a specified case, i.e., death. Also, that condition uncertain to that case must be considered as indivisible, not as a species. For indivisibles are by their nature limited, so that they are not expanded by a subsequent genus; but unenumerated species are drawn to the genus subjected after them, as noted in l. quęsitum, §. vlt., de fun. instru. per Old. and per Dy. subtly in c. generi. Fifth, because it does not seem that anyone repents of what he did in the same disposition, ff. de condit. et dem. l. qui non ad ea.

† Finally, it appears to be expressly stated that the limiting case is understood to be repeated in the subsequent general clause. D. de pactis, l. cum dotis. Which is better here than any other [rule] that is in law. To the contrary, it seems on several grounds. First, from the nature of the general clause, which is extensive, as is fully read and noted in l. quæsitum, §. ult. Second, because [a general term] appended after species amplifies; otherwise, if the genus precedes and species follows, D. de verbis significatis, l. si cum fundum. Third, because the general clause must have some effect, but here it would have no effect, D. de verbis obligantibus, l. quicquid astringendæ. Fourth, this seems to be expressly stated in l. si quis sic, D. de solutione matrimonii. Fifth, because it would follow that the woman would not have an heir in the dowry; therefore, the sons would not succeed to their mother in the dowry, because it would be in the father’s goods, not the mother’s. Therefore, if the father’s estate were burdensome, and it were repudiated, the sons would succeed to the mother. Moreover, they could be burdened by the father in the mother’s dowry, all of which are most absurd. C. de bonis matri, l. 1; de bonis quæ lib., l. cum oportet; de vulgari substitutione, l. cohæredi, §. cum filiæ. This reason being considered above all, and because in ambiguities [interpretation should favor] dowries, it is responded that it is better, D. de re iudicata, l. in ambiguis. And because it is in the interest of women that they do not die without a dowry, so that they may make testamentary dispositions of their dowries, and especially for the soul, as C. de iure dotium, l. si mulieres. It seems to me that those words, “without children,” do not induce a tacit contrary sense, such that it appears added in favor of the husband when children exist, but in favor of the children as heirs. D. de pactis, l. tale pactum, §. si. And thus it is commonly observed, where a general clause is subject, so that women endowed with this dowry could dispose of it by will, even if there is an intestate heir; because a woman is not presumed to make a gift, and especially to her husband. D. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. sed si stipulata. But the words of Martinus Silius, of which I made mention above, are such: “It is valid according to the true opinion of Baldus, when the father stipulates for us, the dowry returns to the father in every case, whether children exist or not. And therefore, when the father stipulates for only one case, namely, non-existent children, the stipulation is interposed in favor of the genus. And it seems the father tacitly agreed on the dowry to be acquired. And therefore, although the sons are not heirs of the mother, they can demand the dowry, as in this § and D. de solutione matrimonii, l. si cum dotem. But according to our opinion, which prevails in practice, when the father does not stipulate, the dowry returns to the father in one case, namely, if children do not exist. And therefore, when the father stipulates for that case, it seems he stipulates for caution and out of abundance for himself, namely, the stipulation is interposed in favor of the father. Nor does it seem to generate a pact on the dowry to be acquired in another case, namely, if children will exist, lest the stipulation, which was interposed in favor, be turned to his detriment. And therefore, this § has no place here. But if the sons were to demand the dowry in the person of the mother, and as heirs, and not otherwise, Martinus Silius. But against this opinion, because the stipulation says, “in every other case for the restitution of the dowry.” But by tacit pact, this is not a case for the restitution of the dowry. I respond: an express general clause, although it does not cause an express special clause to cease, causes a tacit special clause not to be implied. For it is easier to prevent a tacit [clause] than to revoke an express one, l. si, in principio, D. de legatis 2. And especially when it follows the above-mentioned [points], it cannot be denied that the question is doubtful. Nevertheless, in doubt, I think favor should be given to the woman, Inst. de actionibus, §. fuerat; D. de familia erciscunda, l. Pomponius Philadelphus. And thus she can make a testamentary disposition of her dowry. I, Baldus.
In the Name of Christ. Amen.
† One who holds a mortgage is preferred in real execution over all bondholders, and over those prior in time, as is fully known in the law *Privilegia creditorum*, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The right of a *studium generale* is acquired by very long custom.
2. A privilege granted to students is understood to apply to students in *studia generalia*.
3. Milan is said to have a *studium generale*, and it holds the primacy among all the cities of Lombardy, and it is a Metropolitan see.
casus: CASE. In the name of Christ, Amen. The case is as follows: A certain person obtained a favor from the Supreme Pontiff, in which he stated that he was studying civil law, without specifying the place where he was studying, although he was studying in Milan. Although there is no established or general university there, it is read by learned doctors, as it was read in the past and is read today, for such a long period of time that there is no human memory to the contrary. Now the question arises whether the aforementioned favor is fraudulent, because he was not studying civil law in an established and designated university, or not.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The words of Cynus in the preface to his *Flores*, on the word “who made the city,” say thus: by very long custom, as in Padua, where there is a *studium generale* by custom, and thus the privileges are the same as those from the privilege of Emperor Lothar, as they say. What then is it that in the public examination for the doctorate the bishop or archdeacon says: “We also grant you license to teach here and everywhere in the world”? But “everywhere” is taken to mean every place, i.e., every suitable place, as in D. de munere et honore, l. ut gradatim, § 1; and cf. D. de his qui sui vel alieni iuris sunt, l. 1, § quandocunque, with its gloss.

† From this it is concluded that those who study at the University of Milan are said to be studying law in an approved place; nor are the letters considered obreptitious, even though they do not study at Paris or Bologna.

† Because the city of Milan, by custom, of which there is no memory to the contrary, is understood to have a general studium within itself, especially because it is a royal and metropolitan city: as is stated in Extra, De verbis significantibus, l. Super quibusdam, § Praeterea; and because it holds the principality among almost all the cities of Lombardy, of which there is no memory to the contrary: as appears in the Peace of Constance. I, Bal.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A marriage contracted by words of the present tense by the father, and subsequently ratified by the daughter not by words but by acts, prevails over a second contract made by words of the present tense by the said daughter.
casus: CASE. In the name of Christ, Amen. The case of Arancus concerning waters, by words of the present tense spoken in this manner, namely: "I promise you Tiburga, my daughter, in marriage"; and conversely, you accepted her in marriage with a certain dowry established. And then afterwards you approached the girl, knowing the aforesaid, although she did not express her consent by words, and with the consent of the girl's mother and others present, you embraced her; and the said bride received gifts, or presents, from the hand of her sister. Afterwards, the said girl contracted marriage with another by words of the present tense. It is asked: who is the legitimate husband of this girl?
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† And it seems, in the first place, that the second man is the legitimate husband of this girl, because between the first man and the girl there did not intervene the words required for contracting marriage, according to ecclesiastical statutes, and as regards the contentious forum: as in Extra, De Sponsalibus, c. Tua; and although the father of the bride gave her in marriage, and she afterwards tacitly consented, nevertheless these were betrothals de futuro, which do not dissolve a marriage afterwards contracted with another: as in Extra, De Sponsalibus Duorum, c. 1; and Codex, De Sponsalibus, l. 1. To the contrary it seems, because sometimes when a father promises his daughter as a betrothed or wife, the words of the father suffice, followed by the tacit consent of the daughter; otherwise, if no words of the father had proceeded: as in c. 1, § Porro, De Desponsatione Impuberum, lib. 6; and noted in c. Ultima, De Coniugiis Servorum; and in l. Saepe, Digestum, De Sponsalibus; and Distinctio 22, quaestio 2, Honorantur. Solution: The words must be considered, for either the father promised that she should marry, as is in the case proposed; or that the girl herself would promise to marry. In the first case, marriage was contracted, because the girl appears to have wished to release the father from his promise, and to carry out the father’s intention and paternal affection, which seems to have contemplated the effect of marriage. Argument from Digestum, Quod Filius Tutori, Authentica, l. An in patrem. In the second case, this ratification would not induce anything other than betrothals de futuro, because the words sound thus, and ratification regards conformity with the promise. From which it appears that, in the theme proposed, this Tiburga is the wife of the first man, and cannot be the wife of the other while you live, as in c. 1, De Sponsalibus Duorum; to this also contribute all the other allegations made for this party. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an instrument is rendered false, or suspect, or at least provides grounds for torture—so that both parties ought to be tortured—by means of a single superfluous witness who contradicts the instrument.
2. Proof of good reputation prevails over proof of bad reputation.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. It is proposed that from a certain instrument drawn up in public form, in which instrument four witnesses are named, when they were produced in court and the plaintiff wished to found his claim thereon, an exception of falsity was raised, and to prove the falsity one witness described in the instrument was produced, who testified that the said instrument was false. Likewise, he produced certain other witnesses, who stated that the said notary had asked them whether they wished the said notary to describe them in the said instrument. Also, certain other witnesses testified that the notary is of bad reputation. And it is true that the said notary was arrested, and an inquisition was formed against him regarding the fact: and a most rigorous investigation was conducted, and the said notary was tortured, who always remained firm and constant in his instrument, saying the instrument to be true; wherefore the judge absolved him from the criminal charge, and remitted him to the civil judge.

† Now the question arises, given these circumstances, whether the judge in a civil case ought to deem the said instrument false, or at least so suspect that, being otherwise uncorroborated in the instrument itself, it does not yield effective proof. And it seems at first to be said that the said instrument ought to be deemed false: as in C. de probat. l. iubemus. Or at least so suspect that it does not make full proof: as in ff. de edendo l. si quis ex argentariis § 2. Or at least this should remain at the discretion of the judge, as noted by Cynus, according to Jacobus de Arena and Petrus, C. de fide instrumentorum l. in exercendis in 1. qu. On the contrary it seems, because by one witness, who is not of the substance of the instrument, a public instrument is not reproved on the ground of falsity. This is held by Accursius, Inst. de inutilibus stipulationibus § item verborum; and by Bartolus in l. 1 in fine ff. quemadmodum testamentum aperiri; and by Canon in c. cum Ioannes heremita de fide instrumentorum. And because one witness is a single and unique witness, he therefore does not make faith, especially in so arduous a case. As in extra de probat. c. licet causam § quamquam autem; and de causa possessionis c. cum ecclesia; and the text of the law requires a plurality of witnesses for the reprobation of an instrument, and that they be above all exception, as in C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione l. optimam in fine; and noted in ff. de pactis l. iure gentium § pactorum. And this is the very truth, that an instrument is not reproved by one witness above the number: because the voice of one is of no account, as in C. de testibus l. iurisiurandi cum si. It is, however, true that although one good witness does not reprove an instrument, he nevertheless makes an indication for torture, so that both ought to be tortured, both the witness and the notary: and the notary persisting in his instrument is more believed than the witness persisting in his statement, on account of the public authority of the notary. But after the inquiry has been made, and the notary has been acquitted by a definitive sentence, it does not seem that further dispute should be had concerning the crime, as in extra de collusione et detractione c. si. And it seems expressly stated in C. de fide instrumentorum l. fin. in fine. For a sentence passed in a criminal case makes faith in a civil case: as noted in C. quando civilis actio in l. 1; and C. ad legem Iuliam de vi l. si quis a se fundum; and l. 2 ff. vi bonorum raptorum.

† Moreover, the aforementioned other corroborating circumstances do not prevail, because good reputation has been proven against bad reputation, and greater weight is given to this proof, since it is supported by a natural presumption. To this effect: C. Ne de statu defuncti, l. Si mater. Furthermore, corroborating circumstances drawn from the statement of a notary made outside of court do not prejudice the party, as shown by: Extra, De testibus, c. Sicut nobis. Moreover, it is more strongly presumed in favor of an acquittal than in favor of these remote indications, as stated in: Extra, De renuntiationibus, c. In praesentia; and C. De administratione tutorum, l. Si bona. And by this reasoning, C. De probationibus, l. Iubemus, does not prevail, because by means of the acquittal every stain upon the notary has been purged, and consequently the notary’s credibility has been approved, and consequently the instrument must be upheld, as in: C. De probationibus, l. Cum precibus; and C. De edicto divi Adriani, l. Edicto, together with similar authorities. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether, and when, a cleric may bequeath, or otherwise dispose of, all his goods.
body: For the sake of clarity, three cases must be premised.

For sometimes it appears that the property was acquired from the goods of the church; and then it pertains to the successor in the church, as stated in 12 q. 1, *Si manifeste*; Extra, *De testamento*, c. *Cum in officiis*; and fully noted in c. *Praesenti*, *De officio*, lib. 6. Sometimes it appears that it was acquired from other personal goods of the acquirer himself, or from his own industry; and then he may donate it, bequeath it, and transmit it to his heirs, and it is not acquired by the church, as in C. *De episcopis et clericis*, l. 2; and *De sacrosanctis ecclesiis*, Auth. *Presbiteros*. And sometimes it is doubtful from whose goods it was acquired; and then witnesses are to be received and proof made regarding this doubt. For if he has sufficient movable goods of his father, it is presumed to be from paternal patrimony; otherwise, it is presumed to have been acquired from ecclesiastical goods, according to the argument of C. *De arbitrio tutoris*, l. *Si defunctus*; and what is noted in C. *De bonis quae liberis*, l. *Cum apparet*, § 1. Then it is presumed to be half from ecclesiastical sources, by argument of ff. *Ad Trebellianum*, l. *Titius*; and ff. *De petitione hereditatis*, l. *Sed si lege*, § *Quod autem*. Nor does the objection hold from ff. *De negotiis gestis*, l. *Nensenius*, at the end, because there the reason of the law does not permit it, and c. *Hic sic*. The canonists simply favor the churches when the acquirer has administration, as noted in the aforementioned c. *Si manifeste*. I say that this matter is to be tempered by the discretion of a good man, according to the quality of the persons and the quantity of the goods. I also say that this seizure is not reasonable, without any liquidation having been made of the aforementioned matters, since the instrument does not speak of successors in churches, but of proper heirs, as in ff. *De probationibus*, l. *Si pactum*; and C. *De contrahenda et committenda stipulatione*, l. *Secundum responsum Domitii*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a mother may donate all her property to one of her sons, while preserving the legitimate shares of her other children.
body: Mother

† He may donate to one of his sons his entire patrimony, except for the legitimate portion of the other son; and therefore, if the said mother had six hundred in her assets, she could dispose of all her goods to the other son, amounting to five hundred when all is counted; and Antonius must be content with one hundred, which is half of six hundred, nor can he demand more: although there are various opinions on this matter, as in D. de legatis 3, l. Titio Seio, § Imperator; nevertheless, when a donation is made to one of the sons, there is no doubt that it suffices for the other son to have his legitimate portion restored, as in C. de inofficioso testamento, auth. si parens. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. In a vituperative or impulsive [defamation], whether malice is required, according to the prevailing opinion, and so forth.
body: HAVING SEEN

† Given two statutes, one placed under the heading concerning the penalty for invading or occupying a tenement granted by the court, and the other under the heading concerning the penalty for those inflicting expulsive or turbative force; and considering the said point contained therein, it must be observed that the statute regarding the penalty for those inflicting force requires audacity and implies fraud or gross negligence, as in C. unde vi, l. si quis in tantam; and fraud is presumed in one who occupies new possession which he did not previously hold, as in C. unde vi, l. cum quaerebatur. Since, therefore, it is stated that ancient possession of the said vineyard has been proven, the event of the subsequent possession is rightly formed from the beginning of that possession, as in ff. de acquirenda possessione, l. clare possidere, in principio; and as in C. de usucapione transformatione, l. 1. And the possession of the deceased benefits the instituted heir, as in C. de edicto divi Adriani, l. edicto adeo; and so that the new possessor cannot prevent the instituted heir from being put in possession, unless he holds a title of the same kind and superior with respect to final justice. But it is so that the adversaries of the said substitutes do not have older possession prior to the death of Bucia; nor can they claim to have new possession by authority of law or judge; therefore, they rightly ought to restore the invaded possession, as in ff. de acquirenda possessione, l. qui universas, § item cum Praetor; and C. unde vi, l. invasor; and C. de agris et censibus, l. si coloni, lib. 11; and C. ad legem Iuliam de vi, l. si quis ad se fundum; extra, de restitutione spoliatorum, c. saepe. And although those chapters speak of expulsive force, i.e., turbative force, as in C. si per vim vel alio modo, in rubrica, and in l. 1, and therefore judgment should be given against the said injury according to the form of the petitions, since the testament was clearly established. For upon the death of Jacob, having instituted a universal heir, the compendious substitution made during the testator’s life in the testament of the said Bucia passed to an express vulgar substitution, as noted by Cy. in l. precibus. It is certain that in possessory actions, ancient possession is presumed to be more just, as in extra, de probationibus, ca. licet causam; and the aforementioned l. cum quaerebatur, C. unde vi. Furthermore, it is certain that if there are two houses divided into different parts or portions, he who possesses one does not thereby possess the other, as in ff. communia praediorum, l. si quis duas, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. To enact statutes is a matter of jurisdiction.
2. A general confirmation of privileges or statutes does not extend, except to those that are just.
3. A statute excluding a son from the succession of his parent is inequitable and contrary to natural reason; and so too is a statute excluding parents from the succession of their children. See also nos. 6 and 7.
4. A statute excluding a mother from the succession of her children is not valid.
5. It is the same whether something is not done at all or is done less legitimately; hence, a guardianship not legitimately assumed ought not to benefit the mother.
6. An unwritten or harsh extension ought not to have place in statutes.
7. An infant is not properly said to die intestate.
body: For clarity, it must be premised that enacting statutes is an act of jurisdiction, as noted by the gl. on l. 1 ff. de iur. om. iudi. and in Auth. de defenso. ciui. § iusiurandum, around the middle of the great gloss; and therefore any principal people, since it possesses full jurisdiction, at least by custom, as in ff. de tu. et cu. dandis ab ipsis l. ubi, as noted by Cyn. on l. omnes populi de iusti. et iu., and by Bar. on l. 1 de dam. infe., and by the doctors on c. cum dilectus de consue., can establish for itself a singular or special law, as in Inst. de iure natu. § 1, and by Innoc. on c. cum accessissent de constit., contrary to the common law, as in the said l. omnes populi, and by Cyn. and others. But a populace that is a dependency, subordinate to a greater populace, such as a castle or a village, since it does not have jurisdiction, cannot make a statute without the authority of a superior, as in the said legal authorities; but with the authority of a superior it can, as in l. fi. C. de testa., etc.

† Secondly, it must be premised that by a general confirmation of statutes or privileges, none are understood to be confirmed except just ones, according to Cyn. on l. 1 ff. de his, qui sunt sui, uel alie. iur. and by Dyn. on l. legata inutiliter de leg. 1; for this see ff. de rebus credi. l. si quis priore in fi. and ff. de fal. l. diuus § nec generalem, which Guil. de Cun. cites as a singular case.

† Thirdly, it must be premised that just as a statute excluding a child from the succession of a parent is iniquitous and contrary to natural law—that is, contrary to natural reason, as in C. de epis. et cle. auth. nunc autem, in the text there: 'lest anything iniquitous happen concerning children', and as noted by Dyn. on c. indultus de reg. iur. in VI, and by Cyn. on l. sancimus C. de nup.—so too is a statute that excludes parents from the succession of a child, ff. de inoff. testa. l. nam et si parentibus, de bonis damnatorum l. cum ratio, and in Auth. de here. et fal. § 1; for the legitim by natural law is owed not only to children, but also to parents where there are no children, as noted in the text there, etc.

† These things having been premised, I come to the question of whether the said lady Clarutia succeeds to her daughter Paula dying in infancy, or whether by virtue of the aforesaid statute she is excluded from her succession. And it seems that she is excluded: because although by common law a child succeeds to the mother, and a mother to the child, and even to an infant, as in C. ad Tert. l. 1 and l. mater, nevertheless it seems otherwise where a statute provides the contrary, since it removes the common law with respect to the property and the place of those enacting it by the tacit permission of the superior, as noted by Cyn. on the said l. omnes populi, by this ff. communia praediorum l. venditor § si constat, and there is the gl. on ff. de reg. iur. l. nec ex praetorio, and l. neque pignus § priuatorum; but in the aforesaid case the statute provides the contrary.

† The objection is proven thus: it is equivalent that something is not done, or that it is done less legitimately, as in l. quotiens vitiose ff. qui satisda. cog. But this Clarutia, although she undertook the tutorship, did not undertake it legitimately, because it was before an incompetent judge, namely before the judge of Foligno, who could not appoint her as tutor, since in the city of Foligno the said ward had neither her assets nor her domicile, as in l. unica C. ubi pe. tut. vel cura., l. 1 ff. de tut. et cura. dan. ab his. Therefore, it is just as if she had not undertaken the tutorship, in which case she would be deprived of succession, as in l. sciant cuncti C. de legi. haeredi. and l. 2 § confestim and § si autem ff. ad Tert.; and therefore note that a tutorship not legitimately undertaken or administered does not profit the mother. To the contrary, the truth seems to be that the said Clarutia is admitted to the succession of her said daughter, notwithstanding the aforesaid statute.

† Because the said statute, being inhuman and contrary to natural law, is invalid, and consequently does not displace the common law, as in the legal authorities cited above. Nor is it rendered valid by the confirmation of the superior, because the said confirmation is general: for it confirms the ordinances and statutes of the commune of the castle of Carino contained in this volume; and a general confirmation does not include an unjust or iniquitous statute, as shown above. Furthermore, even the one confirming expressly disapproves in his confirmation and [refuses to] confirm statutes that would be contrary to divine and human law or contain what is iniquitous. But this statute is of such a kind, as I have shown; therefore, even granted that the said confirmation extended to all the statutes of the said land of Carino, nevertheless, because it was made at the good pleasure of the superior, it terminates with his death, as in c. si gratiose de rescri. and in l. 4 ff. loca.

† Secondly, it seems to be proven that the said Clarutia is admitted to the succession of her said daughter: because this statute, which excludes a mother from the succession of her daughter, is odious and contrary to the rules of civil law; therefore, I will not extend it except through the heir, as in l. si vero § de viro ff. sol. matri., and there by Bar. in the same title on l. si constante, and by the gl. on l. quod vero contra ff. de legi. and in l. si quis seruo C. de fur.

† For an unwritten or harsh extension has no place in statutes, as noted by Cyn. on l. quicunque C. de ser. fugi. Since, therefore, the aforesaid statute was enacted in favor of agnates, because the law speaks only of them, it therefore does not comprehend cognates, especially where we are dealing with the disfavor and exclusion of another, as in l. 1 ff. de vent. in spi., and as noted by Cyn. on C. de adult. l. 1; for it suffices that the words of the statute be satisfied, ff. de iudi. l. 2 § conueniente; and when the cause of the statute ceases, if it was in favor of agnation, the disposition of the statute itself also ceases, as in Inst. de haere. ab intest. § sed cum uetustas. What was stated earlier—that she was decreed tutor by an incompetent judge—does not stand in the way: because even positing that she had in no way undertaken the tutorship, she ought nonetheless to be admitted, since she has a year to undertake the tutorship from the day of the parent's death, as in l. sciant, and the said daughter died within the year.

† Likewise because an infant is not properly said to die intestate, as in l. 1 in prin. ff. de suis, et legi., although Bar. says there that this strict meaning is not approved there by Julian, and that one who cannot make a will is also called intestate; therefore I do not pursue this further for the present. Yet the doctors commonly say that in an odious matter a pupil is not said to be intestate; and therefore if a custom provides that the fiscus succeeds to the property of an intestate, it is not understood of the property of pupils; and so hold all the Ultramontane doctors and all the Citramontane doctors except Bar. I conclude, however, as is clear from the above, that the said mother is not excluded from the succession, but rather is admitted to it, especially on the ground that the statute does not speak of descendants through the female line as excluding the mother; and because in the new statutes no mention is made of the said statute, by the argument of ff. de test. mil. l. Tribunus § ulti.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The mother and the grandfather are preferred to others in guardianship.
2. A statute contrary to reason is not to be extended to its consequences.
body: VII. It pertains: and especially because this is a matter of law. For if [it were] by a point, and the aforementioned statutes

† I say that the guardianship pertains to the great-grandfather: and especially because this is according to the law. For if the mother and the grandmother are preferred to others: therefore much more strongly the great-grandfather, as in the auth. ma. et auie. And although the statute corrects the common law in succession, nevertheless not in guardianship, concerning which the statute otherwise disposes, or in no way disposes, especially

† because the statute is contrary to reason: and therefore it should not be extended to its consequences, as in D. de legibus, l. quod vero; and C. de appellationibus, l. precibus, in fine. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If a father in his will commands that his houses not be sold, but rather pass in perpetuity to his descendants, and if any of his sons wishes to sell his share, he is to sell it to his co-heir; whether he who, by permission, purchased the share of his co-heir may freely sell it.
2. The term "descendants" includes all persons in infinitum.
body: The words of the testament being premised, and saying: “Furthermore, he prohibited and forbade in perpetuity the sale, alienation, etc., of his houses, etc.” And he, the aforementioned testator Andreas, willed this so that the said houses might come in perpetuity to his sons, his heirs, and to the free descendants of the same heir, etc. Nevertheless, if any of the aforementioned his heirs should wish to sell or in any way alienate from himself that part of the said houses which has devolved upon or fallen to him: then it shall be lawful for him to sell and give his contingent share to all his said brothers for the price of 7 pounds of denarii of lesser currency; and they, wishing to sell and buy that share which has fallen to them, are bound to firmly offer and give to him the aforementioned price of seven pounds. It is proposed that some [of the houses] have been sold, some divided, some left intact, and some mixed.

† And it is asked whether the buyer, the exchanger, and the legatee may freely sell, exchange, or bequeath the goods offered to them to another, or alienate them. And it seems that they may not, because the said goods have a perpetual cause of prohibition.

† Moreover, under the term “descendants” are included all descendants in infinitum, as stated in D. de in ius vocando, l. sed si hac, §. liberos. And this is true, and I have so advised on other occasions. Nevertheless, the contrary view appears to hold, because the sale here was made at the discretion of the testator; hence the purchaser may freely alienate the property to whomever he wishes, as stated in D. de legatis 3, l. pater, §. 15. The reason is that prohibitory words are lacking, and because legal reasoning itself, even by a slight point of reason, clearly demonstrates this. For since the testator permits the property to be sold, it is understood that he permits it to be sold freely and transferred freely. For this is according to the nature of the contract of sale and purchase: for the obligation of the seller is to deliver the property freely, as noted in C. de contrahenda emptione, l. ex prædictis. Hence it is not surprising that the purchaser, who bought the property at the discretion of the testator, may by the very nature of the contract freely alienate it to whomever he wishes, as stated in C. de contrahenda emptione, l. dudum. This reasoning is subtle, and may be assigned among the other reasons in the aforementioned §. 15. And this is the truth with respect to the purchased properties themselves. But with respect to other properties, which by order of succession passed from the person of his ascendant to the descendants, the portion of the last descendant, if he has daughters, passes to his sons, as stated in C. de fideicommissis, l. cum acutissimi, and D. de vulgari substitutione, l. cohæredi, §. qui discretas. But if he has no sons, then considering that the testator used the appellation “heirs,” the portion passes to the sons of the testator who were instituted heirs, as argued in C. de impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus, l. finalis. But if he had used terms denoting nothing other than agnation itself, it would seem that the nearest agnates would succeed to the exclusion of others, as stated in D. de legatis 2, l. cum ita legatur, §. in fideicommissa. And although I have said that the property may be sold freely, the rule is different in the case of partition: for partition appears to be made with its own cause, as fully noted by Bartolus in l. qui Romæ, §. finalis, de verbis obligatorum. Moreover, if that last person, to whom I said the portion passes, were to renounce, the result would be the same as if he had never been the immediate heir. Nevertheless, to whom that portion would pass is clear from the foregoing. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a donation made to absent and specific poor persons is valid.
2. By the resignation of the usufruct and habitation, which the donors make, ownership is transferred.
3. Likewise, whether a donation made to one of the saints, such as to God, is valid.
body: Regarding the aforementioned matters, it seems that one should say,

† that the aforesaid donation was valid and binding, is valid and binding: because a donation can be made by mere agreement between those present and those absent, and a donation can also be made to an absent person, as in D. de donat. l. nec ambigitur and l. absenti; and even to strangers and unknown persons, as in l. in extraneos, C. de donat. Therefore, this donation is rightly valid, and especially so when it was made in evident poverty, and for the benefit of poor recipients, however uncertain and unnamed the poor may be, as in l. id, quod pauperibus, l. nulli, and l. si quis ad declinandum, C. de episc. et cleric., where the uncertainty of the persons does not invalidate the donation. And from this, divine right is acquired through delivery to the poor themselves and to the place where the poor reside, and even without delivery, as in l. si, C. de sacr. sanct. eccl., although in the present case there was delivery.

† For, due to the resignation of the usufruct and the habitation, which the donors made for themselves, ownership was transferred, as stated in the law *Quisquis*, Codex, *De donationibus*. Thus, in the case at hand, ownership was transferred to the poor, and especially to those poor persons who inhabit and will inhabit the property, whose names were received in the said donation, as stated in the aforementioned law *Inter dominium* and the law *Si quis ad declinandum*, and the law *Nulli*. For, according to canon law, an action is acquired even through a stipulator or contractor who is an outsider. Likewise, note the gloss in Decretum, Distinctio 50, Question 8, Chapter *Quotiens*; and it is commonly said in the Decretals, *De coniugiis*, Chapter *Dudum*. And especially in the case at hand, when it is made for their own persons, the donation is valid, because a donation can even be made from God, as in the Authenticum, *De ecclesiis*, Title, § *Si quis autem universorum*.

† where also a donation may be made to any of the saints. And thus it is established that the aforementioned donation was valid both with respect to the person of the said Marmelli and with respect to the persons of the poor inhabitants of the land of Saxiferrato. Accursius wrote.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a legatee of the usufruct of all goods is bound to the creditors.
2. Likewise, add on the matter below in the consultation.
3. From a legacy of usufruct, the Falcidian portion is deducted.
body: On the first point

† Finally, it seems necessary to state that a legatee of the usufruct of all goods and the inheritance is not bound to the creditors. First, because "goods" are understood as the net assets after deduction of debts; therefore, debts and funeral expenses must be paid first, and the legatee must have the usufruct of the residue, as stated in D. 50.16.13 (*sub signa*), § *bona* (On the Signification of Words), and D. 41.1.1 (*mulier bona*) (On the Right of Donation). Second, creditors do not contract with legatees, but with heirs. For the heir is the one who has accepted the inheritance, not the legatee. And creditors do not bring actions for debts except against the person who, by accepting the inheritance, binds himself, as stated in D. 44.7.1 (*maleficiis*), § *haeres* (On Actions and Obligations). Third, this is proven by C. 4.1.1 (If a Certain Thing is Demanded); and C. 6.30.1 (*quotiens*) (On the Institution of Heirs); and D. 36.1.1, § *si haeres* (On the Trebellian Trust); and D. 5.1.1 (*fideicommissum*), § *tractatum* (On Judges); and D. 28.5.1 (*quotiens*), § *haeredes* (On the Institution of Heirs); and D. 28.5.2 (*ex facto*), § *dicebant*. But it is remarkable that, although this appears to be the law and must be said according to the point of reason, nevertheless the case in strict terms appears to be to the contrary, as in D. 7.1.100 (*ult.*) (On Usufruct Bequeathed), according to the interpretation of Bartolus, whom he places there, saying that when a usufruct of the tutor's goods is bequeathed, with mention made of a share of the inheritance, the legatee is bound to bear the burdens of debts and liabilities, if he is a legatee of a share, pro rata; and if he is a legatee of the whole, for the whole. And he says that that case is elsewhere. But I do not see, from the reasons first stated, that creditors have the legatee of the usufruct bound, except by saving Bartolus, who says that the usufructuary is compelled by the heir, not by the creditors, so that the debt may be paid proportionally, which can be understood in two ways: either that both from the ownership and from the fruits—namely, that something be sold wherefrom satisfaction is made—or that the legatee alone pays for his share of the legacy to them for the whole. But this second interpretation seems unjust. Suppose, for example, that there are a thousand in debts, which, according to Bartolus, the legatees are bound to pay. Furthermore, suppose that the legatee dies immediately thereafter; injustice will already result, unless you say that the heir of the usufructuary can claim from the legatee, just as a bona fide possessor recovers from the true heir. Thus he himself says, and according to this, the legatee is not bound to pay, unless he is bound to him for the restitution of the quantity upon the termination of the usufruct. But this opinion does not seem true.

† Because great expenses do not pertain to the usufructuary even in the things themselves, much less do they pertain to things outside thereof. I admit that the aforementioned last law, according to the second gloss in the word "because burdens are divided," says what Bartolus says. However, according to the true gloss, which Doctorus approves, that law does not have this meaning; but the true meaning of that law is this: either a usufruct of a share is bequeathed, and first the debt is deducted, and the usufruct is owed only on the net assets, absent debts, whether the testator said "of goods" or "of things," provided it is by share, as in D. de legatis 1, l. non amplius, §. fin.; or a usufruct of a certain thing is bequeathed, and the debt does not follow the land. For the legatee of the usufruct of a bequeathed land is not bound more than the legatee of the ownership, and the usufruct is the end of the bequest in full right, which is known not to be bound to creditors, as in the aforementioned l. 1, si certum petatur. Therefore, solving the said question, I say that first the creditors and funeral expenses must be satisfied from the fruits which the testator left in his patrimony at the time of death, if they suffice; and if they do not suffice, through the sale of immovables, and afterwards the legatee of the usufruct has the usufruct of the residue. And thus I hold, and especially because the word "revenue" and "proceeds," appended in the bequest, has this meaning: as in D. de usufructu legato, l. fundi Trebatiani. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. In inheritances, the share of the defaulting heir accrues to the other heir who accepts, even against his will.
2. The right of deliberation is not transmitted by one who is ignorant.
3. An inheritance of a mother not accepted is not transmitted.
4. A minor transmits the benefit of restitution in integrum.
body: Regarding the first point, it seems that one should first say that, since the aforementioned Fran. died without having accepted the inheritance, the entire said inheritance pertains to the aforementioned Gul., namely one half by right of institution and the other half by right of accrual.

For this is the rule in inheritances, that the share of the defaulting heir accrues to the other heir who enters upon the inheritance, even against his will and without his knowledge, as is stated in C. de caducis tollendis, §. pars his ita; and in D. de legatis 1, l. Celsus; and in D. de legatis 1, l. ciuitatibus, §. Lucius; and in D. de acquirenda hereditate, l. si seruus communis ab extero, with many others. Nor is this surprising, because the right of accrual is a kind of tacit vulgar substitution, as noted in D. de legatis 2, l. si Titio, et Meuio, §. Iulian. And therefore it is not surprising if the entire estate accrues to the coheir, so that the testator does not die partly testate and partly intestate, contrary to the rules of civil law.

† That the portion of Francis has lapsed is apparent, since he did not transmit the right of deliberation: for he was ignorant of his mother’s death, and the right of deliberation is not transmitted by one who is ignorant, C. de iure delib. l. cum antiquioribus.

† Moreover, an unaccepted inheritance of a mother is not transmitted, as stated in C. ad Orfi. l. non pro numero, unless it concerns children to children. C. de his, qui ante aper. tab. l. 1. And it is considered that, indeed, the benefit of restitution in integrum is transmitted; this does not seem true, because the fact that an unaccepted inheritance is not transmitted is common law, whence it does not seem that a minor is circumvented, because he is protected by common law, as in C. de in inte. resti. mi. l. non uidetur. To the contrary is the truth,

† Because the benefit of restitution in integrum is transmitted, and especially on account of minority. For here the Doctor persuades that restitution is granted. For minority, and just ignorance, and absence, as C. de restit. in integr. l. Valerianus; ff. de acquirenda hereditate l. cum quidam in principio; and l. Pantonius. Or there it speaks of absence on account of public business; for voluntary absence is not of this kind that deserves restitution in integrum. Nor even ignorance, as in the said l. cum antiquioribus; and what is noted, ff. de in integrum restitutione l. finalis, unless he is absent for such a just cause as is probable, for example, on account of studies, or a similar cause: as in the said l. Pantonius. I therefore say that the heir, namely the aforementioned uncle, is restored in integrum on account of the minority of the said Francis. This is proved first by the text in l. qui duos, ff. de rebus dubiis, according to Jacobus de Arena and Bartolus; secondly by reason, because if an absent person on account of public business is restored, then much more so a minor. For he was injured in the last breath of life, in not transmitting a certainty. Since therefore a minor is equated with an absent person on account of public business, indeed he is more favored, as is fully known in the said l. ultima, ff. de in integrum restitutione. If therefore an absent person on account of public business transmits the benefit of restitution in integrum, then much more so a minor. Likewise, if any absent person for a just and probable cause transmits the aforementioned benefit, then much more so a minor, who, as I said, is more favored. For a minor is aided by a special edict, de minoribus, as ff. de minoribus l. ait Praetor. But an absent person for a just cause is aided by a general clause, as ff. qui ex causa maiestatis l. sed et si per Praetorem §. fin. And a special provision does not operate less than a general one; indeed, it operates more, as is clear from infinite examples. And these things apply to one who is older than an infant, as is apparent, C. de iure deliberandi l. si infanti. For the text there wants that an infant transmits nothing. And according to this, an infant is in a worse condition than one older than an infant. Which seems absurd, since an infant is considered as absent for a just and probable cause: as ff. rem pupillarem salvam faciendo l. finalis. Likewise, the younger the age, the more favorable it ought to be, as ff. de administratione tutorum l. 1 §. 1 sufficit. And although it is harsh to respond to l. si infanti, nevertheless it could be said that the disposition of that law would be true in strict law; otherwise by the benefit of the Praetor, as in the said l. Pantonius. I do not dispute here about an infant; this is not the point: but about one older than an infant, in whom sense and understanding fall, which are useful and necessary for entering upon an inheritance, as C. de iure deliberandi l. potuit. I hold that the benefit of restitution is transmitted by two headings joined together, namely, absence and minority. And therefore the more glorious one can be of this succession: and because he succeeds by the benefit of restitution in integrum, if the times allow. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether it suffices for the validity of a will and of disinheritance that the testator merely expresses the causes of ingratitude, even if he does not specify the place or the time; for example, if he states that such-and-such his son laid violent hands upon him, but does not say when or where. Furthermore, whether the heir will be required to prove the place and the time.
body: It is alleged that Luciarellus, in his will, disinherited his son Bartholomew in the following form, namely: "Furthermore, the said testator, knowing and recognizing that Bartholomew, his son, is unworthy of the hereditary succession of the said testator, because he impiously laid violent hands upon the person of the said Luciarellus, beating him and doing him injury and reproach against the will of the said Luciarellus, and laying snares for his person, etc., as is contained in the will of the said Luciarellus, etc." And that afterwards the said testator died, persevering in the same will.

† Now it is asked whether the said will is valid, such that the disinheritance has been properly made. For it is established that unless the disinheritance is properly made, the disinherited son is said to be null as if passed over, as in D. de contrariis tabulis, l. non putauit, §. non quaeuis. And it appears that the said disinheritance was not properly made, for since the said causes of disinheritance contain injury and fraud, the place and time should have been inserted, and the quality of the injury and fraud specified, as in D. de dolo, l. item exigit; and D. de accusationibus, l. libellorum; and in c. pia, de acceptis, lib. 6; and in c. praesentium, de testibus, eodem libro. Just as if one were to disinherit on account of adultery committed with a stepmother, as in l. libellorum. Moreover, he should have stated with which enemies of the father he consorted, so that the person might be demonstrated, as in C. de poena iudicum qui male iudicant, auth. nouo iure; and D. nau. cau. stab., l. licet, §. possumus. For one ought not to wander vaguely in so great a crime as he alleges, as in D. de iniuriis, l. Praetor, in principio; and D. de testibus, l. 3, §. idem Diuus, in illo vero, qui crimina obiecerit.

On the other hand, it seems that no law provides that the father is bound to express the place and time, but only that he is bound to express the causes of ingratitude, as in Auth. vt cum de appel. cogno., §. aliud quoque capitulum.
