But I readily concede that the heir, in order that the proof may be certain and not doubtful, will be bound to prove this, as noted in a similar case, as in D. de deposito, l. 1, §. si quis argentum. Which I believe to be true, because the law does not bind the father to state the place and time, but only the causes and ingratiudes, which are here expressed in that form which the law requires, which prescribes this form. For whatever law prescribes a form, it is not necessary to add anything to such a form, as in D. de verborum obligatione, l. in conuentionalibus. Therefore, I conclude that the said will is valid, and the disinheritance is properly made: nevertheless, the heir must prove that the causes of ingratitude are true, and the place and time in which the son beat the father, or had him beaten; otherwise, the disinherited son obtains success in the querela inofficiosi testamenti, which he must bring within five years after the heir has entered upon the inheritance, C. de inofficioso testamento, l. omnino; and l. si quis filium, §. fi. And thus I hold, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, and when, a person arrested for one debt may or may not be recommitted for another.
2. A person arrested for a debt is to be released upon the provision of a surety, even a son, provided he is suitable.
3. A person arrested for a debt is rather to be equated with a hostage than with a pledge.
4. If anyone is arrested for the debt of a son, he may be recommitted again.
body: The question is,

Whether a person arrested for one debt may be recommitted for another. Answer: If the initial arrest is invalid, he cannot be arrested for another debt; because that which is void in itself cannot give validity to another, as in D. de bonis auctoritatis iudicis possessoribus, l. cum unus. And therefore, in the force or truth of adhesion, recommitment does not proceed; because he who adheres must always adhere in the state in which he found that to which he adheres. Or, if the initial arrest is valid, then either we are speaking of the common law, and then such an arrest of the person cannot be made except in the case of a judgment debtor, as in C. qui bonis cedere possunt, l. 1, and in Auth. ut cum de appellatione cogitur, §. aliud quoque capitulum, vers. si quilibet de prædictis. And there also is the text.

† That, given a surety, one ought to be released from prison, even if his son is given as surety, provided he is suitable. Hence a distinction must be made: either both are of the same title, because both have a judgment in their favor and leave to arrest, and then the arrested person must be recommitted for the debt; for it makes no difference whether he is arrested anew or detained in prison. For it is not fitting to act in a matter of sale for one who is in a snare, regarding the acquisition of property, L. in laqueum. Moreover, arrest is a kind of citation; but he who is present ought not to be cited, but commanded. Hence to add that he shall not depart from prison is to cite him, as in C. quomodo, et quando iu. L. 2. And this is true when the judgments are of the same title. But if one is fiscal for a delict, and the other for a civil debt, then it does not seem that the release of one benefits the other, as noted in the said L. cum unus, and de re iudicata L. a Diuo, according to Bartolus, and C. qui pot. in pign. L. 2 and 3. But if one has a judgment and the other does not, then he who does not have it cannot cause the one who is arrested to be recommitted in prison, unless he himself, while imprisoned, waits to be cited anew and leave is granted, which can be done even though he is in prison, as noted in C. quilibet, de causis maleficiorum, lib. 2. And therefore the arrested person ought to provide for himself, so that he may offer the debts for which he was arrested and consign them, before another leave is granted. And thus, since he is to be released from prison, he cannot be recommitted, as in ff. de procuratoribus L. si reus paratus. One cannot make use of the aid of prison except with his own cause and his own faults. Hence it is necessary that he be first released if he is unjustly detained. But if municipal law provides otherwise, adhere to municipal law.

And note that he who is seized for a debt is rather equated to a hostage or pledge, as is noted in C. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. ob eas, and C. quae res pignori obligatae possunt, l. qui filios. And therefore, although a pledge may be retained for a chirographic debt, in which there is no obligation, nevertheless he who has bound himself to the penalty of imprisonment for one cause, and is detained, cannot be held in prison for another cause, for which he was not seized.

† which is to be noted. However, for a debt owed to the fisc, one may always be arrested; because the fisc is privileged in this regard, so that no order is required once the debt is established, as is clear from D. ad l. Iul. pecul. l. sacrilegii §. si quod non. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a bishop, or his vicar, may impose upon a secular authority that he retain in his prisons the person who is held therein, and not release him without the bishop’s permission.
body: But suppose, let the statute say,

† That a person condemned for contempt of a precept cannot be recommitted for another debt. The question is whether the Vicar of the Bishop can cause him, who is in the prisons of the commune and not in the prisons of the Bishop, to be recommitted for some debt for which no license is given in the court of the Bishop to arrest. And it seems that he can, because the Bishop is superior. And the Potestas must execute the sentence of the Bishop, as noted in ff. de posthu. l. ex ea. and in c. 1. de offi. or. through Innocentius in c. ult. de except. lib. 6. On the contrary, it seems that in execution the authority of the judge is not considered, but the custom of the region where the execution takes place, as in C. de exac. tribu. l. missi opinatores. lib. 10, where there is a golden text, and because the prison, which by its jurisdiction belongs to the city, is not the prison of the Bishop, and therefore he cannot change the law of the prison. Moreover, he cannot order the officials of the prison, who are mere executors, appointed not by him but by another, but he could well order the Potestas to order them to be detained, as argued in c. Romani. §. contrahentes. de fo. competen. etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a substitution made in direct terms in a codicil is valid.
2. Whether the penalty for forgery applies in a will or in nuncupative codicils.
3. Likewise, whether a son under paternal power may be inscribed by his father in a will.
body: Disposition

The codicillary disposition, concerning which the question is raised, contained and contains, by right, a trust (fideicommissum), because a substitution made in a codicil, even if expressed in direct terms, is drawn into the nature of a trust, although the rule is different in the case of an institution, as established in D. ad Trebellianum, l. Scaeuola; C. de codicillis, l. final; and D. de vulgaribus substitutionibus, l. verbis civilibus. Nevertheless, I have never seen a similar codicil in which one burdens a son upon the subsequent birth of a grandson. For this is not the customary practice, as stated in C. de fideicommissis, l. cum precibus. And this concludes the first point.

† But with regard to the second point, it must be premised that these codicils were made by oral declaration (nuncupation) and not in writing. Hence the question arises whether the penalty of the Cornelian Law concerning quasi-falsity and suspect writing applies to a nuncupative will or to nuncupative codicils. It must be said that either faith can be given to such writing through the proof of witnesses or the testator’s subscription, in which case the penalty does not apply; or faith cannot be given to it, in which case the penalty applies by virtue of that rule, because he who produces a suspect writing is punished unless he proves it to be true, as stated in C. de probat. l. iubemus. And thus we hold in l. 1, §. pe., ff. ad l. Cor. de falsis, according to Decius, Jacobus de Arena, Cynus, and Bartolus, and this is the truth. It should be known, however, that even where the penalty of exile

† Nevertheless, a legacy is not owed to one whom a son under paternal power institutes as heir to his father, as stated in the Digest, ad legem Corneliac de falsis, in the law De eo; and in this case, those legacies are not vitiated on account of this useless legacy, as stated in the Digest, in the same title, in the law Filius, section Sequens quaestio. I always presume that the notary speaks the truth; nevertheless, we cannot depart from legitimate witnesses. And I consider it sufficient for the defense of the notary if two living witnesses, who were present at the will or codicil, testify in favor of the notary himself. But this would not suffice for obtaining the legacy. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether an outsider who gives a dowry and stipulates that it be returned for himself, and in the name and stead of the woman and her heirs, whoever they may be, acquires the action for himself alone, or for the woman, or for both.
body: Assuming the tenor of the promise to restore the dowry, which is as follows, namely, the said d. Paulus promised to restore the dowry to the said Vennarello, present and for himself, and in the name and on behalf of the said d. Thomasa, and to render and restore it to the heirs of any of them in every case and event of the dowry being restorable. And so forth.

† It is reasonably doubted whether, in the case of the dowry being due for restitution, the action was acquired by Vannarello, or his heirs, or by the lady Thomasa, or by both for one-half, since both were opposed to the obligation. And that it was acquired by Vannarello and his heirs seems to be proven by the wording of the stipulation. For it is certain that when an outsider stipulates for the dowry to be returned to himself, the action is not acquired by the woman. An outsider is considered to be anyone who does not have the girl in his power, as in C. de rei uxoria actione, l. rem in praesenti, and §. extraneum. But this Vannarello stipulated for himself: therefore, the action was not acquired by Thomasa, nor by her heirs. And it seems that the action was acquired solely by Thomasa. For whenever anyone stipulates for the principal dowry to be returned to himself or to his dowried granddaughter, the action is acquired by the woman herself, as in ff. de solutione matrimonii, l. Gaius. For the dowry is the woman’s own patrimony. And this is presumed from natural affection, lest it happen that, if the stipulator predeceases, the woman remains without a dowry. And therefore, upon the death of the said Vannarello, the entire dowry seems to have been consolidated in the person of Thomasa, as in C. de rei uxoria actione, l. in praesenti, §. videamus. But certainly against the foregoing it seems that the right was acquired by both for one-half, because the conjunction falling between the persons stipulating or promising distributes the obligation into equal shares, as in C. de constitutione pecuniaria, auth. sequens, and C. de duobus rebus, l. reos, §. cum tabulis. So from this stipulation, the action was acquired by each for one-half, and therefore one-half of the aforementioned dowry ought to be restored to the heirs of Vannarello, according to the laws cited above. For this part, the other half remains with Nicolaus, heir of the lady Thomasa. From this stipulation, the lord Paulus is sued, if he is alive, or his heirs, as in ff. de legatis secundis, l. cum ab uno. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the formalities required by statute in making compromises must be observed in the extension of the term of the compromise.
2. An oath does not supply the formalities required by statute in making compromises.
body: Having seen the Statute on contracts between living persons, which begins “We establish and ordain that contracts made by a minor,” etc., and having seen the Statute on contracts of women, etc., and having seen the Statute on the power of arbitrators, which begins “Compromises,” etc., and having seen the Statute on the manner and procedure to be followed by arbitrators appointed and chosen between related parties, which begins “We establish and ordain that arbitrators,” etc., and having seen and considered the said points in question,

It must be said that the prorogation of the said compromise was invalid, and the reason for this is as follows. For, by reason of the prorogation, a new obligation is said to be created, as in D. de arbitris, l. Si cum dies, in principio; although it is said that there is only one compromise, as in D. de precibus, l. Sed si manente, nevertheless in the prorogation it is necessary that a new obligation arise, as in D. de pretio stipulationis, l. Pe, and D. de locato, l. Qui ad certum. But this new obligation cannot be created between persons who are incapacitated. It is certain that the said minors were incapacitated, because the statute incapacitates them unless a certain form is observed: and especially concerning the authority of the general curator, or of two blood relatives, who are to represent or supply the age of the minors, as in C. de in integrum restitutione minorum, l. Si curatorem habentes. Therefore, if that which is done contrary to the form of the statute is not valid, as in D. de fideiussoribus, l. Cum lex, and C. de legibus et constitutionibus, l. Non dubium, neither is the oath valid in this case.

† because we are not in the common law, but in the municipal law: one oath does not represent the presence of relatives, or of the general curator. And one must not depart from the words of the statute, as stated in D. 2.14.1 (qui et a quibus), D. 47.16.1 (prospexit), D. 24.2.1 (si vero), § de viro, and D. 14.2.1 (si is qui navem). And therefore, because the said prorogation did not hold, the award was not valid, notwithstanding the statute speaking of the power of arbitrators, which expires after six months. I, Bal

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given the legal rule that a dowried daughter does not succeed when male heirs are extant, may she, as a pretermitted heir, declare the testament null, in which males are instituted? And whether [this is so]. 2.
body: To be considered

It is that the testator made two substitutions: one from males to females. And this substitution did not take effect, because the males died and the females survived. The second substitution, however, was that he substituted two males and three females, Scholastica and Juliana; this substitution does not take effect, because the females survive, as in D. ad l. Falcidiam, l. si pater filiam, § duobus; D. ad Senatusconsultum Trebellianum, l. heredes mei, § cum ita; and fully in the law and note, C. de impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus, l. penultima; non obstantibus D. de legatis tertio, l. Titia, § Seia; and D. ad Senatusconsultum Trebellianum, l. Lucius, § Gaius. For the interpretation of those laws does not apply when there is some person who, from the presumed will of the deceased, induces a conjecture of substitution, not to brothers dying before others on account of the survivors, as is clear in the said § cum ita. And therefore, in the case presupposed regarding John, Matthew, and Matucia, no substitution is found to have been made of Scholastica and Juliana, and it necessarily follows that, upon the death of the three brothers, the two surviving sisters succeed, with Scholastica, who is the aunt of the deceased, totally excluded; because carnal brothers are preferred to an aunt, as in Auth. de defunctis et de haereditatibus ab intestato, Marco et Amatucia. And from the person of Matthew, who was in a pupillary substitution, the aforementioned Vannis also succeeds to the brother, as in D. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione, l. sed et si plures, § ad substitutos; and D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. qui patri.

Regarding the other point in question, whether Scholastica has the legacy of the said piece of land free, since the male heirs have died, it is sufficiently probable to doubt. It seems that she does not, because it was left to her only for her lifetime; therefore, it does not endure beyond her life, as in C. de legatis, l. si. On the contrary, it seems that she does, because the time of life was added in favor of the male heirs; therefore, if they die in the meantime while Scholastica is alive, the said legacy remains with the said Scholastica free, because the burden opposed to the legacy fails, namely, to restore it after the death of Scholastica to the male heirs, as in C. de caducis tollendis, l. pro secundo; and l. codicillis, in principio; D. de legatis secundo, l. Celsus; and D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. haeres meus.

Solution: The first part is more correct, because this legacy was temporary, for the time of the life of Scholastica herself, as in D. de legatis primo, l. nemo potest, in its gloss; and those which follow, namely, that after the death of Scholastica it shall go to the male heirs, are added to diminish the legacy of Scholastica, not to increase it, and therefore they do not increase it, so that Scholastica might otherwise have the said legacy in perpetuity, as in D. de legatis primo, l. legata inutiliter; and D. de manumissionibus testamento, l. Titia, § finalis.

Regarding the legacy of alimony and habitation left to Scholastica, there is no doubt that such legacies end by their nature upon the death of Scholastica, as in Inst. de usu et habitatione, in principio, cum sequentibus.

It is to be known that the said Scholastica, to whom nothing was left by way of institution, may, if she wishes, declare the father’s testament null, as in Auth. ut cum de appellatione cognoscitur, § aliud quoque capitulum. And this is true according to the common law.

But suppose that the statute states that, where males exist, a dowried female does not succeed; can the person passed over in this case claim that the will is void? I speak of a will in which those males are instituted as heirs. I answer: No. For the reason why the person passed over declares the will void is that, by passing him over in the will, injury is done to him; and because the proper form is not observed in making the will, as in D. de lib. et posth. l. Gallus, § in omnibus, and l. inter cetera; and C. de posth. hær. inst. l. si. But this testator did no injury to the daughter, who did not succeed intestate. Hence the will is valid from the beginning. It is true that if the males were to predecease the testator, then the will would immediately become void; because the daughter, as a female, by acknowledging the will, would break it, according to D. de inof. test. l. pater filium, and D. de iniusto test. l. posthumorum. Hence it may be said that the will is in a sense in suspense. For if males exist at the time of death, the will is valid; but if they do not exist, the will is not valid. And this holds if the statute excludes the female daughter precisely from the entire inheritance; otherwise, if according to the form of the statute she would succeed to something else, and even to a single coin. For that coin ought to be left to her by right of institution; otherwise the will would be void, as noted in D. ad Trebel. l. si quis priorem. The words of the statute must also be weighed, in which case the statute speaks; because where the statute does not speak, we adhere to the common law. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, and when, a compromise made by a minor is valid or invalid, even with the authority of a curator.
2. Whether a ward or a minor may renounce the benefit of restitution, even with an oath.
3. Whether a statute prohibiting any manner of proceeding against the sentence of arbitrators prohibits restitution in integrum.
body: Pupil

† Without the authority of the tutor, he cannot compromise, as stated in the Digest, *De arbitris*, law *Si pupillus*. Therefore, it appears from the contrary sense of that law that he can compromise with the authority of the tutor, whether this is true must be considered: either the compromise is necessary by the form of some statute, and such a compromise is valid, because by the law of the city not only adults but also minors are bound, as stated in the Digest, *De administratione tutorum*, law *Si suum heredem*, section *Lucius*; or the compromise is voluntary, and then either it is evidently damaging to the ward, and such a compromise is not valid with effect, because restitution in integrum is granted, as stated in the Digest, *De minoribus*, law *Si minor viginti quinque annis filio*, section *Minores*; or it is evidently beneficial, and then it is valid, since the authority of the tutor and the decree of the judge are added; and if the decree of the judge did not intervene, such a compromise would be valid, it would not exclude alienation, etc., because without a decree they cannot be alienated. For since a compromise to an arbitrator is a certain transaction under a condition, namely if the award follows, such a compromise is valid, as stated in the Code, *De transactionibus*, law *Praeses*. However, it must be noted that although it was beneficial to compromise upon inspection of the beginning, nevertheless if afterwards the award is unjust and to the prejudice of the minor, restitution in integrum can be sought, because from the event it appears that the minor has been enormously harmed, as we see in a similar case. For although the minor has a just cause for deferring an oath, if nevertheless afterwards he swears inequitably, restitution in integrum is granted, as stated in the Digest, *De iureiurando*, law *Nam et postea*, section *Si minor*. And it must be known,

† If a minor renounces the benefit of minority, the renunciation is not binding if he is a ward, even if he is near puberty, because it cannot be validated by an oath. But in the case of an adult, a distinction is made as to whether he swore an oath or not; and if he did swear, whether he was informed of the benefit of age or not, according to Dy. Io. An. in l. 2. de resc. ven. per Cy. It supports what is noted in ff. de mino. l. si iudex circunuento, and ff. de noua. l. doli. §. diuersum. Furthermore, he cannot renounce an appeal or a reduction to the arbitration of a good man, as stated in the aforementioned §. minoris. Just as he cannot make a gift or dissipate his property, as in ff. de manu. testa. l. qui filium, and ff. pro empto. l. qui fun. §. si tutor.

From the aforesaid, it is concluded that the compromise in question was valid. However, if an inequitable award followed, an action for restitutio in integrum may be brought against the compromise itself, even if a reduction of the award could not directly be sought according to the form of the statute. Therefore, in seeking this restitutio in integrum, a conclusion must be drawn regarding the capture of the compromise. And thus the libel proceeds. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. And if, on account of the disagreement of the arbitrators, a third party is chosen, and the two promise to approve the award that shall please that third party: if afterwards those two agree with each other, the award rendered by them is void. Whether it is possible to compromise regarding penalties for delicts.
2. If there was a compromise concerning a certain penalty, and that penalty was not incurred, the award rendered concerning the said penalty is not valid.
3. If the right to demand a penalty belongs to several persons, no one can demand the penalty except for his own share.
body: It is proven,

† That, on account of the discord of two, a third was elected at the discretion of the compromitter, and those two arbitrators promised to obey and abide by the decision of the third arbitrator. And it is alleged that the said two first arbitrators, despite the contradiction of the third, rendered a sentence in agreement. It is asked whether, having regard to the form of the election and compromise of the said third, the award of the said two agreeing arbitrators is valid or not. Answer: It is valid, because by the election of the third, the first arbitrators were not revoked from their power; but provision was made only in the case of discord, as in the law and note, ff. de arbitr., l. item si vnus, § si in duos. In the gloss, a distinction is made; therefore, since all three are arbitrators, the sentence of two prevails. In the same title, l. sicuti. That the compromitters and those two arbitrators promised to abide by the will of the said third: because this indefinite promise must be understood according to the disposition of the law, namely, in the case where the first two are not in agreement in rendering the sentence. For the third arbitrator is elected in a subsidiary capacity, and by his election the first two do not cease to be arbitrators, nor do they cease to be the majority. And since they retain the name of arbitrators, they retain, conversely, the effect of the name, ar. ff. de feriis, l. nullo, etc.

† On another point, namely whether one may compromise regarding penalties for malefices: it must be said that yes, regarding past penalties, but not regarding future penalties. For a person may bind himself on behalf of another to contribute to the penalty for a preceding malefice, but not to the penalty for a subsequent malefice, as stated in D. 46.1.11 § 2 (Si ar... § pe). On another point, I say that if a compromise was made concerning a certain penalty, and that penalty was not incurred, the award regarding the sharing of the penalty is invalid, because it was not rendered on the matter compromised, as stated in D. 4.8.1 § 2 (Non distinguimus § de officio) and § fin., and D. 4.8.2 § Item in fin. (Quid tamen § Item in fin.).

† On another point, when several persons have the right to demand punishment, I say that no one can demand it except for his own share, as in no. ff. de verb. oblig. l. 5. §. si sortem, and fl. de duobus reis l. reos. §. cum tabulis. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. What is necessary to prove robbery, or plunder, or spoliation of any movable thing. Likewise, how these are to be proved.
body: I presuppose,

† That the accusation was not made for robbery or spoliation, and that the statute speaking of the matter, which is in the chapters of the third book of the statutes under the heading “Concerning Spoliators, Rapists, or Robbers,” has been invoked. Having considered this statute, it is necessary for the accuser to prove and make good faith regarding three things. First, his possession. Second, the removal of the thing. Third, the value and estimation of the thing itself. It is necessary that all these be proven according to the time of the delict, as in D. de vi et vi armata, l. 1, § interdictum. For I do not believe that the judgment of spoliation applies to him who did not possess at that time, because there is no robbery nor spoliation against one who does not possess, although clandestine theft sometimes occurs, as in D. ne quis eum qui vi, l. sed ex mundum, and D. si quis aliter quam in testamento, l. 1, § Sceuola. Now, therefore, having examined the statements of the individual witnesses, the first, named Marcus, said that he saw the table of the said Bartholomew being taken away and carried off. This witness proves the act of removal well, but he does not prove the possession or dominion of Bartholomew, as noted by Innocentius in c. Cum causam, de testibus. Nor does he testify concerning the pertinence of the thing, except by reputation. Furthermore, he does not prove the value of the thing, because he gives the cause of his knowledge, even though not questioned; for just as dominion is not proven without giving the cause of knowledge, so neither is value, because the value of a thing cannot be seen nor touched. And thus, regarding the value of the thing, a reason and cause must be given by the deponent, as noted in l. 1, C. de senatus consulto quod pro eo, and l. 2, C. de rescindenda venditione. Moreover, the purchase is not proven, because he does not testify of a certain price, as noted by Cynus in l. 1, C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione. Another witness, named Johannes Simonis, testifies of the delivery and consignation made to the said Bartholomew, and testifies of a certain time. And I believe that this witness proves possession, but he does not prove the value of the table, especially at the time alleged in the accusation. And because he seems to refer to what had happened two years prior, this does not exclude the estimation of the time alleged; it holds in l. Aquilia, dum habet oculos retro. By this alone it does not follow backwards, yet it was valid. Therefore, it is valid only now, as in D. ad legem Aquiliam, l. 2, in principio. Another witness, named Blapius, testifies more fully, except that he does not prove that possession was delivered to the accuser himself, nor taken by him, because it does not follow that such a person sold, therefore he delivered, as in D. de rei venditione, l. si ager. And thus possession is not proven. There follows another witness, Jacobus Vernossi, who testifies concerning the confession of removal, and concerning the sale and delivery which he himself made, but the value is not proven, because he does not give the cause of his knowledge. Hence, according to what is proposed, the said three substantial elements do not appear to be proven. Moreover, fraud or the reputation of fraud, which is required in theft and robbery, is not proven; nor does any witness testify anything on this point. And those things which by their nature are in no one’s goods, if they are occupied, fraud is not presumed. And even if they are [someone’s goods], but their possession has been neglected, it is not called spoliation, as in D. de acquirenda possessione, l. si rem mobilem. And there could also be a just cause for ignorance, and if it is not just, supine negligence suffices for the excuse of fraud, as in D. si ager vectigalis, l. 1, in fine. And that fraud is required, Bartolus states in l. 2, D. de vi bonorum raptorum. And because no witness testifies of fraud, and if he does testify, he does not testify conclusively, therefore for these reasons the accused ought to be absolved, because knowledge of another’s thing was not alleged in the articles; nor did I see the tenor of the accusation in the depositions of the witnesses, but only the statements of the witnesses, which, upon mere inspection, do not seem to me sufficiently proven, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, when execution of an instrument is sought for damages and interest, such damages ought first to be liquidated.
2. The petition for execution is summary.
3. If execution is sought for damages, whether the judgment of execution is questioned.
body: The words of the statute concerning summary cognition having been premised,

It is asked whether he who fails to execute an instrument confessing damages and interest must first petition that said damages and interest be liquidated in the manner customarily employed in actions for unliquidated sums, i.e., that after liquidation, etc. And I say that he must, otherwise execution ought not to be carried out, because an unliquidated instrument, unless liquidation is petitioned, ought not to be committed to execution, since only that which is pure and liquid ought to be committed to execution. That which is not liquid cannot be committed to execution unless it has been liquidated; and it cannot be liquidated unless it is expressly petitioned to be liquidated, or by stating why he petitions, after liquidation, etc. And this is most well-known. And thus I have practiced in the city of Perugia: and it is expressly proven by the third law, in fine, Codex, de inutilibus stipulationibus; and Codex, de sententiis, quae sine certa quantitate; l. in fine; l. haec autem, § 1, Digestum, quibus ex causis in possessionem eatur; Digestum, de praetoria stipulatione, l. in fine; and Codex, de sententiis, quae pro eo quod interest, in l. unica, § in aliis. And the reason is manifest, that this instrument is not confessed except as to an uncertain amount. And therefore it ought not to be committed to execution as a confessed instrument, but it is necessary that a sentence be rendered, and it will be committed to execution as a sentence, or at least the instrument declared by sentence. Hence the force arises from the sentence in both cases, not from the instrument; and this is true as the gospel: and thus it is observed in all instruments drawn up and not liquidated.

It is true that this cognition is summary; nevertheless, a petition is required. And every order that is required in summary proceedings, although a formal libel is not required, from which a litigation controversy ought to follow, as stated in c. Saepe, de Verborum Significatione, and the aforementioned statute is understood to refer to a summary complaint.

Secondly, it is asked whether, if condemnation in the said damages is sought, this is called an action for execution. I answer: no, because just as condemnation is one thing and execution another, and a petition for condemnation is one thing and a petition for execution another, as stated in C. de executione rei iudicatae, l. Executorem. And so I hold, and so it is true; and this is evident from the conjunction of two laws. One states that if execution is sought, a judgment is not valid against a judgment; the other states that if condemnation is sought, it is valid, as stated in C. quoniam provocatio non est necessaria, l. 1, and in D. de executione rei iudicatae, l. Duobus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a woman is said to become a citizen of the place where she marries.
2. A statute providing that the citizens of Todi are to be treated as citizens of Perugia, and vice versa.
body: Considering that the said Lady Agnes was and is a natural and original inhabitant of Castiglione, and that she, as being of that origin, was united by the force of marriage and became, and is, during the marriage, of Castiglione as part of her husband’s body. For marriage is of such virtue and nature that it transfers the wife’s origin into the husband’s origin, as is stated and noted in the law *originem*, *De mutatione et origine*, Book 10. This is also proven by the force of union, in which that which is stronger draws to itself that which is less worthy, as is fully stated and noted in the extrajudicial law *Ut sede vacante*, chapter 1. But there is no greater union than the conjugal union, by which the husband and wife become one flesh, and are also one substance in two persons, as in law 1, *De rerum amotione*; in the law to the Sillanian law, law 1, § *Si vir aut uxor*; and in the extrajudicial law *De bigamia*, chapter *Debitum*.

And therefore the said lady Agnes, as a natural and original citizen of the said territory of Castellione, ought to be considered, since by divine law she is one flesh with her husband, and divine law consists in truth and not in fiction; it follows that the wife is properly made a fellow citizen with her husband. And so it is held by the gloss in l. ciues, Codex, de Incolis, and by Bartolus in ff. ad municipalia, l. si ita, §. ita rescripserunt.

Secondly, it must be considered regarding the said statute whether it is a penalty for that case against the person who ought to be held and treated in civil and criminal cases in the common court of Castellione as a native of Castellione, whereas she was a native of Montichio. And it must be said that it is not. For the words of the statute under the heading "that natives of Montichio are to be treated as natives of Castellione" have this modification and condition, namely, provided that, conversely, natives of Castellione are treated in any case. And this word, "in any case," we consider either according to the mode of treatment from the disposition of the law, or from the contingency of facts. If from the disposition of certain laws, it appears from the statute that natives of Castellione are treated as natives of Montichio in three cases, namely, civil and criminal cases, and in damages given. And nothing is statuted regarding others, for example, in taxes and levies. And if therefore those words, "in any case," are not verified, because they are universal words, and thus the condition which the said statute requires under the heading "that natives of Montichio" is not fulfilled, therefore the disposition of that statute is also void, as in D. de pignoribus et hypothecis, l. si necessarias, § si annua. Moreover, because it appears that the statute of the natives of Montichio is annulled, and it does not pertain to the woman to dispute on the points of law, it is sufficient that the writing could be said, as in D. de adulteriis, l. si ex lege. But if we consider the contingency of the fact, then if we attend to the proof, it seems proven that there was no such treatment. But if we consider the disposition of the law, it ought and must be proven regarding the said treatment, of which the statute disposes. For since it is a matter of fact, it is not presumed. And that it consists in fact is the text of D. de verbis obligatis, l. quidam cum filium. And therefore for the said homicide, a pecuniary penalty of five pounds of pe. ought to be imposed, and not the penalty of the head. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a pupillary substitution is valid if the instituted heir dies during the lifetime of the testator. Likewise, whether one may be pupillarily substituted to an heir instituted in a specific thing.
2. You add that he subsequently consulted on the same case below in consilium 121.
body: Point: The testator instituted his mother as universal heir and his two daughters in a certain sum, and made a substitution for them. They died in pupillary age, or later, whenever, in the said legacy, namely, because he substituted the said mother, and after the death of the mother, according to the said legacies, it passed to another. Then, while the testator was still alive, one of the daughters died in pupillary age. Then the testator died. Then the other daughter, who was a pupilla. Thirdly, the mother died. Now those others, to whom the said legacies ought to pass, demand the supplement of the legitime as if they were pupillary substitutes. On the other hand, it is said that they ought not to have anything except the legacies of the daughters, with the Falcidian deduction made, and it is said that a pupillary substitution cannot be made in a specific thing to an heir, because institution is equated with a legatee. The question is: what is the law?

Having considered the aforementioned points, it must first be known that there is no need to discuss the pupillary substitution in the person of Catherine, because she died while her father, in whose power she was, was still alive, as stated in D. de capitibus minuendis, l. quod si filius, and D. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione, l. lex Cornelia. Nevertheless, I concede that the legacy made to Catherine remains with Angela, the heir, together with its burden, so that after the death of the said Angela, that legacy is owed to Nicholas and Bonragnus, after the deduction of the Falcidian portion, if Angela made an inventory, as is proven here in C. de caducis tollendis, l. pro secundo, and C. ad legem Falcidiam, auth. sed cum testator. It now follows that we must examine the legacy made to Bonaventura. And it is certain that Angela succeeded to the said Bonaventura, a minor, in full by virtue of the pupillary substitution, and no one else can succeed to him by pupillary substitution, as stated in D. de regulis iuris, l. quod contra, §. vni duo, presupposing that the said substitution is drawn into the pupillary category by the law cohaeres, §. fin., D. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione, which, however, is doubtful in law, and it is not expedient to decide this point here. It therefore follows that the aforementioned Nicholas and Bonragnus do not come by virtue of the pupillary substitution, but only by way of a singular legacy, or bequest, can they demand the quantity left to Bonaventura, likewise without the deduction of the Falcidian portion, if it is applicable, and if an inventory was made, as I said above. For the substitution of a minor can be made by legacy and by fideicommissum, as stated in D. de legatis primo, l. si fundum sub conditione, §. si pater, and D. ad legem Falcidiam, l. in ratione, §. quod vulgo. From these things it is concluded that the said Nicholas and Bonragnus have no right in the said legitima to be claimed, but only in the said quantities bequeathed, as I said above, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a vulgar, pupillary, or fideicommissary substitution expires if the person to whom the substitution was made dies while the testator is still alive.
2. If a posthumous heir was passed over, but who, although born, dies while the testator is still alive, whether the will is revived.
body: Assuming that the said Turea had from the first wife two daughters and one son, and that during the lifetime of the said Turea one of the said daughters and also the male son died, and that thereafter, after the death of the first wife, the said Turea took another wife, from whom he had seven sons, who died during the lifetime of Turea himself, and that finally the said Turea died, survived by Angela, the first daughter from the first wife, and by Peter, the full brother of the said testator. The question is: what is the law?

† Whether Angela succeeds, or the said Peter. And it must be said that the said Angela succeeds in full, and the said Peter does not succeed in any respect. And this appears evident, because either we say that the said Peter succeeds the aforementioned son and daughter, who are mentioned in the will. And this is impossible, that he should succeed them, or in their place. For if he were to succeed, he would succeed either by vulgar substitution, or by pupillary substitution, or by fideicommissary substitution. Not by the vulgar substitution contained in the *compendiosa*: because that was broken by the birth of posthumous children, as in D. de in iustum et omisso testamento, l. Posthumorum. Likewise, not by pupillary substitution, even if he had been a pupillus, because pupillary substitution has no place when the pupillus dies during the lifetime of the testator, as in D. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione, l. Lex Cornelia; and D. de captivis, l. Quod si filius. Likewise, not by fideicommissary substitution, about which there is greater doubt on account of the codicillary clause: because when a fideicommissary substitution is made nominatively to someone, and that person dies during the lifetime of the testator, and thus does not enter upon the inheritance: such a substitution is extinguished, as in D. de legatis tertio, l. 1, § Illud. For it is necessary that he to whom the fideicommissary substitution is made nominatively should enter upon the inheritance, as in D. ad Senatusconsultum Tertullianum, l. 1, in principio; and C. de fideicommissis, l. Eam, quam, with similar authorities. But here this substitution was made nominatively to the son born; therefore it is not extended to another successor, as in l. Is, qui, D. de iure codicillorum. Moreover, it is not probable that the testator intended the property to remain with the posthumous children. Hence the will appears to have been broken not only by the force of law, as in D. de iure codicillorum, l. Qui graui vero; D. de militum testamento, l. Militis codicillis, § Miles in supremis; and C. de inofficioso testamento, l. 3; but against the foregoing, it might be objected: namely, that the vulgar substitution contained in the *compendiosa* is validated by the death of the posthumous children, who were passed over, since they died during the lifetime of the testator. Hence the substitution suffices for him. And it is necessary to acknowledge possession of goods according to the will, as fully set forth in D. de in iusto et omisso testamento, l. Posthumus. Likewise, the affection of the testator extends to this case, in which he ceased to have children, as in D. de pactis, l. Tale pactum, § Si.

But the answer is that the omission of the said posthumous heirs opened up the right to claim that the said daughter has no right, if she is alive, and therefore there is no one who can claim against the will. The daughter herself ceases to have rights according to the will, as stated in ff. si tab. testa. nul. exta. l. 1. in fi. and ff. de secun. tab. l. aequissimum. §. expectandum. And I advise this daughter to claim possession of the estate against the will, even though she may succeed according to civil law, as stated in ff. de contratab. l. si post mortem. §. fi. I, Bal.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a brother instituted as heir, who is prohibited under penalty of forfeiture of the inheritance from giving or granting anything to his disinherited brother, unless perhaps insofar as he was compelled by law, may in some way give something to his brother without prejudice to himself.
2. The word "grant" is more apt to comprehend generally all things than the word "alienate."
3. A brother is bound to provide maintenance for his brother.
body: The premises having been stated, the words of the will dispose in the manner which follows, namely: if the aforementioned Paul, instituted as heir, at any time associates with the said Bartholomew, or gives anything, or grants anything of the above-mentioned goods left to the said Bartholomew or his heirs, he shall fall from the said inheritance, to be entirely applied to the said common hospital of Nursia, as has been said. That is, that the said goods are to be given for the love of God, and [to] the aforementioned Chatelina for 400 florins, unless and insofar as the said Paul is compelled by law and bound by law to give anything of the said goods to the said Bartholomew. But if he gave voluntarily, he shall fall from the said inheritance in the manner and form aforesaid.

† It must be considered first that the testator, expressing indignation against his son, imposed a double prohibition: one concerning alienation, and the other concerning any other act, which ceases. Hence, it cannot be alienated with impunity, nor could it even be leased for a short time. And thus the remedy set forth by the gloss in the law *Codicillis*, § *Instituto*, D. *De legatis* 2, ceases.

† because the word “concede” is more suitable to comprehend all things generally than the word “alienate,” as is stated in the Digest, *De alienationibus*, l. *Plene*. Therefore, it must be considered whether there is any remedy by which a brother may lawfully concede something to his brother. And here the term “permitting” must be considered. For the testator permitted necessary alienation. And I say that such a remedy is to be employed, whereby the son disinherited by his father may claim maintenance before a judge.

† For a brother is bound to support a brother born of the same father, whoever he may be, even if deserving ill, with respect to the father: for he is bound to do so in his own person, as is stated in D. de administratione tutorum, l. cum in plures, §. cum tutor, and l. tutor secundum dignitatem, §. si, where it is expressly set forth. And it is noted in C. de administratione tutorum, l. non omni. Nor can the father forbid this, because such a prohibition by the father would be contrary to natural law, which is unchangeable, as is stated in Inst. de iure naturali, §. sed naturalia quidem. And the judge seized of the matter concerning alimony ought to condemn the wealthy brother to the poor one, always providing alimony, and to assign some possession for alimony, which yields sufficient revenue for the same, as is stated in C. de donationibus, l. si quis argentum. And this will be a necessary alienation, which is not prohibited, as is stated in D. familiae erciscundae, l. alienationes, and D. de legatis 2, l. peto, §. pretium. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a substitute heir may be put in possession by virtue of the last law of the Code on the Edict of the Divine Hadrian abolishing [certain actions], on the strength of a vulgar substitution contained in a summary instrument.
2. A judge, to whom nothing has been proved, cannot at least by means of an oath against frivolous litigation order any putting in possession.
3. A defective proceeding cannot be validated.
4. When a prejudicial question is reserved, the matter is understood to be defective.
5. Where there is a dispute concerning possession, he must prevail who better proves the older possession.
body: Colceta and certain other substitutes appeared in court, having been briefly substituted in the court of Bucia. They asserted that the instituted heir had died during the testator’s lifetime, and that they themselves came by virtue of the vulgar substitution contained in the summary document, and they requested to be put in possession of the goods which the said Bucia possessed at the time of death, namely, in half of certain houses, etc. To this petition, a certain Entia opposed herself, alleging that the said house and other possessions belonged to her by full right. Moreover, the judge, without examining any other matter, but only having seen the said will, decreed that the said petitioners should be put in possession, saving the right of the said Entia, stating that he did not intend to prejudice the said Entia in any of her rights. And finally, execution was carried out pursuant to the sentence, resulting in the putting in possession of the aforementioned houses; which putting in possession the said Entia claims is invalid. And she alleges that the benefit of the law and edict does not pertain to the said substitutes, and that the said decree was, and is, null by operation of law, and that although it was executed in fact, such execution is not binding.

† Now the question arises, what is the law. On which points I answer and say that the vulgar substitution is contained in the compendious one, and for the vulgar substitution the benefit of the law is compatible with the edict concerning the goods, namely those which were possessed by the testator at the time of death, as in l. 1. C. de edicto divi Adriani. That the vulgar substitution is contained in the compendious one, as noted in l. precibus. And this is the truth. Nevertheless, according to what is proposed, the said missio was null by operation of law: first, because it was not liquidated before the judge, nor shown, that the case of substitution had occurred.

For the rule of law is that a judge, to whom nothing has been proven at least by the oath against calumny, can make no delivery into possession, as noted in the Authentica *De ex his rebus*, § *Si vero etiam quidam*; and in the Digest, *De exhibendis*, l. *Thesaurus*; and in the Digest, *Quibus ex causis in possessionem*, l. *Haec autem*, § 1. Especially when the defendant is not pronounced contumacious, but is present, from whom possession may not be taken without cognition of the cause, as noted in the Institutes, *De maioribus et obsequiis*, c. *Inter quatuor*. And because when it is a matter of taking possession from someone, it is necessary that it be claimed against him and proven, as noted in the Authentica *De triennio et semestri*, § *Penultimus*; and in the Code, *De pactis*, l. *Si pacto, quo poenam*. For one must not begin with execution where the defendant has appeared in court, as in the Code, *De executione rei iudicatae*, l. *Nimis propere*. And the commission, which is made by law in the edict, has the force of a delivery which is made in a real action: since by that delivery possession is transferred, as in the said law *Edicto*. But in a real action there is no doubt that proof of the cause and liquidation of the right of the plaintiff are required to transfer possession, as in the Code, *Ubi in rem actio*, l. 2. Thus there is no doubt that the unjust possessor constitutes himself an adversary in court and contumacious, and this must be proven by evidence, as in the Code, *De rei venditione*, l. *Finis*, § *Quibus dummodo praetermissis*. And if not done, in a summary cognition the decree is null by the law itself, as in l. 1, § *Haec verba*, Digest, *Ne vis fiat ei*. And a proceeding is void for non-observance of order and for the judge’s faith not being established, and it cannot be validated, and especially since an interlocutory judgment must be justified by the preceding acts, as in the case *Appellanti*, *De appellationibus*, in the Clementinae.

† Because an invalid proceeding cannot be validated, but must be annulled, insofar as it proceeded in fact, since it proceeded null and void, as stated in l. 1, § 1, ff. de feriis. For that which is null cannot be confirmed, as stated in ff. de obligationibus et contractibus, l. obligationes, quae propriis viribus. And this rule is especially true in judicial proceedings brought for penalty, as stated in extra, de iudicibus, c. exhibita. It therefore appears that the said tenuta, concerning which the question is asked, did not bind, because the judge could not grant it, if the aforementioned narrated facts are true. Secondly, I say that the said Entia did not bind with respect to the said house, because the judge did not wish to grant it. For when he decreed the tenuta, he expressly protested that by the said pronouncement he did not intend that Entia should be prejudiced in any right. For these words are protestatory and reserving, as noted in ff. familiae erciscundae, l. item Labeo, § 1. Hence, if the said Entia was owed any right in possession or ownership, it was entirely reserved to her; and although the messenger reported that he had made mention in the said house, a certain execution of the fact does not enlarge the sentence, but rather ought to be revoked, because the proper measure would be exceeded, as noted in C. quorum appellationes non recipiuntur, l. ab executione. Hence it is concluded that the said pronouncement did not prejudice the rights of Entia.

† Moreover, when a prejudicial question is reserved, the matter is understood to remain intact, as stated above regarding witnesses: Auth. Si testis; D. Qui satisdare coguntur, l. Fideiussor; D. De pactis dotalibus, l. Beblius. Hence, we consider the former grant of possession. Nevertheless, I state that it has prejudiced the said Entity in some respect, since it could not rely on such a grant, as D. De bonis, Auth. Iudicium possessio; l. Cum uidetur. Therefore, it must be done anew from the beginning, and a new grant of possession is requested; and then he will prevail who holds the stronger rights to the grant of possession, whether by bringing the action or by opposing it, as in the aforementioned l. Edicto, § 1.

† In another possessory action, he must prevail who has better proved possession, and more ancient possession; and all other things being equal, he is also presumed to have the more just claim who holds a title, as in Extra, de probat., c. Licet tamen; de testib., l. Obcarmen, § Si testes, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The legitimation of an infant, at the instance and petition of the father, is valid and admitted, so that the one thus legitimated succeeds as if he were legitimate.
2. Add that he consulted more fully on this matter below in consilium 119.
body: First

It must be considered regarding the legitimation of the said infant, whether it is valid. And it appears that it is not. First, because since the infant cannot consent, therefore he cannot be legitimated, as in Auth. Quibus modis naturalis efficiuntur sui, §. Generaliter. Second, because legitimation does not seem to be able to be made through a procurator, as in D. De adoptionibus, l. Post mortem, §. Finis. Third, because the sisters were not duly cited, as in l. Ultima, D. De naturalium restitutione. Fourth, because it does not appear that the mother consented; hence the legitimation does not extend to her: and because he was born from intercourse, for which she could be accused of adultery. Hence he does not succeed to the mother, as noted in Inst. Ad Orphitionem, §. Non inficiatur.

To the contrary, it appears, having regard to the tenor of the privilege, and the power of the one legitimating, and the clauses of rogatory letters appended in the privilege of Caesar, in which it is expressly provided that such legitimation be valid, and that such legitimated person succeeds like other legitimate agnates and cognates. And the Emperor in this matter, by which one returns to simple natural law, when no distinction was made between natural and legitimate children, can do all these things, as noted in Auth. Quibus modis naturalis efficiuntur sui, §. Finis, Collatio 7. And it is treated by the doctors in l. Gallus, D. De liberis et posthumis. Nor does it obstruct that the mother did not consent, because rather she consented, as is evident from the instrument, so that the said legitimated person succeeded to the mother together with the others. And if the sisters died before the inheritance was accepted, it accrues to the said legitimated person, as in C. Ad Orphitionem, l. Non pro numero. And thus I hold regarding the goods of the mother and the sisters. Otherwise, the said legitimation would effect nothing: which is contrary to the tenor of the rescript, and contrary to the law, because where parents petition for legitimation, such legitimation is valid without any others being cited, as noted by the doctors in the said l. Gallus. And this Christopher, father of the said Matthew, for the legitimation of these legitimated persons by imperial power, and as father and legitimate administrator, can bring action on behalf of him, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The father and mother, marrying off their common daughter, bound themselves to provide a dowry to her upon the death of the father. It is asked: to what is the mother bound by virtue of the said obligation, especially if the father is insolvent, or his estate is.
body: Point

† A certain man and his wife married off their daughter, and both bound themselves to provide the dowry. Now the said man has died. Now the dowry of the said wife is being claimed, because she had bound herself together with her husband. She responds that she could not bind herself, etc., since her husband’s goods are insufficient for her own dowry. The question is: what is the law?

There is no doubt that this lady Margaret must have her dowry from her husband’s goods, as stated in C. qui potior in pignore habeat, l. assiduis, §. exceptis. But there is doubt concerning the obligation which the mother, namely Lady Margaret, made to her husband for the dowry of their common daughter. For it seems that the said obligation of Lady Margaret is not binding. First, because she could not alienate or encumber her own dowry in the same instrument to her husband, eod. tit., auth. si qua mulier. But the contrary is the truth, because a woman may bind herself in respect of the dowry, especially in support of the father, as in C. de dotibus promissis, l. finalis, and as noted in C. ad Velleianum, l. finalis. Nor is the woman in this case considered to be deceived, but rather acting out of the duty of piety, as in ff. de conditione indebita, l. cum his, §. si mulier.

Secondly, by reason of the oath, which must be observed, as in c. mulier, de iureiurando. And therefore the said Lady Margaret is bound to pay the said dowry if she has the means. But if she does not have the means, she would not be bound, because since the marriage has been dissolved by the death of the daughter, the nephews claim the benefit of the donation as a lucrative cause. Hence, both because she is the mother and because she is the donor, she is not bound unless a deduction is made so that she may not be in need, when the dowry is retained by the children on behalf of their mother. For the children themselves have a lucrative claim to the dowry, as in l. finalis, ff. quae in fraudem creditorum. But if there were no children, so that the husband should profit from the dowry by agreement: then the father-in-law and mother-in-law would be sued jointly and severally upon dissolution of the marriage, as in ff. de re iudicata, l. quod hoc. Thus, if the marriage is not dissolved, the husband owes no deference to the parents of his wife, but the nephews ought to show deference to their own parents, and should not demand payment from them after the parents themselves, except to the extent that they are able to pay, as in l. patronus, ff. de re iudicata, and l. sunt qui in id, ff. de iure dotium, §. si extraneus.

I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether, and when, a later law is said to revoke an earlier one, and what applies to statutes.
body: To be considered

It is, when laws are diverse, and without a derogatory clause, sometimes they are contrary, or with a derogatory clause. In the first case, the legislator, by enacting the later law, does not derogate from the earlier one. In the second case, he derogates, as stated in the first constitution, C. §. quidam. Hence, it must be examined here whether the statute made last derogates from the first, or not. For whenever a certain form is given, and afterwards such form is changed, it seems that a departure from the form has occurred, as in ff. de Praetor. stip. l. Valerianus. But so it appears in our case, because by the ancient ordinance the bulletini had to be carried on the same day, because they had to be placed at the entrance and exit on that same day. But by that last ordinance it is provided that they should be placed at the will of those to whom it is assigned. Hence, the last statute does not so strictly constrain as the first: and therefore, according to law, it can be defended that the said penalty is not due, as in ff. loca. l. cum in plures. §. lege dicta. and ff. de mino. l. Emilius. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the recipient of money offered and deposited is deemed to approve the contract, so that he is bound on his part to perform it.
body: This one, who

† If he promises to resell to the redeemer at a certain fixed price by a specified term, he is not bound to resell after the term has passed, unless the entire price was offered to him in the meantime, and, being unwilling to accept it, it was deposited and consigned, as stated in C. de pactis inter emptorem et venditorem, l. 2. However, if after the day he accepts part of the price, he is deemed to have departed from the term, and when the remainder is subsequently offered, he can be compelled to resell, as in l. commissoriae, de pactis inter emptorem et venditorem, and l. post diem, ff. de lege commissoria, and by argument from l. 2, C. de iure domus Imperatoris. And therefore, if the said buyer received the said deposited and consigned sum after the day, he is bound to complete the reverse sale, if he received it in the name of the price; because he is deemed to have accepted the deposit under the title under which it was made, and for that cause. For the depositary had no power to release the deposit for any other cause, whence it appears that he paid it under the title under which he could and ought to have done so, as in ff. de solutionibus, l. cum legibus sequentibus. And it must be carefully considered whether he received it after the fixed day or not, as in ff. de minoribus, l. Emilius. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. By what right a widow may claim maintenance.
1. Discharge may be made by a procurator.
2. He is bound to the dowry, into whose hands it came.
body: Regarding the first point concerning the penalty, it must be said that it cannot be claimed, because if it had been incurred on account of the dowry upon the dissolution of the marriage, it ought to be restored to the father of the woman, as stated in the Digest, *De iure dotium*, law *Quotiens res*. And the same rule applies if the marriage has not been dissolved and the dowry is the cause of the reassignment, as stated in the Code, *De iure dotium*, law *Ubi adhuc*.

† But regarding the point concerning alimony, it must be said that alimony comes within the office of the judge. See absolutely Baldus in l. 1, C. de re uxoria actu; l. unica, § praeterea; and ff. soluto matrimonio, l. si marito, § final; iudicis mercenario. And therefore, once the principal is dissolved, its effect vanishes, as ff. de deposito, l. 4. And that they come within the office of the judge mercenary, and not by right of action, is clear, because they are not owed by right of contract, but by accident due to delay, as C. de dote promissa, l. final; and ff. de eo quod certum locum habet, l. centum Capuae; and l. final; and ff. de actionibus emptio venditionis, l. qui per collusionem, § ultimate.

† On the point concerning the discharge, it must be said that it is valid, because through the procurator the exception of fraud is sought for the principal, as in D. de pactis, l. rescriptum, and l. idem in duobus, and D. de liberis legatis, l. non solum, § liberationis verba.

† On the fourth point, I say that if the dowry was lawfully reassigned, it must be investigated to whom it came, whether to Angelus alone, or to A. alone, or to both. For if Angelus receives the whole, or a share, he must reassign it for the burdens of marriage, if it lasts, namely, for that part which he receives, because the dowry ought to be with those who sustain the burdens of marriage, as in D. 23.3.17 (l. si is, qui Stichum, § si dos) and D. 10.2.12 (l. si maritus, etc.). I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a pupillary substitution may be made for a pupil instituted in a specific thing.
2. Whether an emphyteutic right is to be computed to the son in his legitime.
body: Substitution

† The facts in the prelegata are as follows: if he dies in pupillary age, such legacies devolve within [the estate]. And then follows the universal institution of the testator’s goods, with another substitution made to the universal heir; this should not be called a pupillary substitution, because it is made by a common word in a certain thing. And he is regarded more as being in the place of a legatee than of an heir, since the heir instituted universally has entered upon the inheritance, as in C. de haer. inst. l. quotiens non obstat; ff. de vulg. sub. l. cohaeres §. si. Because when an express pupillary substitution is made in a certain thing to an impubes instituted universally, and no other person is substituted universally, and then such a substitution in a certain thing is drawn to the whole, as is said there; sometimes an impubes is instituted in a certain thing, and another universally: and then it is otherwise. The same. It is the law that institution is the same as institution, as in ff. de haer. inst. l. 1 §. si ex fundo; and l. si quotiens §. si duo; and l. ex facto.

Secondly, it was asked whether an emphyteutic estate should be imputed to the son in his legitime. And the answer is that it should be imputed to the extent of the amount into which it can be converted from the emphyteusis itself, provided that it comes to the son as to an heir. Otherwise, if it comes to him simply as a son, unless it was also purchased with the father’s money, as in C. de inoff. test. l. omnimodo § imputari. And thus I hold, and I reduce it to the amount that can be understood from the emphyteusis itself, considering the reverential obligation to its lord, whether he wishes to grant permission to sell, or whether he wishes to buy. And whatever remains beyond that for which satisfaction is made to the lord: this is what is imputed in the legitime, not the thing simply. And it supports C. de collat. l. illud ad instar, where the purchase of military rank, which is transmissible to heirs, is required; so too is the said emphyteusis, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the procedure of the delegated judge, carried out after revocation, is valid.
1. Whether an appeal may be taken from the revocation of the delegation.
body: Procellus

A judgment rendered by a delegated judge who is ignorant of his revocation is valid; likewise, a sentence pronounced by him is valid, as established in D. de iurisdict. omn. iud. l. et quia; D. si cert. pet. l. eius, qui in Provincia; and Extr. de restit. spoli. c. audita. But if he knew, or ought to have known, that he had been revoked, his proceeding is not valid, nor is his sentence, because it was issued by a private person lacking jurisdiction.

And although an appeal was taken from such a revocation, the appeal is not valid, because it is contrary to the law, as in D. de iudic. l. iudicium soluitur. And the reason is that in those matters which pertain solely to the authority of the ordinary judge and not to the right of the parties, such as delegation, an appeal does not proceed, because delegation and revocation are made by operation of law and by the mere authority of the ordinary judge, and are of free will. And it supports what Innocentius notes in c. ultima, extra, de servit. Hence I conclude that in those matters which pertain to the mere authority of the judge, an appeal does not proceed. And thus I conclude, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The disinheritance of a son made in a will on two grounds, namely because he beat his father and because he associates with enemies, is valid, and it suffices to prove one of them. And no. 2.
2. Whether the confession of a general procurator prejudices the principal regarding a crime.
3. Reconciliation is brought about by cohabitation and mutual association, which benefits with respect to preceding injuries, but not with respect to subsequent ones.
4. Disinheritance made of a son because he associated with enemies does not require the expression of the enemies.
5. In enmities expressed in disinheritance, it is required that they be serious and capital.
6. Mere association and dwelling with enemies is a just cause for disinheriting a son.
7. Although the son came to visit his father while the father was ill, and could not visit him, the offense is not thereby considered remitted.
body:
Point: Whether the testament of Lumarellus subsists in law, given the universal disinheritance of his son.

First question: Whether the testament of Lumarellus subsists in law by appending and setting forth the causes in the manner in which he instituted and appended them, and since he always spoke using the gerund.

Second question: Assuming, but not conceding, that the said testament subsists in law, whether all the causes inserted in the said testament are effective, that is, effective for the disinheritance of the said Bartholomew; and if not all are effective, which of them are.

Third question: Whether all the causes must be proved conjunctively by the said Paul, the aforementioned heir, or whether the proof of one cause suffices for the disinheritance of the said Bartholomew.

Fourth question: Since proceedings were taken against the said Bartholomew by the Potestas of the territory on the ground that it was said that the said Bartholomew had struck the said Lumarellus, and a certain defender appeared before the said Potestas in the name of the said Bartholomew and confessed that the said Bartholomew had struck the said Lumarellus: whether the said confession prejudices the said Bartholomew.

Fifth question: Since it was said that the said Bartholomew had struck the said Lumarellus, and the said Lumarellus and Bartholomew were reconciled, having lived together for a long period of time: whether the said reconciliation had and has the effect of invalidating the said cause.

Sixth question: Whether it was necessary for the said Lumarellus to name his enemies in the said testament.

Seventh question: What kind of persons must be capital enemies, or others.

Eighth question: Whether mere conversation and cohabitation with his enemies is an effective cause for disinheritance.

Ninth question: Since the said Bartholomew, during the illness of the said Lumarellus, wished to visit him several times, and the said Bartholomew could not do so because the said Lumarellus did not permit the said Bartholomew to go to him or visit him: whether he could lawfully disinherit him, since it did not depend on the said Bartholomew.

† I have previously opined, and I now opine, that the said disinheritance was valid, and is valid, on account of the causes inserted in the disinheritance. And this is especially so on account of that cause, namely, that the son beat his father, and that he consorted with his enemies against the father's will, etc., as is contained in the will. But if the disinherited son knows that the causes are not true, or if they cannot be proven by the heir, let him bring an action of complaint of an undutiful will, and he will succeed, as is stated in C. de inoffic. testam. l. omnino. And see the notes in ff. de inoffic. testam. l. quinta. And in Auth. ut cum de appel. cog. §. aliud quoque capitulum. And in Auth. de hered. et fals. §. exheredat. And these are my remarks on the first point.

† Regarding the second and third points, I say that it suffices for one of the aforementioned causes to be proven, because the law does not require that they be proven conjunctively. Hence, whether it is proven that the son beat his father, or that he formed an alliance with others who had beaten his father, or that he laid ambushes against his father’s life, this is sufficient against the son himself, C. de inoffic. testam. l. liberi. §. fin.
†Furthermore, I say that such a confession does not prejudice the son, unless it was made by his mandate, as in C. res inter alios acta, throughout.

† Fifth, I say that reconciliation benefits the son with respect to preceding injuries, not subsequent ones, as noted in the Institutes, *de iniuriis*, § *fin.*; Codex, *familiae erciscundae*, l. *in ipsius*; Digest, *de adimendo legatis*, l. 4.

† On the sixth point, I say that it is not necessary to specify the names of enemies in a will; rather, this comes into play in the proofs, which must be more certain, as noted in the Digest, title on deposit, law 1, section "if someone [deposits] silver."
† On the seventh point, I say that enmities must be serious and capital, or nearly so, as stated in the Digest, *De arbitris*, law *Licet*.

† On the eighth point, I say that conversation and cohabitation with the father’s enemies, and association with them, suffice to disinherit the son, as stated in the Digest, De officio præfecti urbis, l. 1, § cum patronus.

† On the last point, I say that it is of no benefit to the disinherited son that he wished to speak with his father and could not, because fault preceded the accident. And because we are uncertain whether the father would have spared him or not. Hence, let the son impute it to himself, who committed the offense. For the father is presumed to have persevered in the same hatred toward the ungrateful son as he had when he disinherited him; since a change of will is not presumed, as argued in ff. de probat. l. cum tacitum. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The will is void in which a daughter who was under the power of the testator was passed over.
2. Whether the will is annulled by the passing over of a posthumous child, if he is born and dies while the testator is still alive.
3. Whether instituting the womb is understood to refer only to the womb that existed at the time of the will, or to a subsequent one.
4. A substitution made by these words, "if he should die before the lawful age for making a will," is a pupillary substitution.
5. Whether the pupillary substitution, mentioned above, vanishes due to the passing over of the posthumous child.
body: It is proposed that a certain Simon, a citizen, made a will in this form, namely that he instituted the womb of his wife Joanna as heir, if she were pregnant and bore one or more male children. However, if she were not pregnant, or if she gave birth and the child was born and it happened that they died before the legitimate age for making a will, and if they reached that age, he made certain particular legacies, and added in this form: “The residue of all his other goods in the said case he judged and left to the work of Saint Michael in Florence, etc.” This same testator also said, willed, and commanded that if the said Joanna, his wife, were pregnant and bore a female child, and she reached marriageable age and was given in marriage, he endowed her with 500 florins, etc. The case occurred that the said Joanna was pregnant and bore a female child, who died during the lifetime of the testator. Subsequently, the said wife became pregnant by the said testator, and while she was pregnant, the said Simon, the testator, died. Finally, the wife died in the eighth month of her pregnancy. And so, although the birth was not mature, a son was extracted by cutting open the womb, emitted a cry, and immediately died. The question is between the work of Saint Michael and those succeeding intestate, to whom the inheritance of the said testator should be awarded. Secondly, it is asked whether the maternal inheritance was awarded to him. Thirdly, it is asked, because in the said will there is a codicillary clause, if it could not be valid by the law of wills, etc., whether the said clause has any effect.

† To the understanding of these doubts, it must be premised that the said testament was null: because the daughter, who was in the power of the testator, was passed over, to whom nothing was left by way of institution, as in Auth. ut cum de app. cogn. §. aliud quoque capitulum. Unless the local statute provided that it would suffice if left under any title, as was the case under the law of the Codex, as C. de inof. tes. l. omnimodo. And although the daughter died during the lifetime of her father, it nevertheless appears that the testament does not become valid, as ff de libe. et posth. l. qui filius, qui in potestate. and Insti. de exhęr. lib. in prin. But the contrary is true in this case, when the son of the testator was instituted heir, as ff. de iniust. testa. l. posthumus. ver. idem et circa. For then it becomes valid by praetorian law as regards the first degree of institution: but because that son died, and did not claim possession of the goods according to the tablets, the institution of the son appears to be in the cause of lapse: since possession of the goods is not transmitted to heirs if it has not been claimed, as ff. de Bon. pos. l. 3. §. et acquirere. By civil law, however, the testament does not become valid, as ff. si tab. testa. nul. exta. l. 1. in fi. and no. de iniusto rup. l. cum in secundo. and C. de contratab. l. posthumo.
