It follows, therefore, that if the testament is null due to the omission of the posthumous child, the vulgar substitution made to the male son does not hold. For it is vulgar: because the testator said, if he is not born, as ff. de ventre inspi. l. qui ventri.

† But a doubt remains, whether a substitution made to the unborn child, if it be male, and if he dies before the lawful age for making a will, has effect. And before I come to this, it is necessary to premise such a question,

† namely, whether the aforementioned will is to be understood as referring only to the womb that existed at the time of the will, or whether it also refers to a subsequent womb. And it seems that only the womb existing at the time of the will is considered instituted, as in D. 35.1.10 (*Si ita scripsisset*). The contrary view is now preferred, because the testator did not say “if she were pregnant”; which is understood to mean whenever she was pregnant by the said testator, by analogy with C. 6.2.1 (*Si*) and D. 28.5.1 (*Placet*). For in case of doubt, we must interpret that the will is valid and that the testator intended to cover necessary cases, as noted in D. 28.5.10 (*Gallus*), § *Videndum*. Hence, when different pregnancies resulted in a daughter and a son, it is understood that the testator intended both, namely, the daughter to receive a legacy and the male son to be instituted heir, as in D. 28.5.11 (*Si ita scriptum*).

† But now let us see what this substitution was. And I say that it was pupillary, because those words, "if he should die before the lawful age of testifying," express this meaning, that is, if he should die in puberty: for that is the age of not testifying, as in the Digest, on Wills, the law "Who of age." Therefore, the substitution is formally and strictly pupillary. But then immediately

† It is asked whether the said substitution fails due to the omission of the said woman. And the glossa says that a pupillary substitution is not vitiated on account of omission, as is noted in the Digest, *de vulgari et pupillari substitutione*, l. 1. And the same is held by Bartolus, although Dino del Garbo holds the contrary. I consider the opinion of the glossa to be true when the pupillary substitution is an institution, and not an omission, as is the case here; but if it were made to an omitted impubes, then the opinion of Dino would be true, from the argument in the Digest, *de legatis tertio*, l. *ex filio*, and in the Code, *de fideicommissis*, l. *penultima*. And therefore, in the question proposed, I am of the opinion, both as to the paternal inheritance, which had entirely devolved to the posthumous child because the sister had died during the father’s lifetime, and as to the maternal inheritance, because the male was the sole survivor. And although he was born in the eighth month, which according to the physicians cannot live, nevertheless it suffices that he lived for a moment, as in the Code, *de posthumis haeredibus instituendis*, l. *uxoris ab ortu*. And so I decide on these points; it is not expedient to treat of the codicillary clause, since the pupillary substitution is valid between direct heirs. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If one of the parties who have submitted to arbitration acts contrary to the award, he is punished with the penalty for his share, unless it has been expressly stipulated that each party is bound for the whole amount.
2. If it has been agreed between the parties submitting to arbitration that half of the penalty of those who contradict the award shall be applied to the common fund, the common fund cannot bring an action, even if a civil law oath has intervened, unless someone has received the promise in the name of the co-parties; but what is the case under canon law? No. 3.
3. In the forum of conscience, delay can always be purged.
body: There are several compromittors on one side, who at the first point

† The ordinary gloss states that when there are several compromittors on one side who have promised a penalty, if one of them breaches, he incurs the entire penalty by the nature of the penal stipulation, which is incurred in full by reason of the part. For, since the penalty is accessory to the principal obligation, its nature is such that it is not divisible, as noted in the Digest, *De verbis obligatis*, l. *Eadem*, § *Cato*; l. *Quinta*, § *Si sororem*, on the word “if one.” And there the ordinary gloss is to the letter. But Jacobus de Arena and Bartolus say that each appears to have promised the penalty for his share, and not jointly and severally (*insolidum*), unless it was expressly agreed that each should be bound jointly and severally, as in the Digest, *De duobus reis*, l. *Reos*, § *Cum tabulas*. The objection based on the note in § *Cato* does not hold, because that passage speaks of a case where there was one promisor, from whose person the obligation descended to several heirs. It is otherwise if from the beginning there are several promisors, for each is presumed in doubt to have promised a part, both of the principal sum and of the penalty, as in the Code, *De duobus reis*, auth. *Hoc ita et ita teneo*.

† On the second point, it must be said that if no one received the promise for the community, no right is acquired by the community, as in D. de arbitris, l. Arbiter intra. But if someone received the promise for the community, then the community could bring an action, as in D. de iure fisci, l. 1, there: “a penalty from a private contract,” etc. However, by those words, “half of the penalty belongs to the community,” the stipulation is not so conceived that something is acquired for the community, because the words are directed to the fisc itself, as in C. de inutilibus stipulationibus, l. 3, and D. de verbis obligatorum, l. Stipulatio ista, § Alteri, and this applies to a private person. But the officials of the fisc can stipulate for the fisc in any manner, as noted in D. de usuris, l. Legare. And this is true according to civil law.

† But some say, according to canon law, that once an oath has been added, §. alteri has no application. And that one can be compelled to observe the oath by ecclesiastical censure, because it is by the office of the Bishop, not by the right of action, as is read and noted in 1 q. 7. quotiens cordis oculus; there, however, it speaks of a case which principally and directly concerns the peril of the soul. Moreover, that the oath must be observed is proved by another reason. For that which is given to another is a pact, although invalid according to civil law. But according to canon law it seems valid, although it is naked. The first is proved from what is read and noted in D. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. quaecunque; D. de verbis oblig., l. liber homo, §. si. The second is proved because, according to canon law, action is taken on a naked pact by the office of the judge, although the civil action praescriptis verbis does not lie, where the naked pact is clothed in no kind of vestment, as in X. de pactis, c. 1. For canon law does not care for the technicalities of law, but for the substance of the faith promised. Thus, D. de mandato, l. si fideiussor, §. quaedam. It must be said that in the secular forum, a pact that something be given to another is not a pact, because it lacks the elements of a pact: since it does not give rise to a natural obligation, as is noted in D. de pactis, l. 1, in principio. Moreover, an oath by itself does not bind naturally, as in D. de fideiussoribus, l. si quis pro eo, which I prove. A natural obligation must arise from consent; but between absent persons, without an intermediary messenger or letter, there is no consent; therefore, a natural obligation does not arise between them, as in D. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. consensu, and l. ex maleficio, §. longe minus; and C. de donationibus, l. nec ignorans; and as is noted in C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, l. illud; and as is noted in D. de contrahenda empt., l. 1, in fine. And this is the very truth in the judicial forum.

† Certainly, even in the forum of conscience, I do not think that a penalty is due if the lot is provided. For I hold that in the forum of conscience delay can always be purged by what is good and equitable, cf. D. de verb. oblig. l. si servum § sequitur; and note 12 q. 1 fraternitatis. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A sui heres does not transmit a conditional fideicommissum to his own descendants.
2. Add below, in opinion 147.
body: Ol Derest in l. si cui, ff. de actionibus et obligationibus, says that his view on this point is that of the ordinary glosses. For the gloss which Ol Derest in l. si cui, ff. de actionibus et obligationibus, says, holds that a predeceased heir transmits a conditional fideicommissum to his descendants. And in support of this opinion is ff. de acquirenda hereditate, l. qui patri haeres extitit. But

Elsewhere, the gloss, in disputing, holds the contrary opinion, as is fully noted in l. 1, C. de his, qui ante aper. tabu.; and this opinion is the very truth. Hence, without further allegations, I state that the said inheritance pertains by right of fideicommissum to Angela and Paulutia, and not to the daughters of the other daughters of the testator who predeceased the aforementioned Iuvenalis. With these substitutes also succeed the male children of Siucia, Vannocia, and Paulocia, or of any one of them; because so does the will declare. But the daughters of the aforementioned Siucia, Vannocia, and Paulocia do not succeed, because a conditional substitution is not transmitted, as I have said. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The guardian is not bound to render an account to the substitute of the ward, whether minor or adult, except concerning the assets that fall within the fideicommissary substitution.
body: to you, unless from the goods which come into the substitution

† He is not bound to render an account to an adult substitute, except concerning the goods which fall within the fideicommissary substitution. For regarding those, he is rightly bound: because the stipulation that the ward’s property shall be kept safe was accepted for the benefit of all who have an interest. And therefore it comprehends universal fideicommissaries, who are regarded as standing in the place of heirs, once restitution has been made to the universal fideicommissary pursuant to the Trebellian Senatusconsultum, as in D. ad Treb. l. 1, in princ. And it is established in D. de adop. l. his verbis. But concerning goods acquired after the father’s death, and concerning fruits which do not fall within the restitution of the universal fideicommissum, an account need not be rendered to the universal fideicommissary, as in D. de vulg. sub. l. cohaeredi, § cum filiae; and C. ad Treb. l. iubemus; and D. ad Treb. l. in fideicommissaria; and C. de fam. ercisc. l. filium, quem habentem. And from this it appears what is the law on the said point. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, and when, an oath validates a contract, supplies for age, or other formalities.
2. When a law or statute prohibits an oath, it is not valid. The useful is not vitiated by the useless, when they are separable.
body: OODC. [A prohibition] does not invalidate a contract by any other reason than by the [prohibition] itself. 91. It is to be said at the first point,

† that the oath of OODC does not validate a contract prohibited by another reason than the reason of age: because the oath represents nothing else but age, and no other solemnity, as ff. de leg. 1. l. si quis inquilinos. §. fin. de leg. l. non dubium. ff. de fideius. l. cum lex praeterita. that statute does not confirm the oath, except in one case: therefore it seems to prohibit it in others, as C. de procura. l. maritus.

And when the law or statute forbids, the oath is not valid, as in D. de iure patronatus, l. adigere, §. fin.; and that which is invalid cannot give strength to another, as in D. de transactionibus, l. cum hi, §. si Praetor. But even assuming that the compromise were valid, insofar as it touches the right of a third party, it is null by the very law of awards, because there is no compromise concerning the right of a third party. For no one can litigate concerning another’s right, as in D. si pars hereditatis petatur, l. 1, in principio; and D. si ususfructus petatur, l. uti frui.

† On the third point, it must be said that the useful is not vitiated by the useless, if they are separable, or rather entirely separate, as in the Digest, *De minoribus*, law *Et etiam*, section *Ex causa*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an executor appointed for the purpose of selling and distributing, after the death of someone, may act or institute proceedings during that person’s lifetime.
2. Whether the property subject to sale and distribution is said to be subject to restitution.
3. Whether the property subject to distribution may in the meantime be alienated by the heir.
4. The knowledge of the first heir prejudices his heir, so that he cannot alienate more than what his predecessor could have alienated.
5. Legacies left for pious causes cannot be diminished, nor can they be changed for other uses.
6. In the reception of witnesses for perpetual record, that mode of citation suffices which would suffice if the fideicommissum itself, pure or purified, were being sought.
7. Universal executors may carry out execution, even without restitution having been made to them under the Trebellian law.
body:
Cale Jacobus Patinus of Este made a will, which is proposed in the following form, namely, that a certain Cale Jacobus Patinus of Este made a will, in which he instituted Laurentius Patinus, his brother, as his universal heir. Furthermore, the said testator wished and commanded that the said Jacobina, his wife, be and should be the dowager usufructuary of all the goods, things, and inheritance of the said testator. Furthermore, he appointed as his executors of the said testament the said Antonius and the Prior of the Society of Discipline, etc. Furthermore, it is proposed that after the said will was made, read, and perfected, the said Jacobus, the testator, uttered these words in the presence of the said Laurentius, the instituted heir, namely: “I wish that the following be added to the said will: if my brother Laurentius should die before my wife Jacobina, that after the death of the said Jacobina, my house and all my things be sold and distributed for the love of God and for my soul by my executors.” These matters are proposed on behalf of the said executors.

Furthermore, it is proposed that the said Laurentius, knowing the aforesaid, sold to Master Bonus one of the foundations of the late Jacobus Patinus. And that the said Laurentius, heir of the said Jacobus, his brother, died after making his will, with the aforementioned Jacobina surviving, who is still alive. And that a certain Dame Charutia, wife and heir of the said Laurentius Patinus, delivered the said house with its foundation, etc., to the said Master Bonus, although, as is said, in fact and for less than just price. And because the said sales were made of a thing subject to restitution, and while a condition was pending, and against the will of the deceased, the said executors ask that the said sales be declared invalid and of no effect, and that no right accrues to the said Master Bonus therefrom, and that perpetual silence be imposed upon him, etc.

On the other hand, in effect, it is requested by the said Master Bonus that the said sales be confirmed, reserving the right of the poor, if any they have or could have in the aforementioned price. And the said Master Bonus grounds himself, first, as to the exclusion of the plaintiffs, due to the restitution under the Trebellian law not having been made, due to the day of the fideicommissum not yet having arrived, and due to the condition, and due to the citation being less than legitimate for the publication of the witnesses of the party in the said judgment. Furthermore, due to the good faith of the said Charutia, the seller, and of the said buyer; because they proceeded to the purchase of the said house out of ignorance that was not gross, but legitimate. Therefore, granted and presupposed that the said Jacobus, the testator, had uttered the aforementioned last words regarding the sale of the things, nevertheless, since the possessor in good faith sold the inheritance, and since he is not bound except to the extent that he is enriched, the price succeeds in place of the thing, and the thing cannot be evicted, as in D. de petitione hereditatis, l. sed et si lege, §. ita si rem dixerit. And because a thing subject to restitution under a condition seems to be able to be permanently alienated by one ignorant of the law, as in l. fi., §. fi., D. de legatis 2, and in D. Ad Trebellianum, l. quidam ita, §. si quis filium. And on these points, it has been argued most elegantly and copiously on behalf of the said Master Jacobus.

It is alleged that before restitution under the Trebellian law, no rights accrue to the said executors, who are considered in the place of universal fideicommissaries, as in Inst. de fideicommissis hereditatibus, §. restituta, and D. ad Trebellianum, l. restituta. For this reason, restitution under the Trebellian law was devised, so that rights may effectively pass through it, as in D. ad Trebellianum, l. 1, in principio, l. facta, per totum. Furthermore, it is alleged that the publication of witnesses does not hold, because personal citation or latitatio did not intervene, which ought to intervene in such a regular, extraordinary, and prejudicial publication of witnesses, as noted in l. 4, §. totiens, D. de damno infecto, per Dynus, and C. de testibus, authent. si quis ab aliquo, and in the corpus, whence it is taken, and noted in Mercatus, in the rule praesumitur. And on this, it has been argued subtly on behalf of Master Bonus.

Furthermore, the said ignorance is alleged, which is presumed in a certain fact, as in D. pro suo, l. fin., whence the act of an ignorant person is valid, which would not be valid if done by one who knew, as in the said l. fin., §. fin., D. de legatis 2, where it seems expressed in a will. And the said l. quaedam, in the gloss.

On the other hand, it is alleged quite copiously on behalf of the said executors. And it seems that while the day or condition is pending, a thing subject to restitution cannot be sold or alienated, as in C. communia de legatis, l. fi., §. si autem sub conditione, and §. si autem auaritiae. The favor of pious causes is also alleged, and that where it concerns bequests to pious causes, only the truth is considered, even if all legal solemnities are omitted, as in Extra, de testamentis, c. cum omnis, and c. relata, and in the Repetitio, l. 1, C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, and many other things are said elegantly and well.

Therefore, these matters being thus narrated and explained, let us extract the points from the said matter, from the resolution of which the truth and what is the law will appear. For first, it must be asked whether an executor appointed to sell and distribute after the death of someone can act during the life of that person. Second, whether a thing subject to sale and distribution is understood to be subject to restitution. Third, whether such a thing can be alienated in the meantime by the heir. Fourth, whether the knowledge of the first heir affects the heir of the heir who is ignorant. Fifth, whether the law l. fi., §. fi., D. de legatis 2, has application in bequests to pious causes, in which the testator provided for certain executors to see to them. Sixth, whether the solemnity of personal citation is required, where one can otherwise proceed summarily and by the office of the judge, both ecclesiastical and secular; as is the case in bequests to pious causes. Seventh and last, whether universal executors of the judgment can carry out their execution without the inheritance having been restored to them under the Trebellian law.

† On the first point, it must be said that executors for pious causes are permitted to act in order to obtain that which they are bound to execute. Hence, before they can execute, it is mandated that they act if the mandate is denied. But it is certain that where, after the death of someone, execution or distribution must be made, in the meantime the executor cannot distribute or execute anything, as in D. de legibus 1, l. si filius; D. de legibus 2, § diuus Seuerus; and D. de legibus 2, l. uniuersali ex familia, in principio. Certainly, neither can restitution under the Trebellian trust be made before the condition, as in D. ad Trebellianum, l. sed si ante. Hence it appears that, while the condition is pending, the day of execution has neither fallen due nor arrived. For in the meantime, with respect to this, the executors are not executors in selling and distributing; although in the meantime they may seek that which pertains to the proof of their office and of the testator’s judgment. Hence they could rightly seek to have witnesses received for eternal memory, because this mode of seeking is available to those claiming a conditional right, so that the means of proof may be preserved against fortuitous events, as in C. de usuris pupillaribus, l. pupillus; and Extr. de testibus, c. significauit. That a condition is here attached, which renders the mandate of the executors conditional, is evident from the fact that the mandate to sell and distribute was conferred upon them after the death of Jacobina, as in D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. haeres vnus, in principio. Moreover, I say further that if a certain day is appointed to an executor, the day of his office does not fall due nor arrive before that day. For since the office does not pass to the heir of the executor, it is in vain if someone departs before the day falls due, as in D. quando dies legati cedat, l. 3. Much more strongly, therefore, is this the case where there is an uncertain time, which is regarded as a condition. And by this, a decisive answer to the question appears, namely, that these executors act wrongly and without effect before the day and the condition.

† On the second point, I say that these matters are connected to each other: the restitution of the thing, so that he could sell it. For he who has the power of selling can act so that it may be delivered to him, so that he may deliver it to the buyer. And we have a similar case, because by the very fact that the executor is given license to sell, the hypothecated thing is deemed to be given to him so that he may sell it, nor can he revoke this license, because it is annexed to the right of hypothec, whereas a simple and bare promise could be revoked, as in D. qui pot. in pign. h. l. creditor. § post divisionem. And this is also supported by the fact that for pious causes everything is understood to be implied by which execution is more easily achieved, as in l. si quis ad declinandam, C. de episc. et cler. On the third point, doubt may be raised.

† For sometimes the testator simply left a legacy subject to a day or a condition; sometimes he adds a prohibition against alienation. In the first case, in the meantime, the heir may alienate with his own title, and the alienation endures as long as the condition of the fideicommissum exists; afterwards it is resolved, as in D. 38.2.1 (*Is cui*), § *Haeres*; D. 39.5.1, § *Secundum*; D. 35.1.1 (*Fundo*); D. 28.5.3, § *Fideicommissariam*; and fully noted in D. 36.1.1 (*Marcellus*), § *Res quae*. Provided, however, that the testator prohibits alienation so that no difficulty may arise concerning the pious execution: then I say that the alienation is not valid, in Auth. *De alienatione et emphyteusi*, § *Sanctissimas*, even if the burdened party is unaware, D. 19.1.2 (*Pro emptore*). Hence it must be examined whether, by the executor’s mandate to sell, the heir is thereby prohibited from selling in the meantime. And I hold that he is not, because they are separate matters, D. 18.1.1 (*Non ideo minus*). Nevertheless, the truth of this point cannot be known unless we know, assuming that the house was not sold, whose dominion it is in the meantime. For if the dominion belonged to the executors for the poor, the property of the poor could not be sold to the prejudice of the poor, as in X. 3.26 (*Filius*). But if it belongs to the heir, then he may sell his right: and the law decides that in the meantime it belongs to the heir, D. 7.5.1 (*Vexori usumfructum villae*), with its gloss.

† On the fourth point, I say that the knowledge of the first heir prejudices his heir, as in C. de fruc. et li. expen. l. 2. in fin., in this respect, namely, that he cannot alienate more than his predecessor could.

† On the fifth point, it must be considered that legacies to pious causes cannot be diminished, nor can they be changed for other uses, as stated in the chapter *Quia contingit* in the title *De religiosis*. I hold this to be true, arguing from the law *Locum* in the title *De usufructu*. For I equate them with legacies of freedom, as noted in the Code, title *De fideicommissis*, law *Eam quam*.

† On the sixth point, it seems to be said that even in the reception of witnesses for perpetual memory, that mode of citation suffices which would suffice if the fideicommissum itself were pure or purified and were being sought, or if security were being sought in the name of a conditional fideicommissary, or one deferred to a certain day. For in those things left to God or for pious causes, one should not dispute on the highest points of law. But since the substance of the truth appears clear through the deposition of lawful witnesses, that subtlety of personal citation does not seem necessary, provided that the citation was otherwise made in such a way that it ought to and could have come to the knowledge of the heir who was to be cited. For since legacies for pious causes, even if the inheritance has not been accepted, are due by the office of the judge, if they are pure or purified, and the inheritance itself, lying as it were, is bound in this manner: and if it is necessary that witnesses be received for perpetual memory, they can be received while the inheritance lies unaccepted. And yet there is no one who can be personally cited, because although the inheritance performs the function of a person, it is nevertheless not a person, nor does personal citation apply to it. However, because this passage and the preceding one are novel, I do not speak decisively, but conclude to that which is the decision of the question. I answer that the petition of the said executors does not proceed, because the aforementioned contracts remain binding during the life of the said Jacobina. Hence, from the petition of the executors, because it is not founded in law, the said Master Bonus ought to be absolved. For certainly the petition of the said Master Bonus does not proceed, because he cannot seek to confirm that which, by the passage of time through the death of the said Jacobina, can be weakened and resolved. For that which an heir alienates while a condition of a fideicommissum is pending, that being so, is void and caducous, as is stated in § Si autem avaritiae, and in the Authentica De restitutione, and that which it generates, § Quamobrem; and see the argument from Codex De legato uxorio, paragraph, and Digest De usufructu, law Sticho, and Digest De legatis 2, law Peto, § Praedium, and Digest De pignoris, law Lex vectigali, and Digest De locato, law Si quis domum, § 1.

† On the last point, I say that, as regards selling, or the sale, and the execution of the mandate, restitution under the Trebellian senatus consultum is not necessary, because such a sale consists in fact, not in hereditary right, and it can be carried out by mere ministerial action, as stated in the Digest, *De legatis secundo*, law *Si quis*, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A father may legitimize an infant son with respect to the succession of both himself and the mother, even if the mother is deceased.
2. Whether anyone is to be cited in legitimation, and whether citation is a matter of civil law, since every act of the forum is a matter of civil law.
3. Whether it suffices in legitimation to state "notwithstanding any laws," or whether a special mention is required.
4. Add to this opinion that which was advised above in opinion 105 regarding the same case.
body: A certain widow, having two legitimate daughters, was married to a man named Christopher, from whom she conceived and bore a certain illegitimate son named Matthew. This Matthew, being in infancy, was legitimated by the said now-deceased widow through the Count Palatine, both as regards the succession of the legitimator himself and as regards the succession of the said widow, by a procurator specially appointed for this purpose by Christopher himself, without citing the said legitimate sisters, nor the paternal and maternal grandmothers of the said legitimate sisters. The said sisters died, with the aforementioned paternal and maternal grandmothers surviving and possessing the inheritance of the said legitimated nieces. And in the said legitimation, no one was cited. Now it is asked: whether the said legitimated Matthew succeeds to the sisters, excluding the grandmothers and the heirs of the grandmothers, who are the Poor of Christ, or a certain fraternity. For it is said that such a legitimation is not valid. First, because it was made to the said Matthew without his consent. Second, because it was made without citation of the opposing party. Third, because it was made in the absence of the person being legitimated. Fourth, because the said legitimated person did not ratify the said legitimation. Fifth, because in the privilege it was not stated by the Emperor, "notwithstanding such law"; nor was there an express derogation from the laws speaking to the contrary; although the one who legitimated did derogate and said "notwithstanding such law," because he could not do more than what his privilege states. Sixth, because the said legitimate sisters were dead before the legitimation was made. Seventh, because their inheritance had already been acquired and applied to others, namely the said grandmothers, before the said legitimation. Lastly, because the procuratorship is not established. Now it is asked: what is the law?

† To the first point, I answer that the father can legitimize the infant with respect to himself, since this is done by the Prince, or by one having authority from the Prince, in the manner of the arrogation of a minor, as in D. de adoptionibus, l. his liberis, and l. si arrogator; and in the manner of the emancipation of an infant, C. de emancipatione filii, l. iubemus. And immediately, since he is legitimized with respect to the father, he is in paternal power; from which it follows that the father, as the legitimate administrator of the infant, can demand that he be legitimized with respect to the maternal succession. And he can do this both personally and through a procurator, from the arguments of those who do not, cited by Cynus and others in l. 1, C. de bonis maternis. But it is doubtful whether, if the mother has predeceased, he can be legitimized with respect to the mother. And it must be said that yes, because the words of the Emperor should legitimize for the living, or even for their deceased parents. And it is certain that the Emperor can do this by virtue of his Caesarean and Imperial power, as noted in Auth. qui modo naturales efficiantur sui, §. si, column 7; and from the arguments in D. de restitutione in integrum, de querelis, and in Dist. 8, c. quo iure.

† But it is doubted whether anyone is to be cited in legitimation. And it is to be said that a deceased parent is not to be cited, because a dead person cannot be cited, as in D. 49.4.10 (quae sine appellatione rescinduntur), l. ultima.

But I ask concerning the living, whose prejudice is at issue, whether they are to be cited. Say that they are, as in the last law of the Digest, *de natalibus restituitis*. To the contrary it seems, because if those whose succession is in question are not to be cited, as has been said, therefore neither are others who are more remote, as in the Digest, *de venditionibus insipientibus*, law 1, § *denuntiari*. Solution: I say briefly, either at the time of the limitation the inheritance had been taken up by others, and the legitimation does not hold, because the rescript does not state that dominion already acquired is of the law of nations in retaining, although in acquiring it is of mere civil law, as noted in the law *ex hoc iure*, *de iustitia et iure*, and in the Code, *si contra ius vel utilitatem publicam*, last law; or the matter is entire, because the inheritance has not yet been taken up at the time of the legitimation, and then the legitimation is valid, because the right to take up the inheritance consists in civil law, to which the Emperor can derogate. Nor do I require citation here, because in the same way I would require consent, and thus the privilege of the Prince would be a mockery. For no agnate or cognate would consent against himself. I therefore equate this legitimated person with one who has passed, who can claim possession of goods without anyone being cited, as noted in the Digest, *de bonorum possessionibus*, law 3, § *tam cognata*. Since therefore the Prince wishes the legitimation to have effect, and not to depend on another’s discretion, but only on his imperial power: such legitimation is valid. And thus the Emperor can legitimize, and confer the benefit of legitimates, without anyone being cited. And this, just as he can do by himself, so he can do through another, his commissioner. And legitimation is more equated to a benefit than to a judgment. And therefore, just as the Pope confers benefits and his privileges, so does the Emperor, and he who acts in the place of the Emperor. See what is noted in chapter 1, *de officio delegati*, in the Clementines.

And if it is said that the citation is of natural law, and by reason of the defense to which it tends, which is of natural law, I answer that, on the contrary, every act of the forum is of civil law, as noted in the Institutes, *De obligationibus*, in the beginning. It does not follow that defense is of natural law, since here no defense arises, because there is no challenge, but rather participation in grace, as argued in the Digest, *De bonis auctoris iudicis possessis*, law *Cum unus*. To some, however, it seems that agnates and cognates ought to be cited, by the law *Nam ita Divus* in the Digest, *De adoptionibus*; the law *Si is, qui*; and the Digest, *De aqua pluviali arcenda*, law *In concludendo*. And what is noted by Bartolus in *De liberis et posthumis*, law *Gallus*, section *Et quid si tantum*. I believe that what I have said can be sufficiently defended, because the right of access is not properly in the mother’s goods, but is a certain faculty of the mind, as in the Digest, *Ad legem Falcidiam*, law *Pretia rerum*, which can be perpetually impeded by the supervening legitimation. For the legitimated person is a certain posthumous child not born, but given, and raised as it were from nothing; nevertheless, he assumes the rights of legitimated children, because he is restored to his birthrights, which restoration is of the Lord Prince and of the law, in which donation it is not necessary to cite another, where the matter is intact, as I have said. But after the inheritance has been entered upon and fixed in the bones, he who is heir ought not to cease to be heir, as in the Digest, *De minoribus*, law *Et si fuit*, section *Sed quod Papinianus*. Moreover, if the mother were living, she could not be legitimated with respect to the mother herself without her consent, and similarly, with the sisters living, he could not be legitimated with respect to the succession of the sisters, unless they consent, whose succession is in question, as in the Authenticum *Quibus modis naturales*, etc., section *Et generaliter*. But with the sisters dead, he can be legitimated even with respect to their succession, because so the Emperor wishes by his privilege derogating from criminal laws. And by the foregoing, I advised that if the mother had consented to the legitimation, this spurious child would succeed his mother together with the legitimate sisters. And if the sisters had died before the mother, he would succeed the mother alone, excluding others, and so the sisterhood. And so I still say and advise, assuming the privilege of the Count. But if the inheritance had been entered upon, as I have said, then those goods pertain to the said sisterhood.

† On another point, I say that in the prince’s privilege there are these words: “notwithstanding any laws in the aforementioned matters, even if such were those which ought to be expressed, or of which special mention should be made, etc.” These words are held to constitute a special expression, as in C. de praescri. 30 ann. l. omnes. Hence, the specification of the laws made by the Count could be done for nothing, because he who adds nothing makes nothing new, but merely declares or expresses. ff. de testamentis l. haeredes palam § sed si totam. And it is pertinent to the above, the chapter quamuis de rescrip. lib. 6. and what is noted, and the law l. ult. C. de sen. pas.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. No one is presumed to make a gift of his own property, but rather to have paid by mistake.
body: Auiclius promised Venanco, as a dowry for Cicilia, that in the event where Cicilia’s goods, which amounted to 70 florins, were insufficient, he, Auiclius, would make good the deficiency. Auiclius paid twenty florins of the said amount. Finally, appraisers were appointed to appraise the goods of the said Cicilia, and they appraised them at 70 florins. After this, the said Auiclius learned of all the goods that the said Cicilia’s brother by blood, Collecta, possessed, except for the said dowry.

† Now it is asked whether the said Aviclius may retain the said 20 florins for himself from the said goods of the said Cicilia. I answer that the said Aviclius did not bind himself simply, but only to the extent that he could not be reimbursed from the goods of the said Cicilia up to the said sum; and therefore, insofar as he can be reimbursed, if the said Cicilia has ratified, the said Aviclius is not bound by the said promise. And if he has paid anything, he recovers it from the said Cicilia by the action of negotiorum gestio; for he does not seem to have made a gift, but rather, having erred, he anticipated payment. To this effect: D. de verb. oblig. l. decem; and D. si certum petatur l. final. Therefore, immediately upon forming the intention to be discharged in part for the said dowry with the intention of recovering, he acquires the action of negotiorum gestio, according to the authorities noted in D. de petitione hereditatis l. si quid possessor. It is certain that during the lifetime of the said Cicilia, the said Aviclius cannot give the goods of the said Cicilia in payment to her said husband; but Cicilia herself, if she has ratified, is rightly compelled to this, as C. de solutionibus auth. hoc nisi. And perhaps in the case of ratification, Aviclius himself, as one bound for the woman, may pay from her goods, as D. de manumis. l. si procuratorem § si ignorantes. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. After the inheritance has been accepted, a pagan cannot directly substitute an outsider.
2. No one can have two direct heirs at successive times.
3. Whether a pupillary substitution may be made for a minor instituted in a specific thing.
4. Add that he consulted on the same case above in opinion 101.
body: It is proposed that a certain Laurentius, having two daughters, namely Catharina and Bonaventura, who were under age, and a mother named Angela, as well as Joanna, his wife and mother of the said wards, made a testament, in which, among other things, he left to the said Catharina and Bonaventura for their dowries one hundred gold florins and a certain house by way of institution, with this condition appended, that if any of his said daughters should die within the age of minority, etc. He ordered the Roman executor, for an appropriate fee, that the remainder of the said share of the dying daughter of the said one hundred florins and the house should remain and devolve upon Angela, the mother of the said testator, and after the death of the said Angela, upon a certain Nicolaus and Bonagnus. And similarly, if both his daughters should die in the age of minority, etc. In all his other goods, he instituted as heir the said Angela, his mother; and he willed and ordered that after the death of the said Angela, one hospital be established in her houses; and he instituted the said hospital as his heir after the death of the said Angela. First, Catharina died during the lifetime of the testator, while still under age. Second, the said testator died. Third, the said Bonaventura died while still under age. Fourth, the said Angela died, who during her lifetime had the said hospital constructed. Now the said Nicolaus and Bonagnus, the substitutes, demand the legacy of one hundred florins and the house, etc., and they demand the supplement of the legitime of the said daughters; because they say they were substituted for them as pupillary substitutes, and in a pupillary substitution, the goods of the minor, and consequently the supplement of the legitime, should also come to them. But on behalf of the hospital, the universal heir of the said Laurentius, it is responded that the said Nicolaus and Bonagnus cannot sue for the supplement of the legitime; because they were substituted in a certain thing and quantity, whence they cannot demand more. And because by the form of the statute, daughters cannot sue for the supplement of the legitime. Now from the foregoing, doubts arise: First, what were the species of substitution made from the mother of the testator to the said minors. Second, what was the substitution made from Nicolaus and Bonagnus, after the death of the mother of the testator, to the said minors, and of what species are these substitutions. Third, it is asked whether the said Nicolaus and Bonagnus can demand the said supplement of the legitime. And the day before yesterday I advised that the said Nicolaus and Bonagnus had no right in demanding the said supplement, because they were substitutes in a certain thing and in a certain quantity. And that their substitution cannot be considered pupillary. And that this is true, I now declare more clearly. For either we say that the substitutions made to the said minors are all pupillary, or that all are in a certain thing and in a legacy; or that one is pupillary, the other singular, namely in a certain thing and quantity. I answer the first, and I say that we cannot say that both are pupillary. For if the substitution of the mother is pupillary, the substitution made afterwards in the case of the mother's death is of necessity a singular substitution, or a fideicommissary one; because one cannot have two pupillary substitutes in solidum, namely one for an even uncertain time, such as the death of someone, and another after death. For it is impossible that the inheritance be certainly applied to one. Afterwards, it will be said by direct right, and it will pass to another substitute, unless in the testament...

† Otherwise it would follow that, after the inheritance had been accepted, a pagan could directly substitute an heir who is an outsider, which is contrary to the rules of law, as in D. de vulgari et extraordinaria substitutione, l. verbis civilibus and l. Centurio; and D. de militum testamento, l. militi ita haerede, §. et quia diximus. Although the law sometimes does this, as in Auth. hoc amplius, C. de fideicommissis; and sometimes a judge, as in the querela inofficiosi testamenti, as noted in D. de vulgari substitutione, l. in substitutione.

† Hence I admit that William of C. holds that one can have two direct heirs at successive times, so that they do not concur in the same time, for example Peter, while Peter lives, and Seius after the death of Peter, as he says, C. de haer. inst. l. extraneum. Whose opinion is not true. Rather Peter transmits the inheritance to his heir, and the substitute of Peter has to come by fideicommissum. And this is the true opinion in the matter. l. haereditas ex die. For by the acceptance of the inheritance a quasi contract is introduced, which of necessity passes to the heir of the one who accepts, and the obligations arising from that quasi contract. Now I come to the second point, and I say that if both substitutions are singular, it is evident that the said Nico. and Bo. can ask for nothing more than what the writing states, as ff. de nego. gesto. l. qui aliena. §. liberos. I come to the third point, and I say that if one substitution is pupillary, it is necessary to speak of the substitution made for the mother. And then it immediately follows that the subsequent substitution will be singular. And I said in the first counsel what I think about this.

† I now state that when a substitution is made to an impubes (minor) instituted in a specific thing under the condition that he should die during his minority, it appears that the substitution is pupillary and that it extends to all assets, as stated in the Digest, On Vulgar Substitution, law *cohaeres*, section *sin*. To the contrary, because there the text speaks of when the impubes is instituted universally or in a share; but if he has a universal coheir, then the impubes is reduced to the status of a single legatee, and the substitution appears to have been made as to a legatee, and he appears to have been requested as a legatee, as stated in the Digest, On Institution of Heirs, law *quotiens*. Which I believe is more correct and more in accordance with the testator’s intent. And then it follows that such a substitution does not hold against the legitime, insofar as it has been left. And if the said bequest does not exceed the legitime of the said Nic. and Bo., they could not claim anything on the ground of the said substitution made to the impubes. Therefore, it must be that if they can claim anything, they claim it on the ground of the fideicommissum left by the testator’s mother, which could be burdened by the testator. And then it immediately follows that she is burdened by operation of law in two ways, namely, individually with respect to the said Nico. and Boneagnus, and universally with respect to the hospital; because all these things accumulated together not only exceed the one-eighth part, but also occupy the entire patrimony. Hence, two fourths arise here, one concerning the singular bequests, which is called the Falcidian deduction, the other the Trebellian deduction. But the first can be deducted by Nicolaus and Boneagnus; the second cannot be deducted, because it has no place for pious causes according to the true interpretation. From which I conclude that, favoring the said Nic. and Boneagnus as much as we can, nevertheless we cannot favor them in this respect, that the Falcidian deduction does not apply, if an inventory has been made. Also, if the mother were understood to be a pupillary substitute, in truth every commission, namely of the bequests in the first and second wills, would appear, as stated in the Digest, On the Falcidian Law, law *in ratione*, section *quod vulgo*. However, this is not our case, because here there are not two wills, since there is no pupillary substitution. But assuming that there were, then one would have to resort to the matter of the said section *quod vulgo*. Indeed, to the matter of the law *qui fundum*, section *cohaeres*, in the same title. I cannot always write in descending order due to occupations, and sometimes due to bodily ailments. But whatever I write, I always wish it to be subject to correction under certain conditions. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A promise made under this condition, for example, "I promise to pay you if the assets are not solvent," fails if the assets are solvent.
body: QIida e Colcetam, and one daughter named Ci¬

† Cobictius, having one son named Colceta and one daughter named Cicilia, made a will, in which he instituted Colceta as universal heir, and instituted the said Cicilia to one hundred and fifty pounds. Then, after the testator died, the said Colceta was captured by robbers, for whose redemption his mother sold one piece of land of Angelutia to the wife of Auiclius. Then the same Auiclius, who was equally related to the said Cicilia, gave her in marriage to a certain Venancus, for whom he promised a dowry, in this manner, namely: 70 gold florins from the goods of the said Cobictius, and if the goods of the said Cobictius were not sufficient for the said amount, he promised to make good the deficiency from his own funds. And then Venancus paid from the said amount 20 florins. Then the same Colceta sold to the said Auiclius, individually and separately, all his own goods and the goods of the said Cobictius, and delivered them. Then the aforementioned Venancus demanded from the said Auiclius 50 florins, the remainder of the said dowry, and 15 florins for the aliment (interest) of the fruits of the said dowry money for the three past years, during which the payment of the said 50 florins had ceased. To whom, in court, Auiclius responded and protested that he assigned the goods of the said Cobictius for fulfilling the said promise. The judge pronounced that the said Venancus, for the said 50 florins, ought to retain all the said goods, if they amount to the said quantity, and if they do not amount to so much, that the said Auiclius ought to make good the deficiency from his own funds, and that two good men were to be appointed to appraise them. Then, having been appointed by the said judges and parties, the said two good men appraised the said goods, excluding the said piece of land, at more than seventy gold florins. Now the said Venancus demands the said piece of land sold. He also demands that the said Auiclius be compelled to pay to the said Venancus at the rate of ten florins per hundred for the aliment of the dowry, and until the insolvency ceases. Now it is asked, what is the law? I answer that the said judge judged wrongly, because Auiclius promised under the condition that if the goods were not solvent; and because the goods were sufficient, the said condition has failed. Hence, Auiclius was bound in no principal quantity. Therefore, neither was he bound in the aliment, which is accessory, as in D. si certum petatur, l. fin. Also relevant to this is D. de fideiussoribus, l. fideiussores, §. pro Aurelio. But since the sentence passed has become res iudicata, although it was unjust, nevertheless the said Auiclius is not bound by the said sentence, except insofar as the words of the sentence say, and for that time, not for the future, as in D. de usuris, l. 1, §. 1. Also, the said Auiclius must either have the said 20 florins, or from the said goods only that which is worth the said 20 florins. For when, namely, 70 florins were paid in possessions, the said 20 florins must be restored, lest payment be made in different things, as in D. de verbis obligatorum, l. 2, §. ex his, and l. si non sortem, §. fin., D. de condictione indebiti. Regarding the said piece of land, there is no doubt that the said Venancus cannot demand it; and that for the ransom of the said Colceta, he could sell it, as in C. de episcopali audientia, auth. si captivi. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Three species of executors are found. And no. 3.
2. When several executors are appointed in a will, whether all must execute, or whether one may act without the others.
3. Whether executors named by their proper names may appoint sub-executors and delegate their functions to others.
4. How it is determined whether a commission is of an industrial nature or not.
5. There are three things that make an execution personal.
body:
The Reverend Lord of Peace, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, made a will, in which he provided and ordered concerning the executors as follows, namely:

I name, make, and constitute as executors of this my will or ordinance the most Reverend Fathers, Messer Angelo, Bishop of Albano, and William, Bishop of Sabina, and John, Cardinal Priest of Saint Mark, and Rainald, Cardinal Deacon of Saint Adrian; also the venerable Fathers, Messer Luca Micerino, Bishop of Perugia, who is and who shall be for the time being, and Niccolò de Anxino, notary and secretary of the Lord Pope; and the venerable and discreet gentlemen, Messer Bernardo de Hero, Apostolic Chamberlain, and John Rubinelli, auditors of the Sacred Palace; and John Fernandez, and Laurence Egidii Angelerii, aforesaid; and Andrew de Monte Leone, vicar of my said chamberlain, canon of Todi, and prior of the said monastery of Mount Olivet, of the diocese of Perugia. I order, willing and disposing, that two or more of the said executors may carry out the ordinance and disposition of this kind in its entirety, and in each of its parts, and freely exercise the business of its execution without contradiction by any of my heirs. And that the others of them may, according to the mode aforesaid, carry out through others, or some of them, whatever has been begun. They may also, each of the aforementioned, with the commission of the others, or some, or any one of them, exercise particular matters of the said execution.

I also will and order that all legacies and whatever I have left in any manner be paid by the hand of the said executors, or those appointed by them, without contradiction by anyone. And because the aforementioned Lord Bishop Micerino, Niccolò de Anxino, John Bernardi, Laurence, and Andrew are more fully informed, by reason of greater association and familiarity, regarding my affairs and will, I beseech my said cardinals that they will and permit that the aforementioned Bishop Micerino, and Lord Niccolò de Anxino, John Fernandez, Laurence, and Andrew, if present, with the counsel and aid of the same cardinals and the other executors named above, or some or any one of them, shall principally bear the burden of this my execution, as it shall seem fitting to the said Bishop Micerino, and Lords Niccolò, John, Laurence, and Andrew, and to each of them.

Furthermore, I will and order that the said executors may review the statutes ordered by me in the said college of scholars, and correct them, and order whatever they shall see as useful concerning the correction of the said house and other matters regarding the same statute, provided that they may not diminish the number of scholars, nor change the places from which I ordered them to be taken.

Now it has happened that all the said executors named by their proper names have died, except for Lord B., now Bishop of Gubbio. Therefore, it is asked: to whom does the administration of the said house of wisdom belong? Whether to the said Lord B. alone, with the counsel of the Bishop of Perugia and the Prior of Monte Morello, or Mount Olivet; or to the said Lord Bishop of Perugia and the said Prior; or to all three; or to any one of them by himself alone. And whether counsel must be followed.

This venerable testator was a man most learned in law; therefore, it is credible that he uttered no word that he had not previously weighed and considered in his mind.

† And if I consider the matter well, there are three kinds of executors, just as there are three appellations for tutors appointed by will. For some are called honorary, who are appointed for the honor of those who appoint them, of the person from whom they are appointed, and of those for whose benefit they are appointed when left as executors; and of this kind were the Lord Cardinals, who were left as executors so that they would be bound to uphold the testator’s will and the House of Wisdom, lest anyone unjustly harass the said House, as in ff. de solutionibus, l. quod si forte, § 1, in the first response, and the first gloss; and as in ff. de testamento tutelae, l. iure nostro. Others, however, are appointed for the sake of knowledge of the matter, either because they knew the testator’s will better, as in ff. de dote praelegata, l. Theopompus, or because they knew the strength of the patrimony better, such as the testator’s freedmen, left as executors, or the testator’s intimates: who are compared in this book to those whose office is to instruct other executors, but certainly they themselves can execute, as in the aforementioned l. quod si forte, in the second response, and the verse “dico igitur.” And certainly, if we consider the said testament, five were named of this kind of executors, namely, Lord Lucas, Nicholas, John, Lawrence, and Andrew, as being fully informed of the affairs and the will of the testator. Here it must be noted that the testator disposed that they, and each of them, should principally bear the burden of execution under two conditions, namely, if they were present, and with the counsel and aid of the same two Cardinals and the other aforementioned persons, or some or any one of them, as it shall seem good to the said Lords Lucas, Nicholas, etc., and each of them. I therefore say that the aforementioned five were appointed as executors for the sake of knowledge, and as principals in the actual office and exercise thereof. But it must be considered that all power of executors comes from the will, as in ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. in conditionibus primum locum, and l. pater seuerinam, § conditionem.

Whether, from the aforementioned five, one can exercise the office without the other: it seems that he cannot, because the words of the testament say "with the counsel and aid," which require concurrence in the act of exercise. For no one aids another by doing nothing, since aid is an act and requires a deed, as in D. de minoribus, l. Auxilium; and D. de excusationibus tutorum, l. 2, §. Auxiliantur autem sic. And a pact is said to be clothed with the aid of the law. And when the law and the pact agree in the same opinion and effect, as noted in D. de pactis, l. Legitima. Unless one should say in this way that it was added not to diminish the office, but rather to diminish the honor, so that he may be supported by the help and aid of another, so that counsel is required by necessity, but not aid. But I believe the former is truer, because this is a certain form of mandate, as in D. de manumissionibus testamento, l. Si ita fuerit, §. Si non simul. Moreover, even if no mention were made of the other, except of counsel, yet where a colleague must seek the counsel of a colleague, it is necessary that they agree in one opinion. For if they contradict each other, they hinder each other, as in D. de administratione tutorum, l. Titium et Mevium, in principio; and D. de cura furiosi, l. Consilio, §. Finis. Nor can there be a case in which counsel is not required: since among the executors there are two perpetual ones, namely the Lord Bishop of Perugia and the Prior of Oliveto. Unless perhaps when the dignity or the prior is vacant. Therefore I say "perhaps," because unless in matters perishable in time, perhaps a citation should be awaited, as in D. de naufragiis et mutuis, l. Praetor, §. Si. For at the dignity there is no execution except in habit; but at the person it is in act, as argued in D. si quis testamento liberum esse ius fuerit, l. 1, §. Scaevola. And although the burden of management is principally committed to the said five in their own name—I say principally, i.e., more principally, as in D. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, l. Quia tamen ita—demum if they are present, D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. Si quis mihi bona, §. Coram, with the counsel and aid of someone, etc. Hence, what is committed jointly cannot be performed separately. For we are not speaking here of pious causes, certainly, and then the form of the mandate is to be followed, as in c. Ultima, de testibus, lib. 6. But it is a matter of form, whatever savors of a condition or is equivalent, as in D. de manumissionibus testamento, l. Si ita fuerit; and D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. Si quis mihi bona, §. Si coram; and l. Eum qui duobus, §. Filius; and D. de arbitris, l. Non distinguemus, §. Cum plures; and Extra de arbitris, c. Cum olim; and de electione, c. Cum in veteri.

† Now I come to the ordination of the House of Wisdom, and I say that it is the third kind of executors, namely those left simply, and as regards the third kind, that part of the testament applies which says: "Moreover, I will and ordain that the said executors may review the statutes, etc." Here it must be noted that the testator says "the said executors." Hence, at least two must participate in the ordination of the house and the election of the corrector: because the plural number requires at least two, as in D. ad Trebellianum, l. Iulius Febus. Nor do I understand the above matters in this chapter to be repeated, because the subject matter is undeniably different in reason; I do not understand a tacit repetition. Indeed, it is far removed from reason to provide for so arduous a matter concerning the house as for other particular matters. And certainly it would be contrary to reason if one person alone could introduce an error there without the other being consulted or objecting: because whenever election pertains to several persons, one cannot prejudice another, nor extinguish the office or voice of another, because one of two is not the greater part. And because it is entrusted to each individually, and the laws are most common in matters of elections. But in every matter the rule is handed down that one of two equals has no power over the other, as in C. de auctoritate praestanda, l. si. For even a donkey swells with pride if he sees himself being apprehended as an equal, as is read and noted in D. de acquisitione possessionis, l. 1, §. veteres. Therefore, rightly, whenever the subsequent provisions differ from the preceding ones in the reason of the matter, so that the latter does not apply, the conjunction of reason is understood to give a new form, not to repeat the superior one, as in D. de legatis 1, l. licet Imperator; D. de legatis 2, l. Seium. Moreover, even if the preceding provisions were repeated, the same conclusion would hold because of the words "with counsel and assistance," as has been proved above. And although the late Lord Vincetinus himself did many things alone, this was perhaps because others were present, and the writing seems to speak of those present, not of those absent. Or perhaps he did not act according to law, because at least the prior of Monte Morello, who was present in the Diocese of Perugia, should have been consulted. Or rather, he certainly acted according to law, because others consented and accommodated patience, as in D. de manumissione testamento, l. Lucius Titius servo. As they ought to have done, on account of the illustrious dignity of the cardinalate. For it was not right to contradict such a Cardinal, whose faith the testator chose above all others, as appears from the order of the writing, arg. D. de usufructu, l. quotiens; and De consensu, dist. 2, c. in Christo pater; and D. de procuratoribus, l. filius, §. sed et filia; D. de manumissione vindicatione, l. pater, in fine; D. de iudicibus, l. si longius, §. ult.; D. de administratione tutorum, l. si plures. Concluding, therefore, I think that before the Reverend Father Lord Laurentius alone, the ordination of the said house is not, but before all three, or at least two of them, on account of the words of the plural number, which plural number is not resolved into singularities: where plurality is required as a form, as in D. de arbitris, l. Pedius, §. in seruum, with the following law, and l. sicuti tribus; and D. de re iudicata, l. Pomponius; and c.

It remains to consider another doubt, namely whether the said executors, appointed by their proper names or designated by titles of dignity, may appoint sub-executors and entrust to others the execution of their will. And it seems that a distinction must be made. For it matters greatly whether the testator chose personal industry and trustworthiness, or dignity and authority. In the first case, that which is personal cannot be delegated, because the rule of law is that those things which are not transmissible are not grantable to another, as in D. de administratione et mandatu tutoris, l. ex pluribus. But those things which are based on industry are not transmissible, as in D. de cura furiosi, l. cuius bonis. Therefore, they cannot be entrusted to another. Those things, however, which pertain to right by authority, seem to be able to be entrusted to another on account of the authority of the dignity, which does not always allow its person to be present at affairs, especially small and trivial ones, as in C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione, l. optimam. For indeed it does not seem that the testator considered that bishops, who sometimes are present for certain causes of the Roman Church and are in the service of the Pope, could not entrust light and moderate matters; certainly, since they are considered to be present, as in D. de excusationibus tutorum, l. iurisperitos. Hence recourse must be had to them, not the contrary, since they cannot depart from the side of the Supreme Pontiff, as in D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. talis, §. praesens. Or else, affairs which are conducted by the determination of the mind, and which require singular industry, are therefore not delegable, because they adhere to the person and are passions of the mind, as in D. de statu liberorum, l. servus si haeres, ver. duae sunt enim causae. But certainly it seems that, since they are such in which the authority of the dignity is chosen, they generally cannot be delegated, as in C. ne liceat potentioribus, l. 1, in fine. But there it speaks in a just Empire, where terrible authority is entrusted for severer punishment. And on account of the magnitude of the affair, it cannot be entrusted to another, as in D. de officio eius, cui mandatum est iuris dicendi, l. 1, in principio. On this matter, Lord Cynus expedites himself in one word. For he says in l. id, quod pauperibus, C. de episcopis et clericis, that an executor appointed for affairs may entrust them to another, just as a procurator constituted for affairs. But this is a very bad similarity, for a procurator substituted for affairs may be revoked by the living master, if the procurator displeases him. But in a sub-executor of a last will it is not so: for the deceased cannot revoke, as in D. de adimendis legatis, l. quod si iterum. Nor could his heir revoke, if the sub-executor had been constituted by the authority of the deceased, as in D. de iure dotium, l. ego, §. 1. A similar reason is given between contracts and last wills, as in l. 1, de legatis 2. And therefore a distinction must be made between necessary and voluntary absence. For one absent due to public necessity may entrust to another, or recourse must be had to him for counsel and information on what is to be done, and also followed, if access is easy. Otherwise, if difficult, for example if he is traveling abroad or is absent on a long embassy, as in D. de pronuntiis, l. aut longa, and D. de statu liberorum, l. cum haeres, in principio, and D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. multa non committitur. Thus I see it in any guardian, although the testator chose him by singular trust and hope, Inst. de satisfactionibus, in principio, as Inst. de cura, §. si, and note D. de procuratoribus, l. neque tutores, and l. actor, rem ratione habita. Also, because one having a universal commission may entrust one case to another in the manner of an ordinary judge, as noted in D. de iure omnium iudiciorum, l. solet praetor. If the testator trusts him, therefore he trusts in his acts and his commission; hence trust alone is not the cause, if the commission is personal, but industrial. It would well be among personal and non-delegable causes, as in Extra, de sponsalibus, de legibus, quoniam appellatio, in fine, through Innocentius.

And if it is asked how I may know whether a commission is one requiring personal industry or not, I answer that this is known from the form of the mandate, as in C. de caducis tollendis, § ut autem, and from the magnitude and quality of the business. For there are certain businesses so great and so arduous that they are not usually entrusted to anyone except those perfect in Christ, as in C. de summa Trinitate, l. epistolas inter claras. I therefore consider that in these businesses of the house of wisdom, some matters are very easy to dispense with, and in these sub-executors may be appointed, for example in the exception of servants, tenants, or lodgers, and in similar cases. But some are arduous, which pertain to the governance and state of the house, and its general reformation. And these cannot be done by sub-commissioners by any executor named in his own proper name. And the same seems to apply to executors appointed under the name of a dignity, if they are absent voluntarily, and not on business, for example in the suburbs, or a nearby village, that they may order that nothing be done without them, nor entrust such arduous businesses as require industry, arg. ff. de ritu nuptiarum, l. generali; ff. de procuratoribus, l. Pomponius; and l. non solum, § si status; ff. de arbitris, l. non distinguemus, § de officio; and l. in compromissis; and l. si cum dies, § arbiter; and ff. de annuis legatis, l. Mevia, in fine.

And in sum, three things make an execution personal, namely, the form of the mandate, because it is commanded to someone that he do it by himself. Secondly, skill, when singular skill is required, which is not acquired by man naturally, but through continuous exercises, teachings, and experiences, as noted in c. Dispendia, in the beginning, de rescriptis, book 6. The third is the magnitude of the business. Hence, visitors and reformers ought to go to the place; and if they are appointed by a person, they ought to go by themselves; but if they are appointed by law, they may commit the office of visitation to others, as having ordinary jurisdiction, 61. distinction, c. Ultima, de rescriptis; c. Dilectus filius. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an inquiry may be conducted for the same homicide both in the place of the offense and in the place of origin of the offender.
2. If execution has been carried out against the goods in the place of the offense against the person who was inquired into and condemned, and subsequently the person is apprehended in the place of his origin, where he too has been condemned: whether execution ought to be carried out against the person.
3. Which judge is said to have first obtained precedence: he who apprehends the person, or he to whom satisfaction is first made.
body: Cagnus of Treviso killed his brother Lidda in the city of Foligno while he was committing adultery. For this homicide, he was condemned in absentia in the said city of Foligno to pay one thousand livres of deniers to the chamberlain of the commune of the said city, under the condition that if, within the days after he came under the jurisdiction of the said commune of Foligno, he did not satisfy the said condemnation, his head should be amputated. At the time the crime was committed, the officials of the said city seized and took from the said Cagnus all his movable goods which he had in the said city of Foligno and its district, and these came into the hands of the chamberlain of the said commune, being worth one hundred florins or thereabouts. After the court of the commune of Treviso had also tried the said Cagnus for the same homicide and condemned him in absentia to pay one thousand livres to the chamber of the said commune, for receipt by the commune itself, the said Cagnus was finally detained by the officials and retainers of the Podestà of Treviso. This occurred after he had, three days later, made a settlement and obtained a remission of the said condemnation from the city of Foligno, so that he was released by the commune of Foligno.

† It is asked whether an obligation has been contracted with respect to the Commune of Terni, or not. And it seems that one should first say that in the court of the Commune of Terni no proceedings could be taken against him, because the same man’s offense ought not to be investigated repeatedly, as in D. 47.10.1 (*Licet*). § *Si*. Moreover, although a person may obtain jurisdiction in several places, yet if there has been a prior seizure of jurisdiction (*praeuentio*) in one place, the matter cannot be cognized elsewhere, as in D. 2.1.1 (*Si quis postea*) and D. 2.1.1 (*Cum quaedam puella*). § *Si*. Furthermore, it is absurd that he should be punished in as many places as he obtains jurisdiction, because a person ought not to be subjected to several full penalties for the same crime, as if they descended from different laws or statutes, as in D. 48.1.1 (*Senatus censuit*). Moreover, when there are multiple accusations for vengeance, one consumes the other, as in D. 47.10.1 (*Quod Senatus*). Moreover, if prior seizure of jurisdiction is considered, the Commune of Foligno proceeded in acting and condemning. Moreover, it proceeded in execution. For the seizure of goods made from the beginning of the time of the offense, although it was done *de facto*, took the place of the annotation of goods, which goods thus annotated ought to be computed in the ban and in the lands in the quantity of one thousand pounds of denarii, in which he was condemned. And it is certain that the perception of part induces executive prior seizure, as in C. 7.71.3. Moreover, under the *ius commune*, remission to the place of the offense has place, as in Auth. *Ut nulli iudici*. § *Si quis vero comprehensorum*. This remission is made for the end that execution be carried out there. But since we do not care about the mode when the end is achieved, and here we have the end, because execution has been made, or is deemed made, because remission and satisfaction are equivalent, as in D. 47.10.1 (*Sed si unus*). § *Si ante iudicem*, rightly after remission, he who remits ought not to interfere. Nor regarding the mode, as in D. 48.1.1 (*Si cui*). § *Si*. Moreover, consider that he who commits an offense ought to be punished by the penalty established in the place of the offense, as fully noted by Bartolus in D. 1.4.1 (*Cunctos populos*). Therefore, he is punished by the law that prevails in the place of the offense; or if he is not punished by the same effect of the law, rightly therefore he ought not to be punished further, because the law has been satisfied, as in D. 48.1.1 (*Diuus*, or *Vespasianus*). § *Si*. Moreover, a pecuniary penalty takes the place of a capital penalty. But if the capital penalty, i.e., of life or limb, had been exacted, no further execution would be made, either because of impossibility by nature, or because of impossibility by law, as noted in D. 47.2.1 (*Vulgare*). In the beginning. Moreover, the fiscal chambers are different, i.e., the chamber of the Commune of Terni, yet they depend from one principal superior, just as from the Roman Church, from which all jurisdiction in the Duchy of Spoleto depends. Since therefore the principle is referred to one, one satisfaction ought to suffice; because whenever many things arise from one source, they are removed by one satisfaction, as in C. 4.14.1 (*Si*) and C. 5.4.1 (*Fin*). On the contrary, it is made certain that a person can become liable in several places by reason of the same offense, i.e., in the place of the offense, in the place of domicile, and in the place of origin. And where jurisdiction is established by appearance, there he is to be condemned, as there the crime ought to be tried, D. 2.1.1. Therefore, the process held in both places, even by inquisition, remained valid, although Speculator says that outside the place of the offense no other judge has power to inquire. And the same is held by Johannes Andreae in the additions to the Speculum. And it was also formerly observed *de facto*. For Lord Cynus, disputing, held the contrary. And the same Bartolus, i.e., that one could inquire against a subject offending outside the territory. If therefore one can inquire, therefore he could also be condemned. Then I argue: and he could be condemned, therefore execution ought to be made, because the decrees of the Praetors ought not to be illusory, as in D. 2.1.1 (*Si praetor*). In the beginning. Moreover, these two fiscs are not joint debtors, but are entirely separate creditors, therefore an inequitable condition ought not to be imposed on one by the other, as in D. 9.3.1 (*In concedendo*). Hence one could not dissolve the obligation of the other, because he has no mandate for this from law or man, nor his procurator, as in D. 46.3.1 (*Qui hominem*). § *Si nullo*. Moreover, this man was condemned for different contumacies, namely, therefore if he is punished by several penalties according to the customs of the places, as in C. 10.4.1 (*Eos*) and D. 48.1.1 (*Nunquam plura*). Moreover, the condition of the prior seizer is better. And prior seizure is said in this case to be he who first exacts, or who is first in possession of the pledge, so to speak, i.e., in possession, or detention, of the person of the condemned. For prior seizure requires a fact, and we consider in prior seizure the effect of the thing, because we are not here treating of prior seizure with respect to jurisdiction to be exercised, according to the notes in D. 9.2.1 (*Si quis a multis*) and C. 7.71.1 (*Cum rem publicam*). Moreover, for this side serves the disputation of Jacobus de Belvis, which he places in C. 7.62.2. Moreover, by paying the ban in one place, one is not released from another place, holds Bartolus expressly in D. 47.12.1 (*Sepulchri violati actio*). In the first place, where he openly decided this question. Moreover, that a person is punished differently by the diversity of places, appears in D. 48.19.1 (*Relegatorum*). § *Constitutum*. Solution. It must be considered first that under the *ius commune*, inquisitions are not premised, except in those cases expressly stated in law, as in D. 48.5.2. § *Si publico*. Although Nicolaus de Tudeschis wished to reduce this matter to certain rules, which I do not pursue. For the law says that where an accuser is lacking, there the judge does not make punishment, as in C. 7.61.1 (*Si filium tuum*) and D. 48.2.1 (*Rescripto*). § *Si quis accusatorem non habens*. And therefore the ancient doctors held that the judge of origin could not inquire into an offense committed outside the territory. For not under the *ius commune*, except in certain cases, nor under municipal law, because municipal law does not give form to offenses committed outside its territory, as in C. 10.32.1 (*Ut animarum*). § *Statuto*. On constitutions. Book 6. And D. 48.19.1 (*Relegatorum*). In the beginning. § *Sicut autem*. And § *Interdicere*. And § *Per contrarium*.
