Moreover, grant that under the *ius commune* one could not inquire preceding form or indications, yet from such an inquisition no definitive judgment could be made against an absent person in a capital case, as in D. 48.19.1 (*Absentem*).

† Nor does the objection hold if it is said that, with regard to the ordering of the judicial process, we look to the place of the court, because rendering a definitive judgment is not a matter of mere judicial order, but is something decisive. And therefore it cannot have such authority unless derived from a statute of the city. And a statute does not extend beyond its territory, whether one speaks of the sentence of the statute itself or of the sentence of a judge by virtue of the statute, as in the law *extra territorium* and similar authorities. From which it would seem to be said that the inquiry conducted in the territory of Treviso was invalid. However, because the Modern jurists commonly hold the contrary, the only remaining doubt concerns the satisfaction, namely, when satisfaction has been made in the place of the delict, which is the principal place: whether another execution can be carried out in another place, especially considering the aforementioned facts, and especially given that preventive action was taken by the prior seizure of goods in the city of Fossombrone. And because a payment for absolution must be regarded as such, as noted in the Digest, *de exceptionibus rei iudicatae*, law *si quis cum totum*, section *plane*; and as noted in the Code, *ad legem Aquiliam*, law *ex morte*; and because the said territories are of the same principal forum of the Holy Roman Church; and because the said penalties are of the same kind and form, since both principal penalties are pecuniary and mutually receive performance, according to the note by Dyther in law 1, section *dixerit aliquis*, Digest, *de publicis*; and because properly speaking the said territories do not have a treasury, but have certain revenues by concession of the treasury, yet according to common law it is as I have said, especially because penalties are lucrative causes, as noted in the Digest, *de exceptione doli*, law *apud Celsum*, section *de auctoris*, which, although they may have accrued from one person or from one principal treasury, the rights of different parties should not be duplicated, as in the Digest, *de legibus secundis*, law *Lucius*, section *impuberem*; otherwise an absurdity would follow. Suppose, for instance, that the commune of Fossombrone paid one thousand pounds, and the commune of Treviso could not pay another thousand, and thus according to the form of the superior sentence it would seem to be said that the said satisfaction would suffice in law to remove the entire obligation arising from the same delict. And although the commune of Treviso might say to the commune of Fossombrone, "As far as you are concerned, I have free hands, and I should not be prevented from my right," as in the Digest, *si servus venditus*, law *sicuti*, section *Aristo*, it is answered that this does not occur by the mere act of a man, but by the act of the law, that is, by legal disposition, as is clear from the laws and reasons cited above. And this opinion could be defended in law, yet by custom in certain places the contrary is observed, Code, *de testamentis*, law *nullum*, I hold that the condition of the one who acts first in execution is the better one.

† Hence it remains only to consider who is said to have preempted, whether he who seized the person or he to whom satisfaction was first rendered, even if satisfaction was rendered only in part, according to the aforementioned third law, C. de noua. Therefore, it being established that the commune of Fuligno preempted first in taking from the goods, as is proposed in the case, the said goods will be extinguished by operation of law through the solution, or discharge, of the double obligation, namely on account of the commune of Fuligno, which I hold to have been removed; nevertheless, as I have said, the lords of the places do not wish their fiscal rights to be extinguished by others. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether those who practice one and the same art or trade, sometimes one person, sometimes another, in a single shop, are called or presumed to be partners.
2. How partnership among certain persons is to be proved, and how partners are bound one for another.
body: A certain John, son of James, purchased certain castrense lands from a certain Gerinus, and therefore constituted himself his debtor in the amount of 29 gold florins. Finally, the aforementioned Gerinus brings an action against Anthony, brother of the said John, as partner of the said John in the butcher’s trade; and he proves this by witnesses, who state that during the time mentioned in the petition they saw the aforementioned John and Anthony together practicing the butcher’s trade, slaughtering beasts, butchering, and selling at one stall; and that they were considered partners.

† Now it is asked whether, on this ground, the said Antonius, as partner of the said John, should be condemned in another action. And it seems that he should, because whenever two persons jointly exercise some craft, and sometimes one, sometimes the other, in the same shop or stall, one is deemed substituted for the other, and the other for the one; thus one binds the other, and the other the one, at least for a half share, as in D. de exercendo (14,1), l. Si tamen plures. To the contrary it seems, for it does not follow that because two brothers together carry on the butchery trade, therefore one, by buying in his own name, binds the other; for he who does not buy in the name of the partnership, but in his own, conducts business for himself alone. And he who buys for himself did not have the intention of binding another, but only himself, who contracted in his own proper name, unless it were proved that the thing was turned to common advantage, as in C. quod cum eo (2,19), l. Ei qui. One thing is that the vendor followed the credit of the partnership; another, that he followed only the credit of the buyer, without mention of the partnership. For just as from such a contract the partnership body does not sue, but only the buyer, so conversely only the buyer ought to be sued, as in D. pro socio (17,2), l. Duobus, § Si fratres; and C. de decuriis (10,32), l. Licet, lib. 10. And the law says that if there are two partners, and one buys in his own name, it is his own, not common; nevertheless, because it is to be shared, he is sued by the action pro socio, as in D. pro socio (17,2), l. Si quis societatem contraxisse. La Pichola. Certainly that law favors Gerino, for if he can sue to have it shared, so too can he be sued.

† Hence, the better opinion seems to be that the form of the partnership initiated is not established, nor that it was initiated for buying and selling at common risk. And it is possible that some stand together to sell in a certain tavern or stall, yet they are not partners, but one of them is the owner and the other the *institor* (manager). Hence, it does not appear that a partnership cohabited for buying has been conclusively proven; because these acts can be performed without the law and name of partnership; and thus partnership is not sufficiently proven. For partnership is proven in two ways: either by the express agreement of the contracting parties, or by social acts. But it is not proven by social acts that they were accustomed to buy in common as partners, that they shared losses and profits with each other, nor that they brought in gain in common. And thus the social acts indicative of a firm partnership contracted for these purposes do not appear to be proven. Furthermore, the custom does not appear to be proven that they were accustomed to concur promiscuously in social acts in forming an obligation. Hence, partnership does not appear to be proven either by words or by the things themselves and facts. For the reality of acts induces a tacit partnership when gain is brought in common. Which does not appear to be proven here, argument from D. de edendo, l. Praetor, §. sed si filius, vers. sed recte Sabinus.

And although I believe conscientiously that these two brothers consented as partners, and that they were accustomed to trade as partners, sometimes one, sometimes the other. Furthermore, it does not appear that the said beasts were bought for the purpose of butchering; for when a partnership looks to a certain cause, that cause must be proven, argument from D. de exercitoria, l. Lucius. Considering all things, therefore, it seems to be said that even if partnership were proven, which however is not proven for this act about which inquiry is made, such proof is not sufficient for the condemnation of the defendant, as in D. de institoria, l. cuicunque, §. non tamen omne; and D. de exercitoria, l. Lucius. For it may be that he bought the castrated oxen for the purpose of reselling them alive, but the purpose of the butcher’s trade consists in reselling the flesh of dead animals, as in l. cum Delanionis, in principio, D. de fundo instrato. Hence, because the proof does not appear sufficient, as in D. de deposito, l. 1, §. si quis argentum; and Extra, de probat., cap. in praesentia. But if it had been proven that they were accustomed to buy or sell as partners, then partnership would seem to be proven, and the act of one partner would bind the other body of the partnership. And the body of the partnership being bound, all partners are bound, each for the part he has in the partnership, as in D. ad legem Falcidiam, hoc servando. To this effect serves D. quod cum eo, l. Titianus. From this it appears that it does not seem to be proven that they were partners in contracting, as in D. de administratione tutorum, l. Titium et Mevium, §. alterum.

Furthermore, if it were proven that the said beasts were butchered in the tavern without the butcher shop of the two brothers, then I would advise against the plaintiff, because in effect it benefited both, as in the said l. ei qui. I do not deny, however, that the said proofs make great conjectures in the mind of a good man. For beasts that are butchered do not live on wind, but must be fed, as in C. de alimentis pupillis praestandis, l. si. And thus partnership in butchering presupposes its necessary antecedent, or from things commonly happening. This is the first question as to the quantity, which is small. Nevertheless, for the understanding of the truth of the law, I have spoken somewhat at length, and I believe that all things considered, it is not conclusively proven, always saving the substance of the truth. For in the libel it was alleged that they acted by authority of commerce. And this is not proven, although the witnesses say that they stood together to butcher and sell beasts. Hence, by strict law, such a thing is not proven, as I said, which was sufficient for the condemnation of the said Antonio. By the said l. ei qui, vers. alioquin, C. quod cum eo. For a brother contracting in his own name does not bind his brother, unless it was transacted in fraternal matters; therefore, much less a partner. And it serves D. pro socio, l. sed nec aes alienum. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
0. A legacy of food, clothing, and lodging made to the rector of a certain church is considered perpetual, and not for the duration of life.
1. Of the rector.
2. Whether bad grammar invalidates a legacy.
body: Tactus Iiciae made his will, in which, as it is thus proposed, he instituted Bartholomew, Francis, and Amador as his universal heirs. And he provided that if any one of them should die without legitimate sons born to them, the other should succeed. Furthermore, he added that the said Amador could not sell, nor alienate, nor in any way donate anything of his goods without the license of two of the nearest blood relatives, and also of the Rector of the churches of Mark and James; and that he must have food, clothing, and habitation in the house.

† Now it is asked whether the said Rector ought to have the said food, clothing, and house habitation, since the said heirs died without legitimate children. The said Rector ought to have food, clothing, and house habitation, which are presumed to have been left in consideration of the church, and not of the person, as in D. de annuis legatis, l. annua, § 1. And such a legacy is perpetual, and does not terminate upon the death of the Rector, unless it were proven that it was left in consideration of the person, and not of the church, as in X. de testamento, c. acquisisti, and D. de excusationibus tutorum, l. tutor petitus, § quae tutoribus, and noted in c. ultima, de testamento, lib. 6. And there the glossa says that if the Rector of the church were a person related to the testator, it would be presumed that the legacy was left in consideration of the person only. To this effect is what is noted in C. de legatis, l. cum alienam.

It is true that this instrument has poor grammar, on account of which it might be doubtful whether those words, “and also of the Rector, etc.,” refer to the license or rather to the legacy. And it seems to me that they refer to the legacy; otherwise, those words which follow, namely “ought to bequeath from his goods,” would be of no effect, which ought not to be the case, as in D. de legatis 1, l. si quando. And in case of doubt, we must interpret so that such a bequest may be valid and not fail, as noted in C. de fideicommissis, l. voluntas. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether legacies made in a testament, in which a living son is instituted heir and a posthumous son is passed over, and a codicillary clause is appended, are owed intestate to the posthumous son; and if so, whether by the instituted heir, or by the posthumous son, or by both.
2. Whether the brothers of Saint Augustine succeed and exclude the mother, if entering that religion excluded her.
3. Whether the Order of Saint Augustine is regarded in the place of children, so as to exclude a fideicommissum left in default of children.
4. Whether one detaining the goods of the deceased for legacies made to him by his own authority falls from his right.
body: A certain man instituted his son Andrew as his heir in his will. But Peter made a will and codicils, and in the will he instituted his son Andrew as his heir, and, unaware that his wife was pregnant, he passed over the posthumous child, who was born after the testator’s death around the eighth month, and whose guardianship the mother assumed. And he died in infancy. Now the question arises whether the legacies left in the said will are due or not. And because the statute provides that the mother does not succeed when agnates exist, except in the eighth part: it is asked whether the son of the said Ser Peter, and the said Andrew, who is a professed member of the mendicant order of Saint Augustine, excludes the said mother in any respect or not. And whether the said mother, by detaining the goods for the legacies left to her and for another right which she now claims in the said succession, falls from her right by judicial authority. On these points, I, Baldus, consulted, say as to the first point concerning the omission of the posthumous child,

† That there are three opinions, presupposing the codicillary clause, in words and acts, for the present and future time: for example, if it were not valid, etc. For some say that the said clause operates for nothing in the omission of a posthumous child, and that legacies are not said to be due in any way on account of an unforeseen case, as argued from D. de testamento militis, l. miles codicillis, §. miles in supremis; and C. eodem, l. sicut certi; and l. si cum vel in utero; and D. de pactis, l. tale pactum, §. fin.; and C. de revocatione donationum, l. si nunquam; and C. de fideicommissis, l. cum acutissimi. Others say that the legacies are valid for the share of the instituted heir, but not for the share of the omitted heir. And this on such reasoning: because the instituted heir has the will of the testator even by succeeding intestate, and therefore he can be burdened, as in l. 2, D. de iure codicillorum. But the omitted heir does not have the will of the testator, neither from the will nor intestate, and therefore the testator did not intend, nor provide, nor ought or could have done so regarding burdening him, since he did not honor him, as in C. de fideicommissis, l. eo; and l. pe; and note in l. 1, §. vel maxime, D. de collatione bonorum; and D. de legatis 2, l. cum pater, §. ex filio. And this is supported by the theory of Dyonisius in l. cum pater, §. cum aestimaret, D. de legatis 2, where he says that when there are two sons, one succeeding according to the will of the testator, the other against, or contrary to, the will, legacies are due for the share of the one succeeding according to the will of the testator, and not for the share of the one succeeding against, or contrary to, the will, as in D. de iure codicillorum, l. is qui. The third opinion says that by the codicillary clause he ought to have considered any person succeeding intestate, as in D. de legatis 2, l. Lucius, §. filiam; and D. de testamentis, l. ex ea; and l. is qui; and D. de in iusto testamento, l. posthumus, §. si paganus. And it seems expressly stated in D. de fideicommissis liberis, l. generaliter, §. ex testamento. I distinguish: either the legacies are left purely, or under a condition which does not regard the lack of children: and then the opinion of Dyonisius in the said §. cum aestimaret is true. Or they are left under a condition of lack of children, for example, because the testator, who did not think he had more than one son, said, if he should die without sons, I leave such legacies; then, a posthumous child being born, and thus the final consideration of the testator regarding the lack of children failing, perhaps the legacies are not due in any way on account of the defect of the final cause, as argued from D. de hereditate instituenda, l. si in ratione sui: because if the institution is vitiated on account of the defect of the final cause, much more is the legacy vitiated, as argued from D. de adimendis legatis, l. ex parte. Someone might say, this is contrary to the case of the said l. si, D. de hereditate instituenda, for there the legacies are valid. But I answer that there the final cause did not regard the legacies, but only the institution. It is safer, however, to say that they are due for the share of the instituted heir, and not for the share of the omitted heir, so that what is the law regarding part to part, the same law is regarding the whole to the whole. For just as they would be due in full if the posthumous child were not born, so they are due for the share if he is born, since the condition of lack of children is not added except to one, and to him alone by name, as argued from D. ad Trebellianum, l. Lucius, §. Gaio; and D. de vulgari substitutione, l. vel singulis: and there is no person who, by the presumed will of the deceased, ought to exclude the legatees, because the omitted heir does not have the will of the deceased, but rather is said to succeed against the will, because he comes by breaking the will, and thus by breaking the mind of the testator. Therefore, he succeeds against the mind of the testator, and against the testator’s consideration and disposition. And hence it is that he has against the will, as in D. de secundis tabulis, l. aequissimum, §. expectandum; and what is noted in C. de collatione, l. ut liberis; and D. de in iusto testamento, l. nam et si sub conditione, §. rumpendo; and l. posthumorum.

† On the second point, I say that the mother does not succeed, except in the eighth degree, because the brothers of Saint Augustine, by virtue of a papal privilege, retain the rights of agnation in succession; since the Order, according to the said privilege, is capable [of inheriting]. It would be otherwise in the case of the Minor Brothers who had professed the order before the death of the posthumous heir: because the Order of the Minor Brothers does not stand in the way of the mother, since they are considered dead with regard to successions, for natural death can effect nothing, as is stated in C. de Ep. et cl. l. Deo nobis.

And from this another doubt is resolved, namely whether the Order of Saint Augustine is regarded in the place of children, so that it excludes a fideicommissum left in default of children: as in the Authentica de sanctis episcopis, § hoc praesenti; and in the Extravagantes, de probat., c. In praesentia. For I say that the said Order would not be regarded in the place of children, unless it had the privilege of taking; but where it is capable of the privilege, since it can succeed, as in the aforementioned chapter In praesentia. I do not say that the monastery is a son; rather, it is a kind of arrogating father. Nor does any civil or canonical law state that the monastery is a son. But it states that one who has entered the monastery is deemed to have a son, in this manner having a successor who has. Thus the laws which they have, as sons, which is introduced in favor of religion, and so that the contemplative life may be found more pleasing than the conjugal life, as noted by Cynus, C. ad Trebellianam, Authentica Nisi rogati. And I speak of the said brother, presupposing profession.

† On another point, whether the mother has lost her right, I say that she has not, because she had a lawful basis for retaining the property by virtue of her office as guardian. Finally, upon the son’s death, she acquired a direct succession to one-eighth part, because the statute speaks of a person dying intestate, whether or not he is capable of making a will. And by this means, another doubt is resolved, namely, whether the words “intestate” are to be understood as referring only to one who is capable of making a will, as in l. 1, ff. de condictione ex lege. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that hearing shall be denied to one who has not paid the tithe in that cause in which he has not paid: whether a sentence pronounced against the non-payer is valid, when no proofs have been made, or they are insufficient.
2. In every cause there is a twofold hearing.
3. Given the statute mentioned above and the sentence pronounced: whether one who has not paid the tithe may appeal, or allege nullity.
4. If a statute compels the judge under penalty to pronounce judgment, and the plaintiff has proved nothing, and the defendant has not paid the tithe: what is the judge then bound to do?
body: † It is provided that one who does not pay the tithe (decima) in a case ought not to be heard, and that the contestatio litis made on his behalf shall not be valid, nor any judgment rendered in his favor, and he shall forfeit his right. Now, a certain defendant who was summoned did not pay the tithe in the case; the judge, without sufficient proofs having been adduced in the case, rendered a judgment against the defendant and condemned him to what was sought. Now it is asked whether an appeal can be lodged, and whether evidence may be given concerning the iniquity of the judge who rendered the judgment without full proofs having been obtained on the part of the plaintiff; and whether the defendant ought to be heard regarding the said appeal notwithstanding the said statute. First, for clarity, it must be premised,

† that in every case there is a twofold hearing: namely, of the plaintiff and of the defendant. And if indeed a hearing is denied to the plaintiff, the plaintiff is not admitted to sue or to make proof, as in ff. de aleato. l. 1. §. quod autem. If, however, a hearing is denied to the defendant, the defendant is not admitted to plead exceptions or to make proof; but he would rightly be admitted simply to deny. For simply to deny is nothing other than to make the matter doubtful, as in C. quibus ad libe. re. non lice t. l. fin. But a matter is doubtful, even if the defendant does not deny it, so long as it is not proved to the judge by the plaintiff; rather, the judge of his own office is bound to supply it. Hence, if the plaintiff proves nothing, the judge ex officio ought to impose silence upon the plaintiff, as noted in C. de transac. l. vbi pactum; and the judge can command nothing against him, as noted by Inno. de sen. excom. c. solet. And that is an obligation of law, and de iure; and the civil law can bind anyone. For the statute which says that he is not to be heard does not pertain to the obligations of the written law; for in such matters the judge supplies that in which it falls short, because he swears to judge according to the laws, as noted in C. quae de sunt aduo. parti. l. 1. But those things that would require proof of fact ought not to be admitted when they are raised by one who ought not to be heard, as noted by Iac. Bu. in ff. de condi. inde. l. eleganter. §. si quis post. From this it is concluded that a judgment rendered against one who ought not to be heard, when no proofs have been admitted, is invalid. But if kinds of proof against him who ought not to be heard—for instance, of witnesses or instruments—had been duly admitted, even though they did not prove fully, the judgment would stand, as in ff. manda. l. si fideiussor. §. in omnibus. Now two doubts arise.

† The first is whether this person who did not pay the tithe ought to be heard when asserting that the judgment is null, and showing the record of the proceedings from which the nullity appears. And I say that a judge can never supply in those matters which are the foundation of the claim. Hence, if the petitioner ought not to be heard in petitioning, the judge cannot supply, just as he could not where nothing was sought, as in ff. de dam. infec. l. 4. §. hoc autem iudicium. And therefore it does not seem that this person to whom a hearing is denied can sue for nullity; and much less can he appeal, as noted expressly by Odof. in ff. qui sat. cog. l. si arbitrio. Therefore, the judge ought to pronounce that the said person suing for nullity or appealing is not to be heard. I consider that the statute says that he ought not to be heard in the case in which he did not pay the tithe. Nevertheless, an appeal and nullity are not that same case, but a new case, as is fully noted in C. de proc. l. inuitus, and especially a case of nullity, which concerns the proceedings and not the principal fact, as noted by Inno. extra, de procu. c. auditis. Hence, if in this second lawsuit the tithe is tendered, although the hearing was denied in the first case, it cannot be denied in the second; and especially because the default committed in the first case can be purged in this second one, as noted in l. 1. in princ. ff. de act. emp. Hence, just as in an appellate case the rule is given to the parties, 'I will allege what was not pleaded, and prove what was not proved,' so it is given to the judge, 'I will hear what was not heard concerning matters connected to the old ones,' as in C. de temp. app. l. per hanc. But against the aforesaid it is objected, and it seems, that the said person not paying the tithe ought in no way to be heard. For he who ought not to be heard in the principal case cannot say that he has received an injury, as in ff. quibus ex cau. maio. l. sed et si per Praetorem. §. sed si, so long as access or entrance to the courts is not open to him by decree, as in C. de iudi. l. sancimus. For this person not paying the tithe, having regard to the statute, seems to be equated with a truly contumacious person, who does not appeal even though he suffers an injustice, as in C. quorum app. non reci. l. 1. and ff. de in integ. resti. l. Diuus. and l. contumaciam. and ff. de re iud. Moreover, the judge of the first case could not and ought not to have rendered judgment for the non-payer of the tithe; therefore, by rendering judgment against him he did not commit an injustice. Hence his judgment ought to be confirmed. For that which was duly and rightly judged ought to be confirmed, as in extra, de test. c. Ray. and c. Raynal. and C. de app. l. eos. in prin. Moreover, the judge of the appeal succeeds into the place of the first judge, as in ff. iud. sol. l. pe.; he ought to pronounce that which the former ought to have pronounced, or that which an upright man ought to pronounce. But an upright man ought to pronounce according to the statute of the city, as in C. quae sit lon. consue. l. 1.; therefore this judge of appeal ought also to follow the statute. But the statute, first, denotes denial of a hearing; second, it invalidates the litis contestatio; third, it annuls the judgment; fourth, it returns to the first, and says that the judge shall not take cognizance of his right. Then I argue thus: of the matter concerning which the judge took cognizance, he ought to pronounce, as in ff. de iudi. l. de qua re; so conversely, of that concerning which he did not take cognizance, he ought not to pronounce; and it is the same not to have taken cognizance and not to have been able to take cognizance. Moreover, whether it be an appeal or an action of nullity, both avenues implore the office of the judge, as in ff. quę sententię sine app. rescin. l. 1. post prin.; but praetorian aid is denied to such a non-payer; therefore, upon such an appeal or nullity he ought not to have been heard in any way. And from the aforesaid a very great absurdity follows: namely, that the judge of the first instance, under this pretext of the unpaid tithe, can effectively condemn even someone who owes nothing; and since he cannot appeal or claim nullity, he will be compelled to pay an undue debt, while a most iniquitous and null judgment will be held as just and valid, even if the defect appears from the very record without any other proof of fact, which is exceedingly iniquitous, as noted in C. de transact. l. vbi pactum. and ff. de pe. haer. l. plane. And therefore, lest the disposition of the statute be drawn to this absurdity, we can first say that the words of the statute speak only of the case in which the tithe was not paid; but the appellate case, when the defendant appeals, seems an entirely new case. Suppose that the first case for which he was sued was a loan (mutuum) case, but the defendant in the appeal does not pursue a loan case, but a deposit case in respect of the proofs, and founds himself upon this. Hence the merits of the cases are not the same, and thus the cases are not the same cases as to the causes of the case; and much less the case of nullity, because nullity does not touch the merits, but only the proceeding.

† For the understanding of these things, I pose this question: the defendant did not deposit the tithe, and the plaintiff proved nothing. The statute, however, under penalty, compels the judge to pronounce. It is asked what the judge of the first instance, before whom this question is pending, ought to pronounce. For he cannot condemn, because it was not proved; nor can he acquit, because the defendant did not deposit the tithe. I answer: he shall acquit in fact, since de iure he cannot, as in ff. de ver. ob. l. quidamcum filium. §. si videamus; or he will pronounce that on this account he cannot pronounce for the plaintiff because it was not proved, nor for the defendant because he did not deposit the tithe. And by this pronouncement the judge will escape the penalty of the statute. Therefore the judge of appeal will pronounce in like manner: namely, that the judge of the first instance ought not to have condemned when no proofs had been made, if this is notorious from the record, wherein the judge can supply ex officio; otherwise the judgment would have to stand. And I say the same regarding nullity: that if it is evident from the record, he shall pronounce the sentence null; but if it is not evident, he would not admit the defendant who did not pay the tithe to prove nullity extrinsically. Nor does any other way appear to me by which justice and the statute can be preserved at the same time. If there were another, better way, let him who sees better look to it. For as often as a defendant's appeal is founded on a mere negative, of which by the nature of things there is no proof, just as the denial was admitted in the principal case, so it is in the appeal, because an appeal does not change the nature of the matter. Nor can any virtue of a reasonably enacted law bring it about that it is not lawful for a defendant to deny a fact which the plaintiff is required to prove. Nor is that denial properly speaking called a defense. Hence there is a difference between simply denying and pleading an exception, as noted in C. de exc. l. si quidem. Thus he who ought not to be heard in the principal case ought, on a new cause and new grievance, to be heard in the appellate case; but a new cause and a new grievance is whatever is brought forward beyond the nature of the first, as in C. si saepius in inte. rest. postuletur. l. 1. And thus a new cause begets a new right, in which new right new matters are founded; and in respect of that, it suffices to deposit the tithe so far as pertains to obtaining this new effect, as in ff. de excep. rei iudic. l. cum quęritur. and l. si mater. §. eandem. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a person to whom power has been granted to reform a statute may entirely reform the statute.
body: It is to be said, to pay in florins according to the second [provision]

† That the said buyer is bound to pay in florins according to the promise made by him, it is to be said, for multiple reasons. For the ordinance made by the consuls has effect with respect to the chamber then present, since the person of Ja. was added uniformly with respect to both; it disposes, as argued from the law *Iam hoc iure*, Digestum, *De vulgari et pupillari substitutione*. Since therefore it has effect with respect to Iaco. as long as he remains at the cash box, so too does it have effect in that chamberlain; where the chamberlain is lacking, this is strengthened by the words of the present tense, namely *teneantur* (they are to hold) and *debeant* (they ought), which are not extended to the future, as stated in the law *Si ita*, Codex, *De auro et argento*; but to the past, while the statute says, for the good state. Moreover, it is understood as referring to the present, as noted by Bartolus in the law *Ambitiosa*, Digestum, *De decretis ab ordine factis*. Furthermore, as the statute dictates, and the same Bartolus notes in the aforementioned place, those establishing such an arbitrium cannot establish anything that is contrary to statutes from the very first merit, since this reform is contrary to the statute, as is clear to one who understands it correctly, it is to be considered null. And because they cannot order anything contrary to statutes, neither directly nor indirectly: since therefore the statute made from the beginning and placed in the volume of statutes says that florins of gold are to be given and received by anyone for so much, and afterwards the reform says that the chamberlain and Iaco. are bound to receive for so much less, it appears contrary to the statute not only indirectly, but directly. Therefore, as has been said, such a reform is not valid. Moreover, and presupposing without prejudice that it is valid, which in truth it is not: nevertheless, they say that the party is bound in florins to make the remaining payment in a similar manner, as stated in the law *Non dubium*, § *Illud*, Codex, *De testamento non obnubentium*. This is not obstructed by what is alleged from custom; rather, it supports the common party, as appears. Furthermore, the aforementioned consuls could not order this to the prejudice of the Republic, as argued from the law *Praeses Provinciae*, Codex, *De transactionibus*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether one who is bound to pay florins may pay the estimated value, and at what time:
body: OIi a vt ff. depo. l. 1. §. si conuenerit. and the obligation is for¬

† Obligations arising from convention receive their law from the agreement, as is stated in the Digest, *de depositis*, law 1, § *si convenerit*. And since the obligation is formed in florins, it is necessary that either florins be paid, or that an estimation of florins, current for the time, be received for the function, so that the condition of the plaintiff, or creditor, does not become worse, as in the Digest, *de solutionibus*, law *Paulus*. And this is noted in the Code, *de donationibus*, law *si quis argentum*, in the beginning; and in the Authenticum, *de fideicommissis*, § *quod autem*; and in the Code, *de solutionibus*, Authenticum *nisi debitor*. Hence, according to the variety of times, the currency varies, and rises and falls, and the time of payment must be considered, or the time of default, as is noted in the last chapter, *de decimis*, in the Clementines. Notwithstanding the disposition of the Priors, or Decurions: because either it was not their intention to provide for changing the estimation of florins in this case, and then their disposition does not extend to this case, as in the Digest, *de administratione tutorum*, law *ita autem*, in the beginning; and in the Digest, *de re militari*, law *milites agrum*, in the beginning. Or it was their intention to provide for every case, and then their said decree is not valid with effect: because insofar as it results in public damage, it is ambitious, as in the Digest, *de decretis ab ordinariis factis*, law *ambitiosa*. Furthermore, it savors of a certain donation, which Decurions cannot make, as in the Digest, *quod vi aut clam*, law *prohibere*, § *plane*; and in the Digest, *de triumphis*, law *cum hi*, § *si Praetor*; and § *si cui*. Moreover, suppose the case now, that the florin was diminished in estimation, its substance and weight being preserved, for example, not being worth more than 16 Antonini. Would the debtor say, "I wish to pay 16 Antonini"? Certainly not at all. Hence, the debtor should not seek the contrary of what he would not be demanding, as in the Code, *de solutionibus*, law *pecuniam*. Certainly, nor could the fisc compel him beyond the florin; with the payment of what he promised, he is released. And the agreement made must be observed, and the debtor is bound to nothing else, as in the Code, *de solutionibus*, law *si operas*. And if the said statute were understood otherwise, it would be inequitable and absurd: which it ought not to be, as in the Digest, *de vulgari substitutione*, law *ex facto*, in the beginning. Furthermore, the said statute was temporary, and designative of a certain office; hence, that office being removed, the statute does not endure, as in the Code, *de fructibus Alexandri*, law *diurnos*, book 12. Furthermore, in those things which change with time, those who enact statutes are not understood to dispose uniformly, but when the reason and due consideration have changed, the statute yields, as in the Code, *de caducis tollendis*, law 1, in the beginning. From which, and other allegations, and what can be said, it must be said that florins are due, as in the Digest, *si certum petatur*, law *cum quid*. Nor can the fisc be compelled to receive less than is due, since the whole debt is liquid, in the same title, law *quidam aestimaverunt*. And in the Digest, *de usuris*, law *tutor*, § *Lucius*, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether, and when a testator leaves something to executors, so that they may give it for his soul, the fourth part is due from such a legacy.
body: When they give for his soul out of love of God, he,

† If a testator left something to executors to be given for his soul out of love of God, the person to whom it is given out of love of God is said to receive it from the testator, not from the executor, except as from a minister. And therefore, if the executor distributes such a legacy to persons, the fourth part is not due; because, granted that what is left to persons of a certain college does not require the fourth part to be paid, as noted in c. 2, extra, de sepultura. But if the executors designate places or pious colleges, then the fourth part is due, unless they designate it for such pious causes or uses that are not subject to the fourth part: as in extra, de testamentis, c. si. For example, if it is declared that something is to be provided to pious places for the building of a church, or similar purposes. This rule fails when it is left to the Minor Friars or other mendicants, where the fourth part is due to the parish priest, and to the diocesan bishop is due through that priest the fourth part of that fourth part, as in extra, de sepultura, c. dudum, ver. verum. Regarding what is left to the poor, there are various customs, and bishops sometimes take the fourth parts, because the poor in general are reduced to the likeness of a college, whose prelate and father is the bishop. And it would be otherwise in what is left for the redemption of captives; because this is similar to what is bequeathed to places for pious uses, and which cannot be converted to other uses, from which the bishop ought not to have the fourth part, nor the parish priest, as in C. de episcopis et clericis, l. ad declinandum. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether, and when, a debtor who entrusts money or another thing to a messenger for delivery to the creditor is liable for the messenger's fraud.
body: Franciscus de Io. Slo, to whom the letter of the Lords Bar. was written, was the creditor of a certain Franciscus de Io. Slo, to whom he had written a letter of the following tenor, among other things, namely: “As for the payment, if it be so, that with your health and mine you see fit to send it to me.” In this manner, that debtor gave that money to a certain noble and trustworthy citizen of Perugia, so that he might carry that money to the said Franciscus. That citizen of Perugia did not notify the said Franciscus of this; nevertheless, he received that money from the said sender. He [the citizen] says that he is not bound, except to assign the rights. The question is asked: what is the law? And it seems to be said first, that the said Ortanus is not bound, for two reasons.

First, because he gave the money to a trustworthy man while carrying the creditor’s mandate. Hence it is as if he had given it to the creditor himself, as in D. 20.1.13 (*Solutum*), § *Solutam*. Second, it seems sufficiently sufficient for the debtor to have entrusted the matter to a trustworthy messenger, as is read and noted in D. 17.1.1 (*Eum*), § *Si*, together with the following law and D. 17.1.10 (*Argentum*). To the contrary, because the said messenger was chosen by the debtor himself, and was the debtor’s messenger, not the creditor’s; and a bad choice is at fault. And that he was a bad messenger appears from the effect: because he did not give the money to the creditor; hence the debtor must impute it to himself, who chose an untrustworthy messenger, as in D. 10.3.1 (*Cum in plures*), § *Servum meum*, at the words “quod si sine distinctione.” Moreover, this seems to be determined by the words of the letter, where it says, “when you see to my and your safety, etc.” For by these words the creditor warns the debtor to send by such a messenger that the thing may be safe for the creditor. These words are understood with effect. But the thing is not safe for the creditor if the money is not paid, as in D. 26.7.1 (*Pe.*) and D. 50.17.1 (*Periculum*) and D. 26.1.1 (*Cum quaeritur*). Moreover, it is fault to entrust money to so powerful a man from whom it cannot be exacted against his will, since he is not suitable due to the ease of suing him, as in D. 46.1.2, § 1 (*Qui satis cogantur*), and this is understood from the quality of the messenger, as noted in the said D. 10.3.1 (*Cum plures*), § *Si*, together with the following law. Moreover, this was a debtor of a generic thing, hence a fortuitous event does not release him, as in D. 14.3.1 (*Incendium*). Furthermore, this debtor did not observe the form of the mandate, as I said, because he did not make payment in such a way that the thing would be safe for the creditor. And therefore he remains obligated as before, nor is he released by assigning the action, if the creditor does not wish to accept such assignment, as in C. 4.5.1 (*Cum a quo*). The debtor ought to have been careful to deliver the money to such a person that he would make the thing safe for the creditor, nor does it avail him that he trusts in a good man and of good reputation, which the words of the letter require as to the fact, as it was considered from the effect, as appears from the very signification of the words. For he said, “with my safety,” unless he had ratified it, that is, if the said Framn., with the addition of the messenger, had demanded the money, he would have had the fideicommissum, for then ratification would have made him the proper messenger, and specifically the messenger of the ratifying party. To this effect is what is noted in D. 13.1.1 (*Si procuratori*) and D. 2.14.1 (*Si quis iussori*), § *Apud Labeonem*, and D. 17.1.1 (*Eum qui*), § *Si*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a statute providing that a debtor cannot prove his discharge unless by means of a public instrument: what if he can prove it by witnesses, and the lay judge does not admit such proof on account of the statute: may the bishop be approached? And may such a debtor compel the creditor to draw up an instrument for him? And whether the aforementioned statute is equitable. And no. 2.
body: CdIIIS LaIIS. 2. florins of gold for the valuation of a cow, someone was condemned to another in CdIIIS LaIIS. 2. florins of gold for the valuation of a cow; finally, the said condemned person satisfied the debt, and came to an agreement with the creditor for 5 florins of gold, and promised the debtor to make an instrument of refutation. Afterwards, the said Victor petitioned that the said sentence be put into execution, against which petition one cannot object on the grounds of the said liberation, because by statute the said liberation cannot be proven except by a public instrument. Hence, the condemned person has recourse to the ecclesiastical court, due to the defect of natural justice not reserved to him in the secular court, nor possible to be reserved, and also on account of sin: because sin is committed, since in the forum of conscience, and in the temporal forum, the forum of conscience is invited to come against the due faith. And since it is a case of restitution, so that the one acting acts to the prejudice of his soul, and to that which, if he were to demand, he would sin, and would be bound to restore.

† Now it is asked whether there is a case in which, on account of sin or due to a defect of justice of the secular judge, one may have recourse to the Bishop, and especially in the lands of the Church. To which I answer that, although against the said sentence, by the form of the statute, proof by witnesses is not admitted to derogate from the said sentence, nevertheless, in order to demand that a public instrument be drawn up regarding the said liberation, one may well proceed, and the statute does not stand in the way. Hence, since justice must and ought to be found in the secular forum among laymen, it is necessary that the secular judge adhere to the Bishop, to whom there is no recourse by leaps, nor when the written justice of that secular law does not fail. For if the judge were to fail in justice, he would make the case his own, and this would not be a case for recourse to the Bishop. For the understanding of these words, it must be noted that where recourse to the secular judge does not fail, the Bishop cannot interpose himself, nor make himself judge of profane causes, as in C. de testamentis, l. consulta diualia; otherwise he would usurp almost all causes to himself, which is ridiculous. Hence, since in this case the creditor can be compelled by the secular judge to make an instrument of settlement and refutation, as in ff. de pac., l. si intra, and C. de libe. causa, l. sic datam, the Bishop cannot be approached by the husband, as noted in c. dispendiosam, de iudic., in the Clementines. And although against the execution of a sentence that which is not liquid cannot be opposed, nevertheless, in bringing an action, that which is not liquid may well be proposed. And this is dictated by civil reason, which also binds the Bishop in his forum, as in C. de compens., l. fi.; ff. ut in pos. leg., l. is a quo; C. de edic. diui Adria., l. 2; and ff. ad exhi., l. 3, §. ibidem. And this is not injustice, but rather it is the justice of judicial order. Certainly, it is not unjust to establish that against a written document proof cannot be made, as in C. de non nu. pec., l. generaliter.

† Nor is the statute unjust, which does not allow exceptions to be raised unless they are certain ones: for the reason of the statute, from which the statute itself arises, is the cause for reducing litigation: and so that no occasion be given to debtors for not paying their debts, as in C. de duobus reis, l. si. And by natural reason it must be considered that where one can find something more just than just, or more equitable than equitable: yet since the statute establishes that the equitable, and not the more equitable, is to be observed, the statute is not inequitable, although it could be more equitable, as noted in ff. de iustitia et iure, l. 1, in principio; and in ff. de legibus, l. cum quidam. Since therefore an open way is provided before the secular judge, and the way of seeking, although not of obtaining, follows the rule that the plaintiff follows the forum of the defendant, he should not be drawn to a prohibited examination, as in C. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, l. in criminali. Moreover, a statute that repels an exception does not repel an action: when it repels an exception because the proceeding is summary; or when the reason for repelling both is not the same, as in ff. de evictionibus, l. sed exceptio; and in C. de evictionibus, l. si; and in extra, de iureiurando, c. debitores. Furthermore, the statute speaks when it is opposed against charters, or the execution thereof. But when it is opposed against the substance, or the cause, and not against the solemnity, it may well be opposed, as noted in ff. de pactis, l. iuris gentium, §. quod ferre. But he who brings an action does not oppose. For one thing is to bring an action, another to oppose. As in delicata, c. vetera, lib. 6; and in Auth. quomodo oportet episcopos, §. si quis autem tales. Hence, the petition that an instrument be made with a promise of refutation is so full and effective as is recourse to the ecclesiastical judge. Therefore, justice does not fail, nor judgment, nor the secular judge. Wherefore, ecclesiastical censure, which is remedial and a refuge for the wretched, has no place here, considering that which is not ordained by sentence is not ordained by statute, speaking of sentence. But sentence is not ordained for cases arising after sentence; therefore neither is the statute ordained to eliminate said cases, because the foundation of the statute is this sentence, as in ff. de conditionibus sine causa, l. si fullo; and noted by Cynus in l. 1, C. de conditionibus indebiti. And therefore where there is a new pact, there is a new action, as in ff. de minoribus, l. minor 25 annorum, cui fideicommissum; and in ff. de re iudicata, l. 4, §. si ex conventione. In which action the secular judge, and the proper judge, and not an extraneous one, ought to be employed. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether, and when, the mere emphyteutic land is deemed to be an emphyteutic building, so that, due to the non-payment of the canon for the land, both revert to the owner.
body: Quid. I. A certain person, selling a certain house built on land, or on a leasehold estate of a certain monastery, bought it from Titius in his own right and in perpetuity. He himself, however, had taken the said land in emphyteusis from the said monastery for 29 years for a certain annual rent. It happened that this person remained for four years without paying the rent. And that the said term of 29 years has elapsed. Now the question is,

Whether the said building, together with the said Casaleno (or land), has reverted to the said monastery, or to the said Casaleno (or land). Nevertheless, on this question, Bartolus says that it must be considered whether the land, or Casaleno, draws the superstructure to itself by necessity, so that both are held under a leasehold (livellare) and the superstructure, i.e., the parts of the land, are truly owned in full property. And in this article, Bartolus says that the land draws the building to itself in such a way that it makes the bishop’s building subject to emphyteutic right. Therefore, just as improvements (emponemata), i.e., enhancements joined and fixed to the land, follow the land, and when the land reverts to the owner, the improvements revert as well. And he says that this is the case in L. 2, C. de iure emph. as noted by him in ff. de superfi. L. 1, § 1. But to me, without prejudice to the substance of the truth, the contrary seems to apply in our case. For it must be known that the reason why the building follows the land is that the building cannot stand by itself. For it cannot stand in the air, as noted in ff. de damno infecto, L. si. And a similar reason applies to the upper part in relation to the lower part. For the upper part follows the lower part because it cannot stand by itself, as in C. de rei vend. L. 2. And yet we see that there can be two owners and proprietors: one of the upper part, another of the lower part, and each has direct ownership of his part, as noted by Cynus in L. si severior, C. ex quibus causis infausta irrogatur, in that common question concerning two persons having a tower divided between the upper and lower parts. And by the same reasoning, it is the same with a tree: for I can have a tree in another’s land with the effect of ownership, so that I can cut it down as my own property and derive fruits from it. And similarly, I can have gold and silver mines in another’s land. And although by natural reason they follow the land, by civil reason they belong to the holder, so that he can freely contract and make a will regarding them, and transmit the right he has to his heirs in perpetuity, as in ff. de acquisitione et obligatione, L. obligatio fere, § placet, ver. sicut, and in tradendo; and in ff. de damno infecto, L. damni, § si is. And it is supported by ff. de contrahenda emptione, L. cum manu sata, and it is expressly stated in ff. de legato primo, L. si fundum, § qui fundus. Although by law itself the building follows the land, nevertheless in effect it does not follow if the contrary is agreed upon between the parties. Returning to the question proposed, I consider that if it had been agreed that the improvements would not be considered part of the land, but could be separated from it, then certainly in that case the agreement and convention would have to be upheld. The case is in the aforementioned L. 2, de iure emphyteuticario. But whenever it is agreed between the parties that the building is owned in full property and in perpetuity, it is agreed that it is not temporary, i.e., for a certain time, as is the land. Therefore, by the force of this agreement, separation of the building must necessarily be permitted upon the expiration of the term of the lease. For we should not depart from the proper meaning of the words, as in ff. de legibus tertio, L. non aliter. And this is especially true in the case of our question, in which the cause of the building came from one person, and the Casaleno from another, and thus from different authors, with different rights, different forms, and different modes of selling. And thus we must consider the effect of the words, and not mere legal subtlety. Hence, just as if he had never taken the Casaleno in emphyteusis, he would nevertheless have the superstructure, because they are different things, so too if one is admitted, the other is not thereby lost, as in ff. de servitutibus urbanorum praediorum, L. si domus; and in ff. de fideiussoribus, L. Vrannius. And the statement of Lord Bartolus would be true if the Casaleno were granted to someone in emphyteusis, and the building were to be erected by the emphyteuta himself in his own right. Otherwise, if he purchased the building already erected at the time of purchase, which did not pertain to the owner of the land, which can be the case by agreement, as has been said. And this is our case. Even if someone wished to entirely deny the statement of Bartolus, it would still perhaps not be an error, because the nature of the contract is removed by a contradictory and incompatible agreement, and by the law which he himself cites, C. de iure emphyteutico, L. 2, post principium. And therefore I say that the said house has not reverted to the monastery, because in that purchase the monastery has no cause, nor is any census due for it, nor does it depend on the census, nor on the censual part. But as far as the reason of law is concerned, it stands by itself by reason of the express agreement. However, I say two things: first, since the land has reverted to the owner, the owner is not bound to anything else, except to suffer that the other remove the building, as in ff. de acquisitione emptionis, L. qui pendente; and in ff. de donationibus, L. sed in saxum. Secondly, if the other wishes to remove it, and the owner only wishes to give him as much as the materials and mortar are worth, it would seem that the owner should be heard according to the equity of the law in fundo versi, constituimus, ff. de rei venditione. And it is well supported by what is noted in L. sine haerede, ff. de administratione tutorum. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a city or a corporation can bring an action against another, so that it may be compelled to obey with respect to jurisdiction, public duties, functions, and taxes.
2. Whether subjects can withdraw themselves from the obedience of their superior and transfer that obedience to another.
body: Between the Castle of Rotarum and the Castle of Sintiglia, a dispute has arisen on account of a certain village called Circiglium, because all the aforementioned villages have submitted themselves to the Castle of Rotarum with regard to real and personal burdens. However, the inhabitants of the said Castle of Sintiglia claim that the said village of Circiglium is subject to them with regard to real burdens, and that it formerly belonged to them with regard to both real and personal burdens. Moreover, it is now a hundred years and more since the inhabitants of the village of Circiglium have performed real services in the said commune of Sintiglia, and have held possessions and goods in the territory of the said Castle of Sintiglia; and the territory of the said village of Circiglium has been subjected by the lapse of time and by boundaries prescribed and possessed from ancient times, and held and reputed to belong to the said Castle of Sintiglia for a time of which there is no memory to the contrary. From this factual premise, devoid of further material or fact, the following doubts arise, upon which legal advice is requested. First, whether the inhabitants of the said village of Circiglium could have made any recognition or submission to the prejudice of the community and the inhabitants of the said Castle of Sintiglia; and whether they could have interrupted their quasi-possession of the jurisdiction and subjection aforesaid concerning tithes, taxes, and other real and mixed burdens. And this question stands thus:

Whether the aforementioned commune of Sintigliano could have acquired dominion, that is, lordship and sovereignty, over the said men and the village of Circiglio. And certainly this is an ancient question: whether someone, as my man and my subject, long possessed by me, becomes my man. And some say that, in general, a person cannot become a slave through time; for it would be foolish to say that a free man can be prescribed, since he cannot be possessed, as in D. de acquirenda possessione, l. cum heredes, § 1. Moreover, this cannot be alienated; therefore, it cannot be prescribed, as in D. de fundo dotali, l. si fundum, and D. de verborum significatione, l. alienationis. Furthermore, an agreement cannot be made concerning another person; therefore, it cannot be effected by time. For what cannot be done cannot be accomplished by agreement, namely that one should become the master of another by the passage of time, as in D. quomodo servus amittitur, l. non satis, ver. nec si forte.

To the contrary, it seems that jurisdictions and dominions can be prescribed, as in C. de diversis officiis, l. viros, lib. 12, and l. emancipato libero, § 1, and notably in D. de iure omnium iudicum, l. more maiorum. Nor does it avail to object that a freeborn man cannot be prescribed; for although jurisdiction can be prescribed, the person prescribed does not cease to be freeborn. Hence, jurisdiction is prescribed, but not proprietary jurisdiction, as in C. de agris et censibus, l. litibus, lib. 11. Hence, one universitas can prescribe against another, so that it may obey it as subject in public burdens and functions, as noted in Auth. qui mores nationum efficiunt sui, § si quis igitur ex qualibet. For long possession has the force of truth, as noted in C. de servitutibus et aqua, l. 1, and D. de aqua quotannis, l. hoc iure, § ductus aquae. And it is natural that the weaker be ruled by him who is stronger. And in this matter, the longest prescription has the force of consent, as in D. de usuris, l. cum de in rem verso, and D. de aqua pluviae arcendae, l. 2, in principio, and Extravagantes, de verborum significatione, c. super quibusdam, § preterea.

† Nor can it be said that subjects, although they withdraw themselves from the obedience of their lords, derogate from their jurisdiction. On the contrary, they invite the case against themselves, because they turn the rebellion of the lords upon themselves. For in a certain sense they commit theft of themselves by withdrawing from the obedience of their superiors. And those who receive them into their own obedience are said to be invaders to the prejudice of the former possessors: and they ought to be punished as invaders, as in C. de Agri. et cen. l. coloni. lib. 11. and they can also be vindicated as detained by invading possessors, as in Inst. de act. §. praeiudiciales. and ff. ad Munic. l. de iure. Indeed, they can be captured and reduced to the obedience of the party from whose obedience they had in fact withdrawn, just as Apostates can be captured who apostatize from the order, as in C. de Decu. l. generali. lib. 10. and no. in l. 1. C. vbi de curiali, vel cohartali conditione. For it ought not to be lawful for subjects to withdraw themselves from their lordships, so that no occasion for sinning is given, nor can the right of creditors be changed by a pact of debtors, as in C. de pact. l. certe. Nor did a Barbarian, who was handed over to the Roman people, obtain the praetorship, and therefore free himself from servitude, as in ff. de offi. praet. l. Barbarius. Nor can one bound by accounting free himself, although he subjects himself to another, because he subjects himself with his cause, leprosy, and disease, as in extra, de oblig. ad ratiocinia. c. 1. Hence neither does the law grant liberty to one who has acquired it, because he has long withdrawn himself from the yoke of vices, as in ff. de acquepos. l. 3. §. si seruus. Hence he who is in the power of another has no commerce of himself, nor can he abdicate himself from him whose he is: just as a son, who is in the power of his father, cannot give himself in adoption, unless he is given by the father, as in C. de ado. l. cum in adoptiuis. For it is always necessary that he consent in the transferring of the right, whose right it is that is transferred or consumed, as in ff. de aq. plu. arc. l. in concedendo. and ff. de natalib. ressit. l. fi. and C. de eman. libe. l. nec auus. And therefore I conclude that the subjection of the said village, which is real and mixed, pertains to the said castle of Sintigliani according to the most ancient custom, as in ff. de aq. plu. arc. l. fi. I, Baldus. Done without allegation of law.
In the Name of Christ, Amen. In the year of His Incarnation 1208, on the 4th day of the month of December, in the same year, under the 11th Indiction, no one, and so forth.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether goods acquired by a widowed mother, living together with her minor children, are presumed to have been acquired from the mother’s property or from that of the minors.
2. If a testator left his wife as usufructuary owner, etc., whether the heirs are bound to assign to her a specific part of the house for habitation.
3. Likewise, whether the paternal grandmother, who possessed the goods of the grandchild, is bound to reimburse the maternal grandmother for the maintenance provided to the granddaughter.
4. If the husband assigned one house to his wife in lieu of 300 [units of currency] which were in the dowry, the heirs cannot repudiate her claim.
5. Whether the maternal grandmother is bound to make an inventory of the goods of the common granddaughter, when the paternal grandmother possesses the granddaughter’s goods; every manager of affairs is bound to make an inventory.
6. The amount of a legacy may be claimed up to 30 years.
body: A certain person purchased certain goods for his wards.

† A widow, after the death of her husband, standing with her own pupils, purchased certain goods in her own name, which the said pupils claim belong to them as having been bought with their money. But the said widow says that she acquired them by her own industry and labor. Now the question arises: on whom does the burden of proof lie? I answer that one must resort to presumptions. For if the pupils were wealthy and the mother poor, it is presumed that she acquired the goods from the children’s assets, if she was administering their property. But if the mother was industrious and the pupils poor, it is rather presumed that she acquired them by her own industry. If, however, these presumptions do not appear, then it suffices for the mother in possession that the children do not prove that the purchase was made with their money, as in C. arbitrium tutelae, l. si defunctus, and ff. de administratione tutorum, l. Titium et Maevium, §. altero. And it supports this what we note in a similar case in C. de bonis quae liberis, l. cum oportet, in principio. For even if there is no presumption in favor of the mother, it suffices for her that there is no presumption against the mother; because when presumptions cease as to either of the two extremes, uncertainty itself suffices for the defendant. Indeed, even if the husband were bringing the action, it would suffice for him to have title, as in the aforementioned §. altero. And therefore it will be said that controversy cannot be made against the mother by the children unless they prove true what they allege. The objection from ff. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. vir, does not hold, because there it speaks of acquisitions during the marriage, otherwise in acquisitions after its dissolution, because the law speaks of the wife, not the widow. And because in the case of a widow the same reason does not apply, since she can acquire by her own work, because she is not bound to work for the heirs of her husband, as she was bound to work for her husband, unless she wishes to receive alimony from them, as in l. sicut, ff. de operibus liberto.

† It is asked whether, if a husband left his wife as owner and usufructuary, etc., the sons can assign to her a certain part of the house in which she may dwell. I answer that they are bound, however, to provide what suffices for her maintenance, both in habitation and in other things, because the full usufruct is not due to her, as is noted in l. j. C. si secum. nu. mu.

† Furthermore, the question arises in such a case: the maternal grandmother provided maintenance for the granddaughter, whereas the paternal grandmother possessed the granddaughter’s property; may the said maternal grandmother recover the maintenance from the fruits collected by the paternal grandmother, considering that she had repeatedly and often demanded maintenance from the said paternal grandmother? Answer: Yes, as stated in the Digest, *De negotiorum gestione*, law *Nesennius*. For, since the paternal grandmother administers the granddaughter’s property, she is bound to provide maintenance to the granddaughter. Hence, the maternal grandmother managed the affairs of the paternal grandmother, which was a duty pertaining to the paternal grandmother with care and solicitude; therefore, she may sue her by the action for management of affairs without mandate, as stated in the Digest, *De negotiorum gestione*, law *Si pupilli*, in the beginning.

It is also asked, if the husband assigned to his wife a certain house for 300 pounds which were in the dowry, whether the heirs of the husband can repel her from the house. And it must be said that they cannot, as in D. de iure dotis, l. ita.

† Furthermore, it is asked whether the maternal grandmother is bound to make an inventory of the goods of her granddaughters, since the paternal grandmother possessed the goods of the granddaughters. I answer that every manager of affairs is bound to render an account, but the head of accounts is the inventory.

† Hence every negotiorum gestor is bound to make an inventory, as in the Digest, under the heading "On the action for management of affairs and on the action for things given," in the laws *Cum seruus* and *Cum tale* in the beginning. And therefore the aforementioned paternal grandmother is compelled by the office of the judge to make an inventory, so that the property may be described, as in the Code, under the heading "On judicial faith," in the law *Facultas*, book 10.
It is also asked, for how long a time the amount of a legacy may be claimed. I answer, for up to 30 years, as in C. de praescrip. 30 ann. l. licet. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a procurator appointed by a Prelate for leasing, for receiving fruits, for alienating, and for doing all things which he himself could do, can renew emphyteutic or feudal investitures.
2. A procurator generally appointed for conducting and administering affairs does not seem to have a mandate to alienate, unless the things are about to perish in time.
3. A general mandate with liberty is not induced from the fact that there is a clause in it, namely, in the aforesaid and concerning the aforesaid.
4. How manyfold alienation is, and which alienation is said to be prohibited to a procurator.
5. What effect this clause placed in a mandate operates, even if the mandate required a special one.
6. Things lawfully done cannot be revoked by a successor. Hence, the son and successor of the king cannot revoke things well and lawfully done by his predecessor; likewise, neither can the Rector of a church revoke a fief well granted by his predecessor.
body: The case of Pactum quondam, §. Adriani, the Cardinal Deacon, is proposed under this form. Gentilis, by concession of the Apostolic See, having obtained the priory of St. Mary of Vallis Fabricae, appointed his procurator, Lord Nicolaus Rugerii, among other things, in the said priory and others, under this form. Therefore, in the said priories and the members dependent upon them, by the tenor of these presents, we make, constitute, create, and ordain him our general procurator and factor of the said priories, and manager of affairs, and special messenger, granting and conceding to him free power, and within the scope of petitioning, demanding, recovering, and receiving any fruits, revenues, and proceeds, whether consisting in money or any other thing, from whatever persons. And afterwards it follows below: and to do all other and each of the things necessary, or even opportune, in the aforesaid matters and any of the aforesaid, and which we could do and exercise if we were personally present, even if the mandate required special authorization. Now, in fact, it is proposed that the said priory has many written instruments, or leasehold or enfiteutic estates, which were accustomed to be granted and renewed for a third generation, and which, having been renewed by predecessors, were accustomed to endure for successors:

† Now it is asked, by virtue of the said mandate, whether the said procurator had the power to lease, grant, and renew the said documents for a third generation, as was the custom to be done by the predecessors and governors of the said places. For the understanding of these matters, it must be premised that the said emphyteusis is called, and it is a certain alienation, whereby the useful dominion is transferred to the emphyteuta, as in C. de rebus alienatis non alienandis, l. si.

† Moreover, it must be premised that a procurator generally constituted for conducting and administering affairs does not appear to have a mandate to alienate, unless the property is about to be claimed at the time, as stated in the Digest, *De procuratoribus*, law *Procuratorum tutorum*. And there the text specifically states that a special mandate is required for alienation.

† or general, not restricted, but given for all matters with full freedom. But here it does not appear to be a general mandate with full freedom, because it is written with those words “in the aforementioned matters” and “concerning the aforementioned matters.” And note Bartolus, Digestum, De verbis obligatorum, l. Qui Romae, § Calimacus. For these words are restrictive, as in Codex, De transactionibus, l. Si de certa. Therefore, such a procurator did not have the power to grant emphyteusis, unless he reported the price to the principal, or otherwise the principal ratified it, or it was applied to the principal’s benefit, by argument from Digestum, De edendo, l. Praetor, § Si servus; and Codex, Quod cum eo, l. Ei qui, in fine. To the contrary it seems,

† For there is a certain gratuitous alienation. And this is not called administration, but dissipation, as in the Digest, De manumissionibus, l. Ab agnato. And this cannot be done not only by a procurator, but certainly not even by the Rector of the church himself: because the procurator is not the owner, as in the Extravagantes, De donationibus, c. 2. There is, however, a certain non-gratuitous alienation, and this in two ways. For there is a certain unusual alienation, and this a procurator cannot make without a special mandate, or without a general mandate coupled with liberty: but with a special mandate, or if it is with liberty, as in the Digest, De procuratoribus, l. Procurator, cui libera. There is, however, a certain usual and customary alienation, and one which the owner, or principal rector, is accustomed to make, such as these renewals, as in the Digest, De aqua quotannis et aestimata, l. 1, §. Permittitur. And then these things, which are usually done, are included in a general mandate, even if they imply a perpetual obligation, as in the Digest, Quod cum eo, l. Titianus. Hence, a general procurator appointed to administer the priory and the members dependent on it, such as these leases or emphyteutic contracts, seems to have been able to make the said reforms and renew them in the customary manner. Since his lord would, most likely, and according to custom, have done the same: and especially because the words of the mandate do not restrict themselves, since the said Do. Nico. was constituted procurator, factor, and negotiorum gestor of the said priory and the members dependent on it: and to this general mandate was subsequently added liberty, and also words appended which have the force of a singular mandate: there, where it says,

And if a special mandate were required, as stated in the extrajudicial collection on procurators, chapter 1, in the gloss, and noted by Bartolus in the Digest on donations, law *filius*; and by Guillaume de Coulanges in the Digest on the question "if someone gives a guarantee," law *sed et si quia*, section *quæsitum*; and it is supported by the Digest on peculium, law *quam Tuberonis*, section *alia causa*; and by the Code on procurators, law *si procurator ad unam speciem*, or law *procuratorem, vel actorem*, where this is noted to this effect. Therefore, it seems to be concluded in law that the procurator of the said Lord Cardinal could reform [the act], just as the said Lord Cardinal could have done if he had been present. Because by these words a most full mandate was given to the procurator, as in the Digest on mandate, law *creditor*, section *Lucius*; and that which was done by the Lord Cardinal, or by his authority, being perpetual until the third generation of the recipient, cannot be revoked by successors, as stated in the aforementioned section *emphyteosim*, and in the extrajudicial collection on prelates exercising their vicarious functions, chapter *finis*; and especially since he was a Cardinal, whose acts, on account of the dignity of his office, ought not to be made a mockery; moreover, power is augmented by dignity.

† Therefore, the son and successor, even of the Queen, cannot revoke what was lawfully and legitimately done by his predecessor, as is fully stated in Archid. 12, q. 2, c. alienationis. And we have a similar rule in feudal law: if the rector of a church enfeoffed a fief that was open to him, the successor cannot revoke it, unless the vassal fails to perform the services of the fief, or it does not depend on him, as in 10, col. qui successores teneantur. The established rules are those which custom has confirmed. For custom gives authority to such emphyteutic contracts, as noted in the rubric of C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, and from the argument in ff. communia praediorum, l. venditor, § si constat, and noted in 10, col. qui feudum dare possunt, in the beginning. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that no woman of the City of Assisi may make a will without the presence of her husband, whether a woman from Perugia married in Assisi is considered to be of the City of Assisi, so as to be bound by the statute. And if the said woman from Perugia made a will in Assisi in accordance with the form of the said statute, and later, being in Perugia, made another in accordance with the common law or the statutes of Perugia, which of them is valid.
2. Whether a woman married elsewhere loses the privileges and common rights of her natural homeland.
3. When a fiction or interpretation of the common law provides for the interpretation of a certain term, whether such interpretation applies to statutes using that term.
body: By the statute of the city of Assisi, or of its county, which is observed by the commune of Assisi, it is provided that no woman, whatever her condition and status, who is subject to the statute of the city of Assisi or its county, may contract or make a will without the presence of her husband, if she is married.
