Now, a certain woman, by paternal and proper origin and nation Perugian, was married in Assisi and there dwelt with her husband for a long time; and finally she made a will in the presence of her husband. Subsequently, this Perugian woman returned, and, with her said husband absent and not consenting, she changed and revoked the said first will; and this second will was made in the city of Perugia, where the common law prevails. It is asked whether her said will is valid or not. From this case two doubts arise. First, whether a Perugian woman married in Assisi is to be called a woman of the city of Perugia or of the city of Assisi. Second, whether the said woman, returned to her own natural homeland, may make a will according to the laws of her own homeland, wherever she wishes; or whether she is not bound by the laws of the forum where she is found to be married.

† This passage seems to me sufficiently doubtful, on account of the words of the statute saying that no woman of the city of Assisi, etc. For a Perugian woman married to an Assisiate retains her own and natural origin, which cannot be extinguished, although it may be changed by a certain legal fiction, which is that marriage draws the wife to the city of the husband, as if she had been born there; where there is a fiction, which does not seem to have place in statutes disposing something against the law of nations and against the common law, as in D. 23.2.10, *Si vero*, § *De viro*. Hence the statute does not seem to speak of this woman about whom inquiry is made, as in D. 50.4.3. To this effect is the common gloss in D. 3.5.3, § *Hoc autem*, D. 3.5.3, where the gloss notes that for fictitious cases it is necessary that a special law be made, otherwise they are not comprehended under a law speaking generally, even under the common law, much less under municipal law, which is to be strictly interpreted. The laws are common. On the contrary it seems, for marriage by its nature renews the origin of the woman, and she is transferred to the origin of the husband by the power of a certain union. For when the husband and wife become one body and one flesh, that which is stronger draws that which is weaker into itself to be totally transferred, as is noted in C. 5.45.1, *Originem*. To this effect is what is noted in C. 1.16.1, *Ne sedes vacent*. But certainly this reason does not seem true, for just as the substance of origin cannot be changed, so neither can the name be taken away. And therefore also the laws treat of the origin of the married woman, and dispose concerning origin according to her own origin, as in the law and the note in C. 5.45.1, *De mulieribus*, and in what place, Book 10.

† Hence, a married woman does not lose her privileges, nor the common rights of her natural country, because natural attributes cannot be changed, as stated in the Digest, *De capitis diminutione*, law *Tutelas* and law *Legatum*; and in the Digest, *Ad municipalia*, law *Assumptio*. For the origin of the fact is established and resides in the fact itself, and facts concerning the cause, with regard to natural truth, cannot be regarded as if they had not occurred, as stated in the Digest, *De capitis diminutione*, law *In bello*, section *Factae*. And although the wife transcends to the domicile of her husband, as stated in the Digest, *De iure omnium iudiciorum*, law *Cum quaedam puella*; and in the Digest, *De iudiciis*, law *Exigere dotem*; nevertheless, she retains her father and her natural kinship, which is inseparable, as argued in the Code, *De adoptionibus*, law *Cum in adoptivis*, in the *Pepercolatio*. And these terms "of the city" or "of the community" signify origin, as noted in the Digest, *De exceptionibus quae rei tutelae*, law *Sed et reprobari*, section *Amplius*, in the word *commanentes*. For one is properly said to be "of" a certain place who is of that place according to origin and natural truth, and not according to fiction, as argued in the Code, *De his qui veniam aetatis*, law *Si*. It would be otherwise if this preposition "of" were applied to a Province, but not to a city: for example, if the words were "whoever is of the Province of Tuscany, etc."

† For the term "province" is most general, and it also includes inhabitants due to its breadth in the mode of signification assigned to it by law, as in the law and notes, ff. de ver. sig. l. provinciales. Here it must be considered first, whether when a fiction, or interpretation of the common law, disposes regarding the interpretation of a certain word, such interpretation has place in statutes using that word: and I say that it does, as in ff. ad leg. Fal. l. 1. § 1. Secondly, it must be considered what is said about the city, whether what is said about the city is understood of those who are governed by the civil law in that manner of the city of which it is said, of the city is understood, and of the place thus bounded and enclosed by walls. For if the words are taken civilly, i.e., in the first way, this woman married at Assisi is truly and properly of the city of Assisi, i.e., of the civility, i.e., under the civil law of that city. For she is truly a citizen, because the nature of civility can be induced by legal disposition, and not only by the common law, but also by the municipal law, as noted by Bartolus, ff. de usuc. l. si is, qui pro emptore. But if these words are understood materially for the place enclosed by walls: then without fiction a citizen cannot be said. Similarly, it seems to be said that the common law is drawn to the municipal, and vice versa. And that this woman should follow the statutes of her husband's origin, by which statutes she was in some way, as to these matters, in the power of her husband, just as also by the Lombard law. And therefore, especially concerning her dowry, she cannot dispose against the statute, although by the common law it would be contrary, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If a legacy to one person is found twice in the same will, especially a legacy of a specific quantity, first of a lesser amount and then of a greater amount, whether both are due or only once, and whether the lesser quantity is deemed to have been transferred into the greater.
2. If the testator left his wife the usufruct of his goods, so long as she remains a widow and lives with his son, whom he instituted as universal heir, what the heir owes the wife while the son is alive, and what after his death.
body: The father left, by way of institution, for his two or three daughters, for each of them, 240 gold florins; and he instituted John, his other son, as universal heir; and if the said John should die in pupillary age, or later, or at any time whatsoever, then he left to the aforementioned daughters, for each of them, by way of institution, 500 gold florins. Then, after the testator died, the case of the death of the said John, his son, occurred.

† It is asked whether each of the said daughters ought to have 500 gold florins for their dowries, or whether she ought to have 200 gold livres from the first head of the legacy and 500 florins from the second head, so that the legacy of the lesser amount is not confused. It appears that the said daughters ought to have, for each of them, all things considered, only 500 gold florins. For when a legacy is left for the same cause expressly stated by the testator, if first a lesser sum is left and second a greater sum, one legacy is understood, namely of the greater sum, and it is not due more than once: as in *l. libertis, quos*, in the beginning, D. de alim. et cib. leg. and noted in D. de probat. *l. quinquaginta*. Furthermore, because when a legacy is left by an instituted heir, although there are different heirs, they are regarded as one, the legacy is not understood to be from each, such that both are to be performed in full, but it suffices that they be performed together. D. de legat. 1, *l. seruo alieno*, § *si quis a primo*. Furthermore, because it is not presumed that the testator wished to burden the heir with so many performances, as in D. de legat. 2, *l. Titia*, § *qui in vita*, and D. de sol. matr. *l. si cum dotem*, § *si pater*. Furthermore, because since in the same will a legacy is left twice, and a legacy consists in quantity, it suffices to pay once. Nor is it presumed that the testator would divide the performances, as noted in D. de adim. leg. *l. Sempronius proculo*. Furthermore, just as the lesser sum relates to the greater sum, so does the composition of one sum relate to another sum, interpreting that both sums appear to have been left. But it is so that in doubt we interpret that less was left; therefore, we shall say in this manner that these legacies are understood to have been made with the intention that the lesser sum be counted in the greater, not that an augmentation of the lesser sum was made in itself. And thus it appears that the said daughters ought to have for each of them only 500 gold florins for their dowries, and not also 240 livres. For thus the testator fixed the dowries, and considered this dowry of 500 florins to each of the daughters to be a competent and sufficient dowry. To this effect is what is noted in D. de adim. leg. *l. cum centum*. Furthermore, the expression of the same dowry, because a dowry does not appear to be duplicable, nor a marriage, whence it suffices that the daughter be sufficiently dowered once, as in D. pro socio, *l. si socius pro filia*.

To the contrary it appears, for whenever several legacies are left in different cases, or one purely and another under a condition: then because there are several dispositions and several forms of disposing, if indeed the legacies consist in quantity, all are said to be integral, as in *l. plane*, D. de legat. 1. But these legacies, concerning which it is asked, consist in quantity, and one legacy is left purely and without the attached condition of the death of a male son, and another legacy is left under the condition after death: therefore they are different legacies and different forms of legating, and one legacy does not refer to the other, and therefore one is not understood to be repeated nor joined in the other; otherwise it would follow that the last conditional legacy by some tacit condition would induce a tacit repetition of the condition in the first legacy. Which is not true nor reasonable. And from this reason it seems to me to be said, saving the substance of the truth, that on account of the substantial formal difference of these legacies, one is not confused in the other. And if it be said that there is no difference in the final cause. I answer that it is true that in the cause of the dowry there is no difference; nevertheless, a dowry is not only constituted from the beginning, but another dowry can also be constituted afterwards, although the marriage had been contracted, as in D. de act. et obl. *l. obligamur*, and C. de donat. antenupt. *l. si constante*. And it supports the foregoing, because testators are more inclined to burden strangers than to burden sons, as in D. de mil. test. *l. militis codicillis*, § *miles in supremis*. And because in wills a broad interpretation is made, as in D. de reg. iur. *l. in testa*. And because that which is left to the same person in different cases is the same as if it were left to different persons. And therefore I conclude, always saving the substance of the truth, that if something else were proved regarding the intention of the testator in the case proposed, seven hundred and fifty gold florins are said to be due to each of the said daughters.

† Another question arises: suppose a testator left his wife the usufruct of his goods, as long as she remained a widow and lived with his son, whom he subsequently instituted as universal heir. Now it is asked what the wife ought to have while the son is alive, and what after his death. I answer that this legacy is of such a kind as if the testator had bequeathed the usufruct to one person and the fund to another. For each has half of the usufruct, as stated in the Digest, *De usufructu legato*, law *Si alii*. And he who has the casual usufruct, upon dying, transmits it to his heir, because it is joined to the ownership; or it may be said that the wife has two-thirds of the usufruct, and the son one-third of the said usufruct. For the son ought to have his legitime together with the usufruct, and with full right, as noted in the Digest, *De usufructu legato*, law *Uxori*, in the last paragraph. Consider that there was one male and three females, who make up the male’s share in the legitime, and therefore the usufruct of the son’s legitime portion would not be more than one-fourth of one-third of all the goods. And thus the wife ought to have the usufruct of 11 ounces, and the son’s heirs the usufruct of 12 ounces, however. And this is taken with respect to the subtlety and meaning of the words. But I do not think that the testator had this intention, namely, to restrict the son to one-twelfth part of the casual usufruct. And because the testator attached the condition “as long as she lives with his sons, etc.,” the testator wished her to have care of the sons; out of regard for this care, he made the legacy to her. And if we were to say that this was not a legacy of alimony, since it was terminated by the death of the sons according to a certain opinion held by Bartolus in the Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, law *Illis libertis*, and in the Code, *De legatis tertio*, law 1, according to which opinion it would be concluded, following Bartolus’s view, that the said legacy of usufruct was extinguished by the death of the son. But if we hold that it was a legacy of alimony, it endures even after the death of the person with whom the legatee was to dwell. And this is a special favor for alimony, as in the Digest, *De legatis tertio*, law *Qui concubinam*, section *Uxori*. And according to Bartolus’s opinion, if a usufruct is bequeathed under the condition that she shall dwell with Titius and Seius, upon the death of one, the legacy would either be extinguished entirely or at least in part. Certainly, this point is doubtful according to Decius: this condition, “as long as she dwells with her sons,” if it is attached for the sake of the daughters, even in alimony, the legacy is extinguished upon the death of the sons. And in doubt, it is presumed thus in the case of a mother, as in the Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, law *Sed si haec*, section *Si*. Finally, I conclude that, upon examination of the words of the said testament, she ought to have the said usufruct, as in the Digest, *De usufructu accrescendo*, law *Si mulieri cum liberis*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a natural son, prohibited by his father from alienating the property bequeathed to him except to the legitimate sons of the testator himself, may leave it to his own natural son.
2. Legitimation by subsequent marriage causes the condition of the fideicommissum to fail.
3. Whether one prohibited from alienating to another person is deemed prohibited from alienating to his own natural son.
body: A certain person left a house to his natural son on the condition that he could not sell or alienate it, except to the legitimate sons of the said testator. Now the said natural son dies, leaving behind a natural son by a certain concubine, who was legitimated through the marriage of his mother, the concubine, to the said natural son of the testator. The question arises whether the said house devolves upon the natural son legitimated by the marriage of the concubine, or upon the legitimated sons of the testator, and what is the law.

† On the first point, I say that if the testator left property to his natural son and commanded that he could not sell or alienate it except to the legitimate sons of the said testator: if the said natural son has a legitimate natural son, or a natural son legitimated by marriage contracted with a concubine retained in the household with the intervention of dotal instruments, the said son thus legitimated succeeds in the said goods. And the reason is that, since he is legitimated by marriage, it is not understood that an alienation has been made, but rather a continuation of ownership. Hence, such a legitimated son, being his own and necessary heir, does not have a simple title as an heir, but ownership, which is understood to be one and the same ownership in number with that of his father, as in D. de usucapione pro herede, l. nihil; and one and the same continuation of ownership, as in D. qui ex causa maiorum, l. cum miles; and note D. de acquirenda possessione, l. cum heredes; and one and the same person is feigned, as in C. de impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus, l. si. Furthermore, even if it were an alienation, it is an intestate alienation, necessary, favorable, and legal, and by it the will of the deceased is not infringed; rather, if the testator had considered this case, he should have permitted this alienation, as in D. de pactis, l. tale pactum, § fin. Moreover, a tacit reason must be considered as if expressed, as in C. de fideicommissis, l. cum acutissimi. But the reason moving the testator was that the property should not be alienated outside the family; but here it is not alienated outside the family, as in C. de fideicommissis, l. voluntas.

† and therefore I say that if the marriage was contracted in the form required for legitimation, it is valid by virtue of the intervening dotal instrument, whereby such nephew, thus legitimated, causes the condition of the fideicommissum to fail. And on account of that legitimation, those goods remain to that son, as in the Institutes, De nuptiis, §. si.

But let us suppose that no dotal instruments intervene, and thus the natural son is not a legitimate son according to civil law. The question arises in any case whether the testator’s natural son, who is prohibited from alienating his goods to another, may transmit them to this his natural son. It seems to be mandated that care be taken and ensured that the property, which is prohibited from being alienated, does not pass intestate to a person prohibited from succeeding, as in D. 35.1.1 (ff. de leg. 2. l.) and C. 6.30.24 § pen. (codi. §. pen.). For since the testator designated the persons to whom alienation was permitted, he is deemed to have prohibited it to all others, as in D. 5.2.1 (ff. de iudi. l. cum Praetor). And this prohibition appears to contain a cause, since mention is made of agnates, and a cause, as in D. 35.2.3 (l. vxorem. §. haeres, vel legatarius).

The question turns on this: whether one prohibited from alienating to another person is deemed prohibited from alienating to his natural son. And certainly it seems that he is not: for, considering nature, the natural son is a son, and the father has paternal affection for him, and therefore he should not be considered another person, but the same as the father, as in D. 47.10.1 (ar. ff. de iu. delide. l. fi.) and D. 36.1.1 § si quis (ff. ad Treb. l. ex facto. §. si quis). Hence he is not called another person, because “another” is a relative term indicating diversity of substance. But father and son are regarded as the same body, so that what is retained and preserved in the same lineage does not seem to be alienated to another person, as in C. 6.42.1 (C. de fideic. l. voluntas).

On the contrary, it seems likely that the testator preferred legitimate and lawful sons, for whom he has paternal affection, as in C. 6.24.1 § fi. (C. de insti. et substi. l. generaliter. §. fi.). And it is held that, since the words of the testament state that the property cannot be alienated to any other person except John and Nicholas, it seems that the words must be followed, so that it cannot be alienated to any other person, as in D. 18.1.1 (ff. de contrahen. emp. l. qui fundum vendidit). This is supported by what is noted in D. 43.2.1 § qui iniuriam (ff. si quis cau. l. si eum. §. qui iniuriam). Hence the legitimate son seems preferable to the natural grandson in a legacy left in this manner, especially if the testator knew of such a grandson and made no mention of him in any premiss, as in C. 6.26.3 (arg. C. de inoff. testa. l. 3.). And although elsewhere the question is formed whether a natural son excludes a substitute, this question does not arise here, because we are speaking of a particular legacy, not of a universal substitution. For in a particular fideicommissum left after the death of someone, that condition is not implied, namely, if the burdened party dies without children, as noted in the laws cited above. And therefore it seems to be concluded, although I am quite doubtful, that the legitimate son succeeds, excluding the natural son, who has no legitimate claim, as in C. 5.27.1 (C. de na. lib. l. fi.). This is supported by the fact that in a last will, contemplation operates only as much as proper demonstration, as in D. 35.2.1 § haec uerba (ff. de leg. 3. l. fideic. §. haec uerba) and § plerunque and § interdum, and D. 36.1.1 in princ. (ff. ad Trebe. l. qui filium. in princ.). Hence, since contemplation was had for the legitimate sons, it seems tacitly left to them by fideicommissum after the death of the natural sons.

The objection from D. 35.2.1 § fundum (ff. de leg. 3. l. pater filium. §. fundum) does not hold, because there the phrase “as long as he lived” resolves the contrary.

I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether he who stood surety for someone that he would faithfully practice the art of exchange is liable for debts contracted by that person on account of cloth, iron, or other merchandise.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A certain Odorisius Campsor promised to carry out the art of exchange well, loyally, and in good faith. And a certain Antonius acted as his surety up to the amount of 500 florins. This Odorisius wrote in his books that he was a debtor to certain persons on account of cloth, pepper, and iron. Then afterwards this Odorisius defrauded and fled.

† It is asked whether the said surety is bound for the said entries written in his books on account of cloth, pepper, and iron, assuming that the said books are titled in this manner, namely: these books are exchange books of such a money-lender. To the aforementioned points, I respond and say that the surety is not bound for several reasons. And first, because the surety acceded to the promise of the principal debtor, namely the said Odorisius. But the said Odorisius did not then promise to conduct the trade of cloth well and loyally; therefore, the surety is not bound for the trade: because a surety cannot be obligated for more, or for something else, than the principal himself is obligated, as in D. de fideiuss. l. Graece, §. Illud. Second, a surety who guarantees for a specific cause is not bound outside that cause, as is presently alleged and noted in D. locati conducti, l. Quo, in principio. But this surety guaranteed for the cause of exchange, and this is not a cause of exchange, but of another trade, namely the trade of cloth; therefore, he did not guarantee for this cause: and thus he is not bound, as in D. de verb. oblig. l. Quicquid astringendae, and D. de fideiuss. l. Fideiussoris magistratuum, §. Pro Aurelio. Third, because a surety is understood to guarantee for an honest cause, and not for these fictitious, simulated, and usurious causes, as in D. ad Municipalem, l. Lucius, §. Fin. Fourth, because this is a necessary guarantee on the part of the money-lender, and therefore it is not held to be a guarantee unless for that cause which the statute provides, as in D. si quis cautio, l. Sed et si quis, §. Fin. Fifth, because different trades have different ends, and obligations are different and separate, as in D. de institutionibus, l. Quicunque, §. Non tamen, and D. quod cum eo, l. Tuccianus. And therefore, a guarantee restricted to a certain type of trade does not extend to another type. On the contrary, if the type for which he guaranteed is of a different kind than what the surety promised, he is not understood to have guaranteed for this trade of mixed kind or mixed exercise, arg. D. de leg. 3, l. Hoc legatum, and D. de leg. 1, l. Titiae textores. Hence, one who guarantees for a money-lender simply in the civil art does not seem to be bound if exchange falls under trade: because principally another trade is contracted, as in D. nautae, cauponae, stabularii, l. 3, §. 2. Hence, if a merchant wrote the price in an exchange book, saying that he binds himself to it by exchange: nevertheless, because the origin is inspected, it does not seem that the surety of exchange is bound by this: because from the beginning of the title, the subsequent event is formed. And because it is not likely that this was considered by the surety, as in D. de donationibus, l. Quicquid, and D. de fideiussoribus, l. Tutor, and C. de impositione lucrae descriptionis, l. 1, lib. 10. Otherwise it would follow that, since every cause in the world can be deduced by stipulation into any other cause, as in C. si certum petatur, l. Si ex pretio, that this surety could be bound from any cause deduced into the figure of exchange, which certainly does not seem true, because it is not the intent of the contracting parties. And assuming that this reason were not true, nevertheless I firmly hold that the surety is not bound in our case, because whether we call money-changers money-lenders or bankers, as in D. de edendo, l. Quaedam, §. Numularios, and in Auth. de fideiuss. §. Pe, and they differ from merchants regarding confession, oath, register, and judge, as in C. de iudicibus omnium iudiciorum, l. Fin, and D. de publicaniis, l. Licitatio, §. Mercatores. And therefore, the exchange magistrate, or the notary of exchange who caused that public document to be received, is not understood to have made or received it, except insofar as it pertains to his public office, and not to the office of a chamberlain of another art, as in l. 2, C. de executionibus, and l. Ex postfacto, lib. 12. It supports what is noted by Innocentius in de clericis conjugatis, c. Dudum. And this appears, because this security contains a guarantee to appear in judgment and to satisfy the judgment. Third, it is not understood to be made except for that which pertains to the jurisdiction of exchange or trade. Hence, it necessarily follows that the said stipulation does not refer to trade, but to that lawsuit which, before the auditors of exchange, must be conducted according to the form of the statutes. Certainly, a judge stipulating simply is understood to stipulate for his own interest, namely his jurisdiction, and not for the interest of a third party, as in D. de verb. oblig. l. 2, §. Fin. With the following law, it is clearly and evidently concluded that the surety of the said Odorisius is not bound for the said trades of cloth, pepper, and iron, nor for other similar ones: and especially in those in which derogation has been made for creditors to contract, because trade and exchange are not exchange, but usurious loan, as John of Andrea says. And truth itself attests to this. And although the ordinance of the exchange art says in it "as he promised as a money-lender": nevertheless, where he himself buys that which he promises, he promises as a merchant, not as a money-lender, as in D. de tabulis, l. Procuratoris, §. Si plures, and D. nautae, cauponae, stabularii, l. Et ita, ver. Caeterum, where the text says that if someone is bound by the edict of a certain trade for the sake of a trader of that trade, if he received something outside that trade, he is not bound by that edict or by the statute of that art.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Bequests to pious causes are said to be entire, and the heir makes no deduction from them.
2. One who bequeaths certain specific items of the inheritance is not said to exceed the capacity of the estate.
3. If legacies made in a quantity exceed the estate, such legacies diminish legacies made in specific items.
4. A legatee may repudiate a universal legacy and accept a particular one.
5. The legatee is not bound to pay the debts of the testator, but the heir is.
6. An heir who denies that the inheritance assets are in the estate cannot avail himself of the benefit of inventory.
7. [Text illegible or missing]
8. If the heir is unjustly condemned, this does not harm the legatees.
9. A promise made to restore something is understood to be in the same degree, if it will be possible, and if a fortuitous event does not impede it. By what penalty is an heir who does not restore a fideicommissum bound?
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. In the case pending between the Brothers of the Holy Cross and Lady Lita, because her procurator, Lord Laurentius, states that this Lady Lita offers herself ready to restore the fideicommissum, if and insofar as the Brothers satisfy the debts and legacies: if Lord Laurentius has a just intention, if they say that they are to be paid, and if they do not say that they are to be paid, that they are not to be paid, he is to be praised for his good intention. But if he had the intention that those things which are not said to be paid should be paid, he ought not to be acceded to in his wishes, but justice should be administered as peremptory. And therefore, for the understanding of the intention, insofar as it pertains to the disposition of the law, certain things must be premised.

† And first, that when the testator does not exceed the assets of the estate in making legacies, there is no doubt that all legacies, and in full, whatever have been left for pious causes, are due; because from such legacies an extraneous heir makes no deduction, as is stated in C. ad l. Falcidiam, auth. similiter, and in c. Si pater, de testamentis, lib. 6. But if the testator exceeds the assets of the estate in making legacies, if indeed the heir receives fruits by the judgment of the testator, to such extent or of such kind, because he left them under a condition or for a future day, then the deficiency must be made up from those fruits. The case is literally covered by ff. de legatis 1, l. Filius, §. Apud Marcellum, and ff. ad Senatusconsultum Trebellianum, l. Ita tamen, §. Ex asse, which begins Haeres ex asse, and there the text and glossa are literally applicable. Hence, since the fruits received in the meantime from the conditional fideicommissum left to the brothers truly amount to the value of the quantities of the pure legacies, on account of these quantities having been paid, no diminution ought to be made of the universal or particular fideicommissum left to the brothers after the death of the instituted and substituted heirs. And there is no doubt about this, because it is the case of C. de substitutionibus, l. Ancillae. Hence, even if the brothers had accepted the universal fideicommissum, the law would be the same; because it is the case of the aforementioned laws, namely, that no diminution is made of the universal fideicommissum, nor of the particular one, on account of the legacies having been paid, insofar as the fruits received in the meantime by the judgment of the testator contribute together with the legacies themselves. But it is most certain that he who is charged with a fideicommissum under a condition, while the condition is pending, receives the fruits by the judgment of the testator, as ff. ad Trebellianum, l. Mulier, §. Alia causa, and note ff. de inofficiosa testamento, l. Papinianus, §. Si conditioni.

Secondly, it must be premised that when a testator bequeaths to certain persons specific hereditary items, it is certain that by making such a bequest he does not exceed his estate, because they are part of the estate and belong to the substance of the estate, as stated in D. de legatis 2, l. cum pater, in principio, and D. ad Trebellianum, l. deducta, § minus.

† Because, if this testator leaves to other legatees quantities in addition to the aforementioned specific items, even if such quantities exceed the estate, the legacies of specific items are not diminished on account of these quantities; rather, the specific items themselves are said to be due. And if the assets are insufficient for the quantities, the quantities are not said to be due; this is the case in the Digest, as in the proposed law, l. si fideicommissor, and there Jacobus de Arena expressly notes that the legacy of specific items of the testator is not diminished on account of a legacy of quantities, especially when the latter were not among the testator’s assets. Therefore, let the heir impute the loss to himself, who paid the quantities, although he could not satisfy the fideicommissaries regarding the specific items; even though, according to the truth of the matter, the inheritance of Cola was most wealthy and enriched. And thus the said brothers suffer most openly.

Third, I premise that when a universal fideicommissum is left to the same person, and it is within his power to accept a particular legacy and repudiate the universal one, and it is within his power to accept a particular legacy and repudiate the universal fideicommissum: because, where two paths are granted by the testator, the legatee may choose whichever path he wishes. The case is found in D. de legatis 1, l. et quidem totum; and D. de legatis 2, l. ult. ad sororem, § pro parte; and D. ad Trebellianum, l. recusare, § Titius; and C. de codicillis, l. si quis agere. And these brothers could, and can, choose the fideicommissum, or the legacy of certain things, and not involve themselves in hereditary burdens, because the case is expressly stated in the aforementioned laws.

Fourthly, I premise, and now I proceed to debts arising from contracts, and I say that it is certain that the legatee is not bound to pay the debts, but rather the heir, as in C. si certum petatur, l. 1, where the case is presented verbatim. And the reason is that the heir, by entering upon the inheritance, as it were contracts with the hereditary creditors; but the legatee has not entered upon the inheritance, and therefore does not as it were contract, nor can he as it were contract, as in ff. ad Trebellianum, l. 1, § si haeres; and ff. de hereditate instituenda, l. ex facto; and ff. de iudiciis, l. fideicommissum, § tractatum. Hence, the exception of alien debt does not hinder legatees from obtaining their legacies, if the assets of the inheritance permit, or even if they do not permit, if the heir has not made an inventory.

† It must be noted here that an heir who denies that certain corporeal things are part of the inheritance cannot avail himself of the benefit of the inventory; because, since he did not include those things in the inventory, the inventory is null by operation of law in all respects and in every way, so that it is of no benefit whatsoever, as is expressly stated in the law and the note in the Authentica *De haeredibus et falsis*, § *Et hoc discimus*, in the gloss beginning *Hoc facit*, at the word where it says: “Moreover, heirs who secretly appropriate [property] are deprived of everything.” And in the Digest, *Ad legem Falcidiam*, law *Haereditas*, § *Si*, where there is a notable case. But since this lady denied that many things were part of the inheritance, when in truth they were, even if an inventory had been drawn up, it would be of no benefit to her.

Fifthly, I premise that when an heir unjustly condemns one who is not a creditor, this does not prejudice the legatees, as is stated in the Digest, *De fideiussoribus*, law *Exceptione*; and in the Digest, *De inofficioso testamento*, law *Qui repudiandis*, section *Si*, with the following section. And having made this premise, I come to the acts of the case, and I accept the article of the lady as the factual foundation. For she states that the mills were destroyed by the force of the river, which could not be resisted. From this it follows that the best thing, which existed, was removed, and that no obligation remained in force, as is stated in the Digest, *De locato conducto*, law *Si fundus*; law *Si merces*, section *Vis maior*. For in mills this can be called *casus* (accident), since they are destroyed from the root, as is stated in the Code, *De iure emphyteutico*, law 1. And the peril of *casus* does not fall upon any contract in the world. This is understood to be the case, because it is contrary to equity, contrary to the nature of the contract,

† And the promise to reassign the mills in the same state contains within itself a tacit condition, namely, if it shall be possible, and if a fortuitous event does not impede it. For these conditions are tacitly implied, as in D. si quis cautionem (46.1), l. sed si quia, § quaesitum; and D. de contrahenda emptione (18.1), l. domum. Therefore, if anything was paid or damaged on this occasion, the heir suffered an injury which does not prejudice the legatees, as in D. de evictionibus (21.2), l. per imprudentiam; just as, conversely, it would not benefit the legatees if the heir acquired something through the wrongful act of a judge, as in D. ad Senatusconsultum Trebellianum (36.1), l. et debitor, § final. I premise that when the first heir is burdened with certain things to be provided to someone, even though those things do not belong to the heir of the heir, nevertheless there is no doubt that the heir of the heir is bound to those things; because in this case they are regarded as a debt, in which it is not examined whether it has come into his hands or not, as in D. ad legem Falcidiam (34.1), l. pater filium. And by this it is evident that, although the massarities did not come to this lady, nevertheless she is bound to all the massarities which were in the goods of the said Cola at the time of his death, which remained in his inheritance, or to their estimation, as in C. de secundis nuptiis (5.18), l. hac edictali, § illo. It does not prejudice the legatees if the heir squandered or sold those massarities. Hence it suffices to prove once that they came to the heir, or could have come to him, as in D. quod metus causa (4.2), l. videamus.

From these points it clearly appears that it is a grave sin to keep these brothers in such distress; rather, the said lady has incurred the penalty of double restitution, as stated in the Institutes, concerning actions, §. item, where it is said that an action is mixed against them. Let the rest be supplied by the good faith and devoted conscience of the judge. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The word "cassare" (to annul) is understood in several ways, and numbers 2 and 3.
2. Given a statute that if the assignment of a will is not requested within a certain time, annulment may be requested, whether the one requesting that the will be declared invalid appears to be requesting its annulment.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The statute of the commune of Perugia provides that if no assignment of the testament has been made within a certain time, its cancellation may be requested; and if such cancellation has not been requested, an assignment may always be made. It happened that, because no assignment had been made, it was requested in this manner, namely, that the testament was invalid and is invalid. In the petition, no mention was made of cancellation using the formal words of the statute. After the petition was presented, the adversary made an assignment and produced the testament with the intention of insinuating it. It is opposed against the said assignment, because first it was requested that the testament be declared invalid as not having been assigned within the proper time. But to this it is answered by the opposing party that, although it was requested that the testament be declared invalid and not binding, nevertheless this is not to request cancellation, as the statute requires. Now the question arises whether the aforementioned words “invalid” and “not binding” carry the force and nature of the requested cancellation, such that the assignment and production subsequently made during the time of insinuations avail nothing.

† To this, we must first note that the word "we annul" and the verbal noun "annulment" are found in a twofold sense. In one sense, annulment refers to the act, as in the Digest, extra de concessione praebendarum, chapter *Proposuit*, on the word "annulment"; and then even that which is null is annulled. And elsewhere the text says: "we have annulled, nay, we have declared annulled and void," as in extra, ut lite non contestata, chapter 2, at the end. To this effect is the Code, de aquaeductu, law *Diligenter*, book 11, on the word "to be annulled," where an obreptitious and null rescript is annulled. To the same effect is extra, de electione, chapter *Cum dilectus*, on the word "you annul." Innocentius says: "you declare it null." The same is said there by Hostiensis. And thus something is annulled insofar as it proceeded de facto. So also the Code, de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, authentic *Cassa et irrita*.

Secondly, it is said that that which holds by strict law is annulled, although it was unjustly done. And in this sense the term is taken in *Extra*, *De restitutione spoliorum*, chapter *Cum ad sedem*; and in *Extra*, *De electionibus*, chapter *Consideravimus*; and chapter *Super eo*; and in *Extra*, *De posthac praelatis*, chapter *Gratum*. For although it holds from the beginning, yet since a cause for annulment exists, such annulment is referred to the primary law, which is annulled and invalidated. Hence, it is the same to say "to annul" as "to invalidate" or "to rescind." Therefore, the text in the *Codex*, *De sacrosanctis ecclesiis*, law 1, states: "It is not annulled, but is invalid and has no force."

Thirdly, something is said to be annulled, or to be annulled, if its execution cannot be carried out; hence the text states that a sentence would be called annulled if its execution were not carried out, as in C. de episcopis et iudiciis, l. episcopale. From these authorities it appears that annulment is understood in several ways. For, as I have said, it sometimes refers to the act, sometimes to the substance, sometimes to the execution, and sometimes to the cancellation of the writing.

† Let us therefore consider what kind of cassation is meant by the statute. It must be said that, since the will is valid from the beginning, the cassation referred to is that which must be effected by judicial sentence, according to the doctrine handed down by Bartolus in C. de precibus Imperatoris offerentium, l. universa; de iure fisci, l. eius qui delatorem. And thus it refers to the substance, because the substance of the will is annulled. For what is it to annul the substance of a will, other than to pronounce that the will is invalid? Moreover, he who does not ask that the will be pronounced invalid does not seem to be asking for that from which the invalidity follows, as shown by the argument in ff. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. illud. Furthermore, does not this person appear to be bringing all his rights into the judicial proceeding, since the words of the libel allow for it, as in ff. de iudiciis, l. si quis in onere? It is also irrelevant whether one says “annul” or “I ask that it be declared invalid” or “null.” Hence, if someone asks in the libel that the election be pronounced invalid, and the judge pronounces using the word “we annul,” is the sentence invalid? Certainly not, because it accords with the intent of the plaintiff and the matter at hand, and the signification of the thing requested is appropriate. Indeed, these terms are synonymous: “to annul” and “to pronounce invalid,” insofar as annulment refers to right or to fact. Therefore, it seems to me, without prejudice to the truth, that by such a petition, namely “the will is invalid,” the right of assigning, not of insinuating, is interrupted and removed. And this petition is founded on the statute, because the statute states that it “shall not be valid, nor shall it bind,” etc. Hence, the statute considers “not valid” and “annulled” to be the same. Therefore, it seems to be said that the libel was clearly conceived, since the signification of annulment is included in the words of the libel, and we must be satisfied with the sense of the words, as in ff. de iureiurando, l. sed et si possessori, § si quis iuraverit. Otherwise, it would follow that if annulment was requested in the libel, and the judge in the sentence did not say “we annul,” but said “we pronounce it null and invalid,” such a pronouncement would be invalid, because it would not conform to the libel, as in C. de fideicommissis, l. si. Which I absolutely do not believe. On the contrary, I say that the sentence is valid, and that these words are conformable and equivalent, and it does not matter whether one speaks properly or by equivalent words, as in ff. de arbitris, l. quid tamen. And it is read and noted in C. de sententiis et interlocutionibus omnium iudicum, l. Praeses Provinciae.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The party bringing an action by way of petition for inheritance, if he does not prove the facts conclusive for his claim, must bear the costs. See also no. 4.
2. Where it does not appear who died first, the father or the son: who is presumed to have died first. See also nos. 3 and 6.
3. One claiming to be an heir by reason of the death of someone must prove that person’s death, since it is the foundation of his claim.
4. Life is rather presumed than death; and death is a matter of fact, and is not presumed, except in cases expressly provided for in law.
5. That the son is presumed to have died before the father is not presumed, unless they died simultaneously in the same event, such as a collapse, etc.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen. In the case pending between Lady Flore Achea Paluella and Vanna, acting on one side, and Lady Lena, widow of Peter and mother of Titia, defending on the other side, and having examined the proceedings in the said case,

† It seems to me, according to Baldus, always saving the substance of the truth, that it has not been proven by the aforementioned agents that the inheritance of Peter, formerly brother of the said women, pertains to them. And this is clear from the following reason. It is certain that from Peter and the said Lady Lena was born Tia, daughter of Peter. It is certain

It is certain that both have died, namely Peter and Titia. It is also certain that it has not been proven by the plaintiffs that Titia died before Peter. And thus it does not appear that the said plaintiffs know that Peter’s inheritance was devolved upon them. Therefore, they cannot enter upon the inheritance, even if in truth it had been devolved, as is stated in the Digest, *De acquisitione hereditatis*, in the law *Quod si dubitet* and in the law *Is potest*; and as is noted in the Digest, *De petitione hereditatis*, in the law *Illud*; and in the Code, *De postliminio reversis*, in the law *Nec nos*. Since, therefore, they cannot enter upon the inheritance of the said Peter, they cannot bring an action for the vindication of the inheritance.

The second reason is as follows: in case of doubt, it must be presumed that the father died first rather than the daughter, as stated in the Digest, *ad legem Falcidiam*, law *Hereditatum*. For it is presumed that a young person lives longer than an old man. This is also proven in the Digest, *de rebus dubiis*, law *Qui duos*, section *Cum in libello*. Hence, since Titia is presumed to have survived her father, her inheritance belongs to her mother, namely the lady Lena, as stated in the Code, *de suis et legitimis heredibus*, law *Apud hostes*. The third reason is this: even if it were not presumed either for or against, nevertheless in case of doubt the defendant ought to be acquitted, as stated in the Institutes, *de interdictis*, section *Commodum*.

† because whenever anyone claims to be an heir by the death of another, who would have been an obstacle if he were alive, he must prove the order of death, namely that the one who would have been an obstacle died first: because this is the foundation of his claim, just as he who claims to be an heir by pupillary substitution must prove that the case has occurred. And the same applies in all similar cases, as C. de edicto divi Adriani tollendo, l. si. Fifth, and finally, in support of this is the general rule stated regarding the burden of proof of time lying on the plaintiff, who must prove the time necessarily concluding to his claim, as noted in ff. de negotiis gestis, l. eum actum; and C. de probationibus, l. matrem tuam. Moreover, although the notary may have erred in the writing, yet because the error is evident from what precedes in the same writing, which speaks of Peter Angeli, the writer’s error does not prejudice the truth, as ff. de re iudicata, l. si liberare. For an error, of which there is proof, does not harm. Otherwise, if it were not evident, as noted in C. de testamento, l. ambiguitatem; and ff. de hereditate instituenda, l. quotiens. And therefore, considering the truth, and also considering the acts, judgment should be rendered in favor of the said Lena. Nor does it matter that the daughter of the said Peter died before reaching puberty: because then it is presumed that she died first, when they were thrown together. But here it is not established that they were thrown together, nor that they were in the same place: and the reason is that when it is presumed that the father survived the impubes, because a child dies more easily, as ff. de rebus dubiis, l. mulier. In support of the foregoing is also the fact that the said Lady Lena is in possession, and is the defendant, and in doubt judgment is rendered for the defendant, as Inst. de interdictis, § commodum. Bartolus says that although someone had children, it is not presumed that he had them at the time of his death, from which words some might perhaps be deceived,

† because life is rather presumed than death, as noted in C. sol. mat. l. si quidem and l. 2 § si dubitatur, ff. quemadmodum test. aper. For death is a matter of fact, and facts are not presumed, except in cases expressly provided for in law.

† But that an impubes is presumed to have died first is not found in the law, except when they were thrown together. And in one and the same case, for example, a collapse, or a fire, or in similar cases, etc. This is held by Jacobus de Arena in l. ex facto, §. pe., ad Trebellianum. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a *suus* heir transmits a conditional fideicommissum to his own descendants. And add the same opinion above, in opinion 115.
2. A renewal of emphyteusis made by the emphyteuta is understood to have been made twice for those who paid the canon, but not for others.
3. The legitime is not deducted from the goods of the emphyteuta
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† On this point there are contrary glosses. The gloss in l. is, cui. ff. de acquisitione et obligatione states that a predeceased heir transmits a conditional fideicommissum to his descendants, and in support of this opinion is l. qui patri haeres extitit ff. de acquirenda hereditate. But another gloss, by way of disputation, holds the contrary, as is fully noted in l. 2. C. de his, quae ante apertionem tabularum. And this opinion is the very truth; hence, without further allegations, it seems that prima facie the said inheritance pertains by right of fideicommissum to Angelina and Paulina, and not to the daughters of the other daughters of the testator who predeceased the said Giovanelli. For even with these substitutes succeed the male children of Suicia, Vannucia, and Paulucia, or of any one of them; because the will says so. But the daughters of the aforesaid women Suicia, Vannucia, and Paulucia do not succeed; because a conditional substitution is not transmitted, as I have said.

It is to be considered more clearly on this point that either we speak of the force of transmission, and while the condition is pending no transmission takes place, as C. de caducis tollendis §. si an conditione and §. pro secundo, and C. de fideicommissis l. si in personam; or we speak by virtue of the disposition in the person herself. And then succeed the males born of those who predeceased, but not the daughters of those women. And this distinction is made by the testator himself, for the masculine gender is put forward here causatively and distinctively. Hence it does not comprehend the feminine, because the testator made mention of males as if they were added to the females. Hence rightly he established one thing for males, another for females, because this provision appears from the mind of the testator, as ff. de venditionibus in possessionem missis l. 1. §. quare. For where sexes are distinguished as things opposed, one is not contained in the other, nor there in any way does the masculine comprehend the feminine, as Inst. de hereditatibus ab intestato §. item vetustas.

† It is nevertheless asked whether the emphyteutic properties, which have been reformed, belong solely to the aforementioned Paulucius, formerly Salualis, acting for himself, and a certain Bartholomew, since the others have not paid the census for eight years or thereabouts. I answer that they belong to the said Bartholomew and Paulucius, to whom the new reformation was made, and that the others have forfeited their right, if any they had, due to the unpaid canon, as provided in C. de iure emphyteuticario, l. 2.

† Furthermore, it is asked whether one should receive the legitime and the Trebellianic portion from emphyteutic goods by virtue of emphyteutic rights. I answer: no, as stated in the Digest, ad Trebellianum, in the law "Quia per vim," because the mother does not succeed her son in ecclesiastical emphyteutic goods, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Certain petitions were submitted to the Pope.
body:
In the Name of Christ, Amen. Most Blessed Father, a dispute having arisen between Lord Lanfranc, formerly son of Zentilin of the Suardi family, a citizen of Bergamo, on one part, and Jacob, his brother, on the other part, concerning and regarding the goods and inheritance of the said late Zentilin, the said brothers compromised to certain laymen as arbitrators, under a certain penalty, and swore that they would accept the awards or arbitral decisions which the said arbitrators would promulgate, and would not go against them, nor would they seek restitution in integrum, nor would they seek to have such awards or arbitral decisions reduced to the discretion of an honest man, nor would they seek to have such oaths relaxed. And having undertaken the compromise upon themselves, they rendered their award between the said brothers, which was spontaneously approved by both parties.

Subsequently, however, the said Jacob, having changed his will, falsely suggested to Your Holiness that at the time of the said compromise he was of an age such that he ought to have had a curator, and did not have one. And that by the said award he had been enormously injured, having been entirely consumed of his goods. And, as is said, he obtained from Your Holiness a mandate to the Lord Bishop of Bergamo, his own name not being expressed, that, the said parties and others who were to be summoned being absent, and notwithstanding the oaths, the said Jacob being restored in integrum, and against the said award, as would be just according to law, that he should decree what would be just, etc. And subsequently, as is said, the said Lord Bishop, proceeding by virtue of such commission without a mandate, pronounced that the oath given by Jacob should be relaxed, and in fact relaxed it, to the end, as he said, that the said Jacob might be restored against the injury, from which pronouncement an appeal was taken on the part of the said Lord Lanfranc. Your Holiness committed the cause of such appeal by its letters to the venerable man, Lord Abbot of the monastery of Alta Valle of the diocese of Bergamo, his own name not being expressed. By virtue of whose commission the said Lord Abbot, proceeding duly in effect, pronounced that the said Lord Bishop had proceeded and pronounced wrongly, and that on the part of the said Lord Lanfranc the provocation and appeal had been rightly made, and that the said oath or oaths given by the said Jacob had been and were to be proven, as is contained more or less in the said pronouncement.

Since, however, it is said that an appeal has been taken and is taken from such pronouncement on the part of the said Jacob to the Holy Apostolic See and to Your Holiness, therefore it is supplicated to Your Holiness on the part of the said Lord Lanfranc, the appellant, that you deign to commit the cause and causes, both of the appeal or appeals interposed on the part of the said Jacob, and of the whole principal business, and of any other whatever which is used and will be used between the said parties on the occasion of the aforesaid matters, both jointly and severally, to one of the venerable men, Lords Auditors of Causes of your Sacred Palace, to be heard, decided, and terminated with a due end, with all incidents, emergences, dependencies, and connections, and with the power of summoning the said Jacob in court and out, and to parts once or several times, and as often as need shall require. Although such cause and causes are not legitimately devolved to the Roman Curia, nor are they of their nature to be treated and done therein, since the said Lanfranc hopes better to obtain the fulfillment of justice in court than out. And if it pleases, let it be committed to the venerable man, Lord John of Cambr., Auditor of the said Palace, to whom the said causes were committed, because it was alleged that the parties were legitimately present in court, although after the presentation of the said commission the said Jacob nor his procurator was not found in court.

Most Blessed Father, it is exposed to Your Holiness on the part of the venerable man, Lord Massiet of Urmano, a prebendary canon of the church of Bergamo. Who formerly was sub-collector of the fruits of the Apostolic Chamber of Your Holiness, in the city with the diocese of Bergamo, that during the time of his said office, a certain Nicorolus of Scampuo, or of Scamo, a canon of the said church of Bergamo, affecting damage to the said Apostolic Chamber of Your Holiness, informed a certain Lord Barnaboe, then vicar of the said city of Bergamo, namely, that the said sub-collector had in his possession 500 gold florins of the fruits of the said Apostolic Chamber. On account of which unjust information, the said sub-collector, by the command of the said late Lord Barnaboe, was imprisoned and detained in prison for 25 days. And finally it was necessary for him to pay whatever he had of the fruits of the said Apostolic Chamber, namely, 30 gold florins, since he did not have more of the said fruits, and 20 florins of his own, because otherwise he could not have exited from the said prisons. For the said Nicorolus said that he would have the said sub-collector burned, because he was performing the office of sub-collector.

It is true, Most Blessed Father, that the said Nicorolus obtained the said canonries and prebends by violence, because at his instance the said late Lord Barnaboe expressly commanded the chapter and canons of the said church of Bergamo that, under penalty of imprisonment, they should elect the said Nicorolus to the said canonries and prebend then vacant in a certain manner. By virtue of whose mandate the said Nicorolus was elected, who otherwise would not have been elected, since he is a man lacking virtues, nor does he know or say the divine office. Moreover, the said Nicorolus during the time of the present Holiness resided continuously in Avignon for two years, and of all the aforesaid there is public voice and fame. Wherefore it is supplicated to Your Holiness on the part of the said Lord Massier, that you deign to commit and mandate to the collector of the fruits of the Apostolic Chamber in those parts, or of that place, that he inform himself of the aforesaid. And if he finds the aforesaid to be true, or at least the greater part of them, that he deprive the same Nicorolus, as one who has obtained them by suppression, of the said canonries, prebend, and other ecclesiastical benefices to be named in the chancery of Your Holiness, or of the Apostolic authority, and of the same canonry, prebend, and benefices. The fruits of all of which do not exceed the value of 125 gold florins annually by common estimation. And if otherwise in any way, or from any person, or if they are reserved specially or generally to the Apostolic See, let him provide for your devout servant Antonio, son of John of Freci, his cleric of Bergamo, with the same authority. For the same Antonio is ready to say that the perpetual benefice called a clerkship situated in the church of Saint Christina of Albino of the diocese of Bergamo, once he has peacefully obtained the priorate, with non-obstantes and opportune clauses, as below.

I have to propose for a certain noble man and graduate, for whom formerly in the roll of your University of Pavia supplication was made. However, according to the statutes of the said University of Pavia, no one in civil law ought to be admitted to any degree unless first he has studied integrally in civil law for 6 years, and afterwards he can have the degree of bachelor. After this, let him read the book of Institutes through entirely, and in one year the new Digest, and in another the Digest anew, and the Decree. And one of the 9 collections of the book of Authentics, or one of the extraordinary books of the Code. Then let him read one lecture for each doctor of the same faculty, and answer one doctor of decrees, and hear any opponents, and argue in the school of each doctor. Since therefore this is a great and arduous form, and this noble man, of whom it is spoken, observed the said form before the signing of the said roll of the work of three days, except which he completed after the signing, and exists licensed, therefore equity suggesting, and because the laws cry out that he ought to have as much as he who is next to be touched, and also another law expressly provides that in the course of a long time very few days are not imputed to fault, D. de fundo dotali. I. si fundum, I come to the aforesaid supplication.

Another supplication presented to the Pope. Most Blessed Father, it is exposed to Your Holiness on the part of your devout orator Matthew Haumet, rector of the parish church of Lanuighur of the diocese of Assisi, for whom in your roll of the University of Pavia concerning a canonry under expectation of a prebend and dignity in the church of Messina, supplication was formerly made, that the signing of the said roll did not extend to his supplication because then he was not a doctor nor licensed. But the work of three days was lacking to him for the time, namely, to read two lectures for two doctors, and to answer one doctor of decrees according to the statutes of the same study. Since therefore he has completed those afterwards, and exists licensed, it is supplicated to Your Holiness on the part of the said Matthew, that, considering the nobility of his birth and his labors in study, in which he has effectively toiled for 16 years and more by hearing and reading in the same study of Pavia, you deign mercifully to grant him the said grace, and also to the dignity, if he should say an elective one, comes a dignity to which one is prefixed by election of the chapter, otherwise not, as in c. cum in illis, de praebendis, lib. 6. And if greater is after pontificals, and under the date of the signing of the said roll, to insert in the said roll his non-obstantes here having for sufficiently expressed with executories, and the rest as below.

I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A father cannot make a substitution for his children who die during his lifetime.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† A father, who is also the testator, could not make any substitution for sons who died during the testator’s lifetime, as stated in the Digest, *de vulgari et pupillari substitutione*, law *Lex Cornelia*; and in the Digest, *de capitis deminutione et postliminio reuersis*, law *Quod si filius*. This rule admits an exception for vulgar substitution, which a father could make for sons who were instituted as heirs and who died during the father’s lifetime. Nevertheless, this vulgar institution, whether express or tacit, when the son dies during the father’s lifetime, does not extend to the son’s property. The reason is that vulgar substitution pertains to the inheritance of the institutor; but the son’s property was not part of the father’s inheritance. Furthermore, although Master Dy. states that tacit vulgar substitution extends to the property of a ward and to a slave held in the property of an adult, it is impossible for this to apply where the ward dies while the testator is alive, because a father could not appoint heirs for a son who predeceased him. Therefore, the same hospital has no right to the property of H. N., the son; rather, the grandmother succeeds to the same son N. intestate in the son’s property. Baldus. Add Baldus’s counsel in the sixth part, beginning *Viso dicto puncto*, where he considers that in the said point it is presupposed that the citation is valid.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a statute providing that if any woman is summoned to a case, she is not bound to go to the palace, but the judge and the notary must go to the street of the episcopal see and hear her there: Whether such a citation of a woman, ordering her to appear at a certain hour of the court sessions, is valid for her legitimate appearance before the judge at the bench of cases.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The statute of the city of Foligno provides that if any woman is summoned to a case, the judge and the notary of the podestà are bound to go to the street of the episcopal palace and hear her there; and if it is done otherwise, it shall not be valid. And that no woman ought to come to the palace for any civil case, under penalty of 100 solidi of denarii. Now, a certain woman was cited in this form, namely, that on such a day, at the hour of cases, she come and appear legitimately before the judge at the bench of cases, etc. It is asked whether such citation is valid or not.

† And it seems, first, that the said citation is invalid, because the woman was cited to a place where she cannot appear without compromising her modesty. For the statute considers such a place to be indecent for women; and even the citation is invalid by reason of the place to which the citation was made, as in D. de arbitris, l. si cum dies, §. quid tamen. Moreover, this place is a prohibited and penal place for women to appear. But it is certain that a penal place is not safe for the person cited, and one is not bound to be cited to an unsafe place, as noted in D. ad Trebellianum, l. de aetate, and in X. ut lite non contestata, c. accedens. Therefore, either we must say that she is in contempt because she did not appear in that place, and this is true, because she could not appear there. Or, on the other hand, because she did not appear elsewhere, and this is not true, because she was not cited to another place, as in C. quomodo et quando iudices, l. ut proponis. Furthermore, either we must say that this woman was in contempt because she did not appear in her own person. And this is not true, because it was not lawful for her to access that place, as in c. 2, de iudicibus, lib. 6. Or because she did not send a procurator. And this does not seem true, because the defendant is not bound to send a procurator if he does not wish to, insofar as the defendant is impeded by law from appearing in that place. To this effect are D. si quis cautio, l. 2, and D. quibus ex causis maior, l. 1, and there noted, and D. de diversis et temporibus praescriptionum, l. 1. Furthermore, the form of the citation does not allow it, because the citation says, "and let her come, and appear at the bench of causes." For the word "come" signifies personal appearance. And if she appears, it is understood, i.e., she appears by coming, so that one is a verb and the other is a gerundive: which has to explain and specify the force of the verb, as in l. vim facit, de vi et vi armata. To the contrary, it is argued, for this citation is considered justified and possible because of the adverb "legitimately." For he who is cited to appear legitimately seems to be cited to appear in the manner in which he can appear according to law, as in D. de bonis autem iudicis possessoribus, l. si minor. But this woman could appear through a procurator; therefore, even if she did not appear, she ought to be considered in contempt. For thus it is in all those who are excused by privilege: they are said to send a procurator, as in C. de procuratoribus, l. si. And no one can be seen to be ordered to do through another what he can do by himself, as in D. de verbis obligatis, l. continuus, §. si ab eo. Solution. It must be said briefly that, since this adverb "legitimately" is uncertain as to the person in the place, not as to the person simply: inasmuch as that act is prohibited from being done in that place, the citation does not hold, nor does the statute derived from it, because the citation errs by reason of form and place, or by reason of the formal place. And therefore the adverb "legitimately," as being impossible, operates for nothing; nor is it necessary to send an excusator, because the disposition of the law excuses, indeed the law even prohibits; for he who is absent has the excuse of the law, which is much, of the sort: for if he had an excusator, i.e., one constituted, and if anyone has an excusator, he is not bound to send a procurator to the cause, because the excusator, alleging causes of absence according to law, relieves the defendant from the burden of constituting a procurator for the cause, as in D. de negotiis gestis, l. liberto, §. si. And therefore I advise for the woman that the citation under the said form is invalid for this added reason: because, since the woman is ignorant of the law, she is excused if she ought to have sent a procurator due to the subtlety of the law, and did not send one, because ignorance of the law should not hinder women, especially in avoiding damage, as in l. regula, and D. de iuris et facti ignorantia. And we have a similar case in one who cannot bind someone personally to appear. If, in citing, he sends to the person who will come by herself, the citation for appearance is invalid. And this is the similarity with respect to the form of the citation, which is questioned in the first question, as noted by Dynus, de iudicibus, lib. 6. And just as there, where there are two precepts, as in D. de arbitris, l. rursus. I answer that that law has no place in a place which cannot be separated from the precept, and from the concomitance and coherence of the act, and is inseparable from the act, as in D. de iure, l. si locus, and Inst. de verbis obligatis, §. loca. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given the statute that a woman endowed by her father or grandfather shall not succeed, if a granddaughter is endowed by her grandfather, may she repudiate the legacy on account of age, when she wishes to succeed to her father?
2. Whether she is said to be endowed who is burdened with the obligation of restitution.
3. If a daughter, who is to be endowed, is burdened with the charge of restitution, whether she is then said to be endowed; or, if the heir of the testator to whom restitution is to be made remits it to her, whether satisfaction is thereby rendered to the law.
4. Whether an arbiter, by his award, may declare who is the heir of the father, i.e., has the right of succession and of being heir, or does not succeed and is not heir, by imposing a condition which neither the law nor the statute imposes.
5. How it is to be ascertained whether a mode is irrelevant or not, by a judge or by an arbiter.
6. Whether a daughter declared heir by award under a condition, dying while the condition is pending, or after it has been fulfilled, transmits the inheritance to her mother in her last breath of life, and what is the law regarding the right of acceptance. And number 7.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. It is proposed that a certain testator, having two sons, instituted them as universal heirs, and if either of them should die without male children, he substituted the survivor. If he should die leaving a daughter, he left to her the right of dowry and of institution. After the death of the testator, one of the sons took a wife, and, while a daughter conceived after the death of the said testator was living, he died intestate. Now the statute says that a dowried daughter shall not succeed to the donor, nor shall descendants from him.

† It is asked whether this girl succeeds to her father. I answer: yes, because this granddaughter is not properly a granddaughter, but only abusively so, since she was not in existence while her grandfather was alive. And the statute, which speaks of a dowry given by the grandfather, must be understood properly as referring to a grandfather who is naturally a grandfather. But after death, no one can begin to be a grandfather, as stated in D. de suis et legitimis heredibus, l. Item Praetor; and D. de bonis liberti, l. Qui libertinus, § Posthumus. And not only would this be true in the matter of successions, but also generally. Hence, if a statute were to say that the grandsons of soldiers could not enter the palace, it would not apply to grandsons who are such in name only, conceived after the death of their grandfather, unless we ought to interpret otherwise according to common usage of speech. For common usage of speech prevails over every mode of signification, as noted in D. de legibus tertio, l. Librorum, § Quod tamen Cassius. However, the mode of speaking must be according to the subject matter. Secondly, it is asked concerning such a question,

† Suppose that a statute provides that a daughter endowed by her father or grandfather shall not succeed; now, the granddaughter, endowed by her grandfather, does not wish to accept the legacy in the will, but wishes to claim succession to her father. The question arises whether she is excluded from her father’s inheritance, given the aforementioned statute. It seems that she is, because she is endowed by a certain designation; hence even a ward is excluded, although the endowment is not repeated in her case. It is also sufficient that the testator complied with the aforementioned statute. He could thereby acquire freedom of testation, as noted in l. cum pluris, de administratione tutorum.

On the contrary, it seems that this legacy carries within itself a burden of exclusion from succession; nevertheless, a legacy must be gratuitous, and the legatee is not bound to accept a burden, as in ff. man. l. haereditatem. Moreover, the testator acts fraudulently. Therefore, with respect to excluding the girl, one may renounce the disposition, as in ff. de leg. 2. l. cum pater. §. litem.

Or, if the statute states that the granddaughter is bound to abide by the content of the will, she is understood to be endowed, although she may otherwise renounce the cause of the testator and succeed as an intestate heir, as in ff. si quis omissa causa testamenti.

Thirdly, it is asked: assuming that she is bound to abide by the testamentary appointment of an arbiter, is she to be understood as endowed, if she is burdened with the obligation of restitution? I answer: she is not to be understood as endowed, since she was not freely endowed, as is stated in the Digest, *De legatis* 2, *Uxorem*, § *Pater naturalis*, where Bartolus of Saxoferrato says that she is not to be understood as endowed unless this burden is remitted to her.

Fourthly, it is asked: what if this burden is not remitted to her during her lifetime, but rather the heir of the testator, to whom restitution is owed, remits it to the same girl? I answer: it appears sufficient, because from this we obtain the effect of the law, as shown in the argument from the Digest, title *Qui modis pignus vel hypotheca solvatur*, law *Sicut*, § 1.

Fifthly, it is asked concerning such a difficult question: since there was doubt both in law and in fact as to whether the said granddaughter succeeded to her father, the matter was compromised according to the form of the statute of the city of Perugia. It was solely inquired into, both in court and in the award, that the said granddaughter was not the heir of her father, notwithstanding the said testament, provided that the dowry was paid at the proper time, namely when she married, and that in the meantime maintenance was provided; but if the aforementioned conditions were not observed, she was declared heir. Now, since the said girl died before reaching marriageable age, it is asked whether she transmits the paternal inheritance to her mother. And for the investigation of this question, I do not call into doubt what I have said above, nor do I call into doubt the effect of the awards, assuming the power to make an award. Because, assuming the power to make an award, the award must be observed in its form, as if it were a judgment, which can produce something from non-existence to existence, and conversely, as noted in the Digest, title *De conditione indebiti*, law *Si non sortem*, § *Si con.*, and in the Digest, title *De statu liberorum*, law *Statuliber a caeteris*, § *Quintus*; or as if it were a transaction, as in the Digest, title *De transactione*, law *Controversia*.

But these doubts arise: first, whether an arbitrator could be appointed to succeed to the right of inheriting, and of being an heir, or of not succeeding, and of not being an heir, to impose a condition which neither law nor statute imposes. And it seems that he could, for the sentence of an arbitrator does not operate except according to the intention of the arbitrator, as is stated and noted in the law *et not.* in the Digest, *De arbitris*, in the law *Qualiter*, in the principal part. But the intention of the arbitrator is that the condition be observed; and if it is not observed, it is not his intention to dispose of anything, as in the Digest, *De manumissionibus testamentis*, in the law *Si quis locuples*. Similarly, if he imposes a mode in the force of a final cause, he wishes that things exist; otherwise, he would not have acted. Hence, a mode has the effect of a condition, although it differs from a condition in this respect: that a condition has occurred in potentiality, but a mode has occurred in a thing existing in act, as in the Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, in the law *1*. A mode which is in the place of the final cause of the entire act, that act has no effect, as is noted in the Digest, *De senatusconsulto et interloquendo omnium iudicum*, in the law *Cum eorum omnibus*. I speak properly of the act of the sentence.

Moreover, because these arbitrators are in the place of judges, and not only of judges who have to judge from the acts, but they can also judge upon the matter compromised, and transact, and compromise, even without certain acts.
