And they succeed not only in the place of the judge, but in the place of the compromising parties: so that they may judge with judicial authority, and compromise the parties with the authority of litigants, and diminish in both great and small quantities. Hence, if he has the power to diminish in quantity, he can also have power in time and in condition, just as from the contrary, from which one remains, the rest is removed, as in the Code, *De inofficioso testamento*, in the law *Qui in prioribus*.

On the contrary, it seems that these arbitrators are said to follow the nature of judgment: and according to that nature, it seems that the compromise was made in them. Moreover, more strongly, they are adapted to the form of the compromise than to the nature of the thing, as in the Digest, *De arbitris*, in the law *Non distinguemus*, § *De officio*, and as is noted by Innocentius in the Decretals, *De officio delegati*, in the chapter *Si pro debilitate*. Moreover, every judgment consists in action and in defense, and in acting, replicating, and excepting. But these modes do not consist in action nor in replication, but are outside the form and nature of the thing about which the case is heard. Hence, just as if the arbitrators imposed a condition, if the heir of second Jacob, the mode does not bind an uncertain thing determined, and which ought to be determined, as it is determined. And I say that it is determined with respect to the opinions of the arbitrators, it does not vitiate the principal disposition, because there are two precepts of the arbitrator, one useful, the other useless. The useful and the useless would not contract, nor ought to be had, or considered in the place of a final cause. And also because although these arbitrators err in the final cause, the award is not vitiated by the form of the statute.

Moreover, a final cause is twofold: namely, of the past. And this does not enter into the award without doubt, as in the Digest, *Familiae erciscundae*, in the law *Cum putarem*. And a cause taken in this way is put for a reason. Moreover, a final cause of the future either concerns the obligation, and then if the cause does not exist, it vitiates, as in the Digest, *De locato conducto*, in the law *Quomodo*, § *Inter locatorem*; or it does not concern the obligation, because the one imposing the cause cannot by himself dispose of a new obligation: and then it does not vitiate, as in the Digest, *De conditionibus indebiti*, in the law *Damus*. But here I do not see that this arbitrator could impose a mode of succession of boundaries, from which it seemed to the arbitrator that such a daughter ought not to succeed, things being so. And thus he declared, even if he declared this wrongly, and erring. For I do not speak of the equity of the award, nor of its inequity: but whether this mode sounding in the figure of a condition is valid, or not.

And I declare thus: either this daughter was not an heir, and the award declaring was not true, just, and possible; or she was an heir, and then the award was not just, but it was possible, not exceeding the powers of the compromise. Hence, insofar as it exceeded the powers of the compromise, the said award was null, and insofar as it did not exceed, it was something. Although nothing can be opposed against an award, this must be understood excepting the exception of an incompetent arbitrator, as in the Code, *De arbitris*, in the law *Si*, in the end, *De sequestro posito*, in the gloss of the Ordinary. But more than incompetent is an arbitrator over a thing not compromised, as in the Digest, *De arbitris*, in the law *Quid tamen*, § *Si*. Hence, it is not said that this exception is opposed against the award, but against the non-award: because award and arbitrator are correlative, if you begin from the award. And here is applicable what is noted in chapter *1*, *De sequestro posito*, in the Decretals. Hence, just as it is written, if not from a competent judge, etc., so it can be written, if from a non-competent judge-arbitrator, etc.

But I again ask how I may know whether the condition is pertinent or impertinent: I answer that if it can indeed inform the principal disposition naturally or by some equity, such a condition is pertinent and falls within the jurisdiction of the arbitrator. Otherwise, if such a condition cannot be introduced as a cause, neither final nor imposed, as is noted in a similar case in the Digest, On Exceptions of Fraud, Law 2, Section "Certa."

† It remains only to inquire about such a question concerning transmission, namely: if she was declared heir under a condition, and died while the condition was pending, or while it existed in the last breath of life, is such an inheritance transmitted to the mother? And here it must be considered, beyond the aforementioned, that those words, “if she provided maintenance,” do not create a *modus*, because a *modus* is to obligate the natural heirs, as noted in D. de iureiurando, l. si quis cum debitore. But by these words no obligation of maintenance is instituted, as in D. si quis omissa causa testamenti, l. si quis sub conditione. Moreover, because by the word “if” a condition is denoted, and not a *modus*, as in D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. qui promisit; but by the word “so that” a *modus* is well denoted, as in D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. qui promisit; but by the word “so that” a *modus* is well denoted, as in D. de manumissionibus testamento, l. Mevia. Since therefore these words create a condition, it must be seen what they do as a condition, and what is the sense of this condition. And here it must be considered that nothing is found to have been disposed of beforehand. However, that which is found beforehand is declared to be true, whether it is affirmative or negative, as noted in D. de iustitia et iure, l. manumissiones. Now the sentence of the arbitrator declared that the granddaughter was not heir, which refers to this sense, that according to the true proposition of terms she is not heir. But nevertheless the arbitrator wished that she should not remain disinherited in consideration of the dowry, unless the dowry was paid, and unless maintenance was paid, which are due to her in the interim, about to be married, according to the measure of the dowry destined, by the tacit will of the deceased, as in D. de alimentis legatis, l. cum unius, §. fin. And it is true that the arbitrator believed that this granddaughter would not succeed, having regard to the mind of the statute: because if one already born does not succeed, to whom is it more due, and to the grandfather to whom the grandfather is more bound, since he provided a dowry in the will? Since therefore the granddaughter succeeds even less, to whom nothing is due by the grandfather. Moreover, because the arbitrator believed that the grandfather is called, according to common usage of speech, even he who died before the granddaughter was conceived in the womb: and because the arbitrator considered the final intention of the statute, which is the favor of agnates, and the preservation of families, which are preserved by males, and not by females, who transfer themselves to the domiciles of their husbands: so that from the source from which the goods proceeded, they may return to the same source, as noted by Cynus, C. de adulteriis, l. 1. And in doubt, where there is common doubt of law, arbitrators may follow equity, which is commonly seen, as noted in C. de transactionibus, l. si maior. But nevertheless arbitrators, even moved by equity, wished to restrain the donation of the legitimate portion to the son, as in D. de poenis legatorum, l. 1, in fine. And therefore, in effect, for the observance of the natural debt of maintenance, they appended a declaration, an affirmation, opposed to the first declaration negatively. Now since it is impossible that two opposed declarations be simultaneous, nor can they concur in successive time, but one first, the other later: because the power of the judge makes the rule, the question of who is heir ceases to be heir, as noted in D. de vulgari substitutione, l. in substitutione. Hence arises a great doubt of the question. And if indeed we consider the time before the sentence, it is doubtful whether the granddaughter is excluded: because she does not seem to be dowered, who takes nothing by the judgment of the deceased, as is this granddaughter, who died before marriageable years. For since nothing is due to her by the natural right of the legacy of dowry, a condition could be appended: and thus the legacy is extinguished by her dying before marriageable age, as in C. de nuptiis, l. sancimus; and D. de fideicommissis liberis, l. Thays, §. Splendolotus; and D. de vulgari substitutione, l. qui habebat. And that such a granddaughter is not due a legitimate portion, is clear, because the father of the granddaughter preceded her, and because she was conceived after the death of the grandfather, as in D. de inofficioso testamento, l. si quis filium; and D. de inofficioso testamento, l. posthumorum; and l. si quis filio exhaeredato; and noted in C. unde liberis, l. qui se patris. Since therefore this girl was not dowered, the declaration of the arbitrator was erroneous, because an arbitrator can do so that laws and statutes have no place in his disposition, as in D. quae sententiae sine appellatione, eo, l. 1, §. item cum contra sacras. On the contrary, because there was no error. Which sentence is held for truth, and law makes from the form of the statute. Hence, concerning the error of judges, there is no disputing, but founding upon the thing adjudged, as if it were the truth itself, as in D. de arbitris, l. qui arbiter; and l. si erraverit; and D. de iudicibus, l. Praetor, in principio; and D. familiae erciscundae, l. cum putarem. And especially because the arbitrator believed his sentence to be aided by municipal law, as in D. de re iudicata, l. cum probatis. It supports what is noted in Inst. de obligationibus ex quasi delicto, in principio. Assuming therefore the sentence, as if it were true in the case. And it remains only to see whether the arbitrator, who according to the form of the statute must judge someone not to be heir, and thus declare purely and simply, can append to that declaration, from which head some condition, by which he infringes the due and made declaration. And on this I say that the form of the compromise must be attended to. For either the compromise says that it is understood to be compromised about all things, about which there was an award in the aforementioned contained in the libel concerning the aforementioned: or it says simply, about all things there was an award. And then he can add a condition concerning the aforementioned, which is not entirely extraneous, but is adjacent. And if that condition is not observed, he can dispose the contrary under a contrary condition: because this is effected by the virtue of the breadth of power. But if the compromise is only upon the libel, and upon those things which touch the libel for and against, then the award declared upon the libel is valid, and the condition which is appended in another clause is not valid: because when the arbitrator does that which he can and must, and adds that which he cannot and must not. And such an award is necessary as to the arbitration and the parties, namely, the useful and the useless is not valid. And because that useless thing is appended as a private person, not as an arbitrator, since there is no compromise upon it in him. Notwithstanding D. quando appellatio sit, l. 1, §. biduum, where it is said that a conditional sentence should not be made, nevertheless once pronounced it holds, because there it speaks of a judge, who has universal jurisdiction in all that about which he judges. Otherwise in an arbitrator. Hence an arbitrator cannot append to his sentence a condition which is outside the compromise, and the disposition remains null, because the condition is inept, and inept conditions do not have to be entered, as noted in D. de legibus, l. 1, l. turpia. Generally remains the declaratory award pure, because that which is declared to be true, it is necessary to be. But against this it is objected. For some things expressed conditionally vitiate, which otherwise do not vitiate, as noted by the doctors, C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, auth. ingressi. But there we speak of the lord, here however we speak of the arbitrator. From the foregoing appears the solution, whether by a condition not observed was made a translation of the inheritance. For if the arbitrator could append such a condition, a translation of the inheritance is made as to effect, as in D. de transactionibus, l. si controversia. But if he could not append, then otherwise.

† Now there remains a doubt, assuming that the condition could be opposed in this way: if he does not pay until the age of marriage, from that time forth the granddaughter shall be heir, and the granddaughter dies before the acceptance of the inheritance: whether she transmits the right to accept; assuming that this right to accept did not previously belong to the granddaughter. And briefly, here I address the extremity of time denoted by the word "from that time forth." For the same must be said, i.e., after the age of marriage, if she marries, she is heir. Since therefore she dies before the age of marriage, she is equated to a conditional fideicommissary, to whom the inheritance is left, if she reaches the age of marriage, who in the meantime does not transmit; but it remains as caducary in the heir, noted in ff. when the day of a legacy ceases, l. ex his verbis.

But here it must be considered whether a sentence is equivalent to a contract, in which a conditional transmission of a debt takes place, or whether it is equivalent to a last will. And it is to be said that, according to the latter, depending on the subject matter, a sentence sometimes accedes to a contract, sometimes to a last will, or to another rule, for example, the rule of intestacy. For if indeed the sentence derives its force from some preceding contract, it accedes to the contract; if, however, from a last will, it accedes to the last will. If, however, it has its origin in intestacy, it accedes to the nature of intestacy, as in l. 1, § si quis sub conditione, and § bellissime, ff. de legatorum. In our case, because of the words “to be released from that time forth, at the age of marriageable years,” in the meantime the girl is not an heir, the laudum being an impediment, as in ff. de verborum obligatione, l. huiusmodi stipulatio, and what is noted in l. 5, in principio, ff. de conditionibus et institutionibus. And therefore, the conditional right is not transmitted by dying before the marriageable age, but remains with the legitimate heirs as a lapsed burden upon the death of the girl transmitting it. And thus it seems to be concluded on this point, which is sufficiently arduous, in which both knowledge and conscience labor. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If the testator bequeaths to Titius those things which are owed to him by Seius, is the legacy valid if Seius owes nothing?
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The doubt in this question arises from two laws which appear to contradict each other. For in l. si sic, ff. de legatis, it is said that if a testator bequeaths to Titius one hundred which are owed to him by Seius, the legacy is invalid, if Seius owes nothing to the testator, because it appears to be a legacy of a false name of the debtor, or a name of a false debtor. Hence, that which is bequeathed is not in the nature of things, because such a legacy, namely a right, is a cession of an action, which action cannot be ceded if nothing is owed. But in the law quidam testamento, in the beginning, of the same title, it is said that if a testator bequeaths 40 gold coins to Pamphila, in this manner: “I wish 40 gold coins to be given to Pamphila, namely by Julius, so many gold coins, etc.,” even if Julius owes nothing, nevertheless the legacy is valid from the beginning, if it was given purely, and the first clause is complete, in which the substance of the quantity bequeathed is contained, and it refers to the thing, not to the right of cession. The contradiction of these laws is thus resolved: for sometimes the clause importing the legacy is complete, and another clause is joined to it demonstrating from where it is to be paid. And then, although the demonstration is false, nevertheless the legacy is not vitiated. Sometimes there is one clause, in which the relative is constructed with its antecedent, for example: “I bequeath to Seius that which Titius owes me.” And then, if nothing is owed, there is nothing in the legacy, as in the aforementioned l. si sic, § 1, and l. legavi, de liberatione legata.

It is resolved in another way, because either the relative is added to a dispositive verb or an executive verb. For if it is added to an executive verb, the legacy is valid; for example, the testator says: “I order my heir to give 10 to Titius, which Seius owes me.” But if it is added to a dispositive verb, then the legacy is not valid if nothing is owed; for example, the testator says: “I bequeath to Titius 10, which Seius owes me.” For the relative “which” refers to the act of that verb “I bequeath,” which verb is dispositive. Hence the law interprets this legacy to be a legacy of a debt (nomen), and if there is no debt, there is no legacy. And thus this contradiction of the said laws is commonly resolved.

Now, in the question proposed, it is sufficiently doubtful whether those words, “to which my lady Stephanella is bound to me,” are placed in the force of a demonstration, and thus a false demonstration does not vitiate the legacy, or whether they are not placed so as to designate a legacy of a debt, such that if nothing is owed, nothing is due in the legacy. And it seems that the first clause is complete in itself, which says: “I leave to my lady Nuta and my lady Bellaflore one hundred”; thus far is the complete clause. And it follows: “to which my lady Stephanella is bound to me.” And these seem to make a demonstration. And thus, if my lady Stephanella owes nothing, nevertheless the legacy is valid.

On the contrary, it seems that because there does not appear to be a difference between these words: “I bequeath to Titius one hundred, which Seius owes me,” or whether it is said: “I bequeath to Titius one hundred, to which Seius is bound to me,” because these words are not placed in the place of a demonstration or designation, but in the place of a determination; because on account of this the legacy seems to refer to the right of the debt, and not to the thing, i.e., the quantity in general or simply, if nothing is owed to the testator, nothing can be due to the legatee, and nothing is seen to be bequeathed. And if it is said that the first part of the clause is a complete clause, this is denied, because the whole is one construction and one disposition. Wherefore, it seems that in the question proposed it should be said that nothing is contained in the legacy.

But what if the writing says thus: “the said testator left to Titius one hundred, which the said testator said he ought to receive from Seius”? I answer that those words, “which, etc.,” are not the words of the testator, but of the notary writing by the command of the testator. And therefore they do not vitiate the legacy of a certain quantity. But this reason does not seem true, because although that word “said” was uttered by the notary, nevertheless it is the same as if the testator had uttered the whole, as is noted in de verbis oblig., l. sciendum, in the glossa ordinaria. And therefore the better reason is that these words, “which, etc.,” are not appended to the legacy, but are demonstrative of from where the legacy is to be paid; hence a false demonstration does not vitiate the legacy of a certain quantity. The case is in the aforementioned l. quidam testamento, and there by Doctor Dy. Hence it is concluded that the said one hundred is due to the legatee, although that Seius owes nothing to the testator, etc. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether, if access to a leased shop cannot be had except through its door or through the lessor’s house, and the lessee has the keys to the door, and a theft has been committed in the shop, and the lessor’s house door has been found open, the lessee may bring an action against the lessor.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A certain person leased a certain apothecary shop by title, to which apothecary shop one could not enter except through the door of that apothecary shop, the keys of which were held by the said lessee, or else through the house of the said lessor, in which house the said lessor dwelt. It is said that a certain window of the house of the said lessor, in which house the said lessor dwelt and which was joined to the said apothecary shop, remained open at night; wherefore through the said window a thief and robber entered, and then proceeded into the said apothecary shop, and stole and took away much money and goods from it.

† It is asked whether the said lessee may bring an action against the said lessor, and for what purpose, and how the libel should be framed. I answer, and it seems at first that the said lessor is not liable in any respect. For, when the doors of the warehouses are broken open and the warehouses themselves are broken into, he is not liable, unless he has promised custody to the lessee, as in D. loc. cond. l. dominus horreorum, in principio, and C. loc. cond. l. ex Divi. It is true, however, that when one cannot enter the warehouses except through the lessor’s house, it would then be presumed against him that he committed such theft, or suffered it to be committed, or at least that he knew the perpetrator, as is proved by the aforementioned laws, and D. de furt. instr. l. si ita supports this. Nevertheless, it must be said that it is not necessary to institute a criminal action in the question proposed, but an action may be brought against the lessor on the basis of the contract of lease (ex locato) on account of fault. Although the lessor is not liable for fault committed in his own property, which is not leased, this is true only if such property is not connected to the leased property. Since, however, access is obtained through the unleased house to the leased house, he is bound to guard his own house in such a way that no damage is caused to the leased warehouse or to the things existing in the warehouse through it or its entry. For he is obligated to this by the good faith which is present in such contracts, as in D. loc. cond. l. si ut certo, §. nunc videndum, and D. eod. l. in l. locationis. For, by keeping his own door open on the occasion of damage given, whereby he himself seems in a manner to have caused the damage, as in D. ad l. Aquil. l. qui accidit, §. pe. Moreover, or rather more strongly, it would seem to be said that if there are two neighbors, each of whom has his own chamber, not leased, and one of them leaves his own door open at night, whereby easy access is had to the other neighbor’s chamber, that such person, on account of gross fault, is liable to the neighbor by the useful action of the Lex Aquilia, as argued from what is noted in D. de usufr. l. si cuius, and D. de praetor. stip. secundum unam solutionem. Nevertheless, the text there seems to say the contrary, and especially because here fault is committed in one’s own property, which is not punished, as in D. sol. matr. l. etiam, §. 1. Finally, I say that the said lessor is liable for the said fault by the action ex conducto, and that suit should be brought against him by the action ex conductione; because, although it appears that there is fault, and although the cause was not immediate, it is so, because it is not sufficient unless something else is added to it, as in D. loc. cond. l. qui demum. Nevertheless, any fault of the lessor is purged by the action ex conducto, without distinguishing whether such fault was the immediate cause of the damage or the mediate cause, because in every case it inflicts damage, and it is contrary to good faith to commit fault in such contracts. And by the nature of the contract it ought to be punished, as in D. de act. empt. l. Iul., in principio, and §. item qui fuere. From these things, therefore, it is clearly concluded that, the facts being thus, the said lessor is liable. For certainly in the aforementioned l. dominus horreorum, it is not expressly stated that the lessor is liable for that custody which remained with him, but rather the custody of the house which he inhabits remains with him. Hence, if he guarded it poorly by not closing the door at night, he cannot be excused from what is in a manner gross fault, as in D. pro soc. l. cum duobus, §. damna, ver. quod si a furibus, and D. ad l. Aquil. l. si servum, §. si fornicarius, and there it is noted that the act of one ought not to drag others into peril. And he who does not do what he is bound to do is deemed to have done the contrary of what he ought to do, as in D. de reg. iur. l. qui non facit. And thus I say, and I advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The testator leaves his wife as usufructuary, etc., provided she remains chaste, honest, etc., and in widowhood with his son, whom he instituted as his universal heir; and if she should die without children, he bequeathed certain goods to the aforementioned wife. This woman, after the death of the testator, and subsequently after the death of her son without issue, married a second time; whether on this account she loses the legacy.
2. Whether a condition appended in the first part of the will is deemed to be repeated in other legacies.
3. There are three causes which exclude tacit repetition.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen. A certain testator, among other things in his will, left Lady A., his wife, as mistress and manager of his property for as long as she lived chastely and honestly, preserved her widowhood, and stayed together with Iacobus, his son. And then he instituted the said Iacobus as his universal heir. And if the said Iacobus should die without children, he bequeathed to his said wife a house with a garden, a certain piece of land, and certain other things; and in these latter bequests he did not repeat that condition, "as long as she lives chastely and honestly," but bequeathed them unconditionally, saying nothing about marrying or not marrying. It happened that this woman, after the testator's death, did not remarry as long as the said son lived; but afterwards, several years after the son's death, she married a second husband.

† It is asked whether she ought to lose the legacy of the said house and the said piece of land, or not. I respond that this question has two points. The first point is whether she loses the legacy because she marries a second time. The second point is whether the condition "if she does not marry," attached in the first part of the will regarding that legacy of being "mistress and manager," is understood to be tacitly repeated in the subsequent legacies made to the said lady, such that from the very form of the will substantially understood, the said legacy is understood to be terminated and lapsed. On the first point, the ordinary gloss says that a woman who has only one son, if she marries after that son's death, nevertheless loses the ownership of the legacies left to her by her first husband; so says gl. C. de secun. nup. auth. ex testamento. But the contrary is true, and that gloss is rejected by the doctors. For either she marries during the lifetime of the son, and then she loses the ownership (though whether she recovers it if the son afterwards dies without children is noted in Auth. de nupt. §. qui infirmitas and Auth. de non eligen. secundo nuben. §. Gregoriam); nevertheless, when she marries after the death of the son and no other children exist, then the woman does not lose the legacy in any way, as in C. de secun. nup. l. feminae §. fi., even if the testator had children by another wife, because a stepmother is not bound to the said continence with respect to the children of another marriage, but the law of continence is imposed upon the mother in favor of her own children, upon whose death she is released and free from the law of continence. And therefore she can marry a second husband in the Lord, as in extra, de secun. nupt. c. fi. From these things it is concluded what the law is on the first point. Now it remains to consider the second point, namely:

† whether the condition attached in the first part of the will is seen to be tacitly repeated in the other legacies. And at first glance it seems it must be said that it is, because things stated in preceding clauses are believed to be tacitly repeated in subsequent ones, as in ff. de uerb. ob. l. Titia and ff. de pac. l. item quia ver. idem Iuliano. To the contrary, it seems not, because every tacit repetition proceeds either by reason of a copula or conjunction—as when there are several legacies joined by the word "and," or by the word "likewise," or by other conjunctive or connective words; or because they are governed by the same verb and determined by the same act of the determining verb that governs the entire sentence; or by reason of identity, when there is an underlying reason for repeating the preceding things in the following ones.

† And likewise, conversely, there are three causes that exclude tacit repetition. The first is an adversative expression, as when the word "but" or "otherwise" and similar words are present. Likewise, the separation of dispositions and times. Likewise, the opposition of the underlying reason—for things not having an adversative reason do not have an interest in tacit repetition, as these matters are proved in the said laws, as in C. de vsu. l. per retentionem and fully noted by Mod. in d. l. repetendis. Now in our case, the same reason for repeating the requirement of widowhood in the subsequent legacies does not underlie it. For that condition, "as long as she lives chastely, etc.," was attached in favor of the son then living, as in ff. de condi. et demon. l. sed si hoc §. fin. Which reason ceases once the son is dead. Likewise, that condition, "if she stays with the son," cannot be understood as repeated, because in this respect the second disposition is adversative to the first. For in the first he said, "if she stays with the son"; in the second he said, "after the death of the son"; and thus in contrary cases repetition cannot be introduced. Likewise, because tacit repetition has no place where an act would be vitiated and rendered impossible, as in ff. de manumis. test. l. fi. From these points it is concluded that the said legacies made to the said lady are owed to her; and likewise the legacies made to Bartholus and Iohannes are owed, etc., which were left in the said will, because those words, "and in the said case," if referred to the legacies made to the lady as long as she lived, mean the death of the lady, but so far as they are referred to other goods, they mean the death of the son, so that the meaning of those words is "in the said case," that is, if the son dies without others. For saving the reasoning and intention of the testator, the said words cannot be interpreted otherwise, because legacies that are transferred from the mother to another have the condition of the mother's death; but legacies that are transferred from the son to another have the condition of the son's death, because the son is the one burdened with these kinds of legacies taken from the son, and therefore the death of the son is looked to. And the said legacies to them—the said Bartholus and Iohannes—are valid, and also the residue of the inheritance, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether several instruments are, and when, to be regarded as one.
2. An instrument is considered in three ways.
3. Whether ignorance excuses one who is required to do something within a certain time.
4. Time limits prescribed for producing instruments do not bind those who are ignorant.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

It is proposed that a certain donation of a certain dowry was made to Lord Andrea de Monte Ubiano and his heirs: if the marriage were dissolved by the death of the wife without children, regarding which donation two instruments appear: in one it is contained that the donation was made to the same Lord Andrea, present, stipulating, and receiving; in the other it is contained that the said donation was made in this manner, because it was promised to the said wife to make an instrument of dowry for the said Lord Andrea, and without heir, if thereafter the marriage were dissolved by the death of the said lady without children. Now it has happened that the said Lord Andrea, by a double instrument of the said donation, with the intention of insinuating it in the first form. It is also proposed that after the death of the said Lord Andrea de Monte, the said condition occurred. It is also proposed that the said instrument in the second form was not produced with the intention of insinuating it, neither by the said Lord Andrea nor by his heirs, whence the cancellation of the said instrument is requested, but the heirs of Lord Andrea raise an exception and say that cancellation cannot be requested: because insinuation was requested. But by the adversaries it is replied that insinuation of the true instrument was not requested: because the insinuated instrument does not contain the true narration of the fact. And to prove this, the notary’s protocol is introduced, to which recourse must be had, as in Auth. de tabellionis. §. si. But against this it is doubled, because nothing is hindered by diversity of narration, provided the substance of the fact is not changed, as extra, de ver. sig. c. nihil obst. where the text says that nothing is hindered by diversity of narration, where the same things are said and those which signify the same in effect. To this also extra, de conuersione coniugatorum. c. dudum. where the text says that if the notary rendered two instruments, one in the first person, another in the third, both are understood as one and the same. To this also contributes what is noted in C. de accu. l. in causis, where the gloss notes that there is no difference whether the notary speaks in the first person or in the third. But to this it is thus answered, that rather there is a great difference between a direct action and a useful one. For Lord Andrea, by stipulating for himself, acquires two hundred. But if another free man were to accept a vile thing for him, assuming that we were in such a case, in which cession was not required, as l. quotiens. in prin. ff. de admi. tuto. and C. de dona. quae sub modo. l. quotiens. nor is the substance of the useful and the direct the same in this case, ff. de acqui. pos. l. possessio quoque. §. hic. Let it be posited that the statute fictions cession of actions, or fictions a mandate of direct actions. For it is one thing to have a direct action in one’s own person and otherwise the libellus is formed: and otherwise judgment is to be rendered, as C. de procu. l. qui stipendia. and C. de dona. l. illam. To this it contributes, because if two writings appear, one says that the testator bequeathed to my slave. another says that the testator bequeathed to me. these writings are diverse, and if one were insinuated, the other would not be insinuated, arg. ff. de stip. ser. l. quarta. Hence the tenor of the writing is the same. nor does it seem that the obligation is the same in its root, but one obligation seems primitive, another derivative, because they take their origin in diverse persons, as ff. de acquiren. haeredi. l. placet. and this seems to be confirmed by l. ff. de solu. l. si cum Cornelius. For it matters much whether the wife employs someone to stipulate for the dowry, as ff. de solu. l. quae dotis: or whether she herself stipulates for another, as the said l. si cum Cornelius.

† It must be considered that an instrument is said to be in three ways. First, figuratively and superficially. Second, intellectually. For the business is instructed by writing, even if it is not expressly written, it is tacitly considered written, as in D. de haer. inst. l. 1. §. 1. Such an instrument is called from instructing. For often when something is written, we understand more than what is written, as in c. rem in praesenti. §. accidit. Third, an instrument is said to be figuratively and also intellectually. And this is primarily an instrument that represents by what is written to be true of the thing. And also the writing itself, which however is in itself true to the act of the notary, as in l. 2. in prin. D. quemad. test. ape.

It is now certain that the instrument produced by the said And. is an instrument in the first sense, namely figuratively: for upon inspection it has the appearance of being so. Moreover, it is an instrument in the third sense, because it concludes to the truth: for even through another writing the same conclusion results in effect, as in D. de negotiorum gestis, l. actio. And even if, in the subtlety of law, the same right did not result: nevertheless, these instruments are not presumed to be contrary, but are akin, and it is possible that the notary was requested in both ways at the same place and time, namely, that both the woman for the lord And. and he for himself were stipulated. It suffices that this appears from a public instrument, because it is presumed true, as in C. de probationibus, l. cum precibus. And thus it must be considered that either the notary attests that he took some writing from the protocol: and then the protocol is to be followed, and not that writing, if it differs from the protocol. Or he does not attest: every writing with its substantial elements, publicly requested originally by a notary, is called a protocol, i.e., the first request, before another does not proceed, as noted by Bartolus in D. de legibus 2, l. Sempronius Proculo. And if it is said, rather, the protocol is called the first and matrix writing, I concede this; however, of the instrument produced by the lord Andrea, no other matrix writing appears. Hence I call it a protocol according to what is noted by Bartolus in the said l. Sempronius. For these writings are not incompatible, especially since the said lord Andrea was present for every writing, as in D. de verbis obligatis, l. si procurator presentis. Moreover, the act is alterable, and therefore iteration is presumed where diversity is found, but not adversity in writings, as in C. de fide instrumentorum, l. scripturae, and in Extra, de testibus, cap. cum tu filii, and as noted by Bartolus in l. 2, § 1, D. si certum petatur. Moreover, in the insinuation made by the lord Andrea, the party was cited, and nothing of the contingencies was omitted or pronounced. And thus it is held for truth, as in D. de regulis iuris, l. res iudicata. For since the woman knew her own fact, as in C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione, l. magnam, she ought to have appeared and opposed, if she knew that the adversary’s claim was not based on truth, as in C. de fide instrumentorum, l. fin. Moreover, since the time has elapsed within which one cannot inquire about falsity by action, as in C. de falsis, l. querela, nor by replication: hence if cancellation is sought, and the exception of insinuation is raised, one cannot replicate on the ground of falsity: because the time for replicating does not last, unless one speaks of the time for action, as noted in C. de exceptionibus, l. licet. Since therefore the instrument produced by the lord Andrea is consonant with the truth of both instruments considering the end, and cannot be said to be untrue, it is manifestly concluded that the insinuated substance of the thing ought sufficiently to be said to be the insinuated instrument: because the truth contained in both instruments has been insinuated in effect. For let us say that, without prejudice to the truth, these would not proceed on account of other reasons made to the contrary: nevertheless, there is another evident and true reason, namely, that the said cancellation cannot be sought.

† For we say either that the said request for annulment is sought on account of the delay of the sons, and certainly not on account of the delay of the lord Andreas, because the donation was conditional, and he ought not to have hoped for the death and adverse fortune of the free woman donor, nor was he bound to rush to insinuate while she was alive. The first point is proven by the wording of the statute, which states and declares that in conditional cases the time for insinuation does not run. The second point is proven by *l. inter stipulantem*, § *sacramenta*, D. de verborum obligationibus, and D. ad Trebellianum, *l. ita tamen*, § *a patre*, where the words of the text say thus: First, because he gives under a condition; second, because it is not proven regarding the heir of the living. To this effect, C. de pactis, *l. fin.*, and D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, *l. cum tali*, in principio, where it says that it is dangerous and sad to await the death of a spouse. But certainly the lord Andreas would also be excused by another reason, because although one is believed to remember one’s own act, this is true only unless a public document contained something different, as in D. de interrogatione actione, *l. de aetate*, § *ex causa*, and D. de institutionibus, *l. sed et si pupillus*, § *proscribere*; or at least the lord Andreas had a just cause for hesitating whether he remembered correctly or not. And one who doubts is considered ignorant, as in *l. fina.*, C. de conditione indebiti. And even assuming that the said lord Andreas had true knowledge, nevertheless, because the condition of the donation did not occur during the lifetime of the lord Andreas, the duty and necessity of insinuation ought to have begun with the heir, namely when the condition was fulfilled. But the heir had just ignorance, indeed the most just ignorance, regarding the fact of the deceased, as in *l. ultima*, D. pro socio, and D. de usucapione, *l. Celsus*. He had a just cause, I say, ignorance, because it concerned another’s fact, as in D. de probationibus, *l. verus*, and *l. eius, qui in provincia*, si certum petatur, and *l. sin.*, § *fin.*, D. de legato secundo. Moreover, it was most just, because of the written document. For among the writings of the deceased father, this instrument with insinuation was found. Hence, they ought not, nor could, believe that any other instrument or different content would appear, except in that form. For they could not divine what had been done, but ought to believe what was written, as in Auth. de testamentis imperfectis, in principio. It is certain that the prescribed times for insinuation require knowledge. For no one can produce an instrument that he does not know. And therefore, the statutory times for producing instruments do not bind those who are ignorant. And especially considering the wording of the statute saying “if anyone ought,” etc., as these are proven in D. de excusatione tutoris, *l. quinquaginta*, and D. de aedilicio edicto, *l. cum sex*, and D. de calumnia, *l. ann.*, and *l. genero*, de his qui notati sunt infamia, and Extra, de exceptionibus, cap. *pastora*, and in cap. *vt circa*, de electione, lib. 6. And especially if the said heirs found themselves ignorant, because where it is a matter of removing an acquired right and punishing negligence, ignorance is proven by oath to excuse fault or negligence, as is read and noted in D. de accusationibus, *l. si cui*, § 1. And therefore, concluding, it seems to me, according to the facts narrated, that whether there are multiple acts of donation, or forms of donation, or whether in effect there is one donation, or whether it is merely a donation that is sought to be annulled, nevertheless the heirs of the said lord Andreas are excused by ignorance. And thus the said petition for annulment does not proceed, and I remain in this last conclusion, given that ignorance is assumed. Regarding the other articles touched upon above, it suffices to have alleged them. And therefore, at the time of insinuations, this instrument, concerning which there is litigation, may be produced with the intent of insinuating. And so I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How and from what circumstances a partnership is presumed to exist among certain persons.
2. Likewise, whether a partner may claim wages for his labor.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. After certain words pertaining to the formation of a partnership were stated, it was subsequently written that certain merchandise was purchased jointly, and that each party bound himself.

† It is asked whether a partnership has been contracted. I answer that it has, with respect to the things purchased. For a partnership contracted by deed does not extend beyond the deed itself. But if a partnership were contracted by a preceding agreement and pact, such a partnership would be of such a kind and extent as the agreement of that pact, both as to the things and as to the time; because acts which are determined by express will are judged according to the pacts, but acts which are regulated by tacit will are binding by virtue of the things and deeds themselves, as in D. de legibus, l. de quibus, in fine; and D. pro socio, l. de illo. But if the partners descend to one another, and the goods remain with one, while the other does not have them, he with whom the goods remain must keep the other indemnified against the obligations contracted. And just as the principal debtor must keep his surety indemnified, because two partners are deemed to have given surety for one another, and he is considered the principal with whom the final benefit remains, and the other is interpreted as his surety, as in Auth. de fideiussoribus, in principio; and D. ad legem Velleianam, l. vir uxori, §. si.

But if it is asked whether this partner, with whom the goods do not remain, ought to receive wages for his labor or some salary, it must be said that he does not, because he did not apply his labor with the intent of a hired worker, but of a partner, as is stated in the Digest, *Pro socio*, law *Cum duobus*, section *Si coeunda*. If, however, someone were to stand with a merchant as his servant, he could never demand that a salary be established for him. This is not our subject matter, because here we speak of partners. For by that reasoning, if one partner were to claim from the other, and conversely the other from the one, nothing would remain due, since an equal obligation would exist on both sides. But when someone stands as a servant or domestic, one must first examine what was agreed upon between the parties. And if this does not appear, one must examine the custom of the place. And if the custom does not appear, one must examine the quality of the persons, their industry, and their skill; and it must especially be considered whether the one who provides the labor is a poor man who has no means of living except from his own work. For it is not probable that he intended to work for free. To this effect, see the Digest, *De variis et extraordinariis cognitionibus*, law 1, in the beginning, and in that verse, *Tam et librarius*, etc., with similar authorities. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. And if, after the confession of the debt and the precept made for payment, the debtor transfers himself elsewhere and keeps there a shop, ought the judge of the place where the debtor is, according to the letters of the prior judge, to execute against him the said precept.
2. A ten-year habitation constitutes domicile.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen. A certain person in the territory of the Borough of the Holy Sepulchre confessed that he was bound to Titius in the sum of one hundred. And the judge issued to him a writ for payment. Finally, this man, fearing that he would be arrested, withdrew from the territory of the Borough and fled to the city of Castello, and there he took a house and a shed, and practiced the art of a spice merchant. Now, at the request of the creditor, the judge of the territory of the Borough writes to the judge of the territory of the city of Castello: that he carry out real and personal execution of the said writ.

† It is asked whether the judge of the city of Castello can execute the letters of the judge of the Burgus, or not. And it seems that he can, as in D. de iudicibus, l. argentarium, § nomine. For since this debtor has established domicile and has a stall or shop in the city of Castello, and also resides there habitually, he may rightly be compelled there to pay the debt wherever contracted; because there he acquires jurisdiction, as in D. de iudicibus, l. haeres ab sensu. And a debtor may be compelled not only where he originally had domicile, but also where he later acquired domicile or jurisdiction, as in C. de iure omnium iudicum, l. 2. And to this effect is what is noted by Cynus in C. de confessionibus, in 10 q. l. 1. It would seem that even without the letters of the first judge, the said debt may be claimed in any competent place, so that in execution also the statute of that place must be observed, as in C. de exactione tributorum, l. missi opinatores, lib. 10. To the contrary it seems. For a debt contracted in one place cannot be claimed in another suitable place, as noted in l. 1, D. de eo quod certo loco; and D. de constitutionibus pecuniarum, l. eum qui; and D. de deposito, l. Lucius. But the city of Castello does not seem a suitable place, because mere residence does not constitute a new domicile, as in D. ad municipalia, l. libertas, § sola.

† unless it were a ten-year residence, as noted in l. 2, C. de incolis, lib. 10. Nor does it matter that he practices the art of a spice merchant: for by this he acquires jurisdiction there only with regard to debts contracted there, not elsewhere: because he who sells and has a shop in a place does not seem to sell as a traveler. And therefore he can be sued there by reason of the contract, or of any act celebrated there, or by reason of the business. However, that law does not state that he acquires jurisdiction with regard to contracts celebrated elsewhere. And it is not an obstacle if it is said that execution can be carried out by letters of the judge pronouncing or commanding: for then that is true, that the judge had already pronounced that the plaintiff should be put in possession. For the judge of the place where the immovable goods are located can and must carry out real execution. As for personal execution, it is not found to be provided for by law, as in ff. de bonis aucthoritate iudicis possidendis, l. cum vnus, §. is, qui; and see ff. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, l. cum quaedam puella. Hence, the letters of the judge are not sufficient, unless the order of pronouncement is observed, as in c. Romana, §. contrahentes, de foro competenti, lib. 6. Here it must be considered that Bartolus says that another judge cannot act without letters, but with letters, so that no injury is done to the pronouncing judge. But it is certain that no injury is done, since he writes that execution shall be made, as in ff. de officio eius, cui mandata est iurisdictio, l. et si Praetor. Therefore, this reason being considered, even if the first judge had not pronounced on putting in possession, the second judge could put in possession by his letters. But this reason of Master Bartolus is not sufficient, because either these letters will be delegatory. And this cannot be according to law, because real putting in possession cannot be delegated, as in ff. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, l. iubere cauere. Or they would be executory, and then it is required that a decree on putting in possession precede. Hence, he who executes such a decree is a certain organ and instrument of the one commanding, as in ff. ut in possessionem legatur, l. is cui, §. missus. And therefore the true reason is that this is valid, because where the judgment has been begun, it must be finished there, not only by sentence, but by execution: because the whole is one structure. And therefore, since verbal execution, that is, the pronouncement on putting in possession, can be made by the first judge, the real execution of that word must subsequently be committed to the second judge, and by this the rule which is in ff. de iudicibus, l. vbi ceptum, is not infringed, because whatever can be done, is done. And therefore in this question I say that such a Florentine must first have it pronounced that the plaintiff be put in possession of the things wherever located, and afterwards obtain letters and produce them; otherwise the due form would not be observed, nor could execution be made. And although Master Cynus and others commonly speak only of letters, nevertheless their statements must be understood with the order of law being observed, which order is declared above. And this is true when the first judge has mixed imperium, so that he can pronounce on putting in possession; otherwise his decree would effect nothing, nor would the letters emanating from him. And then the judge of the place where the debtor temporarily resides, not because he is his judge, nor because jurisdiction is acquired there, but because, jurisdiction being established, execution would be made according to the statutes of the places, not by the authority of any decree of a pedaneus judge or a cartulary, in whom there is no mixed imperium. And thus this matter must be understood. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that a dowried daughter shall not succeed to the donor, nor to any descendant of his: A father instituted his two sons as his heirs, left a dowry to his daughter, and instituted her in that dowry; one of the sons dies intestate, with his brother, mother, and married sister surviving; the question is asked, who shall succeed.
2. Whether a dowried woman may be endowed again.
3. Whether one who renounces a legacy of dowry is to be considered dowried.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen. A certain man, having three sons and a wife, among whom was one female son who was a ward, provided her with a dowry in his will and appointed her as heir to that dowry; but he made the male sons universal heirs and substituted them for one another. Subsequently, one of the said males died intestate.

† It is asked, who succeeds the said male, having regard to the form of the statute of the commune of Perugia, which states that a dowried woman does not succeed the donor, nor do descendants from him. And it is presupposed that the said daughter was, and is, effectively dowried, and is with her husband. Answer: that dowried daughter does not succeed her brother, nor in the legitime due to the brother from the paternal goods, nor in anything, because the statute forbids it. Therefore, there are two successors of the said deceased son, namely, the sister and the mother, who succeed the said deceased son in his legitime and trebellianic portion, as in the Authentica *Defuncto*. But now it must be seen whether the male succeeds in double, compared to the mother. For the sister is excluded in favor of the male; therefore, her portion belongs to the male, so that the statute operates tacitly in the case which is within the intent of the statute, even if the words are lacking, arguing from C. *De rebus dubiis*, l. *Bis solis*, and ff. *De legatis tertio*, l. *Fideicommissum*, § *Interdum*. For the force of this statute appears to be twofold, namely, the exclusion of the sister, and the conferral of succession upon the male; otherwise, if the male ought not to exclude the sister, certainly the sister ought not to be excluded, because when the cause ceases, the privilege ceases.

On the contrary, it seems that this case is an omitted case, namely, with regard to the right of accretion, because the statute does not provide that the daughter’s portion accrues to the male. And thus the male and the mother remain under the disposition of the common law. Hence, the daughter does not obstruct the mother, since she is precisely excluded, as in ff. *Ad Tertullianam*, l. *Aequissimum*. Perhaps it should be said that the first opinion is the more correct, because indeed the law appears tacitly to provide for the right of accretion; for insofar as one is excluded by special favor of another, such favor ought to benefit the one excluding, not another, of whose favor no account was taken. Nevertheless, this point is doubtful.

Now it is immediately asked, if regarding that in which this mother succeeds, and also regarding her own dowry, she can thus make a will in favor of the male, so as to exclude the daughter. I do not say entirely, but that she diminishes the legitime which the daughter can have in the goods of the mother and wife. Say that she cannot, as in C. *De inofficioso testamento*, l. *Quoniam in prioribus*.

† On the contrary, it appears that such a precaution may be employed, namely that the mother leaves a certain quantity to the said daughter as dowry. For even to those already endowed, a dowry may be added and newly constituted, as is shown in C. de donationibus ante nuptias, l. si; and in no. ff. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. obligamur, §. lege. And I say this considering the statute, which provides that a daughter endowed by her mother shall not succeed to her mother when males are extant; a statute which, according to Bartolus, is understood to apply even to one who is endowed in a will, as in ff. de administratione tutorum, l. cum plures, §. penultimo. But this daughter is endowed in her mother’s will; therefore, she does not succeed to her mother, except in the dowry itself, and in the remainder the male son succeeds.

And if it is said that this daughter will not accept the legacy of her mother, I answer that she must be considered as dowered, since it depended on her, ff. de cond. et dem. l. iure ciuili. But to the contrary it seems, that this testament was made in fraud of the legitime, which succeeds in place of alimony: therefore it is permitted to repudiate, so that frauds may be prevented, as ff. de leg. 2. l. cum pater. §. Titio. And according to this, she who is dowered in the testament is not called dowered unless she accepts the legacy, because the law does not compel her to accept. And thus she remains undowered, and can succeed according to the common law, as l. qui autem. in prin. ff. omissa causa test. and ff. si cer. pe. l. prouidere. For the statute, as I said, must be understood as referring to a dowered daughter with effect, who obtains the dowry by the judgment of the testator. In this it must be considered that there is another statute speaking that daughters are bound to remain content with the testaments and wills of their parents: which statute must be observed, otherwise it would seem to be said that the said daughter would be compelled to accept the said legacy made in fraud of the legitime. What therefore must the said mother do? I answer that as to the goods coming to her from the daughter, she can not accept them, and thus if the mother should die, the daughter can claim nothing: and if the mother is of this intention, that the male heir should have them, if he lives, otherwise they should revert to her, let her repudiate, as I said. And finally let the male make an irrevocable donation to the mother of the said legitime and trebellianica under the condition that if it happens that the said male dies without children. And thus the vow of the mother is saved as to the repudiable goods. And so I say, and I counsel, I, Baldus de Perusio, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a legacy may be left to an heir by himself, and, assuming that it may not, whether he is bound by the burden imposed by the legacy.
1. Whether the condition "if he dies without children" vanishes when there is only one child.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A certain woman made a will, in which she disposed as follows, namely: Furthermore, she left to Vannota, her daughter, the entire field situated at Saint Peter of the Ancients, within its own boundaries. And afterwards, she appointed the said Vannota as universal heir in solidum, with this condition: that if the said lady Vannota should die without male children descending from her body, or if the said male heirs should at some point die without sons or daughters legitimately descending from their bodies through a lawful marriage, the right shall belong to the said testatrix, in the event of the aforementioned case occurring, to have two altars made, etc. It happened that the said Vannota married a certain man, from whom she had two sons and one daughter; and after the death of her first husband, she married another, from whom she had two sons and one daughter. This Vannota made a will and instituted as heirs the sons and daughter of the second marriage, and she died. Finally, the sons of the second marriage died. Then the said daughter of the second marriage died, leaving behind one son. Now, the sons of the first marriage wish to claim the said field. Furthermore, they do not wish to perform the said altars. The question is asked: what is the law?

And it seems at first that the said legacy did not take effect with respect to the said field, and consequently neither did the burden attached in the legacy; because an heir cannot make a legacy to himself from his own estate, as stated in the law *Legatum*, section *Haeredi*, in the Digest, under the title *De legatis* 1. But this reason does not stand in the way, because although the legacy does not hold, the burden inserted for the heir does hold, since even caducary legacies remain with him together with the burden, as provided in the Code, under the title *De caducis tollendis*, section *Pro secundo*, and in the Digest, under the title *De legatis* 1, in the law *Ciuitatibus*, section *Lucius*. Although this field belongs to Vannota by hereditary right and not by right of legacy, nevertheless, if the said Vannota had died without children, or if it had happened that all her children died without sons or daughters, her will would have to be observed. However, in our case, because even one son or one daughter suffices to exclude the substitute,

† And he who died with a son or daughter, such a fideicommissum failed as regards the altars, because the condition of the fideicommissum failed, C. de inst. et subst. l. generaliter. and ff. ad Treb. l. ex facto. §. fin. and ff. de leg. j. l. filius. §. cum quis. Moreover, the male children of Vannota from her first husband can claim nothing: because they were not placed in the disposition of the fideicommissum, but only in the manner of a condition. And those who are placed in a condition do not act in their own name, as l. si quis sub conditione. ff. si quis omni causa testamenti. as noted in ff. de haered. inst. l. Titius. For they say that those who are placed in a condition acquire causa mortis, or it is called mortis causa capio. But it is not said that a legacy or fideicommissum is given. As ff. de don. causa mort. l. quod conditionis. And therefore the children of the said Vannota exclude the altars [children] of the first marriage; in this matter they do not succeed, because Vannota could freely make a will in favor of the children of her second marriage, saving the legitime of the prior children, in Auth. de nupt. §. antepen. col. 3. And with the proviso that she could not have left to the second husband more than to one of the children of the first marriage, as C. de sec. nupt. l. hac edictali. And if it is said that the altars ought to obtain a share, by l. Lucius. §. Gayo. ff. ad Treb. It is answered that that §. is of no effect, because there one was burdened, of whom one died without issue. Here, however, one was burdened, who died with issue. And it suffices that he died with one surviving son, so that in the meantime, while he lives, the altars are excluded, or are not admitted, as ff. de verb. sign. l. non est sine liberis.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How the division is to be made among brother laborers.
2. The summary thereof.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† This person asks: since he stood together with his uncle at one bread and one wine, and at one or more laborers and tillages of lands, and from this acquired oxen, sheep, and pigs, and other animals, whether he ought to have a half share in the said animals, and the other half share ought to be held by the uncle.

† Furthermore, he asks whether the adult son of the aforementioned paternal uncle, who worked together with them, ought to receive any share of the fruits of the labor acquired with the common beasts of his father and his cousin. Answer: Assuming the facts as stated, nevertheless, one-half is attributed to the oxen and animals with which the cultivation is carried out, and this pertains to the said uncle and nephew; and the other half is attributed to the labor, and is divided into three parts, and each receives a third. And if any animals were acquired therefrom, the same division would be made of the animals.

† Moreover, someone asks: while he was tending the common livestock, namely oxen, he was captured by robbers; whether the loss of the lost animals and the cost of the splint should be shared in common. He answers: yes.

† Furthermore, he asks whether the daughter of the said paternal uncle is to be dowered from the common fund. I answer: No, because this pertains to the burden of the father alone, and not to the burden of the partnership.

† Furthermore, he asks, since the uncle had 15 florins, from which and from a certain other sum a certain house was purchased, how the said house is to be divided. I answer that the said 15 florins are to be returned to the said uncle, and afterwards the house is to be divided equally, and below with the nephew.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether religious persons may, at least by the disposition of the testator, be placed in charge of the governance of a hospital, and what if the hospital has an attached or annexed church.
2. If the bishop consented to the construction of the hospital simply, whether he may claim the fourth part or any other right.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A certain person, on his deathbed, instituted his mother as his heir and ordered that, after his mother’s death, a hospital with a certain church be established in his houses, which he instituted as heir to himself after his mother’s death. He appointed and left as rectors of the said hospital and the aforementioned church the priors and brothers of Saint Augustine and the prior of the fraternity of the Trinity of Fulgni, who should be in office at the time, provided that the said brothers and the prior of Saint Augustine are bound to celebrate Mass hospitably in the said church each week. After the death of the said testator, the said mother, during her lifetime, had the said church and hospital constructed with the authorization of the diocesan bishop, and this mother passed away. It is now asked whether the said prior and brothers of Saint Augustine and the said prior of the fraternity are the rectors of the said hospital and church, or whether one of them is, and what authority they have by virtue of the said testament. Also, whether any quarter is due to those who consented to the said foundation.

I answer that whether a religious should preside over that hospital was a matter of opinion, as noted in the commentary on c. Quia contingit, de Religiosis domibus, in the Clementines. Some said yes; others said no, because it is not permitted for a monk or religious to be appointed to a position outside the monastery unless it is for the care of souls, according to the Rule, c. Super. Therefore, where the administration of the hospital lacks the care of souls, a religious cannot be placed in charge of it, and it does not appear to involve such care, since he does not possess the power of the keys by virtue of the office of the ordinary, cum satis. And although the testator disposed that Mass should be said there three times a week, it does not appear that such a person, being obliged to officiate in the church, thereby has the care of souls, because he has no flock, nor does he preside over any university.

To the contrary, it seems that this hospital is annexed to the church, and the church is a parish church, since the Divine Office must perpetually be said and celebrated there, which requires a priest, and he will have the power of the keys with respect to those poor persons, whom he can absolve, hear their confessions, and impose penance upon them. Therefore, on account of this care of souls, a religious can be placed in charge. But if this were so, it would follow that the prior of the fraternity, who is a pure layman, could not be placed in charge of the said hospital and church, but only of the hospital, and the care of the poor would be not spiritual but lay. And therefore, we must speak either of the care of the church or of the care of the hospital. Let us thus distinguish between them as if they were separate.

Solution. I say that the said testament is to be observed, just like a statute, because religious orders and houses can have hospitals under them, as in c. Quia contingit, § Praemissa, de Religiosis domibus, in the Clementines. For what is left to the brothers appears to be left to the place and the convent of the brothers, as in D. de rebus dubiis, l. Civibus. Moreover, when the prior cannot officiate in the said church himself, he will send another, as in D. de verborum obligatione, l. Continuus, § Si ab eo. From the foregoing it follows that the administration of the said hospital pertains to the brothers and the said prior of the fraternity, as is disposed in the testament. The Divine Offices, however, were to be performed by the Prior of the said brothers, or by another commissioned by him, so that the form of the said testament be observed.

† Regarding the second pact, namely concerning the episcopal fourth, I say that if the Bishop consented to the foundation of the said hospital church and to the endowment made from all goods, he appears to have remitted whatever right he might have had by reason of the fourth, since he consented to its transfer to another, as stated in the Digest, *De aedilicio edicto*, law *Quare*, section *Si venditor*. Although there is an argument to the contrary in the Code, *De administratione tutorum*, law *Cum quidam*. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a son from the first marriage, by acknowledging the legacy made to him, when he could not claim more, and by making a refutation regarding the legacy, precludes himself from the benefits of the law.
2. Which disposition may be confirmed.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A certain Mecus left two hundred pounds to the son of his daughter from his first marriage by way of institution [of heir], and he wished and ordered that the said nephew could not claim or have more from his goods. The residue, however, he left to his second wife, Lady Philippa.

The aforementioned nephew claimed the said legacy and received a portion of it. He then made a renunciation. Moreover, the said nephew does not wish to claim by means of the action arising from the law *Hac edictali*, that is, what ought to come to him by virtue of the said law. Two objections are raised against the said nephew, namely, that he acknowledged the legacy, and that he made a renunciation. It appears that the said nephew is excluded on account of these two aforementioned grounds. For he who acknowledged the legacy is excluded from every complaint that would have been available to him against the will, as stated in D. de inofficioso testamento, l. final, and l. nihil interest; and D. de minoribus, l. si filius. Likewise, he who released a debtor, even gratuitously, is not heard regarding what he remitted, as noted in D. de pactis, l. emptor, § Lucius.

To the contrary, it appears that the text in l. Hac edictali first provides that it is not permitted to leave more to the second wife than was left to one of the children of the first marriage. Subsequently, the same rule is extended to nephews in the words *quam observationem*. Finally, it removes the said circumvention and every precaution, however devised, intended to impede the effect of that law. Now, it is the case that this clause, whereby he could not claim or receive more, is a certain precaution devised to impede the effect of that law. Therefore, this clause is null by operation of law (*ipso iure*) by virtue of that law.

Furthermore, there is no doubt that this clause was added to diminish the right of the nephew and to augment that of the stepmother; and thus, just as leaving more is harmful, so too this clause is void by operation of law. Moreover, whenever a disposition is invalid due to a legal prohibition, acknowledgment of such a disposition does not induce its validation. It would be otherwise if the disposition were valid, even though subject to complaint or rescission. Since that which is in excess of what was left is regarded by the law as if it were not written, it follows that the stepmother can acquire nothing by right where the testator’s will is infringed; rather, it is deemed to cease, as stated in C. de donationibus, l. sancimus, at the end, where it says that it should be considered as not written or understood.

Furthermore, although the nephew makes a renunciation of the legacy, he does not make a renunciation of the benefit of the law *Hac edictali*. For he does not claim that benefit for himself as a son or nephew of the first marriage who has suffered injury through perfect marriage, but not as an heir or legatee, as noted in Auth. de nuptiis, § optime, in the gloss *hic manifeste*, Collatio 4. For he who has multiple rights does not lose one by remitting another, which he did not remit, as stated in D. de bonis liberis, l. si filius; and D. de servis urbanis praediis, l. si domus, unless he expressly remitted both, as in C. de inofficioso testamento, l. si quando, § final.

It has been stated in the disposition whether it induces a natural obligation, which can be overcome with some benefit, and then it can be confirmed by tacit will, as in C. ad legem Falcidiam, Auth. sed cum testator. Or it is such as to induce only a natural obligation, as in the case of a non-solenn will, and then the will can be confirmed, and thus by delivery or submitted execution, but not by a simple word, as noted in C. de testamentis, l. non dubium. Or it is not such as to induce a natural or civil obligation, but is a certain disposition regarded as not written, and then it is not confirmed, because that which is not, or is deemed not to be, cannot be confirmed. For confirmation cannot exist unless there is a prior firming with something pre-existing, as in D. de libellis legatorum, l. aurea, § testamento. Or it does not hold by any special favor.

† And it can be confirmed with the approval of the person whose interest is at stake, as argued in *l. filio praeterito*, *de iniusto testamento*; or by public favor, and then otherwise, as in *l. 1* and *2*, *ne fideiussoribus dotium dentur*; or by public odium, and likewise, as in *l. a Diuo*, *de ritu nuptiarum*. Solution. I conclude by saying that the grandson is not understood to have acknowledged the said clause of the said testament, which could not be claimed or possessed more than once, because that clause was invalid by the law itself and was considered as not written. Likewise, he is not understood to have waived the benefit of that law in doubt, unless he expressly waived it and referred to those provisions, as in *C. de exceptionibus*, *l. si ex maiore*. But if there had been no waiver, but only a simple claim of the legacy, then there would be no doubt that, for the mere word, the said clause was not confirmed, since it is void, as noted in *d. l. non dubium*. It does not obstruct the fact that he who acknowledged the legacy seems to acknowledge the burden imposed on the legacy, as in *ff. de legatis 2*, *l. sed ex duobus* and *l. Imperator*, § *si centum*. Because this is true when such a burden could be imposed by law. But if it could not be imposed by law, as in *ff. de legatis 3*, *l. vxorem*, § *haeres, vel legatarius*, and in *l. 1*, *ff. de conditionibus et institutionibus*, and *ff. de operis libertatis*, *l. cerdonem*. And thus I say, and I advise, I, Baldus de Peru, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a fideicommissary burdened with restitution after death may, during his lifetime, give away something from the assets subject to restitution.
2. Whether an executor appointed to distribute to the poor, whom he shall choose, is deemed to have chosen them by instituting them in his will.
3. Whether a poor person instituted as heir may substitute another, or others, poor persons.
4. Whether fraternities of beggars are pious places, or places of the poor.
5. Whether the aforementioned executor may choose the testator’s illegitimate son, if he is poor.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A certain Francis Christionis appointed Ange and his son as his universal heirs, and made a pupillary substitution in favor of Lady Sourana, his mother, during her lifetime. Subsequently, he left a bequest to the poor of Christ, to be chosen by her, using these words: that Lady Sourana ought, for the soul of the said testator, to leave and distribute. Finally, after the son of the said testator had died in pupillary age, and the said Lady Sourana, being heir by virtue of the pupillary substitution and having the authority to distribute among the living, gave and distributed to Anthony, formerly the natural or spurious son of the said testator Francis, for his maintenance and out of piety, one house, one estate, and certain massarities, with the burden that the said bastard could not alienate them; and with this condition, that if he should die without sons, the said properties would devolve entirely to the poor of Christ. After the said Anthony died, leaving John Francis, his legitimate and natural son, and after the said Sourana had possessed the goods granted and donated by her to the said Anthony, the said Sourana finally died, having made a will, in which she instituted the said John Francis as heir of the poor, and substituted for a certain portion a certain fraternity. Now several questions are raised.

† And first, whether the concession made by the said Lady Soura to the said Antonio was valid. Answer: It was valid during the lifetime of the said Soura; however, since it was subject to restitution, it lapsed upon her death, as stated in D. de legatis secundo, l. unum ex familia, in principio; and C. de fideicommissis, l. quotiens; and D. de legatis primo, l. filium, § divus.

Secondly, it is asked whether the institution made of the said John Franci by the said Lady Soura was valid or not.
