Answer: He who is bound to choose the poor at his death may choose them also by instituting them as heirs or by bequeathing to them, as in the Digest, *De legatis* 2, *Unum ex familia*, § *Si dos*. However, he must institute or bequeath in such a manner that the testator’s intention is respected; for he cannot choose from those whom the testator did not intend. Truly, he may choose a poor person and institute him, but not in such a way as to exceed the measure of distribution, but only to the extent necessary for relieving his poverty. For he could not give a thousand marks of silver to one person as a poor person, nor does this pretended name of poverty avail, as noted in the Code, *De sacrosanctis ecclesiis*, *Illud*, and *L. 1*, Code, *De mendicis validis*, Book 11, and the argument in the Digest, *De exercendo*, *Tutius*.

Thirdly, it is asked whether a poor person chosen may substitute another. I answer: yes, if he substitutes someone from those promised, that is, from the poor, when the testator ordered distribution among the poor, or to some pious place, where mention was made of a pious place. For the executor may distribute to one poor person during his lifetime, and to another poor person after the death of the former. Just as he may distribute in quantity, so also in time, as in the Digest, *De militum testamento*, law *Miles*; and *Haeres*, § *Et quia diximus*; and noted in the said law *Unum ex familia*, § *Sed si fundum*, by Bartolus.

Fourthly, it is asked whether the fraternities of the Beaters are called pious places, so that what is to be distributed among pious places can be granted to them. And it must be said that these fraternities, living under discipline and a certain Catholic rule, are approved colleges, but they are not pious place colleges: and their houses are not pious houses. Hence, they are not pious places unless they have an attached church or hospital. For their life is rather a certain local and honest mode of living than a pious mode: and their places are not permanently devoted to divine use, since they could sell the house in which they gather, and even destroy the confraternity, as in l. 1 and in l. fin. ff. de collegiis illicitis, and in l. sodales. And therefore the said lady Sourana could not substitute the said society, which is called the fraternity of praises, since they are neither poor nor a pious place, unless, as has been said, the fraternity itself were ordered for the sustenance of the poor, in whose use the bequests made to it would be converted. It would follow, therefore, that after the death of the said Fran., the said goods should be distributed among the poor by the diocesan of the place.

But certainly one must attend to the foregoing. For the said Ant. was the illegitimate son of the testator, and therefore it does not appear that he could have been named as a poor person under the testator’s will. For he who is named is deemed to take from the testator, even if he is named by the executor, as in the cited law *Unum ex familia*, § *Si de falcidia*, *De legatis* 2; and it is noted in the chapter *Dudum*, § *Vero*, *De stipulationibus incertis*; and it is clear in the law *Verum*, § *Cum quidam*, *De rebus dubiis*. And on account of the prohibition of the law, fraud and a mere pretense are presumed, as in *De probationibus*, law *Qui testamentum*. Nor can anything be left to an illegitimate son under the pretext of poverty, since he ought not to be maintained, as in the Code, *De naturalibus liberis*, authority *Liceat*. And although according to canon law maintenance ought to be provided to him, because he himself does not sin, but his father does, as in *Extra*, *De eo qui in matrimonio duxit*, and chapter *Cum haberet*, nevertheless such maintenance does not last beyond his own life, because maintenance ends with death. But these objections do not prevail. It must be said that the legitimate and natural children of the said Ant., conceived after the death of the said testator Francis, could be named by the said d. Soura as outsiders who are poor and in no way related to the testator himself. And to this effect it is noted in the Code, *De naturalibus liberis*, law *Si*; and I by no means say that there is any doubt concerning those conceived after the death of the grandfather, as in *De suis et legitimis heredibus*, law *Item Praetor*; and *De iniuriis testatorum*, law *Si quis filio exheredato*; and it is noted in the law *Si quis filium*, in the principal part, Code, *De inofficioso testamento*, and chapter *Cum*.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a legacy given for the purpose of a dowry, or in lieu of a dowry, is extinguished if the legatee is provided with a dowry during the testator’s lifetime; and what is the rule regarding a legacy made as an augmentation of the dowry; and number 4.
2. Whether a mother may appoint a guardian for her son in her will.
3. Whether a guardian may alienate property, and what property.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen. A certain girl was bequeathed two hundred by the said Lady Sourana in these words: "I bequeath to such a girl two hundred for the augmentation of her dowry." Finally, the said Lady Sourana married the said girl to a certain Antonius, who confessed that he had received from the said Lady Sourana, for the dowry of the said girl, his future wife, two hundred pounds of denarii. Finally, the said Sourana, notwithstanding the said confession, promised the said two hundred pounds to the said Antonius as dowry. And lastly, the said Sourana died, and in her will she left to the said Antonius the said two hundred pounds, which Antonius now claims.

† It is now asked whether the said 200 pounds ought to be paid once only or repeatedly. The learned doctors say that when a testator first bequeaths a certain sum for a dowry, and secondly gives or promises the said sum, it is understood to be one and the same, and not several; because it is manifest that the legacy was made, and the gift or promise given, for the same cause, as in the Digest, *De legatis* 2, *Lucius*, first paragraph; and in the Digest, *De legatis* 1, *Eiusmodi*, § *Cum pater*; and in the Code, *De legatis*, *Filia legatorum*. And therefore it seems that the bridegroom and the bride, or the husband and the wife, ought to agree, so that only one payment be made. For it is not understood that the testator burdened the heirs with several obligations, as in the Digest, *De legatis* 2, *Titia*, § *Qui invita*; for the addition of a certain final cause restricts the dispositions to one consequence. Otherwise it would be if a simple legacy had been left to the girl. It would be different if the dowry were given or promised to the husband, because these would not be two lucrative causes; since that which is in the person of the husband is an onerous cause, as in the Digest, *De acquisitione et obligatione*, *Ex promissione*. In the question proposed, it seems to be said that the two hundred ought to be paid only once.

But certainly that word, which is added in the will, namely "in augmentation of the dowry," gives rise to doubt. For the term "augmentation" signifies an excess beyond the quantity principally established for the dowry, as in C. de donat. antenup. l. si. And therefore it seems that both sums may be claimed. However, the promise made for the dowry and the legacy given in augmentation of the dowry is a matter of the subtlety of the words of the will. This opinion seems true. On the second point, I say that the aforementioned d. Soura cannot appoint a tutor who is a tutor by operation of law; nevertheless, he must be confirmed by the judge, if he is suitable, as in ff. de confirm. tutor. l. 1 and l. peto, § mater, de leg. 2.

† On the third point, I say that a guardian cannot alienate immovable property, nor movable property which can be preserved in its condition and is not consumed by use, without a judicial decree, as provided in C. de administratione tutorum, l. lex, quae tutores. However, regarding property which is consumed by use or becomes worse or cheaper in a short time, he may not only sell it, but is even compelled to dispose of it if he wishes to avoid the risk of negligence, as stated in l. magis puto, § ne passim, de rebus eorum. On the fourth point, the answer is evident from the records and from what has been said above. And I say the same on the last point.

† I am in doubt on the first point because of the phrase “in augmentum dotis,” which seems to imply quantities, and to increase, as in D. de dot. praet. l. qui ita. I say that if the lady of Soura had had another consideration, for example because she believed that the said girl ought to be dowered by her parents, and therefore she used the words “in augmentum dotis”: that, having this conjecture, or a similar one, the said quantity of two hundred pounds ought not to be due except once. And to this effect is what is read and noted in D. de probat. l. quinquaginta, because in different wills the same cause repeated between the same persons usually makes up only one sum, and not several, as is noted there. I do not believe, however, that the word “in augmentum” was added because of the notary’s ignorance. I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If the person promising the dowry, by reason of the contract, paid the tax (gabella): later it is agreed that the son-in-law shall have one plot of land for the dowry: whether he is bound to pay again as if from a new contract.
2. Agreements and burdens diminish and increase the contract; therefore, consideration must be given to the payment and the annual dominion.
3. I
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The husband confessed that he had received 300 as dowry from the father of the woman. Finally, immediately, notwithstanding the said confession, the father of the woman promised the said three hundred to the father-in-law of the said girl, as is customary. In the end, the said father of the woman gave to the aforementioned father-in-law, in lieu of payment, a certain piece of land to the said father-in-law, on this condition: that if within a year he restores the said three hundred, he shall recover the said land, or piece of land; otherwise, it shall remain to the husband. Finally, the tax on the dowry contract was paid; it is requested that it be paid again on the contract of the giving in lieu of payment.

† It is now asked whether a new gabela (tax) must be paid on the said *datio insolutum* (transfer of property in lieu of payment), and, if it must be paid, on what amount it must be paid. And truly it must be said that the said gabela must be paid, because it is a new contract; for a *datio insolutum*, when a thing is given for a certain quantity, is similar to a sale and purchase, as is noted in C. de sen. l. libera quaedam Theodora.

To the contrary it seems, because this is a certain commutation of the dowry from money to a thing, as in ff. de iure dot. l. ita constante. For it is not a commutation simply, but on account of the dowry, as in ff. de iure dot. l. quotiens. For the statute provides that if the gabela has once been paid, and another contract arises therefrom, that a new gabela must not be paid if another contract arises therefrom: but this is the case here, because on the occasion of the dowry another contract is celebrated. Moreover, although this contract is called *insolutum*, the transfer nevertheless accedes to the pledge, because it is not given so that the thing remains with the husband in perpetuity, but so that it may be redeemed within a year. Suppose therefore that it is redeemed; now from this new contract no utility has been acquired, except in the fruits of the intervening time. This also appears from the words of the instrument itself, which state that he must have half of the fruits of that year. The statute on the gabela seems to speak to the effect that the gabela must not be paid again when a contract is made concerning the same matter of the dowry. But here the dowry contract is in itself, and one obligation arises from the first contract, another from the second.

Solution. I say that this solution regarding the gabela depends on the future course of events. For if it is redeemed, because then the dowry stands in pure money, as before, the gabela must not be paid, except on the fruits, as we say in a similar case when the dowry is recovered by the woman. For the gabela is not paid on the interest for the year of restitution of the dowry. But if it is not redeemed, then it will be paid on the whole, because then the thing, estimated at a just price, I do not say by way of pact, l. commissoriae in pignoribus reprobati: the measure is that it remains with the husband in perpetuity, and in the restitution, the husband being released, it would be a quantity, and not a fund. But if it were posited that the fund ought to be restored, then such an estimation would not make a sale, but would be less similar to a commutation, and an action would lie for the first thing evicted, as in ff. de solutionibus l. qui res in principio.

From these things it appears that, while we are within the time of redemption, the said father of the woman is not bound to pay the gabela on the whole thing, since the thing has not been transferred in full right, as in ff. de contrahenda emptione l. cum manusata § nemo.

† Moreover, the aforementioned pact meanwhile diminishes the right of the recipient, at least with regard to the hope of the year; if, in the meantime, any valuation were to be made, it ought to be considered whether it is probable that the price of the woman will be paid or not, as in D. de legatis 3, l. quia habebat, in principio. For pacts and burdens diminish or increase the contract, as in D. de contrahenda emptione, l. fundi partem, and D. de actione empti, l. si similis, § si tibi durata. Even for a year, and not beyond, the thing is to be returned simply into the cause of the dowry, and ought not to be paid unless for as much as the annual dominion is worth, as in C. de donationibus, l. sancimus, § si; D. de pactis, l. ab emptore, according to Guillaume de Cuy. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a person elected as a syndicus may excuse himself on account of illness, or is bound to serve through a substitute.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen. It is proposed that a certain John Gilii has long been, and still is, hindered by a perpetual illness resulting from certain wounds formerly inflicted upon him, on account of which impediment he is unable to attend to his affairs. Now, this man has been elected syndicus of the village, and thus summoned by the village of Saint Peter in Pariete. He excuses himself, stating that he is not able to perform the said office of syndicus. But the opposing party argues that he possesses patrimony, such that another syndicus may exercise the said office on his behalf at the expense of his patrimony. Hence, since he cannot serve in person, let him serve through a substitute. For they say that he may substitute another, and thus cannot avoid the burden. Now the question is asked: what is the law?

And it seems that he ought to serve through a substitute, as in the Digest, *De verbis oblig.*, l. *Continuus*, § *Si ab eo*. To the contrary is the truth, because the office of syndicate is purely personal, as in the Digest, *De muneribus et honoribus*, l. *Munerum*, § *Defensores*; and therefore those who are afflicted by illness, so that they cannot attend to their own affairs, are excused from such an office, as in the Digest, *De vacando muneribus*, l. *Praetor*, in the beginning. These, however, are such duties for which money cannot be given in place of the duty, as in l. *Illud convenit*, *De excusationibus munerum*, Book 10. Therefore, it is not true that such a syndicate can serve through a substitute; because just as a substitute is not admitted to denounce capital crimes, so too is a procurator not admitted. The laws are well-known. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that a person suspected of flight may be personally arrested notwithstanding even solemn holidays: may he be arrested on holidays in honor of God?
2. Whether a statute may abolish holidays in honor of God that are otherwise prohibited.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The statute of the city of Trent provides that if a person suspected of flight is a foreigner, he may be arrested and held personally. And that after he has been arrested and detained, immediately, notwithstanding any holidays, even solemn ones, the official shall briefly, summarily, and without formality, without the noise and formalities of judicial procedure, expedite the case. And if within a short term to be subsequently fixed by the official himself, the debt is not legally established to the official, such detained person shall be released, and the official shall forthwith compel such plaintiff, etc. Now, a certain cleric was arrested in the city of Trent on account of reprisals on a holiday in honor of God.

† It is asked whether, on holidays in honor of God, the aforementioned capture may be valid, and whether the person was captured according to law or not, and whether he is to be released or not; this could be debated, that as to the said release, if he was to be released, the proceedings should proceed, or the capture be confirmed, if he is to be detained. And it seems that on a holiday in honor of God, one cannot cognize the aforementioned matters, because on such days the office of the judge rests, and the clamor of judicial proceedings is entirely forbidden, as C. de feriis, l. dies festos. But this recognition has in itself the clamor of a judicial proceeding, since it has a contradictor and requires cognition of the case; therefore, it cannot be expedited on such days, as ff. si quis in ius vocan. non ie., l. ex quocunque iure; and ff. de feriis, l. si feriatis; and C. de Iudaeis, l. die Sabbati; and ff. quis ordo in bo. pos. ser., l. 2, §. dies.

On the contrary, it seems that the statute says that proceedings shall take place notwithstanding any holidays. Since it says "notwithstanding any holidays" and adds "even solemn ones," it seems manifest that no holidays shall stand in the way; because so says the municipal law, from whose words one must not depart in any way, as ff. de testa. mili., l. in fraudem, §. fin.; and ff. de exerci., l. 1, §. si is, qui nauem. Moreover, this seems consonant with natural reason and common law, for when someone is captured extra ordinem, holidays seem to cease, as de feriis, l. pen., according to one reading, and what is noted there. Moreover, a person captured during a holiday in honor of God may be released at the same time, as noted in ff. de no. ope. nun., l. 1, §. item nuntiatio; and ff. de euict., l. minor, in prin. Moreover, because equality must be observed in judicial proceedings as to time and as to all things, as C. de fruc. et lit expen., l. fi.

† Solution. Although a statute cannot generally abolish holidays instituted in honor of God, it may distinguish them, so that they apply in some cases and do not apply in others, as stated in the Digest, *De feriis*, l. 2, and by Azo in the Summa, and note the Code, *De feriis*, l. 40. And therefore, the statute expressly commanding it, the said holidays do not obstruct. And I conclude generally that, just as one may be arrested on a holiday in honor of God as a suspect, as noted in the aforementioned law *Dies festos*, Code, *De feriis*, so conversely it may be proven that he is not a suspect, and he may be released, because what is not permitted to the defendant is not permitted to the plaintiff, since it is permitted to the plaintiff, etc., as in the rules of canon and civil law. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a donation is broken by the birth of a posthumous child.
2. Whether, and when, a donation of all goods made to a stranger while a son survives, is valid or not; and whether the son can rescind it beyond the legitime.
3. What time must be considered in judging whether a donation is inofficious or not.
4. Whether a father can give his son his legitime in whatever property the father chooses.
5. Whether the insinuation of a donation must be made by the donor, and how the insinuation is to be made.
6. Whether the insinuation of a donation made in one place extends to property existing outside the territory.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A certain Francis, then lacking male children, gave to certain sons of his predeceased brother, by title of remuneration, as he stated; and he specified the causes of remuneration, namely industry and diligence, saying that he had in some manner profited from his uncle’s industry and diligence. He gave almost all his goods, amounting to some 1,000 florins, and specified those things and goods with that clause, that so many were donations, etc., with certain pacts and burdens. And among the rest is such a resolutive pact of the said donation, namely that if the said Francis should die leaving legitimate and natural male children born from him in the future, one of several, and living, and exceeding beyond the time of their pupillary age, that from then on the said donation, or donations aforesaid, shall be understood as revoked, and the things given shall return and devolve to the said male children. And in the said donation many other things are disposed in similarity to the same testament. Provided, however, that the said donation was inter vivos: and it does not contain the institution of an heir, nor can it contain such, which donation, as is presupposed, having been thus made, the said donor afterwards begot many male children born of legitimate marriage, who, however, died in pupillary age. From the said donor, however, there remains one female daughter. Now it is asked concerning the validity of the said donation, whether the said donation is revoked by the birth of the said children, or not. Also, whether it can be rescinded in whole or in part as inofficious. Also, since the said donation was not insinuated according to the form of the common law, but was produced for the purpose of insinuation before the common judge of Perugia after the death of the said Francis, as is said, the donor: whether the said donation is valid with respect to the goods which are in the Arezzo territory, where the common law prevails, or whether another form is given according to the form of the statutes of that place. And whether, according to the common law, a donation exceeding the legitimate portion can be insinuated after the death of the donor. On all these matters, the sole truth of the law being considered, counsel is requested in the Name of God.

† Regarding the first point, I say that either the father did not consider the posthumous child, and then the donation is entirely broken by the birth of the posthumous child. And because it is rescinded by operation of law and reverts to the father, unless he makes a donation inter vivos: and even if the posthumous child dies while the father is alive, the donation does not become valid, as argued from D. 50.16.105 (Inter stipulantem), § Sacramentum, although it argues to the contrary. D. 28.5.1 (Qui solvendo) does not give two Apollonius. It is otherwise in a will, which becomes valid by praetorian law, as D. 28.2.1 (Posthumus). The argument also holds to the contrary, a certain law which says that a contract becomes valid more easily than a last will, as D. 6.24.1 (Receptum). But there it speaks of validation which depends on the will of another, which is more difficult in wills than in contracts, as D. 28.5.1 (Illa stipulatio). I therefore say that by the birth of the posthumous child, whom the testator did not consider, the inofficious donation is broken by the very birth of the son, as C. 8.57.1 (Si unquam). But sometimes the testator considers the posthumous child, and this in two ways. For sometimes he considers the posthumous child and makes a disposition, and then the same applies as I will say regarding the already born child, concerning whom the father was inofficious. Sometimes he considers the posthumous child but does not make a disposition. And this is our case. For this donor considered the posthumous child, but did not dispose anything regarding the posthumous child not reaching adult age, and therefore this omitted case, argued from a will to a donation, seems to render the donation null. For if the testator disposed regarding the posthumous child living up to such an age: the posthumous child who does not live up to that age is not the designated posthumous child. Hence the reason of the omitted case does not hold: because by reason of the omitted person the donation seems to be infringed: because this one is not that posthumous child of whom the donation speaks, as D. 25.2.1 (Commodissime). And thus it is said that when the testator considered the posthumous child, the reason of the said law Si unquam ceases, since another reason is founded on the presumed cancellation of the donor's will upon the birth of the posthumous child. I answer that when the case was unforeseen, the tacit will of the disposer does not increase the effect of gifts, nor is tacit will presumed in an omitted case, as D. 29.1.16 (Militis codicillis), § Veteranus.

† If, however, the question concerns a child already born, with respect to whom the father was inofficious and disposed of his property in fulfillment of the duty of piety: if the donation had been made to other children, it would not be revoked, except up to the amount required by law, as stated in the Code on inofficious testaments, in the Authentic *Unde si parens*, and in the Authentic *De immens. dona.*, Collatio 7. But if it was made to an outsider, and the legitimate portion was not left to the son, and he thereby acted with certain knowledge, not being mistaken about his assets: according to the old law, the donation would be revoked in its entirety, by analogy to an inofficious testament. But after the law of the Code came into force, a son to whom something has been donated or left cannot bring an action for complaint, except for supplementation, according to Jacobus de Belvisio and Petrus, and the same is held by Bartolus in the law *Titia Seio*, § *Imperator*, on legacies, book 2. The Gloss, however, holds the contrary opinion in the aforementioned Authentic *De testamento imperfecto*, because a donation is not as favorable as a testament; hence, it is presumed that the donor was acting out of favor, as argued in the Digest on inofficious testaments, in the law *Titia*, and therefore his consent is condemned. And thus the donation is rescinded in its entirety. And this opinion is held by Dynus. But Bartolus bases himself on the rule laid down in the final law of the Code on donations, where it is said that the rule concerning inofficiousness regarding a donation is the same as the rule of the inofficious testament. But that law does not prove the similarity of the complaint to the complaint, where both are applicable, that is, the complaint of inofficiousness against a testament, or the complaint of inofficious donation against a donation. But nothing is said there about the right to sue for supplementation. This question is doubtful because of the opinions of so many doctors; it would not be doubtful at all if the father had not acted through inadvertence or fear in making the inofficious donation, as often stated regarding his assets, etc., as in the Digest on who and from whom, in the law *Iulius*. Then, on the contrary, without doubt, it would not be revoked, except up to the amount necessary to satisfy the debts of the estate.

But now it is doubted what time we must consider in order to determine whether the donation is inofficious or not, as stated in the gloss on l. 1, C. de inofficiosa donatione. It is said, however, that we must consider the time of the donation, even if the case subsequently developed in such a way that the just donation is not rescinded. And this gloss is consistent with the text and gloss in the aforementioned Authentica de testamentis imperfectis. But to me, by equity, it seems that a distinction should be made: either the testator could or ought to have foreseen the future case, and then the donation is considered inofficious; or he could not have foreseen it, and then the contrary applies, by argument from ff. de minoribus, l. verum, § si locupletior. Especially so in things that are perishable; for money in general cannot perish. Therefore, the situation is different with money than with a specific perishable item.

But immediately the question arises: suppose that the father assigned to the son for his legitime movable property, and gave to an outsider more substantial immovable property; now the son wishes to have his legitime proportionally from all the substance of the testator. The question is, what is the law? And it seems that the father could provide for the son with whatever property pleased the father, whether in things or in money, as noted in D. 36.1.10 (l. si quis priore) and D. 4.4.10 (l. denique), § sed vtrum, at the end; cf. D. 35.1.10 (l. non amplius), § cum bonorum; and D. 36.1.10 (l. deducta), § minimus; C. 10.2.10 (l. filium, quem habentem). The objection from D. 2.13.10 (l. scimus), § repletionem, does not hold, because there it speaks of the extent to which the supplement arises from legal disposition. But insofar as the testator himself provides, he may provide for the son with any property. And I understand the same to apply to a donor. For another question is raised.

† For it is certain among those skilled in the law that, for a donation exceeding the legitimate sum, the common law requires insinuation in one of two ways: either that the donation itself be made before the competent judge who presides over insinuations in the land where the donation is made, as in C. de donationibus, l. Data iam pridem, where it says, “donations to be drawn up before the records”; and l. Donatio sive, § In conscribendis, where it sometimes says, “they are to be preserved before the judge or magistrate”; or that such a donation be brought to the records by the donor himself together with the donee, or by him alone, as in the same title, l. In hac, where it says, “and since the donation itself rests in the will of the donor, it is permitted to him to announce and insinuate his donation before any judge whatsoever.” And to the same effect is C. de testamentis, l. Divus. Hence, if the donor had changed his status, because he had come to a status in which he could not make a donation; or if he had died, such a donation could not be insinuated according to the common law, nor even according to civil law, because that which exceeds the legitimate measure is held as not written and not understood. And thus neither is the instrument understood to have been celebrated, nor has consent been added. And therefore neither does a natural obligation arise, because the law prohibits or resists such an excessive donation. Therefore, without the faith of the records intervening, on the contrary, even according to the gloss, a decree of the judge approving the records is required, if indeed testimony is required for faith, as in C. de donationibus, l. Secundum divi Leonis, in the word “testimony of the highest authority”; and l. De donationibus, where it says, “for private testimony is superfluous.” Moreover, the authority of the judge is required for the solidification of the act; because where a decree is found to have been interposed, fraud is understood to cease, as in C. de praedio dato in dotem, l. 1, lib. 10. And this is the opinion of the gloss, that the donation ought to be by decree, so to speak. And this opinion is held by Guillaume de Cuyck, C. de sacrosancta ecclesia, l. Illud. And I say this when it was made elsewhere, and insinuation arises afterwards; because it is made before the records, no other decree is necessary. And thus is understood what we have in Auth. Ut non fiat pignus, § Illud, in gloss. 1, Ut fiat, col. 5. Otherwise it would follow that every donation would be valid. For if it were in the power of the donee to insinuate at any time, certainly he would insinuate whenever it pleased him. And thus he would mock the law. Therefore, having premised the common law, it is presupposed that the municipal law of the city of Perugia provides that a donation of any sum is valid, if it is produced before insinuation within six months before the judge of insinuation.

† Now it is asked whether a donation thus insinuated, by virtue of the municipal law, extends its effect to property situated outside the territory in which the common law is observed, or a different statute is written in Perugia. And it seems that if the same statute extends its force everywhere as regards matters depending on the consent of the parties, as in C. de donat. l. iam pridem, at the words “gesta autem,” and l. in hac sacratissima, at the words “ubicunque positarum,” and by argument from C. de contrah. empt. l. 1; nor is this surprising, because insinuation is not yet made before another judge, except before the judge of the place where the donation is celebrated, as in C. de donat. l. secundum divi Leonis. Moreover, there it takes its essential and formal principle; therefore it extends throughout all lands. For it is absurd to say that insinuations are made individually for each estate situated in different territories, as in C. de praescript. 30 ann. l. male arguitur. Furthermore, insinuation is an act of voluntary jurisdiction; therefore it extends its force everywhere, as in C. de emancip. secundum legem civitatis est sui iuris ubicunque locorum, as in C. de emancip. lib. l. 1. And we say the same regarding a will, as noted by the doctors in l. cunctos populos, non ob. ff. de bonis, auth. iud. poss. l. cui vis, because there it speaks of contentious jurisdiction.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Within what time the right to claim a legacy is prescribed.
2. Whether prescription runs against a son.
3. Whether a natural child is included under the term "sons."
4. If a brother substitutes his brother and the brother's sons, the father or this brother will not have usufruct in the goods left to the sons.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen. It is proposed that a certain Siannicola made a will and instituted her two sons as heirs; and if they were to die without sons, she substituted for them Mentio, her brother by blood, and his sons. Then the said testator Giamnicola died, with the said two sons surviving. Afterwards, the two sons died, with Mentio, their brother by blood, and his four sons surviving, namely, one male and three females. Afterwards, two of the daughters of the said Mentio died, one married and widowed, and the other unmarried, aged 14 years or thereabouts. The married one, coming to death, left all her rights to the said surviving brother, with the said male son and the said female, who is called Lady Vera, who was married and had remained a widow, surviving. The said Lady Vera stood for 30 years and more, claiming nothing by virtue of the said substitution, nor did she cause any trouble to her father while they lived; now, both being dead, she wishes to claim the portion falling to her by the said substitution.

† It is asked whether it is possible. And it seems that it is not: because after 30 years a legacy or fideicommissum cannot be acknowledged, just as an inheritance cannot be entered upon, as in C. de iure deliberando, l. licet. And if it is said that the situation is different in the case of a legacy and fideicommissum, because they are acquired by one who is ignorant, as in ff. de legatis 2, l. cum pater, § surdo, and that the situation is different in the case of entering upon an inheritance, it is answered that, although acquisition occurs by operation of law, just as a legacy is acquired by the legatee, nevertheless the law provides that the period of 30 years runs for accepting a paternal inheritance, as noted in C. quando non petentium partes, l. 1.

† Moreover, it is not an objection if it is said that prescription does not run against a filiusfamilias, because this is true in judicial proceedings, but otherwise in the acceptance of an inheritance or the acquisition of a legacy, as is noted in C. qui admitti ad bon. pos. possunt, l. 1, and in l. quod non solum, in principio, de bonis quae liberis, and ff. de acquirenda hereditate, l. si quis bona, § ius sumit. Furthermore, when a legacy is left to the father and the son, usufruct is not acquired by the father, as is noted in C. de bonis quae liberis, auth. excipere, together with the following authority. Therefore, the father is then not the legitimate administrator. Hence, the action lies fully with the son, and he must impute to himself the fact that he did not seek to compel his father to consent on his behalf, as in l. sed si pro praetori, § 2, ff. quibus ex causis maior et adulescens, and extra, de electione, c. iis quibus.

To the contrary, it seems that prescription does not run against a filiusfamilias, as in C. de annali praescriptione, l. 1, in fine. But, as I have said, there the text speaks of the case where the father is the legitimate administrator by reason of usufruct; hence, the exercise of the action lies with the father and not with the son. But in our case it is otherwise, because the father had no legal usufruct in the children’s share. Moreover, the sister, who remained silent for so long on account of the father and the brother, appears to have tacitly remitted her right to them, or on their behalf, taking the conjecture from the quality of the persons and the very long passage of time, as in ff. de probationibus, l. procul.

I therefore say that the said substitution was a universal fideicommissum, and that just as a filiusfamilias can acknowledge possession of goods and accept an inheritance without the knowledge of the father or mother, so he can demand, at least not in the form of a judicial proceeding, that the inheritance be restored to him. If he did not do so, he cannot now, after thirty years, claim to be able to demand the said portion of the inheritance in the future. And I speak of the case where usufruct is not acquired by the father, arg. auth. ut liceat matri et aviae, post principium, and C. de collationibus, auth. quod locum. For if usufruct were acquired by the father, and an action on the testament for the restitution of the fideicommissum were brought by the filiusfamilias, prescription for bringing the action would not run; because, when one is prevented from exercising the action in court, prescription does not run, as in the aforementioned l. 1, in fine, de annali exceptione, C. de iure deliberandi, l. si, § donec, and extra, de concessionibus praebendarum, c. cum nostris.

And thus I conclude that, in our case, usufruct of the portion of the said Lady Vera is not acquired by the said Mentio; and that, against the said Lady Vera in her portion, the exception of prescription is to be opposed by the heirs of Giannicola, who would otherwise be bound to restore the said inheritance under the Trebellian action.

And in the aforementioned substitution made in favor of the sons of a full brother, and the brother himself, I do not believe that natural sons are included, if he was legitimate; therefore, the mention of sons made simply must be understood in the better and more significant sense, so that, where there are both legitimate and natural sons, it is understood to refer only to the legitimate ones, as being the more worthy and just sons, as stated in the gloss on l. 2, ff. de iure deliberandi, because these words are used by agnates. But natural sons do not have agnation, as l. hic pro te, ff. unde cognati.

But it must be observed, because I have always said that where a brother substitutes a brother and the children of the brother, the brother, or this father, does not have usufruct in the goods left to his children; and the reason is that the conjunction falling between two extremes must join them equally, as in C. de impub. et aliis sub. l. quamuis. But if the father had usufruct of the children, the conjunction would not join them equally. Also, because a determined provision of the testator causes the legal provision to cease, as in extra, de testamentis, c. requisisti. And this was the opinion of Guarnerius in auth. idem hereditas, C. de bonis quae libera. But others there hold the contrary; and this is proved by the argument from the special: for it is special when the father succeeds the child together with the brothers of that child, so that usufruct is not sought for the father. Therefore, the common law is to the contrary. Hence the gloss says there that the verse "et forsan" and c. Guarnerius wrongly placed in that auth., and from this would follow the contrary conclusion, namely that for the said ladies Vera, while their father was alive, no prescription would have run, d. l. 1. in fin. C. de annis except., namely because they have no action, nor can they compel the father to sue or to institute. Hence the force of this point rests on this: whether, while the father was alive, usufruct of the said fideicommissum was due to the said ladies Vera or not; for if it was due, prescription runs; if not, then it does not. This question is doubtful, and depends solely on the understanding of the said word "forsan"; and perhaps, if from elsewhere, etc. That is certain, that if a brother substitutes a brother and the children of the brother, the words are understood so that they succeed together, not successively, and first the brother succeeds, then his children, as in ff. de usufructu accresc. l. si mulieri cum liberis, and noted in d. auth. item hereditas. The objection from l. lex Gal. § 1, de liberis et posthumis, does not hold, because there it speaks of a testator who disposes in some uncertain manner and order; here it is otherwise, as in C. de inofficioso testamento. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a son can claim that he has been unjustly disinherited, and bring an action against the will, and demand that the paternal inheritance be declared to belong to him for one-half, if another brother was instituted heir; that is to say, whether the complaint of an undutiful will and the claim for inheritance can be combined in the same petition.
2. A statute prohibiting exceptions against the petition, or ordering that exceptions be reserved for the merits of the case.
3. In judging, it is not safe to depart from the ordinary gloss.
4. Whether this petition proceeds, I ask that the oath be relaxed, and upon its relaxation, that the usurious contract be declared void. As for this part, the petition is aptly conceived, and justice... 9 The word "heir," how it is to be understood.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Since Bartholomew, disinherited by his father, had alleged causes that were just and legitimate, the action for an undutiful testament did not lie against him; nevertheless, he brought an action for an undutiful testament against his brother, and in his bill he drew the following conclusion: that the said testament, insofar as it concerned the institution of an heir, should be judicially declared broken, undutiful, and made contrary to the due duty of piety; and that the said testament being broken and rescinded, the paternal inheritance should be restored to the disinherited son for one-half, and that it should be declared that the inheritance of his father pertains to the said complainant for one-half. For there were two sons, one instituted as heir, the other disinherited. Against this bill, the exception of ineptitude is raised, along with other negative and peremptory exceptions; for it is objected that he was justly and truly disinherited. Now this objection is stated in the exception, although it comes simply to deny what is claimed; for the burden of proving the exception lies upon the party raising it, as in C. de inoffic. testa. l. omnimodo. However, it is proposed that the statute provides that, notwithstanding any exceptions of whatever kind that might be raised against the bill itself, the issue should be joined; but the exceptions should be reserved to be proved after the issue is joined. Moreover, the judge of the cause, following the statute, pronounced that the issue was joined on the said bill. Finally, the advice of a learned man was requested in this interlocutory matter, whether it should be revoked in whole or in part, and what the law is.

† On the aforementioned point, it must be said briefly that the said libel contains two parts: one, in which the rescission of the testament is sought; and with regard to this part, the judge pronounced correctly, because as to this part the libel is aptly conceived, and the justice of both the plaintiff and the defendant after the contestation of the litigation must be examined according to both the statute and the common law, which are consonant in this matter, as in C. de probat. l. exceptio. The second part of the said libel contains the demand that, the testament being broken, the inheritance be restored, and that it be declared that the paternal inheritance pertains and belongs to the said querent for one-half. And in this particular, the libel appears somewhat doubtful, as Guli. de Cu. l. 1. C. de inoff. test. [states], because the libel is inept. For in this particular, the disinherited person institutes a petition for inheritance, which does not belong to him, because he is not an heir unless a sentence has been rendered on the querela, as is fully stated and noted in ff. de inoff. test. l. cui de inofficioso. And therefore, since it appears that he is acting improperly and ineptly with regard to this particular, the querela could not proceed.

† Nor does the statute concerning the reservation of exceptions stand in the way: because the statute speaks of exceptions which require proof. But this exception, since it consists in written law, which determines that the complaint of an inofficious will cannot be cumulated with the petition for the inheritance, does not require proof, because [the law] disposing [of the matter] does not require inquiry. Moreover, the very form of the libel demonstrates its inadequacy as regards this first particular, and therefore such a libel is not considered a libel in this respect, as [stated in] l. 1, D. de officio assessoris, and D. de excusationibus, lib. §. quod si libelli, and in l. 1, §. 1, si mensor falsum modum dixerit. And also regarding that particular, the case should not be joined; and even if it were joined, the exception of inadequacy of the libel could be raised at any stage, as [stated in] Extra, de iudiciis, c. examinata. And this according to the opinion of those who hold that the petition for the inheritance cannot be brought unless judgment has been rendered on the complaint, since the disinherited person is not an heir beforehand, nor can he enter upon the inheritance. But nevertheless, the ordinary gloss holds that this libel proceeds, if the complaint is brought simply, and the claim to the inheritance is proposed conditionally: because this is not a cumulation, but a certain order of proceeding first and subsequently. Thus let the gloss in the said l. qui de inofficioso be understood. For when the origin of one judgment arises from another judgment, the first can be stated purely, and the second conditionally, and not simply, for the sake of abbreviating litigation, as we say in the action for production and the vindicatory action. And some hold this in the restitutory action and the rescissory action, by l. si sine herede, §. interposito, D. de administratione tutorum. Others hold the contrary, because they are different judgments, and cannot arise simultaneously: and it is better to bring the action first, before it arises, as D. de iudiciis, in l. non quemadmodum.
† but because in judging it is not safe to depart from the glossa ordinaria.

I say that the aforementioned libel should proceed as against both parties, and that the judge correctly issued an interlocutory judgment, according to the text of l. 1, C. de inoff. test., and this is based more on equity than on the strictness of the law. But this view seems to be contradicted, because if someone requests that an oath be administered to him, and upon its administration declares the contract usurious, and requests that this be inserted into the libel, such a libel does not proceed. And this has often been pronounced. Therefore, in the case at hand, these matters are not similar, because perjury pertains to the person; hence this exception cannot be raised, because perjury is an exception based on the person, as in C. si adversus vendit., l. 1. And therefore, one who is absolved from an oath as a perjurer ought to be repelled, whereas from a usurer restitution is sought, as noted in extra, de iure iur., c. debitoris. But in our case, the exceptions are not against the person, but against the cause, and therefore they do not proceed against the joinder of issue. And thus I say, and I advise, I, Baldus de Perusio. V. l. doc. et C.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a substitute may enter upon the inheritance under a vulgar substitution when the instituted heir dies during the testator’s lifetime.
2. Whether a codicillary clause operates so that a substitute under a fideicommissary substitution may enter upon the inheritance when the instituted heir dies during the testator’s lifetime.
3. Whether a compendious or vulgar substitution expires when the instituted heir dies during the testator’s lifetime.
4. What effect is produced by a clause stating that one may not demand or possess more.
5. The Trebellian action, just as the Falcidian portion, may be prohibited in a will.
6. The legitime is not owed to a brother unless the heir instituted is a person of infamous character.
7. What effect is produced by a codicillary clause, and in what cases; see also number 10.
8. Whether a vulgar substitution is included in a compendious substitution, and if so, when.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A certain Nicolaus made his will, in which, among other things, he ordered as follows: namely, in all his other movable and immovable property, he instituted his daughter Bartholomaea as his universal heir. And if it should happen that the said heir Bartholomaea should die without heirs of her body, then all the goods should devolve, and ought to devolve, to the lady Margaret, wife of the said testator. And he wished this to be his last will and his last testament; and that it should be valid and binding by the law of wills and last testament. And if it could not be valid and binding by the law of wills and last testament due to some omission of legal solemnity, or if it were otherwise infringed in law or in fact: he wished that it should be valid and binding by the law of codicils, and by the law and title of a donation causa mortis, and by every other mode and form of law by which it could better be valid and binding. In which will the said testator left to his brother 5 solidi, and that he could not demand more or have more. Now it has happened that the said Bartholomaea, the minor daughter of the same testator, died before the same testator, her father. Then, having changed his will by another, the said testator departed this life. Now the said Francis says that the inheritance pertains to him as an heir ab intestato, because the instituted heir died during the lifetime of the testator. On the contrary, the said lady Margaret, wife of the said testator, affirms that the inheritance pertains to her by virtue of the aforementioned substitution.

† It is asked what is the law, and it is alleged on behalf of the said Francis that the case is one of intestacy, and that there is no place for the said substitution for several reasons. First, because either the said substitution was vulgar: for a vulgar substitution is made under the condition that the instituted heir will not be, or will not be able to be, an heir, as in the Institutes, De vulgari substitutione, in the beginning; and in the Code, De hereditatibus instituendis, l. Cum proponas; and in the Digest, De vulgari substitutione, l. 1, § 1. But the wording of this will does not express this form; therefore, this substitution was not an express vulgar substitution. And if it is said that it was a tacit vulgar substitution, then it is shown by another reason that the said tacit vulgar substitution has lapsed: for whenever an impubes dies during the lifetime of the testator, the tacit vulgar substitution expires, as in the Digest, De capitis et postliminii reversione, l. Quod si filius; and according to Doctorus and others in the Digest, De vulgari substitutione, l. Lex Cornelia. Furthermore, the said substitution was not pupillary, because no mention was made of pupillary age, as the words seem to sound toward a pupillary substitution, as is fully noted in the Institutes, De pupillari substitutione, § Qua ratione; and consequently, it also does not contain a tacit vulgar substitution. Moreover, it is certain that, assuming the testator had expressly made a pupillary substitution, nevertheless, since the impubes died during the lifetime of his father, the pupillary substitution, with all its force, both express and tacit, vanishes: because he died under the power of his father, and at a time when he could not have an heir, as in the said l. Quod si filius and l. Lex Cornelia.

† Moreover, the said substitution does not appear to be valid as a fideicommissary one, because the codicillary clause does not seem to operate, except in the case where the will fails due to a lack of common solemnity, or because witnesses were not employed in sufficient number for the will, or were not summoned, as noted in the Authentica *Ex causa*, where the gloss interprets these words thus. But here the will fails because the heir instituted died during the testator’s lifetime. Hence, it does not appear that the said clause operates in any way. Moreover, a fideicommissary substitution requires that the inheritance be entered upon by virtue of the will, as stated in C. de fideicommissis, l. *Eam quam*; l. *Si nemo*; ff. de regulis iuris. But in this case, the inheritance cannot be entered upon by virtue of the will; therefore, the fideicommissary substitution is extinguished, and the entire will collapses.

To the contrary, that the said Lady Margaret succeeds by virtue of the said substitution. And first I demonstrate that she succeeds directly, and to the total exclusion of the testator’s brother; and this by the following reasoning. For if we wish to know the effect of the substitution, we must know its species and nature; for nature is that which produces the effect, and every species of substitution has its own nature and interpretation. But it is certain that the aforementioned substitution is a compendious substitution, because under a compendium of words it encompasses multiple matters at the time of the death of the instituted heir; namely, at whatever time, in whatever case he may die. And thereby, because it comprehends all times, it comprehends every case, and also the time and case in which the instituted heir dies during the testator’s lifetime. For a apt substitution comprehends multiple cases and times; it ought not to be restricted to one case, and especially not to the case and time in which the substitution would be vitiated. But it ought to be understood generally in whatever case and at whatever time, because where the testator does not distinguish, neither ought we to distinguish. Hence, the compendious substitution claims its place even if the instituted heir dies during the testator’s lifetime. This is stated by Cynus in l. *Precibus*.

† And if it is said that a tacit vulgar substitution expires upon the death of the minor during the lifetime of the testator. I answer: a distinction must be made regarding what is tacit. For one kind is interpretative, arising solely from the interpretation of the law and an implied extension. Another kind is tacit, but not entirely tacit, because it can be gathered from the extended meaning of the words, even though its form is not formally or specifically expressed, as with pupillary and vulgar substitutions contained in a compendious clause. I therefore say that what is entirely tacit vanishes, because the express provision vanishes; thus, the tacit provision is also annulled. But that which is not entirely tacit does not vanish, because it accedes more to the nature of the express than to the nature of the tacit, since all things are included in a general word. And this is fully known in *l. precibus*, ult., and in the great gloss at the end. Hence, a true vulgar substitution contained in a compendious clause is tacit if it is special, and express if it is general. But because a genus operates the same effect as an expression and an enumeration of species, and especially in the favorable matter of last wills, as in D. de legatis 3, *l. si chorus*, it is therefore manifest and necessarily follows that, although the instituted heir died during the lifetime of the testator, the substitute succeeds by virtue of the vulgar substitution. And thus I have often advised on this point. Now I show that, although the vulgar substitution would not apply, the fideicommissary substitution *ab intestato* applies. For the codicillary clause appears to have been added for every case in which the testament made by one who could make a will fails, and the matter is reduced to the case of intestacy; because a clause added in default of a will is accustomed to burden those who come *ab intestato*, as in D. de legatis 2, *l. Lucius*, § *filiam*. Furthermore, it appears that, assuming the said substitution were fideicommissary and not direct, nevertheless the entire inheritance should be restored to the substitute without the deduction of the Trebellian portion.

† because that clause, that he could not demand or have more, is also repeated even in intestate succession. And by this it appears that the brother is prohibited from deducting or having anything from the legitime, as is read and noted in the Digest, De fideicommissis libertatibus, law Decem.

† And it is certain that the Trebellianic portion may be prohibited in a will, just as the Falcidian portion, although there are differing opinions on this matter, yet this is the truth, as noted by the doctor after the gloss in the Codex, to the Law Falcidia, in the constitution "But when the testator"; and in the Digest, to the Trebellian Law, in the law "Marcellus," section "But what"; and therefore, if the said lady is in possession, because then she does not require restitution under the Trebellian Law, she excludes the said brother entirely, as in the Digest, to the Trebellian Law, in the law "The daughter to the brothers"; and if she is not in possession, she may demand that the inheritance be restored to her under the Trebellian Law.

† It is not necessary to discuss the legitime here, because the legitime is not owed to a brother unless a person of infamous character has been instituted as heir, as is noted in the Authenticum *De haeredibus et falsis*, §. *Primum itaque*. Therefore, concluding from the first point to the last, it follows that the said lady, as substitute, has a right to the entire inheritance, whether she comes by direct right or by the right of a fideicommissum: for these cases do not differ in the effect of the acquisition of the goods, but only in the mode of acquiring and in the subtlety of the law; because one acquires directly, and the other by half. And because she was substituted directly, she takes by her own right. But a substitute by fideicommissum takes through another who adheres and restores the inheritance, as in the Institutes *De fideicommissis hereditatibus*, §. *Restituta*; and in the Digest *Ad Trebellianam*, l. *Facta*; and l. *Cogi*, §. *Idem Metianus*.

† Nor does the gloss in the Authentica “Ex causa” oppose this, because the doctors commonly do not approve that gloss. And even assuming that gloss were true, namely that such a clause does not operate in the case of omission or disinheritance, nevertheless this does not apply to our case, because we are not dealing with a matter of omission or disinheritance. Moreover, that gloss speaks when the codicillary clause is appended simply. But when the testator expressly wills that such a clause shall operate in whatever case may arise, whether in law or in fact, then such a clause operates as the testator willed, as stated in § Filiam and in the Codex, De codicillis, l. Si, and in the Digest, De legatis 2, l. Cum pater, § Filius matrem, where it says that they were seen to extend to every species of succession.

† Having thus set forth the allegations for and against, it remains to proceed to the matter of restitution. And that which causes me to doubt is this: although the vulgar substitution is included in the compendious one, if it was made simply, yet it is otherwise if it was made in the case of an inheritance having been entered upon; for then the vulgar substitution cannot have place, as is stated in C. de impub. et aliis substi., l. post aditam. But this substitution made is valid in the case of the inheritance being apprehended by the instituted heir; therefore it operates only for the omitted case, as appears from the argument in ff. de libe. et posth., l. commodissime. And that it was made only after the inheritance had been entered upon, so that the vulgar substitution does not have place, as in ff. de uulg. sub., l. uerbis ciuilibus, seems to be clear from those words, namely, because the testator said,

† If the case should occur that the said Bartholomew is heir, etc., for the word "heir" seems to be understood with effect, namely after the inheritance has been accepted. Hence it does not seem that it suffices that he is heir by the testator's designation, unless he is heir with effect; because the words of conditions are said to be taken with effect, as in D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. "Hec conditio" from the first; D. de conditionibus institutorum, l. 10, l. "Mulier," § 2.

And by similar reasoning it appears that the codicillary clause also operates to no effect, because when the testator’s will cannot be adapted to the case that has occurred, neither does the disposition of law adapt to it. Hence, if the condition fails, the will of the deceased then ceases, and the codicillary clause can operate to no effect, because the said clause transfers, draws, and devolves only the case of testacy to the case of intestacy: yet without changing the form, the conditions, or the means. And where the condition fails, and the will of the testator, there the said codicillary clause fails, because the intestate substitute cannot obtain more than he would obtain in the will. Hence, those things which were bequeathed under a condition by will appear to be repeated by the intestate under the same condition, and not simply. And this is what the text says in l. si quis agere, in the word transducere; and in l. j. ff. de iure codicillorum, where it says that in that will it was written, etc. And this is more than manifest. And therefore, a fideicommissum left under this condition, if Titius shall be heir, is not due under the contrary condition, namely, if Titius shall not be heir.

But these objections do not stand. Although the testator says, if my heir shall die, this is understood to mean, if he whom I instituted as heir shall die; but it is not understood to mean, if he shall die after the inheritance has been accepted. Whether we speak of a fideicommissary substitution, because in speaking of a fideicommissary substitution the codicillary clause burdens, since the substitute is appointed by law, which does not [apply] in default of the instituted heir, as in the aforementioned § filiam, from which it is clearly concluded that the said wife, being substituted, has the right; or whether we say the case is called by a vulgar or by a fideicommissary substitution. For she has the choice between these substitutions, as in ff. ad Trebellianum, l. recusare, § Titius. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The Apostle, in one continuous context, asking earnestly, more earnestly, and most earnestly, whether it appears that he asked correctly.
1. Whether faith should be given to witnesses who said one thing outside of court, and another, or the contrary, in court.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Point. It is asked whether the petition of the apostolic letters, made often, more often, and insistently in the appeal, is to be considered a proper petition; and whether faith should be given to witnesses who testified one thing outside of court and another in court. Because the reading of the records clearly shows that at the time the appeal was interposed, the appeals were solemnly requested often, more often, and insistently. Although it follows manifestly from one context that, on account of the apostolic letters not having been requested, the said appeal cannot be said to be abandoned; but on this matter the juridical form must be observed, as in the chapter *Quamvis rigor* on appeals in the Clementines. And this is the first point.

I come to the second point, namely, if witnesses outside of court stated one thing, for example, that they did not see it, and in court, after being solemnly examined, stated the contrary, for example, that they saw it and were present, whether the solemn testimony would be derogated by the less solemn statement made outside of court and without oath. There are contrary opinions. For Bartolus says that such witnesses are presumed to have given false testimony in court, since they previously asserted the contrary. Hence it follows that these witnesses should not be believed, but should be punished for perjury; thus he says, D. de falsis, l. eos. But the ordinary gloss says the contrary, X. de testibus, c. cum causam. And this is the truth: because credence is given to what the witness solemnly deposes, not to what he deposes outside of court; because it carries no credibility, as in c. testibus, de testibus, in the Clementines. This is proven from the contrary sense, because the witness in court is compelled against his will to tell the true testimony, and under the bond of an oath, and for both parties, as D. de testibus, l. 1. And therefore the witness is not bound, nor should the party adhere to what he asserted outside of court. Moreover, even if in court, before the litis contestatio, he had not deposed solemnly, he could later depose the contrary solemnly, although in this case the witness would be very suspect, and perhaps not believed without torture, arg. D. de aedilicio edicto, l. quaero, §. si. From the foregoing it is concluded that the appeal is not deserted. Nevertheless, credence should be given to the said attesting witnesses, but by the judge of the appeal; unless another reason constrains the sentence, the sentence should be confirmed, as C. de appellationibus, l. eos. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether, and when, a partnership is deemed to have been contracted among brothers, or uncles and nephews living and working together, and profiting from the fruits or proceeds of their common labor, and whether profits and losses are to be divided among them.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† On the aforementioned points, it must be premised for clarity that when two brothers, or an uncle and nephews, or similar persons live together and in a communal manner, they sometimes acquire property solely through labor: for example, because each of them goes to work and receives wages therefrom, and then whatever they acquire, for instance by purchasing oxen, fields, or other goods with their salaries, is common to each of them, with each having a half share if there are two, or a third share if there are three, and so on for however many there are; for there is no distinction based on strength, since the division is always made per capita. However, if one acquires through labor while the other is not capable of working—for example, because a nephew is a small child and has no, or almost no, capacity for labor—then a partnership is not presumed, and everything belongs to the one who acquired it, as stated in the Digest, De administratione tutorum, l. Titium et Mevium, §. si altero. Sometimes they acquire something from common property, for example from the fruits of the patrimony, and then each acquires according to the quantity of patrimony he holds; he who has more in the patrimony acquires more, just as when one contributes one hundred to a partnership and another fifty: the one who contributes one hundred must have two parts, and the one who contributes fifty must have one-third part, unless the one with the smaller quantity makes up the difference through labor, for then he would acquire an equal share, as stated in the Digest, Pro socio, l. si non fuerint. Sometimes acquisition occurs jointly from both property and labor, as in the case of those who have oxen and perform agricultural labor. Then one-half share is attributed to the property, for example the oxen, and is acquired by each according to the rate he holds in the property; and the other half share is attributed to the labor, and this part is acquired by each according to his capacity, by the reasons of the aforementioned laws. And thus Bartolus advised.

It remains to declare concerning damage given by fortuitous event. I say that if they were partners in all things, such damage is common, even if it befalls only one of the partners: for example, if he is captured by enemies and ransoms himself. For he must be ransomed from the common fund, as stated in the Digest, Pro socio, l. cum duobus, §. finalis. However, if he paid on account of a wrongful act, or if they were not natural partners, then nothing of what was paid must be contributed, for there is no partnership in wrongful acts. Likewise, damage that befalls the person, not the partnership, nor on the occasion of the partnership, must not be shared; but if it occurred by reason of the partnership, because he was captured while working the common field, then it must be contributed, as stated in the Digest, Pro socio, l. socium, §. finalis, together with the following law.

It must be said concerning the fruits of dowries that if they have been shared and consumed on both sides, nothing can be reclaimed; but the dowry itself can well be reclaimed, and must be returned to him who received it, as the capital of the first husband and the wife, who was not a partner, as stated in the Digest, Pro socio, l. actione, §. finalis, and in the Digest, De minoribus, l. 3, §. sed utrum. And for this appears the response to all the questions formulated. As for the small children guarding the beasts, because they are of little value at that time, it suffices that they have food and clothing from the common fund in recompense, as stated in l. in rebus, §. 1, Digest, Commodati, unless some small wage were given to them for their works out of some discretion; and this would be well done. The houses and lands which were purchased by the uncle and the nephew belong to the uncle and the nephew, and the son of the uncle has no share in them, unless the son of the uncle had profited and contributed to the price of said things. However, the maintenance of the dowry of the son by the father is not owed to the nephew. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Laws, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether and when a judgment rendered against the seller prejudices the purchaser, or does not.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The mother donated certain goods to her son, reserving for herself the usufruct; finally, she assigned her rights against the said son in the said usufruct and in the fruits collected by the said son after the said donation. Ultimately, the said assignee sold the said usufruct. Cancellation was sought against the said donee, because the donation by the said mother could not have been made in accordance with the form of the statute.

† It is asked whether prejudice is caused to the aforementioned buyer. And it seems that it does, because when the right of the author is resolved, the right of the successor is resolved, as in D. de pignoribus, l. lex vectigalis. To the contrary, it seems that it does not, because a judgment rendered against the seller after the sale and delivery does not harm the ignorant buyer, nor does any proceeding conducted against the seller, as in D. de pignoribus, l. si superatus; and D. de re iudicata, l. saepe, §. sed scientibus. Solution: Saving always the substance of the truth, it seems to me that the said petition for cassation does not prejudice the said ignorant and uncited buyer; and the reason is that when the assignor assigns the right to another, no right remains with the assigning assignor, as in D. ad Senatusconsultum Trebellianum, l. ex asse. And therefore, an act done in court, even by the assignment of the same assignor selling his said rights, does not prejudice the buyer, since no right remained with the seller that could be annulled without citation, and with the buyer not present in court and ignorant. But if cassation had been sought against both, then, because the buyer could not avail himself of the aid of the seller, the title of both the seller and the buyer would be extinguished simultaneously, as in the aforementioned §. sed scientibus. Nor is it necessary here to discuss whether the fraud of the author causes harm or not, because we are here discussing whether the procedure of the case causes harm or not: not discussing fraud, which is treated in D. de exceptione doli, l. apud Celsum, §. de authoris; and §. si cum legitima; and D. de nova operis nuntiatio, l. doli mali. And it supports this D. de donationibus, l. ut mihi donares. Hence it is concluded that the said buyer is in possession notwithstanding the proceeding conducted against the seller. It supports what I note in Innocentius, Extravagantes, de regulis iuris, c. in causis. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Law and Canon.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a statute prohibiting the alienation of a thing acquired without certain solemnity outside the jurisdiction or territory also comprehends the acquirer himself and the alienating church.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. It must be presupposed that the great Charles, formerly Emperor, first converted the Saxon people to the Christian faith; there he established and ordained that possessions, things, and goods, which belong to anyone of whatever condition, devolve by right of hereditary succession without express consent, solely on account of the succeeding heirs, and cannot be alienated extrajudicially in whole or in part by any person outside the judgment of the lord under whose jurisdiction those goods are situated. And if it is done to the contrary, let it be void and null. And this was and is observed throughout all Saxony, and especially in the diocese of Verden and in a certain town, Lüneburg, because it is also a general custom legitimately prescribed, and from 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, and 60 years and more, as well as from time out of mind, of which contrary memory does not exist in man; and from the time of the aforementioned conversion of that people by Charles, it has been observed immutably and peacefully in those parts among both clerics and laymen. Now it happens that a certain Lord Nicholas, Bishop of Hildesheim, succeeded to certain saltworks in the town of Lüneburg by right of blood from the succession of his father. And these saltworks, which came to him without hereditary right, without the consent of the existing heirs of such goods, he gave extrajudicially, and not in the court of him under whose jurisdiction they are situated, namely the Duke of Lüneburg, but in his chamber, to the church and chapter of Hildesheim. It is asked whether the donation or alienation is valid.

† If there is doubt on this point, whether the said Master Nico. could, without judgment, i.e., without the will of the lord, alienate the said goods which had devolved upon him by hereditary right to a church situated outside the lord’s jurisdiction and outside his territory, I believe that he could not, because this prohibition is in rem. And when a thing is prohibited from being alienated on account of that thing itself, or a quality inherent in the thing, or on account of its location, the alienation to a church is prohibited just as it is to a private person, because it is affected, as in C. non lice. habi. metro. l. 1. and C. de agri. et cen. l. quemad. and ff. de leg. j. l. si quis inquilinos. and C. de iu. fis. l. certa forma. lib. 10. and in auth. de alie. et emphy. §. 1. and what is noted in ff. de verbo. ob. l. si ita quis. §. ea. Nor does it obstruct that churches are privileged in the case of donation, and therefore the said prohibition does not seem to be valid with respect to churches, as if it were the same to enact against privileges and to enact against liberty, as noted by Innocentius in c. norunt. de sen. exc. and the statute of the Emperor is not valid, nor is custom against the liberty of the church, nor over the rights and things of the church, as in extra, de consti. rationibus. ca. ecclesia. For this I answer that the Emperor can impose a statute on his own thing, and the same applies to custom. Moreover, this law is imposed with respect to alienation, to which he is subject who enacts it, and even whose person he can render incapable. For laws which speak that nothing can be enacted against the church have place assuming the capacity of persons, as noted in C. de sac. san. ecc. l. 1. and ff. de mune. et ho. l. si vt gradatim. §. sed si lege. And to this it contributes what is noted by Bartolus in ff. de mu. et ho. l. rescripto. §. fi. Furthermore, custom dictates even concerning clerics, and previously this custom dictated this before the cleric was a cleric. And therefore it bound and rendered incapable him who was to be a cleric, or prebendary. Hence, the statute must be observed, because it bound the subject at a time when it could do so for all time, and in whatever status, as in ff. de iu. do. l. promittendo. Moreover, general and real custom binds even clerics with respect to things which have come to them with their burden, as in C. de sa. san. ecc. l. placet. and l. iubemus nullam. It does not obstruct auth. cassa, et irrita. because that speaks when a special statute is made against clerics, which would contain something derogatory to them, or their privileges: otherwise, however, if a general statute were made, especially by the Emperor: because if the statute affects the thing, it also affects anyone, because in that thing he would succeed universally, since the thing cannot pass except with its cause, its vices, and real burdens, as in c. si tributum. and c. sine censu, vel reliquis. l. omnes.
