And therefore if there is doubt on this point, I say that this doubt is determined by custom, which must be observed: and by the decree of the Prince, to whom also more must be observed, because it is more powerful, as in C. de adop. l. 2. and ff. de offic. Praeto. l. Barbarius. in fi. Moreover, this custom is for the impetration of the imperial statute. And those things are not to be interpreted which have always had a certain interpretation, as in ff. de legibus. l. minime. Moreover, the church ought to be the guardian of justice, and it ought not to desire those things which are against the nature of things: as is clear in fiefs, and in fi. col. de aliena. fen. c. si clientulus. Hence, the church is bound to observe the common law of the country, just as it is bound to observe the law disposing that a minor of 14 years cannot make a will, although malice supplies for age in him. And just as it is bound to observe the law which says that an adult cannot alienate his goods without a decree. And these are especially true, because, as has been said, that was a decree of the Emperor: because in things of his jurisdiction he has the fullness of power, as is clear from what is read, and noted in 8. dist. c. quo iure. These are true, if it is a person wishing to revoke; otherwise the alienation holds, C. de fideic. l. quotiens. de leg. 2. l. cum pater. §. libertis. And it contributes extra, de in integ. rest. l. contest. and C. de contrah. emp. c. dudum. But if another point is asked of me: then I will answer, when I have been certified of that about which it is asked. And I submit this my response in civil matters to one who understands better, and especially to Master Anselmo, father of both laws, and an excellent and singular doctor, my lord. And thus I say, and I advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Laws, and c.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A compendious substitution made to a minor by means of a general term, without an express division of time periods, is valid at all times as a fideicommissary substitution. See also nos. 5 and 7.
2. The phrase "if, however" repeats the quality of the preceding disposition.
3. What are called direct words.
4. Whether a tacit substitution excludes the mother, when the deceased so intended, or this can be inferred.
5. In a universal fideicommissum, only the father's inheritance comes, not that of the son.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Having set forth the words of the will, because the testator, in making his will, instituted the womb of Lady Sabatolla as universal heir, on condition that she bear a male child: but if she does not bear one, or if the child does not come to light, then he instituted his brothers as universal heirs. But if the child comes to light and dies without issue, it is provided that the said brothers of the said testator succeed in the said inheritance. The son was born and died while still an infant, with the mother surviving. The question is whether this substitution excludes the mother.

The question arises whether the aforementioned compendious substitution, made by the universal word "at all times," is valid as a fideicommissary substitution. The gloss, which is found in the Institutes, *de pupillari substitutione*, § *qua ratione*, states that it is valid as a pupillary substitution during pupillary age; afterwards, it is valid as a fideicommissary substitution. And the same was advised by Lord Dy., as I noted in *l. precibus*. And the same was noted by Lo. An. disputing in the Novella in *c. si pater*, *de testamentis*, Book 6. And according to this, those distinctive words are not necessary, namely, "that he was in pupillary age, or afterwards at any time"; but they are added superfluously, because where the testator does not distinguish times, nevertheless the law distinguishes. And this opinion is confirmed in our case, because the word "succeed" can be direct and oblique, i.e., through an intermediate person. For it comprehends every succession of law, both of heirs, and of possessors of goods, and of universal fideicommissaries, as in the Digest, *de edendo*, *l. quaedam*, § *his autem*. For the substitute by fideicommissum is said to be instituted precariously, as in the Digest, *de militum testamento*, *l. quaerebatur*. However, in the stronger meaning, which is direct, it is signified. It seems that the words should be taken, because a doubtful substitution is interpreted as direct, as noted in the Digest, *de vulgaribus substitutionibus*, *l. verbis civilibus*. And in judgment we must understand direct law, as noted in the Digest, *si ager vectigalis vel emphyteuticus*, *l. 1*, § *qui in perpetuum*. Moreover, it is not surprising if the distinction of times induces a division of the will, as in the Digest, *de conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, *l. pater seuerinam*, § *conditionum*.

† Moreover, this is the function of the adversative conjunction *si vero* [if, however], which appears to repeat the quality of the preceding disposition in an adversative case, in those instances where no opposition is found, as noted by Bartolus in the Digest, Title 3, Law *In repetendis*.

† Moreover, direct words are those which are directed from the instituted heir to the substitute, and without the interposition of another person, as is noted in C. de fideicommissis, l. eam quam. But it is not so here, because the words state that he shall succeed to him, as in ff. de secundis tabulis, l. si ita, §. qui filio; and as noted in ff. de vulgari substitutione, l. 2, §. 1, in the gloss: "this condition," whether the word "my" refers to the testator or to the ward. Likewise, those words, "in the said inheritance," seem to manifestly signify this, because an inheritance is a certain integrity of the whole right which the deceased had, as in ff. de hereditatibus instituendis, l. si quis heres institutus fuerit excepto fundo; and in ff. de verborum significatione, l. nihil aliud. Nor does it admit of division, so that one might be heir by direct right in part, and not in part, as is noted in ff. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. servus communis ab extero.

† From these reasons and authorities, therefore, it is clearly concluded that the mother is to be excluded and the brothers are to succeed as pupillary substitutes. This is especially so for the reason that the testator considered his wife and honored her in a certain manner, from which it now appears that he has satisfied his obligation, so that she should not receive anything beyond the legacies. See the argument in the Digest, *De negotiorum gestione*, law *Qui aliena*, section *Liber*; and in the Digest, *Ad Senatusconsultum Trebellianum*, law *Lucius*, section *Quæ habebat*. And it is certain that even a tacit substitution excludes the mother, when the deceased so intended, or when this can be gathered from manifest indications, as is read and noted in the aforementioned law *Precibus*, in the gloss beginning *Imo ex tacita pupillari*. For the father has this authority, that he may exclude the mother, even against due piety, on account of the subtlety of the law, which consists in this: that the entire testament is that of the father, and therefore it cannot be overturned by the wife. See the Digest, *De inofficioso testamento*, law *Papinianus*, section *Sed nec impuberis*. And this subtlety of civil law is approved by the aforementioned Code law *Si pater*.

† To the contrary it seems, because the common opinion is that of almost all doctors, that a compendious substitution made without distribution or distinction of times is at all times fideicommissary: because where the testator does not distinguish, neither should we distinguish, as the noted glossa ordinaria in l. precibus, in I. Centurio, ff. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione; because since it is made under one conflict of words, and is formed by one common word for all time, we should not introduce a division of the will, arg. ff. de his qui ut indigni amittunt, l. cum qui, §. pro parte. Nor should it be judged by different law, since it must be made at any age of the son existing. And thus the objection from l. pater Severinam, §. conditionum, does not hold, because error cannot be left at any age. And therefore the excess of age changes the interpretation of the will, so that the will may be valid and not perish. Moreover, whenever one determination regards several determinable things, it ought to determine them equally, as ff. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione, l. iam hoc iure, and l. Lucius, and C. de impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus, l. quamvis, and l. haeredi. But here one word, "if he succeeds," determines several determinable things and several times: therefore it ought to determine them univocally, because under one word one sense is contained: so that the predication of this word ought to be uniform, and not difform, as noted extra, de testamentis, ca. Raynaldus. Moreover, here the mother is in the middle, hence so that the mother may not be excluded from the burdensome inheritance of the son against natural equity, this substitution ought to be interpreted as oblique, and not direct, as noted C. de institutione et substitutione, l. penultima. Moreover, this seems to be proved by living reason, because if it once assumed the direct interpretation as such, it would also dispose, if after the pupillary age it were valid by no law, as noted in d. l. verbis civilibus. But the consequent is false, therefore also the antecedent. Moreover, this opinion is approved by usage, for therefore the distinction of times is added in wills, so that more substitutions may be made, otherwise that practice would have been introduced in vain: which is absurd to say, since it was invented and approved by all wise men of the law. Moreover, the law seems expressed in the text, because by law it is provided that whenever the father substitutes, if the son is not born, therefore the testator added this condition, lest he exclude the mother from the burdensome inheritance of the son, as d. l. fin. de institutione et substitutione.

And if it is said that the testator here went too far by excluding the mother, even after the birth of the son, I answer that this is by no means true. Although the testator said nothing concerning the son’s inheritance, he spoke only of his own, which alone falls under the universal fideicommissum, as is shown in D. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione, l. Cohaereditate, § Cum filiae, and in C. de inofficioso testamento, l. Ex tribus. But against the mother strongly weighs the statement in c. Si pater, where it is expressly stated that a second substitution made in favor of outsiders and directed to the son during his pupillary age must be understood as pupillary, if it accords with the words and the persons, and that it excludes the mother. But to this it is answered that either we consider the words of the substitution there, and these are indeed direct, because they are made in civil terms, as appears in the word “instituendo” (instituting), whose proper meaning is direct, as in D. de hereditate instituenda, l. His verbis, and throughout. If, however, we consider the reason, namely that it accords with the words and the persons, I answer that the words are altogether common and accord no more with a direct substitution than with a fideicommissary one.

† I have often advised that words simply uttered without distinction of time import a fideicommissary substitution, adhering at all times to one opinion of the doctors: especially where the mother is in the middle. And in our case, at least, it seems this ought to be said by equity, because the mother is in the middle. Hence, in doubt, the father’s authority ought not to be drawn to inequity by totally excluding the mother. Nevertheless, I doubt much on this point on account of the reasons made to the contrary, which, by the strictness of the law, seem to conclude to the opposite, on account of three words, namely: “succeed”; on account of the word “to him”; and on account of the word “in the inheritance.” And because this second substitution is directly joined by an adversative conjunction, hence, by the strictness of the law, the mother would seem to be excluded, unless we say that these subtleties are not admitted against the mother, lest we incur the greatest inequity, because under the authority of legal subtlety natural equity ought not to be removed, as in D. de verb. sign. l. si seruum, §. sequitur. This question is so doubtful that it is not surprising if the doctors vary in it. Nevertheless, I do not think it well safe to depart from the common opinion of the glosses. Notwithstanding the gloss in the said §. qua ratione, yet because other glosses say the contrary everywhere, the interpretation of that gloss ought not to have place where the mother is in the middle. On this point, my beloved colleague, Lord Angelus Marcinelli of Teramo, also wrote at length and very solemnly. And because there are as many minds as heads, the foot cannot be firmly placed on one opinion only. For piety speaks for the mother, but the quality of the substitutes speaks for the substitutes, who were the brothers of the deceased, as noted in D. de vulg. subst. l. Lucius. This question, as I said, I consider doubtful, and I do not determine otherwise, because to determine against the mother seems to me inequitable; and to determine against the brothers seems to me contrary to many reasons, although many reasons also speak for the mother, as assigned above, which the aforementioned Lord Angelus can add to his opinion: because they are difficult to solve, and perhaps even truer in law. Consider the favor of the mother, for who does not diminish himself for her on account of the danger of childbirth for the creation of her children, as in C. qui pot. in pigno. hab. l. assiduis, §. hic omnia, etc. I, Baldus of Perugia, wrote the above, under the seal of my name, and I advise, according to the gloss of l. precibus, that a compendious substitution simply made with common words is fideicommissary at all times; nevertheless, I doubt in our question, and I decide nothing on account of those added words, which make the question difficult.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A statute providing that if any woman was endowed by her grandfather, she may not revert to the succession of the endower or of any descendant of his, so long as any male descendant of the same endower survives; how this is to be understood and how it is interpreted by custom.
2. The common usage of language in testaments is to be given the greatest consideration.
3. Given the statute mentioned above, whether a grandfather who died before his granddaughter was conceived is properly called a grandfather.
4. Whether grandchildren conceived after the death of the grandfather fall under the appellation of grandsons or granddaughters; and what applies in emphyteusis; and no. 6.
5. The term "properly" and the number of ways it is to be understood.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The statute provides that if a woman has been endowed by her grandfather, she may not revert to the succession of the endower or of any descendant of his, as long as any male descendant of the same endowing person through the male line survives. This statute is interpreted according to general custom, even in the case of a woman who is endowed by will, regardless of her age, so that the participle “endowed” is understood to include also the testator’s designation. Hence, custom approves the opinion of Master Bartolus, which he sets forth in l. cum plures, §. cum lator, D. de administratione tutorum, where he also explains this point with regard to the word “father,” when he says, “or the father had assigned in his will, from which she was to be endowed.” For a woman is said to be endowed, however she may be endowed, whether by will, by promise, or by delivery, as in D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Titio centum, §. Titio genero; C. de legatis, l. filia legatorum; D. de legatis primo, l. huiusmodi, §. cum pater; D. de solutionibus et mutationibus, l. si cum dotem, §. si pater; and D. de in rem verso, l. ad nihil. Moreover, common usage of speech is such that one says, “this girl has a large dowry,” even though the girl is not yet married.

† In wills, the most common usage of language is examined, as stated in the Digest, *de legatis tertio*, in the law *librorum*, § *quod tamen Cassius*. For from the common usage of language, the intent is understood, as in the Digest, *de suppleto legato*, in law 3, at the end, and in the law *Labeo*, § *item Tubero*. Moreover, a dowry can be bequeathed even to a ward under guardianship, as in the Digest, *ubi pupillus educari debeat*, in the law *qui filium*; and in the Digest, *de alio legato*, in the law *cum vnus*, § *alimen*. The case is thus formulated: a certain grandfather, having male children, instituted them as heirs, and if any of them should die leaving male children, he wished that his share should pass to the males. But if he died leaving females, he provided them with a dowry of one hundred, and in his other goods he substituted the brothers of such deceased person, and the children of the testator. Finally, it happened that the testator died, and after his death, one of his sons took a wife, and from that very marriage, a daughter was born, and this son died. Now, this girl claims that she succeeds to her father’s goods, and consequently to her grandfather’s goods, since the goods are united by succession, as in the Digest, *de vulgari substitutione*, in the law *sed si plures*, § *fin.*, and noted in the Digest, *de separatione bonorum*, in law 1, § *praeterea sciendum*. But on the contrary, it is said that she does not succeed to the grandfather who provided the dowry, nor to her father, notwithstanding the said statute.

† Now the question arises, what is the law? And it seems to be said that the aforementioned girl succeeds, because the words of a statute that most disposes against the common law ought to be understood properly and strictly, as in D. de negotiorum gestione, l. 3, § haec verba. For in case of doubt, one should not depart from the primary meaning of the words, as in D. de legibus 3, l. non aliter, and D. de supellectili legato, l. Labeo, § idem Tubero. But a grandfather is not properly called he who died before the granddaughter was conceived in the womb; even if we are dealing with succession to be obtained, which is a favorable matter, let alone with its removal, which is an odious matter, as in l. maximum vitium. This is proven in D. de in ius vocando, l. si quis filia, § 1, vers.

† But this is so. For grandchildren who are conceived after the death of their grandfather are not properly, but improperly, called grandchildren, as in D. de suis et legitimis heredibus, l. Item Praetor. For they are not such, as in l. Titius, eodem titulo, because no one who is dead can begin to be a grandfather, arg. D. de operis libertatis, l. Qui libertinus, §. Posthumus, there: “nor can anyone, etc.” To the contrary, it seems. And I premise for clarity that, according to the subject matter at hand,

† Sometimes something is said properly, which according to another matter is said improperly, as in no. ff. de off. procon. in l. 2. in the gloss on this word. And there are set forth concordances, as appears in ff. de condit. et de. l. pater seuerinam. §. conditionum.

† Hence, if anyone receives an emphyteusis or a fief for himself, his sons, and his grandchildren, these words properly and truly include grandchildren conceived after the death of the grandfather, as in the Authentica *de non alienando*, § *emphyteusim*; and in the first Collatio, law *Titio*, 1, § *cum vero*, where Coradus holds the same view; and Bartolus in the said law *Titio*. For in indifferent matters, such distinctions regarding conception are not considered; but only in matters where the grandchild wishes to succeed by reason of proximity. And to the point raised in the law and noted in the Digest *de senatoribus*, law *emancipatus*, § *si*. Furthermore, as to nature, it is certain that the grandchild is from the root of the grandfather, because the flesh of the son is the flesh of the father, and similarly in all things which derive therefrom in the order of birth. Hence, the generation of the grandchild is from the genus of the grandfather, and nothing else could naturally result, just as seed from seed, and a stream from a spring, as in the Digest *de verbis significandis*, law *pronuntiatio*, § *item appellatur*. Moreover, the reason of the statute and custom must be weighed, as the text notes in the Code *quae sit longa consuetudo*, law 1, where it says that the reason which is established by custom ought to be preserved. But what is the reason of the statute, if not the favor of preserving families, which are preserved through males and not through females, as in the Digest *de ventre in utero*, law 1, § *publici*, where it says that the dignity of families may be preserved; and fully noted by Cynus in the Code *de adulteriis*, law *publico*. Moreover, where the reason is stronger, the statute ought to have greater force, as in the Authentica *de consanguineis et uterinis fratribus*. But the stronger reason is to exclude from the grandfather’s goods those not conceived at the time of the grandfather’s death, rather than those conceived during the grandfather’s life. Hence, laws disposing exclusively rather exclude, as in the said law *item Praetor*. Therefore, since we are not here in a matter of exclusive disposition, the said granddaughter ought to be excluded from the grandfather’s goods, much more strongly than if she had been conceived during his life; otherwise, two absurdities would follow. The first is that one conceived during his life would be treated as conceived after his death, which is absurd, as in the Digest *de testamento militis*, law *si filius familias*; for more right ought to belong to one who is acknowledged than to one who is not acknowledged. The second absurdity, evident and intolerable, would follow in such an example. Suppose that the grandfather provided a dowry in his will for a granddaughter to be born, said nothing about a male grandchild, and finally the grandfather died first; then the son took a wife and had a male and a female child; upon these facts, he died intestate. For if the statute is not understood to dispose in this case, would the said granddaughter and grandchild succeed together? And would the posthumous child, already born or conceived during the grandfather’s life, have more? This is contrary to reason, contrary to the authority of the statute, and contrary to the truth of the law. To this point contributes, in its own reasoning, the Code *de liberis praeteritis*, law *maximum vitium*, § *cum etiam*, where it says “and with what injury is it worthy,” etc. And even if this posthumous child were not excluded from her father’s goods, she ought certainly to be excluded from the grandfather’s goods and be content with the dowry, because she was provided a dowry by the grandfather. Nor is it new that sometimes a separation of goods is made, as in the Digest *de separatione bonorum*, law 1. In conclusion, I say that this granddaughter, conceived after the grandfather’s death, ought to be content with the quantity left to her for a dowry, which succeeds in place of the legitime due to her from the person of her father in the grandfather’s goods, as noted in the Code *de nuptiis*, law *sacrosanctum*; and it is proven in the Code *ad legem Iuliam maiestatis*, law *quisquis*, § *ad filias*. And thus I opine on this point. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If one of three brothers living together and sharing a common household dies, leaving behind a son, whether this son ought to receive a proportional share along with his uncles; and if he has been captured by enemies, whether he ought to be ransomed from the common fund.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The point is as follows: there were three brothers and one nephew from the elder brother, aged 14. It is asked whether the said nephew, who was captured by the enemy and ransomed, ought to have [his ransom] paid from the common fund, since at that time he was living together with the said uncles.

† The aforementioned Matthew ought to have his share of the profits jointly acquired, since he was over fourteen years of age, as is stated in the Codex, *De bonis quae liberi*, in the law *Cum oportet*. And the redemption ought to be jointly excommunicated, as is stated in the Digest, *Pro socio*, in the law *Socium*, in the section *Qui in eo*, § *Si*, together with the following law. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, most learned doctor and canonist.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Having the power and discretion from the common statute to act against homicides and other brawls and wounding, whether they can impose penalties on such persons who have not submitted themselves to their authority or have not paid the condemnation.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Arbitration was granted to certain persons to provide for whatever they should deem expedient, whether or not they wished, concerning and for the prosecution and capture, offense, penalties, and common damages, and punishments of whosoever should commit homicide, or wound, or wounds: and concerning and regarding the aggravation, and, or increase, and imposition, and ordination of any penalties, and any offenses, and of those delinquents themselves, concerning and for the prosecution and offense of any condemned and exiled persons of the commune of Florence. And concerning the aggravation and increase of penalties excepting them, or any of them, and concerning the granting of monetary rewards and privileges of arms to all and each offending or capturing exiles, and to ordain and impose any penalties, as and how it should seem to them concerning and for and regarding the aforesaid, and their observance, execution, effect, and efficacy, so that evils and offenses might be provided for, disposed of, and ordained, as and whenever it should seem to them. By the force of which arbitration it was provided that if any person of the contado should offend a citizen, he be punished with double the penalty, and that his associates be held as malefactors, unless they have represented such malefactor to the Podesta, or have paid the condemnation.

† It is now asked whether, by virtue of the said arbitration, the aforementioned legislators could proceed against the said accomplices. And it seems that they could not, because the beginning of the law granting the arbitration expressly provides that the said arbitration is granted against those committing homicide, or a wound, or wounds. But these accomplices do not commit homicide, nor a wound, or wounds; therefore, the arbitration was not granted against them: because arbitration is a certain genus granted to a person, and since it is of strict law, it should not be extended. For the limits of arbitration are to be carefully observed, as is common in law. But this is proven, because by such arbitration that which is likely not to have been enacted by those who conferred the arbitration does not seem to be granted, as in D. quae credi. l. si pater; and D. ad Mu. l. Lucius, §. si; and D. man. l. creditor, §. Luc. But it is unjust that the innocent be punished for the guilty, as in C. de poen. l. sancimus. And those things which are unjust do not seem to be included in the grant: because such a grant must be understood according to the judgment of a good and innocent man. But a good man would not have enacted this. And C. ne uxor pro marito, throughout; and C. ne filius pro patre, throughout. Moreover, it is against natural reason that he who has not offended be punished. And natural reason, just as civil reason, indeed more strongly, because civil reason restricts the arbitration of power, even absolutely, as in D. de admi. tu. l. impuberi filio Centurio; and D. de test. mili. l. in fraudem. Moreover, statutes receive an interpretation avoiding absurdity, and penalties are to be understood as applying to the guilty, as in legi. and no. C. de noxa. l. si serui nostri. Moreover, even if the said provision were valid, it ought to be restricted to accomplices having the power to apprehend, or to pay the condemnation. Hence, those who cannot apprehend, or pay the condemnation due to poverty, or because the condemnation is personal, are excused, as in l. vt D. rui. et nau. And much more are the ignorant excused, because the text says that we wish knowledge, not ignorance, to be bound, as in C. de tabu. l. generali. Moreover, the beginning of the law seems to declare the whole law, as in D. de iu. et fac. igno. l. reguli, §. si. But the beginning of the law speaks of offenders; therefore, etc. Arg. D. solu. ma. l. si vero, §. de viro, with its similar cases.

On the contrary, it seems that those having arbitration can enact good law, although not equitable, for under the definition of law both are contained, and the one and the other, as noted in l. 1, in princ. D. de iu. et iure. But this statute is good, although it is not equitable: for accomplices ought to correct their relatives. And if the offense demands greater severity, the offenders ought to be handed over to the judges, as in C. de emenda. propinquorum. l. 1. It is very likely that accomplices can prevent the bad morals of others; and if they do not prevent it, a penalty can be imposed on them, for this severity tends to this end, that accomplices strive to prevent the younger from offending, and stand ready to prohibit their offenses, as in Specu. Arg. C. de priua. l. 1; and C. ad l. Iul. de vi. l. antep. And this can be done by statute, as noted in C. de deci. in rub. Moreover, in the city of Florence it is customary to do so in many other similar cases; therefore, this is understood to be tacitly granted. Arg. D. de pigno. act. l. vel vniuersorum; and D. quod cum eo. l. Titia. Furthermore, a general arbitration includes all things, as in D. de ver. ob. l. qui Romae, §. Calimacus, at the end, except fraud, which is not included in the arbitration, as in C. man. l. creditor, §. Lucius. Furthermore, the text of the arbitration first sets forth the species, when it says "of whosoever committing," etc.; secondly, it follows with the genus, when it says "on the imposition and ordering of any penalties." And the genus after the species increases, although if placed before the species it is restricted by the subsequent species, if the species is of the same genus, as in D. de penu. leg. l. si; and l. nam quod liquidem, §. si cui; and D. de vino, et oleo lega. l. si, §. cui dulcia. Furthermore, this is evidently gathered from a certain conjunction, which is extensive, as in D. de lega. 3. l. ea tamen adiectione, and from the word "of which," which is implicative. And this when it says "and with those of the offenders." Hence, those who do not offend principally, but are deemed so by patience or ignorance, such as accomplices given power, and this seems pleasing. And this is confirmed by those words "of, and on, and for the prosecution," etc. For this penalty, which is imposed, tends to this end. Hence, all things seem to be granted by which the end is achieved, as in D. de iurisd. omn. iud. l. 2. And just as a reward can be given by the said statute to any captivities, so it seems regarding the penalty. But those who can likely apprehend and do not apprehend, arg. C. de malefi. et Mathema. l. si. Moreover, sometimes the whole household is placed for the offense of one, as in C. si quacunque praedi. potestat. lib. 1. And although one can appeal from the iniquity of the law, as in l. 1, arg. D. de excep. doli, nevertheless this law does not seem iniquitous, since the public good is considered, D. de publi. l. licitatio, §. in licite.

Solution: I say that if such statutes have been accustomed to be made in other similar cases, that in the aforementioned case the power to enact such seems to be granted, although the contrary is more true in law, because where one can apprehend or offend another as a private person, he is nevertheless not punished if he does not apprehend or does not offend, as noted in C. quod me. cau. l. actionis. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a statute excluding a daughter from her father’s succession is to be understood as applying generally even with regard to the legitime, or to something in its place, such as a dowry and maintenance; and whether it is favorable.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. In the Year of Our Lord 1388, etc., begins the book of opinions of the most eminent doctor of both laws, Lord Baldus of Perugia. That dowried daughters are to be content and cannot have recourse to paternal goods. Heading. That a daughter, or daughters, are to be content with the dowry given to them by their father, mother, or carnal brother, grandfather, or grandmother, and cannot, upon the death of the father, or mother, grandfather, or grandmother, while the brother, or brothers, or their children are living, have recourse to the paternal or maternal goods of the grandfather or grandmother, nor claim anything on the occasion of the inheritance of any of the said persons, or for any other reason, whether they have renounced or not; and if anyone should die leaving only several daughters or granddaughters, each shall succeed equally. But if any of them, or some of them, have been married, they shall acquire from the succession only to the extent of the quantity of their dowry; furthermore, if the father, or mother, grandfather, or grandmother have given anything to the said daughters or granddaughters beyond the dowry, they cannot claim anything beyond that on the occasion of the legitime, or for any other reason, while male brothers, or uncles, or their children are living. Concerning sons and daughters remaining together when the father dies intestate. Heading 54. And so forth. When the father dies intestate, making no disposition whatsoever of his goods, and leaves sons together with daughters, the brothers are bound to provide the sisters with a suitable dowry, having regard to the quality of the persons and the condition of the patrimony. The declaration of what constitutes a suitable dowry shall be made, and the declaration of two of the nearest blood relatives of the said sister, or girl under 15 years of age from the time of her birth, shall be adhered to. But if the father has left anything for their dowry, they shall be content with what is left, and in neither case can they, as successors, have further recourse to the paternal or maternal goods; but the male sons shall be universal heirs in the paternal and maternal goods. But if it should happen that any of the said brothers is absent, he shall ratify the house established by the other brothers, nor shall he adhere to the constitution of the dowry made by the brothers; but the woman shall have recourse against the absent brother for the portion of the dowry due to her. But if any of the daughters was under the age of 11 years at the time of the father’s death, within two or three years the brothers are bound to marry her; otherwise she may marry herself, even if the brothers are ignorant or unwilling, since they are under the necessity of providing them with dowries, as is expressed above. Point of the question. And so forth. A certain Lord Gregory died intestate, leaving two children, namely a male named Jacob, and a female named Aluma. This Aluma married, having been given 300 pounds in dowry by her mother, without any renunciation of the goods being made. Afterwards, this Aluma, the daughter, dies, leaving one son named Carbono, and with her said brother Jacob surviving. Afterwards, the said Jacob dies, leaving his three children, namely Christopher and John, males, whom he instituted as his heirs, and another named Alumella, a female daughter. Finally, the aforementioned Christopher and John, male sons of the said Jacob, son of the late said Lord Gregory, die, leaving, namely, Nicholas, son of one of them, whom Nicholas the said Christopher and John instituted as their heir, and to whom Nicholas they substituted the said Alumella, sister of the said Christopher and John, and aunt of the said Nicholas. Last of all, the said Nicholas, nephew of the said Alumella, dies, and Alumella claims that she ought to succeed by virtue of the said substitution made to her by the said Christopher and by the said John, her brothers, in all the goods and the entire patrimony of the late said Lord Gregory. On the other side arises the said Carbono, son of the late Lady Aluma, daughter of the late Lord Gregory, claiming that he ought to be admitted, in the person of his mother Aluma, to the goods of his maternal grandfather Gregory, who died intestate, etc. It is asked, what is the law, having regard to the statutes noted above, etc.

† A statute that totally excludes a daughter from her father’s goods, because it is inequitable and contrary to natural law, is considered most odious, as noted by Dynus in c. Indultum. Nor should it properly be called a favor simpliciter, but an inequitable favor, which ought to be restricted and not extended, as in c. Odia. But if a woman is not excluded simpliciter, but in consideration of a dowry given or to be given, this statute is not called inequitable, because the dowry succeeds in place of maintenance. Hence she has her legitime fixed for her in the dowry, because the legitime can be reduced by statute, C. de nuptiis, l. Sancimus. According to Cynus, from maintenance, therefore the legitime cannot be excluded by statute, without her having to receive from the paternal estate either something else or its equivalent: namely, a dowry. The understanding of a statute ought not to be referred to an impossible interpretation, ff. de verbis oblig., l. Continuus; §. Cum quis sub hac, ff. de legatis 1, l. Apud Iulium, §. Finalis. And therefore the statute seems to be understood as applying to one who was dowered and received something, or is to be dowered from his goods. Succession is dealt with by soundly examining the understanding, which is declared by another statute concerning sons and daughters, and c. Cum ergo. These maintenance rights of Lord Gregory, insofar as she was dowered from the paternal goods, ceased in her case of exclusion. Therefore also the exclusion, ff. de inofficioso testamento, l. Si instituta. Therefore, according to common law, she transmitted her portion, ff. de stipulationibus servorum, l. Liber homo, §. Finalis. This is noted by Cynus, C. de bonis quae liberis, l. Non sive. But if she had been dowered from the father’s patrimony, Carbonus would have no right: because succession transferred to males, and Aluma having died in the meantime, it perpetually endures in the successors of the males, C. de donationibus, l. Si ania. And what is noted by Cynus, de adulteriis, l. Publico. But if the daughter had survived after all the males, with one woman remaining from that line, considering the reason of the statute according to the petition of the prudent, a woman further in degree would not be of better succession than the daughter, C. de bonis matri, l. Si viva matre. And the thing would return to its nature, C. de pactis, l. Si unus, §. Pactus, ver. Quid et in spe dotis. And although by the name of children are comprehended nephews and great-nephews through a daughter, C. de conditionibus insertis, l. 1, nevertheless I say that by the name of children are not comprehended women, nor those descending through a woman: because the testator says, “to his children.” For it is of the nature of conjunction to join equals in speech, C. de servis fugitivis, l. Si fugitivi, and l. 1, de rebus dubiis. But in no way are they similar in exclusive favor, male, female. And the law speaks of the male, unless the female excludes from the person of the male, who would have excluded the female perfectly, and not suspensively. And it ought to be understood thus what Bartolus notes in l. Aequissimum, ff. ad Tertullianam. And thus I say, and I counsel, I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Both Laws, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A surety may bind himself before the principal debtor, and also after; but a guarantor (constitutor) may not do so after.
2. On the ground of the contract, when a person cannot be sued.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. First, it must be said concerning the substance of the obligation; second, concerning the judgment and the forum. And regarding the first, a twofold obligation is to be considered, namely, of loan and of service, and in the matter of arms.

† As regards the loan for consumption (mutuum), there is no doubt that a surety (fideiussor) and a promisor by constitution (constitutor) can bind themselves. A surety can bind himself before the principal debtor and after him, as stated in the Digest, Title "On Suretyship," Law "If one has stipulated," Section "To employ." However, a surety cannot be bound by letters between absent parties, because a stipulation is required, as in the Digest, Title "On Verbal Obligations," Law 5, Section "Satisfactory acceptance," and in the Code, Title "On Suretyship," Law "Blanditus." But a promisor by constitution cannot bind himself before the principal debtor has promised, as in Law "Moreover, that," Section "What is added," Title "On Constitutions of Peculium." A stipulation is not required, for a bare pact suffices, as in the Institutes, Title "On Actions," Section "On Constituted Peculium." Therefore, if anyone says that Master Francis is bound, or says that he is bound to three hundred as a surety, he does not state the truth in law, because a stipulation could not intervene between absent parties. Or if he says as a promisor by constitution, it seems impossible, because the promise of the principal debtor did not precede. It is certainly true that among men-at-arms one should not dispute on the technicalities of law, considering common equity; but on the subtlety of law, the said allegation proceeds well for Master Francis. The obligation made must also be considered, to which Master Francis seems to have referred, namely that phrase "de la fede" (of the faith). And then the promise is not valid, because he promised another's act, as is fully noted in the Digest, Title "On Suretyship," Law "If anyone for him," in the principle. For the sense is, namely, that he will be faithful in the promise, but what was promised was an act and not a giving. And strictly, and the law proceeding through the technicalities of law, it is thus equitable; nevertheless, let it remain in its place.

But that the master was bound, because whether he could be sued in Perugia. And it seems to be said that not, because on this contract the tax was not paid according to the form of the statutes of the community of Perugia. Also this contract does not seem to have been celebrated in Perugia as to the execution of the contract, but outside the community of Perugia, where he had promised to serve. And therefore in Perugia the master cannot be sued, since he is a foreigner, ff. de solu. l. quaero. and there by Bartolus, ff. de fideius. l. si vt proponitur. ff. de ac. et ob. l. contraxisse. The master also has the privilege of foreigners, per Auth. habita. and the benefit of cession, if other remedies failed, ff. de solu. l. Stichum. §. si marito. Another thing is also to be weighed: because it does not appear that the letters of the master were sent by messenger, nor examined, nor accepted, of which it is necessary to make proof, ff. de acqui. pos. l. qui absenti. de ac. et obli. l. consensu. and l. sicut. Hence many reasons make for the master. And especially, because he believed to promise only to keep faith by serving, and he could not promise another's act. And because excussion must be made, if he is sued, where it is said that he is rich, and has very many goods, as in Auth. praesente. de fideius. And therefore from the subtlety of law it seems to me to Baldus, and under seal.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a procurator can cause his principal to incur a penalty.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The matter on which counsel is requested is as follows. It is provided by the statute of the land of Meschia that against the sentence of arbitrators one may not speak or plead of nullity, nor appeal, nor petition that it be referred to the arbitration of a good man, under penalty of one hundred pounds to be taken away from the fact. Now a certain person named Bartholomew of Nursia, in the procuratorial name of Nutius Peter of the well-known district of Nursia, having a general mandate in which were these things, produced before the judge of the podestà of the land of Nursia a certain sentence of arbitrators, and the arbitrators oppose against the said sentence on the ground of nullity.

† Now it is asked whether a penalty can be exacted by law, and if so, from whom, or from no one, etc. If the procurator is appointed so specifically that it appears he is appointed against a certain person and for a certain cause.

† And it must be added concerning that case of nullity, with the penal article expressly stated, when it is said that he has a special mandate: and this causes the principal to incur the penalty. But if no penal case is expressed, then it does not cause the principal to incur the penalty, D. quod quisque iur. l. 3. §. si procu. For a mandate is never extended to prohibited and penal matters, unless it is expressed in the mandate, as in D. si pater. quae in fraud. credi. and note, per Guillaume in D. et si quia. §. quaesitus. si quis cau. And therefore, because there are many nullities, some penal and some not penal, it is not said that he has a special mandate, unless the penal aspect is expressed by itself, or by reference to another matter: for example, in a case which he has with such a person concerning nullity, and he has nothing else except the nullity of the award, arg. D. de libe. et posthu. l. nominatim. and in C. 2. de procu. nisi talis. Then he has a special mandate; otherwise, it does not seem to refer to a prohibited and penal act. This point was proposed to me, and I have otherwise advised the same as now. But the point was not the same in this respect, because in that case it was said that he had a special mandate. And truly, understanding what a special mandate is, there is no doubt that it causes the principal to incur the penalty; otherwise not: unless the principal has ratified it, as in C. de coartalibus. l. si apparitorum. lib. 12. And therefore I said otherwise according to those things which were then proposed in the facts, as answered. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If the Prince granted in fief, and by reason of a donation, a certain income from a certain land, and afterwards the same Prince, for the redemption of himself, grants that land free and clear, etc., from all grants, does it seem that the fief is revoked? and whether he can, and no. 7.
2. The word, above, what it imports.
3. The statutes of the Duke of Genoa have the force of laws, because they do not recognize a superior.
4. A privilege is equivalent to custom.
5. The nature of a fief can be altered and changed by agreement and custom.
6. Whether a fief containing the exaction of a certain income passes to heirs.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The case is as follows. The King of Cyprus granted in fief, and by way of donation to Thomas de Illionibus for himself and his heirs, two thousand Byzantines to be received and held annually from those of Cyprus out of the dye-works of Famagusta. He also commanded all his officials that they should be answerable for the said quantity to Thomas. Moreover, if the said revenues were insufficient to pay the said quantity, he willed also that it should be paid from other real revenues, as the aforementioned matters appear, according to the form of the privilege issued thereon. It happened that the same King, or his successor, being captured by the Genoese through the mediation of two others, came to peace with them, giving up unpaid, and in satisfaction of the debt by which he was bound to them, the city of Famagusta free and clear of all assignments made therein, and of any concessions to be assigned: however, by the said Lord King in the said city of Famagusta in other than royal matters, in which matter truly the King has nothing. Now the doubt arises whether the said Thomas or his heirs can have the said two thousand Byzantines in the said dye-works of Famagusta, and consequently whether the said dye-works is encumbered, notwithstanding the said donation, or donation given in satisfaction by the said Lord King to the said commune. And it seems first that not: because the King donated, or gave in satisfaction, the said city with all revenues free, clear of any assignments to the Genoese commune. But this the King could do, notwithstanding the said concession made to the said Thomas. For the said Thomas had no real right, but only the King commanded that the said quantity be given to him annually: although he assigned it to the dye-works, nevertheless he has no right, just as when an annual quantity is bequeathed from a fund, as in l. Gayus, and there noted, de annuis legatis; noted in l. Lucius, de alimentis et cibariis legatis; de transactionibus, l. cum hi, §. si uni. Secondly, it is proved, because when someone is to receive from the hand of another, he has no real right, but is bound personally. Hence, if a testator commands that annual revenues of a fund be given, the heir can sell the fund, as in ff. de usufructu legato, l. fundi Trebatiani, where the case of this question appears. And what is noted there by the doctors and by the gloss, ff. de usufructu, l. si quis ita. But in our case, that annual quantity must be provided by the officials to Thomas and his heirs; therefore it could be alienated, since it does not seem that a personal obligation follows the singular successor, as in l. 1, §. si haeres, ad senatusconsultum Trebellianum. Thirdly, because this concession of an annual quantity seems to be a fief de caneva, which has the property that it is not given unless it can be given conveniently, as in usus feudorum, de novo feudo, in principio. But the King could not give conveniently, because for freeing his person he gave to the Genoese commune; therefore, etc. Fourthly, because the King can take away his things from another for cause, as in l. item si verberatum, de re vendicata; l. Lucius, ff. de evictionibus; l. si privatus, ff. qui et a quibus; l. totiens, de pollicitationibus; l. Antiochenorum, and what is noted there by Bartolus, ff. de privilegiis creditorum. But the King does this for cause, and there could not be a greater one, namely, by the liberation of his person, and for the peace of the kingdom, etc. On the contrary, it seems that the said Thomas and his heirs have their right saved in the dye-works. And that he had a real right in the thing itself is proved. The King granted in fief, of the nature of which it is that the useful domain passes to the vassal; therefore, etc. Argument from l. 1, ff. si ager vectigalis. Therefore, he has useful domain in the said dye-works, which is a certain civil revenue, and as it is reckoned among immovables, and is called civil year, as in l. inter, C. de sacrosancta ecclesia, and l. 1, §. exactio, C. de re vendita. Secondly, because in the concession it is said that the King granted two thousand Byzantines to be held on the dye-works. Note

† That term, *supra*, is of such a nature that it establishes a right in rem, as is proven in l. codicil. §. instituto, de legatis 2, and there the gloss touches upon it, and Bartolus expressly notes this in l. fundus, de annuis legatis; and Bartolus refers to this in l. Gayus, de annuis legatis, and cites the rubric in the said l. fundus, de rebus eorum, qui sub tutela vel cura sunt non alienandis vel supponendis. This makes the point excellently, because the term *super* denotes the very substance of the thing in question, as noted by Jacobus Butrigarius in l. 1, C. eo, de legibus. Since it is said *super tinctuariam*, the *tinctuaria* itself is that which grants the quantity for two thousand Byzantine gold coins. Thirdly, it is proven, because the right which is for alimony is this right: if an annual quantity is owed for alimony from a fund, the fund is hypothecated, according to the opinion of the gloss and the doctors in the said l. Gayus, de annuis legatis, and in l. Lucius, de alimentis et cibariis legatis. This right is in a donation in favor of liberality. Thus it seems the gloss wishes to say, as noted in l. si quis argentum, in principio, C. de donationibus, on the word *tradiderunt*, there, *quod ergo* and the following. Fourthly, it is proven that he could not be deprived by the King of his right, by the noted gloss in the prologue of the Digestum, which expressly states that the Emperor cannot take away my right from me, except in cases due to my delict, for example to give to soldiers, or unless by those things which are here; therefore, because the Emperor cannot take away civil rights and give them to soldiers, this is by divine law, as noted there, and it is found in the Book of Kings, where it is said, "he will take our estates and give them to the soldiers." And in this case the rights alleged must be understood. Moreover, there it speaks of the Emperor, who has no superior and is unbound by laws, as in l. Princeps, ff. de legibus; but other Kings have a superior. Of these it is not found that they can deprive anyone of his right; for they are under the Emperor, in cap. In alpis, 7 q. 1. Moreover, what more? I say that a fief is of such a nature, whatever it may be in other things, that it cannot be taken away even by the Emperor, except on account of the fault of the vassal, as is the case in the Usus Feudorum, de natura feudorum, cap. unico; it is supported by cap. 1, de feudo sine culpa non amittitur, and cap. primo, quo tempore miles investituram perdat. If therefore it cannot be taken away by the Emperor, much less by a King. Moreover, by another reason, presupposing but not conceding, because all the aforementioned would cease,

† The Lord Duke, or the Genoese Council, in temporal matters within the Genoese territories throughout their entire district, acknowledges no King as superior. For he is Prince there: and whatever he establishes and decrees among his own subjects has the force of law, as stated in l. quod Princ., ff. de constitutionibus Principum; Instituta, de iure naturali, §. sed quod Princeps; and l. secunda, C. de legibus, with similar authorities. But the Lord Duke then, and the Council then, established and decreed, and also ordered that the aforementioned payment be made in the manner aforesaid by the Captain and Massari of Famagusta, both those then present and those who would be in the future. Therefore, every magistrate must acquiesce to the minor [party] by the Prince. Moreover, a certain Lord John Tortor, then Captain of Famagusta, together with his Massari and consuls, decreed and passed sentence that the aforementioned payment be made, as appears in two sentences pronounced by the said Captain, which are to be taken as established. From whose sentences or declaration no appeal or protest was made; which were ordered to be executed, as appears from what has been said above. Therefore, every magistrate is bound to do this, and especially to execute their sentences, which have passed into res iudicata, as stated in l. finalis, C. ut lite pendente; and l. finalis, de errore advocatorum; l. 1, de re iudicata, with similar authorities.

It is not an obstacle to what is opposed on behalf of the other party regarding the peace concluded, as stated by the said commune through the said Lord King, in that part where it appears that the Lord King gave in satisfaction to the said commune of Genoa the city of Famagusta free, etc., because such a giving rather confirms than infringes the said ducal deliberation and the sentences of the Captain. For although the said city of Famagusta, before its withdrawal from communion, was a participant, as is said, in the said peace, subsequently the aforementioned Most Serene Lord King, knowing that the city of Famagusta, situated in the island of Cyprus, with its castle, jurisdiction of mere and mixed empire, and in its other appurtenances, had come into the commune of Genoa and so forth, makes it a matter of state and faith, as stated in l. optimam, C. de contrahenda et communi stipulatione; and l. cum precibus, C. de probationibus. For which reason the said sentence and ducal deliberation are valid, as concerning a matter pertaining to him. And consequently, the said deliberations and executions, and the said giving in satisfaction, or transfer, mentioned in the said sentence, made by the said King with the confirmation of the said ducal deliberation and sentence, even if it had not previously held due to a defect of non-competent jurisdiction in the aforesaid matters, would be confirmed by the supervening authority of the said Lord Duke and Council. These things are proven in l. si a Titio, ff. de rei venditione; and l. apud Celsum, §. si a Titio, ff. de doli exceptione; and l. cum vir, de usucapione; and l. si rem alienam, de pignoris actione ad Macerum; l. sed Iulianus, §. sed; and in l. si filius, de conditione indebiti, with many others. Wherefore, etc.

To the same effect. Subtleties have been elegantly and copiously alleged for both parties. And to this, so that we may see what is the law, let us examine the nature of the thing itself, and the consideration derived from the name given to this matter and act by law from the indicative vocabulary of the contracting parties, if any law seems to call this concession a privilege. And this is stated in the unique authenticum, which sets forth such a case. The Prince Martianus had granted to the city of the Mitenenses, and to certain nobles of the territory of the city of Pammana, that from the revenue, or canon, which the said city of Pammana was obliged to pay to the Prince, they might exact for themselves such a sum. And upon the death of Martianus, this grace was not observed. The Prince and most just Emperor Zeno supervened, who, considering that the said privilege was to be observed, ordered payment for the past and the future: and he established that a rescript obtained to the contrary should be valid. This is the case in C. de divisione praediorum urbanorum et rusticorum temporum et civium et omni redditu civili, l. finalis, lib. 10. And therefore I have described the entire rubric, arguing from that particular phrase, "de omni redditu civili." And it appears that this is a privilege, and that it is perpetual, and ought not to be revoked: and that it passes to subsequent, or successor, regimes. Nor are those laws to be inquired into which speak of bare contracts, because, as the conclusion is from the instructions, it is in rescripts, and affects quarries, ff. communia praediorum, l. venditor.

And if it is established thus from a privilege, which is equivalent to custom, as in Extra, De verbis significandis, chapter Super quibusdam, § Praeterea, "arises how from a privilege, etc.," there, "the written matter," and it affects the thing itself. Hence, if such a performance is withheld, a useful interdict lies, either Uti possidetis or Unde vi, as in Extra, De electione, chapter Querelam. To every possessory action must correspond some petitory action, which here will be a useful accessory action. For a certain quasi-servitude is established by privilege, which can also be constituted with personal performances. And yet it is anomalous, because another is constituted in doing, not in performing, as in Digest, De servitutibus, law Quotiens, § Servitutum. Nevertheless, it fails in the servitude of leading water, because its nature and formal constitution are such. It therefore does the same in similar cases, as in chapter Querelam, De electione, supra allegata. Nor is it surprising. If, however, it is both a real and a personal action, as in Codex, De usufructu, law Corruptionem, the Commune of Genoa does not resist this noble right, except because the Commune of Genoa claims liberty. The latter alleges a quasi-servitude owed to him by the former, as if he were to say, from a certain mill, so many annual payments. And this, using the vocabulary of the law, which here calls it a privilege, and this is the first investigation. I come to the second consideration concerning the fief.

And it must be known that the form of the fief, which gives origin to the fief, gives law to the feudal matter. For the general nature of fiefs, which the custom of fiefs gives to it, can be deduced to another specific and singular one, namely by agreement. For the common custom of things to be contracted can be changed by agreement, D. de aqua pluv. arc. l. si prius, § recte. That text is singular for this purpose, as someone says in law.

† If, therefore, it is asked whether it passes to the heirs: the form of the contract declares this. But if it is asked of which inheritance it is understood: I will recur to the universal nature of fiefs, C. de oper. libert. l. liberti. per Cy. ad tex. ex facto. §. per Dy. If, however, it is asked whether this fief, nevertheless, has some real right: this indeed is of the nature of fiefs, in which corporal investiture falls. But here we are in a most personal prestation. Therefore, there is no reality here, ff. quorum bon. l. fin. To this effect is what Innocent notes, extra de prebend. c. inter cetera. But the contrary is true: which name of fief is expressive of real right by its own definition: because the King wished, and could, that this intinctuary should be affected to this. And this is that reality, i.e., real affection, of which there is C. si aqueductus. ff. de serv. rust. prœd. l. pecoris. de act. empt. l. in venditione. And the burden is perpetual, where however that. Add what makes very well, what Innocent notes, extra de decim. c. quia nobis. However, in the gloss, ver. and the same seems to be said here of the second.

I come to the third inquiry concerning the royal donation, which has the force of law and simultaneously the firmness of a contract, C. de donat. inter vir. et ux. l. pen. de publ. l. Caesar. Nevertheless, I will consider what happens if Titius makes a donation, or if a certain count, holding a toll right in his county, assigns to me ten annual payments; afterwards he sells that county. Whether the toll right pertains to that county: and it is said that in selling it he was free. Does this harm me? And it seems that it does, ff. de contrah. empt. l. si, in fin., where the case appears. But the contrary is true, because this purchase is a succession to the universality, with which personal rights also pass. And it is similar to one who was an heir to the fiscus. C. de haered. vel act. vend. l. 1. This is clear from the opposite, namely that the debtors of the tinctuaria for the time, after the Genoese succeeded, are bound to answer to the commonwealth of Genoa, assuming the validity of the contract, ff. de iur. fisc. l. si, de act. empt. l. Iul. §. si fructus. When the commonwealth’s fiscus of Famagusta was transferred to the Genoese, all debts and credits of that city’s fiscus were transferred, because wherever there is a fiscus, there is a universality, ff. and C. de iure fisci. And throughout the entire body of law, where the fiscus is treated, that tinctuaria was a part of the fiscal or Royal Chamber of Famagusta. It is not clear that the Genoese are strictly by law, as well as by equity, bound to the aforementioned. That station, which pertains to the tinctuaria, C. de comp. l. 1. And for this conclusion it is most fitting that what Innocent notes, extra, de re iud. c. Abbate, in the gloss, is merely alleged. And by this the response to all matters is clear. For it does not obstruct that the king sold as if free, because he could not do this, ff. de aqua pluv. arc. l. in concedendo, and l. in die accedit. And in the aforementioned, because it places under certainty to purchase, or as if some annual perception favorable is established, given an executor, or not given. That “or as if” is tacitly binding; the laws are common in wills, much more so in benefits of Princes. Which is noted, ff. de ver. sign. l. Princeps bonam, and de concept. princ. c. quia iunctis, lib. 6. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a nun of Saint Clare succeeds to her father together with her brother, who is in the secular world; and if so, whether she must collate those things which were given to the monastery upon her entry.
2. A nun transmits an unaccepted inheritance to the monastery, but what about the inheritance of her brother? And number 3.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The following case is proposed, on which legal advice is requested: namely, Lentius has three children, one female and two males. He placed the said daughter, or female, in a monastery of the Order of Saint Francis, in which he gave a dowry, or alms, for her. One of the sons acted and managed his affairs without the father. The other son conducted his affairs together with the father, who resided in the same house. The same son who remained with the father dies, with the said father, brother, and the aforementioned monastic sister surviving. Finally, the father dies, with the son and daughter surviving, all of whom died intestate. Finally, the said monastic daughter dies. Now the matter is in dispute, and the monastery in which the said daughter entered claims that it is owed half of the inheritance of the aforementioned father and brother of the said nun. The other son says that he alone ought to succeed, because the sister did not contribute to the inheritance, because she was made a nun by the father and endowed, because the statute of the city deprives the daughter of succession and makes her content with the dowry provided to her by the father, although the statute speaks of a married woman, because she is of the Order of Friars Minor. It is asked what law can be derived from the foregoing: whether the nuns of Saint Clare of the Order of Saint Francis are bound to observe the rule of Blessed Saint Francis in all things, just as the Friars Minor of the said order, so that they cannot hold anything in private or in common, according to the Clementine *Exiui de Paradiso*. And thus, whether those succeeding intestate ought to be admitted to the goods of the deceased; or, although the said sisters cannot hold anything in private, whether they can hold in common, so that the monastery succeeds to one half and those succeeding intestate to the other half. Saint Francis instituted three orders: first, the Order of Friars Minor, which is the most strict and lacks private property by the rule, and also in common. The second was that of Saint Clare, which differs from the first, because although it is also a very strict order for women, it nevertheless has private property, and can hold and possess immovable property in common. The third was the Order of the Consecrated Virgins, who have private property, and also individually, as noted in *c. Cum ex eo*, de sententia excommunicationis, in the Clementines. From this it appears that the Order of Saint Clare and the monasteries of the said order are capable of spiritual and universal succession.

† Hence it is concluded that, by reason of the person of the said nun, the chapter of the monastery of St. Clare succeeds to the father of the said nun together with her brother, in respect of those things which were given to the monastery by the father of the girl for her entry, or on that occasion, just as a dowry and other things given on account are conferred, as is noted by Bartolus in the Digest, title *Si a patre*, section *Quis fuerit manumissus*, law 1, § *Si parens*. For immediately the said donation inter vivos was valid, by argument from the Digest, title *De fideicommissis hereditatibus*, law *Pompeius Philadelphus*. And this is especially so because he who has been confessed to be in some manner emancipated from his father, as is noted in the Digest, title *De minoribus*, law *Si ex causa*, § *Papinianus*.

† Therefore I say in a certain sense, because he does not lose the right of existence of his heir, from which he transmits the inheritance of his father, even if not yet accepted, to the monastery, C. de epis. et cle. l. Deo nobis.

† Regarding the undevolved fraternal inheritance, whether a nun transmits it to the monastery, it seems to be said that she does not, as C. de iure delib. l. quoniam sororem. and C. ad Orficianum. l. non pro numero. Although while the nun is alive, the monastery may enter upon it against her will, like a father, as l. cum non solum. in prin. C. de bonis, quae lib. because the monastery represents the image of the nun: yet, with the nun dead, since there is no living image of the dead. Moreover, the root and foundation are extinguished by death, whence no offspring remains, as noted in d. l. cum non solum. per Cyn. It makes for de le. 1. l. cum filio. ff. de fide. l. qui contra senatos. ff. de ope. lib. l. qui libertinus. §. posthumus. and C. de praescri. 30. ann. l. cum notissimi. §. sed cum illud. Moreover, the time and right of deliberation are transmissible, l. cum antiquioribus. C. de iure delib. For as far as the real right of acquisition is concerned, the time of addition is considered, but then the immediate person is lacking: therefore also the mediate. And thus it should be limited, 18. q. 1. c. statutum. And although the gloss seems to say there that the monk appears to give and concede to the monastery the right of entering, nevertheless it should be known that this right cannot be ceded, ff. de iure do. l. si mulier. §. ex asse. And this is established by the subtlety of law, as the urgent disputation of the text teaches, so it says there. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. It is enacted in the secular forum that wills shall not be valid unless they are registered. In the ecclesiastical forum it is enacted that wills shall be put into execution, even if they are not registered: which of these shall be observed.
2. Whether the Church ought to support a civil statute where it is fair and good.
3. Whether a statute concerning the invalidation of wills is good and fair.
4. Justice is twofold.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. By municipal law, testaments appear to be required to be intimated; otherwise, they are annulled, as is provided by the episcopal constitution, that they be committed to due execution, notwithstanding that they have not been intimated. In the secular court, annulment is sought. In the ecclesiastical court, it is sought that they be declared valid, notwithstanding the municipal law, as being unjust and disposing contrary to truth and equity. Hence, beyond the alleged injustice of the statute, recourse is had to the ecclesiastical court.
† It is asked whether it is possible. And for clarity, it must first be inquired into regarding justice and law. Secondly, regarding the forum and jurisdiction.

† Regarding the first point, it must be known that sometimes a statute is good and equitable, i.e., useful and equitable. I say that it appears equitable to the wise themselves according to the conditions of the statute; for it is equitable to find equity, not only natural equity, which proceeds from the source of natural law, as in Inst. de iure naturali, §. item variis, and §. apud manum. Certainly, this statute is promulgated by divine nod through the mouths of those enacting it, and is to be observed in every forum, 4. dist., c. erit autem lex. For a statute of this kind is a holy sanction, ff. de legibus, l. nam et Demosthenes. In this case, the Church ought to support the statute, not to impose upon it; for it could have been instituted thus.

Sometimes it is good, but not equitable: and this can be in several ways, and in every power and virtue of law, l. imperare, vetare, permittere, et punire, ff. de legibus, l. 1. The virtue of the law commands that an heir be instituted in full, unless the causes of ingratitude are expressly stated. For it was equitable that an ungrateful person be punished for a cause not expressed, in Auth. ut cum de appellatione cognoscitur, §. aliud quoque capitulum. Suppose that this ungrateful person, for a cause not expressed, declares the will null against the heir. The instituted heir resorts to the Church as having equity. It is foolish to say that the Church should hear him; nor is there any law under heaven that says this, in Auth. de triennio et semestri, §. consideremus. The law forbids a filiusfamilias and a sexagenarian to make a will regarding their own adventitious property; equity dictates the contrary, C. de mandato, l. in re mandata; in Auth. ut liceat matri et aviae, in principio. Should the Church protect the will of the filiusfamilias? Far from it, unless in the case of the chapter Licet, de sepultura, lib. 6. The law permits usucapions and just prescriptions when accompanied by good faith. Here it is good, but not equitable, because usucapion is usurpation. Should the Church rescind it? Far from it; for even before the Church, prescriptions are justified, but they are strengthened by good faith continued until completion, c. 2, de regulis iuris, lib. 6. Suppose the law imposes a penalty for a minor offense: the law is rigorous, so that others may be terrified by the example. Yet it transgresses the bounds of equity. Should the Bishop be the examiner, corrector, confirmer, or infirmer of statutes made by laymen? Far from it; for this does not pertain to the power of the keys; otherwise, the bishop would have to have all statutes presented for confirmation and approval. To say this is not only legal imprudence, but madness.

Sometimes a statute is neither good nor equitable, and yet the secular judge is compelled to observe it, because it has the form of his jurisdiction. According to that, Claudinus says, under him hangs a question from jurisdiction, e.g., the statute says that a debt cannot be claimed after 10 years. I am a liquid debtor, and I know that I owe; the statute benefits me before the civil authority. Yet, because I know I was obligated, and I was in bad faith, ff. de mandato, l. dolus, and I am not purged, according to the iniquity of the law, and by my sin I am drawn to the Bishop. The same applies to my heir, because he is bound to purge my constitution; and because he is the successor of the defects and fault of the deceased, de sepultura, c. parochiano; ff. de publicis, l. eum qui, §. in hac. And this is the nature of prescriptions contrary to the nature of the contract; otherwise in prescriptions according to the nature of the contract: because those are tacitly included in the contract by the tacit consent of both parties, as in the redhibitory action and the actio quanti minoris. Likewise, otherwise in prescriptions from which one does not enrich oneself at another’s detriment. But it effects that another does not enrich himself not with his own, as in the actio iniuriarum, which is abolished by a useful day, for in executions by time, ff. quod metus causa, l. si cum executione, §. 1, noted.

Sometimes a statute, or civil law, is good and equitable; yet something more equitable than equitable is found, e.g., it is good, and the opportunity to accept is given to him on account of the Falcidian and Trebellian laws. For if he had nothing, he would repudiate, and the will would be void, which would be inequitable, as in Inst. ad legem Falcidiam, in principio, and noted in Auth. de hereditate et falcidia, §. si quis autem non implens. Therefore, it would be equitable that the heir fully observe the will of the deceased, and not seek other profit, except to do well; for to profit by doing well is to have acted, Auth. de hereditate et falcidia, §. si vero expressum; just as the profit of virtue is truth itself. Should the Church therefore add, because it is more equitable than equitable? Certainly not, extra, de testamento, c. si potest, lib. 6; a contrario sensu, eo titulo, c. Raynutius et Raynaldus, in antiqua. Against this, Bartolus operates in the extrajudicial Heretici, in the matter of denunciation. That which is deducted by Falcidia is naturally due to the legatee; therefore, the heir detains it with sin; therefore, it can be denounced to the Church. He responded that the testator did not consent that the heir be obligated to this, nor did the heir by accepting; and therefore, no natural obligation. But what he says about the testator is not true, ff. ad legem Falcidiam, l. Titia. I readily concede that although the testator consented to the whole, in that he bequeaths, nevertheless the heir by accepting does not seem to consent to be bound, except insofar as the law disposes; for he is deemed to accept by that law, since everyone is presumed to will that laws have place in his act, ff. de aqua pluvia arcenda, l. si tertius, §. primo. Likewise, granted that legacies are due naturally, nevertheless Falcidia is due to the heir civilly and effectively. And this civil right is stronger than the natural, or it is foolish, because the civil is objected to it. Therefore, not every natural bond induces a pact, especially one pretended in profit to be gained.

Sometimes also, when it induces sin veiled by fictitious truth, as in a res iudicata, the Church does not support it, lest lawsuits arise from lawsuits, and from them crimes, c. ult., de exceptionibus, lib. 6. It is therefore established that on account of injustice and sin, which cannot be concealed by any tergiversation, the Church is resorted to in aid of laymen. Otherwise, if it is not properly sin, or if it may not be proved.

It is established regarding the forum of the bishop and the power of the land that they are distinct by a principal distinction, which is between the Emperor and the Church, of whom these are members; yet the sun is nobler than the moon; yet also, by possessing its own orb, it triumphs. But one should not touch the office of the other, except insofar as. For it is necessary that sacred rules be valid as laws, in Auth. quomodo oportet episcopos, §. 2; indeed, not only valid, but also prevail, because laws do not disdain to imitate sacred canons, in Auth. ut clerici apud proprios episcopos, §. fi. Yet, under the name of sacred rules are not contained fraudulent sentences, nor usury, which are mutable. For sacred rules are immutable, 50. dist., c. domino sancto meretisque licito, cum si. Now therefore, I return to the proposed question.

† It is therefore asked whether the statute concerning the intimation of wills is good and equitable, or not. And it seems that it is a bad statute, which I prove thus: that which is contrary to what is good is bad, by the argument from opposites. But it is good and equitable that wills be observed, C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, l. 1; nor ought the just will of a sane person to be avoided, ff. de legatis 2, l. codicillis, §. si. Therefore, the contrary is inequitable. First, although it has not been intimated, it is nevertheless true and clear; but truth must be followed, ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. hoc modo.
