To the contrary, that this statute is equitable and good. For, since it is recorded in the memorial books, every avenue for malice is cut off, C. de fideiussoribus, l. quaestionem. Otherwise it would follow that all laws which require intimation or writing are inequitable: which is an open error. C. de iure emphyteutico, l. 1; and C. de donationibus, l. sancimus; and fully noted, C. de fideli instrumentorum exhibitione, l. in exercendis; C. de poenis, l. peccatum, quod bona fides. And this is the equity that obstructs frauds: I do not say in individual cases of each kind, but in the kinds of individuals. For laws are not established generally for individual persons, and that which regards the universal is the concern of the law. Although therefore in the case of A. and B. the truth is clear, nevertheless the law does not except any person from its universal consideration. And therefore the law is the same for all, C. de donationibus, l. data iam pridem.

Therefore, the municipal statute is good, because it is good that last wills should not long lie hidden in private chests, but be brought to public notification, ff. quomodo et quando testamentum aperiri debeat, l. 2; because nothing is so proper to the law as clarity, as in Auth. de testamento imperfecto, coll. 8. And on account of the unknown unfaithfulness of men, as noted, ff. de legatis, l. non possunt, it is equitable that they be published among the public records, C. de testamentis, l. publicati. For this pertains to perpetual and irrefragable memory, C. de re iudicata, l. gesta; and to sincere faith, as in Auth. de defensione civium, post princ., coll. 3; and in the same title, §. nulla, in the words “testatorum insinuationes, et donationum.” And although the constitution of the bishop contains something even more equitable, it is nevertheless irrelevant to the point: as I proved above. And that this statute is effective for preservation, Cynus places, C. de collatione, l. ut liberis.

Furthermore, it must be considered, as I have said, that justice is twofold, namely from the perspective of the law: and then that statute is most just and reasonably promulgated. For it does not contain a burdensome provision, but rather a safeguard for both parties: because if it is intimated, it has ready execution; if it is not intimated, it has ready annulment. The second is justice from the perspective of the party, and then although it would be more honorable to obey the testator, nevertheless one ought not to be blamed if he makes use of the benefit of the law. S. de publica iustitia haeres no. in Auth. de haere. et fal. §. ex haereditas. And although the will of the testator ought to be obeyed, this fails in two cases. First, if it is not legitimate. L. cerdonem. de ope. lib. Second, on account of the fault of the honored party, as noted in Authen. de haered. et fal. §. is ergo a nobis. These matters being considered, that the constitution of the bishop does not have an obstructive or restrictive truth against the statute, C. de episco. et cle. l. repetita. de testa. l. consulta diualia. Moreover, I do not say that it is evident that the statutes and the constitution of the bishop are in concord, because they are of different forums. And therefore the concordance in separated matters, etc., between the statutes of Perugia and Siena, is to be observed. Nevertheless, I say that the words of the episcopal constitution ought to be understood civilly, ff. de serui. l. si cui. i. in the cases in which the constitution is valid, such as when it is left to clerics, or to churches, or perhaps to pitiable persons, or when the testator bound the heir to be subject to the bishop, by ordering that he should pay in any ecclesiastical or secular forum. For the heir, by entering upon the inheritance, is deemed to have contracted in that form and to have consented, ff. de separa. l. quotiens. §. fin. Moreover, the constitution of the bishop says, although they are not intimated, I understand this provided that they can be intimated, because annulment has not been sought. For the constitution ought to be understood in such a way that it does not prejudice the right of another. Therefore, from the diligence of the sought annulment, ff. de vulg. sub. l. ex facto. ne quid in loco publico. l. 2. §. si quis a Principe. de vsupallii. c. ex tuarum. And thus I say and advise, I, Bal. de Per. and colleagues, and especially because the statutes of our city are strengthened by apostolic authority and expressly confirmed. ff. de rebus dubiis. l. si quis priore.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a dowry is presumed to have been constituted.
2. Whether ownership is proved by the dowry instrument.
3. If reprisals have been granted to the Pisans against the Sienese, whether such grant extends to the property of a certain Pisan woman married in Siena.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Point. Repressaliae have been granted to the Pisan against the Sienese.

† It is asked whether the aforementioned reprisals extend to a certain Pisan lady married to a Sienese. On the first point, it must be said that if it cannot be proven that a dowry was given to the lord Francisco de Salibelibus, a dowry is not presumed to have been constituted, as stated in the Digest, *De iure dotium*, law *Mulier bona*. However, it would suffice to prove it by circumstantial evidence due to the status of the persons involved. In this way, the statement of the Philosopher, noted there, may be understood. Nevertheless, this is irrelevant to the matter at hand, whether the dowry is proven or not: provided that ownership, or quasi-ownership, is proven, for the sons of both marriages succeed intestate to the male line.

† By means of the instrument of dowry, however, ownership is not proven if the action is brought against third-party possessors, but it must be proven by legitimate modes, as stated in the chapter *Inter dilectos* on the faith of instruments, in the Code, title *De rei venditione*; in the law *Indicia*, in the Code, title *De probationibus*; and in the law *Cum res*. And this concludes the first point. On the second point concerning reprisals, I say,

† That dotal property could not be seized for the husband’s debt, as noted in the Digest, De bonis damnatorum, l. Quandoque legibus; for they ought rather to be restored to the wife if the husband begins to mismanage his substance, Codex, De iure dotium, l. Ubi adhuc. And because they cannot be alienated, Cap. Rem in praesenti, §. Et cum lex. And because this lady was Pisan, and with respect to goods existing in Pisa, the law and name of Pisan status attach to them, Codex, De mulieribus, et in quo loco, l. 1, lib. 10; although as to forum she follows the origin of her husband, as noted in the Codex, De municipibus et originariis, l. Originem. And therefore there is no doubt that the son of Lord Socco can claim from the said goods the portion that falls to him, notwithstanding the proceedings conducted concerning the said reprisals. As to dotal goods, they are invalid by the law itself, nor would they be valid even with respect to Perugian goods of the woman, l. 1, §. Si quis ideo, Ne vis fiat ei; Digest, De re iudicata, l. A diuo Pio, §. Si super; Codex, Fin., videlicet vel alio modo; l. Fin., Codex, Ut uxor pro marito; l. Ob maritorum, De privilegiis, ex literis; Codex, De privilegiis fisci, l. 1; and in the Authenticum, Ut non fiant pignorationes, in the rubric, with black. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If a brother pays the dowry in the name of the woman’s father, and also in the name of the woman herself, and stipulates for himself and his heirs that it be restored: whether the payment or the stipulation is to be regarded.
2. Just as a woman, when her husband is approaching poverty, may demand that her dowry be placed in safekeeping, so too, upon her husband’s death, if the inheritance is approaching poverty. In what form the citation may best be made.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Point. First, it is asked, if a brother pays, in the name of the father of the woman and also of the woman herself, her dowry, and stipulates for himself and his heirs that it be restored, whether the payment or the stipulation is to be regarded. Second, it is asked, whether, just as during the lifetime of the husband, when he is verging toward poverty, the wife may demand that her dowry be placed in security, this may also be demanded after the death of the husband, if the inheritance is verging toward poverty. Third, it is asked, when someone is summoned to a house, whether he ought to be summoned by written citation, or whether a summons by the voice of a crier suffices.

I begin with the foundation of the obligation, namely whether the woman has a claim for the dowry, when the person making the payment paid in the name of the woman’s father, and also in the name of the woman herself, and did not stipulate for himself. Here I say that, considering the payment made in the said names, and even if a direct action had been acquired by the stipulator according to the strict wording: nevertheless, at least in equity, a useful action, which in this case takes precedence over the direct action, would have been acquired by the woman upon the consolidation of rights after the father’s death, as in c. Rem in praesenti, § Videamus, and l. 2, ff. Solut. matrim. To this effect is what is noted in ff. Si cert. pet., l. Certi cond., § Si nummos, and C. Si cert. pet., l. Si absump., at the end, according to Cynus. And this is the truth, especially in favor of the dowry, and on account of the affection between the persons, ff. Solut. matrim., l. Gaius.

I come to the question of time, because the action was brought within a year: and I say that it could be brought, because whether the husband has misused his property, or the inheritance itself begins to decline into poverty, because there is no administrator; and where the assets are being dissipated, action may be taken immediately, and the woman ought to be placed in security. For if an action is granted to her during the subsistence of the marriage, where there is danger in delay, much more so is it granted after the dissolution of the marriage. This is supported by the Code, On Counselors, the authority *quod locum*; and the Digest, On Pledges, the law *quæsitum*. Furthermore, one who brings an action in due time is not barred, unless the person to whom the delay is due raises the exception, as stated in the Institutes, On Exceptions, § *temporales*.

I come to the citations, and I confess that the citation could have been made in a better form and more securely, namely, specifically and in writing, not by the voice of a herald, which is known to incur penalties. Nevertheless, this cannot be objected to by an extraneous opponent, but only by the person specifically cited, as stated in the extrajudicial argument, *de electione*, chapter *Quod sicut*. And even assuming that it may be objected to under the common law, which is the more correct view for anyone having an interest, the municipal law has decided that it suffices to cite the heirs in general. And note that it says "in general." Hence, it speaks of the manner of citing them, *Codex*, *Si quis se ab hereditate abstineret*, *Authenticum Omnis*. And thus one must adhere to the statute. And because this lady has an institution, although it is subtly alleged, whatever may be said against her, nevertheless judgment must be pronounced in favor of the said lady. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given the statutes that a promisor to a surety, who promises to keep him indemnified, may be personally arrested; and also that a woman may not be personally arrested: what shall be done if a woman has promised indemnity?
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Point. There are two statutes: one, that a person bound as a surety may be personally arrested for the preservation of indemnity; the other, that a woman may not be personally arrested. Now, a woman is bound as a surety, for whose preservation of indemnity she may be personally arrested. And thus the special statute regarding suretyship removes the speciality with respect to sex.

Having examined the said statutes, and coming to this point, I say that the said Lady Berta cannot be personally arrested and detained. For the common law states that she cannot be imprisoned for a civil cause, as is stated in the Code, *De custodia reorum*, in the authority *Novo iure*. Nor does the statute say the contrary; therefore, the common law must be followed. See *Extra*, *De consuetudinibus*, chapter *Cum dilectus*; Code, *De noxa*, law *Si secundum*; and the note in the Code, *De iure deliberandi*, law *Si*, section *In computatione*.

There is another reason. For here the statute expressly and specifically provides that women are not to be imprisoned. And this specificity pertains to the person and the modesty of the sex. Another statute concerns compelling the principal debtor personally. And this statute is specific with respect to the cause of intercession. But a statute specific with respect to the person is considered more specific than a statute specific with respect to the cause. See the Code, *Quod inter pupillos et viduas*. And therefore, in this conflict and contest, the person prevails over the cause as being more worthy and powerful. And even if the specificity regarding the matter were equal to that regarding the person, the greater equity, both lay and legal, prevails, which is that a woman should not be imprisoned on account of the modesty of her sex. And therefore I say that a woman cannot be personally detained. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a legacy of a sum of money to the wife of his son, who is entirely uncertain, is valid.
2. What is included in the term "creditors" and the like.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Point. First, it is asked whether a legacy made to the future wife of his son, who is entirely uncertain, is valid. Second, whether the dowry left to the said future daughter-in-law in this manner: whatever and of whatever kind the daughter-in-law of the said testator had, includes dowries or gifts that she received not only from the said testator but also from the testator’s blood relatives and friends.

† The legacy in question is valid and binding, as stated in the Digest, "On Conditions of Institution and of Utterance," in the law "Who from brothers." For the person is declared by a future event. It is true that those two laws speak of certain persons regarding certain things; nevertheless, because the testator referred to a certain fact, by which fact the person is declared, the legacy is valid as if perfect, because the son, in consideration of whom the legacy is made, is certain, as held in the Digest, "On Conditions and Declarations," in the law "To Titius one hundred," section "To the son-in-law." And there is a text stating that if one leaves a legacy to a future wife who is entirely uncertain, the legacy is valid, Digest, "On Legacies," Title 3, law "This legacy," section "At the end." And note the Institutes, "On Legacies," section "But neither this kind of case," in the gloss beginning "As if it said not only." For either the uncertain person is declared by some fact, and then it is valid; otherwise it is not valid, except in favor of the soul, Code, "On Bishops and Clerics," law "To no one."

† As to the second point, I say that in this legacy it is not considered that it was given by blood relatives; because they bestow gifts in various ways, and it does not pertain to a specific affection of the testator. D. de annuis legatis, l. Seuus, §. Modicus. But it is understood as referring to gifts made by the testator himself, or by those whom he names, or who are related to him; because it was left by way of legal compensation, so that there may be no jealousy among the daughters. To this effect: D. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione, l. Qui liberis, §. Hæc verba; D. de alimentis legatis, l. Mella, §. 1; D. de tutela et ratione distringenda, l. 1, §. Sed nonnullus; D. de legatis 2, l. Cum pater, §. Euictis. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. It is prescribed to the right of speaking that a contract simulated, or entered into by fraud, or by fear, or by reverence for a father, is void, but for what period of time.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Point. It is asked, if a daughter, with the authority of her father, sold maternal property, and subsequently the father repurchased it, whether after 30 years she can bring an action for nullity and simulation. Having considered the said point, speaking in the forum of judgments, I say that the said Bella is not to be heard. And the reason is this: for either the sale made by her was true and solemn, and then it must be upheld from the very beginning, C. de bonis, quae lib. l. fin. §. filiis. auth. falsa. a contrario sensu of that letter there, “against the will” etc.; or it was true but not solemn, and the same applies, because it is strengthened by time, as in C. si maior factus sine decreto factam alienationem. l. fi.; or the sale was simulated, and then it must be known that simulation is addressed by invoking the office of the judge for the purpose of uncovering the simulation: because to act on simulation is to act on nullity, and nullity is addressed by the office of the judge, as noted in l. 1. ff. quae sententiae sine appel. rescin. and l. quae sub condi. §. fi. ff. de condi. insti. per Bar. no. That office prescribes within the space of 30 years, C. de praescrip. 30. annorum. l. sicut. and contra adultum incipiendo, C. in quibus cau. in inte. restit. non est neces. l. fin. in fi. and there by Pet. and Cyn. However, this time does not run in favor of the daughter while she is under paternal power: and especially where she must act against her father, because a lawsuit cannot be brought between father and daughter. Hence, prescription does not run during the continuance of paternal power, but begins its course afterwards, C. de anna. excep. l. 1. in fi. and l. j. C. de bonis ma. Simulation, however, is not presumed in doubt, C. de proba. l. cum precibus. What I said regarding simulation, I say likewise if the contract was made through the father’s fraud, excessive reverence, or terror, ff. de dolo l. itaque. ff. quarum rerum actio non datur. l. j. §. quę honorandae. Always reserving recourse to the Church on account of fraud and bad faith, as in ca. vlt. de praescrip. in antiqua. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a purchaser from a husband, whose heirs are bound to him for eviction, ought to be heard if he offers the wife whatever she ought to have in the purchased things in order to free them from encumbrances, and demands that the action be assigned to him by her.
2. By offering the price so that an assignment may be made to him, in which cases a person ought to be heard.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

The aforementioned opinion is true, as the Gospel, considering the acts and proceedings up to now. Now, he who bought from the husband, to whom the husband's heirs are bound for eviction as being later. The creditor wishes, for the release of the purchased things, to offer the woman whatever she ought to have by her instruments, and wishes that she cede her rights to him.

It is asked whether he ought to be heard, when the goods have not yet been adjudicated, and three cases are to be noted. For sometimes a complete stranger offers, in whom there is no interest. And on this point there are opinions. Some say that he is not heard, as noted in C. de solutionibus, l. obsigna, unless he has an interest by reason of his office, for example because he manages the debtor’s business; or by reason of affection, for example because he is a friend or a related person. Others say that any offerer is to be admitted, ff. de solutionibus, l. qui 10, § 1, and l. solutionem et iudicium. Nevertheless, by this he cannot compel the creditor to assign his rights to him, because generally one is not forced to contract unwillingly with him. For a certain contract results, when money is paid in exchange for the assignment, ff. de manumis, l. Papinianus; de solutionibus, l. Modestinus. Sometimes a second creditor offers, and then without doubt he is to be heard. And the first creditor must place the second in his stead, and in possession of the pledges, ff. quae res in pignus obligari possunt, l. Ariston, in the major gloss. Sometimes the possessor sued hypothecarily offers; and then he has the right to offer, and the right of assignment, l. mulier, qui potiores in pignore habeantur; and l. Paulus, § qui pignoris, qui modis pignus vel hypotheca solvatur. If therefore this new act of obligation of the entire debt is made, and is made in reality with the purse in hand, and the costs of the litigation are reimbursed, I say that the purchaser is to be heard up to the sentence, as a second creditor to claim, and even that the rights be assigned to him. I speak when both, i.e., the first and the second, are hypothecary creditors, according to what is noted by Bartolus, ff. de solutionibus, l. si quis stipulatus fuerit decem in melle. And in this the lady will not suffer any damage, because she obtains what is hers. What I said about expenses, I prove by the argument of two laws, ff. de pignoribus actione, l. si necessarios, § si; and C. de bonis auctoris iudicis possessoribus, l. si.
† I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If a judge, ex officio, investigates someone for theft or adultery and acquits him, is the person who is neither a procurator nor a solicitor admitted to appeal as one of the people?
body: ...tator, nor of whose interest it appears. In the Name of Christ. Amen. The judge, ex officio, investigates against Titius for the crime of adultery, or theft, by virtue of municipal law: and having observed the necessary formalities, he definitively absolves said Titius. Gaius, who is neither a solicitor of the office nor a procurator, and of whose interest it is not established, appeals as one of the people.

It is asked whether a proceeding arising from municipal law or custom is to be understood as one of private judgment, as in D. de privatis accusationibus, l. 3, in the beginning and at the end; and therefore, he who does not pursue his own or his family’s injury does not accuse, D. de privatis accusationibus, l. final. Although Bartolus says the contrary, where a pecuniary penalty is imposed, according to the gloss in D. de popularibus actionibus, in the rubric, which gloss speaks of a civil action, where, after the contestation of the lawsuit, it is always in the interest of the plaintiff, because he becomes a creditor, D. de verborum significatione, l. si cuius; otherwise, if the action is brought for vengeance. It supports what we note in l. pen. D. de conditione ob causam. And therefore, he who is not read [in the record] does not appeal from an acquittal, D. de appellationibus recipiendis, l. 1, and D. de collusione detegenda; otherwise, since he has been punished, he is not heard, d. l. 3, and D. de accusationibus, l. si tibi, § his debet. It does not obstruct D. de appellationibus, l. non tantum, because there the appeal is from a condemnatory sentence. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether spelt, and barley, and other edibles for horses are contained under the designation of victuals.
2. The designation of sustenance par excellence refers to human sustenance.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen. A certain man named Vicus, who sold barley and spelt at retail, bought before nones five baskets of spelt, and no more, for the purpose of reselling at retail. Now it is asserted through a major sanction of the city of Perugia, by which it seems prohibited under a penalty of 40 solidi, namely by virtue of the statute that begins "Insuper quod nullus Pizarellus" joined with the statute that begins "Statuimus, et ordinamus, quod nullus faciat": on behalf of the said Vicus it is noted according to the law that a purchaser of spelt for the purpose of reselling at retail is not comprehended under that statute that begins "Insuper quod nullus Pizarellus," but rather under the other statute in which the purchase is permitted up to the quantity of five baskets without the mention of any specific time; and that the said statutes are different in species, because one speaks of victuals pertaining to the use of man, while the other speaks of those pertaining to the use of animals. Now it is asked, having examined the said statutes, what the law is.

† Having examined the said statutes, and having weighed diligently their words, both general and special, and especially the word "victuals" and the word "edible" (and weigh the fact that it says "before nones", and having weighed the place, "in the city or suburbs"), it seems at first sight that it should be said that by the designation of victuals and edibles, spelt and barley are contained; for they are appointed for the food of animals, and also of poor men when they make spelt-bread. And a decretal says that victuals are owed for visitation, and under this name barley and spelt are included for the riding-beasts of those visiting: de censibus, c. Cum apostolis; de offi. ord., c. Si episcopus, in Sext; and at the end of c. Episcopus, de censib., in Sext. Likewise, animals need to eat, otherwise they perish of hunger: C. ad l. Aqui., l. De pecoribus. Likewise, although the statute that begins "Statuimus, et ordinamus" does not designate a time, nevertheless the other statute distinguishes; therefore we also distinguish, as is fully noted in l. De pretio, ff. de pube. Likewise, that statute prohibiting [contains] this specialization of time, place, and things; and thus it is special in several respects, and several specialities overcome fewer: de mino., l. Emilius; and in Auth. de consang. et vteri. fratri., §. in contrarium. I hold the contrary by several ways: first, from the nature of a rule and an exception; second, from the strict signification of words; third, from the nature of a genus and a species enumerated after the genus; fourth, from the nature of a quality; fifth, through natural reason strengthened by common usage. The rule says: "Let no one keep a warehouse/customs-post [douanam]"; this is understood [to mean] neither before nones nor after; this exception [is]: "let this not be understood of hosts and innkeepers, nor of those who sell barley or spelt and worthy things"; thus an exception is drawn from the rule, as in l. 1, ff. de reg. iur.; the rule is concerning all time by its holy/sound signification.

† "Victus" (sustenance/victuals) is referred by excellence to human sustenance, ff. de ver. sig., under the word "victus"; and common usage of speech conveys this; otherwise, if it were understood of the sustenance of animals, it would follow that before nones hay, straw, grass, and similar things, which are the victuals of animals, could not be bought, which is absurd and uncustomary. The nature of a genus, when it is placed before or interposed among species, is to be limited by the species, and the nature of the species placed underneath is to declare and determine that genus, as is fully noted in l. Quaesitum, §. vlti., ff. de fun. instru., and in c. Generi, by Dynus. But after the genus of "victuals" there immediately follows an enumeration/clarification, namely "cheese, etc."; whence it ought to be understood of those and of similar things; to this also pertains the nature of an alternative, l. 1, ff. de rebus dub. The nature of a quality is to qualify all those things that are placed conjunctively in the same action, ff. de vino, tri. et oleo le., l. fi., §. Cui dulcia; and thus it restricts to similar things. Natural reason is this: because when something is granted on account of necessity, it seems to be granted at the time of necessity, as in l. Si semel, §. Si in habitus, quando dies leg. ce. But to innkeepers it was granted on account of the necessity of those lodging with them, indeed on account of public utility; but lodgers need provender for their horses in the morning just as in the evening; whence the ringers of nones are not to be awaited, because the greater part of the day is beforehand, as in l. 2, ff. de annu. leg. And therefore they can buy barley and spelt even before nones, lawfully and with impunity, up to the permitted quantity. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute that a wife may not bind herself without the permission of her brother, whether the brother may grant permission so that the sister may be bound for him.
1. Whether a woman, who appears in the instrument to have renounced, is presumed to have been informed.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Point. It is prohibited by statute that a woman may not in any way bind herself with her husband, or for her husband, or without her husband, unless with the license of her carnal brother, if she has no father. Now, the woman’s brother sold a certain possession, for which the sister and her husband bound themselves principally in the same instrument: and a notary was requested therefor; and the notary died, and in the summary it appears, “renouncing, etc.” Another statute provides that all solemnities which are, or may be, of the nature of contracts, or by law and custom of the land, are to be understood as expressed. Now two doubts arise. The first is whether the brother could give license to the sister to bind herself perfectly; and whether the said renunciation includes the certification of the woman.

† The obligation of the said lady Catherine is invalid for three reasons. First, because she appears to have bound herself to her husband, and perhaps on behalf of her husband, since several debtors seem to guarantee each other jointly and severally according to one opinion. This is not simply the case, but rather in a qualified sense, as noted in D. ad Velleianum, l. vir uxori, §. fin., and in Auth. de duobus reis, in principio, through Jacobus de Belvisis, who sets out three cases. The first is when she acts together with her husband. The second is when she acts on behalf of her husband, either together with him or separately; and the word "or" is used in an expansive sense. The third is where she acts, or without her husband, etc., for any other person. Therefore, the said obligation is not valid, because it is presumed that she was induced or seduced by the request of her husband, as argued in Auth. ut immobilia ante nuptias, circa medium. And there is a good text on this point in D. ad Velleianum, in Auth. si qua mulier. Second, because she bound herself on behalf of her brother, in which case a good man would not have given permission. This is a case of suretyship or intercession, which did not pertain to the woman’s benefit, as argued in D. de pactis, l. in personam, §. qui pecunia. Also, according to l. 1, in fine, D. de auctoritate tutoris, because the brother gave permission for his own advantage, and in an act that usually harms and binds; and he gave permission in bad faith, seeking his own profit, not the woman’s benefit, as stated in D. de negotiis gestis, l. si pupilli, §. 2, and l. qui sine usuris.

Thirdly, because although it is presumed that she renounced, since she says, "renouncing," etc., and on account of the statute which is here feigned: nevertheless, it is not presumed that she was informed of the benefit of the said constitution, because this is not accustomed to be stated in instruments. Nor is it presumed that she was informed of the benefit of the Velleian law, because the word "renouncing" does not include the requirement of being informed. L. Sciendum, D. De verbis obligatorum, in the gloss; and the aforementioned points are confirmed by that which is noted by Bartolus in L. Mevia, § 1, D. De reriun vindicatione (or Soluto matrimonio). I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether property given in dowry and appraised can be restored in the case of restitution of dowry.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Point. First, it is asked, because things were given for 20 florins in satisfaction of the dowry on this condition, that the donor is bound to receive back those things in the event of the restitution of the dowry for the said estimation, provided they are in good condition, which they were at the time of the said donation, or in better condition. Whether, if the husband afterwards bequeaths the dowry simply, the heir of the husband may give the said estimated things against the will of the woman for the said dowry. But there is doubt, because they were left to her by the chapter *Si non nuberet*; and how Masatino must provide security, let us see in what that dowry consists. Secondly, in what the legacy consists. Thirdly, how she ought to be bound. Regarding the first, I say that in the obligation of the dowry to be restored there is quantity; in the payment there is species, if it pleases the debtor. For that which consists in the free will of the debtor is not in the obligation, since the obligation cannot be placed in the will of the debtor. But a certain faculty can be placed, D. de solutionibus, l. *Si quis stipulatus fuerit decem in melle*. Regarding the second, I say that in the legacy, both in the obligation and in the payment, there is quantity according to the form of the legacy, from which, upon the acceptance of the inheritance, arises a new form of simple and precise obligation. And therefore the species, that is, the estimated things, cannot be paid against the will of the woman, l. 2, § 1, D. si certum petatur. Regarding the third, I say that the said woman is bound to provide security for the restitution of 10 florins and the estimation of the cloths and furnishings, as they are worth at the time when she received them, if she marries, as C. de indicio viduae, auth. *Cui relictum*. For she cannot make certain garments and use them, unless to her own damage, if she marries and offends the will of the testator, D. de legatis 2, l. *Filius*, § *Qui amitianam*, and in Auth. de nuptiis, § *Praefacere*, Collat. 1. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. How a statute excluding females from succession when males are extant is to be understood.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The case is as follows: A mother is prohibited by the wording of a statute from succeeding to her son or daughter who dies without issue, in the presence of a sister or an uncle. Another statute provides that when a wife dies without children, the husband shall acquire two or three parts of the dowry, and the remaining part shall be restored to the nearest heir. Now, a certain married woman dies without children, survived by her mother and her sister, the uncle having also died. The question arises whether the dowry ought to be restored to the mother, or to the sister, or to that person to whom that part of the dowry which the husband does not acquire belongs, etc.

He who is prohibited by the wording of a statute from succeeding in the entirety is not barred from another singular benefit conferred by another statute; for a special statute derogates from a general one. Behold, the law provides that a disinherited son does not succeed in the entirety. Nevertheless, another law states that he succeeds in certain singular matters, D. de operis liberti, l. ut iurisiurandi, § si liberi.

Furthermore, I believe that an exclusive statute speaks with regard to intestate succession, but a declaratory statute speaks also with regard to testamentary succession. Hence, an institution of an outsider is valid in the entirety; nevertheless, the residue of the dowry is due to the nearest heir, because the law is so written, cf. D. de contrahenda emptione, l. dudum; and Extr. de restitutione in integrum, c. ergo constitutus; and in Auth. de nuptiis, § optime. And this can sufficiently be defended when the dowry is claimed by virtue of the provision of the law. But if it was granted by stipulation of the donor to be restored to his heirs, the statute must be understood as referring to the nearest heir succeeding, and he who is stronger in intestate succession. For the force of a privilege ought not to disrupt the rights of contract, if both can be preserved, according to that principle: the law does not protect your right, but its own, and c. l. assiduis.

I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A testament among children that is imperfect is valid, but it must be understood in what sense it is imperfect, whether as to the imperfection of the will, or of the omission, or of the solemnity.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Although regularly seven male witnesses summoned are required in a will, and not females, as stated in D. de testamentis, l. heredes palam, §. in testamentis, and l. qui testamento, §. mulier, in the title Qui testamenta facere possunt, l. hac consultissima, and C. de testamentis, l. hac consultissima, §. per nuncupationem, which regulate them, the will is valid before two witnesses, as C. de testamentis, l. ex imperfecto. Even if the aforementioned witnesses are not males, nor females, as noted by the gloss in the said §. mulier, and C. de testamentis, auth. quod sine, and in Auth. de testamentis imperfectis, in the beginning. But if the will were imperfect for another reason than the omission of solemnity, for example, due to preterition, or because the testator did not expressly complete the expression of his will, then it is not valid, even among children. First, when it is imperfect due to preterition, is the gloss, noted in l. si filius, qui in potestate, D. de liberis et posthumis. Second, when imperfect due to the will not being completed, noted in l. fi, C. familiae erciscundae, and in l. filius, qui, D. de testamentis. For this, because one making part of an indivisible whole is considered to have done nothing, as l. furiosum, C. qui testamento facere possunt. Since therefore the aforementioned Angel, the testator, disposed among his children, his will is valid, although less solemn, because only three witnesses and the parish priest, who constructed the will, were present there, as the said §. ex imperfecto. It supports what is noted, Extra, de restitutione, c. cum esses, and c. relatum. However, what is further presupposed in the fact is that after the death of the said Angel, the testator, two children remained, namely one male and one female, and the wife of the testator, mother of the said children, who son was instituted heir in the will of the said Angel, and the daughter was dowered. And the said son died after the death of his father Angel within a month. It was asked, in what manner and for what share the said surviving daughter and mother succeed the said predeceased son. And it is to be said briefly, that equally. Hence the daughter succeeds in half of the ownership and usufruct, since she was joined to the said predeceased son in both, and the mother in the other half, as in Auth. defunctae, C. ad Tertullianum. But if the said mother passed away, or were to pass to second marriage, then she would be deprived of ownership, and would succeed only in the usufruct, as l. feminae, and in the Authen. there placed, C. de secundis nuptiis. The daughter, however, [retains] the aforementioned dowry left to her by her father.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a nun who has not made solemn profession is properly called a nun.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. All agreements which are held by one final conclusion are valid jointly, and one cannot be separated from the other, if they are compatible; otherwise, the last statement prevails, D. si certum petatur, l. lecta; C. de pactis, l. petens. Hence, the chapter appended at the beginning, if it pertains more closely to the end, is considered as the last, and vice versa; and the same applies to the middle part, C. de institutionibus et substitutionibus, l. pen.; de appellationibus recipiendis, l. si res. And therefore, this entire contract with its chapters is one structure, D. de minoribus, l. 3, § 1, and the whole is valid as it stands, and must be observed as it stands in the goods of the donor, D. de mandato, l. Gayus. And the forms which give origin to the contract, those same forms give origin and derivation to the acquisition made by the son, slave, monk, abbot, and abbess, and similar persons, as noted in D. de pactis, l. si autem. Moreover, here there was an abbess and a nun, and the instrument indicates that all were present, C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione, l. 1. And I say that it was valid with respect to the oratory itself and the goods granted by the donor, not with respect to any other effect, because the donor of another's property could not impose a condition, D. de aqua pluviali, l. in concedendo. If it is asked whether it suffices for the condition to exist only in its transferred form, I say that it does, C. de institutionibus et substitutionibus, l. antepen.

† Furthermore, if it is asked whether a nun who has not taken final vows is properly called a nun, I say that she is not; just as a betrothed girl who is underage is not called a wife, although in some respects she enjoys the privilege of a nun, as noted in c. beneficium, de regulis, lib. 6. And she is regarded as a wife in some respects, if one does not violate her chastity. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a defense is valid even when the form prescribed by statute has not been observed, despite the most just cause. And number 3.
2. Whether a father who has inadequately provided a dowry for his daughter can be compelled to make up the deficiency. And number 4.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Point. If, according to the form of the statute, a specific form is required in refutations, whether the refutation is valid if that form is not observed, even though there was a just cause for not observing it. Secondly, it is asked, if a daughter is excluded from her father’s succession on account of a dowry, whether a daughter who has been less adequately provided with a dowry may, notwithstanding the dowry given to her, bring an action and demand that a suitable dowry be supplied to her.

† The aforementioned refutation did not hold, because where the form is lacking, the cause does not suffice, even if it is most just, ff. de trans. l. cum hi. §. si Praetor. C. de sac. san. eccle. Authen. hoc ius porrectum. extra, de in integ. restitu. c. 1. and 3. q. 2. in fine summę. But if the solemnity had been observed, then I concede that the contract was lawful, as was most wisely alleged above, and that the aforementioned allegations made by the most wise allegator were true, if the aforementioned refutation holds, which, however, I said does not hold, because the form was omitted, and the act was condemned and rejected by statute.

† However, by virtue of the promise of dowry, the father is not bound from his own property, except to the extent that he promised from his own property. For even if he had promised nothing from his own property, he could not be sued on a promise that does not exist, C. de dot. promis. l. fin. ff. de verborum obliga. l. quicquid astringendae. But if he gave to his daughter in a small quantity, when he was wealthy, the daughter can demand a supplement to the dowry. For if I owe ten, and I pay five, I am bound for the other five; thus, if the father is bound according to his means to provide a dowry of one thousand, and he provides one hundred, he would be liable for the remainder, C. de actione, et obligatione. l. obligamur. §. lega. And although a dowried daughter does not succeed to her father, nevertheless here she demands that she succeed, because it is a debt owed to her, which is a notable point. Add the notes in the following counsel below and c. Eo Baldus. Another counsel on the same matter.
In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The refutation was ineffective, because the formalities were not observed, ff. de transactionibus, l. cum hi. §. si Praetor. C. de praediis cum, l. fin. lib. 10. and immediately he may annul the jurisdiction on account thereof, because it holds the opposite position, unless reason should persuade otherwise, ff. de iure patronatus, l. adigere. §. fi. and in the sole gloss, nor does an agreement suffice, where a decree is required, ff. de minoribus, l. et etiam. in principio. or the authority which he has in himself, he cannot provide, ff. de auctoritate tutorum, l. 1. in fine. And the father is sometimes acting in bad faith, ff. de dolo. whence then the presence of relatives is required, so that bad faith is not presumed, note in l. polla. ff. de his quibus ut indignis.

† Nevertheless, by virtue of the promise of dowry, the father is not bound, except to the extent that he promised from his own patrimony, l. fin. C. de do. promis. But if he inadequately endowed his daughter, an action may be brought for supplementation, ff. de act. et obli. l. obligamur. Which is noteworthy. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How an investiture made in favor of a person for himself and his male heirs, and in their default for females, is to be understood.
2. What if, in the last place, two brothers remain, one of whom dies leaving a male son, the other dies leaving a daughter; afterwards, that son dies leaving a daughter: whether this daughter is to be preferred in the aforementioned fief over her cousin (the daughter of the deceased brother).
3. On the matter, see below, consilium 202.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen.

† A fief acquired in this form, namely for himself, and for male heirs, and in their default for females, has this meaning: for himself, and for his children and male descendants, as in 10th Collation, *Qui feudum dare possunt*, Chapter 1, § *Quod in masculis*, and the note in *Ad Trebellianum*, *Ex facto*, § *Si*, through the gloss of Dynus. When males fail, females succeed by agreement, as in 10th Collation, *De duobus fratribus a capitaneo investitis*, Chapter *Duo fratres*. Since therefore it extends to infinity, it is not possible to understand it as referring only to those conceived during the life of the person who was first invested with this fief, but whenever they are born, even from a wife whom he later took, after the death of the original ancestor, as in 10th Collation, *De eo, qui sibi, et haeredibus suis masculis, et feminis investituram accepit*, Chapter *Qui sibi*. Just as in contracts, if someone received an emphyteusis for himself and his descendants, and even if they are born a hundred years later, they succeed by right of contract. And the same applies to wills, where mention is made of descendants by right of will; and the same to privileges, and to any disposition of a man. For this proceeds from the form of the disposition. And yet, it stands with this, that if it is required that the successor be an heir, he cannot succeed to ancient progenitors in his own person, unless he was conceived during the life of the person whose immediate succession is in question, *De suis et legitimis heredibus*, *Item Praetor*. That it is necessary that he be an heir of goods, just as he is an heir of blood, is read and noted in 10th Collation, *An filius, vel agnatus repudiata bonorum possessione*, Chapter *Unico*, and noted in *De petitione hereditatis*, *Item videndum*, § *Si*; *De operis libertatis*, *Ut iusiurandi*, § *Si liberi*, through Bartolus. For by the simple nature of a fief, it does not descend to the descendants of the vassal unless they are heirs, as in the said Chapter, § *Filium*, where it is noted.

† Let us suppose that an ancient fief ultimately devolved upon two males, one of whom died leaving a male heir, the other a female. Then the male heir dies, leaving a daughter, who disputes the fief with her paternal aunt. Or let us suppose that first one brother dies leaving a daughter, and afterwards the other dies likewise leaving a female. These natural sisters contend with each other. The question is: what is the law? For the fief was concluded and consolidated in the last male; therefore it passes through him to his daughter, his heir, and does not look back to the degree that was deprived and lapsed. For that which has once been annihilated never rises again, ff. de solutionibus, l. qui res; §. aream, ff. quibus modis ususfructus amittitur, l. si cum in annos. If this applies to those having a perpetual cause of annihilation under the common law, that which is entirely lost by the father is not recovered by the sons who derive their consequence from him, as in Collatio 10, si de feudo defuncti controversia fuerit; c. si vassallus culpam. Moreover, in fiefs, males extinguish females, at least for the time being, as in Collatio 10, episcopum vel abbatem; c. item si episcopus; §. quoniam etiam si quis. Furthermore, when two lines of the nearest descendants exist, there is no regard for other lines unless they succeed, Collatio 10, de natura successionis feudi, c. successionis. The course went thither, and the line of males cannot be prejudiced; therefore the daughter of the last male seems to exclude other females in such a fief and to take it away from them entirely; not because she is a woman, but because she is substituted in the place of her father and succeeds in his status. Thus the pact is to be interpreted so that among females she is preferred who succeeds in the place of the nearer person, without regard to the fact that she is of a more remote degree from the first stipite, in whom the first investiture was made. For this is what the successor edict and legitimate consequence do; therefore the right of the daughter is augmented from the person of the father; nor is this strange, because father and son. Moreover, the daughter is considered by pact in fiefs as one and the same person, and dominion is said to continue, not to be revoked; nor is it understood as a new fief, but as a continuation of it, l. in suis, ff. de liberis et posthumis. If therefore in fiefs the descendant looks to his own ascendant, Collatio 10, in rubrica, Imperator Lotharius; c. si quis miles; others have it under the rubric, constitutiones loca. And thus I hold in this rather doubtful point, because a fief that is continued to posterity is understood to be an hereditary corpus. Hence the first cause is that of the sons, in Authentica de haereditatibus ab intestato, in principio; and in the said c. an agnatus vel filius, Collatio 10, quia conventum non iudicium, unless they cannot divine it except in an enigma. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a precept that has the force of a definition can be revoked by a contrary precept.
2. Whether the exception of set-off can be raised after judgment.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Point. The quantity demanded was the price of certain mountains before the consuls of the fabric, which he confessed, but he alleged that for another reason the said price ought to be compensated by the agreement of the parties, because thus the consuls mutually issued the order for payment, reserving exceptions and defenses according to the form of the statute of that land. And a term being given for proving, certain things were proved by the said objector. Finally, the consuls pronounced that the said order should be executed; afterwards, the succeeding consuls revoked the order; afterwards, the third and last consuls doubt whether the said order should be executed.

It is asked what is the law. The precept, which is in the form of a confession, has the force to be defined, as stated in the Digest, "de iudiciis," in the law "si debitori," and in the Digest, "de re iudicata," in the law "debitoribus." And because it is argued on this basis, an action in factum cannot be revoked by contrary imperial authority, since an obligation has been acquired, and an action belongs to the party. For this is the rule of law, that no sentence, from which an action arises, can be revoked by contrary imperial authority, as stated in the Digest, "de praetoria stipulatione," in the first law, at the end. And therefore, this first precept must be upheld, whose revocation by subsequent consuls was not valid according to law.

But it causes me doubt whether the allegation of compensation, which could be raised before judgment and was reserved from the beginning, can still be raised, or at least pursued in the same manner as already raised. And it seems that it can, as stated in the Digest, De compensatione, l. Si in dies, § Si rationem. On the contrary, because here it was raised, discussed, and finally a decree was pronounced to be executed. Such a pronouncement imposes an end to the controversy, and therefore has the force of a definitive judgment, and thus cannot be revoked. For since from such a sentence one could have appealed according to common law, if no appeal was made, it becomes res judicata: although no action arises from it, because it does not contain an order to give or do. And this is true according to law, and therefore the latest consuls should carry out the said execution. Moreover, this person who wishes to compensate did not prove a certain quantity of dye or price, therefore no compensation is made, as stated in the Code, De compensatione, l. Sin. For although compensation, which must be made from the price, can be raised from non-liquid to liquid due to the consent of the parties: once raised and not clearly proven, it does not help the one raising it; because proofs must be clear, as noted in the Digest, De deposito, l. 1, § Si quis argentum etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How an investiture made in favor of a person for himself and his male heirs, and those female descendants, is to be understood.
2. A collective noun of the feminine gender has the force of a conjunction.
3. Furthermore, assuming the preceding case, if finally two brothers remain, one of whom dies leaving a male son, the other leaving a daughter, and subsequently this son dies leaving a daughter, whether the daughter is admitted to the aforementioned fief, or is preferred to the cousin (daughter of the uncle).
4. Who are included under the term "heirs" in feudal matters.
5. On the same point, as discussed in the preceding consilium 200 and below in consilium 205.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen. The investiture of Lord Lordan had the following form, for himself and his male and female heirs descending from him: so that if the males fail, the females shall succeed.

† The question now arises among the granddaughters of Lord Lordan, namely between Joan, daughter of Bonfrancesco, on one side, and the daughters of Mark on the other. Concerning the son, John, there is no need to deliberate: for either Joan is capable and included in the pact, and she is opposed to her son as being prior to him; or she is incapable, and through an incapable person the fief does not descend to a male, as in § 10, col. qui feudum dare potest, c. 1, there: “this, however, is to be noted.”

As to whether Joan succeeds by virtue of the grandfather’s investiture before the daughters of Mark, and vice versa, it seems clear: for the common phrase “to the females in the degree” encompasses females equally. For when one determination determines several determinable things, it determines them equally, D. de vulgari et pupillaria substitutione, l. iam hoc iure, § sed si aliter; arg. eorum quamvis; and l. haereditatem. Secondly, because the grandfather’s affection was equal, from which the form of such a contract proceeded, and words are to be understood according to the mind and consent. Moreover, the words are clear, and therefore no question of intent remains, as C. de fideicommissis, l. voluntatis; D. de legatis tertio, l. ille, aut ille, § cum in verbis.

Thirdly, because the collective noun "women" has the force of a conjunction and connection; and therefore the parts make themselves by course, C. de impube. et aliis substit. l. fin. Fourthly, because we see this in legal disposition, insti. de haere. ab intesta. §. cum filius. Fifthly, because from the very beginning of the contract under the hope of inquiry included were these women, insti. de verbo. oblig. §. ex conditionali. nor can a new investiture of heirs prejudice Joanna, who did not consent, ff. de aqua plu. arcen. l. in concedendo. Sixthly, and finally this is clearly proven by the natural reason of blood, and equal reason of equity. and because if there had been doubt about this from the beginning, it is likely that it would have been declared by the contracting parties, as in Auth. de nup. §. pen. which is read ff. de pac. l. tale pactum. §. vlti. if one wishes, and turns over in his mind, equal charity is: and according to the charity of parents it is understood that provision has been made for children, ff. de lib. et posthu. l. Gallus. §. idem credendum. On the contrary it is argued thus, the part of Lordan, nephew of Lord Jordan, accrued to Mark, or by some order of mortality devolved to him, as noted by Bar. ff. de verb. obli. l. si mihi, et Titio. and John was excluded both by Lordan and by Mark his uncle, until Mark lived: and this is not doubtful, because the words of the contract so sound formally. hence the fief was entirely consolidated in the person of Mark, and it became a hereditary body from the said Jordan flowed to Mark, removing Joanna, and deprived, and dispossessed. therefore she does not possess it, having once lost it. it makes what is noted de libe. et posthu. l. Gallus. §. et quid si tantum. C. de sen. pas. l. fin. but this does not seem to be able to be removed, because much differs between exclusion and cessation. for a woman while the male lives rather seems to cease than to be extinguished in her hope, as in Auth. de nupt. §. quoniam infirmas. and de non elig. secundo nub. § gregoria. otherwise it would follow that the order given, as first male, then female, would be impassible: because immediately the male would exclude the female in perpetuity, which is false. Also the exclusion lasts as long as the favor of exclusion and final cause, namely the male, last, for when the obstacle is removed the impediment is removed. Also this is the course, and conflux conventional, not by way of inheritance, ff. de verbo. oblig. l. quodcunque. §. si quis ita.

† What if there were no heir from Marco, neither male nor female, would the fief revert to the lord, or to John? Certainly to Joanna rather than to the lord, because the lineage exists and is preserved for the lineage. Therefore, Joanna is not entirely excluded by the male, but a certain order is established, ff. de usufr. l. Io. quor. ff. de ser. l. 4. §. per intervalla. ff. depositi. I. publici. What if the daughters of Marco also repudiated this fief, Joanna would succeed in their name: for who would repel her? Certainly no one, therefore she is not repelled, arg. ff. de contratab. l. si post mortem. §. liberi. And conversely, because the rule of convertibles is uniform, ff. de leg. 3. l. fin. ff. de vulg. substi. l. et si cum ista investitura dubitanti, consideration of words and differences occurs, as in Authenti. de restitutionibus, et ea quae parit. in princip. colla. 4.

† For the words state, for himself, and his male and female heirs. Although the word "heirs," when used in a fief, is placed for blood heirs, that is, for descendants, as in 10th Coll., l. de alien. feud., c. 1, §. et clientulus; nevertheless, this requires that such a descendant be an invested successor to the fief: as in 10th Coll., an agnatus vel filius, c. 1; and noted by Bartolus, de oper. lib., l. iureiur., §. si liberi; and by Petrus and Cynus, de oper. lib., l. liberti libertaeque; and noted, ff. de pet. haer., l. item videndum, §. fin. Now, it appears for the children of Marcus that if Marcus was the final male heir, the entire fief was his, and his right was derived to his daughters. And this follows from the nature of the end of a movement or motion, and derivation to another, ff. de acqui. haer., l. Paulus, §. fi; C. de impo. lucra. descri., l. 1, lib. 10; C. de dona., l. si auia; ff. de vul. subst., l. sed si plures, §. filio; and from a similar note, C. de secum. nup., l. in quibus. For what is assigned to Marcus, it seems taken away from others, ff. de leg. 1, l. quod in rerum, §. si quis post; C. de legi., l. cum quaestio. Observe, the fief in the person of Marcus was conditional, not free. For it was subject to restitution if he died without a male heir; therefore, upon the occurrence of the case, it is returned in part to Joanna, by argument of those things noted in the said Auth. de resti., and those which follow in the beginning and §. quamobrem, provided that said Joanna is in some way heir to her grandfather by hereditary right, as I said: and certainly the daughters of Marcus succeed rather by the tenor of the contract than by the nature of the fief; therefore, by the same tenor, Joanna also succeeds. Solution. All things considered, either the daughters of Marcus alone succeed, as if the entire fief were confused in their father and made hereditary, by argument, ff. de leg. 3, l. pater, §. 15; or the daughters of Marcus succeed for one half, and Joanna for one half, which accords more with equity, although, according to the strictness of the law, the daughters of Marcus have many arguments from the laws for claiming the whole in solidum. From these two opinions, let each choose the one that pleases him more. To exclude the daughters of this Marcus entirely, and to admit Joanna entirely to the aforementioned fief, is impossible in law, whether you wish to uphold strictness or equity. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A substitution having been made by these words, "if the instituted heir shall die without legitimate sons, or descendants from his own body, I substitute such a person": whether a natural son, legitimated, excludes the substitute.
2. This word, "or," is explained as meaning "or else."
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A certain point was raised as follows: Stefano died without legitimate daughters, or indeed without descendants from his body. The question is whether a natural child who has been legitimated excludes the substitute heir.

† Having considered the words of the will, and having considered that natural affection is also owed to natural children, and having also considered legitimation by marriage with such instruments: I hold that the said legitimated children exclude the substitutes, unless perhaps the first testator was of such nobility and authority that it would be a disgrace for him to have such universal successors, ff. ad Trebellianum, l. ex facto, §. si quis rogatus. However, Jacobus de Belvisi places such legitimated children equal in all respects and in every way to those born in lawful wedlock, as he elegantly notes in Authen. de triennio et semestri, §. quod autem, coll. 3. Bartolus also places legitimated children in the place of posthumous children, in l. Gallus, §. et quid si tantum, ff. de liberis et posthumis. The intention of the testator also appears to have been this, on account of the words, "or rather from his own body," because that term,

But truly. It is explained, for "seu" [or]: and thus it shows natural affection, as if saying, whether they are legitimate and natural, or descending from his own body, that is, natural only. For the word "seu" [or], whether placed ampliatively, declaratively, or alternatively, bears this meaning. Those words, "without legitimate children," are understood to include natural ones, ff. de condi. et demon. l. fideicom. And afterwards he adds, "or descending from his own body." It is necessarily understood to mean natural children only, so that the words may have some effect, ff. ad Trebel. l. haeredibus. §. fin. Except in the case of feudal dignities, which do not pass to persons of humble status. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a son transmits an unaccepted maternal inheritance to his ascendants. Likewise, whether and when a father may accept an inheritance on behalf of his son.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

Having considered the above-stated matter, it must first be known that, by law, the intestate estate of a mother devolves upon her daughters equally, as provided in l. 1, C. ad senatusconsultum Tertullianum and l. matrimonium, C. ad Orphitionem. Secondly, it must be known that a maternal inheritance not accepted by a son is not transmitted to ascendants, as provided in l. non pro numero, C. ad Orphitionem and l. 2, § si quis ex liberis, ff. ad Tertullianum. Thirdly, it must be known that if a son is unwilling to accept the inheritance offered to him, the father may accept it and acquire it for himself with full right, as provided in l. cum non solum, in principio, C. de bonis, quae liberis. However, if the son dies before accepting or repudiating the inheritance, the father cannot subsequently accept it, according to the common opinion of the doctors, as reported by Cynus in the aforementioned l. cum non solum; and Bartolus holds the same view based on l. si infanti, C. de iure deliberandi; l. 2, C. ad Orphitionem supports this. Therefore, from the foregoing, the answer to the question is clear. Although the intestate estate of the said mother devolved upon Veronica and Francisca, her daughters, to each of them for one-half, according to the laws cited above, nevertheless, because the said Francisca died intestate without having accepted her mother’s inheritance, she did not transmit her half, either in whole or in part, to her father, as stated in the aforementioned l. 2, C. ad Orphitionem and l. 2, § si quis ex liberis, ff. ad Tertullianum. Nor does the gloss to l. 1, C. de his, qui ante apud tabulas, constitute an objection, because the law apud hostes, which the gloss there also cites, speaks of a daughter in paternal power, who transmits an unaccepted paternal inheritance not only to superiors, as is said there, but also to anyone, as noted by the doctors in the aforementioned l. si infanti. And this is effected by the existence of her heir, as the text says in the aforementioned l. apud hostes. But our case concerns a maternal inheritance, which does not have sons in its power. And if it is said that the father appears to have accepted by alienating or exchanging the dotal property, since such an act cannot be performed without the name and right of an heir, as provided in l. pro herede, ff. de acquisitione hereditatis, I answer that such alienation was made while the mother was alive, whose inheritance is now in question; and thus, by such an act, acceptance was not induced, since there is no inheritance of a living person. But if, after the death of the said lady mother and during the lifetime of Francisca, he exercised such an act, then he appears to have accepted and acquired for himself the inheritance of the said lady mother for one-quarter. From all of which I conclude that the inheritance of the said lady mother belongs by law entirely to the said surviving Veronica by right of accrual, since the said father did not act as heir after the death of the said lady mother and during the lifetime of Francisca, as is clear from the point stated above. I, Franciscus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. He treats the same matter as in the above-mentioned opinions 200 and 202, where see.
body:
In the Name of Christ, Amen. The doubt, on which counsel is requested, is as follows: namely, Lord Jordan was invested with a certain fief by a bishop who was under an interdict from investing, in this form, namely: And the investing lord invested for himself, and for his male and female heirs descending from him: and so that if males fail, females shall succeed, etc. Here Jordan died, leaving three male sons, namely Bonfrancesco, Vitalma, and Marco. It happens that the said Jordan died, no recognition of the fief having been made, for it was not necessary. Likewise, the said Lord Bonfrancesco passed away in the course of time, no recognition having been made. He left, however, one son named Jordan, and one daughter named Joanna. The said Jordan, together with his uncle Marco, recognized the said fief. It happens that the said Jordan died, so that the fief remained entirely with his uncle Marco, since no other male remained in the male line; afterwards, the said Joanna was given in marriage to a husband, from whom she had one male son now living. Afterwards, the said Marco died, leaving no male, but only two daughters now married, and with the male son of the said Joanna surviving. Invoking the name of Christ, and of his glorious virgin mother, and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, of both Johns, and of James, of the holy spouse Catherine, and of Jerome, priest and most excellent doctor, Amen.

And first, regarding the share of Marco, I do not think there is any doubt, omitting prefaces and divisions in fiefs made by the text, gloss, and sayings of the doctors, especially concerning the acquisition of fiefs: as through the first investment made in Jordan, his nephew, which perhaps, both by the words and by the intent, seems rather to be a confirmation of the first: as the words seem to sound openly, not denying that he who confirms seems to give, *l. lege obuenire*, ff. *de verborum significatione*, and in *Authent. de defensione ciuitatis*, § *sed interim*. For since, by the pact appended, or the fief formally appropriated, it is provided that if males do not exist, females are called: but from the said Jordan there are no existing male children, therefore in his share the female daughters called in the investment are altogether to be admitted. And of this I say it is the case in *c. 1*, extra, *de natura successionis feudi*. For since this fief, as regards the persons of Marco’s children, is paternal and ancient, with respect to the person of the first Jordan invested, and the terms of the male children, and divided among the said three male brothers, the share devolved to the said Marco pertains to his said daughters, notwithstanding that at the time of the death of the said Marco there were some males descending through the male line: for it seems more that the ancient Jordan, and the first invested, and Marco, his son, confirmed in the fief the second time, wished to provide for his own heirs, rather than for others, as in the aforementioned *c. 1*, *de natura successionis feudi*, and in *c. 1*, *de duobus fratribus*, from the chapter *investitura*, there, I answered. And this is the will of the text in the first rubric, *qui feudum dare possunt*, *c. 1*, § *notandum est*, *de successionibus feudorum*, *c. 1*, § *filia*, and *de gradu successionis feudorum*, *c. 1*, verse *proles enim*. And this is most clear, since first the said Jordan, the nephew, died, before the uncle Marco, who died last, notwithstanding males, and those born of males.

I come to the second point, namely, regarding the share of Jordan, the nephew, invested, or confirmed, together with his uncle Marco, to whom his portion should come: because he died before the death of Marco, leaving no male descending from himself, or to the uncle, or to the two daughters of the uncle, or to Joanna, sister of the said Jordan, the nephew, or to the male son of the said Joanna, from her and Alberto, her husband, to whom she was married. Concerning which it is to be known, that the acquisition of such a fief, directly or through an intermediate person, is rather by pact than by succession: which would be otherwise if the fief had been given simply: for then, indeed, by succession, as clearly states Jac. de Bel. and Bart. de Saxoferrato, and others in the chapter *per successionem*, *de his qui et haeredi fuis*, in the last question, there, *haec quaero*, alleging the text, as *l. stipulatio ista*, § *sed quaesita*, ff. *de verborum obligatione*. Therefore, by the force of the words of the investment opposed by the ancient Jordan, first invested, and no other male descending from a male existing, upon the death of Jordan, his nephew, to his heirs, namely male or female children, it was necessary that it come to Marco, the uncle, and be consolidated, since this fief was acquired by ancestors, as noted in the text, *de duobus fratribus*, from the chapter *investitura*, in the end, and *de feudo Marc. Duc. et Comitis*, § *si capitanei*, in the end. And even if a new investment was made in Jordan and Marco, it would be, and not a revocation, or confirmation of the first. The same would seem to be the case from the opposition, as noted, and it is the text in the beginning, alleged *de duobus fratribus*, from the chapter *investitura*, in the end, and *de successionibus feudorum*, § *finis*.

But the aforementioned I say do not obstruct, because succession in a fief directly does not ascend, but descends, because the father does not succeed the son, but the son the father, as proves the text, *de natura successionis feudorum*, in the beginning. And thus much less should the uncle succeed the nephew from the transverse line, as proves the text, *de gradu successionis in feudis*, § *his vero deficientibus*, verse *si enim Titij*. To which there is a clear double response. First, because we are not treating of proper succession in a simple paternal fief, newly confirmed, or newly acquired, with a formal pact. Second, because in a fief, even simple, in nephews and uncles, equality of succeeding is observed, if the fief was paternal. That is, if it was of that parent who was the common agnate, as in our case, because it does not speak of a great-uncle, and brother of the grandfather: but of a proquinque uncle, just as the uncle, who was the common agnate to the first Jordan in the fief, and to the nephew Jordan. And this is manifestly proved by the texts alleged above, simultaneously, *institutio de gradu successionis in feudis*, § *his vero*, verse *si enim Titii*, which speaks only of a great-uncle. And the text in *c. de feudo Marc. Duc. vel Comitis*, § *si capitanei*, verse *si vero*, 7. And on this rests Jac. de Bel. and Bart.

Having seen this, it remains, Marco being dead, to whom the share of Jordan, the nephew, seems to have devolved by pact, and in which it accreted, or was consolidated, as I proved above. Let us see to whom this share is acquired: and certainly, without superfluous allegations, it is acquired to the daughters of Marco. And from the form of the first and second investment, it evidently appears that if no males exist, namely descending from a male, because we should not depart from the words of the investment, as *l. non aliter*, *de legibus 3*, and *l. prospexit*, *qui et a quibus*. And because when that case, to which the words of the law and the disposition of the law are adapted, as *l. 1*, § *non omnino*, *de fluminibus*. And because in uncertain, not certain matters, there is room for conjectures, as *l. continuus*, § *cum ita*, ff. *de verborum obligatione*. But from the words of the investment it is clear that if no males exist, the fief passes to females. Therefore, the daughters of the said Marco are said to obtain by the words of the investment of the fief.

It remains now to respond to one chapter, because at first sight it seems as if the case were that the children, or the male child of Joanna, sister of Jordan, the nephew, should have such a share: namely, of him who receives the investment for himself and his male and female heirs. For there the text says beyond the middle, "for the place of the female in the succession of the fief does not appear, while a male remains from him who was first invested from this." Since therefore in the case of the said chapter there is a nephew and a niece from two male brothers, and the nephew claims for himself the place, the sister being excluded in toto: and thus it was judged, thus should the male son of Joanna obtain, the daughters of Marco being excluded, according to the case sought: but as I said, the aforementioned case makes little to the fact, nor was there hesitation concerning it, since such a chapter speaks of a fief devolved to a daughter of the first, and no male existing, and in the female herself totally consolidated. Therefore, from her being born two male sons, and from one a nephew, and from the other a niece, the father of the niece and the father of the nephew being dead, the male nephew claims for himself the place, the niece being excluded in toto. And this holds the gloss, and Jac. de Bel., and Bart. in the matter in *c. praallegato*, *de eo qui sibi et haeredibus suis*.

But we speak in our case, with the said Joanna, or other female, never having had the said fief, or it being consolidated in her. Therefore, in her son it cannot have success. First, by the text in the title *qui feudum dare possunt*, *cap. 1*, § *hoc autem notandum*, *de gradu successionis in feudis*, in the beginning: if he succeeds, the nephew from the daughter succeeds alone, and thus not from the son. The reasons why children from a daughter, who was not a feudataria, or in whom the fief was not consolidated, do not acquire, are given more fully. First, because it pleased the Prince. And this gloss, according to Jac. de Bel., because the intermediate person is removed. Second, Joanna, through whom the children should have been admitted, and thus they should not be admitted, C. *de suis et legitimis haeredibus*, *l. meminimus*. Third, because it is an obstacle to her, or her mothers, according to An. Iser., and according to Jac. de Are., that what is an obstacle to daughters, should more be an obstacle to sons born from her. And all these are noted in the said § *hoc autem notandum*.

Replying, it seems that if we say a new investment of Marco and Jordan, the nephew, I have my proposition, since there was a pact: as in the first investment, if it confirms the ancient one: which I think more necessary. By sacrament is the response § *proximus*. For since the fief is consolidated in the person of Marco, a male, it passes through him to further capable persons of his degree, according to the form of the investment. And thus to his daughters, males failing, which the text and gloss will in the said *c. de eo qui filios masculos et feminas*, alleged § *quem transitum facere non potest*, as in the aforementioned *c. pluribus*, supra. And existing males, and the form of the investment. Which lastly is openly proved by natural reason, the word "from" notes the proximate, material, immediate cause, *l. eo tempore*, in the end, ff. *de peculio*, and *Instit. de actionibus*, § *sed iste*. But daughters, or a daughter born from the first enfeoffed through the masculine generative, and properly, is said to be descending. And according to the order of the family, and agnation, and nature, born, or born from the daughter of the enfeoffed, is not properly, nor generatively, nor according to the order of the family, and agnation, or cognation, from the male enfeoffed, said to descend. Let not physicists and artists say, to whom in their art, as to experts, is to be believed in their art, as ff. *de statu hominum*, *l. septimo mense*, *de ventre inspiciendo*, *l. 1*, in the beginning, because fathers generate and sow, but mothers receive the seed in the earth, as a sack, and grain are.
