And where none could properly operate, unless they operate improperly, C. *de his qui veniam aetatis impetrant*, *l. verbis civilibus*, ff. *de vulgari et pupillari substitutione*, *l. sed cum*, *ad Trebellianum*. Therefore, that text, *non enim et c.*, in the aforementioned *de eo qui sibi et haeredibus*, and *c. cum non possit*, there from the said, cannot operate properly, it will operate improperly: because descending from a female capable, and in whom, by the form of the pacts of the fief, it is consolidated, and through her it made transition to the sons, which in our case is entirely applicable, since from the said Joanna, an incapable person then, having a brother and uncle capable, in whom it was consolidated.

And thus I say, and counsel, as written above, I, Robertus Ricardus de Saliceto, doctor of laws of Bologna, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an emphyteusis may be given in dowry, and whether the giver prejudices himself thereby.
2. Whether prescription may run against a private person on the basis of a title of the Church, and for what period of time.
3. A defendant may allege contrary matters by amending his pleading.
body: Point. Vanni de Castro, acting for himself and his children, was granted a property in emphyteusis to a certain Vanni de Castro, for himself and his children, and up to the third generation, so that the share of the predeceased should pass to the survivors. He died, leaving Archus and Margaret, his children. To Margaret, the aforementioned property was given as dowry; she died, leaving a single son. Upon the death of that son, his father renewed the said property and sold it, and several renewals were made. Now, the said Archus claims that the said property has reverted to him. A sentence was rendered in his favor, and an appeal was taken. Prescription is objected, upon which witnesses were received in the first instance, but they did not prove it. The question is: what is the law regarding the said witnesses to be considered with respect to the renewal and with respect to prescription? Can prescription be acquired by an emphyteuta against another emphyteuta in less than forty years, considering that the property is ecclesiastical, but the emphyteusis is private and pertains to a specific person?

† Since the aforementioned plots of land came into the dowry of the lady Margaret, it is not expressly stated in the point whether her father gave them, or her brother, or she herself. Nor is it stated whether they came into the dowry as her own property or as emphyteutic property. However, I gather from the facts narrated that they were emphyteutic, because they appear to have reverted to Archus upon the termination of Margaret’s generation, according to the form of the original emphyteutic grant. But it must be observed here that this property belonged half to Archus and half to Margaret. If Archus provided the dowry, the half belonging to Archus never reverts to him. This is supported by what is noted in C. de familiae erciscundae, l. Si familiae; C. de fideicommissis, l. Quotiens; and ff. de modo quo ususfructus amittitur, l. Si cum in annos. For he alienated it by renouncing it. On the other point, it must be said,

† That from a pretended title one may prescribe against private persons by long time, and also such useful rights, ff. de damno infecto, l. si finita. §. si de vectigalibus. And thus here proceeds prescription of long time. On another point it is necessary that we observe leniency towards witnesses, if the witnesses are public: because in the lands of the church the church speaks.

† On another point, the defendant may allege the contrary by amending his statement, as here: not by cumulatively asserting affirmatively according to the first opinion of Dynus, unless where he is punished for denying; because then he cannot amend unless he has incurred the penalty for perjury. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether purgation by delay is admitted to avoid the penalty contained in the compromise.
body: Pactum. A certain Archus, son of the philosopher, from the village of Populi in the district of Nursia, on one part, and Lallus, son of the philosopher, from the same village, on the other part, made a compromise regarding a lawsuit and dispute pending between them on account of certain matters; in which the said parties promised each other to obey, comply with, ratify, and accept every sentence to be rendered by the arbitrators, under a certain penalty. The arbitrators elected in the said compromise rendered their sentence and decided that the said Archus was bound and ought to give and pay to the said Lallus 30 gold florins up to the last day of the proximately past month of June, and thereafter at his term and request, under the penalty contained in the compromise. Afterwards, on behalf of the said Lallus, before the said last day of June, it was protested to the said Archus that he ought to pay him the said 30 gold florins. The said Archus, after the lapse of the said last day of the month of June, did not pay the said 30 gold florins. Afterwards, on behalf of the said Lallus, the penalty contained in the compromise was demanded, as against one who had contravened the sentence of the arbitrators, because he had not paid before the said last day of the month of June. And before the contestation of the lawsuit concerning the penalty, the said Archus offered the said 30 florins and the interest thereof to the said Lallus. And since the said Lallus refused to receive the said 30 florins and interest, they were consigned and deposited with a certain priest by order of the judge. Now it is asked whether the said Archus has incurred the penalty contained in the compromise, because he did not pay before the last day of the month of June, notwithstanding those words, "even if he has incurred." Whether, by the obligation, consignment, and deposit of the principal and interest, the delay is purged and the penalty avoided; and what is the law.

† By the words in question, the delay is not rendered more purgable: because they were added in favor of the creditor, as noted in the Digest, On Obligations Arising from Words, in the law Cum stipulatus sim mihi a Proculo, in the gloss, and according to Bartolus; and therefore the case of the question is found in the law Celsus, in the Digest, On Arbitration, and noted in the Digest, If One Provides Security, in the law Et si post tres. According to the common law and civil law, the purgation of delay has no place here. And I emphasize the interpellation made before the day. Nor does it obstruct what is noted in the Digest, On Minors, in the law Emilius. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If a father, after having instituted his son as his heir, added that the son should pay a certain sum to his mother for the administration carried out by the father, and otherwise deprived him of the inheritance: Whether such deprivation, or disinheritance, is valid; and if not, whether at least he appears to be burdened with a fideicommissum.
body: Punctus, after the second marriage, having been a diligent father to the son of the first marriage, Punctus, after the second marriage, having administered the goods of the second wife, and having received much from the paraphernalia and other sources. He made a will, in which he left several legacies to the son of the prior marriage. Then he instituted both as universal heirs. Finally, he appended a condition, that if the wife should demand the administration, the son of the second marriage would be bound to pay her, and if he did not pay, he deprived him of the inheritance, the legitime excepted. Now the question arises concerning the validity of this will. The will, about which the question arises,

It was very cautiously ordered, and the law urges the father to make a will among his sons equally, or with little discrepancy: if one of the sons perhaps wishes for more, nevertheless, if the father does not wish to use this humanity, it suffices that he leaves the legitime. Thus said the text literally in Auth. de nuptiis §. illud quoque at the end of the title. Moreover, the testator can burden one of the heirs to pay a certain debt in full, ff. de legatis 2, l. cum ab uno. Moreover, he can impose a penalty on the one who does not pay, provided that he does not diminish the legitime, C. de fideicommissis, l. quaestionem §. si. On the contrary, it seems that when the testator first instituted an heir, and afterwards deprived the instituted heir because of the act of another, such deprivation or disinheritance is not valid because of its injustice and inequity; and because such disinheritance is odious and captatory, since it is placed in the will and power of another, ff. de heredibus instituendis, l. pater testamento duas, where it says that no one can be disinherited by the act of another. But here this son is disinherited and deprived of the universal institution by the act of another, namely, by the act of his mother claiming her dowry through an action of negotiorum gestio against the heirs of the husband. Hence it seems that the institution of the first part of the will remains firm, and the deprivation does not hold. But to this someone would say that this son is not deprived because of the act of another, but because of his own act, since he contradicts or opposes the will of the deceased. But to this it is answered that one must obey the wills of the testator whether just, unjust, or inequitable, C. de his qui potestati nominati, l. 1; de operis liberti, l. cerdonem; and the aforementioned l. pater, and there noted. But certainly, granted that the deprivation would not be valid, and thus he is the universal heir, nevertheless these writings have another clause, namely, a fideicommissum, and from this clause, as universal heir, he is bound to pay the debt to his mother, d. l. cum ab uno. And on this point I see no remedy in law, although there is no doubt that prelegata are valid, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the statutes of a people can be changed by the reform of the prior statutes of a certain city.
body: The power of the chamberlains does not extend to the conception of...

† The power granted by the general statutes to the Lords Prior and Chamberlains does not extend to the abrogation or derogation of the statutes in general. For this must be expressly mandated, as in the law *constituta*, Cod., § *quibus*, and in the confirmation of the Justinian Code, § *sed si quae*. And therefore, statutes disposing concerning reprisals, and the effects of statutes, cannot be abrogated nor derogated from by the reformation of the Lords Prior and Chamberlains, unless by some supervening cause that is equitable and reasonable, as noted by Bartolus in the law *ambitiosa*, in the second column, *de decretis ab origine factis*. Therefore, privileges derogating from statutes cannot exist, unless they have the power to correct or derogate from the statutes of the people. For the statute of the people is greater than the statute of the decurions. And it belongs to him who made it to correct and derogate from it, not to an inferior, because an inferior cannot abrogate the law of a superior, as noted in the Code, *de usuris*, auth. *ad haec*. Hence, although the reformation is in itself very equitable, holy, and just, yet equity does not suffice where authority and power are lacking; there are no legal forces. And therefore, unless another power appears, the said reformation does not derogate from the execution of the statutes, nor from reprisals, which are to be observed and maintained, although they are rather rigorous than just. And thus, according to what is proposed, it is concluded in favor of Falcino. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a notary who is not from the place can draw up instruments there, and whether faith is given to them.
2. Whether a subject of someone by reason of jurisdiction can be a witness in a contract or instrument pertaining to him.
3. Whether the execution of a prior contract can be impeded on account of a right supervening from a new contract.
4. Whether one renouncing legal exceptions is deemed to have remitted fraud.
5. An appeal may be taken from a judgment on a possessory matter. And by Bartolus in l. 1, ff. de Salviano interdicto. I, Baldus.
body: The subject of the following written opinion is as follows. A certain notary, not from that city but from elsewhere, drew up a certain instrument pertaining to a certain nobleman, in which he placed as witnesses subjects of that nobleman, namely, a certain servant of his. There is doubt concerning the instrument itself, whether it is valid. Furthermore, in the said instrument of sale, license was granted to the buyer to receive the thing by his own authority, and in the said instrument there was a renunciation of all executions, even if they were to be awaited according to law. Now it is asked whether the execution of the said license can be impeded by a new contract creating a hypothec, by that rule, "He who acts in bad faith, you ask," etc. Thirdly, it is asked whether an appeal can be taken from a sentence passed on the execution of the said license, since it is said that it was passed on momentary possession. On the first point, I say,

† But if the notary is of good fame and reputation, such an instrument is valid, because even if there were some slight presumption against the deceased among the witnesses, it is supplied by the authority of the public instrument drawn up by a notary of credible trust, whose legality has been thoroughly examined and long tested, as noted in Auth. de testibus, §. et licet, where the gloss hints at this. To this effect is ff. de edendo, l. si quis ex argento, §. 1. Otherwise, if the notary were unknown or suspect, the judge has the power to inquire into the will from him and the witnesses, C. de falsis, l. si quis Decurio. This, however, is discretionary, just as if the witnesses were to testify orally.
† For subjects are not entirely excluded by reason of jurisdiction, as noted by Cynus in the Code, on the title "De testibus," in the law "Eos." On the second point, I state without doubt,

† that the execution of an old contract may be impeded, and the effect of a granted license suspended, on account of a right supervening from a new contract: because the most recent agreements derogate from prior ones, C. de pactis, l. pacta nouissima; and because a license must be understood as given under the condition that things remain as they are, ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. quod seruius; and on account of the equality of the supervening cause, even the effect of a sentence is impeded, ff. de conditionibus sine causa, l. si fulle; C. de transactionibus, l. si diuersa; and retention is allowed on just cause, ff. de vi et vi armata, l. colonus; and ff. de condictione indebiti, l. eleganter, § si centum; because it is more advantageous to rely on a pledge than to bring an action.

† And although it has been renounced to the exceptions of law, nevertheless it is not understood to have been renounced to the exception of fraud, which you seek, etc., nor is fraud remitted, C. de pac. l. si vnus. §. illud nuda. Moreover, such renunciation does not concern future matters arising from new contracts, ff. de pact. l. si vnus. §. pactus. insti. de replica. in prin.

† On the third point, I say that an appeal may be taken, because although the matter concerns possession, it is not dealt with by a possessory interdict, but by way of contract, just as an appeal lies from a hypothecary action, even though it merely invokes naked possession. This is supported by what is noted in the Digest, De re iudicata, in the law Qui restitue.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a tutor may, and when during the guardianship, bring an action against the ward, and vice versa.
body: Although it is alleged that nothing further can be alleged, yet you have so fully alleged the theme concerning that which is sought, that nothing further can be alleged, nevertheless, repeating the theme, I shall say something. When a tutor, with the authority of a tutor, openly, in good faith, and lawfully purchased from a ward, or from the co-tutor himself, a certain thing of the ward by delivery, and paid the price on a certain day, no interest is due between minors during the guardianship; he brings an action for this thing.

† It is asked whether it is possible. Texts and glosses are alleged that it is not. D. de tutel. et rat. distrah. l. sed non dantur. Wherein consider, that in native actions the words are not referred to the birth [of the action], but to its exercise, because neither the law nor the judge permits the exercise. And that law speaks of theft and damage given in the property of the ward. But theft and damage given are an extrinsic cause, not arising from the administration itself. For he who steals or gives damage wrongfully does not administer, D. pro emptore l. qui fundum § si tutor. And from this it follows that two glosses are true, which do not expressly state it, C. de admin. tut. l. 2 and D. de procur. l. qui proprio § si. Since therefore we have an express text and glosses, there is no room for doubt, as C. de furt. l. ancillae. It is not objected that we do not [find this] in Inst. de auctor. tut. in fin., because it is understood when the action has an older cause, before the guardianship arose. And thus Cyriacus and Raymundus passed over, reconciling the discordant glosses with this distinction, which the gloss also places in the said l. 2. Hence two distinctions are given in the gloss, one concerning causes, the other concerning times: and join them together. Either from the administration itself, and it is not brought, because it does not even arise during the guardianship; or from an extrinsic cause, and then, if it arose during the guardianship while the office was being exercised, it arises, but is not granted; or from a preceding cause, and already arisen and granted, or which, arising during the guardianship from an older cause, can be brought. This is the collection of the aforementioned glosses.

To the contrary, that it can be brought, especially if the term fixed for the delivery of the thing has elapsed. For it is certain that this contract binds, C. de contrah. empt. l. cum ipse. Therefore it binds with its modes and times. For to defer payment would be to increase the price and diminish the thing, because less and later, Inst. de acq. rer. dom. § plus. Therefore if they are not paid, it can be brought immediately. And what opposes this? Certainly no reason in the world opposes it, and to say the contrary is to say that one can sue for the observance of good faith, and expressly against l. bona fides D. de act. empt. For it is absurd that the ward should have both the thing and the price, l. 1 C. si servus extero. And to say this, i.e., that it cannot be brought, would be against the utility of wards, whose interest it is sometimes to have their things sold, D. de minor. l. et sine § 1. Nor is such a contract made with guardians, D. de evict. l. illud § si. Moreover, this guardian seems able to pay himself, D. de contrah. empt. l. fistulas § fundum; D. de admin. tut. l. quotiens § sicut. If therefore the opportunity of fact is not given, let him sue in court, as we note in another matter, C. de agri. et cens. rust. l. si coloni lib. 11. But these are persuasions.

Let us come to the nature of the cognition of this doubt, and similar ones. And it must be known that certain things are done outside the administration, yet against the administration, as when the guardian steals or gives damage. This is done against that clause, "the ward's property being safe," D. rem pup. sal. fidei l. pe. And in these, which are reduced to the consideration of the administration of the guardianship, and in all reducible to such consideration, the rule is given, 56, that every action which lies for good or bad administration requires the guardianship to be finished, either as to birth, as the action on the guardianship and the account of distribution, and the contrary action on the guardianship; or as to exercise, as the simple action for theft and the Lex Aquilia, when the guardian commits theft against the ward or gives him damage with cause, or is not granted.

But certain things are done so outside the administration that they cannot be reduced to the understanding of good or bad administration, and to the judgments therefore proposed by law; consequently they are extraneous and not adaptable to them. Behold, the ward gives a maxillata to the guardian, or steals the guardian's things, or gives him damage wrongfully; this would not be comprehended by any guardianship judgment. Hence no one would say that these judgments are to be deferred to the end of the guardianship, but a curator being appointed for exercising, C. de in l. dando tut. l. 1; D. de tutel. qui hab. § si pupillus; and Inst. de auct. tut. § fin. Suppose, I have undertaken guardianship, and having undertaken it, the ward was instituted heir, and legacies left to me: the inheritance having been entered upon by the ward with the authority of my co-guardian, I demand the legacy: certainly I can, because it is extraneous to the guardianship and my management. And if your co-guardian has authorized, he has authorized rightly and correctly, l. 1 D. de auct. tut. Suppose, I lend money to my co-guardian in the purchase of lands for the ward, not as guardian, but as a friend; certainly even during the office I shall sue, because in my act the office is not represented. And in sum, that which does not come into the contrary action on the guardianship, can be exercised immediately by the guardian, D. de contr. iud. tutel. l. 1 § in hoc. The gloss therefore of the said l. 2 C. de admin. tut. fails in this one member of the subdivision, i.e., when the act cannot be reduced to the understanding of the guardianship and its remedies, it can be brought immediately for this, D. iud. sol. l. l. 2 § et si quidem. And thus I feel about this point, and conversely, if the guardian becomes debtor to the ward extrinsically, not from a cause reducible to the understanding of the administration, it can be demanded during the guardianship, D. de tut. et rat. dist. l. si pupillus haeres. And thus Decius explains it there, saying "during the guardianship," according to Decius.

Concerning the second point, I say that if it could not be brought by common law on account of the open nature of the business, it would not be necessary to plead an exception, because delay and postponement are inherent in the forms of judgment. It is made by what we note through Bartolus, D. de verb. oblig. l. eum, qui ita § qui ita. And on this it is not expedient to speak further, because it is justly brought, and not excepted, and also by common law. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. It is truly said to be inherent that which arises or is understood by reference to something else.
2. Whether a case that arises through interpretation is included in statutes.
3. Whether statutes speaking of substitutions apply only to express substitutions, or also to tacit ones.
body: Those things are said to be contained truly and properly, which come by way of declaration truly and properly. But those which come by way of supplementation are contained by interpretation not truly and properly. D. de testibus, l. haeredes palam, § si notam; D. de legibus, l. si seruus plurium, § 2. Hence, truly and properly, the guarantor promises the same sentence as the principal debtor, although it is not specified in the instrument of guarantee, except relatively to the instrument of the principal obligation. Hence, the nature of reference, just as the nature of demonstration, is the nature of truth, which appears from the conjunction of writings. And whatever is said to be of the nature of something, seems to be proper. D. de libellis et legatis, l. legaui; D. de verbis obligatorum, l. quae sic stipulatur, quod re mihi; D. de edendo, l. si quis ex argenta, § si initium tabularum; C. de institutionibus et substitutionibus, l. pen.; D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. in testamento quidam. And it is a common doctrine that whatever is contained in the term to which the reference is made, is contained in the referring term at least implicitly. He who explains does nothing new, but uncovers. D. de acquirenda rerum dominium, l. adeo, § cum quis. And he who promises to pay interest, truly and properly promises that true quantity which will be proven. D. de praetoria stipulatione, l. fi; and note in l. certi condictio, in principio; D. si certum petatur. Implicitly, however, it is also said truly and properly that which is said implicitly and generally. And this, which is understood by reference to another, is truly and properly said to be understood. D. de dote praegata, l. Theopompus. And therefore there is no doubt about this. And all allegations tending to this are of the nature of the thing, and from the continuation of two writings there results something true and certain, what kind and how much. D. de verbis obligatorum, l. rati. Nor is the case which comes by interpretation entirely to be excluded in statutes. Hence, if a statute speaks of substitutions, it is also understood to apply to tacit ones; and it is not doubtful that it is understood to apply to express ones as well as implicit ones, because a statute presupposing legal terms and using civil words is understood according to the interpretation of the understanding of those terms, as C. de bonis quae libera, l. non sine. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If the value of the florin has changed, so that it is worth more or less at the time of payment than at the time when restitution ought to be made: whose loss is it?
2. If someone is bound to restore one hundred florins, may he restore their value in silver coinage?
body: 1. The question is as follows: Two hundred florins of good gold, of just weight, were given in dowry. It has now been thirty-three years, or thereabouts. At that time, they were worth three pounds and a half. But now, in the case of the restitution of the dowry upon the death of the husband, they are worth four pounds and fifteen deniers.

It is now asked whether the husband’s heirs are compelled to restore 200 florins at the rate of three and a half pounds, as they were then valued, or whether the said heirs may instead make payment of the said 200 florins at the rate of four pounds and 15 denarii, as the florin is now valued; or even whether the said heirs wish to pay in small coin at the rate of three and a half pounds per florin, as the florin was then valued, especially since it was customary in the city, and was so at that time as well, that small coin could be, and can still be, paid in lieu of the florin owed. It is now asked what the law is: whether this loss falls upon the heirs, who were not, nor are, in default of restoring the said dowry, or whether payment may be made in florins at the rate of four pounds and 15 denarii, as is now the value in the said city where the dowry was given, etc.

† This dowry ought to be restored in florins, because florins are specified in the obligation; and the money itself, in its intrinsic good, is not intrinsic money, but extrinsic, that is, in its estimation and value, as stated in the Digest, title *Si certum petatur*, law *Cum quid*; and in the Digest, title *De solutionibus*, law *Paulus*. Just as with wheat, whose estimation has increased, and with wine and other similar things. But if the very species of the money had been changed, then the time of the contract would be considered, as noted in the last chapter of the Decretals on tithes, in the Clementine. And the aforementioned is true, unless at the time of the contract florins had been given at the rate of a pound for each florin, because that estimation ought to be returned, and not a greater one, just as in any thing given in dowry, estimated at a true estimation, as stated in the Digest, title *De re iudicata*, law *Et si aestimatis*. And thus cautious men, looking to the future, have been accustomed to act. And therefore the tenor of the obligation ought to be diligently observed. The objection does not hold, because it is understood according to custom without prejudice to the creditor, as argued in the Extravagant Decretals, title *De consuetudinibus*, chapter *Cum dilectus*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If a house is bequeathed to one person and the right of habitation to another, whether they may concurrently exercise the right of habitation, or what ought to be done.
body: Point: Whether both concur in the habitation. If habitation is bequeathed to one, and a house to another, Point: Whether both concur in the habitation; or whether the legatee of the habitation may have the key and the lock, so that the other cannot enter the same, etc.

† The right of habitation is common to the lady Angela and to Antony, ff. de usufr. l. Semproniae. And because the ownership of the house has been left to the lady Angela, Antony must give her security for the exercise of habitation according to the discretion of a good man, and Antony may not have a key or a saw by which he might inconvenience his mother or husband, ff. de usu et habit. l. ceterum. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a donation of all goods made to a church is revoked by the birth of a posthumous child.
2. Whether one who possesses emphyteutic goods for a period of fifty years as his own property prescribes against the church.
3. If someone enters a monastery and gives himself and his goods to it, and subsequently fathers a posthumous child, whether the donation is revoked.
body: A certain man donated all his goods to a certain Puctuus, a monastery, and received them back from him in emphyteusis. Then a posthumous son was born to him, who, after the father's death, possessed the said goods for a period of 50 years, as one possessing his own property.

† Now the question arises between him and the monastery. For he says that the said donation, having been followed by an emphyteutic lease, was revoked by operation of law upon the birth of a son: although the said donation cannot properly be termed inofficious, because at the time of the contract it was not inofficious. Considering that, although at that time there was no cause whereby it could be said or held that fraud had been committed, nevertheless it is revoked by virtue of the benefit of the law *Si unquam*, Codex, *De revocatione donationum*, which presumes that in the said case the donor did not have the intention to make a gift. And just as the testament is rendered null by the omission of a posthumous child, so too is a universal donation revoked, Codex, *De pactis*, law *Finis*; and Digest, *Pro socio*, law *Cum duobus*, section *Idem respondit*. And just as a donation of all goods made in fraud of creditors is revoked, even if an oath had been appended, because the reason for an oath to the detriment of a third party operates for nothing, in the Authenticum *De iureiurando praestando*, near the middle; and in chapter *Quamvis*, Extra, *De pactis*, Book 6. Furthermore, it is alleged that the legitime ought to be due immediately, in which case prescription runs against the possessor, as in Digest, *Qui ex causa mortis*, law *Si is*. Furthermore, a tacit remission is presumed in favor of children born, by a certain equity and obligation of the ancients, argument from Digest, *De probationibus*, law *Procula*.

† Moreover, the prescription of forty years is excluded, as in the Authentica de ecclesiis, title 1, § 1, and noted in the Code, ne res dominicae vel templorum, l. universitas. I advised on this point and considered that in the instrument of donation, the donation was not made for the soul, but rather as a pure donation, as noted in the Digest, de pactis, l. si tibi, § si pactum, and in the Decretals, de testamento, c. requisisti. And thus, by the birth of a posthumous child, it is revoked in its entirety by operation of law.

And because a monastery is not considered as a son unless one enters it, in which case it would not be revoked except up to the legitime portion, as stated in the Code, on inofficious testaments, in the authority "Wherefore if a parent." I, Baldus de Perusio.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The cadastre makes the law.
body: It is so, because the payment has been made in a confused manner, and there is no distinct doubt as to how much and for what, nor does the literal form of the statute observe this; and therefore, by the subsequent wording of the statute, circumscribing its meaning, I would say that the tenth was not rightly paid. But this is to be seen and considered, for the estimation of the cadastre is, so to speak, an estimation of the law:

† because the tax register establishes the law. There is another estimation of a person, where the legal estimate ceases to apply. Suppose that someone pays, yet with an insufficient amount: and it seems expressly stated that the payment is valid to the extent that it can be valid, D. de transig. l. et post tres. §. si. Moreover, if the petition is considered, there is a certain element of the petition in which a fact is claimed that was not estimated in the tax register, namely that of the said valvassors and others. For these words can refer to the possessory action, D. quod metus causa l. si mulier. in princ. and bare possession was not estimated in the tax register, D. uti possidetis l. si duo. §. si. And therefore, due to the obscurity of the petition, the bailiffs ought to have estimated everything, and thus the tenth is rightly payable. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a bishop’s constitution, which provides that an instrument of restitution of usury is invalid unless the restitution has been made in the presence of the bishop, is itself valid.
2. Whether a renunciation of usury contained in an instrument proves a true remission of usury.
body: Point: the instrument of restitution is not valid.

Whether the bishop’s constitution is valid, namely that the instrument of restitution of usury is not valid unless a refutation has been made before the bishop; and whether it extends to past cases, etc. The bishop’s constitution has no effect on restitutions made before the said constitution: because constitutions are said to give a rule for the future, not to raise disputes concerning the past, as in C. de legibus et constitutionibus, l. leges; and C. de Decurionibus, l. pe., li. 10; and C. de mandatis, l. ab Anastasio; and C. de testibus, l. testium; and in Auth. de testamento imperfecto, §. j. and penult., no. in proemio, clemen. Moreover, the said constitution is contrary to law, because according to law the said refutation is valid, unless it is proven to have been extorted, simulated, or made in fraud of usury. For in case of doubt, one must stand by the instrument, as in C. de probationibus, l. cum precibus. However, the simulation of fraud could be proven if it were shown that such a money-lender was accustomed to receive such instruments in fraud of usury; or if it were established that such money-lenders commonly employ such a precaution in fraud of usury.

For then the refutation is not valid, except in that which would truly appear to have been discharged, C. mandati. l. per diuersas. C. qui pot. in pigno. ha. l. assiduis. C. de donat. ante nup. Auth. sed iam necesse. in Auth. de aequali. do. §. aliud. C. de sac. sanc. eccl. Auth hoc ius porrectum. in fi. nor can the bishop make a general law against the constitutions of the Pope and the Emperor, as C. de offi. Praefe. pręto. l. norma. ff. de fer. l. j. §. j. and no. in c. vlt. de appel. lib. 6 in nouell. per quas rationes if nothing else appears, I think the refutation to be sufficient, and this is accustomed to be noted in c. peccatum. extra, de iureiur. lib. 6. it would be absurd to say that the bishop by his constitution could prohibit the notary from exercising the office which he has from the Prince, as C. de crimi. sacrile. l. instar. unless, as I said, if it appeared that there was a frequency of such acts in fraud of usury. and then, as I said above, granted that the constitution held in future cases, it would not hold in past ones, and in that case, in which the refutation would not be valid, the confessed money could not be claimed back, nor recovered as unduly paid: because such an instrument would not make faith etc. I, Bal.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If the husband confessed in one instrument that he had received two hundred florins as part of the dowry, and in another instrument confessed that he had received three hundred for the dowry, what will be the wife’s dowry? And which of these instruments will be given credence, since they are of different dates?
body: In the year of our Lord 1366, on the 4th day of January, in which instrument was made, it is contained that Raynerius and Franciscus, brothers, and others, certain John Guidarelli of the city of Castello, were confessed and content that they had had and received from the notable man John Guiducci, lord John, Marquis of Montefeltro, for the dowry and in the name of the dowry of the noble maiden Antonina de Ventiolis, that quantity of money: and in that manner and form, as is declared by Lord Branchaleone, knight, noble of the Guelferi, Jacobus Pater Gratiae, and Ser Andrea Lippi, etc. And having seen the instrument immediately following, in which it is contained that the aforementioned Raynerius and Franciscus were confessed to have had and received from the said Marquis, for the part of Andrea’s dowry and declaration to be made, 200 gold florins. And having seen another instrument made in the year of our Lord 1370, by which it is provided that the said Raynerius, in his own name and that of his brother Franciscus, made a settlement and renunciation to the noble man John Guiducci, Marquis, of three hundred and fifty gold florins, which the said John and Lady Petrucia, his mother, were bound to give in the name and cause of the dowry of the said Lady Mina, according to the testament made by Guiducci, Marquis, the question arises whether the said Lady Mina ought to have only 350 gold florins, or rather five hundred and fifty gold florins. And having seen the said instruments, and considering the various quantities, and that in the first promise of the dowry there is no mention of any testament of the dowry of the said Lady Mina being and amounting to five hundred and fifty gold florins, it is to be restored: especially because by the disposition of the law these things are proved, D. de probat. l. quinquaginta; D. de dote praeg. l. si; D. de adm. leg. l. cum centum; and that not in l. ne casu, eod. de discussoribus, lib. 10; and C. de do. promiss. l. si. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Of what the depositary of a deposit of money is held liable.
2. Whether a sudden attack by robbers is to be attributed to fortuitous event.
body: 1. Whenever money is deposited

† It is evident that, according to 1 Ius Civile, whenever money is deposited or an act is performed, either the same amount is to be returned, or the very same body of coins is to be restored; or it is reasonably doubtful what was agreed upon. In the first case, the debtor is not released by the loss of the money, because this goes beyond the well-known limits of deposit. In the second and third cases, the debtor is released, because only fraud and gross negligence are liable, as stated in the Digest, under the title "Deposit," in the cases of "Lucius" and "What Nerva said." And because in our case it has not been proven that anything was done according to the nature of deposit, in case of doubt it must be presumed against the nature of the contract; and thus only fraud and gross negligence are liable. Moreover, the counting has not been proven as a counting, but only to demonstrate what was in the purse, as stated in the Digest, under the title "Usufruct," in the case "But if someone stipulates," § "If they are not in the bag." Otherwise, it is beyond the law; let us still see if the case is proven. And it must be said that it is, by the argument from commonly occurring events.

† because in the sudden onslaught of robbers and tyrannical invasion, the foresight and counsel of the mind fail: even assuming that the most diligent men save their money, such diligence is not required of a depositary, as stated in the aforementioned law *Quod Nerua*; nor is it presumed that he preserved the deposited money rather than his own, as in the Code, title *De communi*, law 1. And therefore, an acquittal should be rendered. And this I say having seen, examined, and scrutinized all the acts and proceedings in the case. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A dying brother cannot, with the consent of his surviving brother, make a will regarding his share of the emphyteutic lease, which was held in common by himself and his brother.
2. Any executor of a usurer's testament appears to have the power to restore the usury in full, even if the others are negligent or unwilling.
body: † It appears to be expressly stated in the Digest, *Qui autem in rem suam* (D. 20.1), § *Sicut*, under the heading *De pignoratitia actione* (D. 20.1), that one who dies first may make a will regarding the consent of the brother to whom the emphyteusis ought to revert, the other brother having predeceased. To the contrary effect is the Digest, *De legatis tertio* (D. 35.2), *Cum quis decedens*, in the principal part. I believe this latter view to be more correct, because the consent, at the time it was given, had no right in that which the brother bequeathed by will. I speak of the portion of the dying brother, who appears to have disposed of a right by will, although it expired by reason of death; and thus the legacy failed, as in the Code, *De legatis* (C.

† On another point, I say that each executor appears to have a mandate in solidum to pay usury when the other is negligent. This operates in favor of the soul, as we say regarding pious causes. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The mother excludes the grandmother.
2. Particular heirs do not deduct the Trebellian portion.
body: It is well known that Margaret, as mother, succeeds her son. 9. In the first points of Bruna and Margaret.

It must be said that Margaret, as the mother, succeeds her son intestate, to the exclusion of Bruna, the grandmother; because Margaret is preferred in degree, as is stated in the Code, *ad Tertullianum*, in the authority *Defuncto*. However, it is true that, on account of the substitution made in favor of James, the said Margaret does not succeed except to the legitime, that is, to one-third of the goods of Andrew. If anything remained above the legitime of Andrioli, she ought to have it by virtue of the substitution, provided that it is rightly considered that it was repeated in the codicils by a general clause of confirmation of the will. This is proven in the Authenticum *De restitutionibus* and in the law *Ea quae parit*, § *Quamobrem*.

† Concerning the Trebellianic action, however, it is not necessary to treat here, because the aforementioned daughters were particular heirs, not universal ones, as in D. ad Trebellianum, l. Mulier, §. Ut Trebellianum. From this appears the response to the second point, because concerning the whole of that which pertains to the said Bruna, the said Bruna could make a will, and it pertains to the monastery both by reason of the person of the nun and by reason of the express substitution, as in Auth. de sancta Ecclesia, §. Sed hoc praesenti. And it is proven in D. de probationibus, c. In praesentia. And in Q. 18, c. Statutum. On the other point concerning the carnal brothers of the said A., it must be said that the daughters of the said Blasius succeed by right to their maternal grandfather, to the exclusion of the carnal brothers. And this for the reason that in intestate succession the cause of children is prior, as in Auth. de haeredibus ab intestato, in principio. And in Inst. de haeredibus ab intestato, §. Cum filius. And thus I say and counsel, I, Baldus of Perugia, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, and when, one is held liable, or not, for accidental homicide.
2. What constitutes the slightest fault, and whether it is punished.
body: After the aforementioned acts have been diligently examined, and the matters in question have been investigated, or if nothing is found in any of them,

† I, having examined the facts and the inquiries made, or any of them, find no cause for condemnation, nor any fault; because even the slightest fault is excused in one who does all that any diligent person would have done, as is stated in the laws and notes of the Digest, under the title *De locato conducto*; in the law *Si merces*, section *Qui calumniam*; and in the Digest, under the title *Ad legem Aquiliam*, in the law *Si putator*. But these men, Druciolus, Josus, and Spumacolus, acted according to what any diligent person would have done in such work, both in fitting the scaffold and binding it carefully, and in giving warning. And although one stone fell, this is rather to be attributed to chance and fortune than to fault; indeed, if fault could be attributed, it would lie with the one who did not keep his eyes below, nor look out from above; as cautious and diligent men do and have done, who ought to consider that an accident could easily occur, and not place themselves too much at risk, as in the Digest, under the title *De locato conducto*, in the law *Si ut certo*, section *Sed interdum*, subsection *Non et si servum*. For it is impossible to foresee all the accidents of fortune. And it is relevant to the Digest, under the title *De his qui deiecerunt vel effuderunt*, in the law 1, section *Summa cum utilitate*, subsection *Ceterum*. Moreover, these men were engaged in a lawful activity, as in the Digest, under the title *De rei venditione*, in the law *In rem*, section *Tignum*. And from those who engage in a lawful activity, any fault is presumed absent, unless the contrary is proven, as in the Decretals, under the title *De homicidio*, in the chapter *Dilectus*; and in the chapter *Ex bonis*; and in the chapter *Tua nos*, where it says, "he applied the diligence he ought to have applied," etc. And to this point, the present testimony of the one who died is of great weight, as in the Decretals, under the title *De homicidio*, in the chapter *Exhibitum*.

†Moreover, because the slightest fault, which is a certain inadvertence, ceases for the reasons aforementioned, and also because under the common law the slightest fault is not punished criminally, and especially not severely, as noted by Cynus in C. de episc. et cler., l. si quis non dicam rapere; nevertheless, I do not base my opinion on this last point due to the general wording of the statute. Rather, I base it on the innocence of mind, and because they were engaged in a lawful activity; and because such a case rarely, and very rarely, is accustomed to occur; and because fortune happened at such a time that those who were below in the bottom of the well could and ought to have taken care of themselves. Therefore, in the aforementioned findings, no fault is found, because all the caution was observed that is accustomed to be observed by anyone diligent, as is notorious to practitioners of the said art. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a dowry advanced by the father always returns to him, provided that children are still living, whether he stipulated for its restitution or not; and whether the wife predeceases the husband, or vice versa.
2. A husband and wife may acquire a right in rem in the same instrument, even if the price is presumed to have been paid from the husband’s funds.
body: As to the opinions, whether a dowry brought by the father returns to the father, it must be said at the first point,

† Although there are various opinions in Bologna as to whether a dowry provided by the father ought to return to the father when children exist, nevertheless, where the father has expressly stipulated for the case of existing children, there is no doubt that the stipulation is valid if the husband dies first, as noted in C. soluto matrimonio, l. dos a patre. When the husband dies first and the daughter remains in the power of the one who provided the dowry, then it may be reasonably doubted. For the agreement does not seem to be valid, since the father is bound to restore the dowry reserved for his daughter, as in l. unica, which begins “rem in praesenti,” § sed quamvis, joined with the gloss on the word “dotis” in C. de rei uxoriae actione. Hence, in this law, it appears that the sons and daughters succeed, as in l. qui filios, ff. de ritu nuptiarum. To the contrary, it seems that the last law in C. communia utriusque iudicii applies. Solution: If the father dies first, then the daughter, and at that time the action of the daughter consolidates with that of her sons, as in the aforementioned l. unica, which begins “rem in praesenti,” § viduas; or if the daughter dies first, then the dowry returns to the father and to his heirs by virtue of the stipulation interposed. And therefore, since Nicollela died first, before Tanus, the said dowry pertains to Obira, heir of Tanus.

† Regarding the second doubt, it should be known that a husband and wife can validly acquire a right in rem in the same thing by means of the same instrument, as is stated in the Digest, *de fide instrumentorum*, in the law *scripturae*. Nevertheless, it is presumed that the price thus paid by the wife was paid from the husband’s money, and from that of Maximus to the stepmother; and therefore, if Tanus and his second wife purchased the property, it is presumed that the entire purchase was made with the husband’s money. And thus, the said price is to be paid to the daughters of the said Tanus, especially since the husband, if any donation was made tacitly, has revoked it, as provided in the law *quintus*, in the Digest, *de donationibus inter virum et uxorem*; and in the law *si non sortem*, section *si centum*, in the Digest, *de conditione indebiti*, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If a husband confessed that he had received a dowry from the father of his wife, which he promised to the father, stipulating on behalf of his daughter, to restore to the same father and to his heirs, etc. Shortly thereafter, the father, in his own name, not in the name of his daughter, promised the said husband a dowry, notwithstanding the aforementioned confession. After the father subsequently died, the husband dies, who bequeathed to his wife 10 [units] above the dowry. Thirty years elapse, during which neither the dowry nor the legacy is claimed. Now it is asked what and how much can be claimed.
1. Bad faith, presumed by legal fiction, does not impede the prescription of the legitimate period, even according to canon law.
body: VITIIl, having promised to the party receiving the daughter, and having confessed that he had received from the father of the woman the dowry, VITIIl, having promised to the party receiving the daughter, and to her heirs, to return and restore in every case and event the dowry to be restored, then immediately another instrument was made, in which the father, in his own name, and not in the name of the daughter, promised to the husband the said dowry, notwithstanding the aforesaid confession. The marriage having been contracted, finally, the father having died, the husband, coming to death, bequeathed to his said wife 10 pounds above the dowry. The husband having died, the said dowry and legacies were not claimed, and 30 years and more have elapsed.

† It is asked whether, and what, can be claimed. And it seems that the said dowry cannot be claimed. And I argue thus: this dowry was not truly paid, as appears from the conjunction of both instruments made in the same place, and almost in the same context. If it was not paid, therefore it ought not to be restored, as C. de dote cauta, l. si; and ff. si certum petatur, l. qui pecuniam. Secondly, this is proven because the father, by not paying, was in default and in bad faith, as ff. mandatum, l. dolus; C. de iure dotium, l. si, §. utranque. But the father’s bad faith regarding the dowry harms the daughter, as ff. solutione matrimonii, l. Mevia, §. fundus. Thirdly, because the father’s confession in the same dowry contract, or immediately thereafter, harms the daughter, as ff. solutione matrimonii, l. quotiens; and C. de pactis dotalibus, l. ex morte; and l. rem in praesenti, §. accedit; C. de rei uxoriae actione; and ff. de iure dotium, l. adoptivum. But the father was, and is, confessed to have not counted out the money: and he confessed immediately. And those things which are done immediately are deemed to be inherent; therefore, etc. Fourthly, because in a legacy of dowry there is contained nothing but the restoration of the father: and it is valid on account of the usurious interest, as Inst. de legatis, §. si vitori; and ff. ad legem Falcidiam, l. sed usufructu, §. dos. But here it would be valid even though it was not counted out; therefore, etc. Fifthly, and lastly, this is proven, for if someone were to confess that he had borrowed 10 from me on loan, and afterwards, notwithstanding the said confession, I promise to lend to him, from this second contract there arises proof that the first confession was made in hope of future payment. To this contributes what is noted in a similar case in ff. si certum petatur, l. certi condictio, §. si nummos.

On the contrary, it seems that the first confession and promise of restitution is a perfect act, and is an absolute and perfect instrument in itself. Therefore, whatever the father does afterwards does not prejudice the daughter, because the father cannot repent to the prejudice of the daughter, and much less the husband. For whether it is considered with respect to the father, as a donation, repentance has no place in a dowry, as ff. familiae erciscundae, l. Pomponius, Philadelphus. Or whether it is considered with respect to the husband, as a stipulation of a certain thing, repentance has much less place, because it is settled that provision has been made by stipulation, as Inst. de verbis obligationibus, in fine; C. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. sicut. Secondly, this is proven because the father is deemed to have counted out the money, given an external promisor, as ff. mandatum, l. inter causas, §. abesse; and ff. de fideiussoribus, l. qui satisdare. Thirdly, the same, if he himself promised, so that the promise is in place of the final cause of the first contract, although the counting out does not follow. Thirdly, this is proven by l. penult., §. si vir sacro, ff. solutione matrimonii, where it is said that whether he released the promisor by law, nevertheless he is bound to the restitution of the dowry. And the same is held there by Lauro de Arezzo and Bartolus. Fourthly, this is proven because the daughter is understood to be dowered, even by promise alone, as d. l. rem in praesenti, §. accedit; and what is noted in C. de legatis, l. filia legatorum; and l. penult. de collatione dotium. Therefore, since the dowry is left to her by legacy, the promised quantity is contained. Fifthly, and lastly, it seems expressly stated in l. si, §. 1, ff. de dote praedata, according to one reading.

Consider that sometimes a dowry is truly counted out, sometimes interpretatively, sometimes neither truly nor interpretatively. The first case is discussed in §. si uxori, cum sequentibus. The second case is the same, and this is our case: because the subscription by the promisor is interpretatively deemed to be counted out. The third case, if the counting out is to be made by the wife, it seems that a release is left to her. Or if it was to be made by another, it seems that the name of the debtor is left to the wife: as these are proven. ff. de usufructu, l. quotiens, §. si colono; and l. socer, §. 1, ff. solutione matrimonii. For the husband, by leaving a dowry, which is a name signifying a right, seems to leave only the right which he has: as ff. de legatis 2, l. Mevio, §. Aniae. Hence, not departing from Lauro de Arezzo, I say that if time permitted, the dowry could be claimed. But because time does not permit. For neither can a legacy be accepted after 30 years, nor can acceptance be claimed. It follows that a certain dowry cannot be claimed. It is considered that the heir is presumed to be in bad faith, and by canon law a possessor in bad faith does not prescribe: because all that is not from faith is sin: as Extra de praescriptionibus, c. quoniam omne quicquid. Bartolus says otherwise on this, and wrongly. ff. de usucapione, l. si quid, §. si viam.

† Nevertheless, presumed bad faith does not, by legal fiction, prevent the prescription of the legitimate time, if this is also the case according to canon law, as noted by Dy. in c. malaefidei possessor, de re iudicata, lib. 6. Moreover, because unless the heir is certain of the acknowledgment of the legacy, he is not certain, as noted in de debito; for in legacies, as regards inducing a personal obligation, acknowledgment of the legacy is required. And these are sufficiently notable points, and the penultimate law of dote praelegata must be understood when a certain quantity is bequeathed by name as dowry: for example, ten, whether it is certain in itself or by reference to another; because she bequeaths to her wife the quantities contained in the dotal instruments. For whether it is an instrument of dowry paid or of dowry promised, that quantity ought to be bequeathed to him, as in l. cum scriptum. Indeed, I say more, even if the instrument were simulated; because in this case the mere appearance of the writing suffices, as in ff. de verbis oblig., l. si diuortio. Now we have the understanding of the aforementioned notable laws. By this it is clear what is the law. And concerning the dowry, principally and delegated in the final cause. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the course of fatal errors avails the appellant, such that he cannot plead nullity.
2. Whether the rector of a province, for example of a March or a Duchy, may commit a cause simply and summarily, and de plano, to a simple president; and whether he may commit a cause at the definitive stage to judges other than the ordinary ones. And number 3.
3. Assuming that the sentence cannot be said to be null in any way, whether it can be said to be null because the legation did not hold.
body: I. In the case of Calla Minoris Caruli de Malatestis, pending before the Magnificent Prince, and in the case of Calla Minoris Caruli de Malatestis between Count Bandinus and Count of Carpieti on one part, and the men and commune of the Castle of Castellatio on the other, in the matter of the regulation of boundaries, these doubts arise: first, whether the lapse of the fatal periods prejudices the appellant, inasmuch as he may plead nullity, having regard to the constitution of the Church under the rubric "How procedure is to be conducted in cases of appeal," in which constitution certain fatal periods are granted. And afterwards it is added in the text of the said constitution in this form: "All these fatal periods begin from the day of the appeal or of the complaint of nullity, etc." And also that after the said fatal periods have elapsed, the cause is understood to be entirely abandoned. And presupposing that the procedure is null on account of the judicial order not being observed, inasmuch as the case was not contested.

† On this point, I say that although one cannot bring an action for nullity, nevertheless such a sentence cannot be put into execution once the nullity is established from the very acts upon which the petition for execution of the sentence must principally be based, and this is proven by the following reason. This sentence ought to be put into execution by the judge from whom it issued, if he is an ordinary judge, or by a delegate, if the one who judged was a delegate. But the latter, seeing that the sentence of his delegate is null, cannot execute it even if no one objects, nor could one object on the ground of nullity, as noted in a similar case in C. de transac., l. ubi pactum. And if he were to execute it, an appeal could be taken from the grievance.

Secondly, it is asked whether the governor of a province, for example of the March of the Duchy or of Romagna, by the simple authority of his office can commit a cause to be tried summarily and de plano; and I say that he cannot, because he himself cannot so proceed. Therefore, he cannot give to another an authority which he himself does not have, as appears in the text, l. quaest. 7, cap. Dyabertum.

† Thirdly, it is asked whether the ruler of the Duchy, by virtue of his simple office of governance, may commit an appeal from a definitive judgment to judges other than the ordinary judges. It must be said that he may not, because the constitution prohibits it. Hence, since the delegation of cases pertains to the magistrate by right, whatever is prohibited in this regard is due to jurisdiction being taken away—or, to speak more accurately, not granted: as stated in the Code, *De iudiciis*, in the authenticum *Ad haec*.

Fourthly, it is asked, assuming that the judgment cannot be said to be null in any way, whether it can be said to be null if the delegation does not hold. And it must be said that yes, because it does not have the name of a judgment, as if someone to whom no commission had been made had judged, as noted in c. 1. de sequestro posito in the Clementines and C. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, l. priuatorum. I, Baldo de Perusio.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a statute of origin prohibiting a woman having sons or daughters from making a will or codicil, or from entering into any contract with persons other than her children, binds a woman subject to the enactors by reason of her origin, although she is married elsewhere. Likewise, whether such a statute is valid and excludes daughters. And number 2.
2. A statute is not valid which provides that a father or grandfather may not leave the legitime to a daughter or granddaughter.
3. The masculine gender includes the feminine in matters that are favorable.
body: Premises being these: No woman having sons, or if the words of the statute provide under this form, no woman having sons or daughters through a son may make a will, a codicil, or any contract outside the persons of her children; and if she does otherwise, the will, codicils, and contracts are null by operation of law. It happened that Lady Sciphania, by origin from Viterbo and married to a man from Baschi, made a will, in which, among other things, she instituted her son Francis and the said late Lord Rayner, her husband, as heirs to one-third of her inheritance and goods, and she instituted three of her granddaughters through Joanna, the late daughter of the said Lady Sciphania, as heirs to the two remaining parts. And she made this, and the said Lady Sciphania died.

It is now asked whether the said will is valid. And it seems that it is not, because by the law of Viterbo, her place of origin, she is not prohibited from making a will, because the truth of nature is not erased by the image of marriage; for whatever adheres to origin is inseparable. As stated in D. 50.2.1 (*Assumptio*) and D. 49.15.24.2 (*In bello*, § *Factae*). Indeed, the truth of nature cannot be changed even by the authority of the Senate. As stated in D. 7.1.1 and D. 7.1.2 (*De usu fructu*) and D. 1.12 (*De rerum quae usu consueant*). Since she is subject by reason of her origin, therefore the statute is valid with respect to her person. Moreover, she remains subject with respect to the goods which have the force of the author’s origin, as stated in C. 5.39.1 (*De mulieribus*) and in the same place, Book 12. Therefore, with respect to such goods, the statute is valid. For if a soldier’s will can be valid on account of certain goods, so also can the disposition of the law, as noted by the doctors in C. 1.1.1 (*Cunctos populos*, *De summa trinitate et fide catholica*). Moreover, this woman was previously subject to the statute when she was married, and therefore marriage does not release her from the bond of the statute. Argument from D. 50.2.1 (*Incola*, *Ad municipalia*). Moreover, a married woman is not released from the father’s power. As noted in C. 8.40.1 (*Si uxor*, *De conditionibus insertis*). Although she has married, she nevertheless retains the rights of her homeland. Just as a patron who did not consent to the marriage does not release the freedwoman, unless he consented, as stated in C. 7.7.1 (*Quod ex liberta*, *De bonis libertorum*). Moreover, to make a statute is not a matter of contentious jurisdiction, but is a kind of prohibition in itself, as stated in D. 21.1.1 (*Sciendum*, *De aedilicio edicto*). And no law provides that one is exempted or released from such a prohibition by marriage; therefore, she remains subject to the statute.

On the contrary, it seems that through marriage the right of origin is changed. As noted in C. 10.32.1 (*Origine*, *De municipiis et originibus*). And it is a certain novation and transumption, as stated in D. 2.1.1 (*Cum quaedam puella*, *De iurisdictione omnium iudicum*). Moreover, she is not bound to obey the forum of her origin. As stated in D. 50.2.1 (*De iure*, *Ad municipalia*). Moreover, this statute disposes with respect to the person, but in this respect she is not subject to her origin. As noted in the aforementioned C. 5.39.1 (*De mulieribus*) and in the same place. And the same applies to a widow as to a married woman. As stated in D. 50.2.1 (*Foeminae*, *De senatoribus*).

Solution. On this point, it must be said that the statute appears to dispose differently, by expressly stating one thing and tacitly conferring another with respect to the sons, in whose favor it disposes. As stated in D. 36.2.1 (*Qui filium*, *Ad Trebellianum*, in the beginning). Hence, in this respect, the statute is valid with respect to the goods which are within its territory. As stated in C. 10.32.1 (*Non licere habitatoribus Metropolitanae*, Book 11). Assuming this to be so, nevertheless in our case the statute does not prohibit making a will in favor of the granddaughter, because she is not said to be outside the sons, whom she instituted as heirs. As stated in C. 8.40.1 (*De conditionibus insertis*) and as noted in D. 24.3.1 (*Si dotali*, *Solutis matrimonii*). For since the inheritance is due to her, it would be contrary to natural reason to say that it could not be left to her. As stated in D. 33.7.1 (*Cuius ratio*, *De bonis damnatorum*).

For the statute does not seem to have weighed the natural sex [of the children] in the charity to be shown toward children, when it says “having sons or daughters.” Behold, the female sex [is included]; yet I do not know whether the wording of the statute is corrupt, because if it were said “having sons or daughters through a son,” then the statute would speak more precisely to the effect of exclusion, since it would weigh the male sex, as is weighed in many cases, as in D. 1.5.1, l. in multis; and D. 1.5.2, de media iuris prudentia, this was formerly the case, as appears in C. 5.27.1, l. maximum vitium; and Inst. 3.1.2, § item vetustas. But it seems unjust to say that a mother cannot institute a daughter or granddaughter. And perhaps if the statute expressly intended this, it could not do so, because it would be contrary to natural law. And suppose a mother has a son and a daughter, and the father died penniless; the mother wishes to make a will, because perhaps she wishes to leave something to pious causes and for the necessity of the salvation of her soul. And she wishes something to be left to the daughter so that she may not beg. If the statute is understood as the word sounds, the daughter, being female, will be forced to beg. For the institution would not be valid, if we attend to the literal surface of the statute. For I say that in the lands of the Church, in which lands statutes that are altogether unjust and contrary to all natural reason are not valid, and which the Pope would in no way confirm, either such a statute is invalid, or it must be understood soundly and supplied by means of natural reason. And Lord Dy. holds this in c. Indultum.

† That a statute is invalid which provides that a father or grandfather may not leave the legitime to a daughter or grandson. Rather, it is even more invalid if it were stated that he is not bound to leave it. And the same is held by Cynus, C. de nuptiis, l. sancimus.

† Moreover, the masculine term encompasses the feminine in a favorable act. Hence, a statute enacted in favor of sons, without mention of daughters or grandchildren, includes women neither for nor against their interest, but not to their detriment. As stated in D. de vend. in poss. mitt. l. 1, § 4. From these authorities it is concluded that either the statute is invalid in this case, or, by just interpretation, it must be understood that under the term “sons” are included, in addition to male children, female children as well. The same applies to contracts concerning children. This is proven by the conjunction of two laws: C. fam. ercisc. l. fin. and C. de testam. l. hac consultissima, § ex imperfecto. For nature is favorable and, by natural law, common. As stated in Auth. de testam. imperfectis, near the beginning. From these authorities I conclude that the will is just and, in accordance with the aforementioned natural equity, made by the said Lady Sciphania, and must be upheld. It is not necessary to speak of another point, because what I have said is true and equitable, so that no injustice may occur regarding children. As stated in C. de episc. et cleric. Auth. nunc autem. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The seller is bound to three things to the buyer, when things are sold for a debt by the creditor, or by a public official.
2. What is meant by a proper cause.
3. Whether anyone is compelled to testify against himself in a proper cause.
body: and to the evening judge, or another official, pu-

† When goods are sold by a creditor for a debt, before a judge or another public official, for the benefit of the creditor, such creditor is bound to defend the buyer in two respects. First, if a dispute arises concerning the buyer, he must declare himself to be the creditor. Second, because he must prove that he has priority over others, if perhaps there were several creditors holding a hypothec. He is also bound, thirdly, to everything that he expressly promised to the buyer. See Codex, "That the creditor ought not to warrant against eviction of the pledge," l. 1. And this is the first point to be premised for clarity. The second is that the act of the judge represents the act of the party. See Codex, de evictionibus, l. si ob causam; and the same applies to anyone selling by public authority. Thirdly, it must be premised that anyone who receives the price by consenting to the seller is bound to the defense of the thing sold. See Digest, de evictionibus, l. quidam ex parte; and note Digest, de regulis iuris, l. aliud est vendere.

Fourthly, it must be premised that a cause is said to be one’s own when a benefit or detriment pertains, or can pertain, to someone. See Digest 44.1.1, § in propria. Fifthly and lastly, it must be premised that,

† That no one is compelled to testify against himself in his own case. For if he will not be compelled against his patron and certain relatives, much less against himself, as in the Digest, On Witnesses, law Iulia. Likewise, he will not be compelled to produce evidence against himself, as in the Code, On Producing, law Ipse despice; and in the Decretals, On Proof, chapter 1; and more clearly in the same title, chapter 2. And this is the rule generally stated: Code, On Producing, law Qui accusare; and law Si; Code, On Proof, law Actor. Likewise, if anyone could be reduced to the position of a witness or deponent for himself, and would not be believed either for or against himself, then he would have to prove his own calumny, and perjury, if he had sworn an oath of calumny, and the matter would be captious, by which he could only be ensnared. And the offices of persons would also be confused for him in judicial proceedings, because the office of a witness is different from that of a litigant, as in the Decretals, On the Signification of Words, chapter Forus, section In omni quoque; and in the Decretals, On Witnesses, chapter In omni; and in the Decretals, On Fideicommissa, law Quaestionem. And this is clear from the general rule: Code, On Witnesses, law Omnibus. And it is not expedient to dwell further on these points, because they are general matters, and error is rash in general rules.

Having examined the aforementioned points thirdly, it must be said without doubt that the said Lady Maya, and especially because she expressly obligated herself, as appears to the careful reader of the instrument in the word there: "And the said Maya is not compelled to testify in the said case of her own accord." It does not obstruct this that the law and notes in the Digest, On Regulating Boundaries, law Eos, are cited, because this is solved there in the ordinary gloss. Likewise, it does not obstruct the argument made to the contrary from the case of a simple procurator, because that is irrelevant, since he is outside the office and outside the prejudice. But this Lady Maya is under an obligation and under a prejudice, as in the Code, Where an Action in Rem Lies, law 1; and in the Digest, On Judges, law Venditor. And therefore Lord Adrian judged rightly and correctly, and otherwise he could not have judged according to law. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How burdens and assessments are to be imposed.
2. Whether a non-resident owner of immovable property is bound to burdens and assessments.
body: In the case of Calla, the action was brought against her; regarding this reception into the Castilians, three things are to be considered.

For, first, in the case of Calla, the reception itself into the citizens of Castillanos, so called because they bear public burdens by sharing with others in that place or city, is considered. As stated in l. 1, ff. ad municipalia. Secondly, I consider the act and the form of the promise: because these individuals from the castle of Carni, holding possessions, etc., promised to pay the said individual tithes to be imposed, just as others of the land of Maleani do, as if they were their own natural properties. As stated in ff. de verbis obligatorum, l. quidam cum filium. I also consider a third point, that this method of imposing the tax was also introduced among the original inhabitants of Maleani regarding the public burdens, which are imposed on persons for things, and which should be imposed according to the quantity of their patrimony. Another method has been superimposed. As stated in ff. de muneribus et honoribus, l. ex scripto, §. enim, where it is said that an estimate should be made there according to the estimate, unless they were personal burdens, which are imposed only on those with obligations. As stated in C. de immunitatibus non concedendis, l. fin., lib. 10. This is supported by what is noted in l. 1, §. quibus, ff. quod cuiusque universitatis, and de senatu et excommunicatione, c. grauem, per Innocentius. Hence, it can be said from equity that those who have little should not be burdened except proportionally, just as those who have nothing should not be burdened at all, even though they have been received as citizens, they should still be treated with them. As noted in C. de annona et tributo, l. in dictiones, lib. 10, l. ubi expressum, and C. ut nemini liceat in emptione specierum, l. unica, eo. lib. Therefore, when it says, "by which each portion has come to be," nevertheless, strictly speaking, I say, considering the said promise, that if those who knew the ordinances in the castle of Maleani, which are for the most part of greater liberality, and that the ordinance is not valid, especially to the prejudice of foreigners, because it is an unjust statute by reason of the statute itself and by reason of the legislators, who deal with their own benefit. As stated in extra de constitutionibus, c. cum omnes. Otherwise, if the said statute had been made for some short time due to sudden necessities of the castle of Maleani, and not in perpetuity, during such necessity, that statute would be valid and would bind those who were received as citizens of the castle of Maleani.

† Otherwise, if a foreigner possessed something there, who was not a guarantor, nor entered in their book: because the statute could not bind him except according to the quality of the thing possessed and the revenues, because the levies must be assessed against him by those who collect the revenues, according to the quantity and quality of the revenues. As in D. de usufructu, l. si pendentes, § si quid. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that whoever fails to pay the tax on saffron shall forfeit the saffron and incur the penalty: what if the tax collector reached an agreement with the carrier, who nevertheless did not pay the amount promised in the agreement? May the tax collector demand the penalty?
2. One who fails to pay the tax out of simplicity does not incur the penalty; otherwise, if done fraudulently.
body: It is alleged that the city of Perugia imposed a tax of 3 lib. of saffron, or of saffron from his own stock, collected in the castle of the parish. And he sold that saffron in Perugia. And because it is said that he extracted it contrary to the duty by not paying, afterwards within three days from the day of the agreement made with the tax collectors, because the tax collectors, who ought to have had perhaps five denarii, made an agreement with the said Benuenuto for 10 and 9 solidi, afterwards they took for themselves four florins from the fact that the said Benuenuto remained in the city of Perugia for several days, when he had already returned to the castle of the parish within the term of three days, which was the agreed term.

It is asked whether the said tax collectors could extort the said four florins. And it seems that they could, because although the tax statutes are harsh and contrary to all equity, nevertheless the law, however hard, must be observed. L. *prospexit*, D. *qui et a quibus unde*; for on account of one merchant defrauding, the entire ship is confiscated, as in C. *de nautico feno*, L. *cum proponas*. On the contrary, it seems that they could not, because the statute does not speak of a hundredweight of saffron.
