Hence, although the tax ought to be paid pro rata, and thus if it is not paid within three days, the penalty is incurred, L. *librarum pro rata*; nevertheless, since afterwards the tax collectors came to an agreement and accepted 19 solidi, they appear to have compromised. And therefore they labored in vain regarding the other penalty, as in D. *si quis cautionem*, L. 2, § 1. And because this person did not commit fraud, but rather acknowledged good faith, nevertheless he could not be restored sooner, as in D. *de publicanis*, L. *Caesar*. But the better reason is: because the statute requires that if he has extracted, exported, or passed contrary to the form of the statute, and conjunctively adds, and has not paid. And therefore it must be conjunctive. For in penalties, although one thing is contrary to the form of the statute, if it is not paid; nevertheless, because they carry their saffron to sell, it is not contrary to the form of the statute, because although the tax is not paid, nevertheless he does not fall into the penalty of the constitution. But it is required that it be extracted contrary to the form of the statute, as in D. *vi bonorum raptorum*, L. *praetor*, § *decem*. In this case, however, and similar ones, one must adhere to custom, and where it would be done in fraud, it would be equitable that every fraud be punished.
But where it is done out of simplicity, or some impediment occurs, then these are extortions, and they are not to be tolerated by superiors. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a will is valid, in which a legacy is left to a rich person, and not to a needy one, in which the solemnity has not been observed, although it is said that the legacy is left for the soul and for pious causes.
body: Testament. C. de testam. l. hac consultis

† regarding which it is inquired, was not valid. Testamentum C. de testamento, l. hac consultissima, in principio, and § ex imperfecto, and l. si unus, and Institutiones de testamento, § 1, and C. de fideiussoribus, l. si veritas, and C. de codicillis, l. si, § si. Nor does it obstruct if it is said that he had left to Jacobutio out of love for God and for the soul, because these words effect nothing, considering that it was left to a man who does not suffer from poverty, but had goods and earned a certain portion of the dowry, as noted in C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, l. illud, and l. si forte, de castrensi peculio. Nor does it avail to simulate poverty, C. de mendicantibus validis, l. 1. And therefore Abundantia was put in possession as heir ab intestato. Moreover, what was left to Jacobutio is not valid by the law of wills, nor by the law of codicils, due to the defect in the number of witnesses. The Church, although it could have left to the church before two witnesses, and even women, and not formally requested, about which, however, there is great doubt, considering that many inconveniences and contradictions in law would concur regarding the number and quality of witnesses and the formal request. Although in codicils it is not necessary that they be formally requested, nevertheless, during the lifetime of Jacobutio, it has no right. And thus it is not admitted. However, it obstructs others, as l. 3, § viri, ff. de usufructu legato. For I say that Abundantia has the right to the property by the act of putting her in possession, notwithstanding whatever is alleged to the contrary. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A woman who enters into a second marriage within the year of mourning: what and what kind of property she loses.
2. In the case of things that are consumed by use, the usufructuary provides security for the estimation or quantity to be restored after the death of the usufructuary.
body: On the seventh day, and the premises being assumed, that the said Lady Luciana, at the said point, and having considered the statutes of the city, married a second time, Magdalen Thomasia and Joan being still alive.

It must be considered whether the said Lady Luciana married within the year of mourning. In which case, by civil law, she would simply be excluded from all succession to the underage son, as in the Authentica *De nuptiis*, § *Si autem tutor*. If, however, she married after the year of mourning, she is deprived of all goods which the said Napoleon wished to pass to his daughters from his patrimony. For this penalty is established because she despised her first marriage and rejected freedom, as in the Code *De secundis nuptiis*, Authentica *In donatione*. And in this regard, the statute, which speaks of the eighth part, does not benefit Lady Luciana with respect to ownership, so that she loses it; because the statute makes no mention of second marriages. Hence, the statute is drawn to the common law, as if this case were omitted by the statute; but because the statute was issued for the purpose of diminishing, not of restricting the mother’s right. And those things which are done for diminution should not operate as an increase, as in the Digest *De legatis primo*, law *Legata inutiliter*. It remains, therefore, that Lady Luciana succeeds in the goods of her deceased children, which formerly belonged to the said Napoleon, only in the eighth part of the usufruct. Which eighth part she ought not to have unless solemn caution has been provided.

† what usufructuaries ought to provide regarding the use and enjoyment according to the discretion of a good man, with respect to immovable property. But with respect to those things which are consumed by use, or consist in money, a guarantee is given regarding the valuation, or the quantity to be restored after the death of the usufructuary: as in D. de usufructu, quemadmodum, l. 1; and D. de usufructu earum rerum, quae usu consumuntur, l. 1 and 2. In the codicils, however, which the said Napoleon made, he could not diminish the legitime of his daughters, nor impose a burden at that time. And the same applies to dowries, if they succeed in place of the legitime: as in C. de inofficioso testamento, l. Quoniam in prioribus. Hence, the said Lady Luciana succeeds to the usufruct of an eighth part of the legitime, and no more, with respect to the sons. But with respect to the male son, who succeeds to the usufruct of an eighth part left to the said Renald, and no more. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a condition attached to a legacy in a will appears to be repeated in the transfer of said legacy made in codicils.
body: Propoitdr, formerly of Andrea of Bingo, in all his goods, instituted his son Barnabe as his universal heir. However, if it should happen that his son should die without heirs before the age of twenty years, he left to Master Francis of Lucignano, by way of legacy, in the event of the aforementioned case occurring, one piece of land. Later, having made codicils, he subtracted from the said testament in this manner: a certain piece of land which he had bequeathed to Master Francis of Lucignano after the death of Barnabe, the son of the said Matthew, he willed that the said Master Francis should have only the said piece of land during his lifetime, after the death of his said son, with three measures of grain to be distributed and given to the poor of Christ for the soul of the said testator every year during the lifetime of the said Master. After the death of the said Master, however, the said testator willed that the said piece of land should pass to Vanna Francisca and her wife, Lady Horrabella, and their children, in full right. In all other respects, he willed that his said testament should have the fullest force and validity. Then the said testator and codicillator died, the said Barnabe and Master Francis surviving. Secondly, the said Master Francis died. Subsequently, the said Barnabe died, being over twenty years of age, Vanna Francisca and Lady Horrabella surviving.

† Now the doubt arises on a point of law, whether that condition inserted in the testament regarding the legacy made to Master Francis of the said piece of land, namely, if the said Barnabas should die before the age of 20 years, is understood to be repeated in the legacy made to Vanna of Francis and to the lady Horrabella after the death of the said Master Francis. At first sight, it would seem to be said that yes. First, from the words of the codicils, it is inferred regarding the said piece of land, which he had bequeathed to Master Francis after the death of Barnabas, son of the said Matthew, that he wished the said Master Francis to have it, etc. And he adds that after the death of the said Master Francis, he wished the said piece of land to devolve to Vanna. If, therefore, in the legacy made to Master Francis, because the condition which is appended in the bequest seems to be appended in its transfer, as in D. de adimendis legatis, l. Legatum sub conditione. On the contrary, it seems true, because in the codicils the testator changed the entire form of the legacy made to Master Francis. For whereas in the testament there was a legacy to Master Francis by way of a proper legacy, in the codicils, since the same thing is also bequeathed for the term of life with a new burden appended for a pious cause, namely, of three measures of grain to be disbursed and distributed to the poor of Christ for his soul in each year during the life of the said Master Francis. This new burden is indeed appended in favor of the testator alone, and it is in the interest of the testator that it be fulfilled. Hence, we ought not to understand any condition to be tacitly implied. For this is the sense of the words: "the thing bequeathed in my testament after the death of Barnabas, I wish to be given to Master Francis, after the death of the said Barnabas, and of the said Master Francis, and also of the said Horrabella." Thus, from the testament, he subtracted two things: first, the condition of age; second, the smallness of the legacy. Hence, upon inspection of the form of the codicils, the entire form of the legacy is changed, both from the part of the legatee and from the part of the testator, who provided for himself differently in the codicils than he had provided in the testament. Hence, on account of the new burden, I do not understand that said age to be repeated in the person of Master Francis, because these words do not sound that way. And because a new burden is opposed there, tacit repetition ceases, as in D. de legatis 2, l. Licet Imperator, and D. ad Trebellianum, l. Quotiens. For the said condition is understood to be repeated in a simple transfer, but not in a mutation of form, as in D. de locato, l. Cum plures, §. Lege dicta. Hence, it must be considered that in the codicils the testator made mention of death twice. First, he said that the thing which he left to Master Francis after the death of Barnabas, he wishes to be given after the death of Barnabas with the burden, etc. He speaks adversatively to the testament. Hence, by that second phrase "after the death," nothing is required other than death. But here it could be alleged on the contrary, because the testator did not wish to diminish the legacy, hence he does not seem to have augmented it, and consequently the condition of the whole ought to be understood as repeated; otherwise, it would be to augment the legacy and to burden the instituted heir more. But I answer that these words suggest not so much a diminution of the legacy as a new provision of the testator made for his soul on account of the inserted burden. Hence, for the soul, this is a new legacy, although the same body of the thing is demonstrated, and he has entirely receded from the first legacy made in the testament, which is evident, because one could not sue from the testament, saying "I sue from the testament according to the form of the codicils," but one must say "I sue from the codicils simply." Hence, he has receded from the testament, and this is the truth. Hence, assuming that the said Master Francis lived after the death of the said Barnabas, the said legacy with the said burden would be due, even if Barnabas had died under 20 years of age; because it is not in the interest of the testator that that age be repeated, since the final reason for bequeathing does not consist in it; but rather it is in the interest of the testator that it not be repeated, so that the bequest for his soul may be performed, and there is a strong reason which supports the first cause, as in D. de religiosis, l. Sunt personae. And by this it is shown that the knowledge of age is not seen to be repeated in the codicils; and even regarding Master Francis, it would benefit him, and consequently neither regarding Vanna nor regarding the lady Horrabella, so that the sense is that he left it after death at a certain age, [but now] leaves it after death simply with this burden, that he is bound, etc. And this I believe should be held in law. And assuming that this were doubtful, and there could also be opinions for and against this if Master Francis were alive, nevertheless regarding Vanna and the lady Horrabella, there does not seem to be doubt about this. Consider, indeed, that Vanna and the lady Horrabella are not truly substituted in the legacy. For whenever one thing is bequeathed to one for a time, and to another after that time, one is not substituted for the other, but there are two legacies distributed by time, as in C. de legatis, l. Finis. But whenever he to whom the legacy is made is asked to restore it to another, this can well be called a substitution, although sometimes in speaking we do not always truncate the proper force of these terms, as in D. de legatis 2, l. Ut haeredibus. All laws which speak of an instituted heir and a substitute do not claim a place here. Likewise, laws regarding transfer do not have a place, because when a thing is bequeathed to two, one until Easter, the other after Easter, they are separate legacies from the very defect. And because in the testament no condition of a new legator was inserted, therefore neither in the codicils do I understand it to be repeated in his person, because the testator wished that Vanna and the lady Horrabella should have more right than the said Francis, because he left the said thing to them without burden and with full right. The doubt of this question rests on that word, "after the death, however." For those adversative words induce repetition according to Bartolus in l. In repetendis, de legatis tertio. But I answer that they induce repetition of those things which are expressed in the script itself. But here nothing is expressed regarding age. Moreover, Bartolus speaks of substitution or transfer, but neither of these is here to be considered more subtly, but it is such a mutation of the legacy and form of bequeathing, saving that it is one and the same. And these reasons, which are based on conjectures of wills, are always difficult; from legal conjectures, we must conjecture, interpreting concise and obscure words, and as the law interprets them, l. Licet Imperator, de legatis 1. Because the testator introduced a new form, and in the codicils made no mention except of the death of the son, and he himself requested, while leaving for his soul upon the death of the son. Arg. D. de donis causa mortis, l. 1. Hence, I do not believe that the codicillator considered anything other than the death of the son without children. For in the order of nature, one is first to consider oneself; second, children; third, him to whom he left in default of children; fourth, that person who comes after them. And D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Publius, §. Ultimo; and D. de usufructu legato, l. Uxori, quotiens. Whenever the last will does not accord with the prior, it seems that he has receded from the first will, as in D. de legatis 1, l. Si mihi et tibi, §. Finis; and D. de iure codicillorum; and D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Nam ad ea. For that which is emended is held as not written, as in D. de adimendis legatis, l. 3, §. Condicio; and D. de militum testamento, l. Tribunus, §. Ultimo. Inspecting the true form of the said codicils: because what he had left in the said testament after death concerning age, he left in the codicils after death simply. And he repeats expressly the death, but not the age in that mutation of the legacy, and he added a new burden. It seems to be said in law that the aforementioned Vanna and the lady Horrabella can sue from the said codicils. And this I believe was the true will of the testator. And thus I hold in law from the conjectured will of the testator, and by points of reason: because the writing speaks no more than it speaks, as in D. de obligationibus verborum, l. Si ita stipulatus, §. Grisogonus. Because if he had wished to repeat the age, he would have expressed it in the codicils, in which no mention is made of age, but only of death. And to presume the judgment of the testator, nothing is to be supplied by implication, as in D. de manumissionibus testamento, l. Finis. Many other laws could be alleged, but it is not necessary. And so that it may be better understood what I said, as if the testator said, "the thing which I left after the death of my son, if he should die within 21 years, I leave after his death with such a burden, etc." For here there are two cases of bequeathing, one in the testament, and that one perfect in the first; the other in the codicils, and this one also perfect. And therefore, to that which is perfect, nothing is to be supplied by implication. Those things are imperfect which are to be supplied by tacit repetition, as noted in the said l. In re petendis. And therefore, in the second act of bequeathing, the age is not repeated, but only the death: and especially because in the person of Vanna and the lady Horrabella, the testator wished the legacy to be greater and more substantial than in the person of Master Francis, as appears from the form of the codicils. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If the testator does not complete his statement, the disposition fails: for example, if he says: if such a person dies, I wish that my goods shall go to such a person.
2. Add also on the matter below in consilium 135.
body: Propositum. He, with his wife, instituted Antonia, namely that the said Antonius instituted Antonia, their daughter. And when he intended to visit the Apostolic thresholds, he made a testament, in which he thus disposed, namely: Furthermore, he left by right of legacy and succession to his daughter, Lady Antonia, beyond her dowry, 100 gold ducats for her share, and after the Falcidian portion and succession to all his goods, commanding her to be silent and content. In all his other goods, however, he instituted the womb of his wife, if she were pregnant and bore one or more male children, and if they came to light, he instituted them as his heirs with full right; and if it were a female, he left 100 pounds for her dowry, and furthermore for her share of the Falcidian portion and succession to all his goods, 100 pounds. And if all the males should die at any time without children in pupillary age, or later at any time: then, in the place and share of his said sons, the testator wished Lady Acholi, his wife, and Bernard, his son, [to succeed]; but he did not add the word "succeed," leaving the scriptural sentence imperfect. Finally, the testator lived well for 21 years, and from the various wombs of his said wife he begot three sons, who died during the lifetime of the said testator, with the said Archolina and Bernard, or one of them, surviving; I do not care which.

† Now the question arises: whether the said Antonia, daughter of the said testator, succeeds; or whether the substitutes ought to succeed; because the said substitution was concise, which under a compendium of words contains an express vulgar substitution. And it seems to be said that the substitutes come in. And if it is said that the will was broken, because the testator made mention of only one womb and passed over others, it is answered by interpretation: because the testator said, if she were pregnant. Hence it is not understood solely of the present posthumous child, but of any whatsoever, as in D. de liberis et posthumis, l. placet; and C. de posthumis haeredibus instituendis, l. fraternae poenam pariatur praetensionis, qui filios suos non instituit. As is said there, the word "were," which is extensive. And the word "if" is placed for "when," which appears because the testator spoke of children in the plural. Hence, since according to the course of nature a woman in the womb does not bear more than one, it is understood of any womb. To the contrary it seems, because I confess that the said substitution is vulgar, nevertheless the will is not valid. And consequently neither is the said vulgar substitution: because Antonia was passed over, since nothing was left to her by way of institution. As in Auth. ut cum de appellatione cognoscitur, §. aliud quoque capitulum. For it was not left to her the legitime, by the name of a share, or by the name of the legitime; but a quantity was left to be compensated with the legitime. It was not said by way of institution; the word "I leave," added and singular, is not understood by way of institution, but of legacy or fideicommissum. As in D. ad Trebellianum, l. cogo, §. et generaliter, per Dynus. Moreover, as I said, in the said substitution the principal word is lacking; because the words say, and the said testator willed that in the place and share of his said children; it does not say more. For it does not say that the substitutes succeed in the place and share. But to this it could be answered by l. 1, D. de haeredibus instituendis. Moreover, that the posthumous child was passed over seems to be proved by l. commodissime, D. de liberis et posthumis. And if it is said that the will convalesces, because the passed-over person died during the lifetime of the testator, as in l. posthumus, de inofficioso testamento, it is answered that this law has no place in this case; because here bonorum possessio secundum tabulas was not sought. Moreover, because that law has no place when the posthumous child opens the way of breaking to one who is still alive, as in D. si tabulae testamenti nullae extant, l. 1, in fine. This question is very difficult; because Antonia was not instituted heir, and could claim nothing from the will as heir, but only by action on the will; hence she was passed over; and thus the aforementioned substitution was null. Hence it seems that the intestate inheritance belongs to the said Antonia. But whether the said substitution, by the codicillary clause, is directed to a fideicommissum, there are very diverse opinions. And especially on account of the birth of the posthumous child, which breaks the codicillary clause according to the opinion of many doctors. But according to others it does not break it, when posthumous children have been considered. I determine that this substitution is not valid by direct right. But whether it is valid by right of fideicommissum, I leave for the present in doubt. Granted, however, that it is valid by right of fideicommissum, and that after deducting the legitime the remainder ought to be restored, and from the Trebellian, I do not determine whether it is valid by right of fideicommissum, because it seems not to be valid. As in Auth. ex causa, C. de liberis praeteritis. And the point is difficult; but it can well be said that direct substitutions are not valid, and the matter is in the state of intestacy, saving the sounder counsel. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Brothers, who lived together with their father and gained much from their industry, seek to recover the penalty which they paid for one of the brothers.
2. Profit made by one of the brothers during the father's lifetime ought not to be shared with the brothers after the father's death.
body: The facts are as follows. The father, namely Peter, had three sons, namely Peter, Colam, and Vallum, who brothers stood with their father, and many were enriched by their labors and industry. It happened that for the said Peter, the other brothers paid 50 pounds from the common profits for a certain penalty and condemnation made against him by the lord of the land. Moreover, this Peter leased a certain mill, and from it he profited several bushels of grain. Now this Matthew, their father, is dead: wherefore these brothers come to division.

† Two questions are raised: whether the said penalty, once paid, can be recovered by the said brothers from the said Peter for that part which was paid out of the assets of those seeking recovery. And it is to be said that yes, by means of the action for management of affairs (negotiorum gestorum).

Secondly, it is asked whether the said Peter is bound to share the said profits. And it must be said that he is not; because it is clear in law that whatever a son acquires for any reason, he acquires for himself alone as to ownership during the father’s lifetime. And after the father’s death, he has both ownership and usufruct, which he is not bound to share with his other brothers. As stated in C. de bonis quae lib. l. cum oportet, and C. de coll. l. si. cum si. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether an imperfect script of a testament invalidates the disposition, and how it is to be interpreted.
body: What is alleged to be beyond puberty, it shall have no effect, as if it were...

† the aforementioned clause. And if the said Antonio Thomas should die before reaching puberty, it would have no effect, as is to be proven. First, on account of uncertainty: because it is unknown what the testator intended. As stated in the Digest, *De iure fisci*, law *Ita fidei*. Second, on account of avoiding conjecture, for in wills nothing is so proper as clarity, as in the Authenticum *De testibus imperfectis*, near the end. Third, on account of the name of the substitute, or substitutes, not being expressed. As stated in the Digest, *De testamentaria tutela*, law *Duo sunt Titij*. For here the person is not certain. As stated in the Digest, *De haeredibus instituendis*, law *Quotiens*, in the beginning. Fourth, because conditional words do not dispose. As stated in the Digest, *Si quis omissa causa testamenti*, law *Si quis sub conditione*. Fifth, because by the same reasoning by which we can understand the lady Margaret, the father of Nicholas, and the poor, or one of them, we can also understand Mary and John. Since therefore the sentence is imperfect, and, preserving the reason of correct speech, does not rightly signify any thing, it does not seem valid. As stated in the Digest, *De haeredibus instituendis*, law 1, § *Pe*, verse *Ergo et si ita*.

On the contrary, it seems: because when there are two sentences, one perfect and the other imperfect, in which the imperfect one does not require to be openly stated, it is nevertheless tacitly understood to be repeated. As stated in the Digest, *De legatis primo*, law *Si servus*, § *Qui Marga*. Second, because here there is a conjunction, which induces a full repetition. As is read and noted in the Digest, *De funerariis instrumentis*, law *Seyae*, § *Gayo*. Third, because a testator who prohibits making a will seems to leave a tacit fideicommissum to those whom he preferred. As stated in the Digest, *Ad Trebellianam*, law *Qui filium*, in the beginning. Fourth, because this word "provided that" here abounds due to the writer's error, and that which abounds does not vitiate wills. As stated in the Code, *De testibus*, law *Testa*. Therefore, all detracting from this adverb "provided that," the substitution is clear: namely, and if the said Antonio Thomas should die before reaching pupillary age, he could make a will concerning two hundred pounds. Then there would be no doubt that from the conjectures of the chapter of substitution an entire and perfect understanding would result: let us say that the testator intended one thing, namely, to substitute. But he intended this differently: because in pupillary age [he intended substitution] in its entirety, afterwards, however, with this reservation, or with this condition, that the burdened party could make a will concerning 200 pounds. And this is the very truth. For when an imperfect writing must be interpreted, the preceding words declare the following. And if we were to say, it is probable that the testator said what is written, and what the writing accords with the disposition: because that which seems imperfect in voice is perfected by the interpretation of the law. As stated in the Digest, *De legatis secundo*, law *Cum pater*, § *Cum imperfecta*. As stated in the Code, *De fideicommissis*, law *Voluntatis*. Fifth also, because when one principal verb determines two sentences, that person who is supposed concerning one act of the verb is necessarily understood in the whole sentence. As stated in the Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, law *Quae conditio*. And therefore, because three substitutes are in the perfect sentence, to which is joined a less significant sentence, the latter is supplied by the former: because always that which is fuller gives understanding to that which is more uncertain. As stated in the Digest, *De haeredibus instituendis*, law *Qui non militabat*, § *Lucio*. And in the Digest, *De legatis primo*, law *Si servus plurium*, § *Finis*. From which I conclude that the said substitutes named in the first substitution are to be understood: indeed, they are tacitly named in the second substitution. For here there is no difference of persons, but of times. And otherwise this writing, according to its understanding, cannot, nor ought it to, be understood in law, nor in fact. And therefore the said substitution, although made in the briefest words, is valid, and cannot be invalidated by any reasoning. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Two depositors do not have the benefit of division among multiple debtors, nor do they have the exception of uncounted money, and number 2.
2. The heir who is sued has the time of inventory, if the times allow.
3. Whether a deposit is presumed to be natural.
4. The debtor is not released due to fire.
5. Occupation of the entire land is a fortuitous event.
body: VI. Having bound themselves in solidum, John and Anthony, with renunciations, with the assumption upon themselves of risk and fortune, and by means of a deposit instrument of the priest P., and presupposing that the land of the niece was occupied and robbed by brigands, and presupposing that the action is brought against the heir of one of the said debtors, the premises of the cause being supposed, without going through circumlocutions, the following are to be sought.

† First: whether the said depositors have the benefit of the new constitution concerning two debtors. Answer: No, because they have waived it, as in the Authentica de fideiussoribus, in the beginning.
Secondly: whether they have the exception of money not paid. I say that they do not: because they themselves renounced the exception: as noted in C. de non numerata pecunia, l. si ex causa.
Third: Whether the heir who is sued has the benefit of the inventory period. And I say that he does, if the time limits allow it, as stated in the final law, § donec, on the right of deliberation.
Fourthly: Whether a natural deposit is presumed. And I say yes, since the exception of *non numerata pecunia* has been waived. Moreover, by the law *Publius*, § *si*, in the Digest on deposit.

Fifth, whether the debtor is discharged by reason of fire. I say that he is not: because those words, “and they renounced the exception,” do not show that what is owed is in kind, but rather in genus. And thus he is not discharged by fire. As in D. 16.3.1 (Die sponsaliorum) and D. 16.3.2 (Lucius). Moreover, it includes within itself risk and fortune, which is the same as saying in our idiom, as if by chance or accident: as in D. 45.1.3 (Sed et si quia), § Quaesitum; C. 8.3.1 (Quae fortuitis). And therefore, since it is not fitting to dispute over legal subtleties in a deposit, the said instrument of deposit must be put into execution: unless the heir of the debtor was found within the time prescribed: as in D. 16.3.1 (Bona fides). But if the deposit had been made only in kind.

† because this fortuitous event of the occupation of the entire land is among those cases which scarcely occur in a thousand years, the renunciation does not prejudice the permissibility of the case and its admission, as noted by Bartolus in l. seyo, ff. de annuis legatis. Nevertheless, I do not see that a deposit was made in specie, nor that the admission was sufficiently proven. And therefore the said depositary Peter has justice, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The heir alone is bound to pay the debts; therefore, the legatee ought not to be joined [in the action].
2. Whether the heir, or the usufructuary, pays the expenses of the fruits. Whether the usufructuary is bound to pay the taxes.
3. Whether a usufructuary of things consumed by use is bound to give security for the restitution of their value.
body:
Palpu Clds in these words. Moreover, he left by way of legacy to the said Plucia in his testament such a legacy, in these words of Palpu Clds: “Moreover, I leave by right of legacy to Plucia, my wife, the habitation of my houses, and the use of all my household goods and furnishings, and all and singular fruits, revenues, and profits which are received and may be received from the goods and inheritances of the said testator, both those left in the present testament above in the instruments of the legatees, as well as from others wherever they may be; provided that the said Plucia lives honorably, observes the widow’s life, and resides for the greater part in the house of the said testator, notwithstanding any legacies made in any manner above in the instruments of the legatees concerning the immovable goods of the testator, she shall have the habitation of the house, and the fruits, revenues, and profits of all and singular immovable goods, and the use of all household goods and furnishings of the said testator. And I have given and granted to her license to hold, seize, possess, and enjoy her goods without the license of my heirs, and without the request of any person. And I have instituted certain outsiders as my universal heirs, etc.”

Now it is asked: whether the instituted heirs are bound to pay the legacies and other hereditary debts and primary expenses from their own proper goods; or whether they may pay from the movable or immovable goods of the said inheritance. Moreover, whether the movable goods, such as grain and fruits existing at that time in the house of the testator at the time of his death, belong to the wife or to the heirs of the testator. And whether the said wife ought to have the fruits and usufruct of the first year. And whether she may use the hereditary household goods and furnishings.
† The heir is bound to pay the debts, and not the legatees: as in C. si cert. pet. l. 1.

† and therefore the wife is not bound for debts, nor for the expenses of the fruits. ff. de usufr. l. fundi Trebatiani. Nevertheless, the usufructuary is properly bound for taxes and burdens on the things: as ff. de usufr. l. si pendentes. §. si quid and c.

† The grain, which belonged to the testator, is owed to the wife, with security to be given for the return of its value: as in D. de usufr. rer. l. si vim. But the grain, which accrued during the time that the usufruct lasted, need not be restored: because the usufructuary has already profited from it. As in D. de usufr. l. si defuncta etc.

† He may use and consume things and goods which are consumed by use, provided that security is given for their restitution. And they ought to be appraised when they are delivered to him: as in l. 1, de usu et habitatione, and de secundis nuptiis, l. hac edictali, §. mobilium. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a notary or a judge may stipulate for another, and whether an action is available to them without assignment.
body: Whether an action is acquired by a notary or a judge without assignment

There are divergent opinions as to whether an action is acquired without assignment from the stipulation of Cl., the notary, or the judge. Nevertheless, no one doubts that a stipulation so conceived is valid: “You promise to me, the judge, or to me, the notary, receiving for such a person.” This matter is fully treated in the laws cited above, and in D. de adoptionibus, l. non aliter; and l. his verbis; and D. de legibus 1, l. huius modi, in principio; D. de obligationibus et contractibus, l. punctus quae grauius.

Furthermore, there is no doubt that he who received such a stipulation for another is bound to assign the action: D. de acquisitione possessionis, l. quoque, § et si primo modo. But if he cannot assign it because he is absent or has died without heirs, then the action lies even without assignment: l. 1, D. de institutionibus; and l. damni, D. de damno infecto. If two persons are named, as is the case here, a fine question would arise: whether, with one present and the other absent, assignment is required. I say that it is not, by bringing a useful action in the person of the absent party.

Therefore, I conclude that a useful action may be brought: either because assignment is not required in the case of a public official: D. de magistratibus, l. 1, § exigent; and C. de episcopis et clericis, Auth. generaliter; and what is noted in c. dudum, de conversione coniugali; or because the person who ought to assign is absent, and his presence cannot easily be obtained, so that assignment is not required. From these authorities I also conclude that, according to the form of the contract, the action lies without any further assignment. And this is the truth. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A mother who did not accept guardianship, when it would have been futile, is not deprived of the inheritance.
body: For he was deceived in that he had been thwarted in assuming the guardianship,

† The mother is not excluded from the succession: for it is excused in her that she would have been frustrated in assuming guardianship, since there was nothing from which she could hold the reins of administration: as in D. ad Tertullianum, l. 2, §. pen., ver. etiam si mater. And therefore the daughters succeed to the said Chaterus in equal shares: as in C. ad Tertullianum, l. matris; and the inheritance of the said Vannucius must be divided in this manner: because the daughters must have two-thirds, one part in their own person, the other by succession from their sisters. But the mother must have one-third: because she must have half of the two-thirds, as heir of Caralina and Palmatia: as in C. ad Tertullianum, Auth. de possessione. I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether those who have been oblates to a monastery, together with their goods, are deemed to have made a donation inter vivos or causa mortis.
body: Which rule states: when they were offered to be married

† The oblation was simple, and it was not a profession of the Regulars, since the oblates were married. The goods did not come into the consequence of the persons, but simply and for themselves. And therefore, as goods given inter vivos, they are said to remain at the monastery, provided that the monastery observes and wishes to observe the pacts appended in the contract: as appears from those things which are read and noted. 27. q. 1. as the law contains. And in the Authent. ingressi. unless it were added that they had withdrawn with the oblated goods by license of the chapter: because then, by a certain notable distraction on account of the defect of the final cause celebrated, they would have recovered them. D. C. de don. ante nup. l. cum veterum. and l. cum te. ff. de pact. l. ab emptore. where there had not been a regular profession. If indeed it had been invalid from the beginning, the oblation of goods would not bind. C. si pend. appel. mors interuenerit. l. 3. And the reason is: because whenever a donation is made on account of the natural case of death, just as is the case with a changed status: because he is held as dead: such a donation seems to have been made causa mortis. And on account of the existence of children, it is revoked: as ff. de don. causa mort. l. senatus. and ff. si cert. pet. l. non omnis. and ff. de cond. ob causam. l. cum quis. But if the profession were valid: then, as if death had followed, the donation is confirmed irrevocably. It is clear, however, that profession is a certain death with regard to the world. In the Auth. de monachis. in prin. and C. de epis. et cle. l. deo nobis. And from these it is openly concluded that, since the said obligation was a lay obligation, and not a regular one, the said goods donated to the monastery ought to remain with the said monastery: unless the said oblates had been licensed by the said monastery. I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the term "provisions" includes spelt, barley, and other edibles for horses.
2. The term "provisions" is referred by way of eminence to human food.
body: The ancient

† advocates, following the Glossa, used to say that where there is a paternal uncle who is a legitimate tutor, the mother was not bound to undertake the guardianship; and therefore, upon the death of the pupil (impubes), the mother succeeded, and not the paternal uncle: as noted in C. ad Tert. l. matris, where the Glossa expressly states that the mother is excused if the son has another tutor, for instance a legitimate one. The lord Bartolus intervened and stated that today the mother is not excused; because she excludes every legitimate tutor; nevertheless, unless she accepts the guardianship within a year or renounces it, she ought to be deprived of the succession—not on the grounds that she did not petition for a tutor, but on the grounds that she was in delay regarding the undertaking or renouncing of the guardianship within the year. And thus the guardianship, introduced in favor of the mother and grandmother, causes that favor to be converted into hatred on account of the mother's delict: because she neither undertook the guardianship herself nor allowed another to undertake it; nor can any fault whatsoever be imputed to the paternal uncle as long as the mother is preferred to him: as in ff. de adul. l. si maritus, in prin. And we, the doctors of this land, agree with this opinion of the lord Bartolus, and among us it is approved by custom. Whence if the said mother was of full legal age, and did not accept the guardianship within the year nor repudiate it on the court record, the mother, if she is over twenty-five years of age at the time of her husband's death, is excluded, and the paternal uncle is admitted, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an instance is said to be new when the execution of a judgment or instrument is sought.
2. Whether an obligation of a penalty, subject to an obligation of an indivisible act, is indivisible.
3. If a free man is given as a pledge and is released, no prejudice is caused to the releaser: since a free man cannot be given as a pledge.
body: Concerning the rent which he has in the condictio, whether the action is brought

† On the first point, I say that every commandment or judgment which is conditional, whether the action is brought for a penalty or for damages, must be liquidated; otherwise, execution cannot be carried out. As stated in D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Qui sub conditione; and D. quibus ex causis in possessionem, l. Haec autem, § 1; and C. de compensatione, l. Fin.; and C. de sententiis quae sine certa quantitate, l. Pe. and l. Fin., where this is expressly stated. Hence, it is necessary that a certain petition precede and that liquidation be made. And from this it is concluded that there is a certain instance here, since no other instance preceded upon which a sentence was passed. Hence, the execution of a judgment properly does not have an instance, for it is a case placed in controversy, otherwise not decided. Just as there are certain matters which have an instance, yet are brought extra ordinem: as when the action for threatened damage is sought, and when alimony is sought, and similar matters. And therefore, the instance requests a term, after which the parties, having proposed a greater intention and maintaining contradiction, require to be in a contradictory contest: as C. de iudicibus, l. Rem non novam. But here it must be observed that after the first petition for execution, execution was again and anew requested. And this can be called a new instance, and as if upon a new instance, the sentence passed is valid: as is noted and appears in D. de exceptione rei iudicatae, l. Duobus.

† On the second point, it must be said that the obligation arising from the aforementioned act is indivisible; but the obligation of the penalty and interest is indivisible. As stated in D. 16.3.14 (Si plures) and D. 50.17.108 § Catho (De verbis obligatis). And therefore the father’s payment releases the others. Nor can the act be claimed anymore. I say that it releases the others up to the concurrent amount, not in solidum.

† On the third point, I say that such a release of the person does not prejudice the released party; because a free man cannot be called a pledge, nor detained in the matter of a pledge. As stated in the Code, *De acquisitione et obligatione*, law *Ob eas*. Hence, the exception of assigned actions did not create the necessity of assigning captives. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The right, or faculty, of collecting a toll, to whomsoever it may belong by law.
2. Whether the holder of the right of passage ought himself to pay.
body: you will receive the right, but not to the sole or ter-

† The right to collect tolls (pedagium) is attached to the soil; however, the utility thereof does not pertain to the mere soil or territory, and therefore the collection of the toll pertains to the fiscus, and not to the castle or to the territory of the castle. Unless it were such a castle as had a fiscus of its own by virtue of a privilege, or by an immemorial prescription, of the contrary of which there is no memory, or to which the right of toll had been expressly granted, as in the Digest, Title "Locare Conductum," Law "Locare," according to Bartolus. For these rights of tolls are specially reserved to the superior as a sign of superiority, as in the Code, Title "De Prescriptionibus," Law "Competit," in the title "30 Anno." The superior, according to the custom of Italy, are the cities themselves, which govern themselves, as in the Digest, Title "De Captivis," Law "Non Dubito," and Law "Hostes." For they are called res publicae, not castles or villages, as in the Digest, Title "De Publicis," Law "Sed Hi." And therefore they alone have those rights which are called regalia, as in the Decretals, Title "Quae Sunt Regalia," Chapter 1. Hence it must be said that such rights, thus reserved and which are not accustomed to be granted to anyone, but are retained by the fiscus, do not come within a general grant, nor within any indefinite words; for from an indefinite grant, honors of this kind are understood to be excepted. This is supported by the Code, Title "Quae Res Pignori Oblatae Possunt," Law "Alumnos."

† But if the city itself were to pay tolls on behalf of its citizens, or if there were certain movable goods belonging to the city which were brought to the city, what would be owed as passage toll for them? This is absurd. As stated in the Digest, *De peculio legato*, law *Si peculium*, section *Sicut*; and it is supported by the Digest, *De verbis significatis*, in law *Censoria*. And this is true, unless an express agreement appears. As noted by Bartolus in the aforementioned law *Sicut*, observe that such passages are leased and sold for a time every day. As stated in the Code, *De vectigalibus et commentis*, law *Si quis*, with the following. Or unless it were proven that that castle had this special right of collecting passage tolls: as are many castles in Italy. It is considered that having the power of the sword is greater than collecting passage tolls. I answer that this "greater" is not of the same species, nor of the same reason: because jurisdiction adheres to the castle on account of its protection. And it is joined to the castle on account of the necessity and utility for those dwelling there: because in this way the castle ought to be defended against evil men. As stated in the Digest, *De officio praesidis*, law *Congruit*. But to collect passages is something separate from the castle: since those who pass through are from elsewhere, and not from the territory of the castle. And by common law, no jurisdiction over them belongs to the castle itself. As stated in the Digest, *De municipibus et honorariis*, law *Rescripto*, section *Si*. Hence, by consensus, it is concluded that those passing through from elsewhere, and their confederates, and any other strangers, are not bound to pay the said tolls to the said possessor of the said castle. And especially here I adhere to the doctrine of Bartolus, which I cited above there: and because they are not said to be of the same territory as the lords of the fisc, the said toll, or passage, by right ought to be paid to the chamber of the commune of Gubbio: because collecting a toll is a certain jurisdiction pertaining in itself to the principal lord. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a person condemned to the ultimate penalty may make a will, even for pious causes? But what if something is ordered to be restored which he had acquired unjustly? And number 1.
body: It is proposed that a certain nobleman, dominus Thomas of Todi, made his will in the year of the Lord 1356, in which he instituted his son Ludovicus as his universal heir, and left certain things to a certain daughter of his by right of institution. To the said Ludovicus he substituted: if he should die in pupillary age under a certain form; or if he should die after pupillary age, he left the greater part of his property to pious causes and for his soul. Eventually, after proceedings were instituted against him, the said nobleman was capitally condemned as guilty of harming the status that then governed, and execution was carried out. After his death, the said called Ludovicus held the said property for a very long time. And finally, the said dominus Ludovicus met his end, survived by a certain full sister of his, who says that she succeeds intestate to the father and the brother. On the other hand, it is said by the legatees and the fideicommissaries of the soul that the said property is owed to them by virtue of the testament of the said dominus Thomas.

† Now it is asked what the law is. I answer: if the said dominus Thomas was condemned after proceedings were duly formed against him, and after he was convicted by witnesses or by confession, his testament was void, even regarding pious causes, because he died a slave of punishment, as in ff. de iniu. testa. l. si quis filio exhaeredato and noted in ca. quanquam. desinas. de testa. lib. 6. in nouel. And there is a twofold reason: first, as I said, because a slave of punishment is intestable; second, because the goods are confiscated, whence he who left no goods in the state cannot have an heir, as in ff. de vulga. substi. l. lex Cornel., for he dies naked, as in ff. de capi. dimi. l. tutelas. §. sub libertate. Nor can anyone by making a will bring it about that, if he offends, the fiscus cannot obtain his property. Indeed, in that crime, which is proximate to the crime of treason [laesa maiestas], immediately when he offends—nay, even when he prepares himself to offend by plotting, or willing, or soliciting anyone for so great a deed—he must already be certain of his punishment, as in ff. qui et a qui. l. quaesitum and de manu. l. qui pęnae. And therefore there is no difference between bequests to pious causes and other bequests. For he who left freedom to his slave and delivers him from the misery of slavery is like him who left money for the redemption of captives, whence it is said to make a will for pious causes, as noted in C. de fideicommis. l. eam quam and ff. de fideicommis. libe. l. in testamento; and yet such legacies made by those condemned to the ultimate punishment are invalid.

† Whence it is clearly concluded that the testament of the said dominus Thomas, condemned to the ultimate punishment, was rendered void, except in that which he might have left by way of restitution of certain things wrongfully taken. For that does not hold force as a testament or codicil, but as a kind of confession inter vivos, unless it was made to defraud the fiscus; and it is so understood in nouel., for offenses do not prejudice creditors, as in C. de pę. fisca creditoris praeferen. l. 1. lib. 10. But because the said dominus Ludovicus held certain paternal property in his own right, he subsequently prescribed that property in his own person over a very long time, as fully noted in C. de sacrosan. ec. l. fi. and ff. de diuer. et tempo. praescri. l. intra quatuor and ff. de iure fis. l. 1. §. diuus pius and §. praescriptio. And therefore the said sister succeeds to all the said property as brotherly property, as argued from ff. de vulg. substi. l. cohęredi. §. cum filiae. versi. nec fideicommisso. And a fortiori the aforesaid are true if the said property had been granted to the said dominus Ludovicus upon certain chapters of peace, because as if from a new grant they would be new property newly acquired by him, not through an inheritance occasion, which was nonexistent; for an inheritance is spoken of with respect to an heir, but he who died a slave of punishment has no heir. Therefore there is no inheritance of his. Whence, granting from first to last, it necessarily follows that all the said property belongs freely to the said sister, and she cannot be compelled by the bishop’s vicar to observe the said testament, but it rests in the liberty of the said sister. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The proceeding is null, having been conducted without observing the required formalities.
2. He who is not bound to appear is not deemed contumacious for failing to appear; nor can he be held as having confessed.
body: This proceeding is not valid for such a reason, for either we [are bound] by the said statutes, and by the said proceeding I say,

† That the said IS process is invalid for this reason, namely: either we say that the said process is based on the common law, and this is false. And because one cannot proceed by inquisition according to the common law, as stated in the rule, ff. de mu. et one. l. rescripto. §. si quis accusatorem. However, because according to the common law a personal penalty can never be imposed on anyone due to contumacy, as in l. absentem. ff. de pę. authen. non, we do not say that this process holds by the form of the statutes. And this is expressly contrary to the form of the statute prohibiting inquisition, and thus the inquisition itself, which is the foundation of the order of the inquisitorial process, is null by law itself, and secondly, whatever follows from it. For when the substantial foundations are destroyed, whatever is built upon them is void and inane. And especially when the person of the judge is lacking, who, as regards inquiring, having the statute prohibiting it, does not have judicial power. Thirdly, the inquisitorial process is null because the nullity appeared from the disposition of the statute, and thus it was an expressed error.

† The person summoned was not bound to appear. And by failing to appear, he is not deemed contumacious. Nor can he be held as having confessed. As noted by Innocentius in the Extravagantes, *De dilationibus*, chapter *Praeterea*; and as noted in the Digest, *Iudicium solutum*, law *Vir bonus*; and in the Digest, *Si quis in ius vocatus non ierit*, law *Ex quacunque*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A term set in a compromise is computed from moment to moment.
2. The word "proxime" denotes the extremity of time.
body: It is proposed that the award was given at the ninth hour. And the award was given at the ninth hour. And the compromise, as appears, was made on the 4th day of the month of November, and the award was rendered on the 4th day of the month of December. The question is whether the said award is valid. I answer: the question turns on this point.

Whether the day of the compromise is to be counted within the term, or rather whether it is to be computed from moment to moment. And the truth is that it is computed from moment to moment; because the wording states "within the term of the next thirty days." And this is proven by two reasons. First, when nothing else appears to have been agreed upon between the parties, the day begins immediately. And thus the computation is from moment to moment; otherwise it would follow that the award could not be made on the day the compromise was executed, if that day were not part of the term. Furthermore, because the day always begins from moment to moment, if the words allow. As noted in the Code, *De appellationibus*, in the constitution *Hodie*. Moreover, because time must be understood as immediate time. As stated in the Digest, *De verbis obligatorum*, in the law *Eius qui calendis*.

† Moreover, this is proven by the word *proxime*, which designates the extremity of the first period. And thus it appears when we say, "this one is *proximus* to puberty." As noted in the Institutes, *de inutilibus stipulationibus*, § *pupillus*. Furthermore, if it were understood as referring to the artificial day, which runs from sunrise until sunset and the twilight of night, the night would not be included. As noted in the Digest, *de feriis*, l. *more Romano*. And the aforementioned sentence is proposed to have been pronounced in the second hour of the night. Therefore, it was pronounced after the term had expired. Hence, it is void by operation of law. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a statute providing that a person is to be condemned to the gallows for three thefts, or that if a person has been twice condemned for theft, the third condemnation shall be to the gallows: who is to be considered twice condemned, or how are thefts to be distinguished so as to be considered multiple? Likewise, what if it is stated that if a person commits theft three times, how is this to be understood?
body: For the sake of clarity, the statute provides that in order to impose

It must be premised that, for the evident purpose of imposing the penalty of the gallows, the statute requires a first, second, and third theft, without any other qualification. And then, if indeed several things or quantities are stolen together before the thief turns to other acts, this is considered one theft, and not several. But if he commits several thefts at intervals of time—for example, one today, another tomorrow, and another the day after—these are nevertheless several distinct thefts, distinguished by things and times. As stated in D. de furtis, l. eum qui, § idem dicit.

When, however, the statute requires not only theft but also condemnation—namely, that one be condemned for the first and second theft, and then, for the third, condemned to the gallows—then for three thefts, or even more, one cannot be condemned to the gallows unless other condemnations preceded. For it is necessary to observe the form of the statute, as in C. de modo mulctarum, l. eas; and to weigh it diligently, as in D. vi bono rapt., l. praetor, § erat; and D. de poenis, l. capitalium, § crassatores, and § famosos.

Therefore, it must be considered whether the said statute requires that one be previously condemned for the first thefts, in order that for the third theft he be condemned to the gallows. And it must be said that the statute does not state this, and therefore it does not require it. As in D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. si servum, § non dixit.

Secondly, it must be seen whether, considering the form of the inquisition, three distinct thefts separated by intervals of time were alleged. And it appears that they were; because the inquisition contains that the mistress of Mag. stole twice in the month of February, 5 ducats in coin on each occasion; and twice in the month of March, 5 other ducats, which quantities she gave to the said Ang. at the said times. And thus she speaks in the plural regarding times, and subsequently, in declaring, adds that the said A. received these moneys, and by receiving them on six occasions, and by contracting, and by moving them from place to place. Therefore, it must be held that what is said "on six occasions" is the same as "six thefts"; because for each occasion one theft is committed, just as in adultery. As in D. de privatis delictis, l. nunquam plura.

To the contrary, it seems that if, before turning to other acts, everything is considered one and the same offense, and not several. As noted in D. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. plures; and D. de furtis, l. vulgaris, in principio. Nor could the said Magd. have stolen and given six times, or more, on the same day, or even on the same night, continuing the same crime. And in doubt, whenever someone is to be condemned from a confession, the confession must be interpreted in the milder sense. As in Extr. de actionibus, c. cum dilecti; and D. de iudiciis, l. si quis intentione ambigua.

Therefore, since the form of the statute was not alleged—for it is one thing to say "so many times," and another to say "so many thefts"—it is not the case that the sentence of the gallows was justly passed. What shall we say, having seen the reasons and considered that these words, "so many times," signify offenses distinct in number and time? And it seems that the case is in its own reason that this is so, in l. agraria, de termino convento, where the enumeration of terms induces the enumeration of offenses; and in l. quicunque, C. de servis fugitivis; and because here express mention is made of several times, as in C. de usuris, l. usurae; and because in momentary offenses continuation is not presumed, so that the repetition is considered a new offense.

Moreover, the said inquisita are said to have committed certain enormities, if indeed they are true and not fabricated; especially this penalty is deserved for rape, corruption of the mind of a daughter of a family, and theft, with the concurrence of mind and body. As in C. de furtis, l. si quis servo.

I have never been accustomed to give counsel in capital cases. Nevertheless, for now, the magnificient Lord my master Charles Malatesta burdens me to write, and I consent. I believe, however, that he may order me to write the aforementioned, whether just or unjust. In this matter, however, let the most excellent prince himself, who has knowledge and judgment, and who has only truth before his eyes, consider my reasons in this my counsel. For I am moved by the aforementioned, and by another, c. veritatis, in which is contained the order and arrangement that several delinquents were to be removed, who were at his order. For this order and arrangement, followed with administration, must be punished by the same law by which theft is punished. As in D. de adulteriis, l. et si amicus; and D. de minoribus, l. auxilium, § in delictis.

I wrote without salary, because it was done for my lord Charles Malatesta. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a donation causa mortis accedes more to a contract than to a last will, and below in the following opinion, number 1.
2. Whether a blind person can make a donation causa mortis without observing the solemnity required in the law *hac consultissima*, Codex, *qui testamento facere possunt*.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

Whether a blind person may make a donation causa mortis without observing that solemnity which is required in his testament. By the law *Hac consultissima*, Codex, *Qui testamento facere possint*: whether, in a donation causa mortis made by a blind person, that solemnity is required which is required in his testament; and whether a donation causa mortis accedes to a contract or to a last will. For a mere and proper donation causa mortis is equivalent to a contract, as noted in the law *Secunda*, Digest, *De donationibus praeter legem*. For a donation causa mortis can be considered in three ways. First, with regard to its very formation. Second, with regard to its confirmation. Third, with regard to its efficacy or effect.

In the first case, with regard to its formation, we say that it accedes to a contract, not to a last will; because it must be made by stipulation, as in the law *Inter mortis*, Digest, *De donationibus causa mortis*; or today by pact, just like a donation inter vivos. And on this point, that singular gloss in the law *Cum pater*, section *Mevio*, Digest, *De legatis*, second, which says that just as a donation is perfected by bare consent, as in the law *Si quis argentum*, Codex, *De donationibus causa mortis*. A similar gloss appears in the law *Ut haeredibus*, same title, although it is said in the gloss to section *Mevio* that it is not found elsewhere. Also, a similar gloss on this point appears in the law *Si stipulatio*, Codex, *De iure donationis*, in the great gloss there. And thus it ought to be understood, and is understood, as noted in the aforementioned law *Secunda*, *De donationibus praeter legem*. Hence, a son may make a donation causa mortis with the consent of his father. And thus it may depend on the will of a third party, which is otherwise in the case of a last will. And this is true if he consents specifically; or otherwise, as in the law *Filius*, *De donationibus*.

Secondly, I said that a donation causa mortis can be considered with regard to its confirmation. Thereupon, I say that a donation causa mortis does not require acceptance of the inheritance, but is confirmed by death, as in the law *Cum pater*, section *Coram*, and there noted, *De legatis*, second. But it is otherwise with legacies to pious causes, which are greater; because they are not due intestate unless the inheritance is accepted, as in the law *Secunda*, *De fideicommissis liberorum*, and the law *Qui filio*, section *Servus*, Digest, *De hereditate instituenda*, in the singular gloss which says that just as legacies require acceptance when left by testament, so do they intestate. Hence, if the inheritance is not accepted, they are at least not due intestate. Thus says the gloss in the aforementioned law *Qui filio*, section *Servus*. And the case is in the aforementioned law *Secunda*, *De fideicommissis liberorum*. Hence, he who [claims] a legacy from Peter Titius, if he does not prove the acceptance of the inheritance, succumbs by the aforementioned gloss, which we note. But acceptance made afterwards would confirm the judgment, as in the law *Haeres quandoque*, *De acquirenda hereditate*, Digest, and there noted by my learned doctor, Master Baldus, illuminator of both laws.

Thirdly, I said that a donation causa mortis can be considered with regard to its efficacy or effect. And then it must be said that from a donation causa mortis, three kinds of actions do not arise. Hence, neither an action on the testament nor a hypothecary action arises. It is true that a vindication of the thing arises; because dominion passes directly, just as in a legacy, according to the singular gloss, and it is in the law *Secunda*, Digest, *De publiciana actione*; [the action] ex stipulatu, or conditional, from the law *Si quis argentarius*. If no stipulation intervened, from all the above it appears that a donation causa mortis accedes to a contract, especially with regard to the solemnity to be observed.

† and consequently I conclude that the aforementioned donation made by the blind person is valid without the formality introduced by l. hac consultissima, C. qui testamento facere possunt, because that law established that formality solely in a testament in which a blind person wishes to institute an heir, and in legacies and fideicommissa which a blind person leaves, and in codicils which he makes, as in that l. hac consultissima, §. in eundem modum. But that law does not apply to a donation causa mortis, which is equated to and accedes to a contract, as I have proved above: therefore, the formality introduced by l. si, C. de donatione causa mortis, suffices, and no other formality is required. Hence, I conclude that the said donation made by the blind person is valid and binding without the formality introduced for those matters by l. hac consultissima, because the formality introduced by the said l. si, C. de donatione causa mortis, suffices, as I said and proved above. And thus I say and advise, I, Alvise de Peru, as above advised by Lord Peter.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a donation causa mortis accedes more to a contract than to a last will, or vice versa.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† My teacher, Lord Baldus, stated in l. cum hi. §. idem erit dicendum, ff. de transactionibus, that when it is asked whether a donation causa mortis is to be considered as a contract or as a last will, and thus whether it accedes more to a contract than to a last will, or as is called forth by the laws cited above and by the notes of Dyonisius in l. cum tam is, ff. de donatione causa mortis: When, however, we speak with respect to the original active cause, then it accedes more to a contract than to a last will; otherwise a filiusfamilias could not make a donation causa mortis, which would be contrary to the aforementioned l. tam is. Or, if we speak with respect to the subject matter, then it accedes to both; because that which can be donated inter vivos, and that which can be bequeathed in a testament, can also be donated causa mortis. This is supported by what Azo notes in his Summa de donationibus. Or, if we speak with respect to the cause of existential perfection, insofar as the form of the contract is considered, then with respect to mode and form it accedes to a contract; because it is made by pact, and sometimes by stipulation, as noted in l. cum pater. §. meo, supra allegata. Or, if we speak with respect to the final cause, with respect to the end and effect, then it accedes more to a last will than to a contract; because it regularly takes effect upon death, just like a last will. And this is supported by what is noted in l. 2, ff. de dote praelegata. Now, to the point at hand, because here in our question it is asked about the form and order of the contract, and about the person acting, namely, whether a blind person can make a donation causa mortis without observing the form and solemnity required in his testament, as was consulted by the aforementioned most excellent doctors. And thus I say and advise, I, Marcus Angebelli de Peru, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether and when a statute of laymen can dispose of an oath, especially by proving it.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

It must be considered that sometimes a statute expressly repudiates an oath, and sometimes a statute opposing the act does not mention the oath, neither repudiating nor expressly approving it. In the first case, it seems that such a statute cannot impede or remove the efficacy of the oath, or annul the oath; because wherever an oath can be kept without loss of life, etc., it must be kept. D. de iureiurando, c. Cum contingat; and c. Severior. But here it can be kept. Therefore, etc. Secondly, because the statute prohibits or annuls, such an oath is contrary to divine and human law. Hence, in this regard, it does not seem valid; because a secular statute issued against divine or canonical law is not valid: as is clear. D. 10, c. Quod autem sit contra legem divinam. That it is contrary to divine law is clear according to the passage: "Render to the Lord your vows," etc. Deuteronomy 5; and Matthew 5. And D. de iureiurando, c. Et si Christus. That it is contrary to canonical law is clear, because an oath which, if kept, does not result in detriment to the oath-taker with respect to eternal salvation, is not to be kept: as by the laws cited above, and Extr. de pace, c. 2, lib. 6. Moreover, the statute is found to have been made concerning a matter which does not pertain to those enacting it: namely, concerning an oath. D. de iureiurando, lib. 6, c. 2; de fideiussoribus, c. Si, eo. lib. Therefore, it does not seem valid. To the contrary, because the law which expressly repudiates an oath has the force of an apostolic constitution. Hence, as if remitted, it does not bind the oath-taker, as is the gloss, no. in l. Adigere, §. Quamvis, D. de iure pacis. Moreover, one cannot renounce public law, which gives a certain form to human acts. D. de pace, l. Ius publicum; and Omissio vitiat, de constitutionibus pecuniariis, l. 1, §. 1. Indeed, the omission of matter or form vitiates the disposition, even in a favorable act. D. de verbis obligatis, l. Qui Romae, §. Flavius Hermes. To the foregoing, it is pertinent: Extr. de rescriptis, Cum dilecta; de restitutione spoliatorum, c. Pisanis. And substantial form is recognized constructively, when it is said to be the being of the thing to be exhibited. Iulianus; and destructively: because if it is destroyed, the being of the thing is destroyed. D. de usufructu, l. Qui ususfructus. And therefore, whatever is necessary for the being of the thing is said to be of the substantial form. Now, in the case at hand, because for the being of the thing, presence and the consent of two nearest blood relatives are required as a substantial form by municipal law; and otherwise the contract or obligation does not hold. Therefore, where this is lacking, the contract is null, as by the laws cited above. What, then, is to be said? Certainly, I do not affirm this for the present; because I do not see that this is our case; because in our case the statute does not impugn the oath, but rather requires the oath for the validation of the contract, or for greater strength. But the above case is when the statute expressly approves the oath; and then one must stand by the oath. As in Auth. Sacramenta puberum. And this also is not our case. Sometimes the law opposing the act does not mention the oath. And then either the law prohibits the consent, and the oath operates nothing, because the annihilation of consent means the oath has no foundation in natural law. D. de pace, l. Iuris gentium, §. Generaliter; de agris et censibus, l. Quam modum; de legibus 1, l. Si quis inquilinos, §. Si. Or it does not condemn the consent, but confers some benefit or privilege, and then either that is of private utility, and the oath ought to be kept; or principally of public utility, and then otherwise. D. de pace, l. Iuris gentium, §. Si paciscor. Now, returning to the point, from the words of the aforementioned statute it appears, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether possession can be proven by the payment of a collected sum, and who may be said to have been in possession and to have the better right.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen. The sentence that we two rendered is grounded, among other things, upon two privileges of the commune of Pavia. The first is that of Frederick I, of which indeed none appears to be null, in which the origin is contained, and in it provision is made that the Emperor, on account of well-earned services, granted the place of Cagnano to the Pavese in perpetuity. But the last one—since there is no other belonging to either of the parties—is that of Emperor Frederick II, in which, even if the origin were distinct, it is found, as is noted in § pactus ne peteret at the end; and in it a similar grant is provided for, with a formal revocatory clause proceeding from certain knowledge, as he states, as in ff. de re iudi. l. quidam consulebat, de excu. tuto. l. idem vlpia., the effect of whose succession was made to another concerning the said place of Cagnano; and deservedly in the court of justice were we moved by the first, and yet more strongly by the second. Behold, from the first, because a right that is not taken away is not forbidden to stand, ff. quibus ex cau. maio. l. sciendum with the following law, and especially a privilege, C. de decu. l. in filiis, book 10. But having examined diligently, and with better and more mature information, the privileges of the Tortonese, according to what we might see, they do not have a revocatory clause under this form: that the subsequent Emperor from certain knowledge revokes all privileges granted to the prejudice of the commune of Tortona. Whence it is true, because an Emperor cannot derogate from a successor who wishes to use the plenitude rather than sometimes the rectitude of power regarding jurisdictional matters, that if the grant made by Frederick I had been made to the prejudice of the Tortonese, certainly the excess of the Pavese would not have implicitly intended this, as is noted in C. de fundis et saltibus rei Dominicę l. si quo loco, book 11; and if it had been valid, it would have been justly revoked by a contrary privilege, and the place of jurisdiction would have been re-transferred to the Tortonese, because this would have been within the will and power, both most equitable and orderly, of the successor, as in C. de legi. l. digna vox; for all jurisdiction and all district resides with the Prince, as in c. omnis iurisdictio, de extra ordinariis capi. feudo., col. 10, and prescription cannot run against him, C. de praescrip. 30. anno., c. competit de postulatione, c. bonę, by Innocent. Now this would be the case if, as was proposed by the Tortonese from the nature of the location and territory, Cagnano had been of the territory of Tortona, ff. de verbo. signi. l. pupillus, § territorium, de resti. spo. ca. cum ad sedem, by Innocent; because territory is part of the city, ff. ad muni. l. qui ex vico, ff. de iudi. l. insulae cum tale, in Authen. quibus mo. na. effi. sui § si quis igitur ex qualibet, ff. de offi. pręfecti vr. l. 1 § cum vrbem, de elec. c. vbi periculum, book 6, C. de episco. et cler. l. nulli. But we do not see that this proves, or alleges, that before the time of that grant Tortona had anything to do in Cagnano; whence the revocatory words cease to apply, because the terminus to which reference is made is not that one, ff. de leg. j. l. Titię textores, ff. de lib. et posthu. l. commodissime; likewise subreption ceases, and thus, since from the first privilege the beneficial ownership of jurisdiction was acquired by the Pavese, and the commune of Pavia has its jurisdiction founded from the very beginning, which is presumed to endure, C. de prob. l. siue possidetis.
