Moreover, from the fact that we find this Cagnano was granted at one time to one party and at another time to the other, no mention having been made of the prior privilege, we do not believe that the first grant was revoked, as in C. de silen. l. decu., book 10; and this is evidently clear, first, by the express text in extra de praescrip. c. veniens; second, because a privilege does not prejudice the justice of others, de priuilegiis parentibus, by Bernard; third, because the Pope or Prince, in granting a privilege, does not intend to harm the right of another, de priuilegiis c. dudum, by Bernard, argument from ff. de vulg. substi. l. ex facto, C. de emancipa. lib. l. nec auus, de autho. et vsu palij c. ex tuarum, C. vnde vi autho. et l. meminerint, ff. ne quid in loco pub. l. 2 § si quis a principe. For if it had been established to us that in the revocatory clause of the Tortonese privilege—especially through the oath of the Emperor, which signifies his precise intention, ff. de leg. 2 l. cum pater § si filius matre, and it is expressly found in the Peace of Constance—it touched the privilege of the Pavese and revoked it, and no subsequent privilege to the contrary appeared, certainly I, Baldus, would have judged in favor of the Tortonese against Pavia; but the Pavese severed all these assumptions of mine, for they said that they have—and so it is true, according to what I perceived—a final privilege, beyond the privilege after all the privileges of the Tortonese, with a formal, full, absolute, and unqualified derogation and from certain knowledge. And therefore, either from the first or from the last, they necessarily have the right, ff. de lib. et posthu. l. Gallus § si eius, ff. de acqui. haered. l. quod si dubitet, argument from both joined together, ff. de pact. l. si vnus § pactus ne peteret, et vult., and Inst. de replicationibus in the beginning, and what is noted in C. ad Tertu. l. omnem; because if the Tortonese had prevailed by a derogation, therefore by a contrary derogation—especially one better drafted—they ought to prevail, and that reason was conclusive for me. Nor could one in truth say otherwise: abide by the rule that you yourself have laid down, ff. si cer. pe. l. lecta, at the verse et si vt ille. Unless I am blind, it cannot be answered otherwise. For I ask: if they had informed me that the commune of Pavia possessed revocatory privileges, would I have given counsel to the Tortonese with arguments expressly concluding against them? Having been elected, they, who are learned men, would not have accepted such allegations. Someone will say: the Tortonese have prescribed; to this it is answered that in these incorporeal things sufficient time is required, concerning which it is not established, together with the knowledge and sufferance of the adversary; but he who daily exercises it himself does not suffer it, as is noted in ff. quod met. causa l. extat, l. 1 C. vti pos.; and therefore one does not prescribe against the other when two possess simultaneously in dispute, and in condition one prescribes against the other, because it would follow that while they were prescribing—which is impossible. As to the use and quasi-possession of the Pavese, unless it was stated through the acts of the case and by the truth itself—granting that even by the Tortonese many, and very many, possessory acts were proved against certain persons as being of the universitas of the place, and in the form of a universitas, where I believe and the evidence of the writings signifies—nonetheless the more just cause ought to prevail, C. de edi. diui Adri. tol. l. edicto § 1, there: qui potiora iura, etc.; for it would be the mark of a foolish judge, when the priority of rights has been commanded, not to choose the more just party and the one having the better foundations, as Innocent notes in extra de prob. c. iurauit. Whence I, Baldus, acknowledge two foundations: first, that by reason of the older title not abolished, the older and more just is presumed and prevails, as is noted in c. licet causam and in l. momentaneis; second, I acknowledge that if the Pavese have the better privileges, they ought to prevail in both the petitory and the possessory. If, however, the Tortonese have the more powerful privileges, they ought to prevail, because just as the opposite holds in the opposite case, so the proposition holds in the proposed case. And that rule is the very rule upon which I, Baldus, formerly founded the case of the Tortonese, when I had not yet seen the privileges of the Pavese, which they could not show me because they did not yet have a copy—perhaps they alleged something else to me; but after I saw the contrary in fact, on the basis of the very same reasons and rules it is precisely necessary to judge the contrary, for nothing has been changed in law, but in fact, from which the law arises, as in l. si ex plagiis § in diuo capitolio, ad l. Aqui. And if we had recognized that there were two Cagnanos, the image of one Caesar would have been given to the one, and that of the other to the other, ff. de rei ven. l. idem pompo. § fi.; but through the notoriety of a permanent fact and through the criminal avenue the contrary seems sufficiently to appear. That fact is established, that the commune of Tortona sued against Pavia in the petitory and the possessory for retention, which can be cumulated in corporeal things. Whence, if the lack of right of the Tortonese is established, or if it is doubtful, the defendant ought to have been absolved, as we did, and silence imposed upon the plaintiff regarding both, as is noted in C. vti possidetis l. j., although Bartolus says that in the possessory suit, about to be shared, it is divided; and it is a kind of trick that it should be divided where neither party intends it; and therefore I did not agree with the opinion of my teacher, ff. si pars haere. pe. l. non possumus; nevertheless, he would by no means have said so when the petitory is cumulated, C. de rei ven. l. fi.; from these things, what justice dictates clearly appears. There is no doubt that in contrary cases and circumstances contrary rules of law are established, and that upon new proofs it is necessary to change one's consideration and understanding, as in l. per hanc admonendi with its concordances. It is true that on another occasion I advised—both well, justly, and holily, and I say the same and ever the same—that through the payment of a tax quasi-possession is proved. But the Pavese also exercised jurisdiction, and indeed contentious jurisdiction, as their documents state, etc.; and he who terrifies and pronounces the law by judging is not less properly said to possess territory than he who struggles for it, because jurisdiction simply speaking is greater than jurisdiction in a certain respect and not simply speaking, l. 1 C. de of. praef. vr. Furthermore, the proofs of the Pavese speak of both, if I am not mistaken, which were newly produced to us at the very end for the supplementation and confirmation of the old proofs; I held the documents of both fathers, on account of the virtue and uprightness of such great communities, to be truest, although many things were said by the parties, dist. 96 c. nobilissimus. If the sentence is supported by the reasons contained therein, even if something were lacking to the sentence itself, it is ours to supply it, ff. quod cum eo l. Titianus, C. de ap. l. ampliorem. The final conclusion is this: that in rights, the cause of the one having the right is stronger when action is brought in both proceedings, or in one partaking of the force of both, ff. de interdi. l. 2 and 3 § quaedam, ff. de iti. ac. priua. l. 3 § hic autem from the preceding; indeed, according to Innocent, one can possess a certain capacity for acts, but not rights, unless indeed he has the rights; whence he who prescribes a servitude is meanwhile well in quasi-possession of the servitude insofar as it signifies a fact—that is, a certain going and driving, or similar acts, l. 2 ff. si serui. ven.—but he is not yet in quasi-possession of the right of servitude except after he has prescribed, which is the very truth, because that which does not exist cannot be possessed, or quasi-possessed. Likewise, in doubtful matters an absolutory sentence ought to be rendered; note on this, ff. de re iud. l. duo iudices dati, de iudi. l. in tribus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a mother, who did not accept guardianship or did not request that a guardian be appointed while legitimate guardians were still living, ought to be excluded from the succession, given the statute in question here.
2. Whether male agnates, who are in a more remote degree of agnation, succeed and are preferred to the aunt, given the statute, etc.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The statute provides that, in order to preserve the agnatic line and the name of the deceased’s household, and for the general good and utility of the citizens and inhabitants of the diocese of Parma, the mother shall not succeed to a son or daughter who dies intestate, if at the time of the death of the deceased whose estate is in question there exist any legitimate or natural male descendants of the father’s household or lineage, up to and including the fourth degree, the degree being calculated according to canonical law, etc. And the aforementioned provisions, which are established regarding the mother, shall apply to all persons in the maternal line, and it is understood that one who is unable to make a testament dies intestate, etc.

Now it happens that a certain Gissa died in infancy, leaving behind her mother, her maternal grandfather, a uterine sister, and two full paternal cousins, as well as two sons of one of said cousins who are under 25 years of age, and an aunt, no guardian having been requested for said infant, and she having died one year after the death of her father.

Now the question arises as to which of the aforementioned persons shall succeed to said ward, and it appears that the mother should succeed. For she succeeds according to common law, because she is prior in degree, as in the Authentica *Defuncto*. And she excludes all collaterals, not only cognates but also agnates, as in the Institution *De senatusconsulto Tertulliano*, § *Sed nos*, and in the Authentica *De haeredibus ab intestato*, § *Reliquum*.

Nor does it avail to object that she did not request a guardian, for if there were male agnates to whom legitimate guardianship is granted, she had no need to request a guardian, as noted in Law 2, Code *Ad senatusconsultum Tertullianum*. Nor does it avail to object that, on the contrary, the legitimate heirs are not an obstacle, because the mother is preferred; for that is true only if the mother wishes to act as guardian. It is otherwise if she renounces the guardianship or remains silent. For due to her silence, the legitimate heirs may approach the praetor. And if she is cited and does not accept the guardianship, they may and must assume the guardianship themselves. Argument from those things noted in the Digest *De tutoribus et curatoribus*, given by these: Law *Tutor si petitus*.

Others say that that glossa does not state the truth, as is clear there through Bartolus, because there is no place for legitimate guardianship as long as the anomalous [guardianship], which is prior, is pending. Argument from the Digest *Ad senatusconsultum Tertullianum*, Law 2, § *Si mater*. The ancient doctors passed over this lightly, upholding the glossa, because since there is an ordinary legitimate guardian, the mother seems to be relieved, which is thus proven: this mother is not bound to request that a guardian be appointed, nor to be compelled to accept the legitimate guardianship, as noted by Cynus in Law *Si*, Code *De administratione tutorum*. Furthermore, she is not bound to accept the guardianship, for this is a voluntary burden for her, not a necessary one. Furthermore, this was introduced as a privilege for the mother against common law. Therefore, it ought not to be turned to her detriment, as in the Digest *De legibus*, Law *Nulla*. Moreover, it was provided by ancient law that she should be excused if the ward had agnates. And this is not found to have been corrected. Therefore, the mother is excused. And if it is said that the mother sins by not accepting or by repudiating: nevertheless, the law posits that the mother is excluded. In this case, you will not find that condition, as I said. Thus the ancient advocates passed over this lightly.

And there is another reason in favor of the mother: for she is not bound to yield in succession to agnates; but rather she should ensure that they are in default, and are excluded from succession, so that they do not exclude the mother.

But Bartolus, as I said, holds that the mother is excluded, because guardianship begins with the mother. And thus she is negligent in legitimately accepting it, because she did not consult for the welfare of her offspring; therefore, she is rightly repelled from succession, as in the Institution *Ad senatusconsultum Tertullianum*, § *Sed quemadmodum*. And just as the ancient laws were conceived with respect to the mother and the grandmother, so too is whatever follows from them and followed from them, as in the Code *De latronibus et liberis tollendis*, Law 1, in the beginning.

But I do not dispute this further, because the mother is excluded by the statute, given the existence of male agnates. And the same applies to the maternal grandfather, and the same to the uterine sister, because the case falls under the statute. Therefore, there is no doubt, as in the Code *Si fur*, Law *Ancillae*. And even if there were slight doubt, one would still have to adhere to the words of the statute, as in the Digest *De exercitu*, Law 1, § *Si is qui navem*.

† Having therefore omitted all other points, which are superfluous, there remains only one point, namely, whether male agnates, who are in a more remote degree of agnation, succeed: or the aunt, who is likewise an agnate, and in a nearer degree. And on this article it is argued both for and against. And first, that the male agnates should come, it is argued thus. To these male agnates a personal privilege has been granted. Therefore, it does not extend to the aunt. Moreover, favor has been granted to male agnates. Moreover, the purpose of the statute concerns only male agnates. This is why it was so established, and so laws are constituted, so that usually these inheritances would flow to males. As in Inst. de leg. agn. succ. § 1, ver. quod ideo. This also seems sufficiently expressed by the statute, when it says for every good and utility of men. For from the preamble one argues to the mind of the law, not only from the writing, but from the writing. As in D. de haer. inst. l. Pacumeius. And for this part is alleged the opinion of my doctor Bartolus of Saxoferrato, which he places in l. 2, § videndum, D. ad Tertull. where he says that this statute disposes two things: namely, that it excludes the mother. And this is the first. And it devolves the inheritance to male agnates: and this is the second. From which follows the exclusion of any other person: because it is impossible for more heirs to exist in solidum. Moreover, there is no reason why she should concur. Hence it is argued thus. Either you say males do not succeed: and you say against the statute. Or you say they succeed. And then of necessity you exclude the aunt. Nor is it new that a person, who is appointed to exclude another, appears appointed to exclude herself. As in l. fideicom. § plerumque, D. de leg. 3. arg. D. de cond. et dem. l. Pater Severinam, § conditionum. Moreover, because the mother is excluded on account of these male agnates, therefore they enter. Maternal favors, and, so to speak, the maternal degree, namely, therefore if they exclude the aunt. Whose opinion I fortified with many other reasons. C. de collat. l. illam in lectu. mea. And not wishing to totally reprehend him, adhering to his opinion in one case. Namely, when the mother is alive. Moreover, this mother is excluded from the inheritance totally. Indeed, she seems to be a singular heir in the usufruct granted to her by the statute. But with her being an heir, and in one coin, it does not seem possible for the aunt to succeed in any way, on account of the prior position of the maternal degree. This question is very subtle. And as many heads, so many opinions. And therefore, examining it more diligently, I premise that the private edict is here manifest. But the dispositive edict, that agnates ought to succeed, is not manifest. And therefore I form such a doubt: whether, the mother being excluded, these agnates come by the seventh extraordinary possession, under that title, as from the law, etc. and Inst. de bon. poss. § septima. I say this, not excluding the acceptance of the inheritance. But understanding from which head this is better declared, if you consider praetorian law. I consider that the said excluding provision opens the way for agnates to succeed by ordinary right, both by civil law and praetorian law, as if the obstacle were removed. And therefore if they are alone with the mother, or the maternal line, by civil law, by praetorian law they come as if the obstacle were removed, which being removed, ordinary right succeeds, but extraordinary right does not accede: thus the removal of the obstacle is well statutory: but the succession is by common law. As arg. Extr. de rescript. c. 2. From which follows that the said aunt is not excluded: because she is prior in the degree of agnation. And although the statute makes a difference between male and female in obstructing the mother, and the maternal line, yet not in obstructing the aunt. For neither the words, nor the mind of the statute disposes this, since she is an agnate, and by common law stronger. Which is not corrected by the statute, and if this were of unwritten mind, since the reason is not the same: as is gathered from the doctrine of Cynus and Nicolaus de Tudeschis, quae sit longa consuetudo, l. 1, in pe. gl. et si dicis. Therefore, the favor of agnates is not favor potentially. For what if the aunt renounced? She excludes the mother, yet she does not exclude the aunt: because this is not dictated by the statute, nor its reason: since it makes no mention of the aunt. Arg. Inst. ad Tertull. § soror. Where it says that the mother excluded the brother, but not the sister: although to that. § posset responderi: because the mother there did not exclude the sister. Thus it seems to be a certain circle: yet in the circle he wins who has the stronger right. I.e. the aunt, who is not found excluded, as in l. aequissima, § 1, D. ad Tertull. From these it appears that the statute has two virtues. Namely, the exclusive of the maternal line. And the opening: but not the devolving to the prejudice of the aunt: because since this statute is against common law, its words are not said to be vulgar. And therefore I am of opinion for the aunt, although for the mother it is most subtly alleged by those of the contrary opinion. For since the statute excludes only the maternal line, therefore not the paternal. Nor can it include more, which excludes: and especially if the decree of the lord wills that statutes be understood as they lie, without supplementation, or extensive interpretation. And the said mother does not exclude the said aunt, but finds her excluded. Moreover, where terms are narrated, which is, when something is added, or diminished, which is not provided for by municipal law, the disposition of the municipal law ceases. But here is added in fact. Namely, the aunt: therefore the disposition of the statute ceases in this, namely, that it is not drawn to the prejudice of the aunt. Nor is this new, that one edict sometimes opens for another. As D. de contrah. l. si post mortem, § si. If the testamentary tablets do not exist. l. 1, in fi. D. de lib. et posth. l. si. D. de inoff. test. l. posthumus, § si quis ex his. Moreover, if C. defeats A. on account of one reason, although A. excluded B, yet C. does not defeat B, who is before him, in whom the reason ceases. As noted by Cynus, de nat. lib. auth. licita. So it is here, that the mother is excluded because she is not of the agnation, with her whole line: but the aunt is of the agnation, and in her is preserved the honor of the family. And the memory of the parents. Wherefore it must be concluded openly that the mother is excluded by male agnates, and male agnates are excluded by the mother accepting the inheritance. But if she did not accept, or the deceased did not transmit: then there would be place for the said male agnates, and it suffices that it could be to their interest to this, that they exclude the mother. Arg. D. de contrah. l. filium. And thus I hold on this point, how the authority of Bartolus and his reasons make it difficult. But the ancient doctors would not have made a question of it: because it is not ours to exclude him: because he does not seem excluded by statute. As in Auth. de trien. et semis. § consideremus. And in d. l. illam, C. de collat.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If a statute appoints a special judge for the cases of hospitals, excluding all other judges: whether it is understood that the judge having general jurisdiction, such as the podestà, is excluded.
2. Whether special and lower jurisdiction derogates from general and higher jurisdiction.
3. Whether and when the genus is derogated by the species.
4. That which is more universal is considered in the place of the genus, and that which is less in the place of the species.
5. The term "special" is said in many ways.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Having considered all the aforesaid matters, regarding the aforementioned doubt, whether the Hospital of Mercy could have brought action before the Podestà concerning the aforementioned causes of occupation and invasion, it appears that it could not. This is because, according to the form of the older statutes, in cases concerning hospitals, a specific judge is appointed, namely the Judge Prior of Saint Angelo, in the event that the office of the Captain is vacant. And thus, jurisdiction appears to be removed from every other judge. D. de iudicibus, l. cum praetor. For a special assignment derogates from a general one. As stated in D. de legatis 1, l. quod in rerum, § si quis, according to Jacobus de Ateneo; and a matter specially entrusted to one person is not to be attended to by others. C. de testibus, l. consulta diualia, because one cannot perform the office of another. As stated in l. 2, de executionibus, lib. 12. Therefore, from the aforesaid, it appears that the Podestà did not have jurisdiction in such a case.

† To the contrary, that jurisdiction pertains to the power in the aforementioned cases, is proved thus. For it is certain that the Lord Power has superior general jurisdiction. As is noted in the Digest, *De iudiciis*, law *Iudicium soluitur*; and by Innocentius, *De electione*, chapter *In causis*. Now, if one has high jurisdiction and another low and subtracted jurisdiction, the superior is not derogated from by the inferior jurisdiction, as stated in the aforementioned laws. Hence, this general office is not removed by any special commission, because everything else is understood to be committed to it, as being subordinate to it. As noted by my lord in the law *Nec quicquam*, at the end, in the Digest, *De officio proconsulis*; and it is openly proved in the chapter *Per hoc*, *De haeresi*, Book 6. Unless it is said that, although general jurisdiction against heretics in some province is granted to an inquisitor, for that reason the bishop is not derogated from. And note the gloss in the law *Si*, in the Code, *Ubi causae fiscales*, in the ultimate gloss, which expressly says this. As in the Code, *De iure omnium iudicum*, law *Si*. It is also proved because we have a law that ordinary jurisdiction competent to one is not removed by attribution of the same jurisdiction to another. As in the Code, *De officio praefecti urbi*, law 1, where the case is. For it is not said that prejudice is done to the superior because jurisdiction is attributed to the inferior, as the text there states. Hence, Bartolus says there, by that law, that although in a city one special official is made over damage given or abundance, the jurisdiction of the power concerning that is not removed. Since, therefore, all jurisdiction which the Lord Captain and his judges had is attributed to the Lord Power and his judges; and the Captain could have cognized by himself of civil causes for the hospital and against the hospital, as has been proved; therefore also the Power, who succeeds in the same jurisdiction, [retains it], notwithstanding the aforementioned law *Quod in versis*, section *Si quis*, because it speaks of those things which cannot be held by two in solidum, so that by giving to one, it is seen to be taken from the other. Argument in the law *Sicut*, *De adicienda lege*. But jurisdiction can be held by several lords in solidum. Code, *De officio consulis*, law 1. Furthermore, the aforementioned law *Cum praetor*, verse *Iurisdictio uni commissa, videtur alii denegata*, does not object, because it speaks of delegated jurisdiction. Thus, Extra, *De maiore et obedientia*, and chapter *Studisti*. But in ordinary jurisdiction it is otherwise. And for the final conclusion concerning this passage, I think it should be distinguished thus: because either the jurisdiction is distributed, and thus the administration is divided, and one does not interfere in the office of the other. As in law 2, *De executione*, Book 12; *De iudiciis*, chapter *Solemus*, section *Latrunculator*; Digest, *De solutionibus*, law *Quaero*. And the example is clear in this city, where jurisdiction is divided. For the division of powers diminishes them. Or it is attributed to one generally and to another specially; and then that special commission is made on account of the excellence of the commissioner, to whom ascending and greater jurisdiction is granted, and it pertains to him alone. Code, *Ne liceat potentibus*, law 1, at the end; Code, *De pedaneis iudicibus*, law *Placet*; Digest, *De arbitris*, law *Non distinguimus*; Code, *De libellis*.

† Hence, if an official is appointed in cases of nullity and appeals, it is forbidden to any other person to interfere in this jurisdiction, since it is granted by way of superiority, and thus discretively and excellently. Cf. C. de iudicibus, auth. ad haec. The same applies when something is committed which does not belong to the magistrate by right, but because the law so appoints it. Cf. de iudicibus, l. insinuationem; and ff. de tutoribus, l. muto, § tutoris. But if a lower jurisdiction is committed to one person, and especially to one who is subordinate to a superior, then it is not true that it is denied to the superior, since it is in the interest of the republic to have more courts. Cf. d. l. 1, C. de officio praefecti urbi. Hence, the law then proceeds by way of accumulation, not by way of novation of office. And so it is in our case. But the foregoing seems to be opposed by the fact that the aforementioned statute goes further by depriving other judges and officials of jurisdiction. But to this it is answered that such deprivation is understood with respect to judges and officials of equal rank, but not with respect to higher magistrates. Moreover, that deprivation is not repeated in the grant of jurisdiction made by the statute to the judge of the power of the prior of San Angelo. And when it happens that the office of the captain is vacant, this should not be extended so that jurisdiction is understood to be granted under the favor of the same quality, as in ff. de legibus, l. quod favore torqueri non debet. For it is expedient for someone, and it is favorable to have more judges, as in auth. habita, C. ne filius pro patre. Therefore, the contrary is odious. Cf. l. 1, ff. de his qui sui vel alieni iuris sunt. Hence, it must be restricted, as in the rule odia restringenda sunt, de regulis iuris. And this is as far as the statute is concerned. But it must be considered further that after the aforementioned statute, a certain ordinance was issued, which in some places is called a decree, in others a reform, which grants jurisdiction to the power in cases of occupations and insinuations. Hence, even if all the above-mentioned matters were to cease, which, however, proceed according to law, yet by virtue of the said reform or decree, the power was and is the competent judge in such cases, as I will prove. For the sake of clarity, I premise that the rule

† The rule of law that a specific provision derogates from a general one, as in the rule *generi*: *de regulis iuris*. Hence, strictness in a specific case prevails over equity in a general case, as noted by Dyonisius in the rule *prior*: *de regulis iuris*, Book 6. Secondly, it is posited that this derogation may occur either because the species is exempted from the genus, and then it derogates from the generality by way of exception; or because it restricts the genus to the meaning of the species, and then it derogates from the genus by specific declaration. Here, *genus* is taken for a predicable, *species* for an individual, or for a lower genus among the legists. An example of the first case is clear when a genus is bequeathed to one person and a species, or a lower genus, to another. For then the more specific derogates from the general by exception. *Digestum*, *de legatis* 3, *lex uxore*, § *codicillis*, and the following §, *de peculio legato*, *servo manumisso*. But if both a genus and a species are bequeathed to the same person, and it is established that the species are added to restrict, and restriction occurs, the genus is derogated by specific declaration. Hence, if a testator bequeaths to Titia two marble statues, and also all marble, and if the testator has a thousand marble statues, none pass under the legacy except the two, as in *Digestum*, *de legatis* 3, *lex heres meus*, § 1; and *de fundo instrato*, *lex cum delationis*, § *cui fundo*; *de auro et argento legato*, *lex 1*, § *item si duo*. In the second case, however, when the species is expressed not to derogate but to specify the genus, and then it is stated in *Digestum*, *de legatis* 1, *lex si domino*, where one legacy of a species does not derogate from another specific legacy, although one is simple and the other is by option, which is of an uncertain species. *Digestum*, *qui et a quibus*, *lex 3*. Thirdly, I premise,

† That which is more universal is regarded as a genus, and that which is less universal is regarded as a species. And therefore, the less universal derogates from the more universal, just as a species derogates from a genus, as noted by Dino del Garbo in the aforementioned rule *generi per speciem*, and in the aforementioned law *uxore*, § *codicillis*, *de legatis* 3. Fourthly, I premise that a case is special with respect to persons, as in the Extravagant *Ad repraesentationem*, on the words *non obstantibus*, according to Bartolus. Moreover, a case is more special with respect to place, as in the aforementioned § *codicillis*, and there by Baldus. Now, coming to the point: the ancient statute, which grants jurisdiction to the judge of St. Angelo in cases concerning hospitals during the vacancy of the office of the *capitaneus*, is a universal and general statute, both with respect to causes and with respect to persons. With respect to causes, because it includes every civil and criminal cause, whether petitory or possessory; and thus it is general with respect to all causes. Furthermore, it is general with respect to all persons against whom the hospital wishes to act, whether they are bound by contract or quasi-contract, delict or quasi-delict. Furthermore, it is general with respect to time, not distinguishing between obligations having their origin at one time rather than another. Furthermore, that statute, with respect to mode and form of proceeding, regularly follows the order given by the ancient statutes. But this ordinance, or decree, newly issued, by which jurisdiction is granted to the *Potestas*, is special, or at least less universal than the preceding ancient statute. First, with respect to the cause, because it grants jurisdiction to the *Potestas* only over causes of occupations and *insinuationes*. Second, with respect to the persons against whom, because it disposes only against invaders and occupiers; therefore, it is more special, as in the aforementioned Extravagant *Ad repraesentationem*, according to Bartolus. Third, it is special by reason of time, because it disposes only of occupations made at a certain and determined time. Fourth, it is special because it establishes a certain mode and order of proceeding differently, and in another manner, than would be disposed by the ancient statutes. Fifth, because it imposes a new penalty against occupiers not imposed by the ancient statutes. And therefore, this new municipal law, as disposing specially by virtue of its evident speciality, derogates by exception to the ancient municipal law disposing generally, according to the rule of law: *generi per speciem derogatur*, whether it precedes or follows, as in the rule *generi*, *de regulis iuris*, book 6, and it is clear from the premises above. From which I conclude, therefore, that the Lord *Potestas* is the competent judge in such causes. Moreover, this is manifestly proven by those things which our noted Lord, my patron, posits. He says that in the city of Perugia there is a statute that the Hospital of Mercy cannot sue nor be sued before the judge of the Gate of St. Peter. Another statute says that the judge of the Gate of Eburna alone has cognizance of cases under ten pounds. Now it is asked whether the hospital can sue for causes under 10 pounds before the judge of the Gate of St. Peter, and the statute has place in other causes, the cognizance of which is not specially assigned to another judge by the form of law or statute, according to Bartolus, who thus notes in the law *in sacris*, Codex, *de proximis sacrorum scrineorum*, book 11, where he says it is a case. These things, therefore, in the present matter, because in causes of occupations and invasions cognizance has been specially assigned to another by the form of the new law, therefore the hospital can sue in such causes before him, and especially before him who has greater imperial authority, and who in the aforementioned matters has a specific and special commission by virtue of the new law. And so I say and counsel, I, Francesco di Baldus of Perugia, and company.

In the Name of Christ, Amen. Regarding the agreements concerning the goods of the late Thadeus, it seems that one should say that the said John, acting as agent, upholds justice, and that the said Lady Isa, who is defending, ought to be condemned to relinquish and release to the said John the said landholding, which is now the subject of a hypothecary action in this new trial.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. What the plaintiff in a hypothecary action must prove: and see the following opinion below.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen. In the case concerning the goods of the late Thadeus, against Lord Isam, who is defending: having seen all the acts transmitted to me, both in the first judgment, in which it was done by the authority of the judge, and the request was made to compromise the cause: and having seen the compromise made to certain arbitrators, and the award that followed therefrom. And having seen the remaining proceedings, and the acts in this new judgment in which a hypothecary action is brought against the aforementioned lady:

It seems that, in law, it must be said that the plaintiff upholds justice. For although the said John, as plaintiff, did not prove in the first trial that the said Thadeus possessed the property and the massaricias contained in the aforementioned award at the time of the award, he proved it in this new trial, in which the hypothecary action is now being brought; therefore, this suffices, because in a real action, the declaration of ownership comes properly by the action itself and by the judgment of the judge. Thus, once a declaratory sentence has been passed, ownership will come with the judgment by the office of the judge, as stated in the Institutes, *De officio iudicis*, § *Si in rem*; and in the laws *Ex diverso* and *Qui restituere*, *De re vendicata*. Such is the execution of such a sentence, etc., if afterwards the defendant begins to possess, as in the law *Minus*, § *Si quis fundum*, *De exceptionibus rei iudicatae*, and there by the gloss and doctors. Moreover, it was pronounced, in the presence of the party of the said lady, and without appeal, that the aforementioned award should be executed; therefore, now nothing can be said, since the sentence has passed into *res iudicata*.

But notwithstanding these arguments, I am of the opinion that the contrary is to be done in law, and that the said Lady Isa is to be absolved from the petition of the said John, the plaintiff. It is certain, as appears from the records, that the said John brings a hypothecary action against the aforementioned lady. But the plaintiff in a hypothecary action necessarily has to prove two things: namely, that the goods are pledged, and that they were in the defendant's possession at the time of the obligation. The first is proved in the law *Contrahitur*, *De pignoribus*; the second in the law *Quae nondum*, § *Quod dicitur*, in the same title, and in the laws *Sed et quod* and *Paulus*, in the same title, and thus the omission of the expressed cause of the pledge does not matter.

But in the case at hand, John made a compromise with Thadeus regarding the judgment of the arbitrators, and among other things, the arbitrators judged that certain movable goods and massaricias belonged to the said John; nor did they condemn the said Thadeus to give or do anything to the said John or to another in his name. Therefore, by virtue of the award, the goods of the said Thadeus are not pledged, because he was condemned to nothing; nor by virtue of the compromise, because only then are goods hypothecated by the force of the compromise. But it is argued against the award, since in the compromise it is stated that he binds all his goods for the observance of the award. But this curator, against whom execution was sought, was pronounced to execute the award; this makes no difference or comes against the award, since he did not possess the said massaricias, as appears from the discussion made, nor did he cease to possess them through fraud, because he who never began to possess cannot cease to possess. Therefore, in no way does he come against the award. Therefore, the goods are not pledged. If, therefore, the goods are not pledged, the hypothecary action cannot be brought, since that which is the medium by which it is produced is lacking, as stated in the aforementioned law *Contrahitur*.

It is no objection that the sentence was passed in the presence of the party of the said Lady Isa, and without appeal; because in the sentence, the competent right of the said Lady Isa in the said piece of land, for which the hypothecary action is now brought, was reserved. And thus, on account of the said reservation, the sentence does not prejudice her. *Digestum*, *Quibus modis pignus vel hypotheca solvitur*, law *Si debitor*, § *Si in venditione*; *Digestum*, *Familiae erciscundae*, law *Idem Labeo*, § 1; *De re iudicata*, chapter *Cum super*; and chapter *Inter monasterium*; and chapter *Suborta*, in the same title, *De fide instrumentorum*, chapter *Inter dilectos*, with many similar cases. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. What the plaintiff in a hypothecary action is required to prove and conclude, and add the preceding opinion.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Having examined the petition of Francis, agent of Master Thomas, on one side, against Peter Lelli Bagutio and Nicholas Ciccarelli, summoned on the other side; and having examined the sentence rendered upon the said petition

It must be considered that the plaintiff bringing a hypothecary action must prove that the thing was in the debtor’s assets at the time of the obligation, if we are speaking of a specific obligation: if it is a general obligation, it suffices to prove that at some time after the contract the obligation was in the debtor’s assets. As stated in D. de pignoribus, l. et quae nondum, §. quod dicitur; and l. si superatus, eodem titulo; D. de probationibus, l. ante omnia. However, if the action is brought against the debtor or his heir, who relies on the support of the author, it suffices to prove simple possession. As noted by my lord in D. de pignoribus, l. rem alienam; and by Cynus in C. si res aliena pignori data sit, l. cum res. Secondly, it must be considered that the plaintiff bringing a hypothecary action must conclude by requesting that the thing be declared obligated and restored to him; just as the plaintiff bringing a rei vindicatio must conclude by requesting that he be declared owner and that the thing be restored. As stated in D. de rei vindicatione, l. ex diverso, §. 1; and D. si servus venditus, l. sicuti, §. sed si quaeratur. For the hypothecary action is a real action, as stated in D. de pignoribus, l. pignoris. Thirdly, it must be considered that the conclusion of the libel must be observed. D. de dolo, l. non debet; D. de foro competenti, c. ex parte; H. de rescriptis, c. super literis, according to Innocentius. Since this Francis, acting in his petition, does not conclude either on ownership or on the simple possession of the debtor, nor does he conclude that the thing be declared obligated and restored to him: therefore, it is certain that he is not bringing a hypothecary action, but a personal action ex stipulatu. For he acts on a promise ad factum and thus ad certum, namely, that the dowry be constituted as certain, or that it be declared constituted. And thus the reason results from the stipulation, and not from the hypothecary action. As stated in Inst. de verbis oblig., in principio; D. de conditionibus indebiti, l. si interius, §. 1; and there, it is not objected that the sentence seems to refer to the hypothecary action, because that sentence does not hold, since it conforms to the libel. D. ut fundus, communi dividundo; C. de fideicommissis liberis, de simonia, c. licet Heli, cum fin.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A proceeding conducted by virtue of a rescript obtained by an excommunicated person is invalid, whether it was conducted by the legate named in the rescript or by a subdelegate appointed by him.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. In the case pending between Lord Franc. Stephani on one side and Lord Pe. Matthucii on the other, concerning the church or priory of the Church of St. Ang. de Capellis, having examined the process of the eminent doctor of decrees, Lord Gaspar, apostolic executor of the said Lord Pe. Matthucii, and the exceptions produced before him, and other acts of the case, it seems that according to law it must be said that the said process is and was null and of no effect or force; because, as appears from the instruments produced on behalf of the said Lord Franc. and other acts of the case, the said Lord Pet. at the time of obtaining his rescript was excommunicated by Lord Benedict, apostolic sub-collector, and denounced as an excommunicated person. Assuming therefore the power of the said Lord Benedict, sub-collector, which appears, as I have said, by public instrument, and the power of the apostolic sub-collector appointing the same, it clearly appears that the said Lord Gaspar was excommunicated.

It must be premised for the sake of clarity that it is certain in law that a rescript obtained by an excommunicated person, and the proceedings conducted by virtue of such rescript, are invalid by the law itself, as in cap. 1, De rescriptis, lib. 6. Secondly, it must be premised that benefice letters obtained by concealment of facts (subreptitiously) are null, and consequently the proceedings conducted by them are null, as in cap. Ad audientiam, Extra, De rescriptis, under the same title; and cap. Dilectus, Extra, De præbendis; cap. Si motu proprio; and cap. Non potest, lib. 6. Thirdly, it must be premised that when a clause appended in executorial letters to persons appointed for benefices sounds as a condition, as is the clause inserted in the aforementioned rescript, namely “sit ex animo” etc. before purification, the hands of the ordinary collator are not bound, as in cap. 1, De concessionibus præbendarum, in the Clementines. From the premises, therefore, I infer regarding the matter at hand, and I say that the proceedings of the said Lord Gaspar, apostolic executor, are null, and do not avail nor hold, for the reasons premised above. For since the said Lord Peter, at the time he obtained the rescript, was excommunicated by the sub-collector of the Roman Church, and denounced as excommunicated, on account of unpaid Papal tithes: of which excommunication and denunciation there is proof by the hand of a public notary. Therefore, the rescript is null, and the proceedings are null, as being made by one lacking jurisdiction, as in cap. 1, De rescriptis, lib. 6. Likewise, for the same reason, the proceedings of the sub-executor appointed by him do not hold, for the same reason, namely, on account of the defect of jurisdiction. And because he has no jurisdiction, he can render no valid sentence, as noted in l. 1, Codex, Qui pro sua jurisdictione. Since, therefore, the said Lord Gaspar had no jurisdiction, he could not delegate jurisdiction to his sub-executor. This is granted first, even if he had had jurisdiction.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. An alienation made by a minor is invalid, nor is the stipulation of a penalty contained therein valid.
2. Let the buyer who defends himself improperly bear the consequences.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† As to the first question, it is to be said, according to the matters alleged, that the alienation made by the said Matthew, a minor, was invalid by operation of law. For either we say that the said portion above the placatum was freehold, and the sale made by him, if no oath intervened, was invalid; because immovables cannot be alienated by a minor under any title without a decree. As stated in the law *Non solum*, Codex, *De praediis minorum*. Or we say that the said portion above the placatum was held by leasehold (libellaria) or emphyteutic tenure. And the same applies, because it cannot be alienated without a decree. As stated in the same title, the law *Etiam vergale*. Therefore, the said alienation made by the said Matthew, a minor, did not hold. If it did not hold, therefore, the penal stipulation was not incurred; for if the contract does not hold, the addition of the penalty does not hold. As stated in the law *Non dubium*, Codex, *De legibus*; and in the law *Cum lex*, and the note in the law *Seius Augerius*, Digest, *Ad legem Falcidiam*.

† Moreover, it is presupposed in the point that the said buyer, having been summoned, defended himself improperly; therefore, let him impute this to himself, as in *l. per imprudentiam*, D. de evictionibus. From the foregoing, therefore, the answer to the two questions appears: namely, whether the alienation made by the said Matthew held good; and it has been said that it did not. Also, whether the penalty appended in the instrument can be claimed against him, because, having been interpellated to accept the defense, he did not accept it; and likewise I say that it cannot, for the reasons already stated. As to the third question, whether the said canoness, by virtue of the aforementioned last solutions, upholds justice; I still say that she does not, and that judgment was wrongly rendered against her, as noted by Bartolus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the profit which a son acquires through his own industry, or in some other way, during the lifetime of his father, is to be shared with his brothers upon the father's death.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The facts are as follows. A certain man named Titius had two sons, namely John and Martin. Martin left home and, traveling about the world, earned some money from his wages and through his own industry. Eventually, he returned to his native city, though he lived separately from his father, while his mother remained in common with the father. Finally, their father, namely the said Titius, died. Now, the other brother, namely the said John, wishes to claim a share, especially of those things which the said Martin earned while traveling about the world. The question now arises: what is the law? Regarding this matter of two brothers, there are two principal cases. For sometimes they dispute over those things which occur during the father’s lifetime, and sometimes over those which occur after his death. And since this second case is not our case, I proceed to the first case, namely, concerning those things which occur during the father’s lifetime. Regarding which

† Several matters must be examined. For sometimes one of them acquires property, or acquires it through some event. Sometimes he acquires it because an outsider makes a donation to him or leaves a legacy to him. Sometimes the father himself grants it to the son. Sometimes the son himself enumerates the paternal patrimony, and thus there are four principal questions. And because only the first question touches upon our case, therefore, omitting the others, I come to it. Regarding this, it must be considered that sometimes a son, while the father is alive, gains something from the father’s property without any labor of his own; he received it from the father’s property, and then there is no doubt that it must be communicated, just like the other things of the father, and just like other profecticia, as in l. si donationem, C. de collationibus; ff. de re vendicata, l. emptor, in fine; C. de bonis liberorum, l. cum oportet, in principio.

But if the son acquires it also through his own labor, for example when he trades with the father’s money and profits, the gloss in C. de bonis liberorum, l. cum oportet, seems to hold that such profit is profectitium and that the whole must be communicated. This was also held by Jacobus de Belvisis and the Speculum in the title de iudiciis, § sequitur, under the words “quid si alter filiorum,” citing principally l. si ita, § fin., de usu et habitatione; de acquisitione rerum dominarum, l. per servum, § fin. But Bartolus says that the profit made with the father’s money is attributed in part to the money and in part to the labor of the person, citing l. lucrum, C. pro socio; l. 1, Inst. de societate, § 1; ff. eodem, l. si non fuerit, § 1. Hence we see daily that when one puts in money and another works, the profit is divided between them equally or unequally, according as they have agreed and according to custom.

Moreover, it is certain that all profit arising from the person of the son is adventitious, as in the aforementioned l. cum oportet, in principio, de bonis liberorum. I therefore say in this case, since the son acquires with paternal money and his own labor, that that part of the profit which is attributed to the money, as profectitium, must be taken into account, whereas that part of the profit which is attributed to the labor and the person, as adventitious, the son retains as his own and does not collate, as in l. fin., C. de collationibus. And on this point is the gloss in l. illud, eodem titulo. Nor does it avail to object with l. si ita, § fin., and l. per servum, in fine, cited by the Speculum, because they speak of slaves who acquire for another through their labor, according to Bartolus in l. nec castrense, de collatione bonorum.

There is also a third case, when the son acquires solely through his own labor, for example from his salary or his craft. And this is properly our case, about which inquiry is made in the aforementioned theme. And this case is beyond doubt, because since that profit which the son acquires through his own labor or work is adventitious, as in Inst. per quas personas nobis acquiritur, and the aforementioned l. cum oportet, it is not to be communicated or collated to another brother after the death of the father, but the son himself has that his profit as peculiar, as in the aforementioned l. fin., C. de collationibus, and l. cum oportet, and according to Bartolus in l. pater filium, de collatione dotis.

But if there is doubt as to whence the son acquired, one must resort to presumptions. For if the aforementioned son was an industrious man and a craftsman, it is presumed that he acquired through his own labor, and thus he does not collate, as noted by the gloss and doctrine in the aforementioned l. cum oportet, in principio.

Therefore, since the said Martin acquired, while his father was alive, through his labor or work, as is proposed in the facts, etc., it is so presumed, considering the quality of the person, and because while he was absent from his father and the aforementioned homeland, he acquired, rightly the other brother has no right in the said acquisitions made by him, but the son himself who acquired the said profit must have it as peculiar, according to the laws cited above. And thus I say, I counsel, I, Francis, etc.

In the Name of Christ, Amen. In the city of Perugia, the following constitution is in force, namely: Furthermore, lest contumacious persons may boast of their contumacy, we have enacted that if anyone, having been duly summoned before us or our vicar, shall be contumacious, and a real action is brought, the plaintiff shall be put in possession of the thing claimed, so that, wearied by this measure, the defendant may come to answer. And if within 30 days he shall come, having provided security for appearing in judgment, and having made adequate satisfaction for expenses, he shall recover possession. But if within 30 days he does not recover possession, then the defendant shall in the meantime be summoned, and a peremptory term of 15 days shall be fixed for recovering possession; which if he neglects to recover after the said 15 days have elapsed, the true plaintiff shall be constituted possessor as to the property only, legitimate defense being reserved to the defendant. But if he is sued on a personal action, and the defendant is contumacious, as aforesaid, the plaintiff shall be put in possession of the movable or immovable goods of the said defendant, according to the amount of the debt declared, and immediately, upon the granting of the tenure of the immovable goods by us or our vicar, the revenues, rents, and fruits of the said goods shall be sequestered. Which if the debtor does not redeem within 30 days, a peremptory term of three other days being assigned and given after the said time of 30 days, and if he does not redeem the said tenure granted, the same may and ought to be substituted at least three times at the door of our episcopal palace, and if a buyer intervenes, the thing shall be sold, etc., as is provided in our Perugian statute on the execution of acknowledged instruments.

The above premises being presupposed, a certain person gave or produced a certain petition before the lord vicar, in which petition it was narrated how a certain person had molested another in the secular courts, on account of which molestations the said plaintiff says that he was and is in damage and harmed, and his interest was, is, and may be 20 gold florins. Wherefore he concludes in the said petition that perpetual silence be imposed on the said defendant sued, and that the said defendant sued shall render, restore, and satisfy, that is, pay to the said plaintiff the said 20 gold florins, and that the said defendant sued, and every person legitimately intervening for him, be condemned to the said plaintiff. Finally, the defendant sued, having been summoned to receive a copy of the said petition within a term, appeared and made his exceptions, which notwithstanding, the judge pronounced himself a competent judge and that proceedings should continue to further steps, the said plaintiff being present, understanding, and consenting, and offering to contest the litigation. And he said that from now on, with the intent of contesting the litigation, he declared the things contained in the said petition to be true, and that he would not use any calumny, the said defendant sued being present, contradicting, and appealing by living voice. Finally, on the 30th day of the month of March, the said defendant sued was summoned to appear legitimately on the following day at the hour of causes, under pain of excommunication, before the said lord vicar to contest the litigation in the said case at the petition of the above-mentioned plaintiff, and the said defendant sued was contumacious; and similarly he was summoned to the same and in the same manner, and similarly he was contumacious in contesting the litigation. Finally, on the 5th day of the month of April, the above-mentioned lord delegate, cognizant in the case, having seen the said petition and the said summonses and contumacies, and the acts and things done in the said case, remitted and granted license to the notaries of the said court, present and understanding, etc., that they go, place, and put the said plaintiff in tenure and in possession of the goods and things of the said defendant sued for the contents of the said petition and for the expenses occasioned by the said contumacy, and this at the petition of the above-mentioned plaintiff against the said party sued, absent, otherwise not summoned nor placed for the said granting of tenure. Finally, on the 7th day of the said month, the said plaintiff was put in possession of the things of the said defendant sued. Finally, on the 25th day of the month of May, the above-mentioned vicar caused the said defendant sued to be summoned at the petition of the above-mentioned plaintiff, that within a term of three days and peremptorily he ought to pay and redeem the said tenure, otherwise after the said term he would proceed to banishments and other things, as the law requires, to which summons the said defendant sued did not appear; finally, proceedings were had to banishments. Now it is asked: since the said defendant sued was not summoned to the said granting of the said tenure of the said things of the said defendant sued, is the said granting null, and consequently is whatever followed therefrom null?

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What and how many things are necessary to obtain the first decree, and no. 4.
2. Whether the delivery of the writ against a defendant who has not been summoned is valid, or whether it is void, and no. 5.
3. What remedy is said to have been initiated when disturbance or defamation occurs.
body: In the name of Christ and of his mother the Virgin Mary, amen. Having considered the said point, it must be premised that four things are necessary for obtaining the first decree.

First, that a convention precede by means of a libel. Second, that the defendant be peremptorily contumacious, if he does not defend himself. Third, that the debt be clearly established in summary form. If any of these is lacking, the first decree is invalid; this is proven in *l. cum proponas* and *auth. ei et iurat.*, C. de bonis auctoris iudicis positis, and as noted by Bartolus in *l. si finita*, § *Iulius*, de damno infecto. Fourth, it is required that the debt itself, which is clearly established in summary form, be a true debt, as in ff. ne vis fiat ei, *l. 1*, § *hæc verba*, and ff. quibus ex causis in possessionem ea, *l. Fulcinius*, § *sed in diem*, according to Baldus. And having set forth these points, it must be considered,

Whether the aforementioned holding from the first decree is valid, and it seems that it is. For since a petition precedes concerning a personal action, which is evident, in that he states that he is being molested, and thus it appears that the decree *uti possidetis* is being invoked. But it is better to say that the interdict does not lie in this case, since it is granted for corporeal things which are possessed and are disturbed. As noted in C. de interdictis, l. 1, in the beginning, and §. hoc interdictum, in l. si, cum si. But in the point at issue, it is not alleged that this molestation occurs in respect of any things; but if someone is molested in respect of certain corporeal rights, which are quasi-possessed, but not truly possessed, as in ff. de acquisitione rerum dominii, l. si servus, §. incorporales, then the interdict *quasi uti possidetis* would lie, as in ff. de servitutibus, l. quotiens; ff. si servi venditi, l. sicut, §. Aristo. For even usufruct is protected by this interdict, as in l. si, ff. uti possidetis. But neither of these is alleged in the point at issue, namely that the plaintiff possesses, nor is it alleged that the molestation occurs in respect of a corporeal thing, nor in respect of an incorporeal right.

† What remedy, therefore, appears to be sought when such disturbance and defamation occur? Bartolus seems to say that the *officium iudicis* is then sought. For unless silence is requested to be imposed, the *officium iudicis* is sought; this he himself asserts as true in *l. si contemnat*, D. de fideiussoribus, and it is also noted in *l. Aurelius*, § *centum*, D. de liberto legato. But it seems to me that either this disturbance and infamy pertains to a crime, or concerns a crime. And if it occurs outside of judicial proceedings, then the defamer is liable to the action for injuries (*actio iniuriarum*), as in D. de iniuriis, *l. item apud*, § *qui incerta*. And we see this in the famous libel, as noted in *l. lex Cornelia*, § final, D. eodem titulo. And in this case, it does not pertain to the *officium iudicis* to impose perpetual silence. Rather, the action for injuries must be brought. Sometimes this defamation and disturbance concerning a crime occurs in court, because one defames another in court of a crime. And then the *officium iudicis* may be invoked, so that within the term of the statute accusation be made, or perpetual silence be imposed, according to the notes in *l. Titia*, D. de accusationibus, and D. si quis eo titulo. But if this defamation pertains to a civil debt and *iudicium competens*, then the *officium iudicis* may be invoked so that perpetual silence be imposed in place of defense, if such defamation can cause prejudice to the defamed party, as in *l. diffamari* and the laws cited above, and there by Bartolus, and what is noted in C. ut nemo inuitus, *l. 1*. I understand this unless another ordinary remedy is available, because the ordinary remedy and the *officium iudicis* do not concern each other, as in § *per hanc*. From this it is inferred regarding the matter at hand that, since the *officium iudicis* is here sought, we are outside the case of the constitution of the episcopate. For the constitution, which must be strictly interpreted, as the common laws say, provides for two cases, namely when a real action is brought. But this is not our case, because no contract or quasi-contract is presupposed, nor any obligation or action resulting from omission and contract. Therefore, according to the doctrine of Bartolus, the *officium iudicis* is here sought; therefore, the first decree interposed according to the form of the aforementioned constitution is not valid, because this case is not comprehended in the constitution, nor does common law appear to have been observed; therefore, the interposition of the said first decree is not valid.

But, assuming without conceding that the aforementioned constitution provided for the case in which the office of the judge is invoked, it must be considered whether the said immissio by virtue of the first decree is valid. And from no. in *euidentiali*, it appears that it is not, because the common doctrine is that one must first make summary proof of the debt, at least by oath, as in Auth. *et qui iurat*, C. *de bonis auctoritatis iudicis possidendis*; and this is noted by Bartolus in the aforementioned law *si finita*, § *Iulianus*. And the glossa says in the aforementioned law *cum proponas* that the oath against calumny suffices to make summary proof of the said debt. And the same is followed by Bartolus and Baldus there. But certainly, the oath against calumny is not a probative oath, but one of purification of conscience and intent, as is noted in l. 2, C. *de iuramento calumniae*. Hence, I believe that it is safer and better that the creditor, given a term to make summary proof of the debt, swear that what he demands is owed to him. This is supported by what is noted in the aforementioned law *thesauris*, ff. *ad exhibendum*. Nevertheless, I readily confess that, although the oath against calumny is regularly one of purification, it nevertheless sometimes makes sufficient proof where that which is demanded benefits the plaintiff and does not harm, or only slightly harms, another. And thus some understand the aforementioned law *thesauris*. And in this manner I understand the aforementioned laws, although Bartolus, Baldus, and other doctors simply follow the aforementioned glossa in l. *cum proponas*. And from this it is concluded that, since no summary proof of the debt appears to have been made, the said first decree and the said immissio are not valid. But, assuming without conceding that some proof of the debt had been made.

It must be considered whether the defendant summoned ought to have been cited to contradict, why possession should not have been granted by the first decree. And it is truly said that citation is not required, and that if the judge, at the plaintiff’s request, gave him possession without the defendant being legitimately cited, such decree belongs to the plaintiff: because although the decree is unjust, it nevertheless stands, as we say regarding an unjust sentence. See l. 1, C. quoniam provoc. non est necess.; it is presumed in favor of the sentence and decree of the judge. See l. Herennius, §. Caya, ff. de evict. cum sim. Moreover, he who possesses with the authority of the praetor possesses justly. ff. de acq. poss., l. Iuste possidet. Moreover, as I said in the evidentiary matter, it suffices that the personal defendant, so that immission may be made by the first decree, was peremptorily contumacious. Thus, it is noted in the said §. Iul. But this defendant was peremptorily contumacious, because, having been cited, he did not appear. See l. Tres denuntiationes, C. quomodo et quando iud. In the contrary, it seems that after the aforementioned contumacy, citation to contradict is required, because possession should not be granted by the first decree. And first, because the said license and precept is interlocutory, which contains something to be done for a party. Therefore, in its granting, just as in its revocation, citation of the party is required. As noted in ca. Suborta, de re iud. Moreover, I have the rule that unless in judgment the judge does something to the prejudice of a party, his citation is required. See l. Nam ita divus and l. De unoquoque. But the said possession is given to the prejudice of the party. Therefore, it is clear that the defendant summoned ought to have been cited. Moreover, he does not seem to possess, nor can he, because, the party not having been cited, he apprehended possession even with the authority of the judge. As noted by Bartolus in the said l. Iuste possidet, and as noted in the said l. Meminerint, C. unde vi. Moreover, I see that if I request execution of a sentence or instrument, and the judge executes it on another thing than that requested, and grants possession by the first decree, it is not valid unless the party is cited. Otherwise, if execution were made on the same thing requested, as noted by Bartolus in l. A divo Pio, §. In venditione, or in §. 1, supra, de re iud., and as noted in l. Ob maritorum, C. ne uxor pro marito. Therefore, the same seems to apply in the said l. 1, because, in summary, in the granting of possession, it seems that the party ought to be cited, since execution is made on something other than what was requested. What is to be said? This point is difficult. Bartolus holds that the preceding peremptory citation suffices. Thus, he notes in the said §. Iul. But against him are the laws above proximately alleged, and what he himself notes in l. A divo Pio. Finally, it seems to me that the truer view is that in the said interlocutory and granting of license, the party ought to be cited. However, according to the strictness of the law, his opinion could nevertheless be sustained, so that we say that either the defendant was peremptorily cited with the threat of a certain and determined penalty, for example, under the penalty of excommunication, as was the case in our matter, and then if the judge, beyond reason, on account of the aforementioned contumacy, imposes another penalty, he ought to grant possession by the first decree. And then, if in imposing this new penalty a new citation is required, as here seems to be proved by the text in c. Quam frequenter, §. 1, where the text says that if the judge, on account of the defendant’s contumacy, excommunicated him, he may proceed to another penalty. Since therefore he proceeds on this matter, citation is required, because where there is procedure, citation is of the substance. As noted in l. 1, ff. de in ius voc. Nor does the text regard immission by fact, but by way of procedure. Moreover, we see in a similar case that he proceeds from a delict and condemns the defendant to a penalty, and wishes afterwards to add another penalty on account of some omission; certainly the party ought to be cited in imposing this new penalty. As noted in l. Senatus, ff. de accus., and as noted in l. Denuntiasse, §. Quid tamen. Since therefore a new burden is inflicted, a new citation is required. And that the judge, after peremptory citation and after contumacy, ought not to hasten abruptly to immission by the first decree, is noted by the gloss ad litteram in c. Quoniam frequenter, §. Quod si super, in fine. See lit. Non conte. And the reason is assigned there, because the defendant, although contumacious, may have legitimate defenses and excuses. And because the judge, by threatening one penalty, gives the defendant the belief that he will not impose another. But if the judge peremptorily cited the defendant and added that, upon the expiration of the said term, it would be proceeded against you to punish your contumacy, as the law requires, then, because the judge threatens all legal penalties, a new citation is not required for immission by the first decree. And in this way the opinion of Bartolus and other doctors can be saved and understood. And the same if peremptory citations were issued without any threat. See l. Consentaneum, l. Cum proponas. From all the foregoing, I conclude that the said granting of the first decree in the case proposed was not valid for the reasons above stated. I, Marcus Angelelli of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Add also below in the following counsel.
2. Those who contract with one of the partners on account of the partnership, or with a person appointed by the partners, are not required to sue all of them, but may choose to sue one.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Since all matters have been fully and substantially addressed by my consulting lords, I shall proceed briefly.

† And I premise that which has also been touched upon, namely, that unless they are exercising the same action jointly and severally, so that they are bound jointly and severally for the act of the other, not one under the other, because one is deemed to have appointed the other, and the other the one, as is stated in the cited law *Cum te iugalia* in the Code, title *Si certum petatur*, and in the law *Insolidum*. Although he does not have a procurator from his partner, because they are co-obligors jointly and severally both actively and passively, according to the Digest and the Code in the cited law *Cum te*. Secondly, I premise, and it is to be noted, that if partners administer through one person, each is bound jointly and severally. Hence, he who contracted with one does not have to litigate with all, but may choose whom he wishes and sue him jointly and severally, as per the Digest, title *De exercitoria*, law *Ne in plures*. Therefore, since Sempronius and his partners exercised the aforementioned act of promise of debt, acknowledgment, confession, and other matters contained in the aforementioned mandate given to the said Vannes, through one person, namely Vannes, he who contracted with the said Vannes does not have to litigate with all, but may choose whom he wishes and sue him jointly and severally, according to the cited law *Ne in plures*.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The beginning of the contract must be examined.
2. What the plaintiff in a hypothecary action must prove, and whether he is preferred over one who has no such right.
3. One who contracts with one of the partners by reason of the partnership may sue any one of them.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The beginning of the contract must be considered. D. de deposito, l. 1; D. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. si servus; D. de act. et ob., l. quaecunque gerimus. For from the very origin of the title, the subsequent event is shaped, C. de impositione lucrativa descriptione, l. 1, in fine, lib. 10. Since therefore it is proposed as a constant in the fact,

† That the mortgaged goods, concerning which the matter is now at issue, were, at the time of the obligation, and before, those of the aforementioned Sempronius who incurred the obligation. Therefore, a real right of mortgage was contracted in the said goods. D. de pign. act. l. si; and C. eod. tit. l. Paulus, in princ.; and l. si ab eo; and d. l. et quae nondum, §. quod dicitur; and cum omnis dictio. And since every expression and omission by which Sempronius was bound to the said Bartholomew through the delivery made to him in satisfaction of the debt has been extinguished by the laws cited by my lord, Master Angelus, therefore, henceforth, there is no need to consider the priority of the mortgage, because, as the eminent doctor of the laws, Master Honorius, notably observed, the said Titius is found not so much as prior, but rather as the sole creditor in the aforementioned mortgage, as is expressly stated in d. l. 2, in fi., cited by him; and the chapter Susceptivum, in fi., de rescriptis, lib. 6, is highly apposite, where an impetrator in one species of vacation is preferred, although he impetrated second, because he is said to be not so much second, but rather unique.

† It must also be observed that if partners administer through one person, each is liable in solidum; hence, whoever contracted with one does not have to litigate with all, but may choose whom he wishes and sue that person in solidum. By the law Ne in plures, D. de exercitoria, which is noted for this purpose. Since, therefore, the aforementioned partners exercised the act of promise of debt, confession, and recognition through the lord Vannes, whoever contracted with the said Vannes does not have to litigate with all, but may choose whom he wishes and sue that person in solidum, by the aforementioned law Ne in plures. From all these things and others done by the aforementioned consulting lords, I conclude that the said Titius ought to obtain in solidum in the hypothecary action. I, Francesco, of the lord Baldus de Ubaldis of Perugia.

CASE

In the name of Christ, amen. The case is presupposed in these terms. Peter made his last will and testament, in which he instituted his two sons, namely Christian and Flor, as his universal heirs in equal shares, with this condition, however, that if one of his sons or heirs should die from this life without legitimate children, he substituted the other surviving one as his heir in the whole. And if both should die without children born of legitimate marriage, he willed that half of his entire inheritance should go to the ladies Benedicta and Margaret, his daughters, and the other half should be given and distributed to the poor of Christ for his soul and for the remission of his sins. And he added the clause: if it is not valid by the law of wills, let it be valid by the law of codicils and by the law of any last will. The case occurred that both of the instituted heir sons died without surviving issue, the said testator being alive and surviving. Finally, the testator died, the said daughters of his being alive and surviving, who entered upon the intestate inheritance of their said father, against whom the poor of Christ act and petition the most reverend lord Bishop of Verona, to whom pertains the execution of last wills for pious causes, that distribution of half of the said inheritance be made to them. Now it is asked whether the same executor can execute the last will, i.e., distribute to the poor of Christ half of the said inheritance, or not.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When the instituted heir dies during the lifetime of the testator, the institution is called, as it were, lapsed; and if there is a vulgar substitution, it is acquired by the substitute heir; if there is a coheir, by him; if neither, the institution vanishes, and all legacies, except certain legacies. And see number 4.
2. When the testator is invalid from the beginning, whether the clause “if it is not valid, etc.” operates to any effect.
3. A fideicommissary substitution made in the event of the testator’s failure appears to be made generally in intestacy.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. It must be premised for the sake of clarity,

† That when a named heir dies during the lifetime of the testator, such an institution is called as it were lapsed. And if there is a vulgar substitute, it is acquired by the substitute. Likewise, if there is a surviving coheir, it accrues to him with his own burden; but if he has neither a coheir nor a substitute who is directly substituted, not only does the institution vanish, but also all legacies and fideicommissa dependent on the substitution, except those which are repeated ab intestato. As in C. de fideic. l. in testamento. In two cases, therefore, legacies and fideicommissa remain, when the instituted heirs die in the lifetime of the testator: namely, when there is a vulgar substitution, whether the substitute is admitted, or whether the heir, or whether it accrues; or when they are repeated ab intestato. As in C. de caducis tollendis l. 1. §. his ita and §. pro secundo. And fully noted in C. de fideicommissis l. eam quam, and C. de codicillis l. si.

Secondly, it must be premised that sometimes a will is invalid from the outset; and then the clause “if it is not valid” has no effect. Or it is valid from the outset; and then the codicillary clause “if it is not valid” has no effect, because it is false. Sometimes the will is invalid from the outset, and then the clause has effect, because it is true. As is fully explained at no. 10 by Mo. in l. 1, C. de iure codicillorum.
