Thirdly, it must be premised that a fideicommissary substitution, which is made in the event of the failure of the will, appears to be made generally as if intestate, as in the Digest, *De legatis* 2, *Lucius*, § *filiam*. These three points being thus clearly premised.

Let us see in what case we are. And if indeed the testator left something purely to the said daughters by right of institution, then it is certain that the will is valid: because the portion of the males accrues to them. As in D. de haeredibus instituendis, l. 1, § si ex fundo; and fully noted by the Moderators in C. de haeredibus instituendis, quo. And although these daughters should repudiate the inheritance under the will and accept it as intestate, they would be bound to the legacies and fideicommissa by the edict *Si quis omissa causa testamenti*. As in C. de omissa causa testamenti, l. 2; and D. eo, per totum. But if nothing was left purely to the daughters, but they were merely substituted under a causal condition, and by fideicommissum, the will was null: because they were passed over. In Auth. *Ut cum*, de appellationibus cognoscitur, § Aliud quoque capitulum; and C. de liberis praeteritis, l. Maximum vitium. I speak of the *ius commune*, and then the codicillary clause operates well. Also Auth. *Ex causa*, as fully explained there by the doctors, and thus the fideicommissum is still due. But let us suppose that, by the form of some statute, females could be passed over when males are extant. Nevertheless, it must still be said that the said fideicommissum left to the poor is due. For those words, “if he should die without sons,” are words of pregnant meaning. For they can be understood whether they died during the life of the testator or afterwards; as there is some reason why it should be restricted to afterwards. Thus the sense of these words is twofold: namely, if he should die during the father’s life, or afterwards. Now take the first time, and argue thus: this fideicommissum was left under a condition quasi of caducity of the will. Therefore, it was left in default of the will, and thus intestate. Hence that it is due is the case in d. § Filiam; and D. de haeredibus instituendis, l. Qui filio, § Servus. Moreover, many would say that the said substitution is direct, and the vulgar substitution is valid in the aforementioned case: because it is compendious. As fully noted by Ioan. And., who determines by disputing in c. Si pater, extra de testamentis; and in c. Raynu. Also, the will of the testator ought to be interpreted broadly, especially for pious causes. Hence, although the testator said, “if it is not valid, etc.,” in favor of the pious cause it appears that he also provided for a similar case; it is valid, if it will not be valid. Arg. C. de posthumis haeredibus instituendis, l. Fina. Sol. Whether the institution is direct or not, the poor have a right not only by reason of piety and consideration of the will, but also by the point of reason, and distribution must be made according to the form of the will. For the testator preferred males alone to the poor, but equated females with them. And therefore the will must be observed, as mistress, as in C. de legatis, l. Quaestio, § Fina. And to that rule which is placed in l. Eam quam; and l. Si nemo, it has been answered by what has been said above. And it does not obstruct D. de captivis, l. Si filius; and what is noted in D. de vulgaribus substitutionibus, l. Lex Cornelia: because there it is in pupillary substitution; here in compendious, or fideicommissary. It also supports the above: that bequests for pious causes do not await the acceptance of the inheritance; but it can be answered that this is true: when there is no other defect than that of acceptance. But here we are in a case of caducity, concluding finally as I concluded above. Also, it does not obstruct the gloss which is in d. l. Precibus, which says, and I do not consider this compendious: because that speaks, since the instituted heir dies after the inheritance has been accepted. Also, granted that it were fideicommissary, nevertheless, as I said, it is fideicommissary intestate in the case of caducity: because there cannot be caducity without defect of the will. And it seems to me that it would be dangerous to advise the contrary in matters concerning pious causes, since the testator wished it to be performed entirely. Arg. l. 1, C. de legatis, in which legacies even two witnesses suffice, of the best opinion, and greater than any exception. As extra de testamentis, c. Cum esses; and c. Relatum. For if they were stained with a light blemish, they would not be believed. Arg. C. de fideicommissis, l. Quaestionum, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a judgment rendered against an instituted heir, or a substitute, on the ground of the nullity of the will, prejudices others described in the will who were not called.
2. Whether a vassal may enfeoff another, and whether an agnate may revoke: and whether an agnate may prejudice another agnate in a fief.
3. In fiefs, the edict of succession from degree to degree has application.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Regarding the exception raised by the sons of Franchinus de Advocatis, who were substituted in the will by Lord Andriolo de Advocatis. The issue is assumed to be as follows: At a certain time, Lord Andreas de Advocatis made his last will, in which, among other things, he instituted his son Martin as universal heir, and the womb of his wife, if a male child were born. And if it should happen that the said Martin, and the son, if a male, should die within the age of pupillarity, or even at any time without legitimate and natural male descendants issuing from him: that then, and in that case, the aforementioned and hereinafter mentioned Franchinus, his brother and son of the late Lord Andreas, shall be his heir in solidum, and he hereby institutes him as his heir and substitutes him for the said sons. He requests them, and each and every one who might succeed him intestate, by fideicommissum, that in the event of the aforementioned case occurring, they restore the said inheritance to the said Franchinus, etc. Later, in another part of the will, he stated that if the case should occur that the said Franchinus should die before the aforementioned Andreas, leaving sons who are free or legitimate descendants issuing from him: that those sons and descendants shall succeed and ought to succeed the said Andreas, and his children and daughters. The daughters, however, he instituted to a certain sum, and ordered them to be silent and content. The testator died, his son surviving, who appealed, and let us say in the Papal Court. He died, the said Franchinus, his uncle and substitute, surviving, and also the sons of the said Franchinus surviving. This Franchinus, by virtue of the said substitution, declared the inheritance of the said Martin, and the goods of the said Andreas, his father, null and void due to the defect of omitted solemnity or caution. And in contradictory judicial proceedings, without the sons of the said Franchinus being cited, they obtained a sentence with and against the said Franchinus, by which it was pronounced that the will was null. It is asked,

Whether this sentence has created a prejudice to the said sons of Franchinus, who were not present in the judgment having been summoned, and with whom the judgment was not litigated. And in law it seems that it has. First: because it is established that those must be summoned in judgment whose interest is at stake. As in D. de adoptionibus, l. nam ita divus; l. in causis, § causa; de minoribus; Auth. si omnes; si ut se ab hereditate abstineant. To which contributes C. de auctoritate praestanda, l. si. And the sons of Franchinus contend that the testament should not be annulled, since they themselves were also substitutes: as appears from the words of the testament. Furthermore, for this part, that the sentence passed against the said Franchinus did not create a prejudice to the said sons regarding the nullity of the testament: the case seems to be in l. 1, D. de exceptione rei iudicatae. But, invoking the name of Christ and of the Blessed Virgin Mary his mother, in law the contrary is true, namely, that the sentence passed against Franchinus, for the sisters instituted, after the contingency of the substitution occurring, was valid against the sons of Franchinus without citation, and fully took effect in law, which is apparent. First, because it is certain in law that a sentence of nullity of a testament passed against the heir, in whom the principal interest lies, prejudices and establishes law against all others, both substitutes and legatees, or anyone claiming an interest from the testament: as is the case in D. de inofficiosa testamento, l. Papinianus, and there noted in the second solution; and D. de pignoribus, l. si superatus, § 1. And this is held by Master Duarenus, Jacobus de Radineis, and Master Jacobus Butrigarius, and all, unless it had been passed against legatees, or him or those in whom the principal interest did not lie: because it would not prejudice the heir, nor others claiming a right from the testament. As in the said l. de exceptione rei iudicatae. To which also is the response by the aforementioned words. But it is established that the said sentence annulling the said testament of Lord Andrew was passed against Franchinus, the principal substitute, and then heir, namely of the instituted pupil and of the testator. Therefore, it could and does establish law and prejudice against all, and further substitutes: as were the sons of Franchinus: and also against any legatees. And thus they cannot stand, nor contravene. For which contributes well the said l. si superatus, vers. cum legata. Otherwise, etc.

Secondly, it is proved: because at the time the sentence was passed against the said Franchinus, the substitute, it was not in the interest of the sons of Franchinus, nor could it be, whether the said testament was valid or not: because upon the advent of the case of substitution by the death of Martin, the impuberal substitute son of the testator, the said Franchinus was living, and had apprehended the inheritance by virtue of the substitution. And thus the sons of the said Franchinus, who were substitutes to the son or sons of the testator instituted, and the said Franchinus would die before Andrew, the son of the testator instituted, and the said Franchinus did not die before Andrew, but rather Andrew died before Franchinus, the substitute. Whether he can revoke, even after a year has elapsed: because this prescription of a year is introduced solely in favor of the possessor, hence if this annual favor cannot aid him, the prescription does not run against the next nearest agnate. Briefly, I say, and according to the mind of the gloss, that if a vassal alienates to an agnate, whom two perhaps precede in successive order: first the right of revocation is given to the nearest agnate, and he is excluded by the lapse of a year from when he knew. And in successive order comes the second agnate, and he is excluded by the lapse of another year from when he knew. When this second year has elapsed, possession will be confirmed to the possessor, who is third in the order of agnates. And so with the rest, as in D. de successione edicto, l. prima, § largius, and § sed videndum. For that these times run is a favor to the possessing agnate, to whom, through the negligence of those preceding him, the fief is confirmed. For if it had been alienated to an outsider, the third would have the right of revocation; therefore, since it is alienated to him, he would more strongly have the right of retaining. Argument: D. de conditionibus indebiti, l. frater a fratre, in principio; and D. de superficiebus, l. 1, § quod ait; and D. de re iudicata, l. iustus, § cui damus. Hence, the successive right has place in the time of the running of the year. And this is the truth, for which, according to what is proposed, the second in order, at the due time, and thus acting, as it is proposed he acted, has justice: he could petition for investiture.

† Moreover, if the feudatory, instead of alienating, enfeoffed another under a similar law, then, as I have said, it might be doubted whether this subinfeudation was lawful or not. For a vassal can acquire another vassal from his fief; and because the first does not cease entirely to be a vassal. From the arguments of those who [are not], ff. ad Trebonianum; l. ex asse. The subinfeudation is valid, as it can be said in c. Imperialem, §. illud quoque, de prohibitione feudorum alienationis, by Federicus, that if the vassal who enfeoffed another died with an heir, the agnate cannot revoke. For the son succeeds to the father’s right in the paternal vassalage, as in c. 1, an agnatus vel filius, collatio 10. And that some remain of the first degree, the following degree is rejected, if those remnants are of some effect, as l. si, ff. de successionibus edicti; and l. si duo patroni, in principio, ff. de iureiurando. Someone will say, what remnants can these be, when all the right of the alienating vassal passes to the successor, when by the way of feuding. As noted, ff. communis; l. si ut certo, §. si duobus vehiculum. Secondly, certainly, indeed, there are great remnants: because the vassal of my vassal is not my vassal, as regards the obligation of the person; but he is bound to his immediate investitor, to those things which come into the oath of fidelity. The gloss, however, of the said §. si duobus, must be understood as regards natural possession and its benefits, whence it is concluded that he ceases not to be a vassal who acquired another vassal. As ff. de hereditatibus instituendis, l. talem, §. si. But if the vassal had died without an heir, the fief would be open to the nearest agnate,

† in which the right of succession from degree to degree would have place. But if there were no agnates, it would revert to the lord by the strict law: because when the right of the grantor is resolved, the right of the grantee is resolved, as in D. de publicanis l. lex vectigali. and in C. 1. §. rursus. qui modis feudum amittitur. But by benign equity it has been received that then the second vassal, by acknowledging the lord, ought to retain the fief. as in C. 1. §. si qualiter. olim feudum potest alienari. and there C. 1. §. porro. But this statement must be understood where there are no agnates, or there are but they are excluded: but where there are nearer agnates, they are preferred to a more remote subinfeudated person: because an agnate cannot prejudice an agnate. as in the said C. 1. de alienatione feudi paterni. And if one consented and the other dissented, the whole accrues to the dissenting party. as in C. de fideicommissis l. quotiens. and D. de legatis 3. l. cum pater. §. libertis. I, Baldus.
In the Name of Christ, Amen. It is proposed that Manfredinus in his testament. Add below in the following opinion: it is proposed, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a substitution lapses if the substitute predeceases the heir.
2. To whom the heirs of those who come into the inheritance succeed.
3. Transmission to the heir does not occur while a condition is pending, nor can one make a testamentary disposition regarding it.
4. Whether a wife instituted by the words “provided she observes a widow’s life” is said to be instituted subject to a condition.
5. Whether a daughter once excluded from succession by virtue of a statute is said to be excluded in perpetuity.
6. Statutes are more closely connected to contracts than to last wills.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. It is proposed that Manfredinus, in his will, instituted as universal heirs Bartholomew and Louis, his sons who were minors, and substituted them for one another. And if both should die in minority, or afterwards at any time, he substituted to them in their entirety, namely, Otto, his father-in-law, or his heirs, for one half; and for the other half, John, his natural brother, or his heirs. Otto and John died after the said Bartholomew had died and the said Louis survived. John died without issue, having made a will in which he instituted his wife as universal heir during her lifetime, provided she observed a widow’s life, and otherwise not. And after the death of his said wife, he substituted the said Louis to her. Then, after the said John died without issue, the said Louis died in minority.

† Now it is asked whether the said substitution made in favor of the said John has failed, because he died during the lifetime of the said Louis, or not. And it seems that it has failed. For not only was the said John substituted for the said pupils, but also his heirs. For the term "heir" includes all heirs, even strangers. As stated in the Code, De hereditatibus instituendis, l. si. But the contrary is true: because when a person is substituted by the testator, and the word "heir" is added:

† or heirs, or another alternative expression, is understood to refer to children, not to heirs who are entirely strangers, such as a wife. As stated in the law and note, ff. ad Trebellianum; l. ex facto, §. fin.; and in Speculum, de testibus, §. in primis, ver. si; and ff. de usufructu accrescendi, l. si quis Titio, according to one customary reading. This is treated in l. gallus, C. de operis liberti; l. liberti, per Cynus. It might be otherwise if the testator had substituted a complete stranger, or the heirs of such stranger: for then the testator did not weigh the right of blood. Nevertheless, Speculum and the ancient doctors held indiscriminately that those words, or heirs, were not to be understood as referring to strangers altogether.

† It is certain, however, that John died before the condition of the substitution was fulfilled. And therefore he did not transmit [the right] to his heir, nor could he make a will regarding it, as in the law *Sed et si plures*, in the beginning, in the Digest on vulgar and pupillary substitution, and in the Code on impuberes and other substitutions, in the last law. From which it is clearly concluded that the wife of the said John does not succeed to anything by virtue of the said substitution in favor of the said Bartholomew and Louis, but those who are closer in degree to the said pubescent heirs succeed. But let us assume, without prejudice to the truth, that she would succeed; as long as she remained a widow, she would lose the said legacy by subsequently marrying, as in the Code on the indication of widows, in the authentic *Cui relictum*, except for a legacy by codicil. And the testator could have left it in all cases, whether she were to marry or not to marry. The text is in the Authentic *De nuptiis*, § *Disponant*, column 4. But as I said, this is not to be discussed, except with regard to the succession of Bartholomew and Louis: because the substitution made to them has failed, at least with regard to the said John.

John made a will, in which he instituted his wife as universal heir, with these words: "Let her have, hold, enjoy, and possess the inheritance and goods only during her lifetime: observing, however, a widow's life, otherwise not." And that no one could, observing a widow's life, as above, repel her from the said inheritance in any way or by any device: and that no one could compel her to render any account of her goods, or to make any inventory: notwithstanding any chapter or law speaking to the contrary. And after the death of his wife, the same testator substituted his nephew Louis in the whole. And if the said Louis should die without legitimate children born of him, he substituted the same Paganinus, or his heirs, in the whole. First the said Louis died; secondly the said John died; thirdly the said wife possessed the goods for some years, finally she married another, and the said lady and the said Paganinus are alive. It is now asked, what is the law regarding the said goods and the inheritance of the said John.

† And it seems that one must first say that the said testament is invalid, because it has no heir. As stated in the Digest, *De his quae in testamento delentur*, law *Proxime*. For the aforementioned wife appears to have been instituted under the condition that she not marry; because those words “observing, etc.” seem to import the condition that she not marry. This condition has failed. As stated in the Code, *De indice vidui*, authentic *Cui relictum*. And this is the opinion held by the gloss in the final law of the same title. It is not an obstacle if it is said that that woman had a substitute, one of whom is alive, because the said substitution was fiduciary. Secondly, it vanished because the inheritance was not accepted by the instituted heir. As stated in the Code, *De fideicommissis*, law *Eam quam*. For she could not accept it unless the Mutian caution had been provided. As stated in the Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, law *Mutiana*. Furthermore, because the substitution was made after the death of the woman, therefore before her death the substitute cannot bring an action. As stated in the Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, law 4 and law *Publius*, section *Si*. It must be noted that the said woman, in the case where she were to marry and were still alive, had no substitute, and an omitted case is considered as omitted. As stated in the Digest, *De liberis et posthumis*, law *Commodissime*. From these points it follows that the intestate heirs of the said John ought to have the said inheritance. As stated in the Digest, *De legatis tertio*, law *Uxorem*, section *His tamen*. Because there is therein a codicillary clause [stating] “the said wife having died, and not before,” they will be bound to restore the said inheritance to the said Paganino, if he should then be alive, or to his natural heir, if he should then not be alive. What if none of these existed? The said goods would remain with the said heir succeeding intestate. But someone might subtly doubt and say that the said substitution made to the said wife was compendious, and thus contains within itself a vulgar substitution, as noted in law *Precibus* with its material, and then it would follow that, without awaiting the death of the wife, the substitute would come in by virtue of the vulgar substitution. For I say that the removal occurs in the direct institution or substitution of the heir, and the pure institution remains. As stated in the Digest, *De hereditatibus instituendis*, law *Hereditas ex die*. But certainly that law is not understood in that way, as noted in the Code, *De hereditatibus instituendis*, law *Extraneum*, through the doctors, because an uncertain day must be awaited, just as a condition, even in inheritances. What, therefore, shall we say? Is this substitution compendious? I answer: No. Because it was made in the case of the inheritance having been accepted. As stated in the Code, *De impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus*, law *Post aditam*. It seems, therefore, that one must first consider whether those words “observing, etc.” import a condition, and then the opinion is true that those succeeding intestate come in, as I have said. If, however, they do not import a condition but rather a certain burden of widowhood, then the wife would have been heir. But because she acted against the will of the deceased by marrying, from that time she would lose the benefits of the inheritance. But to whom would they apply? For she cannot come in intestate, because from the moment the inheritance has once been accepted by testament, the cause of intestacy has vanished. It would follow, therefore, that this woman is liable for fruits by a certain consequence of having accepted the inheritance, since no one was there who could revoke them while she was alive. But upon her death, they would devolve to Paganino, or, if he were dead, to his natural heirs, i.e., his children, if they survived; and if they did not survive, perhaps the fiscus would come in and take them away from the wife as unworthy. As stated in the Digest, *De adimendo legatis*, law *Ex parte ista*. This question is very doubtful, yet in law it can better be defended that the said words import a condition, and thus the inheritance could not be accepted without the Mutian caution being provided, on account of those words “observing a widowed life.” As stated in the Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, law *A testatore*. On this point, however, there are various opinions. As in the said law *Si*, *De indice vidui*, as there by Cynus. But it can be responded to those opinions, because there the testator added the distributive word “quandiu” (as long as). Because this word “servando” (observing), which is in the testament, is not a distributive word, but conditional and continuative, and thus “observing” is explained as “if she shall have observed.” And this is true. But if “observing” were explained as “until she shall have observed,” in which the will of the testator seems more inclined, the inheritance once acquired by the woman by testamentary right would be excluded. I said those coming in intestate, and the said law *Hereditas ex die*, *De hereditatibus instituendis*, in that word “vel ad diem” (or to the day), and the Digest, *De minoribus*, law *Et sine*, section *Et quod Papinianus*, and in law *Si*, *De successione edicti*, *Porro*. If the said wife did not accept the inheritance before she married, then by marrying she seems to renounce the inheritance. Argument from the Code, *De codicillis*, law *Si quis agere*, and the Code, *De fideicommissis*, authentic *Hoc amplius*. And therefore the intestate heirs would take it, saving the right of the substitutes, and thus it seems to me in a paternal or maternal inheritance, of which she was not dowered.

† On this point, it must be said that a daughter, once excluded by her father, cannot succeed in perpetuity, because the statute does not state “as long as the brothers live,” as noted by Bartolus in *l. si* ad *Tertul.* But against this it is objected that the statute appears to have been made in favor of the brothers, and thus constitutes a privilege of those brothers; therefore, others ought not to be excluded, as in *c. Privilegium personale* de *reg. iur.* lib. 6. But certainly, rather, it is a real statute, because it says “or the heir of their parents,” as in *ff. de pactis*, *l. Iuris gentium* § *pactorum*. For although in wills and last wills the word “heir” is used in last wills for our benefit, as I said in other consilia, nevertheless in contracts.

† because statutes are more akin to contracts than to last wills; yet one might doubt what would happen if, before being endowed by her father, she had inherited the estate of her deceased mother: she would not seem to be able to be deprived of her right except with her own consent, as in D. de re iudicata, l. Id quod nostrum. In case of doubt, it is better to adhere to the literal wording of the statute, as in D. de exercitoria actione, l. 1, § Is qui navem. And if the said statute had been put into practice, recourse should be had to customary practice, as in D. de legibus, l. Si de interpretatione, etc. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldo de Ubaldis, Doctor, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a simulated alienation is presumed from the fact that the alienor is found to be in possession after the alienation.
2. The judge must, ex officio, reject the litigant who is acting in bad faith (calumniator).
3. An action on a hypothecary security may be brought for the
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† On the first point, namely whether the said alleged donation should be considered entirely simulated and made in fraud of the lord and of the alimony, it must be said that it should, for whenever, after a contract that is to the prejudice of a third party, the one who appears to have alienated is found to possess, the alienation is presumed fraudulent and simulated. And [see] D. 20.1.13 § superuacuum; D. 13.6.1 § sciunt omnes. The procurators of the court, not to mention the advocates, know this. But so it is: this husband, at the time when the wife was put in possession, possessed the things which he is alleged to have donated; therefore, the donation is presumed simulated and made in fraud, and consequently the donee must be repelled as a calumniator from his claim, and he must take the oath against calumny.

† And if it appears by legal presumption that there is calumny, the judge must, ex officio, repel him, as noted by Innocentius in c. j., Extra, de officio vicarii. If it is certain that the man possessed during the said period of permission; but if this were not certain, it ought to be investigated, because possessions consist in fact, as in D. de verb. oblig., l. stipulatio ista, §. hi quoque. And once this is investigated and established, there is no doubt that a simulated donation would be presumed, as in C. de nat. lib., l. si qui servum, §. j.; C. de repud. haer., l. 2. And just as a simulated donation is presumed, so too is a precarium. And there is no doubt about this. Also, incorporeal delivery, as in D. de acq. poss., l. qui iure familiaritatis; and D. de aqua pluv. arc., l. qui emptor. But assuming that the donation was true, and that true delivery had intervened, and it were later found that the donor possessed, with the donee’s knowledge, it would still seem that it ought to be presumed, as in D. de fideic., l. si testamento; and D. mand., l. si vero non remunerandi, §. idem Papinianus. And assuming that a redonation were not presumed, nevertheless the woman placed in possession ought to be defended: which is thus proven: if she did not possess, she could bring a hypothecary action, as noted in C. de haer. acq., l. haeredem mariti. Therefore, if she possesses, she can use the exception of fraud, as in the rule, dolo facis.

† But that a hypothecary action may be brought for alimony is proved by this reasoning: since a hypothecary action lies for the restitution of the dowry, it therefore also lies for alimony. It is clear that the word “restitute” has a full meaning, as in D. de usur. l. uideamus § in fauiana. And consider that, although the alimony has not yet accrued, nevertheless the time of the alimony ought not to be considered, but the time of the dowry, as in C. de bonis quae liberis l. cum oportet § sed cum tacitas. From all of which, since a dation in satisfaction was made in the presence of the alleged donee, who did not object nor afterwards appealed, and thus his citation was not necessary, the execution already carried out, and whatever remains to be done, ought not to be impeded on behalf of the said wife, as in D. de re iudicata l. cum saepe § et si scientibus etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A judge does not make the case his own where the judgment is void by the law itself.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The sentence of the syndicator contains truth and justice, because it accords with the law. For the said warehouse is bound for the toll, as is established according to what is alleged: because in the first part of the law, in which provision is made regarding the obligation of the warehouse, the aforementioned general rule is stated. In the second part, certain exceptions are set forth, which do not touch our case. And therefore we must adhere to the general rule, l. 1, § quod autem, ff. de aleatoribus.

† On another point, the gloss in l. si iudex, de variis cognitionibus, states that if a sentence is void by operation of law, the judge does not make the case his own. Therefore, it is necessary to examine whether anything was claimed before him by the tax collectors or not. And the claim is sufficiently gathered, because the statement of facts, the production of instruments and of the sentence, and the request of the executor suffice: since in this case the order of law is not required, but the truth, and that it be established, as appears from the statute mentioned above. To this effect, Extra, de veritate sigilli, saepe. And what is said in no. 2, q. 4, quia præsulatus in culpa. Therefore, he was an official, although not acting in bad faith. See: officialis gabellarum, d. l. si iudex, cum si. And c.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a fortuitous event benefits or harms, and when? Likewise, on the effects of fortuitous events.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. This matter of fortuitous events is a matter of great importance. We say that a fortuitous event and absolute force sometimes render illicit that which is otherwise lawful; and especially a storm at sea, as in the Digest, On Public Matters, law Caesar. Sometimes it excuses from judicial penalty, as in the Digest, If One Gives Security, law 2, throughout the law, and in section Quaeritur. Sometimes it excuses from conventional penalty, as in the Digest, On the Rhodian Law concerning Jettison, law If Goods Were to Be Carried, section For This Reason. Sometimes it destroys the very substance of the obligation, as in the Digest, On Hire, law In a Ship. Sometimes it impedes the very origin of the obligation, as in the Digest, On Complaints of Damage, law Of Rivers, section Servius. Sometimes it gives rise to the repetition of what has been paid, as in the Digest, On Hire, law If One, section Moreover, When a Certain. But certainly, on the contrary, sometimes it harms the person in whose person the event occurred, as in the Digest, On Hire, law He, section Ship. But sometimes it grants indulgence for the impediment of fact in its entirety, as in the Digest, On Rustic Slaves, law And Attilianus. Sometimes it preserves one indemnified by the law itself, as in the Code, On Appeals, Prefect, and in the Code, Who May Demand Guardians, law When by Mothers, and in the Extravagants, On Pledges, chapter Signifying. It must be considered

† It is, however, the case that either by reason of a fortuitous event the creditor wishes to obtain something, or according to the form of the contract, e.g., [he] promised me 10 if I come to Rome within a month. I, being impeded by a fortuitous event, did not come; certainly this fortuitous event harms me, because the condition of the stipulation itself fails, which, failing through a chance event occurring to the person of the stipulator, prevents the obligation from arising. And it consumes the contract itself, from the form of which one must not depart: and especially if it savors of a penalty, as in D. de verb. sig. l. cedere diem; and D. de verb. oblig. l. in executionibus, §. ult.; and note by Dy. in the same title, l. continuus, §. cum quis; and D. de fideiuss. l. stipulatus es opus. But if someone wishes to obtain [performance] such that the obligation is already contracted, yet the creditor could not obtain its execution on account of the accident, the obligation is not permitted [to be enforced], but rather it ceases in the meantime, or is deferred, as in D. de verb. oblig. l. inter stipulantem, §. sacram.

Now let us see whether the words of the contract, speaking of a certain and determined time for navigation and for the receipt of freight and goods to be loaded, signify a condition, namely if the ship was ready for navigation at that time, or whether they do not signify a condition, but rather signify the simple addition of time upon an obligation contracted by virtue of conventional law. For in the first case the merchant is not bound to pay freight, because the condition of the obligation fails, even if by chance. But in the second case he would be bound, especially if, to the fraud of the freight, without it being to their interest, they supplanted the master of the ship; because the general rule seems to be that in a right acquired, a fortuitous event does not harm; and if it sometimes does harm, nevertheless restitution in integrum is granted, as in D. quibus ex caus. maior. l. si quis stipulatus. This seems to agree with the words of the contract, because the words of carriage exclude divine force, as in the said §. servus.

Furthermore, it seems very absurd and contrary to natural equity that this master of the ship should suffer such damages and not hope for profits, C. de furt. l. manifestissimi, §. sed cum in secunda, in fine. Moreover, fraud should not be aided to those merchants, as in D. quae in fraud. cred. l. 1. Furthermore, aid should be given to the necessity of things impeded, as in D. qui ex caus. maior. l. non enim negligentibus. The words of the contract do not allow anything to be demanded from those merchants, or to be owed, because they did not use the convenience of the ship, nor could they use it at the predetermined time. And if any damage arises, it is as in the case of one who buys another’s property, who commits himself to the judgment of fortune, as in D. de act. empt. l. si iactum ratis. For this happens to those contracting over uncertain things and fortuitous events, as noted by Mod. in D. de publ. l. quot, §. qui maximos; and especially by Bart. And it is made by C. de inst. et subst. l. si pater; D. de verb. oblig. l. qui Romae, §. Calimacus; D. de cond. et demonstr. l. quibus diebus, in principio, with many similar cases.

But assuming that the merchants were not bound, it nevertheless seems equitable that the Commune of Genoa, which received benefits, should be bound to pay what wages it would have hired, D. de cond. indebiti l. si non sortem, §. libertus; since otherwise it received benefits without cause, because it can be said that the fortuitous event reduced the cause to no cause. This can be persuaded by l. si pecuniam, in principio, D. de cond. ob causam, where it says, “it is nevertheless equitable that identity be rendered to you.”

The contract, our case, about which inquiry is made, can be considered with regard to three things. First, with regard to that which is to be done and observed by the Commune of Genoa. And this was fully fulfilled and observed, and the navigation was completed. And with regard to this, no consideration of that l. si uno, §. item cum quidam, loc. applies, because here the navigation was completed, there it was incomplete.

Second, it can be considered with regard to the merchants themselves, and because a certain time was opposed [stipulated], within which their goods ought to be carried, and freight provided in compensation, that time ceasing, the contract ceases, and the final cause of the payment of freight, as in C. loc. l. si cum Hermes. For one must not depart from the tenor of the contract, neither in thing nor in time, as in D. de pact. l. epistola, §. fin.; and D. de fideiuss. l. fideiussores magistratuum, §. pro Aurelio.

Third, it can be considered with respect to the Commune of Genoa in that which must be provided to the said master of the ship. And that which must be provided contains from the beginning an uncertain quantity to be certified by the loading of goods, which loading was necessary within the designated time. But the time of navigation having elapsed, it was not necessary, but voluntary, and perhaps it would have been dangerous to the merchants themselves, as in C. de nauticariis et naucleriis, l. cum nave clericorum, lib. 11. It would be equitable to distinguish thus: either the said merchants could wait without great inconvenience to them, or not, arg. loc. l. si in lege, §. colonus. But nevertheless, regarding precise justice, it seems that the Commune is not bound indistinctly on their occasion.

Moreover, fatal damages, which happen to prudent men, cannot be relieved by any remedy of law, as in D. pro socio, l. cum duobus, §. damna. Therefore, the damage offered by divine force must be borne patiently, as in D. de damno infecto, l. fluminum; l. Servius; and D. de re iudicata, l. contractus; D. de nautico faenore, l. periculi; and c.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether an emphyteutic thing is to be returned to the church with improvements on account of the canon not having been paid; and whether the delay can be purged by the emphyteuta.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Regarding the case of the church of Saint Stephen of Buguella, it must be said that anyone who is obliged to receive an annual census is presumed, in case of doubt, to hold the ownership of the thing for which the census is paid. Therefore, if the said census is owed to the church and is not paid for two years, the property reverts to the church by full right, as stated in C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, auth. qui rem huiusmodi, and in ff. de publicanis, l. commissa, and l. vectigalia, § non solum. Since, therefore, the non-payment has persisted not only for two years but for four years and beyond, it must be said that the mill in question returns to the church of Saint Stephen by operation of law, as stated in C. de iure emphyteutico, l. 2. And because the said mill was granted for improvement, this emphyteutic contract, due to the improvements made for the church of Saint Stephen, cannot be purged of delay by the said emphyteutic holders, because we are outside the time limits for purging delay, as noted in the cited constitution potuit.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. That which is recorded in the instrument prejudices the person who suffers it to be recorded, unless something else appears.
2. Whether an heir, by transacting or compromising with the legatees, is considered to have entered upon the inheritance; whether an heir instituted in a specific thing ought to await the entry of the universal heir, so that he may enter; and what effect such entry produces.
3. Given a statute that complaints shall not be heard, it is then not lawful to appeal, nor to act on nullity.
4. A prohibition made to an heir in writing is not considered made to the heir of the heir.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. In the case of the most excellent and magnificient lady, Lady Franchina of Verme, and of the noble and most excellent Milan of Saint Nazarius, difficulty has arisen and continues to arise from the tenor of the arbitration award. For, according to the truth of the matter, insofar as it concerns the said lady, it contains justice; but for the other party, it contains, so to speak, grace. For, the acts having been considered, the arbitrators ought precisely to have declared that the inheritance was accepted and that the usufruct was due, as if the inheritance of the testator had been accepted. And this is most clearly proven by the words of the compromise, where it says: “on account of the usufruct competent to the said lady in the goods and inheritance of the aforementioned late Lord Antonius, her consort.”

† For it is certain that that which is described in the instrument prejudices him who suffers it to be described in the instrument, unless something else appears from the form of the writing. As in D. de fideiussoribus, tut. l. cum attendimus, §. si; and C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione, optimam. Especially since the compromise is founded upon the very words. Since, therefore, the parties asserted that the usufruct is due, then also all that by which one arrives at it is included, as in D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. illud. Therefore, also the acceptance of the inheritance, without which the legacy of usufruct cannot be due, where the testator remained within the limits of a simple legacy. From which it follows that the said compromitting parties tacitly asserted that the testator’s inheritance had been accepted. And upon this they founded their compromise, as in c. 1, de probat., in 6.

Secondly, this is proven because the heir, by compromising with the legatees concerning the legacies, since he does not have the right to compromise unless the inheritance has been accepted, because it is not his own interest, performs such an act which cannot effectively be done regarding the right and name of the heir. Therefore, it necessarily follows that he appears to act on behalf of the heir, as in D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. pro haerede, §. Papinianus; and Inst. de rebus quae in actionem veniunt et differunt, §. si certum est. Note that whoever transacts with legatees appears to accept the inheritance, because otherwise he does not have the right to transact with them: for if he transacts before the inheritance is accepted, there is no transaction from both sides, as in D. quorum legatorum, l. 1, §. quod ait; and D. de inofficioso testamento, si proponas, §. pe. For before the inheritance is accepted, it is certain that nothing is owed to the legatee, nor is the heir bound. Likewise, the heir cannot be condemned, nor definitively absolved, if the inheritance is not accepted. Hence, the compromise would be frivolous and void. Since, therefore, the heir gives the arbitrators the power to declare and define that he is bound, he therefore gives the power to declare that he owes; indeed, as was said, by the very fact that he transacts concerning hereditary property, he is understood to accept, because he cannot do this without the right and name of the heir, as in the aforementioned §. Papinianus. The third reason is that whenever a named heir possesses more than his share, unless he claims it from another cause, he appears to accept the inheritance, unless he legitimately protests the contrary, as in D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. duo fratres. But this noble Milanese possessed that which belonged to the testator’s goods; therefore, he acted on behalf of the heir, as in D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. gerit. Fourthly, it is proven because he requested time for deliberation and did not renounce, as in C. de iure deliberandi, l. si, §. si quis autem temerario; and note D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. quandiu, unless it is said that he requested and time was given for deliberation; otherwise, if it was not given. From these and other matters that can be alleged, the acceptance of the inheritance and the management on behalf of the heir appear. But even assuming as constant that he had not accepted, nevertheless, the usufruct is owed to the said lady for three reasons:

First, because the lady was instituted as heir to the usufruct, by which words it is signified that she may take it for herself, as from her own acceptance, as in D. de haeredibus instituendis, l. sed sine conditione, §. si. For in this case, an heir instituted in a certain thing is greater than a legatee, because he can preserve the legacy for himself by accepting, and the acceptance of the universal heir is not awaited. For either the universal heir will accept the inheritance, and the acceptance of the inheritance in a certain thing will be resolved into legacies; or he will not accept, and the institution in a certain thing is drawn to universals, as in D. de militum testamento, l. si certarum, in principio; and D. de haeredibus instituendis, l. 1, §. si ex fundo. Therefore, since no case can occur in which the said usufruct is not due, it is rightly due without awaiting the acceptance of the universal heir: and in this respect the sentence of the arbitrators was just and juridical, with respect to both parties.

The second reason is that where the testator prohibits the deduction of the Falcidian share in the will, it is not expedient that the inheritance be accepted from the will, for even if it is not accepted, legacies are due, as noted by Iacobo de Belvisio in Auth. de haeredibus et Falcidia, §. si vero expressum; and Bartolus, note, in l. 1, D. si quis omissa causa testamento. They say, however, that it is due according to the form of Auth. hoc amplius. Nevertheless, I do not care in what manner it is due, provided that it is due, because the pronouncement of the arbitrators is founded upon the essence of the legacy, not upon the person owing it. And if it is well considered, this is the intention of the said doctors.

Thirdly, this is proved by another reason. For an heir named, who delays accepting the inheritance, ought not thereby to make his own condition better and that of his adversary worse, as in D. de usufructu, l. si usus fructus legatus. And upon this also the equity of the arbitrators could have been founded. But certainly the said award must be observed for another reason, because whenever an award is within the form of the compromise, the arbitrator can decree that he who does not owe must pay. Especially since the award was subsequently ratified, as noted in D. de conditione indebiti, l. si non sortem, §. haeredi; C. communia utriusque iudicii, l. 2. But this award was expressly ratified, because he who approves the quality of the arbitrator is deemed to have ratified the whole, as in D. de negotiis gestis, l. Pomp. scribit. Therefore, one cannot go against it, as in C. de arbitris, l. penultima.

Fourthly, it is proven by the wording of the statute, because the statute provides that complaints are not to be heard. And therefore, it is not permitted to appeal, nor to bring an action for nullity, as noted by Odofredus in *Digestum*, title *Qui satisdare cogantur*, law *Si ab arbitro*; and as noted in *Clementina* 1, title *De sequestro possessionis et fructuum*, through Cynus in *Codex*, title *Locatio conductio*, law *Si quis conductionis*.

Fifthly, it is proven, because the testator intended it to be valid by way of a donation *causa mortis*, and the lady was present and accepting. In this case, it is not necessary that the inheritance be accepted, because if it is not valid as a legacy, it is valid as a pact, and the action lies under the condition of law *Si quis argentum*, as noted in *Digestum*, title *De legatis* 2, with law *Cum pater*, section *Mevio*, and the following law *Quaestio*. And if it is said that the donation *causa mortis* was in a case where it would not be valid by testamentary law, because he said, "if it is not valid, etc.," I answer that this clause also signifies this, namely, "if it is not valid," i.e., "as long as it is not valid." Hence, before the acceptance of the inheritance, because the usufruct bequeathed does not have actual validity, it is valid as a pact; subsequently, upon acceptance of the inheritance, it will be valid as a legacy. Nor is this strange, as appears in *Digestum*, title *Ad legem Falcidiam*, law *Feudo*; and in *Digestum*, title *De hereditatibus instituendis*, law 3, section *Qui fideicommissaria*.

Sixthly, it is proven, because although the usufruct ought not to be due before the acceptance of the inheritance, nevertheless the instituted heir may well consent that it be performed before the acceptance of the inheritance. And he cannot intervene against his own act. For he did not stop at the limits of consent or permission, but a promise intervened, because by compromising he promised; hence he cannot come against his own act, although he contracted before the acceptance of the inheritance, as in *Digestum*, title *De pactis*, law *Et si stipulatio*, and law *Et si ante aditam hereditatem*. Nor does it avail to object from *Digestum*, title *Quorum legatum*, law 1, section *Quod ait praetor voluntate*, because there it was a simple consent, not an obligation, as noted there; and in *Codex*, title *De pactis*, law 1. Therefore, Milan must stand by the premises, and the sentence must be obeyed, however much, as in *Digestum*, title *Familiae erciscundae*, law *Cum puta rem*; and in *Digestum*, title *De peculio*, law *Eo tempore*. For even before the acceptance of the inheritance, the heir may make a pact with the legatees, so that it is not permitted to him or to them to contravene it, as in *Digestum*, title *De pactis*, law *Pactum contra haeredem*. And this is the truth, notwithstanding any subtleties and cavils whatsoever. Hence, to say that the said sentence contains an expressed error is not true, because it pertains to those who compromised. And thus the compromise creates law between them, although it does not create law as regards all, as in *Digestum*, title *De transactionibus*, law *Imperator*; and most fully noted in the same title, law *Controversia*.

Furthermore, certainly, although as regards the transmission the day of the usufruct of the legacy does not arrive, nevertheless, upon the acceptance of the inheritance, it arrives in a certain sense, because the inheritance is in a certain sense bound to the legatees, as the sole text says in *Digestum*, title *De actionibus et obligationibus*, law *Hereditariarum*. And this also considered, there was not an entirely expressed error in the said arbitration. And it is to be noted that from the foregoing it is inferred that the said excellent lady [is entitled], whether the inheritance is accepted or not. Moreover, if it is accepted, it appears that Milan does not have the benefit of inventory due to the passage of time, and therefore the legatee and the fideicommissary [may sue] in solidum, even if it were beyond the assets of the inheritance, as in the *Authenticum*, title *De hereditate et Falcidia*, section *Sancimus*; and noted in *Codex*, title *De testamento militis*, law *In testamento*.

Now there remain two points: one is concerning a certain tacit fideicommissum, the second is concerning the prohibition against alienating. As for the first, it is a matter of the responses made on behalf of the lady.

† As to the first point, I say that a prohibition made to an heir named in the will does not appear to have been made to the heir of the heir, as in the Authentica de restitutione fideicommissi, § manifestum; and in the Digest, de vulgari et pupillari substitutione, l. qui liberis, § hæc verba. And thus I have advised on this point.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The statute of the city of Tervuren provides that, upon the death of a wife during the subsistence of the marriage, the surviving husband shall acquire the dowry, subject to the common right of the children of that marriage in the said dowry, and notwithstanding any right to the dowry under canon or civil law. What if there are no children from the second marriage, but only from the first?
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† On the said point, I say that according to the common law, this question is determined in the Authentica *De nuptiis*, § *Optime*. But because the statute has a derogatory clause, which ought to have some effect, I do not think that the said § *Optime* applies in our case; rather, I hold that the son of the first marriage ought to have his legitime, in accordance with what is noted by the Lord Doctor in *c. Indultum*, Extra, *De regulis iuris*, lib. 6, especially since the statute makes no mention of the legitime. And therefore, it does not appear to have been abolished by general words, as argued in *C. De inofficiosis testamentis*, l. *Si quando*, § *Si*. Since, therefore, in our case there is no other common child, but only the son of the first marriage, he ought to have his legitime, and the husband ought to have the remaining goods by virtue of the statute, notwithstanding the arguments beautifully and subtly alleged to the contrary. For not all objections are answered by the rule *Non obstantibus*, which is retained for the penalties of the second marriage. And if this statute did not exist, because he later told me that there are two daughters from the second marriage, the share would belong to the son, and the other two shares to the two other daughters begotten of the second husband.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether tithes may be granted in fief.
2. Whether a compromise may be made regarding tithes.
3. The penalty for non-observance of the laudemium, or for non-performance: whether and when it is incurred once or repeatedly.
4. Whether one delay is merged with another.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Without calling into doubt whether tithes can be granted in fief, on which matter is fully read and noted in the Extravagantes, de decimis, although it is a grave matter, I say that, presupposing the custom of the church and also of the province, if tithes have been granted in fief, which is understood, that is, the usufruct of the tithes, as in l. necessario, §. fin., de periculis et commodis rei venditae, and it is a question between the holder of the tithes and the feudatory, it is not doubtful that on such a question a compromise and transaction can be made between them to their prejudice. Thus says the text in the title de controversia inter vassallum et alium de beneficio, c. si inter vassallum, col. 10.

† For it is not understood that the compromise concerns the special right of tithes, but rather the benefit, concerning which one may compromise, just as if a usufructuary were to compromise concerning the usufruct. For it is not understood that he compromises concerning the right itself, which is inseparable from the person, but concerning the benefit itself, as is proven from the note in l. 1, C. si pignus pignori datum sit.

But subsequently it must be considered regarding the penalty. And here there are several cases to be noted: for sometimes a penalty is imposed in place of particular interest, and then it is incurred for each individual performance in place of total interest. And then it is not incurred more than once. Sometimes there is doubt, and then if the obligation is distributive, it is incurred for each individual obligation; if it is universal, then the contrary applies, as in D. si certum petatur, l. lecta; and D. de pignoris actione, l. si necessitas, § si annua. Or there is doubt, and recourse must be had to the words of the contract, and also to the intention; for if indeed the solution is distributed in favor of the debtor, so that he may be able to pay more easily, then the penalty is not incurred unless all installments are past due, as in C. de collatione fundi patris, l. placuit. It supports this: Extr. de locato, c. potuit; and C. de iure emphyteutico, l. 2; and D. locati conducti, l. quaero, § inter locatorem. But if a time is appointed by way of necessity and interpellation, which is tacitly implied by the nature of time, as in C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione, l. magnam; and D. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. traiectitia, § de illo; then default is incurred from the person, and afterwards the penalty in the second place, provided that it was promised in a lawful case. And much more so if a penalty is imposed in place of contempt towards arbitrators, as in D. de arbitris, l. si duo, § semel, vers. nisi id actum; or in place of circumvented interest, that is, as a mere penalty, as in § alteri. Therefore, in the question proposed, according to the common opinion, which holds that where there is an express day and a penalty, purification of default is not admitted, especially when the penalty can be claimed together with the principal, I say, as prudently advised, according to what is proposed, that the debtor has incurred the penalty twice, because he failed in two payments at different times.

And thus there are two causes, and two delays concerning different matters committed, and the first delay is not confused with the last delay, because it is not concerning the same thing; the case is in the aforementioned law *Lecta*, *Si certum petatur*; and the law *1*, at the end, *De penus legatorum*, supports this. There is also a case, if it is well introduced, in the aforementioned section *Si annua*; that which is fully noted by Cynus, *Codex*, *De pactis*, law *Si pacto*, *Quo poenam*, and by Dyther and others, *Digestum*, *De verbis obligatorum*, law *Si insulam*, supports this. And these things are true, whether there is one obligation, and the divided preface with the necessity of paying distributively. Otherwise, if by way of faculty, or if there are several obligations, unless it were such a penalty that would induce novation over the whole. For that could not be demanded, except once, as in *Digestum*, *De concubinis*, law *Si duo rei*, section *Semel*, in the first response, unless, etc., as the text says there in the second response. *Digestum*, *De verbis obligatorum*, law *Si sic stipulatus sum*, *Neque parte*; and there fully noted. And law *Si procurator*, *Rem ratam habere*. And thus I say, and I counsel, I, Baldus de Perusio, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If, before a secular judge, an usurious exception was raised against an instrument and the case was remitted to the Church, and if the ecclesiastical judge again remits it to the secular judge, and a sentence is rendered, whether it is valid or not.
2. An exception which renders the judgment retroactively null may also be raised after sentence has been pronounced; the oath creates a presumption that fraud is more likely with a usurer accustomed to lending at interest.
3. While a usury case is pending, the secular judge may not proceed, even with the consent of the bishop.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Given the statute of the commune of Verona, which provides that the vicar and the consuls of the merchants’ house shall have no jurisdiction over usurious contracts, and that they may in no way proceed in such matters, it is asked what is the law if action was brought before them, pursuant to certain instruments which, upon their first inspection, contained permission for a certain quantity on account of commerce and on account of certain other causes. And the exception of usury was raised, and proof was remitted to the bishop, who, having viewed the instrument, did not wish to intervene otherwise in cognizance of the matter. But, having viewed the instrument, he referred the parties to the said judge and consuls, who afterwards condemned the said defendant as they saw fit.

It is asked whether the aforementioned procedure, established on the basis of presumptions that it is usurious, at least for the greater part of the sum contained in the instrument itself, is null by operation of law; and whether the said exception can be raised again, or, if raised, pursued, notwithstanding the said sentence. And it seems that, at first glance, one should say that, although the procedure is carried out without the exception being discussed, nevertheless the procedure, and even the sentence, is invalid, although an appeal may be taken, as in D. de compensatione, l. quod in diem, § si rationem; and D. de negotiis gestis, l. si navem, § fi. To the contrary, it seems that this exception is prejudicial to the jurisdiction itself. Hence, unless the jurisdiction is discussed and established, the procedure is null by operation of law, as in D. de eo qui pro tutore, l. quaeritur; and as noted by Bartolus in D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. multum interest; and what is noted in c. quod super, de officio delegati; and D. de aleato, l. 1, § quod autem.

† Moreover, this exception renders the judgment retroactively null, as appears from the form of the statute. Therefore, it may be raised even after sentence, as in C. de procur. l. licet, and as noted in C. de iur. et fac. igno. l. 1. Furthermore, the order of law was not observed here, since no cognizance was taken of the prejudicial matter, as in Extra, de iudi. c. exhibita. Moreover, since the usurious exception was remitted to the bishop, jurisdiction over this article was transferred to the bishop, and the jurisdiction of the transmitting judge was meanwhile impeded and suspended, as argued in C. de rela. l. 1. And thus, with jurisdiction suspended, the act is null by operation of law, as in C. de dila. cum a nobis. Moreover, from the forms of the instruments it is evidently gathered that the said promise had its root and foundation in usurious wickedness. And thus sentence should not have been rendered by the secular judge, especially a condemnatory one, since this comes in derogation of ecclesiastical jurisdiction, and also contains sin, as is read and noted in c. vlti. de exceptio. lib. 6. Moreover, no one doubts that where a sentence is null, action may be brought and exception pleaded regarding the nullity even after sentence, as in ff. de appella. l. si expressum. And it is literally the text in c. ut calumniis, Extra, de reg. iur. In the gloss, someone will say that justice has been satisfied, because the bishop remitted the parties to the secular judge. But I answer that he could not do this without observing the order of law, as in ff. de transact. l. cum hi. §. cum prętor. Therefore, the ordinary must, whether he wills or not, take cognizance, since the burden of judging is a public authority, as in ff. de mune. et hono. l. munerum. §. iudicandi. It is supported by what Innocent notes in Extra, de regu. iu. in c. 1. Moreover, it is patent from the acts, whence it is not only apparent through indications and conjectures that there was usury, but also through the reading of the instrument, which patiently shows the quality of the thing, as in C. de probat. l. ad probationem dominii. Since therefore it is established before the said vicar and consuls that they lack jurisdiction, rightly, insofar as they have proceeded de facto to the arrest of the person and the seizure of the goods, they must immediately revoke it, as noted in ff. de euic. l. minor. in princi. It is supported by Extra, de purga. uul. c. significantib. and ff. si mulier uentris nomine. l. 1. §. 1. Nor is there any doubt that, the sentence being revoked insofar as they proceeded de facto, all things that followed from it or by it must be revoked, as is read and noted in Extra, de pręca. c. 2. in nouella. Because when the principal is revoked, the accessory is revoked according to Innocent and Hostiensis. Nor does it object to the foregoing that an oath was appended in the contract itself, because the said oath, as being rendered on a base matter, is null by operation of law, as in C. de legi. l. non dubium, and ff. de leg. 1. l. si quis inquilinos. §. fi. Although it is otherwise in the forum of canon law. This is supported by the fact that an oath rendered in fraud of the laws to evade constitutions which prohibit usury must be said by operation of law not to be valid, as noted in C. plus ualere, quod agitur. l. emptione, and ff. de iure patro. l. si libertus minorem, and l. adigere. §. ulti. And therefore the said consuls should not heed the said oath, since fraud of usury is clearly apparent to them.

† For, as Hostiensis elegantly states, fraud is more strongly presumed in the case of a usurer accustomed to lending money, due to the addition of an oath, as he himself notes in the gloss to *extra de pignoribus*, under the word *vos*, and the same is noted there by Innocentius. For an oath makes suspect contracts even more suspect, and this constitutes a violent presumption, as argued in *extra de renunciationibus*, chapter *Super hoc*. From all of which I conclude that the said Baptist is to be released from prison, as he was unjustly captured, by an incompetent judge, and without observing the order of law. And to the presumption of fraud in the aforementioned matters is added *ff. de probationibus*, *Qui testamentum*, and in *l. Sęya*, *ff. de conditionibus institutis*. Furthermore, it must be observed that, although one instrument speaks of a usurious loan and another of a simple loan, this does not double the quantity of fraud, but rather reveals the fraud more clearly, as stated in *ff. de verbis obligatis*, *l. Qui bis idem*. Hence it appears from this that the usury was intended to be converted into principal. Hence deceit and fraud are more openly demonstrated, as I have said, as in *C. de usuris*, *l. Pe*. And it supports this what is noted by Jacobus de Arena in *l. Cum centum*, *ff. de adicienda lege*, in the solution of the contrary argument regarding *l. Plane*, *de legatis 1*. For although the same quantity is repeated in different contracts, in reality there is only one quantity, as in *ff. de constituta pecunia*, *l. Item illa*, § *fina*. This is also clear from the proceedings, the sentence, and the subsequent capture.

ADDITIO. In the name of Christ, Amen. Since, as has been said, the consuls do not have jurisdiction except that which is granted to them by statute, as is noted in *ff. de pace*, *l. Item magistri*; but this statute does not grant it, but rather denies it on account of the turpitude of the case. And because it has a perpetual cause of turpitude, it renders the judgment retroactively null, as in the aforementioned *l. 1*, § *Quod autem*, *de alea*. And jurisdiction fails by operation of law, because it is prohibited, as in *C. de testamentis*, *l. Consulta diualia*, and *C. ne de statu defunctorum*, *l. Si mater*.

† Moreover, because while a usury case is pending, the secular judge cannot proceed, even with the consent of the bishop, since such consent is contrary to law, as argued from the Digest, *De feriis*, l. 1, § 1. Furthermore, the arrest was invalid by operation of law, according to what is read and noted in the Digest, *De suspectis tutoribus*, l. 3, § *tutores*. For these reasons, and others alleged above, I hold that what I concluded above stands, namely, that the judgment is invalid. And this person is to be released from prison, as having been arrested contrary to civil procedure and against the form of both municipal and common law. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a vassal incurs forfeiture by mere sale and alienation of the fief without delivery, and whether the alienation prejudices the son and agnates.
2. Whether agnates offering the price to the purchaser can recover the fief.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It must be stated at the outset for clarity that a vassal sometimes sells but does not deliver, and in that case there is no doubt that the fief is not alienated by the sale alone, as is read and noted in the Digest, *De verborum significatione*, law *Alienatum*. At other times he sells and delivers, and then either without the lord’s consent or with the lord’s consent. In the first case, if he has neither sons nor agnates, there is no doubt that the fief reverts to the lord, so that the lord may have at least this vengeance for his injury, as in chapter 1, § *Denique*, *Quae fuit prima causa beneficii amittendi*, column 10. Or if he has a son but no agnates, some say that the father’s fault does not harm the son in the paternal fief, as in the Digest, *De iure patronatus*, law *Diui fratres*; *De interdictis et relegationibus*, law 4; *De contrahenda emptione*, law *Non tantum*, § *Si emancipatus*. Others say that the father’s fault harms the son, as in column 10, *Si vassallus feudo priuetur, cui deferatur*, chapter *Si vassallus*, and *Quae fuit prima causa beneficii amittendi*, chapter *Finis*; and this opinion prevails according to the custom of fiefs, as in column 10, *Si de feudo fuerit controversia*, chapter *Si vassallus culpam*. Or if he has agnates, here there are differing opinions, because some say that it does not prejudice the agnates if the fief is paternal. And the gloss inclines to this opinion, which is in chapter 1, § *Hoc quoque*, and *De successione feudi*. And this same view is held by Laurentius de Bella. And this seems very reasonable, because the fault of the alienator does not descend to the agnates, since they derive no cause from him, even though he preceded them in some order of preference. Since therefore the fault does not descend to them, nor does the penalty, as in the Code, *De poenis*, law *Sancimus*, and by argument from the Code, *De inofficioso testamento*, law *Si quis in suo*, § *Finis*. Others say, and it is truer according to the custom of fiefs, that it prejudices the agnates, because this is the nature of the fief, for the contract of the fief is rescinded by such alienation. For we would say the same thing according to some in emphyteusis, as in the Code, *De iure emphyteuticario*, law *Finis*. Also for the aforementioned reason, so that at least the lord may have vengeance for his injury; otherwise the offense would remain unpunished, which is absurd. And these are the points concerning illicit alienation, namely when the lord does not consent to the alienation. But sometimes there is a licit alienation made with the lord’s consent, as is read and noted in chapter 1, *De probanda alienatione per Lotarium*.

† And then sometimes the text says that such alienation remains stable and is valid in perpetuity. Sometimes it says that agnates can revoke it with this distinction. For either the vassal has children, and then the nearest agnate can at least revoke it by returning the price. Or he does not have children, and then he cannot revoke it, unless the alienator dies without an heir, in which case he is not bound to restore the price. Thus says the text in c. Titius filios, si de feud. fue. controuer., col. 10. And that this chapter speaks of a lawful alienation appears from the fact that if it were an unlawful alienation, the fief would immediately be opened to the lord, as is clear from what has been said above. Moreover, if the reason for the difference is sought when he has children and when he does not, the glossa says that the wise man should inquire. And elsewhere it says, let Apollo answer. But in fiefs one need not care for strict reason, but for custom. It is therefore by strict custom that the agnate may redeem, as in c. 1, §. sed et res, per quos fiat inuestitura, col. 10, by offering the price within a year, to be computed from when he learned of it, as in c. 1, near the end, qualiter olim feudum poterat alienari, in the same collection. From this, therefore, the decision of our question clearly appears, because the sale, or contract to sell, was lawful as regards the illustrious lord, who consented; nevertheless, agnates are preferred in redeeming, as noted in the said chapters. If, therefore, the said seller completes the sale by delivering immediately and without interval, it must be returned to the redeeming agnate for the same price; the said buyer cannot pursue his intent, with the agnate opposing himself, since the fief is paternal. And this agnate exists and is in such a degree that nothing stands in his way. Hence, not censuring the opinion of the consultant, who however departed from the ordinary glossae, but saving it, I say and assert that the aforementioned agnate, by returning the price paid by the said buyer—which if he does not pay, he cannot demand the thing bought, ff. de act. emp., l. Iulianus, §. offerri—I say that the agnate himself can redeem from the external buyer. Thus, extra, de restitu. in integ., constitutus. And his condition is better than the condition of the said external buyer. Therefore, to save the sentence of the illustrious one, I say that the sentence should be put into execution for a certain moment of time; but immediately, before turning to other matters, the said fief should be resold to the aforementioned agnate; so that the said buyer in the return of the said fief cannot make any cavil; and let him know one thing, that if the agnate wished to offer, the father nevertheless in this contract should not name the son, nor bind him, because many hold the opinion that upon the father’s death the son could recover this fief without offering the price, which seems to be the view of Iac. de Bel. in d. §. sed et res, and Pe. de Ceruetis in d. §. Titius. But of this there is no need to dispute now, but it must be concluded for certain that the said agnate can redeem and compel the first buyer to resell to him for an equal price. And so I hold. I say further that even the son of the vassal would be admitted to redeem, because there is no nearer agnate than the son. But Petrus de Ceruetis in d. c. Titius holds the contrary, arguing from C. de bo. ma., l. si viua matre. And so I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Both Laws, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a wife unjustly accused by her husband may bring an action for injuries against him.
2. Whether fraud is required in an action for injuries, and whether gross negligence is equivalent to fraud.
3. A curator ad litem cannot swear the oath against calumnia unless he has a special mandate.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. In the case of William de Corrado, which he had with his wife, Lady Helena, and her father

It is true, with respect to the action for injuries brought against her, that if no definitive sentence had been rendered, he could have had several remedies, according to what he himself proposes to me, namely that he was bewitched. For it often happens that, in order to impede the love existing between a man and a woman, certain wicked women perform what are commonly called "love spells," which impede intercourse or greatly weaken it, as stated in the Decretals, *De frigidis et maleficiatis*, throughout. And there are many experiences of this: although it is almost incredible, for which reason, and even if not rationally, as I think, yet he had an opinion-based suspicion about his lady, and did wrong by imprudently defaming her.

† However, injury requires intent, and therefore in the action for injuries gross negligence is not equated with intent, just as it is not in theft, nor in other offenses in which intent is strictly required, as in C. de falsis, l. nec exemplum; and ff. de abigeis, l. 1, in fine. And even assuming that it would be applicable, and by oath alone, because in this manner it is never proven unless intent intervenes, as noted in Inst. de verborum obligationibus, §. pe; and vnde vi, l. si quando; and in l. 1, C. de senatus consulto, quod pro eo quod interest. Moreover, just grief excuses from calumny, as noted in ff. de his qui notati infamia, l. athletas, §. calumniator, regarding a husband who accuses of adultery by the right of the husband, for there cannot be greater infamy than this. For the law presumes that the inner grief of the committed or contemplated crime moves the husband; so much so that the law states that the husband grieves more than the father over the killing of a son, as in ff. de legatis 2, l. codicilli, §. pe.

† Moreover, the curator ought not to have been able to take an oath, since a curator ad litem is equivalent to a procurator. Hence, he ought to have had a special mandate, as stated in the Digest, De in litis iurando, law Vulgo. However, since a definitive judgment has been rendered, from which no appeal was taken, nor could an appeal be taken, because it was rendered against a true contumacious party, the strictness of the law is against this William de Corradis; for he poorly knew the verse of Cato: “Prepare yourself for the forum,” a verse learned by boys who study Cato. But this William was not Cato, but rather a goat, because he did not obey the Prince, as stated in the Digest, De re iudicata, law Contumacia, § Contumax; and in the Digest, De in integrum restitutione, the Divine Emperor [states]. And therefore, although he had justice on his side, he deprived himself of it, and there is no remedy by way of appeal. But he may supplicate the Prince, who may, by virtue of the plenitude of his power, grant him a fitting and appropriate form, according to the equity of the Prince himself, as noted in the Code, Res cui non posse, law Si; and it would be good if the parties could be brought back to concord, as noted in the Authenticum, De monachis, § Si vero intra triennium; and in the Extravagantes, Ut litis non contestatae, chapter 1; and in the Code, De his qui ad ecclesias confugiunt, law Praesenti, § Sicubi. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A constitution of a syndic made by the universitas, with a decree and the authority of the consuls, is valid.
