2. Whether a decree interposed in a church is valid.
casus: CASE. In the name of Christ, amen. The case is as follows, concerning the doubt set forth below, namely, whether the syndics appointed by the community of the men of the castle of Rocherii, with the decree of the consuls of that place, were legitimately appointed. And whether they may act for that community against Lady Margaret, wife of Lord Boniface Burlati. Having seen the said instrument, and having seen the objections made against the said instrument by the procurator of the said Lady Margaret, which objections include, among others, that the said instrument of syndication was drawn up without the decree of Lord Baldinus, the castellan, before whom the first principal question was debated. Also, that the said syndics were appointed in the church of Saint Mary of that place, having also seen a certain pronouncement made by the said Lord Baldinus, the castellan, as above, on the advice of the Spectable man, Lord Firilinus Guarlecta of Asti, doctor of laws, from which pronouncement an appeal was taken to the illustrious Prince, Lord Marquis of Montferrat, who, the said Lord Marquis, committed the said cause to the wise man, Lord Ioannes Cortesius, before whom many matters were debated. And having seen certain chapters produced on behalf of the procurator of the said Lady Margaret to prove that the said community of the castle of Rocherii does not have mere or mixed imperium, nor jurisdiction. And having seen other chapters produced by the syndics of the castle of Rocherii to prove that they are accustomed to govern themselves through consuls. And having seen the witnesses and attestations of both parties, and having seen the allegations of both parties,
body: In the name of Christ alone, I, Bal. de Perusis, having invoked,

† I say, and in the Name of Christ I alone, Bal. of Perugia, declare that the said syndic was and is legitimate; and that the sentence of the said Lord Baldus was lawfully rendered. And this chiefly because, in such a constitution of syndics, it suffices according to the usual custom, and in the customary place, for the universitas to be assembled in the due manner, and there for a syndic to be appointed by authority, with the decree of the consuls, who have by ancient custom the power, and that which confers jurisdiction, as C. de emancip. lib. 1, l. 1; and noted in ff. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, l. more maiorum; and C. de decurionibus, l. nominationum forma; and C. de legibus, l. si quod extra ordinarium, lib. 10; and ff. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, l. more maiorum; and l. et quia. Argument: and C. de decurionibus, l. nominationum forma; and C. de legibus, l. si quod extraordinarium, lib. 10; and ff. quod cuiusque universitatis nomine, l. nulli.

† Nor does it matter that the decree was issued in the church, because acts of voluntary jurisdiction, such as decrees of this kind, which do not require clamor or formal inquiry, may be performed, and what is done is valid, as established in C. de his, qui in ecclesiis manu mittuntur, l. 1, and noted in C. de sac. san. ecc., l. nemo apostolorum, according to the doctrine. Nor does the gloss placed there constitute an objection, because it does not state that the contract or decree is invalid, even though it ought not to have been done on grounds of propriety. This is noted in c. decet, at the end, de immunitate ecclesiarum, lib. 6. Since, therefore, the instrument states that the university was assembled in the usual manner and the decree of the consuls was appended, it appears from the very tenor of the instrument that the syndicate is valid. Moreover, the statute and custom of the place can grant mixed and greater jurisdiction to the said consuls, as noted in ff. de pace, l. item magistri. And therefore, it was rightly judged by the consul, and wrongly appealed.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 0. The facts are as follows: A. invested B. subject to the payment of a certain annual ground rent from certain properties. After many years, the said A. sold, or exchanged with C. in this manner, namely that the said A. gave, delivered, exchanged, and sold to the said C. a ground rent of 20 pounds, which is given and paid, and ought to be given and paid every year by the said B. from the said properties. Likewise, for the same price and in the same manner, the said A. gave, delivered, exchanged, and sold to the said C. the above-written properties and things from which the said ground rent of 20 pounds is given and paid, and ought to be given and paid; and by cause and merit of this present sale, delivery, and exchange, the said A. assigned and conveyed right to the said C. regarding all and singular rights and actions, both real and personal, beneficial and direct, which the said A. had, or could have, and seemed to have in all and singular the aforesaid things sold, delivered, and exchanged above to C. himself, against the said B. and against any holders and possessors, and who shall hold and possess the aforesaid things, or anything of the aforesaid things delivered to the above-said C., transferring to the said C. all his rights and actions regarding the aforesaid: which ground rent of 20 pounds and the aforesaid properties, from which the ground rent itself is given and paid, and ought to be given and paid, the said A. from now on agreed to hold and possess for the future, and as it were in the name of the said C., until the said C. shall have taken corporal possession, which [license] of taking and retaining henceforth, and of doing whatever he might wish, the said A. granted from now on to the said C. in every manner, the said A. delivering and giving from now on to the said C. all ownership and all possession of the aforesaid. These things having been so transacted, within three months the said B. died, and immediately the said C., the buyer, entered the said properties and had them cultivated for many years, and holds them continuously and today. Recently, however, a certain D., an old creditor of the said late B., formerly the tenant, wishes to claim the beneficial ownership of the above-written properties by reason of a general hypothec over his assets, saying that the beneficial ownership still endures; for at the time of the sale made to the said C. as above it endured, because, even granted that a thousand acknowledgments of past ground rent appeared at that time, nevertheless the property was not forfeited [?], nor is the said B. said to have forfeited his right of beneficial ownership, unless it had been declared by the said A. regarding his intention that he wished them to have been forfeited, as in l. 2. C. de iure emphy. But that declaration of intention had never been made, therefore etc.; on the contrary, it is said that rather it appears
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The facts are as follows: A invested B with certain properties, subject to the payment of a fixed annual rent. After many years, the said A sold or exchanged with C in this manner: because the said A gave, transferred, exchanged, and sold to C a fixed rent of 20 pounds, which is given and paid, and ought to be given and paid every year by the said B from the said properties. Furthermore, for the same price and in the same manner, the said A gave, transferred, exchanged, and sold to the said C the aforesaid properties and things from which the said fixed rent of 20 pounds is given and paid, and ought to be given and paid. And by reason and merit of this present sale, transfer, and exchange, the said A ceded and made a conveyance of right to C of all and each of the rights and actions, both real and personal, useful and direct, which the said A had, or could have, and appeared to have in all and each of the aforesaid things sold, transferred, and exchanged to the said C above, against the said B and against anyone holding and possessing, and who shall hold and possess, the aforesaid things or anything of the aforesaid things transferred to the said C above, transferring to the said C all his rights and actions concerning the aforesaid things. The said A constituted himself, from now on, to hold and possess the said fixed rent of 20 pounds and the aforesaid properties, from which the said rent is given and paid, and ought to be given and paid, henceforth in the name of the said C, until the said C shall have taken corporal possession, which he is to take and retain henceforth, and whatever he shall wish to do. From now on, the said A granted to the said C every kind of license, transferring and giving to C, from now on, all dominion and all possession of the aforesaid things. Thus, within three months, the said B died. Immediately, the said C, the buyer, entered the said properties and had them worked for many years, and he holds them continuously to this day. Recently, however, a certain D, an old creditor of the late B, formerly the tenant, wishes to claim the useful dominion of the aforesaid properties by general hypothec of the goods, saying that the useful dominion still endures. For at the time of the sale made to the said C, as above, it endured, because even if it appears that a thousand confessions of the past rent were made at that time, nevertheless the property was not openly declared, nor is it said to have fallen from the right of useful dominion of the said B, unless it was declared by the said A, of his own will, that he wished them to have been open, as in l. 2, C. de iure emphyteuticario. But this declaration of will was never made; therefore, etc. On the contrary, it is said that rather the opposite seems to have been intended at the time of the said sale, because the words of the said sale import this, namely, that he sold the rent which is given and is presumed. These are words of the present tense. Therefore, he seems to have done and wished that at that time he was the tenant, and consequently did not wish the property to have been open at that time. As for the subsequent time after the sale, there seems to be little doubt, because if the owner entered possession, as above, therefore it remained through him that the tenant could not use and enjoy; and thus he was not in default, as in l. ex conducto, ff. locati conducti, with similar cases. Therefore, doubt remains concerning the time before the sale for the aforesaid reasons. For it must be observed whether, from the aforesaid words or from some of them, the said A, the seller, seems to have declared anything concerning the opening of the said properties, or not, and whether he wished to transfer them open. Secondly, it must be observed that, because he transferred to the said C the common rights competent to him, etc., as above: whether he transferred to him the right of deliberating and approaching the said properties if open, or not. Also, whether the right of declaring can thus pass to a singular successor.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, after an investiture, sale, or exchange has been made, as in this case, the right to declare properties to be open or not may pass to a singular successor.
2. The property does not fall into forfeiture unless declared by the lord.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† This investiture begins with the fictions, of which the buyer is perpetually invested: there, when it says, one fiction of 20 pounds, which is given and must be provided to be given and provided every year by the said B. from the said properties, these words are to be understood for the future time. For up to that point of the celebrated contract, the pension is owed to the seller, not to the buyer, ff. de actio. emp. l. Iul. §. si fructib. and noted by Bart. in l. sin. C. de iure fisci. and it is clear ff. quod vi, aut clam. l. si is, qui puteum. §. si postea. if therefore the seller receives it, it appears retroactively that the thing did not fall into forfeiture. ff. de pac. inter empt. l. commissorie. and noted in l. 2. C. de iure emp. Finally, the buyer cannot object to this pension of past time, because it is not owed to him, but to the seller. Which is noted by Cy. in l. ex territorium. at the end of his commentary after Pet. and ff. de usufruct. l. defuncta. And although this reason is sufficient, another reason is also assigned, because by selling the future pension, he seems to have chosen this way, not the way of expulsion, just as by testifying about any right, one is understood to choose and accept it, C. de iu. deli. l. si auia. and instit. de haere. quali. et differentia. §. fin. and it works optimally ff. de inoffi. testa. l. si ut proponas. §. si haereditatem.

† Moreover, the third reason is that the thing does not fall into forfeiture unless the lord declares it so, as noted in D. si ager vectigalis, l. 2. But the seller did not declare this, nor does the buyer have the right to declare it for the past period, but only for the future. For this word indicates future time. The same applies to the adverb "deinceps" (henceforth). The same applies to the adverb "ex nunc" (from now on), because it signifies from now on into the future, not from now on into the past, D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. 4. For annuities are in the place of fruits, D. de rei vendita, l. navis. It is certain that for the time during which the buyer possessed, no annuity is owed to him, D. de actione emptoris, l. bona fides; nor does he fall into forfeiture, because he ought not to possess the thing and claim the penalty, D. de exceptione doli, l. apud Celsum, § Labeo. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether and when a person who makes payment, with an addition to the payment, or to a putative heir, is discharged.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. For clarity, it must be stated that according to the tenor of the aforementioned document, it appears that the said Jac. was added to the solution, and this in the first contract. Secondly, the said Jac. either added the vassal to the solution, or merely indicated him as successor, in the manner of knights, as in C. de pac. licet.

Secondly, it must be premised that the person added to the solution either received the solution or did not. In the first case, he is bound to restore it to the creditor and his heir by means of the *actio mandati* or the *negotiorum gestio*, as stated in the Digest, *De verbis obligatis*, in the title of Julius, § *Si quis alii*. Hence the matter stands thus: if Jacob were bound as a fictitious heir, the receiver of the goods would be bound to Jacob as the true receiver, according to the aforementioned laws. Therefore, the order would be such that the heirs of John would sue Jacob, and Jacob would sue the receiver. And this would be the case if the action had not been transferred, nor anything claimed from the receiver. But let us suppose that action was taken against the receiver by the true heirs, so that what was owed to the true heir by the added person was paid by the added person to the putative heir as if he were the true heir. To recover this, the added person sues the putative heir. Can he now sue the debtor, who paid the putative heir? And it seems to be said that he cannot, because he appears to have ratified the payment, as argued in the Digest, *Si certum petatur*, law *Si eum servum*; *De solutionibus*, *Vero procuratori*; and *Si quis offerenti*. And if the defendant satisfies the claim, there is no doubt that he improperly claims what he has in law, as stated in the Digest, *De solutionibus*, *Qui hominem*, § *Si praedictae*. Furthermore, if he has compromised the matter to avoid being afflicted with double damage regarding their property, as stated in the law *Illicitae*, Digest, *De petitione hereditatis*, and in Justinian’s Institutes, *Etiam*, § *Penultimus*. And because a general or indefinite compromise has regard to the judgment, and there was delay in this matter, there should be no doubt that the compromise is drawn to this effect, as stated in the Code, *De transactionibus*, law *Si de certa*, which benefits Jacob, because it is in the interest of the receiver, as stated in the Digest, *De pactis*, law *Fideiussoris*, and *Quod dictum*. But if we say that the receiver was not added by Jacob, but merely indicated as the heir: such indication does not bind, as noted in the Digest, *De infaustis obligationibus*, *Ob haec verba scripta*. It speaks of Jacob’s will; these words do not induce a mandate, but a promise, as noted in the Digest, *Solutione matrimonii*, law *Post dotem*. And Jacob’s will was not the cause of the payment, but error in the person of the heir, because the error of the deceased took the occasion, and therefore it is inequitable that Jacob, in whom no fault is found, should be bound, as stated in the Digest, *De condictione indebiti*, law 3, § *Finis*. And this opinion has in itself the truth of law and equity. Etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If a vassal donates a feudal estate to his uncle and nephew, who otherwise would have succeeded as agnates, with the uncle himself consenting and accepting for himself and the nephew, whether, upon the death of the donee, the said nephew can be excluded on account of the atrocious injuries inflicted upon the aforementioned uncle. And nu. 3.
2. In an ancient fief, the prior agnate succeeds.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. It is proposed that the noble man, Lord Manfredinus Conventuranis of Castello, citizen of Asti, son of the late Lord, otherwise known as Conventuanis of Castello, and lord of the castle and village of Agnati, and of Castello Nuovo, and so forth, in every way and form in which he could best do so, gave, donated, delivered, and as if he had given, donated, and delivered, and as if it were so, confessed by himself and his heirs and successors in perpetuity to the said Lord Gabriel, the nearest agnate and co-heir in the said fiefs, present there, stipulating and receiving in his own name, and for himself and his heirs in perpetuity for one half; and to the same Lord Gabriel, as a joint person, and to Ser Jacopo, public notary, present there, stipulating and receiving on behalf of and in the name of Bartholomew Conventuanis of Castello, nephew of the said Lord Gabriel, who, as I said, was also a co-heir and nearest agnate in the said fiefs; and for the said Bartholomew and his heirs in perpetuity for the other half, certain castles and feudal places, of which mention is made in the public instrument, the words of which are here expressly set forth. Finally, it happened that the said nephew inflicted grave injuries upon the said uncle, who had made the stipulation for him. Therefore, the grantor having died, it is doubted,
† whether anything should pertain to the said nephew from the said fiefs. And it should be known that

† In an ancient fief, the nearest agnate succeeds, as stated in the tenth column on the degrees of succession in a fief, §. His vero. Moreover, the aforementioned uncle, if he had not given his consent to the said donation, would undoubtedly be preferred to his said nephew, as in c. 1 on the alienation of a paternal fief. This chapter was most prudently cited by the excellent and learned Lord Antonio de Alba. But the entire doubt rests on this point: when the lord uncle consented, whereby he is deemed to have lost his right by contravening the rule; it appears, as in c. 1, §. Praeterea si ille, under the heading "By which means fiefs are lost," that he acted through error, as in C. de iure et facti ignorantia, l. Cum falsa, and in D. de constituto peculio, l. Fin. This certainly seems sufficiently derivable from the instrument, in which it appears to have been provided that the said nephew was equally related to the said uncle, words which contain an express error of law. As for what is said concerning the consent of the lord, it must be known that alienation may be made to agnates without the consent of the lord. Hence, Lord Jacobus de Ardizone in his Summa places such a rubric: "Alienation may be made to agnates without the consent of the lord," because then it is not called alienation, as in Auth. de litigiosis, §. 1, and in the tenth column, per quos fiat investitura, c. 1, §. Sed et res, where this is fully noted by the commentators; and cf. C. de fideicommissis, l. Voluntas; D. de privilegiis creditorum, l. 1; D. de contrahenda emptione, Qui officii, with many similar authorities. And this is the common opinion of the doctors, and the true one.

But one doubt remains here, whether the said consent can be revoked on account of ingratitude. For he who consented loses his rights as if by donation. And therefore it might perhaps be defended in law that the said consent ought to be revoked. However, there is an argument to the contrary: D. de regulis iuris, l. aliud est vendere; and D. de manumissionibus vindicatis, l. si pater, §. si; and D. quibus modis pignus vel hypotheca solvatur, l. sicut, §. venditionis; and what is noted in C. de donationibus causa mortis, l. nec fratris. The question turns on this: if I consent to a stranger that he may donate my thing or my right, whether I am truly, or speaking by interpretation, a donor, or similar to a donor, so that on account of ingratitude I may recover my thing. Although this statute seems equitable and reasonable, for the present I suspend judgment. And thus it is concluded that the case in question would have no doubt if consent had not intervened, or if error had intervened; because the uncle is altogether preferred. Hence this question rests not only on law, but on fact. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. He who has suffered a mission in the hypothesis on account of mere contumacy may come within a year: and, having furnished caution, recover possession.
2. Litis contestatio is not necessary, where the judge proceeds ex officio as a mercenary judge.
3. A praetorian pledge and a conventional pledge may concur in the same thing.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† One who has suffered a mission in a hypothecary action on account of mere contumacy may come within a year, and upon offering security recover possession, and undergo the conventional contests, C. de praesc. 30. an. l. si quis emptionis. §. sed si quis. Which text we must weigh, when it says to undergo the conventional contests. For after proofs have been clearly made, it is not to know, but to have known. And then he ought not to depart from possession, unless he be paid, ff. ut in pos. leg. l. si de possessione. §. 1. Nor does it avail if it be said that the proofs were received in a non-concluded litigation, because by the office of the judge and incidentally it was sought that the detention be relaxed. Hence, by contrary office, it may be sought that it be confirmed, C. de Carb. edic. l. 1.

And because the action proceeds on the basis of a mercenary office, a litis contestatio is not necessary, as is stated in the rubric of the Digest, De interdictis et actionibus; this is the opinion of Speculum in the title De contumacia, § Sequitur, verso; and of Bartolus in l. 3, ff. De acquirenda possessione. However, the contrary argument is made, because according to this view it would not be necessary for a hypothecary action to be definitive, which is false, as is shown in the Digest, De evictionibus, l. Si venditor, in principio. And therefore our case rests on a more secure foundation, because the person sent could enter into possession by his own authority, without judgment and without a libel, because it is an executive action based on a liquid and true real right, Codex, De pignoribus, l. Tertia; Codex, De pignoris actione, Qui ratione; Codex, De iure emphyteutico, l. Secunda. And therefore he ought not to be expelled from juridical possession, because to him who is given an action, retention is all the more strongly granted, Digest, De superficiebus, l. 1, § Quod ait.

† Since in the same matter a praetorian pledge and a conventional pledge may concur, as in D. de annuis legibus, l. Fundus; although the praetorian pledge is removed, the conventional pledge remains, D. de seruis urbanis et praedialibus, l. Si domus. For these remedies are not extinguished by election, since one comes to the aid of the other, as in X. ut lite non contestata, c. Quoniam frequenter, §. Finis. And this is because the pledge is liquid; otherwise it would be different if it were not liquid, as in the said §. Si quis. But the giving of something in satisfaction does not obstruct, which, according to what is proposed, was not executed, nor can it be executed: partly because the debt arises from the cause of dowry, D. de solutionibus, l. Qui res, in principio; partly because of the reservation, as noted in l. Libera quidem Theodora and l. Si quis aliam, ad hoc. D. de actione empti, l. Servus quem, §. Finis; D. de exceptione doli, l. Ultima, §. Ex quadrante. The law Iulia, §. Offerri, does not obstruct, because that is true unless a pact is opposed regarding the return of the price upon eviction, eodem titulo, l. Emptorem, §. Idem. And if it is said that the thing has not been evicted, so that it ought to be evicted by sentence, I answer that it is more than evicted, because it cannot be delivered with effect under these circumstances. Or at least it is a similar case. And it applies to D. de periculo et commodo rei venditae, l. Habes, §. Finis. Hence, against the exception of compensation, there is a replication of fraud, D. de pactis, l. Si debitore. Otherwise, it is §. Legis si cum te. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the profits of the dowry are to be shared.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. It is alleged in the facts that Master William of Dulis of Ponte Curono entered into a partnership of all goods with Blasius Dublio, his brother by blood. This Blasius had several sons. And upon the death of the other sons, except for Master William, he observed the aforementioned partnership with the aforementioned Master William, his uncle, concerning all profits. And he continued it until they came to dissolution, which was some time ago. And it is alleged that during the said partnership, the said Master William communicated all his profits arising from his craft, from whatever source, to the said Master William, his nephew. Furthermore, it is alleged that the said Master William had a certain wife, by whose death, during the said partnership, he profited, according to the form of the statute or custom, the dowry of his said wife. Now the question arises: whether the said profit from the dowry ought the said Master William, the nephew, to communicate to the said Master William, his uncle, or not.

† And it seems that the answer is no, because the gain of the dowry ought to be where the burdens of marriage were. For this gain is personal, just as the dowry itself is, D. 10.2.1 (*Si maritus*); D. 16.3.1 (*Si id, quod ego*). Moreover, because when a partnership is contracted simply, gains which do not arise from the contract, but from the disposition of the law, ought not to be shared, as in D. 17.2.1 (*Cohire societatem*) and D. 17.2.2 (*Nec adiecit*). To the contrary is the truth itself, because it is a case of the law, D. 17.2.1 (*Actione*), § *Si unus*, together with the following law, where it is expressly stated that among partners of all goods, the gains of the dowry ought to be shared. To the same effect is D. 17.2.3 (*Cum duobus*), § *Si inter fratres voluntarium*. And this is clear from the reason, because when there is a partnership of all goods and gains, and a general and most comprehensive partnership containing and comprehending everything, since the contracting parties do not distinguish, but act as universal partners, and thus treat and call themselves: nor ought we to distinguish or restrict, as in D. 40.1.1 (*Cum si*). And here there is no room for doubt: because where there is a case of the law, there is no doubt, C. 9.13.1 (*Ancillae*); D. 17.2.1 (*Quod si eo tempore*). Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the differing declarations of arbitrators in an award are valid.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Consider that the second arbitrator, who condemned the debtor to ten [units], condemned him to a lesser quantity but for a longer period: namely, by the feast of Saint Martin, which falls in the current year. Hence, we cannot say that he was condemned to ten, unless with this addition, which entails a greater obligation in terms of time. And in this regard, concerning the longer period, this second arbitrator does not agree with the first, who stated [the deadline] as the 20th day of the month of March. And thus, regarding the longer time, albeit the lesser quantity. Therefore, since they are contrary to each other, it is impossible for the award to be valid, as it is perplexing that they do not agree on the nearer time, yet agree on the greater prejudice to the debtor, which is impossible, as noted by the gloss in the cited chapter 1, *De arbitris*, Book 6. Nor can the time be separated from the sum, because a quality cannot be separated from its subject. And since the day is a part of the sum stipulated, as in law 1, § *Edicto*, D. *De edendo*, therefore I do not see that the clamor of these [arbitrators] is justified, because the said award does not entirely harmonize. And each one ought to remove the matter of dispute, not introduce it; therefore, I do not see harmony. But if two were found to agree, the sentence of the two would be valid. And according to this, the sentence of the one awarding ten would be valid, because it is contained under the larger sum, and [the feast of] Saint Martin, because it is contained under the year and under eight months. According to the gloss of the said first chapter, where it says: if all disagree, the lesser [award] prevails. But harmony, in my judgment, is not found, as I have said. And although it is true that he who grants a delay of a year grants a delay of ten days, insofar as ten days are contained in a year; nevertheless, it is not true to say that [he grants] ten days, because if he condemned to more than he intended. Hence, it would be openly contrary to his intent and contrary to the nature of the delay. Because that gloss considered the lesser quantity of time as contained under the greater, but it did not consider that they are opposed in reason: because that which is less in time is a greater burden, as in the Institutes, *De actionibus*, § *Plus*. Indeed, from the intention [of the law], he who is condemned to less is condemned to more. According to the note in the Code, *De legibus*, *Cum quaestio*. One cannot extend "not more" to "more." From which I conclude that the award of the said arbitrators does not hold. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Each person is understood to be a principal debtor in his own share, when several are bound by a loan as joint debtors pro rata.
2. He is said to have contracted a loan in whose name it was contracted, with his ratification or command.
3. Not only the principal debtor, but also the surety is said to be bound in his own name, by his own obligation.
4. A privilege of forum granted by reason of the person does not apply except to him who is expressly named in the privilege. Cf. Codex, De officiis, l. Quotiens. I, Baldus.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The case is as follows. The nobleman Peter, formerly of the Giberti family of Correggio, while adhering to the commune of Bologna, received a loan of one thousand florins in his own name, made by the nobleman James, formerly of the Raynaldi family of the Blancs, and promised ratification with the appropriate solemnities. It happens that Galasso, brother of the said Peter, ratified it for his part, and promised that certain brothers would ratify it, and under subpoena. James of the Blancs wishes to sue the said Galasso, who pleads that he cannot be sued in the territory of the lord by virtue of a certain chapter made between the most illustrious lord, the Count of Virtues, and himself, Galasso, and his brothers, a copy of which is described immediately below. Now the question is, what is the law? Also, that the aforementioned brothers cannot be bound nor compelled to the payment of any debts contracted by the late respectable knight, their father, Lord Giberto, nor by the said Peter, their brother.

It must be premised for the sake of clarity that when several persons are bound by a loan, each is understood to be the principal debtor as to his own share, as noted in the Digest, *ad Velleianum*, *l. vir uxori*, § *si*. And this is proven in the Digest, *de duobus rebus*, *l. reos*, § *cum in tabulis*, and in the Code, *si certum petatur*, *l. si non singuli*.

Secondly, it must be premised that he is said to have contracted a loan (mutuum) in whose name it was contracted, with him ratifying or ordering it, as stated in the Digest, title "If certain performance is demanded," law "The condition of certainty," section "If coins."

Thirdly, it must be premised that not only the principal defendant, but also the surety is said to be bound in his own name by his own obligation, although the origin of the surety’s obligation depends on the agreement with the principal, as noted in the Digest, *De his qui non in fideiussione*, law *Furti*, section *Si quis alieno*.

Fourthly, it must be premised that the privilege of forum granted by reason of the person does not apply, except to him who is expressly named in the privilege, as is read and noted in l. 1, ff. si quis in ius vocatus non ierit. From these premises follows a manifestly negative conclusion, namely, that the said Galassus does not have the privilege of declining the forum, especially because he is sued as a principal on his own promise. Moreover, by ratification he makes the transaction his own, because it was conducted in his name, as in ff. de negotiis gestis, l. si pupilli, §. item quaeritur. And the aforementioned are proven by those things which are fully noted by Cy. in C. de praescriptionibus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the contract of alienation made by a spendthrift is valid by oath.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

It is proposed that an adult spendthrift had a curator as an adult, with the authority of whom, without any inventory being made, he alienated and dissipated many goods, having taken an oath. The question is asked: what is the law? And it seems that the oath should be observed, as in the Authentica sacra publica in the Corpus, from which it is derived. To the contrary, it seems that those contracting with such a spendthrift cannot be excused from fraud, at least presumed fraud, as in D. de usu et usufructu legato, l. si quis cum sciret; and D. de re iudicata, l. qui cum alio. And an oath extorted by fraud is not valid, as in the aforementioned Authentica sacramenta. Moreover, since he was notoriously a spendthrift, the law immediately interdicted him from his goods, at least as regards alienations to be made, as noted in D. de testamento, l. is cui non. For those who contract with such a person do not seem to contract in good faith. And although the oath represents him ultimately to be of full age, it does not represent him as not being a spendthrift; indeed, it certainly does not represent him as of full age, because he suffers from exile of the mind and is similar to a madman, as in D. de tutela et cura, da. ab his, l. si is qui, §. diuus. To the contrary, it is noted in D. de verbis oblig., l. is cui bonis, where the glossa says that a spendthrift can contract, unless interdiction from his goods has been pronounced against him by a judge. The same is noted in l. 1, D. de cura furiosi. You say that the first opinion is true, because relief is granted to the spendthrift regarding alienations, even before interdiction, as expressly noted in D. de minoribus, l. patri pro filio, near the beginning, joined with the glossa and the text, quam nemo allegat. And it is very noteworthy that, as an abundance of caution, it would be proper to seek absolution from the oath before the bishop, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether one may waive a statute prohibiting the making of a compromise before foreign judges or a magistrate, and before whom such waiver may be made; and where a distinction is drawn.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Suppose that a statute prohibits compromising with a foreigner, or prohibits compromising with a magistrate; can one renounce this statute? And it seems that one can, because the reason for the statute appears to have been in favor of those compromising. For it is not shameful or absurd to compromise with such persons as amicable arbitrators, D. de usufructu, l. aequissimum; C. de praebendis, c. nisi essent; C. de maiore et obediencia, c. humilis; C. de arbitris, c. sed si in servum, § si quis iudex, in the gloss; C. de episcopis et clericis audiendis, si quis ex consensu; and l. episcopale. Moreover, by this renunciation, the matter is returned to the common law. Hence, it does not seem that the condition of those compromising is made worse, but rather restored to its proper form, D. de pactis, si unus, § pactus, ver. quod in specie dotis. And although at first glance this appears to be a prohibition, it is improperly called a prohibition: because that which is prohibited is not of the nature of things prohibited, arg. eorum quae notantur, D. de verbis oblig., l. stipulatio ista, § alteri. Moreover, a woman is prohibited from intervening as a surety, yet she can renounce, D. ad Velleianam, l. si, § si. Moreover, this prohibition does not concern any public right, because compromises are not of public right; therefore, one can renounce such laws, as is fully noted in Auth. ut sine prohibitione matres debitrices creditrices, § quia vero ad hoc; D. de pactis, l. pactum inter; and l. pacisci, D. eo, si quis in conscribendo. For the proper rule of law permits renunciation of one’s own favors, and especially if there were this clause, that they renounced the statute and promised not to use it. For if they used it, they would incur a penalty, D. de transactionibus, l. pacto convento; and l. qui fidem. To the same effect is what is noted in D. de transactionibus, l. de his controversiis. Finally, for this side is the form given by the Speculator in the title de arbitris, § ut autem, in the word sive ex persona arbitri, where he holds this expressly.

On the contrary, the truth seems to be otherwise, for the gloss in the said l. pacisci gives this doctrine, that sometimes one commands or prohibits, and to such a right one cannot renounce. But here the statute prohibits; therefore, one cannot renounce. For such a statute induces a necessity contrary to the will, and resisting consent; and renunciation cannot do more than consent could, as is noted in c. 1, de regulis iuris, lib. 6. Moreover, another rule is that one cannot renounce those things which are introduced for the substance of some act, D. de legibus, l. nemo potest. But that the arbitrator be a citizen and not a foreigner; likewise that he be another person and not a magistrate, is introduced for the substance of the compromise; therefore, one cannot renounce. Moreover, it seems that what is introduced for the removal of dangers to subjects cannot be renounced. And this statute is of this kind, C. si quacunque praedicta potestate, l. 1; ne fiant concussiones per magistratus, et ne fiant baratariae per forenses; C. de episcopis et clericis, l. si qua per calumniam; in Auth. de testibus, § si vero ignoti. Moreover, and without reason, the sole authority of the law suffices to prohibit, D. qui et a quibus, l. prospexit; and it makes D. de postulando, l. quos prohibet, joined with l. 1, § pueritiam, eo. tit.; and what is noted to the same effect, D. de haereditate instituenda, l. si non lex eliescentia; C. ne fideiussores dentur, l. 1 and 2, and there noted; C. ad Velleianam, Auth. si qua mulier. Moreover, this statute is not introduced for singular favor, but is declaratory of a negative rule, which cannot be evaded; especially because general rules do not concern some particularity, D. de haereditate instituenda, l. his verbis, § si. It makes what is noted by Bartolus, de donationibus, l. Modestinus. Consider and know that it is not introduced in favor of those compromising. Consider and suppose the case that it is expedient and useful for both compromising parties to compromise with themselves as a foreigner or magistrate; it would follow that then the compromise would be valid without renunciation, C. de procuratoribus, l. non eo minus; D. de solutionibus, l. cum Stichus. Which is false, D. de ritu nuptiarum, l. a divo. For these prohibited persons are incapable of such compromises; hence they cannot be made capable even by the will of the litigants, although to the contrary is what is noted by Innocentius, de rescriptis, sciscitatus. But there is another case. Moreover, object what is noted in the said l. de his, as there by the doctors; and it makes D. ad Macedonianam, tam et si; and C. non licere habita, Metrodoro, co. l. 1; and by Bartolus in l. cum lex, D. de fideiussoribus.

† And distinguish: either the law is merely favorable, or merely odious, or mixed by reason of favor and odium. In the first case, one may renounce it by a greater right; in the second case, one may not. Say, as I said in the aforementioned law *de his*. Or, the law does not consider favor or odium, but gives a certain and precise form in human acts, and the renunciation is not valid, because it is contrary to the law established. See *de legibus*, law *nemo potest*; *de legibus* 1, law *codicil.*, § *ulti*; *ff. de administratione tutorum*, law *quidam decedens*; *ff. de tutelis*, law *tutela*; *ff. de negotiis gestis*, law *qui aliena*, § *quamquam*, adapting and applying these laws and similar ones, as is fitting. Certain statutes are enacted for the sake of preserving the rigor of the law, and similarly one cannot renounce these, as noted in *C. de iudicibus*, law *properandum*, in the principle. And what Spezzano says is understood when the person of the arbitrator is not so by the law itself, but can be infringed by an exception, for example because he is an enemy or under 20 years of age. Therefore, it is otherwise if it were precisely prohibited to be an arbitrator, as in *ff. de verbis significatis*, law *illa verba*, in the version *non cadunt*, according to Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. In how many ways a simulated contract is said to exist.
2. If the matter of the simulation of a contract was adjudicated before a secular judge, and it was pronounced that the contract was true and not simulated, whether it may be objected in execution that the contract was made in fraud of usury; and whether on this pretext an ecclesiastical authority may prohibit the execution of the sentence.
3. Whether an oath prevents one from alleging a simulated contract.
4. Add the following opinion.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. I would briefly conclude my argument, were it not that the matter deserves a more extensive introduction: for it is a common issue, and I therefore set forth certain points regarding a simple contract, and certain others regarding a sworn contract.

I say that sometimes a contract is simulated, because both contracting parties intend it to be simulated. Sometimes it is true, because both parties here act with the intention that it be a true contract. And here a further distinction is made. For sometimes it is true, yet unjust due to enormous lesion occurring to the ignorant party. Concerning this, the Code speaks in the title *De rescindenda venditione*, law 2. Sometimes [it is void] on account of fraud and the disapproval of law, for example, because it is done in fraud of usury. For the Pope says that what is done in fraud of usury I will not hold valid. This is gathered throughout his treatise, and in the Extravagant *De iureiurando*, chapter *Ad nostram*. Sometimes it is doubtful whether it is in fraud of usury. And then either we speak with regard to jurisdiction, and concerning this doubt the ecclesiastical judge has cognizance, as noted in Question 11, Cause 1, in the Summa; *De foro competenti*, chapter *Licet*; *De iudiciis*, chapter *Dispendiosam*, in the Clementines. And this is by reason of the crime, which is ecclesiastical and not civil: since the laws permit, Code *De usuris*, law *Eos*, nevertheless civil law cannot permit. And as noted by Jacobus Butrigarius in law *Cunctos populos*: if the statute of the law cannot [permit], therefore neither can the municipal judge, namely the secular one, by argument from Digest *De aedilicio edicto*, law *Ad testationem*. And although the secular judge can order usury to be restored, Question 14, Cause 3, chapter *Quicunque*, nevertheless he cannot absolve from the obligation to restore.

† However, it must be considered here that express matters vitiate, but tacit ones perhaps not so. And therefore, if the matter was acted upon before a secular judge regarding simulation, without mention being made of usury, and the judge declares by sentence that the contract was true and not simulated, this sentence is valid by virtue of jurisdiction. Also by virtue of form; for who would deny that a secular judge is a judge concerning the cognition of truth and simple simulation? D. de aqua pluv. arc., l. emptor; D. de reg. iur., l. imaginaria. And if after this sentence the debtor raises the defense of simulation, it is reviewed that what has been decided remains so, even if he adds a new quality, namely that it was in fraud of usury; nevertheless, because that quality cannot be examined separately from the principal simulation which stands in the way, the exception seems to be refuted, because judgment has been rendered on the principal matter, and consequently on the incidental matter, as in l. 1, C. de ord. iud.; D. de iureiur., duobus, §. colonus. It suffices that it has been definitively judged once, C. sen. rescin., non posse, l. 1; C. quando prouo., non est necesse, l. 1; D. nautae, caupo, l. licet, §. fin. Otherwise there would be no end to lawsuits, contrary to l. terminato and D. de re iud., l. post rem. And let the debtor impute it to himself, because from the beginning he did not assert such a quality as he now raises, D. de noxa, l. in delic., §. si detracta; and in l. edita, C. de eden., with its subject matter. And thus, if this is true, it also follows that the ecclesiastical judge cannot enjoin the secular judge not to execute the sentence, because in this matter the secular jurisdiction is not subordinate to the ecclesiastical jurisdiction. Also, because just as it is presumed in favor of the sentence, as in D. de euic., l. Herenius; de renun., in presentia, so consequently calumny is presumed in him who comes against the sentence; therefore, execution should not be enjoined, C. de falsis, l. satis aperte. Also, this is a mere executor in rem itself, who does not have rescissory power. D. de re iud., de certo; de appel., nouit; D. de iud., si praetor; C. de or., l. fin. To this effect is what is noted by Innocentius, de appel., ex ratione. Also, because contradiction requires a higher inquiry, D. de iureiur., l. nam et postea, in princ.; D. ad exhib., l. 3, §. ibidem; D. ad Treb., ille a quo, §. si de testamento; de in inte. resti., suscitata; C. de preci. impe. offer., auth. quae supplicatio; D. vt in pos. leg., is a quo; de re iud., in cle., c. in ratione sui. Also, the last chapter of de execu., lib. 6, needs a grain of salt. For if, on account of the danger to souls, bishops could cognize every unjust sentence, therefore an appeal could be made to them from any unjust sentence of laymen, as to superiors. Which is entirely false. Hence, that chapter concerning the danger to souls must be understood as referring to that by which secular jurisdiction is enumerated, not to any other. D. fami. ercis., cum putarem; D. de pecu., l. eo tempore; D. mandati, l. si fideicom., §. in omnibus. And secular jurisdiction could be sold and given to the poor. Lord Federicus of Siena advised that if a cleric testified before a lay judge and is accused before the bishop of perjury, the bishop cannot enjoin the secular judge not to proceed to sentence on the basis of his statement. Moreover, if I leased to you a house which at first sight was bought, but in truth was pledged, the bishop cannot prohibit me from using it, because it would be a certain spoliation, since the creditor possesses, as noted by Dynus, C. qui ad agendum, even if the personal obligation has been discharged. Quaest. 1. The creditor does not thereby cease to possess by operation of law, because it is possession of fact. Otherwise it would follow that the debtor, without any pledge action, could occupy the possession by his own authority. Which is either entirely false or at least doubtful. And the judge cannot enjoin the possessor except in a definitive judgment, D. de liberali causa, l. libertis, §. fi. And if it is said that the debt has been diminished or absorbed by compensation of fruits, until the compensation is liquidated, the omission is presumed to continue, C. de compen., l. fi. And even if the judge does not wish to admit compensation, it is not done, D. de compen., quod in diem, §. 1. Also, the authority to prohibit the exercise of jurisdiction never belongs to anyone except in cases expressly stated in law, as noted by Archboldus, 11 q. 1, c. de persona. The point concerning jurisdiction is explicit, and I say that the jurisdiction to cognize concerning the repetition of usury pertains to the court of the Archbishop, because it testifies to usury. But nevertheless, he should not prohibit the secular judge from executing the award, especially because I do not find that any rescissory action has been brought against the award.

† The article concerning the oath follows, and I believe that if nothing is opposed against the award, he who swore should not be heard; but if the award states that it was rendered in fraud of usury, he must seek absolution from the oath. On oaths and swearing, c. 1. Moreover, he who does not act in due order is not competent to sue on usury; in recovering, he can act, without doubt. My final conclusion is that on the petition of usury, proceedings should be taken; however, the injunction concerning which inquiry is made cannot be granted. The first point is proved because the foundation of jurisdiction is expressed in the bill, c. Cum sit generale, Extra, on competent forum. The second is proved from what has been said above, and from others, which can be clearly demonstrated. It must not be denied in the preliminary issues regarding the substance of the case to be decided, but reserved for the end. But objections are raised against the foregoing. For we see that instruments which, by the form of statutes, have the force of a sentence, are not committed to execution if the bishop inhibits, when they are said to have been made in fraud of usury. But I answer: it is one thing to be known as having been definitively rendered, another to be subject to being known. Furthermore, that precept is of voluntary jurisdiction. Cynus, in l. 1, on confessions. Considering the acts and all things to be considered, I adhere to what I said in that verse, final conclusion, namely, that the archbishop can take cognizance of usury. But whether the arbitral sentence be committed to execution, he cannot inhibit in these preliminary stages of the litigation, considering what is to be considered. And weighing the bill, as l. Ut fundus, and l. Fin., on fideicommissa, book one, it must not be omitted that in the letters it is asserted that the true price is 5 florins. Therefore, a true sale was contracted, although in fraud of usury, l. Fin., C., on curators of estates; l. 2, C., on pacts between buyer and seller. And thus the award was true. For a contract can be true but not just, because it is in fraud, C., on mandate, per diversas; and l. Ab Anastasio. It supports what Note Bartolus, ff., on oaths, l. In libello. Nevertheless, there was simulation and fraud intended, and on these points I rest.

In the Name of Christ, Amen. In the case of these nobles, there are two opinions of the doctors and advocates. One is precisely affirmative, that the bishop has cognizance, and may and ought to prohibit [the execution], notwithstanding the confessions and the arbitral sentence; and the substantial reason of those holding this view is that, concerning the crime of usury, and consequently concerning the truth of all things and acts, cognizance belongs to the ecclesiastical forum, and the truth of things is not vitiated by errors in the acts, nor is prejudice caused to a greater judge by a lesser one, nor to a competent judge by an incompetent one. But another opinion is precisely contrary to this, because simulation, simply put, pertains between laymen to the lay forum. And upon this a sentence was passed, and it passed into *res iudicata*. And a sentence against a sentence is not valid, nor even ought execution to be impeded on account of certain allegations which were pertinent before the sentence, and especially if they are not clear. A third opinion may be adduced, that the bishop could cognize, but not prohibit, because the authority of the sentence does not suffer these suspensive delays. However, if it finally appears that the execution was wrongly made, it will be retracted. Therefore, one ought not to obey the bishop prohibiting, because he prohibits against the law. A fourth opinion could be that execution ought to be made, however, with caution provided for restitution, if the usurious malice appears.

For the first opinion it holds, for if the bishop can cognize, therefore it necessarily follows that he can prohibit, lest his jurisdiction be violated, since he is not only a superior judge, but the sole one in this ecclesiastical crime, as is noted in Summa, *De foro competenti*, c. *Licet*; *De iudicibus*, *Dispendiosam*, in the Clementines. Therefore, that which was done in the secular court does not hold, as if in a forbidden examination, C. *De iurisdict. omn. iudic.*, l. *In criminali*. Moreover, jurisdiction is never said to be preempted by a forbidden tribunal, because the citation is valid, C. *Ne de statu defuncti*, l. *Si pater*. No one therefore declines the examination of the ordinary seat, C. *De iurisdict. omn. iudic.*, l. *Nemo*. But the ordinary seat is the evangelical one. And thus it is observed everywhere, against the execution of instruments having the force of confession and sentence by the authority of some statute; because this is the nature of a usurious cause: and while it is pending before the bishop, the secular judge ought not to intermeddle, as is fully noted in Speculum, *De usuris*, in the principle; and Extra, *Eo quia in omnibus*; and *De iureiurando*, *Debitores*, *Cum si*.

For the second opinion it holds, that since a sentence has been passed in contradictory examination, it is held for truth, and it engenders execution of the *res iudicata*; nor would a sentence directly passed against such a sentence be valid, I. 1, C. *Sententiam rescindi non posse*; I. 1, C. *Quando provocatione non est necessarium*. For the secular judge, according to the quality of the controversy, was the competent judge, as is noted by Bartolus in l. *Titia*, 2. And it is confirmed by that which is read and noted in c. 1, § *Sic*, *De controversia investiturae*; and in c. *Si fuerit*, § *Pen.*, and *Quae poena teneatur inter dominum et vassallum de investitura feudorum*; *Si inter*, *De controversia feudi* apud partes terminata, capitulo *Ex eo*, *An apud iudicem vel dominum*.

For the third opinion it holds, C. *De ordine cognitionis*, l. *Fin.*; ff. *De divortio*, § *Si post*; C. *De falsis*, l. 2, with similar cases. Expressly, Innocentius *De officio delegati*, *Cum in iure*; Bartolus in § *Si ex actione*. To the same effect, *De iudicibus*, l. *Si praetor*, in the principle; and from the reason, *Ecce*.

For the fourth opinion it holds, *De in integrum restitutione*, c. *Talis*; C. *De precibus imperatoris offerendis*, Auth. *Quae supplicatio*; simul l. *Pen.*, ff. *De rei venditione*, l. *Is a quo*. Nor is it good [to rely on] instruments concerning which there has been no final cognizance, as is read and noted, C. *De transactionibus*, l. *Si diversa*; ff. *De iureiurando*, l. 2. Also, a denial after sentence is not noted, ff. *De transactionibus*, *Post rem*. And from this it is clear that the sentence passed into *res iudicata*. And it holds that which is noted, C. *De inofficioso testamento*, *Qui de inofficioso*; ff. *Ad exhibenda*, l. *Iulianus*, § *Ibidem*; *Quibusdam tamen*, ff. *De iureiurando*, l. *Si duo patroni*, vers. *Nec pati*; and l. *Duobus*, § *Si quis iuraverit*; and § *Coloni*, *Quae iuramenta*, vers. *Contra finem*. For it does not seem to be a doubt at first sight, namely, because it has the figure of being from the state of dispute, and its form, and thus it does not obstruct, ff. *De communi debitorum*, l. *Eleganter*, § 1, *Si, vel in sententia valet*. For even if perhaps the effect of the said sentence could be retracted on account of the peril of souls, which has in itself a permanent cause, from the arguments of those which the doctors note, ff. *De iureiurando*, l. *Eum qui*, § *In popularibus*; although therefore it contradicts, and that law standing in the way, because preceding the definitive judgment, the judge who pronounced cannot be preempted, ff. *De iurisdict. omn. iudic.*, l. *Pen.*; nevertheless this recourse, which is made to the bishop, does not suspend the pronouncement, because it is not a species of appeal, but is as it were a certain querulous supplication. On account of the doubt, however, caution is provided, arguing from the said Auth. *Quae supplicatio*. And this part pleases me. And thus perhaps both the episcopal and the lay are preserved in their justice, in c. *Ultimo*, *De exceptionibus*, lib. 6. For that which we are certain of regarding the peril of souls, but which is in doubt, is to be presumed for the matter solemnly judged. It is established that these arbitrators, having jurisdiction by statute, are judges and definers. The laws are common. And Bartolus places it in l. *Si dictum*, § *Si promiserit*. And all the more is it presumed for their sentence, inasmuch as they were more friendly and all concordant, C. *De transactionibus*; and noted, C. *De his quibus ut indiciis*, l. *Poll.*. The oath, however, which was given in the compromise, because it has a tacit condition, if it was arbitrated equally, depends on the end of the controversy. Arguing from C. *De iudicibus*, l. *Rem novam*, § *Fin.*; ff. *De excusationibus tutorum*, l. *Dixi*; l. 1, *De ordine cognitionis*; Extra, *De restitutione in integrum*, c. 2, § *Fin.*. Let the advocates see what I say, and if it pleases them, well and good; if it does not please them, let them subscribe, omitting their circumlocutions, their reasons, and the libel to be weighed. And therefore I wish to see and read it with the advocates. And because I do not tell you the law which you do not propose to me, you who speak in the manner of a stipulation, which cannot be made unless both speak, "Ask," he says, "and you shall receive." Therefore, if you do not ask, you who have a voice, you shall not receive, unless the requests were connected, as in l. *Ut fundus*, ff. *De fideicommissis*, l. *Prima*, with similar cases.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. In a universal fideicommissum, those goods do not pass which were acquired from a source other than the testator’s estate.
2. Particular legacies are deducted from the universal fideicommissum.
3. The universal fideicommissary deducts the Falcidian portion.
4. Fruits collected by the son are not imputed to the legitime.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Although many points have been raised, in order to respond to all the points in brief words, it must be said,

† That in a fideicommissary substitution, property which was acquired from a source other than the testator’s estate is not included, as stated in the Digest, *De vulgari substitutione*, law *Cohaeredi*, section *Cum filiae*, at the words *nec fideicommissario*. And therefore, the property of the late Galeotto does not fall within the substitution made by Guidone; rather, it is said that it must first be deducted by the Lady Frances, heir of John and Bari, who were the heirs of the said Guidone.

Secondly, it must be known that from a universal fideicommissary substitution, particular legacies are derived, which are owed to the heir of the heir from whom restitution is sought. Nor can the universal fideicommissary deduct the Falcidian share, as stated in C. ad Trebellianam, l. si; and ff. eodem, l. filiam fratribus; and l. 1, C. communia de legatis. And therefore, the said Francesca can deduct all her legacies.

Thirdly, it must be known that regarding the universal fideicommissum, insofar as it concerns Nicolaus and Lucas, the aforementioned Francesca, acting on behalf of Ioannes and Bari, deducts both the legitime and the Trebellian portion. But insofar as it concerns the monastery, she deducts only the legitime, as stated in the Digest, *extra de testamentis*, chapter *Ray.*, and chapter *Raynal.*, and in the Code, *ad legem Falcidiam*, the constitution *Similiter*, and in the Code, *de episcopis et clericis*, the law *Si qui ad declinandam*. And thus, to the said Ser Nicolaus and Lucas are deducted two fourths, according to some, after an inventory has been made; according to others, even if no inventory has been made, as noted in the Digest, *ad Trebellianam*, the law *Detrahitur*. To the poor, however, or to pious places, only the legitime is deducted, that is, one-third of their portion, or of what is left to them. Some say that the Trebellian portion is also deducted from churches, with the first opinion not being the correct one.

Fourthly, it must be known that in the legitime, fruits received by the son are not imputed, as stated in C. de inofficiosa testatione, l. Scimus, §. Repletionem. However, in the Trebellian action, fruits received by the son himself or by the sons are imputed; for this is a special rule applicable to sons, i.e., children of the first degree, as stated in C. ad Trebellianum, l. Iubemus. But if they have died and their heirs have received the fruits, a distinction is made. For if they were in delay, they must restore the fruits, or their value, or impute them to themselves; but if the fideicommissary was in delay in not claiming, the rule is different, as stated in ff. ad Trebellianum, l. Mulier, §. Si haeres. And therefore, the aforementioned opinion of Franciscus, which in this case is not considered to arise from the right of the daughter, because it comes from the person of the brothers, would have imputed the fruits to themselves in the Trebellian action if they had been in delay. But if they had received them before Nicholas and Lucas had accepted the fideicommissum and demanded restitution to be made to them, or even before they had formed the intention to accept, the aforementioned imputation of fruits would not take place, because although it is true that regular delay is incurred after the delay of the churches, this is true only after the acceptance of the legacy, and not before. Thus, C. in quibus causis in integrum restitutionem non est necessaria, l. In minorum, must be understood. And by this, the question asked about fruits received from the things to be restored is answered, not about Trebellian fruits, because those are never imputed, as stated in ff. de inofficiosa testatione, l. Si papa, §. Si conditioni. Fifthly, it must be known that the heir asked to restore is not bound to be, so to speak, a universal procurator of the fideicommissary, as stated in ff. ad Trebellianum, l. Postulante Sticho, in fine. And therefore, upon his request, a term must be assigned to the universal fideicommissary for deliberating and accepting the fideicommissum, as noted in ff. de legatis 1, l. Cum filio. From which it follows ultimately and conclusively what must be done before the fideicommissum is accepted, and what afterwards. And this is the solution to all the questions asked.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the sale of an annual rent can be called a usurious contract.
2. If a husband purchases an annual rent for himself and his wife during their lifetime, whether upon the husband's death the annual rent is owed to the wife, or only half.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen. Because law arises from fact, I shall set forth the matter itself below as noted. Behold, since the commune and the men of the village of Masio were in need of money to pay certain heavy and burdensome usurious debts by which the commune and the men of the said village were continually oppressed with usuries, for that reason the lords Giorgio Dario and Guglielmo Benito, vicars and lieutenants of the podestà of Masio, having called together, etc., and assembled the council of the commune and of the men of the village of Masio in due manner, with the will, counsel, and consent of the elders and councillors of the said village of Masio, and they themselves acting under the authority and decree of the said lords lieutenants, as well as Manfredo Marito, syndic and procurator of the commune and of the men of Masio, having sufficient mandate to perform the underwritten acts: having sought out ways and means by which they could recover money to pay the aforesaid debts, with certain knowledge in their own names, and in the name and on behalf of the entire universitas of the commune and of the men of the said village of Masio, sold to the lord Matteo Scarampi, there present, purchasing and receiving in his own name and in the name and on behalf of Lady Anesina, wife of the said lord Matteo, and for the life of the said Lady Anesina and of either of them, and for as long as the said lord Matteo and Lady Anesina, or either of them, should live or will live, an annual rent of 140 gold florins, to be paid in each year on the calends of March, as long as the said lord Matteo and the said Lady Anesina, or either of them, shall live: so that by the death of either of them, the said annual rent of 140 gold florins shall not be diminished during the life of the said spouses, or of either of them, but shall be paid in full each year to the said lord Matteo during the life of the said lord Matteo, whether the said Lady Anesina be living or not on the said calends of March. After the life of the said lord Matteo, however, if it should happen that the said Lady Anesina survives, it shall be paid in full on the said calends of March each year to the said Lady Anesina during the life of the said Lady Anesina; for the price, and under the name of the price, of one thousand two hundred gold florins, counted out then and there. Which price was applied to the benefit of the creditors to whom the said commune and men were obligated. All and singular which things the aforesaid persons solemnly promised, and also swore upon the Holy Gospels of God on the soul of the commune and of the men of the entire universitas of the said village of Masio, to hold firm and ratified, to heed, observe, and effectually fulfill all and singular the aforesaid things, and at no time to act against or contravene them for any reason or cause, in law or in fact, etc., just as and according as fully appears concerning the aforesaid matters in a public instrument. Now it happens that the said lord Matteo has died, with the said Lady Anesina surviving, who demands from the commune and the men of Masio that the said annual rent be given and paid to her in full. It is objected that it ought not to be paid, on the ground that the aforesaid contract is usurious, and that they have paid so many annual rents that they exceed the principal, and that they are no longer bound to her; and to the extent that they are bound, they say they are not bound except to the payment of half of the said annual rent for the person of the said Anesina alone, after the death of the said lord Matteo. Wherefore it is asked, what is the law. And for clarity, it is assumed as true in fact that the lord Matteo and Lady Anesina were not usurers, nor accustomed to lend money at usury. In the present question, other things being set aside, two principal inquiries are made: First, whether the said contract is and should be deemed usurious, so that the said commune and men are no longer bound to pay. Second, if the contract is not usurious, whether they are bound to pay the full annual rent to the said Lady Anesina, or rather are not bound to pay except for half on account of the death of the lord Matteo.

† And to the first, it is briefly answered that the contract is not usurious, neither in form nor in intention; for usury is spoken of in a contract of mutuum, whether real or fictitious, as noted in 13. q. 1. et 2. and in c. conquestus, extra de usuris. But the aforesaid contract was a contract of sale, since an annual rent, both in money and in kind, can be bought and sold, as in C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, l. iubemus, and in Auth. de non alienandis rebus ecclesiae, § vult enim. Therefore the said contract ought not to be considered usurious. And that it is not a usurious contract is also proved because we have nothing certain from it, since being born today and dying tomorrow is uncertain; for we all die, and are scattered like water, as in c. non aestimemus, 13. q. 2. everywhere. Likewise, because of uncertainty such a contract cannot be deemed unjust, for which what Justinian says in l. sancimus, circa finem, C. de donationibus, serves as a notable authority; where the question was asked whether, if an annual payment of a certain amount were made by way of donation, an excess would be said to arise in the donation from the quantity of the aforesaid sums to be paid annually, so that insinuation would be required. And it is answered there that if the aforesaid donation is made for the life of the donor or of the donee, multiple donations are understood. For the uncertain outcome of fortune suggested this to us in words, that it is possible for either the donor or the recipient of the said donation to survive for the span of only one year, or for shorter, or even for longer periods. And from this I found that the donation does not exceed [the statutory amount] in total. So, therefore, it is in the matter at hand, that the aforesaid contract is so called since we have nothing certain, Auth. de non alienandis rebus ecclesiae, § ultimo, and in l. si ea pactione, C. de usuris. For by reason of uncertainty something is judged just which otherwise, if it were certain, would be considered unjust, as in the said l. si ea, C. de usuris. Therefore, the aforesaid contract is not to be judged usurious, because the said money was not received as interest, with the capital intact, but as the price of an annual rent. Nor must the subsequent outcome be considered, but rather the beginning or inception of the contract, as is proved in l. soleo, C. de usuris, where that which happens casually is not considered; and that which has in itself the potential for more or less is not said to exceed the proper limit, as there stated. Whence the contract is not considered usurious by reason of uncertainty, since the capital does not remain safe, because the risk also falls upon the buyer, just as profit can casually happen to him. It is otherwise in a mutuum, because the capital sum of money remains safe, as in l. incendium, C. si certum petatur; but in our case, nothing is certain. For which also serves what is noted in l. 1, C. pro socio; and this sort of contract is similar to someone buying an expectation of fortune, that is, a cast of a net, D. de actionibus empti et venditi, l. si iactum, and henceforth the risk falls entirely upon the buyer according to the nature of the contract of purchase and sale, as in l. illud, D. de periculo et commodo rei venditae, and l. necessario, in principio, and C. eodem titulo, l. 1, and Inst. de emptione et venditione, § cum autem, with the like. And for this also serves what Bartolus notably writes in l. cotem, § qui maximos, D. de publicanis. It is concluded, therefore, that the said contract is lawful, since an annual rent, both in money and in kind, can be sold, as in l. iubemus, C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, and in Auth. de non alienandis rebus ecclesiae, § vult enim. For just as something annual can be bequeathed and donated, as in C. de legatis, l. in annalibus, and D. de verborum obligationibus, l. Stichum, § stipulatio, so also it can be sold at a suitable and just price, namely, for what such an expectation could commonly be sold for at the time of the contract. Nor is hope worth as much as the thing itself, since hope is subjected to many fortuitous events, just as the crop in the blade is not worth as much as the harvested grain; to this effect, D. de contrahenda emptione, l. fistulas, § frumentum, and what is read by Bartolus in the said l. cotem, § qui maximos, D. de publicanis. For do not those who purchase tolls and gabelles, which consist in annual rents in counted money, purchase lawfully? And it is certain that they do. Why, therefore, could the commune and the men of Masio not sell an annual rent upon their own goods? It happens daily; what difference does it make whether one pays from the hand of the seller or from the hand of his debtor? Surely none, as in D. de pignoraticia actione, l. solutione, § solutam. Whence, for a certainty, such a contract is not unlawful. For what if the buyer had lived for only one day? Then the commune and men would not return the price; wherefore such a contract is similar to someone buying an expectation, as in the said l. si iactum retis, D. de actionibus empti et venditi. Likewise, if the intention was good from the beginning, we do not look at the outcome, but at the beginning or inception of the contract, as in l. sed an ultro, § fin., D. de negotiis gestis. Likewise, if it is through risk, as in l. si pater, D. de inofficioso testamento. Likewise, the mind is not certain to anyone except God alone, as in extra de usuris, c. in civitate, and what is noted in D. de pactis, l. iuris gentium, § pactorum; and the aforesaid points proceed above all because the buyers themselves were not usurers, nor accustomed to lend at usury; whence the said contract is not presumed usurious, according to the things noted and read in l. cum allegas, C. de usuris, where otherwise the contrary could be said, as in c. illo vos, extra de pignoribus, and noted in c. ad nostram, de emptione et venditione, and c. conquestus, de usuris; for the person must be considered, as in l. cum hi, § sed et personarum, D. de transactionibus, l. si quis ex argentariis, § 1, D. de edendo, and l. qui universorum, D. de pignoraticia actione. And that such a contract is lawful is held by Innocent, and more clearly by Hostiensis in c. in civitate, at the word 'sed', and the Doctors hold this same thing in l. si pactio, C. de usuris, and through Albericus in his work Alphabetum super iure canonico, § usura, location 3, at the verse 'quid de illis, qui emunt a communitatibus', etc., and most fully by Oldradus in his questions, in question 119, where he says it was so determined in the Roman Curia. Albericus also notes the same in l. iubemus nulli, § fin., C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis; nor does C. de donationibus, l. sancimus, § fin., conflict, according to one interpretation, nor D. ad legem Falcidiam, l. hereditatum, because those laws speak in a lucrative cause; but in an onerous cause, as is the present case, it must be said that the said contract holds, as appears from the premises. And all the aforesaid things confirm this by virtue of the oath, and they are bound to its observance, as in c. si vero, extra de iureiurando, even if the contract were usurious—which, however, is not true—as in c. debitores, extra de iureiurando, and what is read fully by Bartolus in l. si quis pro eo, D. de fideiussoribus. And from the aforesaid matters it appears concluded that the said contract was and is lawful, and by its virtue the commune and the men are bound to payment.

† But now, for the second point, it remains to be seen whether the said commune and the men are bound to pay the entire annual rent to the said Lady Anesina, or rather half, on account of the death of the said lord Matteo. And it must briefly be said that they are bound to pay in full, because it was so agreed in the aforesaid contract and between the contracting parties themselves, as appears from the provisions written in the instrument of the said sale. For contracts take their law from the agreement of the contracting parties, as in D. depositi, l. 1, § si conveniat, with the like; l. fundi partem, D. de contrahenda emptione, also supports this. Nor is it novel that upon the death of one person, someone is admitted to the whole, as in l. virum, D. de assignatione libertorum, and l. proclamare non licet, and l. 1, C. si socius liberalitatis imperialis sine herede decesserit, book 10. Likewise, we see this elsewhere in the matter of the right of accretion, because where in contracts there would be no room for the right of accretion, according to what is fully read by Dynus and Bartolus in l. si mihi et Titio, D. de verborum obligationibus, yet if an agreement concerning this has been made, by virtue of the pact the share of the one accrues to the other: as is expressly set forth in feudal law, in the title De fratribus de novo beneficio investitis, c. 1, and in the title De duobus fratribus a capitulo investitis, in fine; and it is also so in contracts, as is fully read by Oldradus and other modern Doctors in l. unica, C. quando non petentium partes. Whence I briefly conclude regarding this point that, according to the common law, the commune and the men are bound by law to pay the full 140 gold florins to the said Lady Anesina on the aforesaid ground. And so it appears, and is to be declared according to law, saving a better deliberation, etc. Continue.

In the Name of Christ, Amen. Because I do not find that these contracts are condemned by any decretal, it is not permitted to condemn them; therefore, they must be observed, unless fraud is proven. And this is established by the allegations and laws cited above, and by the same reasons. I have previously advised accordingly, and therefore I consider the aforementioned reasons, allegations, and conclusions to be true. For if we consider the form of this contract, it is not usurious in form; if it is not naturally usurious in the hope of the contract, and if the case of profit occurs rather by opportunity than by necessity, and rather by the benignity of nature than by any certainty, that which might make it doubtful is that it has an aptitude for immoderate extortion. But this is resolved by the contrary aptitude, *extra de usuris*, c. *nauiganti*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If the prince in his will left his wife as mistress and administrator, and that all subjects should obey her and be faithful to her, what do those words import, whether by this a guardian was appointed for the son or grandson, and what power she has.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

The aforementioned clause of the will of the Most Illustrious Prince is divided into three parts. For in the first part is placed the proemium.
