In the second part is placed the statute and the disposition of the will. In the third part is placed a certain conclusion with modification. The second part begins here: "the same lady"; the third part begins here: "therefore to them." In all these, the proemium demonstrates merits both of congruity and of condignity, as in D. de donat. l. Aquilius; Regula; and l. Si pater. It is also signified the cause which urges the disposition of the testator, and that the benefit is to be interpreted most broadly, as in D. de lib. leg. l. Aurelius, §. Titius testamento; and D. de constit. princ. l. Beneficium. For certainly by this will the benefit of the Prince is to be called, as if made by a Prince, arg. C. de don. inter vir. et ux. l. Penultima. Likewise, from the dignity of the person there is a broader interpretation, as in D. de donat. l. Filios; and D. de iud. l. Sed et si susceperit, §. Et si proponas, there: "he wished honor to be had," etc. Nor is this surprising, because utility is increased by dignity, as in D. de iud. l. Si longius, §. Finalis. Therefore, the said will can be named in three ways: 1. Will; likewise, benefit; likewise, law or statute, as in Auth. de nupt. §. Disponat. And this is said proverbially. Now I come to the second particular, in which particular is contained the general providence of the testator. Therefore, "of the illustrious," and "we delight his consort." Where I weigh three things. That word, "and also usufructuary." I therefore explain that word, "and administration." Thirdly, I weigh that word, "and also usufructuary." I therefore explain that word, "true lady," i.e., true mistress. For true dominion is with the son of the testator succeeding in the county, and other principalities, and baronies, concerning which, even if feudal, the testator, if he wished to make a will, could not do so otherwise than according to the nature of the fief, as in c. 1 de success. col. Therefore, these words sound like a certain empire concerning administration, and the principal honor held for such a wife, as in D. mandati l. Creditor, §. Lucius; and D. de ann. leg. l. Qui Marco, alias est, §. Sub l. Titia, D. de leg. 2; and D. ad Sil. l. 1, §. Si vir, aut uxor. And this is approved by the common understanding of words, as noted in Spec. Qui filii sint legitimi, vers. Quid si quis ita; by Cynus and others in l. 1, C. Si secundo nupserit mulier; and by Decius and others in l. Titia, §. Finalis, D. de leg. 2. I weigh that, "and administration." As if he said "dominable administration," so that the sense is that he grants her general and free administration. What, however, those having free administration of all goods can do, is clear in D. de pact. l. Contra iuris civilis regulas, §. Si filius; D. quod vi aut clam l. Prohibere, §. Plane, where Bartolus says that by this power they cannot alienate the lord's castles, nor enfeoff anew. But those usually enfeoffed can well be re-enfeoffed by such arbitrium, because it is not called alienation, but a mode of using, as in Extr. de feud. c. 2. However, the common usage of speaking and interpreting is not such, that by this is understood to be granted to her free procuratio after the death of the testator; but that while the son lives, the usual honors be shown to her, insofar as they are due to a widow, and sustenance suitable for such a noble lady, her dwellings, and her household. Nor can we depart from what has long seemed equitable, as in D. de constit. princ. l. 2; and D. de pollicit. l. Imperatores. Consider: here we are not in mere terms of custom, as I will say immediately; for the difference of persons, the reason, and the condition moving the testator, and the very series of words, ought to be attended to more than general custom. 11. col. de quibusdam aliis extraordinariis capitulis feudorum, c. Sicut miles, §. Item si quis nec. 11. col. which is not commonly held in the Decretals. But whether by the aforementioned words does it seem that a guardian of the son or grandson is left? It would seem to be said that yes, because from this it would seem she has the plenitude of power, as the testator wished. And he who wills one thing, wills the whole by which that thing is attained, as in D. de iur. omn. iud. §. Cum iurisdictio; and C. de fideic. l. Quamvis simpliciter. However, to the contrary, the case expressed in D. de negot. l. Qui aliena, §. Quamquam, seems applicable, where it is said that if the testator, trusting in piety, entrusts to his wife that she manage the affairs of their common son, by this it does not seem he left her as guardian. From which it follows that she does not have the goods as guardian, because the goods have a present owner, as in D. ad Treb. l. Lucius, §. 1. What, therefore, shall we say about the power of such a lady? I answer, we shall say as the testator declares in the third and last part of the said clause of the will. In the word, "likewise that to them." For ambiguous preceding words are explained by subsequent ones, as in l. Si servus plurium, §. Finalis, D. de leg. 1; D. de verb. sign. Cum fundum; D. de leg. 3, l. Haeres meus, §. Duae statuae; D. de vino, tritico, et oleo leg. l. Finalis, §. Cui dulcia, D. de pen. leg. l. Nam quod liquide, §. Si cui. Therefore, the testator explains himself, saying thus: "therefore that to each of them she may use, and ought to use." These words refer to the things, the use of all of which is broad and free, placed in the power of the said lady, without any other moderation to be made by a good man. And although elsewhere the name of use contains ownership, as in D. de alien. leg. l. 3; D. de transact. Cum hi, §. Si uni; and D. de usu earum rerum, quae usu consumuntur, l. Finalis, nevertheless in the case proposed it is otherwise, as in D. de usu, et habit. l. Si habitatio, §. Sed si sic. For otherwise it would follow that the son would not be owner, because ownership cannot be with several in solidum, as in D. de reg. iur. l. Contra, §. Uni duo. Which is not to be said, as in D. de usufr. l. Sempronio, in princ. Thus, therefore, it must be concluded that in the things the son has dominion, and she has dominium (lordship), which she had during the life of the testator, arg. D. de ann. leg. l. Melia, §. Primo; and D. de usufr. l. Sempronio, §. Codicil. And so much more, inasmuch as the son or grandson shows her eminent reverence. For certainly we must say that she ought to have honor from the grandson as from a count, and the count ought to have reverence for her as for a mother, as in D. de iniur. l. Sed si haec lex, §. Si libera. And it supports D. de leg. 3, l. Item in legato, §. Parvi. And what is noted there. And although sometimes these words, "so that," or "so as," do not diminish the legacy: that is true when they are placed consecutively, as in D. de alim. et cib. leg. l. Lucius. But here they are placed by way of declaration concerning the very effect of the disposition, or by way of final cause, arg. D. de lib. leg. l. Aurelius, §. Stichus. Now it follows in the text written, "and all his faithful and subjects ought and are bound to obey her fully and perfectly." These words refer to the persons of the subjects. If anyone withheld obedience from her, they could be punished not only by the lord count, but also by her, as if jurisdiction and power were committed to her. For under the name of majority and obedience, jurisdiction is contained: as in Extr. de mai. et ob. per totum. Which jurisdiction can be committed to such illustrious women, as in the case of Countess Matilda, as in l. and note D. de arb. l. Finalis. And every day we see principalities being held by the said Illustrious ones, Extr. de for. comp. ex parte bonorum. However, by these words nothing can be commanded to the son, because the son is not a subject, but a superior. She can, however, command the subjects that they receive such a governor in the place and name of the lord count, and they ought to obey her firmly. It follows in the text of this clause, "provided that she lives in humanity, and abstains from other marriages." In which words a double limitation is placed. The first with respect to natural life. The second with respect to canonical life. And thus the disposition is terminated, as the testator wished it to be terminated, and not argued against, as in D. de pact. l. Epistola, §. Finalis; and C. de indic. vid. toll. Auth. Cui relictum. Hence, the effect of the said power, even if it has force at present, because if they say "to obey," it is necessary that she can command. For obedience cannot exist unless one holds the rod of commanding, and the other submits his neck by obeying, C. de captiv. l. An duae species; D. de iur. et iur. l. Manumissiones non transirent tempus vitae; as in D. de pign. l. Lex vectigali; and D. loc. l. Si quis domum, §. 1; and C. de leg. l. Uxor patrui. From these it appears that the said magnificent lady can also confer whatever offices are usually conferred for the time in the said county and principalities: namely, potestariates, castellaniates, and if any do not imply alienation, but only good government: saving the authority and power of the lord count, as in D. de pign. act. l. Vel universorum; D. quod cum eo l. Titianus. In common, letters from fiduciary and plenary power, which the testator gave her. Indeed, nature itself makes it so, that she take counsel for her children, as in D. de haer. instit. l. Quidam cum filium, where it is said that no one can have a better friend than a parent, D. de adul. l. Ne in ea, §. Sin, where it is said that the piety of the paternal name takes counsel for its children, D. de excus. tut. Amicissimos, §. Lucius, where it is said that natural impulse compels parents to this. And D. de bon. lib. Nihil, §. Facili, and where it is said that whatever we acquire for our children, we prepare by vow, and D. de leg. 3, l. Paulo Calimacho, §. Pom. eunuchus, in the gloss of Ruggerius, which treats of this fixed and ardent desire. To which also the nobility contributes, arg. D. de nat. rest. l. Quæris. From all of which arises natural equity. Indeed, the wills of soldiers are also to be interpreted most broadly, as in C. de test. mil. l. Ex his verbis fortunato. From these also it is concluded that and c.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a former tutor of a ward may be a surety for the curator appointed to the same person, now an adult.
2. Whether the word "shall not hear" encompasses legal alienation.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen.

† If it is asked whether a former tutor can be a surety for a curator subsequently appointed for an adult, I say that he can, ff. de tut. et cur. da. ab his. l. Roman. populus. Nevertheless, he could not be a curator unless the accounts of the tutorship have been rendered, as in Auth. minor. debitor. From these points it follows that the aforesaid repudiation is permitted, provided it was made in good faith; otherwise it is different, l. qui filiam, de manu. testa. ff. de iu. do. l. cum pater.

† On the second point, I say that the word "audiat" [let him not hear / let him not be heard] does not encompass a legal alienation, ff. de aliena iudic. leg. ex hoc edicto. §. si heredem, ff. de acqui. re. do. l. quaedam. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Both Laws, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a substitution made to an instituted son under the age of puberty by these words, "if my son should die at any time without children, let all my goods be distributed to the poor of Christ through such trustees, etc.," is direct or fiduciary: Bartolus holds that it is direct, while Baldus holds the contrary.
2. Whenever, from the meaning of the word, I must receive something from the hand of another, that word is rather oblique than direct.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen. The facts of the case are as follows. A testator instituted his impubes son in his testament and stated thus: that if my son should die at any time without children and heirs, all the goods ought to be distributed to the poor of Christ for the soul of myself and of other predecessors by such fideicommissaries, to whom he gave full power, etc.; with this saved and reserved, that a third of the said goods and of my said son ought not to be distributed, but should pass to B. and C., my sisters, whom I institute therein to myself and to my aforesaid son. Thereafter, the testator having died first and subsequently the son in pupillary age, the aforesaid son left paternal goods and adventitious goods. These sisters wish to embrace all the adventitious goods of the impubes son himself and to distribute nothing of them, saying that the substitution is fideicommissary. Now it is asked, what is the law?

† For the clarity of which it is presupposed that Bart. was of this opinion, namely, that the said institution is direct. This is clear because the testator says, "all goods," and thus it is clear that the testator wished nothing to be diminished, which must necessarily be understood of a direct substitution; and thus it is clear that the poor are said to be instituted heirs directly, because those executors in that case are said to be instituted on behalf of the poor, as is the case in l. si quis ad declinandam, C. de epi. et cle. Moreover, when a testator commits the distribution of his goods to someone in a last will, he is thereby seen to institute him and to request that he give them for the testator's soul, as is the case in c. cum tibi, extra de test. And these points are true, according to Bart., when the testator appointed executors in the testament, as was done in our case. But if he had not appointed executors, then that substitution would be oblique, because then the bishop, who is the father of the poor, only comes by the same right as the poor themselves. But the poor are substituted through merely oblique words; therefore, the bishop cannot come by any other right than the right of the poor, since he comes from their person, as we say in the case of a father, as in l. fi., C. de bo. quae lib. in prin., and l. si cum filio, ff. de leg. j., and noted in l. iubemus, C. ad Treb. For from this opinion of the lord Bart., it can be noted that the appointment of a testamentary executor enhances the nature of the substitution and makes it direct, where otherwise it would be fideicommissary if no executor had been appointed by the testator himself. But that opinion is false: for similarly, just as a testamentary guardian and a legatee do not differ in the quality of the office, but only in name, as is proved in l. sub conditione, and what is there noted, ff. de te. tute.; likewise, if a testamentary guardian dies, the guardianship devolves to the statutory guardian, as in the said l. sub condi.; likewise, if a testamentary executor dies, it devolves to the statutory one, as in the said l. nulli, C. de epis. et cle. I say simply that the said substitution is fideicommissary, as is proved by analogy in l. fundi trebatiani, ff. de vsufr. leg., and noted in l. si quis ita, ff. de vsufr., and the good gloss there; nor in that case does the executor give from his own property, but from the goods of the heir, and it is taken away from the goods of the heir and applied to the poor through the hand of the executor. Nor does the said l. si quis ad declinandam and the said c. cum tibi stand in the way, because there the testator had not expressly provided himself with an express heir, but in our case, by instituting the son, he had provided himself with an express heir; therefore, an implied heir ceases, arg. l. cum ex filio, ff. de vulg. et pup. Therefore, by the said words the son is seen to be burdened after his death so that the goods of the father-testator are distributed to the poor, from which goods, however, the legitime will be deducted, not the Trebellianic portion, as in auth. similiter, C. ad l. fal., and in auth. si qua mulier, C. de sac. san. ecc., and l. pe. in eo. ti., and l. si fundum per fideicommissum, §. fi., with the following law, and what is there noted, ff. de leg. j., and l. si fuerit, ff. de le. 3. Moreover, I prove that it is fideicommissary:

† For I presuppose that the word "distribuantur" [let them be distributed] is by its nature oblique, because whenever from the meaning of the word I ought to take something from the hand of another, that word is more oblique than direct, as in l. ex facto, in prin., ff. ad Treb., and l. eam, quam, C. de fidei., and l. cohaeredi, §. cum filio, ff. de vulg. et pu., and noted more fully by the doctors in the matter of l. Centurio, ff. de vul. et pup. sub. l. 2., and there another point also by Bart., C. communia de leg. Then I argue thus: I am held to be such an heir as is he through whom I am made an heir, as in l. qui in aliena, §. interdum, ff. de acqui. haere. Since, therefore, these executors are made heirs through the poor, whatever the substitution is in the poor, such it ought to be in the executors: that which is implied is such as that which is expressed allows, as in l. qui ad certum, ff. lo. But since the form of the aforesaid substitution in the person of the poor is oblique, as is clear through this word "distribuantur," as I stated above, it follows that in the person of the executors it is oblique. Therefore, it is clear, contrary to Bart., that this substitution is to be judged fideicommissary rather than direct. From which things, therefore, I conclude that distribution has no place in the adventitious goods of the son, but they are to be applied to the abovementioned sisters.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether an inquiry can be conducted against a deceased person for the crime of extortion.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen. Present before the most excellent lord Philip of Pistoia, Vicar General and Commissioner of the Illustrious Prince and Magnificent and Most Excellent Lord, the Duke of Milan, Imperial Vicar General, Rabaldus and Nicolaus, brothers and sons of the late, of good and praiseworthy memory, Lord Prosello Desartito, of good memory, the said Lord Prosello, and also as procurator and in the procuratorial name of the said Lady Zilia, their mother and widow of the said Lord Prosello, and in every manner, way, and form by which they can do so more effectively, appeared and presented themselves: opposing, and intending to oppose, against and in opposition to a certain inquisition formed de facto and not de iure, against the said Lord Prosello, notary, and against a certain said Zilia, and against the citation therefore issued: and against the entire process conducted, and that which might follow, on account of the contents of the said inquisition, the tenor of which former inquisition and citation appears in the records. Saying,

† That the said inquisition, insofar as it is against the said Lord Prosello, deceased, and the citation of the said Lord Prosello, deceased, do not proceed, nor can they proceed, especially in the form contained therein: as is shown in D. de iudiciis, l. de qua re, § cum absentem; and D. quae sententiae sine appellatione recipiuntur, l. placet, cum si. Secondly: because in the said Lord Prosello no crime of extortion (repetundarum) is alleged, nor can it be alleged, since nothing is proposed to have been given, especially against law and good morals, nor on the occasion of any office, but for a certain simple remuneration, which, however, was not true: because, due to the stipulation to be made to the lord, if anything is received, it is not simony: as appears expressly in D. ad legem Iuliam de peculatu, l. Titio cum esset. Thirdly: because if the report of the said Lord Prosello, made to our most magnificent lord, had been false: after death, one cannot [proceed]: as is shown in D. de accusationibus, l. ex iudiciorum; and C. si reus vel accusator moriatur, l. 1. Fourthly: against the said Zilia, the said inquisition does not proceed. First, because the contents of the said inquisition are denied to be true. Second, because the said inquisition does not contain the substantial elements by which it can be said that the said lady committed any offense. And the present exception is not otherwise declared, but will be declared at the time of the debates. Fifthly: because a layman is not bound to know the law. Hence, assuming without prejudice to the truth that the said Lady Zilia had received something, that alone, as received without cause, would be subject to restitution, and nothing further. For she could believe, according to natural equity, that it was lawful to receive [payment] for renunciation, and that it was lawful and honest. And this is proven by l. auunculo, D. de condictione sine causa. Hence she alleges ignorance of the law, yet without confessing without some warning. For this, it is expressly noted: C. de incestis nuptiis, in principio, col. 3; D. de adulteriis, l. si adulterium cum incestu, § idem Pollioni. Finally, all other exceptions applicable, and to be applied in their proper place and time, are proposed to be reserved. And especially the exceptions of invalidity of the inquisition and of the entire procedure, to be proposed in their proper place and time: and especially because in the said inquisition, regarding the said Lady Zilia, the place of the alleged offense was not specified, which ought to have been specified; otherwise the inquisition is invalid. As is noted by Jacobus Butrigarius, Inst. de actionibus, in principio; and Bartolus, D. de accusationibus, l. liberorum. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a grandfather acquires an inheritance that has been offered to an infant but not yet accepted.
2. Whether one who supports his grandchildren and keeps them in his household is considered to be acting on behalf of the inheritance.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The case is proposed as follows. John had three sons, namely Dolceto, Nicholas, and Bartholomew. Bartholomew had as his wife Lady Fiordellatra; from which marriage were born Floremons and Bartholomaea. The said Bartholomew died first, then Fiordellatra died, then Floremons died in infancy; then Lord John died, then Bartholomaea died posthumously in infancy; after both Floremons and Bartholomew, the said Lord John, their paternal grandfather, after the death of the said Bartholomaea, his daughter, and of the said Fiordellatra, his daughter-in-law, held the house in which they lived together and were accustomed to live as before. Now the question arises concerning the inheritance of the said Fiordellatra, because John and his brothers, carnal brothers of Lady Lucia, mother of the said Fiordellatra, and maternal uncles of the said Fiordellatra, claim that the inheritance pertains to them, because the inheritance of the said Fiordellatra in the name of the said infants was not accepted by Lord John, their former paternal grandfather, nor by anyone who could have accepted it in their name. But to the contrary, the said Dolceto and Nicholas, uncles of the said deceased infants Floremons and Bartholomaea, and their nearest blood relatives, say that the hereditary goods pertain to and are possessed by them. Now it is asked what is the law.

† And it appears that the aforementioned Dolcetus and Nicholas support the right, and that the paternal grandfather acquires the inheritance devolved upon the infant, upon the death of the infant. And thus it does not appear that any acceptance is necessary, but that it was acquired by operation of law for the grandfather himself, and consequently for Dolcetus and Nicholas, whether we consider them as sons of Lord John or as uncles of the said infants, as in C. de iure deliberandi, l. si infanti, ver. sed si hoc parens. To the contrary, it appears that the said inheritance was not acquired by the said Lord John, because he did not accept it, which he could have done by special right. That acceptance is necessary according to the newest law is held by the gloss in the said l. si infanti, and thus Jacobus de Belvisis affirms there.

But on behalf of the said Dolceto and Nicholas it is alleged that the said Lord John appears to have acted as heir, by keeping the said infant nephews with him and rearing them. And to this point such a reason may be adduced: because it appears that he wished to rear them from the goods of the said infants. As in the Digest, *De negotiorum gestione*, law *Nam et servus*. But the said infants had no goods other than maternal ones. Therefore it appears that he accepted the maternal goods. And thus he acts as heir. As in the law *Pro herede* and the law *Gedit*, in the Digest, *De acquirenda hereditate*. Moreover, when the inheritance is profitable, management as heir is easily presumed: because affection of mind proceeds to acquire it. And it is certain that an inheritance is entered upon by mind alone. As in the Institutes, *De qualitate et differentia hereditatum*, § *Finis*. But against this it is argued: because management as heir requires an expressed intention. As in the Digest, *De iure deliberandi*, law *Potuit*, in the words *actus*. And will was necessary. But here no act appears, except one expressed in words, nor one entering into administration. Therefore we cannot judge the inheritance to have been apprehended. For since this is a matter of fact, it is not presumed. As in the said law *Pro herede*, § *Unum*, § 1. According to what is proposed, the said inheritance was not entered upon by word or deed: because nothing was done that could not have been done within the right and name of the heir. As in the law *Pro herede*, § *Papinianus*. And by the rule there laid down, the decision of the question is clear. And therefore, unless something else were proved than by the entry upon the said inheritance, I say that the said John and the children succeed in the inheritance not entered upon of Fiordellatra.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an inquisition against someone concerning perjury committed in an oath to calumnia in a civil case proceeds.
2. What effect the clause "saving the right of impertinent matters not to be admitted, etc." has.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. It is proposed that, concerning certain allegations, in which was contained an article regarding the sentence of a certain lawsuit, a mere witness, who in another trial, concerning those matters contained in the chapters, gave testimony under oath to tell the truth, stated that he did not believe he knew anything about the said lawsuit that had been brought. Hence, to the contrary, since an inquisition for perjury was formed, because it is established that he knew, and had sworn falsely in an oath against calumny, which oath indeed appears to possess all solemnities. It is asked whether an inquisition may be conducted for perjury of an oath against calumny, or not; and subsequently, questions are asked concerning certain other chapters, as I shall say below. And for clarity, it must be premised,

† That nothing is provided for by any law regarding the possibility of imposing any criminal punishment for the perjury of one who has sworn the oath against calumny in a civil case. On the contrary, it is expressly stated that he has God alone as his avenger. This is the gloss on the Institutes, *de poena temere litigantium*, on the word *religione*, where the gloss says that he will be punished in the future world, not in this one. The gloss in the Institutes, in the proemium, on the word *tramites*, wished to note the same thing. Otherwise, the following absurdity would follow: since in every civil judgment an oath against calumny is taken, and the other party is perjurious, and this is evident from the outcome of the litigation, as in C. *de iudic.*, l. *rem non nouam*, §. *si*, it would mean that one of the litigants would always be punished criminally on account of perjury. This is absurd, because the aforementioned oath was not instituted for this purpose, but solely so that the litigants might be restrained from calumnies by the fear of the divine majesty, as in Auth. *de iudic.*, §. *oportet*. Moreover, this is proven by another reason: because since no civil action for fraud arises from the perjurer, no criminal action is brought against him for the crime of stellionatus, unless it were a fraud that would be purged by an action arising from that contract, as we note in C. *de priuatis delictis*, l. *sin*. Moreover, this perjury does not fall under a specific name of a delict, nor even a general one, because it is called the crime of stellionatus, since no law says this. Therefore, an inquisition made on this matter is not founded on laws. And we blush to say anything without a law, as in Auth. *de triennio et semis*, §. *consideremus*. Moreover, this is supported by the doctrine of the doctors, C. *de rebus creditis*, l. 3, according to Cynus, Iacobs, Bartolus, and others. Moreover, it must be considered in our case that the article concerning knowledge is irrelevant; because even if he had knowledge of the letters, nevertheless he would not have been prejudiced, as in ff. *de rei venditione*, l. *etiam inter officium*. And therefore such a position did not support the case, nor ought it to have been answered, as is fully noted in §. *quod obseruari*, and in l. *si quis liberatione*, §. *ult.*, ff. *de petitione hereditatis*.

† Moreover, the response must be made, saving the right of not admitting irrelevant matters. In which case, if one responds to irrelevant matters, it is held as if no response had been given, and as if no oath had been taken; because it is not understood that he swore an oath regarding irrelevant matters: as noted in the Extravagantes, De officio delegati, chapter Cum contingat. There is another reason why the person under inquiry ought to be absolved: because in the inquisition it is stated that he swore to tell the truth concerning the articles. Regarding which oath, the truth is not contained in a response by the word "I believe" or "I do not believe"; because it is one thing to swear to the truth, and another to swear against calumny: as in the Extravagantes, De iuramento calumniae, chapter 1. From which it appears that this response based on belief was unsworn, that is, without an oath. And thus the inquisition for perjury does not proceed. Furthermore, the propositions, which referred to the acts of another case, were uncertain, the acts not having been read. Hence, by reason of the uncertainty, he could probably respond by the word "I do not believe": as noted in the Codex, De iuramento calumniae, law 2, section Quod observari; and in the Digest, De iureiurando, law Iusiurandum, and Ad pecunias. From which it most evidently appears that Thomas Alionus of Ast, concerning whom the said inquisition was made, ought to be entirely absolved, considering the form of the said inquisition seen and read by me, together with the above-mentioned propositions and responses. And so I hold.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the Pope or the Emperor can, by privilege or rescript, grant to one city jurisdiction acquired by prescription over another.
1. The Emperor is lord of the whole world with respect to all jurisdiction and supreme power.
2. Those things which pertain to supreme empire cannot be prescribed by any inferior.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† For the sake of clarity, I premise that the text of the Imperial Constitution of Emperor Frederick states as follows: "All jurisdiction and all coercive power reside with the Prince, and all judges ought to receive their office of administration from the Prince and to take the oath of office as established by law." This is consistent with the Authentica *Iusiurandum quod praestatur ab his, qui administrationem suscipiunt*, in the *Rubro et Nigro*.

† And this is most true, that the Emperor is lord of the world, with respect to all manner of jurisdiction and supreme power: as is shown in the Digest, under the law *Rho*, on jettison; the law *Deprecatio* in the Code, on thirty-year prescription; the law *Bene a Zenone* in the Code, on laws; the law *Si* in the Extravagantes, on major and obsequious matters; and the chapter *Solitae* in the Extravagantes.

† so much so that those things which pertain to the supreme Empire cannot be prescribed by any inferior person: because they are reserved to the prince as a sign of universal dominion. As is fully read and noted in C. de praescri. 30. ann. l. competit. For if anyone were subsequently to prescribe the true Empire against the Prince, he would become greater than him: and he could punish the prince delinquent in that very territory: as in ff. de rerum div. l. si. which is false. For he who is supreme cannot have another above him. Moreover, the supreme Empire itself is indivisible, just as the Church does not divide itself. As noted by Cynus in C. de cap. dim. l. tutelas in his additions.

Secondly, it must be premised that the prince can grant mere and mixed empire in part, just as Frederick granted it to the cities of Lombardy, which came into the Peace of Constance: as noted in Auth. de def. civ. §. nulla. But this must be observed: that either this pact intervenes by way of fiefs, which also binds the prince. As noted in 10. eod. tit. l. qui feudum dare possunt c. un. §. si. However, for this fief to endure, many observances are required: as appears in the matter of fiefs, and it is terminated by many causes; or it intervenes by way of transaction, or peace. And then the Peace of Constance speaks. But it must be known that that peace appears to have been temporary: namely, for 30 years, as in tit. de pace constant. 2. charta. c. in nomine Christi. vers. ego iuro. where the text thus says, "without fraud I will observe all the above-mentioned things from the Kalends of May, up to 30 years." And thus held many ancient and great doctors, although Odofredus is to the contrary. But for the first opinion is the argument in ff. de pac. l. epistola. §. si. and ff. de leg. 2. l. statuliberum. §. stichum. Or it intervenes by way of a simple privilege, either by interpretation, or by the prince's own motion. And then we speak of congruity, or we speak of power. If indeed we speak of congruity, it is fitting that a privilege granted by the prince should remain and be free from all diminution, as in Auth. constitutio quae de dignitatibus. §. illud. and in the rule of law, decet concessum, lib. 6. But if we speak of power, either of ordinary power, and the same applies; or of absolute power: and then the prince can revoke his privilege. For by the very fact that he revokes it, it is presumed that he does so for a cause. As is accustomed to be noted in the proemium of the Digests.

But by Prince I call the Pope and the Caesar. For none of the inferiors participates in this supreme empire. Although for an evident cause they could remove a privilege from an abuser: as noted in the said c. decet.

Fourthly, mere Empire is acquired in some singular city or village by way of prescription: and then, as I said, because this prescription does not conclude against the Caesar, but only against the subjects against whom it is prescribed: the Caesar can remove this prescription. Nevertheless, he acts wrongly, unless those prescribing abuse it, because by prescription a useful dominion of jurisdiction has been acquired against the subjects, and the Emperor ought not to detract from anyone's right: as in C. de eman. lib. 1. l. nec auus. And such rescripts are presumed to be surreptitious, unless they emanated from the certain knowledge of the prince, as in C. de prec. imper. off. l. nec damnosa. there where it says, "nor contrary to right."

Having therefore premised these things, let us come to the point. And first, as regards the jurisdiction of the city of Parma in the said villages, there is no doubt that it held it by prescription of such long time, of which contrary memory did not exist. As most fully noted by the moderns in ff. de iur. omn. iud. l. imperium. and l. more maiorum. and C. de diuer. off. l. vires. lib. 12. But it is true that Charles the Emperor, by certain knowledge and from the fullness of power, removed the said jurisdiction and district from the said city of Parma, and granted it to the nobles Hugoletus and Ramondinus, and therefore from the things already said it appears that he could grant it. But here it must be observed that by the same reason and power he could subsequently remove it from the said Hugoletus and Ramondinus, and grant and confer it to Peter and Maximus by his own motion. However, it must be established that he wished to do so. For when power and will concur in one, the effect of the grant arises; and power alone without will has nothing to consummate or perfect. As in C. de dona. ante nupt. l. cum te sponsae. and l. si filiae tuae. and there noted.

That also must be observed, that this Peter was in possession for a very long time. Hence against the said Hugo and Ramon it seems that prescription has occurred: as in C. de praescrip. 30. ann. l. sicut. and l. omnes. But to this it can be answered that by the said l. omnes. a prescription of 30 years is required, because we are dealing with jurisdiction to be prescribed, a case not comprehended in l. sicut. eod. tit. And therefore if the privilege granted to the said Peter were surreptitious, it does not give cause for prescribing: as in C. de falsis. l. ex initio. That law, however, does not seem to apply to our case: because here there was no surreptitiousness, but obreption by ignorance. For thus it is to be presumed in doubt: as in C. de probat. l. quotiens. §. qui dolo. And thus concluding from the first to the last, if the privilege of the noble lords Hugoletus and Ramondinus is not absorbed by the later one, they have justice. And by those things which we see, this could sufficiently be defended: nevertheless, I do not affirm it entirely. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The Prince, in granting a rescript, or indeed any inferior authority when the right resides solely in him, is not bound to cite anyone.
2. The petition of a prisoner for release from prison, surrendering all his goods to his creditors, is of common law and consonant with common equity.
3. How cession is usually made: and what are its essential elements.
4. One who cedes his goods is to be released from prison against the will of the creditors, in whose interest those who have an interest are to be called in his release.
5. The form of citation to be observed when he who cedes his goods is to be released.
6. Whether a judgment is said to be completed by being sent to prison.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It must be premised for clarity that the Prince is not bound to cite anyone in his rescript of concession; nor indeed is any inferior to the Prince, since this right resides solely in the concluding authority and does not depend on the parties. But when one party uses such a rescript against another, the adversary and those who have an interest must be summoned in the initiation of the case. This appears clearly: because first the rescript is issued, then the citation, as appears in the Speculum de rescriptis, presentation throughout; and Codex, de his qui veniunt aetate imperatoria, l. 2; and Codex, quomodo et quando iudex, auth. qui semel; and also from the style of the rescripts themselves. Secondly, it must be premised for clarity,

† That the petition of a prisoner, that he be released from prison, releasing all his goods to his creditors, is in accordance with the common law and equity: as is evident. D. and C. de cess. bon. per totum. and Inst. de acq. §. fin. which being conceded

It is not necessary that any ignominy be inflicted upon the person ceding his goods, which is customary in certain places: for example, that he be brought into a public place and there displayed to the people. And in certain places it is customary to observe that he strike his kidneys against a column which has iron in it; and yet no utility accrues to the creditors on this account. For these things are not substantial elements of the cession, but certain accidental ones, as is expressly clear from the law *Et notum*, Digest, *De procuratoribus*, law *Actoris*, which the Prince appears to have remitted, since he made no mention of them. For with respect to the Prince, one should not gloss: as is noted in chapter *Ad haec*, *De officio archiepiscopi*, in the Novella *Quoniam*. For the benefits of Princes are to be interpreted graciously and liberally in those matters which do not harm others, and in supplications. And Digest, *De constitutionibus principum*, law *Beneficium*. And as is noted, Digest, *De rerum iudicatarum*, law *In testamentis*.

Thirdly, it must be premised that he who cedes his goods ought to be released from prison, even against the will of the creditors, as is noted in the Code, in the title *Qui hominis cedendi possit*, in the law *I*. However, because this release ought not to be made without a certain order of judicial proceedings, those whose interest it is say that they ought to be summoned.

† For sometimes a person is in prison, and it is not established at whose petition [he is detained]; and then a general proclamation suffices, as noted by Bartolus in *l. si quis uxori*, § *si fugitivum*, D. de furtis, where he sets forth the theory and practice of this matter. Sometimes it is established at whose petition [the detention occurs]; and then that person, or his procurator, must be cited. See D. de lib. agnosc., *l. 1*, § 1; C. de procur., *l. eum qui res agit*; Inst. de poena temere litigant., § *si*; and Auth. de haeredit. et falsis, § *si vero absunt*; D. de re iudicata, *l. de unoquoque*; D. de adoptionibus, *l. nam ita divus*; C. ut se ab haereditate abstin., Auth. *si omnes*; D. de minoribus, *l. etiam*, § *fin.*, cum *si*. And this is most true according to the law. But if another form of citation has been granted by municipal law, and those who are to be cited are subjects of the territory, then either the trial is completed, i.e., perfected, in which case we are no longer in the forum, but outside the forum; and if a new action is commenced, the plaintiff, in making the citation, must follow the forum of the defendant. But if the trial had not been concluded, then, because all citations regard the order of the trial, we would examine the statutes of that forum; see C. quemadmodum testamenta aperiantur, *l. 2*; and fully noted in *l. cunctos populos*.

Whether, however, it can be probably distinguished whether permission into prison constitutes a completed judgment, namely: either the imprisonment is by a definitive sentence, or one having the force of a definitive sentence: and the judgment is said to be completed. Or it is due to mere contumacy, and then the contrary holds: because the end has not yet been imposed upon the litigation. As in l. 1, § quid ergo, ff. de ventre insepulto. Concluding, however, I say that good assessors have the opposing party summoned, and, having summoned it and the cession of goods having been made, they release the imprisoned person; here another order of judicial proceedings is required, and holidays do not apply in this case: as in ff. de feriis, l. si, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an abbot expelled from the monastery can make an agreement concerning the property of the monastery.
2. Bernard was the supreme glossator of the decretals.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It must be stated at the outset for clarity that the Abbot cannot lease the monastery together with its possessions without the consent of the chapter. This consent also suffices, unless a negotiation intervenes, and those requirements which are demanded in alienation. And if the monastery is not exempt, the lease is made for a prejudicial term, during which the goods and rights of the monastery could be dissipated; it would not be contrary to the form and reason of law to decree that this could not be done without consulting the Roman Pontiff. For the reason which prohibits alienation is that the monastery not be destroyed along with its property: as in C. de sac. sanc. eccl. l. iubemus, nulli, which is of the most just Emperor Leo. And therefore, on this point, I say that this Boniface, the monk, and the spoilers of the said Abbot are to be compelled to restore the said monastery, notwithstanding any agreements made to the contrary. which

† Even if Bernard, who was the supreme glossator of the decretals, had done so, or had advised it to be done, they would be null by the law itself: because they come not only to the prejudice of the Abbot, but also of the monastery and the monks; and even to the dispersion and dilapidation of the possessions of the said monastery. This is therefore the conclusion, that the despoiled Abbot be restored to the possession of the monastery. And then, while he is outside possession, he makes agreements with the consent of his chapter, and he cannot have the consent of the chapter. Let him abstain from every contract, saving that which is owed to his person, concerning which he can compromise and make peace. I say the same, that those who intruded themselves and despoiled him are said to be compelled to relinquish the aforementioned possession. It also seems to me that our magnificence may, according to God, and is bound to commit this to the counsel of his nobles: and since the ecclesiastical arm fails, he ought to supply it, and fear God.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A vassal does not forfeit his fief by the mere consent to its sale, or by a contract not followed by delivery. The authorities are helpful: as in the Decretals, *De auctoritate et usu pallii*, cap. *Ex*. 2. Whether the lord’s consent to the alienation of a fief prejudices the agnates, and whether it prejudices the son of a vassal who has alienated. No. 3.
1. Whether and when a seller is bound to make delivery, and whether he is discharged by paying damages.
body: They are beneficial to songs: as in the Decretals, on authority and the use of the pallium, chapter *Ex*. 2. The consent of the lord in alienating a fief does not harm the agnates, and *In Christi Nomine*. Amen. A certain nobleman of San Nazario sold to another nobleman of Lignano his share of the castle, possessions, and lands of Camagno for the price of two thousand and forty gold florins. This contract remained at the stage of mere agreement, so that neither was delivery made, nor was the price paid in full or in part. That castle was, and is, feudal property of the illustrious lord, the Marquis of Montferrat. Permission for the said sale was obtained from him; however, the agnates of the said vendor did not consent, who would have succeeded in the said paternal and ancient fief after his death. Therefore, it is demanded of the said vendor that he deliver the said things sold, and the price is offered to him. But he says that if he were to deliver, he could not transfer full right to the buyer, thus. Hence, it is not in the buyer's interest that such delivery, as it would be, should take place. Now the question arises: what is the law? And it must be premised for clarity,
† that a fief is not lost by the mere consent of sale without delivery: as is stated and noted by Dynus and others in the Digest, *De verbis significandis*, in the law *Alienatum*.

Secondly, it must be premised that the consent of the lord does not prejudice the agnates who do not consent, as in c. 1, de alienatione feudi paterni, col. 10. But if the agnates were to consent, or ratify the act, the delivery could validly be made: as in c. quia supra, § praeterea, qui modis feudum amittatur, col. 10.

But does what has been said regarding agnates apply to sons when the fief is ancient? And it seems that it does, as in D. de in ius vocando, l. adoptiuum; and D. de iure patronatus, l. diui fratres; and D. de liberis, l. quaeritur. For a fief devolves rather by providence than by the father’s judgment, as in C. 1. q. 2, c. feudorum, § cum vero, where Conradus, in the gloss, says so. Therefore, for this purpose the law D. 3, de interdictis et relegationibus, is applicable. But the case seems to be to the contrary, namely, that the father’s act always prejudices the son in respect of a fief, as in c. Si vassallus culpam, Si de feudo controversia fuerit inter dominum et agnatos, col. 10; and in c. 1, Si vassallus feudo priuetur, cui debeat deferri, c. Vasalli, de feudis. But these chapters are not applicable to our case, because in this seller no fault, at least no consummated fault, is found.

† And therefore, returning to the point at issue, I say that it is of the nature of sale and purchase that delivery be made, if the seller has the ability to deliver the thing. As is fully stated in the law and noted in the Institutes, *De contrahenda emptione*, § *Pretium autem*, in the gloss *caute*; and in the Digest, *De re vendita*, l. *Qui restituere*, at the end. Although it is otherwise noted in l. 1, in the beginning, Digest, *De acquirenda possessione*; and in l. 1, Code, *De senatusconsulto quod pro eo quod interest*. And it supports what is noted in l. *Certae condictionis*, in the beginning, Digest, *Si certum petatur*. Nevertheless, in the case proposed, it seems to be said that the seller is not bound strictly to make delivery, because by delivery he could not irrevocably transfer the right which he has in the thing. At, Digest, *De verborum significatione*, l. *Nepos Proculi*; and Code, *Communia de legatis*, l. *Si*, § *Si*, especially because the buyer knew the quality of the thing. Argument from Digest, *De contrahenda emptione*, l. *Si in emptione*, § *Item si emptor*; and Code, *De evictione*, l. *Si fundum sciens solutio*. It seems to me that he cannot be compelled to do anything else than to pay damages according to the laws and reasons alleged on this side. Furthermore, regarding the delivery of allodial lands, he can well be compelled strictly, if this pleases the buyer, whether he has the ability to deliver the thing or whether he ceased to have it through fraud. As in Digest, *De re iudicata*, l. *Parem*. And thus I hold. Between two legitimate buyers, however, the one to whom delivery was made later is preferred. As is fully read and noted in l. *Siue autem*, Digest, *De publiciana*; and Digest, *De re vendita*, l. *Quotiens*.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If the testator prohibited his instituted heirs from alienating, the said prohibition does not comprehend others.
2. A substitution made on the condition that he should die without children expires if the condition does not occur.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The noble man, Lord Guglielmo of Saint Nazario, had two sons, Lord Simone and Zanone. Finally, while the said Lord Guglielmo was still living, the said Lord Zanone died, leaving behind his son Cancirino. Subsequently, the said Lord Guglielmo died, having made a will, in which he instituted the said Simone and his nephew Cancirino as his universal heirs. And upon their dying without legitimate male children, he substituted them for one another. Moreover, the said testator in the same will wished, ordered, and commanded that his universal heirs could not, nor should they be able in any way, to divide the portions of the said testator pertaining to a certain castle, village, and place, etc., as is more fully contained in the said will. It is asked whether the words, "that his universal heirs could not, etc.," comprehend any other person than the persons of Lord Simone and Cancirino. And briefly, without argument.

It must be said that the answer is no; because the text and the glossa ordinaria in the Authentica de restitutione fideicommissi, § nos igitur, in the gloss beginning “note,” state that the prohibition of alienation is not extended beyond the son, unless it is expressly stated. And the same is noted by Cynus through this gloss in the Codex, de fideicommissis, l. voluntas. And to this point, the following authority is most apt: Digestum, de legatis tertio, l. pater filium, § 10. Therefore, the lord Antonio, son of the said Simon, is not included under the aforementioned prohibiting clause, which is most personal by virtue of the words “his heirs themselves,” as in Digestum, de vulgari substitutione, l. qui liberis, § haec verba, and Digestum, de verborum significatione, l. sciendum. For the word “ipsis” [themselves] is not only relative, but also demonstrative to the eye. And this is the truth.

Secondly, it is asked whether the aforementioned substitution is to be understood as having been made in favor of the said Lord Antonio. It must be said that it was not, because the said Lord Simondo died leaving children. And therefore the substitution expired, which had been made on the condition that he should die without children. As stated in the Digest, ad Trebellianum, law *Ex facto*, section *Penultimus*. From these points it follows that the usufruct, concerning which the question is raised in full, is owed to the said noble lady, Doña Francisca de Verme, formerly the consort of the said Lord Antonio, by virtue of the award already rendered. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. He sets forth a certain privilege of Emperor Charles.
body:
In the Name of Christ. Amen. Charles, by the favoring clemency of God, Roman Emperor, always Augustus, and King of Bohemia, for the perpetual memory of the matter, to the noble Peter de Fornariis of Ciuizano of Parma, formerly of the Cataneis of Vindeto, our Count of the Sacred Lateran Palace, and beloved faithful of the Holy Empire, our grace and every good.

The scepter-bearing sublimity of the Imperial dignity, just as it is preferred by office and authority, by election, to inferior powers, so that it may govern the faithful committed to it with the desired support of consolation—by which the throne of the Emperor is so much more solidly established and advances with more abundant prosperity, insofar as it has been endowed with the gifts of its own virtue and a more generous bounty of benevolence toward its subjects—thus, from the flashing lightning of the imperial throne, nobility, like rays proceeding from the sun, illuminates the status and conditions of the faithful, so that the primary integrity of light suffers no detriment of untainted luminosity; rather, it is perfused with more abundant expected splendor of the scintillating halo, when the number of spectable counts and magnates in the circuit of the August seat is increased for the glory of the Holy Empire.

These things, truly, regarding the noble and exceedingly considerable industry of your circumspection, and the experienced constancy of your virtuous faith toward us and the Roman Empire itself, by which you have shone in the Imperial presence, the eyes of our majesty and the keenness of studious meditation, with a certain singular fervor, more graciously regarding them; and also out of love for the venerable Prepositus Lepis of Nonantula, our beloved Apostolic Nuncio, who offered humble prayers for you, wishing to do you a special grace, you, whom the clarity of virtues, as it were sprinkled with the beauty of laudable morals, renders gracious with special splendor: we, with deliberate mind, sound, and with the advice of our princes, counts, barons, and magnates, and the faithful of the Holy Roman Empire, by our certain knowledge, and by the fullness of Imperial power, make, create, erect, ennoble, elevate, and more graciously insigniate you, and your male heirs legitimately descending from you, Counts of the Sacred Lateran Palace, with all honors, dignities, jurisdictions, rights, privileges, graces, liberties, and offices, and all utilities, as well as all emoluments and commensurabilities which, and whatever, our other counts palatine of the Holy Roman Empire are known to obtain, receive, and hold in any way, by custom or by right, aggregating you and your aforesaid heirs into the number and fellowship of those palatine counts, by certain knowledge and the fullness of Imperial power.

We also invest you and your said heirs, legitimately descending from you through the male line, as is premised, with the dignity of count and the office of countship, with the honor and decency which is expedient, by the authority of these presents. Giving and granting to you, and to the same your sons and male heirs, with the same Imperial authority, full and every kind of power, by our certain knowledge, to create notaries, public scribes, and ordinary judges, in all places and throughout our Holy Roman Empire, who are suitable and sufficiently experienced in literature, with plenary power pertaining to the office of notary and judge; and to invest them, and any of them, with the aforesaid by pen and inkhorn, as is the custom.

Provided, however, that from the said notaries, or scribes, and ordinary judges to be made and created by you, or your aforesaid heirs, as is premised, and any of them, in the name and on behalf of the Holy Roman Empire, and for the said Roman Empire, you receive the corporal and due oath of due fidelity; that the notaries and public scribes, both public and private instruments, last wills, and whatever acts of judgments, and all other and singular things which shall occur to them, and any of them, to be done and written by the duty of the said offices, and any of them, they shall write, read, and make those writings which they ought to reduce to public form, on parchments, not on abraded papers nor paper ones, faithfully writing; and also sentences, and the sayings of witnesses, until they are published and approved, they shall keep faithfully under secrecy, and shall do all and singular things rightly and justly which shall pertain in any way to the said office by right.

And that the said notaries, or scribes, and ordinary judges to be made and created by you, or your aforesaid descendants, throughout the Roman Empire, may make, write, and publish contracts and instruments, judgments, wills, last wills, interpose decrees and authorities, in whatever contracts requiring them, or those; and do, exercise, and publish all and singular other things which are known to pertain and appertain to the office of public notary or scribe, and ordinary judge, by Imperial authority, and by certain license, we give, grant, and bestow upon you and your aforesaid descendants, that you may give and constitute guardians and curators to parents wishing to emancipate their children whom they have in their power, and impart authority and interpose decree in adoptions and arrogations for the said children absent from judgment.

Also, with the same authority, we grant and bestow upon you and your aforesaid descendants, and any of you, that you may and can legitimize bastards, spurious children, manzeres, and whoever begotten from illicit intercourse, with their parents living and even dead, illustrious princes, counts, and barons excepted simultaneously, and restore and reduce them to legitimate rights, and utterly abolish all stain of birth, restoring them to all and singular rights of successions, even intestate of cognates, of honor and dignity, and to all legitimate acts, as if they were begotten from legitimate marriage; provided, however, that the legitimations to be made and created by you and your aforesaid descendants, as is premised, do not prejudice legitimate children and heirs, so that they, with those to be legitimized by you, or by any of you, succeed their parents and agnates with equal portions, not obstructing or being able to obstruct, etc., in this case only. By certain knowledge, and by the fullness of Imperial power, we totally derogate to you and your aforesaid descendants, and any of you, granting that, as regards the aforesaid, with our Imperial authority, you may and can request.

Let no one at all infringe this page of our creation, ennoblement, insigniation, investiture, donation, concession, and largess, or contrary to it with any temerarious audacity. But if anyone should presume to contravene or attempt it, let him know that he will incur our most grave indignation, and also the penalty of 50 marks of purest gold, irremissibly, which we wish to be exacted and received from him who has contravened, as often as the contravention has been made, and we decree that half thereof be applied to our Imperial fisc, and the remainder to the uses of the roads.

The sign of the most serene Prince and Lord, Lord Charles IV, most invincible and glorious Roman Emperor, and King of Bohemia. Witnesses of this matter are the venerable Lambert of Spina, Peter of Ciruen, Albert of Padua, John of Brixen, Gerard of Nuremberg, bishops of churches; as well as the illustrious Albert and Leopold, brothers of Austria, Cazinitus of Stettin, Dukes, John called Zobissa, Margrave of Moravia, and the spectable Burchard of Ciruosus, and John of Burgundy of Magdeburg, as well as the nobles John of Papenheim, Marshal of the Holy Empire, and Bernard Asperanet, Lesiem, and Violartum Marinealcus of our court, Hasto desirecturum, and William of Acemburii, masters of our chamber, and many other nobles and faithful of ours and of the Holy Empire, under the golden bull of our majesty impressed, testimony of letters given in Bohemia, in the year of our Lord 1367, in the fifth indiction, on the Kalends of November, in the 22nd year of our reigns, and of the Empire the 13th.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an absent person can be legitimated.
2. Whether legitimation revives if the legitimated person subsequently ratifies it.
3. A legitimation in which the quality of the person effecting the legitimation is not expressed is invalid.
4. Children born during the lifetime of the wife cannot be legitimated.
5. The omission of a child not duly legitimated does not invalidate the will.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. It is proposed that a certain Antoniolus, having a wife and from her a single daughter named Casina, who was married and dowered, and also having from another unmarried woman two sons, Bartholomew and Thomas, and a daughter named Gentilina, constituted himself personally before us, the lord Peter de Fornasariis, Count of the Sacred Lateran Palace, in the absence of the aforementioned legitimate children, and caused them to be legitimized by the said Count. Finally, he made a testament, in which he instituted the said legitimate natural daughter as heir, passing over the said illegitimate sons, who were not named in any way in the said testament. And here it is first asked whether the said legitimation was valid or not. Secondly, it is asked whether the said testament is valid or not. And it is certain that the second question depends on the first. For if indeed the legitimation was valid, the testament, in which sons in power were passed over, was and is null by the law itself, as in the Institutes, On Disinheritance, in the beginning; and in the Digest, On Free and Posthumous Heirs, in the law *Gallus*, section *In omnibus*; the law *Inter caetera*; and the law *Si filius qui in potestate*; and in the Authenticum *Ut cum de appellatione cognoscitur*, section *Aliud quoque capitulum*. If the legitimation was made before the testament, but if it had been made after the testament, it breaks the testament by acknowledging them, as if they were posthumous children born after the testament while the testator was alive, as in the Digest, On Invalid Testaments, in the law *Posthumorum*; and in the Code, On Posthumous Heirs Instituted, law 2; and the aforementioned law *Gallus*. And this holds if the legitimation had been effective. But if the said legitimation was null, then the said illegitimate-born are spurious, and are not to be named as sons, nor could they have been named in the testament, as in the Authenticum *Qui modo necessario efficiantur sui*, section *Ultima*, column 7. And therefore they could not break the testament, as noted in law 1, section 1, of the Digest, On Contracts; and in the Code, On Natural Children, Authenticum *Licet*.

It is therefore necessary to examine whether the aforementioned legitimation was valid or not. In favor of the said legitimation stands the authority of the Prince and the tenor of the privilege. For the Prince can do this both by himself and through another, as is noted in the aforementioned §. fin. and in the extrajudicial title *Qui filii sint legitimi*, chapter *Per venerabilem*. From this it follows that the said legitimation fictions them as being legitimately born; it restores them to the right of nature, by which right all legitimate children were born. As stated in the Authenticum *Qui modo naturali efficiantur legitimi* and in another Authenticum *Qui modo naturales efficiantur sui* at the beginning. Nor does it matter that the said legitimate daughter was not cited; for the father could legitimize the other said children against her will and despite her objection. Therefore, all the more so could he do so while she was unaware, according to the legal rule *Quod potest inuitis*. Furthermore, the said legitimate daughter had no just cause for objecting in law. Moreover, she could not dispute her father’s inheritance while he was alive, as stated in the Code, title *De pactis*, law *Si*. And that the citation of the son is required in a legitimation made at the father’s petition is held by Bartolus in the law *Gallus*, and this is the truth. Namely, that the citation of legitimate children or of any other person is not required.

On the contrary, that the said legitimation does not hold, is evident from this reasoning: for just as no one can be emancipated while absent, as stated in the Digest, title *De adoptionibus*, law *Post mortem*, §. *Si*; nor can anyone be brought back under paternal power. Therefore, it is necessary that the legitimation take place in the presence of the legitimate child and with his consent; otherwise, he does not come into legitimate power, nor is he acknowledged, from which it clearly follows that by acknowledging him, the will is not broken. For agnation does not proceed while the father is alive, except through paternal power; and also that in succession he holds the first place, or among the first, as stated in the Digest, title *De inofficioso testamento*, law *Si quis filio exheredato* at the beginning. Moreover, this seems to be expressed in the aforementioned Authenticum *Qui modo naturales efficiantur sui*, §. *Generaliter*. For just as no one is legitimated without knowledge, so no one is legitimated while ignorant, as noted by Guillaume de Coucy in the Digest, title *De legitimatione*, law *De quibus*.

† But a doubt arises concerning this: because the text in the aforementioned §. generaliter states that the ratification of the legitimated persons suffices, and thus the ratification becomes valid. Argument from the Digest, *De rebus amissis*, *De hereditatibus*, l. *bonorum*. And then the legitimated person breaks the will, not as one never born, but as if posthumous. This passage is very doubtful. For where presence is required, ratification does not suffice. Likewise, where a right has been acquired by another, ratification does not extinguish that right. Moreover, it is certain that the father instituted the said daughter as a legitimate heir by a necessity imposed by law, as stated in the aforementioned §. *in omnibus*. And that which is done in the meantime out of necessity is not revoked, as noted in a similar case in the Digest, *De infaustis*, l. *furti*, §. 1. And the aforementioned points are proven in the Digest, *De solutionibus*, l. *cum r.* and l. *si quis offerenti*, §. *ult.*; and in the Digest, *De pignoribus*, l. *potior* and l. *qui balneum*. There is also a third reason why the said legitimation does not appear to be valid:

† because it does not mention that the said legitimated persons were spurious, and that the said legitimated person had a wife; and therefore the said legitimation was obreptitious, and obtained by subreption; because the truth was concealed, and thus it is not valid: as in D. de in ius vocando, l. si hac, § paterno. For he was fraudulent in concealing the fraud: as in C. si contra ius vel utilitatem publicam, l. et si legibus, and l. fi, and in c. 1, de filiis presbyterorum, lib. 6. And this is expressly held by Oldradus, that obreption in concealing fraud renders the legitimation null by law itself. And there is a fourth reason:

† because, while the wife is alive, children born in adultery cannot be legitimated: for it is impossible that they be feigned to have been born legitimately on account of the obstacle of the existing marriage, and those things which are altogether impossible cannot be feigned: as is noted in the Digest, *de legibus*, in the law *talis scriptura*; and by this there is an argument from the aforementioned authenticum *licet*, *de naturalibus liberis*. This is also confirmed by divine law: for the divine Scripture says, "The son of the bondwoman shall not be heir with the son of the freewoman." The solution, in my view, is that the said legitimation was invalid as being obtained by concealment of facts.

† and that the said testament of the father is valid, and that it could in no way be infringed by the said bastards. And from these points follows the determination of certain other questions: namely, in what manner the said legitimated persons succeed one another according to the form of the common law or of the statutes; for I say that they are not legitimated in law, but only in fact. And therefore there is no question of any transmission of paternal goods: as in C. ad Tertullianum, l. Si qua illustris; and in ff. unde cognati, l. Si spurius, and l. Hac parte. Moreover, according to civil law they are not to be maintained, but according to canon law they are, if the resources of the inheritance suffice: as in Extra, De eo qui duxit in matrimonium quam polluit per adulterium, c. Cum haberet. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether he who produced the instrument in court may seek to have an error contained in the instrument corrected.
1. Whether a notary may commit instruments, concerning which he has been requested, to another for subscription, and subscribe himself.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. It is proposed that a certain notary was requested to draw up an instrument concerning certain sales of revenues of certain territories, and to prepare a summary thereof. Thereafter, another notary, at the command of the aforementioned writer, transcribed said summary, and the aforementioned commander subscribed himself; finally, the said act was fabricated, and the said instrument was produced.

† After which, the aforementioned agent contends that an error occurred in the writing, and he requests that the error be corrected. On the opposing side, it is said that this cannot be done, because the aforementioned instrument was produced in court. And he who produces an instrument in court appears to confess that all things contained in the said instrument are true, as noted by Innocentius in the Decretals, *De censibus*, chapter *Cum olim*. And it is clear from the gloss which is in the Digest, *De editionibus*, law 1, § *Editiones*. Hence, he cannot come against the instrument and his own confession. Argument: Code, *De testibus*, law *Si quis testibus*; Code, *De non numerata pecunia*, law *Generaliter*; and what is noted in the Digest, *De pactis*, law *Iuris gentium*, § *Quod fere*; and in the Decretals, *De probationibus*, chapter *Per tuas*.

To the contrary, it seems on several grounds. First, because the truth of matters is not vitiated by such errors: Digest, *De officiis praesidis*, law *Illicitas*, § *Veritas*. Second, because an erroneous subscription does not harm: Code, *Plus valere quod agitur*, last law. Third, because the contrary is proved here by the protocol itself: Authenticum, *De tabellis*, § *Si*. Fourth, because here the error was made in another’s fact: last law, Digest, *Pro suo*. Fifth, because although one appears to confess those things narrated in the libel: Code, *De libera causa*, law *Vel cum precum*, nevertheless he can correct his error at the proper time: Digest, *Familiae erciscundae*, law *Qui filiae*. Sixth, because he who errs does not appear to confess, because he is rather deceived than confessing: Digest, *De constipulatione pecuniae*, last law, where it seems expressly stated. Seventh, because that which is defectively produced does not appear to be produced: Digest, *De editionibus*, law *Ubi exigitur*. Eighth and last, because the judge ought to follow the truth, once it is established: law and note in the Authenticum, *De tabellis*, in the beginning. And therefore the text says that those who scrutinize the truth of causes do not easily come to blame if they examine the truth: Authenticum, *Ut defuncti seu munera*, column 5. To the aforementioned, it serves: Digest, *De confessionibus*, law *Non fatetur*; and Code, *De iure et facto ignorantia*, law *Error*. And therefore, if the times permit, the producer can correct his error and order the notary to correct it, the truth being clarified. Argument: Digest, *De contrahenda et committenda stipulatione*, law *Optimam*, at the end.

† As to whether a notary may entrust his writings to another and subscribe his own name, it must be said that he may entrust them for transcription and subscribe his name if he is himself impeded; otherwise, he may not, lest opportunity be given to the transcriber to fabricate a forgery. And because a diversity of handwriting is somewhat suspect, as noted by Bartolus in the Digest, *De falsis*, l. 3, from the beginning. However, if one notary is requested, he cannot have another write for him, because the task cannot be delegated, as noted in the Authenticum *De tabellis*, § *Nos autem*. It is necessary, however, that the notary be requested by the parties, not by another notary.

Furthermore, it should be known that if an error is clearly apparent—because one thing appears in the protocol and another in the transcribed instrument—in transcriptions, the protocol must be followed, not the transcription. For transcriptions, insofar as they agree with the protocol, are private writings, as stated in the Code, *De eodem*, Authenticum *Si quis in aliquo documento*, and in the Corpus from which it is taken, and in the Extravagantes, *De fide instrumentorum*, c. 1. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether nullity may be cumulated with the grounds of appeal.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. On the aforementioned point, I say that the judge of the said second alleged appeal could have judged nothing, except that he was not a judge, or that jurisdiction was not established for him, and to absolve the appellant from the observance of the judgment. But those words, “and to be subject to the same defect, etc.,” effect nothing: because they were pronounced by an incompetent judge, and one who asserts himself to be incompetent, since the appeal is not established, and thus jurisdiction has not been devolved. As in c. Romana, § Si vero vocatis, de Appellationibus, lib. 6; and in the Speculum, de Appellationibus, § De officio, verb. Peccatum; and per Compostellensis, de Electionibus, c. Cum dilectus; and it is touched upon in c. Gaudet, de Fide instrumentorum, in the Novels. Hence, the proceeding sentence, from which it is said that the appeal remains firm: as in C. de Appellatione, l. Eos, in principio; and ff. de His qui non sunt informati, l. Furti, § 1; and what is noted there, and concerning nullity. That when an appeal is made from a sentence, and nullity is alleged, the ordinary gloss says that it comes incidentally. C. Quando provocare non est necessarium, l. 1. And therefore it was necessary to make proof of the appeal; otherwise, it does not appear that jurisdiction has been devolved. But according to what is proposed, even concerning nullity, nothing appears to be produced, namely, that nullity was in any way alleged in the appeal. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that, at the commencement of the litigation, suitable security be furnished, if it is found in the records that such a person has stood surety for the plaintiff regarding costs, etc., but it is not found that the plaintiff himself made a promise, whether the suretyship is valid, and how those words are to be understood.
2. A notary may be compelled by the judge, at the request of a party, to deliver the summary in the proper form and to declare himself.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The decree of the magnific and illustrious count provides that, in the principal letters, sportulae shall be paid or adequate security shall be given. Now it has happened that, upon the presentation of the libel, the following words are found written by the notary: namely, for whom the actor provided surety, Percivallus, for the restitution of expenses, renouncing, etc., and nothing more.

† It is asked whether the said suretyship is valid, when it does not appear that the principal has promised anything. And a suretyship obligation does not bind where the principal is found to be bound to nothing. I answer: This question is examined by Cynus in l. 1, C. de satis dando, where he finally concludes that the suretyship does not bind, nor does it seem that one can say that the principal is understood to have promised; because these stipulations require words: as ff. de verb. oblig. l. 1 and l. 5, §. satis acceptio. To the contrary it seems: because that word, "fideiussit" (has given surety), is placed improperly for an expromissor, so that the matter may be valid and not perish: as ff. de dolo, l. eleganter, §. seruus pactionis, and noted in ff. de pactis, l. in personam, §. qui pecuniam. Also, because in judicial proceedings a tacit stipulation is valid: as ff. de fideiussoribus tutorum, l. cum ostendimus, §. ult. Also, those words "promittendo" (by promising) and the rest can be referred both to the principal and to the surety, since they were uttered without any demonstration of the person, so that the matter may be valid and not perish. Argument from C. de liberis praeteritis vel exhaered. lege, l. 1. Also, these words the notary is bound to extend in the common form, so that the obligation binds. Argument from ff. de legibus 1, l. huiusmodi, in princ., with its gloss, and ff. de regulis iuris, l. si librarius, and noted in ff. de statu hominum, l. Imperator, according to Guillaume and Cynus. Also, this is supported by ff. de usufructu earum rerum quae usu consumuntur, l. tribus. For it suffices that the surety accedes to the legal obligation. To the same effect, Inst. de satisdatione, §. si vero aliquis. And because all things are presumed to have been done sufficiently, on account of the authority of the action and to preserve the vigor of judicial proceedings. Argument from ff. si quis cautionem, l. pe. Since, therefore, the defendant obtained victory in the first case, therefore the expenses ought rightly to be reimbursed to him; but under the name of expenses, the sportulae (fees) are included. As C. de fructibus et litis expensis, l. fi. But against this it is objected: because the first sentence seems to have been annulled against the judge of the appeal. Therefore, from it one cannot sue for expenses by virtue of the said satisfaction. As ff. de iudiciis, solui, l. cum apud Sempronium.
