I answer: This does not obstruct, because by the last sentence the first was confirmed. And thus the stipulation that the first [sentence] endures. Nor does it obstruct that in the last sentence there was made an absolution from the expenses of the last litigation. The sentence says nothing about the first litigation. And therefore my reasoning stands firm.

Secondly, it seems to be said that the aforementioned notary, who wrote the document, ought to be compelled by the judge, at the request of the party, to render the said summary in the proper and customary form of that notary and of other notaries, and according to what the decree of the Lord dictates: notwithstanding that he has already rendered it in the form in which he renders it; because by this he is not contradicting himself, but rather declaring himself, which he may do by order of the judge, when the truth is clear. As is fully noted by Cynus in the Digest, *De statu hominum*, law *Imperator*, in his reading. And it is noted specifically in the *Speculum*, *De instrumentis exhibendis*, section *Instrumentum*, subsection *Sed nunquid*. And this is confirmed, because since we do not say for whom he stood as surety, such writing would be in a manner false if it were not understood that the debtor had promised; because it would be impossible for the surety to have stood as surety. Hence, since the writing is most true and is presumed true, as in the Code, *De probationibus*, law *Cum precibus*, from the necessary truth of the words is inferred the necessary antecedent: that both were present at the time of the execution of the instrument of the principal cause, as in the Digest, *De verborum obligationibus*, law *Sciendum*, and in the Institutes, *De inutilibus stipulationibus*, section *Si scriptum*. Furthermore, even if it were assumed that this were not a necessary argument, it is nevertheless a probable argument, on account of which it is said that the notary is ordered to narrate and write the fact fully, just as a witness is compelled to tell the bare and full truth. As is noted in the Digest, *De inquisitionibus*, law *Lutius*, and in the Extravagantes, *De accusationibus*, chapter *Cum dilecti*. Therefore, for the greater clarity of the truth and to remove all doubt, let it be commanded to the notary and let him be compelled, as has been said. And thus the instrument ought to be declared for caution, and the expenses ought to be reimbursed. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 0. The right of patronage is proved by ancient documents. Likewise, whether ancient letters engraved on stones prove, or not
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

Whether the patronage of the church is proved by ancient letters, it seems that it is not, as in C. de relictis, l. monumentorum, where it is said that such inscriptions made on stones or columns do not confer a right. To the contrary are several ordinary glosses, that such writings, with the lapse of long time, make proof. This is the ordinary gloss in c. cum causam, extra de probat.; de praescriptis, c. ad audientiam; el. 2, de censibus; c. cum olim, 24 q. 2; c. sane. For these are called titles, to which credence is to be given, unless the contrary appears, since they are supported by the lapse of long time. Otherwise, if the writings were made recently, it is not established that they are public, as in C. nemo privatus titulus, in rubro et nigro. And thus the said law monumentorum is understood. It pertains to the aforesaid: ff. de probationibus, l. census; ff. de albo scribendo, l. 1. Moreover, what appears in the said written letters is confirmed in the bell tower by letters directed to the said nobles, asserted as uncles. For although the said letters were directed for another purpose and do not induce truth where truth would be, as in ff. de pace, l. epistola, in princ., and C. de probationibus, l. non nudis, l. non epistolis, yet because the said words signify the final cause of that upon which the letters are founded, they provide great assistance regarding the proof of the case. Arg. C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione, l. optimam, especially considering who writes and to whom it is written. For the writing was of that great abbot, with the presence and counsel of whom the abbot and his associates were present; it is not likely that he mixed falsehood into his letters. 96. dist., c. nobilissimus. Rather, the abbot acknowledged good faith, as in ff. de administratione tutorum, l. quotiens, § sicut. Furthermore, in such matters that exceed the limit of human memory, fame sufficiently proves, as noted in C. de rei venditione, l. iudicia, and ff. de negotiis gestis, l. atqui natura, § cum me absente. It supports what is noted by Baldus in c. 1, de appellationibus. From all these, mutually aiding each other in the proof of patronage, it seems to me that the right of patronage of the aforesaid church is sufficiently proved, or can be proved, if urged in court. To the aforesaid it pertains, as noted in c. t., de consecratione ecclesiae vel altaris, in the novella, or ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. in testamento quidam; as in ff. de origine iuris, l. 2, in the words pro rostris; and ff. de institoria actione, l. sed et si pupillus, § proscribere. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. From what presumptions a contract of sale is presumed to be a pledge, and thus made in fraud of usury, up to number 15.
2. The ecclesiastical judge is the competent judge in cases of fraud of usury.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen. In the case of Galuagini the moneylender, it has been prudently alleged that the contracts in question, from their very terms, consequences, and agreements, clearly indicate that they were concluded in fraud of usury, considering that the character of the said Galuagini concurs, and indeed constitutes the foundation for presuming the malice of usury: although the contract was made so cautiously that the fraud cannot be entirely comprehended from its origin alone. Nevertheless, from what follows, the intent declared in the preceding matters is revealed, and the fraud committed through an interposed person. As is shown in C. de natu. lib. l. si quis seu. For it appears that the interposed person intervened as a minister, not as one deriving benefit. As in ff. de manumis. l. 4. §. si ab ignoto. and ff. de do. inter vi. et vx. l. mulier. otherwise beginning sulpicius. and quod no. ff. de le. 1. l. in taci.

† To prove, however, that the said contracts, although made under the words of sale, are nevertheless considered to be pignorative, the following is alleged first: the congruity of the price, from which fraud and simulation are presumed. As in Extra, De pignoribus, c. Illo vos; De emptione et venditione, c. Ad nostram; De usuris, c. Conquestus.

† Secondly, it is proved, because, considering the preponderance of the price, and that pact: if it shall be worth more, he gave it as a gift; and it will be worth double more: and to be worth more than the words sound, it is that they were sold in part, and given as a gift in the greater part. From which the law presumes fraud: as C. man. l. per diuersos. and l. ab Anastasio. and noted ff. de pac. si tibi. per Gul. de Cu.
Thirdly, because the law invalidates the alleged donation: as in the Digest, *De transactionibus*, law *Cum Aquiliana*.
Fourth, because no insinuation took place: as provided in C. de donationibus, l. sancimus, and l. si quis ex argentariis. Fifth, I return to the point at issue,

† And it is argued thus. The argument from the price of resale, and the custom of lending at interest, induce proof of a simulated sale, and prove that in truth there was a pledge. As in c. *Illi vos*, extra de pignoribus, and there noted by the gloss and Innocent. It is made by l. *Vel universorum*, ff. de pignoribus; l. *Qui semissis*, in fine, ff. de usuris; l. *Iube*, in §. *Idem Papinianus*, ff. de actionibus empti et venditi; and noted in l. *Cum allegas*, C. de usuris. But here the price of resale is increased, and the custom of lending at interest is present, as is proved in the case. Therefore, all these things are proved to have been done in fraud of usury.

† Sixthly, it is argued as follows. Where the thing is found to have remained with the seller, the sale is presumed to be simulated: as in l. Sicut, §. Superuacuam, Qui de modo pignoris vel hypothecae solvuntur, and there Bartolus notes; and by the same author in l. Post contractum, D. De donationibus; by Dynus in l. Omnes, §. Lucius, D. De his quae in fraudem creditorum fiunt; by Cynus in l. 2, C. De repudianda hereditate. It is supported by l. Si is qui, D. De acquisitione hereditatis. But this thing never departed from the Seller, but was always with him, as stated in the case. Therefore, the sale is presumed to be simulated. Nor does it avail that the seller declared himself to hold possession in the name of the buyer; because, to escape suspicion, it is required that the thing have truly passed out of the seller’s ownership: as in l. Unica, De suffragiis. Nor is it sufficient that the buyer holds possession by declaration, as noted by Bartolus in the aforementioned l. Sicut, §. Superuacuam.

† Seventhly, it is argued as follows: a penalty added to the principal amount gives rise to a presumption of usury; as stated in l. cum allegas, C. de usur.; l. placuit; l. pecuniae, ff. de usur.; l. Iul., §. idem Pap., ff. de acq. emp. It is also supported by what is noted in l. rogasti, §. si tibi, ff. si cert. pet.; l. si tibi, in princ., ff. de pact., and there by Bartolus. It is further supported by what is noted in l. sed et si, §. quaesitum, ff. si quis caut. But here the penalty was added to the principal amount in case of non-payment, as appears in the instrument of 600 livres and in the final instrument of lease and pact of redemption, because a penalty was stipulated that, in the event of default in payment, could be demanded. Therefore, etc.

† Eighthly, it is argued thus: Unusual clauses give rise to a presumption of fraud, suspicion, and simulation. L. si quis sub condi., ff. de cond. et demonstr. et ibi noted in the gloss and by Bartolus. If in such contracts many unusual clauses have been added. And this is especially evident in the instrument of florins 600 and livres 60, and in the instrument of the last lease, where a pact is added that the debtor is bound to pay the charges. Therefore, etc.

† Ninthly, it is argued thus: nearly all the agreements induce a presumption of usury in favor of the buyer and to the detriment of the seller, as is stated by Hostiensis in the Institutes, on pledges, in the chapter *Qualiter detegatur*, in the sum of the same. But here, almost all the agreements were added in favor of the buyer, as is evident in the principal places, and in the pact of redemption, and also in the last one, and in the sale made to Tonino the tutor. Therefore, etc.

† The tenth argument proceeds as follows. Agreements appended contrary to, or beyond, the nature of the contract give rise to a presumption of usury, especially in the customary practice of lending, as noted in the chapter *Illo vos*, Extra, *De pignore*. But here many things are appended contrary to and beyond the nature of the contract of sale. For, first, it is contrary to the nature of the contract of sale that the seller is bound to pay the tolls and other burdens of the contract and of the thing sold, and is bound to acknowledge them, as stated in the law *Debet*, and the glosses thereon, Digest, *De edicto*. Furthermore, it is beyond the nature of the contract that he has no right, yet ratifies the contract, provides a surety for eviction, as in the law *Caius*, Digest, *De pignore*, *Actiones*. But if the first sale made by the said Parmeria, procuratrix of George, had been true and not simulated, no right would have remained in the said sold things with George, as in the law *Traditionibus*, Code, *De pactis*, and the law *Clauibus*, Digest, *De emptione et venditione*, Institutes, *De rerum divisione*, § *Interest*. And thus the ratification of the subsequent sales would have been futile, and the promise of eviction made by George would not have been necessary. But because it was held in mind that even the pledge and the simulated sale were doubtful, as was said by Galuagin, lest the said George could contravene, he wished to ratify the said contracts and thus to bind himself regarding eviction. Therefore, etc.

† Eleventhly, it is argued thus: the incongruity of the pension, and its smallness in relation to the said things leased to George and purchased by him from Galuaginus, induces a presumption of usury. For it is not probable that anyone would wish to squander his own property: as in l. cum de indebito, ff. de probat. and especially a usurious lender, who is greedy and avaricious: as in d. 48, c. quoniam; and c. si hi, 13 q. 3; c. quam multi. Such is Galuaginus. But here, a much higher pension could have been obtained for these things purchased by Galuaginus than was being paid by George; therefore, if the said things had truly been leased by Galuaginus, he would have leased them at a fictitious price. But because the said things were in truth pledged, and this was a fiction, they were usuries which Galuaginus ought to have received; and he did not care for a higher fiction than the usuries owed to him. And that a higher fiction could have been obtained is evident from the last lease, whose fiction was 150 florins, whereas in the first leases it was only 100; namely, because the usuries owed regulated the said fiction, so that as the usuries increased, the fiction and the redemption prices increased. Therefore, etc. And the aforementioned allegations, or any one of them, although wisely made by another, are nevertheless found in the first part in many consilia given by me in this matter.

12. It must be considered that it is left to the discretion of the judge, based on the quality of the persons, reputation, place, and other proofs and presumptions, whether such contracts are to be deemed usurious. For from the quality and difference of persons something is presumed, which otherwise would not be presumed: as in c. 1, de feudis; Guar. and Castal., col. 10; and note by Bartolus, ff., de donationibus, l. post contractum, in the words "sed quæro quanto tempore" etc.; and thus holds Jacobus de Aretino in a certain question disputed by him. And this is the truth. To this effect is ff., de re iudicata, l. non omnes, § a barbaris; and in the rubric, semel malus. 13
† Moreover, on account of the interdict of the law, fraud is presumed to be simulated: as is stated in the Digest, under the title "On Proof," in the law "He who makes a will."
† Likewise, deceit and fraud are presumed not only from preceding circumstances, but also from subsequent and consequential ones, as in C. de adulteriis, l. Si qui.

† Moreover, the very fact that someone purchases through an interposed person, if that person is suspect, gives rise to a presumption of fraud. See Digest 26.1.14.1, § et si per interpositam. From these authorities it is clearly concluded that the said contracts, by their very nature, sequence, and consequence, and by the course of trade, are to be deemed usurious.

† Regarding the question of who ought to take cognizance of fraud, it must be said that the ecclesiastical judge [is the proper authority], as is stated in the extrajudicial decretals on usury, *Quia in omnibus*; and in the chapter *Prae* on oaths; the chapter *Debitores*; and the chapter *Ad nostram*; and fully noted in the *Speculum* on usury, after the beginning, where a libel is also formulated in this matter. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The defendant, being a usurer, may raise the objection against the plaintiff that the contract was made in fraud of the laws concerning usury.
2. Where both parties are equally at fault, the condition of the defendant is the stronger.
3. Whether proof may be adduced against the cause of an instrument, unless by means of an instrument.
4. If a person detained in prison has property in another territory under the same sovereign, from which he can provide for the debt, whether he should be released. Where bail is necessary, and the defendant cannot easily furnish it there, he ought to be heard if he is prepared to furnish it in another part of the same province.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† In the case of Baptista de Bianchis, it seems to be said that the said Baptista ought to be admitted to prove the exception of simulation regarding the substance, i.e., the cause of the usurious and loan contract. For there is no doubt that whenever the defendant can oppose the exception of simulation: as in C. plus valere quod agitur, l. emptione. Likewise, against a cause inserted in fraud of usury, there is no doubt that proof by instruments and witnesses is admitted: as in Extra de pignoribus, c. illo vos; and de emptione et venditione, c. ad nostram; and de iureiurando, c. ad nostram.

† and thus both are usurers. In equal fault, the condition of the defendant is the better. As is most fully noted by Innocentius in the Extravagant, *De adulteriis*, chapter *Intelleximus*. And it is proven in the Digest, Book 50, Title 17, law *Cum mulier*, and law *Viro atque uxore*. Nor does it avail what I said concerning the proof of witnesses, which is noted in the Code, *De non numero personarum*, law *Generaliter*, and in the Digest, *De pactis*, law *Iuris gentium*, section *Quod fere*.

† where it is stated that nothing contrary to the cause of an instrument can be proved, except by an instrument. For this, three responses are given. First, because this is sufficiently proved by instruments: for from instruments arises a presumption of fraud, from antecedent and subsequent circumstances. Hence it is rightly said to be proved by an instrument, as in C. de apocryphis, l. Quicunque, lib. 10. Second, because those laws speak when simulation of a contract is not alleged. For when the defect of consent of both parties is then alleged, proof by witnesses is admitted, as in d. l. Emptio. Third, because it is a special rule, out of hatred for usurers, that proof by witnesses and presumptions is admitted. A fourth reason is that when a contract is contrary to law, as is a simulated contract in fraud of usury, and any other contract made in fraud of the law, fraud and deceit can be proved by indicia, as in C. de dolo, l. Dolum. But if the contract were not contrary to law, then the contrary laws would have place. This proof shall be made before the bishop, or by a libel presented before him concerning the release of the imprisoned person, or by proceeding more cautiously. The usurious exception shall be raised in the secular forum, and it shall be requested that the proof be remitted to the bishop, as in c. Si iudex laicus, de sententia excommunicationis, lib. 6.

† On another point, even if the arrest had been lawfully made, which it was not: it must be said that, since the said prisoner has in another nearby domicile, and under the same temporal lord, goods sufficient to cover the debt, and since a postponement has been granted with respect to those goods, the said possession takes the place of bail; as stated in the Digest, *De carceribus edicto*, law *De bonis*, § *Qui pupillo*. From this, by every right, the said Baptista ought to be released from prison; otherwise, if the said admission [of the goods as security] had not been made, because goods situated in another territory would not render him suspect; as noted in the law *Si*, Code, *De principalibus agentibus in rebus*, Book 12.

But neither is it to be omitted that, where bail is necessary and the defendant cannot easily furnish it in the place where he is sued, he may be heard if he is prepared to furnish bail in another city of the same province: as in D. qui sat. cog. l. qui fideius. §. si necessaria, and l. pe. dic. §. plena, versi. diuersum. Hence, if this man could furnish bail in Vicenza, the matter would be clearer, namely that he ought to be released upon furnishing bail, unless the custom of the place were otherwise. However, since this detained man does not seek to have the seizure of his goods revoked, but only seeks to be heard on the allegation of simulation, alleging that it was done in favor of usury, and thus, notwithstanding the res iudicata by the secular judge, the first statement remains true, namely that the said possession yields to bail. It is certainly not doubtful under civil law that, where a debtor has sufficient assets, he ought not to be imprisoned for a civil debt: as in C. qui bonis cedere possunt, l. 1, and D. de susp. tut. l. 3, §. tutores qui. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If a compromise has been made in favor of three arbitrators, one of whom cannot serve as an arbitrator, whether the sentence rendered by those three is valid.
2. A sentence rendered without any preceding proof, even if confirmed twice or thrice, cannot be enforced despite the exception of nullity.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. It is proposed that a certain compromise was made to three persons, both in law and in fact, namely to a certain master in theology and two others. And it is contained in the instrument that the compromise was made to the said master with the license of his president; who this president was is not named in the instrument. It is also provided in the said compromise that the parties promised to abide by the sentence of the lords. And a broad power was also granted to proceed in law and in fact, as it pleased the said arbitrators. Now it has happened that the said arbitrators rendered a condemnatory sentence without any proofs being made or received before them. From this sentence an appeal was taken once and twice; and always the said sentence was confirmed without hearing anyone and without receiving any proofs; so that all who pronounced judgment followed the same error, because without knowledge of the case, as they pronounced arbitrarily, and so did these subsequent judges. Now execution is sought, and it is opposed that the sentence of the said arbitrators was [null]. Now it is asked, how execution is impeded by the said exception. And it seems at first sight to be said,

† That only the first sentence of the arbitrators was valid, due to the very broad power granted to them; and also the confirmatory sentences, because no error was expressed in them, and because they appear to have pronounced judgment after cognizance of the cause, since this was presumed from the first sentence. The third sentence even more so, because it was presumed in favor of the first and second, as in Extra, de renuntiationibus, c. In praesentia; and Digestum, de evictionibus, l. Herennius, § 1; and Digestum, de actionibus, l. Si expressum. Moreover, since three sentences have been issued, even assuming that they were null by law itself, execution ought not to be impeded, but ought to be carried out, however, under the hope of retraction, as in c. Ut calumniis, de re iudicata, in the Clementinae. To this point, the last law, de ordine cognitionum, is most apt, and what Innocentius notes in Extra, de officio delegati, c. Cum in iure. But the truth seems to lie to the contrary. And I premise that a Minor Brother, even with the consent of the General Minister, could not act as an arbitrator, just as a slave could not with the consent of his master; because such a compromise does not fall upon a slave, as in Digestum, de verbis significatis, l. Illa verba. And Minor Brothers are prohibited from such secular offices by their own rule, from which dispensation cannot be made by their superior, as in c. Exiit qui seminat, de verborum significatione, lib. 6. Nor can they involve themselves in litigious affairs, as in Clem. Exivi de paradiso, § Cupientes, and § Cumque dicti ordinis professores. Furthermore, in the instrument it is not expressed who this presiding officer was. Hence the instrument is invalid as uncertain, as in Digestum, de negotiis gestis, l. Papius, § fin.; and Codex, qui testamentum facere possint, l. Hac consultissima. For by reason of its generality and indefiniteness, the instrument is obscure and proves nothing. Argument: Digestum, de testamento tutelae, l. Duo sunt Titii.

These things therefore being presupposed as true, I state this doubt: because power was given to two by the compromise. Since therefore all three pronounced judgment, the sentence is valid by reason of the two, as in Digestum, de arbitris, l. Sed si ita, and l. Non distinguimus, § 1, cum in plures; and in Speculum, de arbitris, § Excipitur, ver. Item quod erant plures; and in c. Uno delegatorum, de officio delegati, ult. responsio, and what is noted there by Butrinteus. But in this it must be observed: that although the other two could have acted without this Minor Brother, nevertheless they did not wish to pronounce judgment without him; so that they did not use the power of two, because they did not wish to use it. And therefore I see the award as null, as in Extra, de officio delegati, c. Cum super abbatia. And thus it seems expressly noted there by Innocentius, unless it be said that there is a special case when one proceeds with a colleague who is suspected and recused. Argument: Digestum, quod falso tutor, l. 1, § Idem Pomponius. Also, because they began to cognize together, Butrinteus says there that one cannot act without the other. To this point serves l. 1, Digestum, de officio consulis. Just as therefore if a free man pronounces judgment with a slave, the pronouncement is invalid, as in Digestum, de iudicibus, l. Cum praetor, § Placet, and Digestum, de arbitris, l. Pedius, so it must be said in the case of a Minor Brother, that he is held as dead, since he is a slave of his religion and bound by the rule prohibiting it.

Also, the contracting parties erred in law, since they chose him as a more solemn arbitrator, perhaps not having done so otherwise. And thus the compromise did not hold, as in Digestum, de iure omnium iudiciorum, l. Si per errorem. Nor can the award given by the Minor Brother be confirmed, because there is an expressed error in the confirmation; as if it were said, "I confirm the award given by a slave." This passage is sufficiently doubtful, although it is certain that a Minor Brother cannot be an arbitrator or decider of any litigious matter according to the newest laws, which the Speculum did not see.

But let us assume that the compromise was valid: nevertheless, since the sentence was condemnatory and rendered without any proof, the glossators determine that a condemnatory sentence is void by operation of law (ipso iure nulla) not in an arbitrator, but in a judge, who is of greater authority. As is noted in C. de sententiis et interlocutionibus omnium iudicum, l. prolatam; and in Extra de constitutionibus, c. cum ecclesia S. Mariae; and in 2. q. j., c. nos in quenquam, in the following chapter. And Innocentius says that a judge, to whom nothing has been proved, can order nothing. As in ca. solet, at the end, de sententia excommunicationis. From which it seems clearly to be concluded that the said sentence, having been rendered without any preceding proofs, was void by operation of law, and does not merit execution; nor does the confirmation, which suffers from a similar defect, avail. As is noted in the aforementioned l. si expressim. The aforementioned l. fina., C. de ordine cognitionum, does not obstruct this, because there the nullity was not clear, whereas here it is. Likewise, the aforementioned ca. vt calumniis does not obstruct this, because under civil law it is established that a sentence should never be committed to execution without other proof when nullity is evident; especially when it is void for lack of jurisdiction, or quasi-jurisdiction. As in ff. de re iudicata, l. 3, § si condemna; and as is noted in c. j., de sequestro possessionum et fructuum, in the final gloss. In cle. propter quae, it can be said both equally and reasonably, according to what is proposed, that the said sentences cannot be committed to execution, nor can it be said otherwise, since they are void by operation of law, unjust, and rendered improperly without observing the order of law and without any cognizance of the case. And supporting the foregoing is Extra de confirmationibus, utrum vel inutiliter, c. examinata, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Credit is given to an instrument stating that all things were done with due solemnity.
2. A thing may be purchased in perpetuity, and for a fixed term.
3. A citation made according to the form of the instrument is valid, whatever words are used, provided they are clear.
1. The right to protest passes to the singular successor.
2. A protest made publicly, and brought to the knowledge of those who have an interest, is said to be lawful.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Whether the said contract is presumed to have been solemnly celebrated. It must be said that it is: because the instrument mentions the solemnity, with the intervention of a decree. Hence, one must adhere to the instrument executed with public authority. The gloss is ordinary in l. 1, C. de fide instrumentorum et iure hastae fiscalis, lib. 10. This is also held by Speculum, because wherever a decree of a superior is found appended to a sale, everything is presumed to have been done solemnly, as noted in Speculum, de emptione et venditione, §. nunc dicendum, ver. et breviter scias. Moreover, the said contract did not merely remain within the bounds of a contract, but passed into the force of law, to which one must adhere, as in C. de vendendis rebus civilibus, l. 1, in fine, where the text is literal, and as noted in l. quod semel, ff. de decretis ab ordinariis facienda.

† On the second point, it must be said that a thing can be sold in perpetuity and for a fixed term; likewise, annuities can be sold, as is stated in D. 18.1.17 *necessario* § *si* and D. 18.1.34 *si debitor* § *verisimile*. And that this contract was a contract of sale appears from its terms. This is clearly and fully noted by Bartolus in D. 49.14.1 *cotem* § *qui maximos*. On the third point, it must be said that

† Finally, the citation in question was sufficient, because the form was observed, or at least the effect of the instrument. And it is not of importance by what words someone is said to have spoken, provided that it is clear, as in C. de testamentis, l. quam indignum. And regarding the protestation, see the glossa ordinaria in l. de pupillo §. meminisse, ff. de no. ope. nun. It does not matter what is said by Cy. in C. de in integ. resti. mino., l. in minorum, and ff. de bonis libe., l. Paulus.

† Regarding the fourth point, it must be said that the right of protest passes to the singular successor, if it has been assigned to him by special or general words. The text is noted in the Digest, *De evictionibus*, in the law *Si res quam*; [and in the title] *De iureiurando*. However, I do not think that an oath can be assigned, because it is personal on the part of the one swearing. See the Decretals, *De iureiurando*, chapter *Veritatis*; and the Code, *De rebus creditis*, law *Generaliter*, in the beginning.

† Regarding the fifth point, it must be said that the aforementioned public protests were made and brought to the knowledge of those who govern the city, and were lawfully made, as is stated in the Digest, *de re iudicata*, in the law *Non potest dolo carere*. From these it appears that the contract is lawful and solemn, and must be observed both as against the persons of the contracting parties and their successors, as has been said. I, Baldus.

In the Name of Christ, Amen. It must be stated for clarity that a vassal sometimes sells but does not deliver; and then there is no doubt that by the mere [sale] etc. You will find this opinion above in opinion 376, beginning: "It must be stated for clarity" etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether that which someone receives from a pupillary substitution comes under a fideicommissum.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† On the aforementioned point, if we examine the will simply, in l. ita tamen, §. qui suspectam, the law states that in a fideicommissary substitution, that which one acquires from a pupillary substitution does not come into play, unless he has accepted the inheritance under compulsion. The glossa, however, understands that the heir was instituted, there being substituted to the disinherited pupillus, and he was requested to restore the paternal inheritance: but others do not make this distinction. For they say that even if the pupillus was instituted, and the brother of the pupillus, or an outsider; and even if he was substituted to the pupillus, that which he acquired from the pupillary substitution, because the pupillus predeceased, does not come into the restitution of the fideicommissum, unless he was compelled to accept. And the reason is, because it appears that he acquired from the testament of the minor, as in ff. de inoff. testa. l. Papinianus, §. sed nec impuberis, where the glossa says that the pupillary substitution is truly the testament of the father, but more truly it is that of the minor himself. Also, because it seems absurd that if the pupillus had maternal goods, or goods acquired from elsewhere, that such goods should come into the fideicommissary substitution, unless the pupillary substitute was specifically burdened with restoring these, as in ff. de vul. sub. cohaeredi, §. cum filiae, ver. fideicommisso. For no one doubts that the testator can burden the pupillary substitute with restoring the goods of the pupillus acquired from wherever, if he declares this in his testament: but if he does not declare it, it seems to refer only to the goods of the testator himself, because this is the nature of the fideicommissary substitution in the said §. cum filiae. Others say, and this is the opinion of Bartolus, that if the testator first provides, by substituting pupillarily, afterwards he imposed the burden of the fideicommissum, by stating that in the fideicommissary substitution comes that which is acquired from the pupillary, because the burdened party is understood to be restoring all and the whole of that which was previously left to him by the testator, considering the order of the intellect. Thus notes Bartolus in the said §. suspecta, citing l. scævola, ff. ad Treb., which seems to make little point, because there it speaks of a substitution made in codicils, which turns into an oblique one as regards the mode of succeeding: but as regards the goods, it concerns the same goods of the testator which came into the direct substitution. These therefore conclude that the inheritance of the pupillus must be restored in its entirety except for the trebellianic portion: because the legitime is not owed to the substitute outsider requested in his own person to restore the inheritance of the pupillus, as noted by Cynus according to Dino in C. de inoff. testam. l. tribus. If therefore in the question posed the dispute were to claim a place, when the testator had requested the restoration of only one, namely the instituted heir, and substituted pupillarily. But here he requested the restoration of both instituted heirs, and said, and if both should die without legitimate and natural children from wherever, or in pupillary age, he substituted to them Paul, etc. Since therefore a fideicommissary substitution was made to both, the portion of each comes into the restitution of the fideicommissum, deducting the legitime and the trebellianic portion. Hence the pupillary substitute, not as himself requested, but as the pupillus requested, after the death of the substitute transmits the right of deducting the two fourths, and the other half must be restored to the universal fideicommissary. And this is noted by Bartolus in the said §. cum filiae. And thus I have previously advised on the aforementioned case, and I advise anew. And thus the testator can make a pupillary substitution to his son after the death of the minor only: and add a fideicommissary substitution, in which his brother should die: as was in the case, and these words of the testament declare expressly, from which one must not depart, as in §. cum in verbis, and C. de necess. seruis haered. inst. l. cum quidam pupillum, in fi. And it makes well ff. ad Trebel. haeredes mei, §. cum ita, when it says, that the grandfather wished to have the whole, if he had also received the portion of the youngest brother, and so forth. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the mother is under the necessity of petitioning for a guardian for her ward, to whom a pupillary substitution was made in the father’s will.
2. At the time of the father’s death, the son was a ward; yet, if he dies while an adult, the mother is not excluded from his succession on account of a guardian not having been petitioned for.
3. A mother who enters into a second marriage, when there are no children from the first marriage, incurs no penalty.
4. Whether the blood relatives of a woman entering into a second marriage may give her a dowry, or anything else in which the children of the first marriage cannot have a right.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. It must be premised for the sake of clarity,

† That where a ward has a pupillary substitute, the mother is not burdened with the necessity of petitioning for a guardian, at least from the prince, by that rule that guardianship returns to the person to whom the inheritance comes, as in D. de regulis iuris, l. Quod tutela. However, Bartolus in l. 2, D. qui petant tutores, and in the question disputed by him, which he there recites, [holds otherwise].

Secondly, it must be premised that, although the son was a minor at the time of his father’s death, if he died in adulthood, the mother is not excluded from the succession, as provided in the law *Matres*, Codex, *ad Tertullianam*.

Thirdly, it must be premised that a mother who has entered into a second marriage, upon the death of all her children, suffers no penalties of second nuptials, as provided in C. de secundis nuptiis, l. foeminae, and in the Authenticum de nuptiis, § quoniam infirmas. Fourthly, it must be premised that,

† That a woman cannot do anything in fraud of the children of the first marriage, towards the second husband; but if the brothers of the woman, or other friends, wish to dowry her from the woman’s goods, or other friends wish to dowry her, not from the woman’s goods, with a pact of gaining, this cannot be infringed by the children of the prior marriage, unless fraud were proven, as C. de secund. nupt. l. hac edictali. in fin. Fifthly, it must be premised that there is no question of the legitime of living children, because the legitime is not owed between the living, but after death, as l. fin. ff. de libe. agno. From these, therefore, such a distinction is gathered, that if the children, concerning whom it is asked, are living, there is no question of succession from the dowry, which is given by an outsider. But if they are dead as pubescent, the mother is not repelled from intestate succession, but is bound to restore the inheritance by fideicommissum. But if they died as impubescent, then it would be necessary to go to the dispute of Bart. But it could be said that even then the mother would be excused on account of the pupillary substitutes, upon whom lay the burden of seeking a tutor, as C. de legi. haer. sciant. And because in the theme nothing is declared about age or death, therefore I was obliged to distinguish, as I said above. I, Bal.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a prelegacy made to a son instituted as heir is valid.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. It is proposed that the son alone was instituted as heir, and that in the will the father ordered certain pious offices to be exercised in perpetuity, expressly binding all his goods. Finally, in another part of the will, the father gave a specific house to the said son by prelegacy, and he wishes to sell it.

† It is asked whether he may sell it by right? And it seems that he may not. For an heir cannot be given a legacy by himself, as in D. de legatis 1, l. Legatum, §. Haeredi. And thus the said house comes into the obligation, just like the other hereditary goods, as it would come into a universal restitution of the heir under a fideicommissum left to the wife, as in D. ad Trebellianam, l. In fideicommissis, §. Final, and D. de legatis 1, l. Plane, §. Si duobus. On the contrary, for this is clearly against the will of the deceased. Since the father wished that the son should have the said principal house, as noted by Rogerius in the said §. Haeredi. Moreover, this seems to be expressed in D. de usu, l. In fideicommissis, §. Cum Pollidius. Therefore, rightly, the said house should not be in general obligation, but should be free in the hands of the son, because the specific derogates from the general, as in Cap. Generi, de regulis iuris, and D. de adimendis legatis, Alimenta, §. Basilicae, and l. Stichus nutricis. So, it must be said that if the valuation of this house does not exceed the son’s legitime, that is, one-third part of all the goods, the son may freely sell it. For the father seems to have assigned the legitime to himself in the house itself, as is fully read and noted in C. familiae erciscundae, Filium, quem habentem. But if it exceeds, then the question would be quite doubtful; nevertheless, in the case of a daughter, I think paternal affection should be presumed. And because there are sufficient indications that the father wished the said house to be specially bequeathed, it should be free to the son, arg. D. de minoribus, l. Si in emptione. Therefore, it seems to me that it may be freely alienated by the said son, always reserving the sounder opinion. I, Baldus.

In the Name of Christ, Amen. A certain Nicholas made his will, in which, among other things, he ordered as follows, namely, in all his other goods, etc. See above, in opinion 170, beginning, a certain Nicholas, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether an heir can be instituted for a hospital that does not yet exist but is ordered to be established by executors appointed in the will, or by the bishop. Likewise, before it is established, what is the status of the construction? Likewise, what is the status of the goods of the said testator? This is a beautiful and everyday matter.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. It must be premised for the sake of clarity,

† That an heir may be instituted for a hospital to be constructed by executors appointed in the testament, or by the legitimate executor, namely the bishop: for this institution is similar to the institution of a posthumous heir, as in Inst. de legatis § posthumus, and Inst. de bonorum possessionibus in principio. Nevertheless, there is this difference: a posthumous child may not be born, whereas a hospital cannot fail to be made. For it will necessarily be made; but before it is made, it cannot be an heir, nor can the inheritance be entered upon for its sake, nor can possession of goods be claimed. See Extra de ecclesiis aedificandis, ad audientiam; and D. de servitutibus praediorum rusticorum, si servitus § futuro; and what is read and noted in C. literas de rescriptis inclementia. What, therefore, is to be done in the meantime, before it is built? Response: If the question is asked regarding certain goods to be administered, if we speak with respect to the construction, then the testamentary executor has the duty to have this construction carried out; nevertheless, he cannot, with respect to this, occupy the goods or sell anything, unless with the authority of the diocesan bishop; because the testamentary executor cannot do more than what is permitted to him in the testament, as in D. de alimentis et cibariis legatis, l. alio herede, in the gloss which says note one for commissioners, and C. debebit. Therefore, the executor must provide the money with the authority of the Bishop, so that the hospital may be constructed therefrom, as in D. de manumis, l. si vero non remunerandi § si; and D. de legatis 3, Titius. Without the authority of the bishop, therefore, this cannot be expedited, since it certainly pertains to him to found and establish the hospital, and to lay the first blessed stone, as is read and noted in Inst. de rerum divisione § nullus, on the word Pontifice; and Extra de relictis domibus, C. de xenodochiis. Otherwise, it would not be a canonical hospital, but a profane one, as certain nobles have in their houses. If, however, we speak with respect to all the goods, it must be said that the bishop should take them, not as heir, but as curator of the goods and administrator; as we have in a similar case in D. ad Trebellianum, l. cum haeres instituta furiosa esset; and D. de minoribus, l. et si sine § sed quod Papi. aequiparatur. Therefore, the bishop will appoint a curator, who is appointed for goods possessed in the name of the womb, as in D. de ventre in possessionem mittendo, l. 1 § quo; and all fruits received therefrom must be preserved for the future hospital, after deducting honors. Nor do I believe that the bishop should have a quarter in the matter of the hospital, because a hospital which is not of the diocesan’s jurisdiction is not his, see l. ultima D. de assignandis liberis; and D. de colonis bonis, l. si. From this it appears how one should proceed regarding the seizure of these goods; nor can the testator impede the bishop, to whom it pertains to coerce the brother with the force of the praetor, as in D. de petitione hereditatis, l. haereditas § si; and Extra de testamentis § nos quidem; and in Auth. de ecclesiis tit. § si quis aedificationem col. 9; and C. de episcopis et clericis, l. id quod pauperibus; and l. nulli; and l. si quis ad declinandam. Hence, it is not necessary that the bishop offer a libellus, unless compelled; because he is the inquisitor of such matters, and the fact, namely the testament, is notorious. See what is noted by Innocentius Extra de verbis significandis, C. ex parte. If, however, it is asked about legacies, whether they ought to be paid, it must be said according to canon law that those left for the soul must be paid, because they are confirmed by death alone by reason of piety, and nothing else is necessary except that the death of the testator intervene, according to the Apostle; but other legacies are not said to be due until the inheritance is entered upon by the rector of the hospital after the hospital is constructed, there placing the authority of the bishop, according to the form of the testament. For he can enter upon the inheritance in the name of the hospital, just as a tutor in the name of an infant, C. de iure deliberando, l. si infanti; and a father in the name of his infant son. For the orphanotrophus was assimilated to a father and tutor, as in C. de episcopis et clericis, l. orphanotrophos; C. de bonis matris, l. 1; and in C. quia contingit de relictis domibus in clerico. That the said legacies cannot be claimed, unless the said inheritance is entered upon as stated, is clear from D. de legatis 1, l. ab exhaereditatis § ult.; and D. de venditione inspicienda, l. quae ventri. It should be known that if the bishop is lacking, the chapter supplies his place by such a notable rule, which Paulus de Liazza takes from the words of the Archdeacon in C. 1 de maiore et obedientia lib. 6, namely that in all matters which regard grace, donation, or alienation, according to Paulus de Liazza. Since, therefore, the curatorship of the said goods pertains to justice, it rightly devolves to the chapter as to certain suffragan magistrates, see optimum D. de negotiis gestis, l. cum alicui. Moreover, since the hospital must absolutely be constructed, as I said, the legitimate heir is absolutely destroyed, unless after the hospital is constructed, the rector of the hospital with the authority of the bishop repudiates the inheritance as burdensome, as in D. de venditione inspicienda, l. qui ventri. And by this, a more useful response is given to all things which have been sought. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If the power to render an award has been granted to arbitrators until the Calends of August, and beyond, as long as it pleases them, with the power also to extend the time, whether an award rendered after the Calends without any further extension is valid, with the following opinion.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The words of the compromise are as follows: and they wished that the compromise should last until the Calends of August and beyond, as long as and insofar as it shall please the aforementioned lords arbitrators and umpires to grant, or two of them to grant; the aforementioned parties, from now on, granting and conceding to the aforementioned lords arbitrators, as above, jointly, and to two of them jointly, full authority and every power to extend the present compromise to its term once, twice, thrice, and more often, and as often as it shall please the aforementioned lords arbitrators and umpires, as above, jointly, and two of them jointly, at their free will; and the said parties, from now on, extended the said compromise by the arbitrators, or two of them jointly.

It is now asked whether, after the expiration of the term of the Kalends of August, the said arbitrators, or two of them, could or can render a sentence without any further prorogation. And it seems that they can, on account of the word "placuerit" (it pleased), which is extended up to the time of life, as in l. 4, ff. loca. de leg. 3, fideicom. §. si quis fidei. de fide. lib. l. Thais ancilla. Moreover, it seems that they tacitly consent, because will is not presumed to be changed, as in ff. de proba. l. cum tacita and l. quinquaginta. Furthermore, the mind of the preceding will is declared by the subsequent act, as in C. de insti. et substi. l. reprehendenda. Therefore, by the very fact that they rendered the award (laudaverunt), they declare the past mind of consent, arg. ff. de acqui. haere. l. illud.

On the contrary, it seems that a certain form must be observed, namely, that all agree together, or two of them agree together. But this form was not observed, because no agreement appears, for silence is nothing; one will never find that persons are said to agree by remaining silent, but a declaration of will is required, and that they agree together, as in ff. de pact. l. 1, §. quaestionis. Moreover, since we are in the matter of prorogation, it is necessary that this agreement precede the expiration of the term; otherwise, it would not be a prorogation, because upon the expiration of the term they immediately cease to be arbitrators; therefore, as private persons, they cannot prorogate, as in ff. de precario. l. sed si manente. Furthermore, it appears expressly from the words that the compromittors gave a certain form for extending jurisdiction or authority, namely, by the way of prorogation; by which way and form the arbitrators could not depart, arg. ff. arbi. l. quod tamen and ff. mandati. l. diligenter. From this it follows, and it is true, that an award rendered after the expiration of the term, without prorogation, is null, and from it a penalty cannot be claimed. And this is the truth.

In the Name of Christ, Amen. The truth is to be seen in the fact that there was no hearing after the first term, with no express extension having been made. For an extension must be made expressly, because it is interlocutory, as stated in the law *diem proferre*, and in the law *non distinguemus*, section *dies*, and in the law *arbiter ita*, in the Digest, under the title *De arbitris*. This is because a term must have some effect, as stated in the law *si cum dim.*, with *si*. I do not stand on the words, but on the conclusion, and that which does not exist cannot be extended, because the authority is lacking.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The place where payment ought to be made.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The allegations of the most excellent learned lord Ubertino are most true, and I have already considered that which is contained in the said allegations,

Namely, that the payment ought to have been made at Monte Magno, where the party sued has his domicile, and where the deceased also had his. And I do not repeat the allegations. Therefore, the lady legatee ought to have sent, or to send, to that place. This is also confirmed by the compromise made there, and by the arbitral sentence rendered there, by which it may be said that a contract, or something akin to it, was concluded there. And therefore, if the heirs were not in default of payment, they are not bound to any penalty, nor to interest.

† As for the matter of the privilege, since it was not alleged, even assuming without prejudice to the truth that it would have been available, it cannot now be raised, because it appears to have been tacitly renounced, as stated in D. de iudiciis, l. sed et si susceperit, in principio. And if the judge were to sentence that the heirs should pay in Ast., an appeal could be brought, because the sentence would be unjust, as is clear from the allegations noted above, and it is valid according to D. de transactionibus, l. cum hi, § in causa.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A father, instituted as heir together with his son in his power, does not have a usufruct in the son's portion.
2. The same case is said to apply when the reason and intent are the same.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. All opinions, which are various, in the Authentico, moreover, the inheritance. C. concerning goods, which are free.

† I hold to the text which states that where a father is instituted as heir together with a son or daughter under his power, no usufruct is sought for the father in the portion of the son or daughter. And from this it follows that he is not a legitimate administrator according to the rule set forth in the same title, Auth. Excipitur, and D. De commodato, l. 3, § Si filio. Furthermore, I consider that in the case at hand the reasoning is not entirely the same as that which the doctors assign in Auth. Item hereditas. For the testator does a certain injury to the mother, since she alone would have succeeded to her children intestate, as in Auth. De hereditatibus ab intestato, in principio. And therefore I say that the father ought not to have a usufruct in the daughter’s portion, but the daughter has in her portion both ownership and usufruct. To this also contributes the nature of equality introduced by the conjunction, D. De hereditatibus instituendis, l. Interdum. For it gives to understand that it is for an equal portion; but there would be no equality if the father had the entire benefit and the daughter, while the father was living, had only a bare name. D. De usufructu legato, l. Si alii. Nor does the rule concerning the father acquiring a usufruct in the adventitious property of his children stand in the way; for that was introduced in cases in which formerly the entire full right was acquired by the father. And that rule is false today in the cases expressed in the law. And the case seems, whether one weighs the text, or the gloss of Accursius, or the reasoning of Jacobus de Arena, to be precisely about those exceptions. Therefore, let the daughter succeed in full ownership of the half, not in bare ownership only. Furthermore, if this case were not entirely expressed, there is in the body of the Authentica a case most similar and indifferent to the expressed one: and exceptions of laws and statutes are extended to cases similar to those expressed.

† Rather, the case is said to be the same when the reason and the intent are the same, c. fin. extra de reg. iur. per Dy. C. de reuo. don. l. his solis. and de interdic. I. 1. ff. vti poss. l. j. per Bart. and per Cyn. in many places. And ff. de le. l. iura non, singulas. ad §. de viro. where extension is prohibited, it is answered that there it speaks of an impersonal privilege, here of a natural reason.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether cities having the right to elect a duke for themselves, such as the city of Venice or Genoa, can also depose him; and whether such a deposed duke is considered an enemy, and nu. 2.
2. Whether a duke can be received by those who have peace or are allied with the said community. Join the following opinion.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Regarding the first point, whether the said noble Lord Antoniotus is, or ought to be called, Duke of Genoa, after he was repelled from the government by the commune of Genoa, I do not believe there is much to dispute, because the dispute would be futile and vain. And because, by law, the city of Genoa was not subject to him, but he was rather its creature, except with respect to good government, or good administration by its magnates, or officials, with whom he had full and connected power, as per the doctors, Extra, de iudiciis, c. fin., and his officials. And presupposing that the said city is free, it could remove him from office, as in Digest, de legibus, l. non ambigitur; as in Title 10, col. si de investitura inter dominum et vassallum lis oriatur, ca. 1, post principium. Many doctors, however, say the contrary, because the Roman people cannot depose the Emperor without cause, nor even with cause, since they transferred to him mere and full dominion, as in Digest, de origine iuris, l. 2, § deinde. Nevertheless, this pretended liberty, which certain peoples usurp, is not according to Roman law, because all peoples are subject to the Emperor. And therefore, those elected by the peoples and confirmed by the Emperor, or vicars of the Emperor, could not be deposed by the peoples, because deposition belongs to those to whom institution belongs, as in Authentica, de defensione civitatum, § interim. Wherefore it follows that if Lord Antoniotus did not preside over the Genoese except by the authority of the Genoese, he could be deprived and deposed from office by them, as in the Peace of Constance. Although mere and mixed empire has been granted to certain cities, nevertheless the powers of those lands cannot exercise it without the confirmation of the Emperor, as appears in the text of the Peace of Constance. And therefore this is not a matter to be disputed under the common law, because there are three cases: either one is elected contrary to the form, force, and authority of the laws, and the election is not valid, nor is he said to be despoiled, since he was never in true jurisdiction; or he is elected and not confirmed, as he ought to be confirmed, and the same applies; or he is confirmed, and then the inferior cannot depose him, because the superior confirmed him, and thus he exercises the authority of the superior. Indeed, peoples who expel such rectors incur the crime of lèse-majesté, as in Digest, de captivis, l. hostes. The words of Cynus of Pistoia, Digest, de legibus, l. cum lex in praeteritum, etc.
In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† On the point of whether the said Antoniotus is the Duke of Genoa: I consider it superfluous for anyone other than he himself, who knows best the reality of the government, to dispute the subtleties of law. And the agreements were made with the Commune of Genoa: and the Commune is no less without him than with him, because one swallow does not make, nor destroy, spring. Just as he was introduced by the people, so was he elected, D. de origine iuris, l. 2. Whether this was just or unjust is not a matter for dispute, because since the agreement was made collectively, let them know that line of Virgil: “Easy is the descent to Avernus, but to recall one’s step, this is the work of virtue,” C. de lib. et eorum liber., l. 2.

† On the second point, whether this diligence in pasturing in the name of the commune of Genoa, with the statute of appeal changed to the contrary, includes his person, I say as in D. de pactis, l. cum in eo.

† On the third point, whether the illustrious Lord Marquis can accept him in the lands of the said Lord Marquis, against the will of the Commune of Genoa, I say that he cannot, because he has become an enemy of the Commune. [See] de capt. et post lim. l. amissione, §. qui deficiunt. For the words of the contract are extensive and continuous throughout the entire period, so that peace and goodwill may be preserved. And the words are implicit as to the beginning, middle, and end of the time. ff. de cond. et demonstr. l. cum tale, §. fin., with its gloss. And this appears if one posits the case conversely, that at the time of the initiation of the agreements someone was a rebel. Certainly, if he is reconciled, he can be received; hence the words are to be referred not to the beginning of the time, but to the substance and reality in the territories. Moreover, this pact is a law. ff. de publ. iud. Cæsar, which always speaks; C. de hæret. cuncti. And because the indefinite is equivalent to the universal, ff. de serv. urb. præd. l. si servitus. And it supports what is noted by Dy. de leg. 1, si mihi, et tibi, §. in legatis. And ff. de leg. l. cum lex per Cy. And ff. de reb. dub. l. si cognata. Many things, however, could be argued to the contrary, and especially what is noted by Cyn. C. de sacr. sanct. eccl. placet; l. leges, et constitutiones. ff. de verb. oblig. l. cum stipulamur. And l. si a colono. ff. de lib. leg. Aurelius, §. testamento. But those laws speak when the disposition is limited to the present time. Now, when it is universal and extensive, and having a course extending into the future, ff. de iud. sol. nouissima, and thus they do not obstruct. And it supports the authority iusiurandum, quod præstatur ab his, there: "if anyone, however, is found by me to be of such [character], I shall keep myself free from him and expel him."

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a curator of the estate may be appointed, and on what grounds.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Having examined the course of events as narrated, and presupposing the public instruments mentioned in the aforementioned narration, it must be considered whether the said Robert has better rights in the said castle, or those who claim title through an intermediary person from Lady Blanch, who indeed, Lady Blanch, initiated her legal proceedings on account of her maternal dowry, notwithstanding that her brother was alive and that she herself was already endowed. For it is said that, notwithstanding the statute of the city of Asti placed under the rubric "that a married woman shall not come to the inheritance of her father or mother," which statute begins "If any woman," the said Lady Blanch cannot in any way claim the said dowry. And the reason for this is: the said Lady Blanch was endowed in the manner required by the statute; therefore, she is excluded from the succession of her mother. First, this is presupposed as established in the facts. Second, it is evident, because the statute could exclude her, as is fully noted by the doctors in C. de adulteriis, l. Publico, and C. de nuptiis, l. Sancimus. And since her brother was alive and acted as heir to his mother, everything accrues to him, because hereditary right is such that it accrues even to one person, as in ff. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. Si servus communis ab extero, and C. de caducis tollendis, §. His ita. For indeed, a male cannot come to a maternal dowry, or unless as an heir, as noted by the doctors in ff. soluto matrimonio, l. Si cum dotem, in principio. Therefore, when one is excluded, the other comes, who is not found to be excluded, as in C. ad Orphitionum, l. Non pro numero. The second reason is that, even assuming the facts were otherwise, it is not clear to me; nevertheless, the proceedings conducted on behalf of the said Blanch were null by law itself,

And the reason is that in the appointment of a curator no cause intervened, nor was the form observed; for one never proceeds to the appointment of a curator of goods unless compelled by necessity: and then a curator may be appointed over all goods, as is stated in D. de curatoribus bonorum damnatorum, l. 1; and D. de hæredibus institutis, l. si quis instituatur; and D. de curatore furiosi, l. observare. This is given and urged by the utility of the goods, namely, for the preservation of the goods, not because debt presses, as in l. puta, because the heir is instituted under a condition which he cannot fulfill, as in the aforementioned l. si quis instituatur. Likewise, on account of long absence, as in D. quibus ex causis in possessionem eatur, l. in possessione. Likewise, for the goods of one who has been captured by enemies, as in D. de mutuis et hostibus, l. 1, §. illud. Likewise, in another case, D. quibus ex causis in possessionem eatur, l. si diu. Likewise, when the debtor has surrendered his goods, as in C. de bonis auctoritate iudicis possidendis, l. creditore. But when the defendant is present, a curator of goods ought not to be appointed, but the due form ought to be observed in proceeding against him, as in C. quomodo et quando iudex, l. consentaneum; and C. de iudicibus, l. properandum, §. fin autem reus; and C. ut lite non contestata, l. quoniam frequenter. The aforementioned causes, or similar ones, ought to have been made clear to the ordinary judge in court; otherwise, this appointment of an extraordinary curator is void by the law itself, as in l. hæc autem, in principio, D. quibus ex causis in possessionem eatur. It ought also to be appointed not at the agreement of one creditor, but of the majority of creditors, or at least with them summoned, as in D. de curatoribus habendis non debet; and D. de eo qui pro tutore. And for this reason, in the entire process of the lady Blancha, the rest collapses, which follows from it, l. quæ ex relationibus; as in C. de legibus et constitutionibus, l. non dubium; C. de procuratoribus, l. licet; C. ne de statu defunctorum, l. si pater; D. quod falsum aut turpe, in l. 1, §. idem Pomponius. Moreover, that the said process did not hold is proved by another reason. For either the said lady Blancha comes by legacy, or by contract. In the first case, unless the acceptance of the inheritance, or admission thereto, is proved, it is not established that an action lies, from the will, even if she is an instituted heir: because it is special in legacies of freedom, which is confirmed by the mere existence of one's own heir. Therefore, it is otherwise in other legacies, as in l. sed cum quasi, §. sed et si quis, D. de fideicommissis liberis. Likewise, if she acts from a maternal contract, it must still be established that the inheritance was accepted, as noted in D. soluto matrimonio, l. si cum dotem, §. transgrediamur. And then it immediately follows that, if acceptance was not established, the process was invalid. But if it was established, then, because the adversary is certain and present, he ought not to have proceeded with a curator of goods appointed, but with the debtor himself, as fully proved above. From which it appears that the said process of appointment in satisfaction was invalid. Likewise, by another reason, because assignments of rights are not valid unless up to that quantity which is truly shown to have been paid, as in C. de mandatis, l. per diversas; and noted by Lauro de Butrio in auth. de qualitate donationis, §. aliud; and many doctors hold this according to the strict law, if the exception of non-payment of money, or simulation of assignment, is not added: and I have sometimes seen this opinion observed in courts. Commonly, however, in practice in many places it is not observed: especially when in the assignment itself there is a renunciation of the exception of non-payment of money, from the argument of what is noted in C. de dote causa non numerata, l. 1. Nevertheless, whatever may be said of this point, the process made with the said pretended curator of goods was not lawfully made, nor was the judgment founded with the person of the defendant, and thus it ought to have been founded according to what is proposed. Since, therefore, the said noble man, lord Robert, has his intention well-founded as regards the ownership of the castle, and is in possession, he who has to judge on this matter will pronounce that the process made with the said pretended curator of goods appointed did not hold at all.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a legacy made to a universal heir is included in a universal fideicommissum.
2. A son may alienate a property bequeathed to him, provided it does not exceed his legitime.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The determination of this question depends on two laws which, according to the letter, appear to contradict each other. One is found in the Digest, *De usuris*, law *In fideicommissi*, section *Cum Pollidius*, where it is stated that when Pollidius was approaching, his instituted heir was requested to restore to the testatrix’s daughter whatever had come to him; he had ordered the same Pollidius to retain the estate, because the said estate did not fall within the restitution of the fideicommissum. And yet it is certain that, since Pollidius was the universal heir, he could not have bequeathed to himself from himself, as stated in the Digest, *De legatis* 1, law *Legatum*, section *Haeredi*. The other law states the exact opposite, namely that if a testator instituted someone as heir and bequeathed an estate to him, and requested him to restore the inheritance, that estate falls within the restitution, because the legacy from himself to himself was void. This is the case expressly set out in the Digest, *Ad Trebellianam*, law *Fideicommissaria*, section *Si*. The gloss placed there resolves the contradiction of these laws in two ways. In one way, it is that in section *Cum Pollidius* it expressly stated that he wished the heir to retain the estate for himself; and thus he deducted it from the universal fideicommissum; otherwise, if he had simply bequeathed the estate to the heir from himself. Secondly, it is that in section *Cum Pollidius* the heir had been chosen in the place of a minister, and therefore it does not appear as a legacy from himself to himself, but rather from the person to whom he was obliged to restore the inheritance. In our case, however, the son was instituted, not as a minister. And thus we see that we are in the case of the aforementioned law *In fideicommissaria*, section *Si*. On this point, I have elsewhere advised as follows,

† namely, that the son wishes to alienate the property bequeathed to him, which does not exceed his legitime, and that he may do so, because by the presumed will of the testator he may deduct his legitime from that very property, as in C. fam. erc. l. filium, quem habentem, according to one reading. For in the legitime he is in the place of a creditor. Hence some say that even without the father’s designation he may choose one thing, as in ff. de distr. pig. l. creditores, and in Auth. de rest. et ea, quæ parit. §. quamobrem. Much more so, therefore, by the father’s designation and paternal affection, of which affection it is established. If the thing assigned to the son consisted in affection: for example, a house, as in C. de adm. tut. l. lex, quæ tutores, arg. ff. de min. l. in emptione, and what is noted in de fideic. l. quotiens. Therefore, in the general obligation of the goods, that house assigned to the son by the present estimation is not included. For even what is excepted in fact is not contained in the fideicommissum, arg. ff. de pec. leg. l. cum dominus, §. filius. It is certain that the son’s legitime does not come into the obligation of the testament, as in C. de inoff. test. l. quam in prioribus, and l. scimus, in princ. As for what would be above the legitime, the question is more doubtful on account of the contrariety of the said laws: nevertheless, because among sons the will of the father is considered more than the subtlety of the law, as in C. fam. erc. l. si, and because special provisions derogate from general ones, as in C. fam. erc. l. quotiens, I think it should be presumed from the paternal effect that the father wished the said legacy not to be comprehended in the said fideicommissum: as if he wished the son to retain the bequeathed thing and to have it in full right, and thus it may be freely alienated, since the intention of the father operates something among sons. And so I have also advised otherwise, and now I advise: saving the sounder counsel. Especially if the testator, after the legacy to pious uses, bequeathed to the instituted son, a similar consideration is made, ff. ad Treb. Marcel. §. quidam liberis, cum suis. Therefore, having the legitime in the goods assigned to him by the testator, the remainder is subject to the burdens of the fideicommissum: and the son cannot prevent execution for pious causes in the said remaining goods, because according to the truth, in what is left for pious causes, only the legitime is deducted, although the Archdeacon says the contrary in c. 1, de testam., lib. 6.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a prescription runs against an ignorant person, or against one who is ignorant.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The aforementioned words of a certain statute of the city of Asti, speaking in this form: if anyone has acquired something from any contract, and has held or possessed it for a period of 20 years, let him hold or possess it, which he had acquired or shall acquire, free and absolute, notwithstanding the contradiction of anyone or several; with this, however, being saved, that if anyone has it pledged as security, which is or was acquired, as within the said space of the said 10 years, he cannot claim it or demand the pledge on account of the tenure or possession of 10 years, he does not lose his right. And with the right of those under 25 years of age being saved. It is proposed that certain goods, pledged for restitution of a dowry, were held and possessed with title for a period of 10 years and beyond, the heirs of the woman, to whom the hypothecary action over the said goods belonged, being ignorant. This woman is said to have been ignorant of her rights, which she had in truth, since she was ignorant that the said goods were pledged by the said person for the restitution of the dowry. She was also ignorant of the rights by which she could prove this. Therefore, she says that the said prescription did not run against her. On the other hand, it is said that this ignorance does not prevent the prescription.

† Now the question arises as to what is the law. And that one cannot bring an action seems to be expressly stated in C. de iure dotis, l. in rebus, § omnis, where it appears that if, for twenty years between present parties, from the time when the action could have been brought, the possessor has held the hypothecated thing by title and in good faith, he cannot thereafter be sued; this is supported by C. si adversus traditionem, l. 1 and 2, and C. de praescriptione triginta annorum, l. cum notissimi, in principio, where it is noted that an outsider possessing a hypothecated thing with title and in good faith prescribes within the space of years between present parties; and another law states that in long-term prescription, the knowledge or ignorance of the person against whom prescription is claimed is disregarded, as in C. de praescriptione longi temporis, l. si. Although the said law states that the said prescription runs only from the time when actions could have been brought, this is understood in terms of legal power, not factual power. The text is express in the aforementioned § omnino. And if it is said that the statute determines the contrary, namely that he who could not claim his right shall not lose it, nevertheless the word “could not” is understood as referring to legal inability; otherwise, if it were due to ignorance, it would be different. This time is not useful, but continuous. To this effect, it is noted in ff. quando actio de peculio est annua, l. quaesitum. Otherwise, it would follow that anyone alleging ignorance would be heard perpetually, which is absurd, especially regarding those who ought to have known. Argument: si certum petatur, l. quod te.

To the contrary, it seems that the text of the statute says: if they could not claim their right, they shall not lose it. But wherever these words or similar ones are added, the time is considered useful, at least as regards its beginning, as in ff. de aedilicio edicto, l. cum sex, where the text states that one who is ignorant is not considered to have had the power to bring an action, as in ff. de calumnia, l. auus; and ff. de excusationibus tutorum, l. quinquaginta; and ff. de inofficioso testamento, l. genero; and it is noted in C. de tempore in integrum restitutionis, l. si, unless the ignorance was gross or supine, as in ff. de iure et facto ignorantiis, l. relatio. And according to this, the said statute favors possessors in one respect and those bringing actions in another. Certainly, this distinction is formally found in C. de praescriptione longi temporis, auth. malae fidei, where prescription of long time does not run against one who is ignorant of his right and of the alienation made. However, it is true that this authority speaks of the case where the one who alienated knew the thing was alien; it does not speak of one who knew the thing was encumbered for another. Nevertheless, I do not cite that authority in this manner, but to prove that one who is ignorant of his right and of the alienation made is not said to be able to claim it.

It seems to me that this question is doubtful, and I lean more toward the possessor, by the legal rule that times of civil possession are continuous and run even against the ignorant, as noted in Inst. de diversis temporum praescriptionibus, in principio. And therefore, it is not safe to depart from the legal rule, since statutes in doubt should be interpreted according to the common law, as in C. de noxalibus actionibus, l. servi vestri, and Extra de consuetudinibus, c. cum dilectus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a legacy made by a grandfather to his granddaughter, who was not yet married, for the purpose of assisting in her marriage, is due if her father subsequently provided her with a dowry.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The case is as follows. A grandfather left a thousand [units of currency] to his unmarried granddaughter as a subsidy for her marriage, and he made a will. In the will, he instituted the girl’s father, and his other sons, and his grandsons, as heirs. Then, after the grandfather’s death, the girl’s father married her and provided her with a dowry. The girl, or her heirs, wish to claim the said legacy, notwithstanding that she has been endowed by her father. The question is: what is the law?

† And it seems that they can, because the father appears to have dowered them from his own property, as C. de do. promis. l. si. On the contrary, it seems that he appears to have dowered them with the intention of compensation, as ff. so. ma. l. si cum dotem. §. si pater. or with the intention of freeing himself, insofar as he is the heir, as ff. de neg. ge. l. nesennius. and ff. de pe. hęre. l. si.
