But regarding the shares of the coheirs, it must be said that the legacy remains firm; for they are not released from the debt if the father dowered his daughter, because the day of the legacy had thereby arrived, and the obligation was contracted in the persons of all the heirs. Nor does it matter that she is married; rather, this strengthens the legacy all the more. To this effect is what is noted in ff. de act. et obliga. l. nupta. and ff. de condi. et demon. l. si iam facta. and ff. de verbo. signi. l. boues. §. hoc sermone. C. de leg. l. filię legatorum. ff. de leg. 2. l. Lucius. el primo. in rationibus ipsarumterum. and ff. de colla. bo. l. dedit doti.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Investigating secondly, according to the form of the first, by confirming whether it appears that all the qualities of the first have been repeated.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A certain person was invested with a certain estate for a fixed annual census, with the agreement that he could sell his rights and improvements, provided a certain form was observed, it being saved that he could not sell to a church, or hospital, slave, or valuator, or persons not suitable in terms of resources or ease of being sued. It happens that the said investee sold his emphyteutic rights to Titius. Afterward, the said lord invested Titius, saying thus, that he was investing him, confirming the first investiture; and this was done with the provision that the said fictual, his heirs, and to whom or to whomsoever he shall give, except to a church, hospital, captain, valuator, slave, infirm, and other places and persons excepted by law or custom, shall have, hold, etc. In these very exceptive words, "not suitable in terms of resources or ease of being sued" is not expressly excepted. Now it is asked whether to this said person not suitable, i.e., in terms of resources and ease of being sued, the said fictual, against the will and objection of the lord, can sell his rights and his improvements. And it seems that he can.

For it is certain that the most recent agreements derogate from earlier ones, as C. de pactis, l. pacta nouissima; ff. de acquisitione possessionis, l. si quis ante; ff. de locato, l. cum in plures, §. lege dicta. Likewise, it is certain that exceptions, in certain cases, while not excepting others, confirm the rule, as noted in l. 1, ff. de regulis iuris, and ff. de militum testamento, l. tribus unus, §. ultimo. Since this case was not among those finally excepted, therefore it remains subject to the general rule. Moreover, it is certain that he who uses loose language incurs obvious peril, as C. de donationibus promissis, l. finalis. But this proprietor used loose language, and the word "voluerit," which imports free and mere will, as ff. de legatis tertio, l. fideicommissa, §. quamquam. Furthermore, this appears to be expressly stated in the locus citatus, de feudo non habente propriam feudi naturam, c. 1, in the first response.

On the contrary, it seems that the word "confirming," which is in the beginning of the instrument, manifestly shows that whatever was said in the first investiture is understood to be repeated in the subsequent one, as ff. de liberatione legatorum, l. Aurelius, §. testamento. Moreover, those things which are said in the beginning of a contract or another disposition seem to be repeated in the middle or at the end, as Extra, de appellationibus, c. secundo requiris. Furthermore, we must examine the cause of the words and the intent of the contracting parties and of the laws, as noted in ff. communia praediorum, l. si quis duas, in fine. But the intent of the contracting parties was to except those who were not solvent, or who could not easily be sued; therefore, this intent must be upheld. Furthermore, this arises from the nature of reference, because reference was made to the old investiture, and a recollection thereof, as ff. de legatis secundo, l. legatorum, §. qui plures. Furthermore, the general clause "and other places and persons excepted by law or custom" contributes to this, in which words all those who are not suitable are included, because it is not permitted for one having a fictitious right to make the condition of the lord worse, as Inst. de locato, §. adeo; to this effect, ff. qui satisdare cogantur, l. quotiens vitiose; and ff. de fideiussoribus, l. qui satisdare.

It is also to be considered that the said investee could not sell except his own right, as ff. de contrahenda emptio, l. qui tabernas. But his right was so modified that he could not sell to a poor person; therefore, in the sale, the right of selling to a poor person was not included. For one cannot transfer a right which he does not have, as ff. de pignori, l. lex vectigali.

The reasons made to the contrary do not stand, because this case is not understood to be committed [to the exception], but is understood to be repeated, and especially because of the general words, since even an agreement is held in place of law, as ff. de deposito, l. 1, §. si convenerit. And therefore, this case can optimally be comprehended under the prohibition, under those words "and persons excepted by law." For that agreement makes law between the contracting parties. Nor does that chapter de feudo non habente propriam naturam stand in the way; because it is not said there that it can be alienated. Not therefore, when those words "and whether he gave his right" were added, as appears there at the end of the chapter, as 10. col. de lege Corradi, §. similiter; and C. de iure emphyteutico, l. finalis.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a prince who holds a joint ownership with a certain subject in certain buildings may lease the whole to someone, or even his procurator: and to whom the rent shall belong.
body: First, it is doubted whether our lord, the Duke of Touraine, having a community with another of his subjects in certain buildings and works,

† whether he may lease the whole to someone. And thus it is asked whether l. 1. C. de venditione rerum fiscalium, lib. 10, has application in this case? And there is doubt, because it speaks of sale; hence it must be considered whether, by the reasoning of that law, it extends to the aforementioned case, and whether our lord is called the fiscus. Secondly, if the leases of the governor of Ast., under the aforementioned name of the lord, leased the property in solidum, whether the lease remains valid, because that law speaks of a fiscal procurator; and whether, in doubt, it is presumed that he was a locum tenens and had power for this, presupposing that those works are common because they were made under the public domain, which pertains to the lord, and in part they were made on the land of a certain private person, hence they ought not to be destroyed, but a tax ought to be imposed, as says Bartolus in l. 2, § si quis minime, ff. ne quid in loco publico, and c. Thirdly, because our lord has here one procurator, whom we call the fiscal procurator: if such a procurator, together with the aforementioned locum tenens of the lord, had leased the aforementioned property, whether it is presumed in doubt that he was the fiscal procurator, from the fact that his person appears to have been approved by the said locum tenens and other officials of the lord then present? Fourthly, whether it ought to be that, if more is leased, the whole is leased, rather than not leasing only part: and this with respect to the part pertaining to the lord, or whether this seems doubtful in itself: however, also because that law l. 1. C. de venditione rerum fiscalium, lib. 10, says, the rule is, whenever even the smallest portion of the thing pertains to the fiscus, so that the whole is to be alienated by our procurators. Therefore, etc. ff. de legatis 2, l. Meuius, § in fundo, ff. familiae erciscundae, Meuius, § si, it is presumed that the part is worth less in itself than in the whole. Also, perhaps the fiscus cannot divide or distinguish, so as to lease one part and not another, as is noted in the said rule non debet.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the closer agnate, who accepts a donation of a fief for himself and for the more remote agnate, prejudices himself in the right of priority.
2. Whether the more remote agnate ought to be deprived of his right after the death of the donor on account of ingratitude committed against the closer agnate.
3. Whether, and when, the right of the acceptor is resolved in feudal matters upon the resolution of the donor's right.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The noble man, Lord Manfredinus de Gutturariis, donated to the noble man, Lord Gabriel de Gutturariis, receiving for himself one half, and for the noble man Bartholomew, nephew of the said Lord Gabriel in the transverse line, the other half, certain portions of certain feudal castles, which the said donor held in noble and ancient fief from the community of Ancona; it being expressed in the said donation that the said Lord Gabriel and Bartholomew were the nearest agnates, although in truth the said Gabriel was the nearer agnate of the said donor, and the said Lord Bartholomew was the more remote agnate; so that by the nature of the fief, the said Lord Gabriel was to succeed in the said fief upon the death of the said donor without an heir, and the said Bartholomew was to be totally excluded by the said Lord Gabriel. It is also true that the said Bartholomew is said to have inflicted and committed atrocious injuries and grave ingratitude against the said Lord Gabriel, as has been proven by the records of the case. Now it is asked: whether, because the said Lord Gabriel, joined with the name of the said Bartholomew, together with a notary as a public person, received the said donation, he has prejudiced himself in the right of priority of the fief, which he is recognized as having and ought to have as the nearer agnate after the death of the said donor, then vassal of the prior and superior lord. Secondly, it is doubted whether, since the said Lord Gabriel says, and it is probable, that he erred in law, because he asserted that Bartholomew was equal to him in right and degree, it is understood by such reception, which he made in a joint name, that he derogated in any way from his right. Thirdly, it is doubted whether, even if the said donation was valid during the life of the said donor, it nevertheless lapsed upon his death without an heir, that is, without sons, according to that rule: "When the right of the donor is resolved, the right of the acceptor is resolved." Fourthly, it is doubted whether the text of the first chapter, *de alienatione feudorum*, in the *Partita*, in the response, which permits alienation to be made without the consent of the lord to agnates, is to be understood of agnates who are in the nearer degree, or rather of any whatsoever collaterals, with the consent of the other agnates who, if the alienation had not been made, would succeed in the fief. Fifthly, presupposing that the said consent was valid, whether the said Bartholomew ought to be deprived of the right, if any right was acquired from the aforementioned donation, on account of the magnitude of the offense committed by the said Bartholomew, insulting the said Lord Gabriel with injurious words, as appears evidently from the proceedings in the proofs of the said Lord Gabriel. In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Regarding the first point, I consider three things. First, the limited and temporary power of the donor himself. Second, the express quality of the said Lord Gabriel as recipient. Third, the power or authority of the notary, or public person.

Regarding the first, namely the power of the donor, it is certain that the donor could not donate more than the right he had, as in D. de legatis 1, l. si domus, §. si; and C. de legatis, l. uxor patrui; D. de contrahenda emptione, l. qui tabernas; D. de usufructu legato, l. Sticho. Nor does anything occur here by which the right of the said donor was augmented, because the act proceeding from him toward the donee tended toward the diminution of his own right, not toward its augmentation; hence it must operate the contrary effect, as in D. de legatis 1, l. legata inutiliter; and D. de manumissione testamento, l. sine haerede. Therefore, the donees cannot possess by title of donation, but they must possess by their own right, as argued from D. de hereditate instituenda, l. seruus, §. qui fideicommissariam; and D. ad legem Falcidiam, l. fundo. Now it is so that, if the said donation ceases, Lord Gabriel, as the nearest agnate, ought to obtain the said fiefs, as in c. 1, de gradibus successionis in feudis; and in c. 1, de successionibus feudorum. Therefore, it follows with truth that, when the donation of the dominant party is annulled or terminated, the gift ought to pertain to the said Lord Gabriel.

Secondly, I consider the person of the said Lord Gabriel, insofar as he acknowledges the fief for half in the conjunctive name of the said Lord Bartholomew. And although the rule of law warns that he who consents to another loses his own rights, as in D. de administratione tutorum, l. cum quaedam; and in c. 1, §. praeterea, qui modis feudum amittatur; nevertheless, in the present case it is not so. Lord Gabriel provided only a simple ministry or bare name of a conjunct person; hence he did nothing in his own name, and consequently he does not prejudice himself, as in l. Lucius, D. de institutionibus. Secondly, because he erred both in law and in degree, when he said that his said nephew was an equally proximate agnate, which is not true, as in C. de successione edicto, l. si a me frater. Thirdly, because one who delivers his own thing so that another may receive it does not transfer any right to the recipient, as in l. 3, §. subtilius, D. de conditionibus ob causam; and fully in l. 1, D. de officio procuratoris caesaris; and l. sicut, §. seruum tuum imprudens; in l. cum fundus; and D. de mandato, l. seruum Titij; D. de acquirenda re donata, l. et in corpus; and these are proven in D. de acquirenda possessione, l. si aliquam rem. And from this follows the manifest conclusion that this Lord Gabriel, being added to the donation, or adding himself to the said donation, did not lose his future dominion, since neither was it the intention of the donor other than to donate his own right, nor was it the intention of the recipient other than to receive in the conjunctive name and as a minister; because one who errs in the dominion, which he thought would be that of the recipient, when it is in fact his own, does not lose the dominion, as is clearly proven above.

Furthermore, the reception made by the notary by virtue of his public office ought to operate nothing beyond what the nature of his own office dictates. And see Innocentius in c. dudum, de conversione coniugii; and Jacobus de Belvisio in C. si adversus venditionem, auth. sacramenta. Hence, from the foregoing, it appears evidently that, upon the death of the donor without children, the fief pertains by right to the said Lord Gabriel, notwithstanding that he received it in the conjunctive name.

† Moreover, if we were to say that the aforementioned Lord Gabriel intended to exercise liberality towards the aforementioned Bartholomew, and since every liberality is called a donation, as stated in the Digest, *De donationibus*, law *Hoc iure*; nevertheless, such consent and liberality could be revoked due to ingratitude, which was evidently committed by the aforementioned Bartholomew, as is fully proven, even by the judicial process, as stated in the Code, *De revocatione donationum*, law *Si*. Hence, after the death of the donor without an heir, he would rather seem to have made a donation than the first one, as stated in the Code, *De inofficiosa donatione*, law *Penultima*, at the end.

From these it appears that the response has been given to all the points to which it is necessary to respond, and that the final conclusion is in favor of the said Lord Gabriel against the said Bartholomew. In this conclusion, nothing is included by any intention of the heir or of the law. For when the right of the grantor ends, the right of the grantee also ends, as in the Digest, *De pignoris*, law *Lex vectigali*. Hence, concerning the understanding of this matter, it must be known that when someone receives a thing from a vassal by a contract other than that of a fief, for example by a contract of simple donation, as is the case in our instance: then either the contract is celebrated with the will of the lord, or without it. In the first case, when the right of the grantor is resolved, the right of the grantee is not resolved, because the lord himself is deemed to have given what he has a perpetual right to, as in the aforementioned § *Praeterea*, *Quibus modis feudum amittitur*. In the second case, either the contract was illicit from the beginning, and then the fief opens to the lord from the beginning, as in chapter 1, *De alienatione feudorum*; or the contract was licit from the beginning, and then, when the right of the grantor ends, the right of the grantee ends, as in chapter 1, § *Rursus*, *De controversiis investiturarum*, and there by Jacobus de Belvis and Petrus de Trinitate. And thus is understood chapter 1, *De alienatione feudorum paternorum*. And this is our case, by which it is clear that it is not necessary to say anything further regarding this proceeding, because from this it clearly appears that the said Lord Gabriel upholds the right, since it has been copiously and elegantly alleged by the lord making the allegation.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If three brothers are instituted as heirs, or come to the succession, and two are alive and present, while nothing is known about the third, whether he is alive or dead, what shall be done with his portion? nu. 4.
2. A pupillary substitution may be made to the prejudice of a brother and of the mother.
3. A vassal cannot make a will concerning a fief, nor establish any other disposition of his last will.
4. If a vassal does not request investiture within a year, whether he can be deprived of his portion and it granted to others by the lord.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A certain nobleman named Albertonus de Monte Calvo, in his will, among other things, disposes as follows. Moreover, he instituted his son Francis as his heir in 300 gold florins, etc. Finally, the said testator died, with the said seven male sons surviving, namely Francis and William, instituted as heirs in the aforementioned quantity, having passed the age of pupillary minority, and Anthony and Leo, who were adults; Conrad, Louis, and Petrinus, who were pupillary universal heirs of the said testator. Finally, Petrinus died while still in pupillary minority; afterwards, Leo died in majority; then Anthony died in majority, and all without issue. As for Francis, it is doubtful whether he lives or not.

† Now therefore the question arises between the said William, instituted heir in the said amount, and Conrad and Louis, universal heirs both of the paternal goods and of the fiefs, as well as of the succession of the said three brothers, who are alleged to have died. And I shall begin with the proper goods, and I say that the said William does not succeed by the father’s will, unless in the said 300 florins, provided that they do not suffice for the legitime portion accruing to him, which must be supplied, as is stated in Codex, De inofficioso testamento, l. omnimodo. Bartolus, however, says in l. si quis filium, § fin., eodem titulo, that since this supplement takes the place of the ancient querela inofficiosi testamenti, this supplement cannot be claimed after five years have elapsed from the day of acceptance of the inheritance. Many others, however, claim the contrary, on which point there is no need to dispute here.

† I come to the inheritance of Petrini, who died in pupillary age, and I say that all his goods pass to the pupillary heirs instituted, and not to the said Guglielmo, because he was not substituted, as in D. de inofficiosa testamento, l. Papinianus, § sed nunc impuberis, where it is expressly stated that a pupillary substitution can be made to the prejudice of a brother, and even of the mother, as in C. de impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus, l. precibus. I come to the inheritance of Leo and Antonio, who died outside of pupillary age, and I say that Conrad and Louis, by virtue of the fideicommissum, must have half of the share that fell to the said Antonio and Leo; then the other half must be divided intestate among the number of persons now succeeding to the inheritance of the said Leo and Antonio, so that from the portions of the said Leo and Antonio, dividing them into 12 ounces, the said Conrad and Louis must first have six ounces by right of fideicommissum, and four between them by intestate right, and Guglielmo two likewise by intestate right. And thus, of the 12 ounces, Guglielmo must have two, holding the common opinion of the two fourths, as in Extra de testamento, cap. Raynutius, and cap. Raynaldus, and in the same title, si pater, lib. 6.

† Now I come to feudal goods, and I say that in fiefs this is the rule: that the vassal cannot make a will concerning them, nor create any other disposition of his last will, but all his sons succeed to him in equal shares, even if the hereditary portions were unequal, as in cap. 1, extra de success. feud. and in cap. 1, §. deinde statuimus, de his, qui feud. da. poss. and in cap. 1, de grad. success. in feu. coll. 10. From which it appears that it is as if no will had been made with regard to the succession to the fief.

† Hence they conclude that, since there are now three living sons of the testator, and it is doubtful whether the fourth is alive, just as there are four portions, and each of these three, whose survival is certain, has a quarter share, that portion concerning which doubt arises as to whether their brother is dead will be under the curator of the goods. As in C. de cap. l. nec nos.

† That which is not to be omitted is that if the said William does not seek investiture within a year and a day, the Lord Marquis, who is the lord of the fief, may grant his portion to the other brothers, as in c. j. quo tempore miles inuestituram petere debeat, cum si, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the burden of proof lies with the possessor.
2. The collation of a benefice that is not vacant is null.
3. The expectations of those awaiting grace are easily extinguished by any incompatible person.
4. Benefices reserved by name cannot be exchanged.
body:
In the Name of Christ, Amen. It is proposed that a certain late Master Guidentinus was archpriest of the church of St. Stephen of Lanania in the diocese of Genoa, and he stood in peaceful and quiet possession of that benefice for many years. Then the said archpriest obtained a vicarage of the parish church, which was to be conferred upon him by the said Genoese diocese. Finally, while the said Master Guidentinus was still in full and peaceful possession of the aforementioned archpriesthood, a certain John of the aforementioned church, prebendary of the church of St. Mary of Trigona in the diocese of Albenga, obtained the said archpriesthood from the Supreme Pontiff. The words of the letters state thus: “Heretofore, since we were unwilling to grant special favor to the said son Guidentinus of Faxarengo, archpriest of the church of St. Stephen of Lanania in the Genoese diocese, concerning a perpetual vicarage of the parish church of the said Genoese diocese, in a certain manner vacant, we graciously granted provision. Concerning which indeed apostolic concessions were not made. Since therefore it was hoped that the archpriesthood of the said church of St. Stephen of Lanania, which is a dignity, and which the same Guidentinus held at that time, as he holds it, would become vacant, wishing to grant you special favor in view of the aforementioned merits concerning the said archpriesthood, and below, when it shall happen that the same becomes vacant by the aforementioned or any other means, except by the death of the said Guidentinus, we reserve it to be conferred upon you as a gift, in the apostolic [reservation], etc.”

After a controversy arose concerning the said archpriesthood between the said Master Guidentinus and Master John, who was put into possession by the said executors, and the said Master Guidentinus stated that the said archpriesthood had not been, nor was, vacant, and therefore could not be conferred upon the said Master John, the said parties came to a certain agreement, whereby they compromised under the appellation of the name of honor, namely the said Guidentinus, archpriest of the church of St. Stephen, and so forth. Finally, the said compromissaries made an agreement between the said parties, namely that the said Master John ought to give a certain quantity of money to the said Master Guidentinus, and the said Master Guidentinus ought to exchange the said archpriesthood with the canonry of the said Master John. And thus it was done, because they renounced with the intention of exchanging, and as if by an exchange made, the collation was effected on both sides.

After the said Master John stood in peaceful possession of the said archpriesthood for several years, afterwards it happened that a certain other Master John of Rauacheriis, a cleric of Genoa, obtained the said archpriesthood as vacant in the Curia, or otherwise, as contained in the apostolic letters. Other executors having been appointed, before whom the question is debated, which of these has the stronger rights. And for the evidence

It must be premised that in this case the aforementioned John de Rauacheriis is the plaintiff, and therefore the burden of proof rests upon him to show that this archpriestric is vacant, according to the rule that he who possesses is not required to prove, unless he wishes to displace the well-founded claim of the plaintiff, as stated in C. de probat. l. actor quod asseverat; and l. siue possidetis; C. de exceptionibus l. si quidem; C. de rei venditione l. fi; de interdictis § commodum. It is also relevant what is noted in c. literis de rescriptis in the Decretals, and in c. 1 de regulis iuris lib. 6. Let us therefore examine how the said John de Rauacheriis proves this vacancy: where it must be considered first with regard to the apostolic letters.

† For if indeed this archpriestry had been conferred in fact upon the said Lord John from the aforementioned church before it had become vacant, and he had thereby acquired possession of the said vicarage, then that collation would have been null by operation of law, to such an extent that it could not have been confirmed by any subsequent supervening event, as established in the legal maxim *quod ab initio*, and especially if the executors had not been aware of the collation of the said vicarage, as stated in the law *Haec autem*, § 1, in the Digest under the title *Ex quibus causis in possessionem eatur*, and in the Digest under the title *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, in the law *Multum interest*. On the contrary, the said grace of expectation of the said archpriestry would have been consumed, particularly by the said exchange:

† because the graces of those awaiting them are easily consumed by any incompatible act, as in c. gratiae, de rescriptis, in the Clementines, and in the Digest, de divortio, l. quod ait lex. It is therefore established from the records that the said archpriestry was not vacant at the time of the said collation made by the executors of the said Lord John of the aforementioned church. Hence it appears that the collation to him was rashly made and was null, because a benefice which is not vacant cannot be conferred. Now it remains to be seen whether the said Lord John of the aforementioned church has acquired a right in the said archpriestry by virtue of the aforementioned exchange. For if he has acquired a right by the exchange, the letters subsequently issued in favor of the said Lord John of Rauacheriis would be null, as obtained by concealment of the truth and as impossible, as in c. cum nostris, de concessionibus praebendarum. But if the exchange had been null by operation of law, then without doubt the said archpriestry was vacant at the time of the said letters granted to the said Lord John of Rauacheriis, and it would have been vacant at the time of the acquisition of possession of the said perpetual vicarage, as in c. cum in cunctis, de electione.

† It must therefore be considered whether the said exchange could have been made in this manner. And it appears that it could not, because reserved benefices cannot be exchanged by the person. And the reason is that in an exchange a renunciation is required, with the intention of exchanging, into the hands of him who could confer; but in reserved benefices no one can confer, unless the Pope, or another by mandate of the Pope, as in cap. 1, de renunt., lib. 6, according to the doctors, and especially the more recent ones; and this was also held by Federicus de Senis in his treatise on exchanges. But I doubt this, because it matters greatly whether the Pope makes this reservation simply, as is the case when he makes general or special reservations of his own motion; and then I concede that an inferior to the Pope cannot confer, even by way of exchange. Or whether this reservation was made in favor of the petitioner, and as accessory to the petition itself, or, to speak more aptly, as a kind of preamble; and then, if the petitioner renounces the letters, the intention of the reserving party seems to be ended, arg. ff. de haered. inst., l. si. For, as appears, the Pope was not otherwise reserved, except in favor of the petitioner. And thus, the grace being ended, the reservation ends, because it was not made principally for itself, but for something else. But it seems safer to say that even the grace being ended as regards the petitioner, the reservation still endures, because the authority of the Pope does not depend on the petitioner, and the reservation is perfected in the nature of things before the collation. Although therefore one clause ceases, another remains, arg. ff. de cond. et demonstr., l. haec scriptura. This is held by the Archipresbyter in cap. tibi, qui de rescript., lib. 6, on the word "reserved"; and also in c. inter dilectos, extra de excess. praelat.; and in c. cum dilectus, de iure patronat., according to Innocentius. And therefore the said John de Ravacheriis has the stronger rights in the said archpriesthood, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The fisc may, by virtue of a special privilege, sell in its entirety a thing which it holds in common with another. An appeal from a sale encompasses every contract whereby ownership is transferred.
2. A building accedes to the soil, and the builder has the exception of fraud, if the expenditure was useful to the owner and he acted in good faith.
3. By custom, individual cities have a separate fisc.
4. The right belongs to those on whose soil the building has been constructed.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† I premise, for the sake of clarity, that the fisc may, by virtue of a special privilege, sell in its entirety a thing which it holds in common with another, as is stated in the Code, On the Sale of Fiscal Property Held in Common with Private Persons, law 1, book 10.

† I understand the term "sale" generally to mean every contract by which ownership or perpetual utility is transferred; and much more strongly can he lease, according to the note in C. de Iac. san. ec. iubemus, in the gloss "ut una pars," at the end, because to whom that which is greater is permitted, that which is lesser is also permitted, as stated in the aforementioned law iubemus. That the term "sale" is general is proven in l. statuliberi a caeteris, § 5, ff. de statulib. It is true that the gloss says in l. fi, C. de praediis curia, lib. 10, and that there the disposition is contrary to common law, where by the name of sale other contracts are not included. But I believe that the privilege of the fisc should be interpreted broadly here. It is a special rule for the fisc that it may sell the whole on account of a part, although Martinus said that this is true only when the common thing cannot be divided. And even if this is conceded, our case stands, because here too it could not conveniently be divided. It is true that unless he who has a part receives what concerns him, he can claim it, as the same text says there.

Secondly, I premise that a building accedes to the soil; nevertheless, if the builder has good faith and is in possession, and the expenditure is useful to the owner, he has the exception of fraud, unless the expenses are refunded to him; otherwise, if it is not useful to the owner, as in l. Paulus, de doli exceptione, and l. si area, de condictione indebiti.

Third, I premise that by custom each city has its own particular treasury, since we see that they, or their lords, exercise either mere or mixed jurisdiction, as noted in the Authentica *De defensione civitatum*, § *Nulla*. And this custom being presupposed, that the Lord of Tours can appoint a fiscal procurator in the city of Asti, nevertheless, if there is no proof of a mandate, as in l. 1, § 1, D. *De officio procuratorum Caesaris*.

† Having therefore premised these things, if it is asked what right he has, in whose soil something is alleged to have been built, I say that before the fisc sold, he had the right of ownership in that which was built on his soil; nevertheless, after the fisc sold, believing that the whole pertained to it, or granted it in emphyteusis, it must have that part of the price or rent which falls to it, according to the authority of C. de quadr. praesc. l. bene a Zenone, and according to C. si adversus fiscum l. edicto. And perhaps, according to what is proposed, this is not properly a case of annona, because the estates are distinct, considering the soil alone. But considering the building, which is indivisible, and is made in an inseparable manner, and does not stand by itself, as in this example, it is well a case of common ownership. Therefore, something must be provided to the lord of the said soil, at the discretion of a good man, for his portion of the annual pension of the said emphyteusis; otherwise, he is not bound by reason, and he can vindicate the thing, as in the aforementioned l. j. C. de vend. rerum fisca. For there it is said that if the part of the price which falls to the partner of the fisc is not paid to him, he has the power of vindicating the thing. Moreover, if the fisc was named in the judgment, but not cited in the process, the judgment is valid between the litigants, but it does not prejudice the fisc by the law itself, as C. ubi in rem act. l. j. and 2, and ff. de iudic. l. venditor; just as the sentence is valid between the buyer and the non-cited seller, yet it does not prejudice the seller by the law itself. And this appears to be the response to all the points about which it is asked: it is finally concluded what right the owner of the soil has in the buildings, and what must be done by the emphyteutic party of the fisc, and that he is bound to abide by the contract, provided that the lessee provides what is to be provided, although the aforementioned first law seems to say that this must be done by the fisc, namely, that the fisc receive the whole price and give the part. And similarly I say that it should receive the whole rent annually and give a congruous part, or cede its rights in that part; but if the lessee does this, I do not make much of it, because it is not a matter of force by whom it is paid, provided that it is paid, as ff. de negot. gest. l. si liber. But if there were whole bodies of mills distinct in place and building, although they were made beside the road, yet they would be in the soil of the builder, because the fisc would have nothing to do there, as in this example set before me. One mill. Another mill. Whole outside the road. Whole outside the road.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A statute making mention of a possessor is understood to refer to a lawful possessor.
2. Whether a judicial precept issued to someone, ordering him to relinquish possession or to prove his title, is valid.
3. Whether a judge may protect and defend the true possessor, and decree that he not be disturbed, without a formal petition and ordinary judicial inquiry.
body: Add also the following opinion. In the Name of Christ. Amen.

† A statute, which provides in effect that if anyone is in possession of a certain holding or land, and has held it, the rector may not issue a precept to him, nor place any boundary marker upon that holding; and that he ought not to be disturbed in that holding until the matter is fully adjudicated, is just and reasonable, and conforms to the common law; because such a mandate ought not to issue unless the reason is known, as in C. si per vim, vel alio modo, l. fi.; and C. unde vi, l. meminerint; and Inst. de interd., §. commodum. But it must be considered that this statute was made in favor of the possessor, as appears from the words of the statute. And therefore, if one were not a possessor, but a disturber of the possessor, or of another’s possession, the favor of the statute is not due to him, as in ff. comm. diui., l. communi diui., §. inter praedones; and ff. de usufr., l. aequissimum; and ff. de offi. praesi., l. illicitas, §. ne potentiores. And therefore, if I am in possession, and another injures me by coming to my possession, I can petition the praetor to command him not to injure me; and I can invoke the office of the magistrate, who, being informed of my possession and the adversary’s injury, can prohibit him from approaching in the future, as in l. fi., ff. de offi. procu. Caes.; and as noted in c. in praesentia, extra de prob., by Innocentius. And thus I stated in the counsel that I rendered to the party.

† Recently you sent me the records, and I have considered that the judge issued a certain summary order, requiring either that the defendant relinquish possession or that he prove his title. This order does not appear to have been valid in this form, because the defendant is not required to prove the title of his asserted possession, as stated in C. de petitione hereditatis, l. cogi, and C. de rei venditione, l. si. Nor is he compelled to relinquish possession unless the action is brought by way of a petitory or possessory suit, as stated in ff. de rei venditione, l. qui restituere, and Inst. de interdictis, § hodie. Nevertheless, the gloss on the original canon law states that it suffices against the wrongdoer to bring a simple complaint, saying, "Lord judge, such a person is committing violence against me in my possession," as noted in j. q. 3, quia praesulatus. This is consistent with another statute, mentioned in the point at issue, which speaks of terminating lawsuits and controversies, whether by way of a libel or petition, or by way of contradiction or complaint; I emphasize this word. Therefore, since it cannot be denied that a complaint was filed against the defendant, and a just complaint, because by thus detaining the property the defendant dispossesses the rightful purchaser and possessor, and the said statute does not concern itself with legal subtleties, it seems to be said that, although the order did not hold from the beginning in the manner in which it was made, yet since the merits of the case are now established, the said proceedings should be confirmed as of now, not as of then. But since the first statute of the lord strongly argues against this, and the matter is bound only to the said order, which was issued without any proof being made, it is more consonant with reason to say that the said order was invalid, and that all the plaintiff's rights are reserved, because in doubt it is better to adhere to the words of the edict, as stated in ff. de exercendo, l. 1, § si is, qui navem. Someone might say that this is contrary to my first opinion. But if one considers it well, it is not so, because I gave my opinion when the plaintiff did not assert that the adversary was in possession: but he said that the adversary was in the thing and possession, because he first purchased it and was put in corporal possession. The defendant, however, had only a certain detention, and was molesting the true and reasonable possessor, to whom possession belongs by full right; this is sufficiently clear from what has been said.

† Even without the submission of a libel and without ordinary judicial proceedings, the judge may uphold true possession and decree that no inquiry be made, as stated in the Digest, *De libellis causis*, law *Liberis*, § *Si*. However, it would be more cautious to proceed by means of the interdict *uti possidetis*, and this would be more in harmony with the common law, as found in the Code, *Uti possidetis*, law 1. Nevertheless, turning to the records of our case, which I have now seen and examined, it appears that the litigation concerned only the precept, and nothing was claimed by the aforementioned methods, nor was possession or injury proven. Therefore, although the plaintiff asserts the truth, which ought to be supported by all means and ways, the records I have seen do not permit this, but rather suggest that the matter remains untested; thus, the defendant should be absolved from observing the precept, without prejudice to the right to bring an ordinary action through the proper legal channel.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How manyfold possession is.
2. If I possess naturally, and another comes to disturb me, I may invoke the office of the judge so that he be enjoined not to disturb me; nor is a libel necessary, nor ordinary cognition.
3. Whether a precept of the judge made to someone, that he relinquish possession, or show title, is valid.
4. Whether a sentence passed in a possessory action is interlocutory, and whether a libel and joinder of issue are required.
5. A statute making mention of a possessor is understood to refer to a lawful one.
6. The defendant is to be absolved on account of the inadequacy of the libel, the right of always suing being reserved.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

It must be premised for clarity that there are two types of possession: natural and civil. And natural possession is twofold: most natural, or corporeal, which one holds either personally or through another; and natural, with the cooperation of the disposition of law, such as that held by a usufructuary even outside the land and out of sight of it, as is read and noted in l. 1, in the beginning, D. de aqua pluviae arcendae.

† I therefore premise that if I possess naturally, and another comes to disturb me, I may invoke the office of the judge so that he may be restrained from disturbing me. And in this case, a formal petition (libellus) or ordinary judicial proceeding is not necessary, as noted by Innocentius in the Decretals, in the title *De probationibus*, chapter *In praesentia*. And the advocates say that this is the case referred to in the law *Liberis*, § *Ultimo*, in the Digest, under the title *De libera cautione*.

† But if I am in natural possession, a precept cannot be issued to the one who possesses entirely, ordering him to depart from the possession; rather, action must be brought by means of a petitory or possessory action, because possession and contradiction make him an adversary. Thus notes Innocentius in c. In praesentia.

There are, however, some who say that the judgment rendered in a possessory action is interlocutory. Hence, according to these authors, a libel would not follow, nor would joinder of issue be necessary, according to the note in the rubric of the title *De interrogationibus actorum* and according to Guillaume in the Digest, title *De in integrum restitutione*, law *Omnes*. And the glossa ordinaria says that a simple complaint suffices, as is read and noted in question 4, *Quia praesulatus*. Nevertheless, since the common opinion is that the judgment is definitive, therefore the procedure by which one arrives at it must be ordinary procedure; and since this is a rule of law from which one must not depart except in cases expressly provided for in the law, as in the Authenticum *Offeratur*, in the Institutes, title *De interdictis*, section *Hodie*, and in the Code, title *De sententiis et interlocutionibus omnium iudicum*, law *Post sententiam*, where, if the defendant appears and requests that a libel be offered to him, a libel must be offered in a possessory action, as noted by the modern commentators in the Code, title *De edicto divi Adriani*, law *Edicto*. Now, these premises having been laid down, the records must be considered. For if the plaintiff proved natural possession at the time of the writ, and thus justified the writ, judgment should be rendered in his favor, confirming the writ.

† The statute does not stand in the way, because it speaks in favor of the possessor who is in natural possession; but this person is rather a disturber than a possessor, and he who brings the action is the true possessor. And on this point rested the opinion which I gave, without having seen the other acts of the case at that time. But if it does not appear from the acts that there is proof of the plaintiff’s natural possession, namely at the time of the said precept, then such precept was not valid, as in l. 1, §. necessario, D. si mulier ventris nomine in possessionem mittatur. And this is also proved by the statute of the lord, which prohibits such precepts from being issued against those who hold and possess. Hence, ambitious precepts are not valid, as in C. si per vim, vel alio modo, l. 1, and C. unde vi, l. meminerint. Therefore, having examined the acts, although I am convinced of the justice of the plaintiff with respect to ownership.

† However, if the procedure were irregular and inconclusive, the defendant ought to be absolved on account of the inadequacy of the judgment, without prejudice to the right to proceed openly, as stated in the Extravagantes, De iudiciis, c. Examinata and c. Exhibita, and in the Digest, Si mensor falsum modum dixerit, l. 1. Since the records state that the defendant possesses [the property], the procedure is inadequate; therefore, the defendant must be absolved from the observation of the judgment due to this inadequacy, without prejudice to the right to proceed properly, as I have said above. And if my opinion was well weighed, I said the same as I now say, because I referred to Innocentius.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A loan for consumption is presumed, unless the quality of the preceding words indicates otherwise.
2. The word "to be provided" imports borrowing.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. It is proposed that a certain quantity of pearls was delivered to a certain merchant to sell the said pearls in Genoa at a certain and determined price, which amounted to 355. The merchant, who received the said pearls, had borrowed from the owner of the said pearls 18 florins and 6 gold coins. Moreover, afterwards, the said merchant, being unable to sell the said pearls for the said amount, stated that he had retained them for himself, and that for the remainder of the said amount, in addition to the aforementioned loan, he wished to give a certain sum of money. And thus he entrusted them to another merchant, of whom the said owner of the pearls was not satisfied at that time; but afterwards he went to the said William, the commissioner, and said, “Are you willing to lend me money?” And he said so, and counted out to him the said quantity, which amounted to the said remainder.

† Now it is asked whether, by these words, the stated quantity is understood to have been lent, or received and given under the name of the residue, or indeed under the name of the price to be determined by the discretion of an honest man and good merchants. This question is resolved by what is noted in l. cum quid. ff. si certum pet. For a loan is presumed, unless the quality of the preceding words indicates otherwise. Therefore, this must be examined, and the quality of the person paying must be weighed, because he was the procurator of another, as in l. Lucius. ff. de instito. and ff. de verborum obligationibus. l. ita stipulatus. §. Grisogonus. But these matters require proof of fact, and therefore a clear answer cannot be given unless the proofs are seen and produced.
† But the common and ordinary meaning of the word *præstari* is to lend. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If a father has substituted his sons and grandsons for a son who predeceased him, whether they are admitted simultaneously or successively.
2. When several persons are joined to one under a collective name, whether that one person is entitled to one half and all the others to the other half, or how otherwise.
3. Whether the right to collect tolls can be acquired by prescription, and whether the goods of those who do not pay the toll may be seized after they have left the territory where payment was due.
4. Whether one who has the right to collect from those navigating or traveling by water may demand payment from those traveling by land, and vice versa.
5. Whether, due to non-payment of the toll, the goods fall into forfeiture.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† If a father has substituted his sons and grandsons for a son who predeceased him, the grandson does not succeed together with his father by virtue of this substitution. For among the children themselves, the ordinary order of affection for children is observed, as stated in D. de lib. et posth. l. Gallus, in principio; and D. ad Trebell. l. heredes mei, § peto.

† Moreover, when several persons are joined to one under a collective name, that one must have one-half, and the others named under the comprehensive name must have the other half, as in D. de usufructu accresc. l. Si quis Titio, and C. de impuberibus et aliis substitutis l. Fin. From these, the question is determined, namely, that the living son is called by the said substitution to one-half, and not his sons. But the grandsons from another predeceased son are called to the other half. And by this, a response is given to all matters inquired about; and thus should those words “in eorum” be understood, because according to the order of affection among children, as fully noted in l. Gallus § Quidam recte D. de liberis et posthumis. The objection from D. de usufructu accresc. l. Si quis Titio, and the notes thereon, does not prevail.

† Regarding the question whether the right to collect tolls can be acquired by prescription or by custom of such long standing that there is no memory of the contrary, it must be said that yes, provided the Prince or his representative is aware of it, as stated in the Digest, *De publicanis*, law *Si publicanus*, § *Finis*, and there also by Doctorus, and in the *Speculum*, *De causa possessionis et proprietatis*, § *Quia vero*, under the rubric *Sed quid de colligentibus pedagium*, where it is thus stated: “What about those collecting tolls from those who pass through a public road? Can they be prohibited by law through this interdict, lest the toll be levied?” I answer that if they hinder those traveling on a public road against the law, as in the Decretals, *De treuga et pace*, chapter *Finis*, unless they have a privilege from the Prince, as in the Code, *Nova vectigalia institui non possunt*, laws 1 and 3, and *De vectigalibus omnium*, from which it follows that cities or nobles cannot impose new tolls in their territories except by privilege of the King or Prince, as in the Code, *Nova vectigalia institui non possunt*, law *Vectigalis*, and in the Decretals, *De censibus*, chapter *Innovamus*. And when the country is poor, this privilege is easily granted, as in the Code, *Eodem*, law 1. However, ancient tolls, or salt taxes, established by the authority of Lateran councils, or of Kings or Princes, or introduced by ancient custom of which no contrary memory exists, may be levied, as in the Decretals, *De verborum significatione*, chapter *Super quibusdam*. But whether, after those passing through have left the territory of this noble, their goods can be seized, it must be said that no, even if the said nobles were under the same superior lord; because they have divided territories, and the useful jurisdiction is distinct, one from the other, and confined within its own boundaries, as in the Code, *De bonis auctoris iudicis possessoribus*, law *Cum unus*, § *Is qui*. For all governors have jurisdiction from the Emperor, yet one governor cannot seize a person or property in the territory of another. Indeed, it appears that those to whom a territory is assigned are prohibited by others from doing so, as argued in chapter 1, § *Si quis de manso*, *De controversia investiturae*, collection 10.

But if there is a custom of collecting a passage toll from those passing by water, could it be collected from those passing by land? I answer that this passage toll is collected by reason of the public soil, as noted in l. j. ff. de public. But the public soil is here designated, namely, by water; hence it is not lawful to collect it by land, by argument from ff. de aqua quotidia. and l. hoc iure. §. si aqua. But what if there is a custom that payment is made both by water and by land? I answer that the custom must be observed.
† But does the matter fall into a forfeiture? I answer that it does, provided that the right to collect the toll is presupposed, as in l. commissa, de publicis, and c. Ego Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If an error was made in the name of the judge in a petition submitted to the Prince against a judgment, because the name of the advisor was placed, when the name of the judge should have been placed, whether the petition is vitiated.
2. Whether a false petition vitiates a rescript, and when.
3. Whether a praetorian pledge can be obligated, and whether it is said to be in our goods.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The statute proposed contains that the judge ought to render sentence according to the counsel of a wise man. It is proposed that the wise man gave counsel, who was called Lord etc., and according to that counsel the judge judged, who was called Lord Bernard. For supplication was made as against the sentence passed by Lord Martin, and the supplication was pursued, and the counsel of Lord Martin was produced, whereas the sentence produced speaks in the person of the said Lord Bernard.

It is asked whether the said petition should be executed, since it does not refer to the person of the said consulting lord, but to the person of the said pronouncing lord. And it seems that it should not, because the said stipulation is not true in fact. For he who gave counsel does not thereby render judgment, as is stated in the Digest, De appellationibus, law 1, section Quaesitum. This is clearly apparent, because an action in factum does not arise from counsel, but from judgment. Moreover, counsel does not become res judicata, but judgment does: this is manifest to all, as appears in the Code, De relationibus, law 1, and in the Code, De dilationibus, law Cum a nobis.

On the contrary, it seems that it should be executed, because an error was made in the name of the judge, and an error in the name should not vitiate the act, as is stated in the Digest, De iudicibus, law Si in iudiciis; and in the Digest, De appellationibus, law 1, section Denique; and see the note of the doctors in the Digest, De legatis 1, law Si quis in fundi vocabulo. For when the error is established, and the substance is established, and the quality of the litigation is the same, and the substance is the same, the error should not vitiate the act, as is stated in the Institutes, De legatis, section Si quis in nomine. The person of the one writing the rescript must be considered, who did not consider the person, but the cause: and he would have written the same rescript if the true person had been expressed, according to the note in the Digest, De pactis, law Tale pactum, section Fin.

Furthermore, since this counsel is to be followed by necessity by virtue of the form of the statute, it is said in a certain sense that he who gave counsel pronounces judgment, as is stated in the Digest, De legatis 2, law Unum ex familia, section Si de falcidia. But another reason seems to be able to be given more effectively, because since counsel is in a certain sense called judgment, just as we say that in such a judgment the jurist is present, at least the letters should operate in the rescission of the counsel, if it was not properly rendered: and once the counsel is rescinded, it seems that the judgment too should be rescinded, as is noted in the Digest, De acquisitione hereditatis.

† l. si is, ad quem. This passage is doubtful, because error vitiates rescripts, if it concerns those matters which are substantial, as C. si contra ius, vel uti. pub. l. praescriptione. As also extra de rescrip. c. Rodulphus and c. fi. Moreover, false demonstration vitiates rescripts, as is expressly stated extra de rescrip. ca. significante. And there fully on this point no. per Batt. especially because they are contrary to the common law, arg. in cap. suspectum. de rescrip. lib. 6. and arg. ff. de lib. et posth. l. commodissime. But to the contrary, the laws cited above in the opposing part make for the other side; yet it is harsh to extend the words of the rescript to an omitted person, and because false demonstration is here in the substance, since the substance of the commission is the sentence itself, which sentence is not found in the nature of things.

Furthermore, it must be known that false supplication vitiates a rescript with a certain distinction. For either it is about substantial matters, and then it vitiates, as no. Inno. extra de priuil. c. ex parte abbatissę. Or it is about some demonstration which is not of the substance, because the person is certain, although there is an error in the name. And then it does not vitiate, because the rule of law dictates this, as ff. de condi. et demonstr. l. falsa demonstratio. ff. de haered. instit. quotiens. Similarly we see in public instruments, as C. de testam. errore. and l. præposteri. And from the rule of law one should not depart; but here the person of the judge who passed the sentence is certain, therefore it should not vitiate the rescript for the reason that an error was made in the name. And it seems to be the case of ff. de iudi. l. si in nomine. And this error appears by reference to the records, as l. in summa. ff. de re iudi. Therefore, rather, the records should be followed, to which our most magnificent lord referred himself. For the person did not give place to the rescript, but the cause, because the right is placed in the cause, as ff. ad l. Aquil. l. si ex plagiis. §. si in cliuo capitolino. Nor would the Prince have granted the rescript less, if there had been no error, as extra de rescri. c. super literis. And the laws which say that error vitiates rescripts must be understood of error in the final cause, not of error of a proper name, when the person is certain, because it suffices that by reference to the records the demonstration is true, arg. in l. j. in fi. ff. de dote prælega.

Moreover, even if we consider the true name, this one can be said to have pronounced, i.e., to have disposed what should be pronounced, ar. extra de app. c. nouit. For whenever a special form is given to someone, he who gives it is considered to have pronounced the act subsequently performed by another, t extra de offi. delega. cap. is, cui ab apostolica. and l. si pater. ff. de manumiss. vind. Also it suffices that the rescript is true in law, arg. ff. de haere. insti. l. fi. And sometimes one person is concealed, yet the act is not vitiated, as ff. si certum peta. l. singularia. And thus it seems to me that Bald. de Perusio holds that it is according to the mind of the one writing the rescript, and that this rescript can be aided by reference to the records, although this passage is doubtful, especially because they are written in strict law: nevertheless I see, on account of the connection of persons, that even when one person is expressed in rescripts, two persons concurring in the same cause are understood to be expressed, as C. de diuer. rescrip. l. si libellum. So it is here, because both concur in the same end of the matter.

† On the second point, if this is asked, whether a pretorian pledge can be pledged as security, it seems to be said that yes, because in our goods as a pledge, although we cannot alienate the thing, as in the Digest, on the law, l. si filius. §. idem princeps. resolved with the first decree, both pledges are resolved, because if he is sued hypothecarily, he offers himself to the defense of the first cause with solemn bail and reimbursement of expenses, as in l. cum proponas. with its material. and this by l. Digest, on pledges, l. lex vectigali and c.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The Pope granted a favor to someone, that he might accept one, two, or three, or more benefices up to the sum of 200 florins; how that clause, "or more," is to be understood.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen. The case is as follows: D. B. has a grace whereby he may accept one, two, three, or more benefices, even cures of souls, or dignities in cathedral or other churches, whose revenues do not exceed the sum of 200 florins annually in Milan, if in the province, cities, and dioceses of Padua, Verona, Vicenza, and Cumae. Secondly, he was granted a grace solely in the city and diocese of Bergamo of the province of Milan. A benefice became vacant in the diocese of Bergamo; D. B. accepted it, although he had already accepted under his grace [benefices] exceeding 30 [florins], not reaching the sum of two hundred. It is asked what is the law, etc. In the Name of Christ. Amen.

† On the said point, I say that those words “one, two, three, or more,” etc., are not extended to the acceptance of as many benefices, even if they do not amount to the said sum, because that word “more” refers only to two. No. Arch. in c. ii. de filiis presby. lib. 6. To this effect, ff. de leg. 3. l. fideicommissa. §. si quis decem; and ff. si quis cau. l. et si post tres; and ff. de verborum significa. l. hęc adiectio; ff. de in lit. iur. l. cum furti; and ff. de leg. 2. l. cum filius. §. 2. For the said grace is not only ambitious, and therefore to be restricted, but also inequitable. For if we were to say the contrary, it would follow that one could accept a thousand benefices, which would not be worth more than two hundred florins: which is false and absurd, as ff. de lega. 3. Offilius; and C. de pręposi. sacrorum scriniorum. l. hac parte, where it is notably stated, “let them not occupy more advantages, leaving nothing to the others.” Therefore, according to what has been said, the acceptance made in the said city of Bergamo by the said ambitious petitioner beyond the number was invalid by law itself. And to this effect, the argument from quantity to the number of persons, ff. de nego. gest. l. qui aliena. §. liberos; and ff. de vulgar. substitu. l. qui plures libertos. Considering the letters, namely the first part declaring the second, it appears that “do not exceed” and “are valid up to,” etc., mean the same thing. And this is due to the word “up to.” C. de donatio, sancimus, in princip. It is not an objection that the notaries in cap. quamuis. de praeben. lib. 6. say otherwise, because there it does not say “up to the sum of such value,” but designated a certain quantity, which can be included in a larger sum, not a smaller one, as C. de lega. cum quaestio. in glo. magna, uetsicu. et est ratio. And it supports what is noted, C. de probationibus. rationes. de pactis. si unus. §. si cum; and the said §. libertos. It pleases R. to see the second letters, which say: “whose fruits are worth the sum of two hundred florins,” whether they mean only as much as if it had been said, “whose fruits do not exceed,” as is presupposed in your case. And also see the said Innoc. in cap. cum dilectus. de iure pa. and Archi. in taISOASVS.. In the name of Christ, amen. The case is proposed thus: d. Ugolinus, formerly bishop of Parma, granted in honorific fief to d. A., son of d. Hyllarius of the archers, absent, and to a certain recipient, and to Hyllarius, brother of Begarius, brothers of the said d. A. present, and to the said names of the recipient, one piece of land, etc. Then the said B., bishop of Parma, successor of the said B. Ugolinus, granted in fief to the said d. A., or confirmed the said fief to the present recipient for himself and for the said Hyllarius, absent, for whom he promised ratification, in such a way that each of them should have the said fief. Then d. Ioan., now bishop of Parma, after the death of d. An. and with d. Hyllarius still living, after a few days granted in fief to d. Ant. de Ferro, citizen of Parma, as vicar, on account of the death of the said d. A., and on account of ingratitude, or felonies committed by the said Hyllarius, as well as for negligence in seeking and acknowledging the due oath to be taken within a year and a day, as he ought to have done. For the said Hyllarius never appeared before the bishop now present to acknowledge the said fief and to take the due oath. Which fief, for the aforementioned reasons, the said lord bishop declared vacant in the grant made to the aforementioned A. de Ferro, and held it as vacant; and he deprived the said Hyllarius of the said fief, and from the said piece of land, the said A. de Ferro took possession.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether he who has a twofold interest in divine offices ought to have two distributions.
body: In the name of Christ. Amen. From whose mouth all right judgment has proceeded; treating the matter more broadly than is strictly due, because what ought to be included is not always entirely set forth in the statement of the case, whence opinions rendered are very often found to be harmful.

† I premise that a fief, with which two brothers or similar persons are invested, may have had its origin in the person of one predecessor, such as a father or a grandfather; and in that case, although they may have been newly invested on account of the investiture and recognition that they are bound to seek, that new investiture is not attended to so much as the first, because of many matters, one of which must be addressed here. And therefore, in the case where the father, grandfather, or great-grandfather had been invested for himself, his sons, and his descendants, as is sometimes customary, then if the said A. and Hyllarius were among those descendants, by the death of the said A. the way would not have been opened for the bishop to confer his share, but the descendants of that first invested person succeed in infinitum, although according to ancient law only up to a single degree, as in ti. qui feu. da. pos. c. j. §. hoc quoque, and noted by the Gloss in ti. de suc. feu. §. hoc quoque, unless in the grant the degree of descendants was limited; and thus ought the Gloss in l. item videndum, §. fi. ff. de poe. her. to be understood.

† But in the case where their grandfather, great-grandfather, or father had not been invested, but the fief had begun in the persons of those two, then upon the part of the deceased the way is opened to confer the said fief on another, as in c. 1. qui suc. tene. col. 10. and in titu. de duo. fra. de nouo benefi. inuesti. c. 1. And from this it is clear that the said bishop could by law confer the share of the said A. upon Antonio de Ferro.

† Regarding the share of Hyllarius, however, it must be considered that he is not to be deprived of the fief abruptly, as in c. j. extra de feu. sine culpa non ami. He ought, therefore, to be cited and convicted of fault; and if he has been convicted and condemned, he ought to be deprived of the fief. If, however, the crime was notorious, he should first be called upon, as the doctors relate and as I have written at length on l. ea quidem. C. de accu. Nor do I deem it fitting that he should possess an ecclesiastical fief who knowingly killed a cleric, because he who commits an offense against the law is not aided by the benefit of the law, l. auxilium. ff. de mino. and l. qui sub praetextu. C. de sa. san. eccl.; for he offends the entire clergy who kills a cleric, and especially a priest, as in l. si quis in hoc genus. C. de episc. et cle.; and this with respect to the homicide.

† But with respect to his not having sought investiture within a year and a day, there is no doubt that he could be deprived by the bishop, as in x. colla. in quo tempore miles inuesti. peti. debe. c. 1. From the foregoing it is inferred that, if the words are such as are assumed in the statement of the case, Antonio de Ferro is preferable to the aforesaid Hyllarius. I, Bartholomaeus de Saliceto.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether he who attends the divine offices by a twofold right ought to have double distributions.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen.

† And in support of this opinion of Ioa. And., the case of ff. de annis leg. l. qui Marco seems to apply. But the contrary seems to hold, because daily distributions, which are given to those attending the hours, are called alimony (or maintenance), as in c. 1. de cle. non resi. lib. 6; however, alimony is not owed except once, because it cannot be duplicated, as in ff. de vsufr. l. dominus. §. fi. And here Pe. de Bel. holds that if alimony has been bequeathed to priests and deacons, or to the prior and the brothers of the Hermits, the one who is both prior and brother, or priest and deacon, ought not by reason of the twofold office to have duplicated alimony; so holds Pe. in l. qui Marco, and Bar. holds the same there, and Cy. holds the same in C. de lega. l. cum quaestio; of which legal authorities no mention is made by Io. An. What then shall we say? I reply: on account of the authority of Ioan. An., I do not depart from what he himself determined, because these are not pure alimony. For they are certain compensations for the solicitude of the divine offices, so that divine worship may be increased; and I maintain this especially when this has been observed through the custom of the church preserved over the longest times. For no reason can be given why the other voice should be extinguished. And whenever two rights concur in the same person, it is deemed one, not several, as in ff. de his, quib. vt indi. l. tutorem; nor is it anything new that he who holds several voices can by one common word perform both offices, as in ff. de autho. tu. l. accipientis, and extra de conces. praeben. postulastis, by Bart., and ff. de pac. l. si plures, and ff. fam. herc. l. plane, and what is noted in ff. de eo, per quem factum erit, l. fi. §. si a fideiussore, in the gloss that begins, ex hoc videtur. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If power has been granted to arbitrators to render an award within two months, and within that same time and term there is a prorogation once and multiple times, whether the prorogation ought to be made within the term of two months, and how often a prorogation may be made.
2. Whether a prorogated compromise is the same.
3. Add the two following consilia, and see below cons. 350, beginning with the word "compromissi" and following.
body:
In the Name of Christ, Amen. Quartus, formerly of Berti de Quarto, a citizen of Lucca, and Bertus, his son, and each of them on one part or parts; and Nicolaus, son of the late Franciscus Nicolai de Arlotis, a citizen of Lucca, on the other part. The tenor of this public instrument. By their certain deliberation and knowledge, not through error, they compromised and made a compromise in the wise men, Pierus, formerly of Guidonis de Rapondis, and Landus, formerly of Sancti Henrici de Sartoribus, citizens of Lucca, as in the arbitrators and arbiters of those parties, amicable composers, common friends, and good men elected and assumed by those parties and each of them, to hear, see, know, and terminate all and singular causes, lawsuits, questions, and controversies which were, or might be in the future, or could be, between the said parties for any reason, cause, or mode: and especially on account of the guardianship and care of the said Nicolaus, which the said Quartus and Bertus, and each or either of them, performed, managed, and administered in the person and concerning the goods of the said Nicolaus, and on account of the reckoning of the said guardianship and care, and the rest and residue, and by reason of those things which one party demanded or intended to demand from the other and against the other by the act of guardianship and care, directly and contrary, and for any other reason or mode with the other clause, that those are understood to be the lawsuits and questions between the said parties, on which and concerning which the said arbitrators and arbiters pronounced a sentence or award: giving and granting the said parties to the same arbitrators and arbiters and common friends license and power, authority, bail, and every faculty to see, hear, know, and terminate the aforesaid lawsuits and questions and any other discordances and controversies from hence to two nearest future months and within that time once and many times, and as often and as much as they wish, to prorogue, and to do all and singular of the aforesaid summarily and de plano, and without the noise and figure of judgment, and no solemnity or form of law and statutes being observed, by right and in fact, of good and equity, or by right only, of good and equity, and by arbitration only, and as they wish, the parties being present or absent, cited or not cited, petition or libel taken or not, exceptions and responses made or not: proofs received or not: and in any place, time, and day, festival and non-festival, even in honor of God. To which solemnities and substantial and formalities the said parties shall stand, obey, and submit to every sentence, award, declaration, arbitration, and precept to be pronounced by the said arbitrators and arbiters, and not to appeal, supplicate, or raise a complaint, or oppose nullity, nor to request to be reduced to the arbitration of a good man, or to be reformed for the better. Which compromise, and all and singular other things above and below written, the said contracting parties and parties compromised and agreed among themselves, and mutually, with solemn stipulation intervening, namely, that each party shall have, hold, attend to, fulfill, and observe all that was done and promised and ought to be done by them above, at all times perpetually, firm, rat, and uncorrupted, and firm, rat, and uncorrupted, and not to do or come against in any way, by themselves or others, in law or out of law, by right or in fact, directly or obliquely: under the penalty of one thousand gold florins, and double the whole of that concerning which the action was brought, if anything were done against it, with the solemn stipulation aforesaid, which, paid or not, the aforesaid things shall remain firm. And that penalty, the party not observing shall give and pay to the observing party, and it shall be due, with solemn stipulation, he promised and agreed. Also, to repair, restore, and amend one party to the other, and henceforth all and singular damages and expenses, and interest of the lawsuit and outside: which, or whatever, one party occasioned by the other, therefore made or substituted in case or outside. For all and singular of these to be observed and fulfilled, and damages and expenses and interest happening thereby to be amended and restored, and the aforesaid penalty to be paid, the aforesaid contracting parties obligated themselves mutually and reciprocally, and their heirs, and all and singular goods, present and future, by right of pledge and hypothec. The said parties expressly renouncing the exception of the thing not so done, and not usefully done, and the benefit of restitution in integrum, and the condictio of dolus malus, and indebiti, and sine causa in fac. action, and every other benefit of law, statute, and aid, by which or by which they could in any way defend or aid themselves from the aforesaid, or any of them. And moreover, for greater caution and firmness of all the aforesaid, the aforesaid contracting parties, and each of them, swore on the holy Gospels of God, the scriptures corporally touched, and the hand of me, the notary, subscribed below, to have, hold, attend to, and observe all and singular of the aforesaid at all times perpetually, firm, rat, gratifying, and uncorrupted, and not to do or come against in any way, by themselves or others, in law or out of law: always reserving the same Nicolaus all and singular his rights, which compete to him against others, who formerly were his guardians and curators: which reservation he made at the beginning, middle, and end of this contract. Moreover, the same Nicolaus, under and with the aforesaid oath, said and asserted that he was older than 19 years, but younger than 20. And so it appears from the aspect of his person. And the said contracting parties requested me, the notary subscribed below, that I make a public instrument of all the aforesaid. Done in Lucca, in the apothecary shop of the house of Petrus, formerly of Ioannes, the apothecary of Lucca, situated in Lucca in the arm of Santa Lucia towards Filiungo, before Sanctus Iacobus, formerly of Matthaeus Turchi, Dominicus, formerly of Bendinelsi Castellionis, and Blasius, formerly of Licti Coriario, citizens of Lucca, witnesses added and requested for all the aforesaid. In the year of the Nativity of the Lord 1388, indiction 11, on the day of February.

After this, the aforesaid Pierus and Landus, arbitrators and arbiters, as appears above, elected and assumed by the aforesaid parties, using the bail granted and attributed to them by the form of the said compromise, by their certain knowledge, prorogued the time and term of the said compromise for two whole months beyond the times remaining, with the same clauses, and with all and singular things contained in the said instrument of compromise: reserving the bail to prorogue the said compromise otherwise, as often as they wish, and also reserving all bail and authority entrusted and granted to them by virtue of the said compromise and contained therein: requesting me, the notary, that I make a public instrument of all the aforesaid. Done in Lucca, in the aforesaid place, namely in the apothecary shop of the house of Petrus, formerly of Ioannes, the apothecary of Lucca, before Constantinus, formerly of the Lord Lazarus Sagginae, Nicocolaus, formerly of Landi Praementiani, and Ioannes, son of Franciscus Perfectutii, citizens of Lucca, witnesses added and requested for the aforesaid, in the year of the Nativity of the Lord 1388, indiction 11, on the 12th day of April.
