After the aforesaid, the aforesaid Pierus and Landus, arbitrators, as appears above, elected and assumed by the certain parties, using the bail granted and attributed to them by the aforesaid form: by their certain knowledge, prorogued the time and term of the said compromise, already prorogued, for two whole months beyond the times remaining, with the same clauses, and with all and singular things contained in the said instrument of compromise: reserving for themselves the bail to then prorogue the same compromise, as often as they wish: and also reserving, both within the prorogated times and those to be prorogated, all bail and authority granted to them by virtue of the said compromise and contained therein, requesting me, the notary, that I make a public instrument of the aforesaid. Done in Lucca, etc.

After the aforesaid, the aforesaid Pierus and Landus, arbitrators and arbiters aforesaid, elected and assumed by the aforesaid parties, because it is not yet clear to them concerning the causes and rights of the said parties, and not wishing to leave the said lawsuits undecided. Therefore, they prorogued the time and term of the said compromise for two whole months beyond the times remaining, with the clauses and powers and all other things contained in the said instrument of compromise, reserving for themselves the bail to prorogue again, as often as they wish, and also reserving, both within the prorogated times and those to be prorogated, all bail which was granted to them by the form of the said compromise. Done in Lucca in a certain place, before Ser Cione and Ser Laurentius Miciorini, notaries, and Iacobus Francisci Martini, citizens of Lucca, witnesses requested for this, subscribed above, in the year, indiction, on the 13th day of the month of August.

After this, the aforesaid Pierus and Landus, arbitrators and arbiters aforesaid, elected and assumed by the aforesaid parties, because it is not yet clear to them concerning the causes and rights of the said parties, and not wishing to leave the said lawsuits undecided, therefore they prorogued the time and term of the said compromise until the Kalends of June of the nearest future year, with the clauses and protestations and all other things contained in the said instrument of compromise: reserving for themselves the bail which was granted to them by the form of the said compromise. Done in Lucca, etc.

After this, the aforesaid Pierus and Landus, arbitrators and arbiters, as appears above, elected and assumed, using the power granted and attributed to them by the form of the said compromise, by their certain knowledge, prorogued the time and term of the said compromise for six whole months, beyond the times remaining: with its clauses, and with all and singular things contained in the said instrument of compromise, reserving for themselves the bail and authority entrusted and granted to them by virtue of the said compromise and contained therein, requesting me, the notary, that I make a public instrument of all the aforesaid. Done in Lucca in the palace of the residence of the Lords Antiani, etc.

After this, the aforesaid Pierus and Landus, arbitrators and arbiters aforesaid, as above, elected and assumed between the aforesaid parties, using the power granted and attributed to them by the form of the said compromise, and their certain knowledge, prorogued the time and term of the said compromise: for six whole months, beyond the times remaining, with all and singular clauses appended and contained above in the instrument of the said compromise, reserving for themselves, both within the aforesaid prorogated times and also those to be prorogated, all power and bail, of which and as contained above in the instrument of the said compromise, requesting me, the notary subscribed below, that I make a public instrument of all the aforesaid. Done in Lucca in the aforesaid place, namely in the palace of the residence of the aforesaid Lords Antiani, etc.

CASE. In the Name of Christ, Amen. Since Quartus, formerly of Berti de Quarto, a citizen of Lucca, and Bertus, his son, on one part, and Nicolaus, formerly of Franciscus Arloti, on the other part: compromised and made a compromise concerning all and singular lawsuits, questions, and controversies which were or could be pending between the said parties in any way, and especially the guardianship of the said Nicolaus, which the said Quartus and Bertus managed and administered: and generally for any other reason in law or out of law, in father Guidonis de Rapundis, and Laudus, formerly of Ser Henrici de Sartoribus, citizens of Lucca, as is more fully and largely contained and appears in the public instrument by the hand of me, the notary subscribed below, requested in the year and indiction present, on the 25th day of February. Now, however, the same Quartus and Bertus wished to provide a surety. Therefore, at the prayers and commands of the same Quartus and Bertus, and each of them, Bona Iuncta, formerly of Simonis Bonaiunctae of Lucca, was solemnly surety before the aforesaid Nicolaus, present and stipulating: the instrument of compromise itself, and the contents therein, having been read to the same Bonaiuncta for his full understanding, and fully and sufficiently brought to his knowledge. Promising and agreeing, the same Bonaiuncta, with solemn stipulation intervening, to the same Nicolaus, present and stipulating, by himself, Bonaiuncta, that the aforesaid Quartus and Bertus, and each of them, will observe and fulfill all and singular things contained and deduced in the instrument of compromise by their and for their part, and dependent and connected therefrom: and that they will obey and submit to every sentence and award to be pronounced by the said arbitrators and arbiters. And that they will rather pay, give, and effectively observe all and singular things which will be contained in such sentence and arbitration to be pronounced by the said Pierus and Landus: otherwise, he, Bonaiuncta, of his own, will pay, attend to, and effectively observe all and singular of the aforesaid, every exception being removed. Similarly, the same Bonaiuncta is bound and wishes to be bound by pact to the payment and observance of the aforesaid, if a third arbitrator and arbiter were elected, who with the aforesaid Pierus and Landus, or with one of them, would promulgate such award and sentence: because thus it was acted between them in all things and by all means, with solemn stipulation valid. Which all and singular things the aforesaid Bonaiuncta, by the mandate of the said Quartus and Bertus, present and commanding, promised and agreed to the same Nicolaus, present and stipulating, to have, hold, attend to, fulfill, and observe at all times perpetually, firm, rat, gratifying, and uncorrupted, and not to do or come against in any way, by themselves or others, in law or out of law, by right or in fact, directly or obliquely, under the penalty contained in the said instrument of compromise: which, paid or not, all and singular of the aforesaid shall remain firm, under the obligation and hypothec of his, and of his heirs', and of all present and future goods: renouncing the forum, privilege, and benefit of sureties and mandators, and of two or more things to be demanded, and the epistle of the divine Adrian, and of ceding actions, and every other benefit, law, statute, and aid, by which or by which... that I make a public instrument of all the aforesaid, etc.

After the aforesaid, the Lord Bonaiuncta closed his last day, to whom in the inheritance succeeded the Hospital of Mercy by testament. Finally, however, the aforesaid arbitrators, within the term of the aforesaid last prorogation, awarded and condemned the said guardians in certain quantities and sums, the said parties being absent. Now it is asked, whether the said award is valid or null. It creates doubt, because it was pronounced outside the time of the first prorogation, so that it can be said to be valid or not, the said arbitrators having had some power to make a prorogation outside the time of the said two months specified in the said compromise: having attended to and considered the aforesaid words, namely, "from hence to two nearest future months, and within that time and term once and many times, and as often and as much as they wish to prorogue," and that the said award holds, it is argued thus: it seems that two interpretations can be gathered from those words according to various punctuations or conjunctions of words. For first, those words, "and within that time," can be joined with the preceding, and the point will be after that word, "time." And the following words, which say, "and that term," will be joined and read with the following, and thus punctuating and reading, the question has no doubt, because according to this sense and interpretation, the prorogations are valid, and consequently the sentence and award. And the reason is, because then the power of proroguing is not limited to them in time, and thus they can prorogue whenever within the term limited to them by law: following those words, "and within that time," they can be joined with the following, and thus joining, it must be observed that the conjunction which follows there, "and that term," is discarded, or resolved into a declarative, or after that word, "within," is repeated. So that the reason of correct speech and good grammar is preserved, which is to be preserved, as l. Plautius, ff. de auro et argento legato. And according to this interpretation, however taken, some doubt may arise, because the time within which the prorogation must be made is the time of those two months within which they ought to have terminated the cause. But the arbitrators prolonged after those two months had passed, therefore it seems that the said prorogation did not hold, and consequently the award and sentence did not hold, as d. l. 1, C. de arbitris. And perhaps some, moved by this reason, would say one of two things, either that this interpretation is not good, because it does not proceed without some understood word, or without some violation of the letter. Or that if it is good, all prorogations except the first, which is made within the term, did not hold, and consequently neither the award.

I, however, even granting this interpretation as good, say that the prorogations hold and are valid, and consequently the award cannot be said to have been pronounced outside the juridical term. And the motivating reason is this, because the expression of those things which are tacitly and necessarily inherent in the nature of the thing operates nothing, as C. de fideiussoribus, l. non recte, and ff. de legatis 1, l. 3. But in our proposal, if the power of proroguing had been given simply, without adding those words, "within that time," or "within that term," nevertheless those words were understood, because after the term had elapsed, there was no prorogation, because the first was already finished. And that which is not, cannot be prorogued, as ff. de precario, l. sed si manente, and ff. de arbitris, l. si nonum dies, in principio. Therefore, it follows well that these words, thus added, do not change the nature of the thing: thus, if these words had not been added, namely "within the time" and "that term," but the power of proroguing had been simply given once and many times, and as often as it pleased them, there is no doubt that the prorogations made would hold: therefore they ought to hold now. These are confirmed by the fact that the first prorogation was within the two primitive months given for terminating. And there is no doubt that that held, but with that, the first term of two months is prorogued, and thus successively the others. It follows that the prorogation is considered to be of the first given, as d. l. si cum dies, and d. l. sed si manente. Also, because that which the arbitrators do in proroguing by the power given to them, the parties themselves are said to do interpretatively, arg. l. si per alium, ff. ne quis cum etc., and l. 1, §. rectissime, and ff. de vi et vi armata, cum si. Therefore, Moreover, this seems to be the mind of the contracting parties, otherwise they would have added those words, "and as often and as much as they wish," in vain. Also, because it would be ridiculous to say that within two months they ought to have prorogued many times, and beyond many more, and especially since the first prorogation would exceed the term of two months by an incompetent term, and would suffice, still appearing to the arbitrators. Bal. says the contrary by the subscribed consilia, the tenor of which is such.

In the Name of Christ. Amen. Having examined the subject matter, the acts, and the aforementioned proceedings, and having reviewed the extensions, in the last of which the award was rendered, I state without doubt that the aforementioned award is entirely void and is void by operation of law, and consequently deserves no execution, and that the petition for reduction to the arbitration of a good man shall have no effect: because the award is void, since it presupposes some award, albeit unjust, as in l. si societatem, §. arbitrorum, D. pro socio, together with the following law. That the said award is void is clearly apparent, because the compromise was made on February 20, 1088, and power was granted to the arbitrators to view, hear, cognize, and terminate the lawsuits and questions which were the subject of the compromise within the next two months, and within that time and term, once or multiple times, as often and as much as they wished, to extend it. But the last extension was made by the said arbitrators on October 23, 1089, as I saw it attested by the hand of the said Lord Dominic, servant of Philip Lupardi of Luca. And thus it was not made within that time, within the term of the said two months, but rather after a great space and a sufficiently long interval of time. And in this last term the award was rendered, and thus the compromise and its force being entirely expired, it is void, as in l. cum dies, §. si intra, D. de arbitris. And the aforementioned last extension made upon the said arbitrators was entirely void, because, as I said, power was granted to them only to extend within the said time and term of the said two months. Hence, after that time they could in no way extend it, because arbitrators cannot do anything beyond the compromise, because all their power depends on the form of the compromise, D. de arbitris, l. non distinguemus, §. de officio. And this is especially true regarding the postponement or extension of the day of the compromise. And therefore they are not to be obeyed with impunity; the text is in D. de arbitris, l. non distinguemus, §. si, where is the case of the said question. Hence, from the premises, I conclude that the said arbitration is void, as stated at the beginning, and consequently that the petition for reduction is likewise void. And so I say and advise, I, Angelus, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Succession to a fief, where the degree of descendants is not limited, up to which degree one is admitted.
2. Whether the lord of the fief may grant the fief to another, if the degree was limited in the grant.
3. The vassal must be summoned and convicted of fault before being deprived of the fief.
4. One who knowingly kills a cleric ought not to hold a fief.
5. Whether one who does not seek investiture within a year and a day may be deprived of the fief.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen. After these things he was consulted, because it is doubted by the advocates of the adverse party against the said decision, that although the prorogation was not made within the term of the said two months, nevertheless the said final prorogation was made within the prorogated term, whence it seems to suffice, ff. de arbi. l. Labeo. Which I readily concede to be true if to the arbitrators had been given the power of prorogating as often as it shall seem good to them, without specifying a time in such a manner that the prorogation had to be made; for it runs then from time to time,

† and it is always one and the same submission to arbitration with respect to the parties submitting themselves, ff. de praeca. l. sed si manente. But the formulation of the submission expressly indicates within how much time the arbitrators have the power of prorogating, both once and multiple times and as often as it shall seem good to them; and it prescribes and wills that all prorogations be made within the very time and term of the submission, as appears, within the two months next following, and within that very time and that very term, of prorogating once and multiple times, and as often and as much as they wish. Note, therefore, that it says 'within that very time and term,' etc., because there is no possible rationale except to the said time of two months, since mention was made above only of that; but it cannot be referred to the time of the prorogation of the submission, if any should happen to be made by the arbitrators, since no mention has been made of that. If therefore the parties willed that one or more prorogations could not be made except within the term and time of two months, he would be foolish who believed that, the two-month period having elapsed, a prorogation could be made, since the power of prorogating is ended, as was shown in the consilium. Nor should anyone say that the aforesaid clause is to be punctuated after that word 'the same time', so that it thus qualifies the preceding matters regarding the cognizance and decision of the case, and thereafter those words 'and the same term' qualify the subsequent matters, so that the meaning would thus be that they can prorogate the term as often and as much as they wish, and thus the power of prorogating would have no designated, limited time; because such a form of reading and construing is not good, on account of the unity of the principal verb governing the said single clause, with the adjunct of the participle 'giving,' etc. Whence, because the verb governing the aforesaid clause under the continuation of that participle 'giving,' etc., is single, all its determinable elements determine equally and in the same manner, as in l. iam hoc iure, ff. de vulg. et pup., and l. quamuis, C. eo. tit., and C. de sen. et interlo. l. fin. But the determinable elements are the cognizance, the decision, and the prorogation. Therefore the parties willed that the case be examined and decided within two months, and within the same, that one and more term or terms be prorogated. This is also proved clearly and openly enough from the repetition of the conjunction, for one is placed after that word 'following,' when that word among others is placed after the word 'time,' before the word 'the same term.' Whence it is a conjoined clause that connects them, and thus the time is understood to be continuously repeated on account of the unity of the language, as in l. tamen ea adiectio, de leg. 3, and l. in repetendis, eo. titu. Therefore, if they take this expression as I have said: because it is more fitting, as in l. Plautius, ff. de aur. et argen. lega. In support of this is that, if we say that the power of prorogating lasts in perpetuity and is not limited in time, we will therefore by this interpretation run into infinity, which, whenever possible, must continually be avoided, as in ff. de dam. infec. l. si finita; de leg. 3, l. fideicommissa, §. si quis 10; ut leg. no. capit. l. 1, §. si cui; solu. matri. l. meam; C. de sac. san. eccle. l. fin., by Dynus and Bartolus in the said l. si finita. In support of this is that words that can operate toward obligating for more or less are in doubt always referred to the less, ff. de reg. iu. l. semper in stipulationibus; de verbo. obliga. l. quicquid astringendae. But the interpretation of which I spoke is of this kind; therefore, etc. And therefore what I have said above I confirm, as consonant with the rigor of the law and with all equity and fair interpretation. I, Angelus de Ubaldis, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a statute providing that a person shall be hanged on the gallows for a third theft, whether it is to be understood as referring to thefts committed in the place where the hanging is to take place, or anywhere; and what if he was not condemned for the other thefts, but instead paid the penalty, which was a fine.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Having seen the aforementioned matter, and having seen the following chapters,

It seems that it must be said that, by the payment of what is owed, every obligation is extinguished, l. Soluendo, D. de negotiis gestis; l. Solutionem, D. de solutionibus. For, since he has paid, he ought to be considered absolved for that offense for which he paid, arg. D. de exceptionibus rei iudicatae, l. Si quis, §. Plane, and what is contained therein. Furthermore, it can be said that the tender and deposit, as previously stated, are considered as payment, because otherwise payment could not have been made, and thus it ought not to be imputed to him, because he did what he could, as in the rule of law, Imputari, D. de regulis iuris, lib. 6; l. Qui, D. de solutionibus, and what is noted therein.

Another point must be premised, namely that, just as the aforementioned statute, which is under the rubric De furtis, commands that a notorious thief be punished by hanging, and states that "notorious" is understood to mean one who has committed three thefts: so also is the custom of Italy generally. For, although one cannot be punished by hanging for the first and second theft, he is handed over to the gallows for the third, because such custom considers him public and notorious after three thefts, arg. D. de poenis, l. Capitalium, §. Famosos, and §. Crassatores. Thus, Baldus notes in Auth. Sed novo iure, C. de furtis. By this, I say that the said statute operates nothing else in this regard than customary law.

However, the following statute operates significantly, because it states that the discretion of the authority regarding thefts in Asti is to be followed, and that the commissioners may act. These things being premised, it seems that it must be said that the said John ought not to be hanged. He ought, however, to be condemned to another penalty, not to death nor to the loss of a limb, as in the aforementioned Auth. Sed novo iure. Nor do the remissions mentioned above stand in the way, because, since it is done privately, the right of the public is sought, so that criminal proceedings may be instituted even against the will of the lord. Thus holds Master Bartolus in the aforementioned places.

I would incline toward the aforementioned opinion, first because, for that offense for which, or for the offenses for which he was condemned, he paid, or ought to be considered as having paid, as was first proven. Second, because the theft committed in Alexandria, and in the goods in Tongno, cannot nor ought to be investigated against him by the authority of Asti, because it is outside the territory, etc., arg. D. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, l. Extra territorium; and Extra, de constitutionibus, cap. Ut animarum, with the notes of the Archdeacon. It would be otherwise if he were accused in Asti, where he ought to have his domicile, and thus the ordinary course of law would proceed. The reason between the aforementioned points is that, since he is not accused, the forum of the judge’s domicile cannot be declined, because the reason of origin applies, nor can he prevent being sued there, because he is of that forum, as in Auth. Qua in provincia. Nor does the judge render justice because he commits a crime, but because he is of the territory; for he does not commit a crime there, since one who commits a crime outside the territory of origin does not do injury to the judge of origin, because he vindicates his own injury, not another’s, D. de iniuriis, l. Iniuriarum; and d. l. Sin, D. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum. And thus, after many arguments, Oldradus determines in his own work, which begins, "Quidam Lucanus in territorio Pistorii interfecit Pistoriensem," by many reasons which I omit here, because time does not permit.

Fourth, because for the theft committed by Roannus de Platis, concerning which we now speak, corporal punishment, at least to death, ought not to be inflicted, because that theft was committed before all the other aforementioned thefts. And thus he could not nor ought to be hanged for that theft according to common law, not because it was the first and second, etc., as previously alleged. Nor by that general custom, which dictates the same as the aforementioned statute according to Baldus, because for the first such penalty he ought not to be punished, nor by virtue of the statute, because for that first and second, etc., he was not notorious, but the penalty limited by the statute to the proper theft, or another arbitrary penalty, which penalty ought to be diminished and imposed at the time the crime was committed, not increased afterwards, arg. l. Iniuriarum, D. de iniuriis.

It does not avail if it is said that those thefts aggravate the crime, or that the theft was committed by the said John concerning whom the question is asked; because, on account of thefts committed elsewhere, infamy would remain, and by the theft for which payment was made, as noted by Ganus in the title De furtis, qu. 51; Bartolus in l. Si cui, §. Cum sacrilegium, D. de accusationibus; Baldus more clearly in the aforementioned Auth. Sed novo iure. For the aforementioned eminent doctors must be understood in the case when thefts committed elsewhere preceded, or for which payment was made. The theft concerning which we now inquire, as that theft for whose punishment we are arguing, ought at least to have two preceding thefts committed elsewhere, for which payment or satisfaction has been made. Otherwise, in our case, where the theft committed by the said John, concerning whom the question is asked, preceded all others, or was committed secondly. And this is indicated by the said doctors when they say that for a new theft, or the third, he will be punished, by which he becomes notorious; but not for others, which nevertheless aggravate the last one. Otherwise it would follow that, if he were punished for the first ones, he would suffer the penalty twice for the same crime, where for the first he paid; which ought not to be said.

Furthermore, it would follow that the penalty would not be imposed according to the time of the crime; which would be contrary to the case of l. 1, D. de permutationibus. For the condition of the person does not cause the penalty to be increased or diminished, which according to the form of the statute from the beginning was not corporal, but pecuniary; as the text there says. But this absurdity ceases in the question of the doctors, when he first committed many crimes, and afterwards commits one; for he is punished for the last one as being notorious, having regard to the time of the crime for which he acts; because preceding acts have a greater relation to subsequent ones, so that subsequent ones are limited and aggravated by preceding ones, than conversely, arg. l. Si quis ex argentariis, and what is contained therein, D. de edendo. And therefore the last crimes, for which he paid, and those committed elsewhere, for which he did not pay, cannot aggravate the first one. Nor can he die for breaking prison, because for the theft committed against his uncle he would have been imprisoned, which is a private crime, for which corporal punishment, or at least the death penalty, ought not to be inflicted, or for which he was condemned to a pecuniary penalty. He could not be punished otherwise for breaking prison and fleeing, except that he be considered confessed for that theft for which he was condemned in money; he ought not to be punished corporally, lest he be afflicted with double punishment. And also lest he be questioned twice, l. Licet, §. Finis, D. de nautis, cauponibus, stabulariis; l. Divus, D. de officiis praesidis. Especially since it has been pronounced, as holds Ioannes Andreas in cap. Per hoc, in the gloss Licet, Extra, de haereticis, lib. 6.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether custom can be established outright, and outside of judicial proceedings, and whether it is not necessary that it be pronounced in an adversarial trial.
2. Likewise, whether a statute or custom is valid whereby the writings of notaries are believed both for and against them.
3. For what length of time custom is established.
4. Whether custom contrary to law is valid.
5. Whether the people can enact a law whereby the writings of notaries are believed both for and against them.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen.

† If this is asked, whether custom can be introduced summarily (*de plano*) and outside of court (*extra iudicium*), and it is not necessary that it has been pronounced in a contradictory judicial proceeding, Cynus in his commentary on ff. de legi. l. de quibus states thus: In the second place, I principally ask how custom is introduced. And although a certain jurist has said that custom is introduced only through the judgments of judges, as in ff. de legi. l. nam Imperator and C. de aedifi. priua. l. an in totum, with similar passages; we nevertheless say that custom is introduced not only through judgments and judicial acts, but also through extrajudicial acts practiced among the people without any judgment, as in ff. de legi. l. sed ea; ff. de leg. 1. l. apud Iul.; ff. de leg. 3. l. nomen; de fun. instru. cum delanionis. §. asinam; de ver. sig. vt Alphenus; de reg. iu. semper in stipulationibus. These are the words of Cynus.

† Subsequently, he asks over what period of time it is prescribed or introduced; and he says that on this question there have been and are various opinions. For some have said that it is introduced in such time whereof memory does not exist, by argument of l. de quibus, §. inueterata, ff. de legi. and quae sit long. consue. l. consuetudinis in the word *longeuae*; for a long time is one hundred years, as in C. de sac. san. eccle. l. fi. and ff. de aqua quoti. et aesti. l. hoc iur. §. ductus aquae. Others, as Johannes and Azo, have said that it is introduced by the space of 10 years among those present and 20 among those absent, as noted by Accursius in ff. de legi. l. de quibus and C. quae sit lon. consue. upon the rubric. Others say that it matters whether the custom has a continuous cause, and then it is introduced in 10 years; or a discontinuous one, and then from a time whereof memory is not extant, by argument of those things which are said regarding servitudes in l. seruitutes. Certain others, as Jacobus de Arena and his followers, say that since custom has a proximity to prescription, and in this, that both assume force through length of time, and sometimes prescription is called custom, as in ff. de aqua plu. arcen. l. j. at the end; therefore, arguing from prescription, they distinguish: either custom has a title or cause, and then it is introduced in 10 years; or it does not have a title, and then it is introduced in 30 or 40 years, as in C. praescrip. 30. ann. l. si quis emptionis and l. sicut, or in a time whereof memory is not extant; and thus they understand the first opinion, because at the time of the Digest there was no mention of the 30-year prescription; and they understand the title of a custom to be a legitimate act for introducing custom, such as a judicial or extrajudicial act; Johannes and Azo [held] that it is true, namely, that it is introduced by a long time, yet that the time should be distinguished according to absence and presence is not true, since the people is always present, as in ff. quod cuiusque vniuer. no. l. sicut, and by argument of ff. de iudi. proponebatur and ff. de condi. et dem. l. municipibus, and therefore it is always introduced by the space of 10 years according to Dynus. These are the words of Cynus. For it should be known that custom is sometimes called long-standing (*diuturna*), as in ff. de leg. l. diuturna; sometimes long (*longa*), as in C. quae sit lon. consue. in the rubric; sometimes it is called inveterate (*inueterata*), as in ff. de legi. l. de quibus, §. inueterata; sometimes it is called perpetual (*perpetua*), as in ff. de leg. l. Imperator; sometimes it is called old (*vetus*), as in ff. de polli. l. Imperatores; sometimes it is called ancient (*vetusta*), as in C. de testamentis, l. testamenta; sometimes it is called antique (*antiqua*), as in C. de iur. fis. l. penul.; sometimes it is called most ancient (*vetustissima*); sometimes it is simply called custom, as in C. de offi. exa. trib. l. placet, bk. 10. From which laws one can argue for and against; nevertheless, in the end, the lord Dynus and the said Cynus abide by the aforesaid opinion, having no doubt whatever regarding a custom of the longest time. Wherefore, in the present case, according to those matters which are submitted, it seems to me that the custom of which mention is made in the said point has been proven. Secondly it is asked, assuming,

† that it has been proven, whether the said custom is valid. Concerning which it should be known that a custom contrary to law is valid; it fails in two cases: first, when the law has expressly condemned it, as in C. de furt. auth. nauigia; secondly, it fails when such a custom introduces an offense or a corruption, or incites to offending, because pernicious customs are not to be observed, as in extra de consue. c. fi.; and because it is of pernicious example that anyone by his own hand should be able to create a debtor for himself, as in C. de proba. l. exemplo, such a custom, as prone to offending and offending enormously, seems to be reproved both by positive law and by natural reason. Innocent says that where a statute is valid, a custom is valid; and where a statute is not valid, a custom is not valid.

† And therefore it must be seen whether the people can establish an express law that credit should be given to the writings of money-changers both in their favor and against them. And it seems that it cannot: especially in large amounts, because that is to provide material for fabricating falsehood. For under this pretext, money-changers could easily write a falsehood and enrich themselves through another's loss; which is most iniquitous and contrary to divine law, as in extra de testi. c. in nomine domini; just as we say in the case of one who writes something in his own favor in a testament, because he is presumed as it were to have written a falsehood, as in C. de his, qui sibi ascribunt, throughout, and ff. de falsis, l. j. and l. filius. The contrary seems true, because this can be done by pact of the parties, as noted in ff. de praeto. stip. l. fi.; therefore also by statute, as noted in ff. de regu. iu. l. ex praetorio, and l. neque pignus, §. priuatorum, and C. de decre. decu. in the rubric. This question is sufficiently doubtful, and therefore I do not decide this second step. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When no time limit has been set, for how long the power to arbitrate endures.
2. Whether an extension may be made by the arbitrator without citation or notification to the party.
3. If the power to extend has been granted to the arbitrators within the term given for arbitration, whether they may extend it after the term has expired.
4. How the clause in compromises, "so often," "whenever," etc., is to be understood. "So often," "whenever": and that, however, it does not appear that he considered this; from the sixth sentence, it proves that all things are solemnly done.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen. The words of the compromise are as follows: granting and conceding to the said arbitrators and common friends license, power, authority, and every faculty to view, hear, cognize, and terminate the aforementioned lawsuits and questions, and any other discordances and concordances, from hence for the next two months, and within that time and term, to extend it once, many times, as often and as much as they shall wish, and to do all and each of the aforesaid things summarily and de plano, without the noise and form of judicial process, and without observing any right or solemnity of statutes, or form required by law, and both in law and in fact, and in good and equitable conscience, or in law, or in good and equitable conscience, and by arbitration only, and as they shall wish, the parties being present or absent, cited or not cited, etc. Afterwards, the said arbitrators and arbiters extended the time and term of the said compromise by two full months beyond the remaining time, and in the same manner they made a second and third extension. Later, they made a fourth extension, because they asserted that the matter was not clear to them. Finally, they made a fifth extension of six months. Finally, they made a sixth extension of six months, always saying, beyond the time remaining: and always reserving to themselves the power to extend. Finally, they issued their award without notification. Now it is called into doubt, what is the meaning of those words, from hence for the next two months, and within that time and term, to extend once, many times, as often and as much as they shall wish. And whether by the said words the said six extensions could be made, and especially in that form, and briefly, what is the law regarding the said award.

† And for clarity, it must be premised that sometimes no time is fixed for arbitrators and arbiters in a compromise; and then either we speak of an arbiter only, and he has three years from the day of joinder of issue; and if the issue is not joined, or quasi-joined, and he is given the power to proceed without the order of judicial process, he may judge perpetually, according to the noted rule in the Digest, *De arbitris*, l. *Sed si compromissum*, and l. *Item si unus*, § *Si multo*, afterwards by the gloss and doctors. Or we speak of an arbitrator only, and then according to the ancient doctors, he may render his award up to 30 years, because it is a perpetual office, and no time limited to an arbitrator is found in law, as in the Code, *De tempore appellationum*, auth. *Si tamen*, unless the parties themselves appointed a term, or the judge, at the petition of one of the parties, by argument from the Digest, *Qui satisdare cogantur*, l. *De die*, and the Code, *De iure deliberandi*, l. *Si curatoris*. But according to the said Bartolus, when someone is taken as an arbitrator, it seems tacitly agreed that he shall arbitrate within a year, arguing from last wills to contracts, as in l. *Finis*, § 1, Code, *Communia de legatis*. But Speculum, in the title *De arbitris*, § *Differt*, ver. *Item ut infra triennium*, inclines more to the view that the time for arbitrating is perpetual, because where the contract does not distinguish, nor should we distinguish, as in the Digest, *De verbis obligatis*, l. *Quicquid astringendae*, and *De bonis auctoris iudicis possessis*, l. *In venditione*, § *De tempore*. For this position supports the Code, *De diversis rescriptis*, l. *Falso*, and because if this is so for an arbiter when the issue is not joined, or quasi-joined, therefore the same should be for an arbitrator, since the reason for a difference cannot be given, by argument from the Digest, *De negotiis gestis*, l. *Ex facto*, in the reason of itself. Or we speak of one who is both arbiter and arbitrator, and then according to the opinion of Bartolus, it should be said that as an arbitrator he cannot [act] after a year, but as an arbiter he can. And thus it should be distinguished according to which power he used, according to the note by Dynus in the Digest, *De furtis*, l. *Si dominium*. In doubt, however, it would seem that he chose the way which makes the thing valid, as in l. 3, Digest, *De militum testamentis*, and Extra, *De praebendis*, c. *Nisi essent*. Or it should be said that the perpetual draws in the corruptible, by argument from the Digest, *De donis causa mortis*, l. *Quod debitori*, and *De constitutione pecuniae*, l. *Item illa*, § *Quod adijcitur*. For both powers depend on one root, namely consent, as in the Digest, *De arbitris*, l. *Non distinguemus*, § *De officio*. For we must follow the form, even if absolute, given in compromises, and more so than in judicial proceedings, as in the Digest, *De arbitris*, l. *Diem proferre*, § *Si quis litigatorum*, ver. *Nisi*.

Let us now consider when a term has been specified in the compromise, and then it matters whether the power to extend the term was granted or not. If the power to extend was not granted, then neither party is compelled to extend the term, unless the cause is known—that is, if the cause is not clear—as stated in D. de arbitris, l. si de meis, §. fin.; l. et si qua, §. fi.; and l. non distinguemus, §. dies. If, however, the power to extend was granted, then either it was agreed that the arbitrator may extend the term even in the absence of the parties, in which case he may extend it while they are absent and unaware; or it was agreed that he must extend it only in their presence or after they have been summoned, in which case the extension is invalid unless the parties are present or have been summoned. Or, if nothing was said except that the possibility of extension was granted, then some say that, since an extension is a kind of interlocutory decision, it may be issued, but it must subsequently be notified, as in D. de arbitris, l. si cum dies, in principio. But I say that it is safer for one party to request this, because an interlocutory decision issued without any request by either party is not binding, as in D. de iudiciis, l. ad peremptorium. And even if it were valid, it should be understood to apply only when the time is short, as in D. de iudiciis, l. si debitori. For a long delay should not be granted, because it diminishes the substance of the debt, as in D. ad legem Falcidiam, l. in lege Falcidia, non habetur pro puro; and l. si constante, §. quoties, so. ma.; and Inst. de actionibus, §. plus; and D. de verbis obligatis, l. si ita stipulatus fuero, 10 or 15. It is therefore conceded that the arbitrator may extend the term according to the form of the compromise, and there should be no doubt about this conclusion. Having premised these points, let us now come to the wording in question. The words state: "from hence to the next two months." In these words are contained two full months, as in D. de regulis iuris, l. ubi lex; and l. 1, §. quod dicimus, D. de successionibus edicti.

† The text of the instrument then follows, and within that same time. If these words are to have any effect, they refer to what follows, namely, the extension of the term. It is certain that the extension must be made once or several times within that very term. For it is certain that words must have some effect, and no word should be superfluous, if possible, as in D. ad muns. l. 1 and l. si quando, D. de leg. 1. And note that it says "and the term itself," and does not say "terms." Thus, it seems to refer to one term, as in D. de verb. oblig. l. eum, qui calendis, and D. de verb. sign. l. boues, § hoc sermone. Considering this, two most excellent doctors advised in favor of this position, namely, that the award is invalid. And this can be confirmed by the following reason:

† Because the parties, from the beginning, by setting a brief term of two months, subsequently granted a general and indefinite power to extend the term in any manner in making said extensions, as in D. de verb. oblig. l. si ita quis, §. Scia, in fine. For even if not according to an expressly stated time, nevertheless according to time: as if this, according to, is tacitly inherent in the limits of the mandate, as in D. de iudic. solut. l. non tamen, §. in hac; and D. de verb. signif. l. haec adiectio; and D. de legat. 2, l. cum filius, §. pater. For the discretion of absolute power is similarly to be interpreted non-restrictively, and understood according to the foregoing, as in D. de serv. iust. l. si cui; and D. de oper. libert. l. si libertus. Thus we note in D. de iure iur. c. Quintauallis; and D. de mandat. l. creditor, §. ultimo. Those contracting are deceived who have presumed well of arbitrators, arg. D. de legat. 2, l. vnum ex familia, §. item Marcus. Otherwise they could extend to the entire time of their lives, as in D. de legat. 3, l. fideicommissa, §. hoc autem legatum. Which is irrational, absurd, and contrary to the nature of the compromise and mandate, which ought to have some reasonable limits: because recourse is had to arbitrators for the abbreviation of lawsuits, as in D. de arbit. l. non distinguemus, §. de officio; and l. quamuis arbiter. Moreover, this does not seem to have been an extension, because the second term began upon the completion of the first, and thus there are multiple terms, not the same term continued, because the end of the first is the beginning of the second. And this is not a true extension, since the arbitrators did not derogate from the first term, nor its mode, but added another term, as in D. de locat. l. qui ex certo; just as when a judge says, I assign to you two days for the first term, and two for the second. For here there is no extension, but the assignment of a new term, as in D. de iudic. l. 2, post edictum. Moreover, that which is conferred upon a time seems to be done at that time, and not before, as in C. de donat. ante nupt. l. quod et sponse; and it is similar in D. de fer. l. et oratione; to this effect D. de praecar. l. sed si manente, §. si praeterea. For, inspecting the mind of the arbitrators, after the first two months had passed, and not before, they wished to begin another two months, which they could by no means do, because they referred themselves to a time when they would be deprived of their office, as in D. de iuris omn. iud. l. eum, qui iudicare, in principio and §. fi. But to the contrary it seems, because it is not our place to restrict the form of the mandate or arbitration. And this seems to have been the intent of the contracting parties, that at whatever time it pleased them, they might decide the causes, whether prematurely or after long delays, provided that by the delay the right of the parties has not been made worse; rather, even if it had been made worse, let the compromitters impute it to themselves, as in D. de verb. oblig. l. qui Romae, §. Calimachus, in fine; D. de aedil. edict. l. quod si nolit, §. si quid ita; D. de deposit. l. Lucius Titius. But if the parties had said, once and many times: they would not have added, as often as, whenever. And they could not have extended beyond two or three times, arg. of those who note, Arch. in c. 2, de filiis; Praeb. lib. 6. Rather, perhaps it would be restricted to two times only, so that the first extension is counted in the number of plurality, as in D. de testib. l. vbi numerus. Reason persuades avoiding obligation, and not multiplying it, as in D. de legat. 3, l. in fideicommissa, §. si quis 10. Now I return to our question, and I ask, what is finally to be held? And certainly the question seems to me very doubtful, but because the parties considered a brief term, i.e., two months, as in D. de iure fisci. l. aufertur, §. qui compensationem, from the conjecture at first sight of the compromise it seems that the arbitrators greatly exceeded the form of the mandate, and therefore unless it is established that they proceeded from just cause in extending, all these extensions ought not to be valid, since in many legal articles the infinite is reproved, as in c. cum in multis, de rescript. lib. 6. Always saving the better judgment, as in D. qui pot. in pign. hab. l. Claudius Felix. Those words of good and fair agree with the foregoing, arg. D. de iust. et iur. l. 1, in principio. For if the parties had not considered speedy dispatch, they would by no means have appended a term of two months, arg. D. de his qui sine manumiss. ad libert. peruen. l. Latinus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether those who have promised to honor one another violate their promise and commit an injury if one says to the other, "You lie through your teeth."
2. If some have promised to live equally, whether he who holds more horses than another is said to contravene the agreement, even if the horses are not his own.
3. Whether proof of possession results from proven detention.
4. The presumption and the common course must be observed. Concordance must be established among witnesses to induce proof.
1. Whether instruments may be produced up to the calculation of the definitive sentence.
2. Given a statute that those having disputes between brothers are compelled to make a compromise, whether the said arbitrators elected by virtue of the statute are said to be necessary or voluntary.
3. If it has been agreed that the arbitrators shall proceed both in law and in fact, but they pronounce judgment only in law, whether their sentence rendered against the right of the litigant is valid.
4. The delegated judge must observe the form given to him and appended in the delegation; otherwise, the sentence is null.
5. Two things are enjoined upon the arbitrator, namely, that he praise, and that he praise well.
6. Where a limiting word is appended concerning that which was otherwise disposed by law, it operates to no effect.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. John and Frederick, brothers of the Palavicini family, made a division between themselves of all their goods. After the division, the said Frederick gave to the said John, in satisfaction of a certain sum of money owed to the said John, a certain possession of Frederick’s which had fallen to him by lot in the aforementioned division. Afterwards, the said John and Frederick commuted all their goods and promised not to contravene the said agreement until a certain time, with the following pacts. Among other things, namely, that one should honor the other, and that they should live equally, and that one should not make himself greater than the other in arms, horses, and clothing; and with this pact, that whenever the said John should contravene by deed or word, and not observe all and each of the written terms, he would fall into a penalty of two thousand florins. And it shall be permitted to the said Frederick to withdraw from the said community and return to the portion which had fallen to him in the aforementioned division. After these things, and three years having elapsed, the said Frederick approached the said John, demanding from him four horses common to both, Frederick and John, on the occasion of going to Pavia for the recovery of certain goods which the said Frederick alleged were being wrongfully retained by a certain person from the said brothers. The said John responded to the said Frederick that the horses demanded by him were not his, nor common, but belonged to a certain bastard of the Carini family, his servant, who had lent them to him. And the said Frederick responded, nay, he says the horses are common to you and me. The said John responded, you lie through your throat. He also added and said, you have kept six horses just as I have kept them. And then the said John said to the said bastard, his servant, put saddles on three horses, because I wish to ride; and the said three horses were saddled, and the other two horses remained in the stable. And concerning the aforementioned matters, the notary present there, in the presence of witnesses, made a public instrument. Also, in a certain other instrument of protestation made by the said Frederick to the said John, against which the said [John] among other things said and responded to him, I have five horses here, and others which I have in Cremona, I do not hold as my own horses, but as horses of the bastard of the Carini family, my servant. Finally, concerning other questions arising between the said brothers, the said John filed a libel against the said Frederick, asking that he be condemned in a large quantity of money, because he alleged that he had contravened the said community and the contents thereof. And the said Frederick likewise offered a libel against the said John, alleging that he wished to withdraw from the said community. And after certain proceedings, the said John petitioned the judge, before whom the question had been initiated, to compel the said Frederick to submit himself to compromise in common friends concerning the said libel and its contents, etc., to proceed, and to sentence according to law only, as is more fully mentioned in the said compromise. The arbitrators, having seen and examined the said instruments of protestation and other rights and proceedings before them, condemned the said John in two thousand florins for the penalty incurred by him, and pronounced that it was permitted to the said Frederick to withdraw from the said arrangement and return to the portion which had fallen to him in the first division. Now it is alleged by the said John that the said arbitral awards were not issued judicially, and consequently are null. Presupposing the statute of the commune of Cremona, that in questions arising between brothers, they precisely are compelled to submit themselves to compromise in two friends. And if those two are not in agreement, that a third be appointed, who are to be and may proceed briefly and summarily, no order of law being observed, and to terminate those questions according to law. Also presupposing another statute, that after precepts and arbitral awards have been made between agnates, they cannot be called inequitable, nor can appeal be made, nor complaint filed, nor supplication made, but they must be put into execution by all legal remedies. The following three doubts are elicited. First, whether the said arbitral sentence was issued judicially. Second, whether the said elected arbitrators should be called voluntary, or assumed by necessity of law. Third, granted that the said arbitral sentence was issued contrary to the law of litigation, whether it is null, or valid in some respect.

† Regarding the first point, it seems to be said that the aforementioned sentence was rendered juridically, since the said John acted contrary to what is contained in the instrument of the said union. For, as is mentioned in the said instrument, the said brothers promised to honor each other. Now, John, by responding to the honest petition made to him by the said Federigo as to whether he wished to honor him, ought not to have lied “per gulam”; rather, by lying “per gulam,” he is said to dishonor him and not to defer to him any honor: since the phrase “lying per gulam” is an injurious term, as is noted by Bartolus in l. item apud Labeonem, § 1, ff. de iniuriis. This holds even if he added “saving your honor,” as is noted by Jacobus de Arena and taught in l. si quis extraneus, in principio, ff. de acquisitione hereditatis. In this regard, l. 1, § si filius, ff. de obligationibus et actionibus, is well suited, where it is stated that one who is not bound to honor another ought not to afflict him with insults; and from this, the said John fell into the penalty contained in the instrument of the said union.

† Moreover, from another point, the said John fell into penalty, and consequently the said sentence was lawfully rendered; for he ought not to have made himself greater than his said brother, but ought to have lived equally: and the word “equally” denotes that there should be no excess between them in any respect, as stated in the law *Interdum*, in the beginning, in the Digest, under the title *De haereditate instituenda*. But the said John made himself greater in equal matters and did not live equally. Therefore, that this is true is demonstrated: for he kept more horses than his said brother. And this is proved by the instruments of protestations made to the said John. First, in that the said John said to the said Frederick: “You kept six horses, just as I kept”; and, joining the preceding words contained in the instrument, he confesses that he kept six horses, to which confession against himself effect must be given, as stated in the law *Cum precum*, in the Digest, under the title *De libera causa*. And even if the said John says that the said horses were lent to him by Bastard of Carienis, his servant: from these words it is not proved that the horses were not in the dominion of John. I say that it is not necessary in this case to prove that the said John had dominion over the said horses, but it suffices to prove his possession of them: since dominion is not here principally pleaded in court, as noted in the law *Cum quidam* and there by the doctors, in the Digest, under the title *De condictione instituta*. And that the said John had possession of the said horses is proved by the fact that he said to his servants, “Put saddles on the horses,” in the presence of the said Bastard, who did not contradict him; and by the fact that he used the said horses as his own, as stated in the law *Titia*, in the Digest, under the title *De solutione*.

And if it is said that by this the possession of the said horses is not proved, but only their detention, it is answered that, once the detention of the said horses is proved, possession of them results therefrom. As noted by Innocentius in the chapter Cum olim, number 2, at the end, in the gloss on Magna, de privilegiis; and as noted in the law Stipulatio, section Hi quoque, and there by the doctors, in the Digest, de verbis obligatis. Indeed, if the witnesses were to say that such a person possessed them, this is resolved in the law Detinuit, as noted by Innocentius in the chapter Cum causam, extra, de testibus. Furthermore, from the words uttered in another protestation, it is proved that the horses belonged to the said John, or were held and possessed by him, when he said: “Those horses which I have here and in Cremona, I do not hold as my own, but as the horses of Bastard, my servant.” Therefore, since it is established that he has and holds the said horses, even if he added that he holds them as the horses of the said Bastard, this confession of his is not sufficient, especially to the prejudice of his brother Frederick, to transfer the possession and ownership of the said horses to the said Bastard. As in the law Cum falsa, in the Code, de iure et facto ignorato, and there the doctors teach.

† Moreover, in favor of the said Federico, there is a presumption and the common course of things. For servants are not accustomed to lend horses to their masters. And this ought to be sufficiently considered, according to the note in *l. cum de indebito*, D. de probat., in principio; and in *l. 1*, C. de arbitris. Furthermore, assuming that the horses were lent by the said Bastard, did not the said John, by holding accounts of common expenses for several horses, whether his own or those lent to the said Federico, and by riding with them and with a larger retinue, make himself greater than the said Federico? Certainly so; therefore, from this he incurred the penalty.

Nothing is to the contrary of what is alleged. First, it is alleged that the said Federico objected a crime and infamy to the said John, or at least that from which infamy results; because by saying that he held several horses, he seems to object that he violated the sworn agreement; and thus he objects infamy to himself, as in *l. si quis maior*, C. de transactionibus. Therefore, it was lawful for the said John to say to Federico: "You lie," according to *l. quae omnia*, D. de procuratoribus. To this it is answered that the said Federico did not object infamy or a crime to the said John, nor did he say that he had violated the sworn agreement, in which case perhaps the rule would apply, as in *l. si quis maior* and *l. quae omnia*. Rather, he made an honest claim against himself, to which claim the said John ought to have responded honestly; because since he was bound to honor him, his response ought to have been moderated in words, as the law *non debet* says at the end, D. de dolo. It supports what Cynus notes in *l. si superstite*, C. de dolo.

Secondly, nothing is to the contrary of what is alleged, because it is said that the said Federico lied through the mouth of the said John; the said John would never lie about the said Federico. Therefore, the claim for penalty ought not to belong to the said Federico, because he incurred the penalty, as in *l. cum paribus*, § *illi*, D. de re iudicata. And this is said to be proven by the witnesses produced. To this it is answered that the aforementioned witnesses prove nothing. First, a certain William of the Lake is singular and from another time. A certain Anthony testified twice, and in his first statement he is singular and does not give anyone as a co-witness. In his second statement, however, he does not agree in time with another witness named Tiolus. For the said Tiolus, in the month of June, says that he heard the aforementioned things in the month of May of the three years just past. But the said Anthony testifies in the month of June and says that he heard the aforementioned things three years ago, and more. But this statement of "more," proven by the said witness, accomplishes nothing, as in *l. cum furti*, D. de in iurando in litem.

† Nor does it matter that a concordance must be made for the proof to be established, according to Jacobus de Belvisus in the law Cum de aetate, Digest, On Proof; and in the law Sed si possessor, section Item si iurauero, Digest, On Oaths; and Bartolus in the law Inter stipulantes, section 1, Digest, On the Obligation of Words; and Baldus in the Authentico At qui semel, Code, On Proof. Nor does it matter that this word "more" ought to be explained by what the said witness said in his first statement, when he said that three years had passed since the last month, during which the said Federico lied to the said John. For this cannot be the case: because since in his first statement he does not give any one as a witness, it must necessarily be understood that the act was different; and regarding the other acts, it must be understood in the first statement that they are those acts mentioned in the second. Moreover, the said Antonio is suspect due to the spoliation which he asserts in his first statement was done to him by the said Federico, from which enmity results between them, as in the chapter Item cum quis, Extravagant, On Restitution of Spoliation. Furthermore, the said Antonio and Guilielminus are of the court of the Castle of Cauarani, as they confess in their attestations, which comes to the aid of the said John, in whose jurisdiction the said John has mere and mixed empire, as in the law Idonei, and there not, Digest, On Witnesses. Nor does it matter for anything else that was alleged, namely that the said instruments of protestation were not produced before the arbitrators. And although the arbitrators in their sentence make mention of the said instruments, nevertheless the said sentence does not presume the production of those instruments, as noted by Innocentius in the chapter Quoniam contra falsam, On Proof; and in the chapter Cum in iure peritus, On the Office of the Delegate; and in the Speculum, On Sentences, section Finis, word In summa. For to this it is answered that a sentence does not prove those things which could not have intervened at the time of the pronouncement of the said sentence. Thus speak the laws cited above.

But it well proves those matters, insofar as they could have intervened at that time. And with respect to all those things, they are presumed to have been lawfully done. As noted in l. 1, C. de fide instrumentorum et iure hastae fiscalis; and as noted by Jacobus Butrigarius in auth. Si quis in aliquo, C. de edendo; and l. Optima, C. de contrahenda stipulatione. It supports what is noted in Speculum, de instrumentis, edicto, §. Nunc restat, under the words “in summa.”

But these instruments could have been produced, not only in our case, in which one may proceed summarily both as to fact and as to law, but also in any ordinary trial, up to the point of the definitive sentence, as in the case Cum dilectus, Extra, de fide instrumentorum, unless there had been a renunciation of the production of instruments, as noted there, or a time limit had been set for producing instruments and that time limit had expired; although even in this case instruments may be produced after the time limit, where the plaintiff’s right has not been made worse, as noted by Cynus, after Jacobus de Arena, in the law Iudices, Codex, de iudicibus, whose opinion is confirmed by the gloss in the chapter Clesępe, Extra, de verborum significatione. Therefore, the said sentence makes faith and proves that the instruments were produced, since they could then have been produced.

† Regarding the second point, it appears that the said arbitrators were necessary and assumed by necessity of the municipal law: after the petition made by John that Frederick be compelled to submit to arbitration according to the form of the statutes of the commune of Cremona, the said compromise was made in favor of the said arbitrators. Therefore, the said arbitrators appear to have been elected by virtue of the preceding petition and the urgent statute: as noted by Bartolus and after him by the aforementioned Baldus in l. 2, ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, and by the Archdeacon, dist. 82, c. Proposuisti, where he says that if one summoned to appear before a judge appears, although he does not say that he appears by virtue of the preceding precept, it is presumed that he appears by virtue of the said precept; so in the case at hand, the compromise is presumed to have been made by virtue of the preceding petition, although this is not stated in the compromise. In support of this is the fact that at the time of the compromise there was a statute in force whereby the parties could be compelled to submit to arbitration. But these matters are equivalent, whether one was compelled or feared being compelled, as l. Nouissime, in principio, ff. Quod falsum aut iniquum, and l. 3, §. Pecuniam, ff. De negotiis gestis, where it is equated that something is done out of necessity or suspicion of necessity. If, therefore, the said arbitrators are necessary, they can be called ordinary, since they have power from the municipal law, as noted in l. Et quia, ff. De iurisdictione omnium iudicum. It is supported by what is noted by the aforementioned Baldus in l. Omnes, C. De episcopis et clericis, or that they have the force of delegated judges, as in c. Ab arbitris, and what is noted there, de officio delegati, lib. 6, and noted in c. Legitima, de appellationibus, in the same book, and in c. Suspicionis, and extra de officio delegati, and noted by the doctors in l. Finalis, C. De iudicibus. Since, therefore, they have jurisdiction, although their sentence was rendered against the right of the litigant, it cannot be called null, as will be declared below in the third point. But from it one can appeal, as in the laws cited above. And by this, l. 1, C. De arbitris, which says that one cannot appeal from the sentence of an arbitrator, does not apply, because that law speaks of voluntary arbitrators who do not have jurisdiction and are not assumed by necessity, which is otherwise in our case. Nor does l. 3, and what is noted there by Jacobus Butrigarius, ff. De testibus, where it is said that a witness, even if summoned, is said to testify voluntarily, apply, because to this it is answered that there it speaks of a witness who had a privilege not to be compelled to testify. Hence, if the summoned witness does not allege the privilege and testifies, he is considered to have renounced the privilege and is said to testify voluntarily. But if a summoned witness testifies who had no execution, but could be compelled to testify, then he is said to testify unwillingly. And this is what the gloss and Bartolus intend in l. Post legatum, §. Finalis, de his qui ut indigni. Nor does l. 2, and what is noted there by Cynus, C. Quod meo nomine, where if someone promised out of fear and later paid, he is said to have paid voluntarily, apply. So l. 2 speaks, or he could not defend himself, but could be compelled to pay by necessity, perhaps by virtue of the statute of Vignola. And in this case he is said to have paid under compulsion, as noted by Bartolus in l. Si ob turpem, ff. De conditione ob turpem causam. But so it is in the case at hand, because the parties could be compelled to submit to arbitration by virtue of the statute here disposing. Therefore, if they submitted to arbitration, they are said to have submitted under compulsion; nevertheless, fear and suspicion of necessity always existed, as in the laws cited above and noted by Cynus in l. 2, Quod meo nomine. Regarding the third point, assuming

† That the said arbitrators are voluntary, it must be considered: whether the said sentence, even if rendered against the right of the litigant, is valid, notwithstanding that it was stated that the arbitrators may pronounce judgment, yet whether it is truly null as a matter of law. First, it appears that it is null: because wherever a certain form is given and the power of the arbitrators to arbitrate is limited, if they did not observe the said form, but exceeded it, such excess renders the sentence null: as in *l. non distinguemus*, §. *nunc*, *de officio*; and §. *fin.*, *ff. de arbitris*. It supports this *l. diligenter*, in the beginning, *ff. de mandato*; and *l. Iulius*, §. *et si quis*, *ff. ad exhibendum*, where the text says that the form gives being to the thing. For this, it is well noted in *c. causam*, *de electione*, in the gloss, which gloss here seems to determine that in any case it equates a sentence rendered against the law of the statute and against the form of the compromise. It supports this *c. cum dilecta*, *de rescriptis*; and *c. examinata*, *de confirmatione utili vel inutili*. Nor does it obstruct *l. diem*, §. *stari*, *ff. de arbitris*, because that §. *stari* speaks simply where a compromise has been made, without any form being given to the arbitrators for pronouncing judgment; otherwise, if a certain form is added, namely, that they may pronounce judgment yet according to law: as was in our case. And this is held by Bartolus in the said §. *stari*, although in *l. si societatem*, §. *arbitrorum*, *ff. pro socio*, he says *cogitabis*. Nor does it obstruct if it is said that the sentence cannot be called null by virtue of a statute disposing this, or even a pact appended in the compromise: because this is true, that it cannot be called null, unless on account of a lack of jurisdiction, which in our case the said arbitrators seem to lack, due to the form given to them in the compromise: as noted in *c. fi*, *de sequestro posito*. It supports what is noted by Bartolus in *l. 2*, §. *praetor ait*, *ff. qui satisdare cogantur*; noted by Baldus in *l. si quis exheredato*, §. *si quis*, verse *ergo si quis*, *ff. de in iustis testamento*; and in *l. diuus Traianus*, *ff. de testamento militis*.

On the contrary, it seems to be said that the said sentence is valid. First, for this supports the saying of Cynus, in *l. 1*, *C. de arbitris*, where he asks, if a compromise is made under this form, that judgment be pronounced according to the laws, or that judgment be pronounced yet according to law: as Albericus formats it there, whether one can appeal from the sentence, if it were null before the sentence. And without the remedy of appeal, one ought not to obey it, as if rendered against the form of the compromise, it would be sought in vain: whether one can appeal. For this, it is well noted in *l. qualem*, on the word *videtur*, *ff. de arbitris*; and what is noted by Gozzadinus in the *Summa de arbitris*, verse *item agi potest*. It supports what is noted by Jacobus Butrigarius in *l. prolatam*, near the end, *C. de sententiis et interlocutionibus omnium iudicum*, where he asks whether a sentence rendered by an arbitrator elected with this form, that he must pronounce according to law, without prior cognition of the cause: therefore there Jacobus Butr. weighs only the cognition of the cause. Hence it seems he wishes that, with prior cognition of the cause, it holds, as he says, not assimilating him to a judge. Inasmuch as there Ia. Bu. weighs only the cognition of the cause, it seems well that he wishes that, with prior cognition of the cause, even if he had pronounced against the law, similar to a judge, that his sentence is valid. Moreover, it is proved thus: the expression of things that are tacitly contained operates nothing. As in *l. 3*, *de legibus 1*; and *l. non recte*, *C. de fideiussoribus*. But it tacitly adheres, and by necessity, according to the mind of the compromitting parties, that they ought to arbitrate according to law. As in *l. rem non novam*, *C. de iudicibus*; and also it tacitly adheres by necessity of the statute, assuming that the arbitrators were assumed according to its form. As in *Auth. de iudicibus*, §. *omnis autem iudex*. Therefore, if it was expressed, such expression ought to operate nothing. Nor does it obstruct if it is said that it does not adhere by necessity, as noted by Bartolus in the said *l. 3*, *de legibus 1*, because the parties could have been in agreement in compromising otherwise: because this is denied insofar as they are called my arbitrators. For if the compromise had been that they could pronounce according to law and according to fact: then they would not be arbitrators, but arbitratores. According to the note by Bartolus in the said §. *arbitrorum*. Therefore, since they were arbitrators, and are called arbitrators, it adheres by necessity that they ought to pronounce according to law, therefore, etc. And if it is said that an arbitrator is not bound to pronounce according to law, as in the said §. *stari*, it is answered in two ways. First, because there it speaks of a voluntary arbitrator, who has no jurisdiction: we speak of an arbitrator by necessity, having jurisdiction, as alleged above in the second point. Moreover, although a voluntary arbitrator is not bound to pronounce according to law, as to the validity of the sentence, as in the said §. *stari*, yet according to the mind of the compromitting parties, and as to himself, and so that he is not obligated to the party, he is bound to pronounce according to law, or he makes the case his own. As noted in *l. si iudex*, *ff. de variis cognitionibus*.

Moreover, where something is prohibited as a burden, that by which one comes to the prohibited thing. As in *l. oratio*, *ff. de sponsalibus*; *l. 2*, *ff. de iure omnium iudicum*; and *l. scire oportet*, §. 1, *ff. de tutoribus et curatoribus dandis ab his*. Also, where two things are connected, one being prohibited, the other is understood to be prohibited, as noted in *3. q. 6*, *c. hoc quippe*. These two notes, Innocentius in *c. praeterea*, *de officio delegati*. But by the statute mentioned above, it is prohibited to call a sentence unjust. Therefore, everything by which one comes to calling a sentence inequitable is prohibited. But this is so in our case: because by nullity one comes to calling a sentence inequitable, which is prohibited by the statute. Therefore, the sentence is alleged to be null on the ground that it was rendered against the law. But for a sentence to be rendered against the right of the litigant is nothing other than to say that the arbitrators pronounced inequitably, and their sentence is inequitable. As in *l. eos*, in the beginning, *C. de appellationibus*, joined with *l. praefecti*, *C. de minoribus*.

Moreover, there seem to be two cases regarding this. The first: *l. ne in arbitris*, §. *sed et si ipse*, *C. de arbitris*, where the text says that if a compromise is made in an arbitrator, so that the arbitrator swears to pronounce with common truth, that although he pronounces against the truth, nevertheless the sentence is valid and merits execution. And yet the form is exceeded, which text Baldus there weighs. The second case is in *c. cum ad sedem*, *extra de restitutione spoliorum*, there. n. The Pope delegated the cause pending between the Bishop of Cuman and the Hospital of Jerusalem, regarding another hospital, to its abbot in this form, that he ought to terminate the said question without debt: because the Hospital of Jerusalem said that it was despoiled by the bishop. The said abbot condemned the said bishop to the restitution of all that was demanded. And the cause was brought to the Pope, seeing that it had not been proven against the bishop regarding the spoliation. And that the abbot had pronounced against the right of the bishop, he annulled the sentence of the said abbot: it is clear therefore that the sentence of the said abbot was valid, granted that it was rendered against the right: because it was not proven against him. And thus, however much the form of delegation was exceeded, the sentence is not null. Which is clear: because the Pope would not annul it, but pronounce it annulled and void. Argument: *l. nam et si sub conditione*, §. *fin.*, *ff. de in iustis testamento*; and *l. boven*, §. *placet*, *ff. de edicto edicto*. Although it is decreed that the said chapter, *cum ad sedem*, speaks of a delegated judge: we, however, speak of arbitrators, who have power limited by a man, and under a certain form. I answer, that it is the same in a delegated judge as in an arbitrator.

† For a delegated judge must observe the form given to him and appended in the delegation; and if he does not observe it, the sentence is null. As stated in the cited chapter *Cum dilecta*, and in the cited law *Diligenter*, and in the chapter *Pisanis* on the restoration of spoliation. This must be understood as meaning that he does not observe the form by pronouncing judgment on a different matter, or between different persons; or by omitting some form appended in the delegation and specially prescribed, which was not inherent by law. Thus speak the said chapters. But if the form appended in the delegation is omitted, which was inherent by law—namely, that he pronounce according to law, or that he terminate without debt, which is the same thing—nevertheless the sentence is valid, as in the cited chapter *Cum ad sedem*. For which it is well supported by that which Innocentius notes in the chapter *Si quando* in the Extravagant on the office of the delegated judge, where he makes a distinction whether he pronounces on matters not committed to him, in which case the sentence is not valid, and one may resist it as a matter of fact; or whether he pronounces on matters committed to him, but otherwise than he ought to have pronounced, as is the case in our instance: for example, because it was committed to him that he pronounce according to law, and he pronounced badly and contrary to law; in which case the sentence ought to be valid, and one may not resist it except by the remedy of appeal, as Innocentius clearly reports there. Moreover, granted that the arbitrators pronounced against the right of the litigant, nevertheless they are said to have declared the law. And consequently it must be said that they pronounced according to law. As in the law *Pe.* in the principle, joined with the gloss placed there, in the Digest on justice and law, where the praetor is said, granted that he decrees unjustly, which is against the right of the litigant, as noted there.
