Moreover, these words, that they pronounce according to law, appended in the compromise, do not give form to the compromise itself, since otherwise this was tacitly inherent, as said above. But the parties seem rather to urge the arbitrators and admonish them that they declare the law. Argument from the chapter *Licet*, and what is noted there by Innocentius on the office of the ordinary judge, where if the Pope commands the ordinary judge that he cognize such a case with appeal removed, in which case otherwise appeal was prohibited by law; because it does not seem to make him a delegate in that case, but seems rather to excite his jurisdiction. And thus those words, with appeal removed, appended, otherwise this was inherent in the rescript, do not introduce a new form of jurisdiction; for the reason that even if said clause were not appended, otherwise this was inherent, it is so by law. And in our case it is noted by the doctors in the law *Saepe* in the Digest on the office of the praeses, and by Innocentius in the chapter *Dudum* on prescriptions, in the great gloss in the principle. For this it is well supported by what Innocentius notes in the chapter *Prudentiam* in the Extravagant on the office of the delegated judge, in the gloss on the word *ex communis*, where if the Pope commands a judge that he condemn someone, if such proves etc. It is said that if the judge condemns, granted that it is not proven, the sentence holds. The reason is that the condition does not regard the substance of the jurisdiction, but only the exercise of cognition. And yet in our case, these words "according to law" regard the exercise of their jurisdiction, as we posit the arbitrators to be voluntary or necessary; but they do not regard its substance. For this it is well supported by what Cynus notes in the law *Praescriptio* in the Code on contravening public law or utility, where holding that a rescript obtained by falsehood from the observance of common law is valid. When responding to the last law in the same title, he says that that tacit condition does not regard the substance of the jurisdiction, but only the act of condemning. Therefore it does not render the rescript null, nor does it render the sentence passed by virtue of said rescript null, as is proven there by the doctors. It supports the law *Ita demum* in the Digest on arbitration, where if the compromise is made thus, with the pact: that fraud be absent. That although fraud intervenes, the sentence holds.

† Because, as Lord Baldus says in l. arbitrorum, C. de arbitris, two things are considered: namely, the substance of the award, and its quality, that is, whether it is well or ill done. For two things appear to be imposed on the arbitrator: namely, that he make an award, and that he make it well. This condition, therefore, does not regard the substance, but the quality. Hence, a condition attached to the quality does not render the substance conditional; so it is in the case at hand. Nor does the restrictive word “however” avail, to the effect that the arbitrators may pronounce only on the law, etc. For the sense is the same whether it is said “on the law,” or with the word “only,” or whether it is said “on the law only.” For when the parties wish that judgment be given on the law, they wish that judgment not be given against the law. And thus they appear to have restricted themselves to the law alone, just as if the word “however” had been added. And the reason is that the affirmation of one is the exclusion of the other: l. cum praetor, in principio, ff. de iudiciis; and in c. exiui, §. nos circa, de verbis obligatis. And that this is true is indicated by the preceding words. For it was said that the arbitrators could proceed on the law and on the fact; when it is added, “and to pronounce on the law only, and on the fact only,” whatever fact occurred, they appear to have excluded, and to have excluded themselves, in the law, and to have restricted the arbitrators to the law, just as if the word “only” had been added. For it seems to be rather a removal than the addition of a new form, according to the above-cited authorities. Moreover, where the restrictive word is added concerning that which was otherwise provided by law, it operates nothing: as l. 1, §. 1, ff. si messor falcem modum dixerit; and l. 3, §. interdum, and what is noted there, ff. de negotiis gestis. For by law this is so, that gross negligence is liable: as l. quod Nerua, with similar cases, ff. depositi. But suppose that it is said that one is bound only for fraud. It must be said that he is bound: as in the said l. 1, §. 1, and in the said §. interdum cited above. So it is in the case at hand. For it makes no difference whether it is said “on the law,”

† since this limiting expression is appended to that which was otherwise provided by law, as has been declared above. Moreover, if the words of the compromise are rightly examined, this passage admits of no doubt. For power was granted to the arbitrators by words importing power, namely, “they may and have the power.” But from this, the power to pronounce on the fact, which they have by law, was not taken away from them. Therefore, one case was expressed, and another omitted. They could therefore pronounce on the law only, if they wished. But they were not under any necessity to refrain from pronouncing on the fact, if they wished; because not everything [expressed] and so forth, as in the law *Non quicquid*, D. *De iudicibus*; law 1, C. *Quomodo et quando iudex*. From which it must be concluded that the said sentence is valid, and not void. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A gratuitous pact is called a donation, whence it requires insinuation, and is included under the statute providing that insinuation is required for donations exceeding a certain sum, otherwise that they shall not be valid.
2. A stepson is not considered a suitable witness, since excessive familiarity weakens the testimony of the witness.
body:
In the Name of Christ, Amen. Furthermore, we establish that any donation inter vivos which shall hereafter be made by any person of the city, district, or territory of Pavia; and any donation inter vivos which shall hereafter be made in the city of Pavia or its territory to any person, college, commune, or university, whatever the status and condition of the person making the donation may be, shall not be valid nor have effect by operation of law, but shall be void, null, and of no value, if it exceeds fifty livres, exclusive of that sum; even if it was made once or multiple times in a single instrument by the same donor to the same donee, where each individually is below the said sum of fifty livres, but which together exceed the said sum, unless the said donation has been insinuated, and with such insinuation it shall be valid, as it could and ought to be valid according to law. And insinuation shall be deemed to have been made if the said donation was made in the presence [of the required officials] and at the proper time. Notwithstanding any custom, observance, statute, or general or special law to the contrary.

This statute, thus proposed in the case at hand, sets forth the terms of the question, which follows below.

A certain A. and B., citizens of Pavia, several years ago, by a public instrument drawn up in the city of Pavia, bound themselves jointly and severally with their present and future goods for five hundred florins on account of a deposit, and bound themselves jointly and severally as principal debtors, with due remuneration, to restore the said debt within a certain term which has long since expired. Finally, C., the creditor, seeing that A. and B., the debtors, were dilatory in the payment of the said debt, proceeded against them jointly and severally for the recovery of the said debt; and finally, he had them condemned jointly and severally by sentence of the ordinary judge to the payment of the said debt and expenses. This sentence passed into res judicata. After this sentence, while C., the creditor, was seeking execution of the aforementioned debt against B., the debtor, requesting that certain immovable goods of B. be delivered to him in satisfaction of the aforementioned debt, regarding which he wished to obtain title before the ordinary judge, observing the form of the statutes of the city of Pavia, B., the debtor, wishing to exclude the claim of the creditor against him, alleged that before and after the aforementioned sentence, which, as stated above, had passed into res judicata, the said C., the creditor, had promised to the said B. by an express pact fortified by a solemn stipulation that he would not trouble, molest, or burden the said B., his heirs, or his goods on account of the said debt, the burden of which debt the said A. had assumed upon himself.

These allegations having been thus produced, the said B. produced witnesses; of whom three appear to testify regarding events before the sentence, from a long time ago; and two regarding events after the sentence, one of whom is the stepson of the said B., to the effect that the said C. had promised to the said B. that he would not trouble or molest him, his heirs, or his goods at any time.

Now it is asked: whether such proof and the statements of the said witnesses relieve the said B. so that he is not bound to pay the said debt and cannot be sued therefor.

Secondly, it is asked: assuming that the said witnesses prove the allegation of the said B., whether such a liberatory pact not to sue, given or received for nothing, is called a donation; and therefore, whether insinuation was necessary in such a pact according to the form of the statute; and consequently, whether such a pact is valid without insinuation or not.

Whether a gratuitous pact is called a donation, such that it requires insinuation, just like any other express donation. The gloss on the Digest, *De donationibus*, in the law *Modestinus*, seems to hold that it is not. And the reason is: because a pact not to sue can be made without cause. Digest, *De pactis*, in the law *Tale pactum*, in the principal part. To the contrary, the gloss determines in the Digest, *De regulis iuris*, in the law *Si quis obligatione*; Digest, *Qui in rem actionem non habent, pignus vel hypothecam solvere possunt*, law 1. And it is an express law, because this is a donation. Digest, *De donationibus*, in the law *In aedibus*, section *Potest*. Nor is it a fictitious donation, but a true one: because it is mere liberality. Digest, *De transactionibus*, law 1. And thus the Lord Bartolus frequently advised in fact. And this applies when no cause is expressed in the donation. For if another cause is expressed, the truth of which cause would exclude a donation: then it would not be a donation. In our case, however, I do not see any cause expressed which would exclude a liberal act. Although there are two debtors jointly and severally liable: nevertheless, if a gratuitous pact is made with one, reserving the obligation of the other: this pact is a donation as regards the person who is gratuitously released from the obligation. Hence, if a husband has his wife and Titus bound as two debtors: and he releases the wife gratuitously, the release is not valid: because it is a donation. As noted in the law *Si sponsus*, section *Generaliter*, Digest, *De donationibus inter virum et uxorem*. Likewise, he who remits an exception is said to make a donation. Digest, *De novazione*, in the law *Si quis delegaverit*. Therefore, he who remits an action is also said to make a donation. Digest, *De conditione ob causam*, in the law *Si mulier*. But what is said to be donated: whether only as much as he could have demanded from him, or half.

† On the point of proof, I do not believe that a stepson, who is regarded in the place of a son and is so closely associated with the household that he is not a competent witness in such a serious case, because excessive familiarity weakens the testimony of the said witness, as stated in C. de testibus, l. etiam. Since an insinuation is required, as stated, it must be proved by written document, as noted by Bartolus in the aforementioned l. Modestinus, where it is said that if the liberality itself is a donation. For these two terms, liberality and donation, signify the same thing, as noted in ff. de donationibus, l. hoc iure, in the gloss, and by Bartolus in l. 2, § citra, de exceptione doli, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether it is lawful for a judge to give or promise to release someone from banishment, or whether another person who gave or promised to secure someone's release from banishment may testify.
1. Whether the statement of a witness who does not testify about the day or the place is valid.
2. In interrogations, the place and the month are required.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. It is alleged that the said Prosellus reported to our lord that a certain Mafiolus of Monte, outlawed in respect of his person, had caused to be delivered into the hands of the said lord Prosellus a just outlawry for hanging, and Paul, half-outlawed in respect of his person; on account of which report, our lord caused the said Mafiolus to be discharged from the outlawry.

† It is also stated that the aforementioned report does not appear to have been true: because a certain Albertinus seized the said Justus and delivered him to the said Lord Prosello, and not the said Mafiolus. Moreover, the said Polus was not delivered to Lord Prosello, nor captured, except by the public household of the said Lord Prosello. It is also stated that, because the said Lord Prosello made the aforementioned report and obtained the said grace from Lord Geroldo da Monte, brother of the said Mafiolus, who had been released from the ban, he gave to the said Lord Prosello two rings, and to Lady Gilia, wife of the said Lord Prosello, one string of coral, and also, after a certain number of days, gave and delivered to the said Lady Gilia two hundred gold florins as remuneration for the aforementioned act. And that this is true, signs and indications are alleged: especially because the said Lady, after the death of Lord Prosello, had fifty florins counted out to the said Albertinus on account of certain agreements that existed by virtue of the said banishment with the said Albertinus; and all these matters have been reported to the Lord, and witnesses examined. And John of Saint Gallo says that the said Albertinus delivered the said Justus of Buriis to the said Lord Prosello. He also said that this was at the instance of one of the sons-in-law of the said Lord Prosello. Also, Lord Prosello had the said Paul seized; and that the said Lord Prosello, by simulation and speaking contrary to the truth, said that the said Masiolus had seized the said Paul, which is by no means true. And he believes that for this reason he received up to the sum of 200 gold florins. And that Brother Francischino went to the house of a certain Iouanolo, together with Martino and Silvestro, who Silvestro, in the name of the sons of the said Prosello, counted out to the said Albertinus 50 florins in grossi in his presence. Here it must be considered that this witness does not appear to be telling the truth: because it is not true that the said Prosello never reported to our Lord that the said Mafiolus had seized the said Justus or the said Polus; but rather that he had them delivered. For it is true that he had them delivered through others and at his own expense. And he who bears the expense is said to be the one causing the act to be done. And it is certain that there is a difference between delivering and having delivered; because he who acts through another acts interpretatively, and not truly, as noted in law 1, § deiecisse, de vi et vi armata. Also, the said John of Saint Gallo does not appear to have been questioned regarding the source of his knowledge. Hence his statement is very weak, even assuming it were true. This is denied by Lady Gilia, because it is expressly contrary to the letters of the Lord. Then follows the testimony of Geroldo, who says many words. And finally he says that he, Geroldo, gave to the said Lady Gilia, for service and remuneration for the aforementioned two hundred gold florins, a certain chest. Now the said Geroldo is the brother of the said Mafiolus, who was released from the ban; and regarding this witness there is doubt whether this remuneration is disgraceful on the part of both the giver and the receiver, or on neither; and whether he is to be believed who says that he gave it; and whether, because no year or month is specified, the testimony is rendered null.

† On the first point, it is certain that if there had been a prior agreement to give [money], this would constitute corruption of the judge, and simony, or barataria, and would be a turpitude on the part of both: for he sins who corrupts a magistrate. And thus the witness would confess himself to be a participant in the crime, and his testimony would not be valid, as in the law concerning accusations, the final law; and he is not believed who says that he corrupted himself, unless he proves it. C. de poena iud. Authen. nouo iur. But if no agreement, or hope, preceded, what the law is, is clear from such a distinction, which is that of Antonius de Pisis in law 3, ff. de condit. ob. tur. causam. For he himself says, if you wish to know when it is lawful to give to a judge, or I wish to give money to a judge on account of a decision, and formerly I could recover what was given, but I lost the cause, today I cannot; or if he objects the corruption of the judge, and I cannot; or if he objects the acquisition of friendship, and I can up to the value of food or drink; or if he objects the retention of friendship, and I can, if I am a blood relative, up to one hundred gold coins; or if for remuneration, and ordinary salary to one not absent, I can, if he has a salary from the public, I cannot. l. 6. §. lege iul. ff. ad l. iul. From this it is clear that if it appears that this was a turpitudinous cause: because from the law, reprobated, de legato I can. And other laws proving this, And. de Pis. this, which he says can. s. palam. But this question does not seem to pertain to our case: for this renunciation did not concern the office of Lord Prosello. But the grace emanated from the prince, which Lord Prosello had procured: it is true that if he had procured it fraudulently, the renunciation would be turpitudinous and execrable, whatever it may be. Let us see if this is established. And regarding Lord Prosello, it appeared that he did not wish to receive money, nor did he receive it through an interposed person, his wife. This does not appear in any way, or by any indication, nor is it presumed. But if this crime is attributed to Lady Gilia, his wife, let the acts speak. For they are written, and it does not appear to me that any witness testifies about the month of this crime. Hence the deposition is not valid, as in l. libellorum. and that no. Bar. ff. de dolo. Moreover, it is required.

For even in criminal proceedings the place and the month must be proved; although a general inquiry does not require this as a matter of form, it nevertheless requires proof thereof as a matter of form, as noted by Jacobus de Belvis in his Institutiones de actionibus in the beginning; similarly in the Digest, title de deposito, and in the law Si quis argentum. Moreover, it is rightly true that the corrupted associate of an informer ought to be punished, as provided in the Code, title de accusationibus, law Si quis; and in the Digest, title ad legem Iuliam de repetundis, law In comites; and in the Digest, title de officiis proconsulis, law Observare, section Proficisci. However, this is always understood to apply only if there is legitimate proof of the felony, as stated in Decretum 2, question 1, chapter Nos in quemquam. Furthermore, if I have carefully examined the proceedings, it does not appear to me that anyone else attests to this except G. Toldus, who testifies that this matter took place secretly in a certain chamber. Hence, according to his own statement, he is necessarily a sole witness in his testimony, such that he cannot have a corroborating witness. And it is certain that a single witness is not believed in criminal cases, as stated in the Digest, title de quaestionibus, law Maritus; rather, the proofs must be clearer than daylight, as provided in the law Sciant cuncti.

† Moreover, this man is not a credible witness, since he admits to having aided the crime, indeed to having been the instigator and the cause of the faction, if it can be called a faction; and thus he confesses himself to be criminal. And by his own testimony and personal admission he becomes infamous, at least de facto; to whom no credence is given without torture. As noted in l. cunctos populos, de summa trinitate. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If a testator, after making a formal will, verbally declares that he revokes it, and donates all his property causa mortis to someone, whether by this act the will is revoked.
2. A donation causa mortis may be made of all the deceased’s property.
3. An heir who, after accepting the inheritance, did not draw up an inventory, or drew it up not in accordance with the law, does not deduct the Falcidian portion.
4. Whether the deduction made from a donation causa mortis has the force of the Falcidian portion or of the Trebellian portion.
5. If the testator did not wish the instituted heir to have anything, but rather revoked whatever he had conferred upon him, whether this is equivalent to a prohibition of the Falcidian portion.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It must be premised for clarity that the first testament, by which the said Doctor Iacobus instituted his fifth-named brother as heir, and subsequently declared that he revoked and annulled it, making a donation causa mortis of his goods to his brother Taliolus, was not thereby vitiated with regard to the institution of the heir; because a mere verbal revocation does not remove the institution of an heir, nor does it render a person intestate. As stated in the Digest, De militum testamento, in the law Militis codicilli, § Veteranus. For the said revocation is not solemn, since it is not a testament, inasmuch as it lacks the institution of an heir. As stated in the Digest, De adimendis et legatis, in the law Ex parte. And no last will can revoke a testament unless it itself possesses the same effect and form of institution. As stated in the Code, De testibus, in the law Hac consultissima, § Pe; and in the Digest, De contrahenda tutela, in the law Si duobus, § Si prius. Nor does the Code, De testamentis, in the laws Scimus and Nostram, and the gloss thereon, although it seems to argue to the contrary, namely, that a testament may be revoked by the testator’s presence and reduced to the state of intestacy in favor of those succeeding ab intestato, through a solemn repentance expressed before seven witnesses, such that the praetor does not grant possession according to the tablets. As stated in the Digest, Si tabulae testamenti nullae extabunt, in the law 1, § Fi. If the first opinion is more probable, because the second disposition is not a testament, since it lacks the institution of an heir. As noted in the Digest, De testamentis, in the law 1; and in the Digest, De his quae in testamento delentur, in the law Proxime. For the testator did not proceed to the act of fact in adding the tablets of the writing. For then it would be otherwise, as if the proof were abolished. As stated in the aforementioned law Proxime, and in the laws Cancellauerat and Nostram. And according to the distinction of the said laws, it seems that the aforementioned law 1 of the Digest, Si tabulae testamenti nullae extabunt, which speaks indiscriminately, should be understood. Similar is the Digest, Qui satisdare coguntur, in the law Sciendum, in the principal part.

Secondly, for the sake of clarity, I premise that the donation causa mortis made of the entire estate of the deceased was valid and binding in the person of Tadeolus, his brother; since a donation causa mortis could be made of all the goods of the deceased, as is fully read and noted in the last paragraph of the Code, On Peace, through the gloss and all the doctors. Nevertheless, the Falcidian deduction is deducted from the said donation causa mortis by the instituted heir, as in the Code, On the Falcidian Law, in the law In donations.

† It is nevertheless true that if the instituted heir, after having accepted the inheritance, did not make an inventory, or made one but not lawfully, he cannot deduct the Falcidian portion, as stated in the Authentica *De haeredibus et Falcidia*, § *Sancimus*; nor can he deduct from legacies or fideicommissa. And he can deduct the Trebellian portion from universal legacies, according to the opinion of many doctors. On this point, see fully the Code, *Ad legem Falcidiam*, Authentica *Sed cum testator*, and in the Corpus, from which this opinion is derived, that the Trebellian portion does not cease. Bartolus holds this view in the Digest, *Ad Trebellianam*, *L. Marcellus*, § *Quod autem*, stating that it is not provided by law that the Trebellian portion is lost due to the fault of one who fails to make an inventory.

† Therefore, it must be considered whether the deduction made from a donation causa mortis is to be treated in the manner of the Falcidian share, which is due by right of institution, or in the manner of the Trebellian share. For in the first case, it would be lost by the failure to make an inventory; in the second case, it would not be lost. And it seems that it is to be treated in the manner of the Trebellian share, when the universality of goods has been donated, as in D. 36.1.1 (Cogi) in the beginning. But the truth is that it is treated in the manner of the Falcidian share. For such a donee is equated to a universal fideicommissary, since he does not passively assume the liabilities, as in D. 23.3.1 (Mulier bona); nor is the heir released from the burdens of debts, as in D. 36.1.1 (Hereditatem).

† It must also be considered whether, because the testator did not wish the appointed heir to have anything, and indeed revoked whatever had been conferred upon him, this is equivalent to a prohibition against the deduction of the Falcidian fourth. And it seems that one may argue in the affirmative, by that which is read in the Digest, *de fideicommissis libertatibus*, in the gloss on the last part of the law *Decem*.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that in villages a will is valid if made before four witnesses and a priest, what if a will is made before
2. witnesses according to the common law without a priest?
3. Whether an appeal is permitted from the sentence of an arbitrator chosen by the parties, or accepted by virtue of a statute.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

It must be premised for the sake of clarity: if a statute provides that in the villages wills made before four witnesses and a priest are valid, whether those made before seven witnesses without a priest are valid. And it seems that they are not, on the ground that a certain form of making a will is prescribed, which, if not observed, renders the will invalid, as in the Institutes, *De testamentis*, § *Testes*. But the contrary is true, because this statute contains a dispensation, not a necessary form, by which, namely, one departs from the common law, as in the Code, *De testibus*, l. *Si*, and in l. 3, Digest, *De militum testamento*. That which must not be omitted is that if the priest is employed in place of a notary, he seems to be employed also in place of a witness, and Digest, *De testamentis*, l. *Domitius*, namely when another notary was also present, according to what is read in the Authenticum, *De hereditatibus et falsis*, § *Si vero absunt*, and Digest, *De testamentis*, l. *Domitius*, and Code, *Qui testamento facere possint*, l. *Hac consul.*, § *Si*. Certainly public fame would suffice that he was then a priest, as in the Code, *De testamentis*, l. 1. And although the statute required that he be a priest, nevertheless it can be adapted to the interpretation of the said statute, and the said law 1 and Institutes, *De testibus*, § *Sed cum aliquis*, and it is proved in the Extravagantes, *De consuetudinibus*, c. *Cum dilectis*. From these the doubts are resolved.

† Moreover, regarding the objection raised concerning the final award, to which, upon arriving, I preface the following for clarity: first, what is the rule under the common law; second, what is the rule under the municipal law. I answer the first point, and I say that we are speaking either of an *arbiter* or of an *arbitrator*. In the first case, distinguish: either the statute does not provide that such an *arbiter* be chosen in place of a judge; and then an appeal may be taken from his sentence; because he is akin to an *arbiter* under the common law, and the rules concerning the abandonment of appeals and the peremptory time limits apply. As noted by the gloss and the doctors in D. Qui satisdare cogantur, l. Arbitro. But if we are speaking of an *arbitrator*: then there is no proper appeal, nor do the peremptory time limits for appeals apply; but the rule requiring prompt action does apply. C. De iudicibus. But if the arbitrator is mixed, both *arbiter* and *arbitrator*, by virtue of the form of the compromise and the statute, I extend the entire judgment of appeal to the *arbiter* with regard to the peremptory time limits. For, once the appeal has been invalidated by the abandonment of the entire award, the matter has passed into the force of res judicata, and it is no longer necessary to inquire about the transactional nature of the arbitration. As in D. De conditione indebiti, l. Eleganter, § Si post. But if we are within the realm of statutes that go further, the form of the statute must be observed: as in C. De emancipatis liberis, l. 1, cum si. For local statutes can put an end to lawsuits. And regarding certain statutory time limits, the complaint is understood to be abandoned, and execution may be carried out without any further pronouncement, after the party has first been cited. As noted in C. De appellationibus, l. Eos, in principio, although it is safer to pronounce the appeal abandoned and then proceed to execution. As in C. Quomodo et quando iudex, l. Si praeses quasi desertam. Although it appears that this pronouncement pertains to the judge to whom the appeal is made, and not to the judge from whom it is taken; unless by way of the cause, as when we pronounce the sentence to be executed; because it is established that the appeal is abandoned by the lapse of the peremptory time limits. For what comes by way of the cession of the cause comes incidentally. As in C. De iudicibus, quo. From these things it appears, according to what is set forth in the case, and having seen the decree of the lord, and from what could be gathered from the records, the discussion of which I leave to the advocates: that the award in question should be executed, for the part of the said agent. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How do the sons of a vassal, together with the grandsons, succeed to the fief? And how is the division among them to be made?
2. A father may leave more to one son than to another, provided he does not diminish the legitime.
3. A father’s will, approved by his sons with certain knowledge and without fraud, is not valid as a will, but by the law of pact.
4. The consent of the lord is not required for the division of the fief among the succeeding sons.
5. If the father received the dowry of his son, after his death, in the division among the brothers, the married son must receive the dowry of his wife.
6. Debts contracted by one of the sons after the father’s death must be paid from his own share, unless he contracted them for the common benefit.
7. Feudal goods cannot be alienated without the consent of the lord and the agnates.
8. A legacy appointed for the time and occasion of marriage must not be paid before the marriage has been contracted.
9. If one of the brothers has incurred certain expenses on the common property, he may claim in the division of the inheritance the useful and necessary expenses, but not the voluptuary ones: and if they are small, he will prove them by presumptions; if large, fully.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† If a vassal dies leaving male children, the children succeed equally in the fief, but the grandchildren do not, nor do more remote descendants per stirpes, in the absence of any disposition by the deceased, the fief being valid. As in § 10, col. de success. feud., c. 1, unless it was acquired under a law, and from one having the power, that the vassal could make a will regarding that fief, as in cap. 1, de feudo non habente propriam feudi naturam, same collection; or unless the brothers themselves agreed among themselves, as in c. 1, de alien. feud. paterni. They are said to agree, unless deceit or fraud intervened, for then one is rather deceived than contracting. As in D. de pactis, l. tres fratres; and D. de transactionibus, l. qui cum tutoribus, § qui per fallaciam. And this is the answer to the first point concerning the will, and to the second concerning the division which they would make among themselves. And it supports what is noted in C. de familiae herciscione, l. si familiae.

† As to the third point, if a father left more to one son than to another, it must be said that the father may do so, provided that he does not impair the legitimate portion of the son. As in the Authentica de nuptiis, §. pe., Collatio 4.

† On the fourth point, the answer is apparent from the foregoing: for if, with certain knowledge and without fraud, they approved the will, after the father’s death it is not valid as a will, but by the law of pact; because at the time of the father’s death, as regards the fief, it was null. We have a similar case. C. co. utriusque iud. l. 2. On the fifth point
† I say that among the sons themselves the consent of the lord is not necessary, as in the cited chapter J. on alienation of the paternal fief, in the Siete Partidas, point 6.

I say that the husband ought to receive the dowry of his wife, as in the Digest, *De fund. dotali*, law *Si maritus*; and this applies if the father received the dowry; but if he himself is the heir, then he ought not to receive it from the common estate, nor is anything owed to him on this account by his brothers.

† On the seventh point, I say that the debts which the said heir contracted after the death of his father, he must pay out of his own share, not out of the common property, unless he had expended them for the common benefit. As in D. de negotiorum gestorum, l. ex duobus.

† On the eighth point, I say that feudal goods cannot be alienated without the consent of the agnates; and furthermore, the consent of the lord of the fief is also required, as in c. j. de alienatione feudorum and in the aforementioned chapter de alienatione feudi paterni, together with its similar provisions.

† On the ninth point, I say that when a testator leaves a legacy to be paid at the time of and upon the occurrence of marriage, it ought not to be paid earlier than the marriage has been contracted, as stated in C. de nuptiis, l. Sancimus. And because the day of the marriage is uncertain, namely with regard to the contracting of matrimony, the legatee ought not to have interest for the time elapsed; rather, the heir [is entitled to retain it], unless he has paid it of his own accord, as appears from the rule laid down in ff. ad Trebellianum, l. Mulier, § Si haeres, and ff. de inofficioso testamento, l. Papinianus, § Si conditioni. On the tenth and last point, the answer is apparent from what has already been said.

† On the eleventh point, by the aforementioned law *ex duobus*, D. de negotiorum gestorum actione, for he had recovered good and necessary expenses, but not those incurred for pleasure: as is clear there. Thus, if any common money comes into the hands of the said Henry, he is bound to render an account thereof to the said brothers. As stated in the aforementioned law *tres fratres*, and if he claims to have expended funds on common affairs, he is bound to prove this. But if the expenses are small, he may prove them by presumptions; if they are large, he must prove them fully. As noted in C. de iure delibandi, l. *si*, § *in computatione*; and C. de donationibus, l. *si quis pro redemptione*; and Extravagantes de accusatione, qualiter, in principio; and C. de administratione tutorum, l. *lex quae tutores*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the territory is included under the name of the city, so that one giving or alienating the city is said to have given or alienated the territory.
2. What the words placed in the contract of donation or alienation, namely "those which it holds and possesses, etc.," signify? And whether those which are ruled and governed are comprehended? And what if such things are held mediately, and not immediately.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen. Note for the Duke of Touraine, brother of the Most Serene King of the realm of the French. The illustrious lord Lord Gian Galeazzo, or Beltrando Guasco, proctor and in the proctorial name of the said Lord Gian Galeazzo, knowing, prudent, and spontaneous, and fully certified concerning the law and fact of his said lord, as he states: permits, and in the said case gives, assigns, and constitutes as dowry in the name and for the cause of the dowry of the lady Valentina his daughter, to the said lord Louis, Duke of Touraine, there present, likewise and with the authority and consent of our said lord King solemnly stipulating and receiving for you: to wit, the city of Asti with all its other lands, villages, castles, fortresses, strongholds, rights, and honors pertaining and belonging to the said city, which he holds and possesses from the lands of Annone and Rocca d'Arazzo upward; so and in such manner that the said two lands of Annone and Rocca d'Arazzo and all other lands which are from those lands toward the parts of Alessandria, that is, between the said two lands and Alessandria, [remain] to the aforesaid Lord Gian Galeazzo just as before. The doubt which is raised by the presidents of the said Duke is this: namely, that they say that all lands which are of the territories of the aforesaid lands of Annone and Rocca d'Arazzo upward toward Asti are included in the said assignment. On the part of the illustrious lord Count it is said that they are not, and especially on account of those words which are at the end of the aforesaid clause, namely 'remain to the aforesaid Lord Gian Galeazzo just as before,' and also on account of many other things, which Lord Pietro Del Corto argues more at length on the present sheet. The illustrious lord and his respectable council would wish that by your reverence the aforesaid arguments of the said Lord Pietro should be considered, and those things should be added which seem to your circumspection capable of being added that bear on the point; even if some things should seem to be removed from the said arguments; and that this be done quickly, because the matter imports haste, so that they may be had tomorrow morning. He says, 'the city of Asti.' Whether under the name of 'city' its territory is contained: I say that either we speak according to the nature and proper meaning of words, and it is not contained, as in ff. de penu le. l. nam quod liquide. §. si ita, ff. de verb. sign. l. 2, de rescrip. l. Rodulphus, de senten. excom. c. si cui ciuitas, lib. 6; or according to interpretation, and then either the grantor or disposer proceeds further in granting, and we stand by what was done, ff. de offi. praefecti vrbis. l. j. §. cum vrbem; likewise if from preceding or following words the intention can appear, for the force of preceding words is fourfold: namely, of declaring, ff. de lega. 1. l. si seruus plurium. §. supplendi; ff. de pact. l. Item quia. §. idem iul.; of amplifying, ff. de iu. et fac. igno. l. regula. §. fi.; and of restricting, ff. de verb. sig. l. si cum fundum. If however it is doubtful, the Doctors commonly say that the territory accrues to the city by natural reason, namely that the members ought to be ruled by the head, ff. de iudi. l. insulae Italiae, C. de testamentis. l. fi., ff. ad municipa. l. qui ex vitio, in Auth. quib. mod. natu. effic. sui. §. si quis igitur. ex qualem coll. 7, de capi. qui curiam vendidit. c. 1. coll. 10; likewise by reason of connectedness, ff. de fun. instruc. l. serie. §. tyrannicae; likewise because men commonly so think, ff. de fun. instruc. l. cum delanionis. §. asinam; likewise because that disposition is perfect which consists of all its parts and appendages, ff. de contrahen. emp. l. aquaeductus; likewise because universal terms are to be broadly interpreted, ff. de fun. instruc. l. lucius; likewise through the favorable act of dowry, and the agreement of the parties, ff. de lib. le. l. Aurelius. §. titius. But because we are in a case where the contracting parties proceeded further, therefore let us see concerning the second part of 'city,' which begins 'with all, etc.', which is entirely ampliative and extensive, except for the word 'its,' which is restrictive. Where it is to be noted that the text says 'other lands, villages, etc.,' for the word 'its' coheres with all the following words, ff. de fun. instru. l. serie. §. cayo; nor indeed can it be understood of others with a lawful intention, ff. de leg. 1. l. serui electione. §. cum fundus, extra de testamentis. filius.

† Now follows in the text of the contract the third clause: 'which he holds and possesses.' These are entirely restrictive and limitative, C. de summa tri. l. cunctos populos; and so far as it looks to places, it is understood of true possession, not abusive or precatory, and in doubt the detainer is presumed to possess, as noted in de priuil. c. cum olim, and Archidiaconus in 7. q. 1. c. Pontifices; but so far as it looks to the promised governance, 'which he holds and possesses' is understood as: which he rules and governs, or which are governed in his name, C. de praescr. 30. an. l. male agitur. But those are understood to be ruled which are ruled immediately; whence places that have their own magistrate ruling in the name of the place itself are not comprehended under these words, arg. ff. de pecu. leg. l. cum dominus. §. filius; even if naturally it is of the territory, because they have a certain exception and are not of the same body, but form a body by themselves, and what has been destined to one seems to be taken away from another, ff. de leg. 1. l. quod in rerum. §. si quis, ff. de admi. le. l. alumne. §. qui filias. There follows the fourth clause of the contract: 'from the lands, etc.' That monosyllable is a mark of punctual and immediate separation, ff. de act. emp. l. ratio. §. fin., so that the sense is that up to the point the cession was made of those things, namely only which the city of Asti ruled, or another in the name of the city of Asti; otherwise if in the name of the castle itself or town, because legitimation does not amplify the principal disposition, ff. de vsufru. le. l. generalis. §. vxori. There follows the fifth clause: 'so and in such manner, etc.' This clause does not come corrective, but copulative and reservative, ff. fa. herc. l. Item labeo. §. j., extra de resti. spo. c. olim causam. There follows the sixth and last clause: 'just as.' These words signify that there ought to be the same state, ff. de fun. instruc. l. praedia maritima. §. ita legatum; and if any variation of times had intervened, the last and final habit is looked to, ff. de ali. et cib. le. l. mella ait. §. j. From these, concluding according to the truth, which ought to be honored, and at the end of the appendages it appears which places come toward Asti and which not, that those [places are meant] which come under their own condition, ff. de fundis limitosis. l. 2. lib. 10. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a debtor may give to his creditor the names of his own debtors without payment; and if so, what kind of debts must be given.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. It may be doubted, because the choice appears to belong to the debtor as to in which names he shall pay. D. de iure dot. l. plerunque; D. de cond. indebit. l. cum his, §. si; and what is noted, D. de pact. veteribus. Moreover, because the minimum is in the obligation. D. mand. l. si fideiussorem. To the contrary it seems, for if one promises ten in honey, he ought not to pay the worst honey, but that which is worth ten. D. de sol. l. si ita stipulatus fuero, in melle. In the same way, if he stipulates in names, he ought to assign to me such names as could be sold for ten. D. ad l. Falc. l. quaerebatur. For a void assignment does not release the debtor. As D. de leg. 1. l. quidam testamento; D. de administ. tut. l. cum quaeritur; D. si cert. pet. l. periculum. Moreover, the creditor is not bound to accept such things; but if he were to accept them voluntarily and with certain knowledge, he prejudices himself. D. de fideicom. l. qui satisdat; D. man. l. inter causas, §. abesse. I resolve that, since such a delegation of names ought to take the place of payment, the creditor is not compelled to receive worthless names of debtors unpaid; for that which is given unpaid ought to be suitable for the quantity of the debt. C. de bonis auth. iu. pos.; auth. et qui iurat, de re iudic.; l. a diuo pio. Moreover, the origin of the obligation ought to be considered, which is solidary in its pursuit. D. de fideicom. tuto. Moreover, because it is in the discretion of a good man, it is fitting to receive names with effect. And this matter descends from the discretion of a good man, to whom it does not fit to pay empty things for the security of a true debt; for just as the obligation is effective, so ought the payment to be effective. D. de pig. act. l. eleganter, §. qui reprobos, from which it is concluded that either suitable names must be assigned, or payment must be made. And the wisely cited law supports this. D. qui satisda. cog. l. 1, in the word "securum faciamus." This law was most prudently cited by my beloved, Lord Jacobus de Fabris of Vicenza. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. How many things are required for a pact of repurchase to be deemed a contract made in fraud of usury.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† This passage is touched upon and determined by the Lord Archbishop in 14. q. 3. c. plerique, whose words are these: Titius purchased an estate for a full as; with the condition added that if he wishes to repay the same amount of money to the latter within ten years, the latter is bound to return that land to him. The latter received the fruits, and finally, having received the money, he returned the field, retaining all the fruits perceived. He commits usury. Indeed, if he does this in fraud of usury, he sins mortally, nor is he defended by the pact of usury: although he cannot be condemned for this by the Church. But if he does not do this in fraud, he does not sin: because such a contract is lawful: and such a purchase and sale is lawful. C. de pac. inter emp. et vendi. l. si fundum. ff. de in diem adiec. quot. according to Ugucio. However, if a condition or pact is added that the seller would restore the land if a certain quantity of money, which scarcely contained half the just price, were returned to him within a certain time: such a contract is judged usurious. ar. ff. de transac. l. cum hi. §. modus. C. mandati. l. per diuersas according to Innocentius. What he says, as noted, extra de emp. et ven. ad nostram, but Raymundus says that such a usurious contract is presumed from these conjectures: from the fact that the price is small in respect to the value of the thing. Also from the fact that something is paid beyond the principal received. Also from the fact that the buyer is accustomed to practice usury. These are proven in the aforementioned decretal ad nostram, as extra de pig. c. illo vos, according to Raymundus de pęna sorti. These are the words of the Archbishop. To this last opinion, which holds, among other things, that he was accustomed to practice usury, Jacobus de Arena agrees in one of his disputations, saying that three things must at least intervene: namely, a small price, and a pact of repurchase, and that he was accustomed to practice usury. And thus he understands the chapters cited above. For although the quantity of the price is an argument of fraud, as ff. de transac. l. cum hi. §. modus, nevertheless this argument by itself is not sufficient, nor even the pact of repurchase, unless the buyer was accustomed to practice usury. The same is noted by Cynus, C. plus vale. quod agitur. l. emptione. And this is the common opinion. And thus I hold that the said contract should not be judged usurious unless it was celebrated with usury, i.e., with one who otherwise was accustomed to lend at interest: as in the rule semel malus, and ff. de accu. l. si cui. §. hisdem. Hence, that word which the gloss places in cap. conquestus, extra de vsuris, when it says "especially," does not please the aforementioned doctors, nor do I hold it, unless there were other violences or probable conjectures.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the order of a superior, which prevents the lessee from using the leased thing, causes harm to the lessor with respect to the rent.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Having examined the instrument of purchase of the fruits of certain mills, made by the noble man, Lord James of Novis, in which instrument is contained this pact in the form that follows. And presupposing that the magnificient Lord, the Count of Virtues, commanded the said community of Novara and the aforementioned James that he should make no novelties or works without his special license, which, because of the said James, who could not have the due advantages from the said mill made, nor from another to be made, on account of the impediment that the Terdonians provided, because they said that the said mills were in their territory; and therefore they prohibited the said James from using the said mill made, the use did not exist except for 28 days, because the command was made on the 28th day; considering these presuppositions as firmly as snow, I say,

†that the said Ia. is not bound to pay the hire, except pro rata temporis, i.e., for the said 28 days, and not beyond, as stated in ff. loca l. si fundus and l. si haec, distinctio, and most fully noted in ff. eo. ti. l. si vno, §. item cum quid in. Nor is it expedient to adduce further authorities, because this is the truth, and especially because the stipulations appended in this contract sound thus. It is most certain. Note that the penalty is not incurred, because it did not depend on him, since he ought to obey his lawful superior, who excuses him from the penalty, as in ff. si quis cautio l. 2, §. simili modo. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether those who have an interest are to be cited in the legitimation of someone, and below in opinion 363.
2. Inferiors cannot legitimize by the Emperor to the prejudice of those who have already acquired a right.
3. Contracts of sale from which it is presumed to be usurious.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The words of Bartolus in the law Gallus, section "and what if only," concerning free and posthumous persons, are to be observed here:

Whether, whenever someone is legitimated, those who have an interest must be summoned. I answer: Sometimes a father causes his son to be legitimated during his lifetime; in this case, others need not be summoned, because this principally concerns the father, who may dispose of his property as he wishes. See *L. Adoptio*, *De adoptionibus*. Sometimes the son himself petitions to be legitimated; and then, if the father had provided in his will that he wished the son to be legitimated, the son may seek legitimation without the request of another. See *C. De naturalibus liberis*, *Auth. Item si quis*, and from which the *Corpus* is derived. Sometimes the father made no provision in his will; and then, to the prejudice of those in whom a right has already vested, legitimation cannot occur without their being summoned. Indeed, more than that, the consent of those persons is required. See *L. Si*, *Ff. De natalibus restituitis*, Bartolus. But whatever the case may be regarding the Emperor,

† However, the same rule does not apply to other lords of cities: because they cannot dispense against an Imperial law prohibiting such dispensation. As stated in Auth. qui monachos efficiunt sui, §. si, Coll. 7; and in l. 1, C. de iure annulorum aureorum; and there by Jacobus Butrigarius. Nevertheless, it must be considered that the said Lord della Scala did not use words from which legitimation would appear, but rather words concerning succession: because he wished the said Alexander to succeed, and to deprive the legitimate heirs of their goods; which he certainly could not do, since the right of succession had already been acquired by those legitimate heirs. And a special statute against a certain person is not valid. D. de pollic. l. totiens; and D. qui et a quibus, l. privatus. And even if it had been valid, it was subsequently revoked, and could be revoked, because it was inequitable: for things easily revert to their natural state. As D. de pact. l. si unus, §. pactus ne peteret, vers. quod ad speciem dotis. Furthermore, at the time of the death of the father and the uncle, this spurious child could not succeed: for this is the time that is considered. l. finalis, D. de regula Catho. Also, because in the said rescript there is no mention that he was spurious, but rather that he was a bastard. Who certainly could have been instituted heir by the father, and also by the uncle. As C. de naturalibus liberis, Auth. licet. Hence, it does not appear that the said Lord della Scala had the intention of disposing contrary to the law. Wherefore, that rescript was obtained by concealment (obreptitium), and therefore null. As D. de carbo. edict. l. 3, §. puberi. From these points it clearly follows that the said spurious child could sell nothing to the prejudice of the legitimate successors; nor are the legitimate successors, or those having cause from them, bound to return the price, which did not come to them. But the vendor, who received that price, is bound, from which he has become enriched. As C. de rei vend. l. in civile; and D. quod metus causa, l. 3. But if it were assumed that the decree of the Lord della Scala had been valid, and before it was revoked, the house had been revoked or sold by the true heir, the contract would be valid: even if the grace was subsequently revoked. As D. de acquirenda hereditate, l. quotiens; D. de minoribus, l. interdum; D. de re iudicata, l. ex contractu; D. de conditione indebiti, l. tutores. Regarding the third point, it must be said that

† If the buyer was a usurer at the time of the said purchase, such contract is presumed to be a loan contract; otherwise, it is not. As noted by the Archdeacon, 14 q. 3, c. plerisque; and in C. plus valere quod agitur, l. emptione. And thus determines Jacobus de Arena, disputing in c. ad nostram, de emptione et venditione, and in c. illo vos, de pignore. And yet it is doubtful whether the fact that he was a usurer can be proven by those to whom he lent money at usury. And I say that they cannot testify in their own favor. But they may testify in favor of a third party, and thus, as in Inst. de testamentis, § legatariis cum si; and in ff. de testibus, l. testamento, cum si. If, therefore, these three things are proven—the two which appear in the instrument, and the third, that he was a usurer—it follows that the said pledge could not have been made, and that the true heirs are not bound in any way, as in ff. de pignoris actione, l. rem alienam. I always say that to prove that it was a pledge, three things are required, which I have stated above. But the two things found in the instrument are not sufficient. Finally, I say that if the said heirs paid from another’s use, because of the concurrent value or quantity of the house, if anyone or another has the benefits of the inheritance, they must participate in this honor. As in l. secundum naturam, ff. de re iudicata; and in ff. de conditionibus, l. his qui hereditatem; and l. his qui plus, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Upon the termination of the arbitration agreement, the case is returned to the ordinary judge.
2. A statute ordering that a case be submitted to arbitration should not be understood as applying only to the first instance, but rather as many times as necessary, until the case is effectively concluded.
3. Whether an assignee can be compelled by the exception of set-off.
4. Whether an assignee becomes subject to the jurisdiction of the assignor.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. First, it must be considered whether the assignment could have been made by the lady during the pendency of the litigation in the manner described above: namely, after the compromise was abandoned due to the lapse of the term, or expired by the death of the arbitrator, and the knowledge of the case reverted to the ordinary judge: before whom the lawsuit was initiated by the presentation of the libel and citation: and before whom the arbitrators were elected according to the form of the statute: and whether the parties ought to be compelled to make a new compromise, notwithstanding the said assignment: and whether, if a new compromise is not requested, the ordinary judge may proceed by virtue of his jurisdiction in the aforementioned case. And assuming that the assignment were valid, whether the exception of compensation may be raised against the assignee, on account of goods removed, alienated, or consumed: and whether the assignee is bound to the forum of the arbitrators to be chosen in the person of the assignor, or not. And in sum, the question is, what is the law.

† And it must be premised that, upon the termination of the compromise, the cognizance returns to the judge in that state in which it was at the time of the compromise: because before the arbitrators the matter was still *res integra*, that is, the testimonies had not yet been received. C. de arbi. l. pe. extra de testi. c. praesentata. C. de temp. ap. Item extra de appel. c. quandiu. in cle. So. it must be premised,

† If a statute commands that the cause be compromised, it is understood to be with effect. Hence, if the first compromise has lapsed, the cause must be compromised again until the intent of the statute is fulfilled. D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. haec conditio. And this is concluded, that the same cause must again be compromised with the same lady, notwithstanding the assignment: because judgment was prevented with the lady. C. de nova, l. 3. and the assignee will await the outcome of the litigation. C. de litigantibus, autem nunc si heres. And therefore the assignee in the meantime cannot sue on the assigned right: because he who has once brought an action is compelled to persist until the end. C. quomodo et quando iudex, auth. qui semel. and this is most true. But assuming that the assignment was valid, and that we are in litigation with the assignee himself, it must be seen:

Whether the assignee can be compelled by the exception of set-off. On this point there are differing opinions. Nevertheless, the common opinion is that if the set-off is liquidated, or can easily be proved, it may be opposed. D. de procuratoribus, l. si quis in rem. This is especially so if it does not appear that the assignment was made for an onerous cause. However, this exception is one prescribed in rem, according to Decius, Iacobus de Belvis, Butrius, and Bartolus. And there would be no doubt where the set-off occurs by operation of law. And in delicts, whatever may be said in disputation, it is safer in adjudication to follow the common opinion, as I have stated according to Decius.

† Regarding the right of forum, it appears that if the assignee brings a direct action, he should be compelled to submit to the forum of the arbitrators to be chosen; but if he brings an indirect action, the contrary holds, because his person is not that of which the statute speaks. D. de sol. matr. l. si vero. I say that either the defendant requests arbitration: and since we measure the right concerning the forum from the person of the defendant, and the defendant is of that quality of which the statute speaks, considering his origin; or the assignee requests arbitration, and he cannot, because it is a personal benefit, arg. D. de adm. tut. l. ex pluribus, etc. And thus I say, and I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Both Laws, etc., advise.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the son of a priest can be legitimated by the Emperor, so that he may succeed to the priest.
2. Whether the consent of relatives is required when a father has his son legitimated.
3. Whether a grandson born of a spurious child is said to be a person of infamous character. Likewise, whether he can be instituted as an heir. And number 4.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It is asked whether the son of a priest can be legitimated by the Emperor for the inheritance of the priest. This is a sufficiently doubtful question; nevertheless, since inheritances are granted by civil law, it seems that legitimation [is possible], as stated in the Digest, *De ritu nuptiarum*, in the principal part of the question, § 1, where it is said that the Emperor legitimizes all those born of incest for the inheritance of their father, as explained there by Cynus. And Johannes Andreae says that it is necessary to specify the type of illegitimacy.

† It is asked: whether, if a father wishes to legitimize his son, the consent of the relatives is required. Bartolus says that it is not. D. 28.2.1 (Gallus). And there he treats the matter fully. Nor, according to Bartolus, is citation necessary, even if the son had himself legitimized in the absence of the father, whose signs, however, had preceded his will, and had also followed in the testament. It seems sufficient, and I believe it is sufficient: because a change of will is not presumed. D. 22.6.1 (Testamentum).

† It is asked whether a son legitimated, born of a spurious child, is called a person of infamous character. I answer no, because he is admitted to all honors. And therefore the brother of the testator cannot bring an action of complaint on this ground.

† It is asked whether a grandson, lawfully born of a spurious son, can be instituted as heir. I answer that no law prohibits this, and therefore the institution is valid. C. de naturalibus liberis, l. fin. It is certain that a father can make a vulgar substitution for his spurious son. C. de haeredibus instituendis, l. 2, and see the note there. Alle. Bald. or Sig. for Peter de Burgaro, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether an older creditor has priority over newly acquired assets with respect to the hypothec.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. It is certain that in a hypothecary action, he who is prior in time is stronger in right, whether he brings the action or is sued. As stated in the rules of both laws. Now it has happened that Titius brought a hypothecary action against Seius, the possessor. Seius accepted the judgment as possessor. And when formally interrogated in court whether, at the time the plaintiff’s hypothec was created, the property was in the assets and dominion of the debtor, he answered that he does not believe it to be so. Finally, the plaintiff proved that the property had been in the assets at the time of the said obligation. After the same plaintiff made his position, by which it was secured that it was proven, and the defendant answered that he does not believe it, now the defendant is in the reckoning for rendering judgment. This defendant produces certain instruments of preceding hypothecs, by which he wishes to be bound. It is objected to him that he cannot do so; nevertheless, because of the said denials, and also because nothing is proposed by him as proven on the point in the law *cauetur* clearly, how the matter stands. But it must be imagined that the point stands thus: namely, because in an ancient obligation present and future things are included at that time, and therefore they are drawn to the time of the new owner by reason of the future things. And then another question arises:

Whether, in newly acquired rights, the older one is stronger; and whether he can claim that they are newly acquired, since he denied this being proven, and denied it under oath. For he does not seem able to assert the contrary of what he swore. Argument: in the last chapter, On Oaths, Book 6. You must clarify this matter more fully, how the case stands, and what these instruments are. And whether he has a ceded right, and how the matter stands; because on an uncertain fact, a certain response cannot be given. By law, denials are also accustomed to prejudice, in cases expressly stated in the law. Digest, On the Action for Recovery of Property; in the Authenticum, On the Three and a Half Years, §. Second; Digest, On Fideicommissa; Law, If there is doubt; to the Law Falcidia; Law, Of inheritances; Law, If. Moreover, I do not see that he can derive aid from the proofs of his adversary, which he undertook to impugn. Code, On Witnesses, Law, If anyone with witnesses. Furthermore, regarding priority in subsequently acquired rights, there is a question. Digest, On the Right of the Fisc, Law, Those who; and who, in pledges, Law, If and therefore. You remit the clear point, and I will consider the matter for the possessor, who ought to have the stronger rights. It is established by Law, To two persons; and Law, From the sixth part, §. Of the sides, On the Exception of Thing Adjudged. On the second point, much could be said: finally, Cynus determines in Law, If, Code, On the Velleian Senatusconsultum; there you will see.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Jurisdiction is twofold: and how it is defined.
2. An agreement made with a judge that an offender within his territory shall not be punished by him is invalid.
3. Whether an agreement to decline jurisdiction is valid.
4. A privilege granted simultaneously to several persons is not considered granted to one against another.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It must be stated for clarity that jurisdiction is either special or feudal. The former is an authority introduced by public law, with the necessity of administering justice and establishing equity. As noted in the Digest, *De iurisdictione omnium iudicum*, law 1, in which definition the words "public" are to be carefully considered.

† and therefore the agreement made with a mere judge, that an offender in his territory should not be punished by him, is invalid. D. de pactis, l. si unus, § illud nullam. For this amounts to renouncing jurisdiction into the hands of private individuals, which cannot be done. D. de officio praesidis, l. legatus Caesaris. Indeed, even the King of France may not permit anyone to offend with impunity in Paris: because an agreement that is disgraceful by its nature is not permitted to kings. Moreover, crimes should not be fostered under the pretext of privileges. C. de privilegiis scholarium, l. 2, lib. 12.

† But if jurisdiction were competent by reason of the fief alone, then such jurisdiction could be declined by agreement: because an agreement to decline jurisdiction is valid. As is noted in the Digest, *De iudiciis*, in the law *Heres absens*, in the gloss beginning *abnegative*. For the right of dominion in fiefs depends either on the nature of the fief or on agreement; and agreement in fiefs is of another nature. Let us suppose, however, that the agreement, because it does not suit great lords to dispute over the points of law, is made with A, B, C, that they may not be sued; the question arises whether such an agreement has effect if they sue each other. And on this point it may be alleged that the general rule does not include the person speaking. Code, *De solutionibus*, *Inquisitio veritatis*.

† I say that when a privilege is granted simultaneously to several persons, it does not appear to be granted to one against the other. D. de exc. rei iudicatae, l. sed et milites, near the beginning; and there by Laurentius de Andrea. And this is confirmed by the nature of the fief, which is that one vassal should not offend another, especially in a feudal matter. And the lord has cognizance, because it is special in the fief that the lord has cognizance, albeit mediately; I do not say immediately, since the case touches him. Nevertheless, he could not have cognizance in a case in which he is bound for eviction. D. de actionibus, l. eos. But in this case, if one co-heir expels another, I do not think the lord has bound himself for eviction, nor is he bound by the common law. C. de actionibus emptoris, l. ipullos. But assuming that the pact is valid, and that the contracting parties were included in the pact, it is necessary to premise another point: namely, that the pact is general as regards the active parties. But as regards the passive parties, it contains only certain persons: namely, A, B, C, and their heirs and successors. Such a pact is in no way extended to their children while their fathers are living. D. de pactis, l. et haeredi, and l. si tibi, § si pactus. Therefore, from these premises it necessarily follows that the defendants in question do not have a declinatory exception of forum. And thus is the response to all five articles of the question, that the said Lord Count is the competent judge. And so I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, doctor of both laws, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a mediator, or a prosoneta, as one who writes letters concerning the contract of others, is bound, and whether they prove.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Having examined the opinions of the aforementioned most excellent doctors, and having weighed the status of the person writing:

† because the mediator, who appears to use words in an exhortative and demonstrative manner, not in a binding one, as noted in the Digest, De infamia, l. haec verba. Considering also the nature of the office of these prosonetars, it is certain that they do not bind themselves with the intention of contracting their own faith, as noted in the Digest, De dolo, l. eleganter, in principio. Nor is it likely that they would obligate anyone, when the matter does not concern them. But they merely provide the act of bare ministry, Digest, De institutionibus, l. Lucius. Considering also that he who promises to me for another, at my command, is secure against me on the ground of fraud, as in the Digest, De solutionibus, l. si debitor, and there by Bartolus. Considering also that a remissive letter does not bind, unless its form is observed, Digest, De acquisitione hereditatis, l. eum qui duobus, § filius, without considering that the reason, or rather the final purpose of the writing, ought to be taken into account, Digest, De legatis 2, l. cum pater, § dulcissimis. And because this Guido was not writing his own business, but for the sake of the person to whom he wrote, Digest, Mandatum, l. 1, I say that the said Guido ought to be absolved, as not being a debtor. For his words ought not to be caviled at, but soundly interpreted according to good faith and equity, Digest, Ad Tertullianum, l. 1, § tractari; Digest, Ad exhibendum, l. penultima.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a person legitimated by subsequent marriage excludes him who is substituted to someone, if the latter dies without legitimate children, and without natural children to be begotten in a lawful marriage.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A certain person instituted three heirs, and among them made such a substitution, namely, that if it should happen that any one, or one of the said three, namely A., B., C., of the aforementioned instituted heirs, should die at any time without legitimate and natural children, to be begotten in a lawful marriage, one or more male children; in that case, he substituted for the same, or for those so dying, in the aforementioned matters, another, or others, of the same survivors, vulgarly, pupillarily, and by fideicommissum, etc. After the death of the testator, one of the said instituted heirs died, leaving to himself three male children, born of a lawful concubinage, but afterwards legitimated by lawful marriage. Now it is asked whether the said legitimated children have the right to exclude the substitutes.

† And it seems that this is so: for the force of marriage is such that they are considered legitimately born, as in the Institutes, De nuptiis, §. si; and in the Extravagantes, Qui filii sint legitimi, c. tanta. Moreover, because they appear to be restored to their birthrights and to their ancient legitimacy, as in the Authenticum, Qui monachos efficiunt sui, §. si quis igitur dotalia, and the preceding §. There the text also says: “We say that once they have been made legitimate, they have the same successors as those who were legitimate from the beginning.” Furthermore, some say that those legitimated by marriage succeed to a fief, even though it may seem tacitly established therein that they do not succeed unless legitimated, if there is a dispute concerning the fief, Cap. naturales, according to Jacobus de Belvisio. Others, however, say the contrary, that the original stain always remains in itself. But this is not disputed now. Moreover, because this restoration by marriage would be a very great restoration, and rather it can be called a detection, as noted in a similar case, D. De iustitia et iure, l. manumissiones; but that opinion is not approved there.

On the contrary, it seems: because formerly there was one name, namely, of legitimated persons. Later the contrary name supervened, namely, of illegitimate persons. Thirdly, the benefit of law supervened, namely, of legitimate persons. And thus three kinds of sons began to exist: namely, those legitimately born, and thirdly, those legitimated. Argument from the said l. manumissiones. Moreover, when a certain quality must exist at a certain time, namely, from the origin, it is not sufficient if it supervenes later. Argument from D. De infamia, l. quid ergo. Moreover, the testator considered the dignity of the successors. Argument from D. De contrahenda tutela, l. non tantum, §. si emancipatus filius. Moreover, a legitimated person is not begotten from a legitimate marriage. Hence it is required that he be legitimated from the very birth, which is not the case here, as appeared above from the text, which places these as similar; therefore they are not the same. Moreover, the testator looked to nature, not to accident. D. De legatis 2, l. si ita quis; l. si is cui. It supports what is usually noted, D. Ad Trebellianum, l. ex facto, §. si quis. And this minor premise, namely, that such legitimated persons are not of that kind of sons of whom the testator speaks, and therefore they do not exclude the substitutes, D. De liberis et posthumis, l. commodissime.

Furthermore, the testator expressly named them. Although I did not say above in the hypothesis “natural” in the default of all three instituted heirs, therefore, as long as any natural heir survives, they do not succeed from the origin. This is evident from the text of the writing. For natural heirs are included in only one case; in the contrary case they seem to be excluded. D. De iurisdictione, l. cum praetor. And this is the truth. Nor does the division obstruct: because it contains a certain pact not to claim the fideicommissum, but not to act against the division; nor is it a mention of the will. On this we note fully, D. De verbis obligatorum, l. qui Romae, §. duo fratres; and C. De pactis, l. 1; D. De transactionibus, l. qui cum tutoribus, with similar cases. And the renunciation, which is there, refers to the person by whom the division would be infringed, and refers to the claimant, not to the one who has obtained. D. De verbis obligatorum, l. 1, si a colono; and l. cum stipulamur; D. De transactionibus, l. cum Aquilio; C. De conditionibus, l. si de certa.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a convention or agreement between two lords that neither of them may acquire anything in the land of the other, whether such an exchange is valid if they mutually exchange castles.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† That the exchange made between the nobles George and Hippomphane, Marquises of Ceva, concerning their castles is invalid, seems to be proven by this reasoning: because agreements appended between those who can make statutes among themselves have the force of law. As in C. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. penultima; and ff. de publicanis, l. Caesar. But between the noble Lord William, Marquis, on one part, and Boniface and Odo on the other, an agreement was made that none of them could in any way, by any device or form, acquire anything in the land or jurisdiction of the other, unless this proceeded from the will of both parties. Therefore, the said agreement has the force of law. And if it is certain that the law can prohibit such alienations by operation of law (ipso iure), as in C. non licere habitatoribus Metrochomiae, in rubro et nigro; C. de praediis curialium, l. finalis; ff. de contrahenda emptione, l. si quis sciens; C. de rebus alienis non alienandis, l. viri; since, therefore, none of them could acquire anything in the land or jurisdiction of the other, such a contract of exchange, as contrary to the force and authority of the law, did not hold by operation of law. As in ff. de legatis, l. si quis inquilinos, §. finalis; and C. de agris et censibus, l. quemadmodum, lib. 11; ff. de legatis, l. caetera; and l. apud Iulium, §. finalis; C. de legibus, l. non dubium.

To the contrary is the truth. First, because it is not true that the said agreements have the force of law, but they have only the force of a contract, because they emanated in the form of a contract. And therefore, although the contract ought not to have been made, the contract nevertheless held. As in ff. de verborum obligationibus, l. si ita quis, §. ea lege; and C. de conditionibus ob causam, l. ea lege.

The second reason is: because the said contract of exchange is not contrary to the said ancient agreements; because if the words of the ancient agreements are carefully examined, that clause: that none of them could, does not seem to refer to their heirs, but only to the lords William, Boniface, and Odo themselves. For in the said clause nothing is repeated concerning their heirs. And therefore those words: that none of them, as personal, do not comprehend heirs. As is read and noted in Auth. de restitutione fideicommissorum, §. manifestum.

Thirdly, because even if they did comprehend them, such an exchange proceeded from the will of both parties. And thus we are not in the case prohibited by the agreement, but rather in the permitted one. As in ff. de manumissione testamento, l.
