Titia, §. finalis; and 10. col. per quos fiat investitura et per quos recipiatur, c. 1, §. pe. sed et res; and C. de imponendis lucri desideriis, l. 1, lib. 10, where it must be considered that parties are called those concerning whose dominion the matter is treated. For extrinsically, those who have nothing to do with the dominion are not called partial or co-heirs. As in C. de contrahenda emptione, l. dudum. For as to them, they have free seats, concerning whose right or prejudice the matter is not treated. As in ff. si servitus vindicetur, l. loci corpus, §. competit; and ff. de aqua pluvia arcenda, l. in concludendo.

From which it appears that the said exchange held and must be observed between the exchanging parties; because it is just to keep faith. As in ff. de pactis, l. 1, in principio; and it is grievous to deceive grievous persons regarding faith. As in ff. de constitutionibus pecuniarum, l. 1, in principio; and if faith is not kept, action lies for penalty or interest. As in ff. de actione empti, l. 1, in principio; and l. praedia. Nor does the father excuse himself on the ground that the sons fortified themselves and he did not wish to deliver; because he ought to have provided that this should not come to pass. As in ff. de verborum obligationibus, l. si stipulatio ista; and ff. de locato, l. in lege; and ff. de pactis, l. non impossibile puto. Also, because the difficulty of performance pertains to the inconvenience of the promisor. As in ff. de verborum obligationibus, l. continuus, §. cum quis.

From which I conclude that the aforementioned exchange was valid and must be observed. And supporting the aforementioned is C. de fideicommissis, l. quotiens; and ff. de legibus, l. cum pater, §. libertis. But it is necessary that he who wishes faith to be observed do on his part what he ought. As in ff. de actione emptionis, l. Iulianus, §. offerri. And if it is something movable or money, he must offer it; if not, for example, a fund, or house, or castle, he must offer himself ready and require the other to go to take possession, together with him doing on his part what he ought. As in C. de usuris, l. acceptam; and ff. de solutionibus, l. si soluturus; C. de distractione pignorum, l. si residuum; and ff. de rescindenda venditione, l. fundus qui Lucii Titii erat. And the pledge can be retained in place of the debt, if he who did not fulfill on his part what he ought to fulfill. As in the said §. offerri, in the ordinary gloss.

I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If the seller establishes that he holds the property by permission (precario) in the name of the buyer, yet does not deliver the thing to the buyer for 26 years; then he sells it to another and delivers it, and the latter possesses it for 4 years; now, if the first buyer wishes to claim it from the second, whether he can do so, and who has the stronger right? And whether the exception of prescription bars the first buyer.
2. The buyer, by means of a precarial constitution, immediately becomes the owner and, as it were, the possessor.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The seller constituted himself as holding the sold thing by precarious title in the name of the buyer, although the seller was then in possession. Then he remained in the aforementioned possession for a period of 26 years, the aforementioned buyer being silent and acquiescent. Finally, the said seller sold the said thing to another and delivered it corporally; who possessed it for a period of four years and more, so that in total 30 years elapsed during which the said thing was not claimed.

† Now it is asked whether the said first buyer can claim the said thing from the said second buyer, or not. And it seems that he cannot claim it: because he who remained silent for a period of 30 years loses the real action. As in C. de praescriptione triginta annorum, l. sicut. Moreover, the second buyer seems to have the stronger right: because although he bought second, the thing was first delivered to him. As in C. de rei venditione, l. quot; and noted in ff. de publiciano, l. siue autem, §. si duobus. To the contrary is the truth.

For it must be known that, by the constitution of the precarium, the buyer was immediately made owner and, as it were, possessor, as stated in the Digest, *De aqua pluviae arcendae*, in the law *Cum eo*, in the principal part; and this is fully noted in the Digest, *De pactis*, in the law *Ab emptione*. Hence, ownership and possession were acquired by him, as stated in the Digest, *De precario*, in the law *Et habet*, section *Cum*. Nor did the prescription begin to run against the first buyer until the seller possessed by precarium, as stated in the Code, *De praescriptione triginta annorum*, in the law *Male agitur*. From these authorities it is concluded, and it is true, that the said house can be vindicated by the said first buyer from the second buyer who is in possession. And this is the truth.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a person who has been dispossessed may, by agreement, waive the privilege of restitution.
2. Whether a vassal may be a party in a lawsuit concerning a feudal estate without the consent of his lord.
body: Whether a privilege of a privileged person extends to his spouse. In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It must be premised for clarity that, although the spoliated party is to be restored above all else, considering the order established by law: nevertheless, if the parties agree that the thing should be surrendered and restored through sequestration, the convention to which effect is given by sentence must be observed; because the spoliated party may renounce his privilege, as stated in the Decretals, De restitutione spoliatorum, cap. 1. And this is proven by the reason of the matter: D. De re iudicata, l. Si convenerit; and D. De pactis, l. Iuris gentium, §. Item ne experiar. Since, therefore, in the present case such a pact was made between the parties, this pact must be observed, as stated in D. De dolo, l. Si oleum. Nor can one, after restoration has been made by sentence, be sued on the convention by a new libel, because the exception of res iudicata stands in the way, as stated in D. De arbitris, l. Inter Cassellanum. And this is confirmed by the following reason: once it is established, through legal disputation or by sentence, that the claimant has no right to restitution, the exception of dolus factus may be raised against the plaintiff, because it is clear and deemed proven. This is noted in D. De iudiciis, l. Si idem; and Innocentius notes this in the Decretals, De filiis presbiterorum, cap. Constitutus. Nor can a compromise be sought, since sentence has been passed on the prejudicial question; because such a sentence impedes every proceeding. Therefore, it impedes this petition, which is part of the proceeding, as stated in D. De transactionibus, l. Post rem; and D. De conditione indebiti, l. Eleganter, §. Si post. From which it is clearly concluded that

† that the aforementioned person who appears to have been dispossessed cannot bring a possessory action, nor does it matter that the tenement is feudal: for it was permissible for the feudatory to be in court, to sue, and to succumb, especially in a simple possessory action. As noted by Bartolus in the Extravagantes, De iudiciis, cap. Caeterum. And it is expressly stated in the Decretals, Title 10, Si de feudo controversia fuerit, cap. Si vassallus de suo beneficio. And it is the ordinary gloss in the Decretals, Title 10, De prohibitione feudorum alienationis, per Federicum, cap. 1, § Praeterea, Si de feudo. And this concludes the first point. On the second point, I say,

† Granted that it could be brought to action, nevertheless, when two parties are in court, and one is privileged against the common law, and the other is not: the privilege of the privileged party does not extend to the co-litigant. The same applies if it is a matter of odium, or anything else that deviates from the common law. For example, regarding privilege, if a student and a non-student are sued in the same petition. For he who is not a student should not enjoy the privilege of forum; because a personal privilege does not extend beyond the person, as the rule of law states, and is clearly proven. C. si vnus ex pluribus appellauerit, l. 2, second response. Nor is it new that multiple litigants are judged under different laws, as in ff. de re iudic., l. non idcirco. And therefore I say that the petition would proceed. However, he who is not an affine cannot appeal to arbitration, since that statute is against the common law. And thus, the title concerning matters to be judged by the same judge does not apply here.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a special statute derogates from a special rule, and when.
2. What is contained in the expression "by law" or "according to the laws." See the following opinion, which appears to provide to the contrary.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. In the volume of the statutes of Savignano there is a certain statute, whereby the officials are bound to swear to observe the conventions and pacts made between the Lords of Savoy, on their part, on the one hand, and the Commune of Savignano, on the other; and all the statutes and ordinances of that same Commune, as the letter states: unless they were contrary to the statutes or pacts of the said Lords. Subsequently, there is placed a certain statute, that no woman, after she has been married, may claim anything, or bring or raise any action against any of her brothers or nephews, on account of any succession of her father or mother, or of brotherhood: unless a legacy had been expressly left to her, or given, or promised. Finally, follow the conventions made between the said Lords and the Commune: in which, among other things, it is contained thus: that any person from Savignano shall have the free faculty of making a will, and of disposing as he shall wish of his goods in his last will, and inter vivos. Subsequently follows such a statute, that in the successions of those dying intestate, the law shall be observed, notwithstanding any pact aforesaid or hereinafter mentioned, or any custom whatsoever. Finally, it happened that a certain G. died intestate, with a certain married sister and certain sons of brothers surviving.

† Now it is asked whether the aforementioned sister is excluded from the intestate succession by virtue of that chapter which provides that no woman, after she has been married, may claim anything from her brother or her nephews. And it appears that the aforementioned dowried sister is entirely excluded, because this chapter concerning a dowried daughter is a most special chapter. That other chapter, which provides that in successions of those dying intestate the laws shall be observed, is not so special a chapter. Hence, just as a genus is distinguished by a species, so a species is distinguished by the individuals of the species, as in D. de legibus 3, l. haeres meus, § duae statuae; and as noted in l. quaesitum, § vlt., D. de funerariis instructionibus; and by Dynus in c. generi. And it supports this what Cynus notes in l. 1, C. de adulteriis.

To the contrary it appears, because the power swore to observe the pacts as the letter stands, and the statutes, unless they were contrary to the pacts. But it is certain that, just as whatever derogates from a genus is contrary to the genus, albeit not in its entirety—for it does not derogate by any other reason than by reason of contrariety and incompatibility—so in the present case, if the aforementioned statute, "That no woman, etc.," preceding that chapter, "That in successions of those dying intestate, etc.," derogated from the pact, it would be contrary to the chapters of the pact. And therefore, considering the words of the chapters of the pact, one must adhere to the pact as the letter stands, without any restrictive interpretation. For every restrictive interpretation is contrary to the literal wording, as in D. de servitutibus praediorum rusticorum, l. si servitus.

Moreover, it is true that a lesser species derogates from a greater one when the authority is equal. But here the authority of the pact and the statute is not equal. For a pact is a contract, and by contract one may depart from a statute. Furthermore, a contract of the Prince has two forces, namely the force of law and the force of contract, as in C. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. penultima. Moreover, those words of the pact concerning intestate successions, which state that "the laws shall be observed," are understood to refer to Roman law, as in Inst. de iure naturali, § sed ius, according to Guidus de Suzia and others.

† You, however, for a clearer understanding of this article, state that if these words were used between two private individuals and they were of the same municipality, they could be understood as referring to municipal law; but if they were of different municipalities, they would be understood as referring to the common law, which is common to both contracting parties. Arg. D. de vulgari substitutione, l. iam hoc iure, §. sed si alter. This applies all the more strongly if the words are used between a testator and a substitute: because the statutes of subjects are regulated according to the will of their superiors, by whom they must be confirmed. See C. de testamentis, l. si. Moreover, the common law of Savignano is not the people in their head; hence it cannot make a statute concerning succession or concerning less solemn testamentary dispositions, unless this is obtained by privilege. See D. Comit., C. de testamentis, l. si non speciale. Furthermore, that statute which provides that no woman can be saved [i.e., inherit] when the deceased made a last will, is sufficiently indicated by those words: “unless a legacy had been left to her.” Arg. D. de vino legato, l. nam quod liquide, §. si cui. But where no last will has been made, the chapter of the pact prevails, which appears to have been made between the successors themselves. Arg. D. de legatis, l. sed ea quae. Moreover, this pact has the force of a judicial sentence: because it was made with him who can pronounce the law. See D. de legatis, l. nam Imperator noster. Moreover, the derogatory words effectively support this. For the text of the pact states that rights shall be observed, no custom to the contrary notwithstanding. But a statute and a custom have equal force. And if custom is removed, the statute deduced from custom is also removed. Arg. D. de legatis, l. de quibus, §. finalis. Although, speaking properly, a statute is said to be a law promulgated by written citation, whereas custom arises from unwritten practice. Moreover, it is very unjust that a statute should provide that a sister dowered by her father does not succeed her brother. And therefore, as odious and based on irrational hatred, it is easily set aside even by general words. Arg. l. cum quidam, de rogationibus, especially since, as I said, later provisions are founded on a greater power of the efficient cause. See D. de pactis, l. pacta nouissima, with similar authorities. From which I conclude that the said sister succeeds: because this is the case under the common law, to which things easily return as to their nature. See D. de pactis, l. si unus, §. pactus, vers. quod et in specie dotis. But suppose that from the predeceased brothers there remain several children. It is asked how the said sister succeeds with them. I answer that they succeed per stirpes. Hence the said sister succeeds for one-fourth part, and the children of each brother succeed per stirpes: because all children who descend from one father are considered as one person. See Auth. de haereditatibus quae ab intestato deferuntur, §. consequens. And so I say and advise, I, Balde de Perusio, doctor of both laws, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. This opinion pertains to the question of the preceding opinion.
2. Where a non obstante clause is appended, the disposition of a statute can never be reconciled.
3. How one may enact statutes, and whether all peoples indiscriminately may enact statutes without the authority of a superior.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The contrary opinion was consulted by certain persons, and the opinion begins thus. Assuming, and not calling into doubt, the power of the community and the inhabitants of Sauigliano to enact statutes: and consequently assuming the validity of the statute placed under the heading: that no woman may claim, etc., it must be observed that these persons falsely assume this premise. For it must be premised that the said castle of Sauigliano has no power to enact any statute contrary to the common law, except insofar as it is contained in the aforementioned pacts. For the said castle of Sauigliano is not a free corporation, but is a corporation subject to the Lord Prince of Achaea, and without his authority it can enact nothing contrary to the common law, especially in matters of testate and intestate succession. As stated in C. de testamento, l. fin. and l. si non speciali, cited above in my opinion, and this is observed in all lands throughout the world subject to princes, namely that they do not have more authority or power than the prince wishes. I do not know if this is observed in Savoy or in the Principality of Achaea, which I do not believe. But let us suppose that the castle of Sauigliano was not within the natural jurisdiction of the prince, but was joined or united to him by pacts. No one doubts that the tenor of the pacts must be observed. Now let us see what is the tenor of these pacts. Certainly, the tenor is that every person, etc., shall have the free faculty to make a will. And this is the first chapter. The second chapter is that in intestate successions the laws shall be observed, notwithstanding any pact stipulated in these chapters, nor any custom. Hence it is strange to doubt our question: because the text of this chapter speaks openly of the common law being observed in intestate successions. And where the words are clear, one should not go by circuitous routes, but we must serve the words of the edict. As stated in ff. de exercito, l. 1, §. si is qui navem, and l. ille aut ille, §. cum in verbis, ff. de legibus 3.

And it must be known that where a non obstante clause is inserted, the disposition of a statute can never be reconciled with the obstacle, nor can it be limited by such means. See Digestum, De legibus, Title 3, Law Si quis, in the beginning; Justinian, Codex, De testibus, Authenticum Hoc inter liberos; and Chapter 1, De prebendis, in the Clementines, with its entire common material, and the power of the blind and the deaf. And the minority, as well as other consulting jurists, proceeded through many arguments which are very frivolous and do not contribute to the truth of the question.

Furthermore, it must be observed that the common law is more equitable and more consonant with natural reason than is the excluding statute. Furthermore, it must be observed that what is equally just is found to be more just. See Digestum, De iustitia et iure, Law 1, in the beginning. And in the same way, what is favorable is found among favorable things. Therefore, if we speak, having made a comparison of males to females, the motivating reason of the statute is the favor of families. But if we speak comparatively in relation to the common law and to natural reason, this statute is unjust and injurious, as is the text in Law Maximum vitium. And on the part of males indeed there is favor; but on the contrary part there is odium, as noted in Digestum, De in ius vocando, Law Sed si hac, § Finis; and by Bartolus de Foro competenti, Chapter Si diligenti. And therefore my opinion was the truth itself, and, abbreviating the contrary speech, the [opposing] opinion was very erroneous and founded on frivolous reasons. And I believe that they did not see my opinion; and if they had glanced over it, they did not weigh it according to the words of Bartolus in Law Omnes populi, where these things are to be sought.

† First, who can make statutes. And first, whether every people can do so by itself and without the authority of a superior. And it seems that the authority of a superior is required, as in C. de legibus, l. si quis extraordinaria, lib. x, which is cited in Auth. de defensoribus civitatum, §. et neque. Guillaume touches on this here, but less perfectly. Therefore, say or ask: are you speaking of a people who has no jurisdiction, such as villages and castles which are simply subject to some city or lordship? Or of a people who has all jurisdiction granted by the prince or acquired by prescription, as in Auth. de defensoribus civitatum, §. iusiurandum, in fine, major glossa? Or are you asking about a people who has limited jurisdiction, for example in civil matters, or in minor criminal cases, as is the case with many castles in the March?

In the first case, either such a people wishes to make a statute pertaining to the decision of cases, or to the administration of the people’s own affairs. If it pertains to the decision of cases, then either the authority of the superior people or lord intervenes, and it is valid, as in C. de testamentis, l. si, where the custom of rustics is not to be observed because the prince or the people to whom those rustics were subject approved it. This is supported by extra de consuetudinibus, c. cum accessisset, and C. cum M. speaks thus in the aforementioned l. si quis extraordinaria. Or the authority of the superior does not intervene, and it is not valid, because it lacks jurisdiction. And to make statutes is an act of jurisdiction taken in the general sense, as is clear from the noted definition in de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, l. prima, and cum quid denegatur, etc., as in l. oratio, ff. de sponsalibus.

But if you ask about those matters which pertain to the administration of their own goods and the expenditure of common funds, it can be done, unless the decrees were ambitious, as in de decretis ab ordinariis factis, l. 1, and l. ambitiosa.

In the second case, when the people has all jurisdiction, it can make a statute without awaiting the authority of a superior, as here, and in Inst. eo, §. omnes, de privilegiis creditorum, l. Atheniensium. And that in this case the authority of a superior is not awaited is clear from the example of custom, which is induced by the tacit consent of the people and which is equivalent to a statute, in which it is established that the authority of a superior is not required, as in ff. de legibus, l. de quibus. And that the generality of this law should be understood as referring to a people having jurisdiction is clear from the text of Inst. eo, where it gives examples of the Roman and Athenian people. For by this law and similar ones, license to make statutes seems to be granted. And therefore no other authority is required, although the presidents of provinces in the lands of the church observe otherwise.

In the third case, when it has limited jurisdiction, it can make statutes in those matters in which it has jurisdiction, but not in others, without the authority of a superior, according to what has been said. Thus far Bartolus.

From these things it appears that the said community of Savignano is not among those universitates which can make statutes concerning successions by their own authority; because successions often involve very large sums, the jurisdiction over which is reduced to the likeness of mixed imperium, which does not belong to such municipalities. And in Auth. de defensoribus civitatum, §. iudicare, and noted in l. imperium, ff. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum.

Consider also that chapter to which those words “notwithstanding the chapter” refer. And it does not appear to me that it is anything other than the chapter of the statute which is corrected by these words, as in ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. nam ad ea.

Furthermore, by the same reason by which custom is abolished, a statute is abolished, because both are a kind of agreement of those making the statute, as in ff. de pactis, l. non impossibile.

I think it is good that the lord prince have these opinions reviewed again, both for and against, and that both parties be informed, so that the truth may not perish.

Baldus de Perusio. Innocentius in c. cum omnes, extra de consuetudinibus, says that to make statutes pertaining to the decision of cases is not allowed unless by privilege or by prescription of such a long time that there is no memory of the contrary, which must be proved; nor can they have a magistrate unless confirmed by a superior. Baldus.

In the Name of Christ, Amen. The statute of the city of Pavia provides that there shall be, and ought to be, holidays in ordinary courts, and in those in which proceedings are ordinarily conducted by means of a libel; and also in extraordinary or summary proceedings exceeding the sum of 100 Pavesi pounds: namely, on account of the harvest, from the middle of the month of June up to the calends of August inclusive. Likewise, on account of the vintage, from the 10th day of the month of September up to the octave of St. Michael inclusive: in any cause exceeding the sum of 25 Pavesi pounds, whether it be ordinary or extraordinary.

These matters being thus assumed, it is true in fact that A. on one side and B. on the other mutually compromised with each other, and made a compromise in a certain C. as their arbitrator and adjudicator in law and in fact, and in amicable composition: specifically concerning a certain question and cause pending between the said parties, with the clauses inserted in the said instrument of compromise, appended. And concerning uncertainties, one clause: namely, that the said arbitrator may proceed, cognize, and terminate on holiday days and non-holiday days, on whatever holidays; even those introduced in honor of God and the saints; another clause, namely, that the said parties wished and ordered that the term of the said compromise should last 40 useful days, computed from the day of acceptance.

Now it is found that the aforementioned arbitrator accepted the said compromise on the 18th day of the month of May, and rendered his sentence on the 8th or 7th day of the month of October. On behalf of one of the compromitting parties, it is asserted that the sentence is null, saying that the time of the said 40 useful days has elapsed, asserting that the said holidays introduced on account of the harvests and vintages, with regard to the said compromise and the compromissary himself, ought to be considered as useful days, especially because of that clause appended to the said compromise, that he may grant and terminate on whatever holiday and non-holiday days; since useful days are said to be those whenever access to the judge can be had, as in l. 1, in fine, de diversis temporibus, apud; and because the said arbitrators never refused to proceed in the said holidays.

On behalf, however, of the other of the aforementioned compromitting parties, it is asserted that the said time ought not to be computed as useful, especially because that word "may" is a word of power, not however of necessity. And thus the sentence was rendered within the term, and is valid, unless it appears that the said compromissary proceeded in the said holidays. Now the question is asked: what is the law?

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If a renunciation has been made during the holidays, whether the time of the harvests is said to be useful or continuous, if the power has been given to the arbiter to proceed at a fixed time and at an unfixed time.
2. When the useful time is said to be.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It is asked, if the holidays have been waived, whether the time of the harvests is considered useful or continuous. And it seems that it is useful: because the judge can exercise jurisdiction on these days. As noted in l. 1, ff. de feriis, and ff. de arbitris, l. si feriatis. To the contrary, it seems that it is not useful: because just as the waiver by the parties cannot prejudice witnesses, so that they may still allege their holidays, as noted in the same l. 1, so it ought not to be able to impose a necessity upon the judge. Hence, the judge is not bound to proceed if he does not wish to. And thus it is not useful time. Regarding witnesses, see the gloss in the said l. 1, de feriis. But regarding the judge, no doctor touches upon the matter. I believe the judge cannot allege holidays. And thus the time is useful according to the said l. si feriatis. Because jurisdiction is a power introduced from the public sphere, with the necessity of exercising jurisdiction at a proper place and time. But this is a proper time, since the holidays have been waived for proceeding and deciding the case. Therefore, the statute, which speaks of useful time, applies. If, however, an impediment arises on account of witnesses, because they could not be compelled, this time of impediment would be deducted. As in l. 2, § 1, ff. quando appellatio sit, and l. 1, ff. de diversis et temporibus praescriptionum, as in l. non enim, ff. quibus ex causis maior. And so I say and advise, I, Bal. de Peru., doctor of both laws. And to the truth I have subscribed and signed with the seal of my name. And the same, I, L. de Castellione, Bishop of Vicenza, and to the truth I have subscribed and sealed. And so I say and advise, I, Rapha. Fulg., doctor of both laws. And to the truth of the foregoing I have written and ordered to be sealed, saving the reverence of such great doctors who advise, who say that from the power attributed to the judge or arbitrator to proceed on holiday days, the days are called useful on this ground: because then the judge is bound by the necessity of judging. Who, however, say that this does not apply to witnesses: because they may enjoy the benefit of the holidays. As noted in the gloss in l. 1, ff. de feriis. And they say that no doctor touches upon the judge, that he may allege holidays. They wish to say that if the judge could allege holidays against the will of the parties, that then the days would be holidays: thus it is said regarding a witness. They do not agree well with each other, remembering all the glosses, which is not surprising: because Pope Urban did not have memory of what had been enacted by Pope Leo. 30. q. 3. cap. quod autem. Who, however, Urban ought to have known all laws: because the Pope, cap. 1, de constitutionibus, lib. 6, l. omnes, C. de testamentis. But against the above-mentioned advisors is the ordinary gloss in iudice, and in arbitro, in Clem. saepe, de verborum significatione, in the gloss on the word valeat. Which gloss says at the end that if holidays have been waived in the compromise, the arbitrator is not bound to proceed during the time of the harvest or vintage holidays, alleging the said Speculum. Therefore, against them it is concluded that from the fact that the judge or arbitrator did not proceed, nor could be compelled, that the days are not called useful, but rather holidays. Friend, he who examines poorly, speaks poorly. It seems to you that that gloss determines the question which troubles me: because it speaks of an arbitrator who may be occupied around the harvests and vintages. And the same, in the judge, in whom there would be the same reason, namely, occupation, regarding rural matters. But if there is such a judge who is not occupied regarding rural matters, or cannot be occupied, or ought not to be: then he cannot allege holidays: because the final reason for the allegation of holidays, introduced for the benefit of men, ceases. As noted in c. si, extra de iudicibus, by Ber. and by Io. An. in the apostil, and the same by Host. in the novella. Although therefore the parties cannot bind the judge who has the benefit of these holidays: yet when he does not have the benefit of holidays, he is bound not so much by the pact of the parties as by the disposition of the law.

† Moreover, whether he is bound or not: nevertheless, since he can proceed according to law, the time is useful. As in l. 2. §. dies. ff. quis ordo in bo. poss. seruetur. But it is certain that he can proceed if he wishes. As noted in Spe. de arbi. §. fi. circa fi. versi. sed nunquid. Therefore, he will be held responsible. Furthermore, the party should have approached the judge himself and inquired whether he wished to proceed or not; if he did not do so, let him blame himself. As in ff. quibus ex caus. maio. l. sed et si prpraetorem. §. 2. and extra de elec. ca. eis quibus. And these matters are as clear in law as the midday sun. And therefore, you, who advised the contrary, should have weighed the matter more carefully. And if it were another, I would believe that he would have acted more prudently by not speaking thus, with all due respect to you, who are most ignorant, and thus you criticize others for their ignorance. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. In which cases an election may be said to be void.
2. A person may come against his own act when it is void by the law itself.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

It seems that it should be said that the said election was null by operation of law. First, regarding the defect of age of the elected person: because he was under 25 years of age, and according to the truth of the matter, he was so far removed that he could not be promoted to the priesthood within a year, as stated in Extra, De electionibus, chapter Cum in cunctis, § Cum inferiora; and De praebendis, chapter Si pro cleri, and what is noted there, Book 6. And thus there is a defect of age and order, not only in act but also in potentiality, as stated in Extra, De electionibus, chapter Dudum, and the gloss. And no mention should have been made of the possession of the elected person: because it was an abusive possession, and rather an intrusion, according to what is alleged; and especially since there was a clause, "any unlawful detainer being removed," as noted in chapter Cum nostris, De concessionibus praebendarum. Nor does it matter that the petitioner was one of the electors, for an election null by operation of law does not prejudice itself, as noted in chapter Auditis, De electionibus.

For one may come against his own act, which is null by the law itself, according to the rules of both laws. Nor is this one of the cases in which the elector is suspended by canon: for that seems to speak only of those electing a bishop or a superior to the penalty of three years’ suspension. But if he were suspended, it is certain that the petition regarding age and quality would not be valid, as seen in *Cum bonae*, *De clericis excommunicatis*; *Administrante*, *De consuetudine*; *Cum dilecti*, *De appellationibus*; *Pastoralis*.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an administrator appointed in a testament may receive homage.
2. A guardian has the fullness of power.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† From these points it is also concluded that she may receive homages as an administrator, as described in the will: there, where it is said, homages, superiorities, reverences, fiefs, etc. Nor is it novel that administrators exercise such rights, as in cap. 1, after the principal, Qui feuda dare possunt, col. 10, and in the said cap. 2, De feudis, and it is clear in cap. Grandi, De supplendis negligentia praeparatorum, lib. 6. Hence an interpretation of the words of the aforementioned will may also be derived. Moreover, the said lady called herself in her letters lady, and full administrator, and executrix. I omit not one thing, of which I have newly been informed, that the said lady was the surviving guardian of her nephew in the will of her son.

And therefore there is no doubt that she has, as guardian, the fullness of the guardian’s power. For we say that a guardian has the fullness of power, as is read and noted in the Digest, De appellationibus, l. Cum in una, §. Tutor, provided that he administers well, as in the Digest, De usucapione pro herede, l. Si fundum, §. Si tutor. Moreover, the lord Count, the testator, considering and attending to the pleasing, fruitful, and laudable services faithfully rendered and bestowed upon him by his illustrious and most beloved consort, Lady Bonne of Bourbon, and by which he has hitherto been humanly delighted, made, willed, ordained, named, and disposed that the same Lady Bonne be true lady, administrator, and usufructuary in the County of Savoy, the Duchy of Chablais and of Aosta, and in the Marquisate in Italy, and the Principality, and in all and every city, village, castle, town, place, person, homage, superiority, and reverence, fief, sub-fief, jurisdiction, mere and mixed empire, jurisdiction, all kinds of revenues, fictions, servitudes, censuses, possessions, properties, dominions, and dignities of the aforesaid, and of all and each of the lands, places, castles, villages, boroughs, cities, and towns, and communities of Savoy, Duchy, Principality, Marquisate, pertaining in any way, whether beyond or beyond the mountains, situated in any manner whatsoever; so that she may use and ought to use all and each of these. And all his faithful subjects ought and are bound to obey her fully and perfectly, provided that she lives in humanity and abstains from other marriages.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a donor, having first given certain things to one person, can afterwards give all his property to another, and whether the second donation is valid; and whether a donor, having given all his property inter vivos while reserving for himself the usufruct during his lifetime, can revoke said donation.
2. Likewise, whether he can make a will, and whether by making a will he appears to revoke the donation.
3. Add also consilium 270 in part 3.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A certain woman first made a particular donation of certain things; secondly, she made a universal donation of all her present and future goods to a certain Albert, irrevocably and inter vivos, with the condition added that she might use and enjoy the said donated things during her lifetime, and that after the death of the said donor, the said donee should be bound to distribute half of the said goods for the soul of the said testatrix and of her predecessors who had died before her. Finally, the said donor, coming to death, made a will, in which she instituted another heir. Here, first it is asked whether the said donation was valid. Secondly, whether it could be revoked. Thirdly, whether it appears to have been revoked by the will subsequently made. And there are some who say,

† Those who say that this donation is invalid, because it impedes the free disposition by will, due to the addition of future things, as the noted doctors after the glossa in l. si, C. de pactis, argue from ff. pro socio, l. cum duobus, § idem respondit. Others say that it is valid, if he reserved something for himself: for example, the usufruct. For he can make a will regarding the fruits again perceived and reserved for himself. And this is established by the aforementioned l. si. But this will become clearer from the following question.

† . s. whether this woman can make a will regarding the half destined for the poor. And it seems that she can: because that is a taking causa mortis, in which, just as in a donation causa mortis, repentance has a place. Moreover, this mandate can be revoked, as if given to an executor. D. de legatis 2, l. cum pater; §. Titio, D. de donatione causa mortis; l. senatus; and l. non omnis, D. si certum petatur. And to this effect is what we know through Bartolus, D. de verbis obligatorum, l. qui Romae; §. Flavius hermes, D. de servo exportando, l. 3. And I believe this to be true. As for the third point, the form of the words of the testament must be examined, whether they are revocatory or not. In doubt, it is not understood to be revoked by the testament: because it depends on a contract. arg. D. de inofficioso testamento, l. 2; D. de probationibus, l. cum tacit; and l. quinquaginta. If, however, unless the testament were revoked, it would be in vain. It is understood that he revoked the final cause of giving: therefore also the donation itself. D. de conditione ob causam, l. cum quis; and l. si pecuniam, §. si servum. And thus I say, and I counsel, I, Baldus of Perugia, jurist.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a statute prohibiting an official from taking anything for himself or through another applies to a counselor; and see consilium 190 and part 2.
2. In part 2.
3. A counselor of the Prince is called an official. And number 4.
4. Counselors of the Prince today succeed in the place of decurions.
5. Who is called an official.
6. Officials may not receive anything except food and drink.
7. It is permissible to argue from the words of the rubric.
8. How a donation is presumed.
9. Truth is said to be that which appears from the records.
10. The word "or" stands between different things; and what is its nature.
11. The penalty is applied to the treasury, and not to the party, where the law has introduced something as a penalty.
casus:
CASE. In the name of Christ, amen. The case of the present question: as it can effectively be gathered from the records, is as follows, simply narrating the substantial facts, without any other repetition of words: namely, that in the year of our Lord 1352, in the cause of avenging the death of certain citizens of Genoa, perpetrated by the Cypriots in the place of Famagusta on the island of Cyprus, there was elected Admiral, or general captain, by the commune of Genoa, Lord Peter de Campo Fulgosio: to whom Admiral, before being given by the said commune, were given and elected certain counselors: among whom it is asserted that Lord Damianus Catanen, expert in law, was one; and to the same Admiral was given full power and bailiwick with mere and mixed empire, as appears in a certain ducal document written by the hand of Aldebrandus de Cor., 1352, on the 5th day of June. There was also elected Admiral, general syndic of the said commune, with full mandate: as appears from a public instrument drawn up thereon, written by the hand of Raphael de Guasco, notary. Who, the said Lord Damianus, was afterwards elected captain of certain galleys, with two of the counselors of the Lord Admiral, with his associates, then going to the said island of Cyprus, and to remain in the said office of Captain until the arrival of the said Lord Admiral: as appears in a certain ducal letter, written by the hand of the said Raphael, Chancellor of the said commune of Genoa.

After this it appears that the said Lord Admiral arrived with a very great army of Genoa, transmitted to the island of Cyprus, for the purpose of compelling vengeance against the Cypriots, enemies of the said commune of Genoa. And finally the said Lord Admiral, with his hostile power, entered the said city of Famagusta, and subjected the said island of Cyprus, under certain pacts and conventions. And there, with his counselors and patrons of his armed force, he stayed for a certain time, exercising his office: as appears from the records. Finally it appears that when the patrons of the said galleys wished to be cautious, and to provide for themselves regarding certain pacts and conventions made between the illustrious Lord King of Cyprus on one part: and the said Lords Admiral and the aforesaid patrons on the other: so that wise counsel might be had on the aforesaid matters, especially concerning the manner of drawing up instruments, they had recourse to the said Lord Damianus, that he might give them legal counsel in the aforesaid matters. Who, the said Lord Damianus: as appears from the attestations produced by him, in the affairs of the said patrons, endured great labors in imparting legal counsel. Whereupon, wishing the said patrons to remunerate the said labor, they deliberated that each patron ought to give to the said Lord Damianus eight hundred bezants. And so it was done by certain patrons, up to the quantity of six thousand four hundred bezants. Which aforesaid bezants the said Lord Damianus gave and restored to the said patrons, from whom he had received them: as appears in a certain document of the said account, written by the hand of Vincentius Gallus, notary. It also appears, both from the aforesaid document and from two other documents transmitted together, that the said Lord Damianus, by reason of the kingdom of Cyprus, and by the will of the King, received from certain massars in effect eight thousand bezants. Which came into the possession of the said Lord by the will of the King: as is gathered from the narration of the fact, and also from the said documents: although I am not well experienced in the account books of merchants. It also appears that by the said commune of Genoa certain officials were elected and constituted to view the calculation, and to examine any debtors of the said commune, or those who appear to owe to the said commune from the said bailiwick transmitted, as appears from a public instrument, written by the hand of Petrus de Bargalio, notary.

Now it happens that the said Lord Damianus is being molested and disturbed by the said officials regarding the said eight thousand bezants received by him with the will of the King, from the royal treasury: the said officials saying that the said Lord Damianus could not have received the said bezants, and that they are to be given and restored to the said commune. And this especially by virtue of a certain rule of their statute prevailing in the said city of Genoa, placed under the heading: that no official or rector may receive a reward or gift. On the other hand, it is responded by the said Lord Damianus that he is not bound to make any restitution of the aforesaid eight thousand bezants, from the premises thus succinctly gathered from the records transmitted, effectively collected otherwise in the fact. It is asked, what is the law.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Always reserving the sounder opinion, upon the doubt of the aforementioned question, I say and advise

† It is stated that Lord Damian could not have received the said eight thousand bezants from the royal treasury, as is presupposed, and that the said sum of money must be restored to the said Commune of Genoa, notwithstanding the said rule or statute of the said Commune placed under the heading "That rectors or officials may not accept rewards or gifts," which claims to apply to the aforementioned question. And in this lies the case of the above-mentioned doubt, which is proven by the reasons set forth below. First, because the words of the law and its disposition apply where they have their place. L. si vero, § de viro, D. de solutione matrimonii; L. 1, § is qui navem, D. de exercitoris actione. But the words of the said rule or statute claim to apply to the question at hand, as is proven. Therefore, etc. The minor premise is proven thus: For the said rule provides that no official or rector of any territory or place, during the term of his office, may accept for himself or through an interposed person any gift, reward, present, or favor, etc. But the said Lord Damian, being a counselor of the said Admiral and in the said place of Cyprus, and consequently was an official of the said Commune of Genoa in the said place at that time, as is proven there. Therefore, since the rule speaks of an official, it applies to the case in question.

† and that, since he had been a counselor, he was called and said to have been an official at the aforementioned time. This is proved first by the text in l. consiliarii, and what is noted there, de assessmentibus et domibus, and by l. Titium et Mevium, ff. de administratione tutorum, and l. consilio, de cura furiosi, and it is commonly noted by the doctors in l. j., § si plures, ff. de exercendo, in which it is proved that a counselor is an official and a prince of the office.

Secondly, because today councilors succeed in the place of decurions, as noted in C. de decurionibus, book 10, on the rubric, and in D. de donationibus, l. si ex dolo, and there the gloss notes, and it is noted in l. nulli, D. quod cuiusque universitatis, but there is no doubt that the decurionate is a public office, as C. de decurionibus, l. ne quis, book 11, and throughout the title in C. and D., therefore, etc. Thirdly, to the same effect, it is proven that a councilor is called an official.

For when someone, acting as a counselor, receives a fixed salary and also expenses from the public treasury, even if he does not have them by right, he may be called an official. L. Nemo, §. Sin autem, and L. Qui necessario, C. de posthum. The text supports this when it speaks of notaries, C. de decur., L. Universos, lib. 10, and of what is said about legates or ambassadors, who, however, are officials, as in L. Non alias, §. Legati, ff. de iudicibus. But from the facts stated, it appears that the said Lord Damianus, because as a counselor he received expenses from the public treasury and a certain sum of money for clothing, was clearly an official, especially since the acts and deeds done in the name of the public community of Genoa appear to have been carried out by the Admiral with his counselors.

Secondly, principally to the same effect, it is thus: For it is a matter of law that an official may not accept anything other than food and drink, as stated in the law *Plebiscito*, Digest, *De officio praetoris*, and in the Authenticum *Ut iudices sine quoquo suffragio*, § *Cognitio*, column 2, cited in favor of the common good. But since the quantity received by the said office exceeded food and drink, therefore, etc. Thirdly, it is proven from the intent of the common law and the said municipal law, which forbid and prohibit an official from accepting a reward, gift, or present; for he who administers the office through gold, etc., as our Emperor notably states in the present case in the said Authenticum *Ut iudices sine quoquo suffragio*, § *Considerauimus*. And the mention of the said statute and the law *Habet locum* applies even to a counselor, lest the perversion of counsel bring about an evil outcome, as in Decretum 1, question 1, chapter *Principatus*, and the law *Ex diuerso*, § 1, Digest, *De rei venditione*. This intent, both of the common law and the municipal law, ought to be observed no less than the words, as in the law 2, Digest, *De constitutionibus principum*, and the law *Sin*, Code, *Quae res pignori obligari possunt*. I do not care to set forth other reasons for this side, because I reserve them for the solutions of the reasons advanced on behalf of the said Lord Damia. Now it remains to respond to the objections made to the contrary, in favor of the said Lord Damia. And first, his first reason does not stand: when it is said that the said rule or statute speaks of officials or rectors of some land or place, but he was not an official or rector of any land or place, therefore, etc. To which it is responded first that it is not true that the said Lord Damia was not an official of the land or place. For since he was a counselor and official in the army sent to the island of Cyprus, he is said to have been an official of the said land and place; for wherever the army is, the president is, there the lord has territory, for there he terrors; and territory is said from *terrendo* (to terrorize), as in the law *Si pupilli*, § *Territorium*, Digest, *De verborum significatione*, and there the note makes what is noted in the law *Extra territorium*, Digest, *De iurisdictione omnium iudicum*. Secondly, granted that the said Lord Damia was an official of some land or place, as is asserted: nevertheless, the words of the said rule or statute and its disposition still claim their place; for in the rubric and in the title of the said rule it is said simply of a rector or official without the addition of the words "land" or "place." According to which, the rubric we must understand, the black [text] is in more than black; we understand the black according to the rubric, as noted by the gloss in the law 1, Code, *Ne fideiussor demittatur*, and the law *Ita*, Digest, *De rerum amotione*.

† And it is permissible to argue from the words of the heading, as noted by the doctors in l. 1, ff. cert. pet. From which it appears, from the disposition of the said rule joining the rubric with the black text, that it speaks not only of an official or rector of some territory or place, but also of a simple official. Thirdly, in response to the same point, it is said that the words "territory" or "place" determine the word "rector" and not the word "official." This is proven because a quality attached to a word always determines the word to which it is immediately appended, and not the one to which it is not immediately attached, as in l. si idem cum eodem, §. fin., ff. de iuris omnium iudicum; and in the gloss. Furthermore, because words appended at the end are always referred to the nearest terms, especially where there is a stronger reason for referring them to the nearest, as noted in the said gloss and in l. 1, C. de lib. praet. and l. si propter, ff. eod. tit., as is the case in the present instance. For the nature of a rector is to have a territory or place, and he cannot exist without it, as noted in C. de recto. prov. throughout, and in l. extra territorium, ff. de iur. omn. iud., and in l. 1, §. cum urbem, ff. de iur. omn. iudic. But an official can exist without territory and jurisdiction, as was demonstrated in the first reason given by the commune. Therefore, etc. Secondly, the second objection does not hold, when it is said that the said rule speaks of officials of the territory of the district of Genoa, etc. For it is responded that what is alleged is not true, because the said rule, especially at its beginning, speaks generally of every rector or official of the said commune, without referring to the officials of the district; these words, being general, are to be understood generally, l. 1, §. generaliter, ff. de leg. praest. To the third reason, when it is said by the said Doctor Damian that the said rule speaks when an official receives something by reason of his office, but he asserts that he received it as a private person by reason of his article and expertise, therefore, etc. It is responded that, since it is presupposed from the transmitted acts that the said bisani were received from the king and by royal reason, of which no patronage is shown to have been provided, although patronage expended by the patrons is proven as a precaution against the king, it follows that he ought to have received from the king himself, by reason of his expertise, or no reward by right of dominion. And consequently, since he had the said peace from the king

† Since no cause appears from the transmitted records, the cause of the donation is presumed, as in *l. Campanus*, D. de operis libertatis; *l. Hoc iure*, D. de donationibus; and as noted by Dynus and Jacobus de Arena in *l. 2*, § *Circa*, D. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem. And if it is a donation, then it is contrary to the rule. The aforementioned notes in *l. Qui proprio*, § *Procurator*, in certis actionibus, and what is noted there, D. de procuratoribus, do not stand in the way, because, according to the distinction of Dynus in *l. Si vero*, § *Item quicquid*, D. de solutione matrimonii, in case of doubt, a donation is presumed to have been made in consideration of the office of his city, unless it otherwise appeared that the said Damian had previously known this. Whether this was so, I leave to the discretion of those who ought to judge, as it is unknown to me. And although the aforementioned matters would not claim a place in an ambassador, etc., under the common law, nevertheless the said statute, or rule alleged for the common good, removes the contrary, as is clear from what has been said above. To the fifth reason, when it is said that he received the said money by the will of the admiral, etc., it is answered that this does not appear from the records, with all due respect, as alleged.

† This is the truth which appears from the records. L. illicitas, § veritas, D. de officio praesidis. Assuming that it is established, it is said that although the said admiral has ample power and bailiwick, he nevertheless could not abrogate and revoke the statutes and ordinances of the city. L. bonorum and L. ne procul, D. de iure fisci. Thus we have the opinion of that same Modus, Bartolus de Saxoferrato in L. ambitiosa decreta, D. de decretis ab ordinariis facienda, although that statement was first that of Odoricus and the ancient doctors. To the fifth reason, when it is said that the said statute speaks of salaried officials, etc., it is answered that it is not true that it speaks first of salaried officials, because this does not appear from the tenor of the said rule, and especially in the beginning, if its words are carefully weighed. Secondly, that the said statute does not speak only of officials having jurisdiction, but also of those not having it, is proved there, when it is said that no official,

† or the rector, etc., because the word "or" should stand between different things. L. Ille aut ille, D. de legibus 3; and L. Si haeredes plures, D. de conditionibus institutis. But if the word "official" were understood as referring to an official having jurisdiction, it would be rendered superfluous by the word "rector," which follows, denoting jurisdiction, etc. Moreover, when the disjunctive word "or" is placed between a genus and a species, it is resolved into the copulative word "and," as noted in L. Quintus Mutius, § Plane, D. de auro et argento legato, and there noted. But the word "and," which is placed between different things and determines them differently, as in L. Non, D. de iure et facto ignorato, supra rubricam; L. Fin., C. per quas personas nobis acquiritur. For there is no doubt that the word "official" is a genus, and the word "rector" is a species. For every rector is an official, but not conversely. Therefore, some officials have jurisdiction, others do not. It follows that the said rule speaks generally of all officials, both those having and those not having jurisdiction; and thus it should be understood generally of all officials. L. De pretio, D. de publicanis. To the sixth and last reason, when it is said that, assuming the said rule offended the said Lord Damian, it nevertheless concerns not the common good, because what is received must be restored to the giver, as appears from the word "restore," etc., it is answered, etc., that, with due respect, it cannot be said in the present case, because from the form of the said rule, all things accepted contrary to the form of the said rule must be claimed for the public benefit, as appears there, when it is said: "provided, however," etc.

Secondly, to the same effect, thus: Wherever the law introduces something as a penalty, in case of doubt the penalty is applied to the fisc, and not to the party. As noted in *l. agraria*, D. de terminando; and *l. in lege*, D. ad Sillanum; and there, Dynus notes. But in the case proposed, the rule imposes a penalty on the taker, and that what was received contrary to its form be restored. Therefore, etc. Notwithstanding these reasons, as has been demonstrated above: it is concluded that in law it must be said, as has been advised above, etc. And so I say, and I advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Laws and Canon.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A deposit made under a condition must be returned to the depositor if the condition is not fulfilled by the person in whose favor the deposit was made.
2. What the term "subsequently" signifies.
3. Matters stated in earlier provisions are deemed to be repeated in later ones.
4. A right cannot be acquired for another person through an illicit contract, even if sworn.
5. The period of lordship is consumed by the passage of time: neither does the cure of delay apply, nor does ratification reconcile.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Having set aside the other allegations, I proceed to the following chapter of the said contract, which begins there: "Furthermore, that in the case... up to... Furthermore, that when." And I presuppose that it happened that the ambassadors of the King of France departed from Genoa in discord, as is contained in the chapter. Furthermore, I presuppose that the said Lord Antonius declares that he wishes to depart, as is contained in the chapter; nevertheless, he does not depart. And in the said Duchy, another is not appointed from among the four named, nor is it likely that one will be appointed, nor the contrary. The question is asked: what is the law? The words state: if it should happen that the ambassadors depart in discord, and subsequently it should happen that Lord A. departs from the lordship and abandons it, and B is placed in his stead, that the said Lord A., departing from the lordship, ought to receive 50,000 florins from a certain deposit. Now, by the first departure of the ambassadors, the condition has been fulfilled; by the second, it has not yet been fulfilled. Indeed, he is in possession of the lordship, just as before, having notified the citizens of his intention.
† It is asked whether the said deposit ought to be returned to the depositor. And it must be said that it should: because it is not true that he subsequently withdrew from the lordship.

For the subsequent wording has the immediate or continuous meaning. Cf. D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Haec conditio si in Capitolium. For he who retains possession is not presumed to have the intention of abandoning it, but of continuing it. C. de probationibus, l. Siue possidetis; D. quibus modis pignus vel hypotheca solvatur, l. Sicut, §. Superuacuum. Thus, therefore, four things are necessary: namely, to cede or withdraw, to be subrogated, and to give notice; this last I do not believe to be necessary, because perhaps he could not do so without danger to his life. Nevertheless, it is necessary that something be done in some manner, so that it may be valid in law. As noted in D. de legatis 1, l. Huiusmodi, in principio; and D. de verbis oblig., l. Quidam cum filium; and that these things be done within a short time. As in D. de verbis oblig., l. Si ita quis, §. Ea lege; X. de electione, c. Dudum, §. Eis quibus. Moreover, this pact is not lawful, but rather is punished by the Lex Iulia de repetundis, l. Eadem lege, §. Lege Iulia, where the glossa says: he who receives money in order to arrange matters in council is liable under this law. And in this case, the malicious act is proven by the instrument; and for a shameful gain there is no action. As in D. de fideiussoribus, l. Si a reo, §. Id quod vulgo; D. familiae erciscundae, l. Cedere; D. pro socio, l. Nec quicquam. From which, concluding from the first to the last, it is clear that the said deposit, as having been made without cause, ought to be restored to the depositor, to whom the exception of alleged turpitude does not avail; because it does not avail the owner of the thing, to whom the vindication belongs. But the deposit remains in the ownership and possession of the depositor. Hence, considering that he is the possessor thereof, the condition of the possessor is stronger. As in D. communia omnium, l. Ita ut si fur; and as noted in l. Nam et si fur, D. si certum petatur. And this conclusion is most certain and true, and it supports D. de negotiorum gestione, l. Qui sine usuris, where it says: "They must certainly render full good faith, and abstain from profit." And on this account the glossa elsewhere attacks the prefect of the district. It is also certainly to be considered in this second aspect of the deposit, that on account of the continuity of the contracts, the same final motive is understood to exist; because those things which are ordered to an end are regulated according to the nature of the end. As in D. de sponsalibus, l. Oratio. And therefore this second aspect is tainted and injured by the first.

† [It is sufficient to state it] once, because what is said in the earlier parts is deemed to be continued in the later ones. See D. de verb. oblig. l. tria, § idem respondit; D. de probat. l. cum tacitum; D. de pactis l. item quia, § idem Iulianus; and Extr. de appellat. c. Secundo requiris. And therefore, since the dishonesty of him who wishes to profit from the deposit by a detestable gain is apparent, and thus the exception of fraud permanently stands in his way, the deposit ought rightly to be restored to the depositors, for the reasons and causes expressed above.

† For a right cannot be acquired for another from a contract that is informed by illicit agreements, even if an oath had been interposed. As is stated in the Decretals, *de foro competenti*, chapter *Si diligenti*, § *ult.*; in the Code, *de legibus et constitutionibus*, law *Non dubium*; in the Code, *de agris et censibus*, law *Quemadmodum*, book 11; in the Digest, *de legibus* 1, law *Si quis inquilinos*, § *ult.* It is also to be known,

† That in this point of law, in which the time of the term is consumed by the lapse of time, as that very notable decretal states, Extra, De iudiciis, cap. Si, the purification of delay has no place. Likewise, ratification after the term has expired does not reconcile. As L. Si, § Si, ff. De re iudicata. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, and others.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether and when documentary evidence proves.
2. When contradictory proofs are adduced, which of them prevails.
3. Many presumptions have the force of a single witness.
4. If someone pays another person money belonging to a third party, that money may be recovered by the true owner.
1. A confession made in the absence of the opposing party does not prove.
2. A witness who gives false testimony on one point is false in all respects.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

There are three cases: either a person confesses in an *apodissa* (written acknowledgment) that he is the debtor of a present person, or of an absent person; or it is doubtful whether one party was present or absent. In the first case, the *apodissa* proves the debt, if it appears that it was written by his hand and contains the cause (reason for the debt); but if it is indeterminate (lacking the cause), it does not prove. D. de probat. l. Cum indebito §. Si. In the second case, just as an indeterminate *apodissa* does not prove, so neither is it presumed for it. D. de donat. l. Nuda ratio. But if it is determinate, i.e., contains the cause, then either it was sent by a messenger, and it proves. L. Publia in fine, D. de positis. Likewise, if it was delivered to the procurator of the absent party. D. de verb. oblig. l. Si stipulatus §. Grisogonus. Or the *apodissa* was not transmitted: then either it is found with the creditor, and it is presumed to have been transmitted, and it proves. Arg. C. de pact. convent. l. Pe cum glossa, and D. de procurat. l. Chirographum. Or it is found with the debtor: and then some opinions say that it does not prove. Arg. D. de confess. l. Certum §. Si quis, unless it is for the purpose of releasing, D. de liberat. l. Non solum §. Si liberationis. And for this side, that it is not valid, it is made by what we know, D. de act. et oblig. l. Consensu, and C. de sacrosanct. eccles. l. Illud, D. de act. empt. l. 1 in fine, C. de donat. l. Nec ambigitur. Others say that it is valid, even if made in the absence of the adversary. C. de conveniend. fisci debito l. Si, and Azo in Summa de fide instrumentorum. But against these it is argued: because a testament in writing is in this confession a certain *apodissa* of the testator, and yet it does not prove. D. de legat. liberat. l. Aurelius §. Ul., unless it is said otherwise in the testament: because it is made with the intention of testating, not with the intention of proving and binding the testator himself. On this, by Cynus, C. de non numerat. pecun. l. Generaliter. In doubt, it is presumed that he who produces the *apodissa*, not to say the letter, was present. C. de contrah. stipul. l. 1. Let us therefore examine in our case the form and cause of action, and whether the proof itself suffices or accords with the libel. Speusatus says that it is not sufficient for him who asserts the truth to prove the confession. In Spec. de testib. §. 1, ver. Sed pone egi contra te ad decem. But I say that sometimes a confession cannot operate anything other than mere proof: and then it suffices. D. de deposit. l. Publia in fine. Sometimes it can operate an obligation of letters: and then, because it concludes in an action not intended, it does not prove. Thus Speusatus speaks. And if the exception of non-payment of money is opposed: but if it is not opposed, it proves: as said §. Grisogonus, D. si cert. pet. l. Lecta, D. de institut. l. Si, D. de donat. inter vir. et ux. l. Ea quae. Let us therefore come to our case: here the payment is alleged, proved because the *apodissa* is produced. On the contrary, the payment is denied, proved indirectly by the confessed *apodissa*, with an attached contradiction, because he confesses the *apodissa* as to the writing: and thus on the surface. But the cause and the obligation are denied: and thus it is denied in the marrow and strength.

It must therefore be considered which proofs prevail. For when two contrary proofs are brought forward, the stronger prevails; but if they are equal, the defendant prevails. As to whether faith is to be given, you, the judge, can know. D. de testibus, l. 3, § tu magis; and l. ob carmen, § si. For the mind of judging is formed from conjectures. And if on one side there are three witnesses without conjecture, and on the other two, with many very close conjectures, the three do not prevail over the two.

† because many good presumptions have the force of a single witness. D. de excus. tutor. l. 2, § 1. But, all other things being equal, the greater number prevails: because that which is more usually wins. Not. in Spec. de testib. § postquam, v. si. Let us therefore bring forward negative proofs with their coherent indicia, and weaken affirmative proofs, if reason permits. For a negative sometimes weakens an affirmative. L. optimam, in fin. C. de contrah. et committ. stipul. And sometimes it does not weaken, but is weakened by the affirmative. De caus. poss. c. cum ecclesia. And Not. D. de acq. vel amitt. poss. l. diem, § si plures. And in C. l. 1, de praescript. lib. 6. And l. 1, de vend. insp. per Oldradum. And de itin. et actu privato, l. 1, § 1. And per Cynum in l. 2, C. de errore advoc. And when proofs are contrary, so that they cannot be aided by any other distinction, in case of doubt the greater number is upheld: as fully noted in Spec. de testib. § postquam, in fin. Unless they do not testify probable matters. De testib. l. ob carmen, § si testes. And here I do not extend myself, except as I shall say below. But I consider this negative differently.

It must be known, however, that if anyone counts out another’s money, that money may be restored by the recipient to the true owner of the money, as is fully noted in *l. nam et si fur*, D. *si certum petatur*; and in *l. bona fides*, D. *de deposito*; and by argument from D. *de exceptione doli*, § *si opera*. Since, therefore, it is proved here that the lady confessed that the money was not hers, but that of the said Hugolino — a confession which constitutes proof, D. *de deposito*, *l. publicus* in fine; and § *Grisogonus* — it follows that Hugo, as owner, could have the said money restored to him. That it was indeed restored appears from the instrument of refutation of Hugolino. Therefore, even if it is conceded that the lady has proved the counting out of another’s money, which could thus be returned to the owner, it is not an obstacle that he who denies the counting out is, upon being convicted, compelled to make payment, as in *Auth. contra qui propriam*; for this is true only if the instrument asserts the counting out; otherwise, if it asserts merely a confession, as is noted there. And so it is here, because this chirograph does not attest to the counting out. Rather, it makes me doubt more,

† because this confession was made in Hugo’s absence. Therefore, it does not benefit him, nor does it prove that ownership pertains to him. L. certum, § si quis absente; as is fully noted in L. 1, de interdictis et actionibus, and Codex, de iudiciis et fideiussoribus ignorantibus, L. cum falsa.

† Moreover, because the witnesses who assert this also assert another thing, namely that the lady did not pay the sum, and if they lie in one respect, they ought not to be believed in any respect, as noted in *l. si ex falsis*, C. de transactionibus. Certainly, the entire article is based on confession; and therefore this last point does not obstruct. However, the preceding point regarding absence does not appear to obstruct, unless it is said that Vannolus himself, in whose interest it lies and in whose favor this confession is valid, was present. Conscience dictates that this Vannolus holds the truth; for it is not probable that Hugolinus would have disputed money not his own, nor that this lady would have remained silent during Hugo’s life if she had the truth on her side. Argument: ff. de probationibus, *l. procurator*. And because women also are not accustomed to conducting business, nor to carrying such a heavy purse, and this concurrence, together with other proven facts joined with many others, favors Vannolus: who moreover would not have been so foolish as to throw away his own money by paying it, or to waive that which was owed to him. These are more persuasive than necessary arguments. And therefore recourse must be had to the motion of the judge, so that he may estimate how much faith is to be accorded to the witnesses, and according to the rectitude of his own mind, pronounce sentence. As stated in *l. 3*, § *tu magis*, de testibus. For affirmation and negation cannot simultaneously be true. Hence it must be that some witnesses are truthful, others lying. It also helps that in obscure cases judgment should be for the defendant, *l. in obscuris*, ff. de regulis iuris. For great obscurity is the contradiction of witnesses, as noted in *c. in obscuris*, per Dy. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The confession of a husband made in a will in the presence of his wife, on account of the dowry, is valid and gives rise to proof. nu. 2.
2. Whether a woman who marries within a year, having children left by her first husband, loses what was bequeathed to her in her husband's will.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† A husband’s confession made in a will, with his wife present, on account of the dowry, is valid and gives rise to proof. It is valid by reason of the cause, and gives rise to proof by reason of the wife’s presence: according to the noted opinion of Cynus, C. de non numerata pecunia, l. generaliter; and de legatis 3, l. cum quis decedens, § codicillis, and § Titia. And if it is not valid for proving the cause of the dowry, it is nevertheless valid as a last will for disposing of property: as in l. Lucius, § quisquis, de legatis 3; and l. Aurelius, § si, de liberis et posthumis legatis. And thus, with respect to the said 300 livres, it was valid, either by virtue of the confession or as a last will. However, in the case at hand, it is presupposed that

† That this woman entered into a second marriage, but on this account she does not lose the dowry, but rather she loses the legacy entirely according to civil law: because she married within the year of mourning: as in l. j. C. de secundis nuptiis. But according to canon law, that law is abrogated, as noted there. And therefore it is not stated that she married within the year; but rather that she married having spurned her children. And thus she is punished in the ownership: nevertheless, she retains the usufruct, and having provided security, she could bring an action. ff. de usufructu, ea re, l. si pecuniae; C. de secundis nuptiis, l. feminae; and auth. ibi posita.

It must therefore be considered whether it is regarded as a legacy or as a dowry confessed. And I say that the woman may bring an action for the dowry and prove it by the husband’s confession made in her presence. The exception of “no peculium or dowry” has no place here, because the circumstances do not permit it. C. de dote cautione non num. l. si. and the authority there cited. Nor does the statute concerning possessions not to be transferred unless the right of the community of Gubbio is reserved, stand in the way; for the aforementioned statute speaks of immovable things, not of a quantity in which the community claims no right. Therefore, a right that does not exist need not be observed. ff. de legibus l. si quis legaverit. and the argument in l. ita autem in principio ff. de administratione tutorum. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether counsel given for evil is presumed from conversation.
2. Reputation is to be preferred to all profit.
3. Whether one giving evil counsel for a wrongful act is to be punished: and by what penalty. Item 4. distinguishes there.
4. Whether advising flight is a wrongful act: and whether flight is a wrongful act.
5. Whether one aiding a wrongful act is to be punished: and who is said to aid.
6. Whether one concealing another’s debtor makes himself a partner in the same danger.
7. That which is done within three days is said to be done immediately.
8. Who is said to be a fugitive.
9. To what one concealing the account books, or books of accounts, of someone is liable.
10. How a statute prohibiting harboring is to be understood.
11. Whether one is bound to report and betray a debtor intending to flee.
12. Who is said to be a harborer, and what is required for someone to be punished for harboring.
13. Whether a partner can be punished for harboring the common account book of himself and another who has fled.
14. Cancelled accounts are also said to be common.
15. Whether the penalty of a statute removes the penalty of the common law.
16. How a statute providing that usurious merchants are not to be regarded as merchants is to be understood.
17. Whether a merchant who flees due to poverty arising from a fortuitous event ought to be punished with a lesser penalty.
18. The preamble of statutes is regarded as the final cause.
19. Bankrupts are said to be defrauders.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. In the case of M., who is alleged to have given counsel to V. in his flight and bankruptcy, said V. being a fraudulent and fugitive merchant of the city of Milan, to the prejudice of certain merchant creditors. First, it must be considered according to the common law, whether from the fact that said V. was a friend of said M., and having had a conversation with said M. a few days before, and having disclosed the secret of his flight, he subsequently fled and took to flight, carrying afterwards into the house of M. the account books, and with the horses and servant of said M., it is presumed that M. gave him fraudulent counsel to the detriment of the creditors; indeed, even open aid and assistance; and whether said M. is therefore bound. And especially considering the form of the ordinances of commerce of the city.
