Many, where the aforementioned acts are said to have been perpetrated, ask: or whether he is not bound in any way, and especially since said V. afterwards returned with confidence, and wished to pay up to certain intervals, and to settle the remainder; and if he were bound in any way, in what respect and to what extent, in the name of God, counsel is sought as to what is the law: since said M. says that he gave no counsel for the flight, nor for any evil or damage to the creditors, but rather for good, and with good intent: as appears from the confession of said M. Therefore, in the name of God, on the aforementioned matters, and on each of the aforementioned points, let counsel be given supported by reasons: presupposing that said V. would otherwise have done it, and was obstinate in his flight, if Franciscus had not persuaded him to the contrary: because he did not wish to die in prison; and he considered it more preferable to flee than to die: although it was more dishonorable, as he also made understood by his very act.

And first it must be considered whether counsel given for an evil purpose is presumed from the conversation. And it seems that it is: because whose end is evil, his premeditation is presumed to be fraudulent, as in C. de adulteriis, l. Si qui. Moreover, the end demonstrates the beginning: as in C. de institutionibus et substitutionibus, l. Reprehendenda. Also contributing to this is Bartolus, ff. de privilegiis creditorum, l. Si ventri, §. Eorum, whose words add, as will be seen below: "A certain person was accused of having given counsel for homicide, and the homicide is proven. Also, that he spoke with the murderer, and immediately went and killed; but it was not known what he said to him; certainly, from the brevity of time, it is presumed that he gave counsel." Bartolus.

On the contrary, it seems that counsel is not established. For one thing is counsel, another is conversation. Conversation can be good or evil, and therefore it is presumed good if it is with a good man, as in C. de inofficioso testamento, l. Aviam; ff. de re militari, l. Non omnes, §. A barbaris. Moreover, no one is presumed to commit fraud or deceit, as in ff. de probationibus, l. Quoties, §. Qui dolo, unless it is proven by clear indications. And they are called clear, as if perfectly effective, as in C. de dolo, l. Dolum. Also, in doubt, good is presumed, not evil. C. de inofficioso testamento, l. Omnimodo; ff. pro socio, l. Merito. Also, it does not prove this to be the case, that it frequently and easily happens otherwise, as in C. de probationibus, l. Neque natales; C. unde leges, l. Non hoc.

Nor does the aforementioned statement of Bartolus oppose this, because it should not be understood so indiscriminately, but in that case when causes and indications of hatred preceded; otherwise, he would be saying something false. Also, from friendship it is presumed that one gives good counsel to a friend, because a friend wishes good for a friend, as noted in ff. de fideicommissis libertatibus, In testamento. But counsel for flight is not good counsel, but ignominious and infamous.

† Reputation is to be preferred to all gain. As stated in the Digest, title *Si quis omissa causa maioris testatus sit*, law *Iulianus*. Hence the Apostle: “It is more expedient for me to die than that anyone should make void my glory.” Nor is reputation well sold for gold in its entirety. As stated in the Code, title *De postulando*, law *Quisquis*.

Secondly, it must be considered, assuming that the evil and wicked counsel is established, whether M. is to be punished in any way, given that V. would have acted anyway. And it seems that he is: because when counsel is given to commit a wrong, the one who advised is liable by the action on account of fraud, as one concurring in the wrong, once the wrongful act has been carried out. As is noted in the rule *Nullus ex consilio*, *De regulis iuris*, Book 6; and there, Dyonisius holds that counsel given for a wrongful act is punished indiscriminately, even if the principal would have acted anyway. Likewise, it seems that the gloss in the Digest, *De iniuriis*, in the law *Non solum*, § *Proculus*, and § *Si mandato*, holds the same. But the contrary is held by the most explicit gloss in the Institutes, *De obligationibus ex delicto*, § *Ope*, and in the Digest, *De verborum significatione*, in the law *Saepe*, at the end. These glosses expressly decide that where the principal would have acted anyway, the one who gave evil or contrary counsel is not liable, disregarding the counsel. And there is also the reason that the principal did not follow the counsel, but rather the impulse of his own mind.

It must therefore be said that either the principal had the intention of committing the act, but did not carry his will into action without counsel; in which case the counselor is liable. Or he carried it into action in any manner whatsoever; and then the counselor is not liable, because since he was going to commit the act anyway, it cannot be said that the counselor, by praising him, instigated his malice. That which is complete does not require addition. And this opinion seems true according to equity, because the offender regarded this counsel as nothing, and consequently did not follow the counsel. And this is the reason on which the gloss of the said §. ope is based. This is also held by Paulus de Liaz. in c. j. de poen. in cle. And especially when we judge of counsel from presumptions; because then it is safer to proceed according to Innocentius, who so elegantly states this in c. quia verisimile, extra de praesump. It follows to consider,

Whether to advise flight is to advise a felony. Here it must be considered: whether flight is a felony. And I say that either the fugitive is a slave, or one tainted with servile status: and it is a felony. As in l. 1, C. de servis fugitivis; and l. 1, C. de operis liberto. Or he is freeborn: and then either he flees with another’s property, and it is a felony by reason of the thing, because by carrying it away he commits theft. The same applies if he flees with a thing which at some time was another’s, as with money deposited for counting. Although there is not properly theft there. As in l. Ait praetor, §. Si debitorem, ff. Quae in fraudem creditorum. Or he flees without the removal of another’s property, or quasi-property, and this flight is not a wrong, but is a certain kind of concealment. As in ff. Quibus ex causis in possessionem, l. Fulcinius, §. Quid sit latitare. Hence, even if someone summoned flees and is condemned, he is not said to be condemned for a felony, but for contumacy. As in l. 1, ff. Si quis ius dicenti non obtemperaverit. Hence the doctors say that flight is not imposed on anyone as a felony, but as a suspicion. As noted by Cynus in l. 1, C. de raptu virginum; and it is clear in Auth. de exhibendis reis, §. Si vero; and commonly by all the doctors in ff. de iureiurando admonendi. It follows to consider concerning assistance.

And I say that if my friend, without my knowledge, flees with my horses or with my servant, I am not said to be providing aid. For knowledge, not ignorance, is punished. As in C. de incestis nuptiis, l. Cum ancillis; C. de tabulis, l. Generalis, lib. 10; and the glosses in l. 1, ff. de receptis; and C. de servis fugitivis, l. Quicunque; and l. 1 and 2, C. de his qui latrocinio; and the Lombard Law states that if anyone has presumed to take another’s arms and has committed evil with them, the fault does not lie with the owner of the arms, but with him who committed the evil with them. As in Longobardum, de his qui cum armis alterius damnum fecerunt, c. Si. But more is said in the same title, c. 1: If anyone has simply provided arms to another, and he who received them [committed evil], the fault is not imputed to him who provided them, but to him who perpetrated the evil with them. Therefore, it is required that aid be provided for this purpose. As in l. 2, §. Homines coactos, ff. vi bonorum raptorum. And if anyone, having taken a knife from a butcher’s shop, killed his son, he himself is the murderer, not the butcher. As in l. 12, ff. de origine iuris. From these it appears that the said M. is bound neither by counsel nor by aid, because neither was obligatory nor true. And this I say with certainty according to the common law, in accordance with what is proposed in his case.

It remains to be seen whether he who knowingly conceals another’s debtor makes himself a successor or a partner in the same peril. And it seems that he does, as in l. si, C. de oper. lib. But the contrary must be said: because the laws which provide for this speak of special cases. And there is one special case, another is the debtor of taxes, as in C. de exac. tribu. l. quotiens. Another is when someone by force removes a debtor, ff. ne quis eum qui in ius voc. vi exi. l. pen. The fourth is when someone prevents a defendant or a plaintiff from coming to court, whence prescription runs against the creditor, as in ff. de eo per quem factum erit l. si. Since therefore in these cases there is a special rule and special provision, it follows that the common law is to the contrary, as in ff. de legi. l. ius singulare. This is the opinion of Innocentius, namely, that those edicts do not apply outside their own cases, extra de off. deleg. c. pastoralis, in fi. and something is touched upon there, ti. c. j. Now let us come to the statute of merchants. And I premise that from the receipt of the valises nothing can be imputed to M., because he neither saw nor consented. Moreover, a sleeping person does not commit a fault, unless there was a prior cause why he ought to have been watchful, as in ff. ad l. Aquil. l. si seruus seruum, §. si fornicarius. And if it is said that he was in subsequent fault by retaining the account books with certain knowledge, for he ought immediately to have restored them, as in ff. de adul. l. si adulterium cum incestu, §. incestum autem, and as in C. de incest. nup. l. cum ancillis.

I answer that an act is said to be committed *incontinenti* (immediately) if it was committed within three days, as stated in l. 3, C. de errore advocatorum; otherwise, if it was done for one’s own caution, even if a short interval of time has elapsed, as in ff. de usu, l. sciendum. Moreover, since the creditors have received or accepted the books and account ledgers, even if M. had incurred some penalty under the law or statute, because he labors in vain over a penalty who has obtained the thing, as in l. 2, post princ., ff. si quis cautionem praestiterit; especially because this obligation, which arises from the decree of the merchants, is a praetorian obligation, and consequently arbitrary, in which the aforementioned rule is most true, as in ff. de publiciana, l. hoc edicto, and ff. quod metus causa, l. si cum exceptione, §. satis clementer. And that it is praetorian law is apparent, because it derives from the jurisdiction of the consuls, who are praetors, just as the curule aediles and similar magistrates are, l. 1, ff. de officio consulum, and ff. de verbis oblig., l. stipulationum aliae, §. praetoriae; or at least invented in the manner of praetorian obligations, from which an *actio in factum* arises. Furthermore, when a genus is specified in an obligation, the genus is extinguished with respect to the species, once the species is delivered, as in ff. de pignore, l. si fundus, §. si pluris; and ff. de doli exceptione, l. fideiussor; ff. de legato primo, l. si fundum per fideicommissum; ff. de petitione hereditatis, l. Item veniunt, §. idem recte. But because perhaps some might argue to the contrary in this case, since this action is penal from the beginning, or perhaps they might say that this penalty should be applied to the fisc, therefore, to remove this doubt, I turn to the interpretation of the statutes. The words of the statute are as follows, infra: “Furthermore, that no one from the city, or the county of Mutina, or from elsewhere, dare or presume to harbor or receive such fugitives, nor fathers, brothers, male sons, brothers’ agents, nor their ascendants, nor their descendants, as contained in the preceding statutes, in person, nor in goods, nor in their houses, nor in others; nor to give them, or any of them, counsel, aid, or favor in person or in goods; nor to plead for them, nor to advocate for them. And whoever shall contravene this shall be punished in the sum of 200 livres of *terzioli* for each offense. And nevertheless, such receiver and agent shall be bound to restore the value of the received goods in double. And the aforementioned authority, judges, and consuls of justice of the merchants of Mutina may and must, under the aforementioned penalty of livres of *terzioli* of their salary, inquire into the aforementioned matters, as above, and proceed against them, knowing them to be fugitives. And first it must be seen”

It is so, because the statute speaks of receiving fugitives. Now, a fugitive is one who is caught in the act of flight, such that at least one foot has been moved. Thus, D. 47.16.1 (De edilitio edicto), l. Quis sit fugitivus, § 1, in the gloss: Ita tamen. He, however, who in no way has reached the beginning of the act, although he has mentally conceived the counsel of flight, is not a fugitive; because the statute must be understood as referring to the act, at least commenced. Thus, D. 7.6.1 (Vi bonorum raptorum), l. Cedere, § Subsecare; and D. 50.16.1 (De verbis significatis), l. Fugitivus. Therefore, it is necessary first of all that the act, or the beginning of the flight, be apparent at the time of the reception of the person or of the goods.

But here it is asked, since the statute says that he is bound to restore the price, whether the account books should be appraised according to the names contained in the books, or materially. And it seems that they should be appraised for as much as the book of papers could be sold for, not for what the names are worth: because that consists in a legal fiction. As in D. 22.3.1 (Qui chirographum). But statutes, and especially penal ones, or those departing from the common law, or establishing new law, do not admit of fiction. As noted in D. 3.5.3, § Haec verba (De negotiorum gestorum), in the common and widespread gloss, which is approved by all. On the contrary, it seems that they should be appraised signifiatively, i.e., according to the names contained in the books: as in D. 35.1.1 (De legibus), L. Servum filii, § Eum qui chirographum. For the words of the statute are to be referred to the effect. But the effect of the chirograph consists in the names. As in D. 2.14.1 (De pactis), L. Postquam. For the paper itself is of little value. And thus it would be a small penalty for so great a crime. And therefore, D. 47.2.1 (De furtis), L. Quidam tabularum, and L. Qui tabulas; and D. 9.2.1 (Ad legem Aquiliam), L. In lege Aquilia, § Si delictum. From which it follows that he is bound for as much as the name could be sold for, provided it is proved that he received them with fraud and certain knowledge, knowing the quality of the chirographs, with the intent to intercept them, and not with the intent to return them to the creditors and preserve them in the meantime. And since the interpretation can be turned to either intent, the intent is to be judged according to the quality of the person. As in D. 11.7.1 (De religiosis et sumptibus funerum), L. At si quis, § Interdum, and the following §. And if it would conveniently have come to him, a bad intent would be presumed; otherwise, the contrary. As in D. 4.3.1 (De dolo), L. Quod si cum scires. Moreover, the said statute is to be understood as applying to the receiver who provides aid, counsel, or favor by the very act of receiving: because that clause concerning aid and favor, which follows, declares the quality of the preceding terms. As in D. 7.7.1 (De vino legato), L. Si, § Cui dulcia. However, I do not hold this last point as certain, but leave it in doubt.

† I believe, however, that this is to be understood as referring to odious receipt, i.e., one that may be fraudulent against creditors, and not to that which is made for good reasons, so that creditors do not seize the account books, because the latter has the intention of managing the business for the creditors, so that in some contingency that might occur to them, they do not suffer loss due to the removal of instruments or account books. This, however, is to be presumed from the quality of the persons, and also from the oath of the receiver; indeed, since the merchants themselves may deposit their books with some trustworthy person, and such a depositary commits no fault, as stated in D. de edendo, l. quaedam, §. his autem; and D. familiae erciscundae, l. si quae; and D. de poenis, l. si quis aliquid, §. instrumenta, where it is expressly stated that the books themselves remain the property of the merchants. And although they may go their ways through deceit, nevertheless, in depositing with a trustworthy person, deceit does not intervene. Moreover, where an act is indifferent as to good and evil, and does not harm another, good rather than evil is presumed. But this deposit is an indifferent act. And insofar as the deposit harms no one, but rather aids, see D. quod vi aut clam, l. si alius, §. bellissime, with the following §. unless it is expressly proven that the books were concealed so that the truth might be hidden, or not easily revealed. As noted by Bartolus in D. de tabulis exhibendis, l. locum, §. si quis dolo, where he says that the intent to conceal is presumed only when it is concealed in such a way that it is not accessible to anyone. Otherwise, if it is accessible to a good man, who would likely notify the creditors, as this one did, whom experience of affairs has shown to be a good man, and whose uncorrupted faith and the highest office of the treasury entrusted to him by our illustrious lord, just as to any other whom our lord has chosen, are evident. These things, indeed, do not occur except on account of virtue. Finally, every great and elegant office is a proclamation of virtue: as stated in l. fi., C. de conditionibus in publicum honoris, lib. 10, tit. 12.

† Subsequently, it must be considered whether M. was bound to inform and betray him who was preparing to flee. And it is to be said that he is not bound to inform, nor to betray the secret: as is read and noted in l. idem est, §. si tibi ob indicium, D. de cond. ob turp. causam. For he would act dishonorably, since he gave his faith to keep the secret; because faith is to be kept even to an enemy. The same holds if he had not given his faith, yet he would not be bound to inform: because this does not pertain to his office. As is stated in Extr. de testib. cogend., cap. delictorum, and it is clear in Dist. 6, c. nerui testiculorum leulatam. And fully noted by Innocentius in Extr. de homic., c. ad audien., where he also fully treats the matter of the counsel.

† Moreover, a receiver, according to the etymology of the word, is nothing other than an acceptor of goods. But this M. accepted nothing from the fugitive, because he was entirely ignorant of the matter. And although the household previously received [the goods] through imprudence, or even if through fraud, it does not prejudice M., as stated in the extrajudicial title On Restitution of Spoliation, chapter Cum ad sedem, because the household was not appointed for this purpose. And in the Digest, title On Public Matters, law 1, section Familia, and there by Bartolus. And therefore the statute on receiving stolen goods has no application here, because three things are required in receiving: the person bringing [the goods], the act of delivery, and the thing received, as is noted in the Digest, title On the Significance of Words, law Marcellus. Furthermore, this M. did not receive from anyone, but found [the goods] in the house. Argument: Digest, title On Theft, law Si quid ex domo. He was not present, nor aware. Argument: Digest, title On Nautic Loan, Stable Law, law 1, in the beginning. For thus it is rather a fortuitous event than a human act. Since therefore no fault is found in M., neither is there punishment. The ancients indeed considered fraud as punishment. As in the Digest, title On the Edict of the Aediles, law Cum autem, section Excipitur. And the reason is that the quality of the offense is named from the type of punishment, and conversely the type [of offense] from the punishment, as is clear there. Let us therefore add the common rule that where no fault is found, there is no punishment. As in the Digest, title On Fidejussors, book 1, law Sed si non data, section Si. And it applies in the Digest, title On the Lex Aquilia, law Qui occidit, at the end. And in the Digest, title On Freedmen, law 1, section 1, and following. Nor is it presumed that he has the intent to receive, who received for only a few days, as is clear in the aforementioned law 1, section His autem, and section Final. Furthermore, for the clarification of the truth, and to block the mouths of those speaking against justice and truth—although one cannot shut anyone’s mouth, for as the wise man says, “It is not within our power that each one should speak”—nevertheless truth conquers all and imposes silence on those who speak. It must be known in the facts, and then we shall conclude in law not persuasively, but demonstratively to the eye, that

† Regarding the receipt of the books, nothing more can be alleged against M. And this is demonstrated as follows: in the aforementioned account books there were many accounts, and of great quantity, of receipts and payments calculated between the said M. and the said V. Hence it cannot be denied that the said accounts were common. As stated in D. de edendo, l. 1, § rationes; and l. si quis ex argentariis, § pertinere; and the notes in § editiones; and C. eod., l. 1 and l. si. And by reason of the aforementioned accounts, even the codex itself was common, and it could not be dissolved by quires, unsealed, and kept in custody in part and not in part. Hence, with respect to this corpus, it was indivisible. And especially because the beginning of the accounts, which is contained in the codex, is common to all: as stated in D. de edendo, l. si quis ex argentariis, § si initium tabularum. And by reason of a part, the whole can be kept in custody: as stated in D. communi dividundo, l. Sabinus. I do not say that the whole can be contracted: as stated in D. pro socio, l. merito; and D. de acquirenda hereditate, l. duo fratres. And custody is something indivisible: as stated in D. comm. div., l. si ut certo, § si duobus vehiculum. And if there are two who have a common codex, it is lawful and just for either to keep it in custody and hold it in his own custody, until a common custodian is appointed by a superior: as stated in D. de senatu consulto Trebelliano, l. si quae cautiones; and D. de fideiussoribus, l. fin. Nor ought anyone to suffer that the accounts come into the hands of a stranger, who might disturb them: as stated in D. de in rem verso, l. quidam. Lest perhaps erasures, cancellations, or additions be easily made: as stated in D. de his qui intestati delinquent, l. 1; D. de falsis, l. 1, § qui rationibus; C. de testamento, l. si unus. And therefore it is necessary that the documents be under faithful custody. And Extravagantes, de praescriptionibus, c. ad audientiam. Since therefore these codices are common, and it concerns M., and since he is a faithful person and the master of the accounts of the lord, he undoubtedly could receive the books pertaining to himself and diligently keep them in custody. For even if there are two lords of the same castle, and one departs, the other can keep it in custody: as stated in D. de funere instituto, l. si ita, § villae custos. For no one is bound to neglect his right: as stated in D. de petitione hereditatis, l. illud. And what is offered to him, he ought not to refuse: as stated in D. de legatis tertio, l. 11, § si rem. Even if it is offered in the middle of the night: as stated in D. de feriis, l. more Romano; and C. de transactionibus, l. non minorem.

† Someone might say that these multiple accounts were cancelled. Therefore, the ledger was not common. I answer that this argument is false: because even cancelled accounts are common; for by them it is proved that the debt arose from both sides. Hence, it is in the interest of both parties that they appear. The text is found in l. Fullo, D. de furtis; see also C. de condictione sine causa, l. Dissolutae; C. de fide instrumentorum, l. Plures apocis; in Auth. de mancipiis principum, § Publicorum; C. de apocryphis publicis, l. 1; C. de discussionibus, l. Nec casu, lib. 10. And this is the very truth.

As for the fact that the account books were well kept, this appears from their first reading, which is the primary evidence, free from all suspicion: as in C. de edicto divi Adriani, l. Si. For the appearance of the writing reveals the hidden trust and legality, which, being expressly manifest, need not be proved: as in C. de fide instrumentorum, l. Comparationes; and D. de regulis iuris, l. Si irruptione, § Ad officium. And to abandon sense and proceed by petty arguments is a weakness of the intellect, as say the two luminaries of philosophy, Aristotle and Averroes. And by these means the innocence of M. appears most clearly, and more than clearly, against the slanderers, who sometimes applaud with their voices, but bite with their teeth, with a curved sting: as says Blessed Jerome. But the decretal says that one should not care what the unjust man objects, but what the equitable arbiter decides.

36 Certain other matters were asked of me.

And first, whether the penalty of the statute removes the penalty of the common law. And on this point I say that either it comes derogatively, and it removes it: as in *l. qui cum uno*, § *qui post.*, D. de re militari, where there is a singular and unique text in the law, in all corporal penalties, that on account of humanity and equity it seems to have receded from the harsher penalty: because the harsher penalty is equated to rigor, the milder to equity, and equity, being written last, is preferred to rigor. Or the new law disposes cumulatively, and then it does not seem to have receded: as in D. de sepulchro violato, *l. qui sepulchra*. Or it disposes disjunctively, and then in the same law it seems that the disjunctive is taken for the conjunctive. But in different statutes it is otherwise. But you say that, out of hatred for penalties, it is not taken for the conjunctive, even in the same statute: but the last section is to be followed: as in D. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, *l. si idem cum eodem*, § *finis*. For even if two legacies, which are favorable, are left disjunctively for the same cause, nevertheless the later one is due: as noted in D. de probationibus, *l. quinquaginta*. Therefore, much more strongly in penalties there should be no duplication. Moreover, we ought to be content with the penalties comprehended in the statute: as in D. de verbis oblig., *l. stipulatio huiusmodi*, especially because the magistrate has sworn to observe the statutes: as in Extr. de iureiurando, cap. *venientes*. Some, however, say that one law does not seem to be derogated by another: *l. quia legum correctio est vitanda*: as in D. de actionibus et obligationibus, *l. quotiens*. If, however, execution of one penalty were carried out, the other penalty would cease, unless it were found to be for the supplement of the first: because a delict which is not fully purged ought to be purged: as noted in Extr. de iudiciis, cap. *at si clerici*; C. de sportulis, *l. 2*; D. de accusationibus, *l. senatus censuit*. For even God does not judge twice for the same thing: as the decree says.

† Subsequently, I was asked, since the statute says that usurious merchants are not to be regarded as merchants, how this is to be understood. I answer: In privileges and favors, they are not regarded as merchants, because debt excludes all honor; as in C. ubi senatus vel clarissimi, l. 1; and C. de dignitatibus, l. iudices, lib. 12. Hence, this is a kind of removal from the roll, which takes away privileges, yet does not remove penalties; as in ff. de infamia, l. 2, § ignominiae, and § miles, because no one by committing a crime makes his condition better. Therefore, when a merchant practices usury, he loses his privilege; as in ff. de privilegio creditoris, l. si ventri, § in bonis; but he does not escape the penalties imposed on merchants. ff. de negotiorum gestis, l. sive haereditaria, just as we have seen in the case of an excommunicated person, who is repelled actively, but may be sued passively; as in extra de iudicibus, c. intelleximus. Moreover, an abominable merchant is one who practices usury, because the wickedness and voracity of usury do not befit a good man, since it is a disgraceful gain; as Aristotle says, and the whole school of theologians: and what I said later is for the satisfaction of the eighteenth question of the inquirer.

† But there remains one fragment, or doubt, arising from the aforementioned matter. The statute on commerce speaks preliminarily of defrauders, but speaks indefinitely in its dispositive part. Suppose, therefore, that a merchant deceived [creditors] due to poverty not sought out, but fortuitous: whether the rigor of the statutes ought to be mitigated on account of poverty. And I say that it should: because poverty excuses from perjury: as noted by Innocentius, Extra, de officio delegatorum, c. P. et G. Moreover, to allege poverty is a kind of exception: as in the Digest, de procuratoribus, l. Titius. Furthermore, it does not concern creditors that he fled: because the action is futile: as in the Digest, de dolo, l. nam is. Also, because that which does not harm creditors, but harms another, ought not to be considered: as in the Digest, de aqua pluviali arcenda, l. 2, §. Item varus. Moreover, those who fall into poverty by chance are worthy of mercy: as in the Lord’s Prayer, and also in the Gospel concerning the wicked servant: as noted in the Digest, 19, de infa[ma], l. furti, §. pactus.

† Moreover, the preamble of the statute is regarded as the place of the final cause restricting it: as in D. de her. inst. l. si; D. de pact. l. quod dictum; D. de leg. 2. l. pater, §. dulcissimis; D. de acqui. poss. si is qui animo; D. de iure pat. l. adigere, §. quamuis. To the contrary it seems: because it would follow that it would be necessary to prove fraud. But this is difficult. Also, because the creditors would not be fully provided for. Also, because the reason of the law is usually true in most cases, but not in all. And yet a precise statute does not admit an exception: as in D. qui et a quibus, l. prospexit. Also, if he is bankrupt, therefore he is a defrauder. Thus, the law calls him so, and the edict calls him a defrauder: nor is it new that sometimes there is more in presumption than in truth. The law says that the heir who did not make an inventory is liable in solidum: because it is presumed that he has embezzled: and against this presumption, which passes into the statute of the law, the contrary cannot be proved: and even if proved, it does not avail: as in Auth. de her. et fal. §. sancimus.

Thus, in the case at hand: since deceivers and defrauders are caught by things that commonly happen, it is presumed that what is common to almost all is present in everyone; nor are they excused on account of adverse fortune: as in D. ad Trebellianum, Epistolam, in principio; and D. de verborum obligationibus, Continuum actum, § Illud, and § Cum quis. And this is the safer opinion, because the reason of the law, which is founded solely on presumption, does not restrict the general statute of the law. It supports what we have said, D. de solutionibus matrimonii, § 1, especially according to the learned commentators and Oldradus. I believe I have satisfied not only those questions put to me, but all those that could be asked in this matter. From all these things it is concluded that M. is secure by his very innocence: as in C. de iniuriis, Si non convicii; and C. de his qui ut indigni, Si sororem; and also by living reason, thus by natural equity. And therefore his rivals would do better if they did not harass themselves with great expenses: as in D. de inofficioso testamento, § 1. And because my opinion does not make law, I refer to those who can make law, namely, to the respectable council of the magnificient [lord] and his other magistrates, to whom I submit myself, although I do not think they will rule otherwise: as in D. de iure patronatus, Divi fratres. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Who is called an assassin.
2. Price, properly and strictly, refers to money paid in cash.
3. How the word "I promise" is to be understood.
4. The accomplice of the crime is not admitted as a witness.
5. A mandate is not presumed unless it is proven.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Bectonus de Ceuo, inhabitant of the land of Cadagnano in the district of Brescia, consul of the commune, and the men of the said land, in order to excuse himself and his said commune, notified and denounced that it had come to his ears and knowledge that, when a certain tempest had gone to the courtyard of the habitation of a certain Bectinus, and was saying to him that he ought to vacate and clear out the said courtyard for the said tempest, and in these very words, M. of Verona, corporal of Aldugini de Homis, V., natural son of the said I., and Iac., natural son of the said Iac., behold, the said Bectinus, with a sword which he held in his hands, struck and wounded the said T. in his person, inflicting one wound passing from one side to the other in the left part of the chest, and the aforementioned others with so many wounds that the said T. died immediately: specifying the wounding and the wounds, etc. The said injured party, in effect, testified concerning the said homicide, adding that two horses were sent, etc., as is contained in the records. Afterwards, however, on the same day, he testified how Aldriginus de Homis called the said Iac. and secretly said to him that he ought to be with the said V. and M. at the said place, in the said courtyard, that he ought to do and commit with the aforementioned V. and M. that deed which they wished to commit; and that the said Ald. would send a horse to meet the said Iac., just as he would send one for the aforementioned V. and M., and afterwards, when the said business was completed, he would grant and give to him two bushels of wheat, which he had promised and wished to give to the aforementioned V. and M. And given this order, the deed was carried out, etc. But it is provided by the municipal law that if anyone assassinates, or causes another to be assassinated, he shall be dragged by the tail of a horse to the gallows, and there be hanged in such a manner that he dies. An assassin is, and is understood to be, one who has killed someone for a question or promise received. Likewise, an assassin is, and is understood to be, one who, for a price given or promised, caused someone to be killed.

† Now it is asked, assuming but not conceding, rather entirely denying in the facts, that the said B. de Homis committed and did the aforementioned acts, whether the assassin ought to be judged or not; and truly, that he ought. For the words state that he, Al., was to send one horse for the said Jacob, just as he would send for the said V. and M., for whom it is established that he did send. Therefore, for this homicide committed, something was promised, indeed even executed: because horses were sent. And in the Digest, *De calumniatoribus*, law *Cum est*. Furthermore, it was promised that he would give to the same Jacob those things which he had promised and wished to give to the aforementioned V. and M., and thus it was promised to give. And from the conjunction of the words it appears that it was promised to give and to do. And thus the assassin ought rightly to be judged, as in chapter 1, *De homicidiis*, Book 6. To the contrary is the truth itself, manifest by several reasons. And first, because to him to whom the words of the law do not apply, neither do the law itself. Law *Ut*, Digest, *Solutis matrimonii*; law *Si vero*, section *De viro*. But the words of the statute do not apply, nor pertain to our case. Therefore, the statute ceases to apply. And I take principally three words. For the statute says, *price*.

† This is properly and strictly referred to money counted. As stated in l. si, C. de praediis curialium, lib. 10. And the words of this statute must be taken in their most proper and strictest sense: because this statute is most penal and most odious. And therefore, the proper meaning of the words must be adhered to. See c. odia, de reg. iur., lib. 6, and there by Dy. The second word is the word "dato." But this word signifies the transfer of ownership. For to give is to make the recipient's. As l. 1, C. de fund. dot.; ff. de usur.; l. si stipulatus, ff. de cond. ob cau.; l. si, ff. de ver. ob.; l. ubi autem non apparet §. si. But here no ownership was transferred.

The third word is the word "promise." Here it must be considered that there are four terms, one of which is not the other, namely: said, pledged, promised, stipulated. Provided that the words which are said to have been uttered here were enunciative words, they were not words of promising. For it does not appear that any agreement intervened on this point. As in D. de pactis, l. 1, §. conventionis; and D. de dilatoris edicto, l. sciendum, §. dictum; and D. de pollicitationibus, l. 1, where it is clear that what is pledged by bare voice is improperly called a promise. Moreover, that is called a promise which is certain. For that which is uncertain in thing and in kind is not called a promise, nor a pledge. As in C. de manumissionibus, l. salarium; and D. de verbis obligationum, l. triticum. Hence the learned Federicus de Senis, in his consilia, holds that he who confesses himself to be a usurer in general confesses nothing. To this it contributes that, as noted in D. de legatis 1, l. turpia and l. Titiae textores, it is said that what is obscure is regarded as nothing. And this is confirmed by what is read, that those words "given, or promised" are understood thus: that is, promised to be given; because the word "or" partakes of the nature of a conjunction. As noted in l. in repetendis, D. de legatis 3, by Bartolus; and C. de servis fugitivis, l. si fugitivum; and l. 1, D. de rebus dubiis; and l. 1 and l. fi, §. cui dulcia, D. de penus legatorum. Behold, therefore, that in our case no delivery intervened, no promise to deliver intervened, nor any other. And if it be said that this man said he would send the money: it is not said that he promised to give the money; because these words partake of a loan for use (commodatum), not of a transfer of ownership, as noted in l. cum quid, D. si certum petatur. Moreover, this sending is accustomed to be done by a friend to a friend. As noted in Extravagantes de simonia, c. et si quaestiones. Moreover, it must be observed that the words of the statute say, "shall have caused someone to be killed." For certainly nothing is proven that the said Aldrigius caused [someone] to be killed; because it is not proven that V. and M. had a mandate to kill the said T., nor could they have had a fixed mandate. For that the said T. approached the said courtyard was by chance and fortune, rather by the fault of T. himself, which the said Al. could not divine. As in D. ad legem Aquiliam, l. Item si putator. And if he had this in premeditated thought: because perhaps the said T. had boasted of expelling the said Betinellus, this mandate could be understood in the case in which the said T. could be expelled lawfully, and also repelled with arms. For a mandate, which can be understood according to law and justice, ought not to be understood according to fraud. As in D. de conditione indebiti, l. si procurator, §. Celsus. For it is a most grave crime to assassinate. As noted by Bartolus in D. de iureiurando, l. non solum, §. si mandato nisi specificetur. Now, having considered the words of the law, let us look at the words and deeds of the said Aldrigius. It is said that he called Jacobinus and said to him secretly, etc. For it appears that this witness is singular, by that adverb "secretly."

† Moreover, Jacob’s statement ought not to be believed, because a confession made against oneself is not credited as evidence against another, as stated in Extra, de confessionibus, chapter Primo, and in Digestum, de accusationibus, the final law. And thus it does not constitute grounds for torture, because he is a disqualified witness. Furthermore, the following words are appended, that he himself ought to perform and commit what V. and M. wished to commit. For what intention V. and M. then had is unknown, as noted in Digestum, de damno infecto, law Si bona, section Si quis stipulaturus. Moreover, those words, that he would give to the same Jacob those things which V. and M. had promised and wished to give, similarly avail nothing, because they are most uncertain, as noted in Digestum, de legatis primo, law Legato generaliter. From all and each of these, from the first to the last, I conclude, and also because assassination was not alleged, that the said Aldrigo cannot and ought not to be condemned of assassination, because neither do the words of the statute permit it, nor do the words of Aldrigo signify this. Moreover, concerning the secrets of secrets, which are in no way proven, judgment does not pertain to the Court of the Militia. And this is what is said, that the Emperor and the Church do not judge hidden matters; God knows the hearts of men, nor does mere mental thought suffice in crimes.

† It is certain that a mandate is not presumed unless it is proven, even if the offense is committed by a servant or a friend. The text is in Extra, De restitutione spoliatorum, chapter Cum ad sedem. And note the commentary of Bartolus in L. 1, § Familia, Digestum, De publicis. It is also established that assassination is a certain quality. And therefore, unless the mandate is proven, it cannot be proven that the mandator committed assassination; because no quality can be proven where the subject is not proven. As noted in Digestum, De probationibus, L. Si arbiter, in fine. Moreover, here it is not proven that enmities preceded, from which material for so great a crime would arise. Therefore, the intent to commit a delict is not presumed. As noted in Digestum, Ad Legem Corneli de sicariis, L. 1. Furthermore, even if a mandate to stand in defense of a friend were proven, it is presumed to have been given with the moderation of blameless protection; because this is fitting for an honorable man. As in L. 1, Codex, Unde vi; and L. Ut vim, Digestum, De iustitia et iure; Digestum, Ad Legem Aquiliam, L. Scientiam, § Qui cum aliter. The confession of Aldrigino, which I later saw, does not obstruct the case, granted but not conceded that it was made voluntarily; because it does not include assassination, nor anything similar. Although in this matter one should not argue from analogy. Moreover, if we were to say that he who sends his mercenaries to his friend for his defense is an assassin, it would follow that all lords of Italy, who send their mercenaries to aid other nobles, are assassins; which is absurd to say and contrary to law. As in chapter Domino guerram, in the title Hic finit lex, then Consuetudines Regni, beginning of Collection 10, where it is expressly stated. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
0. and no. D. de iure fisci, l. ita fidei; and l. in tacitis, D. de legibus 1.
1. Moreover, whether the one who orders is liable for homicide under statutes punishing homicide with the penalty of death.
2. A homicide is said in many ways.
3. The difference between the doer and the one who orders.
4. Whether an indefinite term is equivalent to a universal one by interpretation or by the signification of the word.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The statute of the city provides that no one shall be punished corporally unless it is provided for by municipal law; otherwise, he shall be punished pecuniarily at the discretion of the authority. Another statute provides that if anyone commits homicide, he shall be punished by the head, so that he shall die. Now it has happened that a certain person ordered another to commit homicide, and he committed it.
† It is asked whether such a person who orders a homicide to be committed is punished by death, just as the one who committed the homicide. For clarity, I premise,

† That a homicide is said in many ways. For there is one who is a causal homicide, and not a formal one: as he who commands, and whose command is executed. He himself is the cause of the homicide, yet he is not a formal homicide: because he does not kill by his own blow, whence he is not properly a sicarius. But by interpretation, as we note in the Digest, *De vi et viarum*, l. §. *quotiens*. And this as to the subtlety of words. But as to the effect of law and fact, he is more than a homicide: because he sins against himself, and another, whose mind he corrupts by commanding. As we note in the Digest, *De infamia*, l. *Athletas*, §. *Pomponius*; and in the Digest, *Ad legem Aquiliam*, l. *Qua actione*, §. *Celsus ait*. Moreover, the commander is said to be the principal of the crime. As in the Digest, *De servo corrupto*, l. *In hoc iudicio*. Therefore, he deserves to be punished. As in the Digest, *De accusationibus*, l. *Non ideo minus*. Also, he who commands truly and properly acts, causally. And he who is the cause of the cause is the true cause of the caused, although he is a mediate cause. As in the Decretals, *De sententia excommunicationis*, c. *Mulieris*; and in the Digest, *De regulis iuris*, l. *Hoc iure*, §. *Deiecit*. Also, the Decree expressly says that he who commands a homicide to be committed: when it is done, is truly and properly a homicide. *De poenis*, Dist. I, *Periculose decipiunt* and c. Some, however, is a formal and causal homicide: as he who kills someone with his own intent and by his own hands. And this one is a homicide speaking most properly. And from this one begins to arise the obligation. As in the Code, *Si reus vel accusator moriatur*, l. 1, and this is what is referred to. The commander is said to be an accessory, and the one shedding blood is said to be principal.

And this is the difference between the doer and the commander: for the delict of the doer stands by itself, but the delict of the commander does not stand by itself; as in D. de furtis, l. Si is qui rem, § Si tu Titium, unless it were such a delict as is consummated by the mere command, as in D. de servo corrupto, l. 1, § Persuadere. In the third way, one is called a formal, and not a causal, homicide: as if a madman or an infant kills another. As in D. de officiis praetoris, l. Divus. Thus, therefore, someone is called a homicide in many ways: because sometimes someone is called, and is, a homicide naturally and truly. But someone is a homicide with regard to punishment by interpretation of the law, as a madman or one who kills justly. For the name of justice removes the delict, because it is its contrary; as in D. quod metus causa, l. Nec timorem, § Proinde; and D. de iustitia et iure, l. Ut vim. From these things it also appears that homicide is sometimes said strictly, sometimes broadly: so as to comprehend, by the infinity of the word, even the commander or the advisor. Now I return to our case. And the decision of the question will rest on this:

Whether the indefinite is equivalent to the universal by interpretation or by the signification of the word; for, if it is by interpretation, the penalty of death ceases in this statute, because everything that arises from interpretation is tacit, not express: as we say in the case of tacit vulgar and tacit pupillary substitutions, as in D. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione, l. iam hoc iure. But that which arises from the signification of the word is express. Now, on this point, some say that the indefinite is equivalent to the universal by interpretation; others say by signification, as in D. de servitutibus urbanorum praediorum, l. si servitus, where it is said that all things of the same reason are totally included by signification. But if one thing is greater than another and different from it, it is not included, as noted by Doctorus in the rubric of D. de regulis iuris, unless such difference contained within itself a connection of the same equity. And then it is included by interpretation, not by signification. And therefore it has no place in statutes prohibiting extensive interpretation, as is the case in the statute in question, as in D. quod vi aut clam, l. aut qui aliter, §. si; and it is supported by D. de minoribus, l. auxilium, §. in delictis, where adultery and that which is punished for adultery are set forth as different in fact. Therefore, speaking with the subtlety of the law, the aforementioned instigator does not come under the penalty of death, because he is a homicide in a certain respect, and in a certain respect not, as noted in c. 1, X. de officio delegati. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether credence should be given to the notary or to the witness who asserts that he never said that which was written down by the notary.
2. What is meant by a vicinal way.
3. Three witnesses prevail over an instrument: and if they are such as to be above all exception, they are not to be tortured.
4. Whether individual witnesses contradicting an instrument are to be tortured, or whether the notary himself is to be tortured first.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A question of forgery arose from a certain document: because the witness stated that he had never said that the way was private, but had only said that it was a common way. The notary, however, says that he wrote legally word for word, as the witness said. But the witness says that the notary wrote falsely, in that he wrote that the witness said that the way was private. And to prove this, he produces two witnesses, who, with the consent of the parties, were present at the examination, together with the notary, who testify that the said witness said that the way was common, and not private. Now the vicar of the Lord Marquis, cognizant of the case, ordered the said witnesses, present, hearing, and understanding, that within eight days they must make all their defense, which they wish. And it must be said that the said witnesses should not be tortured for three reasons. For behold, Robert should not be tortured, because he said what was probable, and true with the giving of a reason:

† because it is that way which is vinalis, through which access is open to neighbors, and not to others, and which leads out only to the properties of neighbors, and not to the public road, as in ff. ne quid in loco publico, l. 1, § viarum, and the following §. And in this manner do the witnesses and ordinary people understand a vicinal way. And the said witness assigns the reason, to which one must adhere, as noted in C. de testibus, l. solam. And even if afterwards the same witness had said that it was his own, it is understood, namely, for his part; not that it is common to me, namely, for my part, as noted in l. 1, C. qui testamento facere possunt. Hence it is fitting that the said statements be reconciled with the said statements, as in extra de testibus, c. cum tu filii. Therefore, the witness would not be understood to be wavering; because the reason is common to the entire testimony, and to that reason one must adhere; because reason has more effect than a mere statement, as I have proved above.

The second reason why witnesses ought not to be tortured is that they fully prove the truth, since three witnesses prevail over a written instrument: as is fully noted in the Institutes, *De inutilibus stipulationibus*, § *Item verborum*; and in the Extravagant Decretals, *De fide instrumentorum*, c. *Cum Ioannes haeremita*; and witnesses who fully prove are not to be tortured, but followed: as in the Extravagant Decretals, *De probationibus*, c. 2. The third reason why they ought not to be tortured is that they are above all exception: as in the Code, *De communi et contrahentium stipulatione*, l. *Optimam*; and noted by Jacobus de Arena and Cynus in the Code, *De falsis*, l. *Si quis decurio*.

† Where, however, the witness who has testified contradicts the instrument, and has no corroborators, the instrument is to be believed rather than the witness: for it has the force of at least two witnesses, and sometimes of more; whereas the witness is singular. As is fully noted in the chapter *Bonae*, extra, *de electione*; in law 1, at the end, ff., *quomodo testis aperiri*; as in C., *de fideicommissis*, law *Quaestionem*; and C., *de fide instrumentorum*, law *In exercendis*. And then, if one ought to begin with torture, it is true that the witness ought first to be tortured, as being a person of lower status, since the notary is a person of authority. But when there are several witnesses against the notary, the witnesses are not to be tortured, as I said above. And so it is in the question proposed. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If a father states in his will, “I leave to my daughter two hundred and fifty [units], given to her as dowry”: whether, if they were never given as dowry, the daughter may claim the will is void on the ground that she was passed over.
2. Whether a void will may be ratified by the daughter.
3. Whether one is deemed to have interfered in another’s affairs, by way of quasi-mandate, arising from a lease.
4. Whether prescription runs against the right to interfere.
5. Whether a profession made before the fisc, namely that one will pay such sums for the inheritance, prejudices the person making it.
6. Whether an heir, who once possessed the goods after the death of the deceased and subsequently ceased to possess them, has a claim for the recovery of the inheritance against the possessor.
7. Whether one who has knowledge that a thing belongs to another may acquire by prescription.
8. Whether the thirty-year prescription for taking possession, or the year for deliberation, or the time for claiming possession of the goods, runs against a son who was ignorant of his father’s death.
9. Whether one possessing as a negotiorum gestor, or his heir, prescribes during that time.
10. The thirty-year prescription is acquired by a possessor in bad faith against the claim for the inheritance.
11. Whether a son who possessed the goods after his father’s death is presumed to have continued possession until the death of the son himself, following the death of the deceased.
12. If you lease a thing today in my name, and I ratify it, you are not presumed to have possessed it retroactively in my name.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A certain M. died thirty-five years ago and more, having made a will, in which he instituted his three male sons as universal heirs; he also instituted his daughter as heir to 250 pounds, which he asserted he had given her as dowry. The said daughter claims the will is null, alleging that she was passed over and that she was never dowered.

† It is asked whether, assuming that she was never dowered, she can declare the testament null, even if the time limits were favorable; or whether, by raising an exception, she declares it null, because the right to raise an exception is perpetual. I answer: A false description added to a certain quantity does not invalidate a legacy. And therefore, if she was dowered, it is well, if a certain quantity is not owed to her. As in C. de falsis causis adiectis in legatis, l. si non designata; and fully noted in ff. de liberis et posthumis heredibus institutis, l. legavit and l. cum scriptum. But this is doubtful: because it is not the intention of the testator. Just as when I bequeath to T. in this manner: I bequeath to T. 10 which I lent. For this legacy is for the purpose of raising an exception, not for bringing an action. As stated in d. l. legavit. Therefore, from this bequest, no action is given to the daughter. As noted in ff. de re vendicata, l. emptor, § ancilla; and in Inst. de legatis, § si debitori. Wherefore, since she is instituted in nothing, she seems to have a complaint of preterition. As noted in ff. de minoribus, l. denique, § sed utrum; and this is true: because she was instituted in a false thing, which is not in the nature of things; but if by right of institution a dead man, or one never born, were left to herself. Hence, not only if a false description, although demonstrable, because it is not in the nature of things, is it necessarily expected.

† However, it must be observed whether this daughter ratified the will or not: for if she ratified it, she cannot claim it to be void. See D. de inoff. test. l. filio praeterito; and D. de leg. praest. l. si duo. Yet this point remains without scruple: for even if she ratified it, the will does not become valid unless the instituted heirs petition for possession of the estate according to the will under civil law. They cannot avail themselves of it on account of the defect of omission: see D. de lib. et posth. l. Gallus, § in omnibus; and C. de contr. tab. l. posthumo; for the strictness of civil law stands in the way. See Inst. de exher. lib. in principio. Although Speculum and the ancient advocates, not proceeding so minutely according to the letter of the law, held that in this case the inheritance is granted by the equity of civil law: see d. l. si duo. Others do not say this is the general rule, but rather that there is a special rule for children, so that in this case they may intervene under civil law. And thus it is always sufficiently equitable: but the common opinion is that the praetorian benefit is necessary here. And the gloss confirms this: C. unde lib. l. certum; and all the moderns commonly hold this view. Therefore, the case of intestacy applies. Another question follows.

† Because the said lady A., as a person joined with G., one of the brothers, leased certain possessions formerly belonging to their common father, asserting that she did so as a procurator and in a procuratorial capacity, and that this procuratorial authority is established by the hand of a named public notary, on a certain day and under a certain consul. Now the question arises: assuming that no intermixture is founded upon these words—and it seems that none is, because what she has clearly protested in her own voice she cannot deny, as stated in C. de non numerata pecunia, l. generaliter. On the contrary, it appears that this confession was made in the absence of G., and therefore it does not prove the matter, as is fully read and noted in l. 1, ff. de interrogationibus et responsionibus actorum, and l. unica, C. de confessis; because although a confession does not require presence and consent, at least tacit, presence is deemed to exist when it is directed through a messenger or letter, as in ff. de deposito, l. publica, §. si; otherwise, if no messenger or letter intervenes between absent parties, as in ff. de liberatione legatorum, l. Aurelius, §. si. And if it is said that this was a case of negotiorum gestio, because it can be ratified, the adversaries respond that the time for ratification does not avail, because thirty years have elapsed, within which the right of ratification and other rights are consumed, as stated in C. de praescriptione triginta annorum, l. sicut.

† Someone will say that the right of mixing is not subject to prescription: as the gloss in l. 1, C. quando non peten. par. states, and the reason is: because a sui heres and a necessary heir is immediately mixed, insofar as it concerns his own advantage. And thus, once he is an heir, he cannot cease to be an heir by the passage of time. See ff. de minoribus, l. et si sine, §. et quod Papinianus. However, the goods could have been properly prescribed by a prior legitimate possessor. But this sister, about whom the question is asked, did not possess legitimately: because she possessed in another’s name, as she herself asserts. And regarding her own intent, she is believed against herself in the very declaration of her intent. See ff. de negotiis gestis, l. Nesenius. But this passage, whether the right of mixing is subject to prescription, is doubtful. For although the first and legal mixing takes place instantaneously, and this initiatively, nevertheless completively it requires will and act: so that this second mixing, which is more perfect, can well be absorbed by prescription of the longest time, according to the opinion of the gloss, as noted in l. licet, C. de iure delictorum.

† Beyond the aforementioned, it is alleged that the said A. declared before the fisc that she would pay the tallages for the said inheritance and for the said G. And the question arises whether the said declaration prejudices her. And it seems that it does not: as in D. de acquisitione rei donatae, l. quae quisque; and C. de donationibus, l. censualis. To the contrary, it seems: because a desire recorded in public acts cannot be corrected: as noted in l. rura, alias iura, C. de omni agro deserto; because the fisc is understood to be a public person, and its presence benefits those who have an interest. Arg. D. de usuris, l. Gayus; and D. de magistratibus conveniendis, l. 1, §. exigere.

† Another case occurred, whether an heir, who once possessed the goods after the death of the deceased, and afterwards ceased to possess them, has a claim against the possessor for the petition of inheritance. And it seems that he does not, as in the Digest, on the petition of inheritance, the law "and not only," § "who if as a buyer." And according to this, the petition of inheritance is an action for acquiring, and does not apply to one who has obtained possession. Which is false: because by its nature it is a real action, which allows anyone who ceases to possess to bring an action at any time. As in the Digest, on oaths, the law "but also if to the possessor," in the beginning, and § "furthermore we see this in the action for the family inheritance," which imitates the nature of the petition. As in the Digest, on the family inheritance, law 1. The aforementioned § "who if as a buyer" does not obstruct, because there the petition of inheritance was altered and novated, just as the Publician action is novated by completed usucapion, and the vindication of the thing applies: so the petition of inheritance, which was applicable for a thing that was not the deceased's, but possessed by him, passes from imperfect to perfect through usucapion completed by the heir, and in the person of the heir ownership is founded: which if the heir pursues the petition of inheritance, he does not intend. But if it is intended solely from the person of the deceased, he properly intends: because the right of the heir is not made worse by the acquisition of ownership. Finally, it should be known,

† That today, both in canon law and in civil law, which does not disdain to imitate the sacred canons: one who has knowledge of another’s thing from the very beginning, so that he never had good faith, does not acquire by prescription, not even a mere exception; because the right to sin cannot be prescribed. As stated in Extra, De praescriptionibus, c. Quoniam omne; and in c. Malefidei, Extra, De regulis iuris, lib. 6; and note the gloss and Cynus in l. 1, § 1, C. De usucapionibus; l. Sequitur, § Si viam. For he who knows that he is bound never prescribes. As in c. Peccatum, De regulis iuris, lib. 6. And this is the truth, unless municipal law and custom expressly introduced this to the detriment of the negligent; because it is not new that one loses his right through negligence. As in l. Non, n., Quibus ex causis maiores; and l. Pupillus, ff., Quæ in fraudem creditorum. Or say, that prescription is either against a right to be acquired: and then good faith of the possessor is not required. As in C., De iure deliberandi, l. Licet. Or against a right already acquired: and the same applies if prescription is made to the prejudice of the dominion of the prescriber. As in the aforementioned § Si viam, because the dominion itself is the cause. But if someone has no cause, nor good faith, then he does not prescribe. And thus l. Si quis emptionis, C., De praescriptione triginta annorum, is corrected by canon law. For the Pope can do this on account of sin. Argument from Extra, De iudiciis, c. Novit. Others say that each law must be observed in its own forum; because lay judges swear to observe laws, not canons, from which they have no jurisdiction; nor can they transgress the mandates of princes, from whom they have jurisdiction. And in municipal statutes this can well be defended; because they have among their people the force of a pact. As noted in C., De decretis decurionum, in the Rubric.

† Another doubt follows, whether prescription runs against a son ignorant of his father’s death for the thirty years required to accept the inheritance. And it seems that it does: because that period is continuous. Say, however, that it does not run: because it is a case of exception. C. de captivis et postliminio reversis, l. nec nos, joined with l. 1, in fine, C. de annali exceptione. Likewise, the year for deliberation does not run: because it is preparatory to the right of acceptance. Therefore, neither does the right of acceptance itself run. As in C. de iure deliberandi, l. cum antiquioribus. And even assuming that the time for acceptance were running, nevertheless the time for claiming possession of the estate does not run, which is advantageous; for in the case where one accepts the inheritance before the praetor, he is deemed to be claiming possession of the estate, and conversely. As in C. de iure deliberandi, l. puberem; ff. de bonorum possessionibus, l. cum quidam, which latter law is very notable for this purpose.

† It is also doubted whether one who possessed as a manager of another’s affairs, or his heir, can prescribe at any time. And say that he cannot, because he does not have true possession. As in D. de petitione hereditatis, l. estiam, § si quis absentis; and C. de praescriptione triginta annorum, l. male agitur; and l. cum notissimi. For it is as if he had done this by mandate of the person whose affairs are being managed, because ratification, before prescription is completed, is deemed to operate retroactively. As in l. si, § si, D. rem rabiem habere. It is doubted,

† Whether prescription runs against the claim for inheritance after 30 years by a possessor in bad faith. And it seems that it does: because it is a mixed action, and consequently personal. And against a personal action prescription runs by mere silence. As noted by Bartolus in the said § si viam. Hence also the unclaimed inheritance of a debtor is prescribed, if not interrupted, and yet the inheritance does not have good faith: because it has none. But say, that as regards the corporeal assets of the inheritance, it is an action in rem, not in personam. As in C. de pet. haer. l. haereditatis.

† It is also asked whether a son, who possessed the goods after the death of his father, is presumed to have continued his possession until the death of the son himself after the deceased. And say, as noted in l. 1, C. de servis fugitivis, where the glossa says that unless an interruption is proven, it is presumed that he continued [possession] after ten years, i.e., civilly. The same is said by the aforementioned Dyonisius in cap. Sine possessione, and it is proven in ff. de usucapione, l. Furtum, § Fundum, even if someone in the meantime held [the property] corporally without the son’s knowledge. On this, note, although [it is stated in] C. de probationibus, l. Siue possidetis.

† Finally, it is asked whether, if you today lease some thing in my name and I ratify it, you are presumed to have possessed it retroactively in my name. And it must be said that no: because from a contingent matter, which relates to various outcomes, no inference follows, as noted in C. unde legi, l. non hoc. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Both Laws, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the will of a mother who passes over her sons and institutes her own mother, and thus the grandmother of the sons, is valid.
2. Whether the passing over of a son by a mother is to be regarded as equivalent to disinheritance.
3. Whether a codicillary clause has any effect when the will is annulled on account of the passing over of a son.
4. An institution in a specific thing is not extended to the whole estate when there is a defect of passing over in the will.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† A certain lady made a will, in which she passed over her sons and instituted her mother as universal heir. And in the will she appended a codicillary clause, namely, that if it should not be valid by the law of wills, it should be valid by the law of codicils; and if it should not be valid by the law of codicils, it should be valid by the law of any last will, and in every way, law, and form by which it can be more valid.

† The question is what is the law. I answer that it must be known that the omission of a mother is regarded as disinheritance: and formerly the will of a mother omitting her son was valid, but a complaint was necessary, as stated in the Institutes, *de inofficioso testamento*, § *mater*. And once the complaint was brought, all legacies and fideicommissa were rescinded, and even the codicillary clause made by whatever words was rescinded, as if made by one who had died intestate, as stated in the Digest, *de inofficioso testamento*, l. *Titia*. But today, according to the most recent law, the Authentica *testamentum in quo mater praeterit filium sine causa* states that it is null by operation of law, as fully noted in the Authentica *de haereditatibus et falcidia*, § *exhaeredatos*, and by Dy. in l. *Gallus* in the great distinction. Hence, without doubt, the will in question is null by operation of law. And therefore, the said mother, instituted as universal heir by her daughter, is not the universal heir, but the son of the testatrix is the heir ab intestato.

But it is doubtful whether the sons of the testatrix are bound to restore the inheritance to their grandmother. And the doubt arises on account of the codicillary clause. And on this point there are two opinions of our predecessors. For the ordinary gloss in the Authent. Ex causa, C. de lib. praet. vel exhaer., holds that the said clause is of no effect if the institution of the heir is void on account of preterition or disinheritance, because the judgment of the testator is unjust. But where the institution is invalid on account of a defect in some other formality, then the said clause would be valid. And on this point the gloss in the said Authent. Ex causa stands firm. And so held all the ancient doctors and advocates. Of the more modern writers, this is held by William of Suzio in l. ult., C. de codicillis. But Master Dino holds the contrary, namely, that restitution of the inheritance may be demanded on account of a fideicommissum, as is fully reported by Cynus in the said Authent., and he notes this in l. 2, ff. de leg. 3. The objection from l. Titia, cited above, does not hold, because that law has been corrected with regard to legacies and fideicommissa, even universal ones, as in ff. ad Trebellianam, l. ita tamen, §. quotiens, by Dino and others; and this appears from the fact that the reason of the said l. Titia has been corrected, namely, the reason that the will is deemed to have been made by a madman; and where the reason of the law is corrected, the substance of the law is corrected. This opinion is held by Bartolus and many modern writers. And therefore this question is very doubtful. I consider that the tacit disinheritance of the mother is vitiated and contrary to natural equity. And therefore, since one way is denied, another way should not be granted. Moreover, I say that no law provides that the said law is corrected in its case, and the correction of laws is to be avoided. The objection from §. aliud quoque capitulum in the Authent. Ut cum de appellatione cognoscitur does not hold, because there it speaks of other clauses of the will, not of the clause of the institution transferred into a universal fideicommissum by a codicillary clause. Moreover, because that clause has been interpreted by the glossators when there is a defect of external formality, for example, of witnesses; or because the inheritance is not entered upon from the will for any other cause than for the cause of preterition or disinheritance. For when the said institution is odious, it should not be aided by interpretation. Whichever opinion you hold, it has many patrons among eminent men. But if you consider authority, the authority of the glossator is greater. In such a conflict of opinions, a settlement between the parties would be good, arg. extra de probat., c. si. It is not doubtful that the said sons claim to have their legitime, whatever may be the case with the codicillary clause, as in C. de inoff. testam., l. omnimodo and l. sancimus, and in the Authent. de triennio et semis, §. 1, coll. 4.

† What if the said mother had been instituted heir to a specific thing? I answer that the said institution cannot be extended to the whole estate on account of the defect of omission. And therefore it is regarded as a simple legacy, and would be valid only with respect to that thing. As noted in l. liberis, ff. de doli. excep. I, Baldus. In the name of Christ, Amen. Assuming that the Prince of Achaea and the Count of Savoy have, as they do, privileges, etc., see in part 1, cons. 146, beginning “tit. princi. Achaię” etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Regarding a testament containing a derogatory clause directed at a subsequent testament to be made, and in which the first testament was derogated: whether it is valid and derogates from the first, if after the second testament, in which said clause was contained, codicils were made, in which the heirs instituted in the first were confirmed. And no. 7, where he concludes that the codicils are valid.
2. That which is free and absolute in revoking cannot be rendered not free.
3. If the mind of the testator is certain, namely that he wished to abide by the last writing, derogatory words do not prejudice the last will.
4. Ioannis Calderinus was a man of great virtue and learning.
5. Ioannes Andreae was the fountain and trumpet of canon law.
6. What the words or phrases "in every way and form" and the like import.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. It is found that A. once made a will, in which he left certain legacies to B., a notary. It is also said that later he made another will by the hand of C., a notary, in which he revoked the first and derogated from any will to be made in the future, adding that he did not intend to add or change anything in the said will, and that it could not derogate from it in any way, and that if he did so, he did not wish it to be valid in any way, nor is it his intention that it should be valid. Finally, he made codicils, in which he confirmed the heirs instituted in the first will, but reduced certain legacies from ownership to usufruct. And he made these codicils by the hand of the aforementioned notary B., referring to the will written by the hand of the said B., as if to that will, from which arises a certain modification of the contents of the second will, in which derogatory words are contained.

† From this it is argued as follows. Derogatory words expressed in a testament invalidate codicils: because a testament is a more solemn expression of will. As stated in D. de legatis 1, l. si mihi et tibi; § in legatis, D. de iure codicillorum, l. diui; § licet, D. de legatis 3, l. si quis in principio. Moreover, an equal revokes an equal: as a testament revokes a testament, and codicils revoke codicils, by reason of derogatory words expressing the testator’s will to be absent in future acts, as appears in the aforementioned laws. And D. de legatis 1, l. si ita scriptum. For what is not considered in the mind does not seem to have been written subsequently. And therefore that which is found to be not last, but nonexistent, is not valid. As D. de suppleto legato, l. labeo; and D. de testamento militis, l. diuus.

On the contrary, it seems and must be considered that either the testator uses derogatory words of power, and such derogation is invalid, because it is impossible by law. For no one can deprive himself of public right, because public right cannot be conferred or taken away by private agreements. And among these is the capacity to make a testament, as noted in D. de testamento, l. si filius; and l. testamenti factio; C. qui testamento facere possunt, l. Senium; and there I said. It is therefore concluded, regarding this point, that no one can deprive himself of the faculty of making a testament, because it is of public right. Also, because it is of law and by law, and written law cannot be derogated from: as D. de legatis 1, l. nemo potest; and D. de legatis 2, l. codicillis, § si.

Or the testator uses derogatory words of future will. And here consider that this derogation revokes enunciative words, not dispositive ones. I declare what I mean: namely, that the last writing is invalid. This is because the testator, by enunciative and protestatory words, intended it not to be valid; and he is presumed to persist in the same will of mind, because what is not changed is not prohibited from standing: as C. de testamento, l. sancimus; D. de probationibus, l. quinquaginta; and l. cum tacitum. For even if the testator commits his will to oblivion, he does not thereby lose the force that depends on prior arrangements. As C. qui testamento facere possunt, l. hac consultissima, § at cum humana fragilitas.

But if the last will contains disposition of words and mind, so that there is an intent to dispose, and this is established: the truth itself revokes the presumption, and the true disposition removes the enunciative words and their effect, just as a protestation is removed by a contrary act; because since no one can deprive himself of power, the will is mutable, notwithstanding any ingenuity or art of words: as D. de locato, l. cum in plures, § locator horrei; and C. de pactis, l. pacta nouissima.

† From which it is concluded that that which is free and absolute in revocation cannot be made unfree. As in C. de pac. l. si; ff. de verb. ob. l. stipulatio hoc modo; C. de sacrosan. eccl. l. 1, and there by Cy. and me. From these another conclusion is inferred,
† And if it is certain as to the mind, that the testator wishes to adhere to the last writing, derogatory words do not prejudice the last will; this was held by Johannes Andreas in his disputation.
† and John of Calderinis after him, who was a man of great virtue and learning. And finally, the aforementioned John.

† The fountain and trumpet of canon law, likewise concluding, held this in c. 1, *De constitutionibus*, Book 6. For now consider more diligently the words of the codicils. Either the testator by codicil wished, decreed, and ordained; and wishes, decrees, and ordains.
