† in every manner, way, right, and form, by which he could and can better do so, etc., and adds that all other things in the said testament, delivered and requested by the said B., shall take effect and be carried out, as they stand. From these words two points are briefly derived. First, the choice of solemn modes and forms: because he said, "in every manner and form." These words are precise: as in l. qui iure, ff. de mili. test. Hence it is as if he had said, "Notwithstanding any words ordered to the contrary." Second, the reason for the efficacy that the testator wished his codicils to have. Thus, he certainly considered the effect: as in ff. quod quisque iur. l. 1. §. haec verba. And therefore, to wish to break the pious last will under the pretext of certain trifles, which are not worth one obol, seems to be of a perverted mind and not in accordance with sound judgment.

† I therefore hold that effect should be given to the said codicils in accordance with the effect which the nature of codicils produces: as in Inst. de ademptione legatorum and the note in C. de legatis, l. datum; and in D. ad Trebellianum, l. si quis priore and l. Scevola; and in D. de iure codicillorum, l. quod per manus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an infant transmits the mother’s inheritance not yet accepted, or restitution in integrum to the legitimate successors. And no. 4.
2. Whether the mere knowledge of the tutor, who did not make an inventory, induces the transmission of the right of deliberation.
3. Whether one is said to have accepted the inheritance by possessing the maternal goods.
4. One who does not seek restitution in integrum within four years is thereafter barred.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Regarding the question whether the maternal inheritance has lapsed

† The inheritance was not accepted by the infant, nor in the name of the infant. Whether the legitimate successors of the infant can demand restitution in integrum on behalf of the infant: there are contrary opinions. For some say that they can, by the law *Qui duos*, in the Digest, *De rebus dubiis*, and there this point is fully examined by Bartolus. It is in the interest of the infant to have a successor and to transmit the goods, as in the Digest, *De acquisitione hereditatis*, law *Pantonius*, and in the Code, *De restitutione militum*, law *Si Valerianus*. Others hold the contrary, as does Lauro de Bellis, because the text in the law *Si infanti*, § *Parente*, and § *Si vero, vel non tutor*, states that it is as if the inheritance had not been offered to the infant from the very beginning; and in that way it comes to those persons who would have been called if the inheritance had not been offered to the infant at all. And thus the letter of the law speaks precisely, and makes no mention of restitution in integrum. And if restitution in integrum were applicable, the Emperor would have made mention of it. And therefore one should not depart from the text. For whatever may be said about other minors, in whom leniency deserves pardon, it is otherwise with an infant, in whom no leniency can be found. Hence we must adhere to the text. And this is one doubt.

† Another doubt arises, because Bartolus states that the knowledge of the tutor, even if he did not make an inventory, induces the transmission of the right of deliberation. Hence, in the name of the infant, the inheritance may be entered upon within the year; because since the transmission of the right of deliberation is a mere favor, it is not required that the tutor have made an inventory, as provided in the last law of the Code, On Tutors and Curators Who Have Not Given Security. Thus, therefore, the legitimate successors of the infant, not by virtue of the edict but by the transmitted right of deliberation, were able to enter upon the inheritance of the infant’s mother, as stated in the Code, On the Right of Deliberation, in the law Cum antiquioribus.

† and they appear to have come to possess the maternal goods: as C. de repudianda hereditate, l. 1; and ff. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. gerit and l. duo fratres. But whatever Bartolus may say, no law in the world states that the mere knowledge of the tutor, who did not make an inventory, induces the transmission of the right of deliberation: namely, because the inheritance was left to an infant; rather, the text is to the contrary. d. l. si infanti, in the word "neglexerit." But Lord Bartolus says that this law today must be limited by l. cum antiquioribus. But that law can rather be adduced to the contrary: because it says that one who is ignorant never transmits the right of deliberation, but an infant: just as a madman, who sees what he ignores: as l. 1 de falsis monimentis and l. 1 ff. de bonis possidendis infantis delata. Moreover, even if the knowledge of the tutor induces this: it is true, because someone acted as tutor; otherwise, if he neither made an inventory nor acted as tutor. as C. de tutoribus et curatoribus qui satisfactionem non dederunt, l. in dubium; and C. ubi tutor, l. veteris. Also, the rule is that nothing is valid which is done by one who does not have legitimate administration. as noted, ff. de iureiurando, l. iusiurandum quod ex conventione, § 1. Hence, one should not depart from the text of the said l. si infanti, § si vero, or let it be noted, if he is a tutor.

† It is therefore necessary to dwell solely on the first point, concerning restitution in integrum. Nevertheless, whatever may be said about this step, this difficult question ceases to apply in our case: because the uncles, who are the legitimate heirs of the infant, could not have entered upon the inheritance in the name of the infant unless they had sought or obtained restitution in integrum.

† which they did not seek, five or six years have already elapsed: hence they are undoubtedly excluded. O. de temp. in integ. rest. l. supervacuam. Nor does possession of the goods avail them, where restitution has not been granted: as C. unde leg. l. non hoc, and l. 1, C. de iure delib. and leg. and not. ff. quibus ex caus. maior. l. si is cuius rem. The question is therefore settled, whether restitution is available by lapse of time: but if the time had not elapsed, the opinion of the doctors is divided for and against. For we do not find that restitution is available on account of the facility of a minor, or on account of a fortuitous event. As d. l. qui duos. But the natural death of an infant does not presuppose the facility of a minor, nor a fortuitous event: because that which happens naturally is not counted among fortuitous events. As ff. de cond. ob caus. l. si pecuniam. §. si. What I said of the tutor, I say likewise of the paternal grandfather, adhering to the text of the said l. si infanti, presupposing that the said grandfather died with one infant dead and another surviving, no inheritance having been accepted. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A contract concluded by an adult is validated by an oath.
2. Whether a spendthrift may contract with an oath by decree of a judge or curator.
3. In notarial acts, a declaratory judgment is not required, except as a precaution.
4. Whether a contract is confirmed by an oath if the contracting party swears as an adult, and not as a spendthrift.
body:
In the Name of Christ, Amen. A certain G., an adult, requested that a general curator be appointed for him, to which the judge appointed a curator in the following words: “Considering and knowing that the said G. is dissolute and prodigal, and such a person who spends both what ought to be spent and what ought not to be spent, and who is easily induced to alienate his goods and to bind himself to all and singular things that any cunning man might desire; and because it is better to prevent the wound than to seek a remedy after the cause has been wounded; and lest the said G. be reduced to want and poverty, and have a sad outcome, in every manner, way, right, and form by which he could best do so, the judge appointed, constituted, and decreed Master F., present there and consenting, as curator for the said G., saying thus: ‘I give and entrust to you, Master F., present and willing, the general care of the said adult G., as well as the care, administration, and governance of that care, of his person, rights, goods, and all his assets. And I will and command that you give security, take an oath, and make an inventory of the goods of the said G., and all other and singular things that are to be done in such a case, the form of law being observed; in such a way and manner that the said G. in no way, nor by any form, right, or cause, may or shall be able to sell, donate, or alienate his goods, nor in any way bind himself or his goods to anyone without the license, authority, and consent of the said Master F., his curator. And whatever is done by the said G. without the license of his said curator shall be null and void in every way, right, or cause.’”

It is also alleged that the said curator did not take any oath, although this was commanded to him by the judge and imposed by law; and in the same manner, he did not make any inventory. And thus, by operation of law, he lacked the power of administration, as noted in *l. legitimationis*, D. de legitimis tutoribus, in the beginning.

It is also alleged that the said G., an adult and prodigal, with the authority of such a curator as he was, made many contracts, so that he was reduced from a large patrimony to nothing. In some cases, a judicial decree intervened; in others, it did not. An oath also intervened, in which he swore not to contravene in any way or cause.

It is also alleged that he prodigally consumed all the money he received from the said contracts, so that at the present time of the trial, he is found to be richer in nothing.

The question is therefore whether his legitimate heir may validly claim the goods thus and so alienated.

† And for the clarity of what is to be said, it must be premised that sometimes one is an adult only; and then contracts celebrated by him are validated by oath, fear and fraud being set aside. And this effect, namely the validation of the contract, passes to the successors. For such an oath, solemnly taken, represents him as being of full age, as in the Authentica *Sacramenta* (C. 2.19.1) and in the Corpus, from which it is derived, and as noted in l. 2, C. de rescind. vend.

† Sometimes one is merely a prodigal. And then there are three cases. The first is when he has been declared a prodigal by sentence, and a curator has been appointed to him as to a prodigal. The second is when he has been declared a prodigal, and his property has been interdicted; yet no curator has been appointed, or one less suitable has been appointed, or one suitable has been appointed: nevertheless, he has not given sufficient security, has not sworn, has not made an inventory. For these matters are equivalent. And in these two cases, if we inquire whether an oath gives support to a contract, it must be said that it does not; because the oath of a prodigal is equated with the oath of a minor under tutelage. As noted by Jacobus de Arena in *l. qui habet*, D. de tutel., and Bartolus in D. de verb. oblig., in *l. is cui bonis*. For the oath does not remove prodigality, but rather increases it. Moreover, the decree that has been appended in such alienations is null by operation of law; because in the interposition of such a decree many solemnities are required, which have not intervened. As in D. de reb. eic., *l. magis puto*, § *non passim*; and D. de transact., *l. cum hi*, § *si praetor*; and *l. 1*, C. de praediis curial., lib. 10. The third case is when he has not been declared a prodigal, nor has his property been interdicted by a judge, nor has a curator been appointed. And then it matters: either he is a notorious prodigal by the notoriety of the fact. Then there are differing opinions, because some say that this notoriety is equated with a sentence. As noted by the gloss and Petrus in D. de testam., *l. is cui bonis*. Because one cannot be seen to contract in good faith with him, whom one knows will consume his estate on nefarious or reckless uses. As in D. de usucap. pro empt., *l. si qui cum sciret*. But the contrary is held by the gloss and Bartolus in D. de verb. oblig., *l. is cui bonis*, by *l. Iulianus*, D. de cura furios., and notably in the same title, *l. 1*. For notoriety is not equated with a sentence, but with proof, according to Bartolus.

But it is commonly held in the case of notoriety that such a rule applies, namely that in matters of notoriety a declaratory judgment is not required, except as a precaution. As stated in *l. emptorem*, in the beginning, D. de actionibus empti et venditi; and as noted in *l. at qui natura*, § *cum me absente*, D. de negotiis gestis; and in *l. 1* and *l. j*, C. qui et adversus quos. To this effect is the general principle that to add a demonstration to a thing already demonstrated is futile. As stated in *l. 1*, at the end, D. de dote praelegata. This is clear to you from the converse case. Suppose, for instance, that a person has been interdicted as a spendthrift, and he notoriously returns to sound and upright habits without any decree, just as a madman returns to his senses, since even in lucid intervals he does not need a curator. As stated in C. de cura furiosi, *l. cum aliis*. If he is not a manifest spendthrift, contracts entered into with him are valid, unless he was induced to contract by fraud, because neither the law nor the minister of the law, nor any natural or civil reason, prohibits him; otherwise it would be futile. *l. faceret mentionem* speaks of the interdiction by the judge and the appointment of a curator. Yet it would be rash to say so, according to the aforementioned *l. Iulianus*, D. de cura furiosi, and according to *l. si sciens*, D. de contrahenda emptio.

It now remains to proceed to the third principal case, namely, that when a person is an adult and a prodigal, and it is certain that a curator must be appointed for him as for an adult, because this is an ordinary curatorship, but not as for a prodigal, because the nature is rather considered than the accident, as in *l. qui habet*, D. de tutelis, and there by Bartolus and others. Therefore, it may be doubted whether, since he contracts as an adult and not as a prodigal, his oath should confirm the contract. And for clarity, it must be premised that although he has a curator only as an adult, nevertheless the judge can prohibit administration and alienation for two reasons, namely, on account of age and on account of prodigality. Therefore, the oath is not valid, because if the oath of one who suffers only from the defect of prodigality is not valid, much less is the oath of one who suffers from a double defect, namely, of age and prodigality. Moreover, if the above-mentioned document is carefully observed, the judge wisely appointed a curator as for an adult; however, he interdicted the goods not only as for an adult, but as for a prodigal, because so the document states, which must be followed. And thus, concluding from the first to the last, the said oaths are void by operation of law. For a contract is made against good morals with a prodigal to whom administration of his goods is interdicted, and therefore the oath is not valid, as in *c. non est obligatorium*, X. de re iuranda, lib. 6. Nor could the contracting parties claim ignorance, because one who contracts with someone as such is presumed to know his quality, as in D. de regulis iuris, *l. qui cum alio*. Nor must it be omitted that contracts initiated by the authority of those who are not elected or created by law are not valid, as in D. de iureiurando, *l. iusiurandum quod ex conventione*, § *pupillus*, and D. de negotiis gestis, *l. qui aliena*, § *quamquam*. From the foregoing, it is concluded that the said contracts and obligations are void by operation of law, the oath being in no way valid, neither by civil law nor by canon law, because the prodigal is not understood to consent, as in D. de condictione indebiti, *l. interdum*, and D. de fideiussoribus, *l. Marcellus*, and D. de iureiurando, *l. tutor*, § *prodigus*, and D. si certum petatur, *l. certae condictionis*, § *quoniam*, and in C. de cura, § *furiosi*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The leasing of ecclesiastic things may be made for up to nine years, and not beyond, unless with certain solemnity. And what if the annual contract is one for the entire period of several years, whether it can be made simultaneously.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The leasing of church property may be made for a period up to nine years, provided it is done in good faith; but after nine years it cannot continue unless it is made with the solemnity required for the alienation of church property, as in c. Dudum, de rebus ecclesiae non alienandis, lib. 6, and as noted in c. 1, de restitutione in integrum. It must therefore be said that the said contract is to be upheld for up to nine years. Nor does it matter that the abbess was removed, provided that collusion or fraud is not proven, as in D. de minoribus, l. Aemilius Largianus. And it is established in Auth. de non alienando, § Alienationis, with the following § Seu complexive, whether it was made distributively or collectively, provided that it is contained in the same instrument, so long as the same document contains the whole; thus, that which cannot be done by a pact to renew, unless it is a new contract and in itself, D. de legato 2, l. Codicillis, § 1. From this it is concluded that if no deceit or fraud has intervened, the contract is to be upheld until the expiration of the decade; nor is the utility to be hindered under the pretext of detriment, as in D. de minoribus, l. Etsi sine. Furthermore, to clarify this point, it is premised that sometimes an annual contract is one for the entire period of several years, which occurs when there is a single annual stipulation. And then, that which cannot be done simultaneously cannot be done with a reduction of years; because the periods are joined, whether there is a repeated agreement or not; because whatever is done with repetition is one and the same. Nor can it be reduced by verbal division through real plurality; because there is one subject and one intention. D. de verbis obligatis, l. Si stichum, § Stipulatio; D. de donationibus causa mortis, l. Senatus, § Finis. Nor can any art of words or caution be used to make one thing into many; nor can fraud be committed against the law in the conception of living and dividing speech; because whenever there are multiple statements for one thing, there is only one on both sides. D. de evictione, l. Qui libertatis. The objection from D. de verbis obligatis, l. Scire debemus, does not hold, because that is true only if one part of the extremes contains a defect, as we say when a donation is made beyond the legitimate sum. For the division of words does not divide the disposition, lest it make lawful that which is not lawful under a summary, as noted in l. Nomen, § 1, de legato 3, and l. Si libertus, § 1, D. de iure patronatus. Nor should one be circumvented. l. Oratio, D. de transactionibus; l. Cum hi, § Si cum lis. Hence, that clause stating that there are as many contracts as there are years is not valid in the alienation of church property, as noted by Dy. in l. Codicillis, § 1, de legato 2. And consider that every time that is prorogued is joined as a term from which the substantive act proceeds, and by the accession of time it becomes one and the same. D. de precario, Sed si manente. From which it follows that if nine years are added to two years, the authority of the contract ends when the nine years are completed from the day of the first agreement, because that which cannot be done principally cannot be done by prorogation. For whenever the prorogation is of the same form and nature, it is one and the same. As noted in c. Hi qui auctoritate, de praebendis, lib. 6. And if it were not of the same quality, a long time would have to be taken from its beginning. D. de locato, l. Cum in plures, § 1, dicta. From which it follows that an agreement for perpetuity is not valid, because that which is temporary by form and temporary by nature cannot be drawn into perpetuity, as in D. de pactis, l. Epistola, § Finis. From this it appears that by the extension of time there is not another contract, but a certain continuation, unless the law repels it. And because the beginning shows its end, both formal and temporal, recourse must be had to the original production of the act, and from then on it must be counted; because times continue in natural force. D. de verbis obligatis, l. Cum stipulatus sim mihi a Proculo. However, if the renewal were proper, i.e., novatory, and by operation of law, because this act was between the parties, then a new consideration would arise from the new contract, to be begun and terminated, as follows. D. de pactis, l. Si unus, § Pactus; and D. de praetoria stipulatione, l. Valerianus; and l. 4, D. de damno infecto, per Bartolus, D. de arbitris, l. Si cum dies, in principio; per Cynus. One and the same thing therefore appears, either by reason of the context in time or by reason of the continued consent in the mind. D. de pactis, l. Iuris gentium, § Quinimo. But here the continued consent in the mind appears through successive leases, as proved above. Therefore, it is to be considered one and the same contract, which, in that which exceeds nine years, being contrary to canon law, is not to be observed. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an inheritance, according to its proper meaning, is said to exist after it has been acquired by an extraneous heir, or mixed by a sui heres, or fixed by a necessary heir, or whether that which is in the power of being acquired or acknowledged is called an inheritance.
2. A statute providing that no woman shall marry with an inheritance outside the jurisdiction, etc., and how it is to be understood.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It is asked whether the term “inheritance,” according to the proper meaning of the word, is used after it has been entered upon by an extraneous heir, or mingled by a necessary and sui iuris heir, or fixed by a necessary heir. Or whether that inheritance which is in the power of being entered upon or acknowledged, and which has not yet been united and reduced to a single patrimony with the goods of the heir through entry, mingling, or operation of law itself, is called an inheritance. And this question seems to be determined: first, from the definition of inheritance; second, from the decision of the glossa ordinaria; third, by living reason. The law states that inheritance is the right of succeeding. But this word “succeeding” signifies the future. For he who has succeeded does not have the right of succeeding, but the right of having succeeded, or of retaining. As stated in l. 1, in principio, ff. de bonis possessoribus. Secondly, it is proven by the glossa ordinaria, which says that inheritance is also called such when not yet entered upon, as in ff. de acquisitione possessionis, l. 1, §. veteres. Thirdly, it is proven by living reason, because the inheritance represents the person of the deceased. Therefore, the inheritance is not that of a living person, except abusively, or unless it is understood as having once been, as in l. eius qui in provincia, ff. si certum petatur, in principio. And the foregoing are confirmed by the differences that exist between inheritance taken in the proper sense and in the improper sense: as in ff. de stipulationibus servorum, l. servus communis Mevii, and l. ususfructus.

To the contrary, it seems that inheritance is called such after it has been entered upon. Suppose: I have entered upon the inheritance of Titius. Then I say: I sell to you the inheritance of Titius. Is this not proper language both in law and in fact? Certainly so, as in l. venditor, and throughout, ff. de hereditate vel actione venditionis; ff. de donationibus, l. hereditatem; Codex and ff. de petitione hereditatis, throughout. Otherwise, it would be impossible to sell or donate an inheritance not yet entered upon, as in l. si mulier, §. ex asse, ff. de iure dotium. Because, by selling and alienating, the inheritance is informed by the owner, since it necessarily includes the entry upon the inheritance, as in Institutiones, de hereditatibus qualiter et quibus differant, §. si; and ff. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. pro herede, §. Papinianus.

We can speak of inheritance in two ways only: one way, insofar as it is vacant from the person of the heir and represents the person of the deceased, and then it is not called entered upon, because it represents the shadow of the deceased, and not a real person. In the second way, inheritance is called the goods themselves, and then it is called the inheritance of a living person, and in the dominion of a living person, as in l. his verbis, ff. de hereditate; Institutiones. For inheritance is the same as dominion, and dominion belongs to the living. For truly, death dissolves all dominion, as in Authentica de nuptiis, §. disponat. Because, to the point at hand, sometimes we speak of disposing of an inheritance in habit and act, and it is understood as entered upon. Sometimes we speak of a certain provision for disposing or deliberating, and it is understood as to be entered upon. The first consists in administration, and therefore it cannot be understood except of an inheritance that has been entered upon.

† And thus it must necessarily be understood. The statute of Milan. Or say more broadly, the words state, "no woman shall marry with an inheritance," which can be explained in three ways. In one way, that the inheritance is given as a dowry. In another way, that it is not given, but comes accessory and tacitly, as noted in l. mulier, ff. de iure dotis. In a third way, as we say, this woman is peculiated, as in l. si chorus, de legatis 3. Also, this woman is dowered, that is, she has sufficient means from which she can provide a dowry: as in l. cum plures, §. pe., ff. de administratione tutorum. Thus, in the case at hand, a woman with an inheritance, i.e., having property, shall not marry outside [the family]. And so the word "with an inheritance" comes from the part of the subject, not from the part of the adjunct. And thus the statute is appropriate and disposes of our case, namely, of an inherited estate. And so it must be strictly observed. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that a woman could not contract without the presence of her husband and two close relatives, if the husband has absented himself and it is unknown where he is, whether the woman may contract.
2. Whether a woman may recover her dowry if the husband has been absent for a long time and is presumed dead.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The statute of the commune of Pavia provides that a wife cannot contract without the presence and consent of her husband and two of her close relatives.

† The husband has absented himself, and it is unknown where he is. The question is whether [the wife] may contract. I answer that if the husband has been absent abroad for a long time, and it is unknown where he is, [the wife] may contract; because the husband, by thus absenting himself, makes himself alien to presence: as in D. de fideiussoribus, lib. ult., l. si alieno, § 1. Moreover, this is so in order to avoid an absurdity. For the statute ought to be understood as applying to that husband whose presence can be had; because he is in the same domicile, or in a place where he can be required to exhibit his presence. Furthermore, this statute was made in favor of women; therefore it ought not to be turned to their detriment: as in l. 2, D. de lege commissoria, and C. de legibus, l. quod favore. For it would be absurd that, if utility or necessity is at hand, the wife could not contract these goods. We have a similar case in another matter, as appears above: D. si certum petatur, l. cum filius; C. de annua exceptione, l. ut perfectius; C. de senatus consulto Pegasiano, l. si; D. de iure dotis, l. profectitia, in principio; D. de iudiciis, l. si longius; C. de episcopalis audientia, l. tam dementis. But if the husband were in a nearby place, his presence ought to be awaited: as in c. sciendum, in fine, de consuetudine recedendi a feudo.

Secondly, it is asked: this husband remained absent for a long time and was presumed dead; the wife recovered her dowry, or someone having a claim from her did so, and a sentence was rendered: whether it is valid? I answer thus: because the dowry was sufficient in the case of restitution, since the husband does not bear the burdens of marriage, as in C. de iure dotium, l. ubi adhuc. I, Baldus.

In the Name of Christ, Amen. It is manifest from the most firm authorities of Divine Scripture, confirmed in the New and Old Testaments, that natural law prohibits usury, and so forth. See in the third part, consilium 449. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus of Saxoferrato, having been requested by the magnificient Lord Carlo Malatesta.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether it is permitted to entrust or give money to a merchant for the purpose of receiving a share of honest profit.
2. What is called a partnership contract.
3. What kind of contract this is, and whether it is permitted, if I give money to a merchant so that he gives me eight per hundred from the profits he makes with the money; and what if the merchant loses the money, whether he is bound to restore it. No. 4.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It seems to be lawful and permitted to entrust money to a merchant for the purpose of receiving a share of honest profit: as is stated in the extrajudicial decretals, *De donationibus inter virum et uxorem* and *De donationibus post divortium restitutis*, chapter *Per vestras*. Explaining this passage there, Bernardus says: If he converts it into an honest partnership. Hence, he understands that text in the context of a social contract.

† It is said that a social contract exists when the purpose is to share loss and profit. D. 17,2,1, *Si non fuerint*. And therefore Goffredus says in his Summa, under the title *De usu*, *Verius autem*, and in the chapter *Vis dare pecuniam tuam naviganti*, or to one going to the fairs, or to another merchant, without sin. You provide the money, and the other provides personal labor. For often what is lacking in money is supplied by labor. D. 17,2,5, § 1. And you share the particular losses and profits. This is Goffredus. Therefore, where there is no sharing of risk, there is no partnership: as in the aforementioned law *Si non fuerit*, § *Finis*.

† and consequently it is necessary that this be another contract: I give money to a merchant, so that from the profits which he makes with the money he gives me eight per hundred. For the gain of the money can be greater for such a merchant, and it can be less, and it can be equal. Hence, from the event of profit, if he trades more, it is profit: thus he will not be able to say it is compensation for the money. For even in a true partnership, the capital is safe, namely in a favorable outcome, such that what remains is divided. But the capital is not divided; rather, it is assigned back to the giver in full. As is fully read and noted in l. 1, C. pro socio, by the gloss, which says that this is observed by custom. And by Jacobus de Arena and Cynus, and they also say that this is the case in law. I answer: this contract is either a contract of loan (mutuum); and then whatever is added to the principal is usury. ff. si cert. peta. l. rogasti. §. si tibi. Or it is a deposit, and the same applies; because it passes into a credit, with ownership transferred. l. dies sponsaliorum. ff. de posthu. and l. Lucius. Nor can it be a contract of mandate; because the mandatary ought not to receive profit, but must also restore the entire profit, and not retain it for himself. Hence it is not a mandate if he receives gain; because a mandate must be gratuitous. ff. mandati. l. 1.

Here it must be considered whether this merchant, if he had lost the money, would be bound to restore it. And it seems that he is so bound, as in *Incendium*, D. *Si certum petatur*. To the contrary, it seems, as in *L. 1*, C. *Pro socio*, because he is bound only to his labor, not to the money. But that law speaks of a contract of partnership. Here, however, this money is not a partnership, because the entire dominion has been transferred to this merchant. But it favors the merchant more that he is bound if the money is lost, D. *De praescriptionibus*, *L. Titius*, § *Sed nec ipsius*. Since, therefore, the risk is on the giver and not on the receiver, the pact seems to be lawful. Argumentum, D. *Nautici conductio*, *L. Periculi*. Moreover, since the money was given simply for use, a loan (*mutuum*) is presumed, as noted in D. *Si certum petatur*, *L. Cum quid*. And thus the risk is the merchant’s, as in *Incendium*, even if the money is lost by fortuitous accident. Hence the money is always safe for the creditor, and of this he is certain. It is otherwise in a partnership. For he is not certain of his capital unless things go prosperously; if fortune turns adverse, it perishes. Therefore, presupposing that the merchant’s money is in doubt, but that the giver’s money is certain to be restored to him, the contract is defective. And a defective contract is considered usurious, according to Hostiensis, as noted by Archidamus, 14 q. 3, c. *Usura*. To this also contributes the form of the words, “eight per hundred,” because thus usury is accustomed to be made in a partnership; yet a certain quantity cannot be fixed. But a certain quantity thus, as in the said law *Si non fuerit*. And it contributes, D. *Si certum petatur*, *L. Lecta*, with similar cases. And the Lord Recuperatus of San Miniato, for this reason, ordered that certain quantities of florins be restored to certain merchants, being guided by a subtle conscience. For even if that question were doubtful in law, nevertheless good men in the forum of conscience take the safer side. To this it contributes well, as noted in D. *Pro socio*, *L. Cum duobus*, § *Ex facto*, in the gloss beginning *I. Quotitati*. But the merchant does well if he does not demand to the letter, and is discreet in demanding. I, Baldus.

In the Name of Christ, Amen. Two brothers stood together for a long time, and they possessed all goods in common together, and received the fruits, etc. See in the third part, consilium 452, beginning "duo fratres."

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The form of the interrogatories is at the discretion of the judge, just as it is within his discretion to determine whether it is equitable to interrogate in order to cut short the litigation, and thus whether anyone is compelled to take an oath or not.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The statute of Perugia provides that if the plaintiff wishes to tender an oath to the defendant regarding the cause, or the debt, or the defendant to the plaintiff, the judge may compel him to swear, etc. In the present case, P. deposited five florins with M. and is seeking their recovery from him; the latter, in his response, states that he owes nothing to the said P. Thereupon, P. requests the judge to interrogate the defendant under oath as to whether he received the said deposit from him. The defendant declares that he is unwilling to respond in this manner, but only as to whether he owes the sum or not.

† It is asked whether one ought to be compelled. I answer that wherever equity moves the judge, the judge may interrogate. See Digest 4.15.1 (*Ubiique*), under the title *De interrogatione et responsione actoris et rei*. And just as it is within his discretion whether it is equitable to interrogate for the purpose of proceeding to trial, so too is the form of the interrogatories within his discretion. See Digest 12.2.1 (*Ius iurandum*), under the title *De iureiurando*, and § *Si de qualitate* of the same law. Let us suppose that you deposited ten with me, to be returned to you in secret: if the judge has this knowledge, he ought not to interrogate you extra ordinem as to whether you received it, but as to whether you ought to return it. But if the judge has contrary indications from certain signs, he may properly interrogate regarding the fact; in which case one ought not to respond regarding the obligation, but regarding the fact. But if the indication were established according to the ordinary procedure, one ought to respond legitimately to the positions in the proper form; but extra ordinem it is within the judge’s discretion, as I have said. And the gloss in *Ubiique* refers to the obligation. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How an instrument is to be recognized, whether it is simulated. And no. 5.
2. It is forbidden to the Minor Brothers to elect, declare, accept, and declare to whom the rights of money were to be entrusted. And no. 7.
3. The declaration does not endure after a year, nor should it be made without the other party being cited.
4. Whether the power of declaring given by the parties to someone can be revoked by them.
5. [Continuation of point 4]
6. Parties of uncertain identity cannot contract, just as they cannot stipulate.
7. One may compromise with a Minor Brother regarding matters that pertain to the disposition of money.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Regarding the principal instrument, it must be examined whether it is valid or not. And certainly, the said instrument is not valid, neither by divine nor by human law, canonical or civil. And this for three reasons: first, on account of simulation; second, on account of impossibility; third, on account of form and matter.

† Regarding the first point, that the aforementioned instrument was simulated and that no money was involved: this appears from the confession of the parties, made in M. 61. And if it is said that in the said instrument mention is made of another cause, namely a deposit, and of another quantity, namely fifty florins, with due respect to those who say so: they do not speak well; because the said confession is general as to causes, since the words state “the said cause, or any other whatever,” and as to sums, since the words state “the said quantity, or another.” And therefore simulation is clearly apparent from the confession of the contracting parties. For no proof is more certain or more valid than that by the confession of the parties. C. de non num. per. l. generaliter, ver. unusquisque enim; and in the same title, l. in contractibus, in principio; nor even if one wishes, as noted by Innocentius, de immut. eccl., c. quia plerique, there: “for even if it were known, etc.,” where he places our case and determines it according to the letter. And this instrument has no doubt, nor should it suffer that such licit extortions be made. ff. de off. praesid., l. illicitas, in principio. Moreover, that no money was involved, and thus the contract was notoriously simulated, is evident from the quality of the persons. For this Brother Cola Marra Basis—I speak as I have been informed—was first a certain remitted person having nothing, extremely poor and naked; second, he was offered to the Holy Spirit of Rome; third, he was a monk of Saint Benedict; and in every state he had nothing, let alone three thousand lire. ff. de statu lib., l. cum heres, in principio, there: “as if he had given a thousand to the heir.” Hence, with what face and with what conscience this is done, I do not know; and it proceeds contrary to both divine and human law, as well as contrary to the good office of the praesid, as stated in the aforementioned l. illicitas, and by Innocentius, de off. vicar., c. 1. Secondly, I say that this contract did not hold from the beginning on account of impossibility.

† For Brother John of the Order of Friars Minor could not be elected, nor could he speak, accept, or declare to whom the rights to the money were to be entrusted. For this is entirely forbidden to the Friars Minor, because by this means a way could be opened to holding money, since he would declare his friend and the money would come through his hands into the hands of a Friar Minor: which totally contradicts the Rule of the Minorites. Indeed, fraud is presumed through an interposed person; this is expressly stated in c. Exiit, Extra, de Paradiso; and in c. Exiit qui seminat, and de Sepulturis, Dudum, §. Verum ibi facturi; and c. In cle, and ff. de Donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. Mulier. For on account of the prohibition of the law, a simulation of fraud is presumed. ff. de Probationibus, l. Qui testamentum. This is expressly posited by Cynus in l. Quidam decedens, ff. de Administratione tutorum. Moreover, it is certain that every Friar Minor is a religious who can accept no secular office and one foreign to the offices of his order; nor can he declare anything without the license of his superior, since he does not have the will to will or not to will, as in c. Religiosus, de Testibus, lib. 6.

† Moreover, this declaration could not have been made after the lapse of a year, as noted by Bartolus in the law *Si quis arbitratu*, Digest, *De verbis obligatis*, although he elsewhere says otherwise; I do not care about this. Moreover, this declaration could not have been made without the other party being cited, as noted by Bartolus in the same place, and he also determines this by reasoning in his consilia. And this is the true fact and just. Furthermore, Vagnolus died long before, and thus the commission had expired according to some, although this does not please Speculum; and therefore I do not care about this either, just as a mandate for reinstatement expires upon the death of the mandator, Digest, *De iurisdictione omnium iudicum*, law *Et quia*; and also an arbitration agreement, Digest, *De arbitris*, law *Sed si interpella*.

† Moreover, by another reasoning it is manifest that the declaration of this minor brother was invalid, because although he declared, the parties revoked the contract and thus removed his power to declare, which they could do. D. de verb. oblig. l. qui Romae; §. Flavius, D. de cond. ob causam; l. si pecuniam; §. si servum; and D. de serv. expor. l. si quis hac. And this is as clear as the Gospel, nor could the contracting parties agree that they should not be allowed to repent: for by common consent, notwithstanding a prior agreement, it is lawful to repent. C. de pact. l. pacta neuissima; D. de solut. l. stichum; §. naturalis; D. de reg. iur. l. nihil tam naturale. And derogatory words regarding power, since power is introduced by public law, avail nothing according to all learned authorities. D. si quis in pr. testam. D. de leg. 3.

† Moreover, it must be known that when someone counts out his money in his own name and stipulates for himself, as this simulated and frivolous instrument states, and thus the pact whereby the stipulator and the counter are bound to assign their rights to another, even if the instrument were true, before the rights have been assigned, and also afterwards, except in three cases, the assignor may refuse to confess and to release the debtor. C. de noua. 3. ff. de pact. l. si cum emptore. If this can be done after assignment, then much more so when no assignment has been made; for now that the obligation has been removed, assignment is impossible. ff. de sol. l. modestinus. and l. stichum. §. si mandato. and no. ff. manda. l. papinia. Here, certainly, in our case, no assignment was made nor could it be made. And therefore it is not a matter for discussion here whether, when the assignor is not found, one can sue usefully without assignment, because here assignment is impossible by law; this impossibility is clear, and thus it does not obstruct. C. de acti. et obli. l. i. which speaks of casual impossibility of fact, not of law. For no legal fiction adapts itself to a case that is impossible by law, as noted in l. talis scriptura de lega. 1. Furthermore, assignment is impossible because it lacks a title. Furthermore, Guido was added to the solution, not to the obligation, unless an assignment had been made, if we were to say that the contract and declaration are valid, which is not true, and such an addition can be revoked by the consent of the parties. ff. de consti. pecu. l. sed et si §. si vero. And therefore, to that which Guido wishes to know, it is answered that he has no right to see my [opinion]. Nevertheless, if another sees better than I do, I submit myself to law and reason, which I gladly follow in myself as in others. Furthermore, Guido wrote to me in good faith as a friend, and therefore I do not wish that this should harm him in any way, that this money was his father's. And although this is not possible, it does not occur to anyone's mind, because Vagnolus was so wise a man as to be in the duchy and so cautious. Nevertheless, if this were so, he could act even less: for just as one acts against the heirs of Jacob, so conversely there would be conversion or confusion and collation. That also is manifest, that converts cannot contract under such a form. l. 1. §. si seruus. communis. ff. de stip. ser. Still, regarding the very body of the writings, we shall found defenses that are truthful and clearer than light.

† For in that very instrument, the contracting parties could not have made an agreement with those unnamed persons. As stated in §. alteri, since no one received anything on behalf of that uncertain, ignorant, and absent person, the pact is not valid. D. de solutionibus, l. si cum Cornelius. Cynus states this literally in C. de probationibus, l. ad probationem. Nor can one stipulate for an absent person of uncertain identity, unless in a procuratorial or managerial capacity, even if one wishes to benefit another absent person. This is expressly noted in D. de donationibus, l. hoc iure, §. si quis dederit. Nor can a father stipulate for his son that the father himself will pay, just as he cannot promise to the son himself. D. ad Trebellianum, l. Imperator. Therefore, a father cannot make an agreement that rights against the father himself, arising from the father’s provision and thus from a profectitious cause, be assigned to the son, except in the case of a dowry. D. familiae erciscundae et de acquisitione et obligatione, l. actiones adversus. Furthermore, a father cannot stipulate for his son as if he were a stranger, as is the case here where no quality of filiation is expressed in the instrument, as fully noted by Bartolus in D. de verbis oblig., l. quod dicitur patrem, and is the ordinary gloss in D. de solutionibus, l. stichum, §. quaesitum. This is fully read and noted in D. de pactis, l. si tibi, §. si pactus. And this is most true, like the Gospel, that nothing is sought for an absent person through a contract, unless someone intervenes in a managerial capacity. As noted in D. de legatis 1, l. huiusmodi, in principio, where there is an express gloss, and in C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, l. illud, in the ordinary gloss, and noted in l. 1, D. de stipulationibus servorum, in the ordinary gloss. And it is most certain by another reason from the form of the instrument, because the words say “to whomever person and to the same brother he shall say.” But Brother John said nothing to the same brother, as appears in divine scripture: “Say to his disciples, and to Peter,” and this is the ordinary gloss literally. D. de legatis 2, l. miles ad sororem, in principio. D. licet cum fideicommissum, because the testator does not speak, since he is absent. Since therefore he to whom the declaration was committed did not observe the form of the present instrument, his declaration did not hold by the law itself. As expressly read and noted in D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. si quis mihi bona, §. si coram. There is another reason taken from the words of the instrument which begin there “and if he shall have contravened” until the end: which reason is most certain and most true from the tenor of the charter; let us examine this third part of the instrument diligently. And it is to be noted that this third part begins with a contradiction, namely “if he shall have contravened.” And therefore the one to be named, whom Guido asserts, was placed in a condition, if a contravention shall have occurred, if Brother Cola shall have done against Vagnolo contrary to the above pacts. And under this condition the instrument speaks until the end, because this condition is general to all subject clauses and joined to this; this appears from the reading of the writing: it does not need proof but the reading of the fundamental instrument. D. de iure et facto ignorato, l. regula, §. 10. D. de fundo instrato, l. cum delationis, §. asinam. Now it must be seen whether Brother Cola did not contravene, because he did not make a refutation of this quantity, and then the condition of Guido fails. Therefore, nothing could be paid to him, much less that he can sue; therefore, no refutation is necessary for Dame Rache: because it suffices for her that Guido’s condition fails. D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. quod heres, §. si. D. de conditionibus indebiti, l. Iulianus, §. idemque. Or Brother Cola made an end of this quantity and annulled the instrument as simulated. And then no action can be brought from the instrument because it is annulled and void, and by the confession of the parties it appears simulated, null, and unjust. D. de conditione sine causa, l. dissolute. And l. si, D. de doli exceptione, l. 2, §. circa. I do not believe that anyone is so hard-headed as not to understand that these things are most true. Therefore, Guido would act more wisely if he did not vex himself with expenses, since he cannot obtain even the appearance of success. D. de inofficioso testamento, l. 1.

† It could also be alleged regarding the Minor Brother, to whom these claims concerning monetary disposition cannot be compromised, as in the chapter *Exijt qui seminat*, and expressly noted in the *Speculum* under *de arbitris*, at the words “sequitur” and “quid de monacho simplici, et fratre minore,” and by Cynus, expressly noted, in the Code, *de episcopis et audientia*, in the law *Si qui ex consensu*. For the Minor Brother is entirely separated and prohibited from such matters, as expressly noted by Cynus in the law *Quidam decedens*, in the Digest, *de administratione tutorum*, and this is the truth. The objection of the minority of Bartolus, who enabled minors to do the impossible, does not stand; and even one without a head does not know that the money asserted was without a hide, and therefore should also sound without a hide. For whence did that great sum of money come to that little brother? Although in a point of law one ought not to inquire into the origin where the contract is established upon the firm rock of truth, as in the Digest, *si certum petatur*, in the law *Non unde originem*, and therefore before God no one can hide behind a finger. Fictions multiply and fall like little flowers, says Seneca in his letters. And therefore the judge, seeing such things, must of his own office repel what he sees lacks action by the law itself, as expressly noted in the Code, *de transactionibus*, in the law *Ubi pactum*, and *de officio praesidis*, *illicitas*. Who also doubts the statutory prescription which would stand in the way if other arguments failed, which however abound most plentifully and grow like truth before God and men. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A transfer of written instruments made by the debtor two days before he committed fraud should not prejudice the creditors.
2. A treasury record is presumed to be true and not simulated.
3. Fraudulent debtors are not to be believed, because they are prone to lying.
4. Fraudulent debtors, on account of their own fraud, do not have the benefit of cession.
5. The words of an instrument are to be taken as true and without malice.
6. When one thing is simulated and another is done, whether and when the act is valid, see the distinction for the understanding of the title C. plus valere quod agitur.
7. Whether prior creditors are prejudiced by novation or delegation.
8. Which creditor is to be preferred among creditors.
9. A case is decided on the basis of strong supporting evidence.
10. Among merchants, one should not dispute over technicalities of the law, but over the plain truth.
casus:
CASE. In the name of Christ, amen. The case is asserted as follows. Some time ago, A. was and remained a creditor of our Magnificent Duke, etc., on the books of his treasury for a certain quantity of money at a certain term. But A., having confidence in B. and not wishing to appear as a creditor on these books for such a large quantity, had the said Treasurer, by order of Jac., the referendary of the said Lord Duke, write on the said books that B. was the creditor of a certain part of the said quantity at the aforementioned term, so that truly the said B. was a substituted person to receive the aforementioned part for the said A. Then, when the said B. had devised to flee due to the extreme burden of debts incumbent upon him, compelled and not wishing to leave the said A. so grievously deceived, nor believing that the said A. ought to remain in such damage because of that deliberate flight, he found the said A., simulating to him that he wished to go to the baths for the healing of his infirmity. And he said to him that, since he intended to depart for the aforementioned cause, he wished to retransfer to him the writing which in truth had been and was that of the said A., not otherwise revealing to him the contrived flight. To which the said A. assented, and immediately they went to the said Jac. and the Treasurer, and by the will of the said Jac., the Treasurer retransferred the said writing, making in the said books B. the debtor and A. the creditor of the said money at the aforementioned term. After all these things, the said B. immediately took flight for two days, and when that flight was discovered, many creditors appeared, asserting that that credit should be shared and divided equally among those creditors from the goods of the said fugitive, for six months before the flight itself, rejecting any privilege of time, alleging a certain statute of merchants effectively containing that whatever is found to be acquired may be taken from the goods of the said fugitive, or that which he held and possessed at the time of the flight, or within six months before, and be shared equally among those creditors, whether they are creditors or appear to be so by certain public document or condemnation; and that as to the goods of fugitives, among such creditors there is no cause or privilege of time.

On the other side, it is responded by the said A. that the said statute does nothing for the proposition, because it speaks only of the goods of the fugitive, but the name of such a debtor is by no means to be considered among the goods of the fugitive. Rather, the aforementioned A. neither held nor possessed it at the time of the flight, nor within six months before. Especially since in such incorporeal names, detention nor possession does not apply. Furthermore, that chapter speaks only of creditors appearing by public document or condemnation. Therefore, since these appearing creditors are not from these causes, but by writing or viva voce, therefore, etc. Moreover, it is truly evident that the name of that debt of our Magnificent Duke never belonged to the said B., nor did he ever consider that debt his own, because he made no mention of that debt in the bank book of the said B. and his partner, nor in any of his books; for if it had been his debt, he would undoubtedly have made mention of it, as he did of his other debts. For the best argument is from the custom of the fatherland. Furthermore, it must be observed that the bank book and all its business were common to the said B. and M., and they are and were commonly debtors of any creditors; so that if that debt had been true, he would have received the writing, but not only in his own person, but commonly in his and his partner’s, as he did with all others. Moreover, the aforementioned writing is for such a large quantity that if that debt had truly been that of the same B., it would not have been expedient for him to take flight; rather, that quantity alone could have sufficed for all creditors; and beyond that, he would most likely not have taken flight in any way.

Furthermore, and that which is very weighty to consider, by reviewing the books of both the Treasury and the said A., it can be most clearly comprehended that that debt truly always remained the property of the said A. Moreover, that which seems to remove all doubt is that the aforementioned Jac., trustworthy not only in this matter, but in much greater ones, and very experienced in such matters, bore witness to the truth in the presence of the council. Hence, among good and grave men, his assertion ought to be full proof. Indeed, even from the subtlety of law, his testimony will be half-proof, to be supplied by the oath of the said A. Also, this proof or the testimony of the aforementioned Treasurer, who affirmed the aforementioned things to be true by his sacrament, is made by the fact that the said B. had many accounts with the same Treasurer and made various reckonings, yet he would never have made mention of it if he had been a creditor from it. It follows therefore, upon all these things, what is the law.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen. In the first books of the Treasury, A. was described for one thousand; then that entry was transferred to B. for five hundred. Finally, the said B. committed fraud, and for two days before committing the fraud, he had that entry of five hundred in his name transcribed back into the said A. Now the creditors of the said defrauder

They say that the amount of that debt must be divided and shared among the creditors. This is based on the form of the statute of merchants, approved by the Lord’s decree, which provides that whatever is found, or whatever can be obtained or held from the goods of a fugitive, or which he held and possessed at the time of his flight, or within six months prior, shall be equally divided among those creditors, whether they are creditors or appear to be so by public document or condemnation; as to the goods of fugitives, there is no privilege of time among such creditors. The question arises whether the aforementioned retranscriptions made on the eve of flight, two days before the said An., should benefit him in full. It is alleged on behalf of the creditors of this fugitive that it must be shared among the creditors, as the law provides that the peculium to be shared among creditors includes not only the corporeal things of the peculium but also the claims against debtors. This is expressly stated in the text. D. de pec., l. quantuberonis, § in peculio.

† Moreover, the writing of the Treasury is presumed to be true, and not simulated. This holds both under the general law of all public records, as noted in C. plus valere quod agitur; l. emptione, and also under the special law of the public archive and authentic register: as in C. de non numerata pecunia, l. in contractibus; C. de apostolis publicis, l. 1, lib. 10; C. de fidei instrumentis, Auth. ad haec, and in the Corpus from which it is derived. Furthermore, by this transfer of the writing, a delegatory novation was effected, whereby the Treasury was released from An. and bound to Bernar., as in C. de novatione, l. 1. Indeed, more so, because A. appears to have been discharged, as in ff. de mandato, l. inter causas, §. abesse; ff. ad legem Falcidiam, l. quamvis, §. interdum; and ff. de novatione, l. delegare; ff. de donationibus, l. ut mihi donares. And an obligation once extinguished by payment never revives, as in ff. de solutionibus, qui res, §. aream. Furthermore, this transfer from B. to A. is a new contract, which ought not to prejudice other creditors. Argument: ff. de pactis, l. si; and C. de locatio conductio, l. si cum heres. Hence, the beginning of the last convention must be examined. For a new pact makes a new contract, whence Ant. is found not to be the first, but the third creditor, as in ff. qui potiores in pignore habeant, l. creditor, §. si primus, and §. stichum. Furthermore, unless a re-transfer of the re-transferred writing had been made, the other creditors would undoubtedly have a right; because, as I said, one must not depart from the Treasury’s writing, to which recourse is had as to a mirror, and as to a fountain of truth, as in l. 1, C. de exactione tributorum; in Auth. de mandato principis, §. publicorum, Collatio 3. Therefore, on these and other grounds, it may be said that such a re-transfer does not hold to the prejudice of other creditors: as in ff. de iureiurando, l. nam postea, §. sed et si quis in fraudem creditoris. Likewise, from the short interval of flight, fraud appears to be extended; because that which is done immediately is deemed to be inherent. Argument: ff. de privilegiis creditorum, l. si ventri, §. si; and fully noted by Bartolus in ff. de donationibus, l. post contractum. Furthermore, color is not presumed to have been sought in the writing, unless it is proven by clear indications, as in ff. ad legem Falcidiam, l. vir uxori. Nor does anything else appear to have been done than what is written, as in ff. de fideiussoribus, l. fideiussores magistratuum; l. quod Aurelio; C. de probationibus, l. cum precibus; ff. de pactis iuris gentium, §. quod fere, and §. pactorum. These are some of the points that can be alleged on behalf of the body and universality of creditors. Natural equity also seems to persuade this: because these parties could lie about the date given. As in C. de falsis, l. si creditor colludens; ff. ad legem Falcidiam, Scaevola; ff. de edendo, l. 1, §. edictiones; C. qui potior in pignore habeatur, l. scripturas.

† because these deceived persons are prone to lying, and especially because they might collude: which is absurd. For since they cannot testify solemnly in court regarding this matter, all the more so they cannot do so in a contract. Otherwise, it would be easy to reach an agreement on a share. And certainly, no occasion for wrongdoing should be given. Moreover, because they are infamous, and most infamous, who according to the custom of the most ancient law ought to be handed over to creditors to be torn apart. As noted in l. 1, C. qui bonis cedere possunt.

† so much so that, on account of their own fraud, they are not deemed to have the benefit of cession: which is a relief for the wretched, but not a protection for the fraudulent. As in l. si, §. si, ff. quae in fraudem creditorum; and in l. pen., ff. de iure dotium. Moreover, because when the state has changed, it is not permitted to recognize even good faith to the prejudice of a third party, much less when the good faith is suspect. ff. de eo quod certo nomine, l. si quis ex argentariis, in the words humilis, and deploratus; and ff. de mandato, l. quintus.

† Moreover, that which the word of the instrument signifies must be held as truth, and it ought to prevail without calumny. As stated in the extrajudicial privilege, *porro*; in the Code, on the liberation of slaves, or from an heir, l. 3; in the Digest, on the judgment being satisfied, l. *iudicatum solui stipulatio*; the instrumental voices bear witness to the truth. As stated in the Digest, on pledges, l. *contrahitur*. Who, indeed, have we defrauded, both the deceived parties and this Antonio? But rather, let us turn our gaze for greater clarity. And it is evidently shown that An. has a right to the entire aforementioned transcript, without sharing in any manner with the other creditors. And this is demonstrated by many reasons, laws, and also by natural justice and equity, which favor this position.

† And for the sake of clarity, I premise that sometimes something is simulated to be done, and nothing is done; and this is properly a simulated contract, or a simulated chirograph. Nevertheless, one cannot allege this by alleging one’s own turpitude. As in *l. si creditoribus*, C. de servo pignori dato, manumisso; and *l. transactio*, C. de transactionibus. Sometimes one contract is simulated, and another is celebrated. And then the simulated contract is not valid, but the true contract is valid: if the kind of simulated contract is such that it is perfected by consent. Otherwise, if by words: because the words did not intervene; or by writing, because the chirograph did not intervene. As in D. de verbis oblig., *l. quicquid astringendae*; and C. de fidei instrumentis, *l. contractus*. It also fails when the obligation is contracted by the thing, and the thing does not intervene. As in C. si certum petatur, *l. si ex pretio*; because where there is a defect of the substantial form, or of the quality of the matter, that rule has no place, that what is done prevails over what is simulated to be conceived; but the rule should be stated thus: nothing prevails that is done, because it is simulated to be conceived. Sometimes there is no simulation with respect to the obligation, but concerning the person of the stipulator, or the chirographer: and this can be in several ways. In the first way, because from the beginning someone does not wish to be named in the stipulation, or chirograph: but he makes the stipulation, or chirograph, in the person of a friend. Very often. Now, if this is done in good faith, fraud or deceit being absent. D. de hereditate instituenda, *l. quidam cum filium*; and it is expressed in C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione, *l. optimam*. Sometimes, however, it is done with fraud, when namely there is fraud against the law. As in C. de secundis nuptiis, *l. hac edictali*; or against creditors, who had previously contracted, even under a condition, whom the gloss calls future creditors. As noted in C. de donationibus ante nuptias, auth. *sed iam necesse*; or when something is contravened against the mandates of the laws. As in D. de legibus, *l. fraus*; C. de naturali libertate, *l. 1*; D. de auctoritate tutorum, *si pupillus*, § *per interpositam*; D. de aqua pluviali arcenda, *emptor*. Sometimes the name of another is inserted into the contract, or chirograph, ex post facto. And this can be in several ways. In the first way, that it be added to the payment: and this added person obtains the place of a procurator, and between the one adding and him, an action of mandate arises. As in D. de verbis oblig., *l. Iulianus*, § *qui fundum*. In which case this procurator is bound, if the owner wishes to transfer the rights to the owner, or to whomever the owner wishes. This is said in *l. illa not.*, D. de manumissionibus, *l. idemque*, § *si cui*. Sometimes a third person is added to stipulate or to chirograph. And then either he stipulates uselessly, and the same: because it has the force of a simple mandate. Here, in this law, *l. illa unica in iure*; D. de solutionibus, *l. si cum Cornelius*. Sometimes the obligation, or chirograph, is transferred to him usefully, and effectively, and this in three ways. For sometimes it is so that he is a successor to the obligation, and he alone is found in the debt, or credit. And then novation takes place. As in D. de novazione, *aliam*. Sometimes so that he is added to the debt, or credit: and novation does not take place. Hence the first creditor still endures as creditor, until the other of them is paid. Sometimes it is doubtful. And in doubt, novation does not take place, but aggregation. Hence, although you make what you owe to me be promised by a money-lender, you are not immediately released from me, but after satisfaction has followed. As noted by Bartolus, although under doubt, perhaps. D. de novazione, *l. delegare*; and D. de novazione, *l. si debitor*.

† When, therefore, does novation, or delegation, occur? This can happen in several ways, namely, apparently and in reality. In the latter case, the new obligation belongs to the goods of the subsequent creditor, and not to those of the first creditor, as in D. de legatis 2, l. si, § filia, where there is a standard case. Sometimes the transfer is apparent but not real, as when this is done between the first and the subsequent stipulation. In that case, the benefit remains with the first creditor in the same way as when a pure procurator is appointed. For example, a wife, fearing that her husband will compel her to testify, causes the obligation to restore the dowry to be transferred to a certain friend of the woman. For by this she does not cease to be endowed, as is read and noted in D. soluto matrimonio, l. 2, § nec cogitur. Thus, therefore, the transfer of a chirograph can be made according to different intentions, and it operates differently according to the diversity of the minds of the actors, as in l. non omnis, D. si certum petatur. Sometimes it is doubtful with what intention a chirograph or stipulation is transferred. Then it matters whether, when the second creditor begins, the first ceases, or whether he does not cease. If he ceases, novation has been made between the first creditor and the debtor; if he does not cease, novation has not been made, as in C. de novatione, l. si. However, in the case where he ceases, it is asked to whom the final benefit of the contract belongs: to the new creditor or to the old one, so that if anyone new demands payment, he must be restored. On this point, it seems to me that one should say that, since the chirograph and the payment belong to that debtor who first made the payment, because to him belongs the beginning and the foundation of the credit, it is not presumed that he donated his right, but that he contracted, as is fully read and noted in D. soluto matrimonio, l. quae dotis. If, however, a new payment intervenes, which is not to be presumed, as in Extr. de fide instrumentorum, cum Io. heremita, then the second caution would not be second, but sole, nor would it be derivative, but in itself. Since, therefore, our question asks about the obligation descending from the source of the first payment, and another appears to be transferred to another, yet this second caution is affected and subjected to the burden of transferring the chirograph without the intention of novating, it must be further premised for clarity

† Or, that which is owed by B. is paid to A., and A. is owed nothing, or not so much. And then the creditors of B. can reclaim it, because they alone are creditors. As in C. de iure delicti, l. si, §. licentia. Or, it is found that all are creditors, and then it matters whether among them there is a right of priority or a right of order, or whether they claim simple equality. In the first two cases, he who has the stronger right is preferred. As in ff. de privilegiis creditorum, l. privilegia. For it is said that he is stronger; otherwise, without preference, no priority could be assigned. In the third case, however, when they simply claim equality and equality is established, then either he to whom payment was made first claims gratification, or he extorted the money or debt by fraud, and it must be shared or divided with the other creditors pro rata. Or, it was legitimately collected by a judge: and then either the goods were previously possessed by decree of the judge, and the same applies. As in ff. de bonis ab iudice possessis, l. cum unus. Because the praetor wishes his benefit to be open to all. Arg. ff. de contrahenda emptione, l. si post mortem, §. si. Or, the goods are not possessed, because he confesses out of court and a precept is issued to him. And then this person is not bound to share, because he receives nothing of another’s property, but only what is owed to him. As in ff. quae in fraudem creditorum, l. pupillus, and there by Jacobus de Arena and Bartolus. Sometimes the body of creditors claims equality. But someone is there who claims solidarity, and priority, and solidarity. And this is the direct case of our question. For if indeed all things are equal, equality will be presumed. But if they are unequal, because for him who claims solidarity there are strong judgments from a strong presumption, and the treasurer testified, who is a witness of great solemnity.

† then the case is decided on the basis of strong presumptions. See the Decretals, De successionibus ab intestato, chapter Cum dilectus. Moreover, the very nature of the fact supports this, because if B.’s writings were true, he ought not to have deceived or absconded, since the fiscus, which is always solvent, ought to have been a debtor in a sufficient amount to all creditors; thus, the outcome proves the acts. Furthermore, it is not probable that one who is able to pay would abscond. See law Sciendum, in principio, Digest, Qui satisdare coguntur. Therefore, if the matters supposed in the hypothetical are in favor of A., and the judge’s inclination concurs, as it ought to concur, with him, and it is not directly contrary to the tenor of the writing, but rather a certain interpretation and declaration thereof, judgment should be rendered in favor of A., because the said name is not among those of fugitives. See Digest, De solutionibus, law Fugitivus.

† and especially among merchants, among whom it is not fitting to dispute over the subtleties of law: but rather over the bare truth and the custom of commerce. As in D. de fideiussoribus, si fideiussor, § quaedam. And also in L. I do not omit that if Antonius, after this transcription, received from the treasurer the benefits of the credit, and not the said B., it is presumed that the said transcription was made formally and not substantially, because A. was always in quasi-possession. As in D. de pignoris vel hypothecae solutione, l. sicut, § supervacuum. Moreover, whence do ten thousand florins come to this B.? Do they come from the wind? As in C. de educatione pupillorum, l. si. Nor does D. de petitione certae rei, l. non unde origine, stand in the way, because there the counting and the possession of the counter appeared. As in C. de arbitrio tutoris, l. si defunctus. The account books must also be diligently scrutinized, and consequently the writings, because the antecedent demonstrates the consequent, and vice versa. As in D. de legatis primo, l. si servus plurium, § finalis, and C. de institutionibus et substitutionibus, l. pe. And in sum, this pertains greatly to the examination of the judge and the good man, whether we look to the common law or the municipal law. Indeed, what and how much is in each person’s goods can also be investigated through household servants. As noted in l. 2, C. quando et quibus partes debeantur, lib. 10. Furthermore, if the said B. did not have such resources that he could verisimilarly support the said quantity, this is a strong indication that it is not from his goods, but from Antonius, who is solvent and capable. And this is notorious. As in l. si vero, § 1, D. de his qui satisdare cogantur, and noted in l. facultas, C. de iure fisci, lib. 10. Therefore, it seems to me that, according to the foregoing, one should conclude for the said A., and I conclude and hold for him, summarizing my motives briefly. The first motive is the truth of the principle and origin. D. de donationibus, qui id quod; D. de solutionibus, tutor. The second motive is that the first named in the writings is presumed to be the principal, and more principal. As in D. de stipulatione servo, l. si servus communis. The third motive is that from the beginning of the title, the subsequent event is formed. As in C. de imponendis lucris decreti, l. 1, lib. 10. The fourth motive is that by new or newest [writing] there is no novation: even if what is owed to one is transcribed to another for greater caution. As in D. de novatione, l. delegare, per Bartolus; and today it is presumed that tacitly it is agreed that there is no novation, but rather the adoption of new cautions. As in C. de novatione, l. si. Although formerly it was otherwise: because the rule of ancient law was where there is novelty, there is novation. As in D. de novatione, l. si debitor, and Inst. de quibus modis tollitur obligatio, § praeterea. And thus is understood the said Bartolus in d. l. si debitor, namely, regarding the law of the forums. The fourth reason [note: text says "Quarta ratio" again, likely meaning fifth in sequence or a repetition error in source, but translated as written] is that the one added is presumed to be added for the benefit of the one adding, not for his own benefit, which is shown by the obligation that exists between them. As in D. de solutionibus matrimonii, l. quae dotis. The fifth reason is: that it is not presumed that the one adding wishes to throw away his own right, especially in a large sum. As in D. de donationibus, l. cum de indebito. The sixth reason is that although the chirograph is made, the truth of the matter is not abolished. As in C. de iure dotium, l. in rebus. The seventh reason is the natural consideration itself, which obtains force. As in D. de excusatione tutoris, l. scire oportet. And if anything. For from natural indications the truth is proven; for all things agree with truth, and nothing disagrees with it for the one contemplating the true light. As in D. de testibus, l. ob carmen, § si testes. But here all aids assist Antonius, and not only assistively but also impressively, such that the contrary cannot be persuaded to the mind of the judge, nor can his intellect be turned to the opposite conscience. For this is called a vehement aid. As in Extra de successione ab intestato, c. si. Eighth and conclusively, it follows that the effectiveness of this business always remained in the goods of Antonius, and that this name is to be considered as from the goods of A., and separation is to be made from the goods of B. And although it may be said of public writing, "Touch me not," here certainly nothing is objected to the writing, because to know the law is not merely to read its words, but to hold its force and power. As in D. de legibus, l. scire leges. Just as the writing of Aesop and Fulgentius is true, but the fable is not true. So often the writing is true, and what is asserted as the cause is true, yet the denunciation of the cause has another meaning. As noted in D. de pace, l. iuris gentium, § quod fere. Nor is it to be omitted that this writing has the burden of retroceding or retranscribing actions. And this status exists from the beginning, nor is it changed afterwards. As in l. si, D. si ex noxali causa agatur. From these things, therefore, my conclusion appears clearer than light, saving the deliberation of the greater counsel of our Illustrious Prince, to whom I submit myself, as I am subject. To these also assists the tenth, namely, good conscience, without which no man is a good man, which although sometimes it is not sufficient, nevertheless it is never to be despised. As in c. cum aeterni, Extra de re iudicata, lib. 6. I, Baldo.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. No one can make a will concerning feudal goods.
2. A woman does not succeed to a fief unless by custom.
3. What is required to establish a custom to the prejudice of someone.
4. In the prescription of princes' fiefs, the true or presumed knowledge of the prince himself is required.
