body: It is asserted by the Lord Cardinal from the memory of the late Lords John and William, full blood relatives. There existed in the world Nobles, the Lord Cardinal from the memory of the late Lords John and William, full blood relatives; but John died, with Lords William and Opizio, his sons, surviving; then the said Lord William the elder died, leaving Lord Corrado, his son. Furthermore, Lord Corrado died, leaving William, his son. Finally, the said William, son of Lord Corrado, died, having made a will, while the said Lord Opizio and Matthew, nephew of the said Lord Opizio, born of the said Lord William, formerly of Lord John, were alive and left behind. These nobles, already mentioned, were co-owners of one-third (Terzerio) in the castle of Coconato, together with other castles, which are divided among other nobles of the said house of Coconato. And in sum, all of Coconato consists of three territories, one of which is called only the Terzerio Brozoni of the said nobles; the second is called the Terzerio Robella; the remaining one is now called the Terzerio of the castle of Bergono. All these castles are partly Imperial fiefs and partly fiefs of the Church of Vercelli. From all of which it is asked whether the said William, the last of the Terzerio Brozoli, who died having made a will, could make a will concerning the said feudal goods, especially excluding the said Lords Opizio and Matthew, nephew of the said Lord Opizio, and preferring in that Terzerio of the castle of Brozoli others who are not, nor ever were, of his Terzerio, nor of the consortium of Brozoli; rather, they are of another Terzerio and consortium.

And it must be said briefly that the said Guli. could not make any testament concerning those feudal goods, especially by excluding the same lords Opizo and Mat. and conferring them upon someone else from the other two Terzeri, because in a fief no disposition of the deceased is valid or can be valid, as is read and held literally in the usus feudorum, in the title De successione feudorum, chapter 1, and in Merio, because a fief pertains rather by the principal provision of the first ancestor, through the death and annihilation of the immediate vassal, to the surviving agnate, than by the judgment of the succession of the deceased vassal, as is stated in the law and noted in the title An agnatus vel filius defuncti repudianti haeredi possit feudum retinere. For he is understood to hold it more from his ancestors than from the last deceased himself, as there in the singular gloss Paternum and in the gloss Repudiare. Also, argument from the Digest, De adoptionibus, law Si rogata, section 1. And it is the ordinary gloss in the usus feudorum, in the title Qui feudum dare possit, section Cum vero Coradus, in the gloss Frater, which literally determines this question. In the Name of Christ, Amen. In a fief, a woman does not succeed unless by custom. And because custom has two extremes: the first is that it be reasonable, and with respect to this, it suffices that it is not reprobated.

Secondly, it is prescribed, and with regard to this, long-standing customs suffice. Nor does the text require more than these two elements, as in the Institutes, *De iure naturali*, § *Ex non scripto*. However, an objection is raised, and indeed it appears that the knowledge of those who are bound by the prescription of custom is required, as in *L. 2*, Codex, *De servitutibus et aqua*, from which law the rule concerning the prescription of incorporeal things is derived.

Solution: There is one thing in prescription, which is the usurpation of another’s right already brought into existence, and another in custom, which disposes in the manner of unwritten law, *L. Non scripta*. For this is not properly a prescription of any thing, but rather a certain form introduced by the consent of the people, as in the Digest, *De legibus*, *L. De quibus*, which can be introduced generally in that province, and even against wards and infants; hence, the knowledge or consent of individuals is not required, but that of the community itself, as in the Digest, *De administratione tutorum*, *L. Sine haerede*, § *Lucius*. Moreover, if knowledge were required, it is presumed in public acts, because it would be gross negligence not to know what everyone knows, as in *L. Lata culpa*, *De verborum significatione*.

Now, regarding the matter at hand, consider that we are dealing with the extension of a right from males to females, and this extension is easily made because it is of the same nature, as in *L. Maximum vitium*. And since this is favorable and in accordance with nature, it has not only tacit consent but also a title, because natural reason is considered as a title, as in *L. Scire oportet*, § *Sufficit*, *De exceptionibus tutorum*. And I say that what is drawn from towns is extended to cities, even though they are larger, as in the Digest, *De legibus*, *L. Iura non in singulas*, and in the Digest, *De petitione hereditatis*, *L. Item veniunt*.

† Solution. The common opinion is that, in the prescription of the fiefs of princes, the true or presumed knowledge of the prince is required; and the reason is that the prince holds civilly, and prescription does not run against one who holds civilly, as noted in l. 1, C. de servis fugitivis, and by Dyther in c. sine possessione. Moreover, the lord holds as long as possession has not been transferred by him to another, which occurs even by mere tolerance: as in ff. si servus venditus, l. si quis diuturno. Furthermore, the Gebenensis was never in possession transmitted to women, because this possession begins upon a case, and this case never occurred, since it is a recent case and never happened; hence, the custom had neither origin nor beginning, especially by judicial sentence. It is not an objection that there is a custom of transmitting other fiefs to women; for the reason is not the same in the head and in the members, nor is it our practice to extend an unreasonable custom from lesser to greater matters. The argument is drawn from de rescriptis, c. sedes. To this is added that this fief derives its form and origin not from popular law, because this fief is of mere empire. And therefore, the prescription by which mere empire is prescribed must be proved, which has two extremes, one in the prince and the other in the prescriber. And this prescription is derived from the body of fiscal law. And therefore, the knowledge of the fisc is necessary. Likewise, if any lord were to erect a new dignity and enfeoff it, he would assume for himself the nature of the common law, not of particular statutes. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether written documents and the notary’s instrument are rendered suspect, and thus not believed, solely on account of defamation that the notary is of bad character and reputation, and consequently of slight credibility.
2. What effect suspect writings or instruments have.
3. By what means writings or instruments are confirmed.
4. Which prevails in confirming instruments: good or bad reputation.
5. Whether public reputation constitutes evidence sufficient for torture: and what is meant by public reputation.
6. If the day is missing in the instrument, but is stated in the subscription, whether this defect invalidates it.
7. If one witness contradicts the notary, not the instrument, what effect this has.
8. In criminal cases, a single perfect judgment of a person does not arise from the diverse natures of evidences.
1. Instruments pass into perpetual credibility by virtue of a judicial sentence and the observation of the parties.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It is asked whether by mere defamation, namely that the notary is of bad reputation and consequently of little credibility, his writing becomes suspect, to such an extent that no credence is given to it.

And it seems that this is so: because three things make a document suspect. Namely, the person [who produced it], for the reason that he is accustomed to producing false documents; the person who wrote it, because he is accustomed to making false instruments; and the erasure or defacement of the document itself. See C. de probat. l. iubemus. Furthermore, Jacobus de Belvisi stated that when a copy is produced without the original, such a document is considered suspect, because its origin is not established. To this effect is the law and the gloss in Auth. de tabell. §. si; and C. de testam. l. publicati. Moreover, a notary must be above all exception. See ff. de contrahenda et communi stipulatione, l. optimam, in fine; ff. de edendo, l. si quis ex argentariis, §. quid enim; and de senatu, §. Cassius.

But consider on the contrary that there are three or four things which confirm writings: namely, good and unblemished reputation; produce it. Also, the good reputation of the writer. Also, that the writing is clear, without any blemish: as is evident from the same laws. And because the rule is the same for contraries. But if all these three do not concur, but the producer is of good reputation, while the writer is not of unblemished reputation: then in a small amount, the reputation of the producer prevails, but in a large amount, the ill repute of the writer weakens the instrument. Argument from those things which are noted. D. de iureiurando. L. admonendi. C. de rebus creditis. L. in bonae fidei. And this is true in the producer’s own case. For in another’s case, ignorance is presumed. Therefore, the instrument, which is suspect on the part of the writer, is not aided by the good reputation of the producer. Argument in L. ult. D. pro socio. And what is noted. D. de aqua pluviae arcendae. L. Pantonius. § rei perduellionis.

But it must be noted that, where good reputation is proved by one party and bad reputation by the other, if one is better supported by circumstances than the other, and by more probable causes, that one prevails. Cf. C. de edictis divi Adriani tollendis, l. si, §. si autem aliquis, there: “who has the stronger grounds,” etc. But if the causes of ill-repute are not established, good reputation is presumed, and not bad; especially because good reputation is innate, whereas bad reputation is accidental. Moreover, good reputation is continuous from its origin and from the habit of nature, but bad reputation is not continuous. Also, just as one indication removes a contrary indication, and one presumption another, as in D. de in integrum restitutione, divus; D. de ritu nuptiarum, non solum, §. de uno, so too does reputation remove reputation, as in C. ne de statu defunctorum, l. si mater. Bartolus says that when reputations of equal weight conflict, neither is proved. D. de quaestionibus, l. de minore, §. tormenta. I say that that one is proved which naturally coheres, i.e., the foundations of innocence. Cf. C. de inofficioso testamento, l. omnimodo. And see l. non omnes, §. a barbaris, D. de remissione; C. de susceptis et archis, l. si; C. de conditionibus in pupillis, l. fin., lib. 10. It is established that where suspicion is purged, the faith of a public testament remains unimpaired, as in C. de probationibus, l. cum precibus. Nor does there have place this most severe inquiry, of which C. de falsis.

† For then one proceeds to torture by means of public fame, when public fame has arisen from probable causes, from which indications for torture arise. It is said to originate from probable causes, which induce the people to believe or say thus; otherwise it would not be fame, but rather the vain voice of the people, which ought not to be heeded. As in l. decurionum, C. de poenis. Therefore, let the judge be cautious. For I do not believe that it suffices to prove fame simply, but with some legitimate indication, according to Bartolus, who thus notes in the aforementioned §. tormenta, at the end.

But it is still asked concerning the writing, if the day was lacking in the instrument, and is placed in the superscription, whether this defect invalidates it. And I say that there is a difference between defect and vice. For to lack is not being, but vice is a certain depravity. And that defect ought to be supplied by the notary, because it pertains to his office; but not the vice of erasure. Moreover, a greater defect is the vice of the disparagement of the writing than the defect of omission. Moreover, where there is erasure, there is contradiction, diversity, or vacillation, which weaken the faith of the testimony. But where there is error of omission, and not of commission, the faith is imperfect, unless supplied; but not wounded. And certainly, returning to the point, the notary who omitted to place the day in the instrument can supply it from the protocol, because the error of omission is established. And C. de testam. l. errore. Nor from this is it presumed against the notary, since at the end of the writing it is said that it was omitted by error, according to Dyet and others in l. 1. ff. de his quae in testa. delen. And if there were any ambiguity, it is purged in the manner aforesaid. Furthermore, certain other light objections are raised, about which there is no need to care. As ff. de ven. in spi. l. 1. in fi. and ff. de edi. edic. l. si cui deus abest. Because from light causes one does not depart from public faith.

But it is still objected that one of the appointed witnesses contradicts the statement of the notary, not the instrument itself: for the witness says "half a sheet," and the notary says "in a quire." For this makes no difference as to the substance of the matter and the truth. Moreover, both could have been true, that he wrote in one half-sheet, and immediately in the quire, before the notary turned to other acts. D. ad Tertul. l. unum. Furthermore, the witness agrees with the notary in the substance of the fact. Hence it is not necessary that they agree on these other irrelevant matters: and especially because no memorandum is made of these irrelevant matters, so that they are easily forgotten due to the passage of time. As D. de usucap. l. furtum, § 1, with the following law. Rather, this witness confirms the instrument and does not invalidate it, considering the substantial effect. Arg. D. de verb. oblig. l. quae extrinsecus. Moreover, what does not help individually, helps in multitude, for it is true when they agree towards one end of the matter; then they help each other. Otherwise, if they are of different kinds. As noted in l. 2, § 1, de excus. tutor., through the gloss and Dynus, who expressly says,

† That in criminal cases, from indications of diverse natures, there does not arise one perfect indication of the person. As in C. de app. l. aditos. And therefore the indications ought to be clearer, not more perfunctory, as in C. de quaest. l. milites. §. oportet. For it is not fitting to proceed by ambiguities in so great a peril. As in C. de prob. l. si. That also does not obstruct, that the imbreuiatura is shorter than the extrinsic writing. For from the name itself it is clear that it is so according to the nature of the said writings. Moreover, to specify is not to extend. As in ff. de test. l. haeredes palam. §. sed si notam. and in c. 1. §. 1. de noua. for. fideli. col. 10.

† Coming to the last point. Did these matters, by means of the instrument, the sentence, and the observation of the parties, pass into perpetual faith? As stated in C. de fide instrumentorum, l. si, in fine; and C. de non numerata pecunia, l. cum fide. Hence, I do not at all think that the notary should be subjected to torture. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. By how many witnesses is a notary's error or a forged instrument to be proved.
2. Whether proof by witnesses is admitted against public instruments. And whether. 3.
3. A statement that is false in part may be denied in its entirety.
4. If a witness, when asked whether others were present, says that they were not, and it is proved that others were present, is he to be called a forger.
5. Proof of the existence of a case is required when, by statute, one departs from the common law on the basis of the existence of a certain case.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen.

† That the notary’s error has not been sufficiently proven is established by several reasons. First, because some of the witnesses introduced to prove the alleged error contradict themselves. For they state in the first article read out that it was made for Lady Paulina; yet later, on article 6, they state that the words “he wished, however, that the said Lady Paulina, and her sons and daughters, have beforehand one part, a piece of land, etc.” were not uttered by the testator, nor disposed to the said [parties]; therefore, faith should not be given to these witnesses as being variable, as is read and noted in D. ad Tertullianum, l. qui falsa; and D. de falsis, l. eos, in principio.

Second, it is proven thus: a public instrument can be rebutted by four, or at least three witnesses, and not by fewer, as noted in C. de fide instrumentorum, l. in exercendis; and Inst. de inutilibus stipulationibus, § item verborum; and it seems to be proven in Extravagantes de fide instrumentorum, c. cum Ioannes heredi. But in our case, it is not sufficiently proven by so many witnesses; therefore, etc.

Third, it is proven thus: when one wishes to prove an error committed by a notary in an instrument, it is required that it be proven individually and specifically that the writing was drawn up by that notary, especially since the petition regarding the conception of the error is directed against the notary, as is the case in the matter proposed. Otherwise, the proof would in no way conclude. But in the matter at hand, some of the witnesses say they did not know the notary requested for the will in question. Therefore, it is clear that the proofs do not conclude; see D. de hereditate instituenda, l. quotiens, § 1; and D. de regulis iuris, l. si librarius.

Fourth, it is proven thus: one of the witnesses, when asked whether others had been present at the will besides the witnesses described in the article, said that they had not. And it appears that some other person was present. And thus, both of the said witnesses gave false testimony. And thus, faith should not be given to them, as is clear from what has already been said.

Fifth, it is proven thus: when witnesses contradicting the instrument are above the number required for the solemnity of the instrument, the instrument is not rebutted by such witnesses. And thus, the witnesses from whom the instrument essentially depends do not contradict the instrument, as noted in l. 1, in fine, D. quemadmodum testamentum aperiri debeat; and by Innocentius in the said c. cum Ioannes. But in the matter proposed, even if it were granted that some, or any, of the witnesses sufficiently proved the said error, there nevertheless remains a sufficient number of witnesses not impugning [the instrument], considering the statute of Perugia, and also considering that one of the witnesses described in the said will was not introduced in the said litigation, nor examined; and also considering the reasons written above.

Sixth, it is argued thus: as many witnesses are required for the solemnity of a will as are required for its impugnation, as noted in D. de legatis 2, l. cum proponeretur. But here, the error is not proven by so many witnesses; therefore, etc.

Seventhly, against public instruments drawn up in the form prescribed by statute, proof by witnesses is not admitted; indeed, this also appears to be true according to the common law, as noted by Cynus in the Code, *De non numerata pecunia*, in the law *Si ex cautione*, towards the end. To the contrary, it is clearly proven that the aforementioned error has been established. For when one of the necessary witnesses contradicts the instrument, he causes the faith of the instrument to waver, as is the case in the aforementioned law 1, towards the end, in the Digest, *Quomodo et quando testamentum aperiri debeat*. But according to the form of the statute under the rubric *Quot testes*, etc., in the title *De testamentis*, in the *Centum*, supra, at least five witnesses are required. Therefore, one of the five contradicting the said testament causes the said testament to waver. But in the case proposed, not only one, but four of the five testified against the testament, because six of the seven described testified against the said testament; therefore, etc. For only one remained who did not contradict the testament. The first reason alleged to the contrary does not hold, for it says that the witnesses are not contrary to themselves. For in the first article they state that the legacy was made to the lady Paulina. In the sixth, they state that the legacy was not made to the lady Paulina and her children. Nor does this contradict what they had said in the first article, for where the speech

† If a part is false, the entire statement may be denied. And it is true that what is contained in a true statement is not [false]. D. de rebus dubiis, l. Si is qui ducenta; and D. de verbis oblig., l. 1, § Si stipulanti, with the glosses of Bartolus and the same author there. For a legacy made to Domina Paulina is entirely different from a legacy made to Domina Paulina and her children. D. de usufructu accresc., l. Si mulieri cum liberis. The second objection does not hold, for it applies and has force only in the case of witnesses not described in the testament; otherwise, if they are described, as in l. 1, D. quemadmodum testamentum aperiri debeat. To the third reason it is answered that a plurality of testaments is not presumed. Moreover, the original and the protocol were produced by the notary before our prior, in which the aforementioned witnesses are described as contradicting that very testament, and thus it is clear that this is the testament in question. To the fourth reason it is answered.

† The witness, having been asked whether there were any others present besides those mentioned, answered that there were none; he is deemed to have lied, and in truth another person was present. For it is possible that another person was there whom he did not see, unless he had observed with subtlety and diligence. As noted by Bartolus in the aforementioned law 1, at the end, in the Digest title *Quemadmodum testamentum aperiri debeat*. Moreover, the question put to the witness could be understood as asking whether there were any others present who had been summoned and requested for the said testament. For it is true that others were not summoned and requested for the act, even though they were present at the time the act was performed. See the Digest title *De vindicationibus bonorum fidei possessorum*, law 2, section *Homines*; and what is noted by Bartolus in the Digest title *De verbis obligatis*, law *Sciendum*. Furthermore, even if it were granted that the aforementioned fourth objection stood, the number sufficient for solemnity would not thereby remain. For the witnesses who testify in this manner and were questioned as stated in the said fourth objection are only two. Thus, of the four described, those remain who contradict the testament, and so only three remain in support of the testament. And if it is said that three suffice for the solemnity of a testament in testaments under one hundred pounds, according to the form of the statute, it is answered:

† That whenever one departs from the common law by a statute on the existence of a certain case, in order that the statute derogate from the common law, proof of the existence of such a case is required; nor is such existence presumed, since, as the statute derogates from the common law, proof of the existence of such a case is required, nor is such existence presumed, since the statute is of strict law. As stated in the Digest, De verbis obligatorum, "Quicquid astringendae," and "Cum si." Therefore, since in the present case the value of the inheritance in question has not been proven by that particular clause of the statute, one does not depart from the common law; namely, when the said statute, above one hundred pounds, indefinitely and indeterminately decreed that five witnesses would nevertheless suffice. Since therefore the witnesses should at least remain who do not contradict the testament, which in our case do not remain. The fifth objection does not hold, because the response is evident from what has already been said. The sixth objection does not hold, because it would apply to witnesses not written down, as was answered above regarding the second reason. And in the same manner is the answer to the seventh. Moreover, the aforementioned statute concerning the execution of instruments states, "against which instruments and against which charters, etc." Therefore, it is necessary that the instrument be an instrument in order that the statute claim its place. Hence, nullity, and the allegation which renders the instrument ineffective, can well be opposed and proven by witnesses, notwithstanding such a statute. Digest, De re iudicata, Law 4, § Condemnatum, as noted by Bartolus; Digest, Quod vi aut clam, Law 1, § Denique, where it is said that this was held in disputation. And thus the said error ought to be corrected. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What the plaintiff must prove in a petition for inheritance.
2. In a petition for inheritance, although one may be the true heir, he is nevertheless excluded by the singular title of the successor.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† What must the plaintiff prove in an action for the vindication of an inheritance, and what singular article excludes the claim for the vindication of an inheritance when the action is brought? The plaintiff, in the first place, must prove that he is an heir, either by will or intestate. D. de petitione hereditatis, l. 1, 2, and 3. For one to be an heir by will, several things are required; and chiefly, that he knows of the will. As noted, D. de petitione hereditatis, l. Illud. And this applies both to an outsider and to a sui heres, speaking of effective entry into the inheritance. D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. Gerit. But he who denies the will is presumed to be ignorant of the will, unless knowledge is proven. And therefore he cannot enter into the inheritance: because not by will, since he is ignorant; nor intestate, because the cause of being a testate heir precedes the cause of being an intestate heir. C. communia de successionibus, l. Antepenultima. But if someone can succeed by a double path, namely, as a testate and intestate heir, he can nevertheless enter into the intestate inheritance if he does not have a substitute, because he is deemed to have tacitly renounced the intestate cause. D. de actionibus hereditariis, l. Illud. C. eodem, l. Suum. But if he does not know of the will, he cannot do that which requires knowledge; and it is believed against him that he does not know, from his own words: because he says that he does not know or does not believe. C. de liberali causa, l. Cum precum. And because it resides in the mind, which is presumed from words. As in Cap. Humanae aures. And D. de supellectili legato, l. Labeo, § Idem Tubero. From these follows the true conclusion: that if the plaintiff in an action for the vindication of an inheritance denies the will, once the will has been proven; because he acted ineptly as if intestate, and asserted an incompetent right, he must succumb. D. de pactis dotalibus, l. Beblius, in fine. However, saving the right to sue again, having chosen the competent path, as is said there. And D. de institutionibus, l. Habebat. And D. de acquisitione hereditatis, Claudius. And Extravagantes de iudiciis, c. Exhibita.

† Secondly, it must be known that in a petition for inheritance, although one is the true heir, he is excluded by the singular title of the possessor, even if the plaintiff in the petition for inheritance has been admitted to prove his ownership; because when the proofs exceed the nature of the action, nevertheless one does not exceed the nature of the action from them, nor thereby is the effect increased which the nature of the action cannot bear. And this is held by Cynus in l. cogi, in 4, q. The reason, however, why a singular title excludes the principle of the petition and the threshold of the action is: because the possessor by singular title is not an adversary nor a contradictor to the petitioner; because he is not required to deny that the latter is not the heir. For, even if it is conceded that he is the heir, nevertheless this entitled possessor has his own title which is compatible with his position. Hence he can say: "Lord, I am not bound to come with you to conflict, because I do not deny your title; behold, however, my title, which is not enervated by yours." Hence we are not contradictors in matters of law, and consequently we ought not to be adversaries to one another. For qualified possession makes an adversary in a petition for inheritance by denying that he is the heir, because then he would be compelled to contest the litigation as a contradictor; but he ought to say: "I am not bound to contest the litigation, because I do not intend to deny that you are the heir, nor even to affirm it, but I allege a title as a purchaser." C. in quibus causis cessat longi temporis praescriptio, l. haereditatem. And there the glossa sets forth this reason better than elsewhere in the corpus iuris; for the plaintiff in a petition for inheritance claims universal succession, and if he has no traditor nor adversary in this universal aspect, he cannot found it. Hence, when in the universal title he has no adversary, the defendant is not compelled to contest the litigation. The reason, however, why the title excludes the petition itself in effect, and peremptorily, is: because the singular title enervates in this respect the efficacy of the universal title, and is not enervated by it. And the reason is that the universal title has in itself less right to the thing claimed than the singular title, since for the universal title it suffices, and it includes a title not ordered to any real right. Otherwise in the singular title. D. de petitione hereditatis, l. item veniunt. Others say that the reason is that in equal cause the condition of the possessor is better; but they do not know what they are saying, because the singular title has much more right in the singular thing than the universal title has in the thing taken singularly. C. de evictionibus, l. 1. And thus it prevails by its own nature. However, the first case fails when the title is held as not being a title, because things are not to be considered as being what they are not held to be. D. de petitione hereditatis, l. nec ullam, §. omnibus. For the title excludes the petition for inheritance because it has more right; therefore, he who has no right at all does not exclude. And this is to the point, as if a guardian sold without cause and without solemnity the things of the wards. Other cases are noted in the said l. haereditatem. From the foregoing follow two conclusions. The first is that the nuns, who claim to be heirs of Castrone, and deny the testament, exclude themselves by their denial, since the testament is proved, and among free persons two witnesses suffice. And thus it is proved by many, as in §. ex imperfecto. The second is that the sale by the guardian does not favor the possessors, because no cause and solemnity is proved. C. de publicianis, l. quicunque, §. si. Hence the nuns would prevail, except that the testament is proved against them who deny it. And therefore, the defendant ought to prevail, things being thus situated. The nuns also ought to adhere much to God and to the truth, because if the testament appears with its legacies, and on account of the legacies the executrix sold, the purchase was lawful. C. quando decreto opus non est, l. 2. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When a protestation is of assistance, so that one may not be said to have approached.
2. Whenever a single act can be understood in two ways, it is understood in the manner that is declared by the protestation.
3. When one may retain an inheritance by another right than the inheritance right, by an oath or declaration.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† A protestation made before the act by which presumptive acceptance is induced has the effect that the protesting party is not deemed to have accepted by subsequently performing that act. D. de relig. l. at si quis. § plerique. D. de acquir. haer. qui in aliena. § Celsus. Moreover, it is held that one has the right to hold and possess by the right of a creditor, and not by the right of an owner. As noted, C. de repud. haer. l. 1. And therefore, the said woman is not understood to have accepted, but to have possessed by the right of a creditor. D. de solut. Titia

For whenever a single act can be understood in two ways, it is understood in the manner that is declared by a protestation. D. de negotiis gestis, l. Nesennius Appolinaris; D. de constitutionibus, cum M. Ferratiensis per Innocentium; and this is expressly stated in its own subject matter. D. de acquirenda hereditate, l. pro herede, § 1, in the word "protestari."

† Indeed, even without protestation, if one can retain an hereditary thing by another right than by the hereditary right: then, if he declares under oath that he held the thing by another right, his declaration shall be upheld, according to Jacobus de Arena in the said law *Pro haerede*, § 1, who cites in that title the law *Si quis non quasi*, which states that a contract made by another right, although if done simply, does not induce a presumptive acceptance of the inheritance: as is fully noted in the said law 1, C. *De repudianda hereditate*, through the gloss of Cynus and others. Moreover, it does not seem to constitute acceptance, because before the inheritance is accepted, they do not yet add. C. *De iure deliberandi*, law *Si*, § *Si autem*. However, if the inheritance is accepted by him with the benefit of inventory, and the creditors remain silent, the common law applies. C. *De iure deliberandi*, law *Si*, § *Donec*. But if they act, they must observe the statute regarding the term of ten days for exercise. Law 1, § *Si is qui navem*; law *Omnes populi*, *De iustitia et iure*, together with *Si milibus*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The understanding of the sole law in the Code, *Ut ne liceat etiam in emptione spei*, from the tenth book.
2. It is of public interest that the people, when in need, be assisted with provisions; and therefore those who do not come to the aid of the people in necessary provisions are said to be killing the people.
3. The understanding of sentences proceeds from law.
4. What a sentence is.
5. What is meant by a pressing war, such that the free and exempt are bound to the tax; and what is the case regarding the clause "whatever" etc.
6. A free city holds the place of the Prince; and therefore it can grant freedom to an inferior.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A sentence was issued by the Master of the Gate, which declared that A. and his property and goods were free, exempt, and immune from all and several head taxes, poll taxes, levies, tolls, impositions, collections, corvées, and forced labor, whether real or personal, ordinary or extraordinary, rural or otherwise, and from any others whatsoever that can be named or devised; provided that he observes all those obligations to which he is bound according to the form of the chapters and agreements. Furthermore, it was declared that the aforementioned A. is not entitled to this immunity in times of urgent necessity, famine, requisition, or war; and the following are added herein, reflecting the intent and wording of the sole law, together with its gloss, in the Code, "That no one may excuse himself from imperial service," Book 10. Nor does this immunity apply to the repair of fountains, bridges, roads, etc. Most learned men and pillars of the law, you have first asked me for an interpretation

† d. l. vnicę. and the glossa ordinaria placed there, on the word "urgent necessities," which says of famine, or war. And thus on the indiction, etc. And I say first, that the summary intention of the black letter is described by the rubric. However, in too brief a statement. And therefore, when the public necessity of purchasing crops, or grains, more clearly urges, all are bound, according to the mode of their patrimony, to contribute: not withstanding any privileges, and the authority of sentences: I understand, or fortified by any other firmness, so much so that even the inhabitants of Augusta, or Augustae, are bound to contribute. h. d. on the question. l. Andreas de Barulo there figures the case. It sometimes happens, that grain, and public granaries do not suffice for the soldiers. And thus, necessity compelling, money is necessary for purchasing barley, or grain. To gather this money, all ought to be constrained, nor is anyone excused by any privilege, or sentence, even of the divine house of Caesar, or Augusta. This, therefore, he puts as an example, when on account of the army, or war, it is necessary to purchase crops. The glossa, not content with this example, puts an example. And of famine which, by the disposition of the heavens, or by the judgment of God, often occurs. For the common people, too much oppressed by penury, ought to be aided by the purchase of grains, and crops, so that food does not fail them. This, namely, publicly.

† It is useful and necessary. D. de leg. 1, l. ciuitatibus in principio; C. de episc. et eccl., l. 1; D. ad leg. Iul. de annona, l. 1. For man lives chiefly by bread, and the commonwealth is sustained thereby. As is noted, C. de feriis, l. publicas. And those who do not assist the people with necessary foodstuffs are said to be killing the people. D. de lib. agnosc., l. necare; Glossa. Therefore, the aforementioned authority posited an example of an urgent purchase, but did not join cases of different reasoning. Whether, therefore, on account of war, it is necessary for the commonwealth to make provision for grain, lest it fall into famine or scarcity; or whether it has already fallen, by the judgment of God, on account of the sterility of the land; or by the act of man, on account of hostility, the said law *nemini liceat* and chapter *non* have application. The gloss intends there to say nothing about the stipends of soldiers or footmen. Thus, the city makes war or arms itself, because this is not the matter of that law, but rather the matter is treated concerning the granting of stipends. As in Auth. *ut iudices sine qualibet suffragio*, §. *oportet nos quoque nostros*, with the following two sections, where the text says that military expenses and the pursuit of enemies require much diligence, and these things cannot be done without money. And in the following section it says: We consider sufficient revenue for the empire to be that whereby the collectors gather only the fiscal tributes; for tributes were rendered to the commonwealth in mines and gold. As in Auth. *de collationibus*, in principio, col. 10; and as is noted, C. de annona et trib., in the rubric, lib. 10. It is therefore most certain that the gloss does not speak of this office of stipendiary, but only of the office of purchasing commodities. And therefore it said in the singular number *superindictum*. For it would have said in the plural *super indicta*, if the cases ought to have joined two of different quality and reasoning. For it is one thing to speak of solemn stipends, which have an ordered provision; it is another thing to speak of the purchase of commodities, which is rare, and rarely occurs, and cannot be encompassed by certain provision. Argument: D. de contrahenda empt., l. fistulas, §. frumenta. And I say well that that gloss is notable, because it determines the question raised by Cynus in l. 1, in X, q. C. de iure emptionis. That which the text there says, *urgente necessitate*, speaks of a certain necessity, namely, of victuals, not of every necessity: as l. 1, C. de pater qui filios distraxit; and l. ob eas, D. de praed. milit.; and D. de his qui sui vel alieni iuris sunt, l. 2, §. sed dominorum, in the word *famen*; D. ad Rhod. de iactu, l. 2, §. sed cum, in the same, in the gloss which begins *ad comedendum*. There is also another urgent necessity, but for the good of peace, which is opposed to a complaint. Extr. de despons. impub., c. 2. But of this, nothing pertains to our purpose. There is also another necessity of adverse case. D. de publicis; C. de dilationibus, l. 1, where the most urgent reason shall have demanded, and the cause of necessity ceases all, as is noted in Auth. *de non alienandis*, §. *nos igitur*; D. de manumissionibus, l. qui potuerunt; D. de officiis consulum, l. 1. But of these, nothing pertains to the point, as regards our case: because they differ in genus and reasoning from our theme. And I well confess that certain things are permitted in war itself, which are not otherwise permitted. As in the said chapter *domino guerram*, under the title *Hic incipiunt consuetudines regni*, col. 10; and in the prologue of the Institutes and Authenticum. Nevertheless, one case ought not to be drawn to another. D. de liberis et posthumis, l. commodissime; and in c. suspectum, Extr. de rescriptis, lib. 6; and the gloss says: *famis fame necessitatis pecora*, C. ad leg. Aquil., l. de pecoribus, where it says: *nil magis triste fame necare, nil compare fame*. It accords with what Innocentius notes, Extr. ne clerici vel monachi, c. 1, and he adds: *vel guerrae*. Refer to the text, when war induces the necessity of purchasing commodities to be bought in the commonwealth. For on account of wars, estates remain uncultivated. In Auth. *de armis*, in the 2nd column, coll. 6, there where it says: *terrae cursores uitam amittere metuentes, fuga propter timorem utuntur*, etc. Thus they do not have sufficient victuals for the people, of whom the lords and superiors ought chiefly to take care, nor despise those oppressed by poverty. As in Auth. *ut iudices sine qualibet suffragio*, §. *itaque Deo*, there where it says: *non videamus despicere homines oppressos, quos nobis tradidit Deus*. As C. de mendicantibus validis, l. 1, lib. 10. The gloss adds: and this office of purchase and granting is *superindictum* on account of famine, i.e., extreme scarcity arising from the fault of the sky, or of war, which arises from the fault of men. D. locati conducti, l. si merces, §. culpae; and l. ex conducto, §. sed si labes. The gloss therefore referred only to the necessity of coercion and the price. And the alternative, with which the gloss turns, notes the diversity of contingency, not the diversity of extension. And this is the truth. And from this, as I think, satisfaction has been given to the first question asked concerning the understanding of the text and gloss of the said l. 1.

I come to the second point, namely, to the understanding of the words of the sentence. And because the judge went beyond, that is, by declaring and determining himself according to the understanding of the text and gloss, there is no doubt that the sentence does not create a new understanding, but must be understood according to that law: namely, that the understanding of sentences proceeds from the law, especially when a reference is made expressly to the written law. And it supports what we note in *causam*, Extra, *de officio delegati*, and it is expressed in D. *de adquirendo et retinenda hereditate*, l. *Titiae amicae*; D. *de re iudicata*, l. *miles*, § *decem*: “The words of the sentence follow the words and the mind; these words sound interpretively.” C. *de necessitudine servorum*, l. 1, in princ.: “We follow the footsteps of the will,” and c. *Idem est ergo sensus textus et glossae et sententiae*. For it is consonant with the law of the one declaring the law that the sentence should be consistent with the laws, because a sentence should not lead us to an inconvenience. D. *de erciscundis*, l. *et puto*, § 1; and we note through Cynus in l. *si*, C. *de annua exceptione*. Since the judge, in the pronouncement of the sentence, of which he is the efficient and formal cause, interprets its sense, there is no need for an external interpreter or an extrinsic understanding. D. *de appellationibus ab executore*, contrary to the sense of that adverb “male.” And because there, after the sentence is completed in the pronouncement of the words: “But while it is in the making, it receives every mode and form.” C. *de sententiis*, c. *tussis eorum*. For the last word “pronounced” already demonstrates the sentence. For while the judge is still speaking, the matter is imperfect, and at the end of the words, the final end of the cognition stands.

† Opinion. A principal article is one that is perfect in its substance and structure, containing the substantial and accidental elements of the definition, if they are made within the same context. As is clear from l. 1, ff. de re iudicata, and similar authorities, it therefore follows from the foregoing that war is not contained in itself, but only accidentally, when it gives rise to the necessity of purchasing the aforementioned goods. Otherwise, if war were to bring abundance or plentiful plunder due to favorable fortune, where it is customary for wages to be doubled, nevertheless the free and exempt persons are not bound so fully as stated in our case. For the words say “and whatever other things can be said or conceived,” etc., “under whatever name they may be considered, and for whatever reason, occasion, or cause.” Thus, no case has been left untouched, which regards every article as expressed. ff. de testibus, l. qui testamento militari, in the word “hoc tamen animo,” as noted in l. sed et si quia, § quaesitum, ff. si quis cautio.

I come to the third point, which is called an urgent war. And I say that there is a difference between urging and being urged. For if a city, in order to gain glory, initiates a war, it is said to be urging, not being urged, because it is of the active mode. But if it defends its own pressure, it is said to be being urged. Hence, elsewhere the gloss says: admitted, not seen. C. de cond. ob caus. l. 1. But he who defends himself is said to be compelled by necessity, extra de except. c. cum inter priorem, according to Innocentius, ff. ad l. Aquil. scientiam, §. qui cum aliter, and C. unde vi, l. 2. And therefore, an urgent war is said to be one that protects the right of the people. And if the war were not made, the possession of the honor of the city and its district would be lost; nor do I care whether it is near or far, ff. de iudic. l. insulae. Nevertheless, the exempt are not collected for all small wars. And those who, because of the war, are compelled by urgent necessity, are exempt from subsidiary liability so that the privilege and immunity may benefit them; so that whenever the resources of others are not sufficient, or are sufficient only with great scandal, the exempt may be burdened to contribute with the others, as noted by Dynus in l. 2, ff. de iure immunit. Otherwise, they should not be compelled, arg. ff. de leg. 1, l. ab omnibus, in princ., and de mun. et oner. l. ut gradatim, §. quotiens, and extra de immunit. eccles. adversus, and as noted, C. de sacrosanct. eccles. l. neminem, in ult.

Furthermore, in our case, there is no place for this consideration, because the said privileged person cannot be burdened because of the war, except because of the necessity of provisions for the city or fleets. For naval provisions, which are incumbent upon the war that the city suffers, I think he is bound. But for the wages of armed men, I do not think he is bound, because of the general immunity and franchise, and because of those words said or devised. For I presuppose the immunity to be valid, and its validity is not disputed, because it was granted by the Prince or by the royal city, so that what is noted in l. evacuatis, C. de decur. lib. 10, with similar cases, does not stand in the way. City

† For indeed the king can grant a franchise to his subjects, because he exercises the office of the Prince on his throne. As stated in the Digest, title *Quod vi aut clam*, law *Pro haerede*, section *Plane*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the Sienese are bound to keep in the city of Cortona 40 foot soldiers and halberdiers, and whether they are bound to pay them the wage that is given to the stipendiary citizens of Siena, or whether the said stipendiaries ought to be paid a salary as it is now paid to the stipendiary citizens of Siena at the present time, or as it was at the time of the said agreements.
2. Whether one who is exempt from all real and personal burdens, except for a thousand florins, has this exemption apply to property acquired thereafter in the future.
3. Whether the city is bound to expel all traitors and rebels of another city having a distinct territory.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Regarding the matter of the Lord of Cortona, the chapter states that the Sienese ought to maintain in the city of Cortona 40 foot soldiers and 25 armored horsemen, and that they should remain for 25 years, and that they should receive that salary or stipend which is given to the stipendiaries of the city of Siena.

† It is asked whether the said stipendiaries should be paid as stipendiaries of the city of Siena are currently paid at present: or as was the case at the time of the said agreements. And it seems that the commune of Siena is not bound to pay more than what was formerly paid as stipend at the time the contract was celebrated. For a contract is that which immediately gives origin and form to the obligation, and it cannot give any other form than that which it has at the time of the contract. This arises from the convention of the contract and the obligation. As stated in D. de contrah. empt. l. ruptilia and l. in lege. Present things are indeed swifter and more certain for informing [the obligation] than future ones. And therefore everything that is contracted simply is referred to the present time. C. de serv. l. non modus. Hence, accidental augmentations do not change the substantial form of the disposition. D. de verb. oblig. l. insulam. Within two years. Certain. The primary status of the obligation is not changed by the variety of time. As stated in X. de cens. olim causam. And this seems to be proven by those words of the instrument that it be paid what is given, etc., which are words of the present tense. D. de aur. et arg. leg. l. si ita. Moreover, if I promise you ten gold coins for sustenance, or I promise you sustenance estimated at ten gold coins, although grain is dearer, I am not bound to pay more than ten; and although things are cheap, the obligation does not decrease. For estimation defines the obligation. D. de sol. l. si quis stipulatus fuerit decem in mille. C. de iure dot. l. si inter virum. D. so. matrim. l. aestimante. Thus it seems in the case at hand, as if a sum of money had been promised from the beginning, fixed by tax.

On the contrary, it seems that a fact distributed over time receives the promise of time. Hence, at the time of dearth, the heir is thus bound to provide the full sustenance bequeathed, just as at a time of plenty; and the hardship of the time does not harm the creditor. D. de verb. oblig. l. continuus. §. illud. For such things as do not have a certain quantity or nature receive from accidents both increase and, if they are worth less, diminution. X. de usur. cum Apostolus. And l. mutuum. D. si cert. pet. And extrinsic goodness is not considered, but the intrinsic quality of the substance of the thing. As stated in D. si cert. pet. l. cum quid. The substance of this fact is contained there when it says 25 barbutas, etc. Hence, if I owe service to someone with one knight or foot soldier, no one doubts that the difficulty of this stipend pertains to me, since I am bound to a fact whose expenses accidentally vary from time to time. As stated in l. suo victu. D. de oper. liber. And the contract then speaks. Time does not come unless it is about a certain quantity. But the obligation of a fact is uncertain; and therefore interest does not come in a taxed quantity by right of action, but in facts. Thus D. de verb. oblig. stipulationes non dividuntur. §. Celsus. Moreover, the number of soldiers is for the purpose of the defense of the Lord of Cortona: which purpose would perhaps not be achieved if the number were reduced. As stated in X. de constit. cap. ex parte episcop. And to this contributes what is noted in cap. ult. de decimis. in Clem. And therefore in this first point, I am of the opinion for the Lord of Cortona, according to the nature and purpose of the thing promised.

Secondly, it is asked, because it was in the agreements that the Lords of Cortona were to be immune from all real and personal burdens, whether this has application to things subsequently acquired and to be acquired in the future, because the agreements state: "except for the aforementioned thousand florins." I say that this exception, "except for the aforementioned thousand florins, etc.," shows that the preceding terms, or genera, must be of the same quality, that is, those imposed per pound and by estimation, from which they do not extend to tolls (gabella); because the nature of an exception is twofold. For it exempts from action, and declares that the preceding terms of the genus must be of the same quality as the exception. D. de pignoribus et hypothecis, l. Nam quod liquide, § Si cui. And thus the immunity is restricted to things for which payment is made per pound and by estimation. For such immunity cannot be extended to tolls on fruits and contracts; because these are superindicta (levied by special assessment). But from taxes (data) and collections which are assessed by estimation, they are exempt. What, therefore, of those subsequently exempted? Whether purchase benefits them in these matters can be argued both for and against. And first, it seems that it does not. As C. de servitutibus, l. Non modus; and note in l. Fina, Quae res pignori obligari possunt; and Extr. de privilegiis, cap. Porro, and cap. Cum capella. For what if he were to purchase a hundred times a hundred thousand? D. de legato secundo, l. Offilius, accumulating infinite amounts; eodem titulo, l. Nomen, § Filio. It would be inequitable to make a privilege, and against the public good, which ought not to be. D. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione, l. Ex facto. Moreover, this privilege is granted to persons for things. Argumentum D. de damno infecto, l. Damni, § Si is qui vicinas. To the contrary, it is argued, because this privilege is not restricted by the limits of things; therefore, it extends to whatever things, as being universal, according to Petrus and Cynus in the said l. Non modus; and l. Fina, D. de servitutibus rusticorum praediorum, l. Si servitus; de fundo instrato, l. Lucius. And this is the more correct view, on account of the words of the immunity not being restricted by any limits.

Thirdly, whether the commune of Siena is bound to expel from the city of Siena and its county all the traitors and rebels of the said Lord of Cortona. And I say that it is not, because they have not been banned from its territory. For the commune of Siena possesses a free and franchised territory. D. de edict. edict. l. quid sit fugitivus, § apud. However, if these persons were to plot or arrange anything against the Lord of Cortona within the Sienese territory, then the commune of Siena would be obliged to punish them. D. de capt. l. non dubito. For the Sienese ought not to suffer this. D. loc. l. in lege locationis. And I speak of those who are justly banned, and who are not descendants of Bartholomew. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A manifold species of public offices is found. And see below, cons. 410.
2. Whether the collected sum is a personal, real, or mixed public office.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It must be premised for clarity that certain charges (munera) are purely and truly real, in that by their nature and effect they are imposed on the lands themselves or the fruits of the lands without any distinction of persons, whether they are rendered from the very substance of the fruits or in money on account of such fruits. Such are taxes (tributa) and real tithes. See D. de impositione, l. neque stipendium; and D. de usufructu, l. si pendentes, § si quid; and fully noted in C. de annona et tributo, in the Rubric, n. 59; and l. 1, in the word “fructus percipit”; and l. indictiones, in the words “non personis, sed in rebus.” Such are also the charges imposed on possessors according to the number and measure of the iugera: for example, five coins per year for each sextarius of land, or a fixed sum to be paid for each lagena of wine from such holdings, so that they correspond to the resources of a certain locality. See D. de censu, l. forma sensuali; and C. de immunitatibus nemini concedendis, l. perbucinam, lib. 10; and D. de iudiciis, l. fideicommissum, § tractatum. If these are perpetual, they are called taxes (tributa), and they are purely and truly real burdens; and the final cause of payment is the thing itself, and the possession or the revenues thereof.

Certain charges are purely and truly personal by nature and mode of satisfaction: for example, to serve in the army not at one’s own expense but on another’s stipend; to perform guard duty at a certain place by day or by night; to carry grain to a certain place without any outlay from one’s own purse; to act as syndicus at the expense of the community. See D. de muneribus et oneribus, l. munerum.

Certain charges are mixed, as are all the aforementioned ones, if you combine bodily labor with expense from your own purse. See the same l. munerum, § mixta.

† Regarding the collected taxes, it is doubted whether they are mixed burdens. And it seems that they are purely real burdens: because they are paid from the purse. To the contrary, that they are mixed: because the person is obligated, and payment is made from the purse. D. de muneribus et oneribus, l. 1, rescripto, §. si. To the contrary, that they are purely personal. Arg. D. de contrahenda emptio, l. final, §. final. On this, it should be said thus: either the tax is imposed principally, or in place of another burden. In the first case, it either concerns the resources of a certain place. And such a tax is principally a real burden, although it is imposed on persons for things. Or it regards resources in general: and then such a tax is not a real burden, but a mixed one. As noted by Guillaume de Cousseau, C. de sacrosancta ecclesia, l. placet. And it is mixed not by reason of office or work, but by reason of personal and real obligation joined together. In the second case, such a burden, the tax, is substituted for which burden it takes the place of. As noted by Bartolus in l. 4, §. actor, de re iudicata. Having thus premised, I say that truly and properly, in the truth of the matter, by its nature, the money which is perpetually paid for measured lands, according to the tax on fruits, is considered and is a conventional tribute substituted in place of a purely and truly real tribute. And therefore, those having possessions, from wherever they are in the castle of Saltaria, are bound to contribute the said quantity. Also, to the purse taxes which are imposed on the inhabitants of Saltua by the commune of Fano, or of Saltaria, they are bound to contribute for the outer holdings, according to the form of the agreements, and according to the law given to Saltua, according to the manner of those who possess there, as the above writing stated. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a person appointed as a forensic official is a true citizen, notwithstanding that he has given security.
1. What effect the clause "notwithstanding" has in statutes, privileges, and benefits.
2. That which is granted to deserving persons is granted more effectively.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† That the said Ser Orlandus was made a true citizen from the beginning is not in doubt. For true citizenship, although extraordinary, can be conferred by citizens upon foreigners, as noted in C. de incolis; l. ci. ues., lib. 10; and by Bartolus in ff. de usucapione, l. is qui pro emptore. Hence, the said Ser Orlandus has been included in the number and true essence of citizens. For whatever fits the truth of a definition is truly such. Circumlocutions, however, demonstrate accidents; although they contribute greatly to knowing what something is, ff. si certum petatur, l. 2, § appellata. But this person fits the true definition of him and others, and is a true citizen not by nature but by art, because citizenship is something that can be made, and is not only born but created. And that, although he did not provide surety, he remains in his being and is a true citizen, is shown by several reasons. And first: because in the new statutes, in the reviews and reforms of the old statutes, no mention is made of providing surety. Therefore, just as decretals are not alleged in matters decided by the compilers of the new law, and thus this clause cannot be alleged as if decided by the compilers of the new law, C. de novo codice confirmato, § hunc igitur externum, in the word solis in the series of constitutions, it is necessary to use the argument, ff. de testamento militis, l. tribunus in fine; and de legibus, l. legata inutiliter, according to Cynus.

Secondly, on account of the *non obstante* clause, which has the effect of removing not only the obstacle of principles, but also of those who have been granted privileges, because this clause establishes the thing as being in existence and preserves the thing in its being, as is evident. D. de legatis 3, l. si quis in principio; C. de testibus, Authent. inter liberos; de rescriptis, c. cum aliquibus; and c. si propter tua, lib. 6. Thirdly, because if it had expressly stated, "notwithstanding such a particle of reformation," it is certain that it would not have been an obstacle. But here it sufficed to say that these words are equivalent. There it is said, "special mention," and c. C. de quadriennali praescriptione, l. omnes, cum si. Fourthly, this is especially true when such a civil favor was not granted gratuitously, but on account of some notable merit. D. de donationibus, l. Aquilius, and l. pater.

Fifthly, because those things which are granted to those who have well deserved are granted more effectively. D. ad Senatusconsultum Silanianum, l. si quis in graui; §. hi quoque; and l. 1, §. 1, D. de iustitia et iure, according to Guillaume. From these, and many others which civil reason and natural equity dictate—which I omit for the sake of brevity—I conclude in favor of the said Ser Orlando, that he ought to be considered a citizen of Florence and is not bound to give security. C. de hereditate vendita, l. 1. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the prince, or his president, or authority can command his subjects that they may not grind elsewhere than in the mills of the lord himself, or that they may not use other pastures or woods than his own. And number 3.
2. A twofold condition of lords is found.
3. Whether and when the commands and statutes of lords are binding.
4. The authority of the lord and that of the people are equated.
5. A multiple species of duties is found.
6. Immunity granted indiscriminately is understood to apply to personal matters.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It is asked whether a lord may ordain or command that his subjects may not grind grain elsewhere than in the lord’s own mills, or may not use other pastures or woods than his own. I speak of a lord, not of a governor or public authority, concerning whom there is no doubt that they cannot do such things, insofar as they pertain to their own profit. Jurisdictions are not for extortion, nor for gain. As stated in the Authentica “Ut iudices sine qualibet suffragio,” § “Cogitatio,” Codex, De contractibus iudicialibus; L. “Si,” Digestum, Si certum petatur; L. “Principalibus,” Digestum, De contrahenda emptione: it is not permitted. Hence the most pious Emperor says: “Do you think we command that we guard the prejudicial matter of the judge with less care?” in the Authentica “Ut iudices sine qualibet suffragio,” § “Si quis autem.” Moreover, they say that one must render a faith that is certainly whole and abstinent from all profit, Digestum, De negotiis gestis, L. “Qui sine usuris.” But if any official were to presume to do such things in fact, he could be resisted as a robber. Codex, De iure fisci, L. “Prohibitum”; Codex, De metallis, L. “Deuotum.” And note this in L. “Ut vim,” Digestum, De iustitia et iure, § “De dominis.” Therefore, concerning those who hold baronies, castles, and subjects, it is asked of whom he speaks. Codex, De haereticis, Authentica “Si ideo temporalis.”

The condition of lords is twofold. Some are those who have subjects by right; others are those who have vassals, that is, those bound by fealty. In the ancient law, when Justinian compiled the laws, oaths of fealty were not known, nor is this term found in the ancient law. Later, however, the infidelity of subjects and the dire voracity of lords increased, whence the servile name of fealty was introduced, and a stain was cast upon liberty. For the oath of fealty, and this fealty, is a certain obedient servitude, yet without diminution of status. The father of these oaths introduced this bridle on account of rebels. For, as Ecclesiasticus says: "The yoke and the strap bend the stiff neck." But from the ancient laws, whose traces remain among free peoples, these names were hostile to free birth and entirely alien to human dignity.

† It must therefore be said first: whether the lord of a city or castle can compel his subjects who are not feudatories, nor vassals, but simply subjects, to do those things about which inquiry has been made, or not. Secondly, what holds regarding vassals holding fiefs and bound by an oath of fidelity. For when the oath of fidelity was first invented, it was made on account of fiefs and benefices; later it proceeded further. Hence, as you see in the Peace of Constance, all subjects from the age of fourteen downwards swore fidelity to the prince. The question is asked: what is the law? And first, the meaning of this term "lord" must be ascertained: this name was formerly used without any restriction, signifying absolute power by virtue of holding. As in l. 2, §. dominorum, de his qui sunt sui vel alieni iuris, and de liberis et posthumis, l. in sale, according to Petrus and Cynus, in the said l. non modus, and l. si, de servorum iustis suis. But today this name, insofar as it refers to a slave, has been modified; insofar as it refers to a son, it has been removed. But this is not to be considered now; rather, our matter is as it refers from the lord to the subject. And here it must be considered that I am not speaking of the private property of the lord, but of the public affair, i.e., of the patrimony and jurisdiction. l. bene a Zenone. Thus Caesar has two procurators: one fiscal, the other patrimonial, or of private property. The question therefore stands here: whether the public authority of the lord is so great or of such a kind that he can order or command the aforementioned things, or not. It is certain, however, that subjects are bound to obey their lords in that which is juridical and reasonable. Likewise, it is commonly held that subjects are bound to their lords for public duties, and freedmen to their patrons for services. ff. de conditionibus in debendo, l. si non sortem, §. libertus; and C. de negotiorum gestorum officio; and ff. de obsequiis parentibus praestandis, throughout. Freedmen are also bound to their patrons for labor. However, they do not undertake obligations that perpetually burden their freedom. ff. quarum rerum actiones non dantur, l. 1, §. quae honorandae. But that which is not done for the purpose of exercising religion or piety may be imposed from the beginning of freedom. ff. de manumissione testamento, l. Menia. But that which prevents a freedman from exercising his art cannot be enjoined upon him. As in ff. de operis liberorum, l. libertus negotiationis. Nor can he be bound or prohibited from commerce. As in ff. de iure patronatus, l. quaero; and ff. de obsequiis, l. fin.

† The precepts of the jurisdiction of lords are binding if they are clear, if they are issued after the cause has been heard, and if they are based on merits rather than on the luxury of the mind. Likewise, statutes of lords in which fraud is present are not valid: as this is proven. C. communia episcopi. l. interlocutio. and l. praeses. ff. de lega. j. si filius. §. diui. per Dyn. C. de fideicomm. quotiens. per Cyn. and in cap. j. de iud. per Innocen. lib. 6. ff. de manu. vindic. illud. ff. de except. do. l. 1. in fin. and elsewhere it is not expressly found except there, that the exception of fraud can be raised against unjust statutes. But that this ordinance is unjust, indeed null, is proven thus. Either we will say that this ordering or statute is of contentious jurisdiction, or of voluntary jurisdiction: because it is not provided for by any law, nor is it numbered among the examples of non-contentious, nor among the examples of voluntary jurisdiction. Since therefore this statute is of jurisdiction, as appears from the definition of jurisdiction. ff. de iurisd. omnium iudicum. l. j. It is necessary that this statute be of some species of jurisdiction. But it has been proven that it is of no species of jurisdiction: therefore the one who statutes in this regard obtains the status of a private person: and thus obedience is not due, even if the subject is bound by an oath of fidelity. vt ff. de obsequiis. l. nullum. Furthermore, the chapters of the oath of fidelity have their own form. vt in cap. 1. de forma fidelitatis in vsib. feud. and in those chapters this is not included: therefore they are not owed. ff. de verborum obli. l. quicquid astringendae. For regarding other matters, the subject has free houses: because obligation in some things seems to free from others. ff. de aqua pluu. arcen. l. si prius. §. aquae. ff. quemadmodum serui. amit. si sic. and arg. ff. de proba. Procula. ff. de vsu. l. qui semisses. ff. de mili. testamen. l. tribunus. §. vlti. Moreover, to go or come to a place must be within the free power of anyone. ff. de via pub. l. publicam. ff. de condi. et demonstra. l. quibus diebus. in prin. just as fishing in the sea, or sailing. For these are free by the law of nations. vt insti. de rerum diuisi. §. j. and ij. and this right is called natural, which is immutable. vt insti. de iu. natu. §. sed naturalia. The condition, if you go to such a place: is said to be potestative, not necessitative. ff. de haered. institu. l. suus. §. puto. Moreover, he who is ordered to go to one mill is prohibited from all others. ff. de cond. et dem. l. cum ita legatum sit si Titio. but this also cannot be done even by pact. vt ff. de pact. l. nemo. Moreover, the right of drawing water, or pasturing cattle, is accustomed to be an active right, not a passive one. ff. de serui. rust. praed. l. pecoris. de seruitu. vt pomum. nullo. n. iure hoc cauetur, that I can constitute a servitude for you, even if this has it acquired in itself. Therefore someone is forced to contract, and to enter into a contract: I give so that you do: for example, I give one denarius for pasture for each head, but it is certain that no one is forced to contract. vt l. nec emere. de iure deli. and de act. et obl. l. sicut. and ff. commo. §. sicut. and not. in l. 2. de epi. aud. and such things done by the authority of the people are rescinded. ff. qui et a quibus. l. priuatus. ff. de pollicita. l. totiens.

Similarly, if it is done by the command of the lord. For the command of the lord and the command of the people are equated: as is notably stated in the text, D. de officio praetoris, l. Barbarius Philippus. Moreover, the Emperor and the Pope cannot do this without offending justice, unless on account of public necessity. D. de evictionibus, l. Lucius; D. de re vendita, l. item verberatum; D. de legibus 3, qui solidum, § 1; D. de naturalis restitutione, quaeris. And it is noted in the constitution Omnem, where it is said: the Emperor wishes to foster, not to command, those things which are of free will. D. de testamento, Omnium. Moreover, the lord cannot ill-treat his subjects according to law, nor burden them with an exceedingly harsh yoke. C. de nouis vectigalibus, l. 1, because existing things do not wish to be disposed of badly. Hence, he cannot alienate them against their will to a more severe lord, as is noted in D. de fideicommissis libertatis, l. inuitis. Furthermore, even negative conditions must be fulfilled, such as if he has thrown money into the sea. D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Meuius. But commands are not to be fulfilled unless they pertain either to the necessity of the obligation or to the authority of the commander, provided, however, that they do not derogate from public law. D. de annuis legibus, l. Quintus, § Pomponius; D. de operis libertatis, l. Cerdonem. Finally, it is expedient for the lords themselves that reason and equity rule in them. D. de his qui sui iuris sunt, l. 2, § dominorum. Therefore, certain commands are not to be observed, as is read and noted in D. de hereditate instituenda, l. paterfamilias testamento, in the last gloss. Rather, those who hasten to execute what is unjustly done are punished with penalty, as in C. de excusationibus munerum, l. euidenter, lib. 10; and it is established in D. ad Trebellianum, l. facta, § si sub conditione. And if one cannot resist a lord who acts wrongly, nevertheless the key of justice errs, and the crimes of the great are concealed, as is noted in l. ad splendidum, C. de diuersis officiis, lib. 12. It does not befit a good prince to fill himself with the greed of avarice and treasures. For the treasury of the prince is not his own fisc, but subjects who are well-off. In Auth. ut iuvenes sine quoquo suffragio, § cogitatio; C. de caducis tollendis, infra, in the end. For while he cares for the salvation of the flock committed to him, he is a king; but if he is greedy and delicate, he passes into a detestable and harsh name, and becomes a tyrant, as Seneca says in Epistle 105. And just as in our body the head does not abandon the limbs, so in the mystical body the superior ought to provide for and foster his inferiors, who are called the limbs of his body; otherwise, it is necessary that both perish if the head is cut off from the rest of the body. That fat subjects are called the sinews, we have the text in C. de omni agro deserto, l. 2.

† Let us now argue the point at issue; another consideration of this matter is that it is certain that lords impose public duties on their subjects, and the most well-known division of these duties is into real, personal, and mixed duties, as stated in the law *De muneribus*. Furthermore, there are taxes, some of which are levied on property, others on the person; generally, however, "tax" is said to be whatever is contributed, as noted in the rubric of the Code, *De anno et tributis*, Book 10. Taxes on the person are remitted to the poor, because one must first deal with the subjects, as stated in the Digest, under the same title, in the law *Pensitate omnes*. One must also take care that the burden, which ought to be borne by many, is not carried by a few, with others being relieved, as stated in the Code, *De exactione tributorum*, in the law *Actores*, and there noted; and no one is compelled to pay more than what concerns him, as stated in the Code, *Quomodo et quando civilia munera indicantur*, in the law *Ultra medium*, and there noted, Book 10. Personal duties are explained with solicitude, real duties with performance, and mixed duties with both, as noted in the rubric of the Code, *De muneribus patrimonialibus*, Book 10. And burdens are to be distributed according as fortune favors, as stated in the same title, in the first law, in the text and gloss, to the contrary.

† And if immunity is granted to someone indiscriminately, it is not understood to apply to personal offices. In the same title, l. qui immunitatem. In these offices, first, the person who imposes the office must be considered as to whether he has that office. As in C. de iure fisci, l. super creandis. Second, the person to whom it is imposed, as to whether he is subject. As noted in C. quemadmodum civiles munera indicantur, in the rubric, book 10. For always the virtue and power of the efficient cause must be considered, so that it may act upon the passive and the receiving matter. C. qui pro sua iurisdictione, l. 1; ff. de confirmatione tutelae naturalis, §. final; C. ne de statu defuncti, l. si pater; ff. de tutoribus et curatoribus dandis ab his, l. 1 and l. pupillo; ff. de excusatione tutoris, l. iuris peritos, §. cum oriundus; ff. de muneribus et oneribus, l. rescripto, §. final, and l. honor, §. de honoribus. From all of which we infer thus: if the efficient cause can act upon the passive, and if this is a public office, therefore the imposition holds, and the lord’s ordinance is binding, and obedience is due. For a subject is bound to obey, unless he has an excuse, which must be specifically alleged. Hence the Emperor states that all causes by which one is strangled must be specifically set forth. C. de praediis curiae, l. 1, book 10. Furthermore, the lord may establish that a certain amount be paid for every head of livestock, even if it is not driven to the lord’s pasture, and for every bushel of wheat ground, even if it does not go to the lord’s mill. Hence, if he can impose what burdens more, much more so what burdens less. Thus argues the text in another matter. ff. de in litem iurando, l. in actionibus, and l. videamus, §. final. He could also impose a tax on the heads of those born, as in C. de agris et censibus, l. cum antea, book 10, and this is the custom in Sardinia, as noted there. And if it is said, to which species of jurisdiction does this belong, voluntary or contentious? I answer: this is a certain unnamed jurisdiction, which can be called by the general name of superiority; indeed, it is of empire, because these are royal. col. 10. Hence this can be called royal jurisdiction, or quasi-royal. For they rule by hand and mere arbitrium. As in l. 2, ff. de origine iuris, near the beginning. And that arbitrium is exercised imperiously and voluntarily, and sometimes regularly and well, sometimes irregularly and inordinately; nevertheless, a slave cannot object to his master. What shall I say? Finally, I distinguish. Either the lord’s ordinance regards a private thing, that is, his own patrimony: for example, the mills are his, of his private patrimony, and the profit arising therefrom would likewise be of private right, and such a statute or decree is invalid, because it is ambitious and pertains to private advantage. ff. de decretis ab ordinario faciendis, l. ambitiosa. Or it regards a public thing, that is, the fiscal chamber: for example, the mills are fiscal, or the woods are public, as noted in l. sed Celsus, de contrahenda emptio.
