Hence the profit derived therefrom is destined for public necessities. Then such an ordinance is valid, because it is a public office. And this appears in the case of the mill of the city of Bologna. And those who are appointed to collect these offices perform a personal and menial solicitude. de muneribus et oneribus, l. munerum, §. inter personalia. Nevertheless, such ordinances are not just unless public necessity demands it. For on account of public necessity, one departs from the utility of private persons. d. l. munerum, §. item episcopi, and there noted. Finally, the public voice prejudices the private, as noted. ff. de haeredibus instituendis, l. testamento domini. And this is true in the case of those lords who exercise general, free, and arbitrary power. However, if they have a marked and limited jurisdiction, whatever they do beyond the limits is illicit to their own power. C. de decuriis militum, l. diuinorum; ff. de acquirenda rerum dominium, l. in agris limitatis; and noted in l. penultima, ff. de conditione ob causam, according to the reading. For he is justly despised from whom more than is due is commanded, and his honorific status is diminished by that contempt. Hence Fulgentius: he who seeks to be more than is permitted, will be less than he is. And these things suffice. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the City of Venice is an island.
2. What is included under the term "island." And no. 3.
3. Whether the City of Venice is beyond or on this side of the Tiber.
4. What the terms "on this side" and "beyond" signify.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Certain persons purchased at auction certain tolls of the city of Genoa, by these words: "citra Tyberim" [on this side of the Tiber]. Now it is asked: whether the city of Venice is citra [on this side] or ultra [on the other side]. And to me, who am Tuscan and know for the most part the bed of the Tiber, there is no true doubt, that being in the city of Genoa, and speaking thus: "citra Tyberim," that the city of Venice is citra Tyberim. For the word "citra" denotes nearness, at least comparatively. The word "ultra" denotes nearness, at least comparatively, with some term existing in the middle: for example, a tree, a road, a river, or mountains. For instance, if an Italian says "citra montes Alamaniae" [on this side of the German mountains], it signifies towards Italy. But if a German says it, it signifies towards Germany, and there is no question about this. Although sometimes a question is accustomed to be formed, to which of the extremes this middle term is to be applied, which is nothing to the purpose: and this when the word "citra" or "ultra" is applied to a place, just as if it were applied to time. As when we say "citra pasca" [before Easter] or "ultra pasca" [after Easter]. And imagine that there is a certain statue, which has its face towards the Tiber, and speaks: "I am citra Tyberim." And again, let there be another statue ultra Tyberim, which has its face towards the first statue, and speaks: "I am citra Tyberim." For from each will come a true word, speaking of itself. But if one statue speaks towards the other, it will say: such a statue is ultra Tyberim, remote from me, with the Tiber intervening. Since therefore the river Tiber is not in any place between Venice and Genoa, but very remote: even from all Romandiola, not to mention the March of Treviso, it rightly follows that the city of Venice is, with respect to the city of Genoa, citra Tyberim, and not ultra Tyberim. And this argument is proved by location and by ocular demonstration: an argument by which none is more evident. As in the Institutes, de gradibus, §. sed cum magis.

† The second question is whether the city of Venice is an island. Suppose the testator said, “I bequeath all my goods which you have in the islands”; or “I give, or I bind myself to give, all movable property which I shall export from the islands.” Are goods which anyone has in the city of Venice included? And it seems that they are: because Bartolus says that an enclosure made in a river belongs to the builder, just as an island formed in a river belongs to those who own lands near the island. See Institutes, On the Division of Things, § Island.

† To the contrary is the truth: because the name “island” is the name of the soil, not of buildings. Although sometimes buildings are called an island, this is improper; for no more are houses or towers called an island, which is ridiculous to say: because trees are not an island, although they are in an island: and the same applies to buildings. Since therefore the whole city of Venice is founded in the bed of the sea, and not upon land, it cannot be said that it is an island, whether named or unnamed. It is established that some islands are named: such as Sicily, Sardinia, Cyprus, and similar ones; some are unnamed and uninhabitable, where perhaps there are wild men. Of which note, D. de iust. et iur. l. omnes populi. Now the city of Venice cannot be called an island in any of these ways: because no riverbed is called an island. As in Inst. de rerum div. §. item per alluvionem. Moreover, the homeland of the Venetians has in itself the proper name of an illustrious city, and it is said that it is in the March of Treviso. And it is certain that a March is not contained under the name of island, although it is situated next to the living sea or the dead sea. As in c. 1. quis dicatur dux, Marchio, Comes. And it is called a March, because [it is a border]. But an island is not [a border]: just as under the name of wood, that which is submitted under a proper name is not contained. As in D. de leg. 3. l. ligni and D. de ver. sig. l. pali et perticae. Furthermore, if the city of Venice were an island, it would follow that men could be deported and exiled there, which is absurd: because deportations are made as a penalty, not into a certain paradise of delights. Furthermore, if the city of Venice were an island made in the sea, therefore, upon the citizens departing, it would be granted to the occupant: which is false. Furthermore, it would be of the Roman prince: because all islands are of the empire. As in c. 1. quod sint reges, col. 10. and they are of the reservation to the prince, as in l. illicitas, §. quod universas, de off. praesid. and D. de leg. 3. l. 1, §. a praefectis. The contrary of which experience itself teaches.

† Moreover, the term "island" is sometimes used in a simple sense; and then it signifies only land surrounded by water: I mean land that rises above the surface, not that which lies beneath the earth. As stated in the law *In lege* and the law *Ruptilia*, on contracting sale, and in the Institutes, on the division of things, § *Isula*. This also appears from common understanding, to which we must resort for interpreting words. As in the Digest, on the significance of words, the law *Fundi appellatione* and the law *Auunculus*; and in the Digest, on laws, book 3, the law *Librorum*, § *Quod tamen Cassius*; in the Digest, on funeral expenses, the law *L.*; in the law *Cum delationis*, § *Asinam*, with the case *Si non obstat*. Although the term "island" is sometimes used for a house, because there it is not used in a simple sense, but with an adjunct, namely, a work made by hand, and thus the mode of signification is declared by the adjunct. And so understand the gloss which is in § *Insula*, Institutes, on the division of things, which says that it is sometimes taken for a house situated in the sea; because that is true, since it is used with an adjunct. But when it is used naturally, that is, simply, it must be understood in its primary signification, that is, of a natural island, which arises naturally. For words are to be understood properly, and according to the signification of the law. Digest, on the significance of words, *Nepos Proculo*. Moreover, that which is supported by pontoons in the riverbed cannot be called an island. Moreover, he who builds on an island does not make the building his own; but it accedes to the soil; otherwise if in the sea. Digest, that nothing be done in a public place, law 1; and it applies. Digest, on rivers, law 1, § *Insula*, and § *Si fossam*, and § *In flumine*, in the reason of itself. From which it is clearly concluded that the city of the Venetians is not an island, nor can it be called by the name of island. And so I answer the question. Baldus, ACC, whether on this side or that. Suppose, for example, that the words of the contract q76 apply to the case set forth above,

Whether the city of Venice is situated *citra* or *ultra*. Suppose, for instance, that the words of the contract state it thus, and that *Pelagus* is understood to mean every place and land beyond the Tiber River, and that this contract was concluded in Genoa. The question arises as above. It must be said that *citra* signifies this, considering that the contract was concluded in Genoa. This is supported by several reasons. First, because it is expressly evident, there is no need to prove it. As stated in the Digest, *De verborum obligationibus*, in the law *Ubi autem*: "where nature itself declares it manifest." And men believe more with their eyes than with their ears, as stated in the Institutes, *De gradibus*, in the section *Sed cum magis*. And the inspection of the eyes is a firm certainty regarding the matter at hand, as stated in the Digest, *Si regis*, in the law *Si emptione*, section *Si ad officium*. And it is reasonable to argue that where we have sense perception, the intellect is weak, as Aristotle and Averroes say. But this is a manifest, indeed notorious, fact of a permanent nature: because there is no route to Venice that requires crossing the Tiber, or any imaginary line of the Tiber.

† Secondly, this is proven: because the term *citra* signifies “before” or “on this side,” and the term *ultra* signifies “after” or “on the other side,” with something intervening in between; just as we say, “this field is *citra* the Po, and that one *ultra* the Po.” But the city of Venice is *ultra* the river Tiber, as is evident by measuring over land or through the air. To this effect, the gloss is prudently cited in Inst. de rebus divisis, § Insula, and the statement of Bartolus in his work called *Tiberiadis*. Therefore, that which is closer to the wall is *citra*; that which is more distant is *ultra*. The third reason is: because measurement ought to be made by the more convenient routes, not by windings and the circuit of the sea. The text is noted in l. Non tantum, ff. de excusatione tutoris; and ff. si quis cautionem, l. 2, § Quod diximus; and noted in ff. de falsis, l. Eos, § Si, in fine, gloss. But from the city of Venice, one goes more quickly to the face of the Tiber than to its back and, so to speak, its shoulders. Therefore, the city of Venice is *citra* the Tiber. Moreover, he who, by bringing an action, alleges that something is *ultra* or *citra*, must prove it, not he who denies it. ff. de novo operis nuntiatio, l. Non solum, § Sed ut probari; and ff. de pactis, l. Veteribus, with its entire subject matter. From which it is evidently concluded that, whether we speak in the way of truth or in the way of proof, the city of Venice ought not to be counted among the places that are *ultra* the Tiber, and this is demonstratively shown by reference to neighboring cities. For Padua borders on the city of Venice and its lagoon, which is *citra* the Tiber according to the law *Miliaria* and *ultra*; therefore, the city of Venice is *citra* the Tiber, and not *trans* the Tiber, with respect to the city of Genoa. From which it is concluded that the city of the Venetians is *citra* the Tiber, coming towards Lombardy, and this is a demonstration from situation, which is a perpetual demonstration, as in l. Si, C. de servitutibus et aqua; and l. 1, ff. de fluminibus. Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Monosyllables "a" and "ab" should be noted as indicating either separation of time, or conjunction and copulation, and thus whether they include and exclude.
1. The beginning of the year is where the parties intended it to be.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. F. leased to T. in these words: in the year 1382, in the month of May, from the feast of Saint Martin next to come, until nine years next following; paying each year, on the feast of Saint Martin, 40 florins and c.

It is now asked how these words “from the feast of Saint Martin, etc.” are to be understood: whether they include the first Saint Martin, because the contract was celebrated in the month of October, or whether they exclude it. For this is a common question: whether the monosyllable “a” denotes separation of time or conjunction and copulation; for in the first case it excludes, in the second it includes. Let us therefore see what the law says about this monosyllable “a,” or about the syllable “ab.” For some say indiscriminately that this word “a” and “ab” is used exclusively, as in D. de acquisitione et usufructu emphyteuticario, l. Ratio, § Si. Others say that it is used inclusively, as is most fully noted by the Archpriest in c. Statutum, de prebendis, lib. 6. But Johannes Andreae there says one thing in the gloss, and pursues another in the novella; but elsewhere he is very brief in c. Quam sit, de electione, lib. 6, in the novella, in the word “a tempore,” where he says thus: “It is clear from this that even that day was counted,” although Francesco Vercellensis argues to the contrary by the decretal Pia, infra, de exceptionibus, sed exceptio. The exception distinguishes the case, and Johannes Andreae resolves the contrary. The words are brief, but the interpretation is not brief. It must therefore be said that either the intention of the law or of the contracting parties is established by the words, and we adhere to the words that declare it, whether they precede or follow, as in D. de legibus, l. Si servus plurium, § Fin., and as is noted in D. si certum petatur, l. Cum quid. Or, if it is not established by the words, then either, if it were taken inclusively, an absurdity would follow, and then it does not include, but excludes, as is noted by Cynus in C. de nuptiis, l. A caligato; or, however it is taken, no absurdity follows, and then it matters: either the word “a” or “ab” is joined to the beginning, and it is taken inclusively. It is said in l. Instituo nepotem qui nascetur infra decem menses a die mortis filii mei, that the day of death is counted in the ten months, D. de liberis et postumis, l. Gallus, in principio. It is said that the oath of fidelity, “I swear from this hour henceforth to be faithful,” certainly includes this hour, because the act is joined to the beginning of its own time, as in c. 1, de nova forma fidei. The words of the contract, “from this day I promise ten,” certainly include the present day, because it is a certain integrity of time which does not exclude its own beginning, as in D. si certum petatur, l. Lecta, § Fin., and generally, wherever it is joined with its own beginning, it includes it. But if it is joined with a time which is not its beginning, then it is taken exclusively, as if someone summoned is to appear within ten days from today. For today is not part of the judge’s admonition, because it is not part of the just appearance, as in l. 1, D. si quis cautionibus. Similarly, it is said, “Bishop, unless you pay within eight days from this day, I excommunicate you.” For the delay does not begin to run from this day, but the course of the delay begins from the following day, as in D. si certum petatur, l. Lecta, § Sed cum sortis.

From this theory we arrive at the conclusion of our question. I speak by way of motivation that the word “a” is taken inclusively. First, because the lessee received the fruits of the first Saint Martin, which he could not receive by virtue of another lease, because the second was finished; secondly, to avoid absurdity, because there ought not to be two feasts in the same year in which the fruits of the whole year consist. For the fruits of one year are only those of twelve months, as in D. de solutione et liberatione, l. Divortio, in principio, and § Quod in sementem. Thirdly, by the said doctrine, because the word “a” is joined to its beginning, as the script of the contract declares there, “in the beginning of any year.”

† For there is the beginning of the year where the parties intended it to be, as in l. 1, C. quando dies leg. ce. and ff. eo. l. nec semel, §. si in habitatione; and l. firmio, ff. quando dies le. ce. l. si cum praefinitione; and d. l. lecta, ff. si cer. pet. From these, I conclude that the word "from" here is used continuously and inclusively, not separatively, both by the nature of the beginning coming with its temporal progression, and by reason of avoiding absurdity and duplication, and by reason of avoiding declaration, because, as I said, where the word "from" is placed between the beginning and the end of time, it joins from moment to moment. But where it would be placed between contrary terms or those that could not be joined together, then it would be used exclusively, and of the first there are many examples. Behold, if I say from sunrise until sunset is day. Also, if I say from youth the earth is prone to evil. Also, if I say from the sole of the foot to the top of the head there is no blemish in him, for in all these and similar cases the word "from" is used inclusively, as is clear to anyone observing. So in the case at hand, when I say from the feast of Saint Martin until another feast of Saint Martin, since the word "until" is used exclusively, it is necessary that the word "from" be used inclusively, and if the contrary, the contrary. Since therefore the first feast, by the law of this contract and not another, pertained, as has been said, to the lessee, it necessarily follows that the last feast of Saint Martin does not pertain to the same, because where it begins, there the year ends its revolution, for if it is in days, as in ff. de feriis, l. more Romano. Also in months, therefore, and in years which are measured by days and months, as in ff. de statu li., l. cum hęres, §. stichus; and ff. de mino., l. 3, §. minorem. And it supports what is noted in C. de appel., auth. hodie; and in c. pia, de excep., li. 6; and ff. de vsufr., l. defuncta; and ff. si cer. pet., l. si quis nec causam, §. res pignori; and in c. si propter tua, de rescrip., lib. 6; and insti. de verb. ob., §. omnes. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the term "until" includes or excludes the day in question.
2. Against whom the interpretation of words used obscurely by the lessor or buyer ought to be made.
3. On the understanding of the law *Veteribus* in the Digest, under the title *De pactis*.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The words state “in emphyteusis, up to the large vineyard.” Likewise, concerning four or six perches of land planted with vines, partly uncultivated, located in the said quarter known as “at the large vineyard,” to which they adjoin, etc. Moreover, the Lord Pope granted to the same emphyteutary, in a lay fief, the entire possession which he holds, namely the whole of that quarter, and he annulled the aforementioned investitures. Nevertheless, it pleased the illustrious Lord, the Count of Virtues, that it be ascertained whether the said territory is included in the investiture or not.

† Now the question arises as to what is the law. The statement of Bartolus is alleged, who distinguishes that either the intention is proved: because the intention clarifies the doubtful words of contracts and of last wills. As in C. de fideicommissis, l. voluntas; and fully noted in ff. de pactis, l. veteribus; and ff. de regulis iuris, l. semper in stipulationibus. Or the intention is not established except through the meaning conveyed by the words. And then either it cannot be held inclusively, and is placed exclusively, as is the case when the term 'ad quem' cannot be comprehended under the generality of the preceding term according to its proper signification: and then in last wills it is placed inclusively. As in l. patronus, de lege 3; and l. in testamentis, de regulis iuris. Or in contracts: and then it is placed exclusively; because when the words are doubtful, favor should be given to the defendant rather than to the plaintiff; because he who wished to oblige another ought to have spoken more clearly. As noted in the aforementioned l. veteribus. For in contracts, the extension of obligation is to be avoided. And nothing comes into play except that which the matter itself holds. As in ff. de acquisitione emptionis, l. fundus. Do not understand this rule when words are uttered principally to oblige; but when words are uttered to except. For example, because the vendor or lessor excepts something obscurely, then an obscure exception is interpreted against the vendor or lessor; because he is understood to utter obscure words who wishes to act or except from them. And thus l. veteribus is understood.

And the reason for the aforesaid is this: either the lessor or the seller speaks ambiguously to his own advantage and to the detriment of the other party; and interpretation is made against the seller or lessor, as in l. 1, in fine, D. de actione empti. Or, conversely, the lessee or the buyer speaks ambiguously to his own advantage and to the detriment of the adversary; and then interpretation is made against the buyer or lessee, as in l. Si in emptione, D. de contrahenda emptio. For he is understood to have uttered the words whose interest it is that the words were uttered, not he whose interest it is that the words were omitted, as in D. de verbis oblig., l. Quicquid astringendae. Or the words are uttered by a third party, for example, a witness or a notary. Nevertheless, they are not entirely obscure, but can receive a probable interpretation; and in this case they are interpreted in the milder sense. And this is the opinion of Nicolaus de Tudeschis. Or say that there are certain matters which the buyer or lessor himself ought to specify, as one who knows the facts better, such as boundaries, servitudes of the thing, and similar matters; and then an ambiguous word is interpreted against the seller and lessor, D. de contrahenda emptio, l. Labeo scribit obscuritatem, together with the following law, and l. Cum in l. venditionis, and l. Quod saepe, §. Si, and D. de servitutibus urbanis praediorum, l. Si arborem, §. Si. There are certain matters which the seller or lessor has no need to specify, and then interpretation is made against the buyer or lessee, as in D. de contrahenda emptio, l. Si in emptione. From this it is concluded that interpretation is sometimes an uncertainty regarding boundaries, and thus regarding the thing brought into the contract, because the lessor ought to have specified it more clearly, and interpretation is made against the lessor, unless one were to say that there is a special rule in favor of the church, so that interpretation would be made more for the church than against the church, argumentum D. de iure fisci, l. Si. But this exception is not proven by any law. Let it therefore be concluded that the obscurity of boundaries harms the lessor, insofar as it can be comprehended under the words. Hence, if the lessor says "to you such meadows up to one hundred iugera," I understand this inclusively, because the limit to which it can reasonably be included is included. Also, by such doctrine, for either that which is placed in the place of a limit is of the essence or substance of the same thing, and then the limit is included as inward; or it is of the essence or substance of another thing, and then otherwise. For there is a double limit, namely, the inward limit and the outward limit, as noted in C. de evictionibus, l. Si fines agri. Although, as regards the law of that l. Non placeat, the glossa says otherwise, nevertheless in itself it is the truth; yet by this our question is not decided. I therefore return to our case, in which I say that we must consider first what is probable, as noted in the said l. Veteribus. And to this is added the quantity of the rent. For, having made a comparison of the rent to the thing in question, it is presumed for or against, as noted in l. 1, §. 1, D. de superficiebus. It is true that in deserted places this comparison does not properly apply, as in barren sands and similar places. Thirdly, we must consider appellative names or vocabularies. For from the diversity of vocabularies, something is not presumed to have been granted, as in D. de legibus tertio, l. Praediis, §. Balneas, and §. Qui domum. Fourthly, we must consider the quality of the thing itself at the present time of the contract, as in D. de contrahenda emptio, l. In l. hoc. I say this for this reason: because a vineyard is not said to exist where there are no vines, although there once were. For this name "vineyard" is both a vocabulary and a thing. No one would say that an extirpated vineyard, reduced to the form of simple land, is called a vineyard because it once was a vineyard; just as an island is not said to exist because it once was an island but now is not, as in l. Insulam, §. Si, D. de acquisitione rei dominii. For when the form of the thing is changed, its vocabulary is also changed, D. de usufructu, l. Qui usumfructum areae. Hence, because the words do not say "up to the great old vineyard" but say "up to the great vineyard," which is understood as land presently under vine, pure land is included up to the place under vine. But the place under vine is not included unless it is nominally assigned from the great vineyard, because the words say "namely, of all lands, meadows, brushwood, and pastures, gravel lands, situated and lying in those parts to which the said monastery of the Great Vineyard adjoins." Hence, nothing of the Great Vineyard, which at the time of the contract was a vineyard, is included, except those 146 perches of planted vines, as in D. de legibus tertio, l. Heres meus, §. Duas statuas. Nor do I care if some roots of the vine were still under the ground; for that which lies under the ground is not to be considered, but that which is seen, as in D. de contrahenda emptio, l. In l. fundi. From these, it is concluded that the contract of the said investiture of lease extends up to the place under vine of the Great Vineyard, so that it does not include the non-vineyarded land, but excludes the vineyarded land. For that vineyards are included because of the word "up to" is impossible, because when inclusion would include a contrary quality of the thing, the word "up to" is never placed inclusively, but is placed exclusively. On the matter of this word "up to," see the note by Cynus in C. de nuptiis, l. A caligato, and D. de officio praesidis, Meminisse. But because our matter concerns only interpretation regarding boundaries, no other matter is to be treated here, because it has been fully said above. From these, it clearly appears that a vineyard is not said to be that which has ceased to be a vineyard, from which fruits are not gathered, but has become sterile; just as, conversely, if a sterile land had become a vineyard, it would be called a sterile fund, as in C. de alluvione et palude, l. 2, §. 1, and D. de actione empti, l. Si duorum, §. Si, and C. de bonis praescriptis, l. Si quis intra, and D. de solutione matrimonii, l. Divortio, §. Quod in sementem, and D. de censibus, l. Forma censuali. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Security granted to a husband is understood to be granted to the wife.
1. The word "with," when placed between persons, principally conjoins them.
2. He who can go with his goods to one city, whether he can send his goods by another to that city.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A safe-conduct was granted to T. and M., to each of them, to come to the city of Asti, with ten horses and an equal number of persons, arms, goods, and any other equipment, without real or personal impediment: notwithstanding any proceedings, bans, and condemnations, valid for a certain time, etc. Now, one of these sent his wife to the city of Asti with arms and equipment; which things were taken and arrested, notwithstanding the said safe-conduct and security. And this for the reason that the said holder of the safe-conduct did not go, although the wife went with the horses and things of her husband, and to the domicile of her husband, and also of the wife herself.

† The question is what is the law: I answer. In these securities, the form of the words must be considered, and likewise good faith, and the intent of both the grantor and the recipient, who is deemed to hold the same view that prudent men and honest persons would hold. Regarding the first point, arguing from the form of the words, it seems to be said that the aforementioned security does not avail: because no mention is made of the said wife and of the said things in the said privilege. See Extra, de privilegiis, c. Porro; and L. Quicquid astringendae, ff. de verbis obligatorum. Furthermore, because the word "with" joins accessorially, not principally. See L. Si cui, ff. de funerariis instrumentis. Hence, he who did not go, nor can send: because if the principal does not go, the things are not carried with him, but without him. Since therefore the words are lacking, the intent is also lacking, as stated in the aforementioned L. Quicquid astringendae. Furthermore, because fraud and deception could be committed: as say the receivers of the said horses and the said things. But notwithstanding these objections, three things must be considered: first, that the wife enjoys the privilege of her husband. See Codex, de uxore militis, L. 1, and throughout; and Codex, de episcopis et clericis, L. 2, § Si. Secondly, this is proven by another law, L. Nam cautum est, which provides that if one permits a husband to go and act, or to have the right to dwell in a certain place, the wife is also tacitly included. See ff. de verbis obligatorum, L. Si stipulatus fuero per te non fieri quo minus. And as if it were contained expressly in the privilege to you and your wife: or to you, with your wife.

† For the word "with," when placed between persons, principally conjoins them. D. de leg. j. l. titię textores. §. nihil distat. Hence, a woman can go and act both with her husband and without her husband. As D. de vsu. et habi. l. certorum. and l. non solum. and C. de agri. et censi. l. cum scimus. li. 11. and D. de praecar. l. cum pręcario quis. and D. de dolo. l. cum quis. and D. quib. mod. vsufruct. amit. l. si mulieri. Also, by reason of promiscuous use, as l. 1. D. rerum amo. Thirdly, I consider the place to which the wife was going: namely, to her domicile, a consideration founded on the aforementioned l. si stipulatus. Fourthly, I consider that words are not to be calumniated. As l. i. D. ad exhiben.

† Hence, he who may go with the goods may well send the goods: for to whom more is permitted, less is permitted, which is derived from that greater permission and is included under it. As stated in the Digest, *De in iurandum iuramentum*, law *Cum furti*. Hence, if it is permitted to me to transfer myself and my goods, I shall be able to transfer my goods without myself. And because he who cannot prohibit me cannot prohibit my messenger; and he who cannot plunder my goods. As stated in the Digest, *De religiosis*, law *Ossa*, § *Si*. And this is observed in Italy, that he who may go with merchandise may send merchandise by another. Since therefore the said privilege ought not to be diminished in any respect, being general as regards goods, it is most manifest that the said goods could not have been plundered. Nor does the argument from fraud stand in the way: for this argument would apply where fraud is established. As in the last chapter, *Extra*, *De rescriptis*. But here fraud is not established: for it appears that the wife, and that the goods were those of the husband. The same applies if they are the wife’s, by the laws cited above, and it is presumed to be hers, because they were taken from her. As in the Code, *Ne uxor pro marito*, law *Ob maritorum*. Nor is there violence in the dominion: for true detention suffices. As noted in the Code, *De furtis manifestis*, § *Sed cum in secundo*, with *Si*. From these it appears that the said goods, as having been wrongfully seized and arrested, are said to be restored, because the dispossessed must be restored before all else. Moreover, full faith was given regarding the safe-conduct. The foregoing are also confirmed: for that word “who may go with the goods” was added to augment, hence it ought not to operate a diminution, namely that he may not send the goods. As in the Digest, *De legibus*, book 1, law *Legata inutiliter*. Moreover, it is very well supported by the Digest, *De manumissionibus testamento*, law *Si ita fuerit*, § *Si*.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a son follows his father’s accidental domicile, especially with regard to the burdens to be borne there, or rather his father’s original domicile; and at no. 4, where a distinction is made.
2. What is the import of a clause added to a statement with the word “cum” (with).
3. A disjunctive is used in place of a conjunctive.
4. Acquisition is lost by will alone.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† When it is asked whether a son follows the accidental domicile of his father, especially with regard to the burdens to be undertaken there, it is argued first that he does not, by the laws and reasons set forth below. First, because for this side the case seems to be: l. ut filius, especially with regard to the burdens to be undertaken, he follows only the original domicile of the father, not the accidental one. C. de municip. et orig. l. filios, where it is established law that sons are compelled to honors or offices at the origin of the father. And there the ordinary gloss seems to be for this part, where it asks whether a son follows another domicile of the father, and resolves that he does not, especially if the son has chosen a domicile elsewhere. Likewise, secondly, the case seems to be in l. assumptio, §. filius, ff. ad municip., where it says "son of the city from which the father etc.," as if to say, not by the will of the father. And there the ordinary gloss seems to be on this point in the beginning, the great gloss there: "when the son himself has established it for himself by his own will." Likewise, for this part the case seems to be ff. ad mun. l. libertus, §. patris, where it is said that the domicile of the father does not bind the son to civil offices. Likewise, for this part the text seems to be ff. ad mun. l. placet, where it is said that a son can have a domicile not where the father had it, but where the son has chosen. Likewise, for this part it serves ff. ad municip. l. filii, where it is said that the sons of a freedman follow the accidental or original domicile of the patron acquired by their father the freedman. Therefore not both: because for the force of the alternative, it suffices that one part be true; therefore, since both cannot be, it will be the original only, because it is more worthy, and by the laws cited above. To the same effect serves l. assumptio, §. fi., eo. ti., where it is said that the sons of a freedman follow the original or accidental domicile of the patron acquired by their father the freedman. Therefore, etc. Likewise, for this part serves the gloss placed there, which he wished to understand that §. quando pr. has in the same place both original and accidental domicile, so that then the son of the freedman follows the domicile acquired by his father the freedman; as if to say, not otherwise does the son follow the accidental domicile of his patron. To the same also serves ff. ad municip. l. placet, with the note there by Dy., where the text says that even a son can have a domicile, Dy. says: "on account of his own act, and established in the same place where the father has it." According to Dy., therefore, a son in the house of his father does not have a domicile unless he acquires it by his own act. To the contrary, that the domicile of the father, even if not original, binds the son, and especially with regard to the burdens to be supported, the laws inscribed below support: first l. assumptio, §. filius, joined with its great gloss after the beginning on the word "domicile," ff. ad municipales, where it is said that a son does not follow the accidental domicile of the father when the son himself has established it for himself in another place by his own will. But in the case at hand, the son has not established a domicile for himself by his own will. Therefore, he remains under the domicile of the father.

For a clause added to a statement, when joined by the preposition *cum*, denotes the cause of that statement, just as when added by the preposition *si*. For example, in the text of the law *Titius textores*, § *nihil interest*, D. de legibus I. Therefore, there is a clear ordinary gloss on this point. And this is also what Dycus wished to say in the aforementioned §, in his postilla on the word *domicilium*, which he says is constituted voluntarily. But the domicile in question was not created by the father’s will alone, as will be shown below. Therefore, it is subject to the same rule. To the same effect is the law *Assumptio*, in the same title, where the text states that freedmen acquire the origin or domicile of their patrons.

† In this manner, when the disjunctive is used by the law, it is placed for the conjunctive, as in *l. Quintus Mutius*, D. de aur. et arg. leg., because otherwise, as in *l. Foret incerta*, it would be uncertain, which it ought not to be, as in *l. 1, §. Quibus*, C. de novo comp. It is therefore necessary to conclude that the text imports that the freedman follows the original and accidental domicile of the patron; since the disjunctive "or" must be placed between different things, as in *l. Hec verba ille aut ille*, D. de ver. sig. Then it is added in the same §, at the end: "Moreover, those who are born from children." By this end, it is clearly concluded that children follow every domicile of the father, even the accidental one; especially considering the opinion of Azo, where in the gloss he understood the said § when the original domicile of the patron differed from the accidental domicile; and which opinion the gloss approves, rejecting another opinion recited there by the gloss, which wished to understand the said § when in one and the same place was the original and accidental domicile of the father. According to which opinion, the word "domicile" would have been added in vain in the said §, and the disjunctive "or" would stand poorly. Moreover, for this part, I adduce in another way the said §, and *l. Filii libertorum* in the beginning, and *l. Eius* in the beginning, C. eod. tit., in which laws it is said that the freedman follows every domicile of the patron, both original and accidental; but the conjunction of affection and law between father and child is greater than between patron and freedman. Therefore, since every domicile passes from the person of the patron to the freedman, much more strongly it will pass from the person of the father to the child. For this part also makes *l. Libertus, §. In adoptivis*, D. eod. tit., where it is said that the child acquired through an adopted son follows the domicile of the adoptive grandfather acquired by his father, the same son, and he who gave himself in adoption. Behold, therefore, that the child follows the domicile of the father, even the accidental one; because acquired by his father through the giving in adoption, if therefore the domicile of the adoptive father, even accidental, because acquired by adoption, passes to the adopted son, much more strongly does this claim its place in legitimate and natural father and child; because two bonds, etc. Moreover, for this part it seems in *l. Placet cum seq.*, D. ad munic., where it is said that the child has domicile: not where the father lived, but where he himself chose, joined with a certain gloss on the word "habuerit," which says, however, from which it is concluded that the child has the domicile of the father. Furthermore, for this part, the case seems doubly in *l. Libertus, §. Patris*, D. ad munic., where it is said that the child, an inhabitant of another place, does not follow the accidental domicile of the natural father. Therefore, by argument from the contrary sense, if the child is not an inhabitant of another place, he follows the domicile, even accidental, of the father, which argument is valid in law, as in *l. 1, §. Huius rei*, D. de off. eius cui man. est iurisd. But the daughter in the case under discussion does not have inhabitancy in another place. Therefore, from that text, it must be said that she follows the domicile of the father. Moreover, from the end of the same §, the decision of this question is collected; for it is added by way of reason and final cause that in the said § the child does not follow the domicile of the father, because the reason of domicile in the father was temporary; but in the case under discussion, the domicile in the father was not temporary, but perpetual, as I will fully set forth below in the solution of the present question. Therefore, since the reason of the said § ceases in our case, the disposition stands. And this Oldradus wished to understand clearly, who wrote in the same § that the said § must be understood of domicile assigned by the will of the father, and which can be dissolved by his will. But in our case, the domicile was not created in the father by the will of the father alone; rather, it was created by the will of the father and the citizens of the place where he acquired domicile. And considering that it proceeded from the convention and will of two, it cannot be dissolved by the will of one alone, as I will say below. Therefore, it seems undoubtedly to be said that in our case the daughter follows the domicile. And this part is held by Bartolus in the said § Patris, and in *l. Assumptio, §. Filius*, and *l. 2*, C. de mun. et orig., referring to the said § Patris, where he clearly decides this. Moreover, to the same effect makes *l. Ordine, §. Fin.*, D. ad munic., where it is said that the adopted son is bound by burdens by the adoptive father; therefore, in the domicile of the adoptive father. But burdens are undertaken in the place of domicile, especially for things placed there. If therefore this is so in the adopted son, and thus only legitimate, so that from the person of the father the domicile passes to him only, much more strongly must it be in the natural and legitimate son, so that from the person of his father such domicile passes to him; since the rights of the father and legitimate are stronger in the natural and legitimate son, as in *l. Si arrogator*, D. de adop., and because two bonds, etc. For the solution, therefore, of the present question, I make one distinction, from which the clear solution of it will appear, and also the consonance of all the reasons made above for both parts will be induced, which is such:

† because sometimes one acquires domicile for oneself by one’s own will alone, without the intervention of anyone else’s will: which happens in two ways. First, because one transfers oneself to another city with the intention of dwelling there perpetually: or because one transfers the greater part of one’s fortunes to a foreign city. As in l. ciues, with the gloss thereon, C. de incolis. And in these cases, a distinction must be made: because either his son chose to settle in a foreign place by one of those two modes, and in these cases the father’s domicile does not bind the son. And thus are understood the laws cited in the first part. Or he did not choose to settle in another place: and the father’s domicile binds the son. And thus are understood the laws for the second part. And especially l. libertus §. patris, in the first particle, by argument from the contrary sense. But the daughter concerning whom the question arises in our case did not choose to settle in another place: therefore the father’s domicile passes for the cause. Or the father’s domicile was not acquired by the mere will of the father, but by his will and that of another: as was the case in our case. For the father did not acquire domicile by his will alone, which happens in either of the two aforementioned modes: but he chose it also by the will of those receiving him, and thus of the citizens, or their president. And thus by convention: and concerning which l. 1, ff. ad muni. does not speak. And this domicile undoubtedly passes. And it binds the son immutably. And thus also can be understood the laws cited for this part. And especially the aforementioned §. patris at the end of l. libertus. Or such was the choice of domicile concerning which the question arises; therefore it undoubtedly passes, and binds the son irrevocably. The reason for the difference between the first case and the second: namely, that the domicile acquired for the father by the mere will of the father passes to the son, as long as the son has not chosen another, but not afterwards: because such domicile can also be changed by him who acquired it by his own act, by choosing another. As in l. domicilium, ff. ad muni. Therefore much more strongly by him who acquired rights by the act of another. And rights acquired by someone from the person of another ought not to be stronger in him to whom they passed than they are in him who acquired them. As noted in l. princeps, ff. de legi. Nor ought the consequent to be stronger than that from whose consequence it proceeds. On the contrary, as in l. 1, post prin., ff. de auto. praestam. Nor the accessory to its principal. As in l. gręce, §. illud commune, ff. de fideius. But the father, who is principal and from whose person it passes consequentially to the son, can change that domicile. As long as he does not change it, he remains bound by that domicile. Therefore much more strongly the same will be true for the son. And not the difference between the first two cases and the third: because in the first two cases one can change, but not in the third: it is because in the first two cases domicile is created by the sole will, with some act of the acquirer. Therefore certainly by the sole will of the acquirer, domicile is not lost, because nothing is so natural, etc. As in l. nihil tam naturale, ff. de re. iu. Also, because in the first case there was present in creating the domicile the will of one alone. In the second, however, there was present the will of two: and two bonds are stronger than one. As in l. re coniuncti, ff. de leg. 3. And to this serves the matter of l. 1, ff. de pic. Also the matter which Bartol. notes in the proemium, ff. in the rubric on the word imper., where he says that sometimes skill is induced in the artisan by the sole will and act of the acquirer of the skill, as is the art of the advocate, cerdona, pilippar. And then by the sole will of that artisan, with the loss of that art, he ceases to be an artisan. Sometimes there is such a skill, to which one does not come by the sole will of the one assuming it by his act, but another preamble must precede: as is the art of doctorate. For one does not become a doctor by sole will, even with learning, but it is necessary that an examination precede, with license to teach granted by the bishop, along with other solemnities which are observed in such matters. And then when one comes to the doctorate, one cannot cease to be an artisan by contrary will, even with the act of not teaching intervening: because not sole will with his sole act made him a doctor. And therefore, although he does not wish to be a doctor, although he ceases to teach, nevertheless he remains a doctor. The aforementioned conclusions could be proved by many other remote reasons: especially by the infinite qualities which pass from the person of the father to the son. Of which we note in l. 2, C. de episc. et cle. and C. de praefeso. and medi. l. medicos, and l. vlti., lib. 10, C. de aduo. diuer. iudi. l. cum aduocatio, and l. foeminę, ff. de sęnato, which, because the laws speak sufficiently clearly in the case about which the question arises, I did not proceed to further matters. I, Bal. de Perusio. Si. gnorellus de Homodeis, doctor of laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The principal debtors had been condemned to pay 70 pounds for the whole and entire [debt], etc., with reservation of rights against all those who were bound for the said condemned debtors, in case the said condemned debtors did not pay; whether this reservation benefits or prejudices the sureties of the condemned debtors, who were unaware of it.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The case is as follows. By an arbitral sentence, certain principals were condemned to pay 75 pounds for all that in which they were bound by reason of fictitious retentions of the past time, with reservation of right against whosoever was bound for the said condemned persons, in case the said condemned persons did not pay the said sum, in the collection of the said fictitious claims. Thereafter, action was brought against the sureties, who were ignorant of the said arbitral sentence, and they were condemned to pay six hundred pounds or thereabouts. And the plaintiff well knew of the said sentence, but the defendants were ignorant. Now the said defendants wish to pay the said sum of 75 pounds and to free themselves from the whole. The question is what is the law.

I answer that, if the said reservation had not been made, the said sureties could defend themselves by means of the exception of assignment of rights (exceptio cedendarum actionum), which may be raised in the execution of a judgment, saying to the plaintiff: Assign to us your rights; and insofar as you cannot assign them, we raise against you the exception of fraud. For this exception is among those that may be raised in the execution of a judgment, as is expressly noted in *l. si res obligata*, D. de legibus, book 1. And this is the opinion of Speculum and of all authorities. But doubt is cast by the said reservation, the words of which are as follows: that in the case in which the said plaintiffs could not obtain and receive the said 75 pounds, or if they were not paid, all right to demand and receive the said fictitious sum is reserved. It is therefore argued on behalf of the plaintiffs that these words, “if they were not paid,” must be understood to mean up to the time after the litigation has been joined, as in *l. si Titius*, D. de verbis obligandis. To the contrary it seems: because no time was specified, hence those words “if they were not paid” must be understood to mean: if, after the assets have been discussed (i.e., exhausted), they could not be found to be paid. For this is the ordinary gloss in *l. fideiussor obligari*, § fin., D. de fideiussoribus. For this reservation begins with the condition “if it were not paid,” which condition, being negative, does not exist unless discussion of assets has taken place. Moreover, since no day was fixed, it seems that default may be proven perpetually. Which I prove thus: This sum of 75 pounds succeeded in place of the entire fictitious sum. Therefore, by paying it, the whole debt is paid. Hence it can always be paid; because all judgments are discharged if that which is due is paid, as in Inst. de perpetuis et temporalibus actionibus, § fin. The objection based on the text in *l. cum fideiussor*, § fin., is not valid, because there an interpellation of the principal debtor is required, but the principal debtors were never interpellated. Therefore, the condition of the surety’s obligation, nor that of the aforementioned reservation, did not occur. The case is in the said § fin. Moreover, these sureties were ignorant of that judgment, whereas the plaintiff knew it. And thus there was fraud on the part of the plaintiff. Also, these heirs of the sureties are minors, and have suffered injury due to justifiable ignorance and the deceit of the plaintiff; therefore, they are entitled to restitution in integrum under the double clause, as noted by Master Dy. in *l. ad diem*, D. de verbis obligandis. Considering, therefore, that we are not in the case of the reservation, and that the exception of assignment of rights stands in the way, or that at least we are in a case of restitution in integrum, the said judgment for the payment of one hundred pounds ought not to be put into execution, if the facts alleged are true. It is subtly alleged by the advocate that here, by means of the arbitral award, a certain novation has been made, since the arbitral award itself is a transaction. Hence the sureties given do not seem to be bound, as in *l. Valetianus*, D. de praetoria stipulatione, and in *l. cum in plures*, § lege dicta, D. de locato conducto, where it seems expressly stated that, since the form of the first obligation has been changed, the sureties are not bound. But against this, the reservation makes much, as in *l. 2 post principium*, D. si quis cautio, there: “unless the contrary,” where the case seems to be this. But the single answer is: because here the condition of the reservation did not occur, as in *l. si*, § sed si cum seyo, D. si certum petatur, and as noted by Bartolus in *l. 1*, de conveniendo fisci debito, book 10. For when discussion is placed in the form of the obligation, or something which must be understood as discussion is there, unless discussion is solemnly made, the obligation is not contracted. Also it must be observed that where pupils are involved in the case, there, on account of instruments newly discovered, the judgment may be retracted, and provision made for the indemnity of the pupils, even without any petition for restitution in integrum, as noted in *l. 1*, C. de sententiis adversus fidem latam, book 10, and in *l. Imperatores*, D. de re iudicata. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If the parties have been condemned by arbitrators to make a general release of all claims, etc., and if such release has been made, whether said release extends to matters unknown and not contemplated at the time of the award. And number 3.
2. When the intention of the contracting parties is not apparent, what is to be done.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. In the case proposed: having seen the said compromise and award, whereby Guido, as Affictaiolus of the said Brandon, held during the time of the said compromise and award a certain holding called el podere de Columbaia, and used it by the right of the said affictus during the aforementioned times; and concerning that holding, at the time of the compromise and during its course, or ever at any time, there was no controversy between the parties, nor was anything litigated before the said arbitrators regarding that holding. Hence the question arises: since the heirs of the said Guido now hold and possess the said holding, and have held it for a long time as their own and as if it were theirs, whether the heirs of the said Graden, notwithstanding the award in that part which begins: “Anche lodiamo, che luna parte e cadauna de le dicte parte,” may lawfully and without penalty demand the aforementioned holding; considering that, according to the form of the said award as proposed, a general release followed, doubtful on account of the generality of the words of the said award, namely the said words “Anche lodiamo”; secondly, on account of the subsequent ratification of the award by a release made generally according to the form of the said award.

And I premise that if the said release of part had not been made, the clause of the said award binding as to the general release, being captious, ought to be removed from the equation. D. de transactionibus, l. cum Aquiliana, where there is a strong case, and there by Bartolus. But because a general release of all things can be made by parts, D. de pactis, l. tres fratres; more clearly, ibid., l. emptor, §. Lucius; D. de verborum obligationibus, l. qui Romae, §. duo fratres, it must be considered whether the said release extends to the said weight. At first glance it seems that it does, on account of its generality. Against this it is argued: because since the said arbitration is a kind of transaction, C. de iudicibus, auth. si vero contigerit, and in the Corpus from which it is taken, general words, however broad, are restricted to that species about which there was litigation, concerning which there is a specific transaction. C. de transactionibus, l. si de certa. Indeed, the same is said regarding a gratuitous and general pact, when a general rescript of release can be referred to and restricted to specified matters, saving the reason of correct speech. D. de solutionibus, l. si ex pluribus coniuncta; l. Plautius, de auro et argento legato; otherwise otherwise. D. de acceptilatione, l. pluribus, fully by Bartolus. D. de liberatione, l. Aurelio, §. Gayum. And this was the opinion of Johannes in the said §. Lucius, that just as a transaction is restricted, so too a pact should be restricted. But as I said, the said release proceeded not by way of pact, but by way of transaction, since it was made out of necessity, and concerning the aforementioned opinion of release. Because the general words thereof, saving the reason of correct speech, can be restricted to those matters contained in the award, and therefore it seems that only its releases were considered, and not at all others entirely extraneous. And that the same holds for a pact as for a transaction, were the views of Guido de Caylis and Jacobus de Belvisio, although Innocentius seems to hold the contrary. Extr. de officio delegati, c. conquerente. Therefore, it cannot be denied that this question is doubtful.

† However, in its decision, I adopt the following rule: if it can be proven what the intention of the contracting parties was, we adhere to that certainty, whatever the words may sound; for the form of words is never greater than the sense of the contracting parties. C. de libe. praete. l. 3. Hence, if it can be proven that the parties understood that [the claim] was included in the general release, it will be barred by res judicata; if the opposite can be proven, it will not be barred. But if neither party can prove what the parties intended, then we remain in doubt, as I have said above.

† On this point, I say that the said refutation, since it was made out of necessity and according to the form of the award, ought not to be extended to anything to which the award itself does not extend. D. 39,2,1, § si is qui vicinas. Nor to anything else, since no one is presumed to bind himself beyond what is necessary or otherwise than as was necessary for him. As stated in the aforementioned § si is. But the arbitrators who made the award in the said case ought not to have considered the said land, since no controversy concerning this was before them: as is premised in the point. As stated in D. 44,1,13, si de certa. It is established, however, that a judgment or transaction does not extend to a right unknown, about which the judge or the parties have not thought. D. 2,15,1, qui cum tutoribus and the above-mentioned laws. And this is also proven: because a judgment must be conformable to the petition; and it cannot be rendered on matters not requested. C. 8,52,1, vt fundus; and C. 8,57,1, fin. And he is foolish who renders a judgment. As noted there. But an arbitrator is not presumed to be foolish, since he was chosen as a good man. And due to his diligence, he is not easily believed to err. D. 22,6,1, cum de indebito. Who, therefore, would say that the said arbitrators thought about the said land, or about other things not at all thought of? In fact, they thought in general, so that every ground for dispute might be cut off between the parties. In which case, a general release then suffices. And the release is then extended to things not thought of in specie, but presupposing that they were thought of in genere. In our case, it must be carefully observed: because between the parties, according to the clause of the said award, there must be a release of the promise regarding everything that one party could claim against the other, and the other against the one, for any cause, up to the day of the award. But at the time the award was made, all natural and civil possession was in Grandone. Since it is alleged in the facts that even before, the said Guido held the said land as an Affictaiolus (tenant-at-will) of the said Grandone. D. 41,3,1, non solum, § quod vulgo. Therefore, only mere asinine detention was with the said Guido. Thus, the said land could not then be claimed by Guido; because a real action does not proceed unless there is dominion on the part of the plaintiff and possession on the part of the defendant. C. 3,23,1. Therefore, against the one possessing naturally and civilly, there is no action; unless we speak of the avocation of asinine detention, which the said Grandone could recover by his own authority. D. 6,1,1, officium. Therefore, Grandone will have no right of action for the recovery of that possession, because it was his own. And thus, the form of the award does not extend to it. And consequently, neither does the release deriving its origin from the award extend to it. If we say that they thought in genere, but in specie only of simple asinine detention. Hence, notwithstanding the aforementioned award and release, I conclude that the heir of Grandone will recover the civil and natural possession of the said land, of which he was deprived after the award. But the heir of the said Guido will remain in mere asinine detention, which will be of no effect. X. 2,19, licet causam. For, having recovered civil and natural possession by his own authority, he can expel the mere detainer. As in the aforementioned chapter; and as the doctors teach in D. 43,17,1, si duo; and D. 41,2,1, clam possidere, § qui ad nundinas. And thus it was consulted by the most excellent doctor of laws, Master Angelo of Perugia, in the city of Florence.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If a testator bequeaths to someone things that were previously bequeathed to himself, and it is not established that the prior bequest was made to the testator, whether the legacy is valid.
2. How the laws providing that a testator is deemed to have bequeathed only the right which he possesses are to be understood.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Although Lord Auerard, of blessed memory, in his will stated that he was making a legacy to a certain chapel of certain things which had been bequeathed to him by the said Lord F., his father, in his will, which [will] is not found; nevertheless, there is no doubt that a false description does not invalidate a legacy of a certain thing or a certain quantity. And the reason is: because the description is not of the substance of the legacy, which is certain by another description. D. 45.1.1 (De conditionibus et demonstrationibus), l. Demonstratio; for where the thing is certain, then the description is superfluous. D. 32.1.1 (De legatis), l. 1, in fine, there: “nor does a false [description] vitiate.” To the same effect: D. 50.17.1 (De verborum obligationibus), l. Si diuortio; C. 6.38.1 (De falsa causa ad iec. leg.), l. Si non designata, together with the following. And therefore, although it does not appear that the aforementioned legacy [was made], nevertheless the said legacy is valid. But it must be considered: whether the said legacy is valid in its entirety or in part. And it is certain that the said Auerard had a share in the things bequeathed, and he could dispose of that share by making a legacy. D. 32.1.1 (De legatis), l. Serui electione, §. Fin. And this is true if Lord Auerard had ownership; but if he had a formal usufruct, the legacy seems to be void. C. 6.38.1 (De legatis), l. Vxor patrui; D. 7.5.1 (De usufructu legato), l. Sticho.

But all the rules noted in the above-quoted passage of the law, which state that the testator is deemed to bequeath only the right that he possesses, are true when the right lacking to the testator does not belong to his universal heir. But it is otherwise when the heir’s right comes into the legacy in the same manner as the testator’s right. D. de legatis 2, l. *Unum ex familia*, § *Si rem*; and l. *Cum filius*, § *Dominus*, and there, note. And thus it must be concluded that the testament of the said Lord Auerard is to be observed. And so that the chapel may not fall from its right, let the bequest be claimed with diligence and with protests which signify that negligence ceases. D. de libellis dimissis, l. 1; C. de annalium exceptionibus, l. *Ut perfectius*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If the testator bequeaths an estate, and certain houses to someone, and a usufruct to his wife: having appointed a universal heir. If the wife cannot have it in its entirety by virtue of a statute prohibiting leaving to a wife more than 10, to whom will the usufruct left to the said wife apply, whether to the legatee to whom houses and plots of land were left, or to the heir.
1. Monks, from their conscience, ought to fulfill the will of the testator, notwithstanding the strictness of the law or the statute.
2. If the testator commands the heir to allow the wife, who is a legatee, to have, possess, or enjoy, does it seem by these words that he bequeaths? And what kind of legacy this would be.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The testator bequeathed to a certain Benigno a certain plot of land and certain houses. Then, in the same will, he bequeathed the usufruct of the same plot of land and houses to his wife, so long as she conducts herself as a widow and lives chastely. Finally, in direct words addressed to the heir, he added these words: that the heir may not molest or harass the said lady in the said legacies, or any part thereof, but shall suffer her to have, hold, and enjoy in peace, use, and possess the aforementioned judgments and legacies. It is presupposed that there is a certain Pisan statute which does not permit leaving to a wife more than 25 pounds of the currency annually. Now the question arises between the said legatee of the things, the legatee of the usufruct, and the universal heir.

† It is asked to whom the usufruct pertains: whether to the said legatee of the land and houses, or to the said legatee [female], or indeed to the universal heir. And it is argued that that which the woman could not take pertains to the legatee of the things. For he who is not admitted to a share from the beginning does not make a share. As in D. de leg. 1, l. plane, § si duobus. To the contrary it seems: because he who cannot take makes a share. D. de leg. 2, l. si Titio et ei. And thus half of the usufruct pertains to the legatee of the things; and insofar as the wife cannot take, it pertains to the universal heir. But rather it seems that nothing of the said usufruct pertains to the legatee of the things; because the said usufruct, considering the judgment of the testator, seems to have been entirely adempted from him and collated to the wife. And although the collation does not hold, nevertheless the ademption holds. The first is proven. D. de adim. leg., l. sicut. And arg. D. de peculio leg., l. cum dominus, § si. The second is proven. D. de adim. leg., l. licet transferam, where it is said that an invalid translation extinguishes the legacy. There is no obstacle. D. de haered. inst., l. Iulianus. Because it is one thing in an invalid institution of an heir, which does not remove a valid one, since from the invalid one the inheritance cannot be entered upon. As D. de lib. et post., l. si quis filius qui in potestate. It is another thing in a legacy, which is adempted by bare will. As fully noted, D. de adim. leg., l. ex parte. This tenth point is proven. D. de test. milit., l. militis codicillis, § veteranus. There is no obstacle to this. D. de leg. 3, l. si iure facto testamento. Because there was an express translation. And consequently, ademption is considered express. There, however, it was tacit, which does not arise from an invalid will. And therefore it seems that prima facie it should be concluded thus, that the said legatee of the things would have the entire ownership and half of the usufruct. But the other half he would not have, as being adempted. As D. de usufr. leg., l. si alii fundum, and l. Sempronio, C. tit., and there noted. Moreover, the said half which is not due to the wife does not accrue to the legatee of the ownership; because it is due to another, namely the universal heir, as long as the woman lives. Arg. D. de usufr. leg., l. uxori usufructum villae, and D. comm. praed., l. si in venditione. And if that which is bequeathed to the wife beyond what is permitted is said to be pro non scripto, it remains with the heir, insofar as it can be adapted to the heir, and as the limits of the legacy permit. As C. de caduc. toll., § et cum triplici, and noted, D. de leg. 1, l. dictantibus, § Lutatius, and Inst. de haered. inst., l. 3, and D. de donat., l. pen. The legatee of the things therefore ought not to have more than is assigned to him. But it is understood that only the half is assigned to him. Furthermore, although by strict law this legacy is not due to the wife, nevertheless it may be granted to her by the liberality of the heir, dictated by natural equity. As C. de necess. hered., l. quidam, § illo. Which natural equity prevents the right of accrual. As D. de leg. 1, l. plane, § si coniunctim.

† Moreover, monks instituted as heirs ought not to observe this statute. For they ought to fulfill the testator’s wish out of conscience, as appears in the Legend of Blessed Sylvester. Also, because they are not subject to the laws of laymen, but to the law of God, according to which this legacy is valid; and rightly so, because chastity is to be rewarded, as in the Authentica *De non eligendo secundo nubente*, § *Gregoria*. And certain things are said to be done in fact, although they are not binding in law, as in D. *De verbis oblig.*, l. *Quidam cum filium*; D. *De capite diminuto*, l. *Legatum*; D. *De alio legato*, l. *Servos ad custodiam templi*; D. *Non obligat*, l. 1; C. *De secundis nuptiis*. For that [prohibition] is on account of the unchastity of one marrying within a year. But this, which fulfills the testator’s commands and preserves his honor, deserves reward. Argument: D. *De manumissionibus testamento*, l. *Meuia*. The solution of this question does not rest on any of the aforementioned allegations, but something else must be considered. And it must be premised that formerly there were four kinds of legacies, among which was one kind called *sinendi modo* [by way of permitting]; these kinds have not been abolished, but the differences between the kinds have been abolished, as in Inst. *De legatis*, in the beginning.

And therefore, if the testator commands the heir to allow Titius to have, possess, or enjoy peacefully, it is understood that he bequeaths this to him, either in whole or in part, according as the wording indicates. See C. communia de legatis, l. 1. And all actions that are available for legacies are available for him. Because now we are dealing with this legacy, which is called a legacy of permission (sine); namely, because the heir is commanded to allow the legatee to have and hold the usufruct in its entirety, and to enjoy, use, and possess it in peace; and not to hinder the said legatee in the whole or any part thereof, by which it is expressly designated by words that the said woman is left the legatee of the entire and solid usufruct, through that type of legacy which is called a legacy of permission (sine). Now, from this follows such a conclusion: whether this legacy is called a transfer, or whether it is called a declaration of the will not to bequeath the usufruct of the things to the said legatee, nothing is owed to the said legatee from the aforementioned usufruct during the lifetime of the said woman; either because it has been adeemed, or because it does not appear to have been bequeathed to the said legatee.

The objection from ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. non ad ea, does not hold; because there it speaks of a case where there are multiple forms of legacy concerning the same legatee, and they are fortuitously available by alternation, hence the choice falls. But in our case it is not so, because there are different legatees. And since the entire usufruct is left to the woman, and the testator considered the effect of perception, rightly nothing of the said usufruct is owed to the said owner; because it does not appear that the testator burdened the heir with the provision of the public [share]. See C. de caducis tollendis, §. si autem disiunctim; and ff. de legatis 2, l. Titia, §. qui inuita.

Therefore, repeating the conclusion, I conclude that the fruits of the said things, during the lifetime of the said woman, do not in any way pertain to the said owner, by right of ownership, having diligently examined and understood the words of the said testament. See ff. de transactionibus, l. de his controversiis.

However, I would not consider it correctly stated that the legatee of the things appears to be burdened with the performance of the said usufruct; because the burden of a legacy is, in case of doubt, understood to be imposed and attached to the heir. See argumentum ff. de legatis 3, l. si fundus, §. qui Margaritam. The objection from C. ad Trebellianam, l. fin., does not hold; because there it speaks of a universal fideicommissum, when the testator, in making his will, observed this order: because first he instituted [the heir], second he burdened [the heir] with the universal [estate], third he made singular bequests. But here it is not so. And therefore it does not hold.

I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a confession of receipt, accompanied by a promise to restore, creates an obligation after two years from the date of the confession.
body: The case is as follows. F. sold a house to S. for the price of five hundred florins; then the said F., etc., in the first part, consilio 174.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that if the person whose inheritance is in question died testate, leaving a male son, and if he left anything to his daughter under any title of legacy, the daughter must be content with said legacy and cannot claim more; yet, if the father leaves nothing to his married daughter, unless she remains a widow, in which case she may return and reside in her father’s house, as permitted to daughters by statute: whether said daughter can challenge the will, assuming that the daughter is entirely excluded by the male heir.
2. Jacobus de Arena was the light of civil law.
3. Certain legacies, by the nature of the thing, require a condition to exist by necessity, and others do not.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen. The statute of Perugia provides. But if the testator has died, the person whose estate is in question having left a male son, and if he has left something, under whatever title it may have been left, the daughter herself ought to be content with said legacy, and cannot demand more. Now, the father of the married daughter leaves nothing else, except that if she remains a widow, she may return and reside in her father's house, which is permitted to daughters by the statute. The question is whether said daughter can challenge the will and open for herself the way to succeed: presupposing that intestate, the daughter is entirely excluded by the male heir.

† To this daughter, for as long as she remains in marriage, nothing has been left. And therefore, in the meantime, she is passed over, and as one passed over, she declares the will unjust. D. 28,5,1, § ex his, where it says, “they do injustice to her.” It is therefore unjust, and void by operation of law, namely if we employ strict law, that is, civil rules. D. 28,2,1, § in omnibus; D. 28,2,17; and Inst. 2,12,1. But according to equity, it is possible to succeed from such a will, because possibility is considered at the time of death. It follows that one is not precisely said to die intestate: D. 28,5,1, § idem circa; D. 28,5,2; and D. 34,9,1, § quaesitum. And note D. 28,1,1, in principle, gloss on the words “by operation of law.” And what is noted: C. 6,28,1, in gloss; and D. 36,1,1, in gloss, “but on the contrary”; and D. 36,1,2, in gloss, “but how”; and C. 6,28,1, in gloss, “as if he said.” And thus, although in fact the father is said to be intestate, due to the invalidity of the will according to civil law, as noted in D. 28,5,2, gloss here explains; and D. 28,5,1; and according to civil law, this is abusively, and not properly, called a will. D. 28,1,2. Nevertheless, certainly in many respects it is called a will: first, by potential aptitude, as in the aforementioned D. 28,5,2. Secondly, according to common usage of language, as in the aforementioned § testamentum. Thirdly, with regard to the edict of the Divine Adrian, as C. 6,33,2. Fourthly, in another respect: because a tacitly passed-over son has the appearance of being, although not precisely being, as D. 29,5,1. Fifthly, with regard to legacies which are claimed by the right of the testator, on account of the very form of the institution of heir, as in Auth. ex causa. Sixthly, on account of pupillary substitution, as noted in D. 28,6,2.

Therefore, sometimes we are precisely in the case of intestacy, and then the statute concerning intestacy applies. Sometimes we are precisely in the case of a testator, and then the statute concerning a will applies. Sometimes it is a middle ground between these two, as in the case of a passed-over son. And this case is omitted by the statute, and therefore common law applies. D. 29,1,1, § non dixit. The reason for the difference between these cases is manifest. For where one makes no will at all, the law provides in place of the lacking disposition of the person, and the deceased seems tacitly to have felt the same. Hence, the dying person does nothing unjust. Also, where one makes a just will, he uses his right: D. 28,1,1, in principle. But where one makes an unjust will, rightly greater relief is given to the passed-over son, on account of the injustice. For the statute does not seem to have permitted the father to do injury to the laws and to nature, and, like a madman, to cast aside natural affection toward his children. Finally, a natural spur urges fathers: D. 26,7,1; D. 26,7,3; D. 26,7,4; D. 38,1,1; D. 28,1,1; D. 28,1,2. And therefore, this passed-over daughter has recourse to her father’s goods according to common law. The aforementioned statute does not stand in the way.

† And on this point, in strict accordance with the aforementioned statute, Jacobus de Arena, the light of civil law, gave his opinion, a consultation which I had not seen elsewhere until now. Someone might say that this daughter has not been passed over; because, whatever was left to the son, was also left to her, as to the widow, etc. Therefore, however she is named, since the condition is removed, a pure legacy remains. C. de inofficiosa testamento, l. omnimodo; and l. quoniam in prioribus. For an omission arising from the addition of a condition is not considered an omission when the condition is removed.
