C. de inofficiosa testamento, l. sancimus, § cum autem; and noted in C. de institutione et substitutione, l. si pater, in the gloss; and l. suus, ff. de hereditate instituenda, by the gloss and Bartolus.

† For I do not hold this opinion, and especially not in our case, where one must consider that there are certain legacies which, by the very nature of the thing bequeathed, necessarily require an existing condition: for example, if widow’s garments are bequeathed, it is required that she be a widow; if doctoral robes, that she be a doctor; if a dowry, that she be of pubescent age; if fruits yet to be born, nature requires that they be born. D. 45.1.1, in fine. If a pension is granted to the father’s house during widowhood, the nature of separation from the husband’s household requires that she be a widow. For a married woman ought to remain in her husband’s house and follow her husband. D. 33.7.1 (Meuia), § in fine; and D. 38.1.1 (Sicut), de operis libertatis. Therefore, in our case, the condition cannot be removed without impairing the effective benefit of the thing bequeathed, and thus it has necessarily lapsed in the meantime. And this is a sad legacy, the expectation of which is widowhood. D. 45.1.1 (Pater Severina), § Socius. And therefore it has induced the question of preterition. D. 28.5.1 (Si filius). There are certain conditions or delays that can be removed without prejudice to the species and benefit of the legacy. And of these speaks L. Quoniam in prioribus. And this is a subtle, notable, and new statement, and thus I conclude in favor of the daughter, as though she had been pretermitted. Furthermore, it should be added: because she does not appear to have been instituted in the father’s substance, but in the debt reserved to the daughter herself by the statutes: as to daughters, not as to an heir. For the right of return also applies to an unemancipated daughter. And therefore she does not appear to have this right of a legatee. D. 25.5.1 (Si arrogator), § Sed an impuberi.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a wife instituted as heir on the condition that she lead a widow’s life is said to be an heir without having furnished security, according to Mutia, and whether she could enter upon the inheritance.
2. When a universal fideicommissum is imposed on a successor who is a debtor of the testator, whether the debt is extinguished by confusion.
body: Add the case of this opinion in the fifth part of the opinions, beginning: The facts are as follows: a certain piper in his will, etc. In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† That Lady Contesina was truly and properly an heir is not in doubt: because she was instituted universally and acted as an heir. Inst. de her. quali. et dif. §. si. ff. de acqui. her. l. pro herede. And although she was instituted in the will on condition that she lead a widow’s life, nevertheless, by remaining in widowhood, she could enter upon the inheritance, even without having given the Mutian caution, although the gloss seems to hold the contrary. Pet. auth. cui relictum. ut not. in l. si. C. de indic. vidui. because the word “until” signifies a term, not a condition, according to Marsil., Ricard., and Cynus. She was therefore an heir: and because she did not make an inventory, all obligation is merged, because she entered voluntarily. ff. ad Treb. l. postulante. in princ. and l. debitor. in quibus. Here the article is properly examined.

† namely, when he is requested by a universal fideicommissum to succeed to his debtor. Nevertheless, some say that, after the inheritance has been restored under the Trebellian rule, a useful action is revived for the heir, just as when the inheritance is evicted from him. C. de inofficiosa testatione, l. Si maritus; ff. de usufructu, l. Dominus, in principio; and ff. ad Senatusconsultum Silanianum, l. Propter venenum, § Neptis; and by argument, ff. de iure fideicommissorum, l. Sed revocata. But the truth is that, once the action is merged, the original action is not granted, but rather a deduction or retention is allowed. ff. ad legem Falcidiam, Cum emptor; and there by Doctorus and by the ordinary gloss. C. de iure deliberandi, l. Si, § In computatione. For the heir burdened with the duty of restoration does not appear to be burdened in his own rights and assets, but only in the goods of the deceased, over which the testator could dispose by will. ff. de vulgaribus substitutionibus, l. Coheredi, § Cum filiae, ver. Nec fideicommissum; and ff. ad Senatusconsultum Trebellianum, l. A filia; and l. Lucius, § Maritus; and l. Cum hereditas; and C. eodem, l. 1; and C. de petitione hereditatis, l. In restituenda. And it is relevant, de hereditate vel actione vendenda, l. 2, § Si. And if the inheritance is restored without retaining the debt, the condictio incerti is available. ff. de conditionibus indebiti, l. Qui heredi, § Si pars. This has place in those points of law in which retention had place, and not an ordinary action. Moreover, the fideicommissum in question is universal, and executors, or those who live from them, are regarded in place of universal fideicommissa, however, for the benefit of the poor, to whom the final purpose of the testator is directed. C. de episcopis et clericis, Si quis ad declinandam; and Extra, de testamento, lib. 6. Therefore, these goods ought to be distributed to pious causes, the wife’s dowry being saved. For codicils contain the entire substance after the death of the instituted heir, and every contingency. Every contingency is comprehended which can be conceived from the words of the codicils. By argument, ff. de liberis et posthumis, l. Gallus, § Quidam recte; and de vulgaribus substitutionibus, l. Qui plures heredes. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a statute prohibiting an appeal from the execution of an instrument is valid.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It is asked whether a statute prohibiting an appeal from the execution of an instrument is valid. This statute, which prohibits appealing while the cause for appealing subsists, does not prevent an appeal. Extra, De iureiurando, c. Venientes. And therefore this statute is null by the law itself, insofar as it infringes upon appeals that are interposed to the Apostolic See or other superiors. From this it follows that he against whom judgment was pronounced ought to have appealed if the sentence displeased him, and he could have appealed twice; and if he did not do so, let him complain of himself, not of the law. C. Si sepius in integrum restitui, l. 1. ff. De edendo, l. Argentarius, § Cum autem. And if it is said that, by reason of sin, it pertains to the bishop: this is not true; rather, the bishop is bound to execute the sentences and good statutes of laymen, among laymen, c. Ultimam, De exceptionibus, lib. 6, and no. De postulando, l. Ex ea. Otherwise, an appeal would never be necessary, if, by reason of sin, the bishop could always be approached. And since God has subjected all things to sin, all things would pertain to the forum of the bishop, and not to temporal jurisdiction with decisive effect; which is ridiculous. It supports what is noted, Extra, De purgatione canonica, c. Nos inter alios. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the profits made by the wife of an outlawed man, who does not bear the burdens of marriage, belong to the wife.
2. Whether Peter can accept the inheritance of his half-brother, which was offered to the son after the death of said son, or whether the mother, being negligent, should request a guardian.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Whether what the wife of an outlawed man acquires, when he does not bear the burdens of marriage, belongs to the wife. It must be said that yes: because since the husband does not bear the burdens of marriage, what is acquired belongs to her, and not to the husband. D. 39.5.1 (Sicut); D. 24.3.1 (Insulam), § Usuras; and D. 23.3.1 (Si), with the following.

† Furthermore, it must be known whether a father, after the death of his son, can accept the inheritance of his uterine brother, which had been offered to the son as the nearest heir, or, if the mother is negligent, request the appointment of a guardian. And it is to be said that he can: as stated in the law *Si infanti*, Code, *De iure deliberandi*; and in the authenticum *Post fratres*, *De suis et legitimis heredibus*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether full sisters are preferred in a pupillary substitution, or whether the prorogative is to be considered.
2. Whether the mother succeeds to the son, or whether the full sister succeeds to the substituted heir who has died.
3. Whether the mother can purge the delay arising from the non-appointment of a tutor.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

Whether in a pupillary substitution those related on both sides are preferred when all are substituted pupillarily, and whether in intestate succession the mother and the sister related on both sides, or the sister, is preferred to the mother, when all are substituted pupillarily, only on the maternal side: and whether the mother can purge the delay of not having appointed a tutor. On the first point, some said that sisters related on both sides are preferred in this pupillary substitution for two reasons which call them, and for the closer relationship. As in D. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione, l. cohaeredi, §. qui discretas. But the truth is that all daughters succeed by equal right and in equal shares, unless regard is had to the generative bloodline, where an express pupillary substitution has been made. Hence we see the mother excluded, the sisters succeeding. C. de inofficioso testamento, l. Papinianus, §. sed nec impuberis. The doctors touch upon this in D. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione, l. Lutius, and Guillaume in l. precibus.

† On another point, I say that the mother and the sister related on both sides succeeded to the estate of Marinutus intestate, because the substitute had predeceased. And this holds whether the mother assumed guardianship or had another appointed.

† otherwise, if she had been in default, and had not purged it within a year, the mother would have been excluded from the succession of Marinuta, the pupillary heir, and only the sister would have come. L. 2, C. ad Tertullianum. However, since Vanneta died after reaching puberty, the entire share of the daughters devolved upon the mother by the death of the younger daughter. L. 3, C. ad Tertullianum. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether one who harbors enmity and gathers friends and associates so that he may go more securely and justly is said to make a congregation of a certain people.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen.

† The statute provides that no one shall dare to make an assembly or congregation of any people, against the good state of the land of Narni, under penalty of 100 livres. Now, certain persons having enmities have gathered certain friends and associates, so that they might more securely go to certain places to which they went; because by an act remote from the offense, the offense is not proven, nor the intent to commit such an offense. ff. de furtis, l. verum. And because whenever there are other indications of intent, those which induce the crime cease. C. de sicariis, l. 1. It seems to me that this congregation does not appear to have been made against the good state of the land of Narni. ff. de captivis, l. si quis ingenuam, §. in civilibus, where the case is to the letter. Nor do the witnesses produced for the offense prove this by a vile [or insufficient] means. For that which they saw is not of this genus of offense, but is separated for this purpose. C. unde legi, l. non hoc. Moreover, although this witness in the matter of knowledge says by that which he saw, heard, and knew; in that which he says "knew," it signifies rather the judgment of the intellect. Hence in this he is not a witness, but rather a judgment, in which case, unless he says why he knew thus, so that it concludes, he does not prove. As Innocentius notes, extr. de testibus, causam. And because the witnesses for the defense seem to have proven sufficiently well, therefore the accused come to be absolved. Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If the form of the statute provides that a person may not be accused by any particular person, and he was nevertheless accused and, on account of contumacy, was condemned, whether the proceedings and the condemnation are valid.
2. Error cannot be alleged after sentence has been pronounced.
3. Defense in a capital case cannot be conducted through a procurator.
4. Those matters which are to be proved before the litigation is contested must be established according to the order given by the law *debent liquere*; otherwise, the proceedings are null.
5. It is not within our discretion to alter the nature of judgments.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The statute provides that no noble or powerful person may bring an accusation, denunciation, or complaint against any citizen of the city or episcopate of Ancona, or against anyone from elsewhere, except solely for an injury inflicted upon the person of the accuser, denouncer, or complainant, or upon the property which he possesses. And the magistrate or the judge of crimes is bound not to admit any person of the aforementioned condition to bring any accusation, denunciation, or complaint, under penalty, etc. Now it has happened that a certain noble, included within the prohibition of the statute, caused a certain denunciation to be made against several persons who were said to have committed certain offenses; however, not against the person of the said noble, but concerning property not possessed by the said noble. Regarding this denunciation, proceedings were conducted through a procurator, and the said denounced parties were treated as contumacious. They, through their procurator, claim that the said proceedings are null, because they were conducted contrary to the form of the statute. It is asked whether the said proceedings, as stated above, were null by operation of law. And whether, if a capital penalty has been imposed, it can subsequently be challenged through a procurator. And it seems to be said that the proceedings are valid, because the summoned parties did not appear, nor did they allege that proceedings could not be taken, nor were they required to raise a declinatory plea of forum. For they ought to appear and allege their defense in court. As stated in D. Si quis in ius vocatus non iurat, l. Ex quacunque; D. De iudiciis, l. Si quis ex aliena; D. De procuratoribus, l. Qui procuratorem dat, §. Finis; C. De exceptionibus, l. Finis. These are common legal principles, and the rule of civil law dictates this. Moreover, in this proceeding, no express error is found. Therefore, the proceeding stands, and the sentence rendered therefrom. As stated in D. De appellationibus, l. Si expressum; and l. 1, §. Cum contra sacras; D. Quae sententiae sine appellatione rescindantur; and l. 1, C. De errore calculi. And the reason is

† manifest: because error cannot be alleged after sentence, otherwise there would be no end to lawsuits. D. de iudicibus, l. si praetor, in principio. Therefore, it would be futile to allege error or ignorance, if error could not be proven. As in D. de iudiciis et fideiussionibus, l. error. Moreover, the contumacious party is denied access to the courts. C. de iudicibus, l. sancimus.

† Moreover, it does not seem that in a capital case, defense can be conducted by a procurator, as stated in § ad crimen and Codex de accusationibus, l. reos per Cynus; and this was a common question among the Ravennate jurists. Bartolus places it in l. pe, § ad crimen, Digestum de publicis iudiciis. On the contrary, it seems probable that one can be defended. For the laws state that if the accuser is not legitimate, the accused will not be harassed, Extra de accusationibus, c. 1. Furthermore, he who concealed his nobility committed fraud against the praetor by his silence, and also by proceeding fraudulently; therefore, the procedure is null, Digestum de falsis, l. si quis obrepserit. Moreover, this informer was prohibited from informing and accusing, and thus he was prohibited from entering the judgment; and therefore the sentence is invalid, as in Digestum de aleatoribus, l. 1, § quod autem. Moreover, a procurator is admitted to this defense, insofar as it touches upon the substantial matters of true defense, but it concerns only the procedures, which appears from the fact that it does not give rise to the exception of res iudicata, Extra de iudiciis et examinationibus, in fine. The dispute of the Ravennate does not obstruct this, because there a peremptory exception was involved, which must be determined together with the principal issue, not by itself, as in l. 1, Codex de ordine iudiciorum. For it is implicit in the procedures from the crime; and therefore the reason for the prohibition is examined, because it is fuller and greater, as in Digestum de iudicibus, l. per minorem. Moreover, the matter is not understood to be liquidated by contumacy which is null, Digestum de iudicibus solutis, l. vir bonus, and l. fin, § pe, Codex de iuramento calumniae. Moreover, this procedure has no permissive foundation; and it was carried out against a prohibiting law; therefore it does not hold, and whatever followed from it or on account of it, as in Codex de legibus, l. non dubium. Moreover, the statute prohibits ordinary jurisdiction, otherwise accusation; therefore, much more strongly, extraordinary information, as in l. 1, § accusationem, Digestum ad turpia, and Digestum de dilationibus, l. ex varia, and Digestum de iure fisci, l. deferre. It is true that sometimes where an accuser is lacking, it is supplied ex officio by the inquisitor; but that would proceed from some special law, for example, in favor of a minor; for the rule is not handed down thus, as noted in l. querela, Codex de falsis. Moreover, the crime intended is private, which appears from the form of the statute, which does not permit any member of the Roman people, as noted in l. pe, Digestum de conditionibus ob causam. Furthermore, the inquisitor succeeds in the place of a public person, not a private one, and the office of inquisition is not favorable, but rather odious, and contrary to the regular rules of civil law, as in Digestum de muneribus et honoribus, l. rescripto, § si quis accusatorem non habens; Digestum de simoniis, l. licet; Digestum de accusationibus, l. qualiter. Therefore, this procedure was without foundation, indeed against the foundation, l. munici. Moreover, it can be said that this exception, as being odious, can be raised after sentence; because it was introduced out of mere hatred of the magnates, as in Digestum ad Macedonianam, l. tam et si; and this was held by Jacobus de Arena in his disputation, which disputation I have in a similar case. Nor do I omit that the accuser obtained to proceed against the denounced by procurator; therefore, let him use similar right, as in Codex de fructibus et litis expensis, l. fin, which speaks both in civil and criminal matters. Moreover, the name of querela is general, and comprehends all kinds of complaining, as in Digestum qui satisdare coguntur, l. si ab arbitro, according to Odofredus, who so notes there. And from these things it seems sufficiently clear that the said procedures do not hold by the law itself. However, the question of the crime is not entirely suppressed, but only as to the procedure, as in Digestum de accusationibus, l. libellorum, § quod si libelli, and Digestum de adulteriis, l. si accusaturus. Note that the statute enumerates two cases: the first, when against the person; and this word signifies those things which are not separated from the person, as noted by Bartolus in Digestum de publicis, l. licitatio, § quod illicite. The other case is concerning possessed things; and this chapter was not alleged, nor is it true; and he who alleges nothing, obtains nothing. There are, namely, four cases: alleged and true; neither alleged nor true; alleged and not true; also true and not alleged; and especially those which are derogatory to jurisdiction.

† And those matters which are to be proved before the litigation is contested must be clear according to the order given by the law; otherwise, the proceeding is invalid. As stated in the law *Quaero*, in the Digest under the title *De eo qui pro tutore*, and as noted by Innocentius in the Decretals under the title *De foro competenti*, in the chapter *Cum sit generale*, and in the chapter *Verum*. Therefore, it is rightly concluded that an omitted case in the libels is considered as omitted, and that a sentence cannot be based thereon or thereupon. As stated in the law *Ut fundus*, in the Digest under the title *Communi dividundo*, and in the law *Si*, in the Digest under the title *De fideiussoribus*. Nor is it within our discretion to alter the nature of judicial proceedings.

† to alter. D. de petitione hereditatis, l. non possumus. And therefore, according to what is alleged, always saving the determination of the great council, etc., I conclude that the proceedings were erroneous and null: and that the substance of the defense remains valid for the said condemned parties, as in Extravagant de purgatione vulgaris, c. significantibus; Codex de accusationibus, l. absentem. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether one witness testifying to adultery, and three testifying to the woman’s extra-judicial confession, of whom one is the brother and another the father of the accuser, are sufficient to subject the woman to torture. And no. 7.
2. Whether a confession constitutes evidence sufficient for torture.
3. Whether, by reason of the time being at night, one proceeds to torture, and no. 11.
4. Whether one witness as to the truth constitutes evidence sufficient for torture.
5. Crimes committed in a house are proved by household servants.
6. To prove evidence for the purpose of investigation, witnesses free from all exception are not required.
7. Whether the father and brother of the accuser are competent witnesses for the purpose of inquiry.
8. Adultery disgraces the entire kinship.
9. It rests within the discretion of the judge to determine which evidence is sufficient for torture.
1. The judge must employ the measure of unblamable severity in the application of torture.
2. The exception of inscription cannot be raised after the name has been received among the accused.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† A certain woman named Dom. Mita, wife of a certain Mutius, was accused of adultery by her husband; and against her one witness is introduced, testifying to the truth of the fact; and three witnesses asserting that she made a certain confession outside of court before a priest. Of these witnesses, two are proven [to be related]: one the father, the other the brother of the accuser. It is asked whether they constitute sufficient evidence for torture. And because it was pronounced that they do, it is asked whether it was wrongly pronounced or not. And first, as regards the principal cause, there are several pieces of evidence against this woman, not only probable and likely, but sufficiently proving by the argument from what commonly happens, or at least strongly supporting [the charge].

And let us begin with the confession made before honest persons, which constitutes evidence sufficient to justify torture, as stated in the Digest, *De adulteriis*, law *Capite quinto*, and in the Digest, *De edicto*, edict *Quaero*, section *Si*. For, as Innocentius states, in such a confession one is compelled to persist, as he notes in the glosses to the Decretals, *De electione*, chapter *Per inquisitionem*, and chapter *Cum super*, in the Decretals, *De confessis*. Secondly, it appears certain that this woman is highly suspicious on account of the time, because the darkness of night is more conducive [to such acts], as stated in law 1 of the Digest, *De veneficis et insipientibus*, in accordance with the saying: "The adulterer wanders about at night."

† Also, on account of the presumed turpitude. For it is shameful and infamous for a man and a woman to be together at night, especially in secret and hidden places. And if one asks, my friend, for what purpose did you come? It is not a good or plausible excuse to say that he went there unless to commit a crime: according to the saying, "He who does evil hates the light." He more easily comes to torture; because where clear proof is lacking, one resorts to arguments. As noted in *l. non omnes*, § *a barbaris*, D. de re militari. It supports what is noted in *l. si cum exceptione*, § *haec autem actio*, D. quod metus causa; C. de sicariis; *l. furem*, D. ad legem Aquiliam; *l. sed et si quaecunque plus*, because one of the witnesses says he saw the act connected with the crime.

And one witness as to the truth makes an indication for torture, not delative [torture] for one swearing, but purgative by torments, as noted in ff. de quaestio. l. maritus. and C. ad l. Iul. maie. l. si quis ex argentariis. §. 1. For one witness corroborates another, and from many concurring the effect is increased: according to that saying, "What singly does not avail, in plurality harms." As noted in l. 1. C. qui nume. tute. It applies to this the text which says that from a confession made out of court with the party absent, together with one witness as to the truth, a strong supporting evidence is proved, as extra de succes. abintest. c. cum dilectus.

† Moreover, delicts committed in a house are proved by household servants, as in C. de repu. l. consensu. Moreover, maleficium is presumed from several causes, as in ff. ad syl. l. excusantur. Moreover, it is incumbent upon the judge to investigate all matters and to leave nothing undiscussed; nor should he disregard that which is more than half-proved; otherwise, presumptions and indicia would be in vain.

† Furthermore, to prove indications for the purpose of investigation, not for proof, it is not required that the witnesses be above all exception, provided they testify to probable matters. As in C. ad syl. l. si, where it is noted regarding the impubere, and in de quaest. l. milites, §. oportet. Moved by these reasons, and others that may be alleged, I hold that it was justly pronounced that the woman should be subjected to the rack and interrogated: first, regarding the indications; second, regarding the crime; because grave matters must not be concealed. As in l. fi, C. ne sanctum baptisma iter.

Someone will say that credit is not given to suspect witnesses. But these are suspect because they are blood relatives of the accuser, as in C. si rector prouin. l. 1 and C. si quacunque praedi. pote. l. unica. For they seem to pursue their own grief, as in ff. de iniu. l. lex. cor. in prin. Nor does C. de adul. l. ita pudor. stand in the way, because there it speaks of frivolous exceptions or excuses, not of legitimate defense. But notwithstanding this, because it is not a matter of their own interest here, I think that what I said is true as regards the evidence: because many witnesses concur in the same opinion, and because it is not likely that they wish to do injury to their own blood. By injury I mean infamy.
† because adultery blackens and stains the entire kinship. Moreover, no single determinate rule can be given regarding torture.

† because they depend greatly on the discretion of the judge, to whose trust and authority the matter to be examined is committed. As stated in the Digest, *ad turpem*, law 1, § *calumniatoribus*, where it says: "the question of fact is within the discretion of the judge"; and because tortures are substituted in place of witnesses, we may apply to them what is said regarding witnesses: "You are better able to know." Digest, *de testibus*, law 3, § *tu magis*; and also in the matter of delay: Digest, *de usuris*, law *mora*. Nevertheless, statutes and local customs can properly determine the cases, causes, or types of tortures, which is better than leaving everything to the judges. Hence Aristotle says: "Well-established laws should determine all things themselves and leave as few matters as possible to the judges." However, where the law or custom does not determine the matter, the conscience of the judge supplies the deficiency. Digest, *de testibus*, law *scio*. And therefore, in these matters, law 10 heavily burdens the consciences of judges. Moreover, the judge, in tortures...

They ought to employ a measure of unblamable severity, as in C. de cust. reo. l. 2; nor should they proceed to such measures without a discussion of the case and without fury of mind, ff. de q. l. minore. §. tormenta. For excessive fervor of spirit is converted into fury; hence judges are said to have a mind moderated by reason and understanding, ff. de off. praesi. l. Obseruandum. But in the case proposed, we see that by the motion and footprints the quality of wolves and foxes is signified.

† Thus I say in the case at hand: to wander about at night to a suspicious place, and with suspicious persons: and they began from suspicions of torture, and [such suspicions] are necessary. As in C. de dolo, l. dolum, in the word "ex perspicuis indiciis," and from the track of the feet it is recognized whence the thief passed, who does not escape the snare of the watchful hunter. As in l. in laqueum, de acquirendo dominio. The conclusion is that the said woman ought to be tortured. But if she perseveres under torture and steadfastly denies, she is purged by the undergoing of torture, and ought to be absolved, as not proven.

† There is no need to worry about the fact that no inscription was made, because after the name of the thing has been received among the defendants, this exception cannot be raised. D. de adulteriis, l. si maritus, § praescriptiones: because it is a dilatory exception. Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What is required in an inquisition: and whether place and time are required.
2. Whether having two wives constitutes a crime.
3. How an inquisition is to be formulated when a woman is accused of adultery.
4. Whether it is lawful by law to send a repudiation to a wife: and what is the case among Jews.
5. Who is the competent judge among Jews.
6. Jews are under the protection of the Pope.
7. In inquisitions, multiple crimes may be alleged.
8. Whether Jews incur punishment by maintaining a synagogue.
9. What a synagogue is.
10. Heretics cannot have either public or private places.
11. Jews are not properly heretics.
12. By rescript, it cannot be granted to heretics that they hold public places.
body: In the Name of Christ Amen. And of His most holy passion.

† The inquiry, as brought regarding adultery, against the said Vitalutius in no way proceeds. First, by reason of form. For it lacks the place of the crime. And thus the inquiry is null, as stated in the Institutes, *De publicis iudiciis*, in the beginning; and there, the gloss; in the Code, *De accusationibus*, law *Poena*; and there, the gloss; in the Digest, *De accusationibus*, law *Libellorum*; and there, the text. Certainly, the said laws speak of accusation, but in inquiry it seems otherwise, as noted by the aforementioned gloss in the Institutes, *De publicis iudiciis*. What is to be said? Jacobus de Belvis, in the Institutes, *De actionibus*, at the end, says that as regards the solemnity of inscription and of the accuser, that gloss speaks truly, because the judge supplies [for the defect]; but as regards place and time, it is otherwise, because since these are introduced so that the defendant may be informed and made certain, it cannot be done without place and time. Moreover, then in inquiry, the judge supplies the person of the accuser, but when an accuser exists, [the place and time] must be stated. Therefore, etc. And thus he saves that gloss. Some doctors say that gloss should be understood in a general inquiry, of which in law *Congruit*, *De officio praesidis*, and in chapter *Bonae memoriae*, Extra, *De electione*, according to Innocentius. For since by it one does not come to condemnation, but by it one proceeds to a special inquiry, rightly this solemnity of place and time is required. Fittingly, now, generally either concerning persons or concerning crimes. And thus place and time cannot, nor ought they to be, so necessarily described, and here when it is to punish someone; otherwise if it is to remove someone from some office; because the said solemnities are not required, as in the Authenticum *Quo oportet episcopum*, section *Si quis autem talis*. And thus is understood law 3, section *Praeterea*, *De suspectis tutoribus*, and the aforementioned gloss, which is noted by the gloss in the Institutes, *De suspectis tutoribus*, in the beginning. And this is the common doctrine of the doctors.

Furthermore, it lacks another thing: because if the first wife was not lawfully dismissed, with the second [wife] adultery is not committed, but rape (*stuprum*), as in the Code, *De adulteriis*, law *Eum qui duas*, where the text is. For since there is no marriage with the second, adultery cannot be said to have been committed, but rape. Therefore, etc.

Moreover, even if rape had been brought, one could not proceed: because the five-year period has lapsed. Therefore, it is prescribed, as in the Digest, *De adulteriis*, law *Mariti lenocinium*, section *Quinquennium*; and as noted in the Institutes, *De publicis iudiciis*, section *Item lex Iulia de adulteriis*. And if it is said that he continuously held [the second wife] up to the Kalends of March of the present year, it is answered: therefore, it began by reason of time and place, as I said above just now. Therefore, etc.

Having premised this as to the form and manner of inquiry, let us see whether there is a delict. And it seems that there is. For it is prohibited by law to have two wives at the same time, as is stated in the aforementioned law *Eum qui duas*, Codex, *De adulteriis*; and in law 1, § *fin.*, and law *Quid ergo*, § 1, Institutes, *De nuptiis*; § *Affinitatis*; and Codex, *De donationibus ante nuptias*, law *Ea quae*. And there is a special provision regarding Jews, as in Codex, *De Iudaeis*, law *Nemo Iudaeorum*, at the end, and there the text states: "For no subject of the Roman Empire is permitted to have two wives at the same time," as in law *Neminem*, Codex, *De incestis nuptiis*. But Jews are subject to the Roman Empire, as in law *Iudaei*, Codex, *De Iudaeis*. Therefore, etc. Nor was it ever permitted to anyone to have two wives, unless it was granted by divine revelation, as in Extra, *De divortiis*, chapter *Gaudemus*. And this is what is said in Genesis 2, at the end: "For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife, and they shall be two in one flesh," as in the aforementioned chapter *Gaudemus*.

And note that if the inquiry were made solely on the ground of lust, and he had studiously and deliberately repudiated her without any legal order, then without doubt he would have committed a delict. For, in the first place, the wife would have remained his, and consequently he could not have taken a second, since the first was not legitimately repudiated, as stated in the last paragraph of the Digest, *De adulteriis*. But the truth in the case is to the contrary, namely, that she was repudiated in solemn form, according to the rites and customs of the Jews, while the cause subsisted, as will be proved in the facts. Therefore, etc.

And that it is lawful for them according to law to send a repudiation by giving a letter of repudiation, is the text of Deuteronomy 24:1 (cited as 123) at the end, and Distinction 32, question 1, chapter *Dicit Dominus* in the Gospel, and Matthew 19:3 (cited as 18), and Distinction 32, question 7, chapter *Omnes occasiones*, with many others. Hence, since according to their rites and customs they can, for a cause, having given a letter of repudiation to their first wife, take a second; especially since they have this right according to their rites and customs, because they cannot have children from the first, they ought not and cannot be punished. And although, according to divine law, they would sin by repudiating her, as the text implies in the aforementioned chapter *Gaudemus*, at the words *verum absonum*, nevertheless, the law permitting this, they can do it, i.e., by their customs and rites. However, the mere handing over of the letter of repudiation would not suffice, as the text implies in the aforementioned chapter *Deuteronomy*, but the presence of a priest to inquire into this matter is required, who, however, must pronounce a sentence of divorce between them. Indeed, what is less, he ought not perhaps to say, "We permit you to dismiss your wife," but he ought to say, "The law permits you to dismiss your wife, but not without your sin." The priest intervened so that no one would give this letter whenever he wished, but this was permitted only in certain cases. Thus says Innocent III in the aforementioned chapter *Gaudemus*, in the first gloss. And here it should be noted that, although the text in the aforementioned chapter *Deuteronomy* says nothing about the presence of a priest, it must be understood as referring to their priest, not to our judges. And thus not to a bishop or another ordinary. For Innocent would certainly have known to speak of the presence of a bishop or another judge if he had wished. Moreover, this has been derogated by desuetude, which they have and have had for a very long time, of which there is no memory of the contrary. And then, without doubt, the law is derogated and abrogated, as in the Institutes, in the Preface.

† For the cases of the Jews, insofar as they concern their rites and customs, or regarding money and similar matters: whether they are bound to have them heard before their own judges. Thus says Bartolus in *l. Iudaei*, Codex, *De Iudaeis*. For they have their own leaders, elders, and seniors, as stated in *l. nemo exterus* at the end, and *l. nemo*, and *l. si qua* at the end, and *l. Iudaeorum*, and *l. 2* at the beginning, Codex, *De Iudaeis*. Unless other cases arise, the cognizance of which pertains to secular judges; for then, incidentally, regarding their matrimonial cases and cases of superstition, secular judges could properly take cognizance, as stated in the aforementioned *l. Iudaei*, and thus Bartolus understands it there. Certainly, whether cognizance is taken by Christian judges or by others, the matter must be decided according to their rites and customs; for insofar as it concerns marriages and other superstitions, according to their rites and customs, they are not bound by laws or canons. The text is in the aforementioned *c. Gaudemus*. This is proved by another reason. For we see that although ecclesiastical or spiritual cases are heard before a secular judge, they must nevertheless be terminated according to the canons, as noted by the gloss in *c. Clerici*, *De iudiciis*, and is proved in the Authenticum *De ecclesia*, title, § *Si vero ecclesiasticis*, column 9, and *De testamentis*, *c. Relatum*, and is noted by Hostiensis in the Summa, *De maleficiis*, at the end, and is proved in *l. Omni novatione cessante*, *De sacrosanctis ecclesiis*. All their rites, provided they are not in contempt of the Christian religion, must be observed for them by ecclesiastical or secular princes, as stated in *l. Iudaeos* at the end, Codex, *De Iudaeis*, and *l. Die sabbato*, in the same title. Moreover, the Pope confirms their rites and customs for them; but this is most true in fact, that it is their custom to act thus, unless this custom opposes the primitive law and the primitive church, according to which they live, worship, and govern themselves. Therefore, and *c. Unde cum non del*, this Vitalutius does not seek to harm, but is innocent; although he is a Jew, he ought not to be tormented, or molested, or punished, nor harmed without reason, as stated in Codex, *De Iudaeis*, *l. Nullus*: for Jews, attempting nothing turbulent or contrary to the law, ought not to suffer injury, as stated in *l. Christianis*, Codex, *De paganis et sacerdotibus eorum*. For although Jews are, nevertheless they are to be protected by the Church; for they are counted among the sheep of Christ by creation, governance, and redemption in part, of Christ. Hence the Lord said in John 10.

† I have other sheep which are not of this fold. Jn. 10:16. Hence the Pope ought to protect them, just as his own sheep, which Peter entrusted to him among others, when he said, “Feed my sheep,” Jn. 21:17, making no distinction between these and those. Therefore, c. Extra, De maioritate et obedientia, cap. Solitae, as Innocentius holds in cap. Quod super his, De voto. Since therefore he ought to feed them by word, example, and humanity, he ought not to attack them, nor permit them to be harmed. It is also provided in Extra, De natura, lib. 6, cap. 1, where this is discussed. Hence, since the said Vitalutius did not knowingly and deliberately, nor out of lust, nor by omitting the order of their custom, but by observing it, legitimately repudiated her, he ought not to be punished by the aforementioned laws. For the spiritual lord, who is investigated on this matter, ought to pay great attention, because these Jews do not so abruptly rush to oppose their rites and customs. And if a general inquiry or investigation into this crime had been made, it would undoubtedly have been found, as I said, that she was repudiated for a legitimate cause, according to their rites; and thus a special inquiry would not have been resorted to. I descend to the second case of the inquiry concerning the synagogue, as it is said, made by this Vitalutius.

† And I premise that, whatever may be the law in accusations, in inquisitions it is this: that several and diverse offenses may be brought forward in the same inquisition, as in c. In tamen, Extra de collationibus. Having premised this, I say that the said inquisition is defective in form: because it has no place, therefore, and so forth, according to what has been said above in the first chapter of the inquisition.

I descend to the principal fact alleged. And if an inquiry had been conducted, because it would possess its formalities and the facts were truly narrated therein, he would undoubtedly have committed a delict and incurred the penalty of the confiscation of the said synagogue. And the text of *l. li. auri* is found in *l. fi.*, Codex, *De Iudaeis*, where the text states that no Jewish synagogue shall be raised in new construction. And it adds, or shall have built a synagogue, and the rest. And it adds, whoever shall have begun the construction of a synagogue, etc. And *l. in synagoga*, in the same title. And *Extra*, *De Iudaeis*, *c. consuluit*, and *c. Iudaei*. But in truth, this is not correct. Let the place be examined with the eyes, and it will be seen that there is no delict. For although he has in his dwelling house a secluded place, in which he keeps his books and has lamps lit, and he himself, together with other Jews, prays there according to their rites, it is not for this reason called a synagogue. For as Archidiaconus says in *c. fundamenta*, *De electionibus*, in the beginning, Book 6, a synagogue among the Jews is the same as a church among us. For just as a church is an assembly of the faithful, so among the Jews,

† A synagogue is an assembly of Jews. Hence, just as in the church the faithful people are summoned to the true faith and to the banquet of Christ, so in the synagogue the Jews assembled to perform their ceremonies. Therefore, the judgment concerning a synagogue among the Jews is the same as that concerning a church among Catholics. As noted in the Digest, per Arch., de consecratione, distinction 1, chapter Ecclesia; and in Question 2, Cause 1, Question 1, Extra, per Johannes Andreae, in the chapter Consuluit, de iudiciis, in the Novella. And just as any place constructed by Catholics for prayer is not called a church—for it is lawful for any private individual to have a private oratory, in which he may have seats for sitting, and lamps lit for the devotion of the people, and keep books closed in their closed cabinets for the office to be said therein, and open and close them in his house, which is not called a church (de consecratione, distinction 1, chapter Unicuique; and chapter Ecclesiasticos; and Innocentius in the chapter Inter dilectos, de donationibus)—and this we see daily and commonly in the houses of willing men—so also it is lawful for any Jew to have a private place in his own house for praying and contemplating God for himself and his others, which is not properly called a synagogue. Wherefore, where the laws permit ancient synagogues to be repaired and prohibit new ones from being built, they must be understood as referring to public synagogues. They may have other private places. For just as in the building of these Catholic oratories no canonical solemnity is required, whereas it is required in churches, as is stated in the Extra, de electione, chapter Aedificam, so it is with synagogues. And thus, in consulting, they determined this: Lord Johannes de Lignano and the entire college of canonists of Bologna. And that “synagogue” is taken for a public place where they assemble publicly, and not for a private one when they receive themselves in private dwellings, is the text which sets forth, as different species, in the law Nullus, Codex, de Iudaeis; and the law In synagoga; and the law Iudaeorum, in the same title. And this is what the text says in the aforementioned law Si, de Iudaeis: “Let no Jewish synagogue arise in new construction.” And thus the entire text speaks of public synagogues, in public places, not of those which are made privately in their houses; and this is evident.

† For it is expressly forbidden to heretics to have not only public places, but also private ones, as stated in l. 2, in principio, C. de summa trinitate, and in l. 3, C. de haereticis; a prohibition which is not extended to Jews, as noted in l. 2, per doctores.

† for Jews are not heretics in the proper sense: which is evident from the diversity of titles in the Codex, and concerning the Cretans; and because the Jews had the beginning of the truth, as is taught in the 12th note in the aforementioned law 1.

† Moreover, by the rescript, it cannot be granted to heretics, d. l. 2, whereas it would be otherwise in the case of Jews. Furthermore, do we not see this everywhere, and the Church tolerates the Jews themselves not only in their own home and in private, but also in a remote place of theirs, yet not a public one, so that anyone may access it publicly, as is the case with our churches. Indeed, they keep them closed. And thus the Church tolerates them as a testimony to our faith; likewise their rites, according to the noted opinion of Innocent I, d. c. quod super his. Hence, since everywhere, as we see, Jews have such places, they will not be judged as prohibited synagogues. But that prohibition will be understood properly and within its own terms, taking "synagogue" in its strict sense; because these are odious, and therefore rightly not to be extended, etc. And since custom approves this, and the Pope and all prelates of the churches tolerate it. Therefore, and so forth. Johannes de Montegranario, Doctor of Laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. By what punishment one who commits adultery and incest is to be punished.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Regarding the point you have asked me about, namely by what punishment one who has committed adultery and incest should be punished, given that a penalty of 25 florins is imposed for adultery by constitution, and another statute provides that similar cases should be treated similarly, I answer as follows: According to common law, the same penalty should be imposed for adultery and for incest alone, as noted in the gloss on *Si adulterium cum incestu*, D. de adulteriis. As to what this penalty is under common law, the glosses are contradictory. For three glosses state that formerly there was no penalty of the sword, but today the penalty is the sword and death. And so it is noted in *Claudius*, C. de his qui velut indigni; *Qui cum uno*, § *Adulteri*, D. de re militari; *L. 2*, § *Miles*, D. de his qui non in fide; and the text of *Quamvis*, C. de adulteriis, seems to support this. But another gloss says that the judge may, if he wishes, punish with death, but if he wishes to mitigate the penalty for cause, he may deport the offender to an island; as noted in the gloss on *Si quis viduam*, D. de quaestionibus. And this is the view of Cynus in the aforementioned *Quamvis*, and of Bartolus in the aforementioned *Si quis viduam*, which also applies where adultery is joined with incest. These views are correct according to common law. But since the statute and constitution prescribe a pecuniary penalty for adultery, and another statute provides that similar cases should be treated similarly, and since the law equates adultery and incest as regards the penalty, it can sufficiently be tolerated if the judge imposes a penalty of one hundred for adultery and another hundred for incest, thus doubling the penalty due to the duplication of the offenses, as in *Qui de crimine*, C. de accusationibus. It can also be said that this is an omitted case, and that the penalty is discretionary, according to the gloss in *Si quis viduam*. And it will be sufficient to punish at his discretion in the manner described above, or somewhat more mildly, without death or mutilation, according to the text in the aforementioned *Si quis viduam*. Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If someone, after all parties had been summoned generally and no one appeared, was absolved, does the exception of res judicata bar the sisters of the slain, who were not specifically summoned?
1. Whether a sentence removes the perpetuation of the judicial observation.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. An inquiry was conducted by the executor of the Senate against a certain person. The procurator appeared and objected that he could be killed with impunity according to the form of the statute. The executor, having summoned certain relatives of the deceased and generally others in public places, and those competent and some requesting time to deliberate whether they wished to accuse, and with no response: pronounced that no further proceedings should be taken on the case, and that the offense was unpunishable. The sisters of the deceased, who were not specifically summoned, wish to accuse.

† It is asked whether the exception of res iudicata prevails. The glossa ordinaria says: I do not say that individuals are to be cited, but rather that a general and public edict is to be issued, whereby relatives by affinity and friends are cited. L. Hoc autem, §. I, on the word cognati, D. Qui ex causa in possessionem eant. But the injured party himself may properly be cited by name, if he wishes, because his own case is being tried: D. De venditionibus insipientium, L. I, §. Denuntiari; and D. Quod vi aut clam, L. Aut qui aliter, §. Sed et si forte; C. Si quis se ab hereditate abstinerit; Auth. Si omnes, De maioribus et obsequiis; C. Humilis, according to Innocentius. Or say that if the investigating judge does not cite by name those whom he ought to have believed would proceed to accuse, such an inquiry is deemed to have been conducted secretly (clam), because those to whom notice should have been given face-to-face or at their home were concealed. As in C. Causam, De electione, in the Clementinae; and the aforementioned L. Aut qui aliter; and D. De rebus eorum, L. Magis puto, §. In primis; and D. Ubi puer educari debeat, L. Si; and C. De nuptiis, L. Viduae and L. In conventione, in the final part; and the argument in Auth. De haereditatibus et fideicommissis, §. Si vero absint; and D. De adoptionibus, L. Nam ita divus. And this applies to those persons who have the right to accuse. For those among the agnates who do not have the right to accuse do not hinder the inquiry, nor are they to be cited for this purpose, because they are not suitable for this: for example, wards and similar persons, because they would be cited in vain. D. De habilibus. Therefore, the statute speaks of suitable persons. L. Ut gradatim, §. Sed si lege, D. De muneribus et honoribus. The words of the statute say that they are bound not to inquire into the same crime, if it is alleged that punishment has been inflicted, or a decision rendered, or proceedings repeated, provided that the accusation of the injured party has proceeded, or at least that the injured party has been required to act, or, if he is dead, his nearest agnates: which is to be understood as referring to those who are suitable and competent, as I have said. D. De libero homine exhibendo, L. 3, §. Hoc interdictum. Regarding preemption, the statute says that preemption is induced by act or by word: for example, by capture, which perpetuates jurisdiction before the same judge.

But it is asked whether, after sentence has been pronounced, this perpetuation has been removed from the observance of the trial. And briefly, the case is that a sentence of acquittal operates for no such effect as to the beginning of the process already formed. D. de iure fisci, l. Fiscus, in quaestione, according to the true understanding of Lauro de Arezzo. Therefore, is a new accusation to be received ex officio after this sentence of acquittal has been pronounced? It must be said that yes, provided two conditions concur: that the new accuser pursues his own injury or that of his kin, and that he proves collusion on the part of the judge. Others also require proof of ignorance, which is said, as in D. de accusationibus, l. Si cui, §. Finis, which can be gathered from the records. For if the cause was acquitted without being discussed, or on a pretended false cause, or an insufficient one, when certainly the crime was manifest, the fraud of the inquirer is manifest. D. de iudicibus, l. Si filius. But if it is established that the sentence was pronounced on a true and sufficient cause, so that the judge believed he judged well, then the sentence must stand and gives rise to the exception of res iudicata. L. Praeses, and L. Cum prolatis, D. de re iudicata. Provided, however, that if the judge ought to have cited the injured party or his relatives in his process and did not cite them legitimately, the matter must be heard anew. D. de iure fisci, l. Si fiscus alicui. Nor is it necessary to approach the same judge, because as regards himself he has abdicated the exercise of jurisdiction by his sentence. First, because on account of his fault the process is invalid. As C. de accusationibus, l. Ablente. And it supports this, D. de officio delegati, c. Significantibus. Therefore, another judge may hear the case. It supports the foregoing, D. de iureiurando, l. Eum qui in popularibus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The benefit is not lost when a specific quality is required for the exclusion from a benefice or the imposition of a penalty, provided that such quality is alleged and proven.
2. A crime committed with an iron weapon is more serious than one committed with a stone.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Assuming that the proofs do not contain what is contained in the inquisition, I say that from the said inquisition, since an affinity contrary to it has been proven, a condemnation against the defendant for aid and favor cannot follow. And the reason is:

†because when some quality is required for the exclusion from a benefit, unless that quality is alleged and proved, the benefit is not lost. Likewise, a quality that aggravates the penalty must similarly be alleged and proved. D. 47.10.1 (Praetor), § docere; D. 9.2.1 (In delictis), § si extraneus and § si detracta; D. 48.1.1 (Senatus censuit), according to Petrus; D. 48.19.1 (Si praeses); D. 26.1.1 (Hoc), n. and no.; X 5.39.1 (Ex parte abbatissae) per Innocentius. But here the quality of the instrument has not been alleged, nor does it appear. For the quality of the instrument increases the crime and excludes the benefit.

For it is a more serious offense that is committed with an iron weapon than one committed with a stone or a club. Extra, De homicidio, c. Significasti, in fine; and Digestum, De sicariis, l. 1, § Si claua. I conclude that, unless the quality of the instrument is alleged or proven, the aforementioned relative cannot be condemned. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Laws, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the statute concerning an evident scar applies to a blow struck to the head resulting in a deep depression.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Whether a statute concerning an evident scar applies to a blow struck to the head resulting in a great concavity. Having examined the statute, which speaks strictly of a blow from which an ugly mark or an evident scar remains, and which imposes a penalty of two hundred pounds, I say that he who struck by day on the head, with fracture of the bone, and a great concavity remained in the head: because he deformed the head of the person struck with scars, ought to be punished in 200 pounds. For the statute does not restrict itself to a blow to the face: and because it is an ugly mark. L. fin. ff. de his qui deie. vel effu. et si quadr. pau. fecis. dica. L. hac lege. I doubt, however, on account of the word "evident." For a scar which is covered by the scalp or by hair does not seem to be evident: because it is not exposed to the eyes of men looking upon it, but is concealed. But certainly sometimes it is evident. The head is not always covered, but rather uncovered in prominent places, and where there is an assembly of men, as in church. And therefore the reason of the statute, which considers the disgrace arising therefrom, applies here, or at least the judge ought to assimilate it thus: because that which is more similar is that which is more proximate and united in reason to that to which it is assimilated. As ff. de leg. l. non possunt. and l. de quibus. and l. illud. ad l. Aquil. and de verb. obl. l. a Titio. To the statute concerning the doubling of penalties I do not respond: because I have not seen the expenses. Nevertheless, it makes a difference that they do not come to be doubled by virtue of the statute speaking of the doubling of penalties: because this is not a mere penalty, but interest. As said in the aforementioned laws. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether only one penalty, or whether several penalties, are to be imposed on one who struck once in the face with an empty hand, or with a comb, or a pitchfork, or a fork, from which blood issued from four or two places.
2. Add the opinion in part 5, beginning: the case was as follows: the judge of malefices, etc.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The point is as follows. The inquisition states: he struck once with an empty hand in the face, from which blood issued from four parts of the face, etc. In the Name of Christ. Amen.

The ancients commonly held, and Lauro de Arezzo followed them, that one penalty should be imposed: because there is one intent, one act, and one crime. But Bartolus holds that there are several crimes, and therefore punishment should be made for several. This is supported by the argument from effect, which causes several things to be considered as one, as in *l. illud*, at the end, *D. ad leg. Aquiliam*; and causes one to be considered as several, as in *l. qui de crimine*, *C. de accusationibus*. It is also supported by *l. si familia*, *D. de iure omnium iudiciorum*. Thus Bartolus holds in *l. si gemina arbor*. But Cynus aligns himself with the ancients, as he states in *l. finalis*, *D. de excusationibus*, and *C. in fine*. Add this, according to Bartolus: it is supported by the statement of Aretinus, who says that the law looks to the difference in harm. Hence, he who causes harm in several respects seems to offend in several respects. And it seems absurd to say that he who inflicts wounds with one blow—for example, with a comb—should not be punished more than he who inflicts one wound, for example, with a single tooth of the comb. Such absurdity must always be avoided in laws and statutes.

I say that sometimes the law considers the act absolutely, sometimes with respect to the manner. In the first case, the controversy of opinions applies. For example, if a statute says absolutely, "if anyone strikes, etc." In the second case, for example, if a statute says, "if anyone strikes someone with a comb, or pitchfork, or fork, and blood flows, let him be punished in ten [units]." For if several wounds follow from one strike, there is nevertheless one penalty: because the law seems to have considered this, since it disposes regarding an instrument suitable for this purpose; for it seems to speak according to the suitability of that instrument, as we say similarly in *l. 2*, *D. si certum petatur*. So it is in the present case: if anyone, it says, strikes with an empty hand, for the hand has five fingers, like combs or pitchforks, and although each finger causes blood to flow, there is nevertheless one penalty, because that injury does not consist solely in the blood, but in the blow and in the origin. And although there are several flows of blood, there is nevertheless only one hand, and thus one injury: and for this reason, one penalty. And this is confirmed by the word *inquisitio* in the word *semel*, which is used both actively and passively. Also, blood can flow from four parts, and it is not seen as a single cut. For example, if the entire lip is cut, blood flows upward, downward, and to the left. And therefore, the inquiry does not conclude regarding plurality. To this also contributes that word, *ex qua percussione*, which is singular in number. Also, the statute seems to have considered what can happen verisimilarly and usually according to the suitability of that instrument; for the law seems to have considered all things that can easily and frequently happen, as in *l. 3* and *4*, *D. de legibus*. Also, one and several are said in many ways, as noted in *l. patris, et filii*, *D. de vulgo et pupillo*. And this is the conclusion. Here, more could be alleged. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute that grants the right to kill a banished person and the reward for re-banning, is it required, in order to obtain said reward, that one kills him with certain knowledge and voluntarily? And is it required that the killing takes place within the territory?
2. A reward granted for merit is not deserved unless the acts are performed with certain knowledge and voluntarily.
3. Ignorance is proven by oath: so too is knowledge.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.
It must be premised for clarity that there are certain conditions which require knowledge and fulfillment, and which must be fulfilled with one's own intent. See Digest 45.1.2.

And whatever is granted on account of merit does not deserve a reward unless it is performed with certain knowledge and voluntarily. D. ad Sill. l. si quis in graui; D. ad tert. l. 2, § si mater, ver. quid ergo. Therefore, these two things are required, namely, that it be done with certain knowledge and spontaneously. Nevertheless, certain knowledge is presumed when someone is publicly proclaimed, announced in public places, and finally condemned in the council of the people. As it is stated and noted in D. de recept. l. 1. What all commonly know, it is presumed that each individual knows. Extr. de postul. prel. c. 1; and l. pe. C. de peric. tu.; and l. iubemus; and as noted by Dy. in c. ignorantia, de reg. iur. lib. 6.

† Moreover, just as ignorance is proved by one’s own oath, so too is knowledge; for the rule is the same for contrary matters. Hence, he who alleges knowledge in his own favor may also prove it by his own oath. D. 29.2.1 (Pro haerede), according to Licetius of Arezzo. It is pertinent, C. 1.2.10 (Ut circa), X. 6. Item, as appears from the attestations, the beginning of the motion was voluntary. And thus, having regard to the beginning, which is to be considered, as D. 47.10.1 (Quod ait), § 1. Therefore, the said Dominic is owed the reward and the faculty of rebanning another; because the statute does not distinguish from where the slayer of the outlaw comes. D. 48.1.3. And it is pertinent, what is stated and noted by Dyonisius, D. 45.1.10 (Cum servus). And therefore, the said Martin must be removed from the ban. Nor does it avail that he was killed outside the territory. For the killer of a public enemy does not thereby merit the reward less. For it is expedient for the republic that public enemies, against whom war is declared, be killed wherever they may be, as D. 48.9.1 (Transfugas). I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a feudatory can build fortresses in places enfeoffed to him.
2. Whether a feudatory can impose unusual burdens in places enfeoffed to him.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen.

† Concerning that which is asked, whether the noble knight lord Cathalanus can build fortresses in the places enfeoffed to him by the lord Pope, notwithstanding the constitution of the Church. I, the undersigned Ubaldus, say that he can, for the following reasons. First, because by reason of the fief he has beneficial ownership (utile dominium), and just as an emphyteutic tenant can build on the granted ground, as in l. 2. C. de iure emphy. and C. de sac. san. eccle. auth. si quis ruina. Second, because not so much he himself as the Church seems to build, since the direct ownership is acquired for the Church, and the affair of the Church is beneficially managed; whence it must be ratified, for in reality it belongs to the Church, ff. de neg. ge. l. Pomponius scribit. Third, because what he builds, since he holds title from the Church, the Church seems to build, ff. de alie. iud. mu. cau. fac. l. 1. §. opus. Fourth, because it is so by custom, that the lords of jurisdictions build fortresses, as argued in l. vniuersorum. Fifth, because to whom jurisdiction is granted, a place seems to be granted where it can be exercised safely and conveniently, l. 2. ff. de iur. omn. iud.; but on account of the malice of the subjects this cannot be done without a fortress. Sixth, because to whom greater things are granted—that is, the merum and mixtum imperium—all the more strongly lesser things seem to be granted, C. de pac. conuen. l. hac, ff. de serui. rustic. praed. l. 3. §. qui habet austum. Seventh, because a constitution is not understood to impose a law upon one holding a papal grace, ff. de pec. leg. l. si peculium. §. sicut. Eighth, because by reason of jurisdiction it is permissible to build castles and fortresses, l. quicunque. de fundis limitosis and the notes there. Ninth, because in the grant it is said: “we grant to you such things, and greater,” which word is to be interpreted broadly, because it harms no one and benefits him to whom it is granted, C. de consti. prin. l. fi. For he is not presumed to act out of spite, since he has sworn to the contrary, C. ad l. iul. repet. l. iubemus. The constitution is not an obstacle, because for the aforesaid reasons it is understood to apply to one who does not have the right of the soil; but this feudatory has the right of the soil, and because the rationale of spite ceases in him. And although I believe this to be true in law, nevertheless it is safer to obtain a license, so that all occasion of dispute may be removed.

† Concerning the other matter which is asked: whether the lord Catalanus can impose unusual burdens, I say that this does not seem to have been granted to him, C. noua vecti. l. 1. and by argument from ff. de contrahen. emp. l. fistulas. §. frum., unless there were a necessity such that it could not be passed over without a super-imposition; for on account of emergent cases one departs from the usual and passes over to the unusual, because necessity, which has no law, does this, ff. de leg. l. in rebus nouis, l. 1. de off. consu., C. de sa. san. ec. l. neminem. For the lord Catalanus in those lands can be called a prince, l. spadonem. §. si ciuitatis princeps. ff. de exc. tu. For he can use it somewhat more broadly because he has the beneficial ownership, as noted in C. de iud. l. omnis. lib. 10. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether laborers hired to cut wood can be accused of disturbing possession, or are liable under the Aquilian action, or under the interdict *quod vi aut clam*; and what is the case with the hirer of said laborers, whether he himself is liable.
2. One is not said to disturb who does not have the intent to disturb.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen. Given the statute of the commune of Pavia, which imposes a certain monetary penalty on those who disturb anyone in possession of a thing that he truly possesses, it is proposed that A. and B. were hired by C. to cut down a certain forest truly possessed by D., adjacent to another wood of the said C., and that the hirers of the laborers, namely the said A. and B., were thereupon accused, along with the said hirer of the laborers.

† Now it is asked, without calling into question the possession of the said D., whether the said lessors of labor, or the said hirer, are therefore liable to the penalty of the statute; or whether they are liable only by the simple action of the Lex Aquilia or by the interdict *quod vi aut clam*. And it seems that they are liable to the penalty of the said statute; because the statute does not distinguish whether dolus (fraud) intervened or not. Therefore, we ought not to distinguish. D. 47.11.1 (*De publicanis*). Moreover, injury ought not to be done to another under the pretext of error, lest the fool be in a better condition than the expert. As in D. 43.16.1 (*Servius*). Also, because they ought to have inquired, at least by domestic inquiry and among the neighbors, what the nature of the said wood was and who possessed it. For if they had inquired, they would easily have known. As in C. 7.6.1 (*Si aviam*) and D. 43.12.1 (*Prima*), § 1. And not to inquire about that which one is accustomed and ought to inquire about is a species of gross negligence. As in D. 43.23.1 (*Doli mali*), § final. Furthermore, he who causes damage to another’s property is liable not only civilly by the action of the Lex Aquilia, but also criminally to a penalty imposed on the fisc. This is the singular gloss in D. 47.11.1 (*Si*), D. 47.11 (*De privatis delictis*).

On the contrary, it seems that no damage was given if the wood was coppice, provided that the timber was not carried away by them; otherwise, if the wood was not coppice, because then some damage would have been given. As in D. 9.2.27 (*Si servus servum*), § *Si oliva*, and D. 43.16.1 (*Nam et si ramos*). Also, in the interdict *quod vi aut clam*, damage is not distinguished from non-damage; because the very disturbance of possession is held as damage given, as is fully noted in D. 43.26.1 (*Extat*).

On the contrary is the ordinary gloss to D. 18.1.1 (*In rem*), § *Tignum*, D. 18.1 (*De rei venditione*). For these lessors of labor are excused; because they are accustomed to work in such matters and to let their labor. As in D. 47.10.1 (*Item apud*), § *Si quis astrologus*, D. 47.10 (*De iniuriis*). And having regard to their art, they applied themselves to a lawful thing. Also, if any fault could be imputed to the said workmen, it was in omitting to inquire; and this fault in omitting does not fall under the action of the Lex Aquilia, because it is the lightest fault. As the noted text says: “The lightest fault is never punished criminally by an ordinary penalty,” such as this pecuniary penalty also is. This is singularly noted by Cynus, C. 1.3.1 (*Si quis non dicam rapere*), C. 1.3 (*De episcopis et clericis*). And by this, the lessors of labor are excused.

However, the hirer is not excused; because he ought to have known the boundaries and limits of his property, and ought not to err in his own fact. As in C. 3.31.1 (*Si constiterit*), C. 3.31 (*Finium regundo*); and D. 6.1.1 (*Fina*), D. 6.1 (*Pro suo*); and D. 29.2.1 (*Duo fratres*), D. 29.2 (*De acquirenda hereditate*). From these it appears that the lightest fault has a certain latitude, the minimum degree of which, or the least, is in not doing. And therefore, one need not care for trifles; because he who transgresses so slightly is not blamed. As in D. 12.1.1 (*Quamvis*), D. 12.1 (*De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*). Thus, therefore, the lightest fault and the minimum fault are not the same. As the said § *De praeteritis* is to be understood subtly.

Moreover, these lessors of labor are rustics, and leniency is shown to rusticity, except in natural law. As in C. 7.33.1 (*Venia*), C. 7.33 (*De in ius vocandis*). But they ought to have believed the good man hiring their labor, since everyone is presumed to be good, and it is not contrary to natural law to do something. As noted in D. 12.1.1 (*Titio*), D. 12.1 (*De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*); and see, what is noted, C. 11.39.1 (*Quicunque*), § penultimate, C. 11.39 (*De servitute fugitiva*), where lawful contact excuses the erring person; as I said there. It supports the foregoing: because the law says, “We wish knowledge, not ignorance, to bind.” As in C. 4.20.1 (*Generali*), C. 4.20 (*De tabulariis*). For penalties are not imposed on those deceived by the slippery slope of factual ignorance. As in D. 2.1.1 (*Si*), D. 2.1 (*De decretis ab ordinariis faciendis*).

† Moreover, one is not said to disturb who lacks the intention of disturbing. As is elegantly noted in *l. si duo*, in the beginning, *Digestum*, *uti possidetis*; unless they were neighbors, who are presumed to know. See *l. si ita*, *Digestum*, *de fundo instrato*; and *l. 1*, § 1, *Digestum*, *de fluminibus*; and the notes in *l. 1*, *Codex*, *quando fiscus vel privatus*; and *l. dominus horreorum*, *Digestum*, *locato*; and *l. prima*, *Codex*, *ubi de ratiocinatione agi oportet*; and according to Bartolus in *l. 1*, *Digestum*, *si certum petatur*. That which must not be omitted is that if those laborers exceeded the limits of the mandate by sending a sickle into another’s harvest, the master is not liable: because he did not mandate it, nor did he ratify it, as in *Extra*, *de restitutione spoliorum*, c. *cum ad sedem*. The objection from c. *ultimum*, *Extra*, *de homicidio*, book 6, does not hold; because there the mandatary exceeded the limit in a personal offense; here it is in a real one. Moreover, there the limit could not be set in the entry of the sword; because the sword obeys the body more than the mind. And other things are usually more deadly. And death is connected and inseparable from the atrocity of wounds. And therefore it is imputed, because it harms; because fraud precedes accident; otherwise it would be different. See *Digestum*, *ad legem Silanianam*, *l. qui posthumos*. Even those laborers, as I said before, are excused on account of ignorance. And if it is said that rather they should be punished by an arbitrary penalty, because the statute grants discretion? I reply that the discretion to punish is never understood to be granted when there is no crime at all. For arbitrary penalties fall in the selection of punishments between one penalty and another. See *Digestum*, *de poenis*, *l. hodie*. But where there is no crime, there is no penalty whatsoever, and therefore no selection or discretion between penalties falls, since the innocent defendant is safe, and the faith of innocence has the greatest security. See *Codex*, *de iniuriis*, *l. si non convitiis*. But if the type of crime did not fit the quality of the penalty, there would necessarily be a deviation from the ordinary penalty to an arbitrary penalty, ascending or descending to a penalty, or from a penalty, as is appropriate to the degrees of guilt and the reason of the underlying person, and similarly a permutation. See *Codex*, *ut intra certum tempus criminalis causa terminetur*, *l. 2*; and *Digestum*, *de his qui notati infamia*, *l. quid ergo*, § *poena gravior*. And see what Bartolus notes in *l. 1*, § 1, *Digestum*, *si quis testamento liber esse iussus fuerit*. Moreover, it would be absurd to say that he who hires out his labor for one day, or a few, would be bound to investigate the owner; because the investigation would occupy more time than the labor. See *Digestum*, *de damno infecto*, *l. inter quos*, § *si dominus*. The one giving the mandate would also be excused if he did not mandate with certainty regarding the place; because he is not understood to have mandated that which is contrary to law. See *l. si pater*, *Digestum*, *quae in fraudem creditorum*; and *l. si procurator*, *Digestum*, *de conditione indebiti*. I, B.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. It is impossible to know who is the son.
2. How the presumption of filiation is proved.
3. Whether a person is proved to be a son if it is proved that his mother lay with an adulterer.
4. Whether a son is presumed legitimate from the fact that the father calls him son.
5. A witness testifying that someone is a son is said to testify concerning both natural and legitimate status.
6. Whether credit is to be given to the father and mother saying that he who was born in marriage is not a son.
7. He is a fool who believes his mother saying that he will not be a son in the kingdom of his father.
8. Credit is not to be given to an outside woman saying to you that the son she bore is your son: which note, you scholar, because it occurs daily in practice, but beware lest you be very incredulous and act against conscience.
9. Whether an institution made concerning one who is reasonably doubted as to whether he is the testator's son is valid.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Titius had Seia as his wife, who, being in her fiftieth year of age, asserted that she was pregnant, and at the appropriate time asserted that she had borne a son named Peter. Titius treated Peter as his son by rearing and nourishing him. As time passed, the said Titius drew up his will, in which, naming Peter, he instituted him as his natural and legitimate son and universal heir. Finally, it is asserted that Seia, the wife of Titius, confessed to her brother confessor that Peter was not her son, nor the son of Titius, her husband; of this confession it does not appear that Titius had knowledge. Finally, Seia having died, Titius drew up a second will, in which he said thus: "Peter, whom I have always reared and nourished in my house, I institute in such goods as well amount to the legitime." In the other goods he instituted Gaius, his brother, as universal heir, with the burden of providing a certain sum annually to a certain other natural son. Peter asserts that he was instituted in the second will in certain things not as a son, but as an outsider, and as a passed-over son. Therefore, the second will is void on account of the passing over. The question is asked: what is the law?
