The words of Master Guy in the ordinary lecture which he began on the old Digest, in the law *Filium diffinimus*, in the title *De his qui sunt sui vel alieni iuris*, are these: It is opposed first, that no certain definition can be given concerning filiation:

† Since it is impossible to know who is the son, as will be said below in the title *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, in the law *Lucius*. It must be stated that here the son is not defined according to truth, but according to fiction or presumption. For in truth it is impossible, as in the contrary law. Nor does it suffice there to prove by presumption; because the testator attached the condition that he prove himself to be the son, which is heard according to truth; because conditions are said to be fulfilled according to the form of the fact attached. See *Extra*, title *De testibus*, law *Meuius*; and *Qui heredes*, in the beginning. But it is objected: *Digest*, *De liberis agnoscendis*, law 2, § *Si quis longo tempore*. Solution: noted in the gloss. Thirdly, it is objected that here it is said that if it is established that he is not the son, etc.; but this cannot be established, because negatives, by the nature of things, etc., as in law *Actor*, *Code*, *De probationibus*. Solution: here the negative is proved by affirmative proof, from which this results, as appears here in the text itself. *Code*, *De contrahenda et committenda stipulatione*, law *Optimam*, with its following sections.

† The question here is: since filiation is proved by presumption, what must be proved in order for someone to be presumed a legitimate son? Certainly, first the marriage contracted between Mar. and Bar. must be proved, and that they were of marriageable age. Also, that while they were cohabiting together, the woman gave birth to such a son, or that he was born from her womb. From these facts, the son is presumed by a presumption of law, unless an impediment to procreation is proved on the contrary side. As is clear from this law, and it suffices to prove the presumed fact, as here, and below in the Digest, *de his quae in fraudem creditorum*, l. *omnes* § *Lucius*.

But suppose that my mother lay with the husband, whom you call your father, and also with another man before your birth: would you be presumed a legitimate son? This is the argument, which is as follows: although on account of adultery it seems less likely to be presumed, as below, on adultery, l. miles, § quae propter.

† Furthermore, suppose that a father called someone his son: does it follow from this that the son is presumed legitimate? The argument is that it does not. C. de probat. l. Non nudis; and l. Neque; and infra de inoff. testam. l. Si instit. § 1. But say the contrary, as in extra de probat. c. Per tuas; and extra qui filii sint legitimi c. Per tuas; and this law in the beginning. It says: “We define a son,” etc., with “natural and legitimate” understood; so also in the case of a father who calls someone his son. And this is the opinion of Odofredus here, and we note it in Inst. de adopt. § Si. For common presumptions are established, unless the contrary is proved.

And also in the case of a witness who testifies that a child is a son, and says nothing more: for it is understood that he has testified concerning a natural and legitimate son. What if the witness says, "I know for certain"? Some say that he speaks falsely, because such knowledge is impossible. You should say, however, that his statement is saved, so that it is understood that he is certain insofar as human nature permits, that is, by presumption, as the law presumes. See below, *de edicto*, edict, l. *Si venditor*. In support of this is what I said in l. *Iustitia*, above, *de iustitia et iure*, according to Jacobus de Radulphis.

But suppose that the mother or father says that the child born in wedlock is not their son. Should they be believed? Jacobus de Radoneo says no, because this is a presumption of law, which must be adhered to unless the contrary is otherwise proven.

† Hence, a certain king, born in wedlock, was foolish, who believed his mother when she told him, at the time the old woman died, that he was not the son of the king, and he renounced the kingdom. For he ought not to have believed her, but rather ought to believe the law, and according to the law inform his conscience. As in the Authentica de iuribus, §. oportet.

And I say the same to the contrary: if some unknown woman, whom you have recognized, says to you, "Such is your son," you ought not to believe her; because the law does not credit this, except in the case of one born from marriage, for just as he may be yours, so he may be another's. And thus he has no father, as above in the preceding title, the common law. Thus, therefore, one wise man of Bologna believed, for whom, as is reported, a certain person was made by the grace of God Supreme Pontiff; he sent [a message] and said in private: "You are my son, whom I begot from your mother, when at such a time I was a student in Bologna." Hence, since now I am lord, I wish to promote you to the highest honors. He who said this, it does not please God. I am the son of him whose wife my mother was, and she was a good and wise lady. Would that he had said this to a certain friend of ours, Cy. of Pistoia, in his lecture on the words "ad verbum."

† It is therefore asked concerning this person, about whom there can be probable doubt as to whether he is a son: whether the institution made of him holds in whole or in part. And it seems that it does not: because doubt is assimilated to error, as in C. de furt. l. manifestissimi, §. si autem dubius. But if the testator errs in filiation, the institution does not hold, as in C. de fideicomm. l. eam quam, and C. de haer. inst. l. si pater, with similar authorities. To the contrary it seems: because the testator did not institute him with a curse, in which case the institution would not be valid, as noted in l. pen. C. quemadmod. testa. aperian., and in l. turpia, de leg. 1. It seems a distinction should be made: either he was a false son, and the testator erred, and the institution is not valid; or the testator did not err, because he knew him not to be a son, yet loved him as a son: and then the institution is valid, as in l. nemo, §. 1, ff. de haer. inst. Or it is doubtful whether it was by error or from certain knowledge: and then it seems recourse should be had to presumptions. And that he acted from certain knowledge is indicated here by age: because according to the common course of nature, women do not conceive at this age; although sometimes the contrary occurs, as in the case of Master Alberico de’ Gentili of Perugia, whom a noble lady, Lady Becta, conceived upon completing her first year, and he was a youth so notable as if he were in Tuscany: but legal presumptions are adapted to those things which usually happen, not to those which rarely occur, which is to be noted in l. si sterilis, de act. empt. Moreover, knowledge is presumed from conversation, as in l. octavi, ff. unde cog. Briefly, I say that the institution is valid, even if the testator was in doubt about the status of the son, and if there was common doubt about this: because this is not such a doubt as to remove the will or the license of the law from the act, as in ff. de test. milit. l. qui iure militari, and ff. de acqu. haer. l. sed et si de sua. And therefore this person is not passed over, but instituted as a precaution, so that the testament may be valid in every case. And it is supported by ff. de lib. et posth. l. si pepercerit, and l. si posthumus, §. fi. It would be otherwise if error were proven, as in ff. de pact. l. tale pactum, §. fi. But to prove this is very difficult, ff. de condit. et dem. l. Lucius. For paternity can be presumed, but it cannot be demonstrated. And it is supported by ff. de man. testa. l. uxorem. Furthermore, to clarify the above, distinguish the cases. For either he was a true son, and the testator bore a substituted child, and the testament is not valid: because the father did not fulfill the office of a father. And thus intestate, the son, as if passed over, possesses everything. Or, on the contrary, the father believed him to be a son, when he was a substituted child: and then his institution is not valid. But the institution of the coheir is valid, and everything accrues to the coheir: because the share of the substituted child is as if not written. Or he did not think him to be a son, nor was he: and then the institution is valid both of him and of the coheir. Or, on the contrary, he thought him to be a son, and he was a son. And the same. Or it is doubtful what the testator meant. And it is presumed that he believed him to be a son, unless it is proven that he knew such a thing, which by the nature of things does not permit a woman to bear children: because then it is presumed that he believed what nature dictates. For nature is common, and is the natural form of the intellect itself. And therefore it is presumed in esse, unless it appears from other presumptions that he believed him to be a son, and he was not a son? Because then credulity and opinion agree. Or it is established that he always doubted. And therefore he chose the middle way, that the testament be valid in every case. And then the testament is valid. And if this is our case in fact, I advise in law that the testament is valid. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether possession held for a long time after the contract by the seller gives rise to a presumption that the instrument of sale was simulated.
2. When a contract is presumed to be simulated, and on what grounds.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Whether possession for a long time after the contract, held by the seller, gives rise to a presumption that the contract of sale was simulated. Some, such as Guido de Suzza, have stated simply that it does: for it is not presumed that something was sold which is effectively found in the patrimony [of the seller], ff. qui in rem actionem non habent, de pign. vel hyp. sol. l. sicut; §. supervacuam, C. de distractione pign. l. et qui sub imagine; and arg. ff. de probat. l. procul; and ff. de contrah. empt. l. cum mancipata; §. nemo potest. Moreover, he is presumed to be the owner who, for so long a time, acted in all respects as owner, ff. de solutionibus, tutor. de aqua haer. l. qui in aliena; §. 1, ff. si servus ven. l. si quis diuturno; and, with the buyer knowing and acquiescing, he called himself owner. arg. C. de servis et aqua, l. 2; de agris et censibus, l. litibus, lib. 11. Furthermore, if such goods were always in the seller’s estate, and with the buyer knowing and acquiescing, the seller paid the tax, it is presumed, by reason of silence and acquiescence intervening, that the title was simulated. To this effect is what is read and noted, ff. de rei vend. l. si solennibus; to this effect, C. de naturalibus liberis, l. si quis seu §. et quod de substitutione nuda, as in ff. de aqua haer. l. is qui bonis; and what is noted, C. de repudianda haereditate, l. 3, in which laws simulation is presumed from possession. For it is not probable that the buyer would have suffered his loss for so long a time, if the contract had been genuine. arg. ff. de probat. l. cum de indebito. Others have said: for where the seller is found to possess and hold by title of precarium, simulation is not presumed, nor does time prejudice [the buyer]. The first point is proved in the aforementioned §. supervacuam, 2. responso, where a new title excludes the presumption of simulation, if the title of precarium is a new title which the seller never previously had. Therefore, etc. To this effect, C. de praescriptione triginta annorum, l. male agitur; nor can he say that he possessed for himself, who is convicted by a testament that he possessed by name of precarium. arg. C. de non numerata pecunia, l. generaliter. For his affirming or denying his own right changes nothing of the truth of the matter, nor do words operate anything which are spoken by one party after the contract. As in C. de transactionibus, l. si maior; quod metus causa, l. metum. Moreover, he cannot change the cause of his detention for himself. ff. de usucapione, l. non solum; §. quod vulgo; C. de acquisitione possessionis, l. cum nemo. Hence, he cannot transfer himself from precarium to another right of holding; and if he does so, he has bad faith, which does not become valid by time. As in C. de falsis, l. ex initio.

† On this point, it seems to be said that either this contract was celebrated between prohibited persons: and then simulation is presumed. As in D. de probationibus, l. qui testamentum. Or between permitted persons: and then either between related persons, and simulation is presumed. As in C. de donationibus, l. data iam pridem; and D. de bonis liberis, l. nisi, §. facilior. Or between strangers: and then either simulation is alleged by a third party, in whose interest it lies: for example, by the fiscus: because the vendor committed a wrongful act; or by creditors. As in C. de non numerata pecunia, l. si cui. Then simulation is presumed. As in §. superuacuam, and l. qui sub imagine. And note in l. post contractum, de donationibus, by Jacobus. Or simulation is alleged by the vendor himself, for his own benefit; then no law occurs to me stating that simulation is presumed; rather, in case of doubt, it seems that one should adhere to the instrument. C. de probationibus, l. cum precibus. Two are in a manner instruments, because there is one having two heads, namely, of sale and of precarium. And therefore, rightly, two instruments seem to exclude every presumption of simulation, just as if the vendor had leased. D. de contrahenda emptio, l. fundi partem. Just as two presumptions and two reasons overcome one. As in Auth. de consanguineis et affinibus, fratri, and what is noted there. Therefore, more favor is shown to the opposing third party than to the contracting party himself. And the reason is: because one’s own act prejudices someone more than another’s act. D. de adoptionibus, l. post mortem; D. de rei venditione, l. cum amatre; C. de revocanda donatione, l. cum profitearis. Or distinguish: either the price was paid, or confessed. If it was truly paid, then simulation is not presumed; because a confession is more easily overcome than a natural payment. As in C. de manumissionibus, l. ab Anastasio, and l. per diversas. And it supports what is noted in C. qui potiores in pignore habeantur, l. assiduis, l. in quo parva; and C. de non numerata pecunia, l. si extant; and in Auth. de aequalitate donationum, §. il. lud.; D. de acceptilatione, l. si acceptilatio; C. de collationibus, l. si donatione. Or it can be said that either the vendor’s possession is favored solely by the passage of time: then simulation is not presumed. As in l. male agitur. Or the possession is joined with other indications signifying simulation: for example, because the vendor, with the buyer suffering and knowing, always called himself owner: then prejudice is done to the buyer. Argument from C. ad Velleianam, l. si sentiens; and C. de petitione hereditatis, l. si filius. Because from several concurrent indications, the effect is increased: as in D. de edicto edilitis, l. quaero, §. si. Or the possession of the sale is joined with an express confession of the buyer. Then there is no doubt that the contract must be considered simulated. And the confession is valid even in the absence of the possessor; because it tends to free the possessor. And every confession that tends to an exception is valid in the absence of the party. As in Auth. de testamento, §. et licet. And note D. de interdictis actoribus, l. de aetate, and l. non solum, §. si liberationis; D. de liberatione legata; and in l. generaliter, de non numerata pecunia, by the gloss of Petrus and Cynus. C. de iure et facto ignaro, l. cum falsa. Therefore, in our case, from the aforementioned concurrent factors, the contract must be judged simulated. For simulation is proved by indications and confession. Extra, de pignoribus, c. illo vos; de emptione et venditione, c. ad nostram. And it supports what is noted in Speculum, de donationibus, §. 1, ver. item pone aliquis. And by Cynus, and C. de bonis proscribendorum, l. si quis post haec, cum si. Added to the aforementioned is that simulation is of fact and of mind. And those things which are of the mind are proved by a confession made in absence. As in D. de negotiis gestis, l. Pomponius scribit, and l. Nesennius, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Five things are required for a just war, and what they are.
2. 7. and 8.
3. It is not permitted for clerics to wage war for a twofold reason; there is a twofold reason why it is not permitted for clerics to wage war.
4. The Pope can dispense with a murderer in a homicide perpetrated: but not in one being perpetrated.
5. The Pope cannot grant to clerics that they may kill with their own hand, although he may well grant that in a just war they give counsel both of men and of money.
6. The Pope can give a religious person license to use arms: not to shed blood, but for the state of the faith, and of the church, and for the safety of the fatherland.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Five things are required for a just war, namely: the person, the matter, the cause, the intention, and the authority. As to the person: it must be secular; for it is lawful to shed blood; but not ecclesiastical, to whom it is prohibited, 23 q. 8. Clerics, unless in unavoidable necessity, as in c. 1, de homic. in cle.

† Why, however, is it not permitted for clerics to wage war? According to Blessed Thomas, there are two reasons. The first is that the art of war and the tumult of battle draw clerics away from the praise of God, prayer, and divine offices. The second reason is on account of the shedding of blood: for, following the example of Christ, they say that it is better to suffer one’s own blood to be shed than to shed another’s; and for this reason it is established that those who shed blood become irregular, as is written concerning David: “You shall not build me a house, because you are a man of blood.” And again: “Deliver me from blood, O God, O God of my salvation: and my tongue shall exult in your justice.” For a murderer cannot preach justice with an open face, according to that Psalm: “Who are you that tells of my justices, and takes up my covenant by your mouth?” And it should be noted that although the Pope

† he may dispense with a murderer in a homicide already perpetrated, as in c. At si clerici, Extr. de iudicibus. However, it is otherwise in the case of a homicide being perpetrated: because he cannot grant license to commit a crime, nor can he pardon what has not yet occurred. As in D. de fideiussoribus, l. Si a reo, § Si reo; D. de pactis, l. Si unus, § Illud nulla. And it is rightly true that the Pope can declare a just war. D. 1, c. Ius gentium; D. 8, c. Quo iure, 23 q. 7; c. Si de rebus; and c. Quid culpatur, 23 q. 1.

† nevertheless, he cannot grant to clerics that they may kill a man with their own hand: but for the execution of justice they may commit the power of the sword to laymen. Likewise, he may permit clerics that in a just war they give counsel, and aid both of men and of money: for if they can declare a just war, therefore they can grant other things which are of right and the nature of wars, and without which wars cannot be waged. Nevertheless, they cannot alleviate crimes by indulgences, lest the authority of outrages increase. As in C. de priu. schola. l. hac. l. libr. 12. From these it appears. 1. part of the justice of war, which is the person. The second part is the thing. i.

† so that it may be done for the recovery of things and for the defense of the fatherland. 22. q. 3. c. 1. and q. 3. c. fortitudo. and qu. 8. c. si nulla. and note, through Innocentius, extra de appellationibus, c. dilectis. de restitutione spoliatorum, c. olim, de voto. c. quod super. Those who wage such wars take their foundation from the law of nations. ff. de iustitia et iure, l. ex hoc iure.

† The third requirement for a just war is cause, i.e., that one fights out of necessity, so that peace may be acquired through the fight. 23 q. 1 c. Noli. Hence Aristotle says: Make war your last resort. He also says that the end of war is peace. He also says that shedding human blood is fitting only for God or His minister.

Fourth, what is required is the intention: so that it is not done out of hatred or insatiable greed, but out of charity, justice, and obedience, and so that one may live without disturbance in security. As stated in the cited chapter, "What is disturbed."

The fifth requirement is authority, because war cannot be declared without the authority of the prince, as stated in the Digest, *De captivis*, law *Hostes*. These five are the conditions for a just war; if any of them is lacking, the war is not just. Nevertheless, in this age it is necessary that there be wars, and herds of wars, and infinite sufferings; for as Augustine says in *The City of God*: "As long as vices reign, there is no perfect peace."

† From these it is concluded that the Lord Pope can grant license to a reputable religious to use arms: not, however, in such a way that he sheds blood, but for the state of the faith and the Church, and for the safety of the fatherland. I, Baldus.

casus: The case is as follows. Sempronius of Milan had and has jurisdiction to sell iron and steel, and to have it sold in bulk, both in the city of Pavia and in Milan, and no one else besides him. He, however, leased this right and this faculty of selling iron in the city and county of Pavia for two years to a certain Titius for a certain price, with the added pact that the said Titius was bound and ought to purchase from the said Sempronius in the city of Milan any iron and steel to be sold in the city of Pavia, and that the said Sempronius was bound to sell the said iron to the said Titius at a certain lower price than he would sell to others. It happens that during the said two years, the said Titius, according to the form of the lease and agreement, purchased and took up from the said Sempronius all the iron and steel necessary for the smithies of Pavia, and furthermore purchased certain other quantities at the price agreed between them, which he distributed and alienated in Milan to various craftsmen, from whom he received on credit iron variously fabricated. Likewise did a certain Gaius, an apothecary of Pavia, not named in the said condition. The said Sempronius, however, claims to have suffered damage and interest for the alienation of the said iron alienated in Milan, because he claims that if the said Titius and Gaius had not purchased and alienated the said iron in Milan, those craftsmen to whom they alienated it would have been obliged to purchase from the said Sempronius at a higher price, and consequently he would have derived profit therefrom. Now the question is asked: what is the law regarding proven interest? I, Baldus.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† According to the matters alleged, the said lessee is not liable for any interest: because there are three modes of being bound, or owing, namely, by commission, by promise, and by legal provision. Now, he is not bound here by commission: because he committed no fault, since it is lawful for everyone to conduct business freely in any manner, unless the goods were illicit: as in C. de commercio et mercatura, l. mercatores; and ff. de operis liberti, l. libertus negotiatoris; or if something were committed in fraud of the customs duties: as in ff. de publicanis, l. commissa; C. de nauigatio fenore, l. cum proponas; ff. locato, l. penes, §. nauem. Furthermore, action cannot be brought here by promise: because these words do not sound, nor does the sense of the words tend, to this effect. For outside the sense and the words, no obligation is contracted, except in tacit contracts: as is read and noted in C. de pactis, l. post venditionem; ff. communi dividundo, l. is qui, §. si libero; or from the nature of tacit repetition: as in ff. de pactis, l. item quia vel subauditi intellectus; as in ff. de verbis oblig., l. triticum and l. quicquid astringendae; and ff. si certum petatur, l. cum quid. Since, therefore, there are no words of this kind of obligation here, nor is it gathered from tacit understanding, nor should one proceed by circuitous means where interest is claimed: as in C. de sententiis quae pro eo quod interest, l. 1, §. 1, rightly nothing is claimed in law: because nothing is owed. Furthermore, I cannot here act by legal provision, because we are ashamed to speak without law, statute, or custom. And he who alleges the law must prove the law: whether he grounds himself on an affirmative or a negative not having a preceding disposition of law: as in ff. de probationibus, l. ab ea parte; and C. de collationibus, l. illam. From the foregoing, therefore, it appears that this interest has no foundation, nor root of reason. And therefore the defendant ought to be absolved: as in ff. de pactis, l. epistola, §. fin. It supports the foregoing: because although everyone may do in his own thing what profits him, even if it harms another: as in ff. de aqua pluviae arcendae, l. 2, §. Item varus.

† Concerning the tavern of the Fertarriae, we have it in the Digest, *de legatis* 2, *Lucius*, § *quisquis*, through which it is proven that the operation of this tavern is lawful, useful, and honorable. If the testator bequeaths a slave for the use of this tavern only, it seems that the legacy is to the extent required for such use.

† Moreover, know that this right, which is applicable, may be called the militia of Ferrara. For certain militias are venal and mercenary. Moreover, they may be alienated by any title and under any condition or mode, as in C. de pign. l. si; and ff. de leg. 3, l. his verbis, §. alumno; C. de inoff. test. l. omni modo, §. si; and in l. 1, §. nec castrense, ff. de col. bo., ver. sed an id, quod. Hence, the said S. could lawfully sell, and the buyer could lawfully purchase. Moreover, it must be known that every pact which modifies a contract informs that contract:

† and that the limiting words appended in the agreement must be observed. As in D. de serv. expon. l. si cui pacto; and C. de pact. inter emp. et ven. l. si; and D. de verb. oblig. l. si ita quis, § ea lege.

† It is also to be known that the word "for," or its equivalent, is either appended to a final cause, or to a motivating cause, or to a doubtful one. In the first case, it must exist and be fulfilled. In the second case, it is not necessary that it exist, because it is not properly a cause, but rather a certain motive for contracting or disposing. See D. de donationibus, l. 2, § si. In the third case, when it is doubtful, then either the words are appended to the cause of the recipient, and it is a motivating cause, as in D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Titio centum, in principio; C. de iure dotium, l. si mulier dotem. Or it is the cause of the transferor, and then this word "for" denotes a final cause, as noted in C. de episcopis et clericis, l. generaliter, according to Cynus and others. Or it is appended in favor of a third party, for whom one cannot stipulate or make an agreement; and then similarly, from a motivating cause, since no obligation arises from a cause, nor even an exception, and thus no right arises, nor any necessity of fulfillment. See D. de donationibus, l. donationes in concubinam, § species. Regarding this word "for," it is noted in D. de peculio legato, l. dominus Sticho.

† Moreover, when there are two contracts, and one comes into execution of the other, it is not regarded as more than one contract: because the second contract in itself is like a certain pact, which is part of the contract: and thus when two contracts are combined on account of one, there is only one in each case. D. de evict. l. qui libertatis. §. seruus. But rather it seems that it is a certain novation of money into a specific thing. D. de iurisd. l. ita constante. because they proceed from different causes and diversities. as D. de pact. l. ab emptione. and D. de pact. l. si vnus. ver. sed proficiet. and D. de contrah. empt. l. pacta conuenta. D. loc. l. cum in plures. §. lege dicta. And although the second comes into execution of the first, it comes with altered terms, and with one substantial element changed into another. Therefore it is not the same contract. Hence if a statute says that no gabelle is to be paid on a contract of sale, and another field is given in satisfaction for the agreed price, then under the general heading of the gabelle to be paid it will be paid as if made by exchange, with reference from one specific thing to another. as C. de sent. l. libera quidem Thodora. But against this it is argued. D. de don. inter vir. et ux. l. si donare. §. si sponsus. Moreover, this supports our question. D. de solut. l. qui. 10. §. si. and D. de leg. 3. l. pater. §. quindecim. Moreover, when there are two contracts, such that one falls into the other, so that it is its execution, the principal contract is considered, not the secondary one. Hence Master Dino says that if a testator commands the heir to sell to me a hereditary thing, dominion is transferred to me by reason of the legacy, not by reason of the sale. D. de leg. 3. l. vxorem. §. agri plagam. Moreover, Jacobus de Belvis disputed this question.

† The statute provides that a tax (gabella) is to be paid on the contract of sale. The testator in his will ordered the thing to be sold to me, and it was certainly sold: because I have the thing principally by reason of a legacy, I shall not pay the tax. D. de actionibus emptoris et venditoris, l. si haeres. Moreover, a statute that speaks of sale, by making mention of the price, ought to be understood properly and strictly, and does not comprehend exchange, unless the thing is given for a thing in satisfaction, having been estimated. As in l. si, C. praediis curialium, lib. 10; and arg. D. de pignoribus, l. in quorum; and l. 1, D. de rerum permutatione; and C. de iure dotis, l. quotiens; C. de sententiis, l. libera quidem Theodora, with its subject matter. Although sometimes the term "sale" is extended to every kind of alienation. As noted in l. 2, D. de usucapione pro emptore; and D. de statu liberorum, l. statu liberi a caeteris, §. final. And if one of two persons liable for the tax evades it, the other is not relieved. As in D. de legatis 1, l. si ab omnibus, in principio. I, Baldus.

In the Name of Christ, Amen. Having examined the statutes of the common guild set forth above, and having fully considered and discussed the doubts arising therefrom, I proceed to the response. And to the first question asked, it must be premised for clarity, etc. See in Part 1, Consilium 148, beginning "In the case proposed" and so forth.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given the state of affairs, that a sentence ought to be rendered according to the advice of a wise person who is required to advise within 20 days, whether, if the advisor gave his advice afterwards, and the judge judged, the sentence is said to be null.
2. Whether the Ordinary can cognize the nullity of his own sentence.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The statute provides that a sentence must be rendered according to the opinion of a wise man who ought to have given his advice within twenty days. Now, the consultant appointed gave his opinion after the term had expired, and the magistrate judged in accordance with that opinion. It is now said that the sentence is null. The question is whether the said magistrate can cognize the nullity of his own sentence. I answer: there is no doubt that the ordinary judge can regularly cognize the nullity of his own sentence, both incidentally and principally, as stated in C. quomodo et quando iudex, l. si vt proponis, unless the nullity had been devolved to a superior by appeal, as stated in C. de accu., l. absentem, and ff. de appe., l. si expressim.

And therefore, if you ask whether he can take cognizance, it must be said that yes. But if you ask what ought to be pronounced, namely whether the sentence is valid or null, it must be said that, once the term for giving the opinion has lapsed, the opinion could not be rendered. As is stated in D. 6.1.17 (bonorum); D. 18.1.1 (qui fundum); D. 26.16.1 (scire oportet), § consequens. And therefore, since according to the form of the statute the sentence must be founded upon the opinion, it follows necessarily that if the opinion is null, then also the sentence which follows from it is null. As is stated in D. 28.5.1 (nam et si sub conditione), § rumpendo; and C. 1.14.1 (non dubium). But if you were to posit that the consultant could have consulted, then he could not take cognizance of the nullity, unless perhaps on account of holidays: or because it was not pronounced in the place of the elders. As is stated in D. 2.12.1 (in principio); together with its subject matter. For this does not concern whether the opinion is just or unjust. But he cannot pronounce against the opinion, because his power is delegated according to the form of the statute. As is stated in D. 49.16.1 (si plures); and X. 1.6.1 (cum in veteri); as in D. 26.7.1 (Titium et Mevium). I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether witnesses from a university are incompetent witnesses in a case involving the university? And see below, opinion 445, number 9.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† This is an ancient and common question: whether, in a case involving a universitas (corporation), members of that universitas may serve as witnesses. This is posited by Cynus in C. de testibus, l. parentes, and he determines that if the outcome of the controversy concerns the individual utility of each member, they are not admitted to give testimony, nor are they competent witnesses, according to Jacobus de Ravanis, Petrus, and many ancient and modern authorities. However, in l. in tantum, §. universitatis, ff. de rerum divisione, in his ordinary lecture, he states: Either the case is that of a universitas or college with regard to name, honor, and advantage; and then those belonging to the universitas may be witnesses. Nor does it avail to object that for this reason they will contribute less [to the common fund]; because this advantage does not follow anyone principally, but only in consequence. Or the case is that of a universitas with regard to name, but with regard to advantage it is that of the individuals; and then they cannot testify, because the case is considered private. But Johannes Andreae, in his additions to the Speculum, in the title De testibus, §. opponitur, under the words "sed nunquid," says that when individuals from the universitas derive advantage from their own testimony, they cannot be witnesses. I therefore answer the question asked, which inquires: whether two witnesses produced by the community of a certain castle, to prove payment made to a certain creditor of said universitas for a certain debt, are competent. And I say that they are not competent. To demonstrate this, I consider that here there are two obligations. One is that of the universitas towards the creditor, for example, arising from a loan. The other is that of the individuals towards the universitas, because the individuals are bound to the universitas for the collection [of taxes or contributions], as in ff. de munere et onere, l. rescripto, §. si. Now it is certain that if they could prove the payment, their testimony would immediately release them from the obligation by which they are bound to the universitas; because, once the universitas is released, they would necessarily be released as well. Therefore, the controversy immediately concerns them. Moreover, it matters greatly whether the advantage pertains to someone by necessity or by casual contingency. In the first case, whether mediate or immediate, one is not a competent witness; as is clear in the case of a guarantor and a seller who is liable for eviction. And wherever the exception of res judicata is available to a witness, there he would not be a competent witness, as noted in ff. finium regundorum, l. eos, and C. ad Tertullianum, l. omnibus. In the second case, testimony is admitted, as in C. de testibus, l. dictantibus. Since therefore in our case it is a matter of necessary advantage to the witnesses, ancient or modern doctors do not doubt that a witness who wishes to free himself from obligations and prejudices by his own testimony is not competent. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. An instrument executed with two notaries and three witnesses, counting the notary, is invalid in light of the statutes, etc.
2. Whether a notary should be counted among the number of witnesses.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen. A statute of a certain town provides that in any instrument at least three witnesses be employed. Another statute of a certain place provides that if a contract or alienation is made for more than 100 pounds, whereby an instrument is requested: two notaries be present at the contract or alienation, counting the notary who delivered the instrument. Otherwise, no faith shall be given to the instrument. Suppose, therefore, that two notaries and three witnesses were employed: counting the notary who subscribed, yet he did not state from whence they were natives.

† It is asked whether the instrument is valid. I answer that it is not valid, because two witnesses are lacking. As stated in C. de testamento, l. si unus, and C. de fideicommissis, l. si veritas. And it is expressly provided that two notaries together do not suffice. In Auth. de haereditatibus et falsis, § si vero absunt. But although the testament is not valid, nevertheless a contract may well be proved, and a transaction concluded by oral testimony of three witnesses, among whom there was one who knew the contracting parties. For it must be considered that proof is made either by oral testimony, or by instrument alone, or simultaneously by oral testimony and instrument.

First, in the first and third cases, the notary is counted among the number of witnesses, as stated in C. qui testamento facere possunt, l. hac consultissima, §. si. In the second principal case, however, the notary is not counted among the number of witnesses; for it would follow that the notary and one witness would suffice, which is false, although some contradict this, and wrongly. On this point, the authorities note ff. de testamento, l. Domitius, and C. de fideicommissis, l. quaestionem. And this is the truth. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How pertinences, districts, and the boundaries of jurisdictions are to be proved.
2. Jurisdiction consists of four elements.
3. The judge may adhere to whichever side he prefers when both parties have provided proof.
4. That dispute concerning the interdict *uti possidetis, ita possideatis* has no place in an action for the partition of boundaries.
5. Instruments regarding ancient facts prevail over witnesses.
6. What is included under the term "pertinences."
7. Whether salt tolls, pedages, and other similar rights are subject to prescription.
8. How possession of jurisdiction may be proved by witnesses.
9. Witnesses are admitted on behalf of a corporation in a case involving the corporation; see also Consilium 453.
10. Whether a vassal may testify in favor of his lord.
11. He who proves an older possession prevails when the matter is doubtful due to the entanglement of proofs and the mixture of acts on both sides; otherwise, he who holds the title prevails.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† How pertinences and districts are proved: for the elucidation of the entire matter. I premise that sometimes the boundaries of territories are evidently and notoriously distinct. Sometimes by royal roads, sometimes by rivers; sometimes by mountains or valleys; sometimes by stones or very apparent signs; and in these ways territories are commonly distinguished, as noted by Johannes Andreae, according to Gozzadinus, in the Extravagantes, *De probat.*, c. *Cum causam*. Sometimes also the limits of jurisdictions are proved by express or tacit assertions, as in the Code, *De contrahenda et committenda stipulatione*, l. *Optimam*; and in the Code, *De iure deliberandi*, l. *Cum aliquis*. Sometimes by the opinion of the common people and the judgment of the inhabitants of the surrounding area, who in this matter are two witnesses more suitable than others, as in l. 1, § 1, Digest, *De fluminibus*; and the simpler and more rustic they are, the more credible they are, because they do not testify except concerning the possession of fact, as if always standing with their own eyes over those places, as noted in the Digest, *De verborum obligatione*, l. *Stipulatio ista*, § *Hi quoque*. They are proved by the sentences of judges and arbitrators, as in the Digest, *De arbitris*, l. *Inter castellanum*; and in the Institutes, *De officio iudicis*, § *Si*. Sometimes by the collection of revenues, as in the Code, *Finium regundorum*, l. *Si quis super*. Suppose, therefore, that witnesses say that they saw one party possessing from such a river towards the source of such a castle, or from such a large and conspicuous stone, and immovable: whether it is presumed that such river or conspicuous stone is the boundary or not. And it must be said that it is presumed, because it is customary to do so. For custom indicates a great part of what something is, as in the Digest, *De dilapidato edicto*, l. *Quod si nolit*, § *Quia assidua*; and in the Digest, *De funere instruento*, l. *Quod si nolit*, § *Asinam*; and in the Digest, *De lege tertia*, l. *Si chorus*, § 1. Likewise, sometimes boundaries are proved by the appointment of custodians, as in the Digest, *De funere instruento*, l. *Si ita*, § *Villae custos*. Likewise by the exercise of jurisdiction through the exaction of tolls and similar things. For by these means districts are proved both on land and at sea; indeed, in heaven and in the air, because up to heaven the possession of the owner ought to be free, as in c. *Ubi periculum*, *De electione*, lib. 6; and in this way the gallows signifies dominion over the air, because the hanged person hangs in the air; and this is a great signification of mere empire,

† which consists of four elements, just as there are four elements: in air, as I said; in fire, as when someone is burned for sorcery; in water, as when someone is placed in the rack and thrown into a river, as in l. 1 C. de patria potestate qui filium occidit; in earth, as when someone is laid on the ground and beheaded, as in l. 3 C. de episcopis et clericis audiendis cum suis. Because, returning to the point, I say that the party who has the better proof should prevail in the case, because justice of proof makes the better prover stronger, as in C. de edicto divi Adriani l. 1, and there this doctrine is masterfully stated. Sometimes both parties base their claim, but one better than the other. But if they do not base their claim equally, the judge may, from his own discretion, looking only to God, and not adhering through any carnality, friendship, or other passion, choose which party he wishes to prevail, as singularly noted in ff. de re iudicata l. duo iudices dati.

† but if he does not wish to adhere, because his mind is not more inclined to one than to the other, then there is room for that discussion concerning two things equally proven in the context of *uti possidetis*, as discussed in note C. *uti possidetis*, l. 1.

But observe that this dispute has no place in the action for the settlement of boundaries, because it is a possessory action. As stated in the Code, On Interdicts, in the law *Incerti*, the judge cannot therefore say, “As you have demanded, so demand,” because such a sentence contains nothing. As stated in law 3 of the Code, On Sentences and Interlocutory Matters, the judge must therefore define the matter against the will of the parties. But what is this? He may avail himself of the assistance of surveyors and the counsel of prudent laymen, and especially of elders, who are more credible witnesses in this matter, where the memory of things is at issue. As stated in the Digest, On Rainwater, in law 1 at the end, and in the Digest, On Proof, in the law *Si arbiter*.

† Moreover, concerning these ancient facts, written instruments are preferable to witnesses, provided that the instruments were executed with the consent of the parties who were then in place, into whose positions the newcomers have succeeded, like shoots from the root. See D. 10.1 (finium regundorum), l. eos; and D. 22.6 (de probat.), l. Celsus, and the glosses thereon. Therefore, having thus premised these theoretical points, the rules of law must be adapted to the practice of our question, and the statements of the witnesses must be carefully examined. It must also be premised that pertinences consist not only in fact, i.e., in possession, but also in right and in jurisdiction. See D. 50.16 (de verborum significatione), l. verbum pertinere; and the cited canon Cum ad sedem, de restitutione spoliatorum, where Innocentius states.

† However, by the term "pertinences" are understood those things which are assigned by statute, custom, or law so as to be attached. And he adds these words: "But nothing is assigned to a castle by law as being its pertinence; nevertheless, it is customary for men and their statutes to assign a certain territory to a castle, which it ought to have in its jurisdiction and to answer for to others." But in the Speculum, in the title *De restitutione spoliatorum*, chapter *Quia vero*, at the words *quid de colligentibus pedagia*, it is said,

† That certain things are not accustomed to be obtained except by privilege of the Prince, such as tolls, or road tolls, or saltworks. And where there is no proof of privilege, possession is required, and that of such long duration that there is no memory of the contrary. As in Extra, De verborum significatione, chapter Super quibusdam. Nevertheless, I do not believe the same applies to the prescription of contentious jurisdiction: because that belongs to municipalities by common law, as regards simple jurisdiction and certain minor fines. As in the Authenticum, De defensione civium, § Et iudicare. Mere and mixed empire can be prescribed by the longest time. As in the Code, De diversis officiis, law Viros, book 12. Nevertheless, tolls, etc., which are reserved to the Prince, cannot be so prescribed, as in chapter 1, Quae sint regalia, title 10. Furthermore, it must be premised that older possession, which was peaceful in ancient times, even if it has since begun to be disturbed, is stronger than the new disturbance by adversaries: because the older it is, the more just it is; and the force of disturbance should not aid those who disturb. As in Extra, De probationibus, chapter Licet causam.

Having therefore premised the above, I consider that the witnesses on both sides are very varied and discordant regarding possession and quasi-territory; indeed, some attempt to prove jurisdiction and quasi-possession of jurisdiction. I begin with the nobles and the community of Gabiano, because they are the plaintiffs and prove their territory or dependencies beyond the Po River up to the place called Cauezagna. Furthermore, some witnesses state that if beasts were sent into said territories, the lords and men of Gabiano would send men to seize them, and would cause those to whom the beasts belonged to restore the damage and pay the penalty. So say Francis, Gozerius, and Coradus. Moreover, William of Gubio says that said nobles held and possessed, as quasi-estates, goods, possessions, and things in the valley of Valisii inclusive, extending towards Gabiano up to the bank of the Po, freely as their own territory, and within the power, authority, and district of Gabiano. See also John the Judge on chapter 4; Fazinus on chapter 14, who says that the men of Fontanetto by force and violence sent their beasts to destroy the meadows, etc.; William of Lorella on chapters 1 and 4; G. of Raviero on chapter 4, although he says he does not know what quasi-possession of right is. On chapter 1, who, when asked what territory is, answered that it consists of meadows, possessions, and woods. See also Angelinus of Monte; G. of Ranis. However, it must be noted that some witnesses testify fully, others not. Furthermore, it must be noted on behalf of these nobles an ancient public instrument, which records that there was already a lawsuit concerning said boundaries, and it was declared: to which declaration one must adhere. See Digestum, De arbitris, l. inter Castellianum. Now let us examine the witnesses, namely for the community of Fontanetto. And certainly their witnesses testify in effect the exact opposite. There are seven witnesses, or thereabouts, who testify based on their observation that the territory of Fontanetto extends up to the Po River; and they seem to testify that it is held in solidum; and consequently that the lords and nobles of Gabiano have no right in said territory. See Extra, De causa possessionis, c. cum Ecclesia. Now the question arises, what should be said in this matter? It cannot be denied that the variety of witnesses and disturbances on both sides makes the dispute and the possession obscure. As the ordinary gloss says in Digestum, Quod metus causa, l. extat. Furthermore, it cannot be denied that there is doubt in law:

Whether the witnesses of a corporation may testify concerning the territory. Nevertheless, the common opinion is that they may, provided that no benefit or detriment accrues to them. Otherwise, if they were to receive immediate benefit, as noted in the Speculum de testibus, § Opponitur, vers. Sed nunquid in causa universitatis; and in the Digest, De rerum divisione, l. In tantum, § Universitatis, according to Cynus; and l. Parentes, Codex De testibus, according to Cynus.

† Likewise, concerning a vassal, whether he may testify for his lord, is similarly doubtful in law: nevertheless, it must finally be said that these persons are not excluded on any ground, because they are household members and subject to command. The Speculum seems to say that they are excluded, in the Speculum de teste, §. opponitur, versi. Item excipitur, quod est domesticus. But may not a community command, where it concerns the community: and yet it is not excluded according to the same Speculum. Hence, if you consider this, the Speculum seems to contradict itself. Solution. It must be said that this is a matter of discretion. For if the witness is of good life and reputation, and gives plausible testimony, and especially if his statements are supported by those of others who are not vassals, their testimony is believed as though corroborated by good life, reputation, and other external witnesses. As in ff. de testibus, l. 3, §. tu magis; and ff. de edendo, l. si quis ex argentariis, §. 2, there: "quid enim etc." Now it is necessary to gather together all the aforesaid points and come to a conclusion. And I say,

† That when the matter is entirely doubtful on account of the entanglement of proofs and possessions, and the mixture of acts on both sides, he prevails in the case who has the older possession. As stated in the Extravagant, *De probat.*, c. *Licet causam*. And if it is not established which possession is earlier, and one party has a title while the other does not, he prevails, both in the petitory and in the possessory action, who has the title. This is expressly determined by Jacobus de Arena, *Codex*, *De rei vend.*, l. *Quotiens*. And because the nobles of Gabiano demonstrate their title and cause through a compromise and award, it follows that it has the force of a transaction, and consequently the force of a res judicata and a definitive sentence. As noted in the Authenticum, *Ut diff.*, iud., § 1, insofar as their instrument contains nothing doubtful regarding the fact that they have the right. And if there is doubt whether the bodies are the same, let one go to the places and subject the matter to ocular inspection. As stated in the Digest, *Finium regundorum*, l. *Si irruptione*, § *Ad officium*. As for the rest, the said nobles and the commune prevail by virtue of older possession, proven by less suspect witnesses. As stated in the Code, *De edicto divi Adriani*, l. *Edicto*, § 1. And because it has been proven that the men of Desaneto were disturbers, they are therefore later in possession. As noted in l. 1, *Codex*, *De appellationibus*. It is therefore concluded, and necessarily follows, that these nobles of Gabiano and the commune of Gabiano uphold justice, and judgment should be rendered in their favor, and perpetual silence imposed upon the other party. And thus I, Baldus, hold.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether one who produces false witnesses is liable to the penalty of the statute against those who produce false witnesses, etc., nos. 6 and 7.
2. The person who produces a witness, and the false witness himself, may be accused in the same indictment.
3. The judge may punish the false witness and the producer ex officio.
4. In the case of forgery, one is sometimes liable on account of the fabrication; sometimes on account of the use.
5. One is presumed not only to know one’s own act, but also its circumstances.
6. In the crime of perjury, the most rigorous investigation is conducted.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Certain witnesses produced in a certain case are alleged to have given false testimony. Now, assuming without prejudice to the truth that the said witnesses did give false testimony.

It is asked whether the party producing evidence may be accused of perjury, given a certain statute of the city which provides that he is understood to produce a false witness who, when questioned by the opposing party, states that he wishes to use [the testimony], and in the case proposed the producing party used false attestations, by introducing them, producing them, and arguing upon them; although the said producing party was not questioned regarding one witness as to whether he wished to use his attestation, whereas he was questioned regarding the other. Also, whether the said producing party, or the one using [the testimony], and persisting in its use until the arbitral sentence, is liable to the penalty of the Cornelian Law, or to the penalty of the said common statute of Verona. And in excuse of the said producing party it is alleged that it does not appear that the chapter [of evidence] upon which they were produced is false; and thus, since the chapter may be true, it cannot be imputed to the producer that the witnesses spoke falsely. Argument: Codex, Ad Legem Terentiam, l. Si quis testibus. They could also have been produced to prove reputation, or some other corroborating evidence. And thus with good intention, and not with malicious intent. For in punishing perjury, malice is required. See De falsis, l. Nec exemplum. The contrary seems to be the case.

† And I premise one thing, that the one who produces a witness, and the witness himself if false, can be accused by the same libel. As in C. si reus vel accu. mor. fue. l. 1. and ff. de falsis. l. athletas.
† Furthermore, I premise that a judge may, ex officio, punish a false witness and a false producer of evidence, as stated in the Codex, Title "De testibus," law "Nullum."

† Furthermore, I premise that sometimes one is liable for falsity on account of the fabrication; sometimes on account of the use. As in C. de falsis, l. si quis falsos, where it says: he bound only the perpetrators to the penalty.

† Furthermore, I premise that one is presumed to know not only his own act, but also the circumstances thereof, as in the Digest, *De acquisitione hereditatis*, law *Panthonius*, section *rei*, and law *Cum falso*. From this it follows that he who produced a false witness to prove his own act is presumed to have knowledge of the truth, and to have produced the witness contrary to the truth, if the witness gives false testimony. To this effect, in the Digest, *Pro suo*, law *Si*.

From these it is concluded that the aforementioned producer, with respect to the witness upon whom he was interrogated and relied, if the truth is that the said witness gave false testimony, as the records show, must be punished by the penalty of the said statute. But if the witness or the producer could be aided by some division, then otherwise, as in Extra, De testibus, Cum tu filii. And according to Innocentius in Cap. Causam, De rescriptis.

† Moreover, it is certain that in the crime of falsehood the investigation must be most rigorous; hence, when indications have been obtained, one proceeds to torture. See Digest 48.18, *l. Maritus*; and Code 9.11, *l. 1*. There it is also established that on account of a single false witness, even if he is the only one produced and relied upon, he ought to be punished; especially since, when a single witness provides an indication, he thereby injures the opposing party. See Digest 22.6, *l. Lucius*; and Code 4.20, *l. 2*. And therefore, what legal conclusion should be drawn in the aforementioned matters, the conscience of the judge is sufficiently able to consider. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
0. Who is said to be a manifest usurer.
1. The quality which the law weighs is of the substance of proof, just as it is of the substance of the fact.
2. A fact is said to be done in camera when it is done secretly.
3. What is meant by secret.
4. How reputation is proved. And no. 10.
5. A crime is considered proved if it is represented in any of its species.
6. Whether the crime of usury suffices to be proved in general.
7. Whether a confession made to a priest or to a notary proves one to be a usurer.
8. It must be established by two witnesses that the act of confession took place.
9. What is meant by dry exchange: and what is called incantia or emantia.
10. Reputation by itself is not a species of proof.
11. A witness must understand what he is saying; otherwise he does not prove.
12. The word "many" is verified in two.
13. What "manifestly" and "publicly" import.
14. Knowledge is twofold.
15. What the word "who" imports.
16. A private writing does not make one a manifest usurer.
17. Whether a prosecutor, who orders the restitution of usuries or things wrongly taken, is thereby proved to be a manifest usurer.
1. The deposition of an executor is proof requiring proof; otherwise in the deposition of a testator.
2. Whether credence should be given to a dead voice.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It must be premised for clarity, who is called a manifest usurer: so that, according to the disposition of the counsel, his testament, without caution being provided, is void by the law itself. To this it is to be known, that something is said to be manifest in two ways: in one way, so manifest, that it is so notorious by the evidence of the fact, that it does not need proof. As in the Digest, title "Who are to be compelled to give security," law "If indeed," section "Who, according to the quality of the thing"; Digest, title "On appeals," law "Citizens," and in the column; and what is not so, Digest, title "On witnesses," law 3, section "That of the same," also at the end, gloss. In another way, it would be called manifest, because, although it needs proof, it can nevertheless be proved clearly and with certainty, and by many, so that it cannot be denied. As in the Code, title "On penalties," law "When the accused"; and in the Decretals, title "On the signification of words," chapter "When formerly"; and in the Decree, question 2, cause 1, in the last chapter; and noted by the Archdeacon, in the Decretals, title "On heretics," chapter "Accused," section "Truly." From this I say, that this name "manifest" is a genus, and has in itself two species: namely, notorious, and manifest, which stands in its own name, just as we say in the Digest, title "On adoption," law 1; and thus holds Jacobus Butrigarius in the said law "Citizens and inhabitants." From these it is understood: who is called a non-manifest usurer: because a non-manifest usurer is he who cannot be convicted by clear, and perspicuous, certain, and clamorous proofs: but is difficult to investigate, and can only be convicted by conjectures. For whatever is proved by conjectures alone, is not said to be certain. As in the Digest, title "On obligations of words," law "When one," section "When someone," there where it says, "in uncertain matters there is room for conjecture." Hence it appears, that conjectures do not make something manifest, nor are laws speaking of the manifest verified from conjectures: because manifest, and evident, are synonyms. As noted in the chapter "If perhaps," in the gloss "If therefore," title "On election," book 6. Nor is it permitted that, because the truth is proved by two witnesses, or three, it is therefore said to be manifestly proved. Otherwise it would follow, that simple proof would be qualified proof by this quality, which is called manifest, which is false. As noted in chapter 1, title "On the office of a delegated judge," in the gloss, second word "For indeed," for it is necessary to prove two things, namely, to be a usurer, and to be a qualified usurer, namely, manifest: nor does it suffice to prove either one. As noted in the Digest, title "On proofs," law "If the arbiter," at the end, gloss.

† because whenever the law weighs the quality, that quality is not so much of the substance of the proof as of the substance of the fact itself. As in D. de noxa, l. in delictis, § si extraneus, and § si detracta; and D. vi bonorum raptorum, l. 2, § docere; and D. de adulteriis, l. denuncias, § quid tamen; and D. de institutionibus, l. habebat. Let us therefore hold to the foundation, namely, that it was necessary to prove the fact, namely, that he had practiced usury. Also the quality, namely, that he was manifestly, or that he himself is a manifest usurer. This is supported by what is noted by Bartolus in l. diuus, D. de regulis iuris, and in l. 2, D. de furtis. Furthermore, it must be premised for clarity, that a secret confession of the testator made before one or two of his secretaries, and not publicly, does not make him a manifest usurer; therefore, nor does it make him a confessed one. To this effect is what is noted in D. de legatis 1, l. in tacitis; D. de iure fisci, l. non intelligitur, § tacita. It would be otherwise if this confession of the testator were made in court; because what is done in court is public, both in law and in fact, since there are always several persons present, as in C. de testamentis, l. omnium, and l. sancimus.

But that which is done in a chamber and in secret cannot be said to be public, because it becomes known to very few. To this effect, *Extra*, *De ecclesia*, *De beneficiis*, cap. 1, where it appears that what is done in a chamber is done secretly and in concealment. Although the decretal *Quamquam* were understood to mean that, by the very fact that someone is proven to be a usurer, he is understood to be proven manifestly and ought to give security, it would be most absurd to say that he who is not manifest would be bound to make himself manifest through the security itself. For then the decretal would command what is unjust, namely, that he should confess a secret crime, and that he himself should find a snare for himself, to inflict upon his own vices and his own reputation. Hence, that decretal speaks only of a notorious usurer, for whom it is no damage to his reputation to confess that he is a usurer. As in *Codex*, *Ut intra certum tempus*, l. 2. For to add a demonstration to a thing already demonstrated is not to add anything. As in *Digestum*, *De dote praelegata*, l. 1, in fine. Therefore, the decretal *Quamquam* must be understood as referring to a usurer concerning whom it is established that he is either a usurer, and that he is a usurer who is publicly known and noted among the common people for usurious wickedness. As in *Digestum*, *De infamia*, l. *Improbum foenus exercentes*. And by the just judgment of the Church, their testimonies are condemned, like those of certain other infamous persons who are marked by the gravest infamy. As in *Digestum*, *De testibus*, l. *Cum lege*. And see Jacobus de Belvisi in *Authentica*, *Ut non luxurient contra naturam*, although an infamous person may regularly make a will. As in *Codex*, *De secundis nuptiis*, l. 1.

Having therefore premised these things, I come briefly to the question of Ludovicus and Mascius, which question hangs upon the records. Hence, let the terrible writings be proposed in the middle; I have examined them. As in *Codex*, *De iudiciis*, l. *Properandum*, § *Cum autem Heremoditium*. And I do not call into doubt that he who makes a contract in fraud of usury is a usurer, whether the contract be called *emantia* or exchange. As fully and elegantly noted by the most excellent doctor, Lord Ioannes Andreas, *Extra*, *De emptione et venditione*, cap. *Ad nostram*, in the *Novella*. Nor is it found more fully and better elsewhere. Likewise, I make no doubt that where there were many witnesses testifying to public voice and fame among the people, or among the greater part of the people, and with this the exercise of usury was proven, so that the truth was established, and the truth had with it the fame of the people in agreement, that by such proofs joined together a manifest proof would be induced. As noted in cap. 1 and in cap. *Quamquam*, *De usuris*, lib. 6. Otherwise, if it appears that there is a crime, or if fame appears but not the crime, or if fame appears among some but not generally: such a person would not be called a manifest usurer, but rather would be called an occult and secret usurer, even if more witnesses knew this secret, and especially singular witnesses.

† For a secret is that which someone has known, unless it has been done publicly. As noted in Arch. de elect. c. si electio, lib. 6, on the word "occultum." Likewise, it will be called a secret that which is done with certain friends present. As in ff. qui potio. in pig. habe. l. scriptura. We do not say that something is manifest simply because it is known by many. For a secret is said to be that which is known even by many. 15. q. 5. c. j. on the word "secreto." And in the Summa: That which the common people ignore, whether it is not public or openly known, is called a secret. As in ff. de deiect. et effr. l. j. §. summacum utilitate, on the word "secreta." And in ff. ad Sil. l. si quis in graui. §. aperire, on the word "secreto." And that which many know, each individually, so that what one knows, another does not know: that is called a secret, and to be known or done individually. As in extra de ele. c. ubi periculum, on the word "secretum," lib. 6. And de consanguini. et affini. c. j. in prin. And even that which is done before a judge is called a secret as long as it remains public. As in C. ad Teriu. l. nullum, on the word "iudicantis intrare secretum." As noted in the same title, if when in the gloss: thus, an "occultus latro" (hidden thief) would be one who is not notorious; and an "occultus homicida" (hidden murderer) would be one who can hardly be convicted of murder, as in a nocturnal murder, or in a place where there were no public bystanders, as noted in C. de sicar. l. siut allegas, and ff. de uen. inspi. l. j. §. tua lumina.

† Furthermore, there is no doubt as to how reputation is to be proved. For witnesses who testify concerning reputation state that they refer to the saying of the people, or of the greater part, or to the greater part of the community, and that they have heard this from them; this is what the witness must testify. As is noted in the Digest, *De testibus*, law 3, § *eiusdem quoque*, and the glossa ordinaria states that someone being reputed or manifest through reputation is not proved, nor does anything proved in this manner avail, unless it is stated that it is so among all, or the greater part, as is read and noted in the Digest, *De testibus*, law *Cum in lege*, in the glossa ordinaria, which all modern jurists approve. Hence, whenever reputation is to induce some incapacity—for example, regarding the making of a will—it is necessary that the infamy be proved in the aforementioned manner; otherwise, the proof would be of no effect. Thus says the glossa ordinaria there, which is not found elsewhere. Now, if we consider the statements of the witnesses individually and separately, also taking into account three episcopal constitutions that speak on the matter, it is certain that in the proof of truth, all witnesses who testify to something are singular in species, or in the individual.

† Nevertheless, the crime appears to be proven, which is represented in each of its species. According to Jacobus de Belvisio, Codex, *De haeresi*, l. *Arriani*, in the new lecture; although others say the contrary, as noted in the Digest, *De testibus*, l. *Ob carmen*, § *Si*; and by the Archdeacon, 2 q. 9, c. *Nihilominus*. To this it contributes that it is noted by Cynus in l. 1, Codex, *De emancipatis liberis*, where it must be carefully observed.

† And I consider whether, in the matter of the aforementioned chapter *Quamquam*, it suffices for the crime of usury to be proved in general, or not. And truly, it suffices for the crime to be proved in general. For if we were to say the contrary, it would be necessary to prove the place and time of the extorted usuries, as is noted in chapter *Ut circa*, *De electionibus*, Book 6. But this is false, nor is it approved by the practice of courts. Hence, great consideration must be given to whether the witnesses are singular in what they state, or in the reasoning by which they testify. For by the first, witnesses are called singular; by the second, they are not, as is elegantly noted by Bartolus in law 1, § 1, *Digestum*, *Quemadmodum testamentum aperitur*, and by Petrus and Cynus in law 2, *Codex*, *Quae sit longa consuetudo*. This is also approved by the episcopal constitution, which, out of hatred for usurers, holds force, even though it exceeds the modes and orders of the common law. For it does not derogate from the common law, but operates by way of supplementation, as is noted by Ioannes Andreas in the aforementioned chapter *Ad nostram*, *De emptione et venditione*, in the *Novella*.

But it must be known that the constitution speaks regarding the proving of someone as a usurer, but it does not speak regarding the proving of the quality of a manifest usurer. Nor can it be interpreted as intending to dispose of that which it does not speak of, as is noted in the *Digestum*, *De acquisitione hereditatum*, law *Si servum*, § *Non dixit*. Moreover, if it were understood thus, such a constitution would be irrational. For it is against reason that that which is hidden should be manifest. For a constitution cannot change natural truth, as is stated in the *Digestum*, *De liberis et posthumis*, law *Filio quem pater*, and in the *Codex*, *De his qui vel aetate impediuntur*, law *Si*, § *Actor*. Therefore, granted that it were proved by singular witnesses according to the form of the constitution, by this the cause of manifest usury is not proved, unless the effect regarding the clarity of public and manifest proof were increased by other attendant circumstances. Note the *Digestum*, *De excusationibus tutorum*, law 2, § *Aetas*, through the gloss of Decius and other modern commentators. For "manifest" is said in two ways: in one way, that which is manifest to some; in another way, "manifest" is said of that which becomes known to the greater part of the people, or a great multitude of men, by fame and truth, and in this sense "manifest" is taken in the Council of Lyon.

† Let us therefore examine these matters. And first, let us consider the constitution which speaks of a confession made before a priest or a notary. The constitution does not state whether witnesses were present or not, but speaks simply. However, since it would be serious and pernicious as a precedent if, in such a grave matter whereby statutes are infringed, credit were given to only one person, it must be said that the aforementioned constitution should be understood to some extent according to the common law, namely, that at least one other witness of good and proven reputation should be present for the said confession. As stated in C. de testibus, l. iusiurandi, and in Extra, ad Tertullianum, cap. In nomine Domini, and in Auth. de haereticis et falsis, § Si vero absunt, in the words "non credimus." Since, therefore, this constitution testifies concerning the act of confession,

† It must be established by at least two witnesses that the confession itself took place: as stated in the Digest, *De testamento militis*, in the laws *Divus* and *Lucius*; this is the common gloss, and it is noted in the last law of the Code, *De familia erciscunda*; and it is expressly stated in the Code, *De testamentis*, in the law *Omnium*, in its final section, and even more expressly in the same title, in the law *Sancimus*. And certainly, it is not a rule of common law that two witnesses suffice to establish manifest proof; rather, this was introduced by the bishop’s constitution. To this end, it is most aptly stated in the Decretals, *De successionibus ab intestato*, in the chapter *Cum dilectus*, where a confession by which a testament is invalidated is not proven by a single witness, and in an act favorable to religion. Moreover, the said constitution speaks by way of fiction; it does not contain the provision that the testament is invalid. Therefore, the disposition of the chapter *Quamquam*, which speaks in a true case, is not understood to apply to a case that is not truly the same case, but rather improper and strict, especially in penal matters, and in those by which new law is introduced; otherwise, it would not be introduced, as stated in the Digest, *De negotiis gestis*, in law 3, § *Haec verba*, and it is noted by Bartolus in the Digest, *De usucapione*, in the law *Si is qui pro emptore*. It is also certain that the said chapter *Generalis* of the Council of Lyon, and general councils, cannot be altered by the constitutions of bishops, since they cannot even be abrogated by rescripts of Princes, unless a clause of *non obstantibus* is specifically added, according to Archidiaconus and others. Although this is not to be disputed regarding power, but only regarding the interpretation of the constitution, which I understand as I have said above.

† It remains only to descend to the proof of reputation, whether it has been proved, and by whom, and in what manner, and what is the effect of the proof. And for clarity, I premise that that is properly called reputation which accords with the truth and is suitable to the nature of the matter, as is noted in the Digest, *De acquisitione hereditatis*, in the law *Cum quidam*, § *Quod dicitur*; otherwise it is not called reputation, but rumor, as in the Digest, *De restitutione*, in the law *Pacumeius Androtenes*. I also premise that general appellative names have been distinguished by the usage of men into immovable and movable, as in the Digest, *De legibus*, in the law *Si quis in fundi vocabulo*. Furthermore

I premise that in common usage and in truth, a dry exchange appears to exist when something is extorted beyond the principal under the name of a simulated exchange. However, when goods are bought at a higher price and sold at a lower price through the fraud of usury, this is called *incantia* or *emantia*, as noted by Johannes Andreae in the cited chapter *Ad nostram*. And to prove this, it is necessary that the witness testify regarding two simulated acts, namely purchase and resale, and regarding the higher and lower price, as stated in the extrajudicial chapter *Illo vos* on pledges, and note the opinion of Cynus in the Code, *Plus valere quod agitur*, and the law *Emptione*. From these, it appears that the witnesses who spoke of the reputation of a dry exchange erred in the name of the appellation. And the error of a witness vitiates the testimony, unless he immediately corrects his statement, as noted in the Authenticum *Ad Tertium*, § *Quia vero*. Furthermore, *emantia* is not proven by witnesses, especially sufficiently and clearly. And obscure proof by witnesses is held as null, as stated in the extrajudicial chapter *In praesentia* on proof, and especially when testifying concerning a crime or guilt, as stated in the extrajudicial chapter *Praesentium* on witnesses, Book 6, and in the Digest, *De dolo*, law *Item exigit*, and *De accusationibus*, law *Libellorum*, and especially concerning the reputation of someone already deceased. For there, the judge must supply for the absent party and inquire individually, as stated in the Digest, *De poenis*, law *Si non defendatur*. Since therefore the fact, namely *emantia*, is not proven here, neither is the reputation or quality understood to be proven, as noted in the Digest, *De probationibus*, law *Si arbitrer*.

† Reputation, by its very nature, is not a species of proof, but requires supporting evidence and the substance of truth; and it suffices only for the purpose of investigation, not for condemnation. And thus it suffices in preparatory and introductory stages of the trial, but not in the decisive stage. As is fully noted in § Tormenta, and the authorities are common. Therefore, whether we consider the true sense of the words, namely that what the witnesses say about dry exchange does not correspond, or whether we wish to speak of usury, usury is not proven, nor do the witnesses speak of the public reputation of usury.

† And unless the witness understands what he is saying, he does not prove. As noted by Bartolus in l. 1, ff. si certum petatur, and it is expressly stated in ff. de furtis, l. quidam tabularum, at the end. Moreover, Johannes Marini does not prove reputation: because after having spoken of all who knew him, he immediately varies his account. For when asked from whom he heard it said, he names two, and adds that from many others.

And this word "many" can be verified in two ways. It does not necessarily conclude to fame. D. de testibus, l. ubi numerus, with similar authorities. And it is certain, because a witness who varies undermines his own credibility. As C. ad Tertullianum, l. nullum; and D. de testibus, l. qui falsa vel varia. Lord Putius does not testify regarding fame: and it has been said that he is not believed. D. de edicto edilitio, l. quaero, §. fin.; D. de custodia rei, l. divus; and note C. de accusationibus, l. ea quidem; and D. de adulteriis, l. capite quinto; and D. ad Tertullianum, l. ab accusato, §. nunciatores; De sancta Ecclesia, §. si vero crimen, Collatio 9. And if you find anywhere that you should believe only a priest, or a single witness, this is only special due to the reason of slight prejudice. And yet, by this, nothing is ever said to be manifest, which is said to the ear of one person and becomes known to few. As noted by Iac. But. C. quomodo et quando iudex, Authent. qui semel, in the lecture of Lord Ioan. Angelini, does not prove the truth or substance of any act; because he does not testify about it, and because he speaks of a dry exchange.
