And because those adverbs "publicly" and "manifestly" refer to his own hearing, which may occur even if he heard it from one person in public, as noted in the aforementioned §. tormenta. It is true that he later heard it said by the greater part of the people who had knowledge of the matter. But this is not sufficient under the common law, because there might be only two persons who knew him, which would not constitute a reputation.

† Now, knowledge is twofold: either through acquaintance, as in the Digest, On the Edict of the Aediles, law *Ediles*, section *Hic autem*; or through visual inspection. And there is another kind of knowledge through reputation, as noted in the Digest, On Contracting Sale, law *In venditione*; as in the Digest, On Things Doubtful, law *Qui habebat*, regarding the constitution. I answer, because I say that it suffices to prove a usurer, but not a manifest one. Furthermore, I say that the constitution determines the question on this point. For it intends that an oath be administered due to the lack of proof; but where there is a lack of proof, there is no certainty. We proceed through begged support, as in the Digest, On Oaths, law *Admonendum*, in its subject matter. Hugolinus does not prove John, because he says that he heard it said by Sinibaldus Thomas, by Bartholomew, and by many others, who had dealings with the said John. And from this it follows that it was a public voice and reputation; because those words, "because they had dealings," are restrictive words.

† For the word "who," when added to a generality of persons, serves to restrict it. As in the law *Cunctos populos*, together with its subject matter. Franciscus Accursii does not testify regarding manifest knowledge or reputation; and since he claims only to know what he testifies, he states that he does not know anything beyond what he testifies. Mattensius son of Marini does not testify regarding manifest knowledge, nor does Gilius Nardi. Oddo son of Marini refers to a writing not written by this person, but by another. And it is a private writing, by which the credibility of the crime is not proven; because its credibility can be called into doubt.

† And private writing does not make one manifest. D. de legatis 1, l. in tacitis. Sinibaldus Geri does not testify concerning reputation, but testifies concerning his own interest. This is not an objection based on the constitution: because, as I have said, it does not speak concerning the proof of what is manifest. And since it departs from the law in many respects, it ought not to be extended beyond the law. D. de legatis 1, l. in tacitis; and D. de legibus, l. quod vero contra rationem. I do not pursue individually the statements of all the witnesses: because it would be too long. But a prudent reader will clearly understand that a manifest instrument has not been proven. And without doubt this man was a usurer, according to my conscience: nevertheless, as I have often said, he was not manifestly so; because usurers conceal their crimes in such a way that they can scarcely be convicted. C. de usuris; and John of Andrea says in c. ad nostram that remedies cannot easily be found against their cunning. For, as the glossa ordinaria says, this occurs due to the limitation of human intellect. D. de legibus, l. non possunt. But it remains to come to that which moves my mind more, 19 than do the statements of the witnesses concerning the proof of what is manifest.

† For it is certain that if the testator in the testament commands that usuries be restored, as I shall prove, therefore he must be said to have been a manifest usurer. That he commanded usuries to be restored, I prove thus. For he who commands his declaration of will to be declared to someone in the testament by an executor, which is afterwards declared after death: it is valid; otherwise the declaration of the executor would not be valid, unless it were understood to be the mind and declaration of the testator. As in D. 35,1, l. 1 and l. vnum ex familia in principio; and note in C. 3,28, c. dudum § verum, de sepulchro violato. Moreover, it appears openly that after the death of the testator the executors paid, in the name of extorted usuries, not to one, but to several. Hence we do not need other witnesses, since the testator is convicted by his own voice, as in X. 2,19, c. per tuas, and C. 4,37, l. generaliter. But to this I respond and say that the declaration made after death does not operate retroactively, nor does it make that which could not yet be known manifest during the life of the testator, nor could it be declared by executors while the testator was alive: for a testament cannot be opened during the life of the testator. As in D. 28,1, l. 2 § si dubitetur and § et pupillares. And therefore I say and hold that if the testator commands that ill-gotten goods be restored according to the declaration of the executors, that this testament is valid: even if the executors declare that these ill-gotten goods are usuries. And to say the contrary would be to find a way to overturn many testaments, and to say that the executors themselves were not executors, so that they could not declare: the testament would be null. And certainly it would be null if the testator were thereby a manifest usurer. And therefore I say the testament is valid, and this man is not a usurer; otherwise, if he had expressly confessed in the testament that he was a usurer, and had not committed the declaration to be made by another after death. And thus speaks and is understood the said c. quamquam with its glossa in the first response. And I prove this by evident reason. It is certain that if the testator commands that uncertain and ill-gotten goods be restored, the testament is valid. As according to some, as noted in the said c. quamquam in the novella. Furthermore, it is certain that if no executor is appointed, the Bishop is the executor. And that which is declared by him seems to be declared by the authority of the testator and the law concurring. Suppose therefore that the bishop, as executor, restored something in the name of usuries: would the testament be infringed? Certainly not; otherwise the executor could easily find a way to impugn the judgments of the testator and to overturn the whole testament: which certainly is not permitted to him either by law or by the testator. As in D. 29,1, l. si is qui destinaverat. Moreover, l. est expresse states that that which is committed by the testator to the declaration of someone to be made after death is understood to be tacit, and is not manifest until it is manifested by death. As in D. 35,1, in l. in tacitis; D. 49,14, l. non intelligitur § tacita; and what is there said by Bartolus; and l. ita fidei, D. 11,7; l. quae habendi. And yet I well confess that if in the testator’s accounts there is mention of usuries, and the lender caused such a document to be published: then he is a manifest usurer.

And the reason is: because such a writing is proof already established, but the disposition of the executor is proof to be established after the death of the testator; in which proof, according to some, an oath is required. See Digestum, De dote praelegata, l. Pomponius. But only the force of the proofs must be considered. See elegantly noted in c. 1, De haereditatibus, in Clementinis; and in c. 1, in fine, De summa Trinitate, lib. 6. I say that, considering the proofs, whether of witnesses, or of instruments, or all joined together: it is not proven that this John was in his lifetime a manifest usurer, although after his death many things have been proven against his memory, which nevertheless do not suffice for pronouncing and decreeing that he was in his lifetime a manifest usurer. The writings also assigned for the memorial, not written by his hand, nor does it appear that they are private writings of a third party by his order: it is certain that they do not prove, and especially not manifestly. See fully noted in Digestum, De edendo, l. Quaedam, §. Nummularios. Even if they had been written by the hand of a notable person: for example, a money-lender, or a merchant. See there singularly noted.

† For what is believed to be the voice of the dead, Innocentius says that it is not according to natural law: but only in cases expressly provided for in the law, as he notes in the Extravagant Decretals, *De fide instrumentorum*, chapter *Cum P. tabellio*. And therefore, having invoked the name of Christ and keeping the path of the law before my eyes, I say that according to law the defendant ought to be absolved by the prosecutor of the plaintiff. And these ought to be the positions of my lord, the Lord Vicar, in this case: notwithstanding whatever acts were performed after the death of the said John in the court of the Lord Vicar; because whether someone is a manifest usurer ought to be examined at the time of death. For a manifestation made of hidden things after the death of the testator has no effect, as is clear in the aforementioned chapter *Quamquam*, at the end, and in the Digest, *De legatis tertio*, law 2, section *Si filius*, and law 2, *De regula Catholica*, with a similar case. And by this response is answered the refutation, and other things done after death. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Saint Francis established three orders: and whether the said orders are capable of succeeding to inheritances.
2. Whether a nun transmits the inheritance of her father or brother, not yet accepted, to the monastery.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Saint Francis instituted three orders. The first is that of the Minor Friars, which is the most strict and lacks private property, even in common, according to the rule. The second was that of Saint Clare, which differs from the first: although it is also the most strict order for women, it nevertheless has property in common, and can have and possess immovables. The third is that of the continent, which has private property even in the singular, as noted in c. Cum ex eo, in the Clementines. From this it appears that the order of Saint Clare and the monastery of said order are capable of special and universal successions. Hence it is concluded that, on the part of said nun, the chapter of the monastery of Saint Clare succeeds to the father of said nun, together with his brother: making contribution with the brother of those things which were donated to the monastery by the father of the girl, on account of her entry, or on that occasion; just as a dowry and other things given for a cause are contributed, as noted by Bartolus in ff. Si quis a patre, l. 1, § Si parens. For said donation inter vivos immediately became valid, ff. Familiae erciscundae, l. Pomponius Philadelphus. And this is especially so because he seems to have been, in a manner, emancipated from his father by profession, as noted in ff. De minoribus, l. Si ex causa, § Papinianus.

† Therefore, in a certain sense: because he does not lose the right of existence of his heir. Hence, he transmits the inheritance of his father, even if not accepted, to the monastery, as in C. de episc. et cler. l. deo nobis. Regarding whether a nun transmits her unaccepted paternal inheritance to the monastery: it seems to be said that she does not. As in C. de iure delib. l. quoniam sororem, and C. ad orph. l. non pro numero. Although, while the nun is alive, the monastery may accept the inheritance against her will, by analogy with the father, as in l. non solum, in princ., C. de bonis quae lib., because the monastery seeks the image of the nun; nevertheless, it is otherwise when the nun is dead: because there is no living image of the dead. Moreover, the root and foundation are extinguished by death. Hence, no offspring remains. As noted in d. l. cum non solum, by Cyn. It is supported by de leg. 1, l. cum filium; ff. de fideicomm.; l. senatus, ff. de operis lib.; l. libertinus, § posthumus; and C. de praescri. 30 ann., l. cum notissimi, § sed cum illud. Moreover, the time and the transmissible right have elapsed, which is excluded by 50 years. As in C. de iure delib. l. cum antiquioribus. For, as regards the real right of acquisition, the time of acceptance is considered; but then the immediate person is lacking, therefore also the mediate one. And thus it must be limited. 17 q. 1, c. statutum. And although the gloss seems to say there that the monk appears to give and cede the right of acceptance, nevertheless it must be known that this right cannot be ceded. ff. de iure dot. l. mulier; C. ex ass. And this is established by the subtlety of law. It is stated. As the urgent disputation of the text there teaches. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the time limits for appeals run against widows and the poor.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It is asked whether the fatal time limits for appeals run against widows and the poor. And it seems that they do: because we are so much in debt to widows in justice, that we ought not to commit injustice against others. As stated in Extra, de foro competenti, cap. Ex tenore. Although they have the prerogatives of judges, as in Codex, Quando imperator inter pupillos et viduas, l. Unica, nevertheless they do not have the prerogative of time limits: because no law says this. Indeed, the laws state that a woman must stand by the common law, except in the case of the Velleian law. As in Codex, De iure et facti ignorantia, l. Finalis, where there is a notable text. Iacobus de Belvisis. The contrary seems to follow from the reason of poverty: because he is considered negligent who, on account of poverty, does not appeal or does not pursue the appeal. This is the notable text in Digestum, Mandati, l. Idemque, § Si ignorantes. This is expressly held by Innocentius in Extra, De appellationibus, cap. Ex ratione, and by Guillelmus de Conchis in Codex, De appellationibus, l. Eos. Solution. It is left to the discretion of the judge to determine which poverty excuses and which does not. Digestum, De excusationibus tutorum, l. Paupertas. So that in the case where penury is established, relief should be granted on account of poverty: because he is not harmed by the running of time, who was not negligent. As noted in Authentica, De appellationibus, post principium, Collatio 8. And it is supported by Digestum, De statu liberorum, l. Cum haeres, in principio; and Digestum, De hereditate instituenda, l. Servus, § Puto; and Digestum, De verborum significatione, l. Nepos Proculi. And what is noted in l. Succurritur, together with the following law, Digestum, Qui ex causa maiorum, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. When the time begins to run for executors of last wills and testaments.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. D. left his wife, Lady F., as usufructuary of all his goods during her lifetime; so that whatever remained to her from her maintenance should be given to the poor of Christ, and with this usufruct reserved, he instituted the poor of Christ as his universal heirs. He willed and commanded that, except for the aforementioned legacies, all goods should be sold and given to the poor by certain executors appointed for this purpose, to whom he assigned a term of five years for execution.

† It is asked when the aforementioned time begins to run for the said executors: whether after the death of the said wife, or immediately upon the death of the testator. I answer: either we speak with respect to the usufruct left to the wife, and the time begins when the wife dies; or with respect to the sale of the ownership, and the time begins when the testator dies. Thus the intention of the testator is satisfied, and the usufruct is not impaired. As in D. de usu et usufructu, l. 1, “uxori.” Although perhaps it was the mind of the testator that all the aforementioned things should be done only after the death of the testator. But we do not have sufficient knowledge of this intention. And this is clear from the fact that the poor are instituted as pure heirs, and from the day of death the office of the said executors for pious causes begins immediately, without the inheritance being acquired in the name of the poor. For the executors themselves are heirs for the poor. As in C. de episcopis et clericis, l. “si quis ad declinandam.” Baldus. The case is as follows. Passutius in his testament made such a legacy, namely: “I also leave to my lady Lucia, my wife, the habitation of my houses, and the use of all my massarities and household goods, all and singular fruits, revenues, and profits which are received and can be received from the goods and inheritance of the said testator, both those left in the present testament to the above-mentioned legatees, and from others; so that the said Lucia, as long as she lives honorably and observes the widow’s life, and for the greater part of the time dwells in the house of the said testator, shall enjoy these, notwithstanding any legacies made in any way to the above-mentioned legatees from the immovable goods of the said testator. And I give and grant to her license to guard, take possession of, hold, and enjoy my goods without the request of any person, and I instituted certain outsiders as universal heirs.” Now it is asked whether the instituted heirs are bound to pay the legacies and other hereditary debts and funeral expenses from their own goods, or whether they may pay from the movable or immovable goods of the said inheritance. Also, whether the movable goods, such as wine and grain, which are in the testator’s house at the time of his death, belong to the wife or to the heir. And whether the said wife ought to have the fruit and usufruct of the first year. And whether she may use the rural property and household goods of the inheritance.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The heir is bound to pay the debts, not the legatee.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The heir is bound to pay the debts, not the legatees, as stated in C. si cert. pet. l. 1. And therefore the wife is not bound for the debts, such as funeral expenses, as per ff. de usufruc. lega. l. fundi trebatiani. Nevertheless, the usufructuary is properly bound for taxes and burdens on the property, as per ff. de usufruc. lega. l. pendente, §. si quid. The wheat, which belonged to the testator, is due to the wife upon provision of security for the return of its estimated value, as per ff. de usufruc. ea. rerum. l. si vni. But the wheat gathered from the testator’s estate during the usufruct need not be restored, because the usufructuary acquires it as his own profit, as per ff. de usufruc. lega. l. defuncto. As for things and movables which are consumed by use, having provided security for the return of the estimated value, they must be appraised when delivered to her, as per l. 1. de usu et habi. and de secun. nup. l. hac edictali, §. mobilium. 1. Bald.
In the Name of Christ, Amen. Regarding the first point, it seems that one should first say that the legatee of the usufruct of all goods, and the heir. See above, opinion 87.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether all brothers are bound to pay the dowry of their brother's wife: or whether only he who received the dowry is to proceed? And what if they are partners in all goods.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† There were four brothers, heirs of their father, living in common, one of whom took a wife and received from her a dowry and other paraphernalia, whereupon a dowry instrument was drawn up according to common usage. Finally, these brothers came to a division; after the division had been made, the marriage was dissolved upon the death of the husband. Now the wife wishes to have her dowry and other paraphernalia restored to her: the portion of the deceased husband is insufficient; she wishes to have recourse against the property of the other brothers, saying that the dowry was given at a time when all were in communion, and consequently that every particular item of property was hypothecated to her. The question is now, what is the law regarding both the dowry and the other goods. I answer that this is a daily question, and the truth is that only that brother who received the dowry is bound to restore it to his wife. And the reason is that, just as the dowry is not acquired by the brothers, but pertains to the husband in solidum, as in ff. fam. ercisc. l. si maritus, so he alone is bound to restore it, since he alone contracted with the woman, and could not bind his brothers, as in ff. pro socio. l. cum duobus. §. si fratris. And this is expressed in l. licet indiuisam. C. de decu. lib. 10. Someone might say: Suppose that these brothers were partners in all goods; in this case, are the other brothers bound to the woman? And similarly I say that they are not: because he did not contract with them, nor did he intend to bind them to himself. For the rule of law is that one cannot bind another when conducting his own business; yet, as it is the business of marriage and dowry, as in ff. de duo. reis. l. si id, quod ego, and what is noted in ff. de mune. et hone. l. et qui originem. §. fi. Moreover, the woman did not wish to bind the brothers with whom she did not contract, nor in what manner? as in ff. de pac. l. si unus. §. ante omnia. To this adds what is noted by Dy. in l. si cum dotem. §. transgrediamur. And these are true, unless this dowry had been converted to the common utility of the brothers, for then they would be bound to share, or contribute, to the restitution of the dowry, either by an action pro socio, or by an action negotiorum gestorum: as in ff. pro socio. l. si socius pro filia. This action would be granted to the woman as useful, as for a name bound to her by tacit hypothec, which is to be computed against the brothers as debtors of the husband, after the excussion of the husband’s faculties, namely of those things which were possessed by him. as in C. quę res peig. ob. pos. l. nomen. Although others say that excussion is not required, because a useful personal action is brought, which belonged to the principal debtor against his debtor. And this is not provided for in this law, that excussion is required, since he acts as in his own right, as procurator for the one principally bound. But I believe the contrary to be truer: because this useful action partakes of the nature of a hypothecary one, and is substituted in its place. Hence I think the excussion of certain goods is necessary. On this, sufficiently noted by Cy. in d. l. nomen. Concluding, therefore, I say that, both in the dowry and in the paraphernalia, the said husband did not bind his brothers, neither by law itself nor in effect, unless something else is proven to have been done. And therefore, the said dowry and paraphernalia, things being thus, cannot be recovered from the said brothers. On the matter, noted in Spe. de iudi. 4. parte. §. generalia. Also, the general matter is treated in l. titium et et meuium. §. altero. ff. de admi. tuto. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a statute providing that the husband shall acquire all usufructs, even of the wife’s paraphernal property, does he acquire the usufruct that the wife held in the property of one of the children from her first marriage, who had predeceased her?
body: other fruits, even of the paraphernal goods. Wherefore—

† The statute provides that the husband shall enjoy all the use and other fruits, even of the paraphernal goods. The question is asked: if the mother had a usufruct in the goods of one of her sons from her first marriage, who had predeceased her, whether the husband can claim those usufructs according to the form of the statute. And it seems that he can: because the term "goods" also includes usufruct, since it is a part of ownership. On the contrary, it seems that he cannot: because a servitude cannot be subject to another servitude, as stated in l. 1, ff. de usufructu legato. But to this it is answered that the term "usufruct" is used here for the benefit, not for the formal right, as in l. necessario, §. fin., ff. de periculo et commodo rei venditae. Solution: This husband cannot claim even the benefit. And the reason is: because his wife could not claim the usufruct before she had provided security for using and enjoying according to the discretion of a good man, since she was not in possession; therefore, neither can the husband. Although the benefit of possessing is available to the possessor without providing the aforementioned security, the right to claim is not available, as in C. de secundis nuptiis, l. hac edictali, §. is illud; C. ut in possessionem legatorum, l. scire; ff. de usucapione, l. si homo; and fully in l. unica, C. de usufructu, and ff. de usufructu legato, l. uxori. And this seems to me to be the truth: because the security is of the substance of possessing. Although it is not of the substance of possessing if the usufructuary is in corporeal possession, it pertains to the acquisition of fruits, as is subtly read and noted in ff. de acquisitione possessionis, l. 3, §. ex contrario. Also, because the usufructuary does not gain the fruits unless they are separated from the land by him or another in his name, as in ff. qui modis ususfructus amittitur, l. si ususfructuarius messem. For enjoyment and use require an act, as in ff. de usufructu, l. si fur decerpserit, and arg. ff. de furtis, l. si servus communis uni, §. locavi. I, Baldus.

In the Name of Christ, Amen. It is alleged that the once magnificient Lord Bernabos, claiming to be imperial vicar-general, made gifts to several of his concubines. Yet, while he was then married, he acquired many properties; and from these women he had numerous children, both male and female, remaining in the status described above. But when some of these offspring grew up, he gave large dowries to their husbands; indeed, after the dowries were established, he granted and transferred to some of his said children certain goods of great value, as an increase to those same dowries. Hence it is asked, first, whether the aforementioned gifts made by the said Lord Bernabos to those, so to speak, concubines are valid. Secondly, it is asked whether children born, as alleged, from an illicit union can succeed, at least to their free mother. Finally, it is asked, and if it had been lawful to provide them with dowries, whether it was nevertheless prohibited to increase those dowries, as alleged.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether Lord Bernabò, the imperial vicar, may make a gift to his concubine. And see number 12, and add counsel 268 in the first part.
2. The law prohibiting soldiers from making gifts to concubines: concerning which soldiers it speaks.
3. Lord Bernabò was not subject to military law.
4. The contract of a prince has two forces.
5. The reason why a soldier may not make a gift to a concubine.
6. To strive in vain and to seek enmity is the height of madness.
7. A prince who makes a gift to an infamous person appears to dispense with her.
8. Whether Lord Bernabò may provide a dowry for the daughters of his concubine.
9. One may neither make a gift to nor leave a legacy to spurious children, not because of their own fault, but because they suffer from another’s disease; yet one may leave them maintenance.
10. A dowry succeeds in place of maintenance.
11. Baldus does not wish to overturn the world.
12. Whether a gift made to a concubine from the fullness of power existing in paternal authority is valid.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. I recall having been consulted,

† that the once-magnificent knight and lord D. Bernabò, by virtue of the plenitude of power in which he was then, as it were, possessed, could make a donation to his concubine, although a simple knight cannot make such a donation. And the reason was, and is: both

†because the law prohibiting [such conduct] speaks of a soldier of the Roman people, who is enrolled in the register of soldiers; otherwise he is not considered a soldier under Roman law: as noted in C. de officio magistri militum, l. eos. Likewise, of a soldier marked with a stigma: as noted in C. de fabricis censibus, l. stigmata; D. quibus ex causis maior, l. penultima. Likewise, of a soldier who has sworn not to avoid death for the sake of the republic: as Vegetius states in De re militari. Likewise, of a soldier who is subject to the laws and disciplines of soldiers, and who is placed under the law,

But Lord Bernabò was not among these, nor was he subject to military law: he was above the law, because he could derogate from laws, as the glorious princes of the House of the Visconti do daily. Therefore, he could derogate from that law which states that a soldier cannot make a gift to his concubine, especially because that law does not contain necessary law, but voluntary and positive law. For natural laws are those which are immutable; but voluntary laws are abrogated by contrary will, as in D. de legibus, l. non est novum, and l. sed et posteriores. For whatever is bound is capable of being unbound, in Auth. de nuptiis, § deinceps.

† Moreover, the contract of the prince has two subordinate forces, namely, tacit prior permission and express subsequent permission. As in C. de donat. inter vir. et ux. l. pen. Moreover, that law which says,

† That which cannot be given to a concubine assimilates the concubine to a wife; for she is similar in the reason for the prohibition, namely, lest he, having fallen into renewed love, should fall into poverty. But with respect to that noble lady, that donation was less significant than if one common man were to give one silver groat; thus, therefore, by comparing the act to the person, and the person to the act, the reason for the prohibition ceases. And especially because in that lady other merits concurred. And where we elsewhere say: "Another reason reforms the pact," here I say the contrary: "Another reason forms the contract," which is honorable, or at least causative, and not ignominious. Argument: Digest, *De donationibus*, l. *Si pater*; and l. *Aquilius regulus*. And if I were to say the contrary, I would incur the hatred of both the said ladies and their daughters.
† and it is the height of madness to strive in vain and, by wearying oneself, to seek nothing but hatred.

† Moreover, when a prince makes a gift to an infamous person, he is tacitly understood first to restore that person’s reputation and then to make the gift, as stated in C. de nuptiis, l. Imperiales. Hence, it cannot be said that this gift was made to an infamous person. Furthermore, this gift ought rather to be called a privilege than a donation. And no law provides that the Emperor, or King, or any other prince may not grant privileges to a concubine. And since such inability to act would be penal, it suffices that the prohibiting law ceases to apply, as in D. de procuratoribus, l. Mutius, § 1; and see D. de solutione matrimonii, l. Si vero, § De viro; D. de iure patronatus, l. Adigere, § Quamvis; D. de divortiis, l. Quod ait lex. I therefore conclude, saving the substance of the truth, that the said donation was valid.

The following question is: whether the aforementioned then exalted lord and prince could have endowed his daughters, whom he had from that concubine. And the truth is that he could not. As stated in the Code, On Natural Children, in the authority *Licet*, and in laws 1 and *Si*.

† For we cannot make gifts to or bequeath legacies to children born out of wedlock. This is not due to their fault, since they have not sinned, but rather to ours. For they suffer from another’s disease. C. de natu. li. l. legem Anastasii. There, when it says “moved by mercy,” because they are not unworthy, who suffer from another’s fault. Solution. By the same reasons by which I said that gifts to a concubine are valid, and by much stronger ones, I say that dowries could have been given to the husbands of girls; because the husbands have committed no offense. And yet, upon dissolution of the marriage, the dowry is returned to the girls. And because they have once left the donor’s assets. As in l. si. in prin. ff. quae in frau. credi. and arg. ff. de le. 3. l. pater. §. quindecim.

† Moreover, the dowry succeeds in place of alimony, as is stated by Cynus in the Code, De nuptiis, in the law Sancimus. Therefore, what is the law regarding alimony is likewise the law regarding the dowry; argument from Extra, De baptismo, chapter Maiores. But alimony can be given as a gift to spurious children, and bequeathed to them according to canon law, having regard to natural piety; because although a child is spurious, he is nevertheless a son, due to common nature. Digest, De accusationibus, law Hos accusare, section Omnibus; here, the text of the Digest; Extra, De eo qui duxit in matrimonium, chapter Cum haberet. And civil law, by disposing to the contrary, loved chastity so much that it destroyed paternal power; hence, in this article of law, canon law causes natural law to revive, as far as this species of piety is concerned, by which right all were born legitimate; as in the Authentica Qui modo nascantur sui, in the beginning, Collations 6 and 7. Furthermore, what credulity would this be? For if girls could not be provided with a dowry, they would be forced, to the shame of their ancestors, to become prostitutes; which is nearly insanity. Moreover, few are those who are truly natural children, due to the many requirements for concubinage, as in the Digest, De concubinis, law In concubinatu. I therefore conclude that, since such a great prince could establish and interpret laws, and since the cause of the dowry is most pious and favorable, Digest, De conditione indebiti, law Cum his, section Si mulier, that the said girls could be provided with a dowry both according to God and according to the world, by civil law, notwithstanding the strict constitution. Moreover, if anyone wished to revoke all the virtue of lords into their power:
† and I would not be of this opinion, that I wished to overturn the world. It follows

† Another doubt: because the said magnificence donated from the fullness of his power, and by right of full ownership, to a certain concubine of his, who was under paternal power and married to another, certain estates; this being added, that no right shall be sought by anyone else, except by the woman herself. It is asked whether, upon her death, any right may be sought by the daughters of the said donor begotten from the said concubine; and briefly I say that not: because the donation is personal, and restricted until death. As in D. de pactis, l. epistola; and in Auth. de non alienandis, §. emphyteosim. And if it be said that he is deemed to have tacitly intended the children, as in C. de fideicommissis, l. cum acutissimi. I say that this is not true: because that law has no application to bastards. As in C. de institutionibus et substitutionibus, l. generaliter, §. fin. Moreover, this donation is odious: because contrary to the common law, and in a manner contrary to good morals. As in C. de naturalibus liberis, l. 1; and l. fin. D. de actionibus et obligationibus. And it is rather a certain odious dispensation, which ought to be restricted, and not enlarged. As in c. 1, de filiis presbyterorum, lib. 6. It does not avail that note of Bartolus in l. pater, D. de servorum legatis; because there were no restrictive words. And because there the act held by the common law. As in D. de probationibus, l. si pactum. Yet it is probable that the said magnificence did not consider the exclusion of the children, but the exclusion of the parent. As in D. ad Trebellianam, l. haeredibus, §. fin. For this is very probable, being entirely devoid of legal support, as in D. de usufructu legato, l. si alij. Moreover, restrictive words restrict even a favorable act: as in C. de legatis, l. pe; and note in Auth. de restitutione fideicommissi, §. manifestum. Also, in doubt one must stand by the words. D. de solutionibus et mutationibus, l. si vero, §. de viro, with similar cases. Also, because every cause of transmission to another is excluded. Therefore, just as it does not pass to the father, so neither to the heir: because these are equal. Argument from D. de vulgari substitutione, l. qui liberis, §. haec verba; and C. de hereditatibus instituendis, l. cum proponas. And this I hold, compelled by the strictness of the words, in which also the mind of the donor is written. Add that it is said in l. quod pater, that he who provided a dowry does not seem to defraud: because he did it for the sake of piety; because the piety of a father is not to be censured. As in l. 1, §. 1, D. si quid in fraudem patroni. Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Concubinage is properly said to exist between a man and a woman who are both free from marriage.
2. What is included under the term "soldier."
3. To whom fullness of power pertains.
4. Whether credence should be given to letters of the prince asserting that he possesses fullness of power.
5. What resists fullness of power.
6. If the prince legitimizes an act, he legitimizes the person for the act, and vice versa.
7. Whether natural children succeed to their mother: what is the case with spurious or incestuous children.
8. The prince also dispenses even with an incestuous person.
9. Whether the city of Milan can make a statute that spurious children may be given gifts and legacies.
10. Those who do not know how to name their father are not citizens, nor can the city legitimize spurious children, nor make them capable.
11. The city does not have the power to legitimize spurious children.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. For the sake of clarity, I premise,

† For concubinage is properly so called when it exists between a man and a woman who are both unmarried; for since it has assumed its name from the laws, as in D. de concubinis, l. in concubinatu, that which is prohibited and punished by the laws cannot be called concubinage; because a name contrary to law is not a name, according to l. assumptum. For the names of contrary qualities must be contrary: and if indeed the man is married, but the woman is not, or both are married, or some other cause renders the marriage detestable, this is called a fornicatory, adulterous, or incestuous embrace. Nor is it a matter for discussion here regarding laws that speak of a donation made to a concubine, but rather those that speak of adulterers, incestuous persons, or those stained by rape, between whom such persons: for since such donations are made for a most shameful or detestable cause, no liberality, donation, or affection arises; for this is not properly affection, but defection. And let it be for a shameful cause permanently existing in the act, as in C. de natu. lib. l. 1, and l. si quis incesti, arg. D. de acq. et obl. l. si. This is proved by reason. For the children begotten from such union are said to be incapable and nameless, because it is a disgrace to name them, as in Auth. quibus modis natu. efficiuntur sui, §. fin., Coll. 7. It is supported by Extr. de elect., c. innotuit, and note C. quemadmodum testamentum aperiri, l. pen. And certainly these boys are not prohibited because they have sinned for themselves, but on account of the cultivation of chastity, and out of hatred and to the opprobrium of the parents, as in C. de natu. lib., l. legem Anastasii. Then I argue: propter quod unumquodque, et illud magis. But bastards are prohibited on account of their parents. Therefore, all the more strongly, the parents. C. de sacrosan. eccl., Auth. multo magis. And this is true, unless the woman had suffered violence and begotten from it. And she is said to have suffered violence, even one who could be coerced by threats. For the mind and will are lacking in the sin. Hence the Lord Azo says, as reported by Cynus: remove the will from the middle, and every act will be indifferent; as in D. de postul., l. 1, §. remouet; D. de furt., l. qui iniuriae; D. de adulter., l. vim passam, in princ. And I in my conscience would rather consider it good than evil; for such women could be compelled in fact. D. quarum rerum actio non datur, l. 2, §. quae onerandae; D. quod falsi tuto., l. nouissime, unless the contrary appeared from acts and signs showing joy. From this I assume two conclusions. The first is that, in the case of coercion, children born from such an embrace may be given a donation by the mother, because she cannot be accused; by the father, not. The second is that will was absent in the embrace by neither party; because such an embrace could be accused, as noted in C. ad officium, si qua illustris, and Inst. eo, §. nouissime, and D. unde cognosc., l. si spurius. Another conclusion also arises: for it is certain that a father can dower his natural daughter if he wishes, although he is not compelled. D. de leg. 3, l. uxorem, §. pater naturalis. But he cannot dower a bastard daughter except up to the quantity of alimony, so that she has perpetual alimony according to the quality of her status. For that which is permitted on account of a cause is limited and moderated by that cause, which is committed to the discretion of the judge; and thus canon and civil law agree. As in Extr. de eo qui duxit in matrimonium, c. cum haberet, and arg. D. de exercit., l. Lucius. From the foregoing it also appears that what I cannot do, namely I as a father, my children cannot do; because the law prohibits it. From these things it sufficiently appears that it is not to be asked whether a soldier can make a donation to a concubine, as in D. de testam. milit., l. miles, §. mulier. For if she were a true and mere concubine, such a prince could have made a donation:

† Because the term "soldier" does not properly include a prince, due to the difference in the name: although he may call his soldiers his comrades-in-arms. And it is similar to the case where the term "benefice" does not include a dignity. Moreover, as I fully noted in another opinion, the soldiers of our time are not included in privileges; therefore, they are not included in odia either, because where a privilege does not extend, neither does an odium extend. As stated in the Digest, De testamento tutorum, l. Si quis ita tamen. Another reason seems to move the donation: because if it were not permitted between spouses, it would not be permitted between lovers either. But I respond that it would be confirmed by the death of the donor, since it is supported by tradition. As stated in the Digest, De donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. Papinianus. Secondly, I premise

† To the effect that the plenitude of power in temporal matters belongs solely to the emperor, or to a free king in his kingdom, as is stated in the Code, *De captivis*, law *Hostes*. It does not belong to inferiors by right of ordinary power; but they may well have it by special privilege, for example, if a vicariate has been granted to them with the plenitude of power. For what the prince can do by himself, he can do through another, as we see daily in the case of counts. Nor is he considered another, but the very same person, as is shown in the Digest, *De manumissionibus vindicatis*, law *Parte ex provincia*, and *De servitutibus legatis*, as is clear from Bartolus. Since, therefore, the plenitude of power, existing outside all territorial jurisdiction, derives from privilege,

It is necessary that there be proof of such a privilege by means of a princely privilege or an ancient custom. As stated in Extra, De verbis significantibus, cap. Super quibusdam, § Praeterea; and in Codex, De diuersis officiis, l. Probatorias, lib. 12; 96. Dist., cap. Nobilissimus; Codex, De mandato principis, l. 1; Extra, De officio delegati, c. Cum in iure; and as noted in c. Innotuit, De eo qui fraudulenter ordinem suscepit, according to Innocentius.

† Nevertheless, because all the lords of Lombardy, by the custom of Usual practice, and as it were by a certain theory and practice, append these words “of the plenitude of power,” and are in a quasi-possession of the word and the deed: I hold, saving the substance of the truth, that their speech should be believed; for it is not probable that they would use a false voice, as in the law cited in the Code to the Julian Law on Repetundae, in the final law. Otherwise, many past matters could give rise to lawsuits, and whatever and however much had been well settled could be reopened: which is inequitable, as in the Code on the Trinity of Faith, § 4; and the decrees of so many lords would become illusory, as in the Digest on Judges, in the law “If the Praetor,” in the beginning. The third conclusive point: namely, that, assuming the plenitude of power, the acts performed against women and children held without doubt; for nothing resists the plenitude of power except two things only, namely, divine law, and immutable natural law, and necessary natural law, as in the Institutes on Natural Law, § “But natural things,” and in law 2 of the Digest on Usufruct, “That which is acquired by use.” For these prohibitions, of which above, namely concerning giving and bequeathing, are not of natural law, but of positive law; and thus they do not bind the prince, as in the Code on Donations between Husband and Wife, in the penultimate law. And if

The prince validates the act that is celebrated, and validates the person for the act, and vice versa. As in Codex, De nuptiis, l. Imperialis. From these, all the questions raised appear to be resolved, because the plenitude of power supplies all things. Unless it were established that there is not plenitude, but limited power: for every jurisdiction is bounded by limits. As in Digestum, De iurisdictione omnium iudicum, l. Si. I recall that I have already given another opinion in different words, yet with the same effective conclusion. Hence it is the same as the same in effect. As in Extra, De conversione coniugiorum, c. Dudum. For I have always presupposed the plenitude of power, considering the words of so great a lord to be truthful. Argument in c. 1, De probationibus, in Clementinis, and what is noted there. Furthermore, it must be known,

† That natural children succeed their mother, unless she is of illustrious rank: but spurious children, who are born from a condemned union, such that the parties engaging in intercourse can be accused of rape, adultery, or incest, cannot acquire anything from the father or the mother, as stated in the Authentica *Qui modo*, column 7, because that text speaks indiscriminately of any parent, whether the mother. It is no objection if you say that, on the contrary, they can acquire from the mother, unless the mother is of illustrious rank; for that distinction applies to natural children, not to the aforementioned spurious children. There are, however, other spurious children, for example, if the father held multiple wives. For such children, born to a free woman and a free man, can acquire from the mother, unless the mother is of illustrious rank, as noted in the law *Si qua illustris*, and this is the truth. The rule fails if the prince, in whom there resides the fullness of power by right, not merely in fact, had interposed his authority, as noted in the aforementioned Authentica and section.

† For the prince even dispenses with an incestuous person. The case is unique in the law. D. de ritu nuptiarum, l. qui in provincialis, §. divus. Thus it is clear that a juridical and truthful response has been given to all points, saving, however, the judgment of anyone who may think better. But the dowries are said to be with the husband, as long as the marriage subsists: because the women are not said to be undowered. Yet we are still not free from the difficulty of the points, for a scrupulousness remains in the mind: granted that the fullness of power is not established. And to this doctrine one arrives thus: because

I ask whether the people of Milan — I do not say the Emperor — could make a statute whereby gifts and legacies could be made to bastards, even assuming the peace of Constantine to be set aside; and it seems that they could, as regards property situated within their territory, and even as regards sums of money in general, which are not circumscribed by place. And it seems that they could, because all things which are in the territory are subject to the statute of that territory. And if they are not in the territory, nor outside the territory — as is the case with a quantity in general — they are subject to the statute of the place of origin or domicile, as in D. de iudicibus, l. fideicommissum, § tractatum; D. de foro competenti, c. postulasti; D. de bonis auctoritatem iudicis possidentibus, l. cum unus, § is qui. For those who make statutes can impose a general law upon their own property or upon their domiciliaries, as in l. omnes populi and l. cunctos populos; and C. de aedificiis privatis, l. an in totum. Moreover, this is not to make new law, but rather to refrain from disputing about the marks of birth, and to return to the primitive state of nature, before the reins of chastity were imposed, as in Auth. qui modo naturali efficiantur sui, Coll. 6 and 7, in principio; and a thing easily returns to its nature, as in D. de pactis, l. si unus, § pactus, ver. quod et in specie. Moreover, just as it is not permitted to a father to kill his bastard son, so neither is it permitted to deny him alimony, as in D. de liberis agnoscendis, l. necare; because nature is common, as in D. de accusationibus, l. hos accusare, § omnibus; and to kill a son is to sin against nature, to the entire species, as in l. 1 ad Legem Pompeiam de parricidiis; and the city is held in the place of a parent, as in D. de iustitia et iure, l. veluti; and D. de captivis et postliminio reversis, l. postliminium, § filius. And if this is permitted to the people, much more so to its prince, as in D. de officio praetoris, l. Barbarius, in fine; for the people consents fictitiously, the prince truly; and truth is greater than fiction, as in D. de origine iuris, l. 2, § nouissime; and D. de liberis et posthumis, l. filio quem pater. Someone says: this is true if the prince has enacted this concerning another; otherwise if concerning himself; because no one declares law for himself, as in C. ne quis in sua causa iudex sit, l. 1; D. de verborum significatione, c. ex parte. But I answer that this rule fails in the case of the prince and the fisc, as in D. de his quae in testamento delentur, l. proxime. It also fails in voluntary jurisdiction, as in D. de adlegibus, l. si consul. Moreover, to enact statutes concerning voluntary jurisdiction is a matter of voluntary jurisdiction; concerning contentious jurisdiction, of contentious jurisdiction. But we are in voluntary jurisdiction. Furthermore, he does not act so much as the people, from whom jurisdiction proceeds, as in C. de officio eius cuius mandatum est iuris, l. et si praetor; D. de legibus 2, l. unum ex familia, § 1.

To the contrary, it seems, first, from the text of l. omnes populi, if the text is understood there. For there it is permitted to peoples to make statutes who are governed by laws or customs. But in this argument, the people do not use law, because they act against the law, as in the aforementioned Auth. qui modo, § si, Coll. 6; nor customs, because good morals are encompassed by these, and fruits arising from a bad tree and infected root suffer from the same vice, as in C. de naturalibus liberis, l. si. Since therefore in this article the people do not live by laws nor by customs, they cannot make a statute. Moreover, a statute is not valid whereby one lives shamelessly, as in the epistle Rex pacificus. Moreover, a statute is not valid by which crimes are nourished or fostered, D. 4, c. erit lex. For the law must be holy and honest. Hence it is defined in this way: law is a holy sanction, commanding honest things and prohibiting contrary things, D. de legibus, l. 2 and 3. Moreover, among all precepts of the law, this is the first and most important: to live honestly, as in the aforementioned c. Rex pacificus; and D. de iustitia et iure, l. iustitia, § iuris praecepta. Moreover
† Naturally and properly, those are not citizens who were born in such a way that they cannot name their father, as is the case with spurious children. See no. in Auth. de 11 nup. in prin. coll. 4.

† Moreover, the city does not have the power to legitimize spurious children, nor to enable them. As is noted by Innocentius in the extrajudicial collection on the matter of fideicommissa, chapter Cum P. tabellio. Nor can a father arrogate a spurious son, even with the authority of the imperial constitution, unless there were a clause of plenitude of power and ex certa scientia. As stated in the Code on natural liberty, law Legem Anastasii. For arrogation is a legitimate act, by which one does not become a son as if a son, and in the power of the father, i.e., almost imitating nature. But it cannot be as if imitating nature an adulterous, nefarious, or incestuous embrace. As stated in the extrajudicial collection on renunciation, chapter Nisi cum pridem. I fully examined this question in laws 1 and 2 of the Code on the right of annuity, after Jacobus de Belvisio. And although it may be more strongly defended according to the truth of law that the statute is invalid, nevertheless, because eminent doctors who were on the contrary side rendered opinions to some asserting that this is not a gift of the father, but of the law, and conceding the condition from law Non ex contractu; others asserting that the condition arises from law from prohibitions by the advice of discreet friends, it was composed between the parties. And thus the arguments for and against were resolved. Arguments from the Digest on inheritance institution, law Si pater, and law Et haec Thyberius, which seems commendable to me. Nevertheless, according to the truth of law, it is the opinion that the people cannot do so, unless by specific authority of the prince. In the Old Testament, however, these difficulties were not observed, because virginity and chastity were not consecrated to God. Hence, I do not think the Old Testament should be alleged in this matter, because what has grown old, worn out by age, has withered and changed for the better, because life has succeeded death. I, Baldus.
In the Name of Christ, Amen. I ask whether a bequest to a future wife is valid in all respects. See above, opinion 188, beginning "punctus."

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A testator left to his daughter, by the law of legacy and succession, and in other goods, the womb of his wife if she were pregnant, etc., and if they should die at any time before the age of puberty, he substituted Cecholina, his sister, and Bernardino, his son, and did not add who of these should succeed: and whether the testament is null.
2. The word "relinquo" (I leave), when added to a singular thing, is not understood as a matter of institution, but of legacy or fideicommissum.
3. Whether substitution from a codicillary clause is drawn to a fideicommissum, when the testament is null.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. It is proposed that Lord Antonius, from Catalutia his wife, begot Antonia, their common daughter, and when he intended to visit the tombs of the Apostles, he made a testament, in which he disposed as follows: namely. He thus left by right of legacy and succession to Lady Antonia, his daughter, beyond her dowry, fifty gold ducats for her share, after the Falcidian deduction, and for the succession of all his goods, commanding her to be silent and content. In all his other goods, however, he instituted the womb of his said wife, if she were pregnant and bore one or more male children, and they came to light, as his heir or heirs with full right; if it were a female, one hundred pounds for her dowry, and furthermore for her share of the Falcidian deduction and succession of all his goods, fifty pounds of denarii. And if all those born, both males and females, should die at any time without children before the age of puberty, or afterwards at any time: then and in the share of his said children, the said testator wished Ceccholina, his sister, and Bernardinus, his son, [to succeed]. And he did not add the word "succeed" to these, but left in the writing an imperfect sentence. Finally, the said testator lived only twenty years. And from various pregnancies of his wife, he begot three sons, who died during the lifetime of the said testator, with the said Ceccholina and Bernardinus, his son, or one of them, surviving.

† Now the question arises whether the said Antonia, the daughter, or the said substitutes should succeed. And it seems that the substitutes ought to succeed: because the said substitution was concise, which, under a concise wording, contains a vulgar substitution, unless one child in the womb and others are passed over by omission, because the testator did not say, "if then pregnant." But if there were one, it is not understood to refer only to the present posthumous child, but to any child whatsoever. As in D. de lib. et posth. l. placet and C. de posth. her. inst. l. si. So that he may not suffer the penalty of omission, who did not omit his children: as is said there. For the word "were" is extensive. And the term "if" is placed for "when," which appears: because the testator speaks of children in the plural. For according to the course of nature, a woman is seen with one womb when she does not bear more than one. I understand this of any womb. On the contrary, it seems: because I confess that the said substitution is merely vulgar. And therefore the will is invalid, and consequently neither is the said vulgar substitution valid: because Antonia was omitted, since nothing was left to her by way of institution: as in Auth. ut cum de appell. cogn. §. aliud quoque capitulum. For she was not left her legitime by the name of a share, or by the name of a legitime, or of the Falcidian portion. But a quantity was left with the intention of compensating with the legitime, nor was it said by way of institution: for the word "I leave," added to a singular thing, does not

It is understood by the law of institution, but of legacy or fideicommissum. As in D. 38.2.1 (*Eas*), § *et generaliter*, according to Dy. Also, as he said in this substitution, the principal word is missing: because words speak. And the said testator intended that they succeed in the place and portion of his said goods; and he does not say more. For he does not say that the substitutes succeed in the place and portion. But to this it could be answered by D. 28.5.1 (*I*). Also, that the posthumous children were passed over, seems to be proved by D. 28.6.1 (*Commodissime*). And if it is said that the will is validated because the passed-over children died during the testator’s lifetime, as in D. 28.2.1 (*Posthumus*), it is answered that that law has no application when the posthumous child opens the way to break the will of a born child who is still alive, as in D. 28.4.1 (*Si tabulae*), at the end. This question is very difficult: because Antonia was not instituted as heir, which is clear: because she could claim nothing from the will as an heir, but only by an action on the will. Therefore, she was passed over. And thus the aforementioned substitution was null. Hence it appears that the intestate inheritance belongs to the said Antonia.

But whether the said substitution is drawn from the clause of the codicils to a fideicommissum, there are very diverse opinions: and especially on account of the birth of a posthumous child, who breaks the codicillary clause, according to the opinion of many doctors; but according to others it does not break it, when posthumous children have been considered. And therefore, having determined that this substitution is not valid by direct law: but whether it is valid by the law of fideicommissum, and that, after deducting the legitimate portion and the Falcidian share, the remainder ought to be restored by the Trebellian share, I therefore do not determine whether it is valid by the law of fideicommissum: because it is said not to be valid. In the Authent. Ex causa. And the point is difficult: but I say well that direct substitutions are not valid. And therefore to be in the case of intestacy, saving the sounder counsel. And so I say, and I counsel, I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How a prohibition made by a testator to his sons against alienating property is to be understood.
2. Under the term "descendants" are included all persons in perpetuity.
3. The nature of the contract of sale and purchase is that the thing be delivered free of encumbrances.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. With the aforementioned words of the testament saying.

† Furthermore, he prohibited and forbade that any sale, alienation, etc., of his houses, etc., be made in the first instance, but that those houses should pass to his sons and heirs, and even to the free descendants of the same heir, in perpetuity, etc. Nevertheless, if any of the aforementioned heirs were to sell his share of those houses during his lifetime, or were to happen to alienate it in any manner, then it shall be lawful for him to give the share of the said houses falling to him to his brothers for the price of 700 pounds of denarii, and the brothers shall be bound to purchase that share and firmly pay the aforementioned price of 700 pounds. It is proposed that certain properties have been sold, certain divided, and certain left within the permitted degrees of kinship; and it is asked whether the purchaser may exchange with the legatees what he has obtained through sale, exchange, or legacy, and whether he may freely sell or alienate it to another. And it seems that he may not, because the said goods are subject to a perpetual cause of prohibition.

† Moreover, under the term “descendants,” all descendants in perpetuity are included. See D. 2.4.1 (*Quod si hac*); D. 2.4.1 § *Liberos*. And this is correct. And so I have previously advised. But the contrary appears to be the case. For the sale here was made by the judgment of the testator. Hence, the buyer may alienate to whomever he wishes. See D. 33.1.1 § 15 (*Pater*). And the reason is: because the prohibitory words are lacking; and because the reason of the law, even by a mere point of fact, clearly demonstrates this. For since the testator permits the property to be sold, it is understood that it is sold freely and transferred freely.

† For this is according to the nature of the contract of sale and purchase, from which arises the obligation to deliver the thing freely. As is noted, C. de evictionibus, l. ex prędiis. Hence, if the buyer can alienate the thing he bought to whomever he wishes, as C. de contrahenda emptione, l. dudum. And this reason is subtle, and can be assigned among other reasons in the said §. quindecim. And this is the truth with regard to goods purchased; but with regard to others, which by succession from an ascending person came to a descending person, the portion of the last descendant, if he has children, devolves to his children. As C. de fideicommissis, l. cum acutissimi; and ff. de vulgari substitutione, l. cohaeredi, §. qui discretas. But if he has no children, then, considering that the testator used the appellative name of heirs, it devolves to the children of the testator per stirpes. Argument from C. de impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus, l. fin. But if he had used names denoting nothing other than agnation, then it would seem that it would succeed to others, excluding the rest. As ff. de legatis 2, l. cum ita legatur, §. in fideicommissis. And although I have said that in sale it is sold freely, it is otherwise in division: because it seems to have been made with its own cause. As is fully noted by Bartolus in l. qui Romae, §. fin., ff. de verborum obligationibus. Moreover, if that last person, to whom I said it devolves, renounces, it would be the same as if he had never been in the middle. Hence, to whom that portion devolves, is clear from the above. I, Baldus.

In the Name of Christ, Amen. The point is as follows. A certain person left to his natural son one house, on the condition that he could not, etc. See the opinion. 14 1. beginning: the point is as follows.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A prohibition against alienation imposed on a legatee is not understood to extend to alienation in favor of the legatee’s son.
2. Whether a father prohibited from alienating is deemed to alienate if he makes a legacy in pupillary wills by way of substitution for the pupillus.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen.

† When a testator prohibits something from being alienated by the legatee, it is nevertheless not understood that he prohibits alienation to the son of the legatee. For this is rather called a continuation of the same ownership than an alienation. D. de lib. et posth. l. in suis; C. de impo. lucra. descrip. l. 1, lib. 10; C. de fideicom. l. voluntas. Moreover, although the legatee were prohibited from alienating, nevertheless his son, to whom transmission has taken place, is not prohibited from alienating; because the prohibition of alienating does not extend beyond the person of the one prohibited. D. de leg. 3, l. pater, § quindecim; and note in Auth. de rest. fideicom. § manifestum. Now there remains the question whether such a father cannot alienate: because, although prohibited, the son can, because he is not prohibited. Therefore, suppose,

† That the father, in pupillary wills, bequeaths to the substitutes of the pupil. It is asked whether the father is said to alienate, and thus incurs the penalty; or whether, on the contrary, the father is not said to alienate, but rather the son, and thus he does not incur the penalty of the will. I answer that, speaking properly, the father alone does not alienate, but both do; because it is the will of both, as stated in the Digest, *de testamento militis*, in the law *Patris et filii*. Therefore, both persons concur in the act, namely, the prohibited and the non-prohibited. And it seems to be said that the permitted person is to be considered, and that one does not incur the penalty, according to the Digest, *de vulgari substitutione*, in the law *Si is qui*; *de vindicatione manumissionis*, in the law *Si pater*, at the end. For this legatee can be called rather the son’s than the father’s. Code, *de inofficioso testamento*, in the law *Papinianus*, § *Sed nec impuberis*, where it is said that that reason is considered from two contrary reasons concurring, which favors the will more, although in the calculation of the Falcidian share everything is contributed. Digest, *ad legem Falcidiam*, in the law *In ratione*, § *Quod vulgo*. But by a subtle reasoning it can be defended that, through such a legacy made as if by the son and not as if by the father, one does not incur the penalty alone; because the prohibitory words were personal, not written *in rem*; as appears there, when it is said that the said legatees, etc. Moreover, those words “to sell,” etc., seem to refer rather to contracts than to last wills. Digest, *de legatis tertio*, in the law *Pater filium*, § *Fundum*. This is also gathered from those words, “let that one fall, who shall have sold,” etc. For this penalty does not seem to be inflicted upon the deceased; because the deceased cannot fall from the legacy. And thus it does not apply to himself, nor does the penalty apply to the act of the dying. As stated in the aforementioned § *Fundum*. And thus it does not obstruct the Digest, *de legatis secundo*, in the law *Peto*, § *Fratre*, and in the law *Codicillis*, § *Pe*, with similar cases. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a substitute is excluded by a natural legitimate child, if the substitution was made on the condition that the testator should die without legitimate children, or descendants from his body, etc.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A certain person made a substitution in the following manner: If Stephanutius should die without legitimate sons, or descendants from his own body, etc.

† It is asked whether a natural child legitimated excludes the substitute. Considering the words of the will, and also considering that a natural affection is held towards natural children, and also considering legitimation by marriage, together with the dotal instruments: it is said that the aforementioned legitimated children exclude the substitutes; unless perhaps the testator was of such nobility and authority that it would be a disgrace to him to have such universal successors. D. ad trebellianum, l. ex facto, §. si quis rogatus. Jacobus de Belvis places such legitimated children equal in all respects and in every way to those born in lawful wedlock, as he himself elegantly notes in Auth. de triennio et semisse, §. quod autem, col. 3. Bartolus places them in the position of posthumous children in l. gallus, §. quid si tantum, D. de liberis et posthumis. The intention of the testator also appears to have been this, on account of those words “or from his own body,” because that word “or” is explained as meaning “that is,” and thus it shows natural affection. That is, whether legitimate, and natural, or descending from his own body, that is, natural children only. For the word “that is,” “whether,” whether placed alternatively, or declaratively, or ampliatively, here bears this sense. For those words “without other legitimate heirs” are understood to include even natural children. D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. fideicommissum. And afterwards he adds: “or to those descending from his own body.” It is necessarily understood to refer to natural children only, so that the words may have some effect. D. ad trebellianum, l. haeredibus, §. si. Except that in dignitary fiefs, which do not pass to persons of low status. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Where a pupil has a substitute, if it does not appear who died first, it is presumed that the testator died first, rather than the pupil.
2. Whether the word "succeed" is direct or oblique, and when.
3. Whether a daughter transmits an undivided paternal inheritance, and to whom.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Having examined the point at issue, and having reviewed the acts and proceedings in the aforementioned case or cases on both sides, as well as the testimonies of the witnesses: it appears to me that, in the facts of the case, it must be presupposed that Benedicta died in her pupillary age, according to the statements of certain witnesses, namely Cechi, Matthę, Marci Iutii, and Vannis Dominici. Furthermore, it must be presupposed that the said Benedicta survived her grandfather, albeit for a short time; for, as the witnesses state, they were buried together. Moreover, this is evident from the testimony of Cechi Auenturatae, Marci Iutii, etc.

† And it is also a matter of law that where a ward has a substitute, and it does not appear who died first, the testator is presumed to have died first, in favor of the ward, or of the substitutes. ff. ad trebellianicam, l. ex facto, §. pe., where there is a most notable text. Furthermore, I presuppose, based on the confession of the parties, that the said Benedicta was under the power of her grandfather Nutius, and not under the power of her father Vannis; because she was born or conceived before the emancipation of her father Vannis. These premises being taken as true, I now come to the points of law. And I say that here two different inheritances are at issue. For the inheritance of Nutius is at issue. Also the inheritance of Vannis. Regarding the inheritances and goods of Nutius, I say that Martellonus has the right, and not Lady Colutia; because the substitution made to the grandchildren is considered a direct pupillary substitution, as it agrees with the words and the age. as in c. si pater, de testibus, lib. 6.

† And although much could be said about the word "succeed," nevertheless, when the word "succeed" is not placed absolutely by itself, but is placed consecutively with "dies," which is interpreted as direct, then the word "succeed," by virtue of the conjunction, must be considered direct, insofar as the times and the quality of the persons allow. For here the testator establishes several degrees of substitutes, but he does not create different species of substitution. And to this effect: ff. de vindicatione legatorum, l. fin. §. cui dulcia; de legatis 3, l. in repetendis; de verborum obligationibus, l. Titia §. idem respondit; de pactis, l. Item quia §. idem Iulianus; de legatis 2, l. cum pater §. ab instituto; and what is noted in the Institutes, de rerum divisione §. item lapilli. And for this also in §. qua ratione. And the question was disputed by Johannes Andreas in the cited chapter Si pater, and by Cynus in l. precibus in the addition. The gloss is not to the contrary, which distinguishes whether the testator specified the time or not; because that gloss is true where it does not appear from another reason that the substitution is direct. But here it appears from the context of the direct words and the nature of tacit repetition. I therefore say that, as regards the goods and the inheritance of the said Nutius, the said Colutia has no part in succeeding. And this applies to the inheritance of Nutius, or of the said pupillary substitutes.

† Now I come to the goods and the inheritance of Vannes, and I say that in these goods Macellonus has no interest, but Lady Colutia succeeds in full. And thus I declare. Vannes had three daughters, who were not under his power, but under the power of their grandfather. Hence, by the law of the existence of one’s heir, none of these daughters could transmit the unaccepted paternal inheritance. Although, therefore, in a pupillary substitution the goods of a minor come from whatever source they were acquired, as in l. sed si plures, §. ad substitutos, and l. si arrogator, nevertheless the goods of Vannes do not fall within the grandfather’s substitution: because the inheritance of Vannes was not taken possession of by Benedict; and thus he did not transmit it to an external substitute: as in C. de caducis tollendis, §. in nouissimo. Therefore, Macellonus has no right in the goods of the said Vannes. But why Colutia has a right, I say: because Pascha and Margarita, who had no substitute, because they died before their grandfather, transmitted the paternal inheritance to their mother by virtue of the privilege of l. apud hostes, according to the gloss on l. 1, de his qui ante apertionem tabularum. For, following the opinion of the gloss, an unaccepted inheritance of ascendants is transmitted to descendants and ascendants, not to other outsiders. Therefore, the parties to the arbitration, the facts being as they are, are these: that they declare the inheritance of Vannes to belong to Lady Colutia, and that they cause her to enjoy the goods of Vannes. And that they impose perpetual silence on the goods of Nutius concerning the said Clarutia: because they do not pertain to her. And thus I say, and I advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The act of the deceased does not prejudice him who has his own title.
2. One cannot depart from the law regarding the form of the contract, unless both parties consent, whether as to its essence, or its modification, or its alteration. And number 3.
3. An emphyteusis having been granted for himself, and his sons, and his grandsons, if the father sold the emphyteusis, whether the sons as heirs can claim it.
4. Pacts placed in the contract are not understood to be departed from by whatever words.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† To an heir who has his own title, the act of the deceased does not prejudice him. As in D. de diuersis et temporibus praescriptionum, l. an vitium, § ex facto. And this must be premised first. Secondly, it must be considered,

† that the form of the contract cannot be departed from in law, unless both parties consent: whether we speak of a departure as to the essence. C. de act. et ob. l. sicut. ff. commoda. l. in commodato. §. 1. C. de dona. l. siue emancipa. or whether we speak of a change. ff. loca. l. cum in plures. §. lege dicta. or of an alteration, or qualification. C. de dona. quae sub modo l. perfecta. or of a prolongation of the obligation, or right. C. loca. l. si cum hermes. ff. de pac. l. epistola. §. fi. and l. fi. eo. tit. Thirdly, it must be considered,

† Since, when a father and son purchase, lease, or enter into any contract together, whatever is acquired is acquired for each in equal shares, just as in the case of any other persons (Digest, De duobus reis, l. Reos, § Cum tabulis), nothing prohibits the father and son from receiving and stipulating in the same contract: and a share is acquired by each in equal portions. Two solidary debtors can also be constituted, if this were the intention, that they should be two persons contracting or holding credit in solidum. And this can be done purely and conditionally, as the parties agree from the beginning. Having premised these things, let us come to our case. A certain person, namely Master G., prepositus maior of the church of Orvieto, syndic and procurator of the Lord Bishop, gave, granted, renewed, and confirmed to Baldus and Pax, son of the said Baldus, confessing that the thing described below was of the domain and property of the said bishopric, receiving for them and their legitimate male and female children and grandchildren, and his descendants, up to the third generation and the complete person: so that the part of the predeceased shall pass to and accrue to the survivor: one piece of land within its boundaries and confines: to have, hold, and possess: and whatever the said Baldus and Pax, and their children and grandchildren, by the said right, shall hereafter please to do: always saving that the said Baldus and Pax, and their children and grandchildren, cannot sell the said thing, nor alienate it in any manner whatsoever, without the express license of the said Lord Bishop and his successors, etc., as appears by the hand of And. Acharigi, and others. Finally, the said Baldus sold the said thing by emphyteutic right to a certain Galassino Cioni Moschae of Cerchaldo, receiving for the said Cioni his father, as appears by the hand of Ranerolus the notary. Finally, the said bishop renewed the said thing to the same Cioni. Then the said Baldus died. Now the said Pax says that the said thing pertains to him by full right, on account of the pact of accrual by death; it is asked what is the law. This question has been committed to me for consultation by the most excellent man, Master Ludovicus de Bulseno, arbitrator in the said cause, chosen by the parties. On the said point, therefore, I have seen the allegations of both parties faithfully transmitted to me, and having considered all things,

I say that the aforementioned Baldus could not alienate the said thing to the prejudice of the aforementioned Pax, his son, so that after Baldus’s death, Pax might claim it and use it according to his right. Nor could the Lord Bishop renew [the lease] to the new buyer against the form of the prior renewal. I am moved to say this by the premises set forth at the beginning. Furthermore, I am moved by the fact that the son comes by his own pact, not by his father’s. Hence, he does not avail himself of the aid derived from his father’s person, but comes in his own person and by his own right; and upon the father’s death, he is liable to stipulate in solidum.
