Therefore, the act of the thing does not harm him. D. de pactis, l. si unus in principio. Moreover, these are adventitious goods, which the father could not alienate. As C. de bonis matri., l. 1. Furthermore, when the father’s right ends by the father’s death, the right of purchase, or of the acceptor, ends. As D. de pignoribus, l. lex vectigal, which is properly alleged. Moreover, the Bishop’s renewal does not harm Pax, because the emphyteusis had not reverted to the bishopric, especially freely. For it was encumbered by a pact concerning the right of accretion, and it could not pass except with its cause and encumbrance. D. de contrahenda emptione, l. si aquaeductus; D. de actione empti, l. in venditione. But if that pact had not been added, the aforementioned last confirmation would hold for the half part. As d. § cum tabulis.

† The words “and whatever shall seem fit to be done” do not stand in the way of the pact, because they are understood as saving the pacts and the nature of the contract. D. de damno infecto, leg. Et quod in stipulatione. Likewise, the words “without express license” do not stand in the way, as if from the contrary sense permission with license were implied. For this permission is understood as saving the right of the pacts. For it always seems to be implied that pacts arising from the same contract remain firm. D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, leg. Non ad ea; D. de pactis, leg. Item quia, §. Item Iulianus; and leg. Iuris gentium, §. Adeo, D. de contrahenda emptione. And therefore, if the said Pax did not involve himself in the paternal inheritance, he can vindicate the entire said thing. But if he were the heir of his father, then he could not vindicate it, because he would be liable for eviction as the heir of his father, since the father sold as sole emphyteuta and in solidum. D. de rei venditione, leg. Cum a matre, unless he were heir with the benefit of inventory, and the father’s goods were not solvent. As noted, C. de iure deliberandi, leg. Si, §. In computatione; and it is supported by D. de pignoribus et hypothecis, leg. Rem alienam. Since, therefore, it is presupposed that the said Pax renounced the paternal inheritance, I say that the said Pax is admitted to vindicate the said thing in solidum, and that the arbiter ought to pronounce accordingly. And it is supported by C. de secundis nuptiis, Auth. Haec res; and Auth. De nuptiis, §. Quoniam in feminis, Coll. 4; D. locato, leg. Si quis domum; D. de legatis 2, leg. Peto, §. Praedium. But a better and more appropriate text is in the aforementioned leg. Lex vectigali. The objection from D. de pactis, leg. Si tibi, §. Si pactus cum, with its gloss, does not apply, because there it speaks of a paternal contract. Here, however, we are dealing with the son’s own contract, which the son himself interposed for himself and on his own behalf. D. de probationibus, leg. Si pactum; and argument from D. de fideicommissis, leg. Be; leg. Si filius, §. Erit rubricabo; and leg. Generaliter, §. Quotiens. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When a written instrument proves: and thus it is understood. L. *scripturas*. And Auth. *ibi positae*. C. *qui potiores in pignore habendi*.
2. A buyer relying on title, as having a cause from the seller, must use his cause with its own defects.
1. A written instrument that makes proof against the debtor makes proof against any successor.
2. Whether a public written instrument makes it so that a private one is not believed.
3. In merchants' cases, it is not fitting to dispute on the subtleties of law.
4. Whether the subscription of witnesses is required for a written instrument to prove.
5. Whether one having a hypothec from a private written instrument is preferred to a buyer not having a hypothec, or vice versa.
6. When the discussion of two debtors ought to be made.
7. What the word "for" signifies.
8. Whether a hypothec constituted by a procurator is drawn back to the day of the mandate.
9. Whether two co-debtors, equally principal, are seen to stand surety for each other.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† To understand this matter, it is necessary to premise an understanding. L. *scripturas* and Auth. *ibi positae*, C. *qui potior in pignore habet*, by distinguishing. For either a private writing is produced against the writer sued personally or hypothecarily, and it has its own, that is, its usual force, which it had under the old law. For it is taken as constant that it was valid and sufficient for proof if the debtor confesses that he wrote it, even if he denies the rest. As in D. *de pign.* L. *cum tabernam*, § *idem quaesivit*; and L. *fideiussor*, § *pater*; and L. *si is qui bona*, § 1. Hence, from such a writing arises valid proof against the writer of those things which are written in it. As in C. *de non numerata pecunia*, L. *generaliter*; D. *de constituta pecunia*, L. *quidam*; D. *de deposito*, L. *publica*, § *si*; and when it is made between persons present, everything is presumed to be both true and solemnly acted. As in D. *de verborum obligationibus*, L. *sciendum*; D. *si certum petatur*, L. *lecta* and in § *si scriptum*; and C. *de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione*, L. 1; and note in L. 1, C. *de usuris*. Therefore, the judge rightly pronounced against the writer for the servant, L., and finally the discussion proceeded correctly, because it had order in itself, and truth of law and fact. And this is determined in the aforementioned L. *scripturas* in the first part of the writing.

Sometimes a private writing of the creditor is produced against the contrary creditor, who likewise relies on a private writing. And because this is not our case, I do not discuss it. Sometimes it is produced against an extraneous possessor, or another creditor who has a public instrument in his own right; and then either the private writing does not contain a hypothec, or it contains a hypothec. In the first case, either an alienation or a new obligation is contracted in fraud. And although a hypothecary action cannot be brought, because there is no hypothec, nevertheless an action in fact for revocation can be brought, with the distinction of which it is read and noted in Inst. *de actionibus*, § *Item si quis in fraudem*. However, it is necessary to prove the counsel of fraud if the extraneous possessor or creditor possesses from an onerous cause; because fraud is regularly presumed. As in D. *de probationibus*, L. *quotiens*, § *qui dolo*. But if the private writing contains a hypothec, then four things are to be considered. The first is the figure of the letters. The second is the substance of the personal obligation. The third is the hypothec. The fourth is the time. I say that the first inspection is the figure of the letters. D. *de actionibus et obligationibus*. Not *figura*. For the figure is the written speech itself. And of this I do not believe that the defendant denies it to be written by the hand of the writer. And thus it is presupposed by me. The second inspection is the personal obligation. As in D. *de probationibus*, L. *ante omnia*. And this is not denied by the adversary; because it cannot be denied without shame, since it appears from the account books; especially since according to the customs of merchants, account books are held as public instruments. As noted by Bartolus, D. *de donationibus*, L. *nuda ratio*. The third inspection is the hypothec. And here also I presuppose that the hypothec is not denied, but the time, which was the fourth thing to be inspected. Time, however, can be denied in two ways. In the first way, because it is said to have been sold and delivered before it was obligated. And thus in the obligation cannot come that which was alienated earlier; because it is not in the goods of the obligor. As in D. *de pign.* L. *si is qui*, § *quod dicitur*. And this buyer has a public instrument of sale and precary delivery, which suffices for transferring dominion and for preference. As in D. *de acquisitione possessionis*, L. *quod meo*; and fully noted in D. *de pactis*, L. *ab emptione*. In the second way: because the buyer has an express hypothec from a public instrument, which is preferred to the hypothec from a private instrument; because a public instrument is more credible than a private one, which is established by the best reason, for two reasons. First, because more certain proof is to be preferred. As in Extr. *de probationibus*, C. *licet causam*. Second, lest it be in the power of the debtor to take away the right of the creditor by a prior date. As in D. *de fideiussoribus*, L. *repetita*; C. *de falsis*, L. *si creditor*; D. *ad legem Velleianam*, L. *seya mancipia*; D. *de editionibus*, L. 1, § *editiones*; C. *de propositis*, L. *exempto*. And there is a third reason: that a thing done between others does not prejudice others. As in D. *de iuribus et factis ignorantibus*, L. *iniquissimum*. And it seems expressed in the aforementioned L. *scripturas*, § *si*; and Auth. *ibi posita*. Unless the private writing is written or subscribed by the hand of the debtor, and subscribed by three witnesses as true and done in the presence of the subscribers, the public writing derogates from the faith of the private one, and renders it invalid by invalidity of proof and invalidity of existence; and especially concerning the prerogative of time. For a public writing is greater than any exception, except the exception of falsity, simulation, and cause not following. But a private writing is not greater than an exception; because it can easily be colluded, as we say that on account of the fear of subornation the proof of truth is sometimes impeded. As in Auth. *de testibus*, § *quia vero*. But these not withstanding, in our case another consideration seems to be applied.

† For if the buyer relies on ownership as having derived his title from the seller, he must avail himself of his own cause, with its own defects, and with the lapse of time. As is noted in C. si aliae res pignori datae sint; and in ff. de pignoribus, l. si autem, §. si duobus. For I ought not to be in a better position than my predecessor. As stated in ff. de regulis iuris, l. in his, §. non debeo. Moreover, it ought not to be within the power of the debtor to make the creditor’s proof more difficult and worse. As held in C. de iuribus et factis ignorantibus, l. iniquissimum; and in ff. de pactis, l. si unus, §. et in summa. Hence the learned Baldus states that even against the fisc, which succeeds, the aforementioned private instrument proves its case, just as against the debtor himself who wrote it. As he himself places it in d. l. scripturas.

The writing, therefore, which made proof against the debtor, makes proof against any successor, whether universal or particular. arg. D. de usu, l. id tempus, § 1; and D. de acq. po., l. Pomponius, § cum quis; and D. de pign., l. si superatus, § 1; and D. de exc. rei iud., l. si a te, § Iulianus.

† It is not an objection if you say that public writing causes private writing not to be believed: for this is true, unless it is established that the private writing is true: for the law *scripturas* is based on a presumption: because public writing is considered more credible: but presumptions cease where the truth appears to the contrary. As in D. de in integrum restitutione, l. *diuus*. Here, however, the truth appears: for the truth is not called into doubt, but the force, i.e., the validity of the writing. For the buyer does not say that the private writing is not true. But he says that the private writing is not valid, which is false: for rather it is valid, if it is true. D. de pignoribus, l. *contrahitur*. And C. de fideiussoribus in stricto sensu, l. *in exercendis*. For here the writing is not one of substance. And the truth can easily be proved: as I will say below in the conclusion, which I state. Moreover, what does not avail singly, avails in multitude. And what, when collected together, gives credibility. As in X. de probationibus, c. *causam*. Moreover, in cases of merchants, where good faith is at issue, it is not fitting to dispute on the subtleties of law. As in D. de mandato, l. *si fideiussor*, § *quaedam*. And from this I state such a conclusion, that if the said writing, i.e., before the contract of purchase and sale, had been seen and read by three literate and intelligent witnesses, who knew and recognized the writing, before the sale was made, that such writing, thus verified, would suffice against the buyer and any possessor. As noted by Cy. C. de edendo, auth. *si quis in aliquo documento*. And it is proved in X. de censibus, cap. *cum olim*.

† Nor does it matter if you say: witnesses ought to be subscribed; for that is true in the case of dead voice testimony, but it is not necessary in the case of living voice testimony. As stated in D. de testibus, l. ubi numerus. And it is most fitting that what is read and noted in D. de negotiis gestis, l. eum actum, and l. at qui natura, §. Scevola, and in c. ultima, de rescriptis, in the Clementines, is true. And it is probable that the said lord has many witnesses by whom he can prove his case. Moreover, the writer himself is added as a witness. As stated in D. finium regundorum, l. eos, and D. de procuratoribus, l. si actor malit.

† And furthermore, it must not be omitted that this is not a question concerning two hypothecs, because the purchaser has no hypothec over the thing purchased. Hence, the question arises between one who holds a hypothec and a private instrument, and one who holds no hypothec; and thus, the one holding the hypothec is preferred. This is proven by three reasons.

First, because one’s own thing is not regularly encumbered to anyone, as stated in the law *Neque pignus*. Second, because the purchased thing is not here encumbered for delivery, since the thing was delivered, as stated in the Digest, *De solutionibus*, law *In numerationibus*. Third, because it is not encumbered for eviction, since the obligation for eviction does not arise until the thing is evicted and possession is taken away, as stated in the Digest, *De evictionibus*, law *Habere licere*; and see the note by Jacobus de Arena in the Digest, *De solutionibus*, major title, law *Facere posse*. Hence, unless the plaintiff evicts the thing and obtains possession, he does not have a hypothecary right, because the condition has not yet occurred. And it is most certain that, under these circumstances, there are not two hypothecs. And no answer can be given to this reasoning.

Having examined the force of the written authorities, it must be considered whether discussion [of the principal debtor’s assets] is necessary. And for the sake of understanding, it should be known that in contracts involving two co-obligors who are partners, each is bound for his share; because the partnership, which is obligated by such a contract, is distributed into equal shares, just as an inheritance is distributed into shares of inheritance, as stated in D. 17.2.14 (*Si non fuerint*). Therefore, partners are bound through the medium of the partnership and in shares; because a partnership cannot exist without being distributed in understanding, except in the case of a Leonine partnership, unless the act is such that each is bound for the whole (*insolidum*), or unless they are administered by one person, as stated in D. 35.2.1 (*In legato Falcidia hoc observandum*) and D. 14.3.1 (*Ne in plures*). For when one person is the procurator of several, and the matter is conducted indivisibly, and the partnership is administered by that procurator for the whole (*insolidum*), he can bind each person for the whole in the name of any one of them.

Consider, therefore, either we are in a case where each is bound for his share, and discussion of the other is not required; because action is not brought against his share, nor can it be brought, as stated in D. 44.7.1 (*Reos*), § *Cum tabulis*. Or we are in a case where each is bound for the whole (*insolidum*). And then, either insofar as one does not act as surety for the other, but promises for himself, and the same applies; or insofar as he acts as surety. And then there are opinions: one that discussion is necessary to the extent that the other is not necessary, because they would not be properly said to act as sureties, since they are equally principal debtors.

Consider that Titius and Seius can be situated in this manner: that Titius is bound for the whole (*insolidum*) principally for himself, and for Seius as a surety, as stated in C. 5.30.1 (*Romanus*). Furthermore, he can constitute himself as principal for himself, and as principal for another; however, a procurator cannot do this unless he has a special mandate for this purpose, as stated in D. 2.14.1 (*In personam*), § *Qui pecuniam*, and D. 50.17.1 (*Si*).

† Moreover, the term “pro” signifies accession: although one may say, “I constitute myself principal for such a person.” But when an obligation is contracted by two debtors, not by way of accession, he who is bound as principal is not bound as accessory; this is of no concern to the creditor. However, among themselves, several persons bound jointly and severally may well perform mutual offices of suretyship, so that he to whom the business principally pertains is called the debtor, and the other the surety; as in C. si cert. pe. l. si non singuli; and subtly noted in ff. ad leg. Falcid. l. vir uxori, §. fin.; and ff. de his qui non sunt in potestate, l. furti, §. qui alieno; and ff. de pactis, l. fideiussores; and l. si unus, in principio; and l. 1, §. 1, C. de duobus reis. Therefore, the hypothec of one equally principal debtor has nothing in common with the hypothec of the other; and their offers [of payment] are distinct among themselves, as in l. si plures, ff. de pactis. And thus, from one of the separated debtors, no impediment arises against the other, since the creditor may choose; as in ff. de mandato, l. creditor, in principio; and noted in C. de pactis, l. si creditores. This is held by Jacobus de Belvisis in the Authenticum de fideiussoribus; and the reason is manifest, since the one who acts must cede his rights; if he were required to exhaust the debtor, he would never be required to cede the action, unless it were empty due to the debtor’s insolvency; which is ridiculous to say, that only an empty action is to be ceded, and not a full and valid one. See C. de collationibus, auth. quod locum; and ff. de pactis, l. nisi; and ff. de solutionibus, l. stichum, §. mandato. Therefore, exhaustion pertains to the possession of the rights ceded to him; because the benefit of cession of actions should suffice for him to whom rights are to be ceded, not for the one ceding them. See ff. qui potior in pignore habeantur, l. mulier. Finally, it may be said in this case that exhaustion is not necessary, because it is not provided for by any law; and on this point is the ordinary gloss in the Authenticum de fideiussoribus, in principio, in the gloss. Note the difference at the end of the gloss, where it says thus: “This end of the gloss applies when one is bound after another; otherwise, if several are bound simultaneously and jointly and severally, because then they would be two debtors.” Indeed, no one is compelled to sue two debtors before reaching the possessors of the pledges of one; since it is free for the creditor to sue one and not to sue the other. And the end of that gloss was an addition. This opinion is also proven by the text, because it says that three accessory persons are to be exhausted: the surety, the mandatary, or one who promises for another; see ff. de pactis, l. in persona, §. qui pecuniam. But a co-debtor, bound principally and jointly and severally for himself, is not accessory, since he is principal for himself and jointly and severally towards the creditors; as in the aforementioned l. generaliter. And therefore, he is not among those three enumerated persons, nor among similar ones bound by more abundant caution. And this is especially true in contracts of money-lenders, in which things are done quickly and execution is more prompt, as is the noted text in the aforementioned Authenticum de fideiussoribus, §. argentariorum; whose writings, although private, are considered by general custom as authentic and credible, due to the particular fidelity of merchants and public utility. See ff. de edendo, l. quaedam, §. nummularios. Hence, I conclude that exhaustion is not necessary for equally principal debtors. Argument: ff. de conditione indebiti, l. dominus testamento; and ff. si certum petatur, l. cum fundus, §. 1, so that circuitry may be avoided and the creditor may be assisted without so many detours.

Furthermore, regarding another point, namely the article of presumed fraud, certain doctrine cannot be given; and therefore we resort to arguments, as in ff. de re militari, l. non omnes, §. Lucius; ff. quae in fraudem creditorum; ff. de legatis tertio, l. nomen, §. 1; ff. de donationibus post contractum; and argument from C. de manumis, l. per diversas; and l. ab Anastasio; ff. qui in modum pignoris vel hypothecae solvunt; C. de donationibus antenuptialibus, Auth. sed iam necesse; C. plus valere quod agitur, l. emptione; ff. de aqua pluviali arcenda, argument from l. emptor; C. de pignoribus, l. si; C. de donationibus, l. data iampridem; ff. de acquisitione hereditatis, si is; C. de repudianda hereditate, l. 2; and what is there said by Cynus in the Authenticum de aequalitate, do., §. illud; and on this last point I have written most fully in my counsel, and therefore I do not repeat it.

But I conjecture that fraud has certainly intervened; and especially from the unusual and sudden alienation prima facie of all goods. And because in such fraudulent merchants, fraud is to be presumed; as in the rule semel malus; and l. si qui. That also concerning the foregoing is not to be omitted, that exhaustion is required where goods are notoriously insolvent, and the debtor is in hiding; as is read and noted in ff. de verbis obligatorum, decem; and ff. si certum petatur, l. fin., §. sed si cum Seyo; because exhaustion is empty, which is excluded by the debtor’s insolvency. See l. nam is, ff. de dolo; and noted in C. quando fiscus vel privatus, l. non prius. And this person about whom inquiry is made, according to what is asserted to me, left the city naked [destitute]. Hence, it is notorious in the letter that he is not solvent. See ff. de actionibus emptoris, l. emptorem, in principio; and noted in l. 1, C. qui et adversus quos; and ff. qui satisdare cogantur, l. si vero, §. qui pro rei qualitate.

Moreover, consider that these exhaustions of which the new law speaks correct the old law, as appears in the text of the said Authenticum de fideiussoribus; and where the correction of laws is at issue, there we must be content with the words of the correcting law, and not extend ourselves further. See noted in C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, Auth. quas actiones.

† Another point on which a question may be raised is this: whether a hypothec constituted by a procurator is drawn back to the date of the mandate. And it seems that it is so, because the substance of the obligation itself consists in the mandate. Moreover, this obligation was made on account of a past cause, cf. D. de pign. act. l. si rem, §. si. Furthermore, the mandate perhaps could not be revoked, because it was necessary, cf. D. de acquirenda possessione l. fundi, §. 1. Moreover, this supports both the affirmative and the negative, cf. D. de fideiuss. l. si ut proponitur. To the contrary, that it is not drawn back, is the fact that the time of the contract is considered. Moreover, because then, and not before, the consent of the procurator and the creditor intervened, cf. D. de acquirenda possessione qui absentis, §. 1. Moreover, because it concerns the prejudice of a third party, to whom in the meantime a sale and delivery had been made, cf. D. de solutionibus cum decem, and l. si quis offerenti, and l. si, D. rem ramm habere. Moreover, because this fiction would have no limit, since the thing is then not in the assets of the debtor, cf. D. qui potior in pignore habet l. potior, and l. qui balneum. Moreover, ratihabition, which is equivalent to a mandate, is drawn to the date of the contract; therefore also the mandate. I do not determine this article: because the said Lord has a right in every event, according as it was promised, since he has the hypothec, and not the buyer, and no excussion is necessary; and especially since it is held to be notorious as an excussion.

† I ask whether two equally principal parties appear to stand surety for one another. The question is difficult, for if this were the case, the action on mandate would lie to a greater extent for the one who pays. Which the glossators deny: because they say that a useful action on negotiorum gestio lies; therefore I hold for your part. I answer not on this ground: because I promise for you, but rather because I promise for myself alone: but because it is paid to you by my will, it seems to me to be paid, just as if you were to pay another by my will after counting out the money to me. And therefore I do not have the benefit of discussion against the sureties, nor can I demand that the action be assigned to me by suing the promisor for the whole amount: because I am bound principally, and in my own name only, partly by the actual payment made to me, partly by constructive payment. As in D. de pignoribus, actio, l. solutum, § solutam. Because in my own obligation I am alone, and bound for the whole amount: and the other in his: although one final payment suffices for both obligors. And this serves to clarify the point regarding excussio. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a notary may draw up an instrument in a matter in which he himself is a party.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† A certain document of a certain notary is found to have been made in a matter concerning the notary himself, in which all the requirements for an instrument are present. The question is whether this document is valid or not. And it is said that it is not valid: because the notary must be requested (rogatus), as in the Authentica de tabellionibus, §. nos autem. But no one can request himself: because no one gives a mandate to himself, as in D. de arbitris, l. penultima. Moreover, because no one can act in the capacity of two persons, unless in the name of another, as in D. de pactis, l. si plures. Moreover, because no one can be a judge in his own case, as in C. ne quis in sua causa, l. unica, and D. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, l. qui iurisdictioni. On the contrary, the truth is this: for in matters of voluntary jurisdiction, one can act in an official and private capacity, as is fully read and noted in D. de adoptionibus, l. si consul. And one must stand by one’s own writing against oneself, as in D. de testamentis tutorum, l. ex sententia, vers. nec admittendum, and D. de contrahenda emptione, l. non putavit, §. si quis sua manu. Moreover, in this instrument all that ought to be present is present: as appears from the instrument itself, as in the Authentica ut praeponatur nomen Imperatoris, in principio, and noted in C. de tabulariis, l. generali. Moreover, the notary’s sign is there, as noted in Inst. de publicis iudiciis, and C. de assessoribus, l. finalis. Nor does it matter that he was not requested: because rather he was requested by the contracting party with him. And it suffices sometimes that one of the contracting parties request the notary, as the gloss notes in the said §. nos autem. Moreover, since a written document intervenes, the presence of the parties is presumed, and all things are presumed to have been done solemnly, as in Inst. de inutilibus stipulationibus, §. si scriptum; C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione, l. 1; D. de verborum obligatione, l. sciendum, with its common material. From these it follows that the said instrument, as a public one, is to be followed and observed in its effects. Nor does it matter that the said document is not written on parchment, but on paper. For even on paper can a public document be written, as says the Speculum, and it is proved in l. 1, in principio, D. de bonorum possessione secundum tabulas. However, I advise that it be first inquired whether it is in his own hand or not. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What the plaintiff in a hypothecary action is required to prove.
2. Present possession is stronger than past possession when it is a matter of presuming possession.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The facts appear to be as follows: a certain B. sold a certain house, mentioned in the records, to a certain P. of Lausanne for fifty gold florins in the year of our Lord 1383. Then, in the year of our Lord 1388, he sold it, together with John of Brescia, to another certain P. of Fabriano for the price of 25 gold florins. And it is true, as appears from the records, that the said P., the second buyer, sold the said house to a certain F. Malacarne for the price of 37 gold florins in 1388. Furthermore, it is true that a certain Lady Catherine, wife of Peter of Lausanne, had all the goods of the said Lord P. of Lausanne bound by dotal instruments. Furthermore, it is true that the said Lady, another wife of Francis, as heir of the said F., possesses the said house, against which the said Lady Catherine, wife of the late Pe. of Lausanne, brings a hypothecary action, alleging that the said house is bound for the amount contained in the dotal instrument; conversely, the said Lady Catherine, being sued, contends that the said house has come to her. Now the question arises: what is the law? Having seen and considered the records and proceedings in the case: namely, whether the said Lady Catherine, being sued, ought to be condemned regarding the said hypothecary action, or absolved. And we shall not err if we base our argument on the rules of law.

† It is established, indeed, that the plaintiff in a hypothecary action must prove that the debt subsists, that the thing is subject to hypothec by agreement or by law, and that the thing itself remained in the debtor’s assets at the time of the obligation; for these matters are expressly required to be proven. D. de probat. ante omnia; and see the note in Speculum, de obligationibus et solutionibus, § 1, under the words “but what must the creditor prove in a hypothecary action.” Furthermore, it must be premised that when a hypothecary action is brought against a third-party possessor, it must be proven that the thing was in the debtor’s assets in such a manner that the Publician claim for recovery of the thing, or some other similar remedy for defeating possession, would have been available to the debtor himself; for example, the condictio ex lege, as in D. si coloni, de agris et censibus, Book 11, or the officium iudicis, as in D. de condictionibus furtivis, l. et ideo, § Neratius. This rule, insofar as it pertains to the petitory action, is proven by the well-known rule in D. de pignoribus, l. si ab eo. As for the possessory action, it is proven by the points noted with great subtlety by Jacobus de Arena and Cynus in C. si res aliena pignori data sit, l. cum res.

It must also be premised for clarity that when a thing is sold to two persons by the same vendor, the thing becomes part of the assets of the person to whom it is first delivered, as stated in C. de rei vindicatione, l. quotiens; and this is fully read and noted in D. de publiciana, l. sine autem, § si duobus. For the incorporation of a thing into another’s assets regularly requires delivery, or quasi-delivery, as in D. de rei venditione, l. si ager; C. de pactis, l. traditionibus. And if it is delivered to no one, the thing is in no one’s assets, but only a personal action exists, which is not granted against a third-party possessor, because a personal action does not follow the land. D. ad Trebellianum, l. 1, § haeres; C. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. eum.

Let us therefore proceed through the records. For I do not find it proven by the acts of the case that the said P. de Losana possessed the said house at any time, nor was it alleged that he did so by virtue of the said title, as in D. de publiciana, l. eum qui, § pen. For the presumption in l. 2, C. de acquirenda possessione, is rebutted by proof, but not by mere assertion. Moreover, it does not appear to be proven that the house was in the possession of the said Franceschinus before the said P. de Losana, except by one witness, which is insufficient in cases of grave prejudice, especially since an oath was not demanded in default of proof, as in C. de testibus, l. iusiurandum, in fine. And that one witness is noted as unreliable, nor does he testify regarding the priority of possession. It therefore necessarily follows that it is not proven that the said house was in the assets of the said Peter de Losana. Consequently, the said Catherine, formerly his wife, fails in her proof regarding this article, namely that the thing was in the assets of the said Peter de Losana. And therefore, assuming that the said Catherine, the plaintiff, had a right in truth—but this is merely conceded, since it does not appear to be proven—the rule of law applies that when the plaintiff fails to prove his case, the defendant is absolved.

† Moreover, concerning possession to be presumed, present possession is preferred over past possession: because present possession is established by truth, whereas the other is not; see the noted provision. C. de edict. diui Adria. Tol. l. edicto. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Having the authority to execute the instruments of a deceased notary, whether he may extend something without citing the parties. It is clear that the laws agree with the laws. I, Baldus.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. There are two statutes in the city of Lucca. In the first, it is provided that if any draft of a deceased notary, which was not public, or had some defect and could be challenged, such that faith ought not to be given to said draft, said draft may and must be examined by the Vicar of the Lord Podesta and the consuls of the college of judges of the city of Lucca, and four notaries of the same city to be chosen by the Lord Vicar and the consuls of the college of judges. Each of whom notaries must be at least thirty years of age. And if, after diligent examination, it shall seem to them, or to the Lord Vicar and two parts of the others, provided that the consent of at least one judge-consul accedes, that faith ought to be given to such draft: the notary having authority to reduce the rogation and protocols of such deceased notary into public form may and must succeed to the instruments from said draft, and reduce them into public form, and full faith shall be given to said draft thus approved, and to the instrument taken therefrom. And this statute is in the 3rd book of statutes. Then in the 4th book follows such statute: And if any writing in public form is produced, which does not contain the day, or the month, faith shall not be given to it, except in the acts of the court, or of arbitrators, and public writings from the public archive, notwithstanding which, faith shall be given to them in the same manner. It happened that in a certain file of notarial drafts, or protocols, was found a certain draft without day and month: in which file was a certain preceding draft of another matter, in which the year, indiction, month, and day were written by the hand of the same notary. After the said draft had been examined, approved, and adjudicated by the Lord Vicar of Lucca, of the Podesta, and the consuls of the college of judges, and four notaries elected by them according to the form of the aforesaid statute, with the sentence that faith ought henceforth and in the future to be given to said draft, ordering it to be reduced into public form. To which sentence and process made concerning said draft, the intestate heirs were cited: but they were poor by nature, heirs instituted by Christ. Finally, from said draft a public instrument was taken.

† It is asked whether the said schedule proves, or not. And it seems that the said instrument, taken from the said schedule, proves: because since the said schedule ought to be the foundation of the instrument, and the schedule itself is void and empty, especially due to the defect of day and month according to the common law, as in Auth. ut praepona, no. impera, § 1, and C. de tabulis, l. generali, lib. 10, with its matter, faith ought not to be given to the said writings; because from the invalid cannot follow the valid; and because the force of the copy is from the original, as C. de edendis, Authen. si quis in aliquo documento. To the same effect is the later statute, of which I spoke. On the contrary, it seems: because in the notarial acts of a deceased notary, having some defect, power has been given to the said officials to approve such writing and to impose upon it full and perpetual faith. Thus the words say, or having some defect, etc., whence they speak indefinitely of some defect, namely, one not of its substance. For the indefinite is equivalent to the universal, as fully noted by Dy. in rub. de regulis iuris, lib. 6, with its common matter. Nor is it strange if, on account of the death of the notary, the statute introduces more abundant provision than when the notary is living, because sudden deaths often befall men who, if they were living, could perform the solemnities. Argument from C. de inofficioso testamento, l. 3. Moreover, faith is sometimes given to a private writing, although it does not contain the day and the consul, as ff. de pignoribus, l. cum tabernam, § idem quaesivit. Moreover, although this writing does not have the beginning of the day and the consul, because the schedule of the unsealed document has no continuity, nor is it something concrete with this, nor is it even a code having consequence, nor the same business, and altogether different. And from one of the separated things argument is not drawn to another. And thus we are outside l. si quis ex argumento, § si initium tabularum, ff. de edendis. Nevertheless, since there is a sentence, and there was no appeal, the sentence shall be held for truth, as ff. de regulis iuris, l. res iudicata. But what is it, that the heirs of the writer were not cited, and therefore the said sentence does not prejudice them, as noted by the doctors in d. Authen. si quis in aliquo documento, although the ordinary gloss says that citation is not required, C. de re iudicata, l. gesta. But this defect can be supplied by asking anew that the said writing be examined, as it was from the beginning, and by citing the poor to all these things, as C. quomodo et quando iudices, l. si ut proponis, and C. de accusationibus, l. absentem. Whence I think that by virtue of the first statute, these things being done, faith ought to be given to the writing, the form of the said first statute being observed, so that truth rather than legal solemnity may be attended to. Argument from d. § idem quaesivit. The second statute does not obstruct: because it fails in writings of deceased notaries examined and approved as above; because

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If a lender of money states that it is for the benefit of the person whom he will subsequently name or declare, and if he later names and declares that person, whether the person so declared may bring an action for the said money.
2. Whether the power of declaration is transmitted to heirs.
3. Assignment is not valid beyond the legitimate sum.
4. The exception of intent and of fact may always be raised by anyone.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Vanninus of Assisi confessed that he had received and taken from Martin three thousand pounds as a loan from the personal funds of the said Martin, for the benefit and advantage of the person whom the said Martin would name, whom he could name at any time; with the condition added that the said Martin could not be paid nor released by him, but finally only to and by him who was declared the creditor in the said amount. It happened that, after the death of the said Vagnolo, the said Martin declared that the payment had been made for the benefit and advantage of Guidon, who at the time of the said contract was under the paternal authority of the said Vagnolo, his father.

† It is asked whether the said Guido, by virtue of the said contract of nomination and declaration, has the right to bring an action, or not. And it seems that he can bring an action: because in a loan for consumption (mutuum) it is a special rule that an action is sought for one person through another, as in the law *Certi condictio*, § *Si nummos*, D. *Si certum petatur*. Moreover, the notary, as a public person, made a stipulation, as in D. *De adoptionibus*, law *His verbis*, by which at least a useful action is sought without any cession. And if it is said that an action cannot be sought for a son in power against his father, as in D. *De actionibus et obligationibus*, law *Actiones cedi*, that must be understood with regard to the old law; but under the new law, on account of an adventitious cause, an action can indeed be sought for a son, as in C. *De bonis quae libris*, law *Cum oportet* and law *Non solum*, even if the exercise [of the action] did not lie due to paternal power, as in D. *De iudiciis*, law *Lis nulla*; but after the paternal power has ended, the exercise lies well, as in the law cited above. Furthermore, Vagnolus has reached the time from which he can begin [to act]; hence it does not seem that the impediment of paternal power is to be considered here, neither with regard to the capacity to sue nor with regard to actual exercise, as in C. *De collationibus*, law *Si*.

On the contrary, it seems that the said contract was not valid, for it appears to contain contradictory terms: for it states that the money was that of Martin, and it states that no right is acquired by Martin. For these appear to contradict each other, since this contract was not a natural loan for consumption, but a civil one, from which it is clear that first an action must be sought for the stipulator directly, otherwise the contract would not be valid, as in D. *De actionibus et obligationibus*, law *Quaecunque gerimus*: "unless it takes its beginning in our person, they render our act void." Moreover, this pact was added with the consent of Vagnolus, by which he cannot bind himself civilly for a son in his power, as in D. *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, law *Frater a fratre*. For it is certain that either the loan did not intervene, and the contract is simulated, and no action can be brought; or the loan truly intervened, and then Vagnolus immediately became owner of the money paid to him, as in D. *Si certum petatur*, law 2, § *Appellata*, and immediately the money was profectitious [property] of the father himself, and did not leave his ownership. And it is certain that profectitious property cannot be owed by the father to a son in power, so that any action arises; for the case is in the aforementioned law *Frater a fratre*. And this reason seems demonstrative. And if it is said that that specific money is not owed, but only an equivalent amount in kind, I answer that an equivalent amount in kind is not owed, nor anything in that regard; for that specific item is represented in the generic kind and acts in its place, as in the aforementioned law 2 and law 1, in the same title. For even in the law *Frater a fratre*, an obligation in kind is contracted, because it is an obligation of a loan for consumption; and yet no obligation is contracted, except a natural one only.

A third reason is: because this declaration has the force of a certain kind of compromise, which expires upon the death of the compromitter, as in D. *De arbitris*, law *Non distinguimus*, in the principal part. The words "by himself and his heirs" do not obstruct this; for they refer to the word "promised," not to the word "compromised." Hence the sense is that, if it is declared at a suitable time, he himself and his heir are bound to observe the declaration, not that this declaration can be made after death, as in D. *De operis libertatis*, law *Qui libertinus*, § *Posthumus*, and law *Bonorum*, D. *Rem ratam habere*.

A fourth reason is: because this declaration pertains to the substance of the contract. For it is of the substance that the person to whom [rights] are acquired be certain. But when some commission is made, or when someone is given discretion regarding the substance of the contract, this person must arbitrate or declare within a year. After a year, however, the declaration pertains to the adversary. Hence, after the year had elapsed, Vagnolus was obliged to declare the person for whom the instrument was received, as in C. *Commune de legatis*, law *Si*.

† Martinus, however, could not make this declaration, since the power had been transferred to another, according to Bartolus, because so elegantly it is noted in l. si, §. j., comm. deleg. and ff. de verb. oblig. l. si quis arbitratu. And if you say that said l. si speaks of a last will, otherwise in contracts, I answer that this distinction is false, because it is not proven by law. For the law says that contracts and testaments are equated, as ff. de leg. j. l. servum filii, §. eum qui chirographum. Moreover, the discretion for a year should more strongly endure after a year in a last will than in a contract, because it is a matter of greater favor. Therefore, the authority to declare and choose should more readily be extended. But it is so that in a last will it is not extended; therefore, neither in contracts. Moreover, the heir is bound by quasi-contract. Therefore, we come to contract, as ff. de iud. l. omnem. Wherefore the opinion of Bartolus is the very truth, if a year and a year have elapsed, and Vagnolus has died and declared nothing. Therefore, the contract falls to the void, as C. de contrah. empt. l. fin. Moreover, it is also to be observed here. Either the said money lent was not the lender’s, but Guido’s; and this is contrary to the tenor of the instrument. And thus from the instrument one could not act, because it would be to allege contraries, as l. 1, C. de furt. Or the money was the lender’s own; and then either Guido wishes to act as a simple person added to receive payment, and as a bare minister; and he cannot act to obtain the said quantity and to reimburse himself, but finally for the benefit of the heirs, says the lender, and with their consent, as ff. de verb. oblig. l. Iulianus, §. j. Or he wishes to act as one added with the intent of giving; and then the donation was null by the law itself, beyond the sum of the law or statute; because insinuation is of the substantial form of the donation, or at least accidental.

† and therefore if rights are ceded with the intention of making a gift, the cession itself is invalid by law beyond the legitimate portion. The objection does not hold: ff. de don. l. ut mihi donares; for there the party employed did not have a lucrative cause. And that this is a gift is most certain: because no other cause appears: as is fully stated and noted in ff. sol. ma. l. quae dotis. Someone might say, this M. did all this as a negotiorum gestor of the aforementioned person to be named. I answer, let it be so: nevertheless, even assuming this, a gift results, which requires insinuation. Moreover, the matter had not yet reached the stage of delivery, but remained at the boundaries of obligation. Hence the defendant can raise the exception of nullity of the contract: because he does not raise an exception based on the right of a third party, but on the lack of right of the actor; and properly it is not an exception, but nullity.

† Moreover, the exception of fact and intent may always be raised by anyone, as is stated and noted by Cynus in the Code, *De servis fugitivis*, in the law *Cum servum*, because it uproots and annuls the foundations of the plaintiff and renders them less true. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a confession made by a wife to her husband during the subsistence of the marriage, that the dowry instrument was simulated, and fortified by the wife’s oath, is valid or not; and whether the oath produces any effect.
2. Whether an oath and its effect is extinguished with the person who swore it, or whether it binds the heirs; whether a contract between husband and wife is confirmed by an oath.
3. The substance of such a thing is presumed to be of the same quality as its appearance and surface.
4. What absolute ablative phrases denote.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Regarding the question whether a confession made by a wife to her husband during the marriage, that the dowry instrument was simulated, and fortified by the wife’s oath, is valid or not; or whether the oath has any effect: it must be known that either the dowry instrument has a presumption in its favor, or it has a clear and valid payment: if indeed the woman bases her claim on a presumption, or a fictitious payment, as in C. de dot. cau. l. fin., then a confession in writing made to the contrary overcomes such presumption. C. de non num. pec. l. generaliter. And this is true, assuming equal standing of the persons and times: and because both were before the marriage or both during the marriage, since the power of opposites is equal, that which is later prevails, i.e., that which was most recently done. But if the woman or her heir bases her claim on an actual payment, then such a confession, which is therefore against the right of dowry and so that the woman remains without dowry, is not valid. C. si dos constantemat. l. j. Nor can this be induced by the husband, because it is considered contrary to public law: because public law and public utility are said to be involved in dowries. ff. sol. mat. l. j. And therefore it cannot be infringed by private agreements. And this is according to civil law, as noted in ff. de iur. do. l. si prdium. But according to canon law, it seems otherwise, extra de iureiur. c. mulieres.

† And although the oath is extinguished with the person who swears it, nevertheless the effect of the oath is not extinguished, namely, the validation of the act validated by the oath. As in the Authentica *De iureiurando a morte praestando*, after the principle; and in the Digest, *De legatis tertio*, law *Cum quis decedens*, section *Codicillo*. And thus, by reason of law, it appears that proof is made against the heir of the one who swore, and firmness is given to the sworn act, so that it cannot in any way be contravened, neither by the one who swore nor by his heir. Argument: law *Nam et postea*, section *Finis*, Digest, *De iureiurando*. Bartolus also says,

† That a contract not permitted between husband and wife, such as a donation, is permitted and effective upon the addition of an oath. D. de fideiussoribus, l. si quis pro eo, in principio, in its last member. But with all due respect, he disposed of this argument too hastily. For since the law prohibits consent on account of the public good, so that marriages may not be venal, and [so that they] may have perpetual concord in themselves, the oath operates for nothing. As noted by Cynus, C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, l. 1, in the end, although he does not explain it well. And even if it were valid, it ought to be relaxed by the bishop; because natural equity suggests that it be relaxed. But wherever an oath is made, no relaxation is expedited for the heir; because the oath is personal and pertains to the person swearing. X. de iureiurando, c. veritatis. And according to Innocentius, and I consider this opinion more true, in favor of marriages and dowries. D. de legibus, l. assiduis; C. qui potior in pignore habeatur; D. de legibus, l. si quis inquilinus, §. si; and C. ad Velleianum, Auth. si qua mulier. And especially in the lands of the Empire, in which natural equity and the public good are more strongly gathered against the oath. Now applying this to the matter at hand. It must be known that the dowry instrument attests to the payment already made. Therefore, it appears that the true payment of the dowry preceded, and was not simulated. As noted, C. si certum petatur, l. si ex pretio; C. de non numerata pecunia, l. si ex cautione. And thus the contrary confession appears false, and not true, nor is it to be followed in the judicial path of courts, unless other presumptions were present. For sometimes the payment appears superficially false; yet it is criminally and effectively null. D. de solutionibus, l. qui si sic soluit. Nevertheless, in doubt, that which appears is presumed to be. C. de probationibus, l. cum precibus.

† Such. It is presumed that the substance is of the same quality as the quality and the surface: and it is presumed that the invisible is such as that which is figured to be present through the visible. As in the laws *Pediculis*, *Neratius*, and *Si quando* in the Digest, *De auro et argento legato*. And it appears that he does not attest to the counting: because he speaks demonstratively to the eye of the senses, not enunciatively to the eye of the intellect. For an enunciation is sometimes false. Often, indeed, a written statement is enunciative of some act as if past, and commemorative of something non-existent. But a demonstrative writing, which demonstrates to the eye, is such as when he said to note the place and time of the execution of the instrument, that the counting had intervened. And the delivery, which is also made visibly. In the Digest, *De solutionibus*, law *Si pecuniam*: one does not presume to attest except the truth.

† Therefore, those ablative cases of *dante* and *numerante*, when uttered with the present tense or present place — because he said “then” or “there, while counting” — denote a true act. But when uttered absolutely, referring to a determined past, in the pluperfect, such as “confessed that he had received and had from such a person giving and counting, etc.,” they do not signify an act being performed, but rather declare an act already done. The conclusion, unless something else is proved, is in favor of the woman; however, presumptive proof to the contrary would not be valid by itself, but only when joined with the confession, which by itself is invalid; nevertheless, taken together they carry weight. Argument: Extra, de successionibus ab intestato, c. Cum dilectus. Add that the same was formally advised by Consilium 398, in the second part, beginning “Super eo,” etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether posthumous children are included if the testator said, "I give a guardian to my sons who need a guardian."
2. A minor under guardianship is not properly called such before he is born.
casus: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The case is as follows: Titius, having two underage sons kept under his paternal power, made a will, in which he instituted his said sons as heirs and appointed guardians for them in this form: namely, “To my sons who need a guardian, I appoint Martin as guardian and leave him.” After the will was made and the testator died, a posthumous child was born. The question is whether the said Martin is considered to have been appointed guardian for this posthumous child, just as for the other sons born during the testator’s lifetime.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Those words “who need a guardian” are to be referred to the time of the testator’s death, not to the time of the will, and this is because of the nature of a last will, which requires death to follow. And because of the nature of guardianship, a ward who, while his father is alive, stands in his father’s power, does not need a guardian. Indeed, it is impossible for one who is in another’s power to have a guardian, as in the Institutes, De tutoribus, l. Et quod. And that these words of the present tense, i.e., are to be referred to the time of death, is clearly proved in the Digest, De testamento tutorum, l. Tutoribus. This, therefore, is the meaning: I appoint a guardian for my sons who, at the time of my death, will need a guardian. Hence, a guardian is also seen to be appointed for posthumous children, who were born after the will was made but before the testator’s death, as in the Institutes, Qui datis tutoribus possunt, §. Qui filiabus. And note in l. Quia filiabus, in principio, De legibus. And perhaps even for those born after death, so that the word “need” is extended even to those who were in the womb of the wife at the time of the testator’s death. And such persons need a guardian at least in hope. And one who is in the womb is considered as born when it concerns his benefit, as in the Institutes, De tutoribus, §. Cum autem; Facit, De negotiorum gestione, l. Cum pater; Digest, Ad Tertullianum, l. 2, §. Quod si cum praegnans. But this is not without doubt, because of the strict nature of words of the present tense, as in l. Si ita, De auctoritate; and see the argument in Legibus, l. Si cui, §. Si vero.

† Properly speaking, one who is in the womb is not a ward, because he is not yet a person before he is born. L. si, de assignatione liberorum et testatorum. And the testator said, “to those who are wards and need a tutor.” But this one, who was born first, if he was not a ward after the death of the testator, nor did he need a tutor immediately upon the testator’s death. Hence, the proper and strict nature of these words greatly contradicts this; as if the testator had said, “I appoint a tutor for my sons born at the time of my death,” because posthumous children born after death are not included, as in L. Gallus, §. matre, de legibus vel de liberis et posthumis, and ff. de verbis significandis, L. non est pupillus. But the gloss there says that one who is in the womb is not a ward, yet it interprets him as such. In the same title, in L. intelligenda. Hence, since in wills a broad and benevolent interpretation is made, which is called the intent (mens), ff. de verbis significandis, L. quisquis mihi, and considering the equal reason of paternal piety toward the one born and the one to be born, hence the first opinion is stronger in law. Nevertheless, I do not firmly hold this, because I do not know if I was consulted on this matter on other occasions, and therefore I affix my seal. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The law, however harsh it may be, must be observed.
2. How a law disposing of successions is to be considered.
3. When a mother is excluded from succession by virtue of a statute on account of agnates, how the distinction of the sex of the agnates is to be made.
4. The reason why the mother is in a worse condition than the aunt.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Regarding the preceding question, I consider three points in this statute. First, the restriction of the mother to alimony, and the exclusion from the inheritance and succession, and the certain persons expressly named in the statute; and this is the first point, and this is not our case. Second, a certain limitation of the mother succeeding, and a reduction to a small portion according to some universal succession expressly stated, so that the law speaks loosely and impersonally of the remaining part in which the mother does not succeed. And in this second point our question stands: whether the aunt is preferred to the mother, and entirely. Third, further down in the chapter of the statute, I consider another clause which says that if there is any or some relatives on the father's side at least up to the fourth degree, the mother shall not succeed, and that the relative or relatives shall succeed, and be superior in succession. And this chapter of the law seems also to touch our case. The aunt, namely, is the sister of the father within the fourth degree. Therefore, it seems to either restrict the mother, as in the second part of the statute, or exclude her entirely, as in the third part or chapter of the statute. For when there is no doubt in the words, the intention is not added. ff. de legibus 3. ille aut ille. §. cum in verbis. And we must serve the words of the statute. l. 1. §. si is qui navem. de exercitoribus.

† And the law, although harsh, must be observed. L. *Prospexit*, Qui et a quibus. And although the law introduces a great defect, L. *Tamen debet seruari*, it must nevertheless be observed, until the defect of the ancient law is corrected by the legislator, as in L. *Maximum vitium*. Although it befits the legislator to be a patron of equity, as in C. *De pac. conuen.*, L. *Hac lege*. Nevertheless, on account of unwritten equity or humanity, we cannot depart from the text, L. J., FF. *De legibus*, L. J.; nor from its general determination, FF. *De publicis*, L. *De pretio*; FF. *De alea*, L. J., § *Quod autem*. And in those matters which are expressly written against universal reason, we cannot follow a reason that is nonexistent or slender, FF. *De legibus*, L. *Quod vero*, and the argument of L. J., FF. *De constitutionibus principum*. But these are superficial points.

† For this law must be considered differently: for sometimes the law disposes of succession by conferring it upon a certain class of persons, or upon certain degrees. And then those named by the law succeed, while others, as though passed over, do not succeed. For passing over by law is equivalent to disinheritance; for the inclusion of those expressly and specifically mentioned is the exclusion of those omitted. C. de secun. nup. l. 1; C. de ince. nup. l. si quis incesti; C. de bo. dam. Auth. bona damnatorum; Inst. de legi. agna. succ. §. quod ad foeminas. Sometimes the law disposes of succession privatively: for example, that the mother shall not succeed; and then it is necessary to inquire into the reason of the law, even if tacit, in a privative disposition. For wherever the law prohibits, the reason of the law must be inquired into, lest the precept appear naked; and the tacit reason is held as if expressed. As in D. de re mili. l. miles agrum. Therefore, sometimes the law deprives the mother because she has offended against that piety upon which the reason and cause of succession are founded: for example, because she did not seek a guardian for her underage son; then she is deemed to have called all the others in order of degree, and finally the fisc. And if no one accepts, the goods are vacant, and according to the heir. As in D. ad Tert. l. 1, §. videm dum. Sometimes the law does not deprive the mother on account of a delict, but under another consideration. For without a consideration there is no privative law, as I said. Ar. l. filius, §. diui, D. de leg. 1; C. de fideicomm. quot. And this consideration cannot be founded on hatred, because the mother has not deserved it. Ar. D. de condi. inde. l. qui exceptionem. For an exception is not called odious unless when the creditor deserves the protection of the law. So here. Therefore, the reason will be the favor of the agnates. For from the very origin of the laws, when only the law of the Twelve Tables commanded all, the same was the case; therefore, senatorial consultations were necessary in this matter, and the edicts of the praetors. As in Inst. ad Tertu. in prin.; and the new constitutions of the princes. As in Auth. de hęre. ab intest. §. ex his.

But concerning which agnates, whether all of them or only males, so that a distinction of sex is made, here lies our question. For in the second part of this statute, which limits the mother to a fourth part, no mention or distinction of sex is made: and that which is gathered from tacit understanding seems to be written with regard to the matter itself. And thus this Florentine prudence will for the most part be consonant. L. 12. Tab. Moreover, a certain rough and lay equity seems to hold that goods should return to the stock from which they flowed. C. de bonis quae lib. quod scitis. But against this it seems that it should be understood as referring to agnates of the male gender. And this is derived from the conjunction of two chapters of the same law. Arg. de lib. et posthum. I. Gallus. §. ille casus indifficilis. For in the third chapter of the statute it is provided that the mother shall not succeed if there is any one, or some persons. And one must even descend to grammatical details. For sometimes [the term] is of the masculine gender, and in this matter, as in a matter differing according to the reason of the masculine toward its feminine privilege: because in the feminine sex, the same reason of privilege and favor is not found. Hence, if the statute says: agnates exclude the mother, this is not extended to women, but follows males and not females. D. de reg. iur. l. quo tutela. And more to the point is what is said and noted in the title Qui sive. D. de poss. §. hoc autem. in fine, the great gloss. And to this effect, what is noted C. de serv. fug. quisquis, by Cynus de verborum sign. l. 1, by Dyacum with similar authorities. And although it says "any one" or "some persons," and this ablative "some persons" is of every gender, and thus seems to include equally and principally male, female, and neuter, as is noted D. de reg. iur. in rub. and in l. 1, nevertheless, because it precedes with the masculine by saying "any one," and not saying "any one or any one [female]," it is understood as a transition to the plural number, but not to another sex; for the statute retains its proper reason, in whatever number it speaks. D. de neg. gest. l. 3. de verborum sign. in usu iuris. And to this effect is what follows, the conjunction "or" [vel], for it speaks in the masculine, which in this case does not extend to females. But against this it is argued: because this statute wishes doubtful words to be interpreted by custom, therefore it will be interpreted by itself. Arg. de iud. l. si quis intentione ambigua. But to this I answer that this power is restricted to persons whom the statute favors, not to others. D. de iure cod. l. quia omnes referunt. D. de in diem adiec. l. si praedio. The third case is when the statute has two certain and clear extremes: because it includes some, it excludes others; then the included exclude [the others], as in Auth. de haer. et fal. §. si quis autem non in plures. and §. exhaeredatos. de contrah. l. 1. and l. 3. §. si emancipa. C. de leg. haer. l. 12. Tab. Conclusively, however, in our question it must be seen how the said statute was previously understood and practiced. And that which has prevailed for a long time must be observed. D. de leg. minime. si non apparet qua interpretatione civitas usa fuerit. The last argument in favor of the mother is that the laws do not permit her to be excluded by conjecture. As l. precibus. with its material. A benign interpretation ought to be made, even in statutes. D. de leg. l. benignius. And the common intention of prudent citizens is presumed to be such, and the statute is presumed to be such as it ought to be, if those named had been interrogated at that time. And it is probable that in this case they would have provided for the mother. Arg. de pact. tale pactum. in fine.

† Wherefore. The reason that the mother ought to be in a worse condition, and the aunt in a better one, cannot be incurred: namely, what substantial and good reason is there, in which the law is defrauded? 4. There will be, however, many probable arguments in succession for the mother, and many arguments make for her. It is true, however, that the statute is very pregnant, and it would be safer to compose amicably than to choose boldly in difficult passages in law. This difficulty depends on the fact that the reason of the statute is not expressed in the statute. Moreover, the reason is not of the substance. L. ff. de legibus. L. non omnium. And for the justification of the statute, the equity of laymen suffices. As C. ut universalis ex vic. L. j. lib. 12. And this argument is taken there by Andreas de Barulo. And although the third clause speaks in the masculine gender, it speaks as to the total exclusion of the mother, which does not happen through a female, unless through the sole sister, joining the third chapter of the statute with the first. But as to reducing the mother to a fourth part, it seems sufficient for any agnate without distinction of sex, because the determination of the statute is general. ff. de militum testamento. L. in fraudem. §. fin. I doubt much in this question. S. concerning the understanding of the statute: because natural reason, which is certain and undoubted reason, is held for written law, and written equity. ff. de exceptionibus tutorum. L. scire oportet. §. et si maxime. It is. N. natural reason is the same as natural justice, and prevails over joined reasons, unless we say that the text suffices for us without reason, and we ought not to require more than the legislator requires. And the law is so written, that the mother does not succeed except in a fourth part, etc. Nor is it added when, or how, but it is read simply. And therefore it seems that the friend of the deceased restricts the mother to a fourth portion without the form of the statute, so that the reason of the agnate rather than the cognate is considered, and the favor of the house induces this preference. Thus, and otherwise in another matter of this C. de impositione. L. descr. L. 2. and §. fi. and L. C. de colonis. Illam. and L. maximum vitium. cum similibus. And one reason suffices for excluding, although all others fail. ff. de haeredibus institutis. L. si non lex. And according to reason, the disposition of the law itself suffices, as it was formerly, C. de legibus. Hae. L. lege 12. tabularum. The mother has by herself, etc., nature and the highest equity, and certain conjectures the aunt has for herself, the first figure of words. S. of the statute, to which men cling most tenaciously, especially the unlearned, who seize the greatest part of the world from the intelligent: and whatever is said subtly and acutely, they say it is cunning and caviling, of whose words, however, little care is to be taken, provided that one does not deviate from the path of reason. What, therefore, is finally to be said? Response. Let practice and customary interpretation be preserved, which, if it does not appear, the mother has equity, but the aunt has rudeness. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a bishop may grant a dispensation from an oath without prior examination of the case.
2. An oath to observe the father’s will does not exclude the son from his legitime; however, it does exclude him from the Trebellian portion, unless the legitime was expressly mentioned in the oath.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The vicar of the bishop cannot absolve the swearing party from a lawful oath: because no one can be absolved from an oath without a cause proven by laws or canons. Indeed, the swearing party is compelled to observe the oath, as in Auth. sacra, public, and in c. quamuis, de pace, lib. 6, and de iureiurando, c. licet multos, unless it is proven that the oath was extorted by deceit, fear, or excessive reverence, as stated in the aforementioned Auth. and noted in l. 1, quarum rerum actio non datur. Therefore, if deceit or fraud is not established, the said swearing party, even if a minor, could not be absolved from the oath. However, if force, deceit, or violence is established, then the aforementioned nature applies when the oath is relaxed and the contract is annulled in its substance. Otherwise, where the oath is relaxed solely for the purpose that deceit or violence may be alleged: because then, without knowledge of the cause, the vicar of the lord bishop may relax it, as held by Oldradus in his decisions. What, therefore, is the effect of an oath to observe the father’s will?

† Whether the son thereby loses his legitime: I say that he does not; because by general words, it does not appear that the legitime was intended. But special words are required. C. de inoff. test. l. si quando. §. si oportet. It is otherwise in the case of the Trebellianic portion, where a general promise suffices. As in C. ad leg. Falc. l. si, and in Auth. sed cum testator. And it supports what I note, Gul. de Cu. de trans. l. de his. Therefore, this person could dispose of the legitime by will, but not of the Trebellianic portion, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If the father receives an emphyteusis for himself and his sons, upon the father’s death the sons succeed to the emphyteutic property by right of the contract; otherwise, if he receives it for himself and his heirs.
2. The son does not succeed in the paternal fief unless he is an heir, and number 4.
3. Whether a son may accept his legitime and repudiate the other portion.
4. What is imputed to daughters in the legitime.
5. A confession made in a will is not valid to bind the confessor.
6. What is the effect of accepting the legitime and rejecting the remainder.
7. If a son does not wish to be an heir, whether he succeeds in the fief.
8. A woman who enters upon the inheritance with the benefit of inventory receives the maternal dowry and the debts.
9. Whether a simulated confession made in a will with an oath proves anything.
10. A daughter may be instituted in dowry and in legitime.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Bartholomew, formerly of Philip, states that he received in emphyteusis, for himself and his legitimate sons and heirs, from the Bishop of Ferrara a certain house, etc. Likewise, he held, invested by the Prior of St. Michael of Ferrara, the use of certain lands, stipulating and receiving for himself and his legitimate sons and descendants, etc. I omit the remainder of the statement of facts. And in the first part of the opinion, for the sake of brevity, the question is briefly raised: what right would the daughter and repudiating heir of the father have in the whole? Solution: that she has the right, having accepted her legitime and repudiated the rest of the inheritance. Thirdly, what right she has, having accepted the inheritance for one-half, with the benefit of inventory. Fourthly, what right she has, having accepted the inheritance without the benefit of inventory, having investigated that the mother of the daughter will appear as a coheir in law, and of the others to whom it was left. And for the understanding of what is to be said, etc.

It must be known that sometimes a father received an emphyteutic lease for himself and his heir sons. In the first case, upon the father’s death, the sons succeed to the emphyteutic properties by right of contract, not as heirs; and therefore the benefit accrues to the sons even if they are not heirs. In the second case, the sons do not succeed to the emphyteusis unless they are heirs, because the contract was concluded under such form and quality. D. de verb. oblig. l. Quicunque § Si quis ita; and l. Stipulatio ista § Si quis ita; C. de secundis nupt. Auth. Haec res; in Auth. de non alien. § Emphyteosim; C. fam. ercisc. l. Filiae cuius; C. de inoff. testam. Auth. Unde si parens hoc; Bart. D. de oper. libert. ut iurisiurandi § Si liberi; de verb. oblig. What is said by Bart. regarding the father, although La. de Bel. seems to say that it is sought for the son as heir, and not otherwise, because in doubt the sense appears to be of the son as heir, as noted in D. de pact. l. Si tibi § Si pactus, applies also to emphyteusis.

But in a fief, unless the son is the heir, he does not succeed to the paternal fief, as in column 10, whether the agnate or the son, c. j., both according to Jacobus de Belvisio and according to Bartolus. I in all respects follow Bartolus on this point, because his opinion is confirmed by the aforementioned laws, and concerning these words, see the note in the Speculum de locatione, § nunc aliqua, versions 79 and 113, and version 158, and c. Secondly, as I said, let us see what the law is if this daughter wishes only her legitime, and this issue is threefold. First, it is asked whether she can accept only the legitime and repudiate the other part, having been instituted as heir to one-half. Secondly, what is imputed to the legitime, i.e., whether these leasehold goods are imputed. Thirdly, what is the effect of accepting the legitime and rejecting the remainder. Where

† As to the first point, it does not seem that an heir can accept in part and repudiate in part. C. de iure delib. l. quidam Clodio; ff. de acquirenda haereditate l. 1. The contrary is true. For when a son is burdened in his own property, and so that he may not be without it, he does not wish to be a universal heir. But he can, however, with respect to the legitime, by analogy with the patron. And on this there is a unique law: ff. de bonis liberti, si libertus patrono, regarding the debt due. And this is a most special and singular case. And thus I heard Bartolus saying in the schools, although he omitted this in his writings in the aforementioned law l. cautum, because he did not say that he accepts the legitime intestate, since he has a coheir who enters upon the inheritance; but this is due from the testament, and by the benefit of the law. C. de inofficiosis testamentis l. scimus. And in the case at hand it is more manifest in this way: because the daughter was instituted in two ways, namely, in a certain quantity, and this amounts to a legacy. Also universally in one-half. It is certain that one can accept a singular bequest and repudiate a universal one. ff. de legatis 2, miles, §. fin.; de legatis 1, qui filiabus, §. fin., with the following law. And if anything is supplied to the said legitime, it is as if she had been instituted in a quantity and not universally; because it is never considered that one has renounced the legitime, unless one renounces it expressly and by name. C. de inofficiosis testamentis l. si quando, §. fin.

† As to the second point, it is certain that the dowry of the daughter is imputed to this legitime, as stated in the Novella *Quamvis*. However, this does not include the maternal dowry, which constitutes a debt (*aes alienum*), as noted in the title *De substantia testantis*, provided that the dowry is clearly established. For the mere confession of the will does not prove a contract binding the confessor, according to *D. De liberatione legatorum*, law *Aurelius*, § *Si*; *C. De non numerata pecunia*, generally according to Cynus; and *D. De legatis primo*, law *Is qui in potestate*, § *Ei qui dotem*; *D. De legatis tertio*, law *Cum quis*, § *Codicillis*, according to Bartolus. Furthermore, I state that in this legitime, emphyteutic rights are imputed, according to *C. De inofficioso testamento*, law *Omnimodo*, § *Si*; *C. De codicillis*, law *Illud*; and by argument from *C. De pignoribus*, law *Si*, and the note by Bartolus in *D. De collatione bonorum*, law *1*, § *Nec castrense*; and by argument to the Falcidian law, with which it agrees at the end.

† As to the third point, I say that this legitime must be had without the burden of the testament, as is stated in the aforementioned law *Scimus*. Although the burden of a contract is stronger than the legitime, unless the contract acceded to the last will, C. ad leg. Falcidiam, l. *In donationibus*, and l. *Papiam*, § *Quarta*; *Cum onere* and *Iura*. Sometimes the legitime is obtained by right, de iure, in the case of a mother, l. *Si cum dotem*, § *Si pater*, according to Laurentius de Arena.
