But we are here dealing with a burden of the testament, which does not fall upon the legitime in the plural. It is read and noted, C. de rei venditione, l. *Cum a matre*; C. de iure deliberandi, l. *Fin.*, § *In computatione*.

† Therefore, I conclude that if this daughter accepts her legitime by title of institution, she succeeds freely in the said fief of houses; and if the value of the houses and dowries exceeds that of the legitime. For, since the word "heir" cannot, by the nature of the thing, refer to an extraneous heir, it necessarily refers to her own. D. ad Trebellianum, l. Ex facto, through the gloss and Doctor, and noted by Cynus; C. de operibus lib., l. Liberti. For nature must be considered. D. de verborum obligatione, l. Ita stipulatus, § Sabinus. And the laws in which the fault of persons is considered do not extend except to capable persons. D. ad Trebellianum; for she is not bound to provide the legacy in the said houses, since she cannot be burdened with that which she does not receive from the last will, but from an irrevocable contract. To this effect, what is noted in D. de legatis tertio, l. Si mulier, in the beginning. But the extraneous coheir shall redeem and pay. D. l. Si libertus; or the universal heir himself shall pay the estimation of the legacy, as in D. de legatis tertio, l. Non dubium, ad legem Falcidiam, Alienus. And this applies to the houses, considering the form of the contract. But regarding the said usufructs, I am more in doubt; for, as I touched upon, universal succession seems to be required. And thus they would follow the extraneous heir; because it is truly hereditary and transmissible right, unless perhaps one were to say that they should be divided per stirpes, according to D. de usufructu accrescendo, l. Si quis Titio, so that the daughter should have one half by title of filiation, and the other half the universal heir by hereditary right. But the preceding opinion seems to be more confirmed by the text in Decretals, Collatio decima, de feudo non habente propriam naturam, caput primum. But there no mention was made of children. This is both for and against, as noted by Bartolus in D. de solutione matrimonii, l. Gaius. And therefore, this article has no small degree of scrupulousness.

† Now let us come to the third main point, namely, if a woman accepts an inheritance with the benefit of inventory. And then it must be said that she is entitled to receive the maternal dowry and the debts owed to the estate. Likewise, her own dowry, which is imputed to her legitime. And these points are clear. Now the doubts raised succeed. For since the emphyteutic right of the church pertains to the daughter, under whatever title of heir, i.e., taken in an improper sense, on account of the nature of the thing itself, etc. I omit here one column, because the writing burdens me, and because it can otherwise be seen in the exemplar.

† In another point, regarding the confession of simulation, I say that the confession must be upheld: because it serves to free [the party], in the Authentica *De testibus*, § *Licet*; and because it was made under oath, in the word of truth, in the Authentica *De iureiurando*, a mo. prae.; and because, in question 2, cause 7, chapter *Quotiens cordis oculus*, *De successionibus ab intestato*, § *Si*; *De liberatione legata*, law *Non solum*, § *Si liberationis verba*; *De legatis tertio*, *Cum quis*, § *Titia*; and § *Codicil.*; and in both places by Bartolus. It is certain that a daughter can be instituted heir to her legitime.

† Therefore, the same applies to one's own dowry which succeeds in place of the legitime, as is noted in § sed vtrum of the law denique in the Digest on the subject of minors. But in that dowry which is not reduced to the understanding of the legitime and lies outside the property of the testator, the institution made is not an institution; because it is not acquired by the benefit of the testament. Argument: § in arrogato, with similar authorities, in the Code. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The wills and legacies of those condemned to death are void and invalid upon the execution of the sentence, both according to civil law and canon law.
2. Whether the confession of a person condemned to death regarding goods unlawfully taken should be upheld so that restitution may be made after his death, provided it is supported by legitimate proof. I, Baldus.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Wills and legacies of those condemned to death, upon the execution of the sentence, are void and invalid both by civil and canon law. D. de testamentis, l. eius qui; and if he were to leave something for his soul, D. de iniustis et omnino nullis testamentis, l. si quis filio, §. irritum, because he who has no property in civil law cannot have an heir or legatee. D. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione, l. lex Cornelia. And this is true regarding a legacy; but as to another debt or obligation between living persons, he may confess and dispose of it. Nor can the fiscus complain, because the fiscus ought not to seize the property of others. C. de poenis fisci, l. 1; D. de iure fisci, quod placuit; Extravagantes de pignoribus, c. ex literis, according to Innocentius.

† If, therefore, he is released before condemnation for the restitution of goods wrongfully taken, this is considered to be more by right of debt than by right of legacy. And therefore it is owed to him to whom it is owed. And omitting arguments, I cite the ordinary gloss in the chapter *Quamquam*, *De usuris*, Book 6, in the Novels; and the gloss begins: *Dominus meus*. And there this question is not fully decided, nor is it found elsewhere in the law. Since, therefore, here he has been released for illicit and wrongfully taken goods, it is presumed to be so: and the fisc must recognize good faith; because this confession is formal, and with cause, and the absence of the creditor of God is filled by the presence [of the debtor], according to the form of the statute. And the argument from *De iudiciis*, *Properandum*, § *Si autem*. But if fraud were proven, it would be otherwise. D. *Ad Senatusconsultum Silanianum*, l. *Si quis in gravi*, in the beginning. Nevertheless, in doubt, fraud is not presumed. As is noted, D. *De probationibus*, l. *Qui fratrem*. Especially where the sword of man and of God is above the head of the dying man; because no one who confesses is presumed to die with a lie and sin. As is noted, Inst. *De iniuriis*, § *Finis*. Furthermore, it supports the statute, which is noted in q. 7, *Quoties cordis oculus*, *De edilitio edicto*, *Quaero*, § *Finis*. And these things are true if he confesses before condemnation. Although after confiscation, his confession is not believed to the prejudice of the fisc, to which a right has been acquired by the sentence of confiscation. Argument from D. *Quomodo et quando ius in re acquiritur*, l. *Si partem*, § 1. But another way would then be to prove the debt

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the provision of laws 1 and 2 of the Codex *Si adversus creditorem* extends by virtue of the statute of Milan concerning prescriptions, so that what was ten years under the common law is reduced by the statute to the limit of
2. years.
body:
In the Name of Christ, Amen. I recall that I was consulted on this statute of Milan, which begins: “Where the common law prescribes ten or twenty years, etc.,” many years ago, and at that time I stated that the statute, by reducing the prescription to ten years, did not encompass the action of the creditors, because he who prescribes a hypothecary right does not prescribe, and because he is the owner, as stated in the Digest, *De usucapionibus*, in the law *Sequitur*, section *Iana*, unless the Wise Men of Milan had interpreted that statute otherwise; for those things which have had a certain interpretation should not be changed, as stated in the Digest, *De legibus*, in the law *Si de impetrata*. But now, since another reason reforms the pact, here I say the contrary, namely that another reason also reforms the contract, which is this: because I feel that it has always been practiced in that illustrious city of Milan, and the said practice is not without reason; for it must be considered that the statute, when it says: “Where the common law prescribes ten or twenty years in immovable and corporeal things possessed with title and good faith, etc.,” because the words of the statute comprehend the one prescribing hypothecarily just as they comprehend the one prescribing ownership and the vindication of the thing. Therefore, consider that in an encumbered thing there are two prescribable rights: one is the right of ownership, or vindication of the thing; the other is the right of pledge, or hypothec; and both rights are in the immovable and corporeal thing, as expressly noted by Cynus in the law *Corruptionem*, in the second question, in the Code, *De usufructu*, and it is supported by the Digest, *De acquisitione possessionis*, in the law *Si quis fundum*, at the end; the law *In noxalibus*, in the Digest, *De noxa*; the Digest, *De damno infecto*, in the law *Eorum*; the Digest, *De pignoribus*, in the law *Pignoris*; the Code, in the same title, in the law *Pignorum*; the Digest, *De legatis* 2, in the law *Meuius*, section *Pe*, in the gloss, *Ordinaria*. If, therefore, considering these rights simply, the right of ownership and vindication of the thing, or the right of pledge and hypothec, is valid, in this respect the statute would not apply, since both rights are incorporeal, and the statute speaks of prescription which runs in immovable and corporeal things possessed with title and good faith. Hence the law would be imposed on words, which is foolish to say. But if you consider the immovable and corporeal thing in which the said rights consist, and thus in the concrete, and not in the abstract, because the said rights in the abstract are nothing, and in this respect prescription is said to run in immovable and corporeal things, and thus the words of the statute equally adapt to the one prescribing hypothecarily as to the one prescribing ownership, or vindication of the thing. And for this reason it is that an external possessor who, with title and good faith, prescribes against the creditor according to the common law, is said to prescribe in immovable and corporeal things. This also appears from the fact that possession and title, which are also required in such prescription according to the common law, as is the text in the laws 1 and 2 of the Code, *Si adversus creditorem*, do not apply to the right of hypothec, but to the immovable and corporeal thing itself which is possessed with title and good faith. For this supports Cynus, *Quibus non obstat longi temporis praescriptio*, in the law *Neque mutui*, in the ratio of itself, and the law *Ait praetor*, section *Item ei qui*, in the Digest, *Ex quibus causis maiores*. And in this opinion was Bartolus, in the Digest, *De usucapionibus*, in the law *Naturaliter*, at the end, where he expressly holds that for one to prescribe against a real action, and thus a hypothecary action, the possession of the prescriber is required. Therefore, because otherwise one cannot be bound by a real right, or be omitted, unless he possesses the thing. And therefore he says that if he ceases to possess the thing, he ceases to be bound or to obstruct; because there is nothing to be prescribed. And thus Bartolus there holds that in this case prescription runs in the thing which is immovable and corporeal; because where being is the cause, non-being is the cause of its contrary, that is, privation; and that which is the cause of being, if it ceases, is the cause of privation. Furthermore, regarding this question, there is a case in the law *Finis*, in the Code, *De praescriptione longi temporis*, 20 or 30 years, which can be subtly examined and induced for this purpose in multiple ways. But this is certain: that incorporeal things are not possessed, as stated in the Digest, *De acquirendo dominio*, in the law *Si servus*, section *Incorpore*; and therefore they are not prescribed by themselves, but together with the immovable and corporeal thing to which they adhere, as stated in the Digest, *De usucapionibus*, in the law *Si aliena*, section *Hoc iure*. And therefore it is that the statute itself, by a point of reason, is understood to comprehend the external possessor of the immovable and corporeal thing prescribing against the hypothecary action; because such prescription runs in the immovable and corporeal thing possessed with title and good faith; which lacking, as I said, prescription does not run. And therefore the Wise Men of Milan do not incongruously practice thus. Moreover, the rights and actions themselves are considered movable or immovable according to the subjects to which they are added and for which they are competent, as stated in the Digest, *De re iudicata*, in the law *Mouentium*, and there noted, and by Dyther in the law *Potest pupillus*, in the Digest, *De auctoritate tutoris*. Again, whether you consider it from the side of the prescriber, the said prescription runs in the immovable and corporeal thing which is possessed with title and good faith, as above; or from the side of him against whom it is prescribed, it still runs in the immovable and corporeal thing, as stated in the Digest, *De evictionibus*, in the law *Si cum venditione*, in the principle; because by the hypothecary action the possession of the immovable and corporeal thing encumbered by hypothec is claimed, as stated in the Digest, *De pignoribus*, in the law *Si fundus*, section *In vendicatione*. For there are two principles of the hypothecary action: one from the side of the possessor sued, which is possession. For possession gives rise to a real action for the adversary or plaintiff, as stated in the law 1 of the Code, *De alienatione iudicii mutata causa facta*; because real indications are not proposed against anyone as against an obligor, as stated in the Institutes, *De actionibus*, section *Omnium*, where the text and gloss. The second is from the side of the plaintiff, and this is that which is immediately secured by the right which the creditor has in the thing, just as other real actions. And therefore in the libel in a hypothecary action instituted, it must be concluded to the thing, for example, that it be restored to me, according to Cynus, Perusinus, and Jacobus de Ravanis, in the law *Finis*, in the Code, *Si unus ex pluribus haeredibus*. This is not obstructed by the fact that the owner does not prescribe, as stated in the Digest, *De usucapionibus*, in the law *Sequitur*, section *Lana*; because since in an encumbered thing there are two prescribable rights, namely the right of ownership and the right of pledge or hypothec, although the owner does not prescribe the right of ownership, he nevertheless prescribes the right of hypothec consisting in the immovable and corporeal thing, with respect to which it is said that prescription runs in immovable and corporeal things, as I said. For hypothec is a right consisting in the immovable and corporeal thing encumbered and founded on the right which is competent to the debtor in the thing, as stated in the Digest, *De pignoribus*, in the law *Si ab eo*; because it arises immediately from the right which one has in the thing encumbered, as stated in the law *Pignorum*, in the Code, *De pignoribus*. And therefore say that the owner does not prescribe incommutably and with full right. But when he does not have ownership fully incommutable, because it can be absorbed by the hypothecary action, as here; then he can prescribe; because by such prescription the effect is increased; because the irrevocability of the corporeal thing is prescribed, as stated in the Digest, *De captivis et postliminio reversis*, in the law *In bello*, section *Si quis servum*, and noted permeably in my lecture, and also by others, in the Code, *Quod metus causa*, in the law 3. And in this respect, such prescription is in the movable and corporeal thing, of which the statute speaks. And thus, from the foregoing, now better and more subtly considered, I conclude as above. For when I was younger, I spoke as a youth. But now, having become old, I change my opinion; for it is wise to change one’s purpose for the better, as stated in the Authenticum *Ut frater filius*, in the principle, and in the Authenticum *De nuptiis*, section 1, *Qualiter et quando*, in the Extravagant, *De accusationibus*. And thus I say and counsel, I, Baldus de Perusio, etc.

ADDITION.

Since the hypothecary action is a real action, as stated in the Code, *De pignoribus*, I also consider the aforementioned, which cannot be denied, that the hypothecary action is a real action, as stated in the Code, *De pignoribus*, in the law *Pignoris*. From this it follows that the words of the statute, “thus runs, etc.,” congruously adapt to the hypothecary action, from the prescription of which this real action induced to claim possession is removed. Hence you see that he who possesses the thing with just title and good faith excludes you from such claiming of possession. By this reason, not subtly devised, I consider the Wise Men of Milan to be born to interpret their statute thus. For which also supports the law *Si alieni*, section *Sed si nummi*, in the Digest, *De conditione indebiti*, where for the sole claiming of possession, the condictio indebiti is given. And also the actio triticaria, which, however, are personal actions. Furthermore, not ignoring that the hypothecary creditor has a right in the thing. Hence, just as the possessor excludes ownership from the vindication of the thing by long possession; so also he excludes the creditor from the hypothecary action. And therefore the laws observe equality of times both in excluding ownership from the vindication of the thing, and in excluding the hypothecary credit from the hypothecary action, as fully read and noted in the laws 1 and 2, *Adversus creditorem*, in the 7th book of the Code. Hence you see that not only the right of hypothec itself is in consideration, but the thing itself which is possessed. For if the simple right of hypothec were in consideration, the laws would have established a longer time for the prescription of such a right, as established in personal actions, which consist in mere right, as in the laws *Sicut* and *Omnes*, in the Code, *De praescriptione triginta vel quadraginta annorum*; and in the prescription of the right of office, of which in the law *Cum notissimi*, section *Sed cum illud*, in the same title. You also see that ownership and the question of hypothec walk pari passu against the possessor wishing to defend himself by prescription, as in the law *Cum in longo*, in the Code, *De praescriptione longi temporis*, 10 or 20 years. And thus, as above, I say and counsel, I, Christophorus de Castelleo, Doctor of Laws, actually lecturing in Pavia, and in the text premised, I subscribed and ordered my seal to be affixed. And thus, as said and concluded above, I say and counsel. I, Ubertus de Lampugnano, Doctor of Laws, actually lecturing in Pavia, and for greater firmness and strength, I affixed my usual seal and subscribed with my own hand. And thus, by the said Lord Baldus, we counseled, I, Ioannes de Castelleo, Juris Utriusque Doctor, Vicar of the Bishop, and for the faith, we subscribed with our own hand and sealed with my small seal. I, Gualterius de Zazis, Juris Utriusque Doctor, counsel as concluded above, and in the text of the premises, I subscribed and affixed my usual seal.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a husband is entitled to the fruits of the dowry and of the paraphernal property, and which he is bound to restore; whether a wife is bound to support her husband and to provide him with assistance.
2. If a widow remarries, whether the black widow’s garments will belong to the husband’s heir.
3. A woman who refuses to wear widow’s weeds does not thereby become infamous.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Certain things are in the dominion of the husband and in his administration: such as dotal property, and in these the husband profits from all fruits, even those not consumed. ff. sol. matr. l. diuortio; even if there had been a pact that he should not profit. ff. de pact. dot. si conuenerit. Certain things are in the dominion of the wife and in the administration of the husband, and these are paraphernal goods, which the husband administers with his own diligence and at his own risk, and for such administration the husband’s goods are tacitly bound. ff. de pact. conuen. l. fina. In these, the husband does not make the fruits his own, but has the power to consume them for himself, for his wife, and for their common household: and to the extent that he has consumed them, he is not bound to restore them; but to the extent that they remain, or have been converted to the husband’s use and have increased his patrimony, they can be recovered. For something is conceded to the husband in paraphernal goods, because since his administration is at his risk, something should redound to his benefit in compensation for the risk. And although the gloss makes a distinction between converted goods and fruits, nevertheless the doctors do not approve this distinction in industrious fruits. vt d. l. fi. per Cy. Certain things are in the dominion of the wife and in the administration of the wife, such as goods outside the dowry, which she herself lets out and from which she receives the fruits. And then either the woman consumes these fruits for her children, and does not recover them. C. de nego. gest. l. alimenta. ff. de nego. gestis. l. Nesennius. C. de cap. l. lib. cap. Or for the husband himself, and it seems that she recovers them. ff. de donatio. inter virum, et vxorem. l. si stipulata. §. j. and there the gloss. But it seems more correct that either the woman does this to relieve the husband’s necessity, and does not recover them. For she is bound to relieve him when placed in necessity. C. vnde vir et vxor. l. j. and Authen. praeerea. and in the corpus from which it is taken. For they are partners in the divine and human household, and one flesh, and each ought to bear the other’s burdens. But the husband for the wife, because women always seem to be in necessity. ff. de donatio. inter virum, et vxorem. l. quin vxor; but the wife for the husband rarely, and contrary to what commonly happens.

But if, in fact, the husband suffers from poverty, and the wife is wealthy, the husband is bound to support her: unless perhaps the husband has fallen into this state through his own wrongdoing; as stated in Extra, De consuetudine, cap. Ex parte vestra. Or if the wife does this, let her make a gift to the husband; and then the husband is bound, unless the donation is confirmed by the death of the wife. D. l. Si stipulata, in principio, in the gloss which begins "Sive uxo." Having considered these matters, the good husband should render a judgment consonant with equity and the laws. And although the gloss says that the wife is not bound to support the husband, this is understood to apply except in a case of necessity. Ff., Sol. matr., Si cum dotem, § Quod enim tam humanum. Nevertheless, the gloss is supported by C., De iure dotium, l. Ubi adhuc, in the gloss: "Sicut ergo sit," provided, however, that what was done out of mercy is not reclaimed. Arg. Ff., De condictione indebiti, l. Cum his, § Si mulier, with similar authorities.

† Regarding black widow's garments, the quality of the persons must be distinguished. For just as a wife is entitled to maintenance, so too is she entitled to clothing. Hence, without a widow's garment, she cannot pass by honorably. The expense thereof must be borne by the husband. Authority: Nostra in the law Sicut, De operis liberti. And thus the custom observes. Nevertheless, if she subsequently removes her mourning and abandons the widow's habit, she must return the garments which she received and now despises. Authority: Digest, De solutione matrimonii, law In his, § 1.
† However, a woman who does not wish to be clothed in black is not thereby infamous, as stated in the Code, On Infamy, in the law Decree. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a confession made by someone under torture, without prior indicia, is to be believed, and how an indicium is to be proved.
1. A person who voluntarily confesses to a crime is believed, if the crime is established, unless the contrary appears from probable indicia or from innocence.
2. If the confessor states that his confession was extorted by fear of torture, and the judge and notary state the contrary, whose testimony shall be upheld.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. There are three cases.

† First, when someone confesses under torture, or out of fear of torture: and this is established. And then, if there are no prior indications, the confession is not believed. And even if the indications are proven after the confession, the apostolic judge should not follow the confession: because it was extorted illicitly and contrary to the order of law. As stated in the law and note, ff. de quaestio l. meritus. Therefore, the indications must precede, through witnesses who are legitimately received and examined. If, however, they say something extrajudicially without an oath, it does not constitute an indication: because they testified without being sworn. C. de rest. l. solam. and l. iusiurandi. The indications must be proven by two witnesses, concurring, not singular. ff. fam. er. l. fi. in gl.

The second case is when someone confesses voluntarily, and this is established; and then his confession is upheld. C. de pe. l. qui sententiam, unless probable and plausible evidence, or the very innocence of the person, appears to the contrary. As in ff. de quaest. l. probus §. si quis ultro. And in this case, if someone retracts his confession and, before the judge, appeals and reveals his innocence, he must be released: as noted in C. de ap. creditor. §. iussus; C. de erro. adu. l. sin.; C. quorum appel. l. 2, according to Cynus. The third

The case is when the accused himself states that he confessed out of fear of torture, while the judge and the notary state that he confessed voluntarily. Thus, the matter is doubtful due to this contradiction. If, therefore, the crime is proven before the appellate judge, condemnation must follow. But if, after a time limit has been granted to both parties, the crime is not proven, then, because such confessions are commonly accustomed to be extorted by the assessors of the authority through torture, perhaps from the place of what commonly happens, fear of torture should be presumed. To this effect is what Cynus notes, and more clearly Jacobus de Belvisio in l. 2, C. quod meo, in the lecture, where he strongly criticizes the assessors who have it written that the confession was voluntary. Moreover, natural reason dictates this: because no one ought to hate his own life. Hence, it is not credible that one, being in the power of the judge, would confess voluntarily. The terror of those who can inflict lesser severity is sufficient. Therefore, from the confession alone, which has been retracted, and after a time limit has been granted for proof on both sides, and with the crime not proven, I do not believe that the judge can base a condemnation, especially. But the glossators who say that credit is not given to a solitary and bare confession, as noted in C. de captis rebus, l. 2, would otherwise be of little help even to the innocent in appealing, because it is difficult to prove torture which takes place in the chamber of the judges, nor are there present witnesses whose statements can be relied upon, as experience teaches. And thus, the law which permits appeal would make the confession a mockery. From these points, I conclude that, first, the judge proceeded improperly and rashly to torture, without preceding indications. And that the said wretched captive could have had a legitimate recourse. For from the acts, I do not see him convicted; and especially since the contrary witnesses are singular and defective, because they do not testify. I do not deny, however, that the judge, or the appellate judge, through the common path, may follow the truth, which is presumed from the consistency of those things which would be proven together with the confession. But where they are not proven, because the proof lacks substantial elements, as here, he should not deviate from the path of the law solely from the conscience of his own mind. Argument: extra de probat., licet causam, circa medium; and l. illicitas, § veritas; and noted in l. 2, ff. de furtis, cum similibus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the statutory prescription runs against a minor. What is meant by a just title.
2. From what good faith is presumed.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It must be considered whether the aforementioned ten-year prescription is statutory. In that case, it runs against a minor, but restitution in integrum is granted; without which having been obtained, there is no doubt that he cannot bring an action for rescission, which would be brought in an irregular and premature manner. Extra, De restitutione in integrum, c. Constituimus; Institutiones, De actionibus, §. Rursus; according to the gloss. Or whether it is a prescription of the common law. In that case, it does not run against a minor by operation of law itself, as in L. Si, Codex, In quibus causis in integrum restitui licet. The doubt, however, lies in this: because the same term appears to apply to statutes and to the common law. S. 10 annorum. Thus, a statute is not a statute: but the living voice of the common law. Digest, De re iudicata, L. 4, §. Si quis condemnatus; and noted in C. 1, De constitutionibus, Lib. 6. So, since this statute does not distinguish between those present and those absent, and exceeds the terms of the common law, this prescription is deemed to be a statute. Yet it is held that the title is just.

† What is it to say a just title? Answer: that it is true, and tends to the transfer of ownership, and that knowledge of another’s thing ceases. D. de usucap. l. iusto. C. de furt. l. apud. Whether it is also said that every title which the praetor protects, even with knowledge of another’s thing, is a just title. D. de nox. l.

† And generally, good faith is presumed from the title. C. de praescri. long. temp. l. pe. de acque poss. improb. per la. de Are. And from peaceful possession joined with title, good faith is even more strongly presumed. As ff. de min. l. intra vtile. §. venden. He who purchases moved by a written instrument is also presumed to act in good faith. ff. de inter. act. l. de aetate. §. ex causa. Therefore, prescription runs, but restitution in integrum must be sought for the minor. l. qui proprio. §. item quaeritur. Hence, here the matter was handled improperly and in an unordered fashion. Hence, in this judgment the minor will succumb; but if he again acts in an orderly manner, he will prevail. The objection based on the confession of credulity does not hold: because omission does not imply bad faith, nor does it follow that "I believe thus" means "I believed thus in the past": as no. C. de in inte. re. mi. l. de tutela. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the Augustinian Hermits are capable of taking legacies, and if not, to whom the said legacies ought to be applied.
2. When certain persons are prohibited from taking legacies or instituted benefits gratuitously, the heir is bound to give them the value thereof.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A certain person made such an institution in his will: in all his movable and immovable goods, rights, and actions, he instituted his son Peter as his universal heir. However, if the said Peter should die without male issue, then in that case he willed that all his possessions which he holds in the chapel of St. Justina in the county of Rimini should pertain to the convent of the hermit friars of St. Augustine of Rimini. Now it has happened that the above-mentioned Peter died without sons, having instituted a certain Nicholas as his universal heir. Now there is a dispute between the said friars and Nicholas, the heir of the aforementioned brother; the friars claim the said property from the aforementioned will. On the other hand, it is said by the said Nicholas that the said friars cannot, nor ought they to have, nor receive, nor especially retain, from this, because they are said to be mendicants, and ought to lead their life by publicly begging, and to seek with an empty hand, not to seek nor retain ample possessions, neither in common nor individually, and especially immovables; because you know their rule and way of life. And thus, both law and fact, therefore, please your wisdom to give counsel on the aforementioned matter. In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† As appears from that passage in the gloss in the last part of the chapter *Deo nobis*, C. de episcopis et clericis, there were three opinions on this point. Some say that the legacy was considered as not written, and therefore void. In this opinion were Jacobus de Arena and Petrus, by the law *Si in metallum*, D. de his quae pro non scriptis habentur. Others say that it is valid, not so that they may possess, but that they may sell and convert the price into uses lawful and permitted to them, such as clothing, books, and food. D. de legatis 1; and c. *Si duobus*, de legatis 3; l. *Fideicommissa*, § *Si servo*. A third group distinguished between mendicants, to whom it is lawful to have movables, such as, according to them, preachers and hermits; these take and sell as stated above. And other more mendicant orders, to whom it is not lawful to have movables, in which case the legacy is not valid, as far as the benefit of the legatee is concerned. A fourth opinion, which supplements this third, holds that although it is not valid so that possession is acquired by the profession incapable of holding it, nor by the religion itself, it is nevertheless acquired by the Church in general. For every professed person belongs to one Church and is its servant, although Jacobus de Arena [disagrees]. But this opinion, although it seems to have the reason of the laws in itself, does not have equity, in that it is acquired by the Roman Church; because the testators who wished to leave a right to the poor to relieve their necessity would be greatly deceived, and it would go to the treasury of the Roman Church. It supports what is noted in c. *Finis*, de pace, lib. 6. Innocentius places the opinion in c. *In praesentia*, de probat. But he speaks of goods brought in by entering, not of goods left by legacy. Speculator holds that the legacy is valid; because although they cannot hoard, they can nevertheless live well. In Speculum, de statu monachorum, words 3 and 4. And necessity makes this opinion, because they wish to live. D. de captivis et post liminium reversis, l. *Legatum*; argument from D. de manumissionibus testamento, l. *Qui potuerunt*. Bartolus in his Minorica says that legacies are determined, left for a lawful and permitted use and manner, as in the case *Exiit qui seminat*, § *Ad hoc*. And therefore the tacitly understood congruity makes the legacy valid, as in c. *Dudum*, § *Verum*, de sepultura.

† Moreover, let it be assumed that a simple legacy is understood absolutely. Nevertheless, the rule is that when someone is not prohibited from taking on account of hatred or delict, but on account of some other quality, so to speak, he is prohibited from receiving goods gratuitously, not by disinheritance: note, as in the case of these brothers. Then the heir must reduce them to an estimated value, and the legacy of the thing to its value. And a commutation is made by l. fin. ff. de legatis 1; l. si filius § si quis alicui; and d. § si seruo. From which it is manifestly concluded that, if the heir does not wish to deliver possession to the said brothers, he must at least render the estimated value, to be converted by the brothers themselves into their lawful uses, for the soul of the testator. And so I hold: although that decretal de postulando, prelato, book 6, calls them simply mendicants, and strict etymology seems to contradict this, nevertheless this does not contradict, because it is a certain alms made to them in the last will. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How a partnership of all goods is proved.
2. A partnership of all goods can be understood in two ways.
3. How public reputation is proved.
4. Whether public reputation constitutes half-proof? And whether there will be room for the referral of an oath.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† First, it seems that one must say that a partnership of all goods among the above-named brothers has been proven. For it is established that there are six proofs. First, the confinement of the brothers themselves in one house. Second, commensality, that is, that those brothers lived at common expense. Third, common merchants between them, sharing profit and loss. Fourth, the common defense of lawsuits and causes that were brought by them or against them. Fifth, the holding in common of their goods as undivided. Sixth, public voice and fame concerning the partnership of all goods. It is certain that from public voice and fame, regarding the partnership of all goods, a half-proof arises. L. *bonæ fidei*, D. *de iureiurando*, with the note there. From the remaining five mentioned above, it does not seem doubtful that the partnership is at least half-proven, given the length of time, that is, ten years, which has also been proven. C. *de petitione hereditatis*, L. *si filius*. Finally, it cannot be denied that an oath in supplement of proof ought to be tendered to the plaintiff who has something proven to more than half-proof, as stated above. L. *in bonæ fidei*. However, the truth is to the contrary: for which reason, first, it is premised that partnerships of all goods are nothing other than an agreement between two or more persons, either concerning the community of all things acquired in any manner, or those to be acquired in the future through effort or fortune. D. *pro socio*, L. *prima*, § 1, and L. 3, § 1. Second, that from the unity of certain particulars, the unity of the universal statement is not inferred. D. *de rebus dubiis*, L. *si is qui ecclesia*, § *utrum*. Third, that from separated things, nothing is inferred. D. *de minoribus*, L. *pauperi exuli*. Fourth, that when something is gathered from our voluntary acts, it is not tacitly induced beyond the extent of our acts. Argumentum, D. *de itinere actuque privatorum*, L. *prima*, § *Iulianus*; L. *finalis*, C. *ne uxor pro marito*.

Fifthly, that a partnership of all goods can be understood in two ways: one way, as an accidental co-ownership; the other way, as a co-ownership arising from agreement, as is gathered from the gloss on the Digest, On Agreements, in the law *Si unicus*, in the beginning. Furthermore, it can be understood that a partnership of all goods, i.e., a co-ownership of all goods, means present goods. In another way, it means present and future goods, by argument from what is noted in the Code, On Agreements, in the law *Si*, and in the Code, On Things Which Can Be the Subject of a Pledge, in the law *I*. Sixthly, and finally, that an agreement can be made tacitly and expressly, both in the case of a partnership and of contracts of another kind, by argument from the Digest, On Agreements, in the law *Labeo* and in the law *Item quia*, and from the Digest, On Partnership, in the law *So*, in the beginning, according to one reading.

These matters having been thus premised, I say that the partnership of all goods contracted between the said brothers by express agreement has not been proven by the statements of the witnesses, and this appears from their testimony. Nor is it gathered from the acts by tacit agreement, from those things which have been related above. And even granting, without prejudice to the truth, that they had been proven, nevertheless the said partnership would not be understood to be proven, not indeed from cohabitation or common table, by the third and fourth premises. And therefore it does not prove this, as stated in the Code, On Compelling, in the law *Non hoc*. Nor from common business in certain things, by the second, third, and fourth presuppositions. The same holds, and for the same reason, in the case of common litigation or the lack thereof, and the communication of certain present goods, and communication thereof; yet nevertheless they did not reduce all present goods into common ownership. For neither do the witnesses state this conclusively, and the opposite is proven, because it appears that certain things were acquired by one of them in his own name, such that the name of the other was not inserted in the title of the contract. For if a partnership were seen to have been contracted between them regarding those things which were to be common, it would not be so regarding those which one of them had purchased in his own name, according to the gloss by Bartolus in the Digest, On the Administration of Tutors, in the law *Titium aut Mevium*, section *Aliero*. This supports the confirmation of these points in the Digest, On Family Partition, section *Filius*, and in the Digest, On Partnership, in the law *Cum duobus*, section *Papias* (which is also the law *Fratres*), and section *Idem Papinianus* (which is also the law *Si inter fratres*). And these are according to the mind of the doctors, and especially Bartolus in the said section *Aliero* and in the said section *Papias*, and in the Code, On Things Common to Both Judges, in the law *Si patruus*.

All the more so because the witnesses themselves depose that of the two brothers, only one conducted business, while the other devoted himself to study. Whereby it follows, according to Bartolus, following Oldradus and Ricardus Malus, that even in this case a partnership of profit and gain is not understood to have been contracted, lest it appear that one alone was making a donation to the other, to whom nothing was contributed, because he alone conducted business; as is gathered from the gloss by Bartolus cited above.

† Nor does that which is said concerning public reputation stand in the way, because said reputation has not been legally proven. For it ought to have been stated expressly from whom it originated, at least from one or two, according to the note by Bartolus in the law *De minore et tormenta*, D. 48.18 (*De quaestionibus*). Moreover, if one considers the statements of the witnesses, it is understood that now there exists a partnership of all goods between certain persons, holding all their goods, both movable and immovable, in common as undivided, considering more the existence of the fact, to which the partnership, that is, the communion of goods, well accords, which signifies more the present time than an agreement concerning the communication of future goods. And this is apparent from their agreement at that time, especially from the reason which he returned to his own knowledge: because they testify to said communion of all goods as undivided between said brothers for said reason.

† Again, public rumor, according to most, does not constitute half-proof: as is noted by Bartolus in *l. admonendi*, D. de iureiurando; but it assists proof already made. As in D. de testibus, *l. 3*, § *idem diuus*. Finally, even if there were room for an oath to be tendered, which is not true, as has been proved above, nevertheless he who has only public rumor on his side ought not to tender the oath. The remaining matters do not provide assistance, as has been said above, but rather to the defendant. As in D. de regulis iuris, *l. fauorabiliores*, and because he can better know the truth of the fact, since the heir of those concerning whose act the case is, and who has his own accounts, is in a better position than the plaintiff, who more likely knows nothing of a fact entirely alien to him. Arg. in the aforementioned *l. admonendi*, and *l. in bonae fidei*, where the gloss and doctors; and D. de legibus, *l. si quis a filio*, § *si quis plures*, and what is noted there. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The legitimate son is admitted to guardianship and succession, to the exclusion of his illegitimate brothers.
body: A certain person died intestate, leaving behind his daughter Margarita, a minor under the age of two, and his wife Joanna, who is under the age of twenty and the daughter of Peter. Joanna has two legitimate younger brothers under the age of twenty, and she has two bastards from her carnal sister, the aforementioned testator’s sister. There is a certain Martin, aged twenty-five. The question is:

† Which of these ought to be the legitimate guardian of the said ward, Marga? And it must be said briefly that the dowry is not to be admitted, nor is the said guardianship to be conferred upon them, because they would not be admitted to the intestate succession of the said ward. As stated in *l. hac parte*, D. *unde cognati*; and in the Authenticum *Quibus modis naturales efficiuntur sui*, § *filium*. Wherein even a legitimated child, and even a natural child, would not succeed, except to a certain legitimate portion. And this is noted by Speculum, Title *De successione ab intestato*, § *fin.*, which supports the foregoing. Also relevant is *l. 1*, D. *de tutela*, together with similar authorities. Moreover, this appears expressly stated to one who rightly considers *l. si*, C. *quando mulier tutelam officio fungitur*. Therefore, the said legitimate heir is admitted, and the said guardianship is conferred upon him by the aforementioned laws. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If a father conducts business in the name of his son, or credits something to his son, or causes something to be promised to his son, whether he is considered to be making a gift or giving it into the peculium.
2. A father who bears the burdens of his son's marriage makes the fruits of the dowry his own, on account of the burdens he has undertaken.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It should be noted that when a father conducts business in the name of his son, or credits to his son what is owed to the father himself, or causes something to be promised to the son, if the son is not emancipated but remains under the father’s power, it appears that the father grants it to him as peculium. And therefore, unless the father subsequently bequeaths the peculium by way of a legacy in his will, such money is common to all the heirs, according to their hereditary shares. C. de familia erciscunda, l. certum; and l. Titii filii, de peculio legato; and there by Laurentius de Arena, de lege 3, l. nomen, § filio. But if he were to do such things in the name of a son who is mancipatus, a donation would be presumed. l. pe., ff. de donationibus. Therefore, resolving the first doubt, I say that if the said B. and Bonaventura were not mancipati, the said 400 florins, as to one-third part, belong to the said B. And this concludes the first point.

† On the second point, it should be noted that if the father bears the burdens of his son’s marriage, the fruits of the dowry ought to belong to the father, on account of the burdens he has undertaken. And therefore, if the father has received them, there is no doubt that they must be common to all the heirs according to their hereditary share, because they are fully the property of the father’s heir. The same applies if the son received them in the name of the father, because they constitute the son’s *profectitium peculium*, even though he receives them in the father’s name; and therefore they are common to all the heirs, as stated in the aforementioned law *Certum*.

However, if the father intended those fruits to belong to his son, it must then be considered that the father may renounce the usufruct he holds over the *bona adventicia* (adventitious goods); and in that case, the property belongs to the son and not to the heirs, as provided in the Code, *De bonis quae liberi* (On goods which children acquire), law *Cum oportet*, section *Si autem res*. And thus it appears that the aforementioned Alvise would have acquired those fruits of the dowry and should not share them. Nevertheless, the truth is as follows: either the dowry was counted out to the son and given to him from the beginning, in which case it is adventitious property, and the father may renounce the usufruct, and it belongs fully to the son, as stated in the aforementioned section *Si autem res*; or the dowry was given to the father from the beginning, and thus it became fully the father’s property. In that case, either the father returns this dowry to the son, because the son then takes a wife and supports her and bears the burdens of marriage; and in this regard, the son, just as the husband, is not bound to share anything with his brothers, as provided in the Code, *Familiae erciscundae* (On the division of family property), law 2, and in the Digest, *Eodem* (On the same matter), law *Si maritus*.

Or, the father bears the burdens of the marriage, and the son receives the profits; and in that case, such profits are common to all the heirs of the father, because a donation from the father to the son is not presumed if the son is under his power; rather, a mere commission of administration is presumed, as stated in the law *Titii filii*, Digest, *De legatis secundis* (On second legacies), and the law *Cum pater*, section *Pater in pluribus*. And therefore, in this case, property purchased with such profits would have to be shared, unless it were proven that the father intended to make a donation to this son. For then, upon the father’s death, it would be confirmed, unless it had been revoked by the father, as provided in the Code, *Familiae erciscundae*, law *Filiae cuius*, and the Code, *De inofficiosis donationibus* (On undutiful donations), law 2.

Therefore, the second question cannot be answered absolutely, but only with the aforementioned distinction. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Opinion of the most eminent doctor of laws, Master Baldus of Perugia, lecturer
2. at Pavia.
1. A will having been made, in which his children were instituted as heirs, and upon their dying without issue, their property was to devolve upon the grandson, whether the children may alienate.
body: The facts are as follows: Domicius, having died, made a will, providing that if he should die leaving his children without legitimate sons, his property should pass to Titius, his grandson, or to Seius, the son of the said Titius, born of the said Domicius. They sell all their property, and it is not taken away by the will that they, while living, may alienate and sell, and that the said sons may sell the said property. The question is whether, upon their dying without legitimate sons, they could validly sell the property of the said Domicius. And assuming that they could sell, whether the said property, thus alienated, can be claimed by the buyers. In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It is answered that the sale is valid as against those who sold it while they were living, according to the true opinion. But upon their death, if they left no legitimate children, it is rescinded by operation of law up to one-half, the other half remaining valid despite having been alienated on account of the legitime and the Trebellian portion. As stated in C. comm. deleg. l. si, §. si autem auaritiae; and Auth. res quae; and in Auth. de resti.; and ea quae parit, §. quamobrem; and ff. ad Treb. l. Marcellus, §. res quae. And the alienated things could be claimed from any possessors and buyers for the half-share pertaining to the said universal fideicommissaries. Others say that only the legitime is deducted. And then they could vindicate two parts at the appropriate time. On this point there is a difference between the legists and the canonists. Nevertheless, because the Pope can determine doubtful opinions of civil law, it is safer to allow two quarters to be deducted. As in c. Raynu., Rayn.; and c. si pater, extra de test. I, Baldus. COUNSEL CCCCLXXXVI. In the Name of Christ, Amen. On the first point, I say that the mother does not succeed to the male children: because they died in pupillary status. And this counsel you will find in part 3, beginning: “The case was as follows: Ser Gervasius, son of Ser Paulus, of etc.”

In the name of Christ, Amen. Upon that first point I say that the mother does not succeed to the male sons, because they died in pupilage, etc. You will find this consilium in the third part, beginning: "The fact is such: Ser Gervasius, son of Ser Paulus of, etc."

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether Papillus ought to be brought up, maintained, and reside with the tutors appointed in the will, or with his mother.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Ser Francesco, in his will, appointed as tutors for his underage daughter Gasparina, whom he had instituted as his heir for a share, Antonio and Marco de Fanno, without any intention of determining with whom the said ward should reside. Indeed, the said ward sometimes resided with the said tutors, or one of them; sometimes with her mother, and for the greater part, yet by the will of the said tutors. And now she is with her mother. The tutors, considering that the aforementioned ward would reside better, more honorably, and more usefully with them than with her mother, request that the said ward be delivered to them and left to their upbringing. However, the mother wishes to retain her with herself and does not wish to give her to the aforementioned tutors. The question is asked: what is the law? In the Name of Christ, Amen.

The female ward ought to remain where it appears equitable and conscientious to the judge, after the case has been heard. D. 26.2.1; C. 4.4.1. For the praetor ought to act so that the girl is nourished and educated without any malicious suspicion. And first of all, care must be taken that she is not educated with him or her who lies in wait for her chastity: as stated in D. 26.2.1 § 1. For this fear is greater than the fear of death. D. 4.10.1 § fin. Secondly, he must take heed that she does not remain with one who would lie in wait for her life, as sometimes occurs with the substitute of the ward. As stated in D. 26.2.1 § denique; and C. 4.4.1 § fin. The same applies if he were lying in wait for her soul, as in Extravagant de conversione, c. 2, fin.; or for her good morals; for here too he is an enemy of good reputation and good morals, just as the former is an enemy of good life or chastity. D. 26.2.1; D. 26.10.1. The same applies if he were lying in wait for her marriage or betrothal, wishing to betroth her to an unworthy person; for these too are capital injuries. As argued in C. 1.39.1; C. 1.40.1; C. 5.50.1. The same applies if he were lying in wait for her patrimony; for he who strips a ward is not a good man. D. 18.1.1 § si tutor. And in sum, an equitable judge ought to do that which the father would presumably do if he were alive. D. 25.3.1 § tria luminaria, at the words "apud eum educatur". For the praetor stands in the place of the father. C. 2.3.1; D. 23.3.1 pr. And he ought to do the same for an alien daughter as for his own. D. 46.3.1, taking for her an equitable, sound, and irreproachable counsel; just as a father takes counsel for his children, and never thinks of anything but their utility. D. 48.5.1; D. 38.16.1 § facilior. From which I conclude that when a doubt arises between the mother and the tutors, considering the affection, charity, honesty, and chastity of the persons, a good man should determine where the female ward ought to reside; yet let him remember that it is presumed most strongly in favor of the mother regarding the rearing of a female. As the text says in D. 26.2.1, first response. If, however, the mother were a vile and wicked woman, or not prudent, then the judge could rightly grant the girl to tutors of good faith and men of sober life, especially testamentary tutors, whose faith was chosen by the father of the girl. This is supported by D. 42.7.3, c. pen. and fin.; and the aforementioned § tria luminaria. And it is clear there that if neither the mother nor the tutors were free from suspicion regarding the ward, she ought to remain with a woman of noted authority, whose life is a praise and example of chastity, and whose conscience would healthily preserve the ward in all things. The conclusion is that she should remain with him or her who is better and more useful for the girl. And in this the judge ought to be severe and rigorous, and not gracious; nor should he be moved by the mother’s tears, nor by the tutors’ flatteries; but only by the merits of their lives. D. 1.16.1. He would be guilty of fault and liable for the restitution of all damage, both in the judicial forum and in the forum of conscience, if any harm were to befall the ward through his negligence. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A compromise made in favor of someone as an arbitrator and umpire does not expire within one year.
body: The point of silence is as follows. A certain compromise was made between Bructia Morici of the Bailiwick of Strauagiano on one part, and Marcus and Vitalis Rainaldi of the said Bailiwick on the other part, in the noble and learned man Lord Verrus of Termo, as their arbitrator and adjudicator in law and in fact, concerning the litigation and dispute pending between the said parties. Who, Lord Verrus, arbitrator and adjudicator, having assumed the way of arbitration, after the year from the day of the compromise had passed, rendered an award between the said parties within four months. And to this award, on behalf of the said Brunutia, contradiction was made, and it was declared null, and in the prosecution of the said cause it was said that the said compromise was null because it was rendered after the year, as is narrated above. On the contrary, on behalf of the said Vitalis and Marcus, it is said that the said award was and is something valid, and that the arbitrator and adjudicator could render the said award after the year had ended and within four months. Now the question is asked: what is the law, having regard to the award and the compromise aforesaid? In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† On the aforementioned point, I was consulted on another occasion, and I held, and still hold, that a compromise made in favor of someone as an arbitrator and umpire is not terminated by the lapse of one year; and that the award is valid, and that he rendered it as an arbitrator after the year had passed. According to the law *sed si compromissum*, Digest, *De arbitris*; and in the same title, the law *Si unus*, § 1, in the ordinary gloss. And this is an express case. Code, *De tempore appellandi*, Authentica *Si tamen*. Thus also holds the Speculum in the title *De arbitris*, § *Differt*, under the words “item, as within three years.” See Cynus in the law *Properandum*, under the words “but if in the middle,” Code, *De iudicibus*. Although Bartolus, following a certain dream, holds the contrary in the law *Si quis arbitratu*, Digest, *De verbis obligatis*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A great-grandfather who does not petition to compel a guardian within a year to assume the administration of the estate of his great-granddaughter, a ward, is not admitted to her succession if she dies during her minority; but the aunts of said ward shall be admitted.
2. Whether the provisions of law speaking concerning a mother regarding the petition for a guardian apply to a grandfather and great-grandfather.
1. A putative heir cannot sell to the prejudice of the true heir.
2. How a second wife succeeds together with granddaughters and grandsons instituted from a daughter of a prior marriage.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The following is presented in the case: a certain man named Thomasius, being in his last illness, instituted his daughter Beatrice as his heir; in codicils subsequently made, he left Dominicus Lini as her guardian. Then the aforementioned testator died, with the said Dominicus, Beatrice, two sisters of the said testator, and her maternal grandfather, whose name was Nicola, surviving. This Nicola, the great-grandfather of the said Beatrice, did not demand that the said guardian be compelled forthwith to accept the said guardianship legitimately and administer it. Rather, the said guardian delayed accepting it for a year and about that time, and the great-grandfather never made a demand. The said Beatrice having therefore died in the age of minority, it is asked who comes to her intestate inheritance. Whether the said Nicola, the great-grandfather, or the aforementioned aunts. On this point, Baldus, the undersigned, was consulted.

I state that, with the aforementioned grandfather as testator and the great-grandfather of the said Beatrice excluded, the aforementioned aunts shall succeed. The reason is that the said great-grandfather did not fully discharge the duty of piety as he ought to have done. This fullness consists in effect and execution: as stated in the Digest, *ad Tertium*, law 2, § *sed quod diximus*, at the end; § *j.*; and *cum plenum officium*, etc., there, on this matter. Just as it is not sufficient for a mother and other ascendants merely to request a tutor, unless it is also requested that she be compelled to legitimately assume and administer the guardianship (*l. matris pietas*, 2, *responso*, Code, *qui petant tutores*; and the aforementioned § *sed quod diximus*; and note this in law § *si mater*, at the words *quod si pater*; and Code, *de procuratoribus*, law *alienas*), so too it is not sufficient if a tutor is requested from another or given by the testator, unless the duty of piety is fulfilled. For the laws speaking of the mother should not be considered penal, because they were not devised for punishment, but for the provision of the children: as is clear in the Digest, *qui petant tutores*, law 2, § *idem diuus*, at the words *communem adhibere rationem*, etc. That which is found expressed in the mother in one case is extended by identity of reason to another case, namely to a tutor requested from another or to a testamentary tutor: because the reason of the necessity of provision is the same, and the appropriateness of piety is the same.

† Moreover, what is stated regarding the mother is extended to the grandmother and the great-grandmother, because we are dealing with a matter of favor: as in D. ad Tertul. l. 2, § filius autem. Nor is it necessary here to resort to the law Sciant. Those laws, which speak of the mother not having made a petition, are extended to all legitimate successors, because we are speaking here of ascendants, concerning whom sufficient provision was made in § filiis autem. See D. qui pet. tut. l. 2, § ex his. It is also established by the law Idem dicens, even in a matter of odium. D. ad Maced. l. filium habeo. Furthermore, we cannot depart from the words of the text, which says that we desire the full office of the grandfather. Nor does it distinguish from whom it was given or requested. Therefore, it is requested with effect. Moreover, it is absurd to say that the mother who requested but did not compel should be punished, while she who did neither should not be punished: the latter is more contumacious and will be punished less. This is absurd. D. quod vi aut clam. l. seruius ait. D. de in integr. restitu. l. diuus. However, one law seems to raise the opposite argument, namely that the penalty for not requesting and compelling the acceptance of guardianship and administration does not apply unless they were requested by oneself. C. de admi. tut. l. si, § personis. There it says that those whom he appointed are to be compelled. The gloss on l. petierit, et ordinari fecerit says so. But I answer that it speaks by way of example, not by way of restriction. Moreover, assuming that the mother requests, she is bound; therefore, if she does not request, she is bound: this does not follow. It is therefore concluded that the great-grandfather of the female line has made the place. D. ad Tert. l. 2, in fine. And note in our terms. C. qui pet. tut. l. nepotibus, with similar cases. Add to the above Inst. ad Tertul. § quemadmodum. From the foregoing arises the solution of another question.

Whether the minor can vindicate the hereditary assets of Beatrice, sold by the heirs of the said Nicholas; because, since they pertain to her, a presumptive heir could not alienate them to the prejudice of the true heir. D. 5,3,1, § quod si quis cum se. And this applies insofar as the succession of Beatrice is concerned.

† Another question arises concerning the aforementioned goods of the said Nicholas, namely how his second wife, instituted by him together with the nephews and nieces from the daughter of his former husband, succeeds to them; this is determined in the law *Hac edictali*. However, one point must be noted: because the gloss in the first law of that title states that those penalties have been abolished. Innocentius says it is a mere penalty, namely the penalty of infamy, abolished by the said Apostle. But not that which redounds to the advantage of the children, as he himself notes in the last chapter, *extra de secundis nuptiis*, and this is the common opinion. And thus I, Baldus, say, etc.
The case is as follows. E.L. sold a house to F. for the price of one thousand five hundred florins. Then the said F. and C. in the first part of the opinion. 174 IIS Idni

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If brothers are partners in all their property, and one of them has pursued his studies, whether he ought to have studied at his own expense or at the common expense.
body: The question of the doctors arose in the study, whether he ought to have studied at his own expense

† Brothers are partners in all goods, and one of the brothers remained in study; the question is whether he ought to have studied at his own expense or at common expense. And it seems that at common expense, presupposing the aforementioned partnership, as in D. pro socio, l. si societatem universalium fortunarum. Hence, half cannot be claimed from him; for then he would have studied at his own expense, not at common expense, which is contrary to the said law. Baldus and Franciscus de Perusio advised. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If some witnesses state that the road was damaged, while others state that they went along it and thus it was not damaged, and there is doubt as to whether it is one road or several, whether falsity has been proven.
2. One witness is impeached by two: and two by four.
3. If some witnesses testify that they saw water flood over a certain vineyard, while others say that it did not, whether they are false.
4. Whether witnesses may be recalled, or whether they themselves may explain their words.
5. Whether contrary witnesses may be tortured, so that the truth may be elicited.
6. Whether a witness who told a lie that did not benefit the party producing him may be punished for perjury.
7. Whether a witness who said one thing in one matter and another in another may be punished for perjury.
8. Whether records in one case make faith in another.
casus:
In the Name of Christ, Amen. In a certain case, the following doubts arise, on which legal advice is requested.

First, the witnesses are accused of false testimony, because in testifying in a certain cause they should have stated that a certain road was so damaged that one could not travel on it with carts and oxen at a certain time without certain precautions. Although some of the aforementioned witnesses say that one could not travel on it well and conveniently, some say without danger, some say that the said road was damaged in some parts. But for the greater part they say that it was so damaged that one could not travel on it at the said times with carts and oxen absolutely, as contained in the accusation. On the other side, to prove the said accusation and the said falsity, many witnesses are produced, who in effect say that they saw the said road at the said time in good condition, or with the said precautions, so that one could travel on it with carts and oxen laden. And that the witnesses of the bishop were at the said time many times, and saw many persons go with oxen and carts, both laden and unladen. From these it is asked whether the said accusation is fully proved, or whether some subdivision can help, so that they do not fall into perjury.

Secondly, it is asked whether the said witnesses can be interrogated ex officio for the declaration of their testimony, so that they may say of which road they understood; since there is suspicion that one understands one road and another another, because the said road is not clearly defined in the accusation.

Thirdly, that there ought to be more witnesses in number who ought to disprove other witnesses of falsity, as regards criminal condemnation.

Secondly, principally the said witnesses are accused of falsity, because in testifying in the said cause they said that from a certain time back they saw the water of a certain fountain retreat through a certain ditch at the time of rains and floods of waters, at the time when a certain meadow is watered by a certain P., that the said water at the said times rose over a certain vineyard. On the other side, to prove the said accusation and that the said witnesses spoke falsely, it is said that at the said time and before and after dwelling in the village in whose territory the said vineyard is situated, and that they saw many floods full of waters, and in the said P. his meadow watered many times. And that they never saw nor heard that the water of the said fountain in any way retreated and rose over the said vineyard; because rather it descended and went or flowed into some surrounding parts, which are lower than the said vineyard, which is higher; and yet they never saw nor heard that the said water rose nor fell into those lower parts. And furthermore they say that the said water could not have risen over the said vineyard without their seeing it. For the aforementioned reasons, some witnesses assign the reason why the said water could not have risen without their seeing it, saying that they passed daily through the said vineyard, going to work as is customary; others assign the reason by what they believed or saw; others assign the reason because they saw or heard. Others assign the reason saying that they saw the said water daily. Another puts the reason that he saw it as a person who stayed and dwelt for sixteen years in the said village. Another assigns the reason that he saw it at the time when he was conversant in the said village, and that he saw the said floods. Another says because he saw the water of the said fountain continuously and almost daily. Another says because he stayed in the said village and often saw the said water; and another says that if it had to rise over the said vineyard, he would have seen it some time during the time he was conversant in the said village; and that yet he never saw nor heard.

† From these, it is asked whether the said witnesses prove the said accusation or the said falsity, or not; or whether the said witnesses who testified to the contrary can be aided by any defense so as not to fall into perjury. Furthermore, it is asked whether the judge, ex officio or at the request of a party, may refer the matter to two experts in the art who have examined whether it was possible that the said water rose over the said vineyard, or not; and whether their opinion is to be believed rather than that of the aforementioned witnesses. Thirdly, and principally, it is asked, assuming that the said witnesses do not sufficiently prove their case, whether they provide sufficient indicia for torture in the aforementioned circumstances.

Fourthly, it is asked: if they testified in a civil case so that someone might be absolved, and it is proven that they gave false testimony; nevertheless, their statement was not such that an acquittal could follow from it. For example, if someone is condemned to do something within a certain time, under a certain penalty, and an action is brought for the penalty because he had not done it within the specified time; the defendant, sued for the penalty, produces witnesses in his defense who falsely testify that the defendant had done what was contained in the sentence; nevertheless, after the time has passed, they are accused and sued for the said falsity. Now it is asked whether they should be condemned and punished according to the form of the decree presently alleged, or by some other penalty; and the converse.

It is asked: if someone is accused of having given false testimony so that someone might be condemned in some case, and it is proven that he gave false testimony; nevertheless, his statement was not such that a condemnation could follow in that case. Whether he should be punished and condemned according to the form of the said decree, presently alleged, or by some other penalty, as if the said decree does not claim to apply unless the testimony is such that an acquittal or condemnation could follow therefrom.

Fifthly and finally, it is asked: if one witness is accused of having given false testimony so that someone might be condemned in some civil case, and while the said case is pending, the said witness is produced as a witness in the case of another accusation, yet regarding the fact on which he testified, and in this case of another accusation, he says the contrary of what he first said and testified. It is asked whether, by this second statement, he can be condemned in the accusation brought against him, as if he had confessed to having spoken falsely; or whether he cannot be condemned because he testified in another case; and in the case where he cannot be condemned, whether proceedings for perjury can be taken against him ex officio by the judge, who sees his contradictory statements, and for which testimony—whether for the first or the second. And what are the duties of the judge in this matter.

On all and each of these matters, it pleases you to write conclusively the truth, with some brief allegations on each doubt, as truth and justice require.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen. Certain witnesses deposed that a certain road was so destroyed that at certain times one could not conveniently travel along it; but for the most part they say that it was so damaged that one could not travel with carts and oxen. At certain times the witnesses were accused of falsehood, which witnesses say that at the said time they traveled many times and saw many persons traveling with oxen and loaded carts. Likewise, it was doubted whether there is one road or several. Likewise, it was doubted whether witnesses may impeach witnesses.

† I respond: if it is doubtful whether there is one road or several, the falsehood is not proved, as in extra de testi. c. cum tu fili, and C. de fi. instru. l. cum Ioann. haere.; and what Iac. Butr. noted in l. C. de errore aduo. supports this very well, and Bar. in l. insulam. ff. so. ma. and ff. si cert. pet. l. 2. §. item muni., and Iac. Bu. in l. sed si possessori. §. item si iurauero. ff. de iureiu., and by Bar. in ff. de oper. no. nun. l. non solum. §. vt probari. Likewise, it is certain that it is nonetheless one road; yet these witnesses are not contradictory, because it does not follow that because some went, therefore all could go, or the greater part, as in ff. de ver. obli. l. continuus. §. 1. Likewise, inasmuch as it was damaged, one could not go conveniently, as in ff. quemad. ser. amit. l. si locus. §. fi. and ff. de relig. l. si quis sepulchrum. Likewise, that which cannot be done conveniently is not properly said to be done, as in ff. de ver. sig. l. nepos proculo.

† Regarding the number of witnesses, however, it has been said that one witness is impeached by two, and two by four, as noted in insti. de inuti. stipu. §. item verborum, and noted in the said c. cum lo., and C. de fide instru. l. in exercendis by Cy. and others. Likewise, certain witnesses said that they saw water flood over a certain vineyard, and others say that it never flooded, because they were neighbors, and that it could never have flooded without them seeing it.

† It is asked what the law is: whether those who deposed that they saw it flood are false. And consider here that the latter depose to a negative, which they strive to prove also by nature, and also by the site of the place, because the water could run down through the plain, and therefore it could rise to the said vineyard. And concerning this it is asked whether the judge may commit the matter to two experts in the art who may inspect this, and whether their report should be relied upon. I respond that if the witnesses depose negatively in the manner that these did, they do not provide proof, because their statement is somewhat suspect unless it is aided by visual inspection from the nature of the place, as noted after the ordinary gloss by Dy. in l. 1. §. 1. ff. de itinere actuque priua.; but because they add a natural reason, the judge ought to go to the place with skilled men, as in l. si irruptione. §. ad officium. ff. fi. regun. and l. semel. C. de re mili. and in auth. de non alien. §. quod autem. colla. 2. C. de adm. tu. l. lex quę tutores. ff. de off. procon. l. Si in aliquam. cum si.

† However, witnesses cannot be recalled, nor declare anything, once the disputation concerning the testimonies has begun, as in Auth. de testi. in §. quia vero; they could only clarify the words of the words, where clarity or uncertainty allowed it, as Inno. noted in extra de test. in c. cum clamor. Yet they would cause prejudice to neither party, although it would be valid for the excuse of falsehood, as in extra de proba. cap. in praesentia, extra de accusa. cum dilecti; and in doubt, favor ought to be shown to affirming witnesses rather than to denying ones, as noted in ff. de arbit. l. diem proferre. §. si plures.

† Further, it is asked whether in the premises one may resort to torture so that the truth may be elicited, as in extra de accusat. c. cum dilecti; and in doubt one ought to favor affirming witnesses rather than denying ones, as noted in the same ff. de arbi. I respond: here there is sufficient discretion, because you can know better, etc., as in ff. de testi. l. 3. §. tu tortura magis, and C. de fal. l. vbi, and ff. de quaestio. l. quaestionis modum, and l. aedictum due. Nevertheless, the judge may well abstain from torture where some natural reason could excuse the witness, and the confession of a witness ought to conform to natural facts, as in ff. de interro. act. l. confessionibus.

† Likewise, it is asked whether, if a witness deposed a falsehood that does not aid the party producing him, he can be punished for falsehood? I respond: yes, if it pertains to the case, as in ff. de fal. l. si quis legatum, provided that the witness's deposition is not null from a defect of form, as noted in l. 1. C. de sepul. viol., and Bart. in the said l. si quis legatum.
