† Lastly, it is asked, if a witness in one matter said one thing, and in another said another, whether he can be punished for falsehood. I respond: yes, as in ff. ad Tertul. l. qui falsa vel varia; and he is presumed to have spoken falsely in the second testimony, as if suborned, as in Authen. de teste. §. quia vero; and even if it did not appear of necessity that follows, that he is false in the first statement or the second, although it is not established in which of them, as noted in ff. de iureiuran. l. duobus. §. fin., nevertheless on account of that doubt he does not escape a penalty to be imposed at the discretion of the judge, on the grounds that he has offended the ears of the judge, as noted in C. de test. l. nullum; what is noted in C. de spor. l. secunda supports this; and he shall be punished by the judge according to how he offended his ears, as in ff. de falsis. l. eos.

† And although the acts in one case do not establish proof in another between different parties, as noted in C. de eden. l. secunda, nevertheless they do establish proof against the very witness who deposes, as noted by Innoc. in extra de test. ca. veniens, even across different instances. Thus he is rather punished as a vacillating witness by an arbitrary penalty—and by the common law if from the mere office of the judge—rather than by the ordinary penalty, as in C. de test. l. nullum. And thus I, Bal. de Peru., say and advise, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a legacy for a marriage portion is due if the woman is found to be married.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Considering that the testator appears to have bequeathed the legacy in aid of marriage, and not simply and absolutely: I say that nothing is owed to the said daughter in respect of the real right. For she ought to have made her claim before the marriage; nor ought she to have extinguished the final cause of the legacy, which fact, even if it occurred through ignorance, is prejudicial. D. de cond. et dem. l. cum tale. §. pen. and l. si iam facta. And thus it is no objection that a dowry may also be constituted for a married woman; because marriage is the productive cause of the dowry, and not the extinguishing cause. For that statement is true only in the case of a dowry owed simply, or by the law of nature, as is noted in D. de act. et ob. l. obligamur. §. lege. But here the debtor is not bound simply, because the final cause has vanished, as is apparent from the form of the will, from which one must not depart. D. de leg. 3. l. ille aut ille. §. cum in verbis. and D. de suppel. lega. l. labeo. §. idem. And so I say and advise, I, Bal. de Peru. and colleagues.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If a monk to whom an inheritance has been left dies before accepting the inheritance, whether the monastery may accept it or not.
casus: CASE. The case is as follows. A certain A. made his will, by which he left his three sons as his heirs in all his goods, substituting the third son for the one who died without children, and the two sons for the third. For these three sons, if they died without sons or daughters, he substituted his two daughters, or their heirs, in equal shares, in all his goods. The point in question is this: the three sons died in pupillary age, without sons or daughters; his daughters survived them, one of whom married and had a son; the other entered a monastery and became a nun. Neither she nor the monastery entered into the father’s inheritance, and she died during the time of the plague. Now it is asked whether the monastery can enter upon the said inheritance, and for what share.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† A great question arises whether, if a monk to whom an inheritance has been offered dies before acceptance, the monastery may accept it or not. And Jacobus says that either it was an inheritance of ascendants, and it is transmitted to the monastery, which is in the place of a son. C. de his qui ante aper. tab. l. 1. and in auth. de sanctis. epis. §. sed hoc praesenti. Or it was an inheritance of strangers, and then the monastery seems to be excluded therefrom: but it could be restored as if it were a minor. ff. de acqui. hęr. l. panthonius. Thus Cyriacus reports in l. deo nobis. C. de epis. et cle. but it does not seem well said in the first case that the monastery comes by right of transmission: because a monk is said to have nothing which he can transmit. as in Auth. ingressi. cum simi. nor is it expedient that the monastery be held in the place of a son. as noted by Cyriacus, C. ad Trebel. auth. nisi. And therefore, in order to see the truth more clearly, it must be premised that if a slave instituted as heir dies before the inheritance has been accepted, the master is totally excluded from that inheritance. as ff. ad leg. Aqui. l. inde Neratius. primo responso. and if a son instituted as heir dies before he is ordered to accept, the father cannot accept: because, the person of the son failing, the possibility of accepting, which depends on him, fails. argu. l. si. ff. commu. pręd. for it is special when an inheritance is offered to an infant, so that upon his death the father may accept. as l. si infanti. unless the father had ordered the son to accept, and the latter refused: because then the right of accepting would have been acquired by the father for himself. as C. de bonis quę libe. l. cum non solum cum non perderetur. even if the son dies afterwards. arg. ff. de stip. ser. l. 1. §. 1. ff. de contratab. l. si post mortem. §. vltimo. For a preceding mandate operates differently. C. ad Trebell. l. non iustam. From these it is inferred thus: if we compare the monk to a slave, as noted by Innocentius, extra de priuil. c. cum olim, the monastery does not succeed. But if we compare the monk to a son, as noted, ff. de acquir. hęred. l. cum hęredes. §. fin. and noted, insti. de iure personarum, then either an order to accept preceded, and he scorned to accept: then the monastery succeeded. Or it did not precede: then it does not succeed. For how can he accept who does not live in the world? ff. de vulg. subst. l. qui liberis. §. hęc verba. and argu. ff. de iure dot. l. si mulier. §. ex asse. And this argues against the monastery; for the monastery argues, and it must be observed first, that sentence and special reason which favors religion. ff. de relig. sunt personae. The second common reason must be considered: for although a son under paternal power has will and unwillingness, and is therefore effectively bound, except in loan and vow, as ff. quod cum eo. per totum. and de condi. inde. l. frater a fratre. and a slave is also naturally bound: because he retains natural law, i.e., consent, as ff. de pec. l. si damnum. §. peculium. de condi. insti. l. si id quod dominus. cum si. yet it is otherwise with a monk: because he has submitted all his will, and as it were transferred it to his superior, and has divested himself not only of his own goods, but of his own will. and he has no executive will. 12. q. j. non dicatis. and de ele. c. religiosus. and c. quorundam. and de testa. c. 2. li. 6. and de sta. mo. cum ad monachum. and c. 1. and a monk is more stripped of his own will than a slave. For a slave, by refusing to accept, never acquires for his master. potest. n. although, even if ordered by the master, he may refuse to accept. ff. de hęr. insti. l. 3. ad fi. But a monk cannot refuse, and if he does not accept, the monastery accepts. as noted by Archidamus, 18. questio. 1. c. 1. and the right of accepting belongs directly to the monastery itself, just as other rights of the monk. as noted, extra de senten. excomm. c. parochianos. For a monk cannot say this right is mine. 12. quęst. 1. non dicatis. and it seems that a monk is in some way comparable to an infant son. Therefore, just as the father accepts the inheritance offered to him, so here the monastery accepts by similar reasoning. And because, while the disposition of law is pending, and the interposition is by the monastery and not by the monk, it seems to be held that, upon the death of the monk, from whom the necessity of the monastery’s acceptance did not depend, it may accept, not by the judgment of the testator, but by benefit. l. sicut contingit. in l. si infanti. and l. cum non solum. It supports what is noted in Spec. de sta. mo. ver. 8. quaeritur. and especially in a paternal inheritance, which is acquired by the law itself. as insti. de haer. ab intest. §. sui. ff. de acque haeredi. l. necessariis. C. de iu. delibe. l. si fratris. de castr. pecu. l. haered. si filius de mili. test. l. ex militari. §. fi. and l. seq. and noted in l. apud hostes. And granted that, at the time of the father’s death, the existence of the monk as a sui heres ceases, and because he is not in the father’s power, as noted, ff. de min. l. si ex causa. §. pap. yet it is the same, as has been proven. And it supports what is noted by Innocentius, extra de prob. in pręsentia. And if it is said that that which adheres to the person is not acquired for the monastery, and the right of accepting adheres to the person. I answer, it does not adhere in such a way that it does not pass to another. Hence, if the instituted heir dies, it is well transmitted. as l. cum antiquioribus. But the monastery does not succeed the monk as if by death: because monasticism is a kind of death, therefore etc. For one who renounces is carefully held as dead. as in Auth. de nup. §. distrahuntur. Hence I admit that, as regards its origin, this right takes its beginning in the person of the monk. as l. deo nobis. §. 1. and arg. ff. de act. et obli. l. quicunque gerimus. yet it immediately passes in the manner of a spark. ff. de acqui. haer. l. placet. ff. de condi. indebi. l. frater a fratre. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Laws, and counsel.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that, etc., whether the children of the first marriage are excluded by the second husband from the succession to the dowry of the mother who marries a second time, who gave to the second husband the dowry she had given to the first husband: and add in Part 3, consilium 276.
2. When the substance fails, the terms and the subject fail. Law.
3. Whether a statute can remove the right of succession and the legitime portion of a child.
4. The calling of one to succession is the exclusion of the other by law.
5. Whether this edictal law applies even when no agreement has been made regarding the acquisition of the dowry. And number 6.
6. The will of the parties is not referred to what is impossible.
7. He who is bound not to do something is bound to ensure effectively that it does not happen, nor that a cause or occasion be taken by him.
8. Whether the disposition of this edictal law can be removed by a statute.
9. Every incompatibility is a contradiction.
10. The interpretation of the statute that, if children exist, the husband shall not acquire the dowry.
11. The nature of a restrictive term is that whatever it does not except, it includes.
12. One section of a law is explained by another.
13. A relative term refers to all preceding matters.
14. An argument from the nature of a relative term is probable.
15. The words of a statute must be understood in their proper sense.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen. A certain lady Elena contracted a lawful marriage with Thomasio Buglionis, in 1369, in the month of August. The said Thomas died, the said lady Elena surviving, and there remaining from the said Thomasio and the said lady Elena, and Guglielmo Sandri, who had lawfully contracted marriage with each other. And the said Guglielmo received in dowry, or in the name of dowry, from the said Elena, 400 gold florins, of the money of the said lady Elena, and left the same amount, nor did he confer anything upon his said son, indeed he conferred nothing upon himself. Then afterwards he made no pact for the said Bugliono, his son, concerning which confession of the aforementioned dowry, a public instrument exists, in which instrument no pact was made or appended on the part of the said Guglielmo, regarding the gaining of the aforementioned dowry: In the case in which the said lady Elena should predecease. And afterwards the said Elena died, the said lady Guglielmo surviving: and no other goods left or remaining in the inheritance of the said lady: and the said Bugliono, her son, surviving, from the said first marriage: and no other surviving children from the said lady Elena. Who Thomasio, the first husband, and the said Guglielmo, the second husband, and the said lady Elena are from the city of Florence, in which city then, and today, there is a certain statute of the commune of Florence, under the following content thereof, namely. How succession is made in the dowry, and other goods of a predeceased wife.

† That the husband acquires the dowry of his predeceased wife, if no son or sons exist from them; but if daughters or a son exist: sons, or a son or daughter from another marriage, or those born from another marriage, are excluded from the succession of the same mother in the dowry. In the other goods of the said wife, however, which are not dowry, if she died testate, the husband succeeds, at least to one-third part of those goods, notwithstanding any son or daughter from them; but if she died intestate, the husband succeeds to one-third part of the non-dowry goods, and to the residue of the said goods, the nearest relatives in degree on the father’s side of the said wife succeed. Now, on behalf of the said Buglioni, son of the said Lady Elena from the said first marriage, it is requested and said that the said William, the second husband, was and is bound to him and is obliged to restore to him at least half of the said quantity, which he received as dowry from the said Lady Elena, as stated. And he rightly claims this by law *Hac edictali*, in the beginning, Codex, *De secundis nuptiis*, which agrees with § *Optime* in the Authentica *De nuptiis*. Nor does the aforementioned statute obstruct this; for the statute speaks that the husband acquires the dowry of his predeceased wife, if no son or sons exist from them, etc. Because it says “dowry,” and thus, for there to be a place for acquisition, there must be a dowry. And then the right is sought by them; otherwise, lacking the substance of the dowry, it fails.

† the terms and the subject matter of the law: and consequently the disposition of the law. As is shown in D. de testamento militis, l. de diuortiis, l. vlti., §. j. facit; D. de testamento, si quaeramus. And regarding the law, some report: but in the case at hand, it is established that there was nothing else in the goods of the said Lady Elena, nor at the time of her death; and that nothing remained with the son of the first marriage beyond what she had given to her second husband as dowry and to her husband. By the rule that the dowry was acquired as a gain, it is inferred that the said dowry, to the extent of one-half, is considered as not given and as not written, by the authority of l. hac edictali, §. si vero plusquam statutum et dictum, and the said §. optime, ver. et hoc decernens. And if there was no dowry for the said Lady, and consequently no gain of dowry, then the provision did not apply. And thus it appears that the said law, hac edictali, cannot be said to be corrected by the said statute, since this does not state it; rather, it speaks of a different case. Namely, that the gain of dowry presupposes a dowry, as has been proven above; since statutes are to be reduced to the common law insofar as possible, provided they have some effect: as the common laws say, C. de noxa, l. 2, and D. de muneribus et honoribus, l. vt gradatim, §. si lege. Nor should the correction of laws be presumed, unless this is expressly stated in the law being corrected, or at least unless it is prevented by reason of unavoidable contradiction. As in Auth. de administratione officiorum, §. fi, and there noted, coll. 3. facit; l. sed et posteriores, and there noted, D. de legibus. Furthermore, it is not an objection that in the instrument the pact for acquiring the gain was not appended, because it suffices that the gain was truly acquired by law, since the same reason applies. And this is held by Cynus and other Moderns in the said l. hac edictali, in the principal part, in the second question. Furthermore, it is not an objection if one were to raise the complaint of an undutiful dowry: because the sons of the first marriage are entitled to both remedies. The complaint of an undutiful dowry serves to rescind and revoke it for the legitime, and for the remainder of the condition: by l. hac edictali, to reduce the second portion according to the subject matter to the proper rate. And both remedies exclude each other, even as regards the effect of collection. As noted in the said §. optime, in the gloss beginning "hic manifeste colligitur etc.", and noted by the glossator there, C. de inofficiosa dote. What is held there by Petrus Cynus in the said l. eadem hac edictali, in the principal part, in the third question. Or one may respond to this objection by means of "quamuis de solutione," which the gloss places in the said l. 1, C. de inofficiosa dote. Furthermore, it is not an objection if the authority of the Apostle were alleged, where he says that a widow should marry in the Lord: because by that, the penalties imposed in hatred of those who marry a second time were abolished, but not these, which were principally introduced in favor of the children: such as the provision of the said l. hac edictali. As Innocentius expressly notes, Extra, de secundis nuptiis, l. 1. Furthermore, it is not an objection if it were objected that the time of the death of the binubia is considered, as in Auth. de nuptiis, §. quia vero hactenus. And thus it seems that the dowry existed from the beginning. Therefore, the gain of dowry also applies: because I respond that the time of death and the time of the donation of the dowry are considered: as is more beneficial to the sons of the first marriage. The dowry is constituted from the beginning under the condition that the woman be found to have the same amount at the time of her death; otherwise, it is considered as not given from the very beginning. And this is proven in l. si constante, in fine, D. de donationibus ante nuptias. And this is held there by Cynus and other Moderns, and more fully in the said l. hac edictali, in the second question. And thus it is not true to say that it had the beginning of truth, and that it was a dowry from the beginning: because it does not contain a resulting condition, but a suspensive one, as has been proven above. Which suspensive condition renders the disposition null in the meantime, and the effect of the sentence: as D. de conversione operarum, si quis fundum; and D. de hereditate vel actione vendita, l. multum; and D. de die adiecta, and what is noted there. On the contrary, on behalf of the said Guglielmo, it is said and alleged that the said petition of the said Buglioni, which he makes against the said Guglielmo for one-half of the said dowry, by the condition of the said l. hac edictali, does not proceed, in view of the said statute of the Commune of Florence.

† Because a statute can, through paternal or maternal succession, even deprive a son of debts owed by natural law. This is determined by Dy. in cap. Indultum, Extra de regulis iuris, lib. 6, and by Cy. in l. Servus, C. de nuptiis. Moreover, because the statute of the city of Florence could correct and abolish common law: as in l. Hac edictali, in the city of Florence; as in l. Omnes populi, wherever the disposition of a statute not disapproved prevails over the disposition contrary to common law; as in l. 1, C. quae sit longa consuetudo; and l. Fin., de tutoribus; l. 3, §. Divus, ff. de sepulchro violato. And that it intended to abolish and correct is clearly shown by the words of the statute, which state this: the words of which, in every part, deviate from common law. It deviates because it provides that if the wife predeceases, the husband does not restore the dowry, even though he profits; which is contrary to common law: as in l. 2, in principio, ff. solutione matrimonii, and many similar cases. And it also deviates when it expressly states that the children of the first marriage are excluded from succession to the dowry. And thus it deviates in our case, in which it provides that the husband profits from the dowry of the predeceased wife, if there are no children from them. From this it follows that the son of the first marriage, i.e., the said Buglionus, who is not a child of both of them, is not admitted to the said dowry given to the said Guli., the second husband, according to the said l. Hac edictali, or another law. For words must be understood with effect, where the singular gloss says in l. Sed hoc nisi, ff. de iure dotium. But if it were said that the son of the first marriage could claim by the condition of the said l. Hac edictali, the said words of the statute, which say that the husband profits from the dowry, would have no effect; because he does not profit who is bound to restore to others: as in l. Aliud est capere, ff. de verbis significatis; l. 2, §. Peruenisset, ff. de hereditate instituenda, cum similibus. And this is also proven by a certain necessary consequence: because he who disposes of one thing seems also to dispose of another, according to which that upon which the principal disposition rests would not have effect. For he who wills the consequent necessarily wills the antecedent: as in ff. de acquirenda hereditate, l. 4, §. Qui habet, ff. de servo rustico praediali, cum similibus. Therefore, since the statute provides that the husband profits and has the dowry, by necessary consequence it wills that the son or another does not have it. For two cannot have it in solidum. To the foregoing is also induced the text with the gloss in Auth. de hereditate, §. Reliquum, joined with §. Illud palam, where it is held that brothers succeed in succession, together with the brother of another son. The gloss says that the said sons of brothers exclude aunts or uncles from the said succession, although they are of equal degree. And this is so: because since the law calls them to the said inheritance, it seems to exclude others who could have come to the said succession; otherwise the calling would not have effect.

† From which it is inferred that the inclusion and calling of one is the exclusion of the other. In the same matter and part in which another is called: so too, assuming that the statute calls the husband to the dowry profit, it seems thereby to exclude all others from the said dowry. For the aforesaid, it is most fitting that which is noted by Bartolus in the last law, ff. ad tert.

† Moreover, because the law *Hac edictali* does not claim application unless the woman gave a dowry with the aforementioned pact of gaining, which she added by agreement, as the gloss expressly holds in the said law *Hac edictali* and is noted in law 1, *De iure dotis*. From this it is said that, since in our case the wife of the aforementioned Guglielmo made no pact of gaining, the said law *Hac edictali* has no place. Moreover, because it is manifest from the words of the said statute that the intention of the legislator was for the husband to gain that which was given to him as dowry: and he preferred to tolerate inequalities between the son of the first marriage and the second husband, contrary to the said law *Hac edictali*, rather than incur numerous injustices and absurdities, and especially the fear that, under the said law *Hac edictali*, young widows would not find a second husband due to the diminution of the dowry, and thus the faculty of marrying and procreating children would be restricted: which is contrary to the liberty of the law of nations and contrary to many laws in the title *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*. Therefore, the interpretation of the aforementioned statute is to be favored, not restricted.

Nor does the objection to the contrary hold, namely, that whatever was given immoderately by the wife of the said Guglielmo to the second husband was not dowry; and consequently, the statute, which provides that otherwise the dowry gain is taken away from the husband, has no place, since dowry is a term of law, as in law *Quod dicitur*; and whatever the wife gave to the second husband beyond what she gave to the son is annulled by the said law *Hac edictali*; and consequently, since it is not dowry, the disposition of the statute has no place, since its terms are not verified, which is contrary to law: because that which was given immoderately is not dowry. Although in the said law they say as if it were not given, the word denoting property is used. It is one thing to say that that which was given is held as not given; it is another to say that it is held as not given. But nowhere, and especially in the said law *Hac edictali*, is it provided that that which was given immoderately is held as not given. Therefore, it is presumed that it was truly made and was dowry from the beginning. And because, as I said above, the statute deviates from the common law, it should be understood that the legislator intended the place to be governed by natural words rather than by words of the common law, from which common law it had already departed. And especially so that the words of the statute have legal effect regarding that which it disposes, namely, that the husband gains that which was given to him by the wife. And because, for the disposition to have effect, we must take the words naturally and not according to the meaning of the common law, as in law *Hos accusare*, § *Utrumlibet*, *De accusationibus*. And because we must understand words according to how common usage of speech interprets them, as in law *Auunculus*, *De verbis significandis*, and law *Labeo*, *De sponsalibus*. But from common usage of speech, whatever is inscribed in the dotal instrument and given as dowry is called dowry. That instrument also makes great faith in this matter, as in law *Una*, Codex *De fide instrumentorum*. And because that is properly called dowry which is inscribed and narrated in the dotal instrument, as in law *Si quis posthac*, in the principle, Codex *De bonis praescriptionibus*. And because we must also attend to the origin of the thing, and thus to the giving itself, as in law *Cum simul*, § *Haeres*, *De legatis 2*, and law *Qui id quod*, *De donationibus*, and law *Tutor*, *De fideiussoribus*. To this also contributes law *Eum qui*, § *Similiter*, *De iureiurando*.

Moreover, it is also proved by reason: because the law says that the immoderation or equality of the dowry given to the second husband, as regards the son of the first marriage, is inspected at the time of the death of the binubia, as in the Authenticum *De nuptiis*, § *Optime*, § *Quia vero hactenus*, Collatio 4. Hence, if a woman gave all that she had as dowry at the time she married the second husband, and afterwards acquired something at the time of death: she leaves to the son of the first marriage as much as she gave to the second husband, there would be no doubt that the son cannot complain, nor invoke the remedy of law *Hac edictali*. Therefore, it appears that that which was given at the beginning to the said Guglielmo was dowry, and he gained it by the said statute.

Moreover, the objection does not hold that it is alleged, that the woman is deemed to have tacitly added the pact of gaining, although it was not expressly stated in the dotal instrument, from which she knew the pact was induced by the statute. And since the dowry gain is induced by the statute: because it is not true that the woman is deemed to have tacitly added the pact of gaining if she does not expressly place it; it is written that scarcely even the dowry gain would be induced by the statute: for there is a great difference between an obligation which proceeds from contracts, and an obligation which proceeds from law, as in law *Obligamur*, *De actionibus et obligationibus*. And those things which are done by disposition of law are not said to be done by man, nor to proceed from the act of man, as in law *Qui sub conditione*, Institutiones. Therefore, since the husband gains the dowry by disposition of the statute and not of man, the said law *Hac edictali* ceases, and nothing can be imputed to the woman: because laws bind even the unwilling, as in law *Mevio*, *De legibus 1*. And that which is done under necessity is not imputed, as in law *Non uidetur*, § *Qui iussu*, *De re militari*, and law *Qua actione*, § 1, *Ad legem Aquiliam*. Nor is it true that the woman was bound to see to it that the husband could not gain the dowry by making a pact that he could not gain: because she performed an act permitted by law, namely, marriage. And although she was restricted by the common law to preserve the share for the son of the first marriage, she was not restricted by the municipal and special law of the community of Florence. On the contrary, she had open hands by the aforementioned statute. Therefore, nothing can be imputed to the woman, who did whatever the statute permitted. For that which is done by authority of law is not imputed to fault or penalty, as in law *Scimus*, Codex *De administratione tutorum*, and law *Gracchus*, Codex *De adulteriis*.

Say also that we see that an obligation not to alienate exists, yet one can alienate in a special case by permission. And especially in the case of dowry, as is our case, as in law *Mulier*, § *Si proponerent*, *Ad Trebellianum*. Moreover, since it is permitted to the woman to marry and give a dowry to the second husband: whether it follows that it is permitted that she marry according to the custom of the city, and that in her dowry the statute of the city regarding gain, and otherwise disposing, has place. Which is proved by that which is noted by the gloss and doctors in law *Ultima*, Codex *De legatis tutorum*, and by Bartolus in law *Constante*, *De solutione matrimonii*.

Moreover, because it is certain that the disposition of law *Hac edictali*, as proved above, has no place unless a disposition of gaining precedes. Therefore, prior is the disposition of the statute in the conferral of gain in this dowry, than is the penalty of law *Hac edictali*. For since it necessarily precedes the effect, the cause, namely the disposition of law *Hac edictali*, is the conferral of gain preceding. Therefore, regarding the same thing, the law and the statute willed contrary things. Therefore, because the statute wills one gain, and the law wills to take away or diminish the gain. But where the disposition of the common law and the disposition of the statute are opposed, there is no doubt that we observe the statute in the place of the legislator, as said above. Therefore, etc.

Nor does the objection hold from law *Codicillis*, § *Mater*, *De legatis 2*, nor law *Si ita quis*, § *Ea lege*, *De verborum significatione*, which say that he who is forbidden to give to another is bound to see that it does not come to another person against the disposition of law: because this is true when such a person who is forbidden has free will and disposition, and not caused by some necessity: because he cannot marry without a dowry. And wishing to marry and give a dowry, the statute induces dowry gain by necessity: because the statute says, nor gain the dowry. Therefore, such will should not be punished, as in law *Tutoris*, *De his qui veluti indigentes cum si*. Moreover, in law *Codicillis*, they were forbidden by the testator that it should not come to another in consideration of another, to whom the right of fideicommissum was acquired. Nor did a new right or just cause supervene for him who died intestate. But here a new right supervenes, namely, the statute permitting. Moreover, from that law *Si ita quis*, he was bound by permission from contract, nor did anything supervene for which the law, permitting, would be done. But here the woman married while the statute remained, and a just cause supervened, namely, marriage. And this solution is proved in a similar case from law *Mulier*, § *Cum proponeretur*, *Ad Trebellianum*, and in the Authenticum *Res quae*, and better by law *Quaero*, § *Inter locatorem*, *De locato conducto*, in § *Qui seruum*, *De verborum obligatione*, *De legibus*, and law *Quid ergo*, § *Si haeres*.

It is asked, what is the law in the aforementioned matters, having seen the said point, and the statute, and the other above-written things. In the name of Christ, amen.

† L. hac edictali. The profit of the dowry arising from the municipal law is expressly not derogated from by the edictal law. L. hac edic. Nicolaus Mata held this view in his lecture on L. hac edi. on the word glossed there as "de lucrando," saying thus: But what if the husband, who receives the dowry, is to profit from part of the dowry or the whole dowry by the municipal law; can the children of the first marriage avail themselves of the benefit of this law? And I think that they can: since what the gloss says here about the pact to profit, it stated merely by way of example concerning the profit from the dowry and the donation on account of marriage; not, however, in order to restrict the statement of the law, which was general. It is to be understood in every profit which the second spouse derives from the goods of the spouse marrying for the second time. Nevertheless, this profit descends from the will of the woman. For, by willing the antecedent, namely to constitute the dowry, she wills the consequent, i.e., that the husband profits, as in C. de fideicommissis, L. quamuis, and ff. de pactis, L. item quia. But this consequent is impossible by the edictal law L. hac edictali.

† Rather, it does not appear that the will of the parties was directed toward the impossible, as stated in the Digest, *De actionibus et obligationibus*, law *Non solum*. Bartolus holds the same view, and the reason is that what is tacit cannot exceed what is express, Digest, *De locato conducto*, law *Qui ad certum*. I hold the same opinion in law 1, Code, *De inofficioso donatione*, and this is proven by the following induction: this woman is prohibited from doing [it], but the prohibition to do [it] lies in an obligation not to do. Therefore, I argue: he who...

† He who is bound not to do something is bound to see to it that it is not done, when the cause or occasion is taken by him, or even if it is done, by L. ff. loc. in L. locationis. ff. de pac. L. non impossibile. ff. de leg. 2. L. codicillis. §. pe. and note. ff. de verbo. obli. L. si ita quis. §. ea. Moreover, whenever the primary cause is not within one’s power, the secondary cause cannot be in its effect; hence, if the contract does not bind, the obligation does not bind; and say the same of similar cases. But the statute can be called a secondary cause; this is proven, because that which is dependent is not valid, therefore the principal is not valid, nor is the disposition for gain valid, C. de condi. ob causam. 1. 1. But notwithstanding these things, having seen and diligently examined the tenor of the statute, the truth is to the contrary, namely, that according to the form of the statute in its tenor, the husband gains the entire dowry when there are no children from his own [marriage], but from the first marriage. And I premise for clarity,

† That which is established by the law *Hac edicto* may be abrogated by a contrary statute, provided that it is evidently contrary. This is incompatible with the tenor of that law. For not only are affirmation and negation contrary,

† Moreover, every incompatibility is a certain kind of contradiction, as stated in l. 1, § si seruus extero. That the rule of l. hac edictali can be abrogated by statute is evident, because that law contains voluntary and positive law, not necessary and natural law, according to the gloss in C. de secun. nup., auth. sed si quis, at the end of the great gloss. Therefore, the statute is valid according to the gloss in ff. de reg. iur., l. nec ex praetorio, and in l. omnes populi, with its entire subject matter. Having thus presupposed the validity of the statute,

† Let us consider the intention of the statute. There is, however, a division of the parts of the statute regarding its understanding. It is therefore divided into two principal parts: for first it speaks concerning the dowry, secondly concerning other goods. The second part is found at the words "in alijs vero" [but in the others], and this is the distinction of things. The first part, however, is subdivided into three parts: in the first it provides for the husband, in the second it provides for the children of the second marriage; in the third it excludes the children of the first marriage. The second part is found at the words "si vero" [if, however]. The third part is found at the words "qui vel quae" [whoever, male or female], and this is the distinction of persons. I therefore argue from the first part, which pertains to the husband, as follows: if there are no children from them, the husband shall acquire the entire dowry; but here there are no children from them; therefore, the husband shall acquire the entire dowry. And this argument concludes formally: for the major premise is evident from the words of the statute; the minor premise is true in its terms; therefore, the conclusion is necessary. For we cannot gloss this statute by saying that we should supply the words "from them" with the addition "nor from another marriage"; because this would be a cervotina [elk-like, i.e., far-fetched] and extraneous gloss. Moreover, if we were to supply this, the sense would be that if there are children from another marriage, the husband would acquire nothing; which is false. Moreover, here common law cannot be mixed with municipal law because of the word "ex eis" [from them]. And I argue as follows: this is a restrictive and distinctive term; therefore, I argue as follows:

† For restrictive terms, whatever they do not except, they include, as in D. de fun. instruc. l. quaesitum § idem. I answer in one way, and there the sons of another marriage do not derogate from the provision of the statute. The second part, however, is translative, because the gain which the husband had in the absence of children is transferred to the children of the second marriage as well; from which second clause the first is also explained.

† For one head of a law is explained by another, D. de petitione hereditatis, l. utrum; and D. de iure et facto ignorato, l. 1, §. si. The third part of the statute is privative, there: "who or whom," etc. And note that this relative has two antecedents: namely, when free children do not exist from them, and when they do exist.

† And it is certain that a relative term refers to all preceding words, D. de legibus 1, l. talis scriptura; and l. si idem cum eodem, §. si, de iur. omn. iud.; de appellationibus, l. secundo requiris. And this argument from the nature of reference is sometimes probable. But here it is necessary,

† For whenever a conjunctive phrase is found in the antecedent, the same must be present in the subsequent relative clause, as in the preceding conjunction, D. de legatis 3, l. et hoc legatum; and l. ea tamen adiectio. Therefore, this hypothetical proposition, which the dialecticians call the antecedent with respect to its members, receives its meaning through what is added, namely “who or whom,” etc. Moreover, this clause, or these words, “who or whom,” etc., must have some operative effect; and these words must not be superfluous, as in l. si quando, D. de legatis 1; and l. 1, D. ad municipalia. But if, by means of these words excluding the children of the first marriage, provision were not made for the husband but only for the children of the second marriage, these words would have no effect, since in the preceding part sufficient provision had already been made for the children of the second marriage against those of the first, there, “even if from her,” etc. They must be construed with the entire two-membered antecedent, not with only one part of the antecedent, i.e., with only one member. But against this it is thus opposed: this dowry is not a dowry in name but in effect, as noted in D. de iure dotium, l. nulla. For wherever a pactum de lucrando is appended, the donation is not valid, as in Auth. de nuptiis, § optime, col. 4; and there by Jacobus de Belvis; and l. hac edictali, § si vero, there, “as if not written,” etc. Therefore, the statute, which speaks of a dowry, does not seem to speak of this one. That which is not valid as such is not properly called such, but is so called abusively, l. 2, D. quemadmodum testamentum aperiri debeat.

† However, the words of statutes ought to be understood in their proper sense and referred to the law, as noted in C. de iure delib. l. si, §. in conputatione. Solution: He who takes it thus, errs. For truly it is a dowry, and as long as the husband lives, the things are dowry property, and the husband profits from the fruits of the entire dowry for the burdens of marriage. And although the agreement to profit is voided by common law, nevertheless the dowry itself remains intact: and while the mother lives, the children of the first marriage have no claim to it. And if the second marriage were dissolved by the death of the second husband, the dowry would return to the woman, not to the children, as noted in l. 1, de dot. praeleg. and l. 2, ff. de pact. dot. Thus, therefore, the dowry is valid in itself, and the children, while the mother lives, have nothing but a certain hope, as stated in the aforementioned §. optime, in the word "propter speciem" [on account of the hope], and in §. quia, in the word "hactenus" [thus far], there: "not from the beginning." Therefore, under a condition, hence the children are called, if they are grateful until the death of the mother; otherwise, upon the death of the mother. And if they are defrauded by the agreement: but those who are called under a condition, in the meantime, what is done is not rescinded, but only upon the fulfillment of the condition, as C. communia de leg. l. si, §. sed quia nostra, and §. seq. l. 1, §. secundum, ff. ad Sil. Moreover, since the statute permits the profit, it permits the dowry itself: for he who permits, also wills the antecedent, by which one arrives at that, ff. de acquirenda haereditate, l. illud. I also say that by the authority of this statute, an express agreement to profit is valid, ff. de pactis, l. non impossibile. It is not objected that it seems an injustice to exclude the children. For I concede that this right is not equitable; nevertheless, it is good according to the situation of the generative and appetitive faculty. Hence the Apostle: let each one take his own, on account of fornication. Also, l. codicillis, §. pe, and the gloss in l. ea, do not stand in the way, for here we are not in a matter prohibited in the antecedent or consequent, but in a matter permitted by the statute in clear words in both. And thus I say, and I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Laws, etc., advise.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If the will of a son does not have effect by the law of wills, whether it can have effect as a donation causa mortis, if there is a codicillary clause, namely, it does not have effect by the law of wills, etc.
2. The reason why a son under paternal power can make a donation causa mortis, and yet cannot make a will.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Suppose that a son makes a will, and therein makes a donation, and states that if it is not valid by the law of wills, it should be valid by the law of codicils, or of any other form of last will. Now the question arises,

† Whether it is valid as a donation. Dy. says that it is not: because a donation causa mortis requires the special consent of the father, as in l. hoc legatum, supra, tit. i. Also, because we must understand words according to their proper meaning, as in l. hoc legatum, supra, de leg. 3. But a donation causa mortis refers to a contract inter vivos and to a last will. See l. 1, ff. de dote praeleg. The same is held by Spe. in tit. de instru. edi., § compendiose, ver. quid si filius. Ray. says that it is valid as a donation, if it had special concession: and thus he removes the reason. The second objection does not hold, because where words cannot operate according to their proper meaning, they operate according to their improper meaning, so that the thing may rather have effect than fail, as in ff. ad l. Iul. Maiest., l. Scævola; ff. de vul. et pup., l. verbis ciuilibus. Against the opinion of Lord Ray., see the gloss in auth. ex causa, de lib. pręte. et ex haere.

But the contrary reasoning is that a son may make a donation causa mortis, yet he cannot make a will. The gloss in l. 3, C. qui testamento facere possunt, states that the reason is that testamentary capacity is a matter of public law, whereas donation is a matter of private law. The Ultramontani jurists say that this reasoning proves the opposite: for if it is true that testamentary capacity is a matter of public law, then paternal power ought not to be taken into account in it, as in l. filium, supra, de his qui sunt sui vel alieni iuris; l. namque quod, ff. ad Trebellianum. Jacobus de Belvisi, defending the gloss, says that it is well stated, provided one understands that that is not the reason itself, but the reason for the reason is that the son cannot make a will because he is not a person with full legal capacity, as in C. de bonis quae liberis, l. si, § necessitatem. But why is he not restored to capacity by the father’s consent? The gloss continues: because a will is a matter of public law, in which paternal power has no effect. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a master in theology can be deprived of his mastership, or dignity, on account of ignorance, and on account of his bad morals.
2. The word *nec*, what it imports.
body: The case is as follows: The General of the Minor Order, by mandate of the Lord Pope, ought to summon all Masters in Theology who were masters of examination within the province to the General Chapter; and that they should be examined there both in life and in learning; and if they are found to be suitable and sufficient both in life and in learning, they ought to enjoy the graces and privileges of masters. But if they are not found to be sufficient, nor of good life, they ought to be deprived of the said graces and privileges, nor should they be called masters any longer. Now a certain master was summoned, and because he did not appear, he was deprived of his office on account of dishonesty and a certain conspiracy. Then the said General had him examined by two masters, who reported that he was of good life and sufficient learning; although in truth he had not been amended in any respect; and the General restored him to the mastership.

† It is asked whether the restoration was valid. I answer that if the restoration was valid, since from it he incurred infamy both in law and in fact. Moreover, if it had been done by the authority of the Pope, the General could not have restored him in full right; even if this man had become so good, as anyone of most holy life, as is stated in D. de postulandis, l. 1, § de qua; D. de poenis, l. fratres; and fully noted by Innocentius in X. de re iudicata, c. cum te. But if the deposition was null, then, as having been done de facto, it ought to have been revoked as void, as in D. de accusationibus, l. absentem, where it is expressly stated. Now therefore let us see whether this deposition was valid or not: and thus it must be said that either at the time of the said restoration it was otherwise established, not merely by contumacy, that the said master was not sufficient either in learning or in life; and then the restoration held, because it was done after knowledge of the cause and according to the form of the rescript. Or it was not established here, and then for contumacy alone the master could not be deposed from the dignity of mastership: partly because this sentence is capital and of the mere Empire, partly because it is contrary to the order given in the rescript, where it is said that they ought to be examined there; and he was not examined there; but this man was not examined, therefore the disposition did not hold. He could therefore be excommunicated, not deposed, as in X. de iudicibus, cap. 1; and X. de rescriptis, cap. cum dilecta; and l. 1, C. de manumissionibus vindiciarum. For whenever an order is established by law, if the order is omitted, what is done is by law itself invalid, as in D. de transactionibus, l. cum hi, § cum Praetor.

† Furthermore, in support of this matter, the following words are cited: "if, however, they are not found to be sufficient, nor of good life"; for the word "nor" is used conjunctively, as is fully read, and as noted in c. Plerique, de electione, in the Clementines. And therefore, unless both conjunctive conditions are present, namely that he is not sufficient in knowledge, nor in life, he cannot be deposed from his mastership; because in a proposition with a conjunctive extreme, it is required that both parts be true, as stated in the Digest, de rebus dubiis, l. Si is qui ducenta, §. Utrum, and §. Cum ita. And therefore, if he is sufficient in knowledge, although of bad morals, he could not be deprived of the authority of the said rescript, nor by any other authority inferior to the Pope, because he holds his office by the bulls of the Apostolic See, as stated in the Extravagantes, de iudiciis, c. Cum venisset. For what is said that infamy deprives one of his dignities, as in the Code, de dignitatibus, l. Iudices, lib. 12, must be understood when they are condemned for fraud, not for insufficiency. For this reason, he cannot be rejected except by him whose authority conferred the dignity, as in the Digest, de excusationibus tutorum, l. Sed et reprobari. I nevertheless advise the one who wishes to be called master that he amend himself. For if he were noted with infamy due to the turpitude of his life, he would lose his dignity without hope of recovery; because the descent to Avernus is easy, but to rise after the fall is most difficult, as noted in l. 2, in fine, Code, de libertis et eorum liberis. And let these things be said, saving the correction of my lords, the General Master and the other masters in theology, to whom I humbly submit myself. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A decree of the prince can remove an action and an exception when it has the force of a judgment.
2. Public auction is not part of the form of judicial procedure, except in certain cases.
3. Genitives import a condition.
4. An indefinite term placed at the end is equivalent to a universal.
body: It is asked whether the principal should be compelled to renounce, if the creditors [are paid] with interest.

† Decree. Question: Should the subjects of the Prince be compelled to renounce proceedings if they wish to renounce? What is the law? I answer that delay and contumacy do not benefit them; nevertheless, by renunciation it is removed by operation of law, as in C. de pac. l. postquam liti. But by silence and contumacy, by means of an exception, as in ff. ex qui. cau. ma. l. sed si per Prætorem. §. sed si decreto. The force of this difference lies in this: if the Prince were to make a third statute, whereby he returned to the common law, he would return to the same instance; but if an express renunciation had intervened, otherwise, as in ff. de transa. l. cum mota. It is necessary, however, that a precept to renounce has been made to the cited creditors, if the written instrument is of such a nature as to compel, as in ff. de fideicom. liber. l. cum vero. §. subuentum.

Secondly, it is asked. The decree of the Lord provides that the judge must satisfy the creditors by having the property put up for auction. Now it is asked whether the judge may interpose a second decree, or an auction? And it seems that he may: because an auction is not of the form of judicial procedure, except in certain cases, as C. de sac. san. ecc. auth. hoc ius porrectum. ff. de mino. l. et si sine. C. si aduersus fiscum. l. edicto. ff. de rescin. ven. l. fundus. C. de fide instru. et iure hastae fiscalis. l. 1. lib. 10. C. de bonis autho. iu. pos. l. fi. The contrary is true, because the words are placed in the obligation, and to have the goods put up for auction. But the ablative

It is of importance that the condition be observed, as stated in the law *ut*, in the Digest under *De usuris*; in the law *Edictum*, in the Digest under *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*; and in the law *A testatore*. And therefore, unless the condition is observed, the disposition is not valid, as stated in the Code under *Ad Trebellianum*, in the law *Iubemus*, section *Si autem*. However, the clause placed at the end of the aforementioned rescript, when it says "and by having the said goods put up for auction," refers to all the matters to be proven: because the same reason applies, and the condition is common to all the preceding matters.

† and therefore an indefinite term placed at the end is equivalent to a universal one, according to the rule set forth by Lord Dynus in the rubric of the Rules of Law, Book 6, and noted in Speculum, De instrumentis edictis, §. nunc videndum, under the words "Item, except that such a clause." I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If a horse is purchased while diseased, by what action shall suit be brought? And by what means must this be proven, and how may the disease of the horse be ascertained?
2. Farriers are to be believed.
body: Thus, for the sake of clarity, if the matter concerns diseases, it must be premised

† It is thus, that for the sake of clarity, if a pact has been interposed concerning diseases and defects, it must be observed, as is fully stated in the law and noted in *l. quod venditor*, D. de dolo; and D. de evictione, *l. si ita quis*; and D. de edilitio edicto, *l. sciendum*, §. dictum. And from this first point of clarity it appears that if the said horse sold was suffering from a disease at the time of the sale, from which it subsequently died, the buyer may bring an action for redhibition, or at least an action for *quantum minus*, that is, in this case, for the amount by which he would have bought it for less, in which judgments the restitution of the price is contained, as in D. de edilitio edicto, *l. bouem*, §. aliquando; nay more, by virtue of that very pact, an action on the purchase may be brought to the same end, as in D. de actionibus emptoris, *l. ex empto*, §. si quis virginem; and any legal avenue is a good avenue in our case. Now it must be proved that this horse was suffering from a fatal disease at the time of the sale and delivery: once this is proved, the buyer undoubtedly has a right. Regarding this, however, it should be known for the sake of clarity that the existence of diseases in the interior parts can be made clear in three, or perhaps four, ways. First, by the effect from the cause. For he who does not eat nor drink is not healthy; rather, he is like one dead, as in *l. in hac*, D. de triticis. Second, this is proved by the swiftness of death; for that which dies quickly is presumed to have died from a wound or ulcer, as noted in *l. 1*, C. de emendatione servorum. Third, it is proved by the visible and apparent corruption of the internal members: when such corruption exists, the thing was bound to perish entirely, and therefore the seller is liable, especially one who promised that it was sound in head and body, when the exact opposite has appeared, as in D. de edilitio edicto, *l. ediles aiunt*.

Fourthly, it also appears from the judgment of the marshals, to whom credence is to be given, as in l. semel, C. de re militari, lib. 12, from which it appears that the said price is to be restored to the said buyer. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The benefit of cession may be raised against the execution of a sentence: and how the clause, "if they do not pay," is to be understood. Also, whether guarantors are released on account of an arbitration made between the principal debtor and the creditor: and whether the reservation, which he made principally of being able to sue others, is of benefit or not.
2. When and how relief ought to be granted to minors who have been injured by a sentence.
body: The case is as follows: 1. By an arbitral sentence, certain principal debtors were condemned in the sum of 75 [librae] for all that to which they were bound by reason of past transactions, with reservation of rights against all others bound for the said condemnation, in the event that the said condemned parties did not pay the said quantity in the said transactions for collection. Thereafter, action was brought against the sureties, who were ignorant of the said arbitral sentence, and they were condemned in the sum of 600 librae or thereabouts; the plaintiff knew well of the said sentence, but the defendants were ignorant thereof. Now the said defendants wish to pay the said sum of 75 librae and to free themselves from the whole.

† It is asked, what is the law? I answer: if no reservation had been made, the said sureties could defend themselves by means of the exception of assignment (exceptio cedendarum actionum), which may be raised in the execution of a judgment, by saying to the plaintiff: “Assign to us your rights, and insofar as you cannot assign them, we raise against you the exception of fraud.” For this exception is among those that may be raised in the execution of a judgment, as expressly noted in *l. si res obligata*, D. de legibus 1. And this is the opinion of Speculum and of all authorities. But doubt is cast by the said reservation, the words of which are as follows: “That in whatever respect the said authors could not obtain and receive the said 75 pounds, or if they were not paid, all right to demand and obtain the said fictitious sum shall be reserved.” It is therefore argued on behalf of the plaintiffs, because these words, “if they were not paid,” must be understood up to the time when the litigation was subsequently joined, as in D. de verbis oblig., *l. si Titius*. To the contrary it appears, because no time was specified; hence those words, “if they were not paid,” are to be understood thus: i.e., if, after discussion of assets, no source of payment were found. This is the ordinary gloss in D. de fideiussoribus, in *l. fideiussor obligari*, §. ult. For this reservation begins with the condition “if they were not paid,” a condition which does not exist, being negative, unless discussion of assets has taken place. Moreover, since no day was fixed, it appears that default may be purged perpetually; which I prove thus: this sum of 75 pounds succeeded in place of the entire fictitious sum; therefore, by paying it, the whole debt is discharged. Hence it can always be paid, because all judgments are discharged if that which is due is paid, as in Inst. de perpetuis et temporalibus actionibus, §. ult. The text in the aforementioned *l. cum fideiussor*, §. ult., is not to the contrary, because there inquiry is made into the interpellation of the principal debtor; but the principal debtors were never interpellated; therefore the condition of the suretyship obligation, nor of the aforementioned reservation, did not occur. The case is in the aforementioned §. ult. Moreover, these sureties were ignorant of that judgment, whereas the plaintiff knew it, and thus there was fraud on the part of the plaintiff. Also, these heirs of the sureties are minors and suffer injury due to justifiable ignorance and the fraud of the plaintiff; therefore they are restored to their original position under the double clause, as noted by Dyther in D. de verbis oblig., *l. ad diem*. Considering, therefore, that we are not in the case of the reservation, and that the exception of assignment applies, or that at least we are within the benefit of restitution in integrum, the said judgment for payment of 75 pounds ought not to be put into execution, if the facts alleged are true. The advocate also argues subtly, because here a certain novation has been effected by the arbitration award, since the arbitration award itself is a settlement. Hence the sureties formerly given do not appear to be bound, as in D. de praetoria stipulatione, *l. Valerianus*, and D. de locato conducto, *l. cum impuberis*, §. 1, where it is expressly stated that, since the form of the first obligation has been changed, sureties and intercessors are not bound. But against this the reservation weighs heavily, as in D. si quis cautio, *l. 2* post principium, there: “unless the contrary [is agreed]”; where the case seems to apply. But the single response is, namely, that here the condition of the reservation did not occur, as in D. si certum petatur, *l. si*, §. si cum Seio, and as noted by Bartolus in *l. 1*, de conveniendo fisci debito, lib. 10. For when discussion is placed in the form of the obligation with someone, so as to indicate discussion, there, unless discussion is formally made, the obligation is not contracted.

† Furthermore, it must be observed that where minors are involved in a case, the judgment may be retracted on account of newly discovered instruments, and the security of the minors may be safeguarded, even if no restitution in integrum has been requested, as noted in l. 1, C. de sen. aduer. fis. lib. 10, and ff. de re iudica, l. Imperatores. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether one who has the power to provide, elect, present, and make any other disposition is said to have the power of confirming.
2. What confirmation is.
body: CrBa presentation, election, or any other [right] which they call Papal, to the collation, provision, pre-CrBa sentation, election, or any other disposition of the Bishop of Trier in his entire diocese.

† Now it is asked whether a benefice is included in which the Bishop of Tournai has a simple confirmation of election: and it seems that it is, because the words are most general, and therefore they should not be restricted, as in D. 50.17.1 (*Si sic*). But this word, which seems most general, is the word “another disposition.” For he who confirms seems to dispose, as in D. 50.16.1 (*Legem obvenire hereditatem*); and D. 2.15.1 (*Legum*); C. 8.53.1 (*Si quis argentum*); D. 29.1.1 (*Tribunus*), § *Si*. For since confirmation adds something to that which is confirmed, that which is added is rightly called a disposition; likewise the word “provision” has a broad meaning, as in c. *Cum in illis*, de praebendis, lib. 6. Hence Innocentius says that he who at the same time confirms and elects is said to provide, as noted by Innocentius in X. 2.28.1 (*Constituit*), in the gloss *Quidem*.

To the contrary it seems that in such a grace elective rights pertaining to another church and to the bishop’s confirmation alone are not included. First, from the case in c. *Si dignitatem*, § *Ad hoc*, de praebendis, in the Clementines, where these words, “provision” and “disposition,” are expressly set forth, and yet electives are not included. Therefore, by this grace the bishop is burdened, but the churches are not burdened. But if we were to say the contrary, the bishop and other churches would be burdened together: which is certainly not contained either in the words of the grace or in its sense, as argued in D. 10.3.1 (*Per fundum*); D. 10.3.1 (*Receptum*).

Moreover, this is clear from the rule that whenever a statement is predicated of one thing and not of several, it must be restricted to that one thing, as in D. 33.1.1 (*Hoc legatum*). Furthermore, it is proved by another doctrine: for he who confirms by virtue of his own and another’s mixed authority is not said to dispose or to provide; nor is this imputed to him as a benefice, but as justice. For he who renders what is due does not impede a benefice, as in D. 36.2.1 (*Si servo fideicommissaria*), § 1; and D. 36.2.1 (*Proxime*), which are laws notable for this purpose.

† Moreover, confirmation is said to be a firming together with another, and therefore it is not included under the appellation of simple provisions, as in D. de iurisi omnium iudicum, l. et quia; D. de libellis, l. Aurelius, § testamento. Moreover, these favors, so ambitious, or rather, as I may say, so enormous, ought to be restricted and not extended. To this point, the statement in c. cum in illis, § sicuti, is most apt; indeed, there is a case in its own reasoning, de praebendis, lib. 6. To the same effect is what Innocentius notes in the said c. constitutio, because a provision is properly so called when it has the force of election and confirmation simultaneously, not when one elects and another confirms. There is no doubt about the other terms, because they are opposed species, and therefore do not comprehend the case of confirmation. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The writing of a notary already condemned for falsification does not carry credibility, nor is he to be believed.
2. What penalty is to be imposed on the offender when the offense has not been consummated.
3. An offense promised to be committed under a condition is not to be punished as if it had been perpetrated.
4. The crime of lèse-majesté is not committed by a non-subject.
5. An unpremeditated and sudden offense is not to be punished severely.
6. The city of Lanua, and it was held that the city of Sagona was in rebellion against its mother city.
body: of the city of Langua, and he was held in the name of certain lords. A certain Zacharias, formerly a citizen of the said city of Sagona, at the request of a certain Antonius Morandi, went to the said Antonius to certain secret places, where they had many words and conversations for a space of three hours, or thereabouts: from which, in effect, no fraud against the community of the said city of Sagona is found. It is true, however, that the aforementioned discussions tended toward the overthrow of the government of the rector then present there for the said lords, but under certain conditions and modes, and with the advice of some experts preserved. And these things are said to appear from the confession of the said Zacharias on the inquiry formed against him, who Zacharias says that the proceeding is not valid, nor proves anything against him, because the notary who is said to have made the record had been deprived of his office by a sentence of condemnation for perjury.

I answer that, if this is so, the aforementioned writings are invalid and prove nothing, as is noted in C. de probat. l. iubemus, and in Auth. de quaest. §. si, col. 6. The objection based on l. Barbarius does not hold, because there that Barbarian could be made capable, whereas here he cannot. Secondly, it is said that it is not true that he made the aforementioned confession, nor is the statement of the suspected notary believed. I answer that this allegation is good, as is noted in C. de fals. l. si quis decurio.

† Then, omitting those declaratory matters, I proceed to the substantial point of fact: although the aforementioned statements contained in the said confession are true and a penalty would be applicable, nevertheless the penalty of death or of mutilation of a limb ought not to be imposed. For every offense is either completed by its result, and this is not among those, since no effect has ensued, as stated in l. 1, § haec verba, ff. quod quisque su.; or it is completed by the intent, and this is not among those either,

† because this Zacharias consented on the condition that he be advised by prudent and honest men, who certainly would not have consented; and therefore, the condition not having been fulfilled, it cannot be said that this man gave his consent, as in the Digest, *De manumissionibus testamento*, law *Si quis locuples*.

† Moreover, this person does not fall under the crime of lèse-majesté, because he was not a subject of that lord, as noted by Paulus de Leazariis in c. pastoralis, de re iudicanda, in the Clementines. Nevertheless, because this person acted against good morals and caused grave scandal, and is suspected of sedition, although he is not yet seditious according to what has transpired up to now, he ought to be punished extra ordinem at the discretion of the judge, as provided in ff. de effracto et expillato, l. 1, § expillatores, and ff. de penis, l. hodie, and as noted in l. 1, § 1, de seditiosis, where the glossa states that punishment should be imposed according to the quality of the person.

† Add, and argue regarding the quality of the intent, for the intent of this man did not entirely incline toward malice; nor was it a premeditated affair, but rather sudden and unconsidered, as stated in the Digest, *De poenis*, law *Respicendum*, section *Delinquet*. And therefore, one should not proceed so far as to impose a greater penalty on those who committed such acts with prior design and deliberation, as noted by Cynus in the law *Si quis non dicam rapere* and in the law *Is qui cum telo*. Wherefore, this is the conclusion: that the aforementioned Zacharias may suffer the penalty of exile and a pecuniary condemnation. He ought not, however, nor may he by law, suffer the penalty of blood, even if all matters contained in the inquisition are true and have been legitimately confessed.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The legitime is owed to the mother.
body: Because this spiritual man wished plainly for the truth of the opinion, I therefore say briefly,

† that the congregation of the Battuti for Christ's poor ought to have two-thirds of all the goods of the said Ruffinus. For the said Francischina could not be burdened in her legitime, as in Authen. de restit. et ea, quę parit. §. quamobram. and in c. si potest. de te. lib. 6. and in c. Ray. and c. Raynal. extra, de test. I also say that the said Francischina was able to make a testament regarding two-thirds of the said third part, and to leave the said two parts to the said chapel. However, she could not make a testament regarding the third part of the said two parts, because the said third part belongs to the said Lady Ruffina, her mother, by title of the legitime owed to the mother herself by natural law, as in Authen. de triente, et semi. in prin. and ff. de inofficio. testamen. l. nam et si parentibus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A mother’s will, in which a son is passed over in the first degree of institution, is null, even if he is subsequently instituted in the second degree.
2. The word “institute,” when placed in the second degree, is used in the sense of “substitute.”
3. A codicillary clause that operates to break the will by the passing over of a son.
4. A son does not transmit to the heir of his mother who has not accepted the inheritance; but whether, by virtue of the codicillary clause, he transmitted the right to a universal fideicommissum for his half-share.
body: The case is as follows. A certain lady, Catharina, having four sons, one named Brandachus from her first husband and the other three from her second husband, made a will, in which she instituted the three sons of her second husband as her universal heirs, substituting them for one another. Furthermore, the said testatrix ordered and disposed that if it should happen that her said sons should die from among the living without legitimate children from their own bodies, she instituted the said Brandachus, her son, as heir to one half. Moreover, she bequeathed by right of testament, and by other rights by which she could do better, the other half of her said goods to Martinus de Solatio, her brother. Furthermore, she commanded the aforesaid to be valid by right of testament, and of any other last will, and that a public instrument be made thereof, if it should be necessary for the said experts, the substance of the fact, however, not being changed. Then the said testatrix died, leaving all the said sons; the father of the three sons took possession of the inheritance, and still holds it; all three sons died without issue; finally, after some space of time, Brandachus, born of the first husband, died without issue, having not accepted the inheritance of his mother. In the part touching the said Brandachus, he made a will, in which he instituted his agnate brothers. It is asked, to whom does the inheritance of this good lady belong, whether to her husband by the person of her sons, or to those instituted by Brandachus, her son, or to the brother of the said testatrix, or to whom?

† And for the sake of clarity, it must be premised that the testament of the said woman was null by operation of law, because Brandachus, her son, was passed over in the first degree, as stated in the Authentica "Ut cum" on appeals, cogn. §. "Aliud quoque capitulum." It is no objection if it is said that the said Brandachus was instituted under a condition, which condition ought to be removed from the equation, as noted in ff. de haeredibus instituendis, l. "Servus quoque," and in ff. de inofficioso testamento, l. "Quoniam in prioribus," and l. "Scimus," §. "Cum autem." For even assuming that to be true, it is understood that a certain son is instituted in the first degree, as in ff. de liberis et posthumis, l. 3, §. "Si." But this was not the case here, because only three sons were instituted in the first degree. It is no objection that the testatrix said, "I institute Brandachus as heir to one-half:"

†because the word “I institute,” placed after the first degree, is used in place of the word “I substitute.” As in C. de haereditatibus instituendis, l. si; and ff. ad Trebellianum, l. recusare, §. Titius. And although Brandachus did not declare the will null, and died without having transmitted the inheritance, and thus there is no one who, in the person of Brandachus, can declare it null: nevertheless, the will did not become valid, in which observance of law is lacking, unless possession of the estate had been requested according to the common and more correct opinion in l. filio praeterito; and C. de contrahenda tutela, l. posthumo. Although the ancient doctors, concerned with equity and not with this excessive subtlety and scrupulousness of the law, said that by civil equity the will becomes valid in which another son is instituted, as in l. si duo, C. de legatis praestandis; from which the passed-over son either expressly confirms it, or does not transmit the right to declare it null: an opinion that is sufficiently equitable, except in the case of his own passed-over son, where rigor is equity, that is, the continuation of dominion makes the will valid. As in C. de postumis, l. in suis; and no. C. unde legitimi, l. certum. But whatever may be said on the point, it is irrelevant to the matter at hand, because here the instituted heirs died before the passed-over heir, who was in no way confirmed by the maternal will, and thus never had the beginning of subsistence. Secondly, it must be premised that the father of the aforementioned three sons, if indeed any of them was an infant, could act as heir intestate, by l. si infanti, C. de iure deliberandi; and l. cum non solum, §. vbi autem puerilis, de bonis quae liberis. But if they were above the age of infancy, he could act as heir for them while they were alive: and this by the new constitution of the aforementioned l. cum non solum, in the beginning.

Thirdly, it must be premised that the aforementioned words are valid by the law of wills and of any last will, and receive this interpretation: namely, that if they are not valid by the law of wills, they are valid by the law of codicils, as stated in C. de codicillis, l. si. And this is especially so because the testatrix intended them to be adapted to the sense of a prudent person, who can indeed declare but not add, as noted by Iacobo de Arena in l. illa institutio, ff. de haeredibus instituendis. However, it is doubtful whether the said codicillary clause operates when the will is null due to the defect of omission, and thus due to the testator’s fault, especially in the case of maternal omission, which is regarded as equivalent to unjust disinheritance, since it does not contain a cause. And the text expressly states that it does not operate, ff. de inofficioso testamento, l. Titia. The Authentica ex causa is not an obstacle, because we are speaking here of the codicillary clause and its effect; concerning which nothing is found to have been corrected from the law of the old statute. This is the opinion held by the gloss in Authentica ex causa, by Guillelmus de Cuneis, and by the Speculator. But Cynus, Decius, and Bartolus hold that the said clause is valid, in the case of intestacy omission is not considered. And this is the true opinion. Now there remains another point to be premised, namely

† That the said Brandachus does not transmit the unaccepted maternal inheritance, as in C. ad Orficianum, l. non pro numero. But it is doubtful whether, by virtue of the codicillary clause, he transmitted the right to the universal fideicommissum for his half. And the gloss in l. cum filio, ff. de leg. 1, says that he did not. But the contrary is more correct: and there we note through Dy. and others. And C. de fideicom., l. cum secundum, and l. si in personam, with si. And therefore it must be concluded that the said full agnates, in the person of Brandachus, can claim half of the said goods: and the brother of the said testatrix the other half, after deducting the legitime and the trebellianic portion; because the fideicommissum was conditional, subject to a condition, and not after death: and considering the condition of after death, which is future, the father can deduct the legitime and the trebellianic portion, as in c. Ray., with si. And these are subtle matters, and of the niceties of the law. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, by the second rescript of the Prince, the permissive grant appears to be revoked by the prohibitory clause, "notwithstanding," even though no most specific mention is made of the aforementioned initial prohibitory letters: because the Prince is presumed to have in mind what he has done.
1. One is presumed to remember what he does.
2. What effect the clause "notwithstanding" has in the rescripts of Princes.
3. A rescript of the Prince does not render a matter litigious.
4. Three things render a matter litigious.
body: The Lord, most magnanimous, having heard that a matter of scandal could arise between the nobles of Milan, the illustrious Count of Virtues, and the nobles of the Criuelli family, and Lord Antoniolus of Moriciis, on account of a lawsuit commenced by the said Criuelli family concerning a certain mill on the river, willed and decreed that neither of the aforementioned parties could make any novelties, as is more seriously contained in his mandate and decree.
