Finally, the said most magnificent Lord, without making mention of his aforementioned mandate and decree, granted to the said Lord Antoniolus license to obtain privileges from the Emperor for leading water from the said river Olona for the irrigation of certain meadows of the said Antoniolus and for the conservation of one mill, with the clause, “notwithstanding any letters, decrees, or ordinances disposing to the contrary.” When the said Antoniolus had lost these letters, the said most magnificent Lord renewed them. Finally, the said Lord Antoniolus merited and obtained the said privilege from the Caesar. After this, the said Lord Antoniolus had the said mill constructed. Now the said nobles of the Criuelli family say that it was not constructed by right, and against the letters of the said most magnificent Lord first directed; therefore, they ask that the said mill be demolished. On the contrary, however, the said Lord Antoniolus says that the said prohibitory mandate of the Lord was revoked by the subsequent concession of the said Lord, who consented to its being obtained from the Caesar; nor was it necessary to make mention of the said prohibitory decree, since the said most magnificent Lord had knowledge of the fact; and in the mandate and prohibitory letters there was no derogatory clause, but in the subsequent letters there was.

† Now the question arises, what is the law: whether one should adhere to the inhibitory or permissive letters? And it appears that the aforementioned later letters were invalid: because he who deceives the conscience of the Prince derives no benefit from the rescript, as in C. de his qui a non domino manent, l. si; and ff. de in ius vocando, l. sed si hac, §. patronam. But here, the said A. deceived the conscience of the Prince in two ways. First, because he did not make specific mention of the inhibitory letters of the lord. Second, because he obtained the privilege during a pending lawsuit: for the rescript of the Prince induces the pendency of the lawsuit, as is proven in l. 1, C. quando libellus Principi datus; and in l. 1, C. ut lite pendente; and extra, eo, c. si; and in Auth. in medio litis non fieri sacras formas, in rubro et nigro. Moreover, whatever is done against the mandate of the Prince must be revoked as void, as in C. de legibus, l. non dubium; and C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, l. nemo martyres, cum sequentibus. Furthermore, this is supported by the private denunciation of a new work, as in ff. de novi operis nuntiatione, l. 1, in principio; and l. Praetor ait, in principio. Therefore, much more strongly does this operate by the supreme authority of the Prince, which also has the force of law, as in Auth. de mandato Principis, per totum; and C. quae res vendi non possunt, l. 1, cum sequentibus. Moreover, the Prince is not understood to write anything contrary to the rights of private persons, as in ff. ne quid in loco publico vel itinere fiat, l. 1, §. si quis a Principe; and C. de manumissionibus liberorum, l. nec auus; and ff. de vulgari substitutione, l. ex facto, in principio; and extra, de auctoritate et usu pallii, c. ex tuarum. But here it would prejudice those nobles of the Crielli family: therefore, the privilege of the Prince, as being obreptitious, does not hold, since it was obtained while they were ignorant, as in ff. de nativitate rei, l. si; ff. de fideicommissis liberis, l. cum vero, §. subuentis; ff. de adoptionibus, l. nam ita divus. On the contrary, it seems that the Prince is presumed to have memory of what he has done, extra, de probationibus, c. literis, in cle.; and C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione, l. magnam. Therefore, it was not obreptitious to the Prince, because one who knows, or ought to know, should not be informed, as in l. 1, in fine, ff. de actione empti; and de excusatione tutoris, l. idem; and ff. de re iudicata, l. quidam consulebat. To this point, ff. de adimendo legatum, l. filio, where Jacobus de Arena says.

† Note that one is presumed to remember what one does. See *c. Ab excommunicato*, de rescriptis. And this is confirmed by two reasons and examples. And first, because if after a new work has been denounced, permission is granted to carry out the work, the denunciation becomes void, as in D. de novo operis nuntiatione, l. 1, §. inde quaeritur. So here, as in D. de remissionibus, l. 1, in principio, and §. 1. A similar rule applies in the case of a will, because a prohibitory rule is removed by a permissive rule, as in C. de familiae erciscundae, l. in ipsius, and l. si, in principio, D. de legatis 2.

† Moreover, there is here a non obstante clause, not merely general, but also special: because it made mention of the specific species of non obstantia. See *de litteris et decretis*; from which two things are established. See *de scientia*. Likewise concerning intention, and also concerning derogation. And therefore the later provisions prevail, as in C. *de testibus*, auth. *hoc inter liberos*, and D. *de legibus tertio*, l. *si quis in testamento Principis*. And therefore it is concluded that by virtue of the first letters the execution of the second letters is not impeded. It is not an objection, § *si quis a Principe*, because here nothing is obtained to the prejudice of another’s right, since the right obtained pertains solely to the grantor, as in D. *de fluminibus*, l. *quominus*. But if it would injure one’s own right, and the singular right of nobles regarding *criuelles*, the rescript would not be valid: and this would be according to the common law, not by virtue of our magnificent rescript, as in D. *de haereditatibus instituendis*, l. *si non lex eliescentia*. Likewise it is not an objection, l. 1, C. *quoniam libellus Principis*.

† because only a rescript of the Prince does not make a matter litigious, as c. si, ut lite pendente in the Clementines, especially when it emanates from the Prince’s own motion, and not upon interpellation.

† There are three things that become litigious: the thing, the cause, and the action. The thing, in a real action. Likewise, the vindication of a thing is impersonal. Likewise, a personal action is also called a litigious thing even in a mixed judgment, as in D. 50.17.1, *In iudicio*. And just as an action cannot be assigned while the judgment is pending, so too can the thing not be alienated with effect, as in D. 26.7.1, *Chirographis*, § 1, D. 26.7, *De administratione tutorum*. But just as a judgment begins with citation, so does the defect of litigiousness; and if not before citation or admonition intervenes, as in C. 7.31, *De litigiosis rebus*, Auth. *Litigiosa*; and Inst. 4.17, *De poena temere litigantium*, § final; and D. 44.7.1, *De alienatione iudicii*, with similar authorities. And it supports what is noted in C. 2.4, *De transactionibus*, l. *Causas*, or *Lites*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a pact made between co-heirs in their partitions, that none of them shall purchase lands in which any of them has obtained his share, is valid; and whether it passes successively to their descendants.
2. How the clause “unless by common agreement, etc.” is to be understood: whether, if one violates the pact by force, the purchase made is void, or valid, and he is bound only to the penalty; likewise, if this pact is fortified by an oath, whether, if he purchases, dominion is transferred or not. No. 3.
3. Whether a son who committed violence with arms and with his father’s men is presumed to have acted with his father’s consent. [action] in its proper places.
body: Whether a lord adhering to another greater lord appears to grant jurisdiction to himself. Concerning the lord Nanni Marchionis, Oddo, and Boniface, sons of the late Georgino, brother of William, divisions were made, and instruments of division of many castles and jurisdictions, with a pact appended between the said parties in this form, that any of the said parties could not, nor would it be valid for them to, acquire any rights in places belonging to another party, unless they proceeded jointly by the agreement of the aforementioned parties. Here, first it is asked,

Whether, in the aforementioned clause regarding non-acquisition, are included the heirs of the said contracting parties, namely, that these heirs cannot act without violating the pact? And it appears that they are not included, as in D. de pign. act. l. si necessarias, § de vendendo, in the second response. For this pact seems to have been personal; and therefore it ought not to extend beyond the person, as in D. de pactis, l. idem in duabus, § personalem. For since this pact was added contrary to the nature of the contract, it seems to bind only the persons named. We say similarly in a will, that a prohibition in a will does not extend beyond the designated person, as noted in Auth. de restitutione fideicommissorum, § manifestum. Furthermore, this is supported by the opinions of Petrus de Bellapertica and Cynus in C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione, l. veteris, where they state that when a stipulation contains a negative obligation which can bring some benefit to the principal person, the heir is not included.

To the contrary, it seems that when a contract precedes, from the nature of which the heir is bound, the clauses and pacts appended thereto are likewise transmissible, as noted there by the aforementioned Petrus and Cynus. But the contract of division is transmissible to the heir; therefore, the pacts are also transmissible, since the same reason for contracting persists in the persons of the heirs. For this, see D. de verb. oblig. l. stipulatio ista, § sed si se, where it seems expressly stated. Moreover, these words were conceived in rem, which were such, namely, that any of the said parties, etc. For that term, namely "parties," is a name of common appellation, and thus written in rem; hence, all heirs are rightly included, and especially sons, who are considered one and the same person, as in C. de impub. et aliis substitutis, l. si.

To this supports the general rule, that everyone is deemed to provide for himself and his heir, as in D. de probat. l. si pactum, and D. de pactis, l. iurisgentium, § pactorum, and in c. 1, de duobus fratribus a capite investituræ. Furthermore, a special law supports this, assuming that the rule of contraries is the same, D. qui potior in pignore vel hypotheca habenda sit, l. sicut, § si creditori. Moreover, pacts and division are one and the same contract, as in D. de contrahenda emptione, l. fundi partem; therefore, they ought not to be judged by different law, so that for part it is transmissible to the heir, and for part it is not, as in D. de usucapionibus, l. eum qui ædes. Furthermore, the principle of the contract lies in the things themselves, the division; therefore, whatever follows from or on account of this, arg. D. de iure et fact. ignor. l. regula, § pen. And this is the truth. On this point, it is subsequently asked, whether

† by those words, unless there is agreement of the parties, it suffices that there is agreement with one of that party, even if not with all: and it seems that the agreement of one suffices, because among themselves alienation is not said to be prohibited, as C. de fideic. l. voluntas. To the contrary it is said, because it is true with regard to the consenting party, and for his part, as ff. de leg. 2. l. cum pater. §. libertis. nevertheless, to those not consenting the penalty is owed for the hereditary portion, as ff. de ver. obli. l. eadem. §. Cato. The objection l. voluntas does not hold, because here it was expressly acted to the contrary, nor can one heir prejudice the right of another, as ff. communia praedi. l. receptum. and l. per fundum. ff. de ser. ru. praedio. nor interpose dominion beyond his share, as ff. de acqui. her. l. duo fratres. I therefore say that if something was acquired contrary to the pacts, the acquisition is valid, because no one can by pact become incapable, since capacity is of public law: but for the part of the non-consenting party the penalty is incurred, whereas for the part of the consenting party the penalty is not incurred, especially with effect, as d. §. Cato. To the foregoing is added the general rule, namely that when alienation is prohibited by contract, the transfer of dominion is not impeded, if the right of dominion was in the transferor free and unencumbered, as in l. ea lege. and in §. ea. l. and l. si credito. §. fi. ff. de distra. pigno. But here arises a doubt,

† What if this pactum de non alienando is fortified by an oath, does ownership pass? And this question can be considered in two ways. In one way, with respect to the oath-taker. In another way, with respect to the heirs, it must be known. Note that an oath, insofar as it affects the contract, passes to the heir both actively and passively, as in Auth. sacramenta puberum. But insofar as it affects the person, it passes actively, not passively, as elegantly noted by Innocentius, extra de iureiurando, in c. veritatis. What, therefore, shall we say? Speculator said that if a woman swears not to alienate, ownership does not pass, because the oath can be preserved without the loss of eternal salvation. The same is said by Johannes Andreae in c. 2, de iureiurando, lib. 6. And if the said opinion is true, ownership is affected such that it cannot be transferred contrary to the sworn oath. To the contrary, it seems, for either the pact is opposed to my thing during my lifetime simply, or in a qualified sense, or in which I retain some right in the thing, so that it is my interest that it not be alienated: and the alienation does not hold. Or I do not retain any right in the thing, and then the alienation holds, but my adversary is bound to the penalty. This doctrine is set forth by Franciscus Accursius and Cynus in the additions to ff. de pactis, l. nemo. But here the parties exchanging retained no right in the exchanged thing; therefore, the repurchaser could transfer his right notwithstanding the pact, even if sworn: because for the transfer of ownership, the sole will of the transferring owner suffices: and it is transferred by the law of nations, as in Inst. de rerum divisione, §. per traditionem. Nor does the statement of Speculator regarding the woman stand against this, because that is due to the benefit of the woman, who by her first oath preserved her right for herself; nevertheless, the statement of Hostiensis never pleased me, unless the adversary had been notified of that oath, arg. l. 1, in fine, ff. de actione empti. Consider the understanding of that law, si creditor, §. fin., de distractione pignorum. For as the text stands there, our question seems determined by the lack of jurisdiction. For it is certain that for the observance of this contract, goods were expressly pledged; in which pledge are included even the exchanged things, as in C. de servo pignori dato manumisso, l. prima. Therefore, the creditor had a hypothec; thus, the hypothecated thing could not be alienated. And holding that reading, this argument concludes necessarily. Others, however, do not hold this reading, because a pledge has nothing in common with ownership; since alienation takes place with the pledge right reserved; and therefore a hypothec does not make a thing inalienable. To this effect, ff. de usucapione, l. iusto, §. non mutat; and C. de litibus, l. 1. One might perhaps distinguish between a special pledge, and then the alienation is not valid; and a general one, and then it is valid, because a special hypothec affects the power of alienating more than a general one, as in C. de servo pignori dato manumisso, l. ab eo. Unless you say, and rightly, that there is a special favor for liberty. Subsequently

† It is asked concerning a certain violence inflicted by Lord Henry together with the men of his father upon the persons of some of his associates, whether it is to be understood as having been inflicted by the counsel or arrangement of his said father. And it must be said that it is not, as stated in the Decretals, De restitutione spoliatorum, chapter Cum ad sedem. For in case of doubt we ought to presume innocence rather than fraud, as stated in the Digest, Pro socio, law Merito, unless it were proven that the said father had obtained something from the said violence. Here consider that a matter can be transacted for me by the act itself, even if it is not transacted in my name, as stated in the Digest, De negotiis gestis, law Si pupilli, section Peculium. If it is certain that something was fulfilled by the act itself, I am conducting my own business; therefore, I am bound. Thus it is understood in the note of Jacobus de Arena, Codex, De accusationibus, law Non eo minus. Subsequently it is asked whether the said violence was remitted by a contract made afterwards concerning the invaded properties. And it must be said that it was, as if the things had returned to the power of the lord; just as if the lord were to sell a stolen thing, for by a supervening title the thief changes the cause of his possession, as stated in the Digest, De usucapione, law Non solum, section Quod vulgo, verse Sed si eundem. And this is true with respect to the thing itself, but the damages and interest do not appear to have been remitted, as stated in the Digest, Quod vi aut clam, law Is qui in puteum, section Si postea.

† Then it is asked whether, by the adhesion of Lord Christophorus, which he made to Lord Duke of Orleans concerning certain castles, any jurisdiction in the said castles was attributed to the said Lord Duke. And it must be said that, by the nature of simple adhesion, no jurisdiction is conferred upon him to whom one adheres, but a certain confederation is formed, by which the greater of the confederates has jurisdiction only in one case, when the offenders of the other are found in the lands of that superior, so that they are first condemned, and nothing remains but to execute punishment upon them, or to remit them to the place of the crime, as in D. de captivis et postliminio reversis, l. non dubito. Unless it appears expressly that the confederate subjected himself to the jurisdiction of the majesty of the other: which anyone may do to his own prejudice, as in D. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, l. est receptum. And when such submission is added to a named contract, repentance has no place; otherwise, if it were a simple prorogation, as in D. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, l. si convenerit. And note, through Arch. in Extravagantes, de haereticis, c. praesidentis, lib. 6. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether agreements that bind the inhabitants of a single castle, but not the nobles of that same castle, also bind the servants and agents of those lords, who are themselves servants from the said castle. No. 2.
2. A prohibition made with respect to one person is deemed also to have been made with respect to another similar person.
3. What services are considered due, if certain persons are obligated to perform due services.
body: On the one hand, the magnificient lords, the Marquises of Ceva, and on the other hand, the community and the inhabitants of Bagnasco, certain agreements were made concerning the extraction of grain and other provisions, since the said Marquises hold the castle in fief from their superior.

† It is asked whether the said pacts could be made without the authority of the superior; and it must be said that either the said pacts result in detriment to the superior, and they are not valid; or they result in detriment to the nobles themselves, and they are valid, as in the Digest, *De pactis*, law *Inter debitorem*, and there noted.

Secondly, it is asked whether, between the said nobles and the said community, a pact was added that the said universitas may impose a tax on wine, timber, and other goods of their men, binding only themselves and the goods of their men, and not outsiders, nor the lords themselves, nor their envoys, procurators, or factors of the said lords, or any of them, from the goods, things, or moneys of the said lords. It is asked, what is the law regarding the said envoys, factors, or procurators? I answer that, if they conduct business with the money of the said lords, they are not bound to pay the taxes to the said lords, as in ff. de reli. l. ossa. §. fi. Thirdly

† It is asked whether a pact was made between the said lords and the community, that the said men were permitted to fish in the river Tanagro, provided that they did not use the *barcagium*, which is a certain device by means of which almost all fish are caught. Now, the said men do not make a *barcagium*, but rather a certain weir, leaving a small opening through which they catch almost all the fish. It is asked: what is the law? I answer: they cannot do this, because when something is prohibited, its like is also prohibited, as stated in the Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, law *Haeres meus*, section *Cum in fraudem*. For it does not matter in the manner, but in the quality of use, as stated in the Digest, *De usufructu*, law *Item si fundi*, section *Si*. Fourthly, it is asked,

† It was agreed between the said parties that the said men are bound to perform for the said lords, and their heirs in perpetuity, all due service, or the due quantity of clients, and this at the expense of the said community and men: and it is presupposed that before the said agreement they were performing the service, that is, they sent men at the command of the said lords, even against the lands of other nobles. The question is asked, how is the word "due" to be understood? I answer, that is, customary. Hence neither can the lords aggravate, nor the subjects diminish, as in C. de agri. et censi. l. cum scimus li. 11. with some moderation being applied, lest the said lords burden the said subjects beyond their ability, or to less foreign places, as in ff. de annuis leg. l. Meuia. §. fin. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A title, or instrument, does not prove possession, unless delivery is also proven, or unless the instrument was made on the spot, and the writing bearing a seal must be believed.
2. The Prince's seal is considered in place of full solemnity.
3. Whether possession is proven by an instrument.
4. What custody is. One is not said to be an official unless he is in possession of the office.
body: The case of the illustrious John of Montferrat is as follows. We, John, Marquis of Montferrat, etc., by these present letters make known that, by our will and express consent, the noble G., in his own name and on behalf of his brother C., appointed in our castle of Calliano, and in the places of said castle, as castellans and custodians, the noble men Ubert and John, brothers of Coconato, counts. These nobles Ubert and John, in our presence and in our hands, swore corporally upon the holy Gospels of God to keep and guard said our place of Calliano with a solemn promise to do so well, diligently, and faithfully; and to render a good and true account to the aforementioned Guidotto and Corrado, and their heirs, of the fruits, profits, and revenues to be had and received by said Ubert and John from said place and on its occasion; and if we, the aforementioned de Grassellis, shall not have satisfied the aforementioned sum of florins, to which we are bound by instrument to said G. in his own name and on behalf of said C. de Grassellis, or his heirs, said Ubert and John, under the faith of their bodies and the aforementioned oath, promised to freely, absolutely, and without delay surrender, relinquish, and deliver said our castle and place of Calliano at the request of said G. and C., or their heirs, until we shall have fully satisfied them for said sum of florins. We ordered this to be done by C. Gabarinus de Ricobonis, our notary, and to be confirmed with the authority of our seal. Given at Clauasium, on the day etc. Finally, because it is said that satisfaction was not made to said creditors, therefore the heirs of said creditors demand from the heirs of said Ubert and John that said castle be relinquished and surrendered, and that a true account be rendered of the fruits, profits, and revenues according to the form of said document.

† Now it is asked whether the aforementioned document sufficiently proves the matter? And it is said that it does, because the said document bears an authentic seal, which must be upheld, as noted in C. de rebus ecclesiae non alienandis, l. 2. Moreover, it is not credible that the said document, drawn up by the hand of a public notary, namely Notary Gambarinus, and sealed with the seal of such a great Prince, would contain anything other than the substance of the truth, as stated in 1. q. 6. c. Nobilissimus. Furthermore, the said document contains the personal act of the said Marquis, namely his consent; therefore, it proves his consent. This is supported by C. de pactis, l. Pacta novissima; C. de episcopis et clericis, l. Si qua per calumniam; Extra de probationibus, c. Post cessionem; De fide instrumentorum, c. 1 and 2, according to Innocentius. Moreover, it is notorious that the said castle belonged to the said Lord Marquis, and still does, and therefore, by consenting, he appears to have acted on behalf of the said creditors; and thus a right has been acquired for them, even if they had been absent, as stated in ff. de pignoribus, l. Si fundus, § 2. Finally, it cannot be denied that this document carries great credibility and authority, as stated in l. Alibi, ff. de iureiurando; l. Si duo patroni, in principio.

† Moreover, the Prince’s seal is regarded as equivalent to full solemnity, as stated in C. de quadriennii praescri., l. bene a Zenone. Moreover, a notary was summoned, and witnesses were present, along with other solemnities, as noted in C. de usuris, l. 1. Moreover, satisfaction has not been rendered, as in ff. de probat., l. quinquaginta. This is not obstructed by the rule that he who alleges a negative must prove it, for this is true only unless he acts on the basis of a promise, as stated in the aforementioned l. quinquaginta. For a debt is presumed to subsist unless satisfaction has been rendered; and this must be proved by the debtor or by one holding title from him, because rendering satisfaction is an act, which is not presumed, as in ff. de cura furiosi, l. consilio, §. si. Nor does it even matter that the witnesses did not subscribe, because the subscription of witnesses is not required except in cases expressly provided for by law, and especially by custom, as noted in C. de fideicommissis, l. quaestionem. Moreover, the said document attests to the celebration of the contract, and it was made at the time of the contract itself, not at some later interval, because in that case it would be a declaratory rather than an operative document, and it would not make at least full proof, as in c. si Papa, de privilegiis, lib. 6. And not only does the said document attest to the truth, but also to the solemnity, which could have intervened at the same place and time, as in ff. de verborum obligationibus, l. sciendum. And this is evident from the words of the instrument, where it is said, “with solemn promise.”

To the contrary, it seems. It must be premised for clarity that a castellany and custody require an act and a certain corporal delivery made with respect to the castellany and custody; for unless one has come to the thing itself, it is not proved that one is the custodian or castellan. Just as we say in a similar case that investiture is not made by word, but by the subsequent act itself, as in c. 1, de consuetudine recti feudi, col. 10. We say the same regarding a praetorian pledge, that it is not constituted by mere permission, unless possession is taken, because this matter requires reality, as in ff. de pignoribus, l. non est merum, §. sciendum.

† Moreover, by an instrument, corporal possession is not proved, unless the instrument is made in the very thing itself, as in the extrajudicial law on the faith of instruments, chapter *Inter delictos*, § *Si*, and the law *Et nos* in the Digest on acquiring possession, law *Praedia*. From which it is concluded that, since the said writing was not made in the castle itself by right, nor does it prove the cause for entering into the custody or castellanry of the castle, such a thing is not sufficiently proved, from which an action may be brought, as it is brought here, namely, for the release of the said castle. To this effect are the laws which speak of the appointment of a custodian, in the Digest on funeral expenses, law *Si ita*, § *Villae*; in the common law, law *Si ut certo*, § *Si de me petisses*.

For custody is a bodily act, and it is not expressed by words unless an effect follows, as is naturally evident from the good allegation, because since custody is a natural act, we must take it from nature itself, as in *l. ubi autem*, D. de verborum obligationibus and D. de interrogationibus et responsionibus, and *l. confessionibus*, and it is supported by Extravagant, de officio custodis, c. 1 and 2. Therefore, even if the instrument is thereafter believed by me to be good and solemn, it is nevertheless imperfect with regard to the delivery of custody or the castellany; for it is a rule in the exercise of any office in the thing itself that intromission is required.

† Nor is anyone said to be an official unless he is in possession of the office, which must be proved, as in Extra, de iudicibus, c. Si in possessione. I say “in possession” in this sense, as in Digest, de publicanis, l. Eum qui, §. Si. Otherwise, if it arises from another cause, as in Digest, de evictionibus, l. Si rem quam mihi, in principio, unless that title was newly fabricated or acquired in fraud, for example, with the intent of interrupting possession of something not his own; for to interrupt is to betray, as in Codex, de acquirenda possessione, l. Si. Moreover, if it does not appear from a new cause, it is presumed from the preceding one, however slight, as in Codex, de acquirenda possessione, l. 2. Having therefore digested these points in mind, let the one about to render judgment consider two things, namely, truth and proof. For sometimes the right does not fail, but the proof, as in Digest, de testamento tutoris, l. Duo sunt Titii. And if the plaintiff does not prove his case, the defendant is absolved, as in Codex, de edendo, l. Accusare. And conversely, if the plaintiff proves his case, the defendant, who has proved nothing, is condemned, as in Codex, de exceptionibus, l. Si quidem. Let the records therefore speak, because, as I have said, the title of custody is not sufficient unless it is proved that custody was actually taken; just as we say in a similar case that the title is not sufficient unless delivery, or quasi-delivery, is proved, as fully in Institutes, de actionibus, §. Alia. Let the records therefore speak for what is lacking to me. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. From the broad discretion granted to the arbitrator after the sentence, or his award, he may also declare that: and first he posits a very wide compromise.
body: Arbiter, nitor, atque compositor ita sumptus, videlicet quod quicquid dicet, faciet, pronunciabit, et arbitrabitur interdictas partes, semper videatur, intelligatur, et praesumatur venisse, et deductum fuisse in compromisso: et perinde valeat, et teneat, ac si de pronunciandis, et dicendis, ac competendis, et pronuuciandis per ipsum esset in praesenti compromisso specialis, et expressa metio facta: cum pacto speciali dicto, et facto interdictas partes, videlicet quod liceat dicto arbitro, et arbitratori dicere, praecipere, pronunciare, arbitrari, seu arbitramentari inter dictas partes vna vicae, et plurib. super vnoquoque capitulis, et diuersis temporibus feriatis, et non feriatis, praesentib. vel absentib. partibus, seruato ordine iuris, et non seruato ad arbitrium, vel voluntatem eius, sedendo, vel non sedendo etc. et tam in loco compromissi, quam alibi ad ipsius arbitri arbitratoris liberam voluntatem: et ita, et taliter, quod quilibet locus videatur, et intelligatur esse idoneus: et quicquid dicetur, pronunciabitur, arbitrabitur, videatur, et intelligatut ipsis partibus, et cuilibet aliarum partium aequum, iustum, et rationabile: nec possir dici per ipsas, vel aliquam de ipsis partib. iniquum, vel iniustum petendo, defendendo, allegando, et dicendo, quod arbitrio boni viri reduci debeat, vel reducendum sit: de quo iure pe tendi, seu dicendi debere reduci ad arbitrium boni viri, seu bonorum virorum dictae partes sibi adinuicem, et vicissim finem fecerunt, et faciunt per pactum expressum, quod ex nunc, prout ex tunc, et ex tunc prout ex nunc voluerunt intelligi ad factum ex certa scientia, non per errorem dictarum partium, vel alicuius earum, ita quod uoluntas dicti arbitri, et arbitratoris intelligatur esse voluntas, et expressus consensus dictarum partium. Item et eo acto inter dictas partes, quod si aliquod uerbum, ut aliquid aliud in dictis arbitramentis inde fiendis inter dictas partes, et quae fient per dictum dominum arbitrum, et amicabilem compositorem esset ambiguum, uel obscurum, quod liceat, et licitum sit dicto arbitro, et arbitratori illud interpretari, declarare, dilucidare vna vice, vel pluribus ad eius liberam voluntatem: et ipsius declarationi, et interpretationi stare, et obedire debeant, ac obedire, et stare dictae partes sibi adinuicem solemniter conuenerunt, et promiserunt et c. inter partes ita pronuntiauit, atque manda. ita uidelicet quod Ant. unus ex dictis compromittentibus habeat authoritatem, et licentiam intrandi possessionem certi fundi, quandocumque placuerit: et quod altera pars teneatur eis concedere immediate hanc licentiam, quod factum fuit, nulla de fructibus dicti fundi facta mentione in dicto laudo. Post haec dictus arbiter pronunciauit, et declarauit, quod suae intentionis fuit, et est, quod dictus Anio. habeat medietatem fructuum, et aliam medietatem haberent coloni.

† Now it is asked whether the said declaration is valid or not, and what is the law. And it must be said that, once the judge or arbitrator has performed his office regarding the principal matter, omitting the fruits, he cannot make up for this omission concerning the fruits, unless on the same day, as stated in D. de re iudicata, l. Paulus; C. de fructibus, l. expensis; and D. de arbitris, l. terminato. And see the note in D. de arbitris, l. qui arbiter. And this applies when he used such a word in the sentence that included the fruits, such as the word "restore," which has a full meaning. For then the fruits would also be included, because it is the same to say "restore" as in the interdict of restitution, as stated in D. de rei venditione, l. ex diverso; and D. de usuris, l. videamus, §. in fauiana. But here such words or similar ones were not used; hence, by these words, "go into possession," the fruits are not understood to be included, as stated in D. de usu, l. si stipulatus. Nor does a tacit intention suffice, because it has no effect unless declared by word or in writing, as stated in C. de sententiis ex periculo recidendis, l. 2. This declaration or interpretation cannot be made by the arbitrator, as is read and noted in D. de appellationibus, l. ab executore. Moreover, this would not be a declaration, but a non-intrinsic, rather extrinsic, supplementation, i.e., a certain extension to the fruits. This extension is not aptly comprehended by the word of license, and therefore it would seem at first sight to be said that the said declaration was invalid? Indeed, it is null by operation of law, because the arbitrator had already performed his office, as stated in l. iudex, D. de re iudicata; and D. de arbitris, l. dicere, §. si. But the truth is to the contrary, by reason of the express power given to the arbitrator. Although arbitrations are reduced to the likeness of judgments, D. de arbitris, l. 1, nevertheless in some respects they are reduced to the likeness of contracts, because the power of the arbitrator depends on the consent of the parties, and derives its force, form, and origin therefrom. Hence, power can be given to the arbitrator to award, to interpret the award, and also to supplement, as well as to pronounce simultaneously and separately, as it may please the arbitrator, and much more so in the case of an arbitrator, as stated in D. de arbitris, l. non distinguemus, §. de officio. And therefore, since such broad power was given, as can almost be given in any compromise, the said declaration must be upheld between the parties; but as regards others who did not compromise, the said award is not valid, just as a contract is not valid, as stated in l. proprium, D. communia praediorum; and C. res inter alios acta, throughout. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a grant of possession under a will is revoked on account of a defect in the will.
2. Whether a confession made in a will proves that someone is a usurer.
3. The last will revokes the first.
4. One who, due to his own fault, is incapable of making a will is said to die intestate.
body: The plaintiff requests to be put in possession according to the form of the law *Edictum*, C. de edicto, in the case of an heir in the will of a usurer. The will is produced in public form: from the reading or appearance of this will, no defect appears; however, the adversary appears and alleges two things. First, that the testator was a manifest usurer. Second, because the said will was revoked by a later will. He attempts to prove the first by excepting from the confession of the said usurer, who confessed to having extorted usury and ordered in his publicly written will that they be restored to whomever they were due. He attempts to prove the second by the later will, made before a legitimate number of witnesses and a notary. And both of these appear by public document produced in court, namely both the confession and the new will.

† Now it is asked whether the said *missio* should be granted or not. And although the allegations made were numerous, elegant, and true, yet because the one consulting me requests that I add something else, which I do however out of abundance, not because it is necessary, I say that the said *missio* should not be granted, nor can it be granted according to law. And I consider that these are distinct matters: the defect (*vitium*) of the testament and its revocation. Regarding the former, there could be a question whether a general and indiscriminate confession made before a notary and witnesses, but not in court, would prove someone to be a manifest usurer or a simple usurer. For if it proves him to be a simple usurer, this does not invalidate the testament. But if it proves him to be a manifest usurer, then the testament appears to be null, as in the common chapter *Quamquam*. And doubt is raised by the gloss which is in C. *De libellis causae*, l. *Iubemus*.

† Moreover, it gives rise to doubt, because this confession is made with respect to a certain thing and genus. Furthermore, if a confession made in a last will is valid, then the last will is valid, as stated in the Digest, *De liberis et posthumis legatis*, law *Aurelius*, § *Si*. Additionally, from this uncertain confession no action arises against anyone, unless he proves that he has paid the usury, as stated in the Digest, *De legibus*, title 2, law *Lucius*, § *Quisquis*. To the contrary, it appears from other laws and reasons most wisely advanced by the learned person who consulted me, which I do not repeat.

Next, it remains to consider the second point, namely, the last will: and there is no room for dispute on this matter, because when there are two wills, the last one absorbs the first: and nothing can be claimed from the first, as stated in the Institutes, "In which ways a will may be invalidated," §. "Later ones." And therefore, the benefit of the edict does not apply to the first will. The text and the ordinary gloss in the aforementioned law on the edict state: "That will alone is valid which is proven to be the last." And because the claimant and the possessor are of the same title, the stronger one prevails, that is, the last one, as per the Code, "On the Sacred Churches," law 1. Not only in defending oneself, but also in bringing an action, as per the Digest, "On Legacies," law "If to me and to you," §. "In legacies." Here it should be noted that the aforementioned conclusion is true from a sufficient and necessary enumeration of the parts. For either this person was not a manifest usurer: and then the last will is valid, in which the time of death is considered, as per the Digest, "On Possession According to the Tablets," law "First," §. "It requires." And if in the past he was manifest, he is always manifest, unless the defect of usury was purged by restitution, and thus by a similar retroactive act, or by a solemn caution. But if he was a manifest usurer, neither will is valid:

† because he who is intestable due to his own fault is said to die without a will. This is the singular gloss in the said §. exigit. From which it is concluded, and necessarily follows, that the appointment cannot and ought not to be made. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. In an alienation of a church made by a Prelate, whether it is presumed that all solemnities were observed.
2. Whether an exchange is presumed from the passage of half the long period of time.
3. Whether enunciative words make proof, and when.
4. In prescriptions of the longest time, error of law suffices to establish good faith.
body: A certain Prior of Saint Proculus, aged forty years and more, by title of exchange and barter, transferred certain possessions to a certain Andrew, and in return received other possessions with the consent and will of his entire chapter. And although no document appears for each individual transaction, it is clearly shown by the instrument of exchange and barter how the chapter was assembled, or the monks representing the entire chapter of the said priory: and the said exchange was made by a public instrument, in which are these words: "Since diligent deliberation and discussion had been held once, twice, and many times between the said prior and the convent, and also the counsel of faithful friends had been taken, and it had been determined that the said exchange was most useful, etc., as they themselves confessed. Therefore, they made the said exchange, and promised to hold it firm and valid in perpetuity." Finally, after the aforementioned events, after the lapse of a long period of time, and beyond the year 1353, the General Vicar superior of the entire order ratified, approved, commended, and confirmed the said exchange as if it had been newly made; and furthermore, he interposed his authority and issued a decree. It is asked whether the said exchange is presumed to have been made solemnly? Secondly, it is asked whether, by the lapse of time and the alternation of possession, an exchange is induced, even if no other document appears? Thirdly, it is asked whether the said confession and enunciative words make proof? Fourthly, it is asked, if all these things fail, is there prescription? I return to the first point,

† And it appears that solemnity is not presumed: because this is an extrinsic solemnity, as in the Digest, *De publico*, l. *Quaecunque*, § *Si*. Moreover, because negotiations ought to intervene at various times prior to the actual exchange, as in the chapter *Dudum*, *De rebus ecclesiae non alienandis*, Book Six. Hence, it is not presumed to be present. For only those things are deemed present which are done immediately, not those which occur at an interval. And this is the doctrine of Innocentius regarding these solemnities, that they are not presumed unless they could have intervened and cohered with the contract itself, as he notes in the chapter *Cum in iure*, Extra, *De officio delegati*; in the chapter *Quoniam contra falsam*, *De probationibus*; and in the chapter *Innotuit*, *De eo qui furtive ordinem suscipit*.

To the contrary is the ordinary gloss of Accursius, who says that negotiations and such like preliminaries are proved by the instrument made concerning the principal contract, in which the notary, from the will of the contracting parties, makes mention of these solemnities. And the gloss speaks of a fiscal contract: therefore, the same applies in the Church. This is the common gloss, yet unique in law, in l. *Prima*, Code, *De fide instrumentorum* and *De iure hastae fiscalis*, Book Ten.

Nor let anyone say that the confession of the prelate and the chapter does not harm the Church: for rather it does harm, when the entire chapter consents along with the prelate; otherwise, if it were the majority of the chapter, and not the whole chapter. This is the singular gloss, Code, *De sacrosanctis ecclesiis*, Auth. *Hoc ius porrectum*.

Furthermore, this is supported by the fact that presumption favors ancient instruments: for they are more credible because they are older, Distinction 50, c. *Domino Sancto, meritisque beato*. And noted by Cynus, Code, *De fide instrumentorum*, l. *Emancipatione*.

I come to the second point, and it appears that a barter is not presumed: because time is not a mode of contracting, or otherwise of alienating, as in D. 44.1.1 pr. § fin. (pure), although from time the cause may be presumed, if a cause is alleged, as is fully noted in D. 22.1.1 (cum de in rem verso). To the contrary it appears, because although the mere passage of time is not a contract, or quasi-contract, nevertheless continuous acts and the continuation of possession, corresponding correlatively, induce a presumption of barter, as is read and noted in C. 10.3.10 (penulti.). For the division spoken of there is a certain barter of part for part, as is fully noted in D. 41.3.1 (cum solus). To the same effect is what is read and noted in D. 3.5.1 (duae filiae). And not only is the contract, or quasi-contract, presumed, but also its solemnity. This is the case in C. 5.3.1 (si filius) and D. 29.1.1 (qui in aliena).

I come to the third point, and I say that certain words are declaratory, which refer to the essence of the act: and such words, when written down regarding the will of the parties, create faith, as in C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione, l. optimam, unless there was incapacity in the persons contracting, as in ff. de legatis 3, l. cum quis decedens, §. codicillis, and noted in ff. de probationibus, l. qui testamentum. But if the declaratory words are not from the same contract or disposition, then they do not create faith, as in C. de testamento militis, l. ex verbis fortunato, with its material. It must, however, be observed that where writing is necessary regarding each individual act, they would not be proved by general declaratory words. Hence, if individual transactions required writing in themselves, a confession made by declaratory words regarding acts long past would not suffice; because the required oath is not present, as it ought to be, and as is required by form, as in l. 1, C. de iure emphyteutico. Nevertheless, no law says that these transactions could not be proved by witnesses; therefore, writing is not of the substance. Moreover, proof by confession is equivalent to writing, as singularly noted in Authent. de aequalitate dotis, §. aliud. Also, the presumption of law is equivalent to a public document, the text is noted in C. de apographis publicis, l. quicunque. And thus, concluding from the first to the last, I hold that by the change it is presumed that the contract preceded, and all preliminaries were solemnly performed. However, because the decree of the superior did not intervene, the contract did not hold. Someone will say, the superior is the Abbot himself, or the Prior; this one does not understand who the superior is, for he who is one of the contracting parties is not called superior; rather, the superior is he who interposes authority; hence he must be someone other than the contracting party, because no one authorizes in his own contract or his own act, but in another’s, which pertains to his approval and disapproval, as in l. 1, ff. de auctoritate tutoris. Therefore, in this case, the superior will be the general prelate of the order, if these are exempt; otherwise, the diocesan bishop of that monastery, as in d. c. dudum. This being premised, it is asked whether the ratification of the superior validates this contract. Innocentius says that it does not, because whether it is a decree or authority, it must be interposed immediately. This is supported by the fact that a decree or authority is interposed by a certain jurisdiction, or mixed imperium, as in l. nec quicquam, §. vbi decretum, ff. de officiis proconsulis, and leg. But a judge, by his jurisdiction, cannot make something valid which is null by law itself. Hence, for the decree to be valid, everything must be done anew. And this is the common opinion. This is supported by what is noted in l. instar, C. de iure fisci, lib. 10, unless custom gives force to this confirmation; because custom confers jurisdiction, as in l. 1, C. de emancipato libero, and l. 1, C. de servis Reipublicae manumittendis.

I come to the last point, and it seems that there is no prescription, because an error of law does not benefit in prescriptions. But those who are prescribing would be in error of law, because they would consider valid what is invalid by law. To the contrary is the truth itself, because in prescriptions of the longest time an error of law suffices to give good faith: hence even a null title gives cause for prescribing by the longest time, as noted in 16 q. 4 c. volumus. For good faith consists in common appearance, not in the subtleties of law. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. An appeal must be taken from a decisive judgment on the merits of the case; otherwise, it would become res judicata.
body: The facts are as follows: A certain Master Anton obtained from the Vicar of the Podestà of Pavia the issuance of a precept directed to a certain Zanotto, his neighbor, whereby he was required to appear before the said Vicar in order to select estimators who would appraise a certain wall upon which the said Master Anton wished to build. Against this precept, among other things, the said Zanotto objected that he was not permitted to build, notwithstanding a certain arbitral sentence previously rendered between the said parties. It was replied by Master Anton that the said sentence did not constitute an obstacle, because it did not encompass the said wall. Furthermore, because the said sentence was null due to the omission of a certain solemnity. Certain chapters and certain proofs were produced for the validation of the sentence. Finally, it was pronounced by the Vicar that the said precept was valid and binding, notwithstanding the sentence rendered, mentioned above, especially since by the said sentence the said Master Anton is not prohibited from building upon the said wall. Finally, four days having elapsed after the said pronouncement, the said Vicar pronounced that the aforementioned arbitral sentence was valid and not null, and deserved execution, condemning the vanquished party to pay the costs to the victor. From the foregoing, it is asked whether the sentence secondly rendered by the said Vicar, confirming the arbitral sentence, is valid or null. Presupposing that this summary proceeding is established by the form of a certain statute, and coming solely to the sentences,

It must be said that either the said precept was contrary to the arbitral sentence, or it was not. In the first case, if indeed by virtue of the statute the arbitral sentence has the force of res iudicata, since it was clear that it was res iudicata, the precept would not have stood, as in l. j. C. quando prouo. non est neces. But if it were not clear, or if by virtue of the statute it did not have the force of res iudicata, then the precept would stand, as in ff. de iureiuran. l. nam postea. §. si damnaretur. From this precept, since it is decisive of the litigation, an appeal ought to have been taken; and if no appeal was taken, it passed into res iudicata, as in ff. de mi. l. ait Praetor. §. permittitur. And thus the final pronouncement of the said judge would not be valid; because two contrary sentences cannot be rendered from the same instance, as in l. quod iussit. ff. de re iudica. and ff. de arbi. l. qualem. §. fina. And on this point all the doctors agree. But if the said arbitral sentence is not contrary to the said precept, then it is plain that the said precept subsists with its own force; because that which is not changed remains standing and is not prohibited, as in l. praecipimus. cum si. There is no doubt about the fact that this precept concerns the principal controversy; and that the principal matter being settled, the incidental matters, which do not stand by themselves, are settled not only by the termination of the litigation, but by reason of contrariety and incompatibility, as in l. 2. cum simili. C. de ordi. cogni. From these things it appears in the aforementioned question what is the law. For if the precept was valid, the precept must be followed; if it was not valid, it must not be followed. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a sale made of the goods of a debtor who has been summoned and seized in solidum by virtue of the first decree, and following a public auction, can be rescinded by the contumacious debtor.
body: IdCX, they will return the thing received by the first decree after the woman...

† And the creditor, in the execution of a definitive judgment, sells the thing; the thing is awarded by the first decree to the highest bidder after many public auctions, the debtor himself having been cited and not appearing. Now the debtor does not wish to ratify this sale, because he claims that he has been defrauded by more than half of the just price: and he wishes to pay the pure debt. It is asked whether, for this reason, the sale is void, or at least ought to be rescinded by the office of the judge: and it seems that it is void by operation of law, as in D. de rescindenda venditione, l. Fundus, qui Lucii. Or at least it ought to be rescinded by the office of the judge, that is, by contrary imperial authority, by argument from l. 1, in fine, D. de praetoria stipulatione. Or by a useful action on the sale, which is given to the seller to rescind the contract on account of unjust price, as in C. de rescindenda venditione, l. 2. For the act of a judge ought not to operate more than the act of a party, as in C. de evictionibus, l. Si ob causam.

On the contrary, it seems. For one law says that where such solemnity has been observed, no one can complain of the injustice of the contract, or of the buyer. This is expressly and notably stated by the text in l. 1, C. de praediis cursorum, lib. 10. Moreover, the law says that when a judge exceeds the limit in executing, an appeal must be taken; otherwise, the decree must stand, as in C. quorum appellatio non recipitur, l. Ab executione. Furthermore, the law says that he who is contumacious is held to be present to his own detriment; because contumacy is equivalent to presence, as in Auth. Qua in provincia. But he who previously knew the value of the thing does not have the benefit of the said l. 2; for he is not understood to be deceived who knows, as in D. de rescindenda venditione, l. Venditor. Although the gloss placed there suggests the contrary: but this reasoning is not well secured; for whatever may be the case with the owner who is selling off, who could give away if he wished: otherwise it is with the judge, who cannot give away what belongs to another, as in D. de transactionibus, l. Cum hi, §. Si Praetor. Moreover, a contumacious person is not understood to consent to that which is done not according to law, as in D. ne vis fiat ei, l. Prima, §. Haec verba.

I add another reason why he does not seem to be one who should not be heard: because in judicial proceedings equality must be observed, as in the sacred canons concerning the sacred scrinia. But a creditor defrauded by more than half of the just price is not heard, as in D. de re iudicata, l. A Diuo Pio, §. Si pignora. Therefore, neither should the debtor be heard. Moreover, there are four substantial elements in this sale, as noted in l. Fulcinius, §. Hoc edictum, D. qui ex causa in possessionem eatur. Among these substantial elements, just price is not one: therefore, the sale must stand, unless an appeal has been taken, or unless it is a minor, or unless there is an absence that is probable and necessary: as in the case of a soldier and a legate, as in C. de restitutione militum, l. Ignorare, and D. de damno infecto, l. Si finita, §. Si forte. And it is a general rule for all precepts of judges made after hearing the case, that unless an appeal is taken, they pass into res iudicata, as in D. de minoribus, l. Ait Praetor, §. Permittitur. Moreover, if such injustice could be questioned, the decrees of the praetors would be called into doubt and rendered illusory, which ought not to be, as in l. Si Praetor, in principio, D. de iudicibus. The objection from §. Haec verba does not hold, because there the plaintiff deceived the Praetor regarding the substance of the debt; here he did not. Moreover, that §. has no place when the order is issued from a definitive judgment; because by the sentence the debt is established, and thus the Praetor cannot be deceived regarding the substance of the debt, as in l. Res iudicata, D. de regulis iuris. Let the contumacious person impute it to himself, because by his own act he seems to have confirmed the sentence, as in C. quomodo et quando iudex, l. Ab eo. Moreover, it suffices that the form of the statute has been observed, from the words of which one must not depart, as in D. de exercitu, l. 1, §. Si is qui navem, and l. Prospexit, D. qui et a quibus. Moreover, the said l. Fundus, D. de rescindenda venditione, does not obstruct, because there the form of law was not observed, although the cause of the debt was true: and here the form was observed, and more than the form, because there were more public auctions than the statute requires. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How an inventory is proven to be defective.
2. When a witness is said to be singular, and when he proves.
3. Whether witnesses who tend toward the same end of the matter are said to be singular.
4. A decree creates a presumption that all things were done solemnly.
5. How the exercise of jurisdiction is proven.
body: For the purpose of evidence, the discovery of the heir is not to be premised.

† That for the evidence thereof, in the inventory of the heir, no other things ought to be described than those things which were in the estate of the deceased at the time of death, or for which the heir has a claim for the inheritance, as in D. de petitione hereditatis, l. item veniunt. But it is doubted whether it is presumed that they were in the estate simply because they were found in his house: and it seems that this is so, as noted in C. ne uxor pro marito, l. ob meritorum, and D. de iure dotium, l. si ego, § dotis. To the contrary it seems: because it does not follow that, since they are found in the house, therefore they are part of the inheritance, unless it is proved, at least, that the deceased possessed them in good faith, as in l. Titia, § Lucius, D. de legato 2, and C. de probationibus, l. siue possidetis. Likewise, it does not follow that, since they were found in the house after death, therefore they were in the house at the time of death, or that the deceased possessed them, as in D. de negotiorum gestis, l. eum actum. To prove that the inventory is imperfect, one witness testifies concerning a certain blue-colored pelandra, which was not placed in the inventory, and yet was possessed by him at the time of death; another witness testifies concerning a certain other thing.

† Now it is asked whether these witnesses prove the matter: and it seems that they do, because these witnesses agree on the same end of the matter, namely that the inventory is imperfect; therefore they sufficiently prove it, as in C. de probat., l. qui sententiam. But I ask you: would these witnesses prove the theft of the said things? You must necessarily answer that they do not, because they do not testify about the same thing, nor does one separate fact lead to another, as in ff. de rei vend., l. si in rem agat; ff. de except. rei iudic., l. cum quaeritur. For in petitions, testimonies, and judgments, the word "thing" is used as specific, not as general, as noted in l. 1, in fine, ff. si cert. pet. Otherwise it would follow that, on the contrary, if the witnesses testified—namely, one about one item listed in the inventory, another about another item, which are known to have been among the deceased's assets—they would prove the case for the inventory, because they tend toward the same end. And the same applies to a notarial instrument, which is ridiculous to say otherwise, as in C. de bonis praescript., l. si quis intra; and l. tutor, qui repertorium, in principio, ff. de administ. tutorum; C. eod., l. tutores.

† Now, regarding the argument that they tend toward the same end, it must be known that sometimes they tend toward the same end through the same or a similar means of conclusion; and then the rule of *l. qui sententiam* applies. At other times, neither through the same nor through a similar means; and then they prove nothing, because they are singular. And thus should be understood what is fully noted by Bartolus in *l. 1*, at the end, *ff. quemadmodum testamentum aperitur*. Just as we say in the petition, that the means of conclusion makes the petition general or special. And note Cynus, *C. si certum petatur*, in the rubric, why it is concluded that the said witnesses prove nothing against the inventory.

† And therefore, since a decree has been interposed, it is presumed that nothing is lacking in the inventory, but that it is complete and valid, according to the doctrine set forth by the Speculator in the title *De emptione et venditione*, and the common gloss in *l. 1*, C. *De fide instrumentorum*, and *Iure hastae fiscalis*, lib. 10. And for the clarification of the aforementioned points, it must be known that if I wish to prove the exercise of jurisdiction, and one witness testifies to one act, and another to a different act, the common opinion is that the witnesses provide proof, as noted in *ff. De testibus*, *l. Ob carmen*, § *finalis*. And the reason is that the same jurisdiction inheres in both acts, just as a genus inheres in a species; indeed, according to some, singular witnesses prove usury, because the same wickedness, like a certain genus, inheres in any act. And it is certain that what is disproved by different species, as in *l. finalis*, § *Creditum ergo*, *ff. Si certum petatur*. But if I wish to prove the theft of one thing, and I prove it regarding another thing, I prove nothing, because between these things there is no participation of any reason or common medium from which one may be inferred from the other, as in *l. finalis*, *ff. De calumniatoribus*. However, it is not a good example regarding theft, because the law interprets as subtracted that which is not placed in the inventory by certain license; otherwise, if due to ignorance of the fact, which is presumed in this case, because it is not presumed that anyone knows another’s fact unless the contrary is proven, as in *l. finalis*, *ff. Pro suo*. Furthermore, fraud is not presumed, as in *ff. De probationibus*, *l. Verius*. And from one witness, an oath is not transferred to a presumption of fraud, as noted in *l. 3*, § 1, *ff. De minoribus*. Furthermore, that liquidated things must be proven, at least by household witnesses, is evident from what is read and noted in *l. 2*, C. *Quoniam et quibus quarta pars debetur*, lib. 10. It is established that witnesses are called singular because they testify singularly, that is, what one says, the other does not say, nor does he know by what he says, as in *Extra, De causa possessionis*, cap. *Cum ecclesia Sutrina*, and *De electione*, cap. *Bonae*. And this is proven in cap. *Licet causa*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What are the sufficient indicia for torture? and no. 7.
2. Two concurring witnesses are required to prove an indicium for torture.
3. Innocence is proven by absence.
4. Three things are necessary for the imposition of torture.
5. Flight does not constitute an indicium for torture.
6. It rests in the judge’s breast whether the indicia are sufficient for torture.
body: Of which of them, P. or G., he killed him, because he was killed at night, and it is doubtful whether P. or G. killed him, since both fled, although later, having given security, both appeared.

† Against the statement of P., the following indications are alleged: one is that, when questioned, he said, “If I were on the side of the accusers, I would say well who it was that killed him.” For from this statement it is inferred that he himself committed the act; therefore, he may be compelled to tell the truth. Because in the most serious crime of homicide, even those who know the truth and do not speak it must be compelled by torture to testify to the truth; which is proved thus: a witness who first said that he knew, and later says that he does not know, is wavering; but those who waver ought to be tortured. And this is stated by one witness against the statement of P. The same witness says that he was asked by the said P. not to say anything about the said words. Another witness says that the brother of the said P. was an enemy of the said deceased; certainly by this an indication is not proved, although it creates a certain very small and utterly weak presumption, cf. in c. 1, de eo qui interfecit fratrem domini sui. Another witness says that the said P. was struck and wounded the said deceased, who was killed immediately at the same place and time, cf. D. ad l. Aquil. l. si ex plagiis § tabernarius. But certainly the § proves in defense of the said P., for from this it is presumed that the act was done in self-defense; therefore, it was not wrongly done. Therefore, the said P. ought not to be tortured; because no one is tortured for the revelation of his innocence, but for the revelation of the crime, because innocence ought not to harm anyone. Another witness says that the one mortally wounded said to him, the witness, that it was the said P.; but this does not even constitute an indication, cf. D. ad Sil. l. si quis in gravi in princ. Moreover, because the said homicide was committed in the darkness of night; hence the said deceased could not have had a probable knowledge of the person, cf. D. quod mei causa l. si cum exceptione § in hac. Another witness says that the said deceased, with his sword drawn, went toward the said P. and finally fled to a certain place; and there he fell to the ground dead; and it is probable that the said P. had been attacked first; but this testimony tends toward the innocence of the said P., because he was defending himself, cf. D. de iust. et iur. l. utrum. And therefore, similarly, torture ought not to be applied. Another witness says that the said P. was the killer; and when he had questioned the one struck, P. said, “I killed him”; but to this it is replied as above. Another witness says that he saw the said P. then holding a bloody dagger; and that he saw the said P. wounded with two wounds, from which it is presumed that the said P. was struck first and then struck back. To this it seems, as said above, that this pertains to his innocence. Another witness says that he heard it said that Pomorinus said that he had drawn his dagger toward the said deceased, although he did not believe that he had struck him. Another witness says that he heard from a certain woman that the said Peter said that he had killed him; but these testimonies are hearsay. And therefore they do not prove. Now let us conclude in this case according to law that the indications are not proven to justify torture; because if the statements of the witnesses are carefully examined, some, in the order of the blows, infer an indication regarding self-defense, cf. § tabernarius.

† Others, however, are singular witnesses: and what they testify regarding the circumstantial evidence is not proven by a single singular witness; but there must be at least two concurring witnesses, as noted in l. fina. C. fam. ercisc. and there by the doctors. Moreover, the quality of the weapons of this P. is said not to have been consistent with the blow; hence, considering the blow in light of the type of weapons, it constitutes circumstantial evidence in favor of the said P., as in extra de homic. c. significasti. Furthermore, one witness states that for two hours, or thereabouts, before he was killed, the said P. was continuously elsewhere, tending to his own wounds.

† Hence innocence is proved by absence, as in C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione, l. optimam, in fine, and the glosses thereto; and ff. de acquirenda hereditate, l. Pantonius, § rei perduellionis. And therefore, if nothing else appears except what is stated above in the testimonies, speaking according to written law, the said P. ought not to be subjected to torture; especially if he has already been tortured; nor have greater indications supervened, as has been said, although the examination of the facts lies within the discretion of the judge, particularly where the inquiry is most rigorous, as in ff. ad Turpilianum, l. 1, § calumniatoribus.

† However, without departing from the path of the law, three things are necessary for torture to be imposed. First, that the evidence be certain, that is, proven by at least two witnesses. Second, that it be plausible. Third, that it conclude with probability, as in C. de quaestionibus, l. milites oportet, where there is a notable text. Since these do not intervene here according to what is proposed, there is no place for the torture of the said P., given the circumstances, as in ff. de quaestionibus, l. maritus. Likewise

† Flight alone does not constitute presumptive evidence: because there is no one who does not fear torture, as Cynus fully notes in l. 1, C. de raptoribus virginum. Moreover, often someone seeks refuge under a just shield, as the Lombard law says: “We have seen many perish under a just shield.” And I have seen in fact a certain person who was considered guilty, but was not, and was beheaded; and afterwards the truth was discovered; and he who was truly guilty was afterwards beheaded. And this case is notably set forth in the law, ff. de interrogatione et actione, l. qui servum, where it is said that the suffering of an innocent person does not free the guilty from punishment.

† In the aforementioned matters, however, a uniform rule cannot be given in every case to powers or magistrates, because it is written: "You can know better," D. de testamento, l. 3, § tu magis. But this refers to the quality of the witnesses, not to the quality of the depositions.

And therefore, in this question, I conclude that either there is no place for any torture; or, if torture has been applied once and sufficiently, he ought not to be tortured further. Moreover, it does not necessarily follow that, since such a person was killed, therefore such a person is the killer, since several others could have committed the killing. And it does not prove that this is the case, from the fact that this could be absent. Moreover, it is more just to err in acquitting than in condemning, as noted by the Doctors in the Digest, to the Law Aquilia, Law Item mela, § If several, with similar authorities. Hence, according to what is alleged, this man ought to be released. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. While the litigation concerning the rendering of an account of administration is pending, if a judgment has been rendered releasing one from guardianship, whether it is understood that he is released from the administration.
2. Guardianship is something different from administration.
3. The judgment is referred to the petition, and to the records and proceedings, and is to be interpreted so that it may be valid, and not so that it may be void.
4. Words are used in an improper sense so that the judgment may be valid.
body: The case is as follows: Lanfrancus was sued concerning the accounting to be rendered. After many various sentences had been given for and against, finally a sentence was pronounced in this form: "We absolve Lanfrancus from the aforementioned guardianship." Now it is asked whether by these words it is understood, and whether he is absolved from every accounting to be rendered, as well as from every administration both past and future, or rather only from the office of guardianship, namely, that he was not bound to exercise that office, or ought not to have exercised it?

† And it appears that from the office, however, because guardianship is defined by the office. I.e., force and power over a free person for the purpose of protecting him who, on account of his age, cannot defend himself, as in D. de tut. l. 1 and Inst. eod. in princ.

† Moreover, guardianship is one thing, and the administration of guardianship is another: for guardianship is a right; but the administration of guardianship is an act, as in D. de curato. furiosi, l. consilio, §. fina. To the contrary it seems, because the controversy was not about the office, but about the rendering of accounts and about the action of guardianship: and therefore such things are subject, as the predicates demonstrate, as in D. de interro. act., l. si defensor, §. 1.

† Moreover, because the judgment refers to the libel, as noted in *l. hæc enim*, D. de suspectis tutoribus. Moreover, because the judgment refers to the acts and proceedings, as in C. de sententiis quæ sine certa quantitate, *l. pen.* Moreover, because the judgment is to be interpreted so that it may be valid, and not so that it may fail, and not maliciously, by argument from D. de verbis obligatis, *l. si ita stipulatus*, § *Grisogonus*, at the words “the following stipulation.” Moreover, the action for guardianship is general, and therefore, since the claim was general and the prosecution was general, the judgment is understood to be general, as in C. de iudiciis, *l. licet*. Moreover, in these cases, when I absolve from guardianship, the cause is stated for the effect, that is, from the administration performed on account of the guardianship. And it is established in D. de administratione tutorum, *l. quidam decedens*, in the beginning; and in D. de iustitia et iure, *l. pe.* And I hold this part according to the doctrine of the glossator, who says that when words, retained in their proper meaning, would vitiate the sense, the words are not taken properly, but improperly, so that the judgment may be valid according to the nature of the case itself. This is the singular gloss. And D. de familia erciscunda, *l. et puto*, § 1. And thus I hold, finally concluding. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a rescript of the Prince is valid if no mention is made of the proceedings, nor of the sentence, on account of which the rescript was issued: where he distinguishes.
2. Whether a delegated judge, who has pronounced a null sentence, may pronounce again from the same records? and whether the instance is terminated.
3. The clause, with all exceptions excluded, placed in a rescript, is understood to refer to dilatory exceptions.
body: After various attempts, a certain rescript of the illustrious Lord Count was issued. After various attempts, a certain final rescript was issued concerning a certain case, in which a proceeding had previously been initiated, and even a definitive sentence had been rendered by a delegated judge, which was therefore null by operation of law, because it had been rendered beyond the limits of the mandate. In that final rescript, no mention was made of the proceedings, nor of the aforementioned sentence; rather, it was commanded to a new commissioner that he should summarily and de plano restore the petitioner to possession, or quasi-possession, etc., doing justice to both parties summarily and de plano. It is opposed against the said rescript that it is not valid, because the petitioner did not make mention of the proceedings and the sentence.

† Now the question arises, what is the law? And it appears that the aforementioned rescript did not hold for two reasons: because it did not mention the proceedings, and because it did not mention the sentence. For both points, the case seems to be found in the Extravagant Decretals, *De re iudicata*, chapter *Inter monasterium*. Solumnio says that there should have been no mention of the said sentence, because it ought not to be called a sentence: for since it was rendered beyond the limits of the mandate, it was therefore rendered by a private person lacking jurisdiction, as stated in the Extravagant Decretals, *De rescriptis*, chapter *Cum dilecta*, and in the Digest, *De arbitris*, law *Non distinguemus*, section *Nunc de officio*. But I doubt the matter regarding the proceedings, because it does not appear that that instance was concluded.

† For whenever the sentence of a delegated judge is null, because he pronounced judgment beyond his mandate, as in C. si a non competenti iudi., l. si de proprietate, the same judge ought to pronounce judgment again from the same records, and the instance is not concluded, as is fully noted in C. quomodo, et quando iudex., l. si vt proponis, and by argument from ff. de arbit., l. quid tamen de pluribus. And the reason is, as I said, because he pronounced judgment as a private person, not as a delegate; and therefore he did not discharge his office. Moreover, it is certain that while one instance is pending, a different judge cannot be approached, nor can one be obtained, as in C. de asser. tollen., l. 1, in fine; to this effect, ff. de iudi., l. vbi ceptum; and in Auth. in medio lit., non fieri sacras formas, in the red and black. But if the sentence of the delegated judge were null, yet rendered under the pretext of jurisdiction, because within the limits of the mandate, then he would have discharged his office; and the instance would not endure, although the proofs endured. However, Innocentius says that if the sentence were null due to an error of fact, he would not have discharged his office, as he himself notes in extra de leg., in the rubric.

† Consider whether something is committed anew either as to a judge, or as to a mere executor, or whether it is doubtful. In the first case, the rescript is not valid if no mention is made of the proceedings; the same applies in the third case, because in case of doubt it is presumed that the commission was made as to a cognizor, as in C. si contra ius, vel utilit. publ. l. et si non cognitio. But if it is committed as to a mere executor, the rescript for restoring or removing possession by the executor is not valid, as in C. unde vi. l. meminerint, and C. si per vim, vel alio modo. l. fin., unless such execution was committed after a definitive sentence had already been rendered, which had passed into res judicata.
