For then the commission in the execution of the definitive judgment would be valid without any further citation, as in ff. de rei vindic. l. qui restituere, and note Innocentius, extra de appell. cap. ex ratione. Or unless it were notorious that someone had been de facto dispossessed, and the prince, having knowledge of this, ordered the dispossessed person to be restored, as in l. and note, second question, first, in primis. For in notorious cases the order of law is not required, the same cause and question being considered; because a notorious fact has ready execution, and especially where the precise intention of the Prince is established, as in the case of these ladies who were dispossessed, according to the words of the rescript. It is proposed that the Illustrious Lord G. de facto caused them to be dispossessed, and therefore the Illustrious Lord G., by a contrary and subsequent imperial mandate, orders them to be restored; and rightly so, because the first mandate was null by law itself, and therefore rightly to be revoked, insofar as it proceeded de facto. For what is done hastily from impulse of mind is corrected by justice. And by this, in the question proposed, it finally appears that the restoration, of which the letters of the prince speak, although not as a mere executor because of those words, summarily and de plano, which signify a summary cognition of the cause, which cannot be done without a commission of jurisdiction, nevertheless can and should be done as through a mixed commission tending to the mere.

† For in the rescript it is said, "all executions having been rejected." I understand this to refer to dilatory exceptions, such as this one, that no mention was made of the proceedings. For the Prince wished for the points of law to be debated; and this is clearly proven by D. 17.1.13 § quaedam (Si fideiussor). And this is my final reason, by which, having also considered the motive of the Prince, I hold this opinion. I, Baldus. 1

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Upon the lapse of two years, the matter falls into forfeiture: and the emphyteuta may be expelled without any judicial proceeding.
2. One who fails to pay the census for two years does not forfeit his right.
3. A just cause for litigation excuses delay.
4. Compensation operates by operation of law to prevent forfeiture: especially in the case of a woman, who is entitled to restitution.
body: In the castle of Distigii, there is no custom of individual possession by single persons, because the individual possessors do not pay a certain fixed census each year in common, from which census the community itself pays a certain amount to the Lord Bishop of Piacenza for the episcopal court. It is also true that the said individual possessors, or at least some of them, do not receive individually from the said Lord of Piacenza any instrument of investiture; but they imagine that the said community is invested on behalf of each individual. Now it happens that a certain woman, at certain times, pays in common 10 [units] each year for a certain field; however, she later discovered from ancient instruments that she ought not to pay so much, but less; and she truly offered that which she ought to pay. Nevertheless, out of fear of the community, she could find no witnesses nor notary willing to attend and testify concerning the said offer and testimony. Finally, two years ago, the said community sold the right of the said census to a certain member of the said university. Thereafter, the said lady did not pay the said census to the said buyer; wherefore the said buyer claims that the said thing pertains to him and entered into possession of it, alleging that the said thing has fallen into forfeiture. And all these things were done without the said lady being summoned, and without any legal proceedings or auctions having been carried out. The said woman was expelled from possession, and she seeks restitution of the said possession, offering to pay separately in common that which she owes. On the contrary, it is said that she comes too late; that the said field has been transferred to another.

† It is asked, what is the law? And it seems that the said woman should be repelled, because after two years the matter fell into forfeiture, as in the Extravagant, *De locato*, chapter *Potuit*; and in the Code, *De sacris sanctis ecclesiis*, the authority *Qui rem huiusmodi*. And since she fell from her right by the law itself, she could be expelled by the authority of the said community and the said cessionary without any judicial procedure, as in the Code, *De iure emphyteutico*, law 2. To the contrary, it is alleged. And first, that this property is not emphyteutic,

† Although it is subject to a census: hence, although it is bound for the census, nevertheless, by the cessation of two years, it does not fall into forfeiture; because the true and direct dominion belongs to the person paying. And this is proved by a similar case in those owing to pay taxes, which are imposed daily on persons for their property. For no one would say that by not paying one loses dominion, L. Rescripto, §. Si, D. de muneribus et honoribus. Although sometimes dominion of movable things is lost, for example, if the toll or tax for the things being carried and transported is not paid, as in D. de publicanis, L. Comissa. But this is special in the cases expressly stated in the law; therefore, the common rule is to the contrary. To this it contributes that we note in D. de publicanis, L. 1, §. 1, in the gloss beginning "Tanquam," which gloss is very notable. Moreover, this woman had a just cause for litigating on account of old instruments, especially those newly discovered.
† And it is certain that a just cause for litigation excuses delay, as is read and noted in the Digest, title "If a certain thing is claimed," law "That which you."

† Moreover, this woman paid more than was due for many years, and so much that, by way of set-off, nothing remained payable for those two years; hence, by operation of law, the debt is extinguished even without the plea of set-off being raised, as stated in D. de transactionibus, l. et post rem, § 1, and D. de condictione furtiva, l. si servus, § bonae. Furthermore, the woman is aided by newly discovered instruments, as in l. 1, D. de condictione indebiti. Moreover, this sale could not have been made abruptly, as in D. de rei venditione, l. fundus. Moreover, this right could not have been sold, especially without a decree, since it is regarded as immovable property, as in l. si, C. de vendendis rebus civitatis, and in l. 1, C. de servis Reipublicae manumittendis, and as noted in l. potest pupillus, de auctoritate tutoris, by Dy and Pau., C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, l. iubemus nulli. Moreover, even assuming that the property had fallen into forfeiture, it would belong to the church, not to the community itself, which is not the owner, nor to the said cessionary. Moreover, notice of the cession was not given to the said woman, as in D. de deposito, l. si quis inficiatus; hence, unless the Bishop exercises his right of withdrawal, the community cannot exercise such right unless it held a right ceded by the Bishop, as in l. creditor, D. de actione empti. From all of which it appears that the said woman, having suffered injury, ought to be restored; and if any condemnation was issued against her, especially by the authority of the said place, which lacks such jurisdiction, it was null and void by operation of law. I, Baldus.
